en: [The Carakasaṃhitā with the Commentary Āyurvedadīpikā by Cakrapāṇidatta] [Sūtrasthāna] [Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 1 (1 of 120)]
Salutations to the three-eyed Lord, the master of the three worlds, who has assumed the three forms through the differentiation of the three qualities and is the source of the three Vedas.
Salutations to Sarasvatī, by whose grace [one attains success] through meritorious deeds.
The world, reflected upon the mirror of the intellect, is perceived by the Supreme Witness. 2.
Salutations again and again to Brahmā, Dakṣa, the twin Aśvin deities, the Lord of the Bhṛgus, Bharadvāja, Punarvasu, Hutāśa, Veśa, Caraka, and the others.
3. [Salutations] to those refined by the Patañjala Mahābhāṣya and Caraka.
Salutations to the Lord of Serpents, the remover of the defects of mind, speech, and body.
(4) This commentary on the *Caraka-saṃhitā*, following its intended meaning as taught by the preceptor Naradatta, is being composed by Cakrapāṇidatta under the title *Āyurvedadīpikā*. (5)

O members of the assembly, I am not able to satisfy you whose ears are overflowing from hearing the nectar of the True Guru’s words; for the ocean is not satiated by the water of a raincloud. However, if this illumination of the essence of the flavor of the commentary is obtained in this regard, [then it will suffice].
Since there is only a tiny fragment of virtue here and there, let that be placed in the ear for a moment.

For here, in the treatises on Āyurveda composed by Brahmā and others for the purpose of pacifying the diseases that obstruct virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation, there is currently no proper comprehension of the meaning for men of short lifespan and limited intellect due to their extreme prolixity; and because of this lack of comprehension, there is likewise a proliferation of diseases resulting from the non-performance of the practices prescribed therein. Thinking thus, the most compassionate and venerable Agniveśa began to compose a treatise on Āyurveda—primarily concerning internal medicine—that is neither too concise nor too extensive, so that even those of short lifespan and limited intellect might easily attain its benefits.

And since that which was to be expounded consists of the sections on verses (*śloka-sthāna*), etiology (*nidāna*), minor diseases (*vimāna*), anatomy (*śārīra*), the senses (*indriya*), therapeutics (*cikitsita*), and success in preparation (*kalpa-siddhi*), he considered that the section on verses (*śloka-sthāna*) alone should be taught first, as it expresses the primary meaning of the entire treatise.
For he will say: "The *Ślokasthāna* is declared to be the auspicious head of this treatise; in this section, a compendium of the great meanings of the [six] tetrads has been made" (Sūtra 1.2).

Thus, even in that *Sūtrasthāna*, although it was necessary to first state the quartet of medicines that counteract diseases once they have arisen— given the urgency of treating manifest illness— he began by teaching the chapter on "Longevity" (*Dīrghañjīvitīya*), which explains the purpose and the means for the engagement with the treatise, as well as the tradition of Ayurveda, including its causes, symptoms, and remedies, which constitute the seed of the entire system.

In order to demonstrate the subject matter, purpose, and relationship—which serve as the causes for the audience’s engagement—and to focus the minds of the listeners, he has placed at the beginning of the commentary the first sūtra, consisting of eight words and the number eight (which serves as an auspicious invocation), declaring: "Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on Longevity. For it is observed that prudent persons do not engage with that which lacks a subject matter—such as the phonemes *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa*—or with that which possesses a subject matter but lacks a purpose—such as the examination of a crow's teeth; therefore, the subject matter and the purpose must be stated at the outset.
As it has been said: "Virtuous persons, whose efforts are stilled by the lack of knowledge regarding the subject matter and its fruit, do not care to listen to even a small portion of a text.

Therefore, in order to establish that the subject matter possesses significance and that the treatise possesses a purpose, the relationship between the subject matter and the treatise must be stated as that characterized by the signifier and the signified; and the relationship between the purpose and the treatise must be stated as that characterized by the nature of the goal and the means.
In this context, the subject matter (*abhidheya*) is life (*āyus*) in its aspects of being beneficial or harmful;

for it will be stated: "That in which the beneficial and the harmful, pleasure and pain, the life-span, and the measurement of what is beneficial and harmful for that [life] are taught, is called Āyurveda" (Sūtra 1.1).
a.30) Herein, the inclusion of all that is to be denoted should be explained according to its respective place,
and the purpose is the equilibrium of the elements (dhātu-sāmya).
As it has been said: "The purpose of this treatise is stated to be the maintenance of the equilibrium of the bodily constituents" (*Sūtrasthāna* 1).

Furthermore, the relationship between the science of longevity (*āyurveda*) and [this] treatise is characterized by that of the signifier and the signified; and the relationship between this treatise—which has the intermediate function of providing knowledge of what is to be rejected and what is to be adopted—and the equilibrium of the constituents, which is its purpose, is characterized by that of the means and the end.

All of this should be understood as demonstrated by the term *dīrghañjīvitīyam*, which—referring to the word *dīrghañjīvita*—expresses the purpose [of the treatise] through such statements as "the restoration of the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (*dhātusāmyakriyā*) is also taught. Now, one might object: "The statement that the declaration of the purpose is for the sake of initiating the study of the treatise is not logical; for the existence of a purpose is not determined merely by the declaration of a purpose, since we observe a lack of purpose even in those treatises that declare a purpose, such as those propounding the liberation from the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) through deception."

Now, you might think: "This statement of the purpose is made by a trustworthy person (*āpta*); therefore, it possesses truthfulness. But, sir, how is this person a trustworthy authority who states the purpose? If you say, "Because the treatise (*śāstra*) he has composed is true," then alas, as long as there is no determination that the treatise possesses a purpose, there will be no engagement with the treatise; as long as there is no engagement with the treatise, there can be no determination of the treatise's truthfulness; and as long as there is no determination of the treatise's truthfulness, the trustworthiness of its author cannot be determined. And if trustworthiness is not determined, how can there be a determination that the purpose stated by him exists? Thus, a circular argument (*cakraka*) results. Now, suppose you think: "Let there be no determination that it possesses a purpose; rather, the mere doubt regarding the existence of a purpose in the form of a result will be the motivator for engagement. For even in agriculture and similar activities, engagement occurs precisely because of doubt regarding the result; for in those cases, farmers do not possess a certainty of obtaining the fruit, since obstacles such as drought are always possible. But if that is so, even without the statement of a purpose, since we observe treatises that both have and lack purposes, let the very nature of being a treatise (*śāstratva*) itself serve to demonstrate the doubt regarding the existence of a purpose. Even so, enough with the explicit statement of a purpose!

It is not so; for a general doubt regarding the purpose does not incite one who seeks a specific purpose to act in the same way as a doubt concerning a specific, intended purpose does. Furthermore, a doubt directed toward a specific intended object does not arise without the recollection of that specific object. Therefore, for those who have not yet ascertained the authority of Agniveśa, the statement of the specific purpose is intended to generate a doubt of this particular form: "Is this treatise a means for achieving the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātusāmya), or is it not? On the other hand, for those who have ascertained the authority of the supreme sage Agniveśa from the very beginning, their engagement occurs simply through the ascertainment of the possession of the purpose stated therein; thus, the statement of the purpose is appropriate.

However, in the case of a sentence that states a purpose—which is understood with very little effort—activity toward it is justified even from a mere doubt regarding the general nature of that purpose. This is not the case, however, for a treatise (śāstra) which is understood only through the hardship of many years;
thus, the objection that "even when engaging with a sentence stating a purpose, another purpose must be stated, leading to an infinite regress" is refuted.

In the sūtra beginning with *atha*, the word *atha*—though employed to indicate the immediate succession (*ānantarya*) of [the author’s] lack of certainty regarding the limited lifespan, intelligence, and capacity [of students] in the systems composed by Brahmā and others, as well as the sequence following the salutation to the chosen deity and the attainment of the teacher’s permission for composing the treatise—is nevertheless an auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) by its very nature at the beginning of the treatise. Just as the sight of a water-pot being carried for the purpose of fetching water brings good fortune to those about to set out, so too, for the author and the listeners who have performed the service of auspiciousness at the start of the work and are thus freed from obstacles, the attainment of their desired goal occurs without hindrance; therefore, the inclusion of an auspicious invocation is appropriate.

Regarding the auspiciousness of the word *atha*, there is a traditional authority (*smṛti*): "The syllable *oṃ* and the word *atha*—these two emerged from the throat of Brahmā in ancient times; therefore, both are auspicious.
Furthermore, this word *atha* is seen at the beginning of other treatises as being used for the purpose of auspiciousness.
For example: "Now begins the instruction on words" (Vyākaraṇa-mahābhāṣya).
Chapter 1, Section 1, Subsection 1.
1) Regarding the opening statement, "Now, therefore, we shall explain Dharma" (*Vai. A.

1.1.1*), the salutation to the chosen deity at the beginning of the work was indeed performed by Agniveśa, the most refined of sages, as it is required by the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*). Otherwise, by transgressing the conduct of the learned, he would no longer possess the status of a *śiṣṭa*, and there would be the fear of obstacles to the exposition. Furthermore, even though the salutation is not actually included within the text, it is not inserted into the work because it serves to remove the demerit (*pratyavāya*) resulting from such omission.

And just as this composition of the treatise follows immediately after obtaining the guru’s command, so too is it clearly evident in such passages as "Now, he who is devoted to loving-kindness [accumulates] merit" (*Sūtrālaṃkāra* 1).

Furthermore, by demonstrating the preceptor’s authorization for the composition of the work, the worthiness of the treatise is established. As for the interpretation that the word *atha* signifies the sequence following a student’s inquiry, that does not satisfy me; for a scripture is not composed by first placing students before oneself. Rather, the composition of a scripture is appropriate when the audience is present in the mind, and those who are present in the mind are not necessarily those who have posed questions.

Therefore, the word *ataḥ* indicates the limit prior to the current section, meaning: "from this point onward, that which we shall teach is the Dīrghañjīvitīya"; or else, it is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), meaning: "because [this treatise] possesses a connection similar to that of the Ayurveda-tantras composed by Brahmā and others according to the aforementioned logic, for this reason we shall explain the Dīrghañjīvitīya"—thus it should be construed.
Regarding the term *Dīrghañjīvitīya*, the word *dīrghañjīvita* is present in this [section] in the sense of possession (*matvartha*), according to the rule: *adhyāyānuvākayor luk ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.60).
The suffix *cha* [is applied] according to [Pāṇini 4.3.87]:

*dīrghajīvite 'bhidheye granthaḥ kṛtaḥ chaḥ*. Alternatively, if the intention is that the work—whether in the form of a chapter (*adhyāya*) or a treatise (*tantra*)—was composed concerning the subject of "long life" (*dīrghajīvita*), then [the suffix is applied] according to [Pāṇini 4.3.87]: *adhikṛtya kṛte granthe*.
By virtue of the governing rule *ityadhikārāt* (Pāṇini 4.3.87), the suffix *cha* is applied according to the rule *śiśukrandayamasabha-* (Pāṇini 4.3.88) and others.
The same should be understood regarding other similar cases as well.

And here, although there are other words, the designation is made by the word *dīrghajīvita* alone; because the word *dīrghajīvita* is introduced at the beginning of the teaching and because it is preeminent, [the treatise] is designated as such either by the sense that "this [work] contains the word *dīrghajīvita*" or by the sense that it was composed concerning the word *dīrghajīvita*. By this etymological derivation, the term *Dīrghajīvitīya* is to be applied to both the treatise and the chapter.

By the phrase "therefore, we shall explain the *Dīrghañjīvitīya*," a promise to explain the entire treatise (*tantra*) is established. Furthermore, by repeating the word "*Dīrghañjīvitīya*" in conjunction with the term "chapter" (*adhyāya*), it secures a promise to explain that specific chapter; for the repetition of a word to connect it [to a subsequent term] is observed, as in the *Apāmārgataṇḍulīya*: "in heaviness of the head, headache, and coryza" (Sūtra-sthāna 24.3).

2) In such passages, the word "śirasā" (with the head) is connected with "gaurave" (in cases of respect), and by repetition, it is also connected with "śūle" (in cases of pain). Therefore, the objection that for one who has not made a formal declaration regarding the entire treatise (*tantra*), the declaration concerning a single chapter (*adhyāya*) would be deficient in scope, is refuted. Alternatively, let there be only the declaration of the chapter; by that very act, the declaration of the treatise is also effectively established, for a chapter is not separate from the treatise. Thus, when a part is explained, the whole—the treatise—is necessarily explained as well. Just as by grasping a finger, Devadatta himself is also grasped.
However, a promise to explain the other constituent parts [of the treatise] is not obtained; rather, he will do so for each individual chapter (*adhyāya*),
as indicated by the rule *iṅaśca* (Pāṇini 3.3.21) following the prefix *adhi* applied to the root *iṅ*.
[The word *adhyāya*] is derived from the root with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*), meaning "that which is studied" (*adhīyate*).

Nor does this etymological derivation lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to terms such as *prakaraṇa*, *catuṣka*, or *sthāna*; for this designation *adhyāya* is a conventional term (*yogarūḍhi*) that applies specifically to a particular collection of chapters characterized by [sections] such as the *Dīrghañjīvitīya*, just like the word *paṅkaja* [which denotes a specific type of lotus despite its etymology]. It does not apply merely through its etymological derivation (*yoga*).
For it will be said: "This designation of the name 'Adhyāya' is established with reference to this [work]" (Sūtra 30);
the meaning is that the designation of the name is a conventional term based on etymological derivation (yogarūḍha).

Alternatively, the form *adhyāya* is established by the rule "adhyāyanyāyodyāvasaṃhārāśca" (Pāṇini 3.3.122), through the technical designation (*nipātana*) for the meanings of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
An *adhyāya* is so called because a particular subject matter (*arthaviśeṣa*) is studied (*adhīyate*) therein or by means of it;
the prohibition against over-extension follows the logic already stated.
The form "we shall explain" (*vyākhyāsyāmaḥ*) is derived from the root *khyāti* preceded by the prefixes *vi-* and *ā-*, using the periphrastic future (*lṛṭ*).

For in the usage of the root *cakṣiṅ*, since the connection between the action and its result is unavoidable even for an interpreter who does not desire it, the Ātmanepada would occur by virtue of the rule *svaritañitaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale* (Pāṇini 1.3.72).
The prefix *vi* signifies distinction (*viśeṣa*), and distinctions include expansion (*vyāsa*), contraction (*samāsa*), and so forth.

As for the prefix *āṅ*, it is used in connection with action (*kriyāyoga*). We do not understand the intention of those who believe that *āṅ* is used in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*) or inclusion (*abhividhi*), because in the case of a limit or inclusion, the prefix *āṅ* would have to be joined with a nominal stem (*prātipadika*); as in: “of the lords of the earth as far as the ocean” (*āsamudrakṣitīśānām*). (Raghuvamśa)
“Vam.
1) ‘The rain has fallen as far as Pāṭaliputra’—in such cases, and here too, it is the same.”

In the absence of connection with a verb (*kriyāyoga*), the prefix *āṅ* would not possess the status of a preverb (*upasarga*) due to the rule "preverbs [are designated as such] when in connection with a verb" (Pāṇini 1.4.59). Consequently, because of the intervention of the non-preverb *āṅ*, the preverb *vi-* could not be employed.

If a prefix were to become a prefix [of a root] even when not immediately contiguous—whether separated by words of the same class or otherwise—then, since both *vi* and *ā* would not be prefixes, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the excessive conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*) of postulating numerous nominal stems (*prātipadika*) suitable for connection with them. Therefore, it is logical that *āṅ* possesses connection with the action alone;
thus, in the phrase "atha, ataḥ, dīrghaṃ, jīvitīyam, adhyāyaṃ, vi, ā, khyāsyāmaḥ," there is a total of eight words.

1. The Chapter on the Path of Seeing (Dṛṣṭimārga-varga) The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the monks: "Friends, monks! They replied, "Venerable friend," and listened to the Venerable Śāriputra. The Venerable Śāriputra said this: "Friends, those ascetics and brahmins who do not understand as it really is the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the five aggregates of clinging—these I call 'ascetics and brahmins who have not crossed over the flood' and 'ascetics and brahmins who have not emerged from the mire. And why is that? Because, friends, these ascetics and brahmins do not understand as it really is the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the five aggregates of clinging. But those ascetics and brahmins who understand as it really is the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the five aggregates of clinging—these I call 'ascetics and brahmins who have crossed over the flood' and 'ascetics and brahmins who have emerged from the mire. And why is that? Because, friends, these ascetics and brahmins understand as it really is the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the five aggregates of clinging. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda thought: "It is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well has the Blessed One spoken this Dharma discourse concerning the five aggregates of clinging. It would be good if the Blessed One were to speak further on this same subject: the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the five aggregates of clinging. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: "It is wonderful, Blessed One; it is marvelous, Sugata! How well has the Blessed One spoken this Dharma discourse concerning the five aggregates of clinging. It would be good if the Blessed One were to speak further on this same subject: the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the five aggregates of clinging. The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, listen closely and attend well; I shall speak. "Yes, Blessed One," the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, what is the gratification regarding form? Whatever pleasant feeling arises dependent on form—that is the gratification regarding form. What is the danger regarding form? Form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—that is the danger regarding form. What is the escape regarding form? The complete dispassion toward form, its fading away, its cessation, its relinquishment, and its abandonment—that is the escape regarding form. "Ānanda, what is the gratification regarding feeling? Whatever pleasant feeling arises dependent on feeling—that is the gratification regarding feeling. What is the danger regarding feeling? Feeling is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—that is the danger regarding feeling. What is the escape regarding feeling? The complete dispassion toward feeling, its fading away, its cessation, its relinquishment, and its abandonment—that is the escape regarding feeling. "Ānanda, what is the gratification regarding perception? Whatever pleasant feeling arises dependent on perception—that is the gratification regarding perception. What is the danger regarding perception? Perception is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—that is the danger regarding perception. What is the escape regarding perception? The complete dispassion toward perception, its fading away, its cessation, its relinquishment, and its abandonment—that is the escape regarding perception. "Ānanda, what is the gratification regarding volitional formations? Whatever pleasant feeling arises dependent on volitional formations—that is the gratification regarding volitional formations. What is the danger regarding volitional formations? Volitional formations are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—that is the danger regarding volitional formations. What is the escape regarding volitional formations? The complete dispassion toward volitional formations, their fading away, their cessation, their relinquishment, and their abandonment—that is the escape regarding volitional formations. "Ānanda, what is the gratification regarding consciousness? Whatever pleasant feeling arises dependent on consciousness—that is the gratification regarding consciousness. What is the danger regarding consciousness? Consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—that is the danger regarding consciousness. What is the escape regarding consciousness? The complete dispassion toward consciousness, its fading away, its cessation, its relinquishment, and its abandonment—that is the escape regarding consciousness. "Ānanda, for a noble disciple who thus understands as it really is the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the five aggregates of clinging, it is impossible that he will not attain final knowledge in this very life, provided he exerts himself with diligence. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Gone One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: "Friends, monks! They replied, "Friend," and listened to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this: "Friends, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well has the Blessed One spoken this Dharma discourse concerning the five aggregates of clinging. For a noble disciple who thus understands as it really is the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the five aggregates of clinging, it is impossible that he will not attain final knowledge in this very life, provided he exerts himself with diligence. At that time, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita thought: "It is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well has the Venerable Ānanda spoken this Dharma discourse concerning the five aggregates of clinging. It would be good if the Venerable Ānanda were to speak further on this same subject: the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the five aggregates of clinging. Then the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Friend Ānanda, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well has the Venerable Ānanda spoken this Dharma discourse concerning the five aggregates of clinging. It would be good if the Venerable Ānanda were to speak further on this same subject: the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the five aggregates of clinging. The Venerable Ānanda said: "Friend Koṭṭhita, listen closely and attend well; I shall speak. "Yes, friend," the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this: "Friend Koṭṭhita, what is the gratification regarding form? Whatever pleasant feeling arises dependent on form—that is the gratification regarding form. What is the danger regarding form? Form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—that is the danger regarding form. What is the escape regarding form? The complete dispassion toward form, its fading away, its cessation, its relinquishment, and its abandonment—that is the escape regarding form. "Friend Koṭṭhita, what is the gratification regarding feeling? Whatever pleasant feeling arises dependent on feeling—that is the gratification regarding feeling. What is the danger regarding feeling? Feeling is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—that is the danger regarding feeling. What is the escape regarding feeling? The complete dispassion toward feeling, its fading away, its cessation, its relinquishment, and its abandonment—that is the escape regarding feeling. "Friend Koṭṭhita, what is the gratification regarding perception? Whatever pleasant feeling arises dependent on perception—that is the gratification regarding perception. What is the danger regarding perception? Perception is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—that is the danger regarding perception. What is the escape regarding perception? The complete dispassion toward perception, its fading away, its cessation, its relinquishment, and its abandonment—that is the escape regarding perception. "Friend Koṭṭhita, what is the gratification regarding volitional formations? Whatever pleasant feeling arises dependent on volitional formations—that is the gratification regarding volitional formations. What is the danger regarding volitional formations? Volitional formations are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—that is the danger regarding volitional formations. What is the escape regarding volitional formations? The complete dispassion toward volitional formations, their fading away, their cessation, their relinquishment, and their abandonment—that is the escape regarding volitional formations. "Friend Koṭṭhita, what is the gratification regarding consciousness? Whatever pleasant feeling arises dependent on consciousness—that is the gratification regarding consciousness. What is the danger regarding consciousness? Consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—that is the danger regarding consciousness. What is the escape regarding consciousness? The complete dispassion toward consciousness, its fading away, its cessation, its relinquishment, and its abandonment—that is the escape regarding consciousness. Now, one might ask: how will Agniveśa explain Āyurveda, which requires knowledge of every single detail of all things? For the exhaustive particulars of medicinal substances and the like cannot be known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), since the specific qualities of all objects fall outside the scope of direct perception. Furthermore, determining the nature of all things through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is indeed difficult; for instance, honey alone—by its very nature—revives life yet kills when heated and mixed with ghee; it is beneficial for those of a phlegmatic constitution (*kapha-prakṛti*) but harmful for those of a windy constitution (*vāta-prakṛti*); it is wholesome in marshy regions but unwholesome in deserts; it is to be consumed in the cold season but avoided in the heat; it is beneficial when one is not aged but harmful when one is old; it produces benefit in small doses but causes harm when overused; when it reaches a state of rawness (*āmatā*) in the stomach, it causes great confusion due to its incompatibility with treatment; and when combined with *kākamācī* or consumed with ripe *nikuca* fruit, it leads to death or the destruction of strength, complexion, vigor, and luster. Since even the nature of a single substance like honey is so difficult to grasp in such ways, what then can be said regarding the knowledge of every single detail of all things? And if one explains while being ignorant, how can his words be accepted? Anticipating this doubt and wishing to dispel it, [the author], showing that his own work is in the form of a restatement of what was spoken by the Teacher, says: "Thus indeed spoke the Blessed One Ātreya."

Here, the word *iti* refers back to the meaning that is about to be stated, while the word *ha* serves as an emphatic particle (*avadhāraṇe*). For example, in the passage: "Indeed, for one who possesses a body, there is no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant" (*na ha vai saśarīrasya priyāpriyayor apahatir asti*), the phrase *na ha* means "not at all. In this context, by the use of the particle *sma* in the expression *smāha*, the suffix *laṭ* is applied in the sense of the past tense (*liṅ-artha*) according to the rule *laṭ sme* (Pāṇini 3.2.118); it does not apply to the remote past (*bhūtānadyatana-parokṣa*), because Ātreya’s instruction was not remote with respect to Agniveśa. We shall demonstrate later how the suffix *liṅ* occurs in the sense of the simple past (*bhūta-mātra*).

"Bhaga" is honored knowledge; one who possesses that is [Bhagavat]. As it has been said: "He who knows the origin and dissolution of beings, as well as their coming and going, and who knows both knowledge and ignorance—he is to be called Bhagavat. Alternatively, the word *bhaga* denotes the totality of sovereignty, majesty, and so forth. As it has been said: "The designation *bhaga* is applied to the six: complete sovereignty, valor, fame, splendor, knowledge, and dispassion."
The son of Atri is Ātreya; by this, his possession of a pure lineage is demonstrated.

On this point, others explain: "Sūtra is of four kinds: the sūtra of the teacher (guru-sūtra), the sūtra of the disciple (śiṣya-sūtra), the sūtra of the redactor (pratisaṃskartṛ-sūtra), and the sūtra of a particular school (ekīya-sūtra)."

In this regard, an example of a *guru-sūtra* (authoritative statement by the teacher) is: "This should not be viewed thus by one possessed of intelligence, O Agniveśa" (*Sūtra-sthāna*, chapter 4), and so forth. An example of a *pratisaṃskartṛ-sūtra* (statement by the redactor) is: "The Blessed One Ātreya said to him" (*Sūtra-sthāna*, chapter 4), and so forth. An example of a *śiṣya-sūtra* (statement by the disciple) is: "O Blessed One, these five hundred *kaṣāya* [periods] are not yet filled" (*Sūtra-sthāna*, chapter 4), and so forth. An example of an *ekīya-sūtra* (statement of a certain school) is: "The head of the child is formed first; thus says Kumāraśiras Bharadvāja" (*Śārīra-sthāna*, chapter 6), and so forth.
Therefore, the first introductory sutra regarding the promise of exposition belongs to the Teacher alone, because the student Agniveśa lacks the authority to provide the exposition.
And the second sutra belongs to the editor (*pratisaṃskartṛ*);

by means of the word *iti*, which denotes manner, it refers back to the statement: “We shall expound the *Dīrghañjīvitīya*. Consequently, the form *āha sma* (‘[he] said’) refers specifically to the remote past (*bhūtānadyatanaparokṣa*), since the instruction from Ātreya is remote (*parokṣa*) with respect to the editor.
By this same reasoning, the prescription of the *liṅ* (optative) mood is also justified in passages such as "The Blessed One Ātreya said to him" (*anena ca nyāyena tamuvāca bhagavānātreyaḥ*),

and likewise in the Suśruta Saṃhitā, where the commentator— regarding the introductory verse "As the Blessed Dhanvantari spoke" (*yathovāca bhagavān dhanvantariḥ*) as a statement by the reviser— has established the validity of the *liṅ* prescription.

To this we reply: as for what was stated—that because the disciple Agniveśa lacks the authority to provide a commentary, this must be a sūtra of the Teacher—that is not so. For teacherhood does not exist by birth alone; thus, that very Ātreya is a disciple in relation to his own teacher, yet he is a teacher in relation to Agniveśa and the others. Likewise, at the time of composing the treatise, Agniveśa is also a teacher in relation to those students whom he has established in his mind. Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever.

Furthermore, regarding the justification for the rule of the *liṭ* (perfect tense) in the second sūtra as being intended to denote an action that occurred in the past, not in the current day, and out of the sight of the speaker (*bhūtānadyatanaparokṣe*), this must be examined: does this second sūtra form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the preceding statement, or not? If it forms a single syntactical unit, then in the *Suśruta*, one must construe it as: "We shall explain accordingly, just as Dhanvantari said. And thus, since the word "said" (*uvāca*) would be part of a single syntactical unit with the action "we shall explain," it cannot have a different agent; and if so, how can there be a rule for the *liṭ*? On the other hand, if it does not form a single unit, then there is no semantic connection, just as there is none between the sentences "cow, horse, man, elephant."

Furthermore, since there is not even a trace of the word "author" (pratisaṃskartṛ) in the case of Jatūkarṇa and others, how can there be an injunctive suffix (liṅ) in such passages as: "The disciple Jatūkarṇa, whose throat was filled with various scriptures, approached with palms joined and said"?

By this same reasoning, even in the *Caraka-saṃhitā*, there is no instance of the optative mood (*liṅ*) being used in the sense of an authorial injunction within the Sūtra section. Therefore, in the *Caraka*, it was Agniveśa who was the original author of the Sūtras, whereas in the *Suśruta*, it was Suśruta himself. Occasionally, for the purpose of praising or censuring some point, he presents a past account (*purākalpa*) in the form of a narrative and writes a certain Sūtra either as a restatement of what was said by his teacher or as a restatement of the opinion of "some" (*ekīya*). The reviser (*pratisaṃskartṛ*), however, completes the work precisely as if he were the original author of that text.

The prescription of the *liṭ* (perfect tense), however, is ordained by Vedic usage (*chandas*) for the mere past non-recent time (*bhūtānadyatana-mātra*) and should be described as occurring even in the common language (*bhāṣā*); otherwise, the word *uvāca* would not appear in works such as the *Jatūkarṇa*. Thus, in the *Harivaṃśa*, in the *Dhanyopākhyāna*, [the forms] "he said to me" (*mām uvāca*) and likewise "I said" (*aham uvāca*) would not exist. For example: "That water-dweller, the tortoise, himself spoke to me like a human:
'O Sage, what wonder is there in me? And how am I blessed, O Lord? (Harivaṃśa, Viṣṇuparvan 2a.110); and likewise: "By the word of the Self-born, I have indeed approached the Vedas."
And he said to those four:

as for the claim that in the phrase “iti ha smāha,” the word *iti* refers back to the preceding sūtra—that is not so. For if only the sūtras such as the *Dīrghañjīvitīya* and their respective meanings were established as being spoken by the Guru, it would not follow that the subsequent exposition of the subject matter establishes the entire treatise (*tantra*) as a restatement of what was spoken by the Guru, thereby generating faith in the listener.
Rather, it should be understood as explained previously; therefore, that [previous interpretation] alone is logical.

Regarding the phrase "we shall explain for Agniveśa," the use of the plural number is justified because the plural form of the pronoun *asmat* (we) is grammatically correct even when referring to a single person. Indeed, speakers correctly say, "We shall do it.
However, in the expression "the venerable Ātreya," the singular designation is employed because the word "venerable" (*bhagavān*) itself demonstrates the respect due to the teacher Ātreya.

Now, one might object: "Just as knowledge of Āyurveda is not possible for Agniveśa—either through direct perception or through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—due to its difficulty of acquisition, how then could Ātreya possess knowledge of Āyurveda, such that Agniveśa’s own knowledge of Āyurveda can be said to be well-founded? Anticipating this doubt, [the author], demonstrating that Āyurveda is an uncorrupted tradition (*aviplutāgama*), says: "Long life" (*dīrghaṃ jīvitam*), and so forth. Life is the conjunction of the body, the senses, the mind (*sattva*), and the self (*ātman*);
and that [life] is "long," meaning it pertains to a long duration of time. Here, the word "time" (*kāla*) should be understood as being elided.
This is the stylistic convention of the Teacher, in that he employs elisions at the beginning, middle, and end [of compounds], such that even when omitted, the words are indeed understood—

just as the word *māṃsa* (meat) is elided in the phrase "the flavors of village, marsh, and aquatic [creatures]" (Sūtra 21), and likewise the word *viṣa* (poison) is elided in the phrase "burnt and pierced" (*dagdhaviddha*),
and so forth. The term *anvicchan* means "desiring" a corresponding long [result].
"Bhāradvāja" is a name derived from a lineage (gotra);

by the epithet "of fierce austerity" (ugratapas), it is demonstrated that even though Bhāradvāja was human, he possessed the power to approach Indra, as well as the capacity to be perceived as a source of refuge; for the power of austerities is inconceivable, since by means of them Agastya made even the great ocean drinkable from a single mouthful.

Nor should it be said: "Why does he not understand even Āyurveda simply by virtue of his fierce asceticism? For the power of asceticism, being restricted to specific domains, is not efficacious in all matters; moreover, its capacity must be inferred from its effects. Therefore, since we do not observe the effect characterized by the knowledge of Āyurveda independent of a teacher, we conclude that his asceticism is not capable in that regard. Alternatively, the knowledge of Āyurveda bears fruit only through the sequential process beginning with a teacher; thus Bharadvāja approached Indra.

Now, one might ask: since Brahmā and others were present as the original teachers of Āyurveda, why did he approach Indra alone? It is indeed proper to hear [the teaching] from the primary teacher himself; for knowledge, which travels through a succession of disciples, might—due to defects such as incorrect comprehension—be diminished like honey being passed along a series of vessels. Therefore, it is said: "Having understood that the Lord of the Immortals (Indra) was the refuge. Since this very Indra was short-lived, he alone was the protector and guardian for those terrified by fear, unlike Brahmā and the others; therefore, he approached him alone.
By the term *Amareśvara* (Lord of the Immortals), he demonstrates Indra’s suitability for the task of protection; for a king indeed exerts extraordinary effort in protecting his subjects.

Now, regarding the phrase "seeking long life," since "long" is not fixed, for how much time is that "long" intended? In this context, it refers to a hundred years in accordance with the specific Yuga, as it has been stated: "The measure of the lifespan in this age is indeed a hundred years" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.2).
Furthermore, as the maximum duration of life diminishes progressively from the beginning of the Kali Yuga onwards, so too does the lifespan itself decrease.

As it is said: "When a hundred years are complete, one year passes away from the lifespan of embodied beings at the time when whatever measure is intended [for that age]. According to this, there was a preeminence of lifespan in the previous ages.
As the venerable Vyāsa said: "In the Kṛta age, men and all perfected beings have a lifespan of four hundred years; in the Tretā and subsequent ages, it likewise decreases by one quarter at a time.
Thus, lifespan is either fixed or unfixed, according to one's karma.

In that regard, karma initiated with great force is determinate (*niyata*), such as when one dies at this very time or no later than it; however, karma initiated with weak force is indeterminate (*aniyata*). When it encounters a visible lethal condition, such as poison, it then kills once its power has been activated. When it does not encounter a visible lethal cause, it kills upon the attainment of the lifespan appropriate to the age, once the body has been worn out by the influence of that age.

Regarding this, the Teacher has shown an illustration: "Just as a horse, endowed with its own qualities, while being driven, reaches its end at the proper time solely through the exhaustion of its own capacity, yet that same horse, burdened by an excessive load... starting from there up to "...falls into calamity midway; likewise, for those of indefinite lifespan, their vital breaths are obstructed midway due to transgressions" (Vi. A. 3).
However, when those of indefinite lifespan practice *rasāyana*, then by its power, there occurs a transcendence of the lifespan determined by the power of the *yuga*.
As he said: "As many [of those seeds] as one should consume..."
"He shall live for thousands of years, regaining his youth," and so forth;

however, there is no bypassing of a lifespan that is determined by powerful karma. As it is said: "Some great karma is fixed in its ripening at a specific time, while some is not fixed in time and is awakened by conditions. (Viśeṣa-sthāna, Chapter 3)

Well then, if this is so, then in all cases—whether death or life, or likewise illness or recovery from illness—it is karma alone that is the cause. What, then, is the use of this Āyurveda, which merely follows along with the fruits produced by karma? For instance: as for what is called "fixed" (niyata) karma, there is no scope for the operation of Āyurveda therein, since even when the visible factors are assembled, they are rendered fruitless by that very fixed karma. And as for that which is called "unfixed" (aniyata) lifespan because it is initiated by weak karma—that too is not subject to our confidence, since we observe that the efficacy of the visible is overcome by the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa). Thus, even when we see the causal efficiency of the visible in a matter under dispute, we determine that the unseen alone is the cause, and that the visible exists there only as drawn forth by the unseen.

It is not so; for if this were the case, it would follow that all ritual performance must cease. Furthermore, for one who maintains the doctrine of action alone (*kevalakarmavādin*) while denying what is perceived, the very production of the unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*) would be impossible; for the unperceived is produced by perceived [acts] such as the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice, and the perceived cause is what the proponent of action accepts. Now, if they claim that the perceived is caused by the unperceived, then alas, by that same logic, why is it not accepted that burning and other such things possess the power to remove cold or produce blisters? Moreover, for the proponent of action alone, since there is no apprehension of a pervasion (*vyāpti*) regarding a perceived cause, there could be no inference of the unperceived at all. Therefore, both the perceived and the unperceived are causes.

In this regard, in some cases the unseen (adṛṣṭa) is sublated by the seen (dṛṣṭa), and in others the seen is sublated by the unseen. Therefore, where for a person there exists an unseen cause of death that is powerful and certain, Āyurveda is of no avail regarding life or death. However, even in such a case, it certainly exerts itself in pacifying diseases that produce suffering prior to the fixed time of death, provided that the disease itself is not produced by that [fixed] karma. But as for that karma whose fruition is uncertain, the undertaking of Āyurveda is entirely purposeful with respect to it.

As for that lifespan which is determined by the age-cycle (*yuga*), it is not fixed by an exceedingly powerful *karma*, because its subversion through the application of elixirs (*rasāyana*) is observed and thus accepted; however, this is not due to treatments that are beneficial for the healthy or harmful to the sick, and since this point has been thoroughly examined by the author of the treatise himself in detail, it is not elaborated upon here.
He explains why Indra alone is the refuge and not Brahmā and the others, saying "by Brahmā," etc.;
for the word "hi" (indeed) signifies "because," and Prajāpati is the one named Dakṣa.
"Proktam" (proclaimed) means proclaimed thoroughly; "thoroughly" refers to an exhaustive description.
By the word "yathā" (just as), there is an attraction of the word "tathā" (so), which is eternally connected to it; thus, he grasped exactly what was proclaimed in its entirety—that is, exhaustively.
Then the Aśvins received [it] from Prajāpati;
here too, the phrase "in its entirety, exactly as it was declared" should be applied in the same manner.
Likewise, in the passage "the blessed Śakra received it from the two Aśvins," the phrase "exactly as it was declared," and so forth, should be applied in the same way.
The word "ha" is used for emphasis; thus, the meaning is that Śakra indeed attained [the Āyurveda], but he did not give the Āyurveda to anyone.
By this passage, which demonstrates the tradition of the Āyurveda without deficiency or excess, it is shown that just as Brahmā possesses knowledge of the Āyurveda, so too does Indra.
Therefore, whether it is heard that the Āyurveda came from Brahmā or from Indra, there is no difference in substance.

In Indra’s case, however, there is this further distinction: that he was a seeker of disciples because his knowledge had not yet been transmitted to them. As it is said: "He who, having properly received knowledge from his teachers, does not bestow it upon his pupils, indeed incurs a great debt toward his elders and commits a grave offense. Therefore, because he was not yet a teacher and possessed the specific quality of seeking disciples, Indra alone—more than Brahmā and the others—is the one to be sought as a refuge. For as for Brahmā, the supreme preceptor who has mastered all the Vedas and whose intellect is unobstructed in every respect, his knowledge of Āyurveda is self-evident; thus, he has no need for another teacher.

And this presentation of the lineage of teachers beginning with Brahmā is intended to demonstrate that Āyurveda is an uncorrupted tradition, as well as to demonstrate its worthiness of adoption because it has been practiced by great beings.

For it is said: "In that regard, one should follow that scripture which one considers to have been practiced by great, illustrious, wise, and noble persons," and so on, up to "one should resort to that scripture" (Vi.
A. 8). It is declared by the Ṛṣis according to the account that will be related, thus it is "proclaimed by the Ṛṣis."

"Therefore" means because Indra alone is specifically the one worthy of refuge (4–5). Now, as to how this [Ayurveda] was proclaimed by a seer, he states the reason for its arrival in the world of mortals, beginning with the words "obstructive factors" (vighnabhūtā) and so forth.
"Obstructive" means having the nature of an obstacle;
"afflicting" means diseases;
"manifested" means become apparent.
And this manifestation of disease is to be understood as occurring at the end of the Kṛta Yuga;
for he will say [later], beginning with "But in the Kṛta Yuga it declines" (Vi. A. 3), regarding the manifestation of disease in the chapter on the destruction of regions (*janapadoddhvaṃsana*).
Furthermore, this manifestation is the actual appearance of that which was already established previously.
Therefore, even the impermanence of the continuity of disease is not contradictory; this is what should be stated in the *Daśamahāmūlīya* chapter (*Sūtra-sthāna*, 30).
[The term] *śarīram* means "that which perishes" (*śīryate*); that which possesses this is the "embodied one" (*śarīrī*).
By this, it is indicated that the body perishes by its very nature, but it perishes all the more so through its connection with disease.
To whom do they act as obstacles? He says: "Asceticism, fasting, study," and so forth.

For embodied beings seized by disease are unable to perform asceticism and the like because of their impaired state. Likewise, certain maladies are obstructive here because they destroy life-span. In this context, "asceticism" refers to the Cāndrāyaṇa and other such practices; "fasting" refers to the abandonment of anger and the like, as well as the adoption of truthfulness and other virtues. For there is a saying: "He who dwells with those who have turned away from sins is indeed virtuous."

“That should be understood as fasting, not the mere emaciation of the body. Study (*adhyayana*) means the study of the Vedas; *brahmacarya* is the conduct for the sake of *brahman*, i.e., liberation (*mokṣa*), consisting of the restraint of the genitals and so forth; a *vrata* is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) desired for a specific goal. Regarding the usage "longevity is said to consist of austerity and fasting" (*tapopavāsa*), it should be understood that because the rule of non-application (*asiddha-vidhi*) is not always mandatory, the elision of the *y* sound—which was the substitute for the *s* in *tapaḥ*—is established, according to the rule "not [if there is] a penultimate vowel" (*nopadhāyāḥ*, Pāṇini 6.4.7), as in the case of living beings (*bhūteṣu prāṇiṣu*).

"Anukrośam" means compassion. Why? Because verbal roots have multiple meanings, it signifies "placing before" or "honoring. By this, it is shown that the removal of diseases from living beings is the primary fruit for the great sages in undertaking Āyurveda; the prolongation of life, however, is established as a secondary consequence for those high-souled ones—this is the intended meaning.

While it would have been sufficient to say "among men," the fact that he uses the general term "among beings" (bhūteṣu) shows that this compassion is not directed toward those of his own kind, but is extended to all living creatures; thus he demonstrates the impartial vision of the seers (ṛṣis). They are called "Great Seers" (maharṣis) because they are both great and seers. By this, all four classes of seers are included: the female seers (ṛṣikās), the sons of seers (ṛṣiputras), the divine seers (devarṣis), and the great seers (maharṣis). The inclusion of the female seers and others follows from their being followers of the great seers. Those whose actions are meritorious—that is, purifying—are called "the doers of meritorious deeds" (puṇyakarmāṇaḥ).
The side is covered with ribs; thus, it is "pārśva" because it is like a side (*pārśvam iva*).
The word "śubhe" (in a pleasant place) is intended to indicate the conditions conducive to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), for it is in a pleasant location that concentrations become serene.
He asks, "Who are those great sages? and answers with "Aṅgiras" and so forth.

The mention of many sages at the beginning of the text is for the purpose of destroying evil, as well as to demonstrate that Āyurveda itself is worthy of service because it has been practiced by such great persons.

Among these, some were *yāyāvara*s (wandering mendicants), some were *śālīna*s (householders), and some were *ayonija*s (not born from a womb); all such types should be understood to be included here collectively.
"Bhikṣu" is a qualification of Ātreya, for he will state later: "The mendicant Ātreya said, 'That is not so'" (Sūtra-sthāna 25).
"Vaikhānasas" is a designation applied on account of their specific practice;
the "Vālakhilyas," however, are certain sages of very small stature.
Like treasures— treasures in the sense of being an inexhaustible storehouse—
is self-restraint (*dama*), which is the state of being self-controlled;
"this" refers to that which will be described further on.

*Dharma* is so called because it upholds; it is inherent in the self (*ātman*) and is inferable from the observation of its effects. *Artha* refers to gold and the like. *Kāma* is that which is desired, such as the embrace of a woman and so forth. *Mokṣa* is liberation from the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*).
Health (ārogya) is the absence of disease, characterized by the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātusāmya);

it is the "root," meaning the supreme cause, that is, the primary factor. Therefore, health is the principal cause among the four aims of human life (caturvarga), because one who is afflicted by disease is incapable of accomplishing any purpose whatsoever; thus it has been stated.

"Those who rob him" means those who rob him of health; and this very acquisition of misfortune is what constitutes the robbing of health by diseases. It is not, however, that a disease which has already arisen subsequently robs one of health, because existence and non-existence consist of the mutual absence of one another.

Regarding the phrase "and of a superior life" (*śreyaso jīvitasya ca*): a "superior life" is that which will be described in the *Daśamahāmūlīya* (Sūtra-sthāna 30) as being beneficial and pleasant; it should be understood that [the physician] is one who takes away such a life. As for an "inferior life," because it is not beneficial and is a cause of suffering, it is not worth pursuing; therefore, its taking away is not mentioned here.

In this context, the injury to happiness, welfare, and life is obtained precisely through the injury to *dharma* and the other [ends]. Therefore, we see that by the word "welfare" (*śreyas*), which generally denotes worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), *dharma* and the rest are designated; and by the word "life" (*jīvita*), mere life itself is meant, since life is, in its very nature, something to be accepted by all living beings without qualification. For it is said: "And this was the prayer for the self made by Brahmā: 'May I be long-lived.'"

As for the fact that one seized by extreme suffering desires to give up life: because that suffering, which is to be utterly abandoned, cannot otherwise be relinquished, one wishes to abandon even dear life; yet this is not an obstacle to its own nature. This should be understood as the manifestation of disease, occurring within the practice of the means for achieving Dharma and the other goals.
"Of them" refers to those diseases;
"refuge" means a protector, and he is called Śakra because of his power.

Dhyāna is a specific state of meditative concentration (samādhi); because it is the means for attaining that [concentration], it is called the "dhyāna-eye," just as the eye is the means for perceiving form. The construction is: "With the dhyāna-eye they beheld him," in accordance with the statement, "By that [eye], he, the Lord of the Immortals, will declare the means to tranquility as it truly is.
(Verses 15–17)
Now, among these, he explains how Bharadvāja approached Indra with the words beginning with "Who... and ending with "Lord of Śacī.
By this phrase "Lord of Śacī," Bharadvāja demonstrates that he is capable of attending upon [Indra] even though he is preoccupied with the enjoyment of Śacī;
"arthe" means for the sake of a purpose.

"I shall employ" or "I shall apply myself here" refers precisely to the present purpose; the word *atra* (here) has the sense of *yasmāt* (because), as in the expression "come because of [or from] a good harvest" (*subhikṣamityāgataḥ*), which means "he has come because there is a good harvest."
The term *niyojita* is derived from the *cur*-class with the suffix *ṇic*; it does not imply causation.
By this context, it is shown that there was no instigation because Bharadvāja had a particular eagerness for the traditional knowledge of Āyurveda.

The word *provāca* means he spoke correctly (*samyag uvāca*); the prefix *pra-* is not intended to signify elaboration (*prapañca*), as it has already been stated that [the teaching] was given "in few words" (*padair alpaiḥ*).

To the question "Why did he speak in few words?", he says: "Having perceived the vast intelligence" (*matiṃ buddhvā vipulām iti*). The sense is that because he had approached Bharadvāja, who possessed vast intelligence, he spoke in few words. Furthermore, "intelligence" (*mati*) is figuratively called "vast" (*vipulā*) due to its manifold scope. And this intelligence should be understood here as being "vast" insofar as it is endowed with the desire to hear (*śuśrūṣā*), listening (*śravaṇa*), grasping (*grahaṇa*), retention (*dhāraṇa*), reasoning (*ūha*), refutation (*apoha*), and devotion to the truth (*tattvābhiniveśa*).

In this context, Indra, having perceived Bharadvāja’s intention beforehand through his divine vision, taught the Āyurveda; therefore, the dialogue with Indra and so forth was not shown here by Bharadvāja, or else, although it did occur, the dialogue with Indra and other such details were not written down here for fear of excessive length.
(18–23) He now describes that very Āyurveda as it was taught in concise words, beginning with "hetu" and so forth.

"Knowledge of causes, signs, and medicines" (*hetu-liṅgauṣadha-jñāna*) means that by this [knowledge], causes and so forth are known; the meaning is that whatever is expressible in Ayurveda is included within causes and the rest. By the mention of "cause" (*hetu*), there is the inclusion of both proximate and remote causes of disease. By the mention of "sign" (*liṅga*), the entire sign of both disease and health is expressed; therefore, disease and health are also denoted by the word "sign," because even by those two, that sign is indeed made manifest (*liṅgyate*). For it will be said: "Fever is indeed the single characteristic of those whose roots are irregular undertakings."

"Jvara is said to be of one type [in its primary form], rooted in irregular onset and so forth" (Ni.A.8), and so on; by the mention of "medicines," all wholesome regimens (*pathya*) are included, and the body is subsumed here under both the cause and the symptom; furthermore, because it is the supreme, most excellent refuge (*ayana*) or path for both the healthy and the afflicted, it is called *svasthāturaparāyaṇa*.

Is this Āyurveda, consisting of the knowledge of causes, symptoms, and medicines, something different from the Āyurveda of Brahmā-Buddha, or is it non-different? To this he says: "The Three Sūtras," and so forth.
Even the Grandfather (Brahmā) understood that which consists of three sūtras; Indra taught that to him.
That in which or by which the three—beginning with the cause—are set forth (sūtryante) is called the "Three Sūtras" (trisūtra).
In this context, it is called a *sūtra* because it indicates (*sūcana*) and strings together (*sūtraṇa*) a continuous sequence of meanings.

By this, he demonstrates that the tradition is unimpaired, showing that Indra proclaimed the knowledge of causes, symptoms, and medicines exactly as Brahmā understood it through the *trisūtra*; the word "understood" (*bubudhe*) implies that he did not merely compose it.
Therefore it has been said: "eternal"; the meaning is "constant.
And that constancy is to be explained at the end of the Sūtrasthāna.

Now, he explains how Bharadvāja received the Ayurveda that had been taught: "He, who is infinite... and so forth. That which has no end (*anta*) or limit (*pāra*) is called "infinite-limit" (*anantapāra*). Here, by the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), the word *pāra* refers to the beginning (*ādi*); for the word *pāra* can, depending on the speaker's intention, denote both banks of a river. Alternatively, *ananta* is liberation (*mokṣa*), and *pāra* is the supreme fruit; thus, Ayurveda is "infinite-limit" because its ultimate result is liberation. As he will state: "But medical treatment is final when it is free from worldly motives" (*Śārīrasthāna*, chapter 1).

In this context, "triskandha" refers to that which has three parts (skandhas) consisting of the cause, the means, and the goal, where the ultimate goal is the cause for attaining liberation; and "tanmanāḥ" refers to one whose mind is fixed on the study of Ayurveda itself, where "skandha" denotes either a gross limb or a distinct division.

Because he possesses the excellence of knowledge through reflection (*manana*), he is a sage (*muni*). By this it is intended that, since he is of great intelligence and his mind is fixed upon that [knowledge], he—having taken as his object the three aggregates beginning with the cause (*hetu*) within Āyurveda, which is of infinite extent—practiced it correctly and attained mastery in a short time.
"In a short time" (*acirāt*) means "without delay" (*acireṇa*).

And here, by stating that just as Brahmā understood the *trisūtra* and Indra proclaimed the knowledge of causes, symptoms, and medicines, so too did Bharadvāja understand that *triskandha*, the uncorrupted tradition (*aviplutāgama*) of Āyurveda is demonstrated; therefore, there is no redundancy between the *trisūtra* and the *triskandha*.
By "by that" is meant by the Āyurveda received from Indra;
"immeasurable" (*amita*) means immeasurable as it were, because of its extreme length.

The word "āyus" (life) should be understood here as referring to the knowledge of *rasāyana* (rejuvenation therapy), which is the cause of longevity; for it is by means of this that Bharadvāja will later attain immeasurable life through the application of *rasāyana* (note: he did not practice *rasāyana* prior to the teaching of Āyurveda by the sages). Alternatively, it should be understood that Bharadvāja obtained immeasurable life at that very moment due to the power of the merit (*dharma*) generated from having studied Āyurveda for the benefit of all living beings. This is what was "heard. Furthermore, if the reading is "tam" (him), then it means "without leaving anything out," that is, in its entirety.
Having studied Āyurveda, he immediately gave it to the sages for those who desire long life for themselves and for living beings.
"Desiring long life" refers to both [the sages] and living beings.

The "eye of knowledge" (*jñānacakṣus*) is either for the sake of knowledge or is itself the form of knowledge. By means of that eye of knowledge, which is grasped through that *Āyurveda*, what did they see? To this he says: "And the common [nature]," and so forth.
Furthermore, the definition of these six categories (*padārtha*), which possess universal forms, will follow later; therefore, this must be explained in that very place.

The word "that" refers to the general [category] and so forth as taught in the Tantra; "method" refers to the form consisting of the avoidance of what is unwholesome and the adoption of what is wholesome; "bliss" means happiness.
"Supreme" means not overcome by suffering; "not fleeting" means not transitory.
With the words beginning with *atha*, the author demonstrates that Ātreya—who was a disciple of Bharadvāja and bore the alternative name Punarvasu—was the teacher of Agniveśa and the others.

On this point, some consider Bharadvāja and Ātreya to be one and the same person; however, that is not so, because Ātreya is never mentioned by the name Bharadvāja anywhere in this treatise (*tantra*). Furthermore, in the *Hārīta-saṃhitā*, Bharadvāja is mentioned as the teacher of Ātreya and the others, starting with the passage: "I studied [this] from Śakra," and continuing: "From me, moreover, the seven great sages (maharṣis), ending with Ātreya and the rest, learned the three-fold thread (tri-sūtra) which has three purposes."
Regarding what was stated by Vāgbhaṭa in the passage ending with "from Ātreya [it went to] the sage Hārīta," namely: "Brahmā, having remembered the Veda of longevity, taught it to Prajāpati;

he [taught it] to the two Aśvins; they [taught it] to the Thousand-eyed One (Indra); he [taught it] to the sages such as the sons of Atri" (Vā.Sū.A.1)—this [statement] that Ātreya was a disciple of Indra is to be reconciled with the fact that his status as a disciple of Indra will be mentioned later by the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the *Rasāyana-pāda* of the *Āyurvedasamutthāna*.

In that regard, it must be stated that Āyurveda was subsequently taught by Indra to the great sages. One who is devoted to friendliness (*maitrī*) has friendliness as their primary quality; and friendliness is the perception of all living beings as being like oneself.

The "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) of the Buddha refers to his excellence (*utkarṣa*); because of this distinction of the Buddha, there are their respective *tantras*, namely those marked by their own individual names, such as the *Bhelatantra*, the *Jatūkarṇatantra*, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "and [the treatises] were composed," the word "treatises" (*tantrāṇi*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Those such as Agniveśa and others whose deeds consist of the composition of the meritorious treatise of Āyurveda are "those of meritorious deeds" (*puṇyakarmāṇaḥ*); the phrase "desirous of the welfare of all beings" is an epithet of those of meritorious deeds, namely Agniveśa and the others. Alternatively, it may be an epithet of the assembly of sages (*ṛṣisaṅgha*).
The word *sādhu* is exclusively neuter because it does not abandon its original gender (*ajahalliṅgatayā*). For example, as in "the Vedas are authoritative" (*vedāḥ pramāṇam*).
However, some read *anukrośam* (compassion) as neuter as well, in accordance with the neuter gender of the qualifier *sādhu*.
[It is used] in the sense of praise, as in "Ah, how excellent! (*aho sādhu*).
"Smooth" (*snigdha*) means auspicious due to its lack of intensity and its quality of refreshing;
by such auspicious characteristics as "the wind blew," it is shown that even the gods have, in effect, approved the composition of this present tantra.
"Deities of knowledge" (*jñānadevatā*) refers to the deities who preside over knowledge.

Therefore, it is established that Agniveśa and the others already possessed intellect (*buddhi*) and the other faculties prior to the composition of the treatise; however, following the completion of the work, the deities of intellect and the rest entered them with reverence.
"Success" (*siddhi*) means the knowledge of the means and the end to be achieved;

"fame" (*kīrti*) means the knowledge required for speaking—that is, the capacity for eloquent discourse—and not fame in the form of renown, because the latter is of the nature of ignorance (*ajñāna*); furthermore, it is the deities of knowledge who are being referred to here.
"For existence" means for stability; that is to say, for life unafflicted by disease. "Foundation" (pratiṣṭhā) refers to remaining in a state of being worthy of reliance by people.

Now, while providing an exposition on Āyurveda, [the author] demonstrates the subject matter of Āyurveda: "The beneficial and the harmful," and so forth. Beneficial and harmful constitute "beneficial-and-harmful. Likewise, because it is associated with pleasure, it is "pleasure" (*sukha*); because it is associated with pain, it is "pain" (*duḥkha*). These four types will be explained in the *Daśamahāmūlīya* chapter by the passage beginning with "Therein, [regarding] the bodily and mental... and ending with "The harmful is the opposite of that" (Sūtra-sthāna 30). The "beneficial and harmful" of that [life] refers to what is wholesome and unwholesome for life (*āyus*).

And "measure" (*māna*) refers specifically to lifespan (*āyus*); and that measure is to be explained in the *Indriya-sthāna* through the characteristics of morbidity (*vikṛti*), such as being monthly or bimonthly, and likewise in the *Śārīra-sthāna* through the characteristics of normalcy (*prakṛti*), starting with: "This is the characteristic of long-lived youths" (*śā.a.8*).
Furthermore, "lifespan" (*āyus*) in its essential nature is what will be described [in the *Sūtrasthāna*] with the words: "The conjunction of body, senses, mind, and self," and so forth.
By this, it is stated that [this treatise] is called *Āyurveda* because "it makes known lifespan" (*āyur vedayati*).
In this context, by the author of the treatise, only the sense of "knowledge" is intended;
as he will state in the *Daśamahāmūlīya* chapter: "It is called Āyurveda because it makes known that [life-span] (*āyur vidayati*).
The other meanings of the root *vid*, such as "acquisition" and so forth, are not mentioned here, because they are not directly produced from the Āyurveda—this is the underlying intention.
Regarding the term *āyurveda*, the first member of the compound, *āyus* (life), is explained as follows: "The body," and so forth.

The body is that which consists of the transformations of the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) and serves as the locus for the experience of the self (*ātman*). The senses are the eyes and the rest. *Sattva* is the mind (*manas*). The self is the knower who links [cognitions] together. The "union" (*yoga*) is their conjunction, governed by correct perception.
Although the sense organs are indeed included by the very mention of the body, they are stated separately again because of their predominance.

Furthermore, although this conjunction is momentary due to the momentariness of the body—the possessor of the conjunction—it is nevertheless spoken of as a unity because it is established as a continuum (*santāna*).
He states the synonyms for that lifespan, beginning with "the sustainer" (*dhārī*), and so forth.
It is called *dhāri* because it sustains the body and does not allow it to become putrid;
it is called *jīvita* because it enlivens or sustains the vital breaths (*prāṇa*);
it is called *nityaga* because it moves constantly through the momentary nature of the body.

It is called *anubandha* (the bond) because it binds life (*āyus*) by way of conjunction with successive bodies and so forth; thus, "life" is expressed by synonyms that denote the same meaning. Although life is not denoted anywhere by the two words *nityaga* (ever-present) and *anubandha*, nevertheless, these two designations should be understood as being for the purpose of making known the properties of ever-presence and being a bond. As for the designation *dhārī* (the sustainer), it will appear in the tenth chapter on the Great Roots (*daśamahāmūlīya*).

[Objection: But surely, later on [in Sūtra 30], he will provide the definition of life-force (*āyus*) as "the persistence of consciousness" (*caitanyānuvṛtti*); why then is it stated here that it is "the conjunction of body, senses, mind, and self"? [Reply: We say: the persistence of consciousness produced by the conjunction of body, senses, mind, and self is stated in the *Daśamahāmūlīya* chapter as the definition [of life-force] because it is invariably concomitant with the aforementioned conjunction and because it is manifest. However, in the ultimate sense, life-force is simply the form of the conjunction of the body and so forth. In the absence of such a conjunction, death occurs, which consists in the cessation of life-force; for in a dead body, due to the absence of the mind (*cetas*), there is an absence of the conjunction that constitutes life-force.
42. "Of that," and so forth;
it is called "Veda" because it causes one to know (vedayati).
"According to the opinion of those who know the Vedas" means it is honored by those who know the Vedas.
Now, he explains why the Veda characterized as Āyurveda is the most meritorious and is honored by those who know the Vedas, beginning with the words "it will be stated," and so forth.

"Yat" means "because"; thus it is said: because other [scriptures] such as the Ṛgveda and others mostly speak of matters beneficial for the next world, they are meritorious; and this Āyurveda is most meritorious because it will declare that which is beneficial for humans in both worlds—that which is the means for longevity, health, and the accomplishment of dharma—and therefore it is exceedingly meritorious and honored by those who know the Vedas. Some read "vakṣyate yaḥ" (that which will be declared), and in that case too, it should be explained as containing a reason (hetugarbha).

One should understand that Āyurveda is the most meritorious because it bestows life; for that which bestows life, which is the means for achieving the four aims of human existence (*caturvarga*), is indeed the supreme among all things.
And it is said: "Indeed, no gift excels the gift of life" (Ci. A. 1).

Now, since the subject matter of Āyurveda has been introduced by way of its general categories and so forth, and because the general category was mentioned first, and because the causes and other factors to be explained in Āyurveda are rooted in the knowledge of that general category, he points out the general category first,
beginning with "sarvadā" (always), meaning at all times, both in the eternal and the situational.

In the phrase "of all entities" (*sarvabhāvānām*), the word "all" (*sarva*) signifies the totality. "Entities" (*bhāvāḥ*) means those that exist or possess being—namely, substances (*dravya*), qualities (*guṇa*), and actions (*karman*)—and not those that come into existence or are produced. If it were the latter, then eternal atoms such as those of earth, as well as universals (*sāmānya*) and the effects consisting of the growth of binary atomic compounds of earth and so forth, would not be included. Furthermore, the universal has the definition that will be stated later: "The universal is that which produces unity," and so on. "Growth" (*vṛddhi*) means increase; the cause of that is the "cause of growth" (*vṛddhikāraṇa*).

And this "commonality" (*sāmānya*) has been described as the cause of growth by virtue of being the characteristic of the substance of meat and so forth, which is the cause of growth; for the commonality, in the form of a genus such as "meat-ness," does not itself become the cause of growth. If that were the case, then just as the commonality of "meat-ness" exists in the meat that serves as food for the one who grows, it would likewise exist in the bodily constituent (*dhātu*) that is to be nourished; consequently, due to the constant connection with "meat-ness," even those who do not eat meat would have to grow by means of meat. Therefore, it is stated that the commonality is the cause of growth by way of being the characteristic of the cause of growth.
For this very reason, it is stated even in the Vaiśeṣika [sūtra]: "The three are neither effects nor causes.
Here, the phrase "of the three" refers to generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*).

However, for those who, taking "generality" to be identical [to substance], designate substance and so forth by the term "generality," nothing would be said by this [sūtra] regarding the "generality" mentioned in the passage beginning with "Generality and particularity" (VS 1.2.3); thus, the section would be rendered irrelevant.

Furthermore, this state of being a cause of increase is not the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of generality (*sāmānya*); rather, it is an exposition (*nirdeśa*) by means of a property useful for Āyurveda. As for the definition, he will indeed provide it later with the words, "Generality is that which produces unity. In the same way, regarding substance (*dravya*) and the others, after the initial enumeration (*uddeśa*), he will provide the exposition with the words, "The elements beginning with space and the self," and thereafter he will provide the definition with the words, "That in which action and qualities reside," and so forth.

Furthermore, the fact that a general [quality] acts as a cause for increase should be understood to occur only when there is no opposing cause; therefore, it is logical that the acidity and other qualities residing in *āmalaka* and similar fruits do not increase the acidity and other qualities residing in *pitta*, because they are opposed by the specific power (*prabhāva*) of the coldness inherent in *āmalaka*.
This same principle should be understood to apply elsewhere regarding substances that alleviate the three *doṣas*.

In this context, it is stated that the commonality (*sāmānya*) is the cause of increase, but it is not stated that the commonality alone is the cause of increase. Therefore, the increase of intelligence and fire even from ghee—which is not similar [to them]—is established solely by way of its specific power (*prabhāva*), as it has been said: "Ghee produces fire and intelligence. Likewise, the increase of wind (*vāta*) through mental anxiety, and the increase of semen through intention and the application of aphrodisiacs to the feet, and so forth, are established by way of their specific power.

When it is stated here that "the general property (*sāmānya*) is the cause of increase," it is understood as "of the similar" (*samānasya*). For the nature of flesh (*māṃsatva*) is not a general property with respect to blood; rather, because it generates a distinct cognition, it is indeed a particular (*viśeṣa*). Now, since the ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣa*) mentioned by the Vaiśeṣikas are of no use in this science of medicine (*cikitsā*), and because they possess the capacity to differentiate through their specific properties, [the author] speaks of "general-particulars" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) themselves as the causes of decrease—starting with the phrase "cause of decrease" (*hrāsahetu*) and so forth.
Here too, the phrase "of all entities at all times" (*sarvadā sarvabhāvānām*) should be applied.
Diminution (*hrāsa*) means decrease (*apacaya*).
That which is distinguished, or that from which something is excluded, is a "particular" (*viśeṣa*).

Thus, the universal itself—namely, the nature of being a *gavedhuka* grass—is a particular with respect to meat and so forth. For the *gavedhuka* is common (*samāna*) in its quality as a *gavedhuka* relative to other individual *gavedhuka* plants, but it is a particular because it is excluded from meat; for the nature of being a *gavedhuka* does not exist in meat.

In this way, "meat-ness" (māṃsatva) is a generality (sāmānya) because it is inclusive relative to other types of meat, whereas it is a particularity (viśeṣa) relative to blood and so forth, because meats are excluded from one another. Here too, the state of being a cause of decrease should be understood as being like a generality, insofar as it is characterized by substances and other factors that cause decrease.
