Likewise, the state of being a cause of decrease should also be understood—provided there is no contradiction—by the same logic applied to generalities. Therefore, even though sour tamarind (*nikuca*) and similar substances are contrary to *vāta* and other humors, their failure to pacify *vāta* and the rest is to be understood solely due to the unwholesome potency (*prabhāva*) of the substance, despite its qualities such as unctuousness (*snigdhatva*).

In this context, "specificity" (*viśeṣa*) is intended to mean a "contradictory specificity" (*viruddhaviśeṣa*); for he will later teach that very contradictory specificity as the cause of decrease in various places. For example: "The increase of all [doshas] occurs through similar [factors], while the opposite occurs through dissimilar ones" (Vāgbhaṭa Sūtra-sthāna 1); likewise, "by those with contrary qualities, provided they are applied according to place, measure, and time" (Sūtra-sthāna 1), and so forth; similarly, "the wind is pacified by substances with contrary qualities" (Sūtra-sthāna 1), and so forth; and likewise it is stated in the *Jatūkarṇa*: "The increase of all entities occurs through similar [factors], and their decrease through the opposite."

Although a non-conflicting specific quality (*aviruddhaviśeṣa*) is not a cause for either decrease or increase—just as the earth’s non-hot-and-cold touch does not increase nor decrease the coldness of the wind—nevertheless, because it fails to produce equilibrium when the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are being depleted by fire, it becomes a cause of decrease. For when substances that are not homologous (*asamāna*) are consumed, a decrease is indeed observed in perishable entities due to the absence of a replenishing cause; just as, for example, the water flowing downstream decreases when a dam is built across its previous course, thereby reducing the volume of water in the region further downstream.

And seeing that such a thing occurs even when there is the application of non-contradictory particulars, the Teacher has stated here [the cause of decrease] by means of the universal alone. The word "ca" (and) connects this with the phrase "the particular is the cause of decrease for all entities.
Now, one might ask: are the universal and the particular, even if unrelated, the causes of increase and decrease? He says, "But the activity of both... to show that it is not so.

The word "cause" (kāraṇa) is to be supplied [as the predicate] for both the general and the particular; "activity" (pravṛtti) means setting into motion, that is to say, connection with the body. Such activity is the cause for the increase and decrease of the general and particular elements (dhātu).
The particle "tu" (but/then) is used for emphasis; by it, he shows that the general and the particular do not perform their own functions when they are not connected [to the body].

Or rather, what is the appropriate activity? It is the activity of the *dhātus*, which is to say, the equilibrium of the *dhātus*; that [activity] is "to be performed" (*kāryā*)—this is the ellipsis—with respect to both the general and the specific.

By this it is stated that from the use of purely general [substances], there is an increase of the *dhātus* leading to *dhātu*-disequilibrium; and from the use of purely specific [substances], there is a decrease of the *dhātus* leading to *dhātu*-disequilibrium; whereas from the simultaneous use of substances that are both general and specific, the activity results in the form of *dhātu*-equilibrium. The word "but" (*tu*) excludes the prima facie view characterized by the use of a single substance.

44. Now, what are the characteristics of that universal (*sāmānya*), or what are the characteristics of that particular (*viśeṣa*)? To this he says: "The universal," and so forth. "That which produces the notion of unity" means that which produces the cognition of oneness. That universal is [defined as] that which, in multiple individual instances of cows and the like existing in different places and times, produces a uniform cognition of a single form, such as "this is a cow, this is a cow. That is the universal.
The point is this: for a non-erroneous cognition of a single form does not arise with respect to distinct individuals unless there is an undifferentiated universal (*sāmānya*) of a single nature.

Furthermore, even in cases such as "this is a cook, this is a cook," or likewise "this is white, this is white," where a cognition of a single form arises due to a universal of action, quality, and so forth, even there the universal residing in those identical actions, qualities, and so on, is the cause of the determination of a single form.
For the action that exists in one cook does not exist in another cook; rather, it is of the same class (*tajjātīyā*).

Therefore, even in that case, the cause for the determination of oneness is the commonality of action (*kriyāsāmānya*). As for the statement "the characteristic of a particular (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*) is that which produces differentiation," this means it produces a cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛttabuddhi*). Consequently, what is called "cowness" (*gotva*) as a universal because it produces a single cognition in relation to other individual cows, is said to be a "particular" with respect to horses and the like, because it produces a cognition of exclusion toward them. Thus it is explained.

Therefore, "fleshness" (*māṃsatva*) serves as the cause for the growth of flesh in relation to other flesh, because it is common to them; however, that same "fleshness," by virtue of its specific form, becomes the cause of decrease in relation to *vāta*. But in relation to blood and the other [dhātus], it is not such a cause of decrease, since it is a non-contradictory particularity; rather, due to the commonality of qualities (*guṇasāmānya*), flesh also acts as a promoter of blood and the others.

To the question, "How does a universal (*sāmānya*) produce a single, non-deviating cognition across multiple individuals? he says: "For 'having a common object' (*tulyārthatā*)," etc. "Having a common object" means the state of being connected to an object whose nature is a single universal.

The meaning of this is as follows: because there exists a relationship with a single form among distinct individuals, it is logical that a single cognition—which rests upon multiple objects—is possible despite the difference between those individuals;

however, the case of "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) is the opposite. For "particularity" consists in having unequal referents; thus, it is shown that a separate cognition for a cow and an elephant is indeed appropriate, since their respective referents—cowness and elephant-ness—are of unequal nature.

Others, however, explain it as follows: there are three types of *sāmānya* (commonality) and three types of *viśeṣa* (specificity); namely, those pertaining to substance (*dravya*), qualities (*guṇa*), and actions (*karman*). Among these, "always" (*sarvadā*) and so forth refers to the commonality of substance; "commonality produces unity" (*sāmānyamekatvakaram*) refers to the commonality of qualities—for instance, although milk and semen belong to different classes, the commonality of their qualities such as sweetness produces a sense of unity between them; this same principle should be applied to specificities as well. Furthermore, "having a similar purpose" (*tulyārthatā*) and so forth describes the commonality of action: for the action of "lying down" (*āsya*) is not identical to phlegm (*śleṣman*) itself, but because it performs the same functional activity (*arthakriyā*) as substances that increase phlegm—such as water and other *kapha*-increasing items—the action of lying down is also said to be "similar to phlegm. This should be understood to apply similarly to actions such as sleeping and the like.

This very point has been refuted by Bhaṭṭāraka Haricandra himself; for since the threefold universal is obtained by the definition itself through the phrase "at all times" and so forth, it follows that in this position, such statements as "the universal is the cause of oneness" would be inexpressible.

Others, however, observe that there are three kinds of similarity: absolute similarity (*atyantasāmānya*), intermediate similarity (*madhyasāmānya*), and partial similarity (*ekadeśasāmānya*). Among these, "at all times" and so forth expresses absolute similarity; "similarity is that which produces oneness" expresses intermediate similarity; and "for there is equality of meaning" and so forth expresses partial similarity. This enumeration of a threefold division is neither very useful nor consistent with the definition [of the subject], and thus does not inspire much confidence.

Some maintain that there are two types of *sāmānya* (commonality): that which functions in both [the nourished and the nourisher], and that which functions in only one. In this context, meat increases meat because it possesses the commonality of functioning in both. Indeed, "meatness" (*māṃsatva*) functions in both the thing to be nourished and the nourisher, and is thus a commonality functioning in both. However, that which functions in only one is as follows: clarified butter (*ghṛta*) produces fire; likewise, activities such as running produce wind (*vāta*); and likewise, substances such as *āsa* produce phlegm (*kapha*). All of these are not identical to the thing to be increased, but rather increase it through their specific power (*prabhāva*). And this power consists precisely of the commonalities of being "clarified butter," "running," and so forth. Since that [power] takes the form of a commonality functioning in only one, they assert that even here, it is indeed the commonality that is the cause of increase.

But in this [opponent's] position, since the universal (*sāmānya*)—which does not subsist in either [the similar or the dissimilar]—is nothing other than a particular (*viśeṣa*), it follows that both the similar and the dissimilar would be causes of increase; thus, nothing at all would have been said regarding the universal.

In our view, however, the universal is indeed a cause of increase, and so the universal is restricted by its status as a cause of increase. But it is not restricted such that increase must have the universal as its sole cause; therefore, even from the dissimilar, increase occurs without fault.

As for what is said—that in this treatise there is no basis for the increase [of a tissue] through similarity of action (*karma-sāmānya*), because the wind (*vāyu*) is not increased by running; for this very reason, the Teacher has stated similarity of substance (*dravya-sāmānya*) in such passages as, "flesh is nourished by flesh" (Śā. A. 6), and similarly stated similarity of quality (*guṇa-sāmānya*) in such passages as, "the consumption of food-transformations possessing similar qualities" (Śā. A. 6); however, similarity of action was not stated in this way, for the statement is: "Whatever action increases a particular constituent (*dhātu*), that should be practiced" (Śā. A. 6); in that case, no inclusion of similarity was made.

To this we reply: the general inclusion [of sleep and so forth] has been omitted because action (*karman*) is generally the cause of increase through its very power, and not because of an absence of the generality of action itself. For the increase of the wind (*vāta*), which possesses motion, is produced by a body that possesses motion and is engaged in exercise and the like; whereas its decrease occurs through its lack of motion.

As for sleep and the rest, although they are not mentioned by the definition to be stated later—“in conjunction and in disjunction”—they are nevertheless designated by the word ‘action’ (*karman*) due to technical usage in the treatise.

In this context, sleep is said to cause the increase of *kapha*—which is being accumulated solely from its own causes—by acting as an inhibitor of bodily movements and other factors that cause the depletion of *kapha*; however, sleep does not directly produce the increase of *śleṣman*.
This same principle should be considered regarding the mouth and other [organs].
But where it is impossible to conceive of such a causal mechanism, there one must simply describe it as a specific potency (*prabhāva*).

Now, it may be argued that meat increases flesh by virtue of its general nature, and it also diminishes wind (vāta) by virtue of its specific properties; how then can meat simultaneously perform these two contradictory functions? For Devadatta does not fashion a jar at the very same moment he fashions a staff.

It is not so; this principle applies to those who possess action (*kriyāvat*), not to those who lack action. For instance, sound simultaneously initiates many other sounds at one and the same time, and likewise, fire simultaneously performs both illumination and burning. Therefore, it has been stated by the Teacher: "Consequently, a medicine being properly administered brings about the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) that are deficient or excessive; it diminishes what is in excess and replenishes what is deficient" (Śārīra-sthāna, Chapter 6).

As for what is said—that food possessing qualities identical to those of an increasing *dhātu*, or of one who is aged, or of one with many *doṣas*, is not a cause of increase; likewise, in summer, there is no increase of *kapha* even with sweet and similar [qualities] that are identical [to it]—in these cases, because obstructing factors such as old age, the state of having many *doṣas*, and the heat of summer are present, similarity does not produce increase. The established principle is that in the absence of an opposing factor, similarity is the cause of increase; therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Or rather, growth certainly occurs for the elderly and others through food that is similar [to their own constitution]; however, in a person where wasting is being induced by an extremely powerful cause of wasting, that growth is not perceived.

And in this case, it is only the similarity of substance (*dravya-sāmānya*) among the tissues (*dhātu*), which are themselves of the nature of substances, that acts as their nourisher, not the similarity of qualities (*guṇa-sāmānya*), because qualities do not initiate the formation of substances.

However, by virtue of the commonality of qualities (*guṇasāmānya*), a substance (*dravya*) that serves as the substratum for those qualities is inferred; and that substance becomes an increaser of the constituent element (*dhātu*). For example, having observed qualities such as dryness (*rūkṣa*) and so forth, *citraka* is inferred to be predominant in *vāyu*; when that *citraka* is used, it increases *vāyu*. Qualities, however, increase [the element] by generating qualities of the same kind, and it has already been stated previously that commonality is a cause of increase by definition, but is not a direct cause of increase. This is also the case with specific properties (*viśeṣa*).

And this doctrine of generalities and particulars has been stated here merely by way of those principles useful for Āyurveda, for fear of excessive prolixity; its full elaboration, however, is to be understood from the Vaiśeṣika [system].

Having now explained the general and specific [categories], and since the qualities (*guṇa*) must be discussed in accordance with the order of enumeration, [the author] speaks—beginning with "sattva"—to describe the conjunction of *sattva*, the self (*ātman*), and the body, which is the primary factor among the qualities and the beneficiary of Ayurveda. Alternatively, it may be that by means of the general and specific categories alone, the causes (*hetu*), signs (*liṅga*), and remedies (*auṣadha*) have been shown; for since everything everywhere possesses both general and specific characteristics, it is precisely these that constitute the subject matter (*tantra*) when investigated as cause and sign. Furthermore, the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) has not yet been stated; therefore, he states the conjunction of *sattva* and so forth as the substratum for the causes and other factors, beginning with "sattva."
"Sattva" refers to the mind; the word "ca" (and) is used for conjunction.
Since the number is already obtained from the very mention of the things to be numbered, the word "trayam" (triad) is intended to include them only as a combined group.
The word "this" (*etad*) refers to the description just mentioned:
the triple-staff (*tridaṇḍa*), which is held together by their mutual conjunction and serves to support vessels such as water-pots.

Just as this [staff] cannot remain standing if any one of its parts is missing, so too it is stated that the stability of the world cannot exist if even one among the qualities of *sattva* and the others is absent.
It is called *loka* because it shines forth (*ālokata*) from the world (*loka*); by this term, the moving collection of living beings is meant here.
Because it stands through conjunction—that is, through a mutual support—it performs its own causal function and does not fall apart.
However, the sense organs (*indriya*) are not mentioned separately here, as they are already included by the mention of the body (*śarīra*).
In that regard, "everything is established" means that in that world, the fruits of karma and so forth are situated; as he will say: "Herein is the fruit of karma, and herein is knowledge;
herein are delusion, pleasure, pain, life, death, and selfhood" (Śāstrāvatāra 1).
That person refers to those three—sattva and the rest—which are called "the person."

In this regard, although the triad beginning with *sattva* is neuter in gender, nevertheless, because of the inclusion of the gender that will be mentioned later as "the male" (*pumān*), the masculine designation "he" (*sa*) is used; just as in [Pāṇini's rule] "ṇeraṇau yatkarma ṇau cet sa kartānādhyāne" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.67), and so forth.

Furthermore, although the present tense was employed in the phrase "this" (*etat*), nevertheless, its designation as past by means of the pronoun "he" (*sa*) should be understood as not contradictory, since pronouns can denote all times—as the grammarians say: "Whether in the perceptible or the imperceptible, whether in proximity or at a distance..."

If it is argued that "the term *sarvanāman* (pronoun) is employed by the learned for these meanings," [the author] states the reason why that [tantra] is considered the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of knowledge— just as [it is the locus] of consciousness— in the passage beginning with "for the sake of that" (*tadarthaṃ hi*).

"For the sake of that" means for the purpose of assisting it; by this, he shows that the activity directed toward it has the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) rather than the sense of a substratum (*ādhāra*). Here, "existence" (*sattva*) is mentioned first, because the activity of the self and the body is dependent upon it, as it has been said: "The mind is insentient yet possesses activity, while the Supreme is the sentient agent; the activity of that Self is designated [only] when it is joined with the mind" (Śā. A. 1).

Life span was previously described by the passage beginning with "the body" (śarīra), whereas by the passage beginning with "sattva and the self" (ātman), the person who is the substratum of the treatise is being discussed; thus, there is no redundancy here. Furthermore, it should be explained that by the mention of "self," the intellect, ego, and so forth are included, and by the mention of "body," the senses and their objects connected to the body are included.

Now, having bypassed the description of qualities (*guṇa*), which was due in order, the author points out the substances (*dravya*) and thereby asserts the primacy of substance as the substratum of qualities. Furthermore, by mentioning qualities first in the aphorism "Generality and Particularity" (*sāmānyaṃ ca viśeṣaṃ ca*) and so forth, it is demonstrated that qualities such as taste (*rasa*) and the rest are generally the agents of action (*kārmuka*) in this treatise. For this very reason, in the chapter on Ātreya and Bhadrakāpya (Sūtra 26), he will describe all the qualities and actions of a substance by way of its sweet and other tastes. Moreover, life itself—the most primary of all things—is of the nature of the quality of conjunction (*saṃyoga*); thus, the mention of "quality" occurs there [in the definition of *ātman*] first, and that quality of conjunction has already been stated at the outset in the passage beginning with "Existence is the self" (*sattvam ātmā*). However, among specific qualities (*viśeṣa-guṇa*), substance is primary; therefore, the substances are mentioned—beginning with "earth and the others" (*khādīni*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "khādīni" (ether and the rest), why is the *ātman* not mentioned first, even though it is the primary [subject]? It is said in reply: because in this context, the body is the primary subject as the locus of disease and health, only the ether and other elements that constitute it are mentioned, and not the *ātman*, since the latter is changeless (*nirvikāra*). For there is the statement: "But the supreme *ātman* is changeless" (Sūtra, Chapter 1), and so forth. Furthermore, the elements beginning with ether are stated in the sequence "The great elements are ether, air, fire, water, and earth" (Śārīra, Chapter 1); these elements are mentioned here by looking ahead to what follows, whereas among the *ātman* and the others, the more venerable is mentioned first.

"Dravyasaṅgraha" means the compendium (*saṅkṣepa*) of effect-substances (*kāryadravya*), which are divided into innumerable varieties such as hands, feet, *harītakī*, *trivṛtā*, and so forth, by way of their causes.
He states the systematic classification of all effect-substances in the verse beginning with "sendriyam" and ending with "nirindriyam";
here, in the word "nirindriya," the prefix "niḥ" signifies absence, as in the expression "nirmakṣikam" (free from flies).

In this context, although it is understood through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) that "that which possesses sense-faculties is conscious" implies "that which lacks sense-faculties is unconscious," the explicit statement of the latter is nevertheless necessary. This is because such an implication is not invariably certain (*anaikāntikatva*). For example, while sleeping during the day and so forth are prohibited for one suffering from a new fever, it might follow by implication that they are permitted once the fever has subsided; yet this is not the case, as those practices remain prohibited even then. Therefore, for the benefit of disciples of three types of intellectual capacity, even what could be inferred is stated directly. As the masters of logic say: "Direct instruction is better than [relying on] an explanation."

Although it is the self alone that is conscious, and neither the body nor the mind—as it has been stated: "Since the self possesses consciousness, it is therefore designated as the agent" (Śāstradīpikā 1)—nevertheless, like the heat of water, even the body and other such things are conscious through inherence in a conjoined entity (*saṃyuktasamavāya*). This indeed is the consciousness of the self: namely, the possession of knowledge when there is contact with the sense organs; it is not the consciousness of the self in its isolated state. As it has been stated: "The self is the knower; however, knowledge proceeds for it through connection with the instruments" (Śāstradīpikā 1).

In this context, it should be understood that even trees and such possess sentience by virtue of having sense organs (*sendriyatva*). For instance: from the way the sun revolves, the sight of the *sūryabhaktā* plant is inferred as it turns accordingly; likewise, the *lavalī* becomes laden with fruit upon hearing the thundering of clouds; the *bījapūraka* also becomes exceedingly fruitful through the scent of the fat of jackals and other animals; and from the abundance of fruit on mango trees after being sprinkled with fish-fat, their sense of taste is inferred. Furthermore, the touch of the *aśoka* tree—when it has put forth buds—is inferred from its pleasure at being struck by the soles of the feet of a passionate woman. And tradition (*smṛti*) confirms this inference, as in: "He who, having been saluted by a Brahmin, does not bestow a blessing..."

“A tree grows in the cremation ground, frequented by vultures and herons”; likewise: “Various kinds of trees and shrubs, as well as species of grass, grow right there, covered by darkness in the form of unrighteousness due to the cause of karma;
these possess internal consciousness and are endowed with pleasure and pain.”
“Thus, these destinies, beginning with that of Brahmā, have been declared as the limit” (Manusmṛti 1.50).
Likewise, the author of the Tantra will speak of living beings that conform to trees; therefore, by means of reasoning supported by scripture, trees are sentient.
Now, in order to specify the qualities (*guṇa*), he says "sārthā" and so forth;
by this, the three kinds of particular (*vaiśeṣika*), general (*sāmānya*), and mental (*ātma*) qualities are indicated.
Among these, the objects (*artha*) are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
As it has been said: "Objects such as sound and so forth are to be known as the spheres, the domains, and the qualities" (*Śāstrāvatāra* 1).
These, moreover, are the Vaiśeṣika [categories]; for sound belongs primarily to space alone, touch primarily to air alone, and likewise form and the other [qualities] to fire and the rest.
Furthermore, the perception of the qualities of one element in another occurs due to the penetration of one primary element into another.
For there is the statement: "The posterior is pervaded by the prior" (Nyāyadarśana, 3.1.66).

However, the teachers and others [enumerate] twenty qualities—namely, heavy, light, cold, hot, unctuous, dry, dull, sharp, stable, mobile, soft, hard, clear, viscous, smooth, rough, gross, subtle, dense, and liquid—and these are general qualities because they are common to earth and the other elements.
These [qualities] are listed separately from the *para* (supreme) and others in the *Yajja-puruṣīya* chapter because they are primarily utilized in Āyurveda:

*buddhi* (intellect), which is synonymous with *jñāna* (knowledge); by this term, specific forms of intellect such as memory (*smṛti*), consciousness (*cetana*), fortitude (*dhṛti*), and ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) are included;

those whose enumeration ends with effort (*prayatna*) are called "ending with effort" (*prayatnānta*); by this, desire (*icchā*), aversion (*dveṣa*), pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), and effort (*prayatna*) are included.
For there is this statement: "Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, effort, consciousness, resolve, intellect, memory, and egoism are the marks of the Supreme Self" (Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.5).

Here, consciousness and the others are included by the very mention of "intellect" (buddhi); however, in the Śārīraka [Sūtra], consciousness and the rest are listed separately as they serve as distinct indicators of the Self.
And this must be explained in that very same place,
as in the case of [the categories] beginning with "far" (para): "Priority and posteriority, conjunction, number, and also disjunction, separateness, and furthermore dimension."
"Formative activity (saṃskāra) and practice (abhyāsa)— these qualities beginning with 'parā' have been declared" (Sūtra 2.26).
Although these are general qualities, they are mentioned at the end because they are not as essential [to the primary goal] and because of the predominance of the intellect (buddhi).
"Proktāḥ" means they have been specifically described as possessing particular qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) and so forth.
He explains the action that has come down through tradition, beginning with "effort" (*prayatna*) and so forth:

effort (*prayatana*) is "effort" (*prayatna*), which is indeed the primary [action] of the self. As it was explained in the rule "Vowels produced in the same place and with the same effort are homogeneous" (*Pāṇini Aṣṭādhyāyī* 1.1.9), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) expresses a variety of types.
By this, there is an exclusion of all actions produced by the heaviness of the *saṃskāras* and so forth.
Although "movement" (*ceṣṭita*) is said to be the activity of a living being, nevertheless, here "action" (*kriyā*) is intended in its general sense.

Since all types of karma would already be included by the term "movement" alone, and since the prohibition of actions such as vomiting would already be established, the inclusion of the word "effort" (*prayatna*) and so forth is for the purpose of indicating that [the definition] pervades even those karmas consisting of extremely subtle effort.

Others, however, say that "prayatnādi" means "having effort as its cause," and they state that the mention of "effort" (prayatna) is an indicative mark for the cause in general; by this, actions whose effects are gravity and so forth are also included.

Furthermore, the word "prayatna" is seen in Āyurveda as a synonym for action (*karman*), according to the statement: "Activity (*pravṛtti*), however, is purposeful movement; that itself is action (*kriyā*), effort (*prayatna*), and the undertaking of an effect" (Vi. A. 8). 49
He states [the definition of] inherence: "Inherence," and so forth.
This very mention of inherence is its definition; therefore, its definition need not be formulated again later in the definitions of substance and the other categories.

"Inherence" (*samavāya*) is the designation of the definiendum; "non-separateness" (*apṛthagbhāva*) is the definition. Non-separateness means inseparability (*ayutasiddhi*), that is to say, existing together, as in the case of part and whole, quality and possessor of quality, action and agent of action, and generality and possessor of generality. For the whole and so forth are not perceived apart from the parts and so forth. Specifying this very non-separateness, he says: "It is considered [to exist] through the qualities of earth and the other elements."

Regarding earth and the other [elements], as well as the various types of earth: the earth is the substratum (*ādhāra*) for numerous things to be supported (*ādheya*); therefore, it is mentioned as an illustration of being a substratum. For from the earth, all objects—such as heavy things and so forth, as well as qualities like priority and posteriority—and likewise composite wholes, universals, and common properties (*dharma*s) are supported; such a perfection of all that is to be supported does not exist in any other substance.

By this [statement], "of the substrata such as earth and so forth" refers to the loci (*ādhāra*); "by means of qualities" refers to the non-primary superstrata (*ādheya*). For the superstratum is non-primary in relation to its substratum, and the word "quality" (*guṇa*) is used for what is non-primary, as in the expression "this has become subordinate" (*guṇībhūta*), meaning "non-primary. Therefore, the inseparability (*apṛthagbhāva*) of substrata from their superstrata is *samavāya*.

By this, it is stated that although earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and the possession of odor (*gandhavattva*) are inseparable, there is no *samavāya* between them because they lack the relationship of substratum and superstratum.

Therefore, it is stated in the Vaiśeṣika [system]: "Inherence (samavāya) is that relation between inseparable entities standing in the relationship of the supported and the supporter which is the cause of the cognition 'it is here'"; and it is eternal. Thus, inherence is indestructible;
even when the substances that are the possessors of inherence (samavāyin) are destroyed, inherence itself does not perish.
He states the reason for this: "For where," and so forth.

Where a substance (*dravya*) is fixed and eternal—such as space (*ākāśa*)—therein, in that eternal space, no quality (*guṇa*) is unfixed or perishable; the word "any" (*kaścit*) is to be supplied. He thinks thus: first, even the dimension (*parimāṇa*) in the eternal ether is eternal; likewise, the substantiality (*dravyatva*) residing in space is also eternal; and likewise, the relationship characterized by inherence (*samavāya*) between the two eternals—space and its quality—is also necessarily eternal.

Thus, since the permanence of inherence (*samavāya*) has been established there, because inherence is of a single nature, it is likewise permanent elsewhere; nor is there a destruction of inherence upon the destruction of its substrate substance,
just as the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) is not destroyed even when an individual cow is destroyed.

For them, those various earthly substances and so forth serve as the manifestors of the eternal *samavāya* (inherence) in their respective locations, just as individuals are the manifestors of a universal (*sāmānya*).

However, others have explained *samavāya* as being of two kinds, distinguished by being eternal or non-eternal. Furthermore, this text has been explained as teaching only that connection which exists between the qualities and the earth and other [substances], exactly as it is heard in the scripture. But that [explanation] is neither all-encompassing nor does it follow the Vaiśeṣika doctrine; therefore, it has not been elaborated upon here.
He states the definition of substance (dravya): "In which," and so forth.
"In which" means that upon which [qualities and actions] depend and in which they are inherent. "Action and qualities" (karmaguṇāḥ) refers to action and qualities;
"that which is the inherent cause" (samavāyi kāraṇaṃ yat) means that which is the inherent cause. For indeed, only substance is the inherent cause of substances, qualities, and actions.

And that which produces an effect inherent in itself is an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); however, quality (*guṇa*) and action (*karman*) do not produce effects inherent in themselves, and therefore they are not inherent causes.

For this possession of action (*karmavattva*) is stated merely as a definition that distinguishes substance from the other five categories, such as quality (*guṇa*), and so forth; it is not, however, a definition that pervades its own class while excluding those of different classes. Therefore, one should understand that the definitions of substance—namely, the possession of qualities (*guṇavattva*) and being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇatva*)—are consistent with the definition and exclude those of different classes, even though the inherence of action does not exist in ether (*ākāśa*) and the like.

When a substance has just arisen, it is devoid of qualities in its first moment; nevertheless, because it possesses the capacity for them—since qualities are necessarily present in the second moment—it must be understood as being indeed possessed of qualities.
This is also stated in the Vaiśeṣika [Sūtra]: "Substance is that which possesses action, possesses qualities, and is an inherent cause" (VS 1.1.15).
And in that case as well, it is explained in exactly the same manner as has been explained here.
He states the definition of a quality (guṇa): "Inherent," and so forth.

"Substantially inherent" (*samavāyin*) means that which is contained within a substance by way of inherence (*samavāya*); by this, the quality is distinguished from all-pervading, inactive substances such as space (*ākāśa*) and the like, for space and the others are not contained within a substance by way of inherence.

"Devoid of motion" (*niśceṣṭa*) means free from movement; by the exclusion of movement, both the state of being devoid of movement and the state of being distinct from movement are expressed here. By this, its distinction from action (*karman*), which consists of movement, is established, as well as its distinction from material substances (*mūrtadravya*) which possess the capacity to be the substratum of activity. Furthermore, by the phrase "the cause of a quality," its distinction from non-causes—namely, universals (*sāmānya*), particulars (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*)—is established.

However, causality does not exist in qualities such as the dimension of all-pervading substances (*vibhudravyaparimāṇa*), ultimate parts (*antyāvayavin*), or color (*rūpa*), which are themselves to be defined; therefore, the definition would be "partially unestablished" (*bhāgāsiddha*) in those cases. Consequently, by "causality" here, one should understand "the possession of generality" (*sāmānyavattva*), which is invariably concomitant with a positive cause. And this possession of generality pervades all qualities while excluding universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, because universals and the like lack the possession of generality.

Alternatively, since it is observed that all-pervading substances (*vibhudravya*), dimension (*parimāṇa*), ultimate wholes (*antyāvayavin*), color (*rūpa*), and so forth, possess causality [toward their respective effects], all-pervading substances, dimension, ultimate wholes, color, and the like, also certainly possess the fitness for causality even with respect to [their own] color and so on; thus, there is no lack of pervasion (*bhāgāsiddhatā*) regarding the property of being a cause. Or rather, one should understand that all-pervading substances, dimension, and the rest also possess causality by virtue of being causes of the direct perception (*pratyakṣajñāna*) of yogis.

And although such causality is sometimes observed even in universals (*sāmānya*) and the like, nevertheless, by the phrase "but [that which is] inherent" (*samavāyī tu*), both the state of being the substratum of inherence and the state of being the superstratum of inherence are simultaneously intended. By this, the exclusion of all-pervading substances (*vibhudravya*), which are mere substrata of inherence, as well as universals and the like, which are mere superstrata of inherence, is established.
(51) He states the definition of action (*karman*): "conjunction," and so forth.
It is the simultaneous cause of both conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*).

Therefore, its exclusion from conjunction is established: [conjunction] is that which produces a subsequent spatial conjunction and is not the cause of disjunction; likewise, [disjunction] is that which is the cause of mere disjunction born of disjunction and is not the cause of conjunction.

As for the statement "it is dependent on substance" (*dravyam āśritam*), this should be explained as a mere description of its essential nature (*svarūpa*); however, its exclusion from substance is already established by the very statement, "action does not depend on anything else."

The meaning of this is as follows: when an action (*karman*) has arisen, it requires no other cause existing at a subsequent time for the purpose of effecting the disjunction from its own substrate-substance from a prior location and the conjunction with a subsequent location. Although a substance, while being the cause of both conjunction and disjunction, may exist simultaneously [with them], nevertheless, only when that [substance] has arisen and is joined with an action does it become the cause of conjunction and disjunction. An action, however, once arisen, necessarily effects conjunction and disjunction; it does not require any other cause to follow later, though it does require proximity to the substrates of conjunction and disjunction, and since that [proximity] is already established beforehand, there is no requirement for an action to depend on another cause occurring at the final moment.

Now, since the word "karma" (action) denotes emetics and the like, as well as the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and ritual performance (*kriyā*), one might ask: "Of which action is this the definition? To this he says: "The action of that which is to be performed is *karma*.
By this, it is shown that this is the definition of *karma* in the form of an action, and not of the unseen force and so forth.

He concludes the section with "iti" and so forth; "iti" signifies completion. Therefore, this alone—the sixfold set beginning with generality (*sāmānya*)—is the cause of every class of effect, and there is no other cause.
Having stated the cause in general terms, he now describes the effect as it pertains to Āyurveda: "The effect," and so forth.
The equilibrium of the *dhātus* is health (*ārogya*). For he will state later: "Disease is the imbalance of the *dhātus*; their equilibrium is called the natural state (*prakṛti*)."

"Health is the perception of happiness" (Sūtrasthāna, A. 9), and so forth; "here" refers to Āyurveda. [An objection is raised: "In other contexts, other effects such as pots and the like are also mentioned; why then is that [specific] effect not mentioned here? To this he says: "The equilibrium of the *dhātus*, etc."
The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*);

because the very act of balancing the bodily constituents (*dhātu-sāmya-kriyā*) is the purpose of Āyurveda, therefore, in Āyurveda, the balancing of the constituents alone is stated as the task (*kārya*) and is declared to be the purpose (*prayojana*). Other [tasks] are not mentioned here as tasks because they are either unintended to be expressed or are secondary in importance.

Now, the cause has been stated in general terms; it must now be explained by way of its application to Āyurveda. Among these, the cause of disease is first addressed, beginning with the word "time" (*kāla*), in accordance with the sequence of the aphorisms, for the aphorism states: "Knowledge of the cause, signs, and medicine" (Sūtra 1). Here, "time" refers to the seasons characterized by cold, heat, and rain; "intellect" (*buddhi*) means wisdom (*prajñā*); "objects of the senses" (*indriyārtha*) are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, along with their concomitants—substances, qualities, and actions—which are utilized through the medium of the sense organs. The "conjunction" (*yoga*) of these factors, such as time and the rest, is their relationship.
It has three qualifiers: "false," "not," and "excessive.
By these, "false application" refers to [the application of] time and so forth incorrectly; "non-application" means no application at all; and "excessive application" means an over-application.
"Of those based on the two" means those based on the mind and the body.
Furthermore, this state of the mind being the presiding factor over the body should be understood as both separate and combined;
"threefold" refers to the summary of causes— the concise enumeration of causes consisting of under-application (ayoga), over-application (atiyoga), and improper application (mithyāyoga).

Furthermore, these excessive, deficient, and perverse applications of time and the other factors are clearly explained in the section on the three types of seeking (*tisraiṣaṇīya*) by the passage beginning with "In that regard, those who possess excessive power... (Sūtra-sthāna 11); thus they are not elaborated upon here.
However, time is mentioned first in this context because it is so difficult to avoid.

Following that, the intellect (*buddhi*) is discussed, because it is precisely the fault of the intellect that serves as the cause for the excessive engagement with sense objects and so forth; for it will be stated: "Indeed, due to intellectual error (*prajñāparādha*), one indulges in five harmful things" (Sūtra 28). Thus, although unwholesome contact with sense objects is included within intellectual error, nevertheless, because it is the most proximate cause, it is indicated separately in this treatise by the term "unwholesome contact with sense objects"; intellectual error, however, pertains to errors in the actions of body, speech, and mind that are distinct from unwholesome contact with sense objects.

In this context, unrighteousness (*adharma*) is also a cause of disease, as it has been stated: “Diseases born of action are destroyed by [correct] action” (Śārīra Sthāna, Chapter 1), and so forth. Some maintain that this unrighteousness is already included within the category of time (*kāla*); however, that is not correct, because in the *Tisraiṣaṇīya* chapter, unrighteousness is specifically mentioned alongside intellectual error (*prajñāparādha*).

For in that context, a specific kind of intellectual error (*prajñāparādha*) consisting of improper mental and verbal applications—such as speaking untruths and covetousness—is stated [as the cause]; however, it is not that speaking untruths and so forth act as causes of disease by their own nature, but rather only through the intermediate operation of producing demerit (*adharma*). Therefore, in diseases born of karma, it is intellectual error itself, acting through the intermediate operation of producing demerit, that is the cause, just as sacrifice is the cause of heaven through the intermediate operation of producing merit (*dharma*).

As for what is said—that because they arise from the transformation of time, the disorders born of karma are "born of time"—it has been stated: "By the transformation of time, those caused by old age and death [arise]."

“Diseases are seen to be natural (*svābhāvika*); nature (*svabhāva*) is beyond remedy” (Śārīra-sthāna 1). This is not so; for if that were the case, then even those diseases arising from the contact of the senses with unsuitable objects (*asātmyendriyārthasaṃyoga*), which manifest after a certain period of transformation, would have to be classified as caused by time (*kālaja*).

Furthermore, in the *Tisraiṣaṇīya* chapter, which discusses the excessive application of time (*kālātiyoga*) and other factors, there is no mention whatsoever of an obstruction by karma (*karmāvarodha*).
However, in the *Katidhāpuruṣīya* chapter, it is stated: “The impairment of intellect, fortitude, and memory is the onset (*samprāpti*) of time and karma.”

Having stated, "Unwholesome contact of the sense organs [with their objects] should be known as the causes of disease" (Śārīra Sthāna, Chapter 1), the inclusion of both natural diseases (*svābhāvika*) and those born of past actions (*karmaja*) is made within the category of time (*kāla*) alone.

For it is said there: "Diseases arising from the causes of old age and death through the transformation of time are seen as natural; nature (*svabhāva*) is beyond remedy. Likewise: "That which is designated as destiny (*daiva*) is the action performed in a previous body."
"Even that [time] is found to be a cause of diseases at a particular time" (Śā.
A. 1). Here too, the transgression of wisdom (*prajñāparādha*), in the form of an improper application of the intellect, is indeed the causal factor for the karma that generates disease.

However, regarding those diseases whose onset occurs upon reaching a specific time—whether they be produced by an improper application of time and so forth, or produced by unwholesome sense objects and the transgression of wisdom—all of them, without distinction, are described as "produced by the arrival of time" because they are understood simply as being manifested by time.

For instance, even continuous (*santata*) and other types of fever are said there to be produced by time alone; for the statement is: "Continuous, quotidian (*satata*), tertian (*anyedyus*), quartan (*tṛtīyaka*), and quaternian (*caturthaka*) fevers manifest at their respective times, for it is at those times that their strength arises" (Śārīra-sthāna, Chapter 1).

Furthermore, improper application of time (*kālasya mithyāyoga*) and the like are not observed as causes in the case of *santata* (continuous) and other such fevers; rather, it is only the unwholesome contact of the senses with their objects (*asātmyendriyārthasaṃyoga*) and intellectual error (*prajñāparādha*) that are the causes. Similarly, in the case of natural diseases (*svābhāvika-roga*), improper application of time and the like are not observed as causes. Therefore, those [fevers] are not intended by the Teacher to be "born of time" (*kālaja*) in the sense of being produced by improper application of time and so forth; rather, they are "born of time" in the sense of being manifested by time. For this very reason, it is stated there: "The onset (*samprāpti*) is of the actions of time" (*śā.a.1*), and not "Improper, excessive, or deficient time."

Furthermore, even there, although time has been mentioned, the word "of actions" (*karmaṇām*) is recited separately, thereby indicating that what is born of time is distinct from what is born of action.
Moreover, in the section on the etiology of insanity, the Teacher himself explicitly states that what is born of action is produced by transgression of wisdom (*prajñāparādha*);
for the statement says: "When a disease arises from transgression of wisdom, it is 'born of action' for the self."
“A wise man should not cast blame upon the gods, nor upon the ancestors, nor upon the *rākṣasas*” (Nirukta 7).

Furthermore, regarding the destruction of a country, it is said: “Its root is unrighteousness (*adharma*); its root is improper action performed in the past; and the source of those two is precisely the error of intellect (*prajñāparādha*)” (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3).
Thus, two factors dependent on karma have been demonstrated; as for their relative strength or weakness, the learned will examine this for themselves.

But here it must be considered: where would there be room for natural afflictions such as hunger and thirst, as well as the accumulation and provocation of the *doṣas* that arise even when time is properly joined? They cannot be caused by time, because time is indeed properly joined in those cases, and the established doctrine is that the proper conjunction with time is not a cause of disease. If, on the other hand, it is held that the cause there is specifically the unwholesome contact of the senses with their objects (*asātmyendriyārthasaṃyoga*) which is restricted by time, even so, this being the case, one could likewise say that in the improper conjunction with time and so forth, the cause is simply the unwholesome contact of the senses with their objects. Therefore, the understanding turns toward this very path: that since innate disorders (*sahajā vikārāḥ*) are incurable, they are not included among those produced by improper application (*ayoga*) and the like; for even those born from the nature of time are indeed innate. However, regarding the remedies for these innate conditions—whether for future states born of the nature of time, consisting of the service of *sattva*, virtues, and substances, or for natural hunger, thirst, old age, and so forth, consisting of timely eating and elixirs—if these are not performed, the manifestation of a disease born of the nature of time is indeed produced by intellectual error (*prajñāparādha*), for the non-performance of what ought to be done at the appropriate time is itself intellectual error. For it is said in the *Katidhāpuruṣīya* chapter, in the summary of intellectual error: "The transgression of the time for action and the improper commencement of actions. (Śārīrasthāna, A. 1)

Others, however, explain that because of the existence of false application (*mithyāyoga*) and so forth during the period of emptiness, these morbid transformations (*vikāra*) are contained within time itself; this is based on taking the literal meaning of the text to be stated in the *Katidhāpuruṣīya* chapter.

Furthermore, by the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "not... and," one includes deficient application (*hīnayoga*), for it will be stated: "The disease which arises from false, excessive, or deficient signs" (*Śārīrasthāna*, Chapter 1).

However, for one of inferior yoga (*hīnayoga*), not reciting [the mantra] directly constitutes a form of non-yoga because it is a deviation from the practice; even in the case of a very slight yoga, it becomes non-yoga, just as eating a single grain of rice is called "fasting.
With the phrase "of those who rely on the two," he shows the basis (*āśraya*) that was mentioned—namely, "the body," and so forth.
In this context, the body is mentioned first because this treatise proceeds specifically under the heading of bodily diseases (*śarīra-roga*).

By the term *sattva-sañjña*, the mind (*manas*) is expressed. Alternatively, since the mind is already understood by the word *sattva* alone, the word *sañjñā* indicates that the mind here is that which is connected to the self and the body; for a mind that is not connected to the body and so forth cannot be a locus for disease.
Furthermore, by using a non-compound form, he demonstrates that both the body and the mind are independently loci for disease.
Since diseases such as leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) are purely physical, while desires (*kāma*) and the like are mental, and conditions such as insanity (*unmāda*) depend on both;
[the author] states the basis and cause of health: "Likewise, of pleasures," and so forth.
"Of pleasures" means of healths.

For there is this statement: "Health, which is designated as pleasure, is indeed a modification, but it is nothing other than suffering" (Sūtra 1.29). Likewise, [this applies to] the body and the mind; therein, the body is the substratum for health, which consists in the absence of physical disease, while the mind is the substratum for the absence of mental disease.
Furthermore, the "equilibrium" (*sama*) of time, intellect, sense organs, and objects—consisting in their proper application—is likewise the cause of pleasures and states of health.

Regarding the phrase "of pleasures" (*sukhānām*), the multiplicity of those things denoted by the term "pleasure"—which are the absences of disease—should be understood precisely from the multiplicity of the diseases being negated. For this is indeed the multiplicity of absences: namely, the multiplicity of the entities being negated. Now, one might object: "In the summary of the chapter's subject matter at the beginning of *Sūtra-sthāna*, Chapter 1, where it says 'the source of Āyurveda is the cause' (*āyurvedāgamo hetuḥ*), the substratum of disease was not included; so is this [present statement] unauthoritative (*anārṣa*)? No, for by the word "causes" (*hetavaḥ*), the cause in the form of the substratum of disease is also included therein.

By the statement, "The *sattva*, the self (*ātman*), and the body," a triad is established. Here, the body and the mind are described as the substrata of disease; however, as to what the status of the self is, he says: "changeless," and so forth.
"Changeless" means free from modification; by this, the self's state of being free from disease is indicated.

The word *para* means subtle or supreme; it excludes that which is denoted by the term *ātman*—the form consisting of the union of the *sattva*, the body, and the self—as stated: "In the case of the person as a conjunction, the distinction produced by sensation is accepted" (Śārīrasthāna 1).

Furthermore, even when there is a conjunction [of the self] with the mind, sensation occurs in the mind alone; yet it is said that this [sensation] is also connected to the self which is conjoined with the mind. Therefore, the statement "when the inner self is free from pain" (Sūtra 2.22) would effectively mean "when the mind is free from pain. Likewise, the word "self" (ātman) is also used for the body and so forth; to exclude these, the word "supreme" (para) was stated elsewhere: "The word 'self' may apply to twelve things: to Brahmā, Indra, Vāyu, Agni, the mind, the earth, dharma, fame, glory, prosperity, the body, and the embodied being."

Now, if the self (*ātman*) is immutable, does it possess even the modification consisting of consciousness (*jñāna*), or not? To this he says: "Sattva," and so forth. *Sattva* is the mind (*manas*); the qualities of the elements (*bhūtaguṇa*) are sound and the rest; the sense organs (*indriya*) are the eye and the rest. With these serving as instruments, the self becomes the cause of consciousness;
and consciousness arises or is manifested within the self.

For this very reason, because the causes of cognition—such as attention (*sattva*) and so forth—are not present everywhere, cognition does not occur in every location even though the self (*ātman*) is omnipresent.

[Objection: If the self possesses consciousness, then it would be non-eternal, being sometimes possessed of knowledge and sometimes ignorant. To this he says: "eternal. Although the self is eternal, its cognition is non-eternal; and the non-eternality of an attribute (*dharma*) does not entail the non-eternality of the substratum (*dharmin*). The point is that even though the quality of sound (*śabda*), which is an attribute of space (*ākāśa*), is non-eternal, space itself is not non-eternal.

The permanence of the self [is established] because of the synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) of objects experienced in prior and subsequent states; for a subsequent knower does not synthesize an object previously experienced by one who is impermanent. Indeed, Yajñadatta does not synthesize as something known an object perceived by Devadatta. [Objection: Is it not observed that in the experience of pleasure there is a modification characterized by attachment in the possessor of knowledge, and likewise in the experience of pain there is a modification characterized by aversion? Therefore, how can this self be changeless during the experience of pleasure and pain? [Reply: He says: "The seer sees, for [seeing] is an action."

The "seer" (draṣṭṛ) is the witness (sākṣin). Therefore, just as an ascetic (yatī), being supremely tranquil, observes all the activities of the world as a witness and is not affected by passion, aversion, and the like, so too the Self (ātman), although perceiving pleasure, pain, and so forth, is not affected by passion and the like. The sense is that the observed modifications such as passion occur in the mind (manas) or in the primordial intellect (buddhi), according to the acceptance of the Sāṅkhya philosophy.
And in the Sāṅkhya system, by the word "mind" (manaḥ), both the intellect (buddhi) and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) are understood.

Having now described the substratum of the morbid transformation (*vikāra*) as well as its remote cause, he states the immediate cause in the form of the *doṣas*, beginning with "Vāyu... and so forth.

Here, Vāyu is mentioned first because of its predominance; its predominance is due to its being the agent of swift, frequent, and severe morbid transformations. For it is said: "It acts swiftly and moves repeatedly" (Su.Ni.).
a.

1) Thus; likewise, he will indeed describe eighty disorders born of wind (vāta), forty disorders of bile (pitta), and twenty disorders born of phlegm (kapha) in the chapter on major diseases (Mahārogādhyāya). (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 20)

2) Pitta is primary with respect to vāta because it is the cause of the fire that constitutes the root of the body, because it produces disorders characterized by an excess of kapha, and because its action is more rapid than that of kapha.
The use of the non-compounded form [of the terms] is intended to demonstrate that vāta and the other doshas can act as causes of disease even independently.
The term "bodily" (*śārīra*) is used for the purpose of excluding mental defects (*mānasadoṣa*).

The term "summary" (*saṅgraha*) refers to a concise statement of the detailed exposition (*prapañca*) that will be described later, beginning with: "There are six [types of fever] caused by two being aggravated and one being dominant, and another six by their being diminished, moderate, and excessive" (Sūtra-sthāna 17).

Now, one might object that this summary is not correct because blood (*rakta*) is also a *doṣa*, since specific instructions regarding its causes, symptoms, morbid transformations, and treatments have been provided—just as they have for *vāta* and the others. In that regard, the instruction on its cause is as follows: "Due to lack of bloodletting at the proper time" (Sūtra 24.9), and so forth. Its symptoms are as follows: "Having the luster of refined gold or an *indragopa* insect, resembling a lotus or lac," (Sūtra 24.22), and so forth. Furthermore, blood-related disorders such as hemorrhoids, menorrhagia, and hemoptysis have been mentioned, and its treatment has been stated beginning with: "Bloodletting, however, [is the remedy]" (Sūtra 24.18). Moreover, the designation of blood as a *doṣa* was established by Caraka himself, as it is said: "When *kapha* and *vāta* have been mostly conquered, [one must treat] *pitta* or indeed blood."

"If, while the treatment for vāta is being performed, [the condition] becomes aggravated, then medical therapy should be applied there according to the predominant doṣa" (Cikitsāsthāna 5.27). Likewise, in another treatise on surgery (śalya), blood is also mentioned as a doṣa, based on the statement: "By these [doṣas], with blood as the fourth" (Suśruta Saṃhitā, Sūtrasthāna 21).

This is not so, for a "defect" (*doṣa*) is defined as that which is inherently corrupting. Thus, wind (*vāta*) and the other humors become corrupted independently, without depending on anything else; blood (*śoṇita*), however, becomes a corrupter only by coming into contact with corrupted wind and the others. Indeed, blood does not become morbid without a connection to morbid wind and the rest; for blood is always corrupted by those very factors that produce wind and the others. Likewise, blood is always considered corrupted only when it possesses the characteristics of wind and the others. Furthermore, the specific causes and so forth mentioned apply only to blood that is already associated with wind and the others. Therefore, in that case as well, it is wind and the others that are the agents of corruption, while blood—even when exceeding its own normal measure—is merely the object to be corrupted (*dūṣya*). Nor is it the case that the causes and so forth are not specific to the object to be corrupted, for even in the case of flesh and the other tissues, there are specific causes and so forth. For instance, regarding the corruption of flesh, he will state: "The vessels carrying flesh are corrupted in those who sleep during the day after eating [heavy food]" (Vi. A. 5), and so on. He will describe the symptoms of flesh-corruption in the *Vividhāśitapītīya* chapter (Sū. A. 28) starting with: "Listen to the disorders born from the corruption of flesh," and these disorders are to be understood as such. This is because he will later designate these very disorders of flesh-corruption as the symptoms of flesh-corruption through an extension of the principle (*atideśa*) in the *Srotovimāna* chapter, and the disorders of corrupted flesh, such as *adhimāṃsa* and *arbuda*, have already been mentioned. Furthermore, the treatment is stated as: "For disorders born of flesh, purification, surgery, alkali, and thermal cautery" (Sū. A. 28).

Therefore, when an action is produced by a *doṣa* (morbid humor) acting upon a *dūṣya* (vitiated tissue), it is designated by the name of that *dūṣya*—such as "this is blood-born" (*raktaja*) or "this is flesh-born" (*māṃsaja*). This is just as fire, when it burns using oil as its fuel, is designated as "burnt by oil" (*snehadagdha*). However, the designation "*doṣa*" may be applied even to what is not a *doṣa* due to the commonality of causing affliction (*pīḍākartṛtva*); for instance, in the statement, "One should ignore that *doṣa* which has become spontaneously active through wholesome diet" (Ci. A. 5.46), feces itself is referred to as a *doṣa*. In Suśruta’s work, however, the status of blood as a *doṣa* is mentioned only figuratively, based on the frequent observation of blood vitiation in wounds.

Because in another section concerning wounds (*vraṇa*), only the three—wind (*vāta*) and the others—are mentioned there as well, beginning with: "Vāta, pitta, and kapha alone are the causes for the manifestation of disease" (Su.Sū.A. 21).

Furthermore, if blood (*śoṇita*) were a humor (*doṣa*), it would, like vāta and the others, be a constituent of the primary constitution (*prakṛti*); yet it does not so constitute it. Therefore, it is established that there are only three humors.
He now describes the mental humor (*mānasadoṣa*), beginning with "The mental, however," and so forth.

The word "punaḥ" (again/furthermore) is used for emphasis; by it, it is meant that the mental [doshas] have merely been mentioned, but not elaborated upon like the bodily doshas, because mental defects are irrelevant to this treatise, which is in the form of a manual on internal medicine (*kāyacikitsā*). This is the intended meaning.
At the beginning, *rajas* was mentioned because of its predominance; for it is said: "Tamas does not function without *rajas*" (Vi. A. 6).
By the word "eva" (only/merely), he emphasizes that the quality known as *sattva* is not a *doṣa*, for *sattva* is non-transformative (*avikāri*).
Now he states the cause for the pacification of the defects, beginning with "praśāmyati" (it is pacified), etc.;
"pūrva" (the former) refers to the bodily [defect].
By the mention of the *doṣas* (humors), the diseases produced by them are also included, because diseases are not distinct from the morbid *doṣas*.

*Daiva* refers to the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*); that which one performs as a remedy for disease by relying upon it—such as offerings (*bali*) and auspicious rites (*maṅgala*)—is called *daivavyapāśraya* (reliance on the divine). And this is mentioned first because it pacifies disease immediately and without causing distress.

*Yukti* means application; that which depends on the proper union of the body and the medicine regarding purification (*saṃśodhana*) and pacification (*saṃśamana*) is called *yuktivyapāśraya* (reliance on rational therapy).

*Jñāna* is knowledge of the self (*adhyātmajñāna*); *vijñāna* is knowledge of the scriptures; *dhairya* is the absence of mental agitation; *smṛti* is the recollection of experienced objects; and *samādhi* is the withdrawal of the mind from sense objects and its restraint within the self.

(58) Now, since this treatise is concerned with the topic of bodily diseases, he describes the characteristics of *vāta* and other [humors] that produce such diseases, as well as their remedies, beginning with the word "dry" (*rūkṣa*).

Vāyu is mentioned first because of its predominance; the qualities beginning with roughness (rūkṣa) are mentioned because they are most significant, by which other qualities such as hardness (dāruṇa) and so forth are also to be understood. Furthermore, roughness is predominant in vāyu, since vāyu is to be treated with unctuousness (sneha); therefore, roughness is mentioned first.

Although according to the Vaiśeṣika school air is neither hot nor cold, nevertheless, because an increase is observed here through cold and a subsiding through heat, and because cold is observed in a disease initiated by vāta alone, air is indeed cold; as for its heat when associated with pitta, that is due to its capacity for association (yogavāhitva), just as a stone assumes the qualities of whatever substance it comes into contact with—whether cold or hot—so it is with air as well.

That which possesses qualities contrary to the qualities of *vāta*—that is, qualities that are the opposites of *vāta*—is called "possessing contrary qualities" (*viparītaguṇa*). Here, by the word "quality" (*guṇa*), which denotes attributes, all factors including taste (*rasa*), potency (*vīrya*), post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*), and specific action (*prabhāva*) are included. Consequently, anything that is contrary to *vāta* even by virtue of its specific action (*prabhāva*) is also included. Others, however, suggest that by the elision of the single word "contrary" (*viparīta*), both "contrary" (*viparīta*) and "possessing contrary qualities" (*viparītaguṇa*) are understood. Thus, through the inclusion of "contrary," that which is contrary by specific action is grasped, and through the contrariety of "qualities," [the contrariety of] post-digestive transformation and so forth are grasped.

But surely, even by substances abounding in qualities contrary [to the doshas], there occurs the pacification of vāta and the others, because not every medicine is entirely antagonistic to vāta and the rest; for it has been said: "When substances with contradictory qualities meet, the one that is more abundant overcomes the one that is less" (Vi. A. 1). Why, then, is that which abounds in contradictory qualities not included? It is replied: because even that which abounds in contradictory qualities is already included under the very term "qualities contrary" (viparītaguṇa).

Even when [the doshas] are predominantly characterized by contrary qualities, those qualities that are contrary, minor, or weak are not even designated as such because they do not perform their own functions; or rather, tranquility (*śānti*) is superior and more praiseworthy when it is increased by contrary qualities in every respect. For this very reason, the two words *sam* and *pra* have been employed to denote the meanings of "swift" and "perfect" pacification respectively. Tranquility does not occur in such a manner through [qualities] that are predominantly contrary; therefore, that [state] was not explicitly stated by the two words *sam* and *pra*. This same explanation should also be applied to bile (*pitta*) and phlegm (*śleṣman*).

"Sasneham" means slightly unctuous; by this, it is established that ghee, being unctuous, serves as a medicine for pitta. Furthermore, the sour taste of pitta is mentioned here because pitta is composed of water and fire (*aptejaḥ*). However, in the *Suśruta*, pungency alone is stated for pitta, while its acidity is said to belong to pitta when it is "burnt" (*vidagdha*), as it is stated: "That which is burnt is indeed sour" (*Su.Sū.A. 21*).
Thus, even regarding its viscidity (*sasnehatā*), there is no essential juice (*svarasa*) of *pitta* [in that quality];

moreover, this viscidity and acidity of *pitta* are indeed logical because it is originated from water and fire. However, in the *Suśruta*, that [viscidity] is rejected solely with the intention that *pitta* is of the nature of fire (*tejas*).

It is said that the pacification of qualities occurs through qualities contrary to those of *śleṣman*, but the pacification of *śleṣman* itself is not what is being described. Why is it stated thus? It is for the purpose of indicating that by the pacification of qualities, the substratum of the qualities (*guṇin*) is pacified, and by the increase of qualities, the substratum of the qualities increases.
Since, when cold is being pacified by heat, the watery portion that constitutes the substratum of the cold must necessarily be pacified as well (vv.

59–61), [the author] states "viparīta... and so forth, explaining that pacification does not occur even with substances of opposite qualities if they are present in only small quantities, or if they are obstructed by factors such as place and time that are not contrary [to the disease].

The place (*deśa*) refers to the location and the patient; the measure (*mātrā*) refers to the quantity that does not deviate from the proper limit; time (*kāla*) is both the ever-moving [time] such as the seasons, and the situational [time] such as childhood and so forth. "Prepared" (*upapādita*) means fashioned according to what is appropriate with respect to place and the other factors, brought about by place, measure, and time; the suffix *ṇic* is used here according to the *caurādika* group (meaning "to bring about"). Alternatively, it may mean "prepared by the physician."

Here, by the mention of "place" (deśa), there is the inclusion of strength, body, diet, suitability (sātmya), and temperament-nature (sattva-prakṛti); by the mention of "time" (kāla), age is also included; the "humor" (doṣa) is included precisely as that which is to be pacified; and "medicine" (bheṣaja) is mentioned explicitly. Thus, there is the inclusion of all ten types of factors to be examined—humor, medicine, place, time, strength, body, diet, suitability, temperament-nature, and age—which are accepted by authoritative authorities as being curable, and are thus known as "those considered curable. By this, those cases which are taken as curable by the ignorant due to their lack of knowledge are refuted.

As for the claim that by the inclusion of the word "properly" (*samyak*) the maintenance of a palliative state is meant, that is not very elegant, because of the statement "they turn back. Furthermore, the maintenance of a palliative state is not the same as "turning back. [The author] speaks of the cessation of treatment in the case of the incurable, starting with the words "the means," etc. Now, it may be argued that even for the incurable, a means of treatment is observed; for instance, one who possesses fatal signs (*ariṣṭa*) is indeed incurable because he is seized by death. As it has been said: "There is no such fatal sign which can occur without death."

"And there is no death that does not have *ariṣṭa* as its precursor" (*Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya*, Sūtrasthāna 2). Furthermore, the means for counteracting manifested *ariṣṭa* is stated in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā*: "Death is certain when *ariṣṭa* has arisen, O Brāhmaṇa; however, it is indeed averted by those who are stainless and devoted to *rasāyana*, austerity, and recitation [of mantras]" (*Suśruta*, Sūtrasthāna 28). Likewise, the venerable Agastya said: "Even timely death is conquered by wise, high-souled men perfected through *rasāyana*, austerity, recitation, and yoga, but not by idle men. Similarly, it is stated elsewhere: "One may live even after *ariṣṭa* has appeared."

On this point, some say: fatal signs (*ariṣṭa*) are of two kinds—certain and uncertain. Among these, that which is certain is indeed incurable; for this very reason it is said: "But there is no destruction of a manifest fatal sign except by death" (*Caraka Saṃhitā*, Indriya-sthāna 2). Here, from the expression "of a manifest [sign]," it is understood to mean "of a certain [sign]. As for the uncertain fatal sign, the statements of Suśruta and Agastya regarding it are meaningful; Caraka also mentions uncertain fatal signs, as in: "Ātreya considers his life to have reached a state of doubt" (*Caraka Saṃhitā*, Indriya-sthāna 9).

Others, however, say that the phrase "when [death] has reached the state of uncertainty" is merely a difference in expression; therefore, all *ariṣṭas* (fatal signs) are indeed fatal unless there is the use of elixirs (*rasāyana*) and the like. For elixirs, asceticism, and so forth, by virtue of their extraordinary power, accomplish even that which cannot be achieved by other treatments. Furthermore, this prevention of *ariṣṭas* is observed only in rare, exceptional persons such as Nandikeśvara and others; it is not possible for all people. Therefore, it is stated in the treatise that for those in whom *ariṣṭas* have arisen, the condition is simply incurable.

As for what some say—that for those with a fixed lifespan death is preceded by *ariṣṭas* (signs of approaching death), whereas for those with an unfixed lifespan death occurs even without *ariṣṭas*—that is not so, because of the statement: "And there is no such death that is not preceded by *ariṣṭas*" (*Indriya-sthāna*, chapter 2).

Furthermore, it is said that even for one with an unfixed lifespan, although *ariṣṭas* may appear, life must continue if proper treatment is administered; for in the case of those with an unfixed lifespan, death occurs only due to the failure of human effort (*puruṣakāra*), and in the case of proper treatment, there is no failure of human effort.

That is not so; for those with indefinite lifespans are not always achievable through human effort (*puruṣakāra*), but rather are achieved through human effort consisting of the service that promotes the welfare of the healthy and the sick when performed at the appropriate time. Therefore, regarding a disease that is incurable because beneficial treatment was not administered at the proper time, once the fatal signs (*riṣṭa*) have appeared, what can medicine do when applied after the time has passed? It would be like building a dam after the water has already flowed away. Thus, it is correct that the treatment of incurable diseases is not taught.
He asks: Are these alone the functions of the qualities (*guṇa-karmāṇi*), or are there others as well? He says "Furthermore" (*bhūyaśca*) and so forth;
"functions of the qualities" (*guṇa-karmāṇi*) means the activities of the qualities.

"According to the substance" (*yathādravyam*) means that whatever quality or action belongs to whichever particular substance—whether it be food, drink, and so forth, or the entire treatise (*tantra*)—that will be explained by the "Teacher" (*ācārya*), as is the understood remainder of the sentence. The use of the verb *vakṣyate* (it will be told) is from the substitution of *vac* for the root *brū*. Alternatively, "according to the substance" may mean "according to the cause. For example: an earthy substance (*pārthivadravya*) is characterized by an abundance of qualities such as heaviness, roughness, and hardness; and the action of those earthy qualities consists of accumulation, cohesion, heaviness, and so forth.

Having now described the defects, he proceeds to state the tastes (*rasas*), which are primarily intended for their pacification; first providing the definition of taste, he describes the sequence of its production, beginning with the words "the object of the sense of taste" (*rasanārtha*).
Taste (*rasa*) is that which is tasted or relished.
"The object of the sense of taste" means that which is perceivable by the tip of the tongue.
And this [definition] follows all six tastes; because it is excluded from color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest, it is the correct definition of that [taste].
"The substance of that" means the substantial cause (*ādhārakāraṇa*), which is the taste.
The word *dravya* indeed denotes a substratum or a causal basis; as in the statement, "the five material sense organs" (Sūtra 8).

Just as water is a substratum, so too is earth. Although one might expect the expression "water and earth," the use of the phrase "earth is likewise" indicates that earth's status as a substratum is not primary.

For water is naturally flavorful; thus, in the *Ātreya-Bhadrakāpyīya* chapter, [the text] beginning with "Water is indeed gentle" (*saumyāḥ khalvāpaḥ*, Sūtra 26) demonstrates that the manifestation of taste occurs in water alone.
It is also stated in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā*: "Therefore, taste is composed of water" (*tasmādāpyo rasaḥ*, Sūtra 42).

The earth is said to possess taste because it is constantly permeated by the essence of water alone, since the connection between earth and water is eternal; for there is a statement: "The subsequent is indeed pervaded by the preceding" (Nyāya-sūtra 3.1.60).

Its meaning is this: in each successive element—ether, air, fire, water, and earth—there is the eternal penetration of each preceding element, and this causes the increase of qualities within ether and the others.

He asks: "Are water and earth the cause for the manifestation (*vyakti*) of taste, or rather for its specific differentiation (*viśeṣa*? He replies with the words beginning "in its production" (*nirvṛttau*), etc.; by saying "and in its production," he means "in its manifestation. By this, he demonstrates that when taste is manifested, it is manifested as having water and earth as its very substratum.
