Because of the word "and" (*ca*), even in the case of specific qualities characterized as sweet and so forth, water and earth are the material causes (*pratyaya*).

Therefore, the fact that water and earth will also be stated to be specific causes—as in the passage beginning, "Sweetness arises from the predominance of the quality of soma; sourness arises from the predominance of the qualities of earth and fire" (Sūtra 2.26)—is justified.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that space and the other elements are the causes in the case of specific qualities, space, air, and fire are the efficient causes (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) for the production of specific qualities such as sweetness, but they are not the substrative causes (*ādhāra-kāraṇa*).

Since the number three is already established by the word "khādayaḥ" (beginning with space), the further mention of "trayaḥ" (three) is for the purpose of showing that these very elements—both individually and collectively—are causes. For this very reason, the internal distinctions among tastes, such as being sweeter or sweetest, are logically accounted for through the different combinations of space and the other elements, both individually and collectively. Furthermore, by the word "ca" (and) in the phrase "viśeṣe ca," he shows that space and the others are also instrumental causes in the manifestation [of taste].

For it will be stated: "Falling from the intermediate space and having fallen, endowed with the qualities resulting from the transformation of the five great elements, they nourish the forms of mobile and immobile beings; in them, the six tastes become manifest" (Sūtra-sthāna 26).

Others, however, connect the word "ca" (and) in the phrase "viśeṣe ca" (and in the specific) with the preceding "khādayaśca" (and the ether etc.); by that "ca," time (kāla) is also obtained as a cause for both the specific and for manifestation.
However, by not explicitly mentioning time, its status as a cause is shown to be even more subordinate than that of the ether and the other elements.

Alternatively, as before, water is the substance of taste and earth is likewise [the manifestor]; and regarding its "manifestation," it is earth alone that is the cause for manifestation—that is, for the appearance [of taste], not water. For water is indeed of unmanifested taste, and taste is perceived as manifested only through its connection with earth.
And it has been said: "They nourish the forms of moving and stationary beings, and within them the six tastes become fully developed" (Sūtra-sthāna 26).
Therefore, the taste of water is manifested only through its connection with an earthly substance, and not otherwise.

Regarding the phrase "and in the case of a specific [taste]," the word "and" (*ca*) implies that although water and earth are the causes of a specific taste, nevertheless—as in the statement, "it is sweet due to the predominance of the quality of soma" (Sūtra 2.26)—the elements beginning with space (*khādayaḥ*) themselves arrange themselves in such a way that *soma* becomes predominant; therefore, even in that case, it is the elements beginning with space, arranged in a state of deficiency [relative to *soma*], that are the causes of the specific taste.

Even though manifestation may sometimes occur devoid of specific qualities such as sweetness and so forth, nevertheless, that cause which is observed to be invariably present for manifestation everywhere in a general sense—whether it be the nature of earth or the nature of water and earth—is the cause of manifestation. However, that through whose presence the perception of specific qualities like sweetness arises is called the cause of those specific qualities.
(64) He states the specific tastes, beginning with "sweet" and so forth.

Here, because it is desired by all living beings, the sweet (*madhura*) is mentioned first; thereafter, the sequence of the enumeration of the sour (*amla*) and other tastes should be understood according to the very order of increasing desirability for living beings.
The repetition of the number "six" (*ṣaṭka*) is for the purpose of negating the number seven and other such figures asserted by opposing schools.
By the phrase "this summary," he demonstrates both the great number of intermediate subdivisions as well as the great number of combinations of tastes that will be described hereafter.
65. He states the most effective application of the tastes: "Sweet, sour," and so forth.

In this context, it should be understood that even though *vāyu* is devoid of taste, its pacification occurs through qualities such as unctuousness (*snigdhatva*) which accompany the tastes and are contrary to its own nature.

In the same way, the increase of phlegm (*śleṣman*), which possesses a sweet taste, occurs precisely through its association with qualities such as unctuousness (*snigdhatva*) and obstructiveness (*abhiṣyanditva*) that accompany sour and salty tastes.
Furthermore, in this context, those tastes that have not been mentioned as pacifiers of *vāta* and the others should be understood as their augmenters.
As Vāgbhaṭa said: "Among these, the first [sweet taste] destroys wind (*māruta*), while the three beginning with bitter destroy phlegm (*kapha*)."

"Those that are astringent, bitter, and sweet produce pitta, while others do so differently"— by this extension of the functions of tastes (*rasa-karma*), the functions of qualities (*guṇa*), potencies (*vīrya*), and post-digestive transformations (*vipāka*) have indeed already been specified.

For Ātreya-Bhadrakāpya will describe all the qualities, potencies, and post-digestive effects by means of the sweet and other tastes alone, starting with: "Among those, the sweet... (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 26); likewise: "The post-digestive effect of pungent, bitter, and astringent [tastes] is generally pungent" (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 26); likewise: "The sour [taste] is digested as sour, the sweet as sweet, and the salty likewise" (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 26); and likewise: "That substance which is cold in potency and sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect... that which is sour and hot... and that which is pungent and hot... (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 26), and so forth.

Therefore, in order to state the remaining function of substances—which is produced by their specific potency (prabhāva)—he describes the classification of substances according to the classification of their potencies, beginning with "kiñcit" and so forth.
"Kiñcit" means not everything;
it refers to the pacification of one humor (doṣa), two humors, or all three humors, which is called "doṣapraśamana."
By the mention of "defects" (doṣa), the corrupted tastes and so forth are also included;

therefore, by virtue of the greatness of the substance, those things such as *āmalaka* and *durālabhā* which pacify the defects, the corrupted tastes and so forth, or the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are understood.
For *āmalaka*, due to its auspicious nature, removes the three defects (*tridoṣa*), and *durālabhā* also removes wind, bile, and phlegm.

Although the *Āmalaka* fruit is said to alleviate the three *doṣas* through its properties—such as the statement, "It destroys *vāta* because of its acidity" (*Suśruta Sūtrasthāna*, A. 46)—nevertheless, this must be understood as being augmented solely by its specific power (*prabhāva*).

For while its acidity and other qualities might logically lead to the provocation of *pitta* and the rest, such provocation does not occur due to the power of the *āmalaka*. Thus, there is no corruption whatsoever of the *vāta* and other *doṣas*, which maintain the body through their equilibrium, nor of the *rasa* and other tissues (*dhātu*), as is the case with substances such as *yavaka*, *mandaka*, or poison.

One is "healthy" (*svastha*) because one remains well through the state of being free from disease; the "conduct of the healthy" (*svasthavṛtti*) is the persistence in that state of health. In this context, "approved" (*mata*) means desired or honored.
Since the number three is already obtained from the very mention of the items to be counted, the inclusion of the term "threefold" (*trividha*) is for the purpose of restriction;
by it, various types of treatments such as purification (*saṃśodhana*) and pacification (*saṃśamana*) are included within these very categories.

Regarding *rasāyana* and *vājīkaraṇa*, however, it is stated within the very context of *svasthavṛtti* (the regimen for the healthy)—specifically in the first chapter of the Cikitsāsthāna—“That which promotes vigor (*ojas*) for a healthy person is aphrodisiac (*vṛṣya*) and that is *rasāyana*” (Ci. A. 1, pāda 1).

This mention of "some" [qualities] is intended to demonstrate that the various actions, such as the removal of *doṣas*, depend upon different substances. For if only one [quality] were mentioned, a single substance would have to be simultaneously a remover of *doṣas*, a corrupter of the *dhātus*, and a constituent of the regimen for the healthy—which is not the intended view.

Now, it may be argued that even for those who maintain a healthy regimen (*svasthavṛtti*), red rice (*raktaśāli*), sixty-day rice (*ṣaṣṭika*), barley (*yava*), and so forth, are observed to pacify the *doṣas*, since the author will prescribe the use of red rice and other such grains in various instances for fever and other conditions. Furthermore, even that which pacifies the *doṣas* becomes a cause of *doṣas* when combined with [inappropriate] constitution (*prakṛti*), body, place, time, or dose—as should be understood from statements such as "an excessive quantity of *āmalaka* causes weak digestion" (*agnimāndya*). Likewise, the aggravation of the *dhātus* is seen to result in the pacification of the *doṣas*, as poison destroys abdominal diseases (*udara*). Similarly, that very substance which causes *doṣas*—such as indigestible food (*mandaka*)—becomes a pacifier of *doṣas* for one whose *doṣas* are diminished, by increasing the *doṣas* and thereby restoring equilibrium. Thus, because of this lack of fixed rule, the statement that "some things pacify the *doṣas*" and so forth is contradictory.

To this it is replied: Red rice (*raktaśāli*) and other such grains, while belonging to the category of *svasthavṛtti* (regimen for the healthy), also serve to pacify the *doṣas*; however, because they are generally beneficial for the maintenance of health, they are categorized as *svasthavṛtti*.
For there is a saying: "That which promotes vigor in the healthy is generally considered aphrodisiac (*vṛṣya*) and elixir (*rasāyana*);
it is generally beneficial for the pacification of diseases."
"The word 'mostly' (prāyas) is for the sake of distinction, for both [types of causes] indeed produce both types of effects" (Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 1).

Substances that pacify the *doṣas* certainly perform the pacification of the *doṣas* when there is an absence of obstacles such as an abnormal constitution (*prakṛti*); however, they do not act when such obstacles are present. Yet, this does not mean that their inherent nature (*svabhāva*) ceases to exist. For fire is not taught to lack the quality of burning simply because it sometimes fails to burn due to obstacles such as mantras. Likewise, even for a substance that generally vitiates the *dhātus*, its occasional pacification of the *dhātus*—occurring through the application of another cause—does not destroy its essential nature as a vitiator of the *dhātus*, just as water possesses heat when in contact with fire.
Therefore, it is appropriate to designate a thing by that very nature which is its predominant characteristic and not produced by any external condition.

As for the fact that substances such as *mandaka* (sour gruel) act as pacifiers of the *doṣas*—despite their actually increasing those *doṣas* in those whose *doṣas* have been diminished—it is not designated as a pacifier because this quality occurs only occasionally (*kādācitkatva*) and because, at a later time, they actually bring about an increase in the *doṣas*.

Now, one might object: even if this is so, where then does that category of many substances belong which remedy one disorder while producing another—for example, black pepper (*marica*), which removes phlegm (*śleṣman*) yet produces bile (*pitta*)? On this point, some say: that which possesses both natures is both a remover of disorders and a producer of disorders; however, this does not undermine the threefold nature of substances. For, when diseases arise from the combination of *vāta* and the other doshas, the threefold classification of diseases based on their being produced by *vāta* and so forth is not thereby invalidated. Alternatively, the dual action of substances like black pepper is not caused by the specific potency (*prabhāva*) of the substance itself, but rather by its taste (*rasa*) and other qualities; therefore, such cases should not be cited in the discussion of the potency of substances. Furthermore, there is no substance whatsoever that, by its potency alone, produces one disorder while simultaneously pacifying another; thus, there is no fixed rule regarding the potency of pacifying disorders and so forth. This very position is the correct one.

Now, one might instead say: "one [substance] pacifies certain defects while another aggravates certain defects," or "one pacifies certain bodily constituents (dhātus) while another aggravates certain bodily constituents."

It is not so; for if that were the case, since the word *doṣa* (defect) would primarily apply only to wind (*vāta*) and the other humors, and the word *dhātu* (tissue) would apply only to the tastes (*rasa*) and so forth, the inclusion of both would not be achieved. By employing both terms, the skillful author of the treatise intends to include both categories: through the application of the terms "corrupting" and "sustaining," he indicates that medicine—as will be described in the chapter on various foods and drinks—is that which pacifies defects by pacifying corrupted tastes and the like, and likewise, as will be described in the chapters on etiology (*nidāna*) and so forth, it is that which corrupts the humors such as wind by corrupting the tissues.

The prefix *pra-* here denotes a particular manner (*prakāra*); thus, aggravation (*prakopaṇa*) by that manner—such as mild, moderate, and so forth—is expressed, as well as pacification (*śamana*) by that manner—such as purification (*saṃśodhana*), palliation (*saṃśamana*), and so forth. Alternatively, these two prefixes (*pra-*) may simply follow the root meaning (*dhātvartha*), as in the expression “the fallen portion runs” (*cyutāṃśaḥ paridhāvati*), where the meaning is simply “runs.

Why is the pacification of the doshas mentioned first? Because that alone is intended here. [Objection: But surely, a substance belonging to the regimen for the healthy (*svasthavṛtti*) is indeed a pacifier of doshas (*doṣapraśamana*) by virtue of removing doshas that are yet to arise.

It is not so; for it is not called "doṣa-haraṇa" (the removal of morbid humors) because it produces the persistence of health, but rather because it maintains the equilibrium of the *dhātus* by not increasing them and by preventing their depletion, while being conducive to the channels of the *rasa* and other elements. For there is this statement: "That which does not deviate from the path is wholesome (*pathya*)" (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 25).
Now he states the difference between substances in another way, beginning with "tat punar" (that, moreover):
"tat" refers to substance;

"jaṅgama" is that which moves; "audbhida" refers to trees and the like, which are born by breaking through the earth; and "pārthiva" is a transformation of earth distinct from the two aforementioned types.
In this context, the term "mobile" includes worms and the like born of moisture, as well as *kukuṇḍaka* insects and so forth;

and here, by the word "substance," only an earthy substance is intended. Therefore, one should not allege that there is an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) because water, air, fire, and the like are not included.
Furthermore, by the word "mobile," that which originates from mobile beings—such as cow's milk, honey, and so on—is also to be understood.
In this same manner, the inclusion of *audbhida* (salt from saline soil) and *pārthiva* (earth-derived substances) should also be stated.
*Rocanā* refers to *gorocanā* (cow-gallstone);

and these, such as honey and the rest, are mentioned because of their predominant utility and importance. By this, the inclusion of *aṇḍa* (egg), *vasti* (bladder), and so forth should also be understood.

Although the vegetable kingdom (*audbhida*) was taught immediately after the mobile kingdom because it is more extensive and primary, nevertheless, because there is not much to be said about it, only the mineral kingdom (*pārthiva*) is explained immediately after the mobile kingdom; following that, the vegetable kingdom—which has much to be said—will be discussed.
By the phrase "the five metals," such as gold and so forth, copper, silver, tin, lead, and black iron are included.

Regarding the term *samalā* (with impurities), by the word "impurity" (*mala*), bitumen (*śilājatu*) in the form of metal dross is intended; and according to the view of Suśruta, that is understood to be of exactly six kinds, originating from gold, silver, and so forth. For in the Suśruta, bitumen is indeed said to be of six kinds, whereas here in the context of *rasāyana*, it is stated to be of four kinds, based on the statement: "Its origin is from four elements: from gold, silver, copper, and even black iron" (Ci. A. 1).

Furthermore, this statement demonstrates that the four types of *śilājatu* are eligible for use as an elixir (*rasāyana*), but it is not intended as a prohibition against the six types of *śilājatu*; thus, there is no contradiction with Suśruta.
Alternatively, [the term "metal" refers to] pure gold (*suvarṇa*), while the impure ones are silver, copper, tin, lead, and iron (these five metals taken together);
the inclusion of *śilājatu*, stone-impurities (*pāṣāṇa*), mud (*paṅka*), and so forth, is indicated by the word "specified" (*uddiṣṭa*); for "specification" (*uddeśa*) indeed means a brief mention.
Lime,
realgar, yellow orpiment, collyrium, and antimony.
"Vanaspati" refers to those [trees] that bear fruit without flowers, such as the *vaṭa* (holy fig) and *udumbara*.
As stated by Hārīta: "Those which bear fruit without flowers are known as vanaspatis.
Alternatively, "vānaspatya" refers to those that bear both flowers and fruit; the meaning is that they possess fruit immediately following their flowering.

Those such as sesame, mung beans, and so forth, whose end is destruction through the ripening of their fruit, are called *phalapākāntāḥ* (those ending with the ripening of fruit). On this point, some say that *auṣadhyaḥ* (medicinal herbs) are both those ending with the fruit and those ending with the ripening [of the fruit]; by this, even those such as *dūrvā* grass, whose end occurs through ripening alone even without fruit, are included.
By the word *pratāna* (creepers), both *latās* (vines) and *gulmas* (shrubs) are included, as stated by Hārīta: "Vines, shrubs, and spreading plants (*vīrudhaḥ*)."

In the passage beginning with "mūlatvak" (root-bark), "niryāsa" refers to resinous exudates such as lac (*lākṣā*) and sal tree resin (*sarjarasa*); "audbhida-gaṇa" means a group of substances produced from plants. 68–73.
Now, regarding the substances here that are mobile, vegetable, and mineral, he states what among them is most excellent: "those with roots" (mūlinyaḥ), and so forth.
Those which have roots as their most excellent part are called "root-bearing" (mūlinyaḥ); likewise for those with fruits (phalinyaḥ).
The word division is "ṣoḍaśa" (sixteen).

Regarding "mahāsnehāḥ" (great unctuous substances), since milk, meat, and so forth will also be described as unctuous substances in the chapter on *Sneha*, the term "great" (*mahā*) is used for ghee and the others because they possess a greater degree of unctuousness than those.
The phrase "only five salts" is intended to show that, although many salts will be described in the *Vimāna* section (Vi. A. 8), only these five are considered commendable.

In this manner, a knower of the Vedas (*vedavit*) should infer the predominance [of specific elements] among their respective homologues even in the case of urine and so forth; thus, one who knows Ayurveda (*āyurvedavit*).
Regarding "hastidantī" and so forth: *hastidantī* is the large-fruited *goḍumbā*; some say that this very plant is called *nāgadantī*;
[and] *haimavatī* is *vacā*.
Śyāmā, śyāmamūlā, trivṛt, adhoguḍā, pradhvāraka, saptalā, and carmakaṣā.
Śvetā, aparājitā, pratyakśreṇī, dantī, bimbī, and oṣṭhopamaphalā are the names of the white [variety].
Śaṇapuṣpī, ghaṇṭāravā, viṣāṇikā, āvartanī,
and ajagandhā are known as ‘aphokāndī’.

Regarding the application of emetics and other therapies for plants with roots, such as *dravantī*, *dantī*, *cīritapatrā*, *kṣīriṇī*, *dugdhikā*, and others, he says: "The *śaṇapuṣpī*," and so forth.
Śaṅkhinī is white Buhnā (or Dhunā).

*Klītaka* is *yaṣṭīmadhu*. Although its root is praised in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*, and it is indeed used by means of the root, nevertheless, regarding purgation, it should be understood that for both types of *yaṣṭīmadhu*, the fruit alone is recommended.
*Dhāmārgava* is *pītaghoṣaka*;
*ikṣvāku* is *tiktālābu*.
Jīmūta is a variety of ghoṣaka;
kṛtavedhana is jyotsnikā;
and prakīrya and udakīrya are the two types of karañja.

*Pratyakpuṣpā*, *apāmārga*, *antaḥkoṭarapuṣpī*, *nīlabudhnā*, *hastiparṇī*, and *moraṭa*; and of this [last one], only the fruit produced in the autumn season is to be taken; therefore it is said: "and of *hastiparṇī*, that which is autumnal."
Although *kampillaka*, *guṇḍārocanikā*,
and the leaf of *āragvadha* are mentioned in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā* as being primary, nevertheless, here the fruit is taken because of its supreme importance;
thus, by the words "dhāmārgava" and so forth, its application in the five purificatory procedures (*pañcakarma*) is stated.
Nastaḥ-pracchardana (nasal emesis) is used for head-purgation (śirovirecana). 80–85.

Ghee and other substances are listed among the great unctuous substances (*mahāsneha*) because of their preeminence; for it is said: "No other unctuous substance conforms to processing (*saṃskāra*) as ghee does; therefore, ghee is considered the best of all unctuous substances" (Ni. A. 1).

— Although among salts *saindhava* is preeminent, since he will state in the section on the foremost [substances]: “*Saindhava* is the best of salts” (Sūtra-sthāna 25), nevertheless, because of the excellence of *sauvarcala*’s power to clarify the eyesight (*rocanatva*), it is mentioned first after *saindhava* for the purpose of proclaiming its importance.
*Audbhida* is salt from saline soil (*autkārika-lavaṇa*); some call it *śāmbhara* salt.
"Sāmudra" means produced from the southern ocean, known as "karakaca";
"for anointing" (abhyañjana) refers to an oil massage,
and "for the purpose of wicks" (vartyartha) refers to the purpose of medicinal wicks.

In the passage beginning with "the urine of a sheep" (avimūtra), [the author] indicates through the inclusion of the feminine gender that the urine of a female alone is recommended; for since women have lighter limbs, their urine is also light. Indeed, there is a statement: "Lightness is common to both genders, but there is heaviness in men compared to women" (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 27).

As for what is said—that the urine of men is heavy due to its connection with semen—that is not correct, because the connection with semen is equal for women as well, since they possess semen too. For there is a statement: "When a woman indeed approaches another woman for sexual intercourse, they both emit semen; from that, a child is born without bones," and so forth. Furthermore, the urine of a neuter person is not taken in anti-toxic formulations (*agada*) because of its inauspiciousness; thus, there is no redundancy between the phrase "suitable for the application of anti-toxics" (*agadaprayogayaugikatvam*), which indicates its fitness for use in such preparations, and the phrase "it destroys poison" (*viṣaghnam*), which indicates its power to neutralize poison even when used alone.
It is called *śarma* because it produces the happiness of health (*ārogya-rūpa-sukha*).

Regarding "the lower part," one should draw down the *pitta* by means of the downward path. Alternatively, it purges only that *pitta* which has moved downward and not that which moves upward, according to the application of its capacity—just as is the case with the capacity of urine.
"Generally sweet" means primarily sweet.

By this, it is shown that even when other tastes are present as secondary factors—as in the case of camel’s milk being slightly salty, goat’s milk being astringent, and so forth—their association still occurs within the milk.

This is indicated by the word "mostly" (*prāyaśaḥ*), which connects with the terms "nourishing" (*bṛṃhaṇa*) and "unctuous" (*snigdha*), as well as with "cold" (*śīta*). Therefore, the description of the camel's milk as dry and hot is not contradictory.
Furthermore, the term *stanya* means that which increases breast milk.

It is called *manaskāra* because it produces mental clarity (*prabhāva*) and because it bestows vigor (*ojas*). For through the increase of vigor, the mind—which conforms to that [vigor]—also gains the capacity for its own functions.
And this alone is the "making" (*karaṇa*) of the eternal mind here: namely, the production of qualities such as excellence of intellect and preeminence in the mind.
It "destroys blood-bile" (*śoṇitapitta*); it destroys only that blood-bile which has reached a particular pathological state.

For the statement is as follows: "When blood-bile (raktapitta) does not subside despite the various aforementioned applications of decoctions and oleaginous substances once the fire has been kindled and the phlegm (śleṣman) has been conquered, then wind (anila) would follow; in that case, goat's milk should be used as the supreme application, or cow's milk boiled in five parts of water. (Ci. A. 4)

And thus, that which is said—that in cases of *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders) moving downward, milk is unsuitable due to its fluidity, and in those moving upward, it is unsuitable because it increases *kapha*—is refuted.

In the statement "it is wholesome for all living beings," the word "all" (*sarva*) refers only to all humans under discussion here as subjects of treatment; therefore, one should not raise the objection that milk is unwholesome for beings born from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*) and so forth. Alternatively, this word "all" is used in the sense of "many.

In the phrase "by those who subsist on fruits and roots," the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*) due to its connection with the word *pṛthak* ("separately").
*Aśmantaka* is a tree with leaves resembling those of the *māluyā*.
Pūtīka is the thorny karañja;

*tilvaka* is *lodhra*. By the qualifying term "its tree" (*tasya taruḥ*), he excludes *paṭṭikālodhra* and indicates that *śābaralodhra*—which is of great size and worthy of the designation "tree"—is intended; alternatively, by the qualification "tree," he excludes young *lodhra*.

Regarding the statement "six trees are purificatory" (*ṣaḍvṛkṣāñ śodhanāni*): although *kṛṣṇagandhā* is not mentioned among the [drugs] used for the five purificatory procedures (*pañcakarman*) and thus does not possess the status of a purifier [in that context], nevertheless, it should be understood that it acts as a purifier of external humors through external application as an ointment. Alternatively, by the force of the word "also" (*api*), its lack of purificatory action [in internal administration] is also indicated. (116–119) Demonstrating the primacy of knowledge regarding the formulation of the aforementioned medicinal herbs, he says: "The medicinal herbs... and so forth.
"Attaining the highest state" means the most excellent and correct application (samyagyoga) with respect to the disease,
the body, and so forth; "yoga" is the complete and correct joining of the medicine in every way through its names, forms, and applications.
Demonstrating that yoga alone is distinguished, he says "yogam" and so forth.
The phrase "deśakālopapāditam" means produced by place and time.

By the repetition "puruṣaṃ puruṣaṃ vīkṣya" (observing person after person), he shows that because of the differences in *prakṛti* and other factors, there is generally a difference in yoga for each individual.
By the word "puruṣa" here, the person associated with yoga (saṃyogapuruṣa) is intended.

Since yoga depends upon knowledge of medicine, [the author] demonstrates through many examples the great harmfulness of ignorance regarding medicine, beginning with the verse: "Just as poison... and so forth.

By means of many examples such as poison and so forth, he demonstrates that a medicine unknown [to the physician] may kill by destroying consciousness like poison, or kill by cutting vital points (*marmans*) like a weapon, or kill by producing boils and the like like fire, or kill instantaneously like lightning.

By the phrase "by means of the qualities of name and form" (*nāmarūpaguṇaiḥ*), although a triad is already established, the further mention of "by three" (*tribhiḥ*) is for the purpose of excluding the knowledge of each one individually; thus, he shows that a medicine known through all three combined is truly excellent. (124–125)
He praises yoga with the words beginning "even from yoga," and so forth.
That even poison becomes medicine through proper application should be understood from such clinical applications as "one should give a sesame seed of poison" (Ci. A.

1). It is not only that a physician must not withhold medicine from a patient; rather, he states with the words beginning "to one who is suffering" that a physician must also not administer medicine to a patient if it is outside of rational application.

Now, he explains what the characteristics of a properly administered medicine are, and likewise the characteristics of an excellent physician who is to be accepted—beginning with the words "tadeva" (that very same) and ending with "yaḥ pramocayet" (who would liberate from diseases). By this, it is stated that the removal of disease occurs through the administration of medicine preceded by knowledge. Therefore, the practice of a quack who achieves success by mere chance should not be described [as medical practice]. For in the case of accidental success, the physician is not the cause of liberation from disease; rather, it is simply the proper application of medicine that has arrived by chance, according to the maxim of the "worm in wood" (ghuṇākṣara-nyāya).
How is correct application of the medicine known through health? To this he says: "proper administration," and so forth.

By the word "of all," he indicates that the success of other actions as well—such as the making of images—is due to correct application, which is their cause; for indeed, when the cause is not correctly applied, the effect cannot be correct.
"It is declared that there is accomplishment" means that the accomplishment described is specific and determined, not accidental;
for it is heard [in scripture] that it is characterized by all qualities such as purity and so forth, as will be explained in the *Khuḍḍaka-catuṣpāda* (Sūtra 10).

Regarding the phrase "there are verses" (*tatra ślokāḥ*), this is the convention of the author of the treatise: wherever he expresses a previously stated matter in summary form, he uses the expression "there are verses"; however, wherever something is stated that is not redundant with what has been said before, he uses the expression "and there occurs here" (*bhavati cātra*). This is not purposeless, for it is the characteristic of a treatise (*tantradharma*) to express in summary at the end of a chapter the subject matter discussed within that chapter—beginning with the words "The tradition of Āyurveda," etc. Furthermore, the statement of this summary is for the purpose of grasping the previously explained meaning in brief, as well as for the purpose of preventing [the meaning] from being difficult to understand.
Whatever may be difficult to understand here will be ascertained by cross-referencing it with the meaning established in this [work],

for there is this saying: "When a matter expressed in prose is subsequently sung again in verses, that repetition is not to be censured, as it serves the purpose of clarifying the determination of the meaning" (Nirukta 1.1).
And here, the phrase "stated in prose" (*gadyokta*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for what has been stated in detail;
therefore, it is not contradictory that the meaning of the *āragvadhīya* and other sections, though already stated in verse (*śloka*), is again summarized by means of a verse.
*Vyakti* means clarity; *vyavasāya* means ascertainment.

“Scripture” (*āgama*) refers to [the verse] beginning with “seeking long life” (*dīrghañjīvitamanvicchan*); “reason” (*hetu*) refers to the reason for the scripture of Āyurveda, and that [reason]—namely, the manifestation of disease—is stated in the passage beginning with “when diseases act as obstacles” (*vighnabhūtā yadā rogā*). Alternatively, the verse beginning with “seeking long life” serves as a summary-sūtra specifically for the scripture of Āyurveda as well as its reason; whereas the textual portion beginning with “for by Brahmā” (*brahmaṇā hi*) establishes the scripture of Āyurveda, and the portion beginning with “acting as obstacles” (*vighnabhūtā*) establishes the reason, exactly as described.

"The propagation of the tradition" means that Bharadvāja, having received [the knowledge] from Indra, propagated it in the mortal world until its mastery; "the formulation of the aphorisms" refers to the composition of the Ayurveda treatise; and "the authorization of Agniveśa and others" refers to the passage beginning with "And those were approved."
The remainder is easy to understand (136–140).
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Longevity Chapter" (*Dīrghañjīvitīya*), in the *Carakatātparyaṭīkā*, known as the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Chapter 2 of Sūtrasthāna (2 of 120):

On Longevity] In the chapter on longevity (*dīrghañjīvitīya*), the plants with roots and those with fruits that serve as components for the five therapeutic procedures (*pañcakarma*) have been described; furthermore, other agents for the five procedures such as *pippalī* and *marica* also exist. Likewise, the specific subject matter regarding the five procedures has not yet been stated there. Therefore, immediately following this, the chapter titled "On the Seeds of *Apāmārga*" (*apāmārgataṇḍulīya*) is now declared, which describes the remaining substances useful for the five procedures and the scope of their application.

Although the *apāmārga* and other [plants] have already been mentioned previously, the reason they are stated again here is that the Teacher himself will resolve this at the end of the chapter with the two verses beginning “First, roots and fruits” (*pūrvaṃ mūlaphala*).

When the designation *apāmārgabījīya* would have been expected, the name *apāmārgataṇḍulīya* is employed in order to include only the dehusked seeds of the *apāmārga* and others. By using the word *taṇḍula* (grain) for the chapter title, he then uses the word *bīja* (seed) in the phrase "the seeds of the *apāmārga*" in order to include only those grains which are capable of producing sprouts.

Although, as a general rule (*utsarga*), the engagement in the five purificatory therapies (*pañcakarma*) begins with emesis (*vamana*), as stated: "The application of emesis and the other therapies occurs during the common seasons" (Vi. A. 8), and likewise in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā*: "For in one who has not vomited properly, even if they have been purged, the *śleṣman* (phlegm) displaced downwards covers the *grahaṇī*" (Su. Ci. A. 33), and so forth; nevertheless, in certain cases, depending on the predominance of the *doṣas*, the sequence may be otherwise—such as purgation (*virecana*) and so on when *pitta* is aggravated in autumn, or enemas (*basti*) and so on when *vāta* is strong in the rainy season (*prāvṛṣ*). It is for this reason of non-fixity that head-purification (*śirovirecana*) is mentioned first here. Alternatively, head-purification was performed first because it cleanses the head, which is the primary organ.
As it has been stated: "That which is the foremost among limbs is called the head" (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 17);
and it is also said in Śālākya-tantra: "Just as a tree grows properly when its root is free from disease, so too the body grows properly when the head is free from disease."
*Apāmārga* is mentioned first because it is preeminent among head-purgatives (*śirovirecana*), as it has been stated: "The *pratyakpuṣpā* [is the best] of head-purgatives" (Sūtra-sthāna 25).
*Ajagandhā* is *ajamodā*; some call it *phophāndhī*.
Pilu is the fruit from the northern region (auttarāpathika).

The two salts—sauvarcala and saindhava—are those recited in the section on salts and the like. This group [of drugs] may be used for head-purgation (śirovirecana) either individually or collectively, because it constitutes a medicinal category (gaṇa).
As it has been stated: "Even if a substance has been specifically enumerated, one should take it if one considers it non-essential" (Viśeṣa 8);
and elsewhere it is also said: "The entire group, or half, or even according to availability" (Sūtrasthāna 37).
The term "of the head" (*śirasaḥ*) is connected with both "heaviness" (*gaurave*) and "pain" (*śūle*).
In this context, the disease caused by worms (krimivyādhi) should be understood as being located specifically in the head, since it is precisely there that head-purgation (śirovirecana) is effective;
furthermore, "delusion" (pramohaka) refers to fainting (mūrchā) or the dullness of the sense organs (indriyāpaṭutva).

Among emetic substances, *madana* fruit is mentioned first because of its preeminence; for it is said: "Among emetic substances, *madana* fruits are declared to be the very best because they are free from complications" (Ka. A. 1).

"Presented" (*upasthita*) should be explained as having reached the upper part of the stomach (*āmāśaya*), the seat of *śleṣman*, and having become provoked (*utkleśa*). "Kapha and pitta" (*śleṣmapitta*) refers to both *śleṣman* and *pitta*.

Although *pitta* is not directly an object for emesis (*vamana*), it nevertheless becomes an object for emesis due to its connection with *śleṣman* (phlegm) by virtue of having reached the site of *śleṣman*.
As it has been said: "One should treat a *doṣa* that has reached the site of another *doṣa* as if it were residing in its own site.

Although it was stated [in the context] of emesis that one should act "without vitiating the body," this should also be understood to apply to purgation (*virecana*) and other procedures, because there too the suspicion of bodily vitiation through excessive, deficient, or improper application is equally present.
And it is stated by those learned in logic: "When the subject matter is the same, a rule prescribed in one instance should be applied elsewhere as well.

Thus, following the description of emesis, the mention of purgation occurs in the sequence of describing the purification of the head and the upper body; and immediately after the purification of the upper part of the stomach (āmāśaya), [it follows] because it removes the *pitta* situated in the lower part of the stomach.

In this way, although the enema (basti) is mentioned immediately after purgation (virecana), it is discussed [first] in the section on trivṛt and other drugs because of its superiority among purgative substances; for it has been said: "Trivṛt is the best among pleasant purgatives" (Sūtra-sthāna, chapter 25).
Nīlikā, nīlabuhnā, kṣīriṇī, dugdhikā,
and dravantī are varieties of dantī.
*Nicula* is well known as *hijjala*. "Located in the *pakvāśaya*" (*pakvāśayagata*) means it has reached the *pakvāśaya*;
therefore, the impurity (*doṣa*) that is the object of purgation is located specifically in the *pittāśaya*, which is characterized as the lower part of the *āmāśaya*, and not in the *pakvāśaya*.
In this context, by the word *doṣa*, either *pitta* or *kaphapitta* is intended, because they are suitable for removal by purgation;

as it has been said: "The laxative (*sraṃsana*) should remove *pitta* or *kaphapitta* located in the receptacle of *pitta* (*pittāśaya*); the enema (*basti*) should remove the three impurities (*malas*) situated in the receptacle of digested food (*pakvāśaya*)" (Ci. A. 3).

Alternatively, a *doṣa* (humor) that has reached the vicinity of the colon (*pakvāśaya*) and is thus inclined toward downward movement is said to be "located in the colon," just as one says "the hamlet is on the Ganges.

The description of the non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*) prior to the unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*)— beginning with the verse "pāṭalām" and so forth— is because the *nirūha* is primarily intended for the removal of the *doṣas*.

In the chapter on the physician’s victory over disease (Viśeṣa-sthāna 8), *kattṛṇa* and *gandhatṛṇa*, as well as the unctuous substances— clarified butter (*sarpis*), oil (*taila*), muscle fat (*vasā*), and marrow (*majjan*)— and salts such as rock salt (*saindhava*) and others, are stated as the primary items for enemas (*vasti*) according to their respective groups.
The phrase "for this very reason" refers to the group of drugs beginning with *pāṭala* mentioned in the context of the *nirūha*;
by the statement "the *anuvāsana* is to be prepared [from that]," he declares the means for preparing the unctuous substance (*sneha*). For the *anuvāsana* consists of the unctuous substance itself;

thus, a separate substance for preparing the *sneha* for the purpose of *anuvāsana* has not been mentioned, since it is accomplished by the very same group of medicinal drugs prescribed for the *nirūha*.

By the term *mārutaghnam* (wind-destroying), he indicates the scope for the application of non-unctuous enemas (*anuvāsana*); the meaning is that when wind (*māruta*) is to be subdued, a non-unctuous enema should be prepared.

Alternatively, it suggests that from the group of drugs beginning with *pāṭalā* which remove wind, a wind-destroying non-unctuous enema should be prepared; whereas from other groups—specifically those removing bile (*pitta*) or phlegm (*śleṣman*)—a bile-destroying or phlegm-destroying enema should be prepared, as indicated by the word *saṅgraha*.

Furthermore, by this [term], he indicates the detailed exposition of the five medical procedures (*pañcakarma*) that will be discussed in the chapters on *kalpa* and *siddhi* within the *Rogabhiṣagjitīya* section (Vi. A. 8).
He shows how the five procedures (*pañcakarman*) are to be performed by means of the words beginning with "those" (*tāni*).
The word "those" (*tāni*) refers to those previously mentioned.

The plural number in the phrase "by means of oleation and sudation" (*snehasvedopapādanaiḥ*) is for the purpose of indicating various types of oleation and sudation. "Of the provoked humors" (*upasthitadoṣāṇām*) refers to those humors that have abandoned the peripheral branches (*śākhā*) and moved into the visceral cavity (*koṣṭha*), as well as those that have abandoned their state of latency (*līnatva*) and reached their primary state (*pradhānāvasthā*). In that regard, the very fact of having provoked humors is the reason for proceeding with the five purificatory therapies (*pañcakarma*); for if it were otherwise, even without the application of oleation and sudation—as in the case of fever, where [it is said]: "the humors, dominated by phlegm, being excited and situated in the stomach..."—[the therapies would still be indicated].

"Having recognized the causes of fever at the appropriate time, one should eliminate them through emetics for those cases where emesis is indicated" (Ci.A.3). In this regard, although the onset of emesis can indeed occur even without the prior administration of oleation and sudation, the prescription of oleation and sudation is stated as being the general rule; furthermore, it is taught that even when the morbid humors (doṣas) are present in another manner, these procedures may be performed in small doses to overcome the vāta produced by the agitation caused by the initiation of the five purificatory therapies (pañcakarma).

The mention of *mātrā* (dose) and *kāla* (time) is for the sake of their being subjects of investigation due to their preeminence; by that, it should be understood that *doṣa* (humors), *bheṣaja* (medicines), and so forth are also to be understood here as subjects of investigation. Alternatively, as before, the inclusion of the remaining factors such as the *doṣas* should be explained as being implied by the very mention of *kāla*.

Even though the word "those" (*tāni*) has already been used, the explicit mention of "five" (*pañca*) again is for the purpose of instructing on the application [of therapies] when all five are present as morbid humors;
here, in procedures such as emesis (*vamana*), the characteristic of the action is the superior power of eliminating the *doṣas* associated with extensive procedural requirements.

Therefore, when it is stated in another tantra that there are "seven procedures" by adding oleation (*sneha*) and sudation (*sveda*), that is not the case; for oleation and sudation do not effect the external expulsion of the *doṣas*, but rather they effect their pacification (*saṃśamana*). However, when oleation and sudation function as ancillaries to the five procedures (*pañcakarma*), they function solely toward the provocation (*upasthāna*) of the *doṣas*, and not toward their expulsion (*nirharaṇa*) which is accomplished by emesis (*vamana*) and the other procedures.

Although *anuvāsana* (oil enema) does not cause the elimination of many morbid humors (*doṣas*) like emesis and other therapies, it nevertheless fulfills the definition of a therapeutic action (*karma*) because it expels feces and wind located in the colon (*pakvāśaya*).

However, in the case of spitting, eye-salves, and similar treatments, there is no application of extensive procedural requirements as in oleation or sudation, nor do they eliminate many morbid humors; therefore, they are not denoted by the term "action" (*karma*).
As for the *uttarabasti* (urethral/vaginal enema), being of the nature of an oil-based enema, it is included within the category of *snehavasti*.

Alternatively, if this technical term refers to the five purificatory procedures (pañcakarma) such as emesis and so forth by virtue of being both etymological and conventional—like the word "lotus" (*paṅkaja*)—then it does not apply to oleation, sudation, expectoration, and the like.
[The author] states the result of considering the dose and time, beginning with "mātrākāla... and so forth.
*Rukti* (reasoning/application) is the application of medicine in consideration of the bodily humors (*doṣas*) and other factors.
He praises this *yukti* with the verse beginning "Success" (*siddhi*), etc.;
here, "success" (*siddhi*) refers to the accomplishment of the goal to be achieved, namely the pacification of the disorder (*vikāra*).

Now, with the preliminary statement "hereafter," etc., he prescribes gruel (*yavāgū*) for the purpose of kindling the fire that has become weak due to the improper administration of emetics and other therapies, as well as for the purpose of pacifying colic and other ailments produced by the non-application of emetics and such;
for it has been said: "Just as a tiny spark of fire, when fanned by grass, cow dung, and so forth, becomes [large] gradually..."
"In the case of a person who is large, stable, and a consumer of all kinds of food, the internal fire of one who is pure [should be stimulated] with drinks and so forth" (Siddhi-sthāna 1)—

this statement regarding the preparation of the *pippalyādi-yavāgū* (rice gruel with long pepper and other ingredients) uses the term "prepared" (*upasādhitā*) for the purpose of taking the appropriate quantities of the constituent substances, such as the medicinal drugs, water, and rice;
the specific measure of the medicinal drugs and other components is not explicitly stated here, because the dosage (*mātrā*) is not fixed due to variations in the digestive fire and other factors.
As it has been said: "There is no fixed rule for dosage; one should administer the dose after considering the [patient's] humors, digestive fire, strength, age, disease, substance, and constitution.

Although this is so, nevertheless, based on the observation of technical definitions and the practice of experienced physicians, the manner in which it should be done is now stated: the substances used for preparing gruels (yavāgū) are of two kinds—medicinal substances in which potency (vīrya) is predominant, and food substances in which taste (rasa) is predominant.

In that regard, medicinal substances are also of three types according to the difference in their potency (*vīrya*): those of sharp potency (*tīkṣṇavīrya*), such as ginger (*śuṇṭhī*) and others; those of medium potency (*madhyavīrya*), such as *bilva* and *agnimantha*; and those of mild potency (*mṛduvīrya*), such as *āmalaka* and others. Regarding these, the general rule is that one *karṣa* for the sharp, half a *pala* for the medium, and one *pala* for the mild [should be used].

As stated by Agniveśa: "One should cook half a *karṣa* of long pepper (*kaṇā*) and ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), or one *pala* of any paste-like substance (*kalkadravya*), having dissolved it with a *prastha* of water, using the appropriate method."
In this context, although a dose of half a *pala* for those of medium potency (*madhyavīrya*) is not explicitly stated, it should be understood by taking the medium measure as the standard.

Likewise, in the case of the *peyā* beginning with "with *jīvantī*, *ajājī*, *śaṭī*, and *puṣkaramūla*" (Ci. A. 12), the nine substances combined in the measure of a *kola* result in a total that is not far from one *pala*; and this is intended specifically for those of mild potency (*mṛduvīrya*). [As it is said: "Having boiled one *añjali* of crushed decoction-ingredients in one *āḍhaka* of water..."

In the passage, "Then one should prepare gruel (yavāgū) and so forth with that [decoction] boiled to half its volume," the mention of four *pala* of the substance is intended solely for substances where the juice (*rasa*) is the primary constituent. Therefore, this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) should be understood in such cases as, "Gruel prepared in a decoction of pork is considered nourishing. Regarding the technical rule for the six-ingredient preparation (*ṣaḍaṅga-sādhana*), it is stated: "When the six-ingredient [decoction] and others are employed in water that has been boiled and then cooled, one should prepare one *karṣa* of that substance in one *prastha* of water."

Regarding the statement, "It should be used half-boiled for drinking or in the preparation of *peyā* and other [gruels]," the mention of a *karṣa* measure of the medicinal substance in relation to the *peyā* must be understood as intended for a person with weak digestion, even though the six-ingredient (*ṣaḍaṅga*) preparation possesses moderate potency.

As for the quantity of water, a *prastha* of water for a *karṣa* of substance is specified in the technical definition of the six-ingredient method; following that rule, an increase in water should be understood to apply elsewhere as well.
However, where a gruel (*yavāgū*) is to be prepared from a paste (*kalka*), the amount of water should be taken according to the proportions stated in the culinary treatises (*sūdaśāstra*).

As it has been stated: "Solid food (*anna*) is prepared with five parts [of water], gruel (*vilepī*) with four parts, scum (*maṇḍa*) with fourteen parts, and rice-gruel (*yavāgū*) with six parts of water";
and this [proportion] of "five parts" and so forth should be understood as being from the total aggregate of rice and medicinal ingredients.

The quantity of rice that serves as the base for gruel (*yavāgū*) should be understood from the words of Suśruta, which state: "The physician [should prepare] *vilepī* made with a fourth part of the usual amount of cooked rice" (Su.Ci.A.
39), and likewise, "gruel (*yavāgū*) contains very little rice."

A gruel prepared with the *pañcakola* group is mentioned first; because it causes the increase of the digestive fire diminished by the five purificatory procedures (*pañcakarma*), the *dadhittha* (wood-apple) is used.
In this context, *takra* (buttermilk) acts as a substitute for water;
the word *grāhiṇī* is to be split [as *grāhiṇi*]; and *savāte* refers to diarrhea accompanied by wind (*vāta*).

The "five roots" (*pañcamūla*) here refers to the *sthirādi-pañcamūla*; as stated in the *Jatūkarṇa*: "With *dhruvā* and others in cases of wind-type diarrhea. *Dhruvādi* refers to the *vidārigandhādi* group.
Regarding the statement "pṛśniparṇī, round-leaved [plant], siṃhapucchī, and sour pomegranate," this indicates that the quantity of pomegranate should be such that it provides the desired acidity.

In the verse beginning with "payasyardhodake," *nāgara* and *musta* are included; as stated by Jatūkarṇa: "In the case of bloody diarrhea (*raktātīsāra*), [the gruel is prepared] with goat's milk and water, along with *ghana*, *jala*, and *utpala*. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and with *pṛśniparṇī*," it should be understood that this refers specifically to the sour gruel (*yavāgū*) for curing bloody diarrhea, which is made sour with pomegranate (*dāḍima*).
Regarding the verse beginning with "śvadaṃṣṭrā," Jatūkarṇa states: "Pṛśni, gokaṇṭaka, and jaggery [cured] urinary distress and bladder pain.
Here, *suvarcikā* refers to *sarjikākṣāra*, and the word is split as *pipāsāghnī*.
Somarājī, avalguja,
gavedhuka, and ghuluñca; and in place of gavedhuka grains,
śyāmāka— a specific type of grass— is used, and its seed-grains are to be taken.
In the Yamaka (combination) formula, where ghee and oil are present,
wine should take the place of the liquid; otherwise, gruel (yavāgū) should be understood as being used with equal parts of vegetables and other such ingredients.
By the term "sour wood-apple" (*dadhitthāmla*), he shows that it refers specifically to the state of the *kapittha* fruit when it is sour;
"alkali" (*kṣāra*) means barley-alkali (*yavakṣāra*);
and "prepared with buttermilk" (*takrasiddhā*) means that which has performed the function of water made from buttermilk.
*Piṇyāka* is sesame paste;
by the term *yamaka*, he demonstrates roasting with a double layer [of paste].

In the phrase beginning with *samāṣavidala*, the quantity of split black gram (*māṣavidala*) is equal to that of rice; milk takes the place of water, and ghee is used for the roasting. Alternatively, this [preparation] may have black gram as its primary ingredient.

By the word *mada* (intoxication), all three types—poison, blood, and liquor—are included, as there is no specific distinction made in the statement "one should destroy hunger" and so forth; in such cases, *apāmārga* seeds take the place of rice grains, while milk and the meat-broth of a monitor lizard (*godhā*) take the place of water.
He provides a summary of the chapters by means of the *pratiloma* (reverse) method of tantric reasoning, beginning with "twenty-eight," etc.
(verse 34).

He states the justification for the repetition of plants such as *apāmārga* and *jīmūta*, which were already included in the list of the *mūlinī* and *phalinī* groups in the *Dīrghañjīvitīya* chapter, starting with "previously," etc.

"Because of the need for knowledge of the root and the fruit" means: "in order to know that 'the practical application of this is by way of its root' and 'the practical application of this is by way of its fruit. It is the locus of the five activities; and the word "locus" (āśraya) emphasizes the state [of being]. Therefore, it results in the meaning: "for the sake of knowing the state of being the locus of the five activities."

Although plants with roots and those with fruits are also mentioned as bases for the five types of medical procedures in the *Dīrghañjīvitīya* chapter—starting from the passage, "Śaṇapuṣpī, Bimbī, and so forth" (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 1)—nevertheless, because they are not included here among the groups of substances being described primarily as the bases for the five procedures, one might suspect that plants such as *Apāmārga* are secondary in their role as bases for the five procedures. Therefore, it is said: "That [group] is proclaimed again for the purpose of providing knowledge regarding the bases of the five procedures.
(Verse 35)

Since the engagement in the five therapeutic procedures (pañcakarma) taught in this chapter is difficult to master, [the author] describes the kind of physician by whom medical treatment must be performed: "possessing memory" (smṛtimān), and so forth. "Possessing presence of mind" (pratipattimān) means one who possesses immediate knowledge of what ought to be done when a crisis arises.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Seeds of Apāmārga," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the first section on Medicaments (*Bhaiṣajyacatuṣka*) of the *Sūtrasthāna*.
[Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 3 (3 of 120)]

Indeed, medicine is twofold: internal cleansing and external cleansing. Having described internal cleansing—consisting of the five purificatory procedures (pañcakarma) and medicinal gruels (yavāgū)—in the chapter on *Apāmārgataṇḍula*, [the author] states the remaining external cleansing, such as topical applications, in the chapter on *Āragvadha* with the words, "Now, therefore, the Āragvadha chapter," and so forth.

Although the treatment of leprosy (kuṣṭha) will appear separately in the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsā-sthāna), and it would have been appropriate to mention these [drugs] such as āragvadha and others there, since their occasion arises then; nevertheless, by mentioning the formulations for leprosy separately here, [the author] proclaims its status as a major disease due to its persistent nature. For a matter that is highly esteemed is indeed stated again and again.

And this treatment for leprosy (kuṣṭha) is stated with reference to leprosy as characterized by its causes, symptoms, and so forth in the Section on Etiology (Nidānasthāna), according to the methodological principle of "anticipating the future" (anāgatāvekṣaṇa-tantrayukti). Therefore, the objection that "treatment being described for what has not been characterized is improper because its subject matter is unknown" is refuted.

Furthermore, although there are other major diseases such as pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman) and others, they do not require such extensive external cleansing as does leprosy; thus, it is specifically regarding leprosy that these formulations for external cleansing are prescribed.
By way of introduction to the external cleansing treatments that cure skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), those remedies that alleviate *vāta*, such as "kola, kulattha," and so forth, will be described.

Furthermore, this is the essential nature of the applications for external cleansing that cure skin diseases: they become effective only when administered after the body has been purified (*śodhana*). As it is said: "Those ointments (*lepa*) which are applied for skin diseases [are successful] for those whose blood and *doṣas* have been eliminated."

"For those whose internal receptacles have been purified, success occurs immediately" (Ci. A. 7). By first describing the purificatory therapies (*saṃśodhana*) in the preceding chapter and then here presenting the formulations for *kuṣṭha* which had reached their proper occasion, the Teacher has performed an excellent arrangement of the text.

Furthermore, although the statement "Khadira is the foremost among those that remove *kuṣṭha*" (Sū. A. 25) establishes Khadira as the primary agent among medicines for curing *kuṣṭha*, the Teacher nevertheless teaches Āragvadha first, setting aside Khadira, in order to demonstrate that Āragvadha alone is the primary agent among external cleansing medicines (*bahiḥparimārjana*) for removing *kuṣṭha*.
1–2 He states those very formulations for removing skin diseases (kuṣṭha), beginning with *āragvadha*:
*śryāhva* is well known as "the *khoṭi* of fresh butter."
And *granthi* is *bhaurja*, meaning a knot made of birch bark;
*salomaśa* is *dhātukāsīsa* (green vitriol); and *phaṇijjhaka* is a variety of *parṇāsa*.
Sumanaḥ-pravāla, Jātī-pallava, Nikumbha, Dantī, Āla, and Haritāla.
Regarding the term *ardharūpaiḥ*, this means by half-verses (*ardhaśloka*).

The compound *gopittapītāḥ* means "yellowed by cow-bile" (*pītagopittāḥ*), where the former member is placed first according to the rule governing compounds such as *mayūravyaṃsaka*. Alternatively, they are called *gopittapītāḥ* because they have acquired a yellow color through the infusion of cow-bile (*gopittabhāvanayā*). Although all formulations composed by great sages are effective within their own respective domains, these are here described as "supremely effective" (*para-siddhāḥ*) because they quickly eliminate many diseases that are otherwise difficult to treat.

"Powders and plasters" (cūrṇapradehāḥ) refers to powders that are applied as plasters; or alternatively, "powder-plasters" refers to plasters made from substances that have been reduced to powder. A "plaster" (pradeha) is an ointment, and the method of application for these formulations—such as cow's urine, cow's bile, and so forth—should be understood as being for the purpose of removing skin diseases (kuṣṭha).

Regarding "sureśalupta" (Indralupta), although it is already included under the term *kuṣṭha*, it is mentioned again along with *kiṭibha*, *dadrū*, *pāmā*, and others in order to demonstrate specifically the power of these applications to cure those conditions.
Tumburu is well-known by its own name;
Vanya is Kaivartamustaka; and Caṇḍā is Corapuṣpī.
The word "first" (prathamam) is connected with the phrase "smeared with oil" (tailāktam).
Furthermore, in this section concerning the treatment of skin diseases (kuṣṭha), the oil to be understood here is mustard oil (sārṣapa).
"Amṛtāsaṅga" refers to blue vitriol (tutthaka).
Kaṭaṅkaṭerī is dāruharidrā;
saugandhika is gandhatṛṇa or sulphur (gandhaka);
and ārkam is the milk (payaḥ) of the arka plant.
Similarly, the medicinal paste for curing leprosy consists of *prapunnāḍa*,
*eḍagaja*, *hayamāraka*, and *karavīra*; the bark of these should be taken, as well as their inner pith, separately.
*Tuṣodaka* is sour gruel (*kāñjika*) made from barley grains with their husks through a specific process of fermentation.

*Palāśanirdāharasa* is the juice obtained by the burning of the *palāśa* tree; specifically, when the primary root of the *palāśa* has been cut and a jar is placed beneath it, the natural sap that drips from the burning of the tree above is collected.
*Caturaṅgula* is the golden *hālī* plant.

A single formulation consists of *aśvahana*, *karavīra*, *caturaṅgula*, *kākamācī*, and the leaves of *aśvahana*; for if there were two [of this], the number thirty-two mentioned hereafter would be contradicted. (3-17)

Fruits that are sources of oil, such as castor seeds, sesame, and so forth; "sour" refers to [substances] through their association with sour gruel (kāñjika) and the like; and the flesh—meaning meat—of marsh-dwelling animals such as rhinoceroses and the like, as well as of fish, constitutes "marsh-dwelling fish-meat."

*Vesavāra*: "Boneless meat, ground and steamed, combined with jaggery and ghee, and mixed with long pepper (*pippalī*) and black pepper (*marica*), is known as *vesavāra*. *Gandhauṣadhāni* are fragrant medicinal substances; these include agallochum (*aguru*) and others, which are explained in the chapter on fevers (*jvarādhyāya*). The phrase "prepared with fragrant medicinal substances" (*gandhauṣadhaiḥ siddhaiḥ*) should be applied accordingly; thus, the unctuous substances (*sneha*) should be prepared with both the *daśamūla* and the fragrant medicinal substances. Alternatively, this poultice (*pradeha*) consists of the *daśamūla*-prepared fragrant medicinal substances mixed with unctuous substances.
They desire to speak;
*vidārī* is the tuberous root (*vidārīkanda*),
and *sitopalā* is white sugar (*sitaśarkarā*).
The remainder of the honey, along with beeswax, is prepared; that is, having been combined with ghee and milk, it is cooked slightly over the fire.
*Nata* is *tagarapādikā*; in its absence, *śīulīcoppaḍaka* is taken;
*prapauṇḍarīka* is *puṇḍarīka*.
Iron, aguru, erakā, hoggala,
and this [iron] together with prapauṇḍarīka and the others, ending with coraka— this is one formulation.
*Coraka* is *corapuṣpikā*, well-known by its own name;
*nalada* is *māṃsī*; and the two called *śatāhvā* are *śatapuṣpā* and *madhurikā*.
Tuṅga, punnāga,
amṛṇāla, uśīra, kāleyaka, and kāliyākāṣṭha.
Latā, mañjiṣṭhā, aindrī, gorakṣakarkaṭī,
and nalinam (the lotus).
The root of *yavāsa*, the root of *durālabhā*, the roots of *kuśa* and *kāśa*,
and *sitādirerakā*— this constitutes one formulation.
Water, bālaka,
sindhuvāra, nirguṇḍī, viṣa, and so forth— this is another formulation.
Lāmajjaka, uśīra,
hema, nāgakeśara, abhaya, and uśīra.
Summary of the meaning of chapters 23–29: Here, the passage beginning with "Atri" and ending with "powders and plasters" (cūrṇapradehān) is to be explained as before.
The specification of the number as "thirty-two" is for the purpose of eliminating confusion regarding fewer or more numbers.

Thus ends the third chapter, named "On Āragvadha," in the first section on Medicaments (Bheṣajacatuṣka) of the Sūtrasthāna, within the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
3 [Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 4 (4 of 120)]:

In the chapter on *apāmārgataṇḍula*, internal cleansing was described; and in the chapter on *āragvadha*, external cleansing was described. Now, the *Ṣaḍvirecanaśatāśritīya* chapter is being expounded to state the remaining category of medicines for both types of cleansing, which was not yet presented in the two preceding chapters and must necessarily be explained.
The term *āśrita* means that which is resorted to, in the sense of a "basis" (*āśraya*).

This chapter is titled *Ṣadvirecanaśatāśritīya* because it was composed with reference to the six hundred purgatives delimited by the number six, which constitute the bases. By this it is meant that one should understand that this designation was formulated with reference to these two categories: the six hundred purgatives and the six bases of purgation.

Furthermore, although the word *iha khalu* (here indeed) is heard at the beginning of the chapter, nevertheless, because it is not the primary subject, it has not been included in the formal designation of the chapter.
The word *iha* (here) refers to the *Agniveśa-tantra*, which is neither too concise nor too prolix.

By this, it is indicated that even in the detailed formulation of the six hundred purgatives to be described hereafter, as well as the fifty great *kaṣāyas* and the five hundred *kaṣāyas*, there may be further expansion; for this very reason, he will state in the section on pharmaceutical preparations (*kalpa*): "This [list] of six hundred should be regarded here as merely a brief enumeration."
"One may thus imagine thousands or even ten million [worlds] by one's own intellect" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.6);
likewise, he will say in this very context: "For there is no limit to its extent," and so forth;
indeed, the word *khalu* is used here for the purpose of clarification.

In this context, by the term *virecana*, both emesis (*vamana*) and purgation (*virecana*) are intended, since the author will state in the *Kalpa-sthāna*: "Both [emesis and purgation] receive the designation *virecana* because they expel the humors (*doṣa*) and impurities (*mala*)" (Ka.A.1).

Nor should it be argued that if the name *virecana* is applied due to the expulsion of humors and impurities, then the name *virecana* would also apply to enemas (*basti*) and head-purgations (*śirovirecana*); for this is a technical designation established by the author of the treatise, and does not function merely through its etymological derivation like the word *pācaka*. Furthermore, the author of the treatise applies this name as a conventional term (*rūḍhi*) specifically to emesis and purgation, and nowhere else; so how could there be any such extension elsewhere?
The teacher himself will explain "six hundred purgatives" and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "five hundred decoctions" (*kaṣāya*), by the word *kaṣāya* is meant the medicinal substance that serves as the substratum for those tastes—sweet and the rest, excluding salt—which have been designated as "decoctions" (*kaṣāya*). These are the sources of decoctions, the classes of decoctions.
The preparation (*kalpanā*) of decoctions (*kaṣāya*)—that is, the processing of the aforementioned substances for the purpose of administration—is called "decoction-preparation" (*kaṣāyakalpanā*).

The term "great decoctions" (*mahākaṣāya*) is the designation for a group of medicinal drugs (*auṣadhagaṇa*) consisting of ten items, which are grouped together for the sake of performing a single function. As he will state: "These ten are the vitalizing [drugs]," and so forth (Sūtra 1.3).

"Kalpopaniṣad" means that the ritual manual (*kalpa*) itself is the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*), by way of summary or mere indication. In the Veda, "upaniṣad" refers to a place of instruction for extremely useful secret knowledge; likewise here too, because the ritual manual is extremely useful as it teaches the applications of emetics and purgatives, the ritual manual itself is called the "secret doctrine."

Nor should it be argued: "Since six hundred purificatory procedures will be described in detail in the *Kalpasthāna*, let that suffice; there is no need for this brief statement, as it does not serve as a means for complete understanding. For this is the nature of a treatise (*tantra*): first there is a concise summary (*sūtraṇa*), followed by its detailed exposition (*prapañca*). And it is said by those who know the rules of logic: "Those subjects are well-grasped which possess both a summary and an expansion. Thus, one hundred and thirty-three formulations constitute the "three hundred and thirty-three formulations" (*trayastriṃśad-yoga-śata*).
The formulations ending with *kṛtavedhana* are for emesis; the remaining ones are for purgation.
Here, "śyāmā" refers specifically to *trivṛt*, where "śyāmā" means *trivṛt* with dark roots, and "trivṛt" means *trivṛt* with reddish roots.
"Six," and so forth:
there are exactly six bases for purgation, that is, the substrata for purgation.
For here, milk is placed first because it is a sharp purgative; as it is said: "The milk of *snuk* is for those who require sharp purgatives" (Sūtra-sthāna 25).
By the word "bark," the bark of *lodhra* is understood;
by the word "leaf," the leaf of *ikṣvāku* and others is meant.

As he will state in the Kalpasthāna: "One should administer a fistful of sprouts from a flowerless plant, cooked in one *prastha* of milk, for a fever arising from *kapha* with a predominance of *pitta*" (Ka.A. 3).

Although it is possible that castor oil, copper, mercury, and the like—even when present in quantities exceeding milk—may serve as bases for purgation, nevertheless, because they are not mentioned here in this treatise within the Kalpasthāna as bases for purgation, the statement "the six bases" in this context refers to the formulations (*yoga*) established at the beginning of the chapter; thus, there is no contradiction.
The five hundred types of *kaṣāya* are to be explained by means of the exposition of the great *kaṣāyas*; therefore, bypassing those, the five sources of *kaṣāya* are now stated.
That which is both sweet (*madhura*) and an astringent (*kaṣāya*) is called a sweet-astringent (*madhurakaṣāya*); the same applies to the remaining [types].

By the term "sañjñā" (designation) in the tantra, it indicates that with the exception of the salty taste (*lavaṇa-rasa*), the tastes beginning with sweet (*madhura*) are designated by the term "astringent" (*kaṣāya*); thus, this is the independent convention (*svatantra-samaya*), and here there is no usage according to other systems (*paratantra-vyavahāra*).

Now, for what reason does the Teacher again abandon the designation "kaṣāya" for salt—which, like sweet and other tastes, has been taught by its qualities and so forth; which is taught in formulations such as the *citraka-guḍikā* by the statement "the two alkalis and the salts" (*Ci. A. 15*); which is taught as a whole category in the *Rogabhiṣagjitīya* (*Vi. A. 8*); and which is taught in various sections on tastes just like sweet and the rest? It is said: this designation "kaṣāya" was established by the Teacher for those tastes that function as medicinal substances.
In this context, there is no use of salt alone, whereas sweet and other tastes may be used even by themselves; however, salt is employed only when combined with other substances.
Furthermore, pharmaceutical preparations characterized as fresh juices, pastes, and so forth are possible for sweet and other tastes, but not for salt.

To begin with, salt possesses no natural juice (*svarasa*). A paste (*kalka*) is also prepared by grinding a substance with a liquid, but that is not possible for salt; for when salt comes into contact with water, it becomes water itself. Even though powder (*cūrṇa*) is a variety of paste, and the state of being powder is possible for salt, nevertheless, the powdered form of salt does not produce any specific potency (*śaktiviśeṣa*) distinct from its prior non-powdered state. We shall demonstrate later that a conceptualization is made for the sake of postulating a specific potency, and therefore even the "powderedness" of salt is like a mere conceptual construction. Furthermore, decoctions (*śṛta*), cold infusions (*śīta*), strained extracts (*phāṇṭa*), and astringent infusions (*kaṣāya*) are taught for the purpose of introducing small portions of a substance into liquids through various processing methods, when that substance cannot be used in its entirety. This is not possible for salt, because when in contact with a liquid, salt permeates the liquid in its entire essence. Therefore, because salt lacks separate application and because a [technical] preparation (*kalpanā*) is impossible for it, it was excluded by the Teacher when he formulated the designation "decoction" (*kaṣāya*); thus, this activity of the Teacher is not without purpose.

*Kalpanā* refers to the preparation for administration, meaning the processing [of medicinal substances], characterized by various features such as *svarasa* (fresh juice) and so forth; as it is said: "Fresh juice (*svarasa*) is declared to be the natural sap; a paste (*kalka*) is that ground on a stone;
a decoction (*śṛta*) is that which has been boiled; and a cold infusion (*śīta*) is considered to be that which has stood overnight."

Regarding the statement, "That which is crushed in hot water and then squeezed is called *phāṇṭa*," the verse of Śaunaka, however, says: "The decoction (*kaṣāya*) that emerges from a substance that has been soaked in heated water overnight is declared to be *śīta* (cold)."

Regarding the statement "the *phāṇṭa* is a decoction" (*kaṣāya*), this term *kaṣāya* is connected with the expressed juice (*svarasa*) and the other preparations as well. Therefore, it should be understood that the expressed juice is a decoction, the paste (*kalka*) is a decoction, and so forth.

Among these—the expressed juice and the others—there is an increasing degree of potency in the order mentioned; thus, the cold infusion (*śīta*) is heavier than the *phāṇṭa*, and the boiled decoction (*śṛta*) is heavier than the cold infusion, and so on.

Since the preparation of the decoction becomes progressively heavier in this sequence, for that very reason it must take into account the strength of both the disease and the patient; the meaning is that it depends upon the strength of the disease and the patient.
Regarding this, he states the justification: "But not so," and so forth.

The meaning is that a fresh juice (*svarasa*)—which is extremely heavy and performs many functions because it consists of the essential part of the substance—is appropriate for a person of strong constitution or for a severe disease; however, this [same juice] is not suitable for a person of weak strength or for a mild disease, because it causes a loss of strength and acts as a fault by way of being incompatible with the medicine. This should be explained similarly in other cases as well; likewise, not all [forms of administration], such as fresh juices and the rest, are suitable for every person. For some are averse to fresh juices, while others are fond of fresh juices and averse to other preparations, and so on.
Furthermore, the administration of extremely bitter medicine is not desired, because it causes immediate defects such as vomiting and loss of appetite;

likewise, the preparation of decoctions (kaṣāya) depends on the disease, the patient, and their strength—this is for the sake of illustration—and by this, it should also be understood that it depends on the substance (dravya), since he will state the rule regarding substances in the section on Rasāyana: "The fresh juice of maṇḍūkaparṇī should be used, and the powder of yaṣṭīmadhuka with milk."

Regarding the statement, "The juice of *guḍūcī* [should be used] together with its roots and flowers, and indeed the paste (*kalka*) of *śaṅkhapuṣpī* should be employed" (Ci.A.1), the powder (*cūrṇa*) must be understood as being included within the paste itself; for paste is of two kinds: liquid and non-liquid. Therefore, in passages such as, "Whether left overnight, or made into a fresh juice, or made into a paste, or as a powder, or boiled" (Ci.A.4), the occurrence of a separate mention of "powder" should not be raised as a point of contention regarding an additional formulation.

He cites the "great decoctions" (mahākaṣāya): beginning with "fifty," etc., that which is beneficial for life is "life-promoting" (jīvanīya); likewise, elsewhere, that which is prepared from six [ingredients] is a "hexad" (ṣaṭka), and this should be understood for the "tetrad" (catuṣka) and so forth as well.

In this context, the classification of the great *kaṣāyas* (medicinal decoctions) into groups of six and so forth should be understood through the pursuit of a specific purpose. For example: in the group beginning with *jīvanīya*, there is the suffix *-eya*; in the group beginning with *balya*, there is the suffix *-ya*; in the group beginning with *tṛptighna*, there is the suffix *-ghna*; and in the group beginning with *stanyajanana*, the subject matter concerns breast milk and semen. Such examples are to be inferred.

Furthermore, this detailed enumeration of various sub-classifications by means of suffixes such as *-eya* and others is intended to provide the treatise with a wealth of designations through its diversity;
