and this must necessarily be done within a scientific work (*śāstra*).

As was stated right here in the description of the qualities of this treatise: "Words that are not fallen [into error], words that are not strained, and abundant expression" (Vi. A. 8), and so forth; by the term *jīvanīya* (vitalizing), longevity (*āyuṣyatva*) is intended here. Furthermore, regarding the quality of the sweet taste (*madhurarasaguṇa*), he will state: "It is vitalizing (*āyuṣya*) and life-sustaining (*jīvanīya*)" (Sū. A. 26). In that context, its status as *jīvanīya* should be explained as the power to generate consciousness in one who has fainted.

*Tṛpti* (satiety) is a disorder of *kapha*, by which one feels as if one has overeaten. That which destroys it is *tṛptighna*. Regarding the term *snehopaga*: they are called *snehopaga* because they approach (*upagacchanti*) as auxiliaries (*sahāyatvena*) to the unctuous substance (*sneha*), such as ghee (*sarpiḥ*), during the act of oleation. The meaning is that when ghee and other substances are combined with *snehopagas* such as grapes (*mṛdvīkā*), their power for oleation becomes more intense. Similarly, regarding *vamanopaga*, honey, licorice (*madhuka*), and so forth serve as auxiliaries to emetic substances such as the fruits of *madana*. This should be explained in the same way for *svedopaga* and the others.
In the section on head-purgatives (*śirovirecana*), however, one should understand that the substances are primarily those used for head-purgation;
it is called "purifying the feces" (*purīṣavirajanīya*) because it effects the cleansing of the feces by removing their association with the *doṣas*.
This should be explained in the same way for the "purifying the urine" (*mūtravirajanīya*) section.

That which causes the evacuation of urine is *mūtravirecanīya*. *Udarda* is a swelling resembling the bite of a *varaṭī* (gadfly); that which pacifies it is *udardapraśamana*. However, the disorder of wind (*vātavikāra*) mentioned here is not the one listed in the chapter on major diseases (*mahārogādhyāya*), because substances such as *tinduka* and others, though they pacify *udarda*, are not favorable toward [excessive] wind. That which, having removed the corruption of vitiated blood, establishes the blood in its natural state, is called *śoṇitasthāpana*.

When sensation has arisen, by suppressing it, one establishes the body in its natural state; thus it is the "establishment of sensation. By establishing perception and knowledge, it is the "establishment of perception. By removing the affliction that harms living beings, one establishes the people [in well-being]; thus it is the "establishment of the people."
It establishes youth, thus it is "youth-stabilizing" (*vayaḥsthāpana*). He concludes [the section] with the words beginning "iti" (thus) and so forth:

"of the great decoctions" (*mahatāṃ kaṣāyāṇām*) refers to those indicated by the statement that there are fifty great decoctions (*pañcāśanmahākaṣāya*); "their characteristics" (*lakṣaṇam*) means their essential nature, such as the life-promoting group (*jīvanīya*) and others; "their illustration" (*udāharaṇam*) means their detailed exposition; the meaning is that they have been explained by the commentator through specific instruction. Alternatively, the "characteristic" of the great decoctions is the accomplishment of a single purpose—such as the life-promoting group—by combining many decoctions; [the phrase] is for the sake of illustrating that, that is, for the sake of providing an example.

By this, he indicates that other major formulations (*mahākaṣāya*) as well—such as those for pacifying *vāta* or pacifying *pitta*, which consist of multiple substances (*anekadravyamaya*)—are likewise accomplishing a single purpose.

The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "of the great ones" (*mahatām ca*) should be understood here as serving the purpose of providing an illustration; by it, he combines [the meaning] "and for the practical application of those of limited intellect. This will become clear later on.

Later, when he will say, "And they are explained for the purpose of defining and illustrating the great impurities (*kaṣāya*)," that is intended to explain the meaning of the passage beginning with "tadyathā" (for example). Alternatively, here the word "vyākhyātāḥ" (are explained) functions as a mere designation in the description of the great impurities, whereas there the word "vyākhyātāḥ" functions in the description of each individual substance such as *jīvaka* and so forth; therefore, there is no tautology.

The parts themselves are the possessors of parts; the meaning is that those very fifty great *kaṣāyas*, when multiplied by ten parts and existing as individual substances, become five hundred *kaṣāyas*.
First, the *jīvanīya* (life-sustaining) group is mentioned, because the benefit of sustaining life is intended above all else for everyone.
The list ending with *mudgamāṣaparṇī* is easy to understand.

*Jīvantī* is well-known by its own name and has a golden-yellow luster; *madhuka* is *yaṣṭīmadhuka*; *kṣīriṇī* is *kṣīralatā*; *rājakṣavaka* is *dugdhikā*; *vāṭyāyanī* is white *balā*; *bhadraudanī* is yellow *balā*; *bhāradvājī* is wild cotton (*vanakārpāsī*); *payasyā* is the tuber of *vidārī*; and *ṛṣyagandhā* is *ṛṣyajāṅgalaka*.

Kaṭukā is kaṭurohiṇī; cirabilva is karañja; haimavatī is white vacā (3). Suvahā is trivṛt; agnimukhī is known as ‘lāṅgalikā’; citrā is dantī; śaṅkhinī is white buhnā; śakulādanī is kaṭurohiṇī; svarṇakṣīriṇī is aṅguṣṭhaprabhā (4);

ambaṣṭhakī is akarṇaviddhā; samaṅgā is varāhakrāntā; kaṭphala is well-known by its own name; *sandhānīya* refers generally to that which is astringent (*saṅgrahaṇa*); however, that which is astringent for feces (*purīṣasaṅgrahaṇa*) specifically refers to that which binds the excrement alone. (5)
Śṛṅgavera is ginger; hiṅguniryāsa is asafoetida;
aindrī is gorakṣakarkaṭī; ṛṣabhī is śūkaśimbā; atirasā is śatāvarī or ṛddhi; ṛṣyaproktā is māṣaparṇī; atibalā is pītabalā; and payasyā here is either kṣīravidārī or kākolī. (7)

Tuṅga is *punnāga*; sitā is white *dūrvā* grass; latā is dark *dūrvā* grass (8). Sārivā is *anantamūla*; ikṣumūla here means the root of sugarcane or *moraṭa*; vidārī is the tuber of *vidārī*; kaiṭarya is *kaṭphala*; haṃsapādī is well known by its own name (9); āmrātaka is *āmrāḍaka*; vṛkṣāmla is large-sour (*bṛhadamla*) (10).
*tṛptighna* is *vyakta*; 11. *dhanvayāsa* is *durālabhā*.
Aruṣkara is bhallātaka (13).

Nalada is māṃsī; kṛtamāla is suvarṇahali; naktamāla is karañja (14). Akṣīva is abdaka or śobhāñjana; gaṇḍīra is śamaṭha-śāka; nirguṇḍī is sindhuvāra; kiṇihī is kaṭabhī; ākhuparṇī is mūṣikaparṇī; and vṛṣaparṇī is a variety of it known as ‘phañjipatrikā’ (15).
Suvahā, rāsnā, hāpharamālī, or pālindī, śyāmalatā, śleṣmātaka, and bahuvāra (16).
Ikṣuvālikā, khāgālikā, darbha, uluyātṛṇa, gundrā, and guluñca (17).

*Stanyaśodhana* is *vyakta*. (18) *Vṛddharuhā* is *śatāvarī*; in the reading *vṛkṣaruhā*, it refers to *bandāka*. *Jaṭilā* is *uccaṭā*, and *kuliṅga* is a variety of *uccaṭā*. (19) *Kadamba* is the many-fruited tree; its resin is used. *Ikṣuraka* is *kokilākṣa*. *Vasuka* is *vasuhaṭṭaka*. Here, Jatūkarṇa reads *elavāluka* in place of *kaṭphala*. (20)
12. *Vṛścīra* (21), which is clear and an adjunct to oleation, is white *punarnavā*. (22)

The *kovidāra* is well known by its own name; the *karbudāra* is the white *kāñcana*; the *vidula* is the *hijjala*; the *śaṇapuṣpī* is the *ghaṇṭāravā*; the *sadāpuṣpā* is the *arka*; the *pratyakpuṣpā* is the *apāmārga* (23);
the three types of *badarī* (24); and the *vyakta* (25).
Vyakta (26) is the kṣavaka plant, which causes sneezing; śvetā is aparājitā, and mahāśvetā is a variety of it, or else kaṭabhī (27).
Manifest (28),
manifest (29), manifest (30).
14. *Anantā* has an infinite root; *kaṭvaṅga* is *śyonāka*; *mocarasa* is the gum of the *śālmalī* tree; *padmā* is *brāhmaṇayaṣṭikā* (31);
*śallakī* is well-known by its own name; *kacchurā* is *śūkaśimbā*; *śālmalīveṣṭaka* is *śimilīāṭhā*; *śrīveṣṭaka* is *navanītakhoṭī* (32).
*Kapītana* is *gandhamuṇḍa*; *aśmantaka* is *amlaloṭa*; *somavalka* is *khadira*.
(33) There are four varieties of *padmabheda*: *saugandhika*, *śundhī*, *vṛkṣādanī*, *bandāka*, or *vidārikanda*; *vaśira* is *sūryāvarta*. (35)
*tāmalakī*, *bhūmyāmalakī* (36), *caṇḍā*, *corahulī* (37).
(38) Vyakta, (39) Vyakta,
(40) Phalgu Kāṣṭhodumbaraka.

Because of the reading in the *Jatūkarṇa* regarding parched grain (*lāja*) and other items, *padmaka* is substituted for *guḍūcī*; or else, although *guḍūcī* is indeed hot according to the statement, "The pungent substances—*arka*, *aguru*, and *guḍūcī*—are desired to be hot" (*Sūtra-sthāna* 26), nevertheless, its capacity to pacify burning sensations must be understood as being due to its specific potency (*prabhāva*).
(41) *Bhūtīka* is *yavānikā*. (42)
*Tinduka* is well known as *kendu*; *kadara* is *viṭkhadira*; *arimeda* is a variety of *khadira* (43); *vyakta* (44);
*ajagandhā* is *phokāndī* (45).
17. *Rudhira* is saffron (46);
*vañjula* is the cane-plant (*vetasa*) (47).

*Kaiṭarya* is *parvatanimba*; *vayaḥsthā* is *brāhmī*; *golomī* is *bhūtakeśī*; *palaṅkaṣā* is *guggulu* or *jaṭāmāṃsī* (48). *Śatavīryā* and *sahasravīryā* are types of *dūrvā*; *amoghā* is *pāṭalā* or *āmalakī*, or *lakṣmaṇā*; *avyathā* is *kadalī*, *guḍūcī*, or *harītakī*; *ariṣṭā* is *kaṭurohiṇī*; *viṣvaksenakāntā* is *priyaṅgu* (49); *muktā* is *rāsnā*. Some say that in place of *śvetā*, there is *śreyasī*, which is a variety of *rāsnā* (50).

Now, showing that these very substances beginning with *jīvaka*, when enumerated individually as distinct entities, constitute five hundred decoctions (*pañca-kaṣāya-śata*), and when enumerated in groups of ten, constitute fifty great decoctions (*pañcāśan-mahā-kaṣāya*) specified by their specific names, he concludes with the words "iti" and so forth;
"abhisamasya" means having grouped them into a single category by the number of tens.

Regarding the illustration of the definition (*lakṣaṇodāharaṇa*): previously, the designations such as "vitalizing" (*jīvanīya*) were stated with reference to the definition; now, for the purpose of illustrating that definition, *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, and others are explained by way of example. By means of these ten, beginning with *jīvaka*, the "vitalizing great decoction" (*jīvanīyo mahākaṣāyaḥ*) is characterized—that is, known.
And the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "of the great [decoctions]" serves to include the illustrations of the definitions of the hundreds of fivefold decoctions (*pañcakaṣāyaśata*).
In this context, each of these substances, beginning with *jīvaka*, constitutes the defining nature of one hundred fivefold decoctions respectively.

"Either for the sake of definition (*lakṣaṇa*) or for the sake of illustration (*udāharaṇa*). In this context, "for the sake of definition" means for the sake of the knowledge of the five hundred and fifty *kaṣāyas* for those of dull intellect; however, "for the sake of illustration" means for the sake of providing examples for those who possess intelligence.

[Objection: "Surely, as many *kaṣāya* substances as exist should be mentioned, or at least two or three for the sake of illustration. Why then is this neither too extensive nor too concise? To this he says: "Not indeed," and so forth.
For there is no limit or measure of detail; therefore, the meaning is that the detailed exposition is not being stated here.

Furthermore, even an extreme brevity consisting of the mention of only two or three characteristics is not sufficient for the capacity or for the clinical practice of those with limited intellect who are unskilled in inference.
Thus, [the details] are stated as follows.
"Alam" means capable for practical application;
"cikitsā-vyavahāra" refers to the practice of medical treatment.

"Svālakṣaṇya" is the state of having its own specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa). Inference based on that is "tenānumānam. The meaning is that those who are skilled in this are the "abhijñās" (those with higher knowledge).

The meaning is as follows: Intelligent persons, having ascertained through repeated observation that substances such as *jīvaka* and others—possessing qualities such as being unctuous, cold, sweet, and aphrodisiac—perform the function of sustaining life (*jīvana*), infer that other substances of the same class, such as *drākṣā*, *payaḥ*, and *vidārī*, which also possess those qualities, are likewise "life-sustaining" (*jīvana*). Just as *jīvaka* and others are considered "great decoctions" (*mahākaṣāya*) because they perform the single function of sustaining life, so too are *pāṭhā*, *samaṅgā*, and others—which cure diarrhea—considered "great decoctions" that cure diarrhea. Thus, by means of inference, they comprehend the entire category of decoctions.
He raises the prima facie objection (pūrvapakṣa) with the words "In this way," and so forth.

"Those various [substances]" refers to *jīvaka*, *kṣīrakākoli*, and others. Regarding those various [qualities] such as vitalizing (*jīvanīya*), nourishing (*bṛṃhaṇīya*), and generating semen (*śukrajanana*), these very same substances recur and are mentioned again and again. Since a single substance is mentioned in multiple contexts yet remains one and the same, the number [of distinct substances] is not fulfilled; such is the prima facie objection. He establishes the final position (siddhānta) with the words "This is not so," and so forth.
He provides an illustration for expressing a single thing as many, beginning with "just as," and so forth.

A single person is capable of performing various activities—such as cooking rice, making pots, using a spade, or digging the earth; the word "yaḥ" (who) is to be supplied [in the text], and it refers back to the person possessing the aforementioned qualities. Whatever action he performs—whether it be the cooking of rice or the like—for each and every such action, he receives a specific name associated with the agent, such as "cook" (*pācaka*); associated with the instrument, such as "digger" (*khānitrika*); or associated with the effect, such as "potter" (*kumbhakāra*). These are secondary names derived from the connection with specific qualities. The connection with qualities is as follows: in the case of "cook," there is the agency (*kartṛtva*) in the act of cooking; in the case of "digger," there is the agency in the act of digging by means of a spade; and in the case of "potter," there is the agency directed toward the pot. The sense is that, though not distinct [from the person], he is designated and conventionally treated as distinct through these three qualities.

In the same way, even a medicinal substance like the *kṣīrakākolī* plant, though being a single entity, is designated and referred to by various terms such as "life-promoting" (*jīvanīya*) because it possesses multiple qualities characterized by vitality, nourishment, and the generation of semen.

Now, for what reason is this very same single substance mentioned in various places due to its association with many qualities such as those of the life-promoting group, when there are indeed many other substances that possess each of these life-promoting qualities individually and are distinct in their own nature? Why are they not mentioned separately instead? To answer this, he says: "And if it were only one," and so forth.

Just as many substances are each capable of performing a single action such as *jīvanīya* (vitalizing), so too there exists a single substance capable of performing multiple actions such as *jīvanīya*. In that case, it is more appropriate to teach and to cause students to master a single substance that performs many functions, because it can be understood with little effort and retained with little effort; whereas it is not [appropriate] to teach many substances restricted to a single function, because they require great exertion to prepare, great effort to understand, and great effort to retain. Furthermore, the purpose—such as vitalization (*jīvana*) and nourishment (*bṛṃhaṇa*)—is identical for both positions. This is the meaning of the sentence.

Thus endowed with such qualities, it is capable of performing numerous functions such as those that sustain life (*jīvanīya*). He explains this very possession of qualities: "Who would desire anything other than that single entity which performs many functions, when there exists something else that performs many specific, distinct functions? The meaning is that no one would so desire. This is to be understood by means of repetition, so that it may be firmly established in memory.
To the question "Whence [is this]? one must supply the word "then" (*tadā*) at the beginning.
He states the summary of the meaning of chapters 21–22, beginning with "Since," and so forth.
For, from the *madanaphala* and other such substances,

there are three thousand three hundred formulations and so forth; by whichever substances these six hundred purgatives are produced, it is by those very same *madanaphala* and other substances combined that these six hundred purgatives are said to be declared.
The passage beginning with "for the sake of definition" (*lakṣaṇārtham*) summarizes the arising of the fifty great afflictions (*mahākaṣāya*) without being either too concise or too prolix.
The word "alam" means "sufficient.

In the phrase "this [is] for one of small intellect," the word "this" (*ayam*) is connected with the preceding "excessive conciseness" (*atisaṅkṣepa*). Although there is no excessive conciseness here, nevertheless, that which has been firmly established in the mind is being reflected upon.

Regarding the phrase "for this [treatment] consists of fifty [parts]," the word "this" (ayam) is indeed easily applicable to both external applications such as ointments and internal procedures such as emetics and digestive stimulants.
The conjunction (*saṃyoga*) of substances is their appropriate meeting; the application (*prayoga*) is the coordination based on considerations such as time and nature. 23–29.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Six Hundred Purgatives," within the section on the Fourfold Group of Medicines, in the first part, the Sūtrasthāna, of the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the essential meaning of the Caraka Saṃhitā, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 5 (5 of 120)]

The purpose of this treatise here is twofold: the removal of disease in the afflicted and the preservation of health in the healthy. As it has been said: "It is the refuge for both the healthy and the afflicted" (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 1). Therefore, having explained the fourfold set of medicinal factors (*bheṣaja-catuṣka*) by means of the counteracting of arisen diseases for the protection of the afflicted, the fourfold set for the healthy (*svastha-catuṣka*) must now be explained. Among the causes for the maintenance of health, food in the proper measure (*mātrāvad-anna*) is paramount. As it has been said: "Furthermore, food is the root of living beings, as well as of strength, complexion, and vitality" (Suśruta-saṃhitā, Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 1). Since that very food in the proper measure is prescribed here, it is discussed first in the chapter on eating in proper measure (*mātrāśitīya*).

The chapter concerning eating in the proper measure is called the *Mātrāśitīya*. Although the word "mātrāśī" (one who eats in measure) is heard at the beginning of the chapter, nevertheless, this technical name (*saṃjñā*) was formed using a synonym for that meaning rather than the term "mātrāśīya," out of fear of its difficult pronunciation—just as the names such as "Navegāndhāraṇīya" (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 7) and others are formed.
One whose habit is to eat food with moderation is called *mātrāśī*; or rather, one whose habit is to eat and consume with measure (*mātrayā*) is likewise so described.
In this context, "moderation" (*mātrā*) refers to a quantity that does not cause harm; here, it applies without distinction to the consumption of all types of food—solid, chewed, licked, and drunk.

By this, it is stated that one should eat in moderation (*mātrāśī*); thus, any objection raised to the effect that "the consumption of what is chewed, drunk, licked, and sipped in their proper measure has not been explained" is refuted.

Furthermore, this fire is observed in the process of consuming food such as what is chewed; for example, in the *Daśamūlaharītakī*: "Having consumed one *abhayā* fruit and then a spoonful (*śukti*) of the electuary (*lehā*), one destroys even advanced swelling" (Ci. A. 12); likewise: "One should administer that while subsisting on milk" (Ci. A. 1).

It should be understood from this that "aśita" (eaten) refers to all types of consumption, since this explanation is made in general terms: "Furthermore, the measure of food (*āhāra-mātrā*)," rather than "Furthermore, the measure of what has been eaten (*aśita-mātrā*).
He explains the measure as follows: "In food," and so forth;

the measure is superior, middling, or small in dependence upon whether the strength of the digestive fire (*agni-bala*) is superior, middling, or small. Thus, it depends on the strength of the digestive fire.

The word "again" (punaḥ) excludes the dosage of medicines and the like, as well as the dosage of physical exercise. Therefore, not every dosage depends solely on the strength of the digestive fire (*agni-bala*); for the dosage of medicine must be stated as depending on the strength of the disease and the patient, whereas the dosage of exercise must be determined with regard to the depletion of the *doṣas*, the increase of the digestive fire, and so forth, as well as the non-production of fatigue, exhaustion, and the like.
Alternatively, if the word "again" refers to repetition (*paunaḥpunye*), then the dosage of food repeatedly depends on the strength of the digestive fire.

This is what is meant: the quantity established for a single person at one time by the strength of his digestive fire (*agni*) does not remain constant at all times. This is because that very fire sometimes increases due to differences in season and differences in age—such as in winter and in youth—and sometimes it becomes weak, such as in the rainy season and in old age. Therefore, due to these variations in the strength of the digestive fire, the quantity of food is not of a single uniform form; rather, depending on the digestive strength prevailing at that particular time, the quantity is modified again and again. 3
He explains precisely the dependence upon the strength of the digestive fire (agnibala) with the words beginning "yāvadhi," etc.;
"yāvat" means "to whatever extent," and the word "hi" indicates the reason.
"Of this" refers to the enjoyer;
"eating" means that even the fourfold food, whatever is eaten or consumed, is the object of enjoyment.
"Without impairing the natural state"— meaning without causing a disorder— of the humors such as wind (vāta) and the tastes such as sweet (rasa);
"at the proper time" means at the end of the night.
The word "tāvat" (so much) refers back to the meal delimited by the previous means of knowledge;
the second mention of "asya" (of this person) is for the purpose of excluding [the rule] from others.

Therefore, whatever measure is non-disruptive for one specific individual, that alone should be considered [appropriate] for him and not for others, because the digestive fire (*agni-bala*) differs for each person.

And although there may be a variation in digestive power (*agnibala*) even in a single person due to differences in time and other factors, nevertheless, once a person has determined a specific measure (*mātrā*), as long as that same measure is maintained for some time in the absence of any cause for a change in digestive power, practical activity (*vyavahāra*) certainly proceeds. "Measure" (*mātrā*) here refers to the quantity or limit of the measure; by the term *mātrāpramāṇa*, it should be understood here as "that which possesses the measure of the amount. Otherwise, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word *mātrāpramāṇa*, which denotes a quality, and the word *tāvat* (so much), which denotes eating delimited by that [measure].

Now, one might object: the qualification "without impairing the constitution" (*prakṛtim anupahatya*) should not be made. For food that undergoes digestion at its proper time does not produce a disorder due to a defect in quantity (*mātrā-doṣa*); rather, it produces one due to defects such as the nature of the substance (*dravya-svabhāva*), processing (*saṃskāra*), and so forth. For example, even if mangoes and other fruits ripen at their proper time, they still invariably produce a disorder; yet, in that case, the quantity is not at fault. As he will state in the *Trividhakukṣīya*: "It is not possible to obtain the full excellence of the results of food merely through the possession of the correct quantity, because the eight specific bases for the rules of diet—beginning with constitution (*prakṛti*)—have distinct results. (Vi. A. 2)

It is not so; for two kinds of measure (*mātrā*) must be explained in the *Rasavimāna*: that which consists of the total intake (*sarvagraha*), and that which consists of the individual components (*parigraha*). Therein, the measure of the entire food aggregate is the "total intake" (*sarvagraha*); the taking of each constituent part of the food, such as the sweet, sour, and others, according to its own proportion is the "individual component" (*parigraha*). Therefore, even where the measure of the food aggregate is taken exactly as appropriate, if the measure of the individual food constituents—such as the sweet and others—is not as prescribed, even if they are naturally wholesome, then due to the imbalance in the measure of those food constituents, an imbalance of the bodily elements (*dhātu*) certainly occurs, and there would also be the onset of premature aging. Thus it is said: [the term] "without impairing the natural constitution" (*prakṛtimanupahatya*) is used as a qualification.

Others, however, explain it thus: the three words "of this" (*asya*), "eating" (*aśanam*), and "eaten" (*aśitam*) are understood from the context itself; that which is stated [explicitly] is for the purpose of indicating specific distinctions. By the word "of this," the investigator who is the eater is designated; by the word "eating," excellent food—uncontrary to its nature, preparation, combination, place, and time—is expressed; and by the word "eaten," eating according to the prescribed rule is expressed. Thus, food endowed with all these qualities is said to be possessed of the proper measure (*mātrāvān*). 4

Having taught the definition of *mātrā*, he now demonstrates the variation of *mātrā* according to the different substances useful for daily practice—beginning with "In that regard, *śālī*" and so forth.

Among those, the light category (*laghuvarga*) is recited first because it is the most wholesome (*pathyatama*). Even within that, red rice (*raktaśāli*) is mentioned at the outset because it is the primary substance among foods.

The *kapiñjala* is the grey partridge (*gauratittiri*); the *eṇa* is the black antelope (*kṛṣṇasāra*); the *śarabha* is the large-horned deer (*mahāśṛṅgī hariṇa*); and the *śambara* is a specific variety of that same species.

In the section on the rules for food and drink, regarding the description of the qualities of *ṣaṣṭika* rice as "cold, unctuous, light (*aguru*), and sweet" (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 27), the term *aguru* should be understood as containing the elided vowel *a* (i.e., *a-guru*). Consequently, there is no contradiction here in establishing the lightness (*laghutva*) of *ṣaṣṭika* rice; rather, it is used in a cumulative sense. Thus, it is understood that parched grains (*lāja*) and the like, which are light by nature (*prakṛti-laghu*) and light through processing (*karaṇa-laghu*), depend upon their quantity (*mātrā*). Similarly, in the case of things heavy by nature (*prakṛti-guru*), one must also mention items such as balls of roasted flour (*śaktupiṇḍa*) which are heavy due to processing (*saṃskāra-guru*).
In this context, the word "ādi" (and so forth) denotes a category, since there is no fixed group such as "śāli-rice" or "ṣaṣṭika-rice.

The word "vikṛti" (modification/derivative) is connected with flour, sugarcane juice, and milk; thus, "kṣīravikṛti" refers to foods prepared from milk. The word "piśita" (meat) is connected with both the meat of marshy animals and aquatic animals.

Now, one might object: "If even that which is light and wholesome requires the proper dosage (*mātrā*) to produce its own specific qualities, and if even that which is heavy and unwholesome becomes wholesome when taken in the right measure, then what is the purpose of teaching regarding heaviness and lightness? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And it is not so," and so forth.

Although light substances abound in the qualities of ether (*ākāśa*), air (*vāyu*), and fire (*agni*), nevertheless, because ether lacks such capacity for igniting the digestive fire (*agni-dīpana*), whereas air and fire do possess the power to ignite the fire, it is said that they abound in the qualities of air and fire.

For that reason, light substances kindle the digestive fire to a small degree; moreover, due to their own quality—the predominance of the qualities of air and fire—they possess a nature conducive to igniting the fire. Even when the transgression of measure (mātrā) is equal, [the author] demonstrates the distinction of the light substance from the heavy substance: they are said to cause "few defects" even when consumed to satiety (*sauhitya*). *Sauhitya* refers to satisfaction through the transgression of measure. In the phrase "heavy [substances]," the word "again" (*punaḥ*) serves to exclude [the previous case].

The negative particle (*nañ*) in the phrase "due to non-commonality" (*asāmānyāt*) has the sense of contradiction, as in the word "unblack" (*asita*); therefore, "due to non-commonality" means "due to an abundance of qualities of earth and water which are contrary to fire.

Even in the reading "due to the commonality with another" (*anyasāmānyāt*), the word "another" (*anya*) likewise signifies something contradictory; thus, even in that case, the meaning remains the same.
With the words beginning "and for this reason" (*ataśca*), he demonstrates that when there is a transgression of the [proper] proportions, the fault is more serious in the case of a teacher.

Now, one might object: "Are there not some individuals, such as porters and the like, who remain free from harm even when consuming heavy foods in quantities that bring full satisfaction? Why, then, is it said that [excessive food] is inherently defective? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In other cases," and so forth.
The term *vyāyāmāgnibala* refers to the digestive power (*agni-bala*) produced by physical exercise (*vyāyāma*).

Although the digestive fire (*agni*), when its strength is augmented by time, becomes capable of digesting heavy substances in large quantities—as it is stated: "In the winter season, the digester (*pakta*) becomes capable of tolerating heavy substances in terms of both quantity and nature" (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 6)—nevertheless, the fire whose strength is induced by exercise becomes exceedingly powerful; it is for this very reason, as the primary factor, that this [capacity] has been mentioned.

However, for those who describe two reasons—namely, "due to physical exertion" and "due to the strength of the digestive fire"—it would follow that the quantity of food would depend upon physical exertion; thus, their position would contradict the subject matter of this section.

He concludes the point established by reasoning with the words "saiṣā" and so forth: "sā" refers to the quantity previously asserted as depending on the strength of the digestive fire; "eṣā" refers to that same quantity as it has been resolved through logic based on the requirement of the digestive fire.

Now, although the dosage depends on the strength of the digestive fire (*agni*), why is it that for light substances a larger quantity is prescribed when the fire is of a single (average) form, whereas for heavy substances only a third or half of that is appropriate? To this he says: "And not," etc.;
the meaning is that [the fire] does not depend solely on the substance.
One should eat until one-third full with heavy foods;

in this way, other considerations may also be inferred based on the degree of heaviness. Even with light foods, one should not eat to complete satiety; here the word *sauhitya* refers merely to satisfaction. Therefore, light foods should not be consumed beyond the point of satisfaction, for in this way there will be no transgression of their proper measure (*mātrā*).
The application of fire is its maintenance at its own measure; for that purpose.

Now, one might object: let it be granted that the excessive use of heavy substances is prohibited for the sake of protecting the digestive fire (*agni*), since heavy substances are not equal to fire; however, light substances are indeed equal to fire, so how can their excessive use bring about a weakening of the fire? We reply: it is the very state of excess (*atimātratvam*) that, by overwhelming the common nature of light substances, causes the weakening of the fire. For example, the eye is composed of fire (*taijasam*), and it sees when assisted by fire; yet that same fire is impaired by an excessive application of fire. Likewise, a weapon is produced from stone, and it becomes sharp through contact with stone; yet it is blunted when applied improperly to the very stone itself. As it is said in *Śālākya*: "That brilliance which is the radiance of the luminaries and that which is the bodily [fire] of living beings..."
When that light is conjoined with [the internal] light, it indeed perceives forms;
that alone is the eye, and those alone are the luminaries. However, for one who looks [too intently], it undergoes excessive modification or even perishes.
Just as stone is the source of a weapon, and that weapon, though sharpened upon the stone, becomes blunt through excessive use and is blunted right there; so it is with this.

Thus, the measure (mātrā) that depends upon the digestive fire and the food substance has been explained; it was also stated that one should eat food endowed with the proper measure. To explain what benefit lies in eating according to measure, he says: "For that which is possessed of measure," and so forth.

In this context, the restriction "necessarily" (*avaśyam*) must be understood to apply provided that no other opposing causes are present. For although food endowed with the qualities of its constituent parts, processing, and so forth may be obtained through words such as *pūrvavad-aśana* and *aśitopayoktṛ*, which denote excellent eating and the like, there nevertheless exist—due to the adverse timing [of digestion], intellectual error, and unwholesome factors—the qualities of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, which act as obstacles to the strength and other benefits produced by food. As it has been said: "Indeed, there are other predispositions for disease even in the absence of unwholesome food" (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 28). Therefore, since even naturally wholesome factors, when taken in the proper measure (*mātrā*), generally become causes of strength and so forth, the word "necessarily" is used here for the purpose of praising food that is possessed of the correct measure.

"Life joined with happiness" is *sukhāyuḥ*; alternatively, it should be understood as "happiness and life. Furthermore, it has already been established previously that life must be sought even in its own nature.
And here [the following verses] occur:

This is the convention of the author of the tantra: whenever he begins to state, by means of a verse, a summary of the meaning already explained previously, he uses the expression “And here there occurs” (*bhavati cātra*).
This is because it is a derivative of flour, like something made of flour; therefore, due to its heaviness [it requires this introductory formula].

"Pṛthukas" are those commonly known in the world as "flattened grains"; "never"— that is, at no time— should he eat them "in measure," meaning he should eat them in such a quantity that it does not exceed the proper limit.
One should not eat dried meat (vallūra) continuously; one should not consume it constantly.
He states the reason for not practicing [this]: "Because of heaviness" (*gauravāt*).
This means that the meat is thin, undernourished, and derived from animals such as deer that have recovered from illness;
and this is prohibited precisely because it is unwholesome (*apathya*), not because of its heaviness—so they say.
*Kūrcika* is curd or buttermilk cooked together with milk; *kilāṭa* is a lump of *kūrcika*, or according to others, the thickened portion of milk that has lost its liquid consistency.
*Śaukara* refers to the meat of a boar; by association with "boar," it should be understood that the meats of cows and buffaloes are also intended.
*Yavaka* is a specific type of awned grain.

For it will be said: "Among the awned grains (*śūkadhānya*), barley (*yavaka*) is the most excellent in being the most unwholesome" (Sūtra-sthāna, chapter 25). Having stated this, he now demonstrates the [other] cultivated grains with the words beginning "ṣaṣṭikān" and so forth.
Here, *ṣaṣṭika* is mentioned first in order to demonstrate its preeminence among red rice varieties.
Regarding "atmospheric" (*āntarīkṣa*): atmospheric refers to water; *payaḥ* means milk.

"Jāṅgala" refers here to the meat of wild animals and the like produced in the Jāṅgala region. Its use in this context is intended to be moderate as a seasoning for food. Therefore, there is no contradiction with what will be stated later: "One should not excessively consume three substances: long pepper, salt, and alkali" (Viśeṣa-sthāna, Chapter 1), because in that passage, excessive consumption of salt is specifically prohibited.

By the passage beginning with "mātrāśī" (eating in moderation), the means for preserving health is stated. Furthermore, the preservation of health is a subject that must be discussed extensively in this treatise (*tantra*); however, if it were explained here in full detail, it would result in excessive bulk of the work, and if left unexplained, it would leave the treatise incomplete. Therefore, he says "taccetyādi" (and that... and so forth to indicate it by way of a mere aphorism (*sūtra*).

One who remains perfectly in a state of being free from morbid change is *svastha* (healthy); the state of such a person is *svāsthya* (health). The meaning is the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (*dhātusāmya*), which is the absence of the disharmony of the constituents that causes agitation.

And that health is maintained in two ways: by nourishing the body which is constantly wasting away through pure diet and conduct, and by avoiding the causes of affliction (*pratyavāya*). Just as the maintenance of a lamp is performed by nourishing it through the supply of oil and wick, and by avoiding causes of extinction such as moths or wind, so too the cause of bodily affliction is twofold: that which arises from intellectual defects (*buddhi-doṣa*), such as improper posturing of the body which provokes *vāta* and the other *doṣas*; and that which is difficult to avoid, namely specific times of the year, such as winter (*hemanta*) and others, which by their very nature provoke the accumulation of *kapha* and so forth.

In this regard, he states the cause that nourishes health (*svāsthya-poṣaka-hetu*) with the first half of the verse, and the avoidance of causes that obstruct health (*svāsthya-vighātaka-hetu*) with the second half, beginning with "of those not yet arisen" (*ajātānām*). Although the non-arising of disorders (*vikāra*) that have not yet arisen is indeed established by their very nature (*svabhāva-siddha*), and while [the agent] exists, the primary meaning of the verbal root *kṛ* (to do) does not apply; nevertheless, the very avoidance of the causes of those disorders, as well as the removal of humors (*doṣa*) produced by specific times that are difficult to avoid, constitutes the "causing of the non-arising of unarisen disorders. As he will state: "In the first month of Mādhava, and again in the first month of Nabhasya..."

"And during the first month of the month of Sahasya, one should eliminate the accumulation of morbid humors" (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 7); likewise, collyrium is for the purpose of removing phlegm from the eye that arises independently of other causes;
such is the meaning of "from this point forward," and so forth.

Therefore, following the explanation of the causes for maintaining health, "that which must be done" (*kāryam*) refers to what is necessarily required for the practice of the regimen of the healthy (*svasthavṛtti*); the meaning is that eye-salve (*akṣyañjana*) and so forth must necessarily be performed. Although the word *añjana* also applies to oil massage (*abhyañjana*), it is specified as "eye-salve" for that purpose. Salve alone is applied first because it protects the eyes, which are the primary constituent [of the senses].
And it has been said: "The wise know the eyes to be the most important of all the sense organs."
"Like the sun [is to] the luminaries shrouded by thick mist.

Alternatively, this refers to collyrium and such when applied to one in a state of health (*svasthavṛtta*); however, as for collyrium and such used during diseases, that should be discussed under the treatment of diseases (*rogacikitsā*).
Although this collyrium and such should also be mentioned as removing disease, it is stated "with reference to the regimen for health," because this is generally considered the regimen for health.
Regarding "sauvīra" and so forth: sauvīra is that which originates from the Suvīrā river.
The dual number in "of the two eyes" (*akṣṇoḥ*) is used for the purpose of applying collyrium to both eyeballs;
the mention of "five nights" or "eight nights" is intended to demonstrate that the rule applies within a period not exceeding that duration.
Therefore, having regard for the time of the disorder, the application of the purgative collyrium (srāvaṇa-añjana) should be performed in the morning, at midday, or in the evening; thus it is said.
He states the justification for this section on purgative and therapeutic collyriums, beginning with "the eye," and so forth.

Because the ocular faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), which is of a fiery nature (*taijasa*), is opposed to phlegm (*śleṣman*), which is of a watery nature (*āpya*), there arises a greater fear of wind and bile due to that opposition; and since the conquest of phlegm requires drainage (*srāvaṇa*) as the primary treatment, the meaning is that it must be drained.
He then restricts the time for this draining collyrium (*srāvaṇāñjana*) with the words "at night," and so forth.
"Surely" means necessarily at night, because collyrium is applied when it is near [the eyes];
Jatūkarṇa also prescribed *rasāñjana* for inducing lacrimation specifically at night, as it is said: "For seven days, *rasāñjana* at night.
It is also stated in *Śālākya*: "The vision weakened by purgation fails upon encountering the sun."

"By the virtue of sleeping at night, the eye nourishes [the medicine] even when rubbed with collyrium. Thus, *sauvīrāñjana* is not a purgative; it merely clarifies the vision. Therefore, its application during the day is not contradictory.

Others, however, explain it thus: *sauvīrāñjana*, which is a constant duty (*dhruva*), must be performed at night; whereas *srāvaṇāñjana*, in cases of an excess of phlegm (*śleṣman*), should be administered in the forenoon alone, just like emetics.
He states the quality of collyrium (añjana) with the words "Just as," and so forth.
Purity is inherent; it shines forth when it becomes stainless through the removal of adventitious dust and other impurities.

"Irrigation" (āścyotana) refers to the administration of liquid medicine for the purpose of purging the eyes; although not explicitly mentioned here, it is included because its result is the same [as the aforementioned treatments]. By the word "etc. (ādi), procedures such as *puṭapāka* are understood. 18–19.

Right here, in the section on collyrium (*añjana*), the inhalation of smoke (*dhūmapāna*) will be prescribed by the passage beginning with “at the end of nasal drops, collyrium, and sleep,” and so forth; therefore, smoke is described immediately after collyrium. And it is said in the *Śālākya*: “The vitiated phlegm located in the head which does not exit from the eye of one whose eyes have been anointed with a sharp collyrium attains peace in an instant as soon as the smoke has been inhaled.”
Regarding the passage beginning with "hareṇukām": *hareṇukā* is *reṇukā*, also known as *pṛthvīkā* and black cumin (*kṛṣṇajīraka*).
Keśara is nāgakeśara; padmaka is padmakāṣṭha;
and dhyāmaka is gandhatṛṇa.
The barks of trees beginning with the *nyagrodha* and ending with the *plakṣa*, which are characterized as "pure" (*śubhā*); wild [fragrance] (*vanyam*), *kaivarta*, *mustaka*,
peacock feathers (*śukabarha*), and *granthiparṇaka*.

The *śareṣīkā* is the stalk of the *śarapuṣpa* plant, commonly known as *śarikā*. The method for its preparation is as follows: the medicinal drugs should be ground into a paste and wrapped [around a core] so that the resulting wick (*varti*) is eight finger-breadths long and has the girth of a thumb. Once it has dried, the *śareṣīkā* stalk is removed; the wick is then smeared with oil, one end is singed over a fire, and it is inserted into the front opening of the smoke-inhalation tube (*dhūmapānanalikā*) to be described later. From this, the smoke is to be inhaled; this is called the *prāyogikī* wick, which is intended for daily inhalation.
By the word "pleasant" (*sukham*), he demonstrates that it is not harsh and is free from danger.
He describes the unctuous medicinal smoking wick (snaihikadhūmavarti) beginning with "vasā" and so forth:
*madhūcchiṣṭa* is beeswax;
*varauṣadhaiḥ* is an adjective qualifying the sweet substances (*madhuraka*); the sweet substances are the life-promoting (*jīvanīya*) drugs, such as *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, and others.
By the phrase "with those that are logically appropriate," it is shown that the fat and other substances should be taken in such a way that a wick can be made;
and the preparation of the wick is, as before, a lubricating (snaihikī) treatment that effects oleation.
He demonstrates the wick for inhaling purgative smoke (virecanika-dhūmapāna-varti), beginning with the words "white" (śveta) and so forth.

"White" refers to *aparājitā* and fragrant substances (*gandha-sugandhadravyāṇi*). Their specific qualifiers are "aguru, patra, and so forth" (*agurupatrādyāḥ*), meaning aguru, patra, and others. Regarding aguru, patra, and the rest, the group to be understood here is the one that will be mentioned in the chapter on fever, beginning with "aguru, kuṣṭha, tagara, patra" (Ci. A. 3). The term was not rendered as "agurvādyāḥ" (aguru and so forth) because *kuṣṭha* and *tagara* are extremely sharp (*atitīkṣṇa*) and must be avoided for fear of causing the discharge of brain matter (*mastuluṅkakasrāva*).

And it will be stated in the *Trimarmīya*: “One should inhale a medicinal wick (*dhūmavarti*) with fragrant substances such as *akuṣṭha* and *tagara*” (Siddhisthāna, Adhyāya 9). It is also stated in *Śālākya*: “When a medicinal wick is applied, it causes the *nata* and *kuṣṭha* [plants] to discharge the brain matter (*mastuluṅga*) specifically; therefore, one should not use them at all. It is likewise stated in *Suśruta*: “[Use] the *elādi* group, excluding *tagara* and *kuṣṭha*” (Sūtrasthāna, Cikitsāsthāna, Adhyāya 40). 26
He demonstrates the benefits of smoking (dhūmapāna) with the words beginning "heaviness" (gaurava), etc.;
"hair" (śiroruha) refers to the locks of hair, and "skulls" (kapāla) refers to those of the head itself.
"Even though they are strong" means even though they have powerful causes;
although they are already included by virtue of being located above the clavicle (*ūrdhvajatruja*), they are mentioned again for the purpose of specifying particular rules.
It indicates the times for inhaling medicinal smoke (dhūmapāna): "In the case of *prayoga*," and so forth.

These eight times apply to *prāyogika-dhūmapāna* (habitual inhalation). However, in the case of *snaihika-pāna* (oleaginous inhalation), the time should be understood as characterized by the increase of *vāta*, whereas in the case of *vairecanika-pāna* (purgative inhalation), it should be understood as characterized by the increase of *śleṣman*.

In the section concerning the regimen for the healthy (*svasthavṛtta*), it is generally only the *prāyogika* [smoking] that is explicitly mentioned by name at that specific time; or rather, the term "regimen for the healthy" refers to the continuous use during the course of treatment (*prayogapāne satatapāne*). Therefore, these timings apply to all three types of smoking (*dhūmatraya*), as the term "consisting of wind and phlegm" (*vātakaphātman*) includes those consisting of wind, those consisting of phlegm, and those consisting of both wind and phlegm.

In the passage beginning with "the drinks should be," the inhalations of smoke consist of the intake and release [of breath]. At each instance—during the time of bathing and so forth, or during the time of smoking—one must perform three repetitions. Furthermore, even within those three repetitions, each should be performed three times over. Thus, at each single occasion of smoking, nine intakes and releases of smoke must be performed. The meaning is that after performing three intakes, a rest should be taken in between.
He demonstrates the specific rule for the time of drinking— how much [smoke] should be taken at each of the eight times during a single day— in the passage beginning with "param" and so forth,
regarding the application of the preparatory smoke (*prāyogika-dhūma*) at those times such as after bathing and so on.

Regarding the statement "in the unctuous [fumigation], however, one [time]," it should be understood that one should inhale the smoke for only a single duration in the case of unctuous fumigation. As for "three or four [times]," this is an alternative option in the case of purgative fumigation, depending on the strength of the doshas.

Regarding deafness and other such conditions caused by smoke— meaning those produced by the improper use of smoke— if the *vāyu* is aggravated and follows the *pitta*, then nasal drops (*nāvana*), collyrium (*añjana*), and nourishing treatments (*tarpaṇa*) prepared with unctuous substances (*snaihika*) should be administered; likewise, cooling treatments made from cooling substances should be applied as nasal drops and so forth, and even drying treatments (*virūkṣaṇa*) should be administered as nasal drops and so forth.
In passages such as "not one who has been purged" (na virikta), the employment of the negative particle (*na*) serves to indicate the weightiness of the prohibition.

Furthermore, in the phrase "having eaten smoke" (*dhūmaṃ na bhuktvā*), the repetition of the word "smoke" (*dhūma*) is for the purpose of specifying a particular exception regarding one who has eaten with curd (*dadhi*).
In the passage beginning with "fit for smoke" (dhūmayogya), the word division is "by means of the nose" (ghrāṇena).
"Has gone in the reverse direction" means it has entered the mouth and reached the nose.
The two occurrences of the word *hi* indicate a reason;

therefore, the meaning is this: since smoke has gone in the reverse direction—that is, by a wrong path—it would injure the eyes; and because it would injure them, one should not exhale it through the nose.
Being properly seated is "well-seated."

Although it was already stated previously by the phrase "three inhalations, three times three," he nevertheless indicates by restating it that one must keep the limbs straight and the eyes fixed until the end of the smoke-inhalation cycle, and not merely at the beginning; furthermore, there is a rule that one should inhale through the nose while closing one nostril, but one should not inhale through the nose alone.
The nozzle and the tube are twenty-four units long, that is, twenty-four finger-breadths.

"Adhyardha" means "with a half. Here, the purgative nozzle (*virecanika-netra*) itself, which measures twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), becomes thirty-six finger-breadths when it is "with a half" for the habitual inhalation of smoke (*prāyogika-dhūmapāna*). This should be understood based on the authority of Jatūkarṇa, who says: "In the case of habitual [smoke-inhalation] and other such uses, a full *hasta* [of twenty-four fingers] plus three-quarters [of a finger] is required.
"Trikoṣāphalitam" means provided with three distinct joints (*parvan*).
He demonstrates the benefit of drinking through the aforementioned tube with the verse beginning "dūrāt" and so forth.
Some recite a text characterized by such things as the correct inhalation of smoke.

In this context, the passage beginning with "when [the smoke is] like a thief" (coraśca) describes the characteristics of correct smoking (*samyagyoga*); that beginning with "impure" (*aviśuddha*) describes the characteristics of deficient application (*ayoga*); and that beginning with "the palate" (*tālu*) describes the characteristics of excessive application (*atiyoga*).
Because the nose is the common gateway for both smoking and nasal therapy (nasya), he speaks of nasal therapy following the discussion of smoking: "In the rainy season," and so forth.
"Beneficial for the minute channels" refers to *aṇutaila* (minute oil), which will be described further on;
it [reaches] the veins, joints, ligaments, and tendons of the cranial bones themselves.

The plural number in "uttamāṅgeṣu" (on the superior parts) is used because the head is the most honored part; or alternatively, it refers to "old age"—characterized by wrinkles, grey hair, and so forth—which, having reached its highest degree (*utkamā*), is prohibited from being present in the limbs, such as the head and other parts.

In the passage beginning with "candana," *dārvītvak* is the bark of the *dārvī* tree; *jīvantī* is the plant known by its own name as *suvarṇanālā*; *surabhī* is *śūkaśimbā*; *padmakeśara* is the filament of the lotus (*padma*);
and it should be understood that [the potency] is increased a hundredfold in *māhendra* (the atmosphere) compared to oil.
The phrase "tenfold" (*daśaguṇam*) should also be construed as "from oil" (*tailāt*).

However, in this context, the quantity of the medicinal drug to be boiled should be taken such that the water added for decoction becomes four times the measure of the medicine, because the rule "water is four times the quantity of the substance to be boiled" remains uncontradicted. It should not be explained as "water ten times the quantity of the medicine," as Jatūkarṇa has stated: "Having boiled [the drugs] in one hundred *prasthas* of water until ten parts remain, one should cook one *prastha* of oil with that [decoction] combined with goat's milk."

Alternatively, the quantity of the substance to be boiled should be determined by inference from the measure of the oil itself, according to the technical rule that "the decoction should be four times the amount of the oil.
This is done with a *picu*— meaning a tuft of cotton— by means of three *nāvanas*, which signifies three applications.
"Every three days" means having omitted one day at a time; "for seven days" means excluding the omitted days. Thus, in each season, the application of the food offering is completed in thirteen days.
He demonstrates the qualities of the tooth-stick by its proximity to the [preceding] topic: "crushed," and so forth.
It purifies the teeth twice—namely, in the evening and in the morning—and thus it is called *dantapavana*, or a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*).
The connection is "having extracted the impurity";
*kakubhaḥ* refers to the *arjuna* tree;
the meaning is that such [trees] possess such a flavor (*rasa*).
71–75 – Kaṭuka is *latākastūrī*.

Although the stalk of the clove (*lavaṅga*) was intended [by the author], nevertheless, because many fruits are to be taken, it is referred to generally as "fruit" according to the maxim of "those with umbrellas are walking.
(Verses 76–77) Regarding "between the jaws," etc., these are the qualities of the oil gargle (*snehagaṇḍūṣa*).
The section beginning with "nityam" and ending with "niṣevaṇāt" describes the benefits of head oil (*śirastaila*).

Although it is stated that [the benefit comes] from the application of oil on the head (*mūrdhni tailaniṣevaṇāt*), the phrase "one whose head is moistened by oil" (*snehārdraśirasaḥ*) indicates that one should apply as much oil to the head as is required to keep the head moist; this is further clarified by the passage beginning with "snehābhyaṅgāt."
Because of the application of lubricating oil to the axle—the wooden pin that fastens the wheel to the chariot.

The employment of many examples is intended to show that while something may be well-known to some person, it is not necessarily well-known to everyone; or else, it is for the purpose of demonstrating the capacity of oil to produce various effects: in the case of touch, or the tactile sense organ (*sparśana*), air is predominant, meaning that according to the medical view (*vaidyaka-darśana*), the sense organ is composed of all five elements (*pāñcabhautika*).

"Skin-beneficial" (*tvacya*) and "supreme massage" (*paramabhyaṅga*); by the word "and" (*ca*), it is also beneficial for *vāta*. By this, it is stated that it is beneficial for the sense organ of touch (*sparśanendriya*) when it is dependent [on the skin] and dominated by *vāta*, as well as for its substrate (*āśraya*), which is the skin.
"Action to be accomplished through strength" (*balakarma*) refers to tasks such as carrying heavy loads and so forth.
Regarding the passage beginning with "roughness" (*kharatva*) and so forth:

the first occurrence of the word *pādayoḥ* (on the feet) is for the purpose of qualifying roughness and the other attributes; the second is to indicate that strength and the rest arise after some time; the third is for the purpose of qualifying the cracking [of the skin]; the fourth is for the purpose of qualifying the veins and ligaments; and the remaining word *pādābhyaṅgena* (by foot-massage) is for the purpose of recalling the foot-massage that occurred long ago. (90–92)
Since rubbing with fragrant unguents (*udvartana*) is preceded by anointing (*abhyaṅga*), he describes rubbing after that: "Foul odor," and so forth.
The meaning is that it effects the joining—that is, the restoration—of the body's strength through the removal of the loathsomeness caused by perspiration (*sveda-bībhatsatā*).
"Śrīmat" means endowed with beauty;
"pāriṣada" means praised in an assembly.
Auspiciousness, calamity, affliction by serpents, piśācas, and the like,
and ornaments such as jewels; "jewel" refers to pure rubies, diamonds, pearls, gold, and so forth.
The establishment of purity through water and clay,
performed repeatedly and again and again,
is pure and brings about the state of purity.

*Kalpana* means cutting; *samprasādhana* means adorning. This should be applied according to what is appropriate: for the hair, *samprasādhana* refers to proper binding and so forth; for the beard, it is simply *kalpana* (trimming); but for the nails, *kalpana* consists of trimming, while *samprasādhana* consists of applying lac-dye and the like.
By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the trimming of the nasal hairs and other such things are understood.
Regarding the feet, [the terms] are connected with both "beneficial to touch" (*sparśanahita*) and "removing distress" (*vyasanāpaha*).
*Pādatram* means footwear, that is to say, sandals (*pādukā*);

and in this context, it is beneficial for virility and the eyes due to its medicinal power. Alternatively, it is beneficial for the eyes because it removes the affliction of the channels (*nāḍī*) connected to the feet which nourish the eyes, thereby warding off misfortune such as diseases and the like.
Protection (*gupti*) is defense against piśācas and other such beings; it is auspicious (*śaṅkara*), bringing about well-being, providing support, bestowing strength,
and destroying fear from snakes and other dangers.

In order to summarize the rules for the healthy that have not yet been mentioned, and so that what has been taught may be carried out with attention, he says: "In cities," and so forth—regarding those duties (kṛtya) to be performed, whether already stated or unstated.

By means of the analogy of the city, he demonstrates attention toward an action that destroys the internal causes of transgression; and by means of the analogy of the chariot, he demonstrates attention toward an action that avoids external contacts and the like.

For in the destruction of a city, the cause is generally the internal association with wicked people, whereas in the breaking of a chariot, it is the external falling into a pit or onto uneven ground.

Having performed the primary examination of the body, he states what else must be done by one who is healthy: "The means of livelihood," and so forth. "Livelihood" (*vṛtti*) means subsistence; its "means" (*upāya*) are agriculture and the like, which are to be discussed in the section on the three pursuits (*tisraiṣaṇīya*) within the inquiry into the desire for wealth. "Tranquility" (*śama*) means peace. "Study" (*adhyayana*) refers to the study of the Vedas. The connection [of the sentence] is that one should practice these.
This being so, one enjoys and attains happiness;

by this, it is shown that there is wealth from agriculture and other such means, dharma from tranquility and study, and desire—characterized by happiness—from both wealth and dharma; thus, the practice of the three aims of life (*trivarga*) is demonstrated.
The summary of the chapter’s contents begins with "mātrā" and so forth; it includes [the section] beginning with "as much as is his food" (*yāvad asya aśanam*) as taught by the Mother [Goddess],
as well as [the section on] substances beginning with "there, śāli rice" (*tatra śālī*).

"Depending on the dose and its relative weight" means that even substances naturally light depend upon the dose alone; it is in this manner that the "measure of the drink" (*pānamāna*)—such as "three [drops] for each inhalation," and so forth—is stated. That which is to be administered through the nose is *aṇutaila*.
The word "yathā" refers to the passage beginning with "picunā," and "yadā" refers to the passage beginning with "prāvṛṭśarad"; the remainder is easy to understand.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "On Eating in Moderation" (*Mātrāśitīya*), in the second section on the regimen for health (*Svasthavṛtta-catuṣka*) within the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta. 105–111.

[Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 6 (6 of 120): On Eating in Moderation] In the chapter on eating in moderation (*mātrāśitīya*), it is established that food taken in the proper measure is the cause of strength and other qualities; and this occurs when food is prepared with regard for seasonal suitability (*ṛtusātmya*). Therefore, preceded by the classification of seasons, he speaks of the chapter on eating in moderation which describes seasonal suitability.

Regarding the phrase "from what is eaten, etc.": from what is eaten (aśita), drunk (pīta), licked (līḍha), and chewed (jagdha), strength (bala) and complexion (varṇa) are mentioned; by the word "and" (ca), the happiness (sukha) and longevity (āyus) mentioned in the previous chapter are also included. Alternatively, by means of strength and complexion alone, the entire effect of the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātu-sāmya), such as happiness and so forth, which is invariably concomitant with them, is understood.
By the word "known" (vidita), he demonstrates that the practice of seasonal suitability (ṛtu-sātmya) must be preceded by correct knowledge.
By the inclusion of "activity" (ceṣṭā), activities such as sexual intercourse, physical exercise, and massage are included;
[this refers to] that which depends on activity and diet, having activity and diet as its sphere.

Since knowledge of seasonal suitability (*ṛtusātmya*) is not possible without knowledge of the seasons (*ṛtu*), he says "here," etc., for the purpose of knowing the essential nature of the seasons as they are applied. In this context of explaining the seasons, the statement "one should know the year" is intended to establish that the seasons themselves, when combined, constitute the year;
and this combination is a conventional designation of the intellect, for in ultimate reality there is no such thing as a combination of seasons.

In this context, the fact that the seasons constitute the year—that those very same seasons revolve again and again—must necessarily be explained for the sake of knowledge. Here in this section, one should know [the year] as having six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*); however, in other places such as the *Rogabhiṣagjitīya*, it is described differently according to the requirements of specific tasks.
As it has been said: "Time is characterized by cold, heat, and rain," and so forth.

"Six-limbed" (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a collective aggregate, because there is no year apart from the seasons; alternatively, one may form a *bahuvrīhi* compound based on the principle that the aggregate is distinct from its constituent parts. In that context of describing the division of the seasons, "northward" (*udak*) means toward the northern direction, and "course" (*ayana*) means movement; thus, "northern course" (*udagayana*) refers to the movement toward the north.
It takes away and exhausts the mild portion of the earth and the strength of living beings; thus it is called "appropriation" (*ādāna*).

Although the phrase "the three beginning with *śiśira*" already implies that they end in *grīṣma*, the expression "ending in *grīṣma*" is used to prevent the analysis of the compound as "the beginning of *śiśira*" (which would imply starting from *śiśira*) and to exclude the sense of the word *ādi* as indicating a mere type or category.
The same should be understood for the expression "ending in *hemanta*."
The *dakṣiṇāyana* is the movement toward the southern direction;
it is called *visarga* because it emits, generates, or releases the watery portion and the strength of living beings.

Furthermore, the application of designations (*saṃjñā-praṇayana*) is for the purpose of practical usage and for the purpose of explaining the meanings as they are understood through etymological analysis (*nirukti*).
He explains the nature of emission (*visarga*): "Furthermore, regarding emission," and so forth.

Although appropriation (*ādāna*) was recited first, nevertheless, the qualities of emission are explained first according to the logic of the *pratiloma* (reverse) system. Alternatively, while appropriation—being of the nature of the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*)—was mentioned first because of its excellence, here emission is mentioned first because it is intended as that which generates strength.
"Not excessively harsh" means that they blow with their harshness mitigated due to their connection with the time of the gentle emission (*visarga*);
"the others, however, are inhalations" means they are unappeased and excessively harsh, because their harshness is produced by their connection with the fiery inhalation (*ādāna*).
The phrase "Soma, etc. is connected to the aforementioned emission.
"Of unimpeded power" means that at that time, because the sun— the adversary of the moon— is deprived of its power by the path of time, clouds, wind, and so forth;
[the phrase] "constantly with cool, cold [rays]" is the grammatical split (*cheda*).
"Saumya" means that which has the qualities of the moon as its primary characteristic;
"āgneya" means that which has the qualities of fire as its primary characteristic, in the sense of possessing unimpeded strength.
To the question, "In this much alone, how do the sun, the moon, and the wind come to possess strength or lack thereof? he says: "Those two," and so forth.

Time is the form of the deity; although it is eternal in nature, being grasped by the various unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings, it at times produces the power of the sun, the power of the wind, the power of the moon, and so forth. Its inherent nature (*svabhāva*) consists of the sun’s function of causing the waning of gentle portions, the wind’s function of drying, and the moon’s function of nourishing. The paths are the southern and the northern; therein, the southern path begins with Cancer and ends with Sagittarius, while the northern path begins with Capricorn.

Furthermore, these—time (*kāla*), intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and the path (*mārga*)—are to be understood as being grasped according to their respective possibilities. For in the case of water (*soma*), the grasping of the path does not bring about any particular distinction; and in the case of air (*vāyu*), there is no grasping of the path at all.

Those [factors] that are grasped, connected, and serve as the conditions for the manifestation and the causes for the completion of time, seasons, and so forth, are taught by the "Teachers"—this is the ellipsis. Time consists of the year and the two solstices (*ayana*); the seasons (*ṛtu*) are the cool season (*śiśira*) and the others; and bodily strength is *dehabala*.

Others, however, say: since the year and the two solstices consist of a combination of seasons (*ṛtu*), they are already included by the mention of "season" alone; therefore, the mention of "time" (*kāla*) serves as a qualifier for the season. Thus, the term "season" refers to that which is of the nature of time, thereby excluding the appearance of menses (*ārtava*) in women—which is also called a "season"—in the phrase "they are the cause (*pratyaya*)," where the word *bhūta* is used in the sense of a comparison (*upamāna*).

Some explain: by reading "the sun and the wind" as a single unit and then reading "and the moon" separately, he shows that the sun and wind together are the cause for appropriation (*ādāna*), whereas the moon alone is the cause for emission (*visarga*);
this should be understood similarly regarding the taking away of strength, the bestowing of strength, and so forth.
In that regard, "and so forth" means taking up— that is, drying out—
the world of both the stationary and the moving.
The meaning is that "moisture" (*sneha*) refers to the essence or the watery portion.
The connection is that it is not only the sun, but also the winds that dry up this moisture.

They are "intense and dry" (*tīvrarūkṣāḥ*); or alternatively, those whose dryness is intense are "intensely dry. This occurs because of the wind's association with the intensely [hot] sun during its withdrawal, owing to the wind's quality of acting as a vehicle for conjunction (*yogavāhitva*).
For it has been said: "The wind that carries [the qualities] is supreme; through its conjunction, it effects both purposes" (Ci. A. 3), and so forth, according to the sequence.

Thus, in the *śiśira* season, dryness is slight, the bitter taste is slight, and debility is slight; likewise, in spring (*vasanta*), dryness is moderate, the astringent taste is present, and debility is moderate; likewise, in summer (*grīṣma*), it shows that dryness is intense, the pungent taste is present, and debility is great.

Although the astringent taste (*kaṣāya-rasa*) is the most parching (*rukṣatama*) and the pungent taste (*kaṭuka*) is more parching—as it has been said: "Because of its parching quality, the astringent is the best among parching tastes, while the pungent is middling" (Sūtra-sthāna 26)—and although the intensity of parchingness is greatest in summer and moderate parchingness occurs in spring, nevertheless, due to the predominance of the qualities of air (*vāyu*) and fire (*agni*), the pungent taste arises specifically in the summer season, which abounds in the qualities of air and fire; whereas in spring, where there is an excess of air and earth (*pṛthivī*), the astringent taste arises, being produced by that excess of air and earth.

As for what was stated: "It is pungent because it abounds in the qualities of air and fire; it is astringent because of the predominance of air and earth" (Sūtra 26), the increase of earth and the other elements is to be inferred from the observation of their effects as being caused by the influence of specific times.

By the statement "they cause [the tastes] to increase," the growth of bitter and the other tastes at their respective times is indicated; therefore, there is no state of having only a single taste at that time.

And here, the gradual production of dryness (*raukṣya*) and the production of bitterness (*tikta*) and so forth are also causes for the production of debility (*daurbalya*); for this reason, having employed two qualifying attributes containing the underlying cause—namely, "producing dryness" and "increasing the bitter, astringent, and pungent"—it is stated that they "bring about debility.
[The passage beginning with] "the rainy season," etc., follows.
The word "tu" (but) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

When the sun is facing south—that is, precisely when it is intent on going toward the southern direction—even though the sun is situated to the north of the Middle Land (*madhyadeśa*) as marked by the equinoctial sunrise, it becomes one whose strength is waning at the very moment it is intent on going toward the southern direction. However, because its excellence of strength was produced by the excellence of its movement toward the northern direction, even though its strength is diminishing little by little in that sequence, it is not perceived as being so weak.
This should be explained in the same way for the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*) as well.

Time (*kāla*) has been explained previously; here, the path (*mārga*) is directed toward the south; "cloud-wind" (*meghavāta*) refers to the wind from a cloud; "rain" (*varṣa*) refers to the act of raining. The connection is that the sun's heat (*pratāpa*) is struck by these [factors].

Here, the wind—due to its association with clouds—becomes cool and acts as an adversary to the sun's heat. Because the moon possesses unimpeded power and because it is associated with the cloud, wind, and rain which counteract the sun's heat, [the moon's influence prevails] over the world of both the stationary and the moving.

And regarding this, it has been stated that "sourness arises from an abundance of earth and fire," and "saltiness arises from an abundance of water and fire" (Sūtra 26). One should not ask how these two [qualities] can arise from the fiery elements during a lunar (saumya) emission; for it has already been established that even though the sun’s strength wanes, it remains powerful until the equinox due to its possession of superior force.

Now, the decrease of strength at the beginning of the cold season (śiśira) and the increase of strength at the beginning of the rainy season have been established; in that regard, in order to refute the misconception that living beings become weak in the cold season and strong during the rains, he says: "At the beginning and at the end," and so forth.

The connection is as follows: one should indicate that weakness has reached its peak at the beginning of the period of emission (*visarga*) during the rainy season, and that excellence [of strength] has been attained at the end of the period of withdrawal (*ādāna*) during the summer. Likewise, it should be applied that one should indicate the strength to be moderate—neither excessively diminished nor excessively increased—at the middle of the period of emission during autumn, and at the middle of the period of withdrawal during spring. Similarly, the construction is that one should indicate the strength to be excellent at the end of the period of emission during winter, and at the very beginning of the period of withdrawal during the cool season (*śiśira*).

He thinks as follows: A person whose excellence of strength has been established by the excellence of excretion (visarga) becomes strong at the beginning of the period of intake (ādāna), even though his strength is slightly diminishing during the early winter (śiśira). This is just as the night, having reached its peak of increase at the end of the month of Pauṣa, remains very long even while diminishing during the months of Māgha and Phālguna.
By this logic, one should understand that weakness occurs during the rainy season, while moderate strength prevails in spring and autumn.

Thus, the role of the sun and other factors as causes for time, seasons, tastes, body, and strength has been established; however, their role as causes for the humors (doṣas) will be explained later in the description of the seasonal regimen.

Because winter is intended [as the primary season] due to its possession of the excellence of increasing strength, he first speaks of its suitability (*sātmya*) with the words beginning "In cold... and so forth.

Regarding "cold" (*śīta*), which possesses the quality of coldness during the winter (*hemanta*): although the specific qualification "cold" is not explicitly stated, winter is inherently understood to be cold. Nevertheless, since coldness had not been previously established for winter in this context, it is now being set forth. Alternatively, it is precisely when the cold becomes great in winter that the digestive fire (*vahni*) becomes especially strong, and not merely at the onset of the season; furthermore, the phrase "cold" implies that there is an absence of cold during the seasonal derangement (*ṛtuvyāpatti*).

The "cold wind" (*śītānila*) is specifically cold due to its connection with frost (*himasambandha*). Although the specific coldness of the wind is already understood from its association with the cold season because it carries that quality, it is stated again here because it is the cause for obstructing the digestive fire (*agni*).

For when the wind goes out through the body in connection with frost, it blocks the internal heat, thereby causing an increase in the internal fire—much like the application of clay paste by a potter's breath increases the heat of the fire within.
By this, the objection—"How can there be an increase in the fire from a cold wind which is not of the same nature?"—is refuted.

For in this case, cold wind does not transform into fire; rather, the meaning is that the touch of the cold wind—which has become an adversary to the emerging heat—is what comes into contact with the body.

This [touch] becomes stronger for powerful living beings due to the very nature of the winter season; by this, he demonstrates that the strength of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the cause for the strength of the digestive fire (*agni*).

And it is said in the *Hastivaidyaka* (The Science of Elephant Medicine) regarding the establishment of health in young elephants: "From unimpeded intention comes joy; from joy, strength; from strength, digestive fire (*agni*); and from digestive fire, the strength of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).
