Indeed, the Fortuitous Originist does not accept even a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Consequently, because his [position] lacks a basis in valid cognition, the speech of one who says whatever comes to mind without any *pramāṇa* is not to be trusted; therefore, the intention of this section is that he should simply be ignored.

"By chance" (*yadṛcchayā*) means by way of having no settled position; "one whose self is ruined by chance" (*yadṛcchopahatātmā*) refers to one whose self is ruined and thus useless for both this world and the next. The meaning is that for such a person there is no investigation (*parīkṣā*), because of the absence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which are the causes of investigation; nor is there even an object of investigation, precisely because of the absence of the investigator's means of valid cognition. Likewise, the sense is that there is no agent and no cause for that [action], due to the non-acceptance of valid cognition. Thus, by stating that even gods and other beings established by all people do not exist, he shows that the nihilist (*nāstika*) is to be avoided.

"From sins," such as the killing of a Brahmin and so forth; "supreme" means the best; "the grasp of nihilism" refers to the conviction that there is no world beyond and the like; for the sense is that a person who is unrestrained by the intellect of a nihilist commits every kind of sin. (14–15) He states what ought to be done after abandoning nihilism, beginning with the words "Therefore," etc.
The phrase "this" refers to the nihilistic intellect; those who have set out upon the wrong path, which is unrighteousness (adharma), are "those who have set out upon the wrong path.

"Intellect-lamp" means the intellect itself is the lamp; the meaning is that one should perceive by means of that, namely through the instruments of valid knowledge such as direct perception (pratyakṣa).
"Yathātatham" means according to its true nature (yathāsvarūpam).
Having now refuted the opposing position, he introduces the proofs for establishing his own position and the existence of the next world, beginning with the words "dvividham" and so forth.

"Everything" refers to whatever is cognized through the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*); that is twofold. He states this twofold nature: "existent and non-existent. "Existent" is that which is positive in nature, accessible through a means of valid knowledge whose object is affirmation; "non-existent" is that which is negative in nature, accessible through a means of valid knowledge whose object is negation. "Parīkṣā" (examination) refers to the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), by which the true nature of reality is investigated and established. These [means], such as authoritative instruction (*āptopadeśa*) and so forth, will become clear in the subsequent text. 17
In order to demonstrate authoritative instruction (*āptopadeśa*), he first speaks of the authority itself—beginning with "the authorities" (*āptāḥ*) and so forth.
"Completely liberated" (*niḥśeṣeṇa muktāḥ*) means "freed" (*nirmuktāḥ*);
this should be construed as the cause for being freed from *rajas* and *tamas* by the power of austerity and knowledge.
"Three times" means having as its object the past, future, and present; "immaculate" means being unobstructed by virtue of grasping things as they truly are;
and "unimpeded" means having its power unblunted with respect to any object whatsoever.

"Āpta" means the destruction of defects consisting of *rajas* and *tamas*; those endowed with this are "the authoritative" (*āptāḥ*). They are "the disciplined" (*śiṣṭāḥ*) because they instruct the entire world through the teaching of what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, and through the injunctions for engagement and withdrawal from action. They are "the fully awakened" (*vibuddhāḥ*) because they have specifically awakened to that which is to be known. By these three designations—authoritative, disciplined, and fully awakened—he shows the renown of the authoritative ones in the world. The speech of those authoritative ones is "without doubt," meaning it is certain, true, and in accordance with reality. He states the reason for the truth of their speech: "Why would they speak untruth, being free from *rajas* and *tamas*?"

The word *nīrajastamaḥ* ends with the superlative suffix *-tama*; by this, through the excellence of being free from *rajas*, even *tamas* is excluded. For *tamas* does not exist in a person who is entirely free from *rajas*. As it has been said: "There is no *tamas* that is without *rajas*" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.10).

They will say, "Why [do they speak] untruth?"—the meaning being "for no reason at all. Untruth is spoken either from false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), or even when right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is present, it is spoken due to passion and hatred (*rāga-dveṣa*). And that triad—consisting of false knowledge, passion, and hatred—is not possible in one whose consciousness is stainless due to the predominance of the quality of purity (*sattva*) and who is free from the qualities of passion and darkness (*rajas-tamas*). Alternatively, the reading "nīrajastamaso mṛṣā" is easy to understand.

This definition of an authoritative person (*āpta*) is intended with reference to those such as Brahmā who are authoritative by birth; however, for ordinary persons, their status as authoritative should be understood as arising from the occurrence of correct knowledge regarding specific objects and the absence of attachment or aversion toward those objects. By this, the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of verbal testimony—namely, "the instruction of an authoritative person"—is stated. But in the view that cognition itself is the means of valid cognition, it should be understood that "cognition produced by the instruction of an authoritative person" is the means of valid cognition.
(Verses 18–19) He states the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*): "The self, the sense organs," and so forth.

"From proximity" means from a relationship; and that relationship is to be understood as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), inherence in what is inherent in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*), inherence in what is inherent (*samavetasamavāya*), and the character of the qualifier-qualified relation (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).
By the word "manifested," he excludes erroneous cognition (*ayathārthabuddhi*)—which is errant—and doubt (*saṃśaya*).

"At that time" (*tadātve*) means at that very moment (*tatkṣaṇam*). By this [specification], the author excludes, by way of a traditional sequence, inferential knowledge (*anumānajñāna*) and memory (*smaraṇa*), which arise immediately after perceptual knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*), from being produced by the contact of the self, the sense organ, and the object. Furthermore, the mention of the "contact of the fourfold" (*ātmādicatuṣṭayasannikarṣa*) is intended to state the causes of perception; therefore, the definition should be understood as simply: "that which proceeds from the contact of the sense organ and the object. By this, perception whose objects are pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth is also included; for in those cases, there is no contact of the fourfold, while the contact with the self (*ātmasannikarṣa*) alone is not useful for the definition because it is common to all forms of valid knowledge (*pramāṇajñāna*).

And here, although cognition has the nature of a result of perception, it is designated by the word "perception" (pratyakṣa) because of common worldly usage; however, in the ultimate sense, that from which such a cognition arises—namely, the sense organs and so forth—is perception. [The author] states the nature of inference, beginning with the words "perception," etc.

The mention of "perception" (pratyakṣa) is intended as an illustration for any means of valid cognition that grasps pervasion (vyāpti); therefore, "preceded by perception" means preceded by whatever means of valid cognition grasps pervasion.

By the phrase "of three kinds," he demonstrates the threefold nature of inference (*anumāna*). By this, [he shows]: (1) inference of a cause from an effect, as for example, the inference of sexual intercourse from the sight of a pregnancy; (2) likewise, inference of an effect from a cause, as for example, the inference of a fruit from a seed when it is joined with other auxiliary causes; and (3) likewise, inference from the general observation of things that are neither effect nor cause, as for example, the inference of fire from smoke based on its connection with the present moment. This threefold inference is thus understood. By the phrase "pertaining to the three times," he demonstrates that the object of inference extends across the three periods of time.
Regarding the statement "it is inferred" (*anumīyate*), the ellipsis of the sentence is "that by which it is inferred is inference" (*yena tadanumānam*).

Therefore, inference is that by which a remote object is measured—that is, correctly ascertained—subsequent to the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*). The meaning is that it is the perception of the logical mark (*liṅga*) aided by the recollection of pervasion.
To show an example of what was stated as being "threefold," he says: "Fire," and so forth.
And this has indeed been explained:
[the term] "hidden" (*nigūḍha*) means "not being seen" (*adṛśyamāna*);
thus they determine it as "past"—this is the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*).
"From the seed" (bījāt) should be understood as being conjoined with other auxiliary causes such as water and cultivation;
the connection [of the sentence] is that they determine the future fruit to be similar [to its cause].

By the statement, "Having seen that a fruit has arisen from a seed," he demonstrates the pervasion (*vyāpti*) characterized by the cause-and-effect relationship between the seed and the fruit. Although a cause may deviate from its effect—since a fruit does not necessarily arise even when a seed exists—the intended meaning should be understood as follows: a seed endowed with other auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*) does not deviate from its fruit; and the causal totality (*kāraṇa-sāmagrī*) certainly does not deviate from its effect.

Since reasoning (*yukti*) is well-known from other treatises, he first presents its examples alone, with the intention that once the examples are known, the definition of reasoning will be easily understood: "From the conjunction of water, plowing," and so forth.

By the word "plowing" (*karṣaṇa*), land prepared by plowing is meant; the knowledge that the production of grain occurs from the conjunction of water, plowing, seed, and season should be construed as "reasoning.
[Likewise,] from the conjunction of the six elements—that is, the conjunction of the five great elements and the self—...
The word *tathā* (thus) draws forth the following terms:

*mathyam* (the object to be churned), *manthana-kāṣṭha-yantrakam* (the churning-stick mechanism), *kāṣṭham* (the wood), and *manthanam* (the act of churning); or else the reading is *manthaka*, in which case *manthānam* refers to the wood being rotated. It should be understood that this occurs "from conjunction" (*saṃyogāt*), meaning from a meeting; for the conjunction of the act of churning, which is of the nature of an action, is not possible [in the literal sense]. Alternatively, by the word *manthana*, the churning-rope (*manthana-rajjū*) is meant; it is called *yukti* because by it one is joined (*yujyate*) or connected; thus, "joined with that" means *yukti-yuktā*.
Although it should have been stated as "four-footed" (*catuṣpāda*), the inclusion of the word "perfect" (*sampat*) is for the purpose of including that which possesses the four excellent qualities.
Now, he states the definition of reasoning (*yukti*): "Intelligence," and so forth.

That intellect which perceives—that is, takes as its object—entities, which involves a connection with many causes and a connection with many logical proofs, and wherein this "janis" (arising) has the sense of "knowing," such an intellect that perceives objects known through the connection with many logical proofs, characterized by reasoning (*ūha*), is *yukti*; it serves as an auxiliary to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

In this context, the term "reasoning" (*yukti*) refers to such a form of deliberation as "it must be so. Although this reasoning is not, in the ultimate sense, a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is nevertheless described here as a means of knowledge because it functions as an auxiliary to the valid means of knowledge in determining the nature of things. Furthermore, since the worldly transactions of people generally proceed by means of this very form of reasoning, it is spoken of here as a means of knowledge.

For this very reason, in another passage he will show the three aforementioned means of knowledge without including reasoning, based on the statement: "Or [investigation] is threefold, together with instruction" (Viṃśatikā, Chapter 4).

Likewise, having taken up analogy (*upamāna*), [the author] will describe the four means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—sound and the rest—in the chapter on "Diseases Conquered by Physicians" (*rogabhiṣagjitīya*). It pertains to the three times (*trikālā*), namely the objects of the present, past, and future. Its status as pertaining to the three times is established precisely by its teaching of the objects of inference across the three times, and its accomplishment of the three aims of human life (*trivarga*) follows from that very accomplishment of the three aims. For it is primarily through reasoning (*ūha*) that one engages in the practice of the three aims; indeed, its application through the formal determination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇapariccheda*) is quite rare.

As for the claim that the knowledge of a future crop arising from the conjunction of many causes—such as water, plowing, seeds, and the seasons—is called *yukti* (reasoning), this is not distinct from inference (*anumāna*). We do not take seriously the difficulty of distinguishing it from inference in that case; furthermore, an effect perceived through its causes is never perceived as existing in the present, and thus [the claim that *yukti* operates across] the three times would be contradicted. Regarding the acceptance of *yukti* as a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), Śāntarakṣita and Kamalaśīla state the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) as follows: "When X exists, Y necessarily occurs; when X does not exist, Y does not occur."

Therefore, this follows from that; this reasoning is stated: "The Sage Caraka says that this is indeed a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is not inference, since no corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) exists here" (Ta.Saṃ.Kā. 1692–93).

This statement by Śāntarakṣita was explained by Kamalaśīla as follows: "The cognition of something being an effect of another because it occurs only when that other exists is *yukti* (reasoning). And this, because it is conceptual (*savikalpa*), is not perception (*pratyakṣa*); nor is it inference (*anumāna*) due to the absence of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*). For even an example would have its status as an effect of that [cause] understood through the very fact of occurring only when that exists; in that case too, another example would have to be sought, and for that yet another—thus there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, the physician Caraka says that reasoning is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). Having thus raised the prima facie objection, [the following] was refuted: 'The comprehension of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is not tenable.'"
Therefore, there is no difference between the probandum and the probans in this case;

rather, when establishing the capacity for the conventional usage of their existence, the object known at the time of the convention serves as the illustrative example. (Tattvasaṃgraha, Verse 1696–48)

This was explained by Kamalaśīla: "In the case of *yukti* (logical reasoning), there is no difference between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*). For instance, here the probans is the fact of 'occurring when that occurs' (*tadbhāvabhāvitā*), and the probandum is the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇatā*); yet no difference is perceived between these two, because they are synonyms, like the words 'tree' (*taru*) and 'plant' (*pādapa*). Now, if it is thought: 'It is not the relation of cause and effect that is being proved, but rather the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding its existence,' to this he says: 'In the conventional usage regarding its existence,' and so forth. The existence of that causal relation is 'its existence' (*tadbhāva*); the conventional usage therein is 'the conventional usage regarding its existence' (*tadbhāvavyavahāra*), which consists of the application of cognition, designation, and activity. Fitness for that [usage] is what is being proved for the sake of one who is confused. Those things whose nature is such that they are invariably perceived immediately after the operation of something else are fit for the conventional usage of being its effect. For example, jars and the like, which were experienced at the time of the convention [of naming], have a nature of being perceived immediately after the operation of a potter and so forth. And likewise, sounds have a nature of being invariably perceived immediately after the operation of the palate and other vocal organs; thus, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Consequently, since it serves as an example, there is no difference between this logical reasoning (*yukti*) and inference (*anumāna*)."
And these two— the prima facie view and the established conclusion— are beyond refutation precisely because such reasoning is not accepted;
he concludes [the section] with the words beginning "this," etc.
By the statement "there is no other," he negates the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) accepted by other schools, such as presumption (*arthāpatti*), impossibility (*asambhava*), and so forth;
he then applies an investigation to the subject at hand: that there is and is perceived a future existence (*punarbhava*).

In this regard, he demonstrates that verbal testimony (*śabda*) establishes rebirth: first, by stating "therein, authoritative scripture" (*tatrāptāgama*) and so forth, he shows the validity of the Veda, which is free from any suspicion of error; then, with the passage beginning "and whatever other," he demonstrates the validity—determinable through reasons such as its non-contradiction with the meaning of the Veda—of the Ayurveda, the Smṛtis, the Śāstras, and so on.
"Śāstravāda" refers to discourse in the form of a treatise (*śāstra*).
"From authoritative scripture" means from the Veda:
sacrifice refers to the Agniṣṭoma and other rites; celibacy refers to the restraint of the genitals and so forth;
"prosperity" is heaven, and "the supreme good" is liberation. Here, it should be understood that these are the causes of heaven and liberation respectively, according to their suitability.
The meaning is that by this teaching of heaven to be experienced in another birth and of liberation attainable through many births, the existence of the self in the afterlife is stated.
(27) He states another scriptural source, beginning with "na ca" and so forth.

Those for whom the defects of existence (*sattva-doṣa*) and the defects of the mind (*manas-doṣa*), consisting of *rajas* and *tamas*, have not been transcended and have not subsided, are "those [who are thus]. Furthermore, rebirth is [what is meant by] liberation (*mokṣa*). The connection is that this is not taught by the great sages (*maharṣi*) who are free from defects—that is, those whose mental defects have ceased—within the "gates of Dharma," meaning within the treatises on Dharma (*dharma-śāstra*). Therefore, the meaning is that rebirth is what is taught [by them].
(28) He states the words of another sage from a different scripture, beginning with "dharmadvāre" and so forth.

"Brahman" is the knowledge of the supreme self (*adhyātmajñāna*); those devoted to that [knowledge] are "those who know the ritual acts," meaning those who know the rituals to be performed such as sacrifices.
Those whose mental activity, characterized by awakening, has its quality of purity (*sattvaguṇa*) unimpaired are "such [persons]. By this, he demonstrates their state of pure intellect.

Those who possess the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*)—an eye consisting of knowledge in the form of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that perceives objects beyond the reach of the senses—are "those with the divine eye.
The meaning is that [the teaching] was taught by them after seeing [it], that is, after having experienced it for themselves.
The word "iti" is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).

Thus, although perception does not itself apprehend rebirth through scripture (āgama), he nevertheless demonstrates how it functions in the apprehension of the mark (liṅga) for the inference that grasps rebirth— starting with the words "perception also," and so forth.

"Disimilar" means that among those produced from similar origins—that is, having identical causes of production—one is ugly while another is beautiful; likewise, among those of equal birth, one is fair-skinned while another is dark-skinned. In this way, a distinction should be understood regarding voice and other such qualities as well.
"Slavery and sovereignty" means that for one there is slavery, while for another there is sovereignty.
In the same way, the opposite should be understood elsewhere according to the distinction between individuals.
"Pleasure and pain" is a qualification of life.

These [states] such as weeping and so forth are to be understood as being within the domain of unlearned children; and these states, such as weeping and so forth, do not occur without the recollection of what is desired or undesired, and recollection does not occur without prior knowledge. Thus, because they lead to the inference of knowledge from a previous birth, they serve as inferential grounds for the existence of a future world (*paraloka*).

The diversity of dissimilarity and so forth previously established, as well as the characteristics and origins to be explained later, must be understood as inferring causes performed in a previous birth— thereby inferring the existence of another world— since no other causes for such characteristics or their arising are observed. Here, "the arising of characteristics" refers to the manifestation of physical marks as described in the *Sāmudrika* treatises on physiognomy,
occurring when there is a similarity of karma or a similarity of service and so forth.

*Medhā* is the recollection of a past birth regarding some activity, such as painting, weaponry, or the sciences (*vidyā*); this very recollection he demonstrates by saying, "the coming here of those who have fallen from there. The meaning is that *jātismaraṇa* (recollection of births) takes the form: "I was born in this family, and I have come from that family. Alternatively, it may mean the returning to this birth of those who have fallen from this birth; and by this, the returning of one who was led away by the servants of Yama due to a confusion of names is observed.

In the case of equal vision—that is, when things appear as identical—there may be affection for one person and aversion for another; thus, within this equal vision, there exists the distinction between the pleasant and the unpleasant.
However, due to the fear of prolixity, these internal distinctions of inference have not been shown here.

Having thus demonstrated the apprehension of the mark (*liṅga*) through direct perception, he states the inference: "For this very reason," and so forth. "Self-made" means made by oneself; "indestructible" means not subject to destruction without [the exhaustion of] experience.
"Paurvadehika" means performed in a previous body;
"ānubandhika" means that which follows into other births;
"this fruit" refers to results such as the birth of dissimilar offspring; and this has already been explained in brief.
The connection [of the verse] is as follows: "from this" means from the action performed in this life; "another" refers to a future subsequent birth; and "will come to be" is what is inferred.
To the question "How is it inferred?", he says "From the fruit," and so forth.

From the fruit—that is, from the observation of offspring resembling the fruit—the seed, which is the cause consisting of actions and so forth performed in a previous birth, is inferred. Likewise, the fruit—namely pleasure, pain, and so forth—in a future subsequent birth is inferred from the seed, which is the action performed in this birth. This is the construction [of the argument].
He demonstrates that the existence of the next world is an object of logical reasoning through the passage beginning with "And this is the reasoning," etc.

By stating that the birth of an embryo arises from the collection of the six elements, it is shown that consciousness cannot arise in the embryo without a connection to a self (ātman), and since the self is indeed connected to the next world, this reasoning is presented as proof for the existence of the next world.
Regarding the statement "action arises from the conjunction of agent and instrument," since an action characterized by sacrifice and so forth is not observed to exist without the self as its agent,
[the author] demonstrates the necessity of the self with the passage beginning with "of what has been done" and ending with "not from a seed.
By means of the visible fruits such as servitude or sovereignty, he shows that they have their causal origin in actions performed in previous births.
"The fruit is similar to the action" means that from previously performed virtuous action, there arises a virtuous fruit such as sons, wealth, and so forth.
Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "not from another," etc.;
the meaning is that from a seed other than a rice seed, such as a barley seed, a rice sprout does not arise.
He concludes the reasoning: "Thus is the reasoning.
Although there is much that could be said regarding this object of knowledge (*prameya*), no detailed exposition has been provided due to the lack of such utility here and for fear of prolixity.
Having now explained the next world, he states the means for accomplishing the dharma conducive to it, beginning with the words "In this way" (*evam*).
Regarding the "gateways of dharma" (*dharmadvāreṣu*), which are the gateways for accomplishing dharma:

although practices such as honoring guests and so forth have already been mentioned in the *Sadvṛtta*, they are stated again here for the sake of illustration, as they are pertinent to the present context.

From the statement, "One should be attentive during the examination of the body and so forth," it is intended that by demonstrating attentiveness and defining the qualities of the body and so forth—such as their perishability—one brings about an understanding and a lack of attachment to sense objects.
Having restrained the mind's addiction to sense objects, one effects its stabilization within the Self; this is "mental concentration" (*manaḥsamādhi*).
And here, the connection with the phrase "one should be attentive" applies throughout all these instances.
"Leading to heaven" (*svargyāṇi*) means beneficial for heaven, that is to say, producing heaven.

"Nourishment of livelihood" (*vṛttipuṣṭi*) refers to the increase of wealth. Furthermore, the mention of "nourishing the livelihood" within the pursuit of dharma is for the purpose of instructing that one should practice the causes of dharma without contradicting the causes of livelihood. "Fame" (*yaśas*) consists of such renown as, "This person is righteous."

The desire for the other world (*paralaukaiṣaṇā*) is indeed the third; and the repetition of the word "third" is for the purpose of precluding the possibility that the desire for *dharma* (*dharmeṣaṇā*)—because it is the cause of life and wealth—is itself the desire for life and wealth (*prāṇadhanaiṣaṇā*). Now, by way of an introduction limited to the number three, [the author] states the following other things also delimited by the number three, which are to be discussed here as being beneficial to the healthy and the sick, beginning with the words "atha khalu": [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the portion available.]

First, the supports (*upastambha*) are described, as they sustain the body which serves as the foundation; following that, strength (*bala*), because it is produced by the supports, food, and so forth; after that, the seats of disease (*rogāyatana*), because they act as obstacles to strength; after that, the diseases (*roga*), because they are produced by those [seats]; after that, knowledge of their pathways (*tanmārgajñāna*) is well-established; after that, for the purpose of preventing disease, the mention of the physician (*vaidya*) as the primary cause; and after that, the medicine (*bhaiṣajya*) as the instrument for that [physician]. 34

"Upastambha" (support) means that which, being itself supported and held by another, goes near the primary cause (*pradhānakāraṇa*) and supports or sustains it; just as a secondary pillar situated near the main pillar appointed to support a house acts as a support by providing strength to it, so too here, food and other such things—which sustain the body already being maintained by the karma that initiates its lifespan—are called "supports" (*upastambha*) in the sense of being sustainers or causes (*āyatana*, *kāraṇa*), with the word "of disease" (*rogasya*) understood as the remainder of the sentence.
By the term "celibacy" (*brahmacarya*), those factors conducive to the knowledge of Brahman—such as restraint of the senses, mental serenity, and so forth—are intended.

In this context, food and the rest are understood as being exclusively commendable by way of primary conceptualization; therefore, one should not raise the objection that sprouted food and such things do not support the body. For this very reason, he will provide the qualification "properly joined" (*yuktiyuktaiḥ*). "Properly joined" means conjoined with a commendable method (*yoga*); for celibacy improperly joined—consisting of lack of practice or excessive restraint of the senses and so forth—is a cause of mental agitation and the like, whereas what is accumulated [in the right way] is "properly joined."

The meaning is that the cause of life (āyuḥkāraṇa) is dharma and adharma, which lasts until the exhaustion of the *āyuḥ-saṃskāras*. The word *saṃskāra* here denotes a cause; and food and so forth are mentioned as being primary. Therefore, it is not at all contradictory for oil massages and the like to be sustainers of the body.

[Objection: But even for one who practices food and other necessities correctly, premature death is observed due to specific diseases born from the improper contact of the self with the senses and their objects; to this he says: "the *saṃskāra*," and so on.
The formative force (*saṃskāra*) is the cause that is detrimental "to the body"— this is the ellipsis;
it is that which will be taught right here in this very text, beginning with the passage "the three bases" (*trīṇyāyatanāni*).
*Yukti* is the proper application of food and activity to the body;
*sattva* is the mind, or rather, that which is the strength of the mind called "enthusiasm" (*utsāha*).

"Natural" (*prākṛta*) refers to that which has proceeded from birth and so forth, increased through the growth of natural bodily constituents (*dhātu*) independently of other causes. Indeed, some are seen to be strong by their very nature, while others are weak; this is as stated regarding the seasonal variation [of strength], such as "weakness at the beginning and at the end," and regarding food—such as meat, ghee, and so forth—and activity—such as appropriate rest and exercise—the application of these is "the application of diet and activity" (*āhāraceṣṭāyoga*). Others, however, take the word "application" (*yoga*) to mean the administration of rejuvenative therapies (*rasāyana*).
Of the objects— namely, the objects of the senses— and of action— the activity of body, speech, and mind.
Since time— characterized by cold, heat, and rain—
and highly powerful entities such as sunlight and fire do not produce any disorder here even when observed in diminished measure, for this reason it is said "in every respect" (*sarvaśas*).

Non-perception should be understood as belonging only to those things that possess excessive power, whereas the perception of things lacking such power, such as jars and the like, does not constitute a fault even due to excessive conjunction; in this way, it should be explained in all other cases as well.

"Excessively close" means situated near the eyes; "excessively distant" means located very far away; "fierce" means having a marvelous cause and being fear-inducing; "terrible" refers to non-marvelous things that cause fear, such as tigers and the like; "destined" means whatever is hateful to a particular person; "disgusting" means causing agitation to the mind; "deformed" refers to those with missing limbs and so forth; "terrifying" means producing immediate fear; by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," impure substances and the like are also included.

Although *raudra* and the others are not color (*rūpa*) but rather specific configurations (*ākṛti-viśeṣa*), they are nonetheless objects of the eye because they are inherent in the same substrate as color. Furthermore, it has already been explained that by the mention of "sense-objects" (*indriyārtha*), it is specifically colors and the like that are being grasped; for if there were a correct or incorrect contact with the senses of touch and taste, many factors other than touch and taste—such as bathing, anointing, and so forth, as well as natural dispositions, conjunctions, and refinements—would have to be stated as causes.
Excessive thundering is the intensified roar of clouds. *Paṭaha* refers to the sound of a drum. *Utkruṣṭa* is a loud cry uttered out of pride. *Pradharṣaṇa* is an act of insult or contempt.

A sharp odor is one that causes the eyes to water, such as that of black cumin (*kṛṣṇajīraka*) and similar substances; a pungent odor is one that induces vomiting, such as that of *vaca* and similar substances; a *abhiṣyandi* odor is one that causes a sense of numbness or heaviness, such as that of whey, wine, fermented liquors (*āsava*), and so forth; *pūti* is an excessively putrid smell; *viṣayukta-pavana* is wind charged with poison; and *kuṇapa* refers to a corpse, [in the context of] "of tastes," meaning of substances accompanied by their respective flavors.
By stating here that "non-appropriation" [is required], he shows that even a low-level practice causes a transformation of the bodily constituents (*rasa*).

The specific bases for the rules of diet are those which will be explained in the *Rasavimāna* [chapter]: "Nature (*prakṛti*), processing (*karaṇa*), combination (*saṃyoga*), quantity (*rāśi*), place (*deśa*), time (*kāla*), application (*upayoga*), preparation (*saṃsthā*), and administration (*upayoga*) are the factors to be considered" (Vi. A. 1). Among these, by the statement "excluding quantity (*rāśi*)," he sets quantity apart; for any defect of food as a quantity—whether it be under-measured (*hīnamātratva*) or over-measured (*atimātratva*)—is already included within excessive application (*atiyoga*) and insufficient application (*ayoga*). An improper application (*mithyāyoga*) is not possible for quantity alone. For it has been said: "Quantity (*rāśi*), moreover, is for the purpose of determining the results of proper and improper dosage" (Vi. A. 1).

However, regarding [faults] such as *prakṛti* (nature) and so forth, only improper application (*mithyāyoga*) of food is possible. This is because eating beans and other substances that are contrary to one's constitution (*prakṛti-viruddha*) constitutes improper application of food; likewise, even a lump of roasted flour (*śaktu-piṇḍikā*) that is contrary to its processing (*saṃskāra-viruddha*) is improper application, as is the use of honey and ghee in equal proportions when they are mutually incompatible (*saṃyoga-viruddha*). Similarly, all examples of incompatibility regarding time (*kāla*) and so forth, as established in the *Rasavimāna*, are entirely of the nature of improper application, because these—such as cold and hot things—act as defects independently of under-application (*ayoga*) or over-application (*atiyoga*). Thus it is said.

Although even a deficient application of coldness, heat, and so forth, as well as of massage and the like, can cause disease, the statement "not using [them] at all" is intended to refer to total non-usage which produces manifest disorders in great abundance. This includes acting out of sequence—that is, by violating the prescribed order—such as applying an ointment after bathing, or suddenly immersing oneself in cold water when afflicted by heat;
likewise, injury such as being struck by a sword, and *bhūtas*, meaning living beings such as *piśācas* and others.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), whatever is connected with touch that may cause injury to the body—excluding both non-application (ayoga) and excessive application (atiyoga)—is included.

Now, one might object: "Since there are five sense organs, such as the eyes and so forth, their respective contacts with the five types of unwholesome sense objects (asātmya) are distinct; how then can there be what is called 'a single contact between an unwholesome sense object and a sense organ'? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] demonstrates that the sense of touch (sparśana-indriya) pervades all the senses, and shows that the tactile sensation (sparśa), which is the cause for perceiving objects and is common to all senses, is uniform in nature. Consequently, he demonstrates that a single, uniform contact between an unwholesome sense object and a sense organ is logically established through its connection with that one [tactile] organ—this is shown by the passage beginning with "Therein, one... and ending with "...for the meaning of wholesomeness (sātmya) is the meaning of therapeutic suitability (upaśaya)."
"One touch" means the tactile faculty (*sparśanendriya*) alone, and not the others such as the eye and so forth. The genitive case here is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*).

It is "pervading the faculties" (*indriyavyāpaka*) because it pervades the faculties, such as the eye and so forth. For touch exists in all the faculties; therefore, the faculties grasp their objects only after having touched them.

If that is so, why is there not a perception of objects at all times? To this he replies with the words beginning "cetaḥ" (the mind): "In our view, the auditory organ (*śrotra*) consists of the five elements and is of the nature of space located within the ear-cavity; therefore, it also possesses touch (*sparśa*). [The term] "inherent in the mind" (*cetaḥ-samavāyi*) means related to the mind (*manaḥ-sambandhi*). By mentioning its connection to the mind, he demonstrates that touch has the capacity for the apprehension of objects, because the sense organs, when presided over by the mind, are the perceivers of objects.

In that case, since the mind—though of atomic dimension—is situated in one place, does it not cause all the sense organs to function through its connection with the tactile organ (*sparśana*), which pervades all the senses? If that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the simultaneous arising of five cognitions. To this, he says: "And the mind, though pervasive, [functions] because of the pervasion of the tactile organ."

The pervasion of the sense organs by the tactile organ (*sparśanendriya*) is "tactile-organ-pervasion" (*sparśanendriyavyāpti*); the mind (*cetas*) also pervades that [pervasion]. What is meant is this: in whatever spatial extent the tactile organ resides, the mind also moves through that much space for the purpose of grasping objects through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, whenever the mind is present in a particular location, it then perceives the object through that location via the visual organ and so forth; thus, there is no simultaneous arising of cognitions. This is applied to the subject at hand: "Therefore," and so on.

"Pervasive contact" (*vyāpakasparśa*) means that which is pervasive and is contact; "produced by that" (*tena kṛtaḥ*) means having that as its basis. The meaning is: a specific state (*bhāvaviśeṣaḥ*), a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣaḥ*), of all the sense organs, which serves as the cause for the apprehension of objects; with reference to this, it was said: "Contact is twofold—contact with the tactile organ and that which is purely mental—and it is the initiator of pleasant and painful sensations" (Śā. [Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya]).

Thus [it is said]. In this verse, the contact of all the sense-faculties produced by the connection with the tactile faculty is expressed by the term "contact of the tactile faculty" (*sparśanendriya-saṃsparśa*). However, since mental contact can also occur even when the object is merely being thought of, that specific distinction must be explained in that very context;
in the phrase "there is a distinction" (*viśeṣa*), the word "exists" (*asti*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.

Thus, for a single sense organ, there is one type of contact with an unsuitable object—namely, touch—which acts as a cause of suffering because it is not conducive to well-being (*anupaśaya*). Furthermore, this contact takes five forms, such as contact of the eye with an unsuitable object, contact of the nose with an unsuitable object, and so forth. Moreover, it is further divided into three categories: non-contact (*ayoga*), excessive contact (*atiyoga*), and improper contact (*mithyāyoga*).
In this way, contact with an unsuitable object of the senses is said to be of one kind, three kinds, and fifteen kinds.

By the term *anupaśaya*, one should understand the specific *anupaśayas* of the eyes and other senses, because it is taught that there are five types of causes for the unwholesome contact of the sense organs with their objects (*asātmyendriyārthasaṃyoga*). Indeed, a single uniform *anupaśaya* would not be capable of accounting for the fivefold nature of the unwholesome contact of the sense organs with their objects; for the eyes and other senses have their own specific damaging factors, such as excessively brilliant forms and so forth. Consequently, even though the sense of touch pervades them all, the eyes and other senses do not constitute a single sense organ (*sparśana-indriya*). For if they were one, a factor that damages one sense organ would necessarily damage the others as well; this is how it should be understood.
He demonstrates that *sātmya* (wholesomeness) and *upaśaya* (therapeutic suitability) have the same meaning: "For the meaning of *sātmya* is indeed the meaning of *upaśaya*.

By this, having shown that *anupaśaya* (non-suitability) refers to the contact between the sense organs and their objects, it is demonstrated that the application of the designation "unwholesome contact of the sense organs with their objects" (*asātmyendriyārthasaṃyoga*) is not contradictory.

Having described the deficient application (*ayoga*), excessive application (*atiyoga*), and improper application (*mithyāyoga*) of objects, he now describes those same [faults] regarding action (*karman*), beginning with the words "karma" and so forth.

Although, in this context, it would have been more appropriate to describe bodily action first—since it is the primary cause of diseases of the body—it was nonetheless mentioned later because speech and mental actions are minor. However, when describing the improper application for each individually, the improper application of the body is shown first due to its predominance.

In this context, excessive engagement (*atipravṛtti*) in the form of *atiyoga* (excessive application), as well as non-engagement (*apravṛtti*) in the form of *ayoga* (inappropriate application), should be understood as pertaining to prescribed actions of body, speech, and mind; for all harmful conduct must be described as *mithyāyoga* (perverse application).

Furthermore, the terms *vegodīraṇam* (urging of natural urges), *aprāptavegodīraṇam* (urging of urges at an inappropriate time), and *viṣamaśabdaḥ* (the word "uneven") are to be connected with everything ending with *aṅgapraṇidhāna* (application of the limbs).
Defiling the body by excessive scratching and so forth;
causing distress by exposure to wine, heat, water-sprinkling, and so forth;
and incoherent speech, which is the uttering of whatever comes to mind without logical connection.
In this context, speech that is not figurative refers to untruthful speech and the like, which cause disease by way of demerit (adharma).
To include those [practices] that were not mentioned which are joined with falsehood, he says "in brief," and so forth.

By the phrase "harmful in this life" and "not taught," he indicates that [practices] such as serving the wives of others—which cause sin by being causes of unrighteousness (*adharma*) in the next world—are included. Thus, the claim that "this description of the bases (*āyatana*) is deficient because it does not include unrighteousness" is not valid.

Because it is through the improper engagement (*mithyāyoga*) of bodily, mental, and verbal actions—acting as an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) that produces demerit (*adharma*)—that the various transformations produced by demerit are brought about; just as heaven is produced by the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice precisely through the intermediate operation of producing merit (*dharma*). Others, however, attribute demerit to the improper engagement with time (*kālamithyāyoga*), on the grounds that demerit indeed bears fruit only through the power of time and not at the very moment [of its commission]; and this has already been explained in detail in the first chapter.

Now, since improper application of action (*karmāsamyagyoga*) is rooted in intellectual error (*prajñāparādha*), it is described as being that very error itself. By stating "it is threefold," etc., [the author] demonstrates that there is no contradiction with what was previously stated in the enumeration of the three causes: "Improper contact of the senses with their objects, intellectual error, and transformation (*pariṇāma*). Likewise, regarding what will be stated later—"Time, moreover, is called transformation"—one should explain it as demonstrating the absence of contradiction with what was said before. Thus, the threefold classification here consists of excessive application (*atiyoga*) and so forth.
He demonstrates the connection with the excellence of time and other factors through the verse beginning with "cold and heat," etc.
"Excessive specific characteristic" refers to excessive cold and so forth;
that which has characteristics contrary to the specific characteristic of cold and so forth—for example, rain in the winter, or cold during the rainy season, and so on.

He brings together the forty-two bases—this is the connection with the phrase "thus, etc., they become the causes of the morbid transformations. Likewise, it should be applied that those joined with proper application (*samayoga*)—that is, joined with correct application (*samyagyoga*)—become the causes of the primary nature (*prakṛti*); *prakṛti* here means health (*ārogya*).

Having now established correct application (*samyagyoga*) and lack of application (*ayoga*) as the causes for the equilibrium and imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), he says "of all," etc., for the purpose of providing an illustration that even for external objects such as trees and jars, correct application and lack of application are the very causes of their proper maintenance and destruction, and for the purpose of knowing the nature of entities (*bhāvasvarūpa*).

Existence (*bhāva*) is correct establishment; non-existence (*abhāva*) is incorrect establishment or destruction. From "conjunction" (*yoga*), meaning correct conjunction, there is existence; from "non-conjunction" (*ayoga*) and so forth, there is non-existence. The connection is that these two depend upon their respective principles—that is, the principle of whatever existence or non-existence there may be, which is the principle of its own cause.

For example, regarding the existence and persistence of a tree, the logical reasons are such things as its connection with a sufficient supply of water; whereas regarding the non-existence of the tree, the logical reasons are its lack of connection with water and its excessive connection with heat, as well as such things as a lightning strike. Therefore, one should conceive that the existence and non-existence of the tree depend upon those factors.
(44) He states the diseases: "There are three diseases," and so forth.

From the attainment of the desired arises desire, joy, and so forth; and from the loss of the beloved or the acquisition of the undesirable arise grief and so forth. Alternatively, there is the reading: “from the non-attainment of the desired and the attainment of the undesirable. In this reading, however, the conjunction *ca* (and) should be understood to indicate that the attainment of the desired is also a cause. Now, since the treatment for mental disease requires little to be said, he explains its treatment right here, beginning with the words *tatra* and so on.
"Even by one afflicted with mental disease"—by the word "even" (api), it is indicated that even one possessed of physical disease should perform what is about to be described.
This triad, consisting of dharma, artha, and kāma, results in either mental happiness or mental suffering; thus it should be construed.
"One who knows that" (tadvidya) here means one who knows the medicine for mental disease.
"Knowledge of oneself," and so forth:

"Who am I? What is beneficial for me? is knowledge of the self; "What is the place? What is appropriate here? is knowledge of the place; in this same way, knowledge regarding time and so on is to be understood.
Now, for the sake of easy comprehension, he states this very same point in verse, beginning with "mānasam pratītya" (depending on mental [states]):
the meaning is "mental transformation," referring to the three aims of life, such as dharma and the rest.
47. Here he describes the pathways of disease: "three," etc.; one pathway consists of the vital points (*marmans*), the bones, and the joints.

In this context, the designation "branches" (*śākhā*) is for the sake of conventional usage; likewise, it is intended to indicate that the blood and other elements denoted as "branches" are external, being comparable to the branches of a tree. Furthermore, by the term "skin" (*tvak*), the rasa (nutritive fluid) residing therein is also included. However, rasa itself is not explicitly mentioned here in order to exclude the rasa located in the heart from the designation of "branch," for that is indeed included by the very term "viscera" (*koṣṭha*). By this same principle, it should be understood that the blood residing in the liver and spleen is also intended to be included within the "viscera," as the underlying logic is identical.
And it is stated in the *Koṣṭhavivaraṇa*: “The locations of undigested matter (*āma*), digestive fire (*agni*), and digested matter (*pakva*), as well as those of urine and blood—
the heart (*hṛd*), the duodenum (*uṇḍuka*), and the lungs (*phupphusa*)— are designated as the *koṣṭha* (thoraco-abdominal cavity)” (Suśruta Saṃhitā, Cikitsā-sthāna, chapter 2).
Regarding the opening of the bone-joints: "the unions of bones," and so forth;
therein, in the context of the bone-joint, *kaṇḍarā* refers to the thick tendons (*sthūlasnāyu*) according to this treatise.
The receptacle for the undigested and the digested is the *āmapakvāśaya*;
this description of the division of the pathways is for the purpose of knowing the relative ease of treatment and other characteristics of the diseases located therein.
Now, he demonstrates which disease is located in which pathway—beginning with "there, abscesses" (*gaṇḍa*) and so forth.

The phrase "arising in the external pathways" (*bahirmārgajāḥ*) is an adjective qualifying *visarpa* and the others, for *visarpa* and such may also reside in the internal pathways; thus, it is used to exclude them.
The word *pakṣa* (side/paralysis) is connected with both *vadha* (paralysis) and *graha* (seizure), while *śoṣa* (wasting) refers to the wasting of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).

Although fever indeed pervades the entire body, it is nevertheless specifically described here as arising from the stomach (*āmāśaya*) and so forth, as well as those born in the internal channels (*antarmārgaja*), which are particular types such as *visarpa* (erysipelas).
Hemorrhoids (*arśas*) are located in the external folds or in the limbs (*śākhāgata*), while others are situated in the visceral cavity (*koṣṭhagata*).

A gulma that arises externally, which is perceived as protruding outward and suppurates on the outside, should be known as such; all others, however, are located solely within the abdominal cavity (koṣṭha).
Those who practice under the guise of physicians are those who move about in the dress of physicians.

"Siddhasādhitāḥ" means those who have been accomplished or proven by one already established as a Siddha. "Vaidyabhāṇḍam" refers to medical instruments such as enema nozzles and the like; "pratirūpakāḥ" means those who are counterfeits or mere imitations of physicians.
Designation (vyapadeśa) is the mention [of something] by way of connection with another;
those who do not possess that [knowledge] are devoid of knowledge.

*Daiva* refers to the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*); that which relies upon it is *daivyapāśraya*. This consists of mantras and the like, which counteract diseases by producing the unseen. Alternatively, by the word *daiva*, the gods (*deva*) are meant; that which benefits [the patient] by relying upon them is likewise [called *daivyapāśraya*]. For mantras and so forth remove disease precisely through the power of the gods, and the gods themselves, being pleased by offerings of oblations and the like, destroy diseases through their power. Here, *daivyapāśraya* is mentioned first because it removes disease quickly. *Praṇipāta* is physical prostration to the gods and others; *gamana* is traveling to distant places where gods and others reside.
Now he describes the threefold classification of medicines in another way, beginning with the words "In the body" (*śarīra*) and so forth.

The word "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*) is connected with the phrase "aggravation of the bodily *doṣas*"; by this, he shows that even for mental disorders such as insanity (*unmāda*) and epilepsy (*apasmāra*), treatments like collyrium (*añjana*) and others are applicable. Alternatively, by the phrase "mostly threefold," he indicates that even for physical diseases, there are divine-based (*daivavyapāśraya*) treatments such as propitiatory rites (*svastyayana*).
In the context of describing the different types of physicians, he states the different types of patients, beginning with "the wise" (*prājña*): *śarma* means happiness, that is to say, health.
Negligence consists in failing to provide treatment even after recognizing the disease;
"perception" refers to correct knowledge in the form: "This is a disease and must be treated with urgency.
[The sense is that] having failed to find a physician who acts as a protector, the physician does not approach such a patient. This is the underlying meaning.
It shows that the ignorant fool, like the example of the lizard, perishes even while making an effort for the sake of survival;
[the word] "should counteract" implies "an effort."

In the phrase "by the wise one, states [are] for the sake of gathering," there is a word division (*cheda*); the connection (*sambandha*) is that there are eight states (*bhāva*). Regarding these states, which are the objects (*viṣaya*).
By one who is unattached and not clinging to these eight things, such as seeking and so forth— wherein "all" refers to dharma, artha, and kāma.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Threefold Quest" (*Tisraiṣaṇīya*), in the *Nirdeśacatuṣka* (Section on the Four Instructions) of the *Sūtrasthāna*, within the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta.

[Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 12 (12 of 120)] In the preceding chapter, diseases were described in terms of their essential nature, pathways, external causes, and medicinal treatments; however, the Vāta and other factors that serve as their causes were not mentioned because they require extensive explanation. Therefore, they are now discussed in a separate section titled "Vātakalākalīya"; therein, Vāyu alone is addressed first due to its preeminence.

*Kalā* means a quality (*guṇa*), as it has been stated: "consisting of sixteen parts" (Sūtra, A. 10); *akalā* refers to a fault (*doṣa*) which is the opposite of a quality. Therefore, *vātakalākalīya* means pertaining to the qualities and faults of Vāta. Alternatively, *kalā* is a subtle portion; *kalākalā* is a portion of that [subtle portion]; thus, it means an even more subtle part of that. 1–2. Here, the description of the qualities of Vāta and so forth is presented in the form of the words of many sages in order to demonstrate the consensus of numerous seers and to establish the work's adherence to the principles of the treatise and its consistency with traditional authority (*aitihya*).

"Non-composite" (*asaṃghāta*) means being devoid of a collection of parts, like bile or phlegm; "unstable" (*anavasthita*) means having a fluctuating nature; and "unattainable" (*anāsādya*) should be understood as being so due to its mobility and its lack of dense constituent parts.
The terms *rūkṣa* (dry) and so forth are primarily expressive of states (*bhāva*); therefore, they should be understood as qualities (*guṇa*), such as dryness and the like.

Because of its mobility (*calatva*), it possesses harshness (*dāruṇatva*) and mobility; thus, the mobility described in the *Dīrghañjīvitīya* chapter is here stated. Alternatively, because of its desiccating nature (*śoṣaṇatva*), it produces hardness (*kāṭhinya*), which constitutes its harshness.
"Kumāraśiras" is an epithet of Bharadvāja, intended to exclude the Bharadvāja who was the teacher of Ātreya.

"By such powers" refers to activities such as running and staying awake, which produce dryness and other effects; the mention of "powers" is used because actions themselves are devoid of qualities (nirguṇatva).
"By those being practiced" means by those employed repeatedly;
"of bodies" means of the limbs of the body.
Those things which produce cavities and openings constitute the basis; being nourished and accumulated, they remain in a state of similar qualities.
The opposite of harsh is soft; the opposite of porous is dense;

"non-adhering" means not remaining fixed, which is to say that its constituent parts are wasting away. By this it is meant: even if there is no direct connection between the wind (vāyu) and the causes of wind or the pacifiers of wind, nevertheless, through those factors connected to the body, a connection with the wind moving within the body is established. Consequently, an increase of the wind is logically possible through association with qualities similar to its own, and a decrease through association with contrary qualities.
"Moving within bodies and outside of bodies" is a description of the nature of *vāta*. By this, it is shown that there is no tautology in saying it moves "within bodies" or "outside of bodies.
Furthermore, by mentioning "parts" (*avayavān*) here, he demonstrates that it is impossible to describe [the wind] in its entirety because of its vast manifoldness (*bahuprapañcatva*).

Having established and demonstrated that speech and other functions are perceptible in the activities of the vital air (*vāta*), while the mind’s impulsion and so forth are inferable, and the body (*tantra*)—which is the mechanism (*yantra*)—is knowable through scripture because it effects the formation of the embryo and so forth;
as it has been said: "When the mechanisms of the body have broken down, for those about to enter into ultimate darkness... (*Iṃ.*).

Thus [it is said], that itself is the *yantra*; or else, the *yantra* of the *tantra* refers to the joints (*sandhi*), whose nature consists of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth— that is, having the form of the vital breaths and so forth—
which are the specific movements of various kinds, meaning diverse, or rather, auspicious and inauspicious.

He is the controller of the mind as it operates toward objects not desired, and the leader—that is, the instigator and impeller—of the mind itself toward the object that is desired; or alternatively, there is the reading "udyogakāraka" (the maker of effort), which has the same meaning, or "abhivoḍhā" (the bearer), in the sense of being the grasper of the objects of all the senses; and this [leadership] of his should be understood through the logic established in the previous chapter, because he pervades all the senses by means of the tactile organ, which consists of air.

The *prakṛti* (primordial cause) is that which arranges, aggregates, and structures—meaning it is the cause. And the quality of being the cause of sound belongs eternally to air (*vāyu*), because of its constant entry into space (*ākāśa*). For, after mentioning the elements beginning with space, it has been stated: "Among them, the first possesses one quality; there is an increase of qualities in each subsequent one" (Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.6).
Furthermore, it is stated as a redundancy after mentioning earth and the other elements: "For the subsequent is pervaded by the preceding" (Nyāyadarsana 2.1.66).

The ear is the root of the vital air (vāyu) because it functions in the specific formation of the auditory canal; "root" means the primary cause. Enthusiasm is the application of effort toward tasks, and it is the womb—that is, the cause of manifestation—of the mind.
It is the dryer of the humors, the dryer of the bodily fluids,
the breaker, and the maker; and here, at the time of the body's production,
the word *bhūta* denotes its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
The word *upaghātāya* (for the sake of destruction) is a [separate] compound;

it is connected with the phrase *garbhān vikṛtim āpādayati atikālaṃ dhārayati* (causes the embryos to undergo transformation and retains them for too long); and *santānagatividhānam* refers to the regulation of the movement of the sun and other [planets] by way of their continuous, uninterrupted progression (*santāna*).
"Of the streams" means of the rivers;
"the classification" (pravibhāga) is the distinct definition (vibhaktalakṣaṇa).

"Of the elements" (dhātūnām) refers to earth and so forth; the elements are the constituent substances such as stones and the like. "Measure" (māna) is dimension, and "configuration" (saṃsthāna) is shape; their "manifestation" (vyakti) is their appearance, which is to say, the cause thereof.
The "processing" (*abhisaṃskāra*) of a seed such as rice is its capacity to produce a sprout;

"non-moistening" (*avikleda*) is the state of not being decomposed prior to the time of ripening; and "drying up" (*upaśoṣaṇa*) refers specifically to the drying of moist grains like barley through the process of ripening.
By means of non-moistening and drying up—without undergoing any transformation that causes ruin—it asserts that the nature of seeds is the cause for the entire world in its primordial form.
A mountain has peaks;
a tree is an anokaha; moving upward is *udvartana*.
*Pratisaraṇa* means going against [the current];

*visarjana* and *visarga* mean emission, and this is connected separately with *nīhāra* and the others: *nīhāra* is a mass of cold [fog]; *nirhrāda* is thundering without clouds; *aśani* is fire that pierces like a thunderbolt;
*asaṅghāta* is non-aggregation, or rather non-arising or non-accumulation.
"Upasarga" refers to the manifestation of pestilence and the like;
"visarga" in the passage beginning with "meghasūrya" refers to creation.

Here, "Vāyu" is intended in the sense of a deity; therefore, its acting as the wind that brings about the end of the four ages in the form of a physical element is not contradictory. In this same way, whatever else may appear inconsistent regarding Vāyu should also be resolved by understanding it solely in its capacity as a deity.
Now, the nature of Vāyu, both in its provoked and unprovoked states, is described in general terms: "For he is the Blessed One," and so forth;
*prabhava* means the cause, and *avyaya* means imperishable or undecaying.
The term "of beings" (*bhūtānām*) is connected with what follows.

The various divisions, such as Mṛtyu, Yama, and others, are to be understood from the *Āgama* as pertaining to all *tantras* and all ritual actions (*karmas*). The word *tantra* is also used in the sense of "action," as it has been said: "the bladder is the *tantra* of [the *tantras*]" (Sūtra).
a.25); the meaning is "of karmas.
The passage beginning with "Having heard that" and so forth is easy to understand.

By the statement "it possesses brilliance and luster" (9–10) and by the phrase "situated within the bile," [the author] demonstrates the existence of fire in the form of the heat of *pitta* within the body, while negating the presence of fire characterized by flames and the like. However, this does not imply non-difference from *pitta*, because the impairment of digestive fire (*agni-māndya*) by *pitta* will be explained in the chapter on the *grahaṇī*, and likewise because clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*), which pacifies *pitta*, is stated to increase the digestive fire.

"Digestion and non-digestion" refers to the functions of the digestive fire (*pācaka-agni*) through its divisions into unmodified and modified states; "seeing and not seeing" refers to the perceiving fire (*ālocaka*) located in the eyes; "the measure and non-measure of heat" as well as the various colors refer to the radiant fire (*bhrājaka*) located in the skin; "fear, courage, and so forth" refer to the accomplishing fire (*sādhaka*) located in the heart; however, no example is given for the coloring fire (*rañjaka*), because its manifest external effects are not perceived.
Soma is the deity of water, or alternatively, it is the moon.
"Because of the word 'exclusive' (aikāntika)" means because of the restriction; [it refers] to the highest good, which is happiness.
The three seasons—characterized by cold, heat, and rain—are the time of affliction by means of a season consisting of four months;
this refers to the time of the destruction of the country (deśocchedakāle).
The qualities in the context of *saṅgraha* (compendium) are six, beginning with *rūkṣa* (dryness) and so forth.
The cause is twofold: the cause for the provocation of *vāta* and the cause for the pacification of *vāta*.

All the various types of action of *vāta* without exception are manifold; furthermore, that which is fourfold—distinguished by being provoked or unprovoked, and moving within the body or outside the body—should be understood as having been stated [previously]. For no distinct action of *vāta* has been taught apart from these four types.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Quantities of Vata," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the section of four instructions in the *Sūtrasthāna*.
Thus ends the tetrad of explanations.
3 [Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 13 (13 of 120)]

In the *Nirdeśavātakalākalīya*, the [doshas] such as *vāta* have been described. To explain how their remedies (*bheṣaja*) should be prepared, the "Quadruple Section on Formulations" (*Kalpanācatuṣka*) is now set forth. The preparation of medicines is called "medicine-preparation" (*bheṣajakalpanā*). Furthermore, that preparation cannot be formulated without first naming the substances that serve as its basis; therefore, the preparations for oleation (*sneha*), sudation (*sveda*), emesis (*vamana*), and purgation (*virecana*)—which concern substances such as unctuous agents—are discussed here. However, the preparation of enemas (*bastikalpanā*) is not mentioned here because it requires extensive explanation.

In this context as well, since oleation (sneha) alone is prescribed first for the initiation of therapies such as emesis, and because Vata—which predominates among the humors—is the primary therapeutic target, the chapter explaining that very subject is designated as the "Chapter on Oleation" (Snehādhyāya); thus, the chapter explaining oleation is the Snehādhyāya.

*Sāṅkhya* means correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*); those who conduct themselves by means of that are *Sāṅkhyas*. Alternatively, they are so called because they have reckoned (*saṅkhyāta*)—that is, known—the *saṅkhyeya*, which is the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). Or, if the reading is *saṅkhyātasaṅkhyeyam*, then it is an adjective qualifying Punarvasu; however, the meaning remains the same.
This [mention of] the Sāṅkhyas is intended to demonstrate Ātreya’s state of mental composure, which is appropriate for answering the questions regarding what is to be done.
By the term "doubt" (*saṃśaya*), he indicates the object by means of the subject; thus, "doubt" means the object of doubt.
To the question "What is this doubt?", he says: "Of what origins? and so forth.
What are their sources, what are their supporting causes,
and what is the consideration regarding time and post-drink (anupāna)? Regarding the administration of oleation (sneha), one should avoid drinking unadulterated oil or fat alone.
What is measure? Of what kind is measure? And what is it? It is the excellence of quantity and the excellence of time.
Regarding "snehane" (in oleation), it refers to the procedure involving the application of unctuous substances.
"Ke na ca" means who are not to be oleated?

What is beneficial or harmful from "sneha-pāna" (the drinking of unctuous substances) first or initially? Furthermore, one should apply this same principle to what is beneficial or harmful when the unctuous substance has been drunk and when it has been digested.

The *siddhis* (therapeutic successes) are medicines that accomplish cures; because "purification" (*saṃśodhana*) is mentioned separately from "pacification" (*saṃśamana*), the term "pacification" refers to those [remedies] by way of the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*). Thus, "treatment" (*vṛtti*) is the application of palliative measures.
Knowledge is the scripture;
Abhiṣuka was a teacher from the northern region.
*Citrā* is *gorakṣakarkaṭī*, its seed being used here; or alternatively, *citrā* is red castor (*lohitairaṇḍa*);
*atasī* is known as *umā*; and *āruka*, *nikocaka*, and *akṣoḍa* are products of the northern region (*auttarāpathika*).
The "receptacles of oil" (snehāśaya) are the locations where oil resides;
these have been mentioned as the most prominent ones, and by this [principle], neem oil (nimbataila) and others are to be understood.
"Āmiṣa" means meat.

Regarding the phrase "of those born from oil" (9–11), the word *jāta* denotes a class or type. As in the passage, "O Agniveśa, whatever is born from food" (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 25), although by etymological derivation (*yoga*) only that which is produced from sesame seeds is oil, nevertheless, by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), all vegetable fats here are called "oil."
As stated in the Suśruta-saṃhitā: "Because of its production and because it possesses those qualities, the nature of oil exists in others as well" (Su.Sū.A.
45). It is distinguished, excelled, or preeminent; thus, it is connected with the word *airaṇḍa* (castor oil).

Regarding the phrase "the best of all unctuous substances" (*sarvasnehottama*), the word "all" (*sarva*) includes curd, milk, and so forth. Furthermore, the status of clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) and other substances as the best of all unctuous substances is due to their possession of an excellence of unctuous qualities (*sneha-guṇa*).
This excellence consists of the imposition of another quality through processing (*saṃskāra*); "conformity" (*anuvidhāna*) means following after that [excellence], which is to say, its acceptance.

This is what is meant: substances such as oil do not carry the qualities of processing (*saṃskāra*) in the same way that clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) does. For this very reason it was said: "No other unctuous substance follows [the effects of] processing in the same way as clarified butter; therefore, clarified butter is considered the best of all unctuous substances" (Ni.).

a.1) For this very reason, even when conforming to the qualities of the processing substances such as turmeric and others, ghee does not abandon its own qualities, such as unctuousness (*sneha*) and coldness (*śaitya*); moreover, it carries both its own qualities and those of the processing agents. Since the prefix *anu-* denotes "subsequently," it is said that after the carrying of its own qualities, there follows the carrying of the qualities of the processing agents.
Therefore it has been stated: "It pacifies *vāta* due to its unctuousness, and *pitta* due to its sweetness and coldness."
"Ghee possesses qualities equal to those of the [kapha] dosha, yet it overcomes kapha through processing. (Nidāna-sthāna, Chapter 1)

Nor should it be argued: "Since ghee (*sarpiḥ*) has become dry and hot through processing with dry, hot substances such as *citraka* and others, how then can its natural unctuousness (*sneha*) and coldness (*śaitya*)—which are contradictory to those qualities—persist? For the dryness and heat reside in the particles of *citraka* that have entered into contact with the ghee, whereas the unctuousness and coldness reside in the ghee itself; thus, because they have different substrates (*bhinna-āśrayatva*), there is no contradiction. This indeed is what constitutes the ghee’s conformity to processing (*saṃskārānuvartana*): that even a quality contrary to its own nature is maintained within it without being destroyed. Furthermore, although the ghee carries the qualities of the processing agents such as *citraka*, its coldness and so forth may occasionally be overcome by the hot qualities of those processing agents, but its unctuous quality is not. This is because unctuousness, being established in all its parts throughout the ghee, is more powerful. For this very reason, ghee and other such substances are called "unctuous substances" (*sneha*) because unctuousness is their predominant characteristic.

Others, however, maintain that the persistence of a processing (saṃskāra) consists in the carrying of the processing-quality by means of the suppression of its own qualities; they say this applies to oil but not to clarified butter (sarpiḥ). As for the persistence of processing mentioned in the case of clarified butter, that occurs because no quality whatsoever in the clarified butter is suppressed by the processing-quality. For instance, in the case of fever, oil processed with cooling substances such as sandalwood is prescribed for the purpose of pacifying burning sensations; for oil processed with cold substances remains cold by its very nature, even though it is hot [by its substrate]. 13
He states the qualities of unctuous substances: "Ghee," and so forth; "extinguishing" means the alleviation of burning sensations;
"subduing Vāta," and so forth, are the qualities of oil.
Know that it makes [the body] firm and stabilizes the limbs; such are the qualities of muscle fat (vasā):
the increase of virility and the increase of semen.
Regarding "sneha" (oleation), which refers to the application of unctuous substances to the body, the qualities of marrow begin with "strength and semen," and so forth. (Verses 14–17)
He states the time for drinking ghee and other substances: "ghee in autumn," and so forth;
"in spring" refers to Vaiśākha, and "the rainy season" refers to Āṣāḍha and Śrāvaṇa, as it is said: "The rainy season is to be known as [the months] Śukra and Nabhas. (Siddhānta 6)

In autumn, due to the predominance of pitta, ghee alone is appropriate as it is not antagonistic to pitta, whereas other substances such as oils are not; as for muscle fat (*vasā*) and marrow (*majjā*), they are considered neutral because they are neither excessively cold nor hot. This is because no specific instruction regarding their coldness or heat was given in the context of vehicles (*anupāna*); however, the statement, "One should determine the coldness and heat of muscle fat and marrow according to the nature of the living being" (*Sūtra-sthāna* 27), mentions coldness and heat only in a general sense. Since this does not specify heat or coldness in the same manner as oils and ghee, it does not establish an extreme degree of coldness or heat.

Therefore it has been said: "Among oil, muscle fat, marrow, and clarified butter, superiority exists in descending order for disorders of Vāta and Kapha, while it exists in ascending order for disorders of Pitta" (Vi.

A. 8). Here, it is established that clarified butter, being cool, alleviates Pitta; oil, being hot, alleviates Vāta and Kapha; and muscle fat and marrow, being intermediate in nature, occupy a middle position.

Thus, because fat (*vasā*) and marrow (*majjan*) are common [to both seasons], and because they are non-extremely cold or hot due to their qualities of providing strength and increasing the *dhātus*, as well as being associated with the loss of strength and the depletion of the *dhātus* [in spring], their application is appropriate in the month of Mādhava.
However, although Caitra possesses the primary common qualities, it is not a subject for oleation (*sneha*) due to its abundance of phlegm (*śleṣman*), and thus it is not mentioned.
He states the time generally recommended for the use of oleation: "not too hot," and so forth.

This rule regarding the timing should be understood to apply when there is no urgent disorder—neither during the excessively hot summer, nor during the excessively cold winter and early spring, nor during the rainy season characterized by rain-induced chill; for it will be taught later that unctuous therapy (sneha) is prescribed for both hot and cold seasons.
He demonstrates the sequence of drinking according to specific times and specific doshas with the words beginning "vāta" and so forth:
"vāta and pitta" is *vātapitta*; one in whom that is predominant is *vātapittādhika*.
"At night" means in the evening.

The mention of "excess of *kapha* in the hot summer" is for the purpose of indicating a person afflicted by an extreme cold disorder; by this, those with an excess of *vāta* and *kapha*, as well as those with an excess of *kapha* alone, are included. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*: "One with an excess of *vāta* and *pitta* [should drink] at night, while one with an excess of *vāta* and *kapha* [should drink] during the day" (*Su.Ci.* 31).
