Thus, for those with an excess of *vāta* alone, as well as for those with an excess of *pitta* or *kapha*, the time for drinking the potion mentioned below is established as the general rule for the common seasons such as autumn.
For he will say: “One should drink pacifying unctuous substances at mealtime,” and so forth.

Others, however, maintain that by the mention of "predominance of Vāta," even simple Vāta is included; and by the designation of "predominance of Kapha," both Vāta-Kapha and Pitta-Kapha are also included—this refers to the cold season, such as Hemanta and others.
The sun with its powerful rays when it is in that part of the day which is spotless—that is the "spotless sun," meaning midday (19).
He states the fault in deviating from the prescribed rule regarding time: "or when it is excessively hot," and so forth.

Oil drunk during the day in an excessively hot season causes the aforementioned disorders even in one of a *ślaiṣmika* constitution; likewise, when drunk during the cold season by one in whom *vāta* and *pitta* predominate, it causes the aforementioned disorders. The same principle applies to drinking at night. However, when there is a combination of a prohibited time and a [specific] *doṣa*, as well as in cases of excessive intake, the intensity or mildness of the resulting disorders should be inferred through reasoning. (20–21) He now states the after-drink (*anupāna*): "Water," etc.

Regarding oil as an adjunct (anupāna), the quantity of the adjunct, when prescribed for the purpose of ensuring the proper cooking of the medicine, should be inferred from the very fact that the medicine has been cooked correctly; this is also established by the practice of experienced physicians.
He describes the various preparations by way of enumeration and their essential nature in a single section, beginning with "odana" and so forth:
*vilepī* is a thin liquid; *yavāgū* is to be known as that which is thick with many *siktha* (rice-particles);
and *khaḍa* is a soup (*yūṣa*) made with vegetables and sprouts.
*Kāmbalika* is prepared with curd, salt, oil, sesame, and so forth, and is slightly sour.

An example of these two is as follows: "This well-cooked *khaḍayūṣa* (sour soup) made with buttermilk (*takra*), wood-apple (*kapittha*), sorrel (*cāṅgerī*), black pepper (*marica*), cumin (*ajājī*), and *cittraka* is considered *kāmbalika*."

"The boiled [mixture] combined with curd, sour gruel, salt, fat, sesame, and black gram" refers to a *leha* (linctus) prepared through the cooking of sugar and other ingredients; it is called a *leha* because it is licked (*lihyate*). "Pravicāraṇā" refers to that by which food such as rice (*odana*) and the like is processed, applied, or utilized according to a secondary method (*anukalpa*). Furthermore, in the context of "fat-processing" (*snehapravicāraṇā*), rice and similar foods should be understood as being necessarily mixed with fats. Although unguents (*abhyañjana*) and the like are produced from pure fats, they are nevertheless referred to by the term "processing" (*vicāraṇā*) in this treatise because they do not function in connection with the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*).

However, the drinking of oil alone (*kevalasnehapāna*) is not designated by the term "investigation" (*vicāraṇā*) because of its superior capacity for oleation; this very point is stated as follows: "clear and drinkable" (*acchapeya*), etc.
"Clear and drinkable" means that which is clear and fit to be drunk when there is no connection with boiled rice (*odana*) and the like; that is to say, it is to be drunk on its own.
By the statement "they do not call that [state] investigation," he shows that this is a convention established by the tradition of physicians (*vaidyaparamparā*).
"Seen by physicians" means *bhiṣagdṛṣṭa*; "belonging to the first alternative" (*prāthamakalpika*) means belonging to the first or best option, which signifies "excellent."
He describes another way of classifying the variations [of *vicāraṇā*] with the words "by tastes," and so forth.

"Concise" (*samāsa*) refers to the mutual blending of tastes, while "detailed" (*vyāsa*) refers to their non-blending. When *sneha* (unctuous substance) is endowed with—that is, joined by—the six tastes, both concise and detailed, as present in boiled rice and other foods, it attains the number sixty-three.
And that which is single and pure—this being excluded from drinking—is to be used for purposes such as massage and the like.

The sixty-three varieties of taste-differences are to be understood from the statement to be spoken later in the *Ātreyabhadrakāpyīya* chapter (*Sūtra-sthāna*, Chapter 26): "The sweet [taste] undergoes combination with the sour and so forth.
Thus, there are sixty-four permutations of unctuous substances when combined with tastes.
The term "sixty-four" is connected with the word "oils"; by this, the singular number in "pravicāraṇā" (application) becomes justified.

It means that not every application of every oil should be performed everywhere; rather, having examined suitability (*sātmya*), season (*ṛtu*), disease (*vyādhi*), humor (*doṣa*), and the individual (*puruṣa*), whichever [oil] is appropriate for a particular case should be applied there. He says "okaḥ" and so forth;
"okaḥ" means habitual practice (*abhyāsa*).

By the mention of "the person" (puruṣa), it should be understood that the location is also restricted through an examination of where this person resides; furthermore, factors such as age, strength, and so forth must also be understood.
(Verses 27–28) He states the number and the measure of the *mātrā* as follows: "day and night," etc.

The term *ahorātra* (day and night) is an indication for eight *praharas*; likewise, the terms *ahaḥ* (day) and *ardhāha* (half-day) are indications for four *praharas* and two *praharas*, respectively. Therefore, even when a *mātrā* has been drunk on a day where the [specific] *prahara* has already passed, it should be understood as being digested on another day, either during the day or at night, through the attainment of the aforementioned *prahara*-time. Others, however, say that by the term *ahorātra*, a night joined with even a deficient day is expressed by the word *ahorātra*, while *kṛtsna-ahaḥ* (the whole day) and *ardhāhaḥ* (half-day) are indications for the *praharas*.

In this context, when the dosage is made to last for a full day and night, one must not consume food on that day; for this very reason, it is stated in the description of the specific types of persons [suitable] for this drink that they "are capable of enduring hunger and thirst," and by the statement that they are "constantly accustomed to abundant fats" and "properly disciplined," [the author] indicates the great risk of complications associated with this [therapy].
All the channels, joints, vital points (marmas), and branches are rejuvenated by its quality of removing all defects without exception;
"aruṣkā" and so forth refers to the qualities of the medium dose; "aruṣkā" means "arūṃṣikā" (scab).

"For the purpose of purification" means for the purpose of performing oleation as a branch of purification (*śodhanāṅga-sneha*). By this, he shows that the maximum dose is intended only for palliative treatment (*saṃśamana*), and not for oleation performed as a branch of purification.
As for the phrase beginning with "but those who," etc., the quality of the short dose is that it is "easy in terms of avoidance" (*parihāre sukha*), meaning it requires little avoidance.
He states for whom and where oleation (sneha) is to be employed: "In those with vāta-pitta disorders," and so forth.

Although those of vāta-pitta constitution are already included by the mention of vāta-pitta disorders, their specific mention again is for the purpose of prescribing the drinking of ghee even when there is only a slight kapha disorder in those of vāta-pitta constitution. In the same way, this should be explained in the passage: "those afflicted by vāta diseases and those of vāta constitution."
In the phrase "those seeking strength" (*balārthinaḥ*), the word *bala* is connected with the Smṛtis and so forth;
"afflicted" (*ārtāḥ*) means tormented, and the connection is with [suffering] such as burning and the like.
He states the scope regarding oil: "In the increased [doshas]," and so forth.

"In a cold season" means even in a cold season due to the heat of the oil itself; thus, this does not contradict the general prohibition: "A person should not drink unctuous substances when it is excessively hot or cold. Alternatively, "coldness" should be understood in relation to the time for drinking clarified butter (ghṛta).
He states the scope of the *vasā* (fat): "wind, sun," and so forth.
The words *saṃśuṣka* (completely dried) and *niṣpīta* (squeezed out) have the meaning of "wasted" (*kṣīṇa*) alone;
[the term] *mahārujaḥ* (greatly painful) is connected with "bones" (*asthi*) and the other [tissues].
The cavities and channels (47–49),
and the passage beginning with "those with a blazing digestive fire" (50) and so forth, concern the drinking of marrow.
The gluttons, those who eat much, would obtain [it] and consume it. 50

The two terms "excessive" (*prakarsa*) refer to a lesser excess and a greater excess. Thus, by virtue of being lesser, there is an excess lasting three nights, and by virtue of being greater, an excess lasting seven nights.

This should be understood as referring to applications other than the immediate application of unctuous substances (*sadyah-sneha-prayoga*) which will be described later. Alternatively, even the immediate applications of unctuous substances provide oleation within just three days; however, the term "immediate" (*sadyah*) was used in their case for the sake of praise.

As it has been said: "A person who has undergone oleation should be subjected to sudation for a minimum of three days and a maximum of seven days; beyond this, they do not prescribe further oleation, for after seven days, it becomes habitual. (Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 1, Verse 51)
He states those who should generally be oleated: "those to be sweated," and so forth.

"Those to be sweated" refers to those afflicted by Vata-pain and others who are curable by independent sudation; however, those who are to be cured by sudation as an ancillary to purification are already included by the term "those to be purified.
"Those who are anxious" means those who are full of worry.
Regarding those who should not be oleated, he says: "Except for those requiring purification," and so forth.

For those for whom drying therapy (*rūkṣaṇa*) will be described in the chapter on lightening and nourishing therapies (*laṅghanabṛṃhaṇīya*): "Those with excessive secretions (*abhiṣyanda*), those with great *doṣas*, and those diseases located in the vital points (*marman*)."

By the statement, "Those suffering from ūrustambha and similar conditions are indicated as requiring drying therapy" (Sūtra-sthāna 22), it is meant that for them, oleation is not recommended except after purification; however, when they are dried by means of purification, then oleation should be administered specifically as an adjunct to that purification—this is the intended meaning.
Those in whom phlegm and fat are *utsanna* (elevated) or increased are described thus; this qualification shows that those who require drying therapy are indeed of such a nature.
One who is excessively moistened, one suffering from a disorder of phlegm characterized by fluidity, one afflicted by artificial poison (gara),
and one whose liquid tissues are extremely depleted.
"In the present" means while they are being performed (verses 53–56).
He states the characteristics of one who is not affectionate: "feces," and so forth.
"Soft" is an adjective qualifying the cook;
"favorability to the movement of wind" and so forth are the characteristics of proper oleation (snigdha);
"pallor" and so forth are the characteristics of excessive oleation (atisnigdha).
Dullness (*jāḍyam*) refers to the sluggishness of the sense organs (57–59). Regarding what is wholesome prior to [the application of] oleation (*sneha*), he says: "liquid and hot," and so forth.
"Unmixed" means not having its potency counteracted;
"on the morrow," meaning at the time for food on the coming day,
characterized by the two watches (praharas) and so forth, hunger might perhaps not arise— therefore, for that purpose, the qualification "desired" is added.

The meaning is that for the purpose of purification (*śuddhi*), one should drink oil only in the morning, provided that the food consumed the previous day has been digested; this refers to oil intended for pacification (*saṃśamana*). If pacifying oil were administered in the morning immediately after digestion, then because the morbid humors (*doṣa*) coating the digestive tract would not have been eliminated, the provoked humor (*doṣotkleśa*)—being bound by that coating—would cause further provocation rather than pacification. However, in the case of oil intended for purification (*saṃśodhana*), the provocation of the humors is indeed required. This statement regarding the timing is a general rule (*utsarga*); therefore, it does not contradict the specific timing mentioned in the passage: "One with a predominance of *vāta* and *pitta* [should take it] at night."
"One who sleeps only at night" is *kṣapāśayaḥ*;
"and where there is no draft" is an adjective qualifying the bed and seat.

"Consuming another unctuous substance while the previous one is being digested" means that even when the first unctuous substance has been digested, one consumes another unctuous substance that is compatible with the administration of unctuous therapy and endowed with qualities such as non-contradictory potency (*vīrya*).

By this, the answer to the two questions—"What should be eaten after the unctuous substance has been drunk? and "What is beneficial or harmful [at that time]?"—is provided: "One should resort to warm water," and so forth.
He states the characteristics of a soft bowel (*mṛdukoṣṭha*) and so forth—beginning with "soft" (*mṛdu*) and so on.
Because knowledge of the bowel is highly esteemed, he states its characteristics in another way as well, beginning with "molasses" (*guḍa*) and so on;
*ulloḍita* refers to the whey (*dadhisara*) of curdled milk.
*Kṛśarā* is a gruel (*yavāgū*) prepared with sesame, rice, and black gram (*māṣa*). For it is stated: "Kṛśarā and *trisara* are made with sesame, rice, and black gram.
[The author] states the reason for purging those with hard bowels: "It becomes," and so forth.

The *grahaṇī* is the channel located in the abdomen that serves as the seat of the digestive fire (*agni*). As it has been said: "Because it seizes (*grahaṇa*) food, the seat of the fire is considered the *grahaṇī*" (Ci. A. 15).
The passage beginning with "udīrṇapitta" (with aggravated *pitta*) describes the nature of one with a soft bowel (*mṛdukoṣṭha*).

In one with a hard bowel (*krūrakoṣṭha*), the wind (*vāyu*) located in the *grahaṇī* obstructs the laxity of substances such as jaggery (*guḍa*). For in one with a soft bowel, there is no obstructing wind in the *grahaṇī*, the binding *kapha* is minimal, and the *pitta*—which possesses the quality of laxity—is predominant. Therefore, the meaning is that by means of jaggery and similar substances, purgation occurs easily.
Now he demonstrates the complications arising from oleation (snehavyāpada), beginning with the verse starting "udīrṇa":

*ojas* is the essence of all the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), residing in the heart; by the term "powerful" (*balī*), he shows that the fire, having oil as its fuel, becomes exceedingly strong as it washes away, displaces [the *ojas*] from its site, and depletes it.

For there is this saying: "Even very heavy food is not sufficient to bring peace to one whose body is replete with fat," referring to an excessive dose that is fraught with complications and calamities.
*Kakṣa* means a heap of wood.

Regarding the instruction "one should cause vomiting": first, one should induce vomiting of the unctuous substance (*sneha*) itself which caused the thirst; then, having drunk cold water and eaten dry food, one should "scrape" (*ullikhet*). This is how it should be construed; it does not refer to clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*), etc.

Clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) should not be drunk when *pitta* is associated with *āma*; however, it should especially not be drunk unrefined (*asaṃskṛta*) when *pitta* is associated with *āma*. This is the construction [of the sentence]. He thinks as follows: clarified butter that has been refined by being combined with bitter substances (*tikta*) and the like may, on occasion, be suitable for *pitta* associated with *āma* because it possesses the digestive (*pācana*) qualities of those bitter substances and so forth; but unrefined butter is entirely contradictory [to such a condition]. Alternatively, unrefined clarified butter alone should not be drunk in *pitta* generally—whether associated with *āma* or free from *āma* (*nirāma*)—but especially not when *pitta* is associated with *āma*. This is the construction.

By this [principle], even where ghee is prescribed in a general sense—as in passages such as, "Henceforth, when kapha is diminished, when vāta and pitta predominate, and when the fever has become chronic and the doṣas are fully ripened, the drinking of ghee is like nectar" (Ci. A. 3)—there too, it should be understood that it must be processed with appropriate medicinal substances.

Alternatively, the meaning is that not only should ghee specifically not be drunk during the *sāma* stage of pitta, but even oils and other substances prescribed for vāta and kapha should not be drunk during the *sāma* stages of those two.
In this commentary, the elision of the vowel *a* in the word *apeya* (undrinkable) should be understood; "it would color" means it would produce a bilious (pitta) hue,
and "consciousness" here refers to memory, the destruction of which occurs due to the influence of the disease.
Stagnation is like being enveloped in a moist cloth;
it includes disorders such as *āmapradoṣa*, *alasaka*, and *visūcikā*,
characterized by waiting for the time [of digestion] and abstaining from food until the elimination of the morbid humors produced by unctuous substances.

The connection is that there is the administration of buttermilk (*takra*) and the fermented liquors (*ariṣṭa*) to be described in the medical treatment, as well as the consumption of the urines and *triphalā*. (70–78)
Due to improper application— that is, failing to carry out the prescribed method— and because it has been practiced excessively over a long period of time. (79)
Regarding the conduct during the administration of purification and oleation, he says "from oleation," etc.;
"from oleation" means from the application of oleation;
"having abstained for three nights" means having ceased the drinking of oleation for three nights.
Regarding the emetic and purgative procedures, it indicates that food should be taken only after three nights have passed since the cessation of oleation— starting with "snehavat," etc.—
where *rasaudana* refers to rice cooked primarily with meat broth.
Regarding the regimen following oleation for emesis, he says "eka" and so forth;
the construction is "having abstained from oleation for one day."
In the same way, on the very day that the oil has been digested, one should consume rice with broth that is oily, liquid, and warm. 81.
He states the procedure for pacification: "It may be," and so forth; in this context, "treatment" (vṛtti) refers to the therapeutic application intended for pacification rather than purification.

By the phrase "like one who has undergone purgation" (*viriktavat*), he refers to the regimen to be prepared and described later in the passage beginning with "And when he has been properly purged" (*samyagviriktaṃ cainaṃ*, Sūtra-sthāna 15), and not merely the sequence of gruels (*peyā*) and so forth.

Although the high-pitched speech and other factors mentioned in the context of emesis are extended (*atidiṣṭa*) to the procedure for purgation as well, nevertheless, here the extension of the purgation procedure—setting aside the specific rules for emesis—is intended to prohibit the inhalation of medicated smoke (*dhūmapāna*). For in that [context of purgation], it says: "excluding the inhalation of smoke" (*dhūmapānavarjam*, Sūtra-sthāna).

Thus it is established; furthermore, the inhalation of medicated smoke is prohibited after drinking unctuous substances in the *Mātrāśitīya* chapter, by the passage beginning: "Nor after drinking wine or milk, nor after [drinking] unctuous substances" (*Sūtra-sthāna*, chapter 5).
He states the subject of deliberation with the words beginning "snehadviṣaḥ" (those who dislike fats).
He describes the processing of the aforementioned liquids such as meat-broth and so forth with the words beginning "yava" (barley).
Regarding the phrase "rasasaṃyogāḥ": those whose appropriate combination is for the purpose of providing fat in a liquid are called "rasasaṃyogāḥ"; the collection of these is "saṅgrahaḥ".
"Before" means prior to eating; "tilakāmbalika" refers to a *kāmbalika* (a type of sweet dish) in which sesame seeds are the primary ingredient;
and in the phrase beginning with "phāṇita," "śṛṅgavera" refers to the juice of ginger (*śṛṅgavera*).
With the cooked [grains] made into balls,
the *pañcaprasṛtikī* (the five-prasṛta mixture) which will be described below,
and *māṣamiśraka* (food prepared from mung beans and rice).
The gruel should be drunk (82–90) as appropriate; that is, whichever unctuous substance, such as ghee and so forth, is suitable for a particular case.

The term "siddhaiḥ" (prepared with) should be applied separately to *pippalī*, *harītakī*, and *triphalā*. Some authorities maintain that the oil prepared with *pippalī* and the others is used for skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*) and so forth respectively.
The word *yūṣa* here signifies a decoction (*kvātha*), and "containing *vyoṣa*" means having a paste of *vyoṣa* as its internal ingredient.
In this case, the fourfold proportion (cāturguṇya) is formed by combining three substances;
in the formula beginning with *yavakola*, there are six substances equal in quantity to the oil,
and the alkaline powder (*kṣāra*) is that of barley-alkali (*yavakṣāra*), which serves as the paste (*kalka*).

Regarding "tailamajja" and so forth—this refers to the four unctuous substances (*catuḥsneha*) without any medicinal paste (*akalka*). Because "oil, marrow, muscle fat, and ghee" (*tailamajjavasāsarpiḥ*) is treated as a singular compound, it is used in the accusative case.
Now, just as the body is seen to become more supple when oil has been applied, he says "it grasps," and so forth;
and this is stated by the author for the benefit of the student, even though it was not asked at the beginning of the chapter.
The phrase *yathāgni* means "not exceeding the digestive fire.

Now, one might object: if [the oil] exceeds the digestive fire, it flows out; moreover, the definition of unctuousness (*sneha*) has been stated as "the observation of unctuousness below," which implies that the intake of excessive unctuousness should be done on a single day. To this, he says *yathā ca* and so forth:
*ākledya* means having moistened slightly.
The meaning is that oil consumed too hurriedly, without first lubricating the bodily tissues (dhātus), slips away and passes downward; merely by that much, true oleation does not occur.
(96–97) Regarding oleation, he states the application of salt for all types of unctuous substances: "Combined with salt," and so forth.
That, namely salt, is moistening, it breaks up the accumulation of the *doṣas*,
it is pervasive (*vyavāyi*), and it reaches digestion after first spreading throughout the entire body.

Therefore, he states the precedence of oleation (*sneha*) prior to sudation (*sveda*) and the other therapies—thereby indicating the connection between the present chapter and the subsequent chapters on the preparation of sudation—with the words beginning with "oleation" (*sneham*).
Cāndrabhāgī and Punarvasu [100].

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Oleation," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta, within the section on the four types of pharmaceutical preparations (*kalpanācatuṣka*) in the *Sūtrasthāna*.
[Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 14 (14 of 120)] Since sudation is preceded by oleation, the chapter on sudation is now described.
The chapter on sudation (Svedādhyāya), chapters 1–2:

[Diseases] consisting of vāta and kapha that arise from unmixed vāta and kapha, as well as abdominal enlargements (udara) and other conditions arising from vāta and kapha, are not pacified by sudation; therefore, it says "curable by sudation" (svedasādhya). By this, abdominal enlargements and similar conditions that are unsuitable for sudation are excluded.
"Preceded by oleation" (*sneha-pūrvam*) is an adverbial modifier.
"They do not adhere" means they do not become obstructed.

"According to the rule" (*yathā-nyāyam*) and "according to the tradition" (*yathā-āgamam*) connect with the phrase "by means of the application of oleation and sudation. Alternatively, the connection is: "they bend [the body] according to the rule and according to what is natural" (*yathā-sahajam*).
"Dependent on disease, season, and the afflicted person" (rogartuvyādhitāpekṣa) means that it depends on the disease, the season, and the patient by way of their strength and other factors;
[it is] neither too hot nor excessively scorching.

"One who possesses substances" (dravyavān) should be understood as one who possesses substances such as the unctuous (snigdha) and the dry (rūkṣa), prepared according to the requirements of the disease and other factors; that is, it should be considered as having been prepared with appropriate substances in a location such as the stomach (āmāśaya) according to what is suitable.
He demonstrates the aforementioned conceptualization in consideration of disease and other factors with the verse beginning "In disease," and so forth.
In the case of a very powerful disease, as well as in very powerful cold produced by time (*kāla*),

the term "great" (*mahān*) should be understood as referring to an intense heat (*caṇḍatāpa*) because it is applied repeatedly and possesses a higher degree of heat compared to mild sudation (*mṛdusveda*).

"Debilitated" and likewise "middling" should be applied as before to diseases and other conditions. That which is produced by unctuous (*snigdha*) and dry (*rūkṣa*) substances is "unctuous-dry"; unctuous and dry substances and so forth should be understood in their respective order with respect to *vāta*, *śleṣman*, and the others. This discussion of unctuousness, dryness, and so forth is an illustration of a formulation based on the consideration of substances: [the treatment] for *vāta* is unctuous, and for *kaphe* (phlegm) it is dry.

Demonstrating that [the treatment] may vary according to the specific location, he states the conceptualization based on the site: "In the case of wind located in the stomach (āmāśaya)," and so forth.

When wind is situated in the stomach, one should first apply dryness with respect to the site, and subsequently apply oiliness with respect to the wind. In the same way, when kapha is situated in the colon (pakvāśaya), it should be explained as beginning with oiliness. By the term "stomach" (āmāśaya), the seat of kapha is to be understood; for, with respect to the seat of kapha, dryness is applied first, as it has been said: "One should first conquer the site, because that which resides in its own site is not contradictory [to the site]. (9)

In a disease located in the scrotum or similar areas that is curable by sweating alone, one should apply mild sweating; however, it should be understood that if other therapeutic means besides sweating are available, one may not do so.
The term "iṣṭataḥ" (according to what is desired) refers to desire, meaning according to the patient's wish and the physician's wish.
The word "icchā" (desire) here denotes the state of wishing.
Regarding the method for avoiding sweating of the eyes while sudation is being performed, he says "suśuddhaiḥ" and so forth;
*naktaka* refers to a piece of ragged cloth.
While the sudation is being performed, he speaks for the purpose of protecting the heart: "With strings of pearls," and so forth;
*jalajāni* refers to lotuses and the like.

In this way, the protection of the testicles should also be inferred because they share the common quality of being unperceivable by touch; however, the protection of the heart and the eyes is mentioned specifically due to their preeminence.
[Regarding the verse beginning with] "cold pain," etc. (12).

Regarding the statement "sweat," by teaching that "cessation from sweating is intended when there is heat in the absence of sweat," he instructs on two points: that sweat should be discontinued once the cold and other factors have ceased, and that sweat should be applied when the cold and other factors have not ceased. Consequently, it follows that the production of the cessation of cold and other factors—which is the object of the cessation of sweating—is the characteristic of proper application (*samyagyoga*) of sweat; likewise, the non-production of the cessation of cold and other factors—which is the object of the non-cessation of sweating—is stated to be the characteristic of improper application (*ayoga*). Thus, one should not raise the objection that the characteristic of improper application has not been described.

He states the treatment for excessive sudation: the phrase "it has been said," etc., up to "the regimen for the summer season," is stated again—despite being already established—to prohibit the drinking of liquor that was taught in the passage "wine should be drunk in small quantities or not at all" (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 6), and to prescribe specific formulations characterized by sweetness, unctuousness, and coldness.
Regarding those for whom sudation is prohibited, he says "kaṣāya" and so forth.

Wine made from astringent substances is "kaṣāyamadya. Alternatively, the word *kaṣāya* signifies that which is not sweet (*amadhura*). If it were otherwise, it would follow that one who habitually consumes astringent substances (*kaṣāyanitya*) would have a predominance of *vāta*, because astringents cause *vāta*, and sudation is prescribed for *vāta*; how then could there be a prohibition of sudation for one who habitually consumes astringents? Thus, that objection is refuted.

Alternatively, those who habitually consume astringents (kaṣāya) have limbs that become dry and excessively rigid due to the drying and stiffening properties of astringents; consequently, for them, sudation brings about a splitting pain in the joints. Therefore, there is a prohibition against the habitual use of astringents.

Since fomentation (sveda) is already prohibited for those suffering from *raktapitta* by the very fact that it is not prescribed for them, the repeated prohibition of fomentation for *raktapitta* patients is intended to forbid it even when another disorder arising from *vāta* and *kapha* might be treatable by fomentation; furthermore, it is intended to prohibit the application of fomentation that might otherwise be obtained as an ancillary part of emesis (*vamana*) or purgation (*virecana*) for *raktapitta* patients. This same principle should be explained for cases such as *pittameha* and *āmaya*.
The term "for those with *pitta*" (*pittinām*) refers to those of *pitta* constitution (*pittaprakṛti*).

By the term *madhumeha*, all types of *meha* (urinary disorders) are included, for the word *madhumeha* applies to all *mehas*; this is to be seen in the chapter on "How Many [Diseases] Are in the Head" (*Kiyantaḥśirasīya*). Furthermore, since all *mehas* involve a loosening of the body, sweating is specifically inappropriate as a cause for such bodily laxity. The specific mention of "those with *pittamēha*" is intended to demonstrate the particular prohibition based on the connection with *pitta*. Regarding "the scrotum and anus of those with alcohol-related disorders," this is for the purpose of prohibiting sweating in cases of *vāta-kaphaja* intoxication caused by habitual drinking (*madātyaya*).

In this context, for one who is wealthy yet afflicted by gout (vātarakta) and other such conditions where sweating is otherwise contraindicated, if the condition is curable by sweating alone—such as in cases of paralysis (sannyāsa) and the like—then sweating must be prescribed even while disregarding the minor transgression, out of fear of a greater transgression. This is established by logic; as those learned in logic say: "When there is a conflict between many factors, a minor [transgression] is not unjust.
By the words "in cases of catarrh" and so forth, [the author] indicates those who are fit for sudation:
*vināmaka* is wind that causes the body to bend;
*vijṛmbhaka* is external extension, or an excessive frequency of yawning.
Pain in the feet, knees, thighs, and shanks, as well as their individual stiffness, are described;
*khallī* is the contraction of the hands and feet,
while *vātakaṇṭaka* is the wind located in the ankles.

Although "absence of lightness" (*alāghava*) was mentioned previously, the repetition of the term "heaviness" (*gaurava*) is for the purpose of establishing that the limbs are exceedingly heavy. On the other hand, the statement regarding "absence of lightness" has the sole purpose of negating lightness and does not express extreme heaviness; for in all cases, the negative particle (*nañ*) does not denote the opposite quality. For example, in the passage: "It is neither dry (*arūkṣa*), nor causes secretions (*anabhiṣyandi*), and is characterized by sitting and nodding off" (Sūtra-sthāna, chapter 21), the word "not dry" (*arūkṣa*) does not intend to mean "moist" (*snigdha*); rather, it signifies merely the negation of dryness. (20–24)
He states the substances for the types of sudation such as *piṇḍasveda* (bolus-sudation) and others that will be described: "sesame, black gram," and so forth.
*Piṇḍasveda* is sudation in the form of a bolus.
*Karīṣa* is dried cow dung. *Āyasa* is an iron product; in this context, it should be understood as something suitable for making a cup (*puṭa*).
By the phrase "by the former ones," [the author] indicates that sesame, black gram, and so forth—

specifically those mentioned for vāta by the words "according to their respective [nature]," and those mentioned in the text regarding cattle, donkeys, and so forth for kapha— are to be employed in prastara-sveda (bed-poultice fomentation).
"In underground chambers" (*bhūgṛheṣu*) refers to houses intended for sweating on the ground;
"in warm inner rooms" (*uṣṇagarbhagṛheṣu*) indicates *kuṭī-sveda* (enclosure fomentation).
"Well-anointed" (*svabhyakta*) means properly anointed.
*Bastaśiras* means the head of a goat;
*snehavantaḥ* refers to castor seeds and the like; *tilāśca taṇḍulāśca* means sesame seeds and rice grains; *snehavattilataṇḍulāḥ* [refers to] oily sesame seeds and rice.

By the verse beginning with "grāmya," tube-sudation (nāḍīsveda) that removes vāta is described; by the verse beginning with "vāruṇa," that which removes kapha; and by the verse beginning with "bhūtīka," that which removes vāta and śleṣman.
"Vāruṇa" refers to Varuṇa; "amṛtakā" refers to guḍūcī. In the phrase "with mustard seeds" (sarṣapaiḥ), it is connected with "leaves" (patraiḥ); "vaṃśa" refers to bamboo (veṇu).
Furthermore, by the mention of *śobhāñjana*, the second type, *viṭapa-śobhāñjana*, is included; *saitreya* is *jhiṇṭī*.
These three alone are those mentioned in the section on tubular fomentation (*nāḍīsveda*).

A water-vat (*jalakoṣṭha*) is a large water vessel made for the purpose of immersion; in the same way, vats for ghee, milk, and oil are explained. (34) [One may also use] wheat fragments or wheat flour.
*Kiṇva* is the fermenting agent for *surā*.

*Upanāha* refers to wrapping a diseased limb with leather or similar materials after applying a thick medicinal paste; in the phrase "it should be bound with hides," *upanāha* here should be understood as a non-thermal fomentation (*anagni-sveda*), where the binding is performed using fragrant substances (*gandha*).
"By those of hot potency" means by those originating from animals such as deer that possess hot potency;
"āvikaśāṭaka" refers to a woolen blanket (*kambala*).
He shows the limit for binding and releasing in the case of poultice fomentation (upanāha-sveda) with the words "bound at night," etc.;
in the phrase "done by day," the word "binding" is to be understood as the ellipsis;
"vidāha" refers to the burning sensation caused by blood and other humors.
In the phrase "when it is cool," the word "time" is to be supplied as an ellipsis;
"excess" refers to the duration of the imprisonment being longer than the previously mentioned time of imprisonment.
Now, in order to state the definitions of *saṅkara* and other types of sudation involving fire and steam, he first enumerates these sudations by name, beginning with "saṅkara" and so forth.

The terms *saṅkara* and the rest are established through the tradition of Āyurveda. In this context, in certain cases such as *nāḍīsveda*, the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) should also be followed as "it is administered by means of a tube" (*nāḍyā praṇīyate*); however, *jentāka* and others are independent of such a connection.

"With the aforementioned boluses" means with boluses made of sesame, mung beans, and so forth, as well as with boluses in the form of *puṭakas* mentioned in the texts concerning cows, donkeys, and other animals; "gentle fomentation" (*upasvedana*) is simply fomentation (*svedana*).
(41) *Pulāka* is worthless grain.
*Utkārikā* is a specific kind of side-dish made from black gram (*māṣa*) and other ingredients, shaped like a puff of steam;
*prastara* is the spreading out of the materials for fomentation over a surface equal in size to a bed.
Upon that *prastara*, which is covered with silk and woolen cloths—meaning it is spread over with silk and woolen fabrics.
*Pañcāṅgula* is a variety of *eraṇḍa*.
With the words "by means of fomentation" (*svedana*) and so forth, he describes tubular fomentation (*nāḍīsveda*).

The sudorific substances mentioned in the group of *svedopaga* (accessories for sudation) are also stated here for the purpose of preparing the decoction for tube-sudation (*nāḍīsveda*). The term "head" (*śiraḥ*) refers to the skull.
By the phrase "without emitting steam," it is shown that during the time of boiling, one must act in such a way that the steam does not escape.
The connection is that one whose body is smeared with oil should apply the steam of the boiling substances by means of a tube (*nāḍī*).
He states the procedure for making the tube: "with reed, *iṣīkā*, etc.";
"bamboo-slice" (*vaṃśadala*) means a split bamboo.
The shape of the tip of the tube should be understood as being like the trunk of a lordly elephant.
A *vyāma* is the measurement of the span of two arms extended horizontally; the length of the tube should be made one *vyāma* when there is profuse perspiration.

The measurement of the tube should be known as one-fourth of a *vyāma* at the base and one-eighth of a *vyāma* at the tip, respectively. It is so called because its channel or aperture has a circumference—that is, it is encircled by that [measurement].
He states the benefit of performing the channel-construction (*nāḍīkaraṇa*) as previously described: "For steam... and so forth.
That the violent force has been destroyed should be understood through the length and curvature of the channel-body.

He states the procedure for sprinkling (pariṣeka): "Vātikāni" and so forth. "Vātikāni" means those that alleviate wind (vāta). "Uttaravātikāni" refers to those beneficial here in cases of "uttaravāta"—meaning predominant wind—or in the combination of wind and phlegm (vāta-śleṣman); these should be understood as such. "Varṣaṇikā" is a small jar; others say it is a "sahasradhārā" (a vessel with a thousand streams). "Praṇāḍī" refers to bamboo, reed, tubes, and the like.
"Exactly as described" means that the immersion-sudation (avagāhasveda) is precisely that which is well-known in the world.
He states the procedure for the *jentāka* (steam bath): "Now," and so forth.
The word "now" (*atha*) indicates either auspiciousness or immediate succession.
"Either to the east or to the north" means it should be situated outside the village.
"Possessing qualities" (*guṇavatī*) refers to being endowed with the growth of crops and so forth; its state as an excellent portion of land refers to being free from husks, charcoal, and the like.
*Parīvāpa* is a long pond.
In that which has a "good bathing place" (*sūpatīrtha*)— meaning a bathing place (*tīrtha*) very close at hand—
the cubit (*aratni*) or hand is directed eastward when [standing] facing west, and northward when facing south; for in this way, the bathing place becomes directly in front of one.
"Kūṭāgāra" refers to a circular building; by the phrase "up to the door," he indicates the area including the doorway;
"kiṣku" means a cubit (hasta).
"Puruṣapramāṇam" means [measuring] a man's height.

"Kandu" refers to a place for fire in the shape of a pit; that which has a chamber or space for the purpose of charcoal is an "aṅgārakoṣṭhaka. That very thing is a pillar, thus it is an "aṅgārakoṣṭhakastambha" (a pillar consisting of a charcoal-pit chamber).
The genitive case in *khādirāṇām* is used in the sense of completion (*pūraṇe*).

Regarding the word *saḥ*, one should supply the word *tvam* (you); the meaning is "you should know. Alternatively, the reading is *jānīyāt* (he should know), and in the subsequent passage as well, the reading is *praveśayet* (he should cause to enter). In this way, it becomes easy to understand;
*picchā* is simply the slimy portion of the sweat.

"Released from all streams" means released from all currents; "one who has removed obstructions" should be understood as one who has removed the obstructions of impurity. This is for the sake of protecting the eyes; the intention here is that if one who is heated suddenly enters cold water, the heat struck by the cold water will cause injury to the eyes.

In this *jentāka* (sauna), the selection of a specific ground, the proximity of water, and so forth, serve for the sake of auspiciousness; furthermore, the proximity of water is for the purpose of protecting the vision by observing the person undergoing sudation, as well as for the purpose of counteracting excessive sweating and for the comfortable operation of the chamber when water is nearby.
*Kaurava* [cotton] is made from *kārpāsa* (cotton).
A *karṣū* is a pit that is wide at the bottom and has a narrow opening.
'Not excessively high or wide' means having a very small measure of height and width;
'a window' means one without a lattice."
Regarding the phrase "with kuṣṭha and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) denotes a class; by this, it means "with warm and fragrant substances.
*Hasantikā* refers to a charcoal-heater. The word "surrounding" (*parivārya*) is connected with the word "by means of *hasantikās*.
"That" (*tām*) refers to the hut (*kuṭī*) which is the prepared bed; the connection is that one should "ascend" (*ārohet*) it.
Regarding the phrase "and there, the bed above": here, the bed, such as a couch (*khaṭṭā*) and so forth, should be placed upon the *kumbhīka* in such a way that the *kumbhīka* is not broken.
"Situated therein" means situated on the aforementioned bed and seat.
"Like a well" means it is like a well; because of its depth, it should be understood as being double [the size] in terms of its width.
"By the measure of digging downwards" refers to the depth of excavation;
"well-spread" means well-covered or lined; it should be understood that the well is covered by a bedstead placed upon it. 59–60.
By the passage beginning with "dhītīkā," *holāka-sveda* is described;
*dhītīkā* is a specific type of fire-receptacle made from dried cow dung and similar materials.
"Of those previously mentioned" refers to those originating from elephants, horses, and so forth, as stated before.
One should supply the word "having made" (*kṛtvā*) and connect it with the phrase "of the measure of the interior of the bed";
"as described" means not too thickly furnished.
He concludes with the words "thus," and so forth.
Relying directly on the quality of heat belonging to fire, [the agent] causes perspiration; thus, it is "dependent on the qualities of fire" (agniguṇasaṃśraya).
Now, he describes non-fire-based sudation (anagnisveda), beginning with the words "physical exercise" (vyāyāma) and so forth.
"Hot chamber" (*uṣṇasadanam*) should be understood as a house that induces perspiration through its lack of lattices and thick walls, even in the absence of direct heating by fire.
"Excessive drinking" (*bahupānam*) refers to the consumption of large quantities of wine.

There are two types of poultices (*upanāha*): those with fire and those without fire. Among these, the poultice with fire should be understood as being included within the category of "mixed" (*saṅkara*), as stated in the *Āragvadhīya* chapter (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 3) beginning with: "Jujube, horse gram, deodar, and *rāsnā*... On the other hand, the poultice without fire is that which induces perspiration here by creating a blockage of the body's heat through its thickness.
And although sunlight is indeed hot, its heat is not produced by fire; therefore, it is called "non-fire-induced perspiration" (*anagnisveda*),
meaning "without the quality of fire" (verse 64), that is, apart from the heat produced through direct contact with fire.
He summarizes all this sweat with the words "Thus it was said," and so forth;
[this refers to] the *saṅkara-nāḍī*s and others located in a single limb, as well as the *prastara-jentāka*s and others located in all limbs.
Sudation prescribed for vāta is unctuous (snigdha), that prescribed for kapha is dry (rūkṣa),
while that prescribed for both vāta and śleṣman is both unctuous and dry; since it does not differ from these two, it has not been mentioned separately.
A *dvandva* is a pair of mutually opposed things.
(65–66) He now states what should be done with one who has undergone sudation (*svinna*), beginning with the words "one who is unctuous" (*snigdha*).

Regarding the statement "one should eat wholesome food" (*pathyāśano bhavet*), although wholesome food has not been specified here by way of individual enumeration (*śṛṅgagrāhikā*), nevertheless, one should understand that it is precisely that which is wholesome for the specific *doṣa* involved in the process of inducing sudation (*sveda*).
As stated in the *Saṅgraha*: "Sudation is effective when administered preceded by oleation," and so forth.
The phrase "from whom and of what kind" summarizes [the treatment] such as "unctuous for vāta," and so forth;
"in which place and in what manner appropriate" refers to [treatment] such as "preceded by dryness when vāta is located in the āmāśaya";
the remainder is easy to understand.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, on sudation (sveda), in the Nirdeśacatuṣka section of the Sūtrasthāna, within the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka-saṃhitā composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.

[Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 15 (15 of 120)] Because of the connection already stated in the phrase "purification follows for one who has undergone oleation and sudation," the chapter that sets forth the procedure for purification must be presented immediately after the chapter on sudation. Thus, he says "Upakalpanīya" (The Preparatory Chapter), meaning the chapter composed concerning the preparation for purification.
One whose retinue and equipment are like those of a king is a "king-like person" (*rājamātra*);
however, a merchant or similar person who possesses abundant wealth is not so.
Having calculated this— that is, having understood that the purchase is the commodity and the non-fixed price is the cost—
the undertaking, when properly begun, either succeeds or fails.

*Prayogasauṣṭhavam* (the excellence of application) means the proficiency of application; the construction is: "it can be taught correctly by us or by those like us"—this refers to the excellence of application.

"Thus" (*evam*) means "in accordance with reality" (*yathāvat*); "to comprehend" (*upadhārayitum*) means, according to the text, "to maintain" (*dhārayitum*) and "to practice" (*pratipattum*), which in terms of meaning is "to grasp."

"Subtle," and so forth: they are "subtle" because they are difficult to comprehend. Among these, the various states of the *doṣa* (humor) include: decrease (*kṣaya*), increase (*vṛddhi*), and equilibrium (*samatva*); likewise, movement upward in the body, downward in the body, or horizontally; likewise, localization in the peripheral branches (*śākhā*), the visceral trunk (*koṣṭha*), or the middle path (*madhyamārga*); likewise, movement to one's own site (*svadeśa*) or to another's site (*paradeśa*); likewise, independence (*svatantratva*) or dependence (*paratantratva*); likewise, the distinction between parts and sub-parts (*aṃśāṃśavikalpa*); likewise, localization in specific tissues (*dhātu*); and likewise, conformity with time (*kāla*), constitution (*prakṛti*), and the affected element (*dūṣya*), as well as all other factors expounded in the entire treatise—these are to be known. Similarly, the various states of the medicine (*bheṣaja*) include: youthfulness, old age, moistness, dryness, being combined with other substances, suitability for preparation as a fresh juice (*svarasa*) and so forth, and its capacity to perform specific actions upon the *doṣa* and other factors in that particular body through its taste (*rasa*), potency (*vīrya*), post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), and specific action (*prabhāva*). As for place (*deśa*), it is divided into categories such as marshy (*ānūpa*), arid (*jāṅgala*), intermediate (*sādhāraṇa*), and commendable (*praśasta*). The various states of time (*kāla*) consist of the divisions of seasons, the forenoon and so forth, as well as the stages of disease (*vyādhyavasthā*), such as the eight-day period of fever (*jvarāṣṭāha*) and others. Strength (*bala*) is divided into innate (*sahaja*), acquired through practice (*yuktikṛta*), and produced by time (*kālakṛta*), further distinguished as superior, inferior, moderate, and so on. The body (*śarīra*) is distinguished by stoutness, leanness, substantiality (*sāravattva*), and lack of substance (*niḥsāravattva*), as well as by specific parts requiring protection, such as the vital spots (*dṛṣṭimarma*) and others. Diet (*āhāra*) is distinguished by its nature (*prakṛti*), processing (*karaṇa*), combination (*saṃyoga*), and quantity (*rāśi*). Habituation (*sātmya*) is distinguished according to place, time, disease, constitution (*prakṛti*), natural disposition (*svabhāva*), and repeated practice (*abhyāsa*). The mind (*sattva*) is distinguished by its association with fear, courage, despondency, joy, and so forth. The variations in constitution (*prakṛtibheda*) are to be understood as being composed of wind (*vāta*) and the other humors in many different combinations. The variations in age (*vayobheda*) include childhood, youth, old age, and their internal subdivisions. These various states of the *doṣa* and other factors are required in the application of treatment according to their respective needs. Examples of this should be followed in the authoritative scriptures (*śāstra*); however, they are not stated here as they would result in excessive length for this work.
The construction is as follows: "We shall explain both of these later in the section on the accomplishments (siddhis).

Regarding the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even various kinds" (*vividhān api*), it should be understood as implying "even in summary. By this, both aspects are well-established: that houses and so forth are described in detail, while the *saṅgrahaṇī* and so forth are described in summary. Alternatively, if the reading is "both two-fold" (*dvividhān api*), by that, those things intended for enjoyment as well as the means for overcoming calamities are included.
An *anupatyaka* is that which is distant from any other large house;
that by which water is drunk is a well (*udapāna*).
Pradakṣiṇya is circumambulation; ānukūlya is compliance; ullāpaka is praise (stotra); itihāsa is the instruction of a trustworthy person whose author is unknown;
mṛgamātṛkā refers to a doe; pṛthūdara means a deer.

*Śaraṇa* is a house; *ācamanīyodakoṣṭha* is a water-room for the purpose of sipping water; alternatively, *ācamana* refers to the vessel by which one sips. A *maṇika* is a large water-jar; a *golaka* is a small jar; a *piṭhara* is a cooking pot; a *paryoga* is a cauldron; a *kumbha* is a sturdy, narrow-mouthed jar; a *kaṭa* is a seat made of grass and similar materials; an *udañcana* is a shallow bowl used as a lid; a *paripacana* is a vessel for boiling oil;
and *ūrṇā* refers to the woolly hair of a goat.
In the passage beginning with "suprakṣālita," the *upadhāna* is commonly known as a *śilāputra* (a stone grinder); *dṛṣadaḥ* are stone slabs;
and the tools for the purpose of preparation include implements such as spades and scissors.
A *kuśahastaka* is a broom; others, however, explain it as the cooking of moist substances.
The vessel for measuring is the standard [of weight];
and in the phrase "in this interval," it refers to the time of applying oil and fomentation.

"For that same duration of time" means for as long as it takes to effect the pacification of the disease that has arrived; "desired" means it is prescribed for the administration of medicine in accordance with the asterism (*nakṣatra*) and other factors of the person administering the purification therapy. As it is said in *Jyotiṣa*: "One should employ Puṣya, Hasta, Jyeṣṭhā, Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Aśvinī, Svātī, and Saumya (Mṛgaśiras) for medicinal treatment, and avoid others," and so forth.
"Having caused [the rite] to be performed" means having caused the recitation of the *svastivācana* (benediction) to be performed.
By the phrase "they are to be considered for each individual," he demonstrates that there is a difference in the dosage of purification for each person.

The passage beginning with "as much as" (*yāvad-dhi*) and so forth should be explained according to the commentary on the text starting with "for as much as his food" (*yāvad-dhy-asyāśanam*), as stated in the *Mātrāśitīya* chapter (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 5).
The term "he should desire" (*anukāṅkṣet*) means he should maintain [the body] by examining [its needs];
"unconfined" (*asaṃbādham*) means not crowded or obstructed.

"Receiving" (*pratigraha*) means those things that are received, such as alms-bowls (*patadgraha*), forehead-receivers (*lalāṭapratigraha*), and so forth; they are not objects of shame, being matters that do not provoke modesty.

"Upavegam" means near the onset of the force (*vega*). By this, he prohibits the initiation of a force that has not yet manifested in any way. The meaning is that one reflects upon the future occurrences of yoga, ayoga, and so forth regarding the force, having perceived them through the passage beginning with "because of observing the specific characteristics of the force" (*vegaviśeṣadarśanāt*). Alternatively, the purification resulting from the force (*vaigikī śuddhi*) must be explained in the section on success (*siddhi*), as in: "In inferior, moderate, and superior [cases], four, six, and eight forces are desired for emesis" (*Si. A. 1*); he demonstrates that by means of this [verse]. 12.

"Non-functioning from some cause" means the non-functioning of the entire [medicine]; likewise, it refers to the non-functioning of the whole of the impurity to be purified; and likewise, the "displacement" of the medicine, which is its movement in the opposite direction—for example, downward in the case of emesis and upward in the case of purgation. This very point is stated in the *Siddhisthāna* (Chapter 6): "Inadequate administration is movement in the opposite direction, or movement that is insufficient. Alternatively, "non-functioning from some cause" means the movement of only a small portion of the impurity; the construction is thus: "and likewise, the functioning of the medicine alone [without having expelled the impurity]."

"In due order" means that in emesis, phlegm (*śleṣman*) comes first, followed by bile (*pitta*), and then wind (*vāyu*). As it is said: "He from whom phlegm, then bile, and then wind emerge in succession is considered one who has vomited properly" (Sūtrasthāna 1).

Furthermore, showing that even a proper administration (*samyagyoga*) is of three types—mild, moderate, and intense—depending on whether the morbid humor (*doṣa*) to be expelled is small, medium, or excessive, he says: "By [proper] administration," and so forth.

The word *tu* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). Therefore, the meaning is: by that specific dosage of yoga—such as a small dose and so forth—and not by under-dosage (*ayoga*) or over-dosage (*atiyoga*). Furthermore, this classification of sharp (*tīkṣṇa*) and other dosages is for the purpose of advancing through the stages of liquids (*peyā-krama*); for he will state in the *Siddhisthāna*: “Pejā, vilepī,” etc. (Siddhi-sthāna, Chapter 1).

In that context, regarding over-dosage and so forth, distension (*ādhmāna*) and other symptoms occur in the *Śodhana-siddhi* [chapter] concerning one with "excessive morbid humors (*bahudoṣa*) and who is dry (*rūkṣa*)" (Siddhi-sthāna...).

These [topics] are to be explained extensively by means of the textual passage beginning with "a.6)" and so forth; therefore, in that context, the specific varieties of smoking—such as the oily (*snaihika*) and others—which arise from proper application (*yoga*), excessive application (*atiyoga*), or lack of application (*ayoga*), should be clearly understood.

This conceptualization of smoking depends upon the individual nature (*prakṛti*) of the person. For this very reason, it is said "by virtue of capacity" (*sāmarthyataḥ*), which means whatever is appropriate for a particular individual.
"Excessive standing" means remaining in a prostrate position for too long;
"measured eating" is the practice of consuming only a single flavor;
"excessively inferior" refers to grain and other foodstuffs that have lost their potency.
By the word *guru* (heavy), there is a prohibition against eating even the prescribed quantity of naturally heavy foods such as *laṭṭuka* and *cipiṭaka*.

(14–15) Regarding the phrase "in the evening" (*sāyāhne*) and so forth: it refers to the evening characterized by the complete purification of the digestive fire (*agni*); however, if there is some slight lack of purity, it may be on another day.

As it is stated in the Siddhisthāna: “One should cause [the patient] to fast after vomiting, carefully observing the signs of proper digestion; once those signs are seen, one should follow the regimen of thin gruel and so forth, not further fasting. (Siddhi-sthāna, Chapter 6)

This sequence, beginning with *maṇḍa* and having *maṇḍa* as its primary element, is to be understood as that which must be completed over twelve time-periods (*kāla*) when there is purity through the purification of the principal [tissue]; however, in the intermediate case, it lasts for eight time-periods, and in the minor case, for four time-periods. For it has been said: "Gruel (*peyā*), thick gruel (*vilepī*)," and so forth (Siddhisthāna, Chapter 1).

Regarding the qualities of food—such as sweetness and so forth, or heaviness and hardness—one should proceed toward a return to the normal diet after seven nights following the sequence of gradual re-introduction (*saṃsarjana-krama*), provided that no purgation (*virecana*) is to be administered immediately after the emesis (*vamana*). However, if it is performed, then the intake of unctuous substances (*sneha-pāna*) must occur precisely after the sequence of gradual re-introduction. As it has been stated: "On the ninth day, one should have him drink ghee after he has consumed mixed rice, or else administer an oil enema (*anuvāsana*). (Siddhisthāna, Chapter 1).
Likewise, it is stated in the Suśruta Saṃhitā: "Purgation occurs after a fortnight for one who has undergone emesis" (Su.Ci.A.

If the unctuous therapy is administered after performing the regimen of gradual dietary restoration (*saṃsarjana-krama*) and practicing appropriate habits, then purgation would not occur for the one who has vomited after a fortnight.
Then, having been thus subjected to the process of thorough mixing,
it was stirred and well-blended.

The *doṣas* and so forth are to be explained as before; "and disorders" refers to those such as leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), fever (*jvara*), and others that are curable by purgation (*virecana*). However, in the previous passage beginning with "for they are subtle," disorder (*vikāra*) was not mentioned, because it is included simply by virtue of being the object of examination. Alternatively, by the mention of the *doṣas* itself, the disorder is also included therein. Regarding "desires"—that is, things wished for—one should "let loose," meaning one should act without restraint.
Now, he describes the performance of purification even by a poor person who has not gathered the aforementioned equipment, beginning with the words "the poor person" and so forth;
by the expression "difficult to obtain," it is indicated that these [substances] are easily obtained and can be produced even by a poor person.
19–21 He states the qualities of performing purification, beginning with "removing impurities" (malāpaha), etc.

In the *Saṅgraha*: "The lords are full of playfulness; by that, one should cause the inclusion of the king and the royal ministers"—the word "requisites" (*sambhārān*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Quadruple Instruction," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka Saṃhitā* composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 16 (16 of 120)]

In order to describe in detail the characteristics of correct administration and so forth regarding emesis and purgation mentioned in the preceding chapter, as well as the many types of persons with excessive *doṣas* who are the subjects for their application, the *Cikitsāprābhṛtīya* [chapter] is now declared.
It is called *Cikitsāprābhṛtīya* because it contains *cikitsā* (therapeutics) as its essential substance (*prābhṛta*), which must always be applied with effort and presented to the patient.
Through the application— that is, through correct application—
one easily brings about health; in this context, it should be understood that "virecayati" (purges) also implies "vamayati" (emesis), since the term *virecana* is applied to emesis as well.
"From excessive application," and so forth, refers to suffering as modification; as it has been said: "Modification, however, is indeed suffering" (Sūtra 9).

Now, why is "wrong application" (*mithyāyoga*) not mentioned in the context of emesis and other therapies? For, the application that is appropriate for a given substance is called its "proper application" (*yoga*); a slight application or no application at all of that [substance] is called "non-application" (*ayoga*); an excessive application of that very same [substance] which causes disorder is called "excessive application" (*atiyoga*); and an application of a substance through an inappropriate connection is "wrong application. Therefore, in this case as well, for a person characterized by aggravated *kapha* and so forth, purgation is entirely non-appropriate; when administered, it moves in the opposite direction, and thus this is considered "wrong application" (*mithyāyoga*) in the case of purgation. This should be understood to apply similarly to emesis and the other therapies as well.

This is not so, because such a false application is grasped precisely as a non-application; for it has been said: "When one proceeds with difficulty and only slightly toward that which is designated 'non-application' (ayoga-sañjñā), because the defects have been removed in reverse order, yet not entirely" (Sūtra 6).

When a purgative drug intended for a harmful evacuation is administered with the tongue, its causation of disease—occurring independently of both under-dosage and over-dosage—is due solely to improper application (*mithyāyoga*); as stated in the *Tisraiṣaṇīya*: "Improper application shall be explained regarding the specific rules for the administration of food, excluding the [three] groups" (Sūtra 11).

This is true that this refers to the improper application of the medicine itself, but in the case of emesis, it refers to the improper application of the act of expelling the humors (*doṣa*); the same should be understood for purgation and other such procedures.

Although a false application (*mithyāyoga*) could somehow be postulated here as well, it was not treated separately by the Teacher because it lacks practical purpose; however, in the case of sound and other [objects], it was treated separately for the sake of avoiding even the mere connection with those who apply [the senses] falsely.
"Weakness" (*daurbalya*) and so forth are the characteristics of purgation that is properly applied, improperly applied, or excessively applied.
"Absence of debility" means the non-disappearance of corpulence;

by reading it as "in due order," he shows that it occurs precisely in sequence—as it has been stated: "In one who has been properly purged, there shall be the sequential restoration of feces, bile, phlegm, and wind" (Sūtra-sthāna 1).
The construction is: "after those who have arrived, [the signs] are supreme.
(5–10) He extends the characteristics of excessive application (*atiyoga*) to emesis with the words beginning "in emesis," etc.

In the context of excessive emesis (*vamanātiyoga*), the phrase "of feces, bile, phlegm, and wind" is not to be applied in such a way that it would imply a sequential order of the emergence of phlegm, bile, and wind during the administration of emetics—
as it has been stated: "He whose [emesis] proceeds in sequence— first phlegm, then bile, and then wind— is considered to have undergone successful emesis" (Siddhisthāna, Chapter 1).
1) Thus,
verses 11–12 state the characteristics of many morbid humors (doṣa) that are subjects for purification, beginning with "indigestion" (avipāka), etc.
Fatigue (*klama*) is exertion performed without effort; however, in this context, fatigue should be understood as occurring with even slight exertion.
Dejection of mind (*mano'vasāda*) is a state of despondency caused by a humor dominated by *vāta*, or it may be the loss of sleep. Excessive sleepiness is caused by a humor dominated by *śleṣman*.

Regarding the capacity of purification (*saṃśodhana*) to remove the humors (*doṣa*) along with their roots, and the fact that although lightening (*laṅghana*) and digestion (*pācana*) also remove the humors, they do not eliminate them as thoroughly as purification does, he says: "The humors," etc., and "sometimes" (*kadācit*), meaning due to the occurrence of other causes.
It should be understood that "there is no further arising for them" means [it does not occur] without the presence of powerful causal factors consisting of the *doṣas*.
Regarding this stated point, he provides an illustration with the words beginning "of the *doṣas*," and so forth.

The sense is as follows: when a disease has been cured merely by removing the provocation of the *doṣas* that serve as its cause through jumping (*laṅghana*) and digestive treatments (*pācana*), it may recur because the *doṣas* residing in the fundamental substratum (*āśaya*) have not been eradicated; thus, upon encountering some favorable time or other conditions, the provoked *doṣa* arises once again.

Now, through purification (*śodhana*), just as there is a depletion of the *doṣas*, there is also a depletion of the *dhātus*. Therefore, he states the remedy for that [condition] with the words beginning "bheṣaja" and so forth.

The word "eva" (only) is used for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*); by this, he excludes nourishing therapy (*bṛṃhaṇa*) by means of medicine, because at that time, medicine—being primarily characterized by its potency (*vīrya*)—is difficult to tolerate.
In the phrase "sānuvāsanaiḥ," the word "ca" (and) is to be understood; by this, nourishing therapy through massage and other such means is also indicated as wholesome.
(22–23) He now describes the treatment for excessive application and so forth, beginning with the words "atiyoga... and so on.
By the phrase "remembering the previous sequence," he instructs one to avoid that which was previously the cause for unsuccessful practice;
the ellipsis to be supplied here is "it will be explained" regarding how this constitutes a means when it is performed on an improper path or not according to the prescribed rule.

Now, in connection with this treatment of diseases that will be described in the section on successful therapy (*siddhi*), and as a corollary, in order to demonstrate that all medicinal substances possess curative power for diseases even under the view that they are subject to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), he begins the chapter with the words "They are born," etc.;
[the word] "of them" refers to those irregular (*viṣama*) and regular (*sama*) bodily constituents (*dhātu*).

Destruction is the cessation [of an entity] by its very nature, independent of a cause of destruction; this "cessation of nature" means it exists as such, without delay. Therefore, the meaning is that things perish at the very moment they have arisen.
Regarding this very point, he states the supporting argument, beginning with "pravṛtti" and so forth.

There is a cause for the activity and the arising of entities, but there is no cause—that is, no external factor—for their cessation or destruction. This is because all entities depend upon a cause for their production, like the flame of a lamp; however, regarding destruction—characterized by non-existence in the second moment—they do not require any other cause, as it is spontaneously established. Since there is no dependence on another cause for an inherent nature, a sword that has been forged does not require any further cause for its inherent metallic nature. Thus, the point is that for all entities, since destruction is inherent, even the destruction of those with discordant humors (dhātus) is likewise inherent.
Regarding the pacification of disease, he states another position that requires medical treatment, beginning with "some" and so forth.

Even in that case, regarding destruction (*vināśe*), the construction is: they consider the cause (*hetum*)—that is, the reason—to be the non-operation of the cause (*hetor avartanam*), meaning the absence of the productive cause.

Even so, because the succession of causes is momentary, their effects also, by their very nature, possess causes for destruction in the form of the destruction of their own causes which are eternally present; thus, there is no need for medical treatment directed toward a cause of destruction. This is the underlying sense.
When such a doubt has arisen, he asks the Guru: "In this way," and so forth;
the word "what" (*kim*) is used here as an interrogative particle.
The meaning is that [only] action is to be accomplished; since intrinsic nature has ceased, I do not see anything to be accomplished.
As for the phrase "whom does he equalize?": the intention is that because they are unstable and thus unequal, it is impossible to establish equality among them.
And as for the question "what is the remedy?": the sense is that there is no remedy, because it cannot be a cause for the pacification of disease.

Or for what purpose is it applied? If that which is intended to be eliminated by the application of medical treatment has already ceased of its own accord due to the imbalance of the *dhātus*, then there would be no purpose for applying the treatment (vv.
To show that the destruction of the previously mentioned cause is itself caused, he states "not [by] destruction," etc., providing an illustration.

The cause of the destruction of entities is not known; is it because of their non-existence, like a rabbit's horn, or because they exist but are not perceived due to being unfit for cognition, like a wooden peg driven deep into the earth? To this he says: "due to the absence of a cause of destruction. This means it is not due to being unfit for cognition, but rather due to non-existence itself. Here he provides an example: "of that which moves eternally," etc., referring to that which moves eternally in the form of moments (*nimeṣa*) and so forth.

He thinks as follows: Just as time, being ever-present, does not depend on any other cause for its destruction because it is perishable by nature, so it is with all entities whatsoever. For that which depends on another cause is not necessarily inevitable, just as the dyeing of a cloth [depends on a cause]. If destruction were to depend on another cause, it would not be inevitable; and from the opposite of this, the independence of destruction is established.

Now, destruction occurs without a cause immediately after arising; since things are unstable, even the application of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) cannot be effected in entities later on. Thus he says, "Because of its swift movement," and so forth:
"Just as it was when it arose, so too does it perish. Why? Because of its swift movement, that is, because of its instability.

He concludes that [the self] is not subject to conditioning (*asaṃskāryatva*), which was previously established by the absence of a cause for destruction and likewise established by the cause of its rapid movement, with the words beginning "cessation" (*nirodha*).
"Of that" refers to the entity (*bhāva*);

"alteration" (*anyathākriyā*) means making otherwise, which is to say, the imparting of a conditioning (*saṃskārādhāna*). By this, one should understand that even medical treatments of the form "let equilibrium be imparted as a conditioning in an imbalanced constituent" are refuted.

This being the case, they address the previously raised objection regarding medical treatment: by the words "by which," etc., the objection "what is medical treatment? is resolved by the phrase "that is medical treatment."
By the phrase "that is karma," the first objection raised was resolved; by the phrase "action is performed for this purpose," the objection "for what purpose? was resolved;
and the objection "whom does it equalize? was resolved by the passage beginning with "because [it acts] through equal causes."
Therapeutics is that by which, through specific actions, the humors that have become imbalanced are brought back to equilibrium.

He thinks as follows: although the imbalance of the elements (*dhātuvaiṣamya*) is perishable due to its momentariness, nevertheless, even while perishing, that imbalance of the elements initiates its own effect, which is indeed another imbalance of the elements; and so on, one after another, there is no cessation of the continuum of the imbalance of the elements without a cause that produces the equilibrium of the elements (*dhātusāmya*). However, when the cause for the equilibrium of the elements is applied, then that cause, even though it belongs to the continuum of imbalance, initiates a continuum of elements that is indeed balanced, accompanied by that [cause]. Just as the continuum of the atoms of a jar, when struck by a hammer, initiates a dissimilar continuum of shards—this being the established state, the passage beginning with "How, in the body... and so forth is to be explained.
"Disparity does not occur" means that it does not arise;

"the continuity of equals" refers to arising as a continuum (*santati*). Since disparate [factors] do not follow one another, there is no arising of a disparate continuum due to the absence of a cause.
"And by the cultivation of equals" means by the practice of equal causes (34–36).

One becomes a giver of virtue and so forth because of the bestowing of bodily happiness and longevity; the underlying sense is that virtue and the other goals are accomplished through the perfection of the body.

[The discussion concerns] that which pertains to success (*siddhi*), that which pertains to failure (*vyāpatti*), and that which pertains to both success and failure. Among these, that which pertains to success is based on the locus of success; that which pertains to failure is stated by the passage beginning with “those followed by excessive application” (*atiyogānubaddhānām*).

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Section on Therapeutics," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the fourth section, the "Quartet on Formulations" (*Kalpanācatuṣka*), in the *Sūtrasthāna*. [End of Sūtrasthāna Chapter 16 (17 of 120)]

The fourfold set of four [chapters] previously dealt with medicine (*bheṣaja*); now, for the purpose of naming the diseases that are its objects, the fourfold set of diseases (*rogacatuṣka*) must be stated. Furthermore, since treatment (*cikitsā*) is the primary subject as that which is to be performed, it was mentioned first. Moreover, this very relationship was demonstrated in the first chapter itself. Thus, among the limbs and vital points (*marmans*), because it denotes the diseases of the head and heart—the most important parts—it is called "Kiyantaḥśirīya" (On How Many Heads).

[Verse 1-2: The measure of the *doṣas* consists of their decrease, maintenance of status, and increase; its variation (*vikalpa*) is the distinction created by their association or non-association with other *doṣas*.

Regarding the term *mādhumehika*, the word *madhumeha* here is used as a general designation for *prameha* (urinary disorders), since it is stated in this very context in a general sense: "These [boils] arise even without *prameha* in those with vitiated fat (*duṣṭamedaḥ*). Otherwise, it would have been stated as "without *madhumeha*. Likewise, in the section on therapeutics (*cikitsita*), he will speak in a general manner: "The seven types of boils that I have described separately for those suffering from *prameha* in the chapter on diseases," and so forth. (Ci. 6)

Furthermore, because the treatment for the pustules (*piḍakā*) of *madhumeha* is taught, it follows that these pustules arise from all types of *meha*. For if they arose specifically from *madhumeha* alone, then since *madhumeha* itself is incurable, there would be no point in prescribing a treatment for the pustules arising from it. Moreover, in another section, he has referred to all types of *prameha* by the term *madhumeha*, as in: "A man suffering from abdominal tumors (*gulma*), *madhumeha*, or pulmonary consumption (*rājayakṣman*) becomes incurable when his strength and flesh have wasted away" (Iṅguda 9).

For if, in this context, *madhumeha* were intended to mean the vātika type, then the qualification "when there is a wasting of strength and flesh" would be redundant, since that [vātika] type is incurable by its very nature.
