Furthermore, Suśruta has described these carbuncles (*piḍakā*) in relation to *prameha* in general; as it is said: "In that regard, ten carbuncles arise in a patient suffering from *prameha*, whose body is overwhelmed by fat and marrow and whose bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are affected by the three *doṣas*" (Su.Ni.).

6) All these types of *prameha* are called *madhumeha* because they arise after the body has been rendered sweet (*madhurīkṛta*). For it is said: "The body and urine are followed by bees and ants" (Nidāna 4). And likewise Vāgbhaṭa states: "That which is sweet in all [types] generally excretes like honey."
"For all [types] are indeed called madhumeha because of the sweetness of the body [in that condition]" (Vāgbhaṭa-nighaṇṭu 10).
"In detail" is connected with the word "listen.
"From suppression" means from the suppression of the natural urges.
"Green" refers to ginger and similar substances;

this term is connected both with the preceding [phrase] and with the subsequent phrase "by the use of cold water. It means from corrupted *āmadoṣa* (i.e., *duṣṭādāmāt*). Alternatively, there is the reading *uṣṇāmāt*, in which case the meaning is "from heat and from *āma*."

Regarding the phrase "due to the reversal of place and time," the "reversal of place" refers to the location being afflicted by an *upasarga* (malignant influence); by stating that "the blood also becomes vitiated," [the author] demonstrates that vitiation of the blood occurs in all diseases of the head.

By the passage beginning with "the vital breaths" (*prāṇā*), [the author] demonstrates the preeminence of the head among the limbs, thereby showing that diseases of the head specifically are extremely harmful. Thus, the statement regarding the preeminence of the head is not contrary to the sūtra. The term *śritāḥ* means "resting upon"; because of the injury to the head, the head is the supreme limb (*uttamāṅga*) following the injury.
He describes the primary diseases of the head with the passage beginning with "ardha-" and ending with "krimisambhavāḥ";
this is an elaboration of the statement, "various diseases arise with diverse characteristics."

Since diseases such as those of the nose could also be included under the category of being "located in the head," [the author], setting those aside, speaks in detail of those very diseases characterized by headache that were mentioned in the *Aṣṭodarīya* chapter—beginning with the words "separately" (*pṛthak*) and so forth—in the *Saṅgraha*. Therefore, conditions such as *nārūṃṣikā* (scald-head) are not referred to here by the term "disease of the head" (*śiroroga*); for the term *śiroroga* is used specifically for those painful conditions that cause a piercing pain (*śūla*).
"Drinking sharp [liquor]" means drinking strong intoxicants; or alternatively, "sharp" refers to black pepper and the like, as they are said to kill, meaning they cause extreme affliction. 15–21.
One who is cold is treated with cold; one desires cold. (22–23) The pleasure of sleep is to be understood as resulting from improper daytime sleep.
As if asleep, it is indeed asleep; due to its lack of awakening, it is like a porter burdened by a load. 24–26.

By the terms "one who eats mixed food," "one who consumes incompatible foods," and "one who is *doṣala* (having many *doṣas*) and of evil deeds," [the author] demonstrates that this extremely painful disease of worms occurs only for one who possesses unrighteousness (*adharma*).

The definition of the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) is the discharge of pus and other such substances from the nose and other orifices (27–29). "Sorrow, fasting," and so forth, are the symptoms of heart disease (*hṛdroga*).
Enveloping is like unwrapping;
a crack is a fissure; lack of thought is slight thought.
Covered by stone, overrun by stone;
it is like a knot— a "granthi"— and that is produced by a disorder of the vital fluids (rasa-doṣa) in a specific part of the vital organ, namely a specific part of the heart.
The second point, the word *marma*, functions as the object [of the verb].
This is the answer to what was stated in the passage beginning with “And how many of the [doshas] such as wind? (30–40): “By two being excessive,” and so forth.
The phrase "by those inferior, middling, and superior" is to be analyzed as "in association with the old, the older, and the oldest.
The explanation of this very point begins with "six from them," and so forth.
"Dependent on the equal" (*samāśraya*) is the explanation of the phrase "caused by increase and decrease through the equal" (*samair vṛddhikṣayakṛta*).

Regarding this, although "equality" (*samatā*) is also listed among the alternatives of increase and decrease, it is nevertheless stated as "caused by increase and decrease" because equality does not independently produce modification.
By the statement "the increase of one, the equality of one, and the decrease of one," the six transformations are indicated;
by the statement "the increase and decrease of one through the pair," three are indicated;
and by "the increase of one and the decrease of two," another three are indicated.
Thus, there are sixty-two varieties [of the humors].
An illustration of the passage beginning with "the increase of one" (41–44) is as follows: "When the *pitta* is situated in its natural state," and so forth.

In this regard, some read only this as the supreme example for the sake of illustration, while the remaining examples are to be understood throughout the entire treatise (*tantra*). Others, however, because the conceptualization of increase and decrease is difficult to comprehend, maintain that the Teacher has provided the definition for all twelve conceptualizations alike, and thus they recite the whole.

[An objection is raised: "But if *pitta* is situated in its natural state (*prakṛtistha*), how can there be burning at that time? For a humor (*doṣa*) situated in its natural state does not cause a disorder, nor is burning possible for *vāyu*."

It is said: because of the statement "wherever [the wind]," wherever the *pitta* has been carried by the provoked *vāyu*, in that part of the body the *pitta*—even though it was present in its natural state (*prakṛtimāna*)—is indeed increased. For in that region, such an extent of association with *pitta* is simply not appropriate; thus, burning (*dāha*) is entirely logical due to the excess *pitta* there. This should be explained in the same way for other *doṣas* as well, even when they are situated in their natural state, regarding their involvement in a disorder (*vikāra*). Others, however, say: even for *doṣas* situated in their natural state, the capacity to cause a disorder arises through association with a vitiated *doṣa*; as, for example, in the case of blood (*rakta*) and so forth.
The passage beginning with "of one who has deficient vāta" and so forth is an illustration of the rule: "There is increase of two and decrease of one.
*Dehaujas* means the essence of the body (*dehasāra*); alternatively, *dehaujas* refers to both the body and the vital essence (*ojaḥ*).
He describes separately the signs of the increase, equilibrium, and decrease of the *doṣas*, beginning with the words "the *doṣas*" and so forth.
"Their own characteristic" (*svaṃ liṅgam*) refers to their morbid manifestation.

"According to their strength" (*yathābalam*) means that when they are excessively increased, [the symptoms] are excessively increased; when moderately increased, [the symptoms] are moderately increased, and so on.

By the statement "it abandons its own characteristic" (*liṅgaṃ svaṃ jahati*), he demonstrates that for those [humors] that have diminished, there is no capacity to produce morbid transformations (*vikāra*) apart from the exhaustion of their natural characteristics (*prakṛtiliṅgakṣaya*). For it is the aggravated humors moving along improper paths that, while corrupting the bodily constituents (*dūṣya*), produce fever and other disorders, not those that are diminished, because they are themselves in a state of instability.
"Its own action" (*svaṃ karma*) refers to the natural function (*prākṛtaṃ karma*).

Furthermore, these sixty-two varieties are mentioned as being the most manifest; therefore, in cases of the diminution of one humor and the aggravation of two humors, a greater degree [of morbidity] should be inferred based on the distinctions of increased, further increased, and so forth.

Now, let it be so regarding the number [of the humors] if there were a conjunction of the *doṣas*; however, that cannot be the case, because the qualities (*guṇa*) of *vāta* and the others are mutually contradictory. Indeed, for those with contradictory qualities, there occurs mutual destruction, as in the case of fire and water.

It is not so; for the contradiction between entities is to be inferred from their effects, and it cannot be postulated merely by observing something else elsewhere. Since a distinction between water and fire is observed in other contexts, does it follow that a substance composed of the five elements would not exist because of the contradiction between those two? Or would sour taste not exist because of the predominance of the qualities of water and fire? Therefore, since such a contradiction is not perceived in the mixture of defects, it is not proper to question its inherent nature.

Now, if you think that even for defects with contradictory qualities there is no mutual opposition—based on the statement, "When there is a conjunction of qualities with contradictory attributes, the greater overcomes the lesser" (Vi.
1), and likewise the statement, "But the specific cause is diminution" (Sū. 1)—then those [statements] would be meaningless.
No, because these two have fulfilled their purpose by functioning with respect to objects distinct from those already established through their own power.

However, the specific potency (*prabhāva*) of these two [fruits] is indeed antagonistic. For example, the qualities present in the *nikuca* fruit—which produces the three *doṣas*—produce the *doṣas* equally, yet they do not perform the removal of *doṣas* due to their contradictory nature, because of the potency that acts as a producer of the three *doṣas*. Similarly, the acidity of the *āmalaka* destroys *vāta*, while its sweetness and coldness destroy *pitta*, and its pungency and bitterness destroy *kapha*; however, in the *nikuca*, the acidity is overwhelmed by astringency and coldness and thus does not destroy *vāta, and the sweetness and coldness, being overwhelmed by acidity, do not conquer *pitta*, and so forth.
Therefore, the power of the *doṣas* is determined by observation to be this: that they do not destroy one another.

Since their power is of such a nature, the cause for this is indeed the *adṛṣṭa* (unseen force); for they are established in non-opposition by the *adṛṣṭa* which produces suffering in living beings. For this very reason, he will say: "Even though these qualities (*guṇas*) are contradictory, the *doṣas* do not destroy one another because of their innate naturalness (*sahaja-sātmyatva*), just as [the qualities] in a potent poison do not [destroy each other]. (Ci.)
26) Thus, *sahajasātmyatva* refers to that which is innate (*sahaja*), natural (*svābhāvika*), and habitual (*sātmya*) by the power of destiny (*daiva*).

By this explanation, all that is asserted by some— namely, that "just as the *doṣas* do not mutually afflict one another, so too the *rasa*, blood, and other constituents shall not be impaired"— is refuted.

But surely, it will be stated in the section on therapeutics: “For a disorder that is constant, lacks an antidote, and is equal to the time, the humor, and the constitution, causes [suffering]” (Ci. 3). By this, it is said that the constitution (*prakṛti*) is the counteragent to the morbidity (*doṣa*); and the constitution is defined as the Vāta and other humors increased since birth, for it is said: “The bodily constitution of these [humors] is said to be that which is permeated by the morbidity” (Sū.).

7) Because of such statements as these: "How then is this contradiction of a defect by a natural [quality] logically established? It is said in reply: In that context, the "antagonism" of the *prakṛti* (nature/constituent) is to be understood as being non-conducive (*ananuguṇatva*). For a defect, having encountered a similar *prakṛti*, becomes increased in strength; however, having encountered a dissimilar one, it does not become so strong, nor is it destroyed by a dissimilar *prakṛti*. This should be inferred in other cases as well.

When the vāyu is excessively aggravated and the śleṣman is weakened and vitiated, a conflict certainly occurs in some cases; however, this does not mean that *saṃsarga* (combined disorders) and *saṃnipāta* (complex disorders) are impossible.
Now, he describes the eighteen types of *kṣaya* (depletions), beginning with "of vāta and the others," etc.
Here, by the term "of the impurities" (*malānām*), there is the inclusion of urine, feces, and the impurities of the five sense organs;

from the expression "specifically" (*viśeṣeṇa*), the dryness of other limbs is also obtained. The phrase "of the joints" (*sandhīnām*) and so forth refers to the symptom of depletion (*kṣaya*). The phrase beginning with "hair" (*keśa*) and so forth refers to the depletion of the bones.
And because it afflicts this [body], the genitive case is used in the sense of a residual relation (*śeṣalakṣaṇā*).

By the term "exits for impurities" (*malāyanāni*), the respective excretory passages for the five sense organs—the mouth, nose, eyes, and ears—as well as those for the skin organ—the hair follicles, the generative organ, and so forth—are included.
As stated by Jatūkarṇa: "Of the humors (*doṣas*), the tissues (*dhātus*), food, urine, feces, and the impurities of the sense organs..."
"Those eighteen types of wasting (kṣaya) are to be identified by the destruction of their own specific qualities and functions.
Thus [ends verses 63–72]. He states the symptoms of the wasting of *ojas* (vital essence) beginning with "he fears," etc.
Dejected and deprived of mental strength, he describes the characteristics of *ojas* due to its difficulty of discernment, beginning with the words "in the heart" (*hṛdi*), etc.

"Pure" (*śuddham*) means white (*śuklam*); "slightly red" (*raktamīṣat*) means somewhat red; "with yellow" (*sapītakam*) means slightly yellow. By this, he shows that *ojas* is white in color, while red and yellow are colors associated with it as secondary qualities. Alternatively, "slightly" (*īṣat*) refers to a small quantity; thus, he indicates that *ojas* consists of eight drops.

As stated in another tantra: "The eight drops of *ojas* that reside in the heart are the substratum of *prāṇa*. This [eight-drop *ojas*] should be understood as the supreme *ojas*; however, that *ojas* which measures half an *añjali* is secondary. As he will state in the *Śārīra-sthāna*: "Such is the measure of the *ojas* belonging to the phlegmatic (*ślaiṣmika*) type" (Śā. 7). Therefore, *ojas* here is of two kinds.

For this very reason, he will state in the *Daśamahāmūlīya* chapter: “That is the locus of the supreme *ojas*” (*Sūtra* 30); the meaning is that it is the locus of the supreme, most excellent [blood] consisting of eight drops.

Furthermore, here the characteristic of depletion should be understood as pertaining only to the measure of half an *añjali*, whereas death occurs even upon the loss of a single part of the eight-drop [measure]; this he demonstrates with the passage beginning with “in the heart,” and so forth.

And this *ojas* consists of the aggregate of all the *dhātus*; therefore, it is subsumed within the seven *dhātus* themselves, so there is no over-extension [of its definition] to an eighth *dhātu*. For this very reason, it is also stated in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*: "That which is the supreme *tejas* among the *dhātus* beginning with *rasa* and ending with *śukra*, that indeed is *ojas*" (*Su.Sū.* 15).
It is also stated elsewhere: "Just as honey is gathered by bees from fruits and flowers, so too is the vital energy (*ojas*) of men gathered from their bodies by the qualities (*guṇa*).
However, the reading beginning with "first it is born" (*prathamaṃ jāyate*) is not very well known.

These eighteen types of wasting (*kṣaya*) have been described as the most prominent; therefore, the non-mention of wasting of water (*udakakṣaya*), wasting of voice (*svarakṣaya*), and so forth, should not be raised as an objection. For it has been stated: "Wasting of the voice and disease of the chest" (Vi. 74). Likewise, the characteristic of wasting of water is as follows: "Upon seeing the drying up of the tongue, palate, lips, throat, and *kloma*, and observing excessive thirst, one should know that his water-carrying channels are vitiated" (Vi.
He states the general cause of wasting diseases (*kṣaya*) with the words "exertion" (*vyāyāma*), and so forth:
eating in measured amounts, the habitual consumption of a single taste,
and "over-exertion" (*ativartana*), which means excessive activity or going outdoors.
Time, old age, grasping, and injury to living beings—injury to living beings here refers to injury caused by *piśācas* and the like.

The cause for the depletion of *vāta* is not explicitly stated here because it is of a different nature; however, it should be understood as lack of mental reflection, sleeping during the day, and so forth. Alternatively, due to fasting there is an absence of *kiṭṭa* (waste); consequently, because *vāta* in the form of *kiṭṭa* is not produced, its depletion should be understood.

Now the seven types of piḍakās (eruptions) are to be discussed; therefore, first, by way of their primary cause, he describes prameha itself according to the sequence beginning with its etiology, starting with "heavy" and so forth.
"Fresh drink" means fresh liquor.
In this context, at the end of the phrase "sleep, [and] pleasures of sitting," the word "abhajatām" (of those who indulge in) is to be supplied;
"ojas" refers to the clarity of the bodily constituents (*dhātus*);
and "kṛcchre" means that which is difficult to cure.
Through neglect and lack of treatment,
the sequence of perceptions beginning with *śarāvikā* is clear in the commentary;
the perception of *alajī* is that which has become chronic.
These have been mentioned by way of prominence;
therefore, the statement in the *Suśruta* regarding the abundance of pustules (*piḍakā*) is not contradictory.
"The network of vessels" (*sirājālam*) refers to a collection of vessels (*sirāsamūha*).

By the statement "two types of abscesses" (vidradhi), he demonstrates that even internal abscesses are classified as *vidradhi*, and thus there is no contradiction in the number of *piḍakās* being seven.

Having described internal abscesses as being more severe than those resembling tendons (kaṇḍarā) or thick ligaments (sthūlasnāyu), he states the etiological factors, beginning with "cold" and so forth;
[the term] *saṅkliṣṭa* means afflicted by the humors (*doṣa*).
One who consumes spoiled and excessive liquor is called "one who uses spoiled and excessive liquor";
"within the body" refers to the impurities and humors (doṣas) in the visceral cavity (koṣṭha).
It is called a "knot" (granthi) because it is like a knot;
piercing and so forth are types of affliction (vyathā).
That which is cold itself becomes sourish; having reached a state of acidity, it undergoes a burning sensation,
resulting in *tamaka*, a specific type of dyspnea.
Pain in the abdomen, flanks, and between the shoulders": this refers to pain in the abdomen, flanks, and between the shoulders.
By listing separately those pains arising in the heart, navel, and bladder, he indicates that the *sānnipātika* type—whether matured (*pakva*), immature (*āma*), or undigested—is incurable.

From the three examples of the weapon and so forth, it should be understood that [prameha] is like a weapon in its cutting of the vital points (marman), like a serpent in its swift deprivation of consciousness, and like lightning-fire in its rapid lethality.
(101–103) He demonstrates the possibility of the aforementioned carbuncles occurring even without prameha, beginning with the word "vinā" (without).
By this, it should be understood that the statement previously made regarding the "diabetic nature" (mādhumehikatva) of pustules is intended as a general rule; furthermore,
"vāstu-sthāna" and "vidradhi" refer to external abscesses (bāhya-vidradhi).

104–107. In connection with the topic of carbuncles (piḍakā) of urinary disorders (prameha), he describes the characteristics of other manifested carbuncles as well: "Likewise, others," and so forth. "Pale" (pāṇḍura) means greyish; however, those of "pale color" (pāṇḍuvarṇa) should be understood as having a dry, pale hue.
"Having a variegated luster and a glossy black color—
one should treat [them] with medicines for wind and the other [humors]" implies, by context,
that this applies before the appearance of complications; by this, it is shown that a carbuncle (piḍakā) accompanied by complications is incurable.
Decomposition is the state of putrefaction (108–111).
Now, he explains the movement of the *doṣas*— beginning with "decrease" (*kṣaya*), etc.

In this context, the word *pra* is indicated as being elided [after *caya*]. Thus, *sthāna* means one's own state or location; *gati* means manner, mode, or condition; and *caya* means accumulation. Therefore, *prakṛṣṭacayaḥ* means an excessive accumulation. Likewise, *prakopaḥ* is an excessive provocation (*prakṛṣṭaḥ kopaḥ*); similarly, there is also *praśamaḥ*.

By this, it is shown that in the rainy season (*varṣā*) and so forth, there occurs a predominant accumulation (*prakṛṣṭa-caya*) of *pitta* and the other [doshas]; furthermore, it is indicated that even for the other doshas, there is an accumulation to some small degree as far as possible. By this, it is understood that in autumn (*śarad*), due to its residual strength (*anubala*), there is an aggravation (*prakopa*) of *kapha*, and so on. "In due order" (*yathākramam*) means according to the sequence of the rainy season, autumn, winter, spring, summer, and the monsoon (*prāvṛṭ*). Alternatively, "in due order" means according to what is appropriate (*yathāyogyatayā*).
"Of bile and the others" refers to bile (*pitta*), phlegm (*śleṣman*), and wind (*vāta*);

"one by one" means not simultaneously. This should be understood according to their predominance; therefore, there is no contradiction with the fact that in the rainy season (*prāvṛṣ*), phlegm and bile may be provoked as secondary factors.
As it has been stated: "In the rainy season, when the strength of the digestive fire is diminished, the wind and other [humors] become aggravated" (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 6).
Here, the phrase "the wind and others" refers to those for whom wind is predominant; in the same way, this should be explained regarding the provocation of wind and bile in the spring.

And here, among the six seasons, the powerful accumulation (*caya*) and other states of *pitta*, *kapha*, and *vāta* are to be distinguished accordingly: thus, at the time of the accumulation of *pitta*, there is the aggravation (*kopana*) of *vāta*; in autumn, during the time of the aggravation of *pitta*, there is the pacification (*praśama*) of *vāta*; in early winter (*hemanta*), there is the pacification of *pitta* and the accumulation of *kapha*; but in spring, there is only the aggravation of *kapha*. Furthermore, it should be noted that in summer, which is the pacifier of *kapha*, there is the accumulation of *vāta*. This has been established because, since the emission (*visarga*) is intended to be discussed later—where it will be stated that *pitta* and the others [are emitted] while setting aside *vāta*—and because in that emission, only the accumulation of *pitta* occurs.
He states another distinction regarding the types of destinies (gati) with the words "And destiny," and so forth.
Here, bile (pitta) is mentioned first because it is the cause of the maintenance of the body;
digestion (pakti), which is the act of cooking (pāka),
is mentioned next because it is the cause of strength (bala).
It is called *mala* because it defiles the body;

it is called *ojas* because it is the essential essence. Alternatively, it will be described as *ojas* because it is the secondary cause of the phlegmatic (*ślaiṣmika*) *ojas*, for it will be stated in the *Śārīra-sthāna*: "Such is the measure of both the phlegmatic [essence] and the *ojas*" (Śā. A. 7).
Because it is the cause of suffering, every activity is indeed evil; thus, when unmodified movements and so forth are obstructed, one dies.
In the phrase "ātmanvān," the suffix *matup* is used in the sense of praise;
"yukta" means one who is diligent.
"Without haste, without going," and so forth; regarding this, there are two verses beginning with "there."

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "How Many Diseases of the Head," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā*, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the section on diseases (*rogacatuṣka*) in the *Sūtrasthāna*. 120–121.

[Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 18 (18 of 120)] In the preceding chapter, the *piḍakas* were described, and they are of the nature of swelling (*śotha*). Therefore, following this section on swelling, the "Chapter on the Three Types of Swelling" (*Triśothīya*) is now expounded.

Although the two-fold and other classifications will be described later, the mention here of the triad caused by wind (*vāta*) and the others is for the purpose of demonstrating the predominance of those caused by *vāta* and the rest.

3. *Bhedana* is the tearing of the internal receptacles (*āśaya*); *kṣaṇana* is the pulverizing of the bones; *bhañjana* is the shattering [of limbs]; *picchana* is excessive crushing; *utpeṣaṇa* is like being ground upon a stone; *veṣṭana* is the binding of non-knots by snakes and the like.
The "barb" (*śūka*) of worms that possess barbs is the "barb of the barb-worms" (*śūkakrimīśūka*);
this should be applied [as a treatment] for those with poison through methods such as sudation (*svedana*).

By the statement that [symptoms] "are perceived at the outset," it indicates that even those [symptoms] which arrive later possess a similarity to the innate ones, as it has been said: "An adventitious [symptom] follows the innate morbid change" (Sūtra 19). Regarding the phrase "by those that are partially contrary to the innate characteristics": a portion of the adventitious symptoms becomes contrary to the innate characteristics; this should be understood as being due to color changes such as dark-brown (*śyāva*), etc., produced by Vāta and the other doshas. Alternatively, an adventitious [disease] is preceded by pain and is subsequently followed by Vāta and the others, whereas an innate [disease] is first associated with the characteristics of Vāta and the others and only later becomes painful; this constitutes the partial contrariety.
Bandha (bandaging) includes the ariṣṭābandha (protective bandage), vraṇabandha (wound bandage), and other types of bandages, which should be understood according to their respective suitability.
Vomiting and other such conditions are causes of swelling by their very nature;

however, for one who has been excessively weakened by physical labor and so forth, the sudden consumption of very heavy food and the like is the cause of swelling. "Labor" refers to the five purificatory procedures (pañcakarma);
the words *virūḍha* and *nava* are qualifiers of *śūka* and *śamī-dhānya* respectively.
"Of those who have given birth" means of those who have recently delivered;
"cleansing" refers to purging by means of emetics and so forth.
Its color is that of the primary elements; it is the same color as the body;
it is mobile, capable of transition, quivering, and trembling.
One dwells as if with a fire situated at one's side; one is burned,
one is scorched, one emits smoke as it were,
one steams, and even by others one is perceived externally through its heat.
It perspires and becomes moist with sweat; it does not heal easily and does not tolerate [treatment]; it cannot endure touch, nor can it endure heat;
its onset and subsidence are difficult, meaning its onset and subsidence are protracted.
"By means of the primary elements" refers to the causes;
"height" means loftiness.
The statement beginning with "they swell" (*śūyante*) and so forth is a further definition provided by means of a verse for the purpose of showing the characteristic that generally occurs;
"as if sleeping" (*svapantīva*) indicates the absence of sensation (*nirvedana*).
By this, it should be understood that because of the mobility of wind (*vāyu*), there is pain at one moment and its absence at another;
"from the middle" means from the center of the body, its movement is obstructed and it does not spread.
"From being cut by a weapon or *kuśa* grass" means from an incision made with a weapon or *kuśa*.

When a swelling produced in the feet of men arises in a light lower region and is not overcome, then, having moved to a heavy upper region, it cannot be conquered. For that which cannot be conquered in a light location is certainly even more impossible to conquer when it has reached a heavy location. It should be understood that the same applies to that which spreads from the mouth of a woman.
For there is this statement: “The lower part of women is heavy, and likewise the upper part of men is heavy” (Suśruta Sūtrasthāna 46).
He now describes the aforementioned complications, beginning with vomiting: “chardiḥ” and so forth.
Now, based on the similarity of swelling (utsedha), he describes localized swellings (prādeśika-śotha) beginning with "yasya" and so forth;
*kākala* refers to the root of the palate (*tālumūla*).

By the word "gradually" (śanaiḥ), [the author] shows that the doshas which cause goiter (galagaṇḍa) act slowly; whereas in conditions such as throat-obstruction (galagraha), the doshas act quickly. Although visarpa and piḍakā share identical causes, in visarpa the dosha is characterized by its tendency to spread (sarpaṇaśīla), while in piḍakā it should be known as stable (sthira). For this very reason, regarding the pathogenesis (samprāpti) of piḍakā, it is stated that [the dosha] "remains" (avatiṣṭhate).
In the passage beginning with "whose pitta... (yasya pittam), the construction should be understood as: having reached the blood, the agent (kartṛ) [which is the pitta] dries it up.
The *piplava*, known as *jaṭula*,
is a severe disease that kills quickly due to lack of treatment;

it is difficult to conquer, either because it is difficult to treat when approached in the proper sequence, or because it leads to death through improper treatment— this is how it should be understood.

This very swelling (śotha) is also mentioned elsewhere: "At the conclusion of a fever caused by the derangement of all three humors (sannipātajvara), a most severe swelling arises at the root of the ear; by means of it, only some person is liberated [from death].

Although conditions such as abdominal tumors (gulma) and others would require extensive explanation, they are mentioned here only briefly because they share the common characteristic of being swellings (utsedha).
"Collection of swellings" (*śothasaṅgraha*) means a collection in the form of swelling (*śotha*), characterized by elevation; "elevated" (*samucchritāḥ*) means exceeding the normal measure;
[it is] "causing extreme pain" (*bhṛśam atyarthaduḥkhakāriṇam*).

The word "quickly" (*kṣipram*) is connected with the preceding term "is prescribed" (*anukrānta*). Therefore, the objection—namely, how there can be a rapid subsiding for one whose [condition] has been struck down for three nights—does not arise. Alternatively, it means that he becomes happy quickly; this occurs by the power of the disease itself, for it is the very nature of this disease that it kills quickly and subsides quickly, as it has been said:
"Because of its quick action, it either subsides or kills quickly" (Ci.).
3) Thus,

[the author] states "santi" and so forth, indicating that this very quality of rapid action exists in other conditions as well, such as ear-infections (*karṇaśotha*), ear-rings (*valaya*), and the like, which terminate fevers (*jvarāntaka*).
Those considered "severe" are termed *dāruṇasammatāḥ*.

By way of discussing their severity, he also mentions the distinctions such as "mild" (*mṛdu*) and so forth—beginning with the words "and those to be cured" (*sādhyāśca*). [The term] *yātrākara* means that which sustains life.
"By the foolish" means by the ignorant; the meaning is that only the ignorant engage with what is incurable out of enthusiasm.

The curability or incurability of an incurable disease is distinguished by whether it is palliable (*yāpya*) or rejectable (*pratyākhyeya*), as well as by whether it takes life immediately (*sadyaḥ-prāṇahara*) or at a later time (*kāla-antara-prāṇahara*), and so forth.

The phrase "ta eva" (those very [factors]) and so forth refers to the distinctions in etiology based on the distinctions in their origination; the underlying sense is that wind (vāta), being produced by distinct causes such as dry food, staying awake at night, and so forth, must be treated with distinct therapeutic measures (upakrama).
The distinctions in location (sthāna) refer to the stomach (āmāśaya) and other sites, as well as the rasa and other bodily constituents.
Configuration (*saṃsthāna*) refers to the shape, such as a tumor (*gulma*), a fleshy growth (*arbuda*), and so forth;

difference in name (*nāmabheda*) refers to designations such as "royal consumption" (*rājayakṣman*) and "wasting disease" (*śoṣa*) for what is in fact a single condition. [The author] asks: "If they are thus innumerable, how is there any practical usage? To this he says: "The systematic arrangement," and so forth.

The establishment [of categories] is for the purpose of medical practice and involves stating the number [of diseases], specifically regarding those that are "gross" (*sthūla*), meaning those which are gross such as abdominal enlargement (*udara*), urinary retention (*mūtrakṛcchra*), and so forth. As for the summary, the meaning is that they are "indicated" in the summary of the eight types of abdominal diseases (*aṣṭodarīya*). He asks: how is the establishment [of categories] made for disorders that are not gross and are not mentioned by name in the *Aṣṭodarīya*? To this he says: "In the same way," and so forth.

The commonality of nature (*prakṛtisāmānya*) refers to having a common cause. Therefore, even when specific primary humors (*doṣas*) such as wind-born (*vātaja*), phlegm-born (*śleṣmaja*), or blood-born (*raktaja*) are not explicitly mentioned regarding a disease, a systematic classification must be established for the purpose of clinical practice—such as "this is wind-born" or "this is phlegm-born," and likewise "this is rasa-born" or "this is blood-born. This is the intended meaning. For this very reason, it will be stated in the chapter on the eight types of abdominal enlargements (*aṣṭodarīya*): "All disorders do not transcend [the influence of] wind, bile, and phlegm" (Sūtra 19).

He states that even when the specific name [of a disease] such as fever or internal hemorrhage (*raktapitta*) is unknown, one should proceed by knowing its origin from *vāta* and the other doshas—beginning with the words "In a disorder" (*vikāra*) and so forth.
In the phrase "and having moved to another location" (*sthānāntaragataśca*), the word "and" (*ca*) conjoins the idea that even while remaining in a single location, it produces many disorders.
For it will be stated: "Residing in the pharynx, it causes constriction of the throat, cough, hoarseness of voice, and loss of appetite" (Ci.
The various bases and various dispositions are preceded by knowledge— that is, preceded by medical knowledge—
in accordance with reason and in accordance with scripture.

He thinks as follows: "In the treatment of diseases, it is precisely the knowledge of [the humors] such as *vāta*—beginning with their being the initiators—that is beneficial; however, the knowledge of their names serves merely for the sake of conventional usage and is not beneficial to the treatment in its own right.

(Verses 44–47) Now, since the knowledge of disease was indicated by means of the knowledge of *vāta* and the others, he says—"They are eternal," etc.—in order to state, by way of introduction (*upoddhāta*), the characteristics of *vāta* and the others when they are in their natural state (*prakṛtistha*) and when they are not in their natural state (*aprakṛtistha*).
One should desire to know;
"movement" refers to movement that is free from distortion.
"Dhātugati" (movement into the tissues) refers to the movement toward the nourished tissue (*dhātu*) of [substances] such as *rasa* (nutritive fluid).
"Of those possessing movement" (*gatimatām*) refers to excrement and so forth as they exit externally.
"Clarity" (*prasāda*) refers to clarity of mind (*manaḥprasāda*).
Bandha is the binding of the joints,
stability, and lack of laxity; gaurava is natural heaviness of the body.
Forgiveness, endurance, and fortitude— the steadiness of the mind—
are produced by the influence of phlegm (kapha); in this same manner, it should be understood for the other [humors] as well.
49–51. He states the characteristics of decline (*kṣayalakṣaṇa*): "In *vāta*, etc.
[This refers to] "from natural action" (*prākṛtāt karmaṇaḥ*), meaning from enthusiasm and so forth as described according to the actions of the *prakṛtis* such as *vāta*.

"Decrease" means diminution, while "increase" refers to the increase of those factors that oppose the previously mentioned natural characteristics (prakṛta-lakṣaṇa); for example, upon the decrease of vāta, there is an increase of despondency (viṣāda), which opposes enthusiasm (utsāha); upon the decrease of pitta, there is an increase of non-vision, indigestion, and so forth; and upon the decrease of śleṣman, there is an increase of dryness (raukṣya) and other such qualities.

In this context, since the destruction of ordinary karma does not necessarily entail an increase of its opposing karmas, it is said: "or an increase," and so forth. For indeed, a slight loss of enthusiasm does not necessarily lead to an increase in despondency, nor does a slight deficiency in non-greed necessarily lead to an increase in greed. Alternatively, the statement "destruction of ordinary karma" is made from the perspective of negation (abhāvamukhena) for the sake of understanding the absence of enthusiasm and the like; whereas the statement "or an increase of the opposites" is made from the perspective of affirmation (vidhimukhena) for the sake of understanding the increase of despondency and the like.

As for what is said—that there is an increase of opposites, meaning the increase of opposing doshas—such as, for example, that when pitta increases, a decrease of kapha occurs, and so forth; that is not correct. For when one dosha increases, another does not necessarily undergo depletion. If that were the case, then whenever pitta increased, there would always be a depletion of kapha. Furthermore, it has already been established that the doshas are not mutually destructive. Moreover, in other sections, it is stated that the very definition of the depletion of the doshas is the loss of their own specific characteristics: "When depleted, they abandon their own signs" (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 17). 52
He states the characteristic of increase (vṛddhi) with the words beginning "doṣa" and so forth.

*Prakṛti* means innate nature (*svabhāva*); its *vaiśeṣya* is its excess. The specific quality (*vaiśeṣya*) of phlegm (*śleṣman*), such as its natural unctuousness, coldness, sweetness, and so on—namely, an excessive degree of unctuousness, coldness, sweetness, and so forth—is the characteristic of increase.

This is "fixed" (*niyatam*), meaning it is specifically determined (*pratiniyatam*): whatever is the characteristic of a particular [dosha] in its normal state, that very same characteristic when intensified is the characteristic of its increase. Others, however, say it means "certain" (*niścitam*).

53. Regarding the curability of swellings in the summary [of the chapter], this refers to their being curable by specific medicinal treatments; that is to say, it refers to the therapeutic suitability (*upaśaya*). This should be understood as stated in the passage: “And that which is cured by oleation, heat, and massage is of the Vāta type,” and not as non-curability, such as in the passage beginning: “And that which is produced in the feet,” and so forth.
By stating "of those various [diseases]"— referring to swellings such as *upajihvā* (ranula) and others—

as "previously arisen," he demonstrates that in cases such as *upajihvā*, swelling occurs first, and only subsequently does the specific disease manifest. For this very reason, after stating "it quickly produces swelling," it is said, "from this, *upajihvikā* arises."
That which is to be awakened to— the modifications, primordial matter, and so forth— is to be understood;
its threefold compendium is that which was stated in the verses beginning with "Therefore, the modifications and primordial matters," namely the triad [of verses] 54–56.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Three Types of Swelling," in the Section on General Principles (Sūtrasthāna) of the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka Saṃhitā* composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Section on General Principles, Chapter 19 (19 of 120)]

In the preceding chapter it was stated: "The systematic classification of these [diseases] is their grouping according to the gross [categories]" (Sūtra 18). Following that inquiry, the grouping according to the gross categories—beginning with "the eight types of abdominal enlargements" (aṣṭāvudarāṇi)—is now described; this is also the meaning-based designation for the chapter titled "Aṣṭodarīya."

The discussion of abdominal enlargements (udarābhidhāna) comes first because of the similarity of swelling (śotha) described in the preceding chapter; these are indeed varieties of swelling due to the commonality of their protuberance (udārāṇi).

In this context, the number eight is taken first by setting aside numbers such as one and so forth, because the number eight possesses primacy due to its multiplicity. The number twenty is not placed at the beginning for the mehas and other conditions, because there is no possibility of a descending sequence starting from nineteen and below.
Although there are eighteen types of *kuṣṭha* mentioned in the section on therapeutics (*cikitsita*), here seven are stated with reference to the major types of *kuṣṭha*.

Regarding the six types of *udāvarta*, those arising from the suppression of natural urges such as feces and so forth are what are meant here, according to the principle established in the *Navegāndhāraṇīya* chapter.

"Explained by the [chapter on] *gulmas*": just as there are various types of *gulma*, so too are there five types of *plīhadoṣa*. Regarding "thirst," even those produced by overeating, unctuous substances (*sneha*), and so forth, are included within those born of *vāta* and the other *doṣas*.

"Location" (*sthāna*) is like a location; it refers to the cause. By this, the causes of anorexia (*arocaka*) are indicated through their effects. Therefore, the objection that it is improper to mention the causes in the summary of diseases (*rogasaṅgraha*) does not hold.

"Summarizing the previous enumeration" means condensing what was stated in detail in the *Kiyantaḥśirasīya* chapter; or alternatively, summarizing and setting aside those [symptoms] enumerated in the *Kiyantaḥśirasīya* itself, such as "there may be hemicrania" (*Sūtra* 17), and instead describing the five types of pain located specifically in the head. In the reading "excessive restraint, depletion, and irregular eating," the fourfold *śoṣa* (wasting disease) is described by its causes as the effect.

In passages such as "two types of fever," the desire for heat is already understood by virtue of [fever] arising from cold; for a person suffering from fever desires that which is contrary to its cause (*nidāna*). Therefore, the specific qualification "desire for heat" here is intended to exclude the possibility that even a fever caused by *pitta*—which arises during the cold season—is considered to arise from cold. The same should be stated regarding the "desire for cold. Regarding the phrase "raw matter (*āma*) is of two kinds," this is because *āma-poison*, which will be described in the chapter on the three types of abdominal enlargement (*kukṣīya*), is included within *alasaka*. Others, however, maintain that *āma-poison* is not mentioned here because, being a type of poison, it falls under the domain of other treatises on poisons (*viṣatantra*).
Adherence to what is unreal is a mental distortion, and because it is the cause of all the suffering of those in cyclic existence, it is called a "disease.
One should understand that the names "worms," "ants," and "ticks" are generally used as conventional designations.

The "association of the *doṣa* with the *dūṣya*" refers to the contact of the humor (*doṣa*) with the affected tissue (*dūṣya*), such as blood and so forth; "nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to the cause. In this context, conditions such as *raktayoni* (menorrhagia) are to be explained by the description of the association between *doṣa* and *dūṣya*, while conditions such as *prākcaraṇā* are to be explained by the description of the nature [of the disease], after examining the treatment for disorders of the female reproductive tract (*yonivyāpatti*).
Here, since these very intoxicants themselves take on the form of alcoholism (*madātyaya*), they have not been mentioned separately as cases of *madātyaya*.

And although the number of these diseases mentioned here could be stated differently according to another classification—for instance, "there are eight fevers" or "two types of insanity, distinguished as endogenous and exogenous," and so forth—nevertheless, these very divisions have been adopted here with the intention of emphasizing the primary ones; and their primacy is to be understood by following the respective sections dedicated to each disease.

Now, in order to demonstrate this aphorism useful for the treatment of diseases— namely, that for abdominal enlargements (*udara*) and so forth, as well as for the major diseases (*mahāroga*) to be described later, and for those diseases not mentioned here in this treatise, the *vāta*, *pitta*, and *śleṣman* alone, either individually or combined, are the causes— he says "all" and so forth.
Although the term "all" includes both those mentioned and those not mentioned,

and although the connection with the *doṣas* does not deviate even in the case of exogenous (*āgantu*) diseases, nevertheless, because one should not treat an exogenous disease based on the *doṣas*, the word "endogenous" (*nija*) is used to exclude the exogenous.
By using its own specific term (*svaśabda*), he refutes the notion that [disease] is caused by external factors or by an imbalance of the *dhātus*.

Now, one might ask: "If all disorders are indeed produced solely by *vāta* and the other [humors], for what purpose are abdominal enlargements (*udara*) and so forth described otherwise—as being born from the spleen (*plīha*) and so on? To this he says: "*Vāta-pitta-* etc. [refers to] location (*sthāna*), which includes the *rasa* and other tissues as well as the bladder and other organs; configuration (*saṃsthāna*), meaning shape or characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); and nature (*prakṛti*), meaning the cause. Having observed the specific variations of these, they teach them accordingly—thus they teach such things as 'the eight types of abdominal enlargements'."
"Even those consisting of that [same nature]" means even those produced by wind (vāta) and the other doshas therein.

The teaching is according to specific locations, such as thigh-stiffness (ūrustambha), disorders of the female reproductive tract (raktayoni), jaundice (kāmalā), and so forth; according to specific morphologies, such as carbuncles (piḍakā), abdominal tumors (gulma), and so forth; and according to specific constitutional types (prakṛti), such as phlegmatic dropsy (śleṣmodara), splenic enlargement (plīhodara), and so forth.

Others, however, explain it thus: they designate them as "produced by wind and the others" because they arise from those very [doshas]; and "even those consisting of that" means even those possessing the aforementioned numbers of eight and so on.

Although diseases may be distinct due to other causes such as the spleen (plīha) and so forth, nevertheless, because they arise from the locations of vāta and the others, because they possess the characteristics of vāta and the others, and because they are produced by vāta and the others as their causes, all disorders are indeed born of vāta and the others— this is the meaning of the statement. He expresses this very point in a verse beginning with "svadhātu" and so forth.

The word "own" (sva) refers here to the body, which will be discussed later; by this, the disharmony of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) is understood, while mental factors are excluded. Furthermore, since the constituents do not cause disease in their natural state, the term "disharmony" (*vaiṣamya*) has been employed.

For exogenous diseases, such as fever caused by trauma and the like, arise from an imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu-vaiṣamya*); therefore, the term "cause" (*nimitta*) is used to exclude them. Although an imbalance exists in exogenous cases, it is not designated as the cause because it is secondary; rather, the exogenous factor itself—such as the blow of a club—is the cause that necessitates a specific treatment. In endogenous diseases, however, the imbalance itself is the factor that necessitates treatment.

Furthermore, the term *nimittaja* (caused by a cause) is a *karmadhāraya* compound with the word *svadhātuvaiṣamya* (imbalance of one's own constituents); otherwise, if it were interpreted as a *bahuvrīhi*, it would be redundant.

Regarding the phrase "the groups of morbid transformations" (*vikārasaṅghāḥ*), such as "the eight types of abdominal enlargements" (*aṣṭāvudarāṇi*) and so forth: although plurality is already established by the plural suffix itself, the explicit mention of the word "many" (*bahavaḥ*) is intended to negate the notion that the function of the plural number is fulfilled merely by its denoting a group of three.

The statement "they are not distinct from bile, phlegm, and wind" means that they are simply bile, phlegm, and wind themselves, assuming the specific roles of the *dūṣya* (vitiated elements) and so forth.
Here, *pitta* is mentioned first out of metrical necessity; alternatively, it is placed first to indicate that there is no fixed rule regarding primacy.

Furthermore, here only the mere imbalance (*vaiṣamya*) of the *dhātus* is not called "disorder" (*vikāra*), because that is already established as being of the nature of the imbalance of *vāta* and the other *doṣas*. However, that specific imbalance of the *dhātus* which arises from the imbalance of the *dhātus*—such as fever (*jvara*) and so forth—is explained here to the student as non-different from the disordered *vāta* and others, by means of the phrase "from that" (*tataḥ*), referring to the previously mentioned collection of disorders.
"Distinct" means those other than bile (pitta), phlegm (kapha), and wind (anila). Now,
he explains the relationship between the two distinct types, the endogenous (nija) and the exogenous (āgantu), beginning with the words "The exogenous," and so forth.

One's own innate disorder (*nija-vikāra*), which arose first, is followed by—that is, becomes accompanied by—an adventitious disorder (*āgantu-vikāra*) produced by spirits (*bhūta*) and other such factors. For example, in a fever born of the *doṣas* or in insanity (*unmāda*), the subsequent entry of a spirit may occur; likewise, in a fever arising from an external injury (*abhighātaja*) or in insanity born of a spirit that has arisen adventitiously, one's own innate disease, characterized by the symptoms of the *doṣas*, subsequently manifests once it encounters its own specific cause.

By the expression “even though increased” (*api pravṛddhaḥ*), it is shown that although one's own [innate] defect (*nijadoṣa*) indeed exists even in the adventitious state (*āgantvavasthā*), it does not become "increased" because it does not perform its own characteristic function; this is indicated by the word "even" (*api*). Here, the connection between the innate and the adventitious is signaled by the innate through itself, and likewise by the adventitious through itself. Regarding this connection between the innate and the adventitious, the effect is stated in the passage beginning with "in that case" (*tatra*).
*Anubandha* is that which arises at a later time, while *prakṛti* is the fundamental or primary cause;

"having correctly understood" means by way of their relative strength or weakness. Alternatively, *anubandha* is the secondary factor, whereas *prakṛti* is the principal factor—that which is to be attended to.

As it was said: "One who is independent, whose gender is manifest, and whose arising and cessation are as previously described, is to be followed; that which is the opposite of this is a continuity" (VI.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Eight Types of Abdominal Enlargement," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of Caraka’s work, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the section on diseases (*rogacatuṣka*) in the *Sūtrasthāna*.
[Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 20 (20 of 120)]

Previously, diseases produced by *vāta* and the other [doshas] were described in general; now, in order to describe those remaining diseases produced solely by *vāta* and so forth, the "Chapter on Major Diseases" (*Mahārogādhyāya*) is set forth.

(1–2) Although exogenous (*āgantuka*) diseases were already mentioned in the "Chapter on the Three Types of Swelling" (*Triśothīya*), they are stated here again for the purpose of specifically describing their characteristics and other details.
In this context, *prakṛti* (nature) means inherent constitution (*svabhāva*).

Since [diseases] arise from specific states of mind and body, both the mind and the body serve as the substratum for endogenous (*nija*) diseases as well as for exogenous (*āgantuka*) ones. By including the term "exogenous," mental factors such as desire and the like are also indeed included.
Having thus established the fourfold nature [of diseases], he further states that diseases are innumerable by means of another classification, beginning with the words "vikārāḥ" (disorders), etc.
The word "again" (*punar*) indicates another method that will be explained:

*prakṛti* (nature) refers to the proximate cause such as wind (*vāta*) and so forth; *adhiṣṭhāna* (substratum) refers to the bodily constituents (*dūṣya*); *liṅga* (signs) refers to the symptoms (*lakṣaṇa*); and *āyatana* (bases) refers to external causes, namely corrupted diet and lifestyle (*duṣṭāhārācāra*). The term *vikalpaviśeṣa* (distinction of variations) refers to the specific variations among these, which are innumerable.

In this regard, the defects (*doṣas*) are innumerable due to variations such as their combinations, constituent parts, and individual portions; the affected body parts (*dūṣyas*), when divided by their minute components and mutual associations, are likewise innumerable; and the symptoms (*liṅgas*) encompassing all pathological changes are indeed innumerable, though only those manifested [in clinical practice] have been described in this treatise; and the causes (*hetus*), through their internal subdivisions, are clearly innumerable.

Some, however, read "eṣāṃ vikārāḥ" (these are their transformations), but that reading is not accepted for now. If it were so, then the word "eṣām" would refer to the body and mind (*dehamanaḥ-pratyavamarśaka*), while the plural number would be intended to express the multiplicity of the mind and body.
The "mouths" are the causes; as in: "approaching a woman in her menses is the mouth of misfortunes" (Sūtra).
25) Thus,
"impelling" (preraṇa) is the cause, because verbal roots have multiple meanings.

They adhere to and follow [their respective objects] and do not fall into doubt; that is to say, they do not become objects of uncertainty. The meaning is that even when mixed together, they are known distinctly by their own individual, distinct characteristics.
He states the distinguishing characteristic of the exogenous (*āgantuja*) [disease] from the endogenous (*nijaja*): "The exogenous," and so forth.

Being exogenous, it arises having first produced pain (*vyathāpūrvam*); subsequently, there is the "disorder of the *doṣas*" (*doṣāṇāṃ vaiṣamyam*), which is said to be the defining characteristic of the *doṣas*. The sense is that the disorder (*vaiṣamya*) which produces its own specific characteristics, though present from the very beginning of the exogenous [disease], is ineffective [in comparison].

Having stated the distinguishing characteristics of the exogenous (*āgantuka*) and endogenous (*nija*) [diseases], he speaks in order to provide knowledge of the distinctions among the endogenous morbid humors (*doṣa*), such as *vāta* and the others— beginning with the words "Of these," etc.—
the receptacle of feces (*purīṣādhāna*) is the colon (*pakvāśaya*).

Although the author will later describe the distinct locations of the vital air (*vāyu*) as divided into *prāṇa* and the other types—such as: "The locations of *prāṇa* are the head, chest, throat, tongue, mouth, and nose" (Ci. 28)—nevertheless, this should be understood as its specific location, because here wind disorders (*vāta-vikāra*) generally arise and living beings are difficult to conquer; furthermore, when the wind is conquered here, all wind disorders are conquered.
*Lasīkā* is the slimy portion of water.
Regarding the locations of pitta, "āmaśaya" refers to the lower portion of the stomach; regarding the locations of kapha, "āmaśaya" refers to the upper portion of the stomach.
Those arising from common causes are those produced by vāta and the other doshas individually or in combination.

Those which are called "born from various causes" (nānātmajā) are produced by the humors (*doṣa*), such as wind (*vāta*) and others, when they are not associated with other humors; these include *vipādikā* (cracking of the hands and feet),
*pāṇipādasphuṭana* (splitting of the hands and feet), and *pādabhraṃśa* (dropping of the foot), which is the falling of the foot to a place other than its intended position.
Numbness of the feet, lack of motor function, or insensitivity to touch is known as *vātakhuḍḍatā*, commonly called *āluka*;
by the term *gṛdhrasī*, the pain of *gṛdhrasī* (sciatica) is understood.

In the case of *ūrustambha* (stiffness of the thighs), only the stiffness itself is understood as being caused by *vāta*; likewise, in earache and eye pain, it is only the pain that [is so understood],
and even in diarrhea caused by *vāta*, it is only the breaking of the stool (*viḍbheda*) that is considered *vātaja*.
And thus, there is no commonality of origin for the *gṛdhra* and the others, because the aforementioned portion [of symptoms] arises solely from wind (*vāta*);
"stomach-constriction" (*udarāveṣṭa*) is like the wrapping of the abdomen;
and "hearing sounds" (*śabdāśravaṇa*) is the perception of sound even in the absence of sound.
*Uccaiḥśruti* is the hearing of sounds only at a high pitch; *alpaśabda* is the failure to hear sounds altogether;
*bādhirya* is the non-hearing of all sound whatsoever;
and *timira* is caused solely by wind (*vāta*), with the involvement of other humors (*doṣas*) occurring only as secondary complications (*anubandha*).

Regarding "disease affecting one limb" (*ekāṅgaroga*) and "disease affecting all limbs" (*sarvāṅgaroga*): among fevers and other conditions, when heat, cold, and so forth sometimes pervade only a single limb, it is a disease of one limb; when those same qualities sometimes pervade all the limbs, it is a disease of all limbs. Furthermore, even when there is an association with other *doṣas*, the pervasion or non-pervasion is caused by *vāta* alone, according to the statement: "Wherever they are led by the wind, there they rain, like clouds. Likewise, vertigo (*bhrama*) is caused by *vāta* and consists of a confusion of memory.

In this context, pain and other symptoms are mentioned for certain parts such as the feet, but not for the hands and so forth; among those that are mentioned, they are primary because they occur most frequently, whereas those not mentioned should be understood as included due to the fact that the disorders of *vāta* are innumerable.
In the passage beginning with "This is of *vāyu*," the term "this" refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) or intrinsic form of *vāyu*.
"Unchanging" means that it is established by its own nature and not produced by any other limiting condition (*upādhi*).
And "of action" refers to the specific characteristic of the action of the modified wind; that is, its own defining mark.

Here too, the term "non-transforming" (*apariṇāmī*) is connected [to bile and phlegm]; "non-transforming" means independent of the connection with bile and phlegm, but not independent of the body parts, since it says: "entering each respective body part. For this very reason, because falling out (*sraṃsa*) and so forth depend upon body parts, they do not exist at all times. In this way, the nature of bile and phlegm—such as their formlessness (*amūrtatva*)—should also be explained as being invisible (*adṛśyatva*).
The phrase "because it is of such a nature" connects with "because wind is characterized by dryness and so forth.
*Sraṃsa* is a slight movement from its own location; *bhraṃśa*, however, is a distant displacement;
and *vyāsa* is expansion.
Joy is produced by the power of the wind’s instability;
"varta" refers to circular motion, movement, or vibration.
Taste and color are produced by the wind (*vāyu*), even though it is devoid of taste and color, due to its inherent power (12).
He states a sūtra on therapeutics as it arises in this context: "That [wind] is [pacified] by sweet [substances]," and so forth.
"From the very beginning" means immediately;
"merely transformative" means that which causes all transformations.
*Oṣa* is like the pain caused by fire situated at one's side;
*ploṣa* is like a slight burning;
*dāha* is like the burning of all the limbs.
*Davathu*, known in common parlance as *dhakadhakikā*, is *dhūmaka*, which is like the emission of smoke;
it is the cracking of the skin, specifically the cracking of the outermost layer of skin alone; whereas *carmāvadaraṇa* is the splitting of all six layers of the skin.
When *raktapitta* is not associated with other *doṣas*, it should be known as purely *paittika* (bilious) *raktapitta*; likewise, in the case of thirst (*tṛṣṇā*), it is merely thirst;
and the eruptions (*sphoṭa*) that tear the flesh in the armpit region are the *kakṣā*, as described among the minor diseases (*kṣudraroga*) by Suśruta.
Foul odor is the smell of raw meat;
"according to its own" means similar to one's own smell, color, and taste; a house with fire is a fire-house.
*Balāsaka* is that by which one always feels as if satiated, as though the self were already full;
it is a wasting of strength (*balakṣaya*). Alternatively, *balāsaka* is a state of mild fever due to the excess of phlegm (*śleṣman*), or corpulence of the limbs.
The accumulation of vessels, the coating of the vessels,
coldness of the digestive fire, weak digestion, softness, and smoothness.
In the functions of *śleṣman* (phlegm), numbness occurs due to its lack of activity; however, in the case of *vāta* (wind), it is due to the lack of perception of touch.

By the statement "having entered the *āmāśaya*," the *āmāśaya* is shown to be the primary site among the locations of *śleṣman*. Yet, previously, by the statement "there too, the chest (*uraḥ*) specifically," the chest was shown to be primary. Thus, both [the *āmāśaya* and the chest] should be understood as equal.
Now, he explains the utility of the knowledge of disease in the context of treatment, beginning with the words "the disease" and so forth;
the connection is that one should examine the medicine.
The examination of the medicine is dependent upon the disease; therefore, the sense is that it must occur immediately thereafter.
Then, "action" refers to medical treatment;
"preceded by knowledge" means preceded by the knowledge generated from the observation of the action.
Regarding "compendium" (*saṅgraha*), the concise statement is "the four diseases," and so forth;
regarding "nature" (*prakṛti*), it is by means of the passage beginning with "furthermore, [it is] twofold";
and regarding "location" (*deśa*), it is by means of the passage beginning with "and their substratum is twofold."

"Vikāramukha" refers to the modifications (*vikāra*) and the openings (*mukha*). Among these, the modifications are explained by the passage beginning with "Furthermore, the modifications..."; the openings by the passage beginning with "The openings...";
the movement (*īraṇa*) by the passage beginning with "But of the two...";
and the absence of doubt (*asandeha*) by the passage beginning with "Nor mutually... and so forth.
By the words "in all" (*sarveṣu*) and so forth,
it is stated that "all those born of various selves" (23–25) refers to defects produced by other unassociated defects.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Great Diseases," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of Caraka, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the section on the quartet of diseases in the *Sūtrasthāna*.
[Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 21 (21 of 120)]

The diseases have been described in the "Quadruple on Diseases" (*rogacatuṣka*), and the remedies in the "Quadruple on Remedies" (*bheṣajacatuṣka*). Now, the "Quadruple on Application" (*yojanācatuṣka*) is stated in order to explain how the application of diseases and remedies should be carried out.

Furthermore, since that application generally depends upon the body itself in relation to the diseases and remedies, the "Chapter on the Eight Types of Bodies" (*aṣṭau-ninditīya*) is stated to demonstrate the different types of bodies.

By the phrase "with reference to the body," those who are censured with reference to the mind—such as the unrighteous, the miserly, and so forth—are excluded here as being irrelevant. Furthermore, six [defects] beginning with "excessively tall" are mentioned here because they fall under the topic of censure. Their state of being censured arises simply from public reproach.
The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "excessively tall and so forth" is intended to include other censured types, such as the hunchbacked and others.

In that regard, he says "tatra" and so forth in order to state the specific details useful for the medical treatment of those who are excessively obese or emaciated. The phrase "bhūya eva" (furthermore) refers to those who are censured because they exceed [the norm]— being like those who are excessively tall and so forth— and these censured ones are the "censured particulars" (*nindita-viśeṣāḥ*).
He states the cause of excessive corpulence with the words "that," etc.: "excessive filling" means overeating;
"due to the nature of the seed" means because it is produced from a large mother and father.
Now, he describes how even from common food, excessive fat is produced in one who is obese: "Of him," etc.

The term "medasvin" (one who has much fat) is an attributive epithet containing a reason; the meaning is that because in an excessively obese body fat has acquired its function by pervading the entire body, therefore it is primarily that which increases, and not the other elements such as *rasa* and so forth, because they have been overwhelmed by it.
The word "tasmāt" (therefore) refers to the state of having discordant bodily constituents (*viṣamadhātutva*).
"Due to the defect of fat" means that fat is foul-smelling by its very nature;
"even by nature" means that fat is foul-smelling due to its raw stench;
and "because of being sweaty" means that when there is sweat, the state of foul odor is established by direct experience—this is the meaning.
The affliction of perspiration (sveda) is to be understood as arising from causes such as the association with phlegm (śleṣman).

In the passage beginning with "by fat" (medas), because the wind (vāyu) is not excessively increased, it acts as a stimulator of the digestive fire (agni) rather than producing a state of imbalance; for it is only when the wind is excessively increased that it causes an imbalance of the fire.
The word "sa" refers to the obese person.

"Due to the lapse of time" means due to the passing of the proper time for eating; thus he describes the characteristics of one who is excessively corpulent with the verse beginning with "medo-māṃsa... and so forth.
5–9 – *vācya* means that which is to be expressed; or rather, "what is to be said" refers to that which is censured, meaning that which is blameworthy (*avadya*).
Measured eating is the consumption of food in small quantities; excessive application of therapy refers to the excessive administration of emetics and other treatments;
and *prakṛti* is the seed that generates the body.

The latent tendency (*anuśaya*) is the persistence (*anubandha*); it is the characteristic of one who is emaciated— “withered,” and so forth, ending with “reduced to skin and bone”— the word “is seen” being understood as the ellipsis.
"Having thick joints and thick knots" refers to [the two types of bamboo] by way of "emaciating" and "nourishing" respectively.
"Better" (*varam*) means slightly desirable;

[the author says] "one should rather afflict the gross one excessively" because the gross is difficult to treat. For, in the case of the gross, nourishment (*santarpaṇa*) causes excessive obesity, while depletion (*apatarpaṇa*) cannot be endured because of his increased digestive fire (*pravṛddhāgni*); however, for the weak, nourishment is indeed appropriate—this is the intended meaning.
16–17 Now he describes the praiseworthy person: "sametyādi" and so forth.
Here, by the word *māṃsa*, accumulation (*upacaya*) is intended; thus, one whose measure of accumulation is equal to that [of the body] is described as such.
*Saṃhanana* means a combination;
he now describes other qualities regarding the equal proportions of the flesh as well, beginning with "hunger" (*kṣud*) and so forth (verses 18–19).

Having thus explained the obese and the emaciated, he states the appropriate medicine for each: "Heavy," and so forth. That which is both heavy and non-satisfying—such as honey—is prescribed because its heaviness sustains an increased digestive fire, while its non-satisfying nature destroys fat (*medas*).
In this way, foods such as *praśātikā* rice and others, which are non-satisfying, should be given after their heaviness has been induced through processing (*saṃskāra*) and other means.

For those who are emaciated, light and nourishing food should be given; for that [light food], due to its lightness, increases the digestive fire, and due to its nourishing nature, it provides nourishment—both of these qualities being most desirable. Therefore, for the obese, that which is light and non-nourishing, such as *praśātikā*, *priyaṅgu*, and so forth, should be administered; likewise, even for the emaciated, heavy and nourishing food such as new grain (*navānna*) and the like should be administered. However, in those cases, the lightness or heaviness must be counteracted through processing (*saṃskāra*) and other means.

"Of *mākṣika*" means of honey. Nor should its nourishing (*bṛhaṇa*) quality be asserted simply because it is seen in aphrodisiac formulations (*vṛṣya-prayoga*); for honey is "conveying by association" (*yogavāhi*). When joined with an aphrodisiac, it produces aphrodisiac action; when joined with a scraping agent (*lekhana*), it performs scraping; likewise, even by its own nature, due to its association with qualities such as dryness (*rūkṣa*), it causes emaciation (*karśana*). For it is said: "And because it consists of various substances, honey is supremely 'conveying by association'" (Suśruta Sūtrasthāna 45).
The formulation beginning with *viḍaṅga* removes excessive obesity regardless of the patient's heaviness (*gaurava*), due to its specific potency (*prabhāva*).
*Praśātikā*, commonly known as *uḍikā*,
refers to small barley grains.
Cakramudgaka is commonly known as Ṛṣimudgaka; Āḍhakī is tuvarī.
He describes the treatment for emaciation (kārśya), beginning with "sleep" and so forth;
"śamaḥ" means tranquility.

Now, one might object: since heavy foods such as new grain (navānna) and the like must be counteracted through processing (saṃskāra) and other means for fear of weakening the digestive fire (agnimāndya), why are only light grains such as red rice (raktaśāli) not prescribed there? For these are light by nature and nourishing due to their association with sweet substances.

No, because both types are intended [as causes of nourishment]: red rice (*rakta-śāli*) and the like are light by nature (*prakṛti-laghu*) yet cause satiation (*tarpaṇa*); new grain (*nava-anna*) and the like are light through processing (*saṃskāra*) and the like, yet produce nourishment (*santarpaṇa*).
This same principle should be applied to the previously mentioned *praśātika* and other grains.
Furthermore, by the phrase "due to lack of reflection" (*acintanāt*) and so forth, the preeminent cause of nourishment (*bṛṃhaṇa-kāraṇa*) is stated.
29–34. Regarding the constant occurrence of dreams and excessive dreaming:

now, in accordance with the present context, he thoroughly examines sleep—which consists of the form of *nidrā*—as it is the primary factor in the treatment of corpulence and emaciation, beginning with the words "yadā tu" (but when).
"In the mind" means in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); or alternatively, the Self joined with the mind is called "the mind," and in that [mind] being "exhausted" means being inactive,
while the "karmic selves" refers to the senses being possessed by exhaustion and devoid of activity.

The sense is that when the mind does not engage with objects such as forms and so forth, the senses also do not function; at that time, one "sleeps," meaning one becomes endowed with the quality of sleep. And sleep is the abiding of the mind in a region devoid of the senses.
Or rather, the phrase "the selves whose nature is action" refers to the transmigrating selves (*saṃsāry-ātman*);

when the mind is fatigued, the selves become fatigued, because the activity of the selves is dependent upon the mind. Consequently, through the cessation of the mind, the selves no longer perceive objects, and the sense organs likewise do not function, simply because the selves do not engage them.

Now, he describes the virtue of sleep when practiced according to rule and the fault when practiced contrary to rule, with the passage beginning "Sleep-dependent" and ending with "and not. Here, pleasure and so forth are the fruit of sleep practiced according to rule, whereas pain and so forth are the fruit of sleep practiced contrary to rule; he analyzes this very point with the passage beginning "At the wrong time," and so on.

"Improper time" (*akāla*) refers to a time prohibited for sleep, such as at the beginning of the day; by this, "false application" (*mithyāyoga*) regarding sleep is expressed. "The night of Time" (*kālarātri*) is the dawn of Time, which is true intellect (*satyā buddhi*), that is, the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
Now, he describes those by whom sleep should be indulged in even during the day: "By singing," and so forth.
Here, for those exhausted by singing, health results when the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are nourished through daytime sleep.
In cases such as diarrhea, sleep even during the day is beneficial due to its specific therapeutic power (*prabhāva*).

For one suffering from indigestion (*ajīrṇin*), however, daytime sleep is for the purpose of digesting the undigested food (*ajīrṇapāka*); for sleep, by obstructing the channels, strengthens the digestive fire (*agni*) and thus quickly digests the food. For those accustomed to daytime sleep, there would indeed be a disorder if that habit were suddenly abandoned.

For those who have remained awake at night, daytime sleep is prescribed to pacify the agitation of the bodily winds (*vāta*) produced thereby; and that sleep should be undertaken according to the words of Kṣārapāṇi, as it is said: "As long as one has not slept during the night, [one should sleep] for that duration appropriate to one's sleep."

“Then, for that same duration, sleeping during the day (divāsvapna) is prescribed for half of that measure. And this daytime sleep is intended only for those who have not eaten, as stated by Hārīta: “One should not indulge in sleep after eating; even if one is healthy, one will become uncomfortable. It is also stated elsewhere regarding the prescription of daytime sleep following physical exercise and the like: “One may, at will, put men to sleep during the day while they are fasting. This is to be observed at all times, even excluding the summer season. Furthermore, by the phrase “because of the extreme brevity of the nights,” it indicates that there should be only a small amount of sleep.
Because of the statement, "They should never sleep [during the day]," daytime sleep is prohibited even in the summer for those who are obese and the like; however,
in cases such as exhaustion from singing, one should either engage in or abstain from daytime sleep after having carefully assessed one's strength and weakness.
"The onset of the force of poison" should be understood as pertaining to those afflicted by *dūṣīviṣa* (latent or slow-acting poison).
"One should sleep comfortably" means one should sleep in such a way that there is comfort; and that occurs through the abandonment of unwholesome sleep and the cultivation of wholesome sleep.

By the passage beginning with "rātrau" (at night), the dryness (*raukṣya*) and unctuousness (*snigdhatva*) of waking and sleep are metaphorically attributed [to them] because they perform their respective effects. Furthermore, waking—whether at night or by day—is inherently dry; however, waking during the day does not cause excessive dryness in the body because it is moistened by the sleep of the night. Waking at night, on the other hand, produces dryness; therefore, it is called "dry. The same should be said regarding sleeping during the day.
In connection with sleep, he states the qualities of the various types of sleep, beginning with "arūkṣam" (not dry).
"Non-stimulating" means not unctuous.
"Drowsiness while seated" refers to the indulgence in slight sleep by one who is sitting; as people say, this is the foremost among diversions.
He states the reason for the predominance of dreams in the verse beginning with "dehavṛttau" (in the functioning of the body);
"sukhe" means the cause of happiness. 51
He states the cause that produces dreams: "By massage," and so forth.
"The time is likewise appropriate" means that whatever time a person has become accustomed to sleeping is the appropriate time for him.
