The statement "due to the disappearance of [normal] causes" is intended to exclude sleep produced by *ariṣṭa* (fatal signs), for in the medical treatise (*śāstra*), *ariṣṭa* is said to be without [ordinary] cause.
52–54. Here he states the reason for the prohibition of sleep: "of the body," and so forth; *sattvaudāryam* means the abundance of the qualities of *sattva*.

"Conquest of darkness" means the conquest of the quality of *tamas*, and that occurs through the practice of yoga and so forth; it should be understood that these [remedies] are to be applied when one is in a state of health (*svastha*). However, if excessive sleep (*nidrātiprasaṅga*) has occurred, those [remedies] being applied serve to prohibit that excess.
He further states other causes for the destruction of sleep, beginning with "the task," etc.
"Work"—being attached to work, he does not go to sleep;
"time"—old age, for the elderly are by their very nature wakeful; "disturbance"—disease, such as colic and the like.

*Prakṛti* means inherent nature (*svabhāva*). Some people remain awake by their very nature. Although *vāta* (wind) is already understood through the mention of "disturbance" (*vikāra*), the explicit mention of *vāta* again is for the purpose of specifically demonstrating that wind is a remover of sleep.
He describes the specific types of sleep, beginning with "tamobhavā" (arising from *tamas*): Sleep arising from *tamas* is produced by the predominance of the *tamas* quality (*guṇa*).

However, sleep arising from fatigue of the mind and body occurs when, due to the exhaustion of the mind and body, the activities [of the senses] cease; consequently, neither the sense organs nor the mind engage with their objects, and thus sleep ensues. This fatigue intended here is not excessively increased, as it does not provoke the wind (*vāta*). Therefore, one should not ask why sleep is not destroyed by fatigue, given that fatigue generates *vāta*; for it is observed that sleep indeed occurs in those who are fatigued.
It is adventitious, acting as a portent of misfortune,

following after disease, and causing effects such as fevers arising from the derangement of the humors (sannipāta); because it arises from the very nature of the night, it is called "arising from the nature of the night" (rātrisvabhāvaprabhavā).
Sleep that manifests during the day arises precisely from [excessive] darkness and so forth (58).
Regarding these types of sleep, he describes the commendable and the censurable, beginning with the words "rātri" and so on.

It is called *bhūtadhātrī* because it sustains (*dadhāti*) and nourishes (*puṣṇāti*) living beings (*bhūtāni*). It is a *dhātrī*, like a nurse, in that it is the root—that is, the cause—of evil (*agha*), which is to say, sin. For one who is seized by *tamas* never performs virtuous conduct (*sadvṛtta*), which ought to be practiced due to its nature of being characterized by sleep; from that, unrighteousness (*adharma*) arises. Regarding "in diseases" (*vyādhiṣu*): these refer to bodily diseases; phlegm (*śleṣman*) and the others are indeed diseases, and among them, the element of sleep (*bhūtā nidrā*) is itself of the nature of a disease.

It is adventitious, arising from an incurable disease, and is itself of an incurable nature in the form of a disease; therefore, they designate it among diseases. Alternatively, the meaning should be understood as "they designate it among the bases (ādhāra) of diseases.
(59) In the *Saṅgraha*, "for one who is sleepless" means for a person in whom sleep is absent.
"And according to their respective powers" refers to the powers described in the verses beginning with "the supporter of beings" (bhūtadhātrī), etc.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Fourfold Application: The Eight Things to be Avoided," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the section on the fourfold application in the *Sūtrasthāna*.

21 [Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 22 (22 of 120)]: Having described the body as that which requires application (*yojanā*), this chapter titled "On Lightening and Nourishing" (*laṅghanabṛṃhaṇīya*) is now expounded in order to explain, both by way of its subject matter and its essential nature, lightening (*laṅghana*) and other such therapies, since application itself has lightening and the rest as its domain.
"Impelling" means instigating for the sake of knowledge; in the phrase "done," etc., "done" means properly performed.
In the passage beginning with "roughness" (raukṣya), roughness alone should be understood as the primary factor; coarseness (kharatva) and clarity (vaiśadya), however, are subordinate to it.
"Flowing" (visyanda) means liquefaction (vilayana).
It causes perspiration, it causes heat,
it obstructs— that is, it restrains—
what is moving, that is, whatever possesses motion.
"Gatimantam" means having a manifest movement;

this should be understood to apply to cases of diarrhea, hemorrhage, poisoning, burning sensations, pain, and so forth, and not merely to vāta alone, because a stabilizing agent increases that which possesses movement.
In the phrase "guru" and so on, it means abundant or dense.
"Slow" (*manda*) means acting over a long period of time;
"gross" (*sthūla*) means having compact constituent parts, such as *laḍḍuka* sweets or flour-based preparations.

Although it has been stated that whatever qualities characterize a lightening (*laṅghana*) substance also characterize a drying (*virūkṣaṇa*) substance, nevertheless, the quality of dryness (*rūkṣa*) is predominant here, whereas in lightening, the quality of lightness (*laghu*) is to be understood as predominant. Furthermore, lightening can be accomplished by fasting (*upavāsa*), which is not a [substantial] drug, whereas drying is stated to be predominant precisely because it is an action produced by a substance. Therefore, lightening and drying are not identical.

As for what will be stated—“The sign of ‘excessively performed’ (kṛtātikṛta) is that which occurs when [the treatment] has been surpassed and [the body] has become parched (virūkṣita)” — that is said by way of a general rule (*prāyovāda*).

For the primary objective of parching (*virūkṣaṇa*) is the removal of unctuousness (*sneha*), whereas the objective of fasting (*laṅghana*) is the removal of heaviness (*gaurava*); thus, the distinction between them appears quite clear.
In the description of the qualities of sudation (*svedana*), the terms "unctuous" (*snigdha*) and "parched" (*rūkṣa*) mean either unctuous or parched, respectively.
In this way, *saras* and *sthira* should also be understood through their respective alternatives:
*pipāsā* refers to the suppression of thirst,
and although *māruta* does not constitute fasting (*laṅghana*) due to its connection with *soma*, nevertheless, by its very nature, it is indeed fasting.

That which causes digestion by counteracting opposing factors and providing strength while the digestive fire is already cooking is called *pācana* (digestive); it is predominantly characterized by the qualities of air (*vāyu*) and fire (*agni*).
There are four types of purification (*saṃśuddhi*), excluding *anuvāsana* (unctuous enema), because the latter is nourishing (*bṛṃhaṇa*).
He states the distinct scope for the ten types of fasting already mentioned— beginning with the words "prabhūta" and so forth—
the word "first" (ādau) is used because emesis and other therapies are to be pacified [only] once they have become free from morbid humors (nirāma).
"Rogas" refers to diseases that require fasting (*laṅghana*).
"Of the strong" (*balinām*) is a term intended to indicate that those with great strength alone may practice physical exercise (*vyāyāma*) and so forth.

"Of moderate strength" (*madhyabalān*) means even those of moderate strength; by this it is implied that, directly speaking, only diseases of minor strength are the objects for physical exercise and the like.
For those who are obese or require nourishment,

lightening therapy (laṅghana) is recommended; thus, all ten types [of therapies] are indicated during the "cold" season— that is, during both Hemanta and Śiśira, which possess the qualities of coldness— and in this context, lightening therapy should be performed because living beings possess strength.
*Adigdhaviddha* means pierced by a weapon smeared with poison;
*sātmyacāriṇaḥ* refers to those that roam in their accustomed habitats.

"Laghava" means light [substances] by virtue of their processing (*saṃskāra*); alternatively, it refers to the meat juices of those birds of prey that are light, such as hawks and the like. This is to be construed with the phrase "the consumption of honey and so forth. (25–28)
Khali refers to mustard-seed dregs (sarṣapakhali); piṇyāka refers to sesame dregs (tilakhali), or alternatively, oil-cake (piṇyāka) and potherbs (śāka).
By the inclusion of the word "etc. (prabhṛti), wealthy persons, those suffering from vāta-type urinary disorders (vātaprameha), and others are to be understood.
That which is thin and not thick is *sara*;
it moves or goes, thus it is *sara*. That which is not *sara* is *asara*, meaning stable.
The term *kṣutpipāsāsahodayaḥ* refers to the arising of hunger and thirst as causes of affliction that one is unable to endure, rather than the simultaneous arising of hunger and thirst.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*: "One whose wind, feces, and urine have been discharged, who can endure hunger and thirst, and who is light [of body]... (*Su. U.*).
"Taṃ" (39), etc.;
"in the inner self" means in the mind.
Agitation of the mind is indeed delusion; wind in the upper part of the body is upward-moving wind (ūrdhvavāta).
"Abandoning the defects of emaciation" means the avoidance of those defects associated with emaciation, such as intolerance of cold, heat, and so forth.
"When strength is regained" means when the person becomes strong as described by the statements beginning with "those who have been burnt by bile, alkali, or fire";
"distress" refers to the upward rush of wind (ūrdhvavātavega), or alternatively, a lack of desire for medicine.
Regarding the phrase "then of the medicinal substances," this refers to those [diseases] treatable by fasting and similar measures;
and "only an increase" occurs because the mere agitation of the *doṣas* has been produced by the performance of actions such as fasting for only a small duration.

Regarding the term "dhātūnām," it refers to the *doṣas*, because of the statement: "The *doṣas* also receive the designation 'dhātu'. (41–42) Now, he describes the combination (*saṃsarga*) of the aforementioned treatments such as fasting (*laṅghana*) with respect to the specific morbidities (*vikāra*), beginning with the words "of the *doṣas*" and so forth.

Since there are many combinations of the *doṣas*, for that reason the therapeutic measures (*upakrama*) intended to treat them also become combined and reach a state of mixture—such as, in some cases, fasting and sudation, and in others, nourishing and oleation—and so forth. However, even when combined, they do not transcend the nature of the sixfold [therapeutic measures]; thus, even when mixed, they do not abandon their essential character as fasting and the rest. The point is that fasting and the other measures, when joined with one another, do not initiate a different effect independent of their inherent qualities (*prakṛti-guṇa*), unlike the combination of honey and ghee.
Regarding this very point, he states an illustration: "The state of being three," and so forth.
And this illustration serves merely to show that the number of the related entities is not abandoned.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "On Lightening and Nourishing Therapies," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the section of four chapters on application (*yojanācatuṣka*) in the *Sūtrasthāna*.
[Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 23 (23 of 120)]

Having explained the six therapeutic measures, which are of two types—namely *santarpaṇa* (nourishing) and *apatarpaṇa* (depleting)—the person to be nourished (*santarpaṇīya*) is now described in order to demonstrate their application to two distinct categories of subjects.
[Verse 1–2:
"He nourishes" means he practices nourishment (*santarpaṇa*).

The statement beginning with "by unctuous [substances]" (*snigdhaiḥ*) is intended to prohibit nourishing therapy (*santarpaṇa*) even by substances such as parched grain flour (*śaktu*), which, though not unctuous, produce mere satiety; for the term "nourishing" (*santarpaṇa*) is indeed applied to that which produces satiety, as seen in this very context regarding the administration of nourishment: "One should drink sixteen parts of parched grain flour as a nourishing agent.

Furthermore, although aversion to activity is already implied by the phrase "delighting in the comfort of beds and seats," the explicit mention of it serves to prohibit activities such as moving the limbs or singing while remaining on one's bed or seat.
The disorders arising from undigested food (*āmadoṣa*) include cholera-like conditions (*visūcikā*) and others.
Constant drowsiness and deep reflection (3–7);
"the consumption of *abhayā* with honey" means the consumption of *harītakī* along with honey; or alternatively, the consumption of the *agastyaharītakyādi* formulation.
Regarding the phrase "and those which have been mentioned" in the *Āragvadhīya* chapter (Sūtra 3):

"by that" means by that decoction acting as the instrument (*karaṇa*); "of one practicing" means of one performing the practice (*abhyāsa*). Alternatively, the construction may be: "practicing the *triphalā* and so forth with that decoction."
"According to the [nature of the] dosha" means that it is taken into account in relation to the measure of the dosha;
"udvartana" (rubbing) consists merely of what is grasped, preceded by anointment (*abhyaṅga*), whereas "uddharṣa" (massage) is not preceded by anointment;
"with substances combined with unctuousness" means those employed as the means for achieving unctuousness.
Gomedaka is a specific kind of gem;
krauñca is a bird known as 'koñca';
kharāhvā is ajamodā.
"Plunged in iron-water" means plunged in *aguru*-water;
and the preparation of the water is according to the six-limbed water-rite (*ṣaḍaṅga-jalavidhāna*).

In this application, the quantity of the powder and so forth should be understood through association with the proportions stated for the *vyoṣa* (the three pungents) and other ingredients that will be mentioned hereafter.

"Santarpaṇa" (satiating) refers to its form as *śakti* stirred with water; by this, it should be understood that even that which is designated as "satiating" (*santarpaṇa*) possesses the quality of "desiccation" (*apatarpaṇa*).
"Śvaitrya" means the state of being white-spotted (*śvitrita*); in the reading "śvaitya," it means the appearance of whiteness.
"Upward-moving wind and so forth" refers to those mentioned in the preceding chapter, beginning with "upward-moving wind [causes] darkness in the heart" (Sūtra 22).

*Ūrdhvavāta* refers to conditions such as dyspnea (*śvāsa*) and others where the wind moves upward; alternatively, it may refer to a specific disease mentioned in other medical treatises (*tantrāntara*), such as: "When the downward-moving wind is obstructed by aggravated phlegm (*śleṣman*), it causes constant belching; that is called *ūrdhvavāta*" (26–30).

He states the distinction between the scope of the two types of *tarpaṇa* (satisfying therapy) mentioned—namely, *sadyastarpaṇa* (immediate satisfying) and *abhyāsatarpaṇa* (habitual satisfying)—with the verse beginning with "sadyas" and so forth. By the expression "not hurrying," he indicates that if *tarpaṇa* is administered with haste to one who has been weak for a long time, it causes defects such as the destruction of the digestive fire (*agni*). The terms "*tarpaṇās*" and "*atarpaṇās*" refer to those things, such as *mantha* (a churned drink), which produce the effect of *santarpaṇa* (over-saturation). Therefore, here only those substances designated by the name "*tarpaṇa*" that cause over-saturation are intended; those such as *vyoṣa* (the three pungents) and others which cause desaturation (*apatarpaṇa*) are not to be included. Rather, it refers specifically to those described in the passage beginning with "śarkarā-pippalī" and so forth.
Other churned drinks (*mantha*) mentioned here should also be understood according to the measurements stated in the *Śarkarādi-mantha* [formula] (verses 31–38).
With the verse beginning "sweet and sour" (*svāduramla*), etc., he describes an immediate satiation (*sadyastarpaṇa*).

Regarding the term *amla* (sour): due to the addition of sour pomegranate and other such ingredients, even a churned drink (*mantha*) made from dry roasted barley flour (*rūkṣasaktu*) possesses an immediate satiating quality through its liquidity, coolness, and capacity to permeate the body; for this very reason, the word "immediately" (*sadyaḥ*) is used. However, through the addition of unctuous substances and other nourishing (*bṛṃhaṇa*) ingredients, it also possesses the quality of providing satisfaction over a period of time.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "Those Requiring Satiation," in the *Yojanācatuṣka* of the *Sūtrasthāna*, within the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of Caraka composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 24 (24 of 120)]

Now, because blood, like wind and other humors, is the cause of many disorders, this chapter on the "Proper Treatment of Blood" (vidhiśoṇitīya) is being expounded in order to specifically demonstrate the previously mentioned therapeutic measures for blood disorders, such as lightening (laṅghana), nourishing (bṛṃhaṇa), and so forth;
this designation is also intended to convey its specific meaning.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the rule": it becomes pure through the correct rule of diet and conduct; here, the word *bhavati* (becomes) has the sense of "exists" (*vidyate*), because the act of arising has already been expressed by the word *jāta* (born).
To the question "By what rule?", he says: "place," and so forth.

The term *sātmya* is to be construed individually with "place" (*deśa*) and the others; thus, "habitat-sātmya" (*okasātmya*) and "habituation-sātmya" (*abhyāsasātmya*) have been elucidated in the chapter on the "Eighty [Substances]" (*tasyāśitīya*, Sūtra-sthāna 6). Regarding the word "elucidated" (*samprakāśita*), the word "by that" (*tena*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis; therefore, the connection is: "by that procedure which has been elucidated."

Others explain it as follows: first, blood comes into being; and that, having become corrupted by other causes, becomes pure again through the prescribed method—this is how the connection should be understood.
He states what purified blood does: "That purified [blood]," and so forth.

By that method it is purified; that which is purified is what? It is blood, for the vital breath (prāṇa) follows the blood; thus it conforms to the positive and negative concomitance of the blood, as it has been said: "They say there are exactly ten bases in which the vital breaths are established."
"The two temples, the three vital points (marmans), the throat, blood, semen, ojas, and the anus" (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 29).
Having thus stated the causes of purification, he now states the causes of corruption, beginning with "praduṣṭa... and so forth.

"Corrupted" means contrary to its own nature and by other things of that same kind, such as corrupted drinks and so forth; or rather, there is a reading "by foods," and some describe this as referring to medicinal substances, since the phrase "by things of that kind" includes foods and drinks that are excessively salty and so on.
Niṣpāva is the white-podded grain;
over-eating (atyādāna) is eating beyond satiety;
and "at the [wrong] time" refers to the autumn season when blood is corrupted.

*Ajīrṇādhyāśana* means eating while there is indigestion (*ajīrṇa*). Alternatively, *ajīrṇāśana* refers to the consumption of food when it is undigested (*apakva*), whereas *adhyāśana* is that which is eaten upon the remnants of a previous meal. As it is said: "That which is eaten on top of what has already been eaten is called *adhyāśana*" (Ci. A. 15). *Upakuśa* is a specific type of mouth disease. As stated in the Suśruta Saṃhitā: "There is burning and suppuration in the gums, and because of these, the teeth become loose."
"In which [fever], the disease named upakuśa, caused by pitta and blood, occurs" (Sūtra-sthāna, Nidāna 16).
Although "kuṣṭha" is mentioned, the specific term "carmadalābhidhāna" (the designation of skin-scaling) is used for the sake of precision.
By the expression "having their seat in the blood" (*śoṇitāśrayāḥ*), he refutes the independent causality of blood as a disease, similar to that of vāta and the other humors.
He states "cold, heat," etc., in order to include the many diseases of the blood not previously mentioned.
By the inclusion of the word "first" (*ādi*), the sharp (*tīkṣṇa*), mild (*mṛdu*), and other qualities are included;
the word "properly" (*samyak*) is to be construed with the preceding term.

In this context, by the phrase "by cold, hot, unctuous, dry, and so forth," it should be understood that these are employed solely for the purpose of overcoming *vāta* and the other humors, without regard for an increase in blood (*śoṇita*).

Since even the pacification of blood disorders occurs through the aforementioned treatments for *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic diseases) and so forth—which involve procedures such as cold, hot, and unctuous applications—it follows that blood diseases are also alleviated by cold and other such measures that are antagonistic to blood. However, when Vata and the other doshas have become established in the blood, they do not subside through their own specific treatments alone due to the influence of their substrate (*āśraya*).
(Verses 11–17) He describes the treatment for blood diseases, beginning with "one should perform," etc.
Therapeutic measures for the pacification of *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders) and so forth should be understood according to their appropriateness.
(18) He states the prescribed measure for bloodletting: "In strength," and so forth.

"According to the measure of strength and the morbidity" means having observed the measure of the patient's strength as well as the morbidity in the form of the blood disease; for this word "morbidity" (doṣa) refers here to the disease, as in the phrase "and by the purification of the blood," meaning by whatever amount of bleeding the blood becomes purified from its seat or location, that is, from the site where the corrupted blood resides.

For example, in the case of a minor skin disease (kuṣṭha), only a small amount [of blood] should be taken for the sake of purification; whereas in a major skin disease, a large amount must be drained.
As it has been said: "Scraping (pracchana) is recommended for minor skin diseases, while venesection (sirāvyadhana) is praised for major ones" (Cikitsā-sthāna 7).
And among these alternatives, whatever is not contradictory in a given case should be accepted there.
(19) He states the characteristics of vitiated blood: "having a reddish luster," and so forth.
It thickens and becomes solid;
*tapanīya* is red gold; *indragopa* is a specific type of insect well-known by its own name.
The various colors on a pure red *liṅga* arise from the human constitution (*prakṛti*) consisting of wind (*vāta*) and the other [humors].
(22) He states the reason for not consuming food that is excessively hot and so forth, beginning with "tadā" and so on.

Excessive cold causes a deficiency of digestive fire (agni-māndya), while excessive heat causes the already mobile blood to become excessively agitated; therefore, food that is neither too hot nor too cold, but light and digestive-stimulating, should be consumed solely for the purpose of kindling the digestive fire.
Now, even in the absence of visible blood, he states the diagnostic signs for the purpose of knowing pure blood: "prasanna... and so forth.
One whose digestion is unimpeded and whose urges of feces and so forth are likewise unobstructed is described as such.
Now, he describes those diseases that arise from the vitiation of blood-carrying vessels, beginning with the words "When, however," and so forth.

"Carriers of consciousness" (*sañjñāvahāni*) means carriers of the mind which is the cause of consciousness; for the mind has the body alone as its vehicle. As it has been said: "Furthermore, the body alone is the vehicle for *sattva* and the other [qualities]" (Vi.
5), and so on. Alternatively, they are called "carriers of consciousness" because they carry the constituent element known as *rasa* (nutritive fluid).
The heart is the seat of the rasa-carrying vessels (rasavahā dhamanī), and from its impairment, delusion (moha) necessarily arises.
The term "impurities" (mala) is a designation for the vitiated doshas; as it has been said: "They are called impurities because they cause defilement.

One should understand that the form of delusion increases progressively through intoxication (mada), fainting (mūrchā), and the loss of consciousness (sannyāsa). For even in intoxication there is a slight degree of delusion, whereas in the latter two states, delusion is manifest.
Speaking harshly is harsh speech (paruṣābhāṣa).
He states the nature of intoxication (mada) with the words beginning "is born" (jāyate), etc.
Regarding the fourfold nature of intoxication (*mada*) resulting from the excessive indulgence in liquor, poison, and the three *doshas*, he says "yaśca" and so forth.

"From the triad of vāta, pitta, and kapha" means from vāta, from pitta, from kapha, and from vāta-pitta-kapha combined. By this, the intention is that their characteristics are likewise produced by vāta and the other *doshas*.

He states the characteristics of fainting (mūrchāya): "Blue," and so forth. Regarding that, some raise the objection that in vāta-type fainting, the complexion is dark-brownish-red (śyāvāruṇā), which, because it is of the nature of a fatal sign (riṣṭa) and due to its association with vāyu, would lead to death; for it has been said: "That [complexion] belonging to vāyu leads to destruction or even to great suffering" (Indriyasthāna 7).

That is not so; for a shadow is an ill omen (*riṣṭa*) only when it is causeless, but not when a visible cause is perceived, and here the connection with the wind is indeed seen as the cause. Alternatively, by the very statement "or even to great affliction," the deadly nature of the shadow of the wind is shown to be inconsistent [with the general rule]. Or, "by dense darknesses" means *tamoghanaiḥ*; or rather, "by dense darknesses alone," meaning without the loathsome movements such as gnashing teeth or contorting limbs.
He states the defining characteristic that distinguishes *saṃnyāsa* (collapse) from fainting (*mūrchā*) and other conditions, beginning with the words "when the humors... and so forth.

The phrase "having produced their impulse" (*kṛtavegeṣu*) means that after having manifested their force, the humors have become depleted in strength; for the impulse of the humors is the cause of the loss of strength. As it is said regarding irregular fever (*viṣamajvara*): "Having produced its impulse, [the fever] has lost its strength" (Ci.).
3) "They renounce" means they make [the body] motionless;
"the abode of the vital breaths" refers to the heart.
The word "muktvā" (excepting) means "not having attained immediate results";
"sadyaḥphalāḥ" (yielding immediate fruit) refers to sharp collyriums and the like that cause instant awakening;
and "with needles" is connected with the act of piercing.
"Sammūrcchitāni" means mixed together;
"gālayet" means one should strain them and carefully pour them into the mouth.
Some say that *sauvīraka* should be used in place of *sauvarcala*.
The continuous consequence [is understood] from the cause of dissolution, that is, from the cause of delusion. 42–53.

The connection is as follows: "of the twenty-eight-ingredient [ghee]," "of the Pānīyakalyāṇa," "of the Mahātiktaka," and likewise "of the Tiktaka-ṣaṭpala" and "the Mahātiktaka. These two—the Tikta-ṣaṭpala and Mahātiktaka ghees—are to be described in the treatment of skin diseases (kuṣṭha-cikitsita), along with the Kaumbha-sarpis and the Daśābdika.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Bloodletting," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by the venerable Cakrapāṇidatta, within the section on the Fourfold Application (*yojanācatuṣka*) in the *Sūtrasthāna*. 54–58.

[Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 25 (25 of 120)] These six therapeutic measures mentioned within a distance of four *yojanas* are capable of removing disease only by means of food and drink; therefore, the "Quadruple of Food and Drink" (*annapānacatuṣka*) is described.
Within that, the chapter titled "The Origin of Man" (*Yajjaḥpuruṣīya*), which briefly explains the qualities of food and drink, is now set forth.

In this regard, first, the chapter concerning the determination of the causes of human disease—which was composed primarily with reference to the question "From what is a person born? for the purpose of introducing the inquiry into the qualities of food, as well as for the purpose of knowing the previously mentioned six causes of diseases that require treatment—should be known as the *Yajjapuruṣīya* (On Whence a Person Is Born). Although the sequence of the question is "A person is from what" (*puruṣo yajjaḥ*), nevertheless, the meaning of the question is taken up here [as *yajjaḥpuruṣa*].
The state of having dharma directly perceived through the power of asceticism—
this refers to the narrative to be told hereafter—
and the mutual questioning for the sake of desiring to know the truth.
"Rāśi" means a collection; that is to say, the aggregate of the self, the senses, the mind, and objects.
The connection [of the sentence] is that a discourse concerning the determination of the origin of this aggregate and of diseases appeared.
He demonstrates that very dialogue in the form of mutual questioning with the words "tadantaram" and so forth.
The word *antara* here denotes time; as in: "After a short interval (*kiñcid athāntaram*), they bring on the paroxysm of epilepsy" (Ci.
10). The meaning is "after some time"; therefore, "tadantaram" means the time at which the dialogue begins.

Kāśī is Vārāṇasī; its lord is [the Sun]. Because there are many such lords, a qualification is given: "Vāmaka. Since he was born from that, he is "Yajja" (born of sacrifice). From that very cause, the person-generating source, those born are "Tajjāḥ" (born of that);
or else, they are not so born, meaning the person is born from one source and his diseases from another.
By the lord of men, that royal sage named the Lord of Kāśī (5–6),
those whose doubts have been severed by the two immeasurables— namely, knowledge (*jñāna*) and realization (*vijñāna*)— are thus described.
The reading “*bhavantaśchettumarhanti kāśirājasya saṃśayam*” is straightforward.
However, in the reading “*bhavantoarhanti naśchettuṃ kāśirāje ca saṃśayam*,” the word *naḥ* means “of us,” and *kāśirāje* means “in the King of Kāśī who is among us.
By this, he instructs that one should not utter words of delusion regarding the King of Kāśī within one’s own faction.
By the word "ca" (and), he combines the doubts of other sages as well.
However, others explain it as: "our doubt and the doubt regarding the King of Kāśī.

Regarding these two doubts, one is shown here by the verse beginning with "ātmendriya... (the self, the senses, etc.); they explain that this doubt concerns the prior origin—that is, the first production—of both the person and diseases. The second doubt, however, is exactly as stated concerning the Lord of Kāśī.

7. This is the answer to the two questions beginning with "Is the person born of the self? and so forth. Among them, the answer to the first question—namely, the question regarding from where the person and the diseases arise—is: "The person and the diseases are born of the self. Even though this was merely a question posed by the Lord of Kāśī, the answer is this very same point: that from the very source from which the person is born, from that same source the diseases arise.
Thus, the fact that this text serves as an answer to the question is indeed easy to understand.
He states the reason for its being a cause: "It accumulates," and so forth.
The construction is as follows: it accumulates karma and experiences the fruits of karma, such as the body's health or its various transformations.
The intended meaning is that the self, assisted by karma, possesses causality because it is the agent of the body's transformations and so on.
He states this very point by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka) with the words "nahyṛte" and so forth.

The element of consciousness (cetanādhātu), which is the self (ātman), [is not affected] "by pleasure and pain"— that is, by the causes of pleasure and pain, meaning by the bodily changes consisting of health and disease.

If "eight or nine *manas*" is stated, one might suspect that the *ātman* is also intended, based on the etymology "that by which one thinks" (*manyate 'nena*). To this it is said: [the term] "designated as *sattva*" [is used] because the bodily afflictions such as emaciation, produced by wind and other humors, do not exist apart from the body; likewise, it should be construed that the mind does not persist apart from the body.

For a mind perpetually enveloped by *rajas* and *tamas* remains fixed within the body itself; however, that mind which is free from defects is neither the cause of the person (*puruṣa*) nor of disease—this is the intended meaning.

In passages such as "born of *rasa*," it is stated that they are the causes of manifestation (*nirvṛtti-hetu*). Thus, because water is the cause of the *rasas* which generate both disease and the person, water serves as the cause of the modifications of the person by way of being the cause of the cause.
Or rather, the construction is: "Are water the causes of the manifestation of tastes? or "Since water possesses taste, it is therefore the cause of their manifestation.

(10–13) Regarding the passage beginning with "not the self," the construction is: "the mind is not remembered as being born of taste, for it is beyond the senses. Since the mind is beyond the senses and the self is also beyond the senses, they are not born of taste. The meaning is that whatever is born from taste would necessarily be perceptible by the senses, because it follows the qualities of its cause.
He states another reason, beginning with "santi" and so forth;
the meaning is that taste is not the cause of the transformation produced by harmful sounds, forms, and so on.
The six elements (dhātavaḥ) are the self and the five [elements] beginning with earth.
As it has been said: "The elements beginning with space, with consciousness as the sixth, are traditionally held to constitute the person" (Śā.

The objection "Why is the name of Hiraṇyākṣa 'Kuśika'? implies that, since the collection of the six elements exists in all living beings regardless of their parents, there would be no distinction between humans, cattle, horses, and so forth. This is the intended meaning.

He states another reason: "The hereditary diseases such as urinary disorders (meha) and others have been mentioned. They are called *pitryā* because they pass from the father to the offspring; by the word "others" (*ādi*), leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), and so forth are to be understood.
He shows his own position [on the matter] by saying: "In this case, those two are the cause"; that is, the mother and the father.
"For indeed, not being blind," and so forth;
the meaning is that if the mother and father were the cause [of sight], then one born of a blind person would necessarily be blind.
He states another reason: "Of the mother and father as well," and so forth.

For you, who maintain that the parents are the cause, there would be no production of the mother and father "previously"—that is, at the beginning of creation. The sense is that since there are no bodies at the beginning of creation, the production of the first mother and father is not logically tenable.

Regarding the passage beginning with "The agent was previously," the ellipsis is "the agent existed prior to the action. Since that person by which [an action] is to be performed must exist prior to that action, the status of being a cause must be admitted for the person. Consequently, the point is: if the person existed without the action, how can the action be the cause of the person?
Now, it might be suspected that there exists some uncreated action (*akṛta-karman*) at the beginning which produces the person; to this he says: "And [it] is not seen," etc.
An uncreated action is not seen, meaning it is not apprehended by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The sense is that all things, consisting of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), arise solely from the performance of auspicious and inauspicious actions.
The cause of existence is the cause of origination.
Regarding its inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*), he provides an illustration beginning with "solid" (*khara*) and so forth:
"Solidity, fluidity, mobility, and heat are the [respective] qualities of earth, water, air, and fire" (Śā. 5.38). "Of those ending with fire" (*tejo'ntānām*).
1) It would occur in the manner to be explained in the following verses (20–21).

Regarding the phrase "from their own nature" (*svabhāvāt*), the word "if" (*yadi*) must be supplied at the beginning. Thus, the meaning is: if the success or failure of entities—such as bodies and so forth—were to occur solely from their own nature, then the fruit of undertaking [actions] would not exist, because entities would be inherent by nature; consequently, these undertakings of sacrifice, agriculture, study, and so forth, which are established in the world and in the scriptures, would become purposeless, since they would lack a cause.
In the passage beginning with "the creator" (*sraṣṭā*), the construction is as follows: Prajāpati is the creator of the world and of pleasure and pain;

and he is the offspring of Brahmā, possessing immeasurable resolve. This means that by virtue of being the agent who simultaneously produces effects in the form of infinite stationary and moving beings, his resolve to generate them is likewise immeasurable.
"Asādhuvat" means like one who is unrighteous; "apatyadrohakārī" means one who harms his offspring.
"Pakṣasaṃśrayāt" means due to partiality arising from attachment.

"Uncertain" means that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), they are indeed uncertain; however, due to attachment to one's own position (*pakṣarāga*) and the excellence of one's intellect, they are merely designated as "positions" (*pakṣāḥ*) as if they were certain—this is the meaning. "The end of the position" (*pakṣāntam*) refers to the determination of the correct meaning.

A "sesame-presser" (*tilapīḍaka*) is a person standing upon a press for the sake of oil. Just as a sesame-presser, even when moving—that is, while walking—does not reach the end because he does not reach his destination, since he continues to revolve in that very place; so too is the case for the disputant who relies on a [dogmatic] position. This is the meaning.
*Saṅghaṭṭaḥ* is a collision that causes mutual pressure; *melakaḥ* is a meeting; *adhyātmaṃ tattvaṃ* is the internal reality; *skandhaḥ* is an aggregate.
In this context, attachment to one's own position (*pakṣarāga*) is called a "mass of darkness" (*tamaskandha*) because it acts as an obstacle to the knowledge of reality.
He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words beginning "of those" (*yeṣām*):
"of those" refers to those of a particular class; and these [beings] consist of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth.
By that very fact of being the great elements (*mahābhūta*), the inclusion of wind and the others is accomplished;
"excellence" (*sampat*) refers to the state of possessing praiseworthy qualities,
and "man" (*nara*) refers to the person who possesses those [qualities].
The statement "misfortune" means that one would bring about a deficiency;
and the presentation of these words of the sages is for the purpose of removing the student's doubts through hearing the prima facie arguments and the established conclusions.

By the restrictive statement that "the consumption of wholesome food is the only [means]," [the author] demonstrates its primacy, not by way of excluding other factors; for conduct, sleep, and so forth, as well as sound and the rest, have also been stated to be causes [of disease].

The term *vyādhinimittam* (cause of disease) should be understood through the elision of the middle term (*madhyapadalopa*) as meaning "the cause of the increase of disease," since it is specifically the cause of increase that was inquired about. Furthermore, the fact that unwholesome food is a cause of disease has already been stated by the verse: "These very [factors], when impaired, would arouse various diseases."

Or rather, by the general term "cause of disease" (*vyādhinimitta*), both the primary cause (*janaka*) and the contributory cause (*vardhaka*) are denoted without exception. To state the reason why it is difficult to discern what is beneficial or harmful, he says: "Of those things designated as beneficial," and so forth.
"Contrary action" means that wholesome food becomes unwholesome, and likewise unwholesome food becomes wholesome, depending on factors such as dosage (*mātrā*).
In this regard, wholesome items such as red *śāli* rice become unwholesome due to the fault of dosage when they are taken in excessive or deficient amounts.

Similarly, by virtue of time (*kāla*), those same red *śāli* rice grains are not beneficial in the winter for those with strong digestive fires because of their lightness. Here, by the word "time," only the ever-changing (*nityaga*) time is intended, since the situational (*āvasthika*) time is already included under the term "person's state" (*puruṣāvasthā*).

The term *kriyā* refers to processing; by that [processing], red rice (*raktaśāli*) becomes affected by defects of the cooked grain (*odanadoṣa*), such as being improperly steamed or not having drained its water. Likewise, that same [grain] becomes unwholesome when grown in a marshy region due to its connection with the soil. Furthermore, in relation to the body, red rice is not beneficial for those who have an excess of fat (*medasvin*) because of its lightness. As it has been said: "It is considered heavy and non-satisfying, and is intended for the emaciation of those who are corpulent" (Sūtra 21).
Likewise, that same [principle] applies when the fault (*doṣa*) is located in the wind (*vāyu*); here, by the word "fault," disease (*vyādhi*) is also to be understood.

Similarly, for a person in the state of childhood, which is dominated by phlegm (*śleṣman*), bitter and other such substances are wholesome; however, those same substances are not wholesome in old age when wind is aggravated.
Furthermore, the term "different state" (*avasthāntara*) is connected with each of the factors, beginning with the measure (*mātrā*).
In this way, even that which is unbeneficial should be understood as beneficial through its inclusion [in the category] of mother and so forth.
He establishes the final position (siddhānta) with the words beginning "whatever food... and so on.

And by this passage, it is shown that the quality of being beneficial or harmful does not belong to things by their own nature, but rather depends upon factors such as the dosage; however, [the phrase] "not this," etc.—
where "this" refers to the beneficial and the harmful— is stated.
The connection is as follows: they will not understand that which has been taught—namely, the category of food and so forth characterized by such descriptions.

Without knowledge of the various conditions such as dosage (*mātrā*) and so on regarding these characteristics of what is beneficial and what is harmful, it is impossible to know the wholesomeness or unwholesomeness of wholesome items like red *śāli* rice and the like, or of unwholesome items like *yavaka* grain and the like. The implication is that because the states of dosage and so forth are difficult to discern, all physicians are incapable of knowing them.
33–34 This very point— that the characteristic is not known by all physicians— is stated in the passage beginning with "yeṣām hi" and so forth;
"guṇataḥ" here, in this context, means according to qualities such as heaviness, lightness, and so on.

"By substance" means by way of its cause, as for example: "this is watery, this is fiery," and so forth; or alternatively, "by substance" refers to the dietary substance such as red rice and the like, while "by action" (karma) means by way of its effect, as for example: "this is life-sustaining, this is nourishing," and so forth;
and "in all its parts" refers to its taste, potency, post-digestive transformation, and specific power.
The sequence beginning with *mātrā* (measure) and ending with *puruṣa* (the person), as mentioned immediately above, is to be understood;
the construction is that the true nature of food (*āhāratattva*) is known through its qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, and the measures (*mātrā*) and other factors are also known.

Alternatively, by the word "qualities" (*guṇa*), the tastes (*rasa*), potencies (*vīrya*), and so on are also included; and the phrase "in all its constituent parts" (*sarvāvayavaśaḥ*) is connected with the knowledge of the measures and the rest.
In the passage beginning with "yathā," the word "etad" refers to the beneficial and the harmful.

"Most numerous types" (bhūyiṣṭhakalpāḥ) means of various kinds—superior, inferior, and middling. By using the term "most numerous types," there is an inclusion of all [categories], specifically for the purpose of including the distinctions among the superior, more superior, and most superior, etc.; or else, for the purpose of including physicians who have studied the eight branches beginning with surgery (śalya); or else, "most numerous types" refers to those who have understood many examples of what is beneficial and what is harmful. For in the section on the foremost [topics], much that is beneficial and harmful must be stated; and the sense is that this serves for practical application by those of limited intellect, and for the knowledge of the unspoken by those of superior intellect.

"By way of characteristic" (*lakṣaṇataḥ*) means that the characteristic is the state of being nutriment (*āhāratva*), such as consisting of both the stationary (*sthāvara*) and the moving (*jaṅgama*). This he will explain with the passage beginning "For example, the state of being nutriment" and ending with "due to the multiplicity of instruments.

"By way of constituent part" (*avayavataḥ*) means by way of a single portion; and the single portions are red rice (*lohitaśāli*) and so forth. These, however, he will explain with the passage beginning "For example, red rice.
"Because there is no difference in meaning" means because there is no difference in the sense of being consumed (*abhyavahriyamāṇatva*). "Of two origins" means having two sources.

"Having a future result that is either beneficial or harmful" (*hitāhitodarka*) means a future result (*udarka*)—that is, a consequence occurring at a later time—that is either beneficial or harmful; that alone constitutes the distinction. *Udarka* refers to the fruit (*phala*) belonging to a subsequent period.

The pairs of qualities, such as heaviness and lightness, should be understood as being mutually contradictory; however, because they are pervasive— as will be explained in the chapter on Ātreya and Bhadrakāpya (Sūtra 26)— qualities such as priority (*paratva*) and so forth do not assist in this context in that same way, and thus are not mentioned here.

However, those factors which are of great utility in the preparation of combinations and the rules for food have been included here by way of their manifoldness and as the cause of innumerable variations; yet, "measure" (*mātrā*) is the actual limit, and it was declared here not to be illustrated, according to the statement: "not illustrating such matters as measure," because of the vast number of substances used in combinations, preparations, and processing—where "substance" (*dravya*) refers to awned grains and the like, "combination" (*saṃyoga*) is the blending of dietary ingredients, and "processing" (*karaṇa*) is the refinement.
"Vikārāvayavāḥ" means parts of a transformation;
"bhūyiṣṭhakalpānām" means those that are slightly less than many. For this word "kalpa" signifies a slight incompleteness, as in the expression "rājakalpa" (one who is almost a king).
By this, the meaning is that those who are generally beneficial or harmful to many are being described.
Others, however, say "of the majority of kalpas" means "of those with similar elemental natures" (*samānadhātuprakṛti*);
and by "by nature" (*prakṛtyā*), they mean not by artificial conjunctions and so forth, but by their inherent essence (*svabhāvena*).
In expressions such as "lohitaśālī raktaśāliḥ" (the red rice is the *raktaśāli*) and "śūkadhānyānām" (of the awned grains), the genitive case is used in the sense of specification (*nirdhāraṇa*).

The use of the superlative suffix *tamap* in the term *pathyatamatva* indicates that it is the most excellent among its own class (*sajātīya*), meaning "the very best. For example, as in "the most praiseworthy" (*śreṣṭhatama*). Alternatively, the inclusion of *tamap* may be pleonastic (*svārthika*), as in "Yudhiṣṭhira is the best among the Kurus. Similarly, regarding the phrase "one [of the] tongue-perceptible [tastes] is another" (Sūtra 26), although the *kākamācī* plant destroys the three *doṣas* and acts as a rejuvenator (*rasāyana*), here the *jīvantī* is mentioned because of its superior benefit for those in good health (*svastha*). And this superiority in benefiting those in good health is understood from the statement itself.
The same should be explained elsewhere as well;
however, this is the distinction regarding the *kākamācī*: that the *kākamācī* [plant] when stale leads to death.

Although the monitor lizard (*godhā*) and the *arohita* increase *kapha* and *pitta*—for it is said, "Animals that dwell in the earth and those born in water increase *kapha* and *pitta"—nevertheless, they are mentioned here among their own kind because of their excellence as wholesome foods. Likewise, even for a substance that slightly increases the *doṣas*, wholesomeness can indeed occur depending on the specific season. Furthermore, the quality of being beneficial for a healthy person (*svastha-hitatva*) is a distinct attribute of a substance; it does not depend upon its capacity to either produce or remove the *doṣas*. As it has been said: "One thing pacifies the *doṣas*, while another aggravates the *dhātus*."
"In the state of health, a certain substance is considered and declared to be of three kinds" (Sūtra 1); thus says Cullukī, who is known as Sugṛha.
The *pākahaṃsa* is the white swan (*śvetahaṃsa*). The suffix *-tamap* [in *prakṛṣṭatama*] is used in the sense of the superlative; as before, it is an affix added in its own meaning (*svārthika*).

Although the superlative suffix *tamap* in the term *apathyatama* already conveys the sense of excellence, the word *prakṛṣṭatama* is nevertheless used here to manifest its preeminence among many things that are extremely unwholesome (*apathyatama*).
"Not to be drunk during the rains" (*varṣānādeya*) refers to water produced in saline soil (*ūṣara*), which arises from a salt-waste region (*ūṣaradeśa*).
In the term *kāṇakapota*, the word *kāṇa* signifies "small"; as in the expression "the small cloud.
*Cilicima* is a large-scaled fish, a variety of *rohit*; for he will describe *cilicima* specifically as a variety of *rohit* later in this very same section.
*Kākamadgu* is the water-crow.
The sparrow (*caṭaka*) is well-known as having beneficial and harmful constituent parts, and so forth;

here at the beginning, the word *iti* is to be supplied, whereby it should be construed with the preceding [text] as follows: "Thus, the sparrow is explained as having beneficial and harmful constituent parts among the various transformations of food."
"More than this" (*ato bhūyaḥ*): the word "from this" (*ataḥ*) indicates the reason (*hetau*), meaning that [the body] is joined with what is beneficial and harmful, but not with their *karma*.
The word "more" (*bhūyas*) has the sense of "again" (*punar*). "Karma" means "effect" (*kārya*). Therefore, the "karma" of the transformations of food is more than this.

For example: "Food is for those who provide sustenance," "Water is for those who provide relief," and so forth; likewise, the action of medicinal herbs, such as "Trivṛt is for those who require easy purgation," and so on—we shall describe these according to their primary importance.

By the phrase "according to their primary importance," he shows that this is not an enumeration of the actions of all food preparations and medicinal herbs, but rather [of those] according to their predominance.

The term "with their consequences" (sānubandhāni) means "with their purposes," such as "indigestion is for those who must be cleared out," and so forth; for the description of the actions of indigestion, fever, and the like is clearly useful for medical treatment.

"Substances" (dravyāṇi) refers to the great elements (mahābhūtāni); for example, water is [the primary substance] for solidifying agents, and air is the cause for providing vital breath and consciousness, and so forth.

The term "substances" is an illustration (upalakṣaṇa); furthermore, it serves as a qualifier for the phrase "together with their concomitants" (sānubandhāni). By this, even that which is not a substance is said to be "with its concomitants"; for example: "Logic accompanied by the scriptures is [the primary means] among the means of proof," and so on.

Alternatively, "consisting of beneficial and non-beneficial parts" is an adjective qualifying *karman* (action); by this, it follows that action is a specific form of a portion of the beneficial and non-beneficial [qualities] of food and its transformations. In this context, beneficial action is exemplified by "food is for those who seek sustenance," and so forth; non-beneficial action is exemplified by "sheep's ghee is unwholesome for those with heart disease," and so forth;
and the action of medicinal drugs is exemplified by "Trivṛt is for easy purgation," and so forth—the explanation of which is exactly as before.
The term "for those who seek sustenance" (*vṛttikara*) refers to those who maintain the stability of the body.

Regarding the phrase "of those that create a relish for food substances," the meaning is that salt, when combined with food, creates a relish for the food. Regarding "sour [is best] among heart-tonics," this refers to those things that create relish; for sourness itself is inherently pleasing.

Regarding "honey [is best] among those that pacify phlegm and bile," this refers to liquid substances; and regarding "durālabhā [is best] among medicinal substances. Therefore, there is no contradiction in the determination that durālabhā and honey are the most excellent among those that pacify phlegm and bile.

"Basti" refers, without distinction, to both *āsthāpana* and *anuvāsana*. "Without milk" is stated among drinks for those who generate *pitta* and *śleṣman*; "black gram (*māṣa*)" is stated among foods for those who generate *pitta* and *śleṣman*; and "sweetmeats (*śaṣkulī*)" is stated among edibles for those who generate *pitta* and *śleṣman*. Alternatively, all three of these are mentioned together because they are equally generators of *pitta* and *śleṣman*. In the same way, elsewhere too, the statement regarding the excellence of a particular type should be understood as referring to the excellence of that specific class, as well as its relative equality. "Mandaka" means that which is produced from sour gruel (*manda*).
Uddālaka is wild kodrava;
guḍaśotha is hemorrhoids (arśas);
and gandhapriyaṅgu is simply priyaṅgu.
One who eats raw flesh (*kravya*) or meat (*māṃsa*) is a *kravyād*, such as a tiger or other predator;
in the phrase "together with ghee" (*samaghṛta*), the word *sama* has the sense of "with" (*saha*);
and "trembling" (*udvepana*) means shaking (*vepana*).

Although it should have been stated as "water for soothing and immobilizing," the fact that he treats them separately—saying "water for soothing" and likewise "water for immobilizing"—shows that water possesses a unique efficacy for both of these two actions. For if they were listed together in the enumeration of qualities, primacy would belong only to those substances that perform both actions simultaneously. Thus, in other cases as well—such as with *pippalī* root and others where primacy is declared regarding the performance of multiple actions—one should understand that primacy belongs specifically to those instances of performing multiple actions concurrently, and not to each action individually.
*Lāmajjaka*, *uśīra*, and the two types of *muśīra*—both fragrant and non-fragrant—are taken together.

"Eating at one sitting" (*ekāśana-bhojana*) means eating at a single time. By this, only the fact that eating at one sitting leads to easy digestion is stated; it does not constitute a prohibition against a second meal. By this [principle], it should be understood that even when eating twice, factors such as unimpaired digestive fire and sleep serve as causes for easy digestion, provided they are among the "gates of drying" (*śoṣa-dvārāṇi*), meaning they are among the causes of drying.
"Parāghātana" means a place of execution; for upon seeing a living being being put to death, one might lose faith in food out of compassion.
Some read this as "yathāśitam," which is not very accurate;
it refers to eating at the wrong time (*atītakālabhojana*) or eating too little (*stokabhojana*).
Irregular eating refers to eating at improper times or in improper quantities; censurable diseases include leucoderma, leprosy, and the like;
and the "faces of misfortune" refers to the causes of misfortune.
False application is the threefold yoga other than right application;
it is volition, specifically the volition for sexual union with women.
Fever is the foremost among diseases, that is, among those things that cause affliction.
Furthermore,
the Soma, the king of herbs, which has fifteen joints, is the inherent consequence of the ritual actions that lead to rebirth.
"Of the characteristics of the means of livelihood" refers to the characteristics of health;
"knowledge" refers to the specialized knowledge of medicines and so forth;
"of the means" refers to the means for attaining knowledge.
*Sampratipatti* is the performance of duties according to what ought to be done;

*tṛpti* (satisfaction) refers to the qualities of food, where the word "quality" (*guṇa*) denotes praiseworthy attributes. The phrase "the practice of a single taste for those who are emaciated" is stated with the exception of specific prohibitions; therefore, it does not contradict the statement that "the practice of ghee [is beneficial] for rejuvenative therapies" (*rasāyana*).
Regarding the phrase "of the immortals," this refers to those causes that bestow life;
total renunciation is the abandonment of all ritual action, for that is the cause of liberation, the supreme bliss, which must be explained in the context of the body.
In the passage beginning with "of the foremost" (*agryāṇām*), the word *agrya* signifies "excellent.
The term *alam* means "capable.

Here, even diseases such as fever (*jvara*) and urinary disorders (*prameha*)—when recognized by their essential nature, their excessive afflictiveness, and their secondary associations—become useful in medical treatment; therefore, the knowledge of fever and other such conditions is also capable of effecting the destruction of disorders.

Furthermore, the statement that these [remedies] are the foremost because they pacify disorders (*vikāra*) is made either on account of their preeminence or for the sake of praise. Therefore, the objection that "if these alone, as prescribed in the section on the foremost, pacify disorders, then what is the use of mentioning other medical treatments? is refuted;

for here, the destruction of disorders is to be understood as occurring through the application of medicine for those already arisen, and likewise through the preservation of health for those not yet arisen.
He states in brief what was taught in the section on the foremost [qualities]: "Equal," and so forth.
"Of equal performers" means those whose actions are similar.

"The characteristic of the superior" means the characteristic of the praiseworthy; here, however, "characteristic" refers simply to the textual recitation, for by the recitation the superiority is indicated—that is, it is known.

*Jyāyastva* (superiority) means greatness; this should be understood as the greatness of unwholesome qualities. For this very reason, when describing unwholesome practices (*ahitādhikāra*), the term *śreṣṭhatama* (most excellent) was omitted, and it was stated that "they are the most preeminent in being the most unwholesome. By this, the definition of the "excellent" (*śreṣṭha*) should be understood as applying to wholesome foods such as red rice (*raktaśāli*). Furthermore, *jyāyastva* refers to the state of possessing excellence in being the most unwholesome among unwholesome foods like *yavaka* and others; it is the state of being better in performing its [harmful] function, and thus it is the preeminence in action. This is to be understood as what has been stated in passages such as "food is the foremost among those that provide sustenance."

In passages such as "of wind, bile, and phlegm," one should understand that "enema is for those [substances] that remove wind," "purgation is for those that remove bile," "emesis is for those that remove phlegm," and "non-unctuous enema is for those that remove wind. Regarding "that which removes a disease," one should understand examples such as "khadira is for those that remove skin diseases" and "puṣkaramūla is for those that remove hiccup, dyspnea, cough, pain in the flanks, and abdominal distension. Alternatively, there is the reading "inferiority" (*avaratvam*); in that case, inferiority means acting contrary to what is intended, and this should be understood through examples such as "sexual intercourse with a menstruating woman is for those [results] beginning with misfortune."
It should be explained that by virtue of being "excellent" (*śreṣṭha*) and "superior" (*jyāyastva*), both praiseworthy and blameworthy actions are also included [in this definition].
(42–44) Now, he states the definition of the wholesome regimen (*pathya*), which is also known as "beneficial" (*hita*): "Wholesome," and so forth.

"Pathya" means not departing from the "path," which is the bodily route in the form of the channels (*srotas*). "Departed" (*apeta*) means harmful; "not departed" (*anapeta*) means non-harmful—this is the meaning. By the mention of "path," both the *doṣas* and *dhātus* that are outside the path are included, as well as those *dhātus* that constitute the path itself. Thus, the entire body is encompassed; consequently, that which does not injure the body is "wholesome" (*pathya*). Alternatively, the "path" consists of the preservation of health in the healthy and the liberation from disease in the sick; therefore, that which does not depart from this path is "wholesome."
Even so, one might still not obtain the state of being non-injurious to the mind; therefore, he says:

"That which was called 'pleasing to the mind' means that which is desired through the mind's extreme delight; by this, it means 'beneficial to the mind. Through this, qualities such as tranquility, knowledge, and lack of sharpness are included.
By this, the definition of 'wholesome' (*pathya*)—namely, 'that which does not injure the mind or body'—is stated without exception."

Others, however, recite these two characteristics of wholesomeness (*pathya*) and say: "If there were only one characteristic, then a bitter medicine in cases of fever and other ailments would not be wholesome because it is unpleasant to the mind; yet this is indeed accepted, in that the application of the bitter at that time is not agreeable to the mind, and yet by that much it does not become unwholesome for the body. Therefore, only that degree of mental agreeableness which does not produce mental disturbances should be designated [as a characteristic]; or rather, that degree of mental disagreeableness which does not produce mental disturbances should simply not be so designated.

Regarding this state of being unwholesome (*apathya*), he asks whether it is fixed for foods and behaviors, or not; he says "whatever," etc., meaning that there is nothing of such a nature that is invariably certain—such as "this is always unpleasant" or "this is always unwholesome.
He asks why it is not so, and says "only in regard to the mother," etc.
The term "other qualities" (guṇāntara) is connected with the "mothers" (mātrā) and so forth;
thus, "this and that" refers to the various other qualities of the mothers and so forth,
while "those and those" refers to the beneficial and harmful foods and behaviors.
In this way, even things spoken as beneficial may be either beneficial or harmful; likewise, things spoken as harmful may be either harmful or beneficial.

Similarly, that which is pleasant—such as sweet things—and unpleasant—such as bitter things—may be illustrated here as follows: ghee is indeed wholesome (*pathya*), yet it becomes unwholesome when taken in excess, unwholesome during the spring season, unwholesome when prepared with incompatible substances, and unwholesome on marshy ground. Likewise, it is unwholesome for a body that is excessively obese, and unwholesome when the bodily humor (*doṣa*) is dominated by phlegm (*kapha*).

Even unwholesome food (*apathya*) becomes beneficial through proper dosage and other factors, as stated in the section on rejuvenation (*rasāyana*): "One should administer a sesame seed's worth of poison" (Ci. A. 1), and so forth;
other cases should be inferred in this manner.

Since absolute unwholesomeness is thus uncertain, while general unwholesomeness is certain, the "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) is therefore specified—meaning the intrinsic nature of wholesome items such as *raktaśāli* rice and unwholesome items such as *yavaka* grain; that is, their wholesomeness or unwholesomeness by their very nature (*prakṛtyā*).
The connection is that "the basis, such as the measure and so forth, is thus specified"; "measure and so forth" refers to the measure, time, action, and so on,
which serve as the basis for what is wholesome and unwholesome.
The meaning is that, depending on factors such as dosage, the wholesomeness or unwholesomeness of entities becomes ultimately real;
"both" refers to both the intrinsic nature and the dosage and so forth.
Now, because this section concerns the foremost [liquors], those among the infinite *āsava*s that are the most excellent are being described.

Having listed *dhānya* (grains) and the others as a single category, he lists *śarkarā* (sugar/molasses) separately, because *dhānya* and the others possess internal sub-varieties (*avāntarajāti*), whereas *śarkarā* has no such internal sub-varieties. As for *yāsa-śarkarā*, it is not heard of in scripture as a cause for *āsava*; however, *madhu-śarkarā* is already included within honey (*madhu*) itself.
Honey, moreover, is not listed separately as a source of *āsava*, so that an *āsava* made from it is already included under "grain-based *āsava*" (*dhānyāsava*) due to its connection with grain.
The same should be understood regarding *gauḍāsavas* and other such substances.
"Substance, conjunction, and instrument" (*dravyasaṃyogakaraṇa*) refers to these three factors; from these, there would be innumerable varieties.
*Sauvīra* is made from dehusked barley; *maireya* is wine made from fermented grain; *medaka* is white wine known as *jagala*; and *dhānyāmbu* is sour gruel (*kāñjika*).

*Tṛṇaśūnya* is *ketakī*; *mṛgaliṇḍikā* is *vibhītaka*; *kuvala* is the large jujube (*sthūlabadarī*); *karkandhu* is the wild jujube (*śṛgālabadarī*); *kadara* is the white acacia (*śvetakhadira*); *aśvakarṇa* is *śālabheda*; *arimeda* is *viṭkhadira*; *kiṇihī* is *apāmārga*; *śukti* is *badarī*;
*padma* is a red eight-petalled lotus; *nalina* is a white eight-petalled lotus; *puṇḍarīka* is a white hundred-petalled lotus; and *śatapatra* is a reddish one.
Although the *puṇḍraka* is already included under the term "sugarcane" (*ikṣu*), it is mentioned again for the sake of indicating its preeminence with respect to *āsava*.
*Kramuka* is *guvāka*;
*tilvaka* is *śābaralodhra*.

If it is argued that because they are "distilled" (āsutatva)— that is, because they possess the nature of fermentation— the term "of these" (eṣām) in the passage beginning with "the conjunction and disjunction of substances" refers to liquors (āsava) made from individual substances such as grain,
and thus their "disjunction" is untenable due to their being of a single uniform nature; that is not so, for even in those cases, there exists a disjunction of substances belonging to the same genus.

Furthermore, because even the separation of the substances used for processing is possible therein; for liquor and the like are not produced by a single substance alone, but rather grains and such are mentioned because of their predominance, and the processing involves many kinds of options—this is the construction [of the sentence].
He states the purpose of performing the processing through conjunction with the words "according to their respective [natures]," etc.

"According to their respective [conditions]" (yathāsvam) is what is appropriate: place refers to heaps of ash, heaps of grain, and so forth, as will be described in the section on combinations (sandhāna); time refers to the determination of fortnights, months, and so forth; measure refers to the quantity of the substances for the combination; by the inclusion of "and so forth" (ādi), there is a collection of the nature of the substance and the procedure;
and "that specific effect" refers to the state of wholesomeness (hitatva) which differs according to place, time, the body, the doshas, and other factors.
By means of the passage beginning with "mind and body," the description of the qualities of the liquor that has been drunk should be understood through reasoning.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "On What Constitutes Feces," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka Saṃhitā* composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the section on Food and Drink (*Annapānacatuṣka*) of the *Sūtrasthāna*.
[Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 26 (26 of 120)]

Having stated one portion of what is beneficial and harmful, the *Ātreyabhadrakāpyīya* chapter—which explains taste (*rasa*), potency (*vīrya*), and post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*)—is now set forth for the purpose of knowing the entirety of what is beneficial and harmful regarding substances.
Furthermore, since the characteristics of post-digestive transformation and the other factors are generally indicated by taste alone, the section on taste is placed first.

Having established the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) according to the opinions of the sages, the formal determination of the final conclusion (*siddhāntavyavasthāpana*) for the sake of the student's comprehension is the "Determination of Nutritive Essence as Food" (*rasāhāraviniścaya*). Alternatively, this is the "Determination of Nutritive Essence" (*rasaviniścaya*), while the section beginning with "Furthermore, beyond these, [the determination] of the post-digestive effects" (*paraṃ cāto vipākānām*) and so forth constitutes the "Determination of Food" (*āhāraviniścaya*).
Regarding the phrase "only one" (*eka eva*) and so forth:
the genitive case in *indriyārthānām* is used for specification (*nirdhāraṇa*).

The word *anyatamam* means "one"; for this word *anya* is used in the singular, as in "one went by the south, another by the north," meaning "one. Furthermore, the superlative suffix *-tama* is pleonastic (*svārthika*), having no additional meaning beyond the sense already expressed.
Regarding the phrase "pertaining to the domain of the tongue": that which is graspable by the tongue is taste;
since even the absence of taste is grasped by the tongue, he says "a positive entity" (*bhāva*).
The expression "not different from water" is for the purpose of demonstrating the identity between taste and water; it is not faulty because it represents the opponent's position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The prima facie view is according to the doctrine of Kapila; for they maintain, by such statements as "the subtle element of taste" and "the subtle element of smell," that substance is not distinct from its qualities.
[In this context,] "to be cut" means that which causes emaciation, and "to be pacified" means that which causes nourishment.

"Common" (sādhāraṇa) means that, due to its similarity to both the fiery (āgneya) and the lunar (saumya), it is the performer of both lightening (laṅghana) and nourishing (bṛṃhaṇa) actions, or, because of their mutual opposition, it is the non-performer;
"palatable" (svādu) is intended [as a quality]; "wholesome" (hita) refers to that which does no harm over the long term;

"substratum" (āśraya) refers to the substance (dravya); "qualities" (guṇāḥ) refer to unctuousness, heaviness, and so forth; "action" (karma) refers to the increase or depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātus); and "taste-variation" (saṃsvāda) refers to the internal subdivisions of tastes (rasas)—the meaning is "of these specific varieties."

In this regard, due to the difference in substance (*dravya*), there is also a difference in the taste (*rasa*) which is supported by it, through the difference in its substratum (*ādhāra*); for the substratum is the cause, and the meaning is that from a difference in the cause, a difference in the effect necessarily follows. Furthermore, the differences in qualities such as heaviness (*guru*) and so forth, as well as the differences in action (*karman*), are produced solely by taste;
therefore, from the difference in the effect, there must necessarily be a difference in the cause—this is the intention of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

As for the distinction in taste (*saṃsvādabheda*), even within a single sweet category—such as that found in sugarcane, milk, or molasses—a difference is perceived directly through experience. That distinction in taste is indeed self-evident; as it has been said: "The difference between the sweetness of sugarcane, milk, and molasses is great, yet even Sarasvatī herself would be unable to describe that distinction.
He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) by means of the words of Punarvasu: "Only six," and so forth.
He states the arrangement regarding the oneness of taste and so on as asserted in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Of those six," and so forth.

"Source" (*yoni*) means the foundational cause. The point is that because of the difference between cause and effect, the distinction of tastes in water is established as being directly perceptible (*pratyakṣa*).

Just as water alone, distinct from earth, is the source of taste (*rasa*), so too has this been explained in the *Dīrghañjīvitīya* [chapter] under the aphorism "Taste is the object of tasting" (*rasanārtho rasaḥ tasya*) and so forth;

for while the mixing of those two [qualities] is impossible because they are formless actions (*karman*), it should be understood that their mixing occurs through the mixing of the two substances (*dravya*) which serve as their substrates.
"Common" means being connected to a common effect; "devotion" (bhakti) means desire (icchā). By this [it is meant]:
"Whoever desires this, for him it is sweet-tasting, and for another it is otherwise"—thus these two properties depend upon the person, not upon a difference in the taste itself. This is the meaning.

In the phrase "the five great elements" (*pañcamahābhūta*) and so forth, the word "but" (*tu*) is used for emphasis; thus, the meaning is that these are only the substrata (*āśraya*), not the tastes themselves.

To the question of what kind of elemental transformations—earth and the rest—are the substrata, he says: "dependent upon nature, modification, consideration, place, and time. The word "dependent" (*vaśa*) means "subject to," and it should be construed with each of the preceding terms, such as "nature" (*prakṛti*).

Among these, that which is due to *prakṛti* (intrinsic nature) is as follows: mung beans (*mudga*), being astringent and sweet, are light by their very nature; this lightness is not due to their taste, for if it were so, they would be heavy because of their astringency and sweetness. Furthermore, the lightness of rice puffs (*lāja*) compared to rice is due to *vikṛti* (transformation), as is the heaviness of roasted barley flour (*saktu*), cooked balls (*siddhapiṇḍaka*), and the like. *Vicāraṇā* means deliberation or the combination with another substance; thus, that which is due to *vicāraṇā* is as follows: honey and ghee combined become poison, and likewise, poison combined with an antidote (*agada*) produces an effect different from its own natural action. *Deśa* (place) is twofold: the geographical location and the patient’s body. Regarding the geographical location: "The white *kāpotī* plant growing over an anthill is an antidote to poison," and likewise, "Medicines on the Himalayas possess great virtues. Regarding the location of the body: "The flesh of the thighs is heavier than that of the shoulders, chest, head, and feet" (Sūtra).

27) And so forth; as for the influence of time (*kālavaśa*), it is stated with reference to the radish (*mūlaka*): "The young [radish] removes the *doṣas*, while the old one aggravates all three *doṣas*" (Sūtra 27); likewise: "One should gather flowers and fruits according to the season" (Kalpa 1), and so on.

And here, those [factors] mentioned in a single section that have not been explicitly stated elsewhere should be included within [the categories of] nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*).

As it has been said: "In this [context], movement (*cara*), the parts of the body, nature (*svabhāva*), the elements (*dhātu*), actions (*kriyā*), gender (*liṅga*), measure (*pramāṇa*), refinement (*saṃskāra*), and proportion (*mātrā*) are examined" (Sūtra).

27) Thus, in that context, the elements (dhātu) of the moving body and its parts are grasped by way of location (deśa); they enter into consideration by measure (mātrā), while the remainder enters into their own nature (svabhāva). Furthermore, the "basis of specific foods" (āhāraviśeṣāyatana), which will be described in the *Rasavimāna*, must be included here as appropriate.
