By the use of the term "etcetera" (ādi) in the phrase "unctuous, dry, etc.," he demonstrates that even those not explicitly mentioned—such as sharp (tīkṣṇa), mild (mṛdu), and so forth—are not tastes (rasa), but rather distinct qualities of substances (dravyaguṇa).

Because it flows—that is, because it is associated with the action of moving downward—it is a substance (*dravya*) called *kṣāra*, not a taste (*rasa*). For it is impossible for a taste, which is itself devoid of action, to possess an action; this is the meaning. Furthermore, the flowing of *kṘāra* occurs through its downward movement when combined with water, as worldly people say: "We are draining the lye. And the medical scripture states: "Having repeatedly cut [the wound], the lye, by virtue of its corrosive nature (*kṣāratva*), causes it to flow downward" (Cikitsā-sthāna 5).

He states another reason: "That substance is produced from many tastes"; "produced from many tastes" means produced from *muṣkaka*, *apāmārga*, and so forth. And because it is produced from many tastes, for that very reason it possesses many tastes, since the quality of the effect conforms to the qualities of the cause—this is the intended meaning. He expresses its possession of many tastes as "abounding in pungent and salty [tastes]";
by the word "abounding" (*bhūyiṣṭha*), he shows that there is a connection with other subordinate tastes.
He states another reason: "It is endowed with the objects of multiple sense-faculties.
For alkali (kṣāra) is indeed accompanied by touch and smell; therefore, it is a substance (*dravya*). The point is that in the quality (*guṇa*) of taste, there is neither touch nor smell.

He states yet another reason: "It is produced by an instrument"; the meaning is that it is brought about or made by an instrument such as a strainer for ashes. The point is that taste is not produced in this manner.
He refutes the position that there is an unmanifest taste (*avyaktarasa*) with the words "unmanifest state" (*avyaktībhāva*), and so forth.

By the suffix *cvī* in the sense of "becoming what it was not" (*abhūtatadbhāve*), the meaning is that the unmanifestness of tastes—such as sweet and the rest—which are indeed manifest, occurs in some substratum; there is no other unmanifest taste apart from the sweet and the others.
The term "of tastes" (*rasānām*) refers to the six [tastes] beginning with sweet.
"In the primordial substance" (*prakṛtau*), and so forth:
"in the primordial substance" means in the cause, that is, in water.

"Unmanifestness" (*avyaktatvam*) is the perception of the mere generality of taste, devoid of specific qualities such as sweetness and the like; and this occurs in water. For it is stated by Suśruta in the description of the qualities of water: "The defect of taste is the lack of manifest taste" (*vyaktarasatā rasadoṣaḥ*).

As it is said [in Sūtra 45], and here too he will say "and having an unmanifest flavor" (*avyaktarasa*); furthermore, in common worldly usage, when people taste a substance with an unmanifest flavor, they say, "Its flavor is like that of water; no specific quality such as sweetness is manifest," because it is not manifested (*anudbhūtatvena*).

Just as when an object whose specific color is not discerned from a distance, there occurs a perception of the general form (*rūpasāmānya*) but no cognition of specific qualities such as whiteness, so too does there occur a state of being unmanifest (*avyaktībhāva*) in the secondary flavor (*anurasa*). It is called *anurasa* because it follows (*anugata*) the primary manifest flavor (*rasa*) in its state of unmanifestness. For example, in a bamboo sprout that is sweet, astringency is the secondary flavor, as it has been said: "The sweet [taste] is dry, has an astringent secondary flavor (*kaṣāyānuraso madhuraḥ*), and destroys phlegm and bile" (Sūtra 27).
“Endowed with secondary tastes” (*anurasa-samanvita*) means possessed of all secondary tastes, as in the case of poison; for the statement says: “hot, with an indefinable taste,” and so forth.
Alternatively, there is the reading *aṇurasa-samanvite*; by that, in a sugar-drink containing a single minute secondary taste—namely, black pepper—the pungency would be unmanifest.
He refutes the position that they are innumerable with the words beginning "innumerable" (*aparisaṅkhyeya*).

Regarding the phrase "of them," it refers to the tastes (*rasas*); their being innumerable is not tenable. Regarding the phrase "of the entities such as the substratum" (*āśrayādīnāṃ bhāvānām*), it refers to the substratum, qualities, actions, and flavors. He states the reason for this: "because the distinctions are innumerable" (*viśeṣāparisaṅkhyeyatvāt*), meaning because the variations of the substratum and so forth are innumerable.
He provides the logical ground for this with the words beginning "for even each one... (*ekaiko 'pi hi...*).

Among these—substratum (*āśraya*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*karman*), and taste (*saṃsvāda*)—each one, such as sweetness and the rest, assumes its particularities; yet, despite that difference of substratum and so forth, no distinctness arises for the sweetness and the rest that reside therein.

This is what is intended: although rice, mung beans, ghee, milk, and so on, are different substrata for sweetness, nevertheless, there is only a single taste pervaded by the universal (*jāti*) of "sweetness" (*madhuratva*), just as the color white remains the same in cranes, milk, cotton, and the like.

Likewise, even though qualities such as heaviness, sliminess, and oiliness are distinct from one another, or even though actions such as increasing the *rasas*, producing longevity, and imparting complexion are different, there is no difference in the sweet *rasa* itself. Since it is a single sweet *rasa* that possesses those various qualities and performs those respective functions, what contradiction is there?

Similarly, although there are differences in the sub-varieties of taste within the sweet, they do not transcend the genus (*jāti*) of sweetness, just as there is no transcendence of blackness despite the differences among the sub-varieties of the color black.

Now, one might object: "Let it not be that the *rasas* are innumerable; however, the specific taste (*āsvādaviśeṣa*) resulting from their mutual combination is also capable of producing a specific effect. For what is produced by sweet and sour together cannot be achieved by the sweet alone or the sour alone. Therefore, through those mutual combinations, there will be innumerability. To this, he says: "paraspara... and so forth.

The term *saṃsṛṣṭam* (mixed) is formed with the suffix *kta* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). Therefore, the construction is as follows: because these [flavors] such as sweet (*madhura*) and others are produced through a preponderance of mutual blending, the primary qualities (*guṇa-prakṛti*) of these flavors do not become innumerable. This is the meaning: although flavors, being joined by an extreme degree of mutual blending, arise in substances consisting of two or more flavors, nevertheless, their qualities—such as heaviness, lightness, and so forth—or the specific natures (*prakṛti*) of the sweet and other flavors, such as longevity or the promotion of the vital essence (*rasa*), do not become innumerable; rather, it is only those very qualities and natures of the sweet and others that were individually specified which, when mixed, come together.

"Or rather, of the *prakṛtis* of the qualities" means of those whose nature consists of the six qualities beginning with sweet (*madhura*). By this, it is meant that there is no lack of enumerability for tastes when they come into contact with other tastes, just as there is none for the *doṣas* when they come into contact with other *doṣas*.
By the word *prakṛti*, action (*karman*) is expressed; thus, it means "of the qualities and actions.
It should be understood that even the specific internal variations of taste among the sweet and others are produced by their mutual contact.

For this very reason—that when tastes are combined, no other qualities or actions arise—it is said that the specific action of combined tastes has not been stated even in other treatises: "Therefore," and so forth.
By the word "action" (*karma*) here, one should understand both the causal factors such as heaviness and lightness, as well as the production of blood and so on from the tastes.
He further states, "And that indeed," and so forth, to show that not only have the actions of combined tastes not been taught by the authors of other treatises, but we too shall not teach them.
And that very reason is as follows: even when tastes are in mutual combination, they do not possess additional qualities or actions.

"Distinctness by definition" (*lakṣaṇapṛthaktvam*) means distinctness through their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); that by which something is characterized is its "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*). Therefore, everything that is to be expressed by the passage beginning with "sweet taste" (*madhuro rasaḥ*) and likewise by the passage beginning with "moistening, satisfying, and gladdening" (*snehanaprīṇanahlādana*) is included here.

Alternatively, by the word "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), the definition expressed in the text beginning with "sweet taste" (*madhuro rasa*) is meant; and "distinctness" (*pṛthaktva*) refers to what will be stated later for the purpose of knowing the distinctions among tastes, namely the passage beginning with "moistening and pleasing" (*snehanaprīṇana*).
As for the phrase "but further," etc. [the following applies].

The meaning is that, among the tastes (*rasa*) which are the objects to be expressed, the mention of substances (*dravya*) was made first because they are to be presented with the intention of distinguishing between them, and because the knowledge of tastes is dependent upon the knowledge of substances.
"Something" (*kiñcit*) refers to the nature of substances useful for Āyurveda, not everything, because of the fault of irrelevance (*aprasaṅga*);
"all substances" (*sarvadravya*) refers to functional substances (*kāryadravya*).
In this context and within this section, by the statement "ending with fluidity," he refers to the twenty qualities previously mentioned.

Furthermore, by not mentioning here qualities such as priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*), he demonstrates that these are not primary in the science of medicine (*cikitsā*). Even though conjunction (*yukti*), dimension (*parimāṇa*), refinement (*saṃskāra*), and practice (*abhyāsa*) are extremely useful for medical treatment, they are not inherent (*sāṃsiddhika*) to substances such as earth in the same way that sound and the other [sensory qualities] are; rather, they are adventitious (*ādheya*). Therefore, they are not mentioned here in the enumeration of natural qualities.

Regarding the phrase "it has been said," this is stated because of its predominance in the *Apāmārgataṇḍulīya* chapter; by this, it should be understood that nourishing [therapies] and so forth are also included.

The word *bahula* (abundant) is connected with each of [the qualities] beginning with heaviness (*guru*); or alternatively, it is connected with odor (*gandha*) alone, since earth alone is characterized by an abundance of the quality of odor. For this very reason, even in the definition of other substances, a specific quality is mentioned last, as in "abundant in the quality of taste" and so forth. Therefore, in those cases as well, the word *bahula* should be applied specifically to taste and the others. Although all effect-substances (*kāryadravya*) are composed of the five elements (*pāñcabhautika*), their status as "earthy" and so on should be understood according to the predominance of earth and the other elements. *Saṅghāta* is solidity (*kāṭhinya*); *sthairya* is immovability (*avicālya*).
*Bandhana* is mutual conjunction; *prahlāda* is the gratification of the body and the senses;
*sūkṣma* is that which follows subtle channels;
*prabhā* is the radiance that illuminates color; and *dīpti* is brilliance. As it has been said: "Chāyā pervades color, while prabhā is the illuminator of color" (Indriyasthāna 7), and so forth.
Vicāraṇa means *vicāra*, which signifies movement.
*Sauṣirya* is the state of having many cavities;

here, it should be understood as the predominance of space (*ākāśa*), due to the relative paucity of other elements such as earth and so forth, and because of the extensive manifestation of space within the substance. That which possesses abundant cavities is of the nature of space (*nābhasa*); alternatively, it is called a space-substance (*nābhasa-dravya*) because of the abundance of the qualities of space.

"By this" means by the instruction regarding specific substances and qualities; the meaning is that whatever substance, such as an earthy one, possesses certain qualities, that substance becomes the medicine when the body is to be restored to those same qualities.
Furthermore, he states that such earthy and other substances are not medicine in every way nor for every disease, beginning with the words "that particular application," and so forth.

"Reasoning" (*yukti*) means the method (*upāya*); "purpose" (*artha*) means the objective (*prayojana*); "intending" (*abhipretya*) means with reference to (*adhikṛtya*). Therefore, by some method for some purpose, a certain substance becomes a medicine, but not in all cases. Consequently, the statement that "there is no substance that is not a medicine" because contradictory substances are always unwholesome is not a contradiction. This is because contradictory substances depend upon factors such as combination, processing, place, and time; however, in the absence of such contradictory combinations and so forth, even [substances considered] contradictory may sometimes be wholesome.

Even those things which are inherently unwholesome, such as poison or [excessively] slow food, may at times become wholesome when combined with the proper means; for example, regarding abdominal diseases, it is said: "One should administer a drop of poison" (Ci.
13), and so forth.

As for grass, dust, and the like, which are not employed [internally], they are therefore not called medicines; yet that is not so, because even these possess the nature of medicine by virtue of being means such as sudation and other external therapies.

It has been stated that substances such as earth possess the status of medicine due to their association with qualities like heaviness and roughness; therefore, in order to dispel the doubt that a substance becomes medicine solely through the power of its qualities, he says: "But not alone," and so forth.
This means that just as there is the purgative action of *dantī* due to the power of the substance itself, likewise there is the capacity of gems to destroy poison and other ailments, and so on.
By the power of quality (*guṇaprabhāva*), for example: "bitter taste" in the context of fever, or "fire" in the context of cold, and so forth.

By the power of substance and quality (*dravyaguṇaprabhāva*), for example: "upon a black antelope skin" (*kṛṣṇājina*); here too, both the blackness (*kṛṣṇatva*) as the quality and the antelope skin (*ajina*) as the substance are intended. Or, for example: "milk boiled with discs of gold" (*maṇḍalaiḥ jātarūpasya tasyā eva payaḥ śṛtam*). (Cikitsā-sthāna, chapter [number]).
pāda 3); therein, it is only gold endowed with the qualities of a circle that possesses the nature of a bow.
To explain how they act, he says: "In each respective case," and so forth;
"having attained that respective reasoning" means having reached that respective application.

Regarding the examples beginning with "that which they perform" (*yat kurvantīti*), it is as follows: those substances which perform head-purgation (*śirovirecana*) constitute the action (*karma*) of head-purgation. That by which they perform head-purgation—namely, heat (*uṣṇatva*) and so forth—is the potency (*vīrya*); potency is power (*śakti*), and that [power] belongs either to the substance (*dravya*) or to its quality (*guṇa*). That wherein they perform head-purgation is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), namely the head; the meaning is that the substance for head-purgation is effective only in that locus and not elsewhere. "When" (*yadā*) refers to the time such as spring (*vasanta*) or when there is heaviness of the head and so forth; by this it is implied that at an improper time, such as during the cold season, head-purgation is not effective because of stiffness, but rather only at its own proper time. "In what manner" (*yathā*) refers to the method, such as by means of blowing (*pradhamana*) or pressing (*avapīḍana*); likewise: "With limbs extended, lying supine on a bed strewn with a mattress... (*prasāritāṅgamuttānaṃ śayane saṃstarāstṛte*).

The method (*upāya*) consists of performing [the treatment] according to the procedure beginning with, "having laid [the patient] down with his head slightly hanging and his eyes covered," and so forth. That which is accomplished—the cessation of heaviness of the head, headache, and so on—is the fruit (*phala*). The fruit is the objective;

the action (*karman*) is that which is to be done, the means (*sādhana*), while the objective is the fruit to be achieved (*sādhya*). For example, dharma produced by a sacrifice is the action insofar as it is something to be performed, whereas heaven and the like, produced by that [action], are the objective fruit. In the same way, regarding emesis and other such treatments, the action, the locus, and so forth, should be inferred accordingly. 13
Having now described substance (*dravya*), he states the specific classifications of the transformed tastes (*rasa*) with the verse beginning "And their classification...

and so forth. The term *prabhāva* (potency) is to be connected individually with substance, place, and time. In this regard, an example of the potency of substance (*dravyaprabhāva*) is: "It is sweet due to the predominance of the qualities of the *soma* plant," and so forth. An example of the potency of place (*deśaprabhāva*) is: "Grapes, pomegranates, and other such fruits are sweet in the Himalayas, but sour elsewhere," and so forth. An example of the potency of time (*kālaprabhāva*) is: "The young mango is astringent, the tender fruit is sour, and the ripe fruit is sweet"; likewise, "medicinal plants are sweet in the winter (*hemanta*) and sour during the rainy season (*varṣā*)," and so forth.
Other causes of taste, such as contact with fire and so forth, should also be included within either time or substance. (14) He states the classification: "sweet," and so forth.

In that regard, there are five combinations for the sweet (*svādu*) taste through its association with sour (*amla*) and the others; "by the remaining" means by those other than the one already employed as the first. Thus, there are four for the sour taste through its association with salty (*lavaṇa*) and the others; likewise, three for the salty taste through its association with pungent (*kaṭu*) and the others; two for the pungent taste through its association with bitter (*tikta*) and astringent (*kaṣāya*); and one for the bitter taste through its association with the astringent. Thus, there are fifteen combinations of two tastes (15). He states the combinations of three tastes, beginning with "separately" (*pṛthak*), etc.

When the sweet taste is combined individually with each of the four remaining tastes—sour and so forth—and then further combined with the rest, such as salty and so forth, there is a total of ten combinations. Specifically, when the sweet taste is joined with the sour, it has four combinations through its subsequent union with the remaining tastes, such as salty and so forth. Likewise, when the sweet taste is joined with the salty, it has three combinations through its union with pungent and so forth. Similarly, when joined with the pungent, it has two combinations through its union with bitter and so forth. Likewise, when joined with the bitter, it has one combination through its union with the astringent. Thus, with the sweet taste placed first, there are ten combinations.

Thus, for sour (amla) situated first, there are three [combinations] through its conjunction with salt and the pungent (kaṭu) and so forth; likewise, for that conjoined with pungent, there are two through conjunction with the remaining two [tastes]; similarly, for that conjoined with bitter (tikta), there is one through conjunction with astringent (kaṣāya). In this manner, there are six combinations for sour.
By this same logic, there are three for salt, and only one for pungent. Thus, totaling twenty combinations consisting of three tastes. 16.

When the four tastes—sweet, sour, salty, and so forth—are situated as the base and combined individually with salt and the others, they become six through conjunction with the remaining pungent and other tastes.

Sweet and salty, when combined and situated as the base, are joined separately by the pungent and bitter [tastes]; "by the remaining" refers to the bitter and astringent [tastes]. Therefore, the plural number here should be understood as referring to the genus (*jāti*). Thus, there are three [combinations].
By the phrase "so too, sweet and pungent," one [type] consisting of sweet, pungent, bitter, and astringent is indicated;
likewise, in the passage beginning with "by pungent and so forth," the plural number is used in reference to the genus (*jāti*).

Sour and salty, when combined with pungent and joined with the remaining two, constitute two [types]; similarly, sour and salty, when joined with bitter and joined with the remaining [two], constitute one [type].

By the phrase "sour and pungent likewise," one [combination] consisting of sour, pungent, bitter, and astringent is established; and by the phrase "but they are joined," etc., another [is established]. Thus, there are fifteen combinations of four tastes each.
"From relinquishment" means from abandonment.
And here, the inherence (*samavāya*) of the tastes as qualities within a single substance is expressed by the word "conjunction" (*yoga*).
He states that the combinations of tastes (*rasasaṃsarga*) are innumerable by way of another method: "There would be sixty-three," and so forth.
The secondary taste (*anurasa*) will be explained later;

however, in this context of the sixty-three-fold tastes, there is no conceptualization of a primary taste and a secondary taste, because such a distinction is absent in the case of the simple [single] sweet and other tastes. Therefore, the conceptualization of primary and secondary tastes should be understood as applying to the fifty-seven combinations, as far as they are possible.
Alternatively, even in that which has a single primary taste (*ekarasa*), there certainly exists a secondary taste (*anurasa*) that is merely unnameable;
he also expresses their innumerability by another method in the passage beginning with "tastes [vary] by degrees" (*taratamābhyām*).
The meaning is that tastes become innumerable due to distinctions such as sweet, sweeter, and sweetest.

Alternatively, regarding the very innumerability [of tastes] due to their being primary and secondary (*rasānurasatva*), this is the reason: "The tastes [vary] by degrees of intensity (*taratama*)," and so forth (22–23).
Even though they are innumerable, the teachers have devised here exactly sixty-three types of conceptualization for the purpose of clinical practice; thus he says, "The combinations," and so forth.
In that context, "due to suitability" means that it is beneficial because the application of medical treatment for the healthy and the sick is neither too concise nor too prolix.
He states that very application of medical treatment, beginning with the words "in some cases," and so forth.
Here, by the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of unmentioned factors such as place, time, and potency.

Demonstrating that this very same determination of combined and uncombined tastes arises either from the blending of substances with different tastes, or from the administration of a single substance with multiple tastes, or from the administration of a single substance with a single taste, he says: "Substances," etc. [This refers to] those with two tastes and so forth—those established by nature as having two, three, or more tastes. An example of one with two tastes is the mung bean (*mudga*), which is astringent and sweet. An example of one with three tastes is: "It is sweet, sour, and astringent, causing constipation, heavy, and cold."

“...the *bhavya* fruit alleviates *pitta* and *kapha*” (Sūtra 27), and so forth; sesame has four tastes, as it is said: “Sesame is unctuous, hot, sweet, bitter, astringent, and pungent” (Sūtra 27); *āmalaka* and *harītakī*, however, possess five tastes, based on such statements as “*śivā* (harītakī) possesses five tastes”; moreover, a substance with six clearly manifest tastes is not mentioned here [in this text], whereas poison (*viṣa*) is endowed with six tastes that are not clearly manifest; in the *Hārīta-saṃhitā*, however, the meat of the black antelope (*eṇa*) is stated to be endowed with six clearly manifest tastes.

Thus, from the combination of substances possessing two tastes and so forth, there is the utilization of those with two tastes and so forth; likewise, regarding "combined tastes," they prepare and employ combined tastes individually through the blending of substances with one taste each, primarily for the purpose of countering diseases. Therefore, this should also be understood to apply to the maintenance of health (*svasthavṛtta*). Alternatively, the distinction of having two tastes and so forth pertains only to disease, whereas in the healthy person, there is indeed the employment of all tastes. As it has been said: "A diet containing all tastes in equilibrium is praised as wholesome (*sātmya*) for one whose *dhātus* are balanced" (Sūtra-sthāna).
7) Thus, when explained in this manner, there is no tautology with the statement beginning “in some cases there is one rasa,” etc.;

or rather, the statement beginning “in some cases there is one rasa,” etc., expresses his own view, while here, regarding this very same point, he demonstrates the agreement of other teachers with the passage beginning “substances [may] have two rasas, etc.”; for this very reason it was said that they “conceive [it] according to the intention of other teachers,” and therefore there is no tautology.
25–26 He states the fruit of the knowledge of tastes, beginning with "yaḥ syāt" (he who...).

Here, by the very knowledge of the variations of taste, the entire knowledge of the substances that cause disease is encompassed; for it will be explained that, through the knowledge of taste alone, almost all the qualities of substances are [determined].
From the knowledge of the variations of the *doṣas* arises the knowledge of the *liṅgas* (signs), for every *liṅga* is connected with the variations of the *doṣas*.

From the knowledge of the variations of the *rasas* and *doṣas*, however, arises the knowledge of the medicine (*bheṣaja*); because from the *rasa* comes the knowledge of the essential nature of the medicinal substance, and from the *doṣa* comes the knowledge of the scope for the application of that medicine.

Alternatively, the knowledge of causes and so forth should be stated separately from the classification of tastes and the classification of the *doṣas*; for by the differentiation of tastes, its effect—the diagnostic sign (*liṅga*)—is also known. Furthermore, the knowledge of causes and medicines must be derived solely from the knowledge of the differentiation of tastes, because it is the substance possessing a specific taste that serves as both the cause of disorders and their remedy. Likewise, having understood the differentiation of the *doṣas*, one perceives their corresponding cause and understands that the substance which opposes those *doṣas* is the medicine.
Thus, it is rightly said: "He shall not be deluded regarding the causes, signs, and pacification of disorders. (27)

He states the definition of the primary and secondary tastes (rasa and anurasa) as previously mentioned: "Manifest" (*vyakta*), etc. The word "and" (*ca*) in "of the dry" (*śuṣkasya*) implies "and of the moist" (*ārdrasya*); the word "and" (*ca*) in "at first" (*ādau*) implies "and at the end. Therefore, whether in the case of something dry or moist, that which is perceived either at the initial contact with the tongue or at the conclusion of the tasting, through its manifest nature by means of such alternatives as "this is sweet" or "this is sour," is called "manifest" (*vyakta*). However, that which is not perceived as manifest during any of the four aforementioned states, but is instead measured by its indefinability, by its mere appearance, or by the observation of its effects, is a "secondary taste" (*anurasa*). This is the meaning of the sentence.

Since sweet and the other [tastes] themselves take the form of primary tastes (*rasa*) and secondary tastes (*anurasa*) through being manifest or unmanifest, there is no such thing as a seventh taste called "unmanifest.
Although this point was previously refuted, it is refuted again here because a favorable and clear reason has been obtained.

Others, however, say: by the phrase "and of the dry," that substance which is used both in its dry and moist states—the taste which is unmanifest in the dry state is called *rasa*; whereas that which is manifest in the moist state but does not persist in the dry state is not *rasa*, but rather a *anurasa*.

For example, the sweet taste of fresh long pepper (*pippalī*) is manifest, whereas that of dried long pepper is pungent. Therefore, pungency alone is the primary taste (*rasa*) of long pepper, while sweetness is its secondary taste (*anurasa*). However, in the case of grapes and similar fruits, where the taste remains sweet in both the fresh and dried states, there is no disagreement [regarding this]; thus, in those cases, sweetness alone is the taste. Furthermore, regarding substances like fermented rice water (*kāñjika*) or buttermilk (*takra*), which must always be used fresh, the taste that is perceived clearly at first is the primary taste, while the taste subsequently perceived—such as bitterness—is correctly termed the secondary taste. Likewise, in the case of long pepper, that taste which is the opposite of its dried state (i.e., the sweetness present in the fresh state) is called the secondary taste.

However, we observe that even when fresh, long pepper (*pippalī*) possesses a sweet taste (*madhura-rasa*), since it will be stated: "Fresh long pepper is phlegm-forming (*śleṣmalā*), sweet (*madhurā*), heavy (*gurvī*), and unctuous (*snigdhā*)" (Sūtra 27).

If sweetness were merely a secondary taste (*anurasa*) in that case, its heaviness and its capacity to produce phlegm would be untenable. Therefore, it is logical that fresh long pepper possesses a manifest sweet taste, whereas the dried variety has sweetness as a secondary taste.

Now, he states the ten qualities such as priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*), which were not included among the previously mentioned qualities of the guru and so forth, and which are to be taught as properties of *rasa*—beginning with "priority" (*para*) and so on.
That "priority" (*paratva*) is preeminence (*pradhānatva*), and "posteriority" (*aparatva*) is non-preeminence (*apradhānatva*).
Its explanation begins with "space and time" (*deśakāla*) and so forth.

In this regard, location (*deśa*) consists of the desert (*maru*) as the superior (*para*) and the marshy land (*anūpa*) as the inferior (*apara*); time (*kāla*) consists of the period of release (*visarga*) as the superior and the period of withdrawal (*ādāna*) as the inferior; age (*vayas*) consists of youth as the superior and all other stages as the inferior; and the measurement of the body (*māna*) is the superior when it corresponds to what will be described in the *Śārīrasthāna*, while any other is the inferior. Furthermore, those maturations (*pāka*), potencies (*vīrya*), and tastes (*rasa*) which are appropriate for a particular person are superior for him, whereas those that are not suitable are inferior. By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the constitution (*prakṛti*), strength (*bala*), and so forth are also included.

Alternatively, *paratva* (remoteness) and *aparatva* (nearness), as described by the Vaiśeṣikas, are to be understood as follows: with respect to space, *paratva* occurs in that which is related to a distant location relative to something related to a proximate location, while *aparatva* occurs in that which is related to a proximate location. Likewise, with respect to time, *paratva* occurs in an elder relative to a younger person, and *aparatva* occurs in a younger person.

Regarding age and so forth, *paratva* and *aparatva* are produced by time and space as appropriate; they are mentioned here even as metaphorical because they are useful, since it is impossible for one quality to exist within another quality, such as measurement (*māna*).

Regarding the phrase "yuktiśca" (and *yukti*), it refers to the proper formulation (*yojanā*) of a medicine in consideration of [the patient's] defects and other factors. For this very reason it is said: "That which is joined"; that formulation which is appropriate (*yaugikī*) is called *yukti*, whereas even if a formulation is present, if it is inappropriate (*ayaugikī*), it is not called *yukti*—just as a son who is not a son [is not considered a son]. Furthermore, although this *yukti* is included within [the categories of] combination (*saṃyoga*), quantity (*parimāṇa*), and processing (*saṃskāra*), it is mentioned separately because of its extreme utility. He defines number (*saṅkhyā*) with the words beginning with "saṅkhyā."
He states the calculation here—beginning with one, two, three, and so on—as "conjunction" (*yoga*) and so forth.

The word "together" (*saha*) means the conjunction or attainment of substances that have been combined; by this term "together," he excludes a mere mutual contact that is ineffective for the purpose at hand.
He states its divisions: "dvandva" and so forth.

Among these, that produced by the action of two [entities] is, for example, [the conjunction] of two rams fighting; that produced by all actions is, for example, the conjunction of beans being thrown into a vessel arising from their frequent contact with the act of throwing; and that produced by the action of one is, for example, [the conjunction] of a tree and a crow.
By stating "it is non-eternal," he demonstrates that conjunction is non-eternal because it is produced by action.
He states the classification: "But the classification," and so forth.
"Vibhakti" means division (*vibhajana*). He explains *vibhakti* itself as "separation" (*viyoga*); separation is the dissolution of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

Is disjunction (*viyoga*) simply the absence of conjunction (*saṃyogābhāva*)? To this he says: "perception by parts" (*bhāgaśo graha*). The meaning is that it is because there occurs a perception [of objects] as distinct, that is, as divided. Therefore, this cognition of "separation" (*vibhakti*) is a positive entity (*bhāvarūpā*), and does not consist merely in the absence of conjunction; rather, the meaning is that it is endowed with the positive quality of disjunction (*vibhāga*). As for "distinctness" (*pṛthaktva*), it is that from which the cognition arises, such as "this substance characterized as a cloth is distinct from the jar"; that is distinctness.
The Teacher explains this through a threefold classification, beginning with "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*) and so forth.
Among these, that separateness which exists between things like Mount Meru and Mount Himavat, which are as if never joined in any way, is what is expressed by the term "non-conjunction" (*asaṃyoga*).
Likewise, there is also separateness among things that are conjoined, such as different species like buffaloes and boars; this he expresses with the words "distinctness" (*vailakṣaṇya*) and so forth.

The meaning is that "distinctness" (*pṛthaktva*) is characterized by being endowed with specific characteristics; thus, distinctness exists even among things of the same genus that are otherwise indistinguishable, such as beans. He says, "by way of multiplicity" (*anekatā*); for when things of the same genus are conjoined, there is neither difference in characteristic nor non-conjunction, yet there is still multiplicity in the form of distinctness—this is the sense.

Alternatively, one who maintains that separateness (*pṛthaktva*) is a distinct quality (*guṇāntara*) demonstrates, for the sake of worldly convention, that separateness is indeed of the nature of multiplicity distinguished from non-conjunction (*asaṃyoga*), as exemplified [in the text]: "The measure is the *prastha*, *āḍhaka*, and so forth; the instrument is that which is measured by scales and the like;
the meaning of 'refinement' (*saṃskaraṇa*) is the imparting of another quality. As he will state: "For refinement is said to be the imparting of another quality" (Vi. 1.2.9).
1) Thus,
"practice" (*abhyāsa*) is the repeated cultivation of states such as the sixty [virtues] or physical exercises (*vyāyāma*).

He explains this very practice through two synonyms well-known in the world— cultivation (*śīlana*) and constant performance (*satatakriyā*)— the sense being that what people designate by these two terms, cultivation and constant performance, is "practice."
And although this [treatment] consists of a specific modification of the combination of factors, it is mentioned separately because it is specifically useful for medical therapy;

furthermore, by the statement "it does not proceed as it ought," he indicates that among sound and other objects, as well as among teachers and others, the qualities such as "otherness" (paratva) and so forth are not primary.

Now, the mutual combination of tastes has been described as a quality (*guṇa*), and subsequently, qualities such as unctuousness (*snigdhatva*) and so forth are to be discussed; however, since such qualities do not exist within a taste that is itself of the nature of a quality, he states the following—beginning with "the qualities"—to explain how the designation of qualities for tastes is to be understood:
"The qualities have not been stated as being the substrata of qualities," because in the *Dīrghañjīvitīya* [chapter], it was stated: "But a quality is an inactive, inherent cause" (Sūtra 1).

Regarding the phrase "the qualities of taste" (*rasaguṇān*): one should understand these as being precisely the qualities—such as unctuousness (*snigdha*) and so forth—that have been specified for taste, which are actually the qualities of the substances that serve as the substrates for those tastes. Now, one might ask: "If these are indeed qualities of substance, why are they spoken of as qualities of taste? To this, he says: "Of the author" (*kartuḥ*), etc. "Of the author" means of the author of the treatise (*tantrakartuḥ*). "Intentions" (*abhiprāyāḥ*) refers to the intentions regarding the composition of the treatise, expressed through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) here and there, as well as through the employment of general terms and the like. The employment of general terms, metaphors, and so forth is carried out on account of the context and other factors, as well as for specific purposes, since such usage becomes clear through the force of the context.
We shall demonstrate that [contextual factor] and others in passages such as "therefore, having understood what is under discussion" (*ataśca prakṛtaṃ buddhvā*);

and here, regarding the metaphorical application (*upacaraṇa*) of substances and qualities onto tastes, this is the intended meaning: by the very mention of "sweet" and so forth, qualities such as "unctuous" (*snigdha*) and "cold" (*śīta*), which generally do not deviate from being sweet and so on, are already indicated in the substance; thus, after mentioning sweetness, there is no need to perform a separate presentation of unctuousness and the like.
He states "ataśca" and so forth to explain how the text is to be understood when there is a difference in intended meaning (*abhiprāya*).

Having understood what is relevant to the context (*prakṛta*), for example, in the passage "alkali, milk, fruit, flower," because the group of *udbhid* plants is the subject under discussion, one should understand that by the word "milk" he means specifically the milk of the *snuhī* plant and others. Having understood the specific location, for example, when purification of the head is being prescribed, [one understands] "in the case of worm-disease" (*krimivyādhau*) [from the context].

2) Thus, that [instruction] applies specifically to the disease caused by worms in the head, as stated at another time during the context of emesis: "And one should offer vessels" (Sūtra 15). In that context, by the word *pratigraha*, a vessel (*pātra*) is meant, and not the act of receiving (*grahaṇa*).
"The intentions of the author of the tantra" should be understood as the superimposition of qualities upon the tastes (rasas), as previously stated;
"the means" refers to the means of the treatise in the form of tantric methodology (tantrayukti);
and "the meaning" is the subject matter to be expressed.

Although the *prakṛta* (the primary) and so forth are also indeed the intentions of the author of the *tantra*, nevertheless, wherever the status of being *prakṛta* and so on is not clearly perceived, it should be understood as the intention of the author of the *tantra*.
"The six case-divisions" means the sixfold divisions beginning with *madhura* (sweet).

The construction is as follows: "The six [tastes] originate from the five elements" means that, while originating from the five elements, they become numbered as six—defined by the number six—in the manner already described, beginning with the phrase "due to the predominance of the quality of soma," and so forth; this is what I shall now explain. (38) Now, he first states the primary cause of the tastes, beginning with the word "saumya" (lunar).

By stating that "the gentle ones, having Soma as their deity, are falling," it is shown that apart from their connection with the earth, a connection with the atoms of earth and other elements impelled by the intermediate space (antarīkṣa) becomes the originator of taste;
[the word] "mūrtīḥ" refers to individual entities.
"Abhiprīṇayanti" means they satisfy; or rather, they produce and coalesce as "rasas," thereby attaining manifestation.

In this context, atmospheric water is mentioned because it is the primary cause of *rasa*; therefore, even the water situated on the earth certainly becomes the cause of *rasa* in the production of both stationary and moving beings.

'Due to the predominance of the quality of water'—by the word 'predominance' (atireka), he shows that while all elements are present in all tastes, a specific taste arises due to the predominance of the quality of a particular element in certain cases. Furthermore, this predominance of the quality of water with respect to sweetness should be understood as the cause for the production of that specific quality; whereas the fact that water serves as the substratum is common to all [tastes].
In the same way, the causality of water should be understood even in the case of salt."

In the *Suśruta*, however, salt (*lavaṇa*) is taught as having an excess of earth and fire. Regarding this contradiction, is it not the case that there is no contradiction in terms of its functional effect?

For salt, being produced by heat and cold—namely, fire and water—should itself possess both heat and cold; how then can that salt be hot? It is not so, because this is the inherent nature of the elements (*bhūta*): that when they are arranged in a particular manner, they initiate a certain quality, but not every [quality].

Just as a sweet taste is produced from makuṣṭhaka beans by water, but not oil; and likewise, even by fire, heat is not produced in rock salt—so too, this arrangement of the elements is brought about solely by the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa). That arrangement is to be inferred from the observation of its effects; therefore, it is postulated wherever an effect is observed. For example, in the case of salt, fire is inferred from its heat, and water from its fluidity.
Furthermore, this matter is to be known through scripture (*āgama*), and here the conceptual constructions of those like us do not extend;

by this, that which is said—namely, "Why do earth and the other elements not produce a distinct taste just as water does? and likewise, "Why do other tastes not arise from the conjunctions of water, air, and so forth?"—is also refuted precisely because one cannot subject the inherent nature of the elements (*bhūta-svabhāva*) to questioning.

And here, the causality of the elements (*bhūta*) with respect to taste is said to consist in their specific qualities such as sweetness, which function as instrumental causes (*nimittakāraṇa*); by this, the causality even of tasteless things like fire is established as entirely logical. Demonstrating the differentiation of tastes through an analogy, he says "in this way" and so forth: the sixfold nature of tastes is established due to the specific variations in the predominance and deficiency of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), arising from the six productive causes—such as the predominance of the quality of *soma* (water) or the predominance of earth and fire. The sense is that it is indeed logical that six effects arise from six causes.
Just as among the primary elements (mahābhūtas) there are various distinctions of color and form due to specific variations in their relative deficiency or excess, so it is with the tastes (rasas).
To explain the cause for these aforementioned variations in the primary elements, he says: "Because of the six seasons," and so forth.

Time, by virtue of having six seasons, promotes a particular element (*bhūta*) in a certain way through its various forms such as winter (*hemanta*) and so forth; and that [promoted element] causes its own effect, *rasa*, to become nourished. For example, in the winter season there is an excess of the quality of *soma* (water), and in the cool season (*śiśira*) there is an excess of air and space (*vāyu* and *ākāśa*). In this manner, the predominance of elements in spring and other seasons should also be understood according to the sequence for the production of *rasa* stated in the chapter on the "Eighty Topics" (*Aśitīya*). By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "from the six seasons," the predominance of elements caused by day and night should also be understood, as well as that caused by unseen destiny (*adṛṣṭa*). Consequently, the production of a different *rasa* in a certain substance even during winter and other such times becomes logically possible.

And although, even in the case of different seasons, the specific excellence of the elements alone is the cause— as stated in the passage beginning, "Those two, namely sun and wind" (Sūtra 6)— nevertheless, due to the beginninglessness of saṃsāra, the causal relationship between the specific elements and the seasons must be described as being like that between the seed and the sprout.
He states another property of tastes produced by specific elements, beginning with "Therein," etc.;
[the phrase] "mostly" implies that not all tastes [are so produced], referring to substances endowed with tastes.

"Because of floating" means because of possessing motion; although motion could also be downward, nevertheless, the motion characterized by lightness causes the air here to move only upward. He states another reason: "And because fire has an upward flame"; the meaning is that fire also possesses an upward motion. "Downwardness" is simply the state of moving downward.
"According to the substance" (*yathādravyam*) means that one should not deviate from whatever substance serves as the substratum for a particular taste; by this,
he demonstrates that the qualities and actions of tastes are to be understood as residing in the substance which is the substratum of those tastes.
Regarding the passage beginning with "therein," *madhura* (sweet) is mentioned first because it generally possesses qualities such as being conducive to longevity and is beloved by living beings.
The six sense-faculties together with the mind constitute the life-force (*jīvana*); for one who has fainted due to physical trauma and the like, it is the life-force;
however, it is the vital principle (*āyuṣya*) because it brings about the prolongation of life.

It acts as a restorative for what has been depleted by nourishing the bodily constituents (*dhātu*); alternatively, it is both "depleted" (*kṣīṇa*) and "wounded" (*kṣata*). Thus, it heals chest wounds (*uraḥkṣata*) in those who are both depleted and wounded.

The description of its qualities—such as being desired by bees and other insects—is useful for the knowledge of the premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*) of urinary disorders (*prameha*), as it is said: "ants swarm toward the urine" (Ci.).
6) Thus, as he will state regarding the *riṣṭa* (fatal signs): "That upon which flies greedily" (I.5).
By this, its sweetness is known.

Furthermore, although *abhiṣyanda* is already included within *akṣyāmaya* (eye disease), it is mentioned again for the sake of specifying a particular distinction; or else, *abhiṣyanda* should be understood as occurring in the nose and other parts as well. (1)
It is called *hṛdya* because it satiates the heart;
it is called *sārayati* because it expels what has been eaten; likewise, it moistens and digests that which has been eaten.
It is defiled by creatures with poisonous urine, and infested by insects such as *kāraṇḍas* and others with their specific modes of touch; it causes expansion, moisture, and cutting.
It is expansive, moistening, and corrosive.
"Flowing downwards" means having the nature of trickling; it is the opposite of all other tastes. Thus, wherever salt is present in excess, no other taste is perceived there.
"Associated with food" means it is always conjoined with food.
It deludes, it causes mental distraction, and it causes fainting; thus, it brings about the destruction of consciousness. (3) 43

The power of the post-digestive transformation (vipāka) is the "power of post-digestive transformation" (vipākaprabhāva); and the post-digestive transformation of pungent [substances] is indeed pungent. The power of taste (rasa) and potency (vīrya) is the "power of taste and potency" (rasavīryaprabhāva). This is the cause throughout everything that will be stated hereafter. The explicit mention of "action" (caraṇa) and so forth is because, in those cases, there is generally the manifestation of a disorder of Vāta; whereas here, the mention of the power of post-digestive transformation and so on is for the sake of illustration, by which the effects of post-digestive transformation and the rest in sweet and other tastes are to be inferred.
It causes exhaustion, brings about the destruction of joy, acts as a pressure by afflicting the wound,
and is called "the sucker" because it consumes the moisture of the body.
Because of the elision (praśleṣa) of the vowel 'a' in the phrase "cold, light, and [not] heavy" (*śīto'laghūśca*), "not heavy" (*alaghuḥ*) means that one "grasps firmly," i.e., makes them bound.
"By way of distinction" means one by one, part by part; "by way of unity" means having unified them, that is, as a mere aggregate;
"part by part" means by means of parts (*mātrayā*).
And that unification of the internal world with all objects of knowledge— whether two, three, or more— is to be understood as being "otherwise" (i.e.,
incorrectly) if it is done without proper measure.
44. Now, he describes the potency (*vīrya*) of substances specifically by means of their taste (*rasa*): "Cold," and so forth.

That substance which is sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect (*pāka*) should be known as cold in its potency; likewise, that substance which is sour in those two—taste and post-digestive effect—is hot in its potency; and likewise, that substance which is said to be pungent in those two—taste and post-digestive effect—is also hot in its potency. The word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied [as the verb].
Alternatively, there is the reading: "And that which is hot and pungent, of those two...

In this case, while it should have been stated that "that which is sweet by taste is cold by potency," he says "of those [substances] which are [sweet] by taste and post-digestive effect" (rasapākayoḥ) in order to establish that even a sweet substance whose post-digestive effect is appropriate for its sweet taste possesses a cold potency. The same should be stated for sour and pungent substances as well.

"Of these" refers to those [substances] such as *madhura-pāka* (sweet post-digestive transformation) and so forth. "By the instruction on taste" means by the mere mention of the taste alone, because the post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*) is also generally known from the taste itself; as he will state: "The post-digestive transformation of pungent, bitter, and astringent [tastes] is generally pungent," and so forth.
And since this is not the case everywhere, he says: "By potency (*vīrya*), etc."

The knowledge of potency (*vīrya*) is obtained through the gateway of taste for those substances whose potencies are not contradictory to their tastes, but this does not apply to substances such as the *mahāpañcamūla* group, whose potencies are contrary to their tastes. Furthermore, the collection of qualities that will be taught according to post-digestive transformation (*pāka*)—such as "pungent in its post-digestive state, it destroys semen, binds feces and urine, and increases *vāta"—is to be understood as applying to those substances whose potencies are not contradictory. If, however, the potency therein were contradictory, then even the post-digestive transformation would not produce the aforementioned qualities.

Alternatively, the collection of qualities characterized by coldness and heat should be taught according to the post-digestive transformation (*pāka*) for those substances that are not contrary [to their primary taste]. However, in the case of long pepper (*pippalī*), which—though pungent—is contrary in having a sweet post-digestive transformation, there is no heat due to its pungent taste; this is the meaning.
And in this view, the phrase "it will be taught" is connected with the passage beginning "just as milk," etc.
He now states those very substances whose potencies and post-digestive transformations are not contrary: "Just as milk," and so forth.
For substances such as milk and others, when describing their qualities, should be taught as having non-contradictory potencies (*vīrya*) and post-digestive effects (*vipāka*).
Now, he states that case where, due to contradictory potency, heat (*uṣṇatva*) and so forth should not be indicated by means of the taste (*rasa*): "sweet," and so on.

The construction is: "astringent and hot," and "bitter and hot. An illustration of astringent, bitter, and salty [tastes] has been provided here even though they were not explicitly mentioned in the aphorism, by virtue of the context.

Here, the *mahat-pañcamūla* (the great five roots), namely the *bilva*-group of five roots (*bilvādipañcamūla*), serves as an example for the hot potency of both the bitter and the astringent tastes; whereas the meat of aquatic and marsh-dwelling animals serves as an example for the hot potency of the sweet taste.
In connection with *vīrya* (potency), he states another [quality] that is contrary to sourness and so forth, beginning with the words "Furthermore" (*kiñcit*).
Regarding the phrase "other than this in the case of *abhayā*": the meaning is that in *abhayā*, the taste is astringent (*kaṣāya*), it is disintegrating (*bhedana*), and it is hot (*uṣṇa*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "due to dryness" (*raukṣyāt*):

because of its dryness, the astringent taste (*kaṣāya*) is "supreme," meaning it is the driest (*rūkṣatama*); the bitter (*tikta*) is dry (*rūkṣa*); and the pungent (*kaṭu*) is moderately dry (*madhya-rūkṣatara*). The same applies elsewhere as well.
"Acrid and last" means inferior; likewise, "salty and last" means inferior. "Salty and inferior" means [inferior] by way of its heaviness.

Regarding the passage beginning with "sourer than sour" (*amlāt kaṭu*), [it means]: sourer than sour is light; therefore, bitter, which is superior to that excellent sour, is the most excellent (*uttamottama*) in terms of lightness. Regarding the statement "superior to the excellent sour" (*uttamāt kaṭukād uttama*), he states the opinion of some (*ekīyamatam*)—accepting the view of certain authorities through a particular phrasing of the words—beginning with "heaviness" (*gaurave*).

By this, while accepting the inferiority of salt both in terms of heaviness (*gaurava*) and lightness (*lāghava*), one accepts that salt is heavier than sour, pungent, and bitter substances through the phrase "inferior in heaviness" (*gaurave 'vara*); and through the phrase "inferior in lightness" (*lāghave 'vara*), one accepts that the lightness of salt is less than even that of the sour, which is light.

Nor should it be argued that since earth is the cause of sourness while water is the cause of saltiness, it is more appropriate for salt—which is produced from water—to be lighter than [sourness] in comparison to earth; for heaviness and lightness cannot be determined by the mere inclusion of elements. For instance, sweetness produced by an excess of water becomes heavier than the astringent taste produced by an excess of earth.
Now, since even the post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*) possesses the nature of taste (*rasa*), he states its definition beginning with "param" (supreme), etc.
By the inclusion of the word "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*), he demonstrates that *pippalī*, *kulattha*, and others undergo a transformation that is inconsistent with their [original] tastes.

Furthermore, by the term "bitter" (*kaṭuka*) and so forth, the substance (*dravya*) which is the substratum of that taste is expressed; for it is not the tastes themselves that are transformed, but rather the substance alone.

"Lavaṇas tathā" means that salt (*lavaṇa*) also generally has a sweet post-digestive effect (*madhuravipāka*). As for the definition of post-digestive effect (*vipāka*): "The quality that arises at the time of completion of the food through its contact with the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*) is the post-digestive effect. For it is said: "That other taste which arises from contact with the digestive fire at the end of the transformation of food is proclaimed as the post-digestive effect" (*Vāgbhaṭa*).
Sūtra 9) 57–58

Now, regarding the characteristics of post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*) to be described, he states the reason why sweet and sour transformations do not obstruct wind (*vāta*), urine, and feces, whereas pungent transformation does cause their obstruction—beginning with the words "sweet" (*madhura*).

Here, the meaning of the sentence is that sweet, sour, and salty tastes, even when they have reached their final state of digestion (*niṣṭhāpāka*), facilitate the easy discharge of wind, urine, and feces due to their association with the quality of unctuousness (*sneha*).
Therefore, this is a common characteristic of both sweet and sour post-digestive transformations.
In this way, the meaning of the sentence regarding pungent, bitter, and astringent [tastes], or their opposites, is established (vv.

Now, in order to state the characteristic of post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*)—which has been explained through its causes and is characterized by specific qualities such as being "white" (*śukra*) and so forth—he says: "śukra-hetu... and so on.
"Otherwise than this" (ato'nyathā) is the brief [explanation] (laghu).

Now, regarding the various substances characterized by the aforementioned results of maturation (vipāka), he explains how there occurs in some cases a small degree, in some a middling degree, and in others a superior degree: "The result of maturation," and so forth.

One should observe the small, medium, or predominant degree of the characteristic of maturation (*vipāka*), meaning that this occurs due to the specific excellence of the qualities (*guṇavaiśeṣya*) of each individual substance.

By this it is stated that, among substances, whatever specific excellence of quality there may be—such as sweetness, greater sweetness, or greatest sweetness—it is from that cause that the distinctions of the maturations, such as their smallness and so forth, arise.

In this regard, some say that there is a distinct transformation for each taste, such that the six tastes—sweet and the rest—undergo six transformations, namely sweet and so forth. Others say that the weaker tastes fall under the influence of the stronger tastes, and consequently, the transformation is not fixed.
Disregarding both these views regarding the determination of transformation, Suśruta has accepted two types of transformation: sweet and pungent.

Furthermore, there is a twofold nature in substances composed of the five elements: when there is an excess of the heavy elements, earth and water, a sweet post-digestive transformation (*pāka*) occurs; however, when there is an excess of the remaining light elements, a pungent post-digestive transformation occurs. As it has been said: "In those substances being digested wherein the qualities of water and earth prevail, the post-digestive transformation is called sweet; but in those being digested wherein the qualities of fire, air, and space [prevail]..."
“Where the products are more abundant there, that digestion is called pungent” (Suśruta Sūtrasthāna 40).

In the case of a substance that undergoes transformation during digestion (*pratirasa-pāka*) as well as one whose digestion is unstable (*anavasthita-pāka*), the substance remains identical to its original taste and quality even at the stage of digestion; therefore, since no distinction is perceived therein through the resulting transformation (*vipāka*), Suśruta rightly set aside those two positions.

The rejection of the third [position], namely that there is no sour post-digestive transformation (*amlapāka*), however, brings forth a logical flaw; for it is observed that rice, horse gram (*kulattha*), and other such grains produce *pitta* due to their having a sour post-digestive transformation. If you think that the production of *pitta* in the case of rice and the like is due to their possessing a hot potency (*uṣṇavīrya*), that is not so. For, according to your own view, although sweet rice possesses a sweet post-digestive transformation and even a hot potency, its production of *pitta* would not be tenable; this is because a single potency must be overridden by either the taste (*rasa*) or the post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*).

Furthermore, because rice and other grains have an acidic digestion (*amlapāka*), bile (*pitta*) arises with an acidic quality (*amlaguṇa*); if, however, that were caused by their hot potency (*uṣṇavīryatā*), then the bile would be predominantly pungent (*kaṭuguṇa*). Yet it is observed that from eating rice, there is an abundance of acidic qualities, such as acid eructations (*amlodgāra*). Moreover, in the view that a sweet digestion results from an excess of the qualities of earth and water (*soma*), while a pungent digestion results from an excess of air, fire, and space, how can the production of an acid [digestion] consisting of both *soma* (water) and fire when there is an excess of mixed qualities be rejected?

Alternatively, what need is there for these two authors of the tantras to engage in this mere verbal contradiction? For that which Caraka describes as having an acidic post-digestive transformation (*amlapāka*) is reconciled by Suśruta on the grounds that its potency (*vīrya*) is hot (*uṣṇa*); thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever regarding the properties of substances.

As for the objection raised in the Suśruta-saṃhitā to refute the existence of an acidic post-digestive transformation—stating, "Indeed, bile, when it is improperly digested, attains acidity" (Su.Sū.)—[it is addressed as follows].

By such statements as these, [the objection] is refuted precisely because that [position] is not accepted. Now, one might object: "If salt has a sweet post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*), its being a producer of bile, blood, and so forth is illogical; likewise, if bitter and astringent tastes have a pungent post-digestive transformation, their being destroyers of bile is illogical. This is not so. Even though salt has a sweet post-digestive transformation, the fact that it produces bile, blood, and so forth is due to the salty taste and the hot potency (*vīrya*) present therein. As for the post-digestive transformation, since it is sublated in relation to the effect characterized by the removal of bile and blood, it is indeed characterized by the definition beginning with "it causes the evacuation of feces and urine."

By this, the following objection is refuted: "If salt has a sweet post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*), yet because it is overridden by its taste (*rasa*) and potency (*vīrya*), it does not produce its own effect, then what is the point of teaching that [sweetness]?
For indeed, the existence of a sweet post-digestive transformation in that salt is to be inferred by the resulting state of having passed stool and urine that are sweet;
in this same manner, the rebuttal of the prima facie argument regarding bitter and astringent tastes is also established.

Others, however, fearing this objection, explain that salt also transforms into sour (*amla*). They argue that in the phrase "salt likewise" (*lavaṇastathā*), the word "likewise" (*tathā*) draws in the distant term "sour" (*amla*).

But that is not correct, because of the statement of Jatūkarṇa: "The post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*) of pungent and the others is pungent; that of the sour is sour; and for the remaining two, it is sweet.

Nor should it be asked why there are only three transformations and not bitter (*tikta*) and the rest as well; for this is simply the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of the elements (*bhūta*), by which only the three beginning with sweet occur, and the nature of the elements is not subject to questioning.

Now, one might object: let that post-digestive transformation (*pāka*) which is contrary to the taste be stated—such as the sweet transformation of salt, or the pungent transformation of bitter and astringent tastes. But what is the purpose of describing that which shares the same quality, such as the sweet transformation of a sweet substance, the sour of a sour, or the pungent of a pungent? For in those cases, the quality of the post-digestive transformation will already be known through the qualities of the taste itself.

It is not so; for even in that case, a corresponding *vipāka* (post-digestive transformation) must indeed be stated, in order to dispel the suspicion that a dissimilar taste might arise—as occurs, for example, with salt and other substances. Furthermore, a taste born of *vipāka* (*vipākaja-rasa*) occurs at the end of the digestion of food, whereas the natural (*prākṛta*) taste should be understood as being contrary to the *vipāka*, except during the period of transformation itself. Thus, the pungent taste of long pepper (*pippalī*) serves a purpose by initially clearing phlegm from the throat and purifying the mouth; its sweet *vipāka*, however, serves a purpose by indicating its aphrodisiac properties and other effects through its final transformation.

Likewise, it should be understood that where the tastes of the metabolic transformation (*vipāka*) are concordant with the qualities of the substance, the resulting effect is powerful; however, in the opposite case, it is weak. Furthermore, these three types of transformation are determined by the substance itself; therefore, they are distinct from the transformations of the state of food (*āhārāvasthāpāka*) which will be described in the chapter on the *grahaṇī*. For in that context, all tastes without exception are said to undergo three transformations according to their state, as stated in the passage beginning: "Of food that has just been eaten, consisting of six tastes, through its transformation... (Ci. 15).
According to the opinion of some, he states the definition of *vīrya* (energy), beginning with "weak" (*mṛdu*) and so forth.
Furthermore, these two opinions of certain [teachers] proceed by prioritizing a technical (*pāribhāṣikī*) designation for *vīrya*.

In Ayurveda, the term *vīrya* (potency) is designated for a quality that performs a significant action distinct from taste (*rasa*), post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), and specific influence (*prabhāva*). Therefore, according to the view that there are eight types of potency, qualities such as sliminess (*picchila*) and clarity (*viśada*) generally do not produce effects contrary to those of taste and the other factors; thus, they are understood through the very instruction of taste and so forth. However, qualities such as softness (*mṛdu*) and others do possess the capacity to override taste and the rest. For example, in long pepper (*pippalī*), the action of pungent taste—which is the provocation of *pitta*—is overridden by its soft and cold potency (*vīrya*), which pacifies that very *pitta*. Similarly, in the great five roots (*pañcamūla*) which are astringent with a bitter after-taste, the action of wind-provocation is overridden by their hot potency, which produces the opposite effect—the pacification of *vāta*. Likewise, in sugarcane, which is sweet, there is an increase of *vāta* due to its cold potency, and so forth.
As stated in the Suśruta-saṃhitā: “Indeed, these potencies, by the excellence of their own strength and qualities, overcome the taste and manifest their own specific actions,” and so forth (Su.Sū.

The doctrine of those who maintain that [the gunas] possess the potencies of cold and heat should be understood as arising from the view that the world belongs to Agni and Soma, and because cold and heat alone are predominant;

for it has been said: "Even though a substance consists of diverse natures, it never transcends the two mighty ones, Agni and Soma, just as the world does not transcend the manifest and the unmanifest" (Vākyapadīya).
(9) Thus,

both of these two views are indeed accepted by the Teacher as established by technical convention (*paribhāṣā*), since he will later refer to *vīrya* solely in its technical sense in such passages as: "where a commonality of taste, potency, and post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*) is observed."
Abandoning the conventional designation of *vīrya*, he states the definition of *vīrya* as a synonym for *śakti* (potency) in the passage beginning with "Vīrya, however," and so forth.
*Vīrya* is *śakti*.

That by which—whether by its taste (*rasa*), its post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*), its specific potency (*prabhāva*), or by qualities such as heaviness (*guru*) and so on—a specific action (*kriyā*) consisting of nourishment (*tarpaṇa*), exhilaration (*hlādana*), pacification (*śamana*), and the like is produced; in that action, that taste and so forth is *vīrya*.
Therefore, it has been stated in the Suśruta Saṃhitā: "That by which they act is their potency" (Su.Sū.
Right here, he states the reasoning well-known in the world: "Not by the powerless," and so forth.
"Powerless" (avīrya) means lacking capacity.
"Produced by power" (vīryakṛtā) means produced by one who possesses power (vīryavat).
He states the definition for the purpose of knowing the distinctions between taste (*rasa*) and the other [qualities] when they are present in a single substance: "Taste is a *nipāta*," and so forth;
here, "*nipāta*" refers to its occurrence in conjunction with the sense of taste.

"By the culmination of action" (*karmaniṣṭhayā*): the culmination (*niṣṭhā*) of action is its completion (*niṣpatti*), which is the finalization of the process. When there is the utilization of the essence (*rasa*), there occurs a specific transformation of the food resulting from the final stage of digestion, characterized by the increase of *kapha*, semen, and so forth; by this, the "maturation" (*vipāka*) is determined. "Co-dwelling" (*adhīvāsa*) means co-existence; "as long as the co-dwelling lasts" means as long as one resides in the body. This should be understood as occurring after the maturation and prior to the falling [of the body].

The phrase "and from the falling" (nipātāt) means merely from contact with the body. By this, some potency is perceived through impregnation (adhīvāsa), such as the heat of the meat of marshy animals; some is obtained from the falling alone, such as the pungency of *marīca* and other spices; and some is obtained from both the falling and impregnation, such as that of *marīca* and others.

By this it is meant that *rasa* (taste) is perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) alone; *vipāka* (post-digestive effect), however, is always imperceptible and is inferred through its effects; *vīrya* (potency), moreover, is sometimes known through inference—such as the coldness inherent in rock salt (*saindhava*) or the heat inherent in the meat of marshy animals—and sometimes *vīrya* is known by direct perception itself, such as the pungency in black mustard (*rājikā*) perceived by the sense of smell, while qualities such as sliminess, clarity, unctuousness, and roughness are determined by both sight and touch. This is the meaning of the statement;
furthermore, this *vīrya* should be understood as being both innate (*sahaja*) and artificial (*kṛtrima*).
And this definition of *vīrya* (potency) is to be understood as applying to substances according to their respective heavy, light, and other qualities;
that is, it refers to the substances being employed.
Furthermore, this definition of *vīrya* pertains exclusively to the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) sense of *vīrya*.
He states the definition of *prabhāva* (potency): "Taste, potency," and so forth;
"general" (*sāmānya*) means similarity (*tulyatā*).
The phrase "the distinction of actions" refers to the general characteristic observed in those actions based on dental and other [articulatory] places, such as purgation and so forth.

By this, he indicates that whatever effect cannot be determined as being produced by taste (*rasa*) and the like, that effect is brought about by *prabhāva* (specific potency). Therefore, it is said: "Potency is called inconceivable"; the meaning is that it is inconceivable in terms of being an effect of taste, potency, and post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*).
Because this very [subject] is difficult to comprehend, he provides many examples beginning with "kaṭuka" and so forth.

Similarly, regarding the statement that [the substance] possesses qualities equal to those of *citraka* and is called a "poison-destroyer," [it is said]: "Therefore, the primary poison is from the fangs" (Ci.).

23) By the phrase "ascending and descending" (*ūrdhvānulomika*), it refers to that which simultaneously removes [impurities] from both parts; alternatively, it refers to action (*karman*) that is of a dual nature, namely, that which removes [impurities] from above as well as from below, such as the removal of poisons, the removal of pain, and so forth.

This is merely an illustration; by this, it should be understood that all the inconceivable effects of substances such as living organisms or impure materials—such as their tastes and so forth—are termed "prabhāva" (specific potency).

Here, *prabhāva* is intended to mean the power (*śakti*) of a substance, and that power is the very particularity (*viśeṣa*) of substances, being the individual entity itself characterized by qualities such as *dantī*-ness. For power is indeed the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of entities, not some separate or additional attribute. This same principle should be applied to the qualities, potencies, and so forth mentioned in other passages; as it has been said: "For substances [act] through the potency of the substance and the potency of the qualities," and so on.

Nor should it be argued that *dantī* purges by its very nature, so what is the point of [stating] that it does not purge when impaired by water and the like? For it is only potency (*prabhāva*) as qualified by the absence of an obstructing factor that functions as the cause; thus, one must follow the reasoning that in the case of *dantī* impaired by water, the impairment by water acts as the obstructing factor. Furthermore, the explanation given in the Nyāya theory of potency regarding how poison counteracts poison—characterized by the contradiction between upward and downward movement—occurs precisely through potency because it is internal.
In this same way, it should also be stated regarding the description of being composed of earth and so forth, starting from the upward and downward sequences.
"Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) means that by which one cognizes; the meaning is "characteristic.
"Dissolving" (*pralīyan*) means becoming dissolved;
"flowing forth" (*saṃsrāvī*) means causing to flow out.
"Expansive" (*vikāsī*) means having the nature of expanding the heart; for it is said in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*: "It pains the heart" (*su.
74–79 Now, in order to speak of incompatible food (viruddhāhāra), he says "evam" and so forth.

Those which produce opposition to the bodily constituents (dhātu) are called *vairodhika* (incompatible). That by which incompatibility is characterized is the *lakṣaṇa*; thus, the very text that expresses the incompatible is itself the definition.
"Whatever causes the discharge of impurities," and so forth— this should be understood as the characteristic of antagonism (vairodhika).

"Being antagonistic to the bodily constituents" means having a nature that is opposed to the bodily constituents, such as the *rasa* and others, as well as to the *vāta* and others when they are in their natural state (*prakṛtistha*).
"They encounter opposition" means they act in opposition to the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), that is to say, they corrupt them.
Regarding how substances encounter opposition with the bodily constituents as they truly are, he says: "Some are mutually opposed," and so forth.
Among these, those whose qualities are mutually opposed are, for example, those stated in such passages as: "One should not consume fish with milk, for both of these... and so on.

An example of contradiction through association (*saṃyogaviruddha*) is as follows: "That very same *nikuca* fruit, when ripe, is not like *māṣa*," and so forth—this was not stated [as such]. When something is called contradictory merely by its coexistence (*sāhitya*), without mentioning qualities such as preparation (*saṃskāra*) that are contradictory, that is contradiction through association.

Although the simultaneous consumption of fish and milk is indeed stated to be contradictory, nevertheless, since that is described as a contradiction of qualities (*guṇavirodha*), it is an illustration of that alone.

Furthermore, contradiction occurs only in certain cases despite the presence of opposing qualities, due to the specific power of the substance itself.
