Therefore, when consuming food containing all six tastes, one should not raise an objection regarding the contradiction between sweet and sour tastes, which possess respectively cold and hot potencies (*vīrya*), because such opposition is neutralized by processing (*saṃskāra*). An example of what is contradictory due to processing is: "One should not eat pigeons fried in mustard oil," and so forth.
Place (*deśa*) is twofold: the external environment (*bhūmi*) and the body (*śarīra*).

In that regard, what is contrary to the place (*bhūmiviruddha*) is, for example: "that very [thing] covered with ashes and dust"; or whatever has become unsuitable for that region is contrary to the place. What is contrary to the body (*śarīraviruddha*) is, for example: honey for one afflicted by heat leads to death.

What is contrary to the time (*kālaviruddha*) is, for example: stale *kākamācī* leads to death. What is contrary to the measure (*mātrāviruddha*) is, for example: equal quantities of honey and clarified butter lead to death.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), those things that are contradictory by way of their nature, such as defects and so forth, are included.
An example of a contradiction of essential nature (svabhāvaviruddha) is: poison.
"Regarding that which is antagonistic" means with reference to antagonism;
"because of coldness and heat" refers to milk being cold while fish have a hot potency (*vīrya*). The remainder, such as sweetness and so forth, is common [to both].
And this [antagonism] is due solely to the specific power (*prabhāva*) of the substance.
By the passage beginning with “That *śakalī* again,” the fish known as *nāndini* is described (verses 82–83).
Even [the flesh of] domestic animals and so forth are incompatible with any one of the substances such as honey and the rest.
"Kalamūkatā" refers to the state of being mute or having indistinct speech.

The consumption of *pauṣkara* and other such items together with honey and milk is contradictory; *pauṣkara* is the vegetable known as *puṣkaravratarūpa*, and *rohiṇī* is *kaṭurohiṇī* (a collection of vessels, a knot of veins).

By the phrase "jātuśākaṃ vaṃśapatrikā vairodhikatvāt" (jātuśāka and bamboo leaves [are incompatible] because of their incompatibility), there is a restatement of the incompatibility—which was already established by the context—for the purpose of demonstrating that [these] act as causes of diseases such as impotence (*ṣāṇḍhya*) mentioned in general terms. This same principle should be understood elsewhere as well, where even when only incompatibility is mentioned in a general sense.

Similarly, in the passage beginning with "amla" (sour), although [fruits] such as the *āmla* and *āmrātaka* are already included by the mention of "sour," they are mentioned specifically for the purpose of indicating particular types of incompatibility.

Since both liquid and non-liquid sour substances are already included by the very use of the word "all" (*sarva*), the explicit mention of "liquid and non-liquid" is for the purpose of negating the idea that the word "all" refers to the totality of liquid and non-liquid sour things; for indeed, within a specific context, the designation "all" may apply even to a single part, as in the expression, "one should feed everyone. Alternatively, the inclusion of the word "all" is for the purpose of including grains (*vrīhi*) and other substances that have a sour post-digestive transformation (*amlavipāka*).

Since the sense of "together" (*saha*) is already obtained by the instrumental case *payasā* itself, the explicit mention of the word *saha* again is for the purpose of demonstrating that the contradiction [of milk] applies only when it is combined with sour substances such as *amlā* alone. Therefore, when there is a combination of milk and sour substances, if there is also a combination with jaggery (*guḍa*) and so forth, there is no contradiction regarding milk, mangoes, and the like.
*Vanaka* is a type of *kodrava* grain;
*padmottarikā* is safflower (*kusumbha*).
The term *śārkara* is an adjective qualifying *maireya*;

by the statement "it excessively aggravates *vāta*," it indicates that it also slightly aggravates *pitta* and *kapha*. Similarly, this should also be stated for the two [other drinks]: "it excessively aggravates *pitta*" and "it excessively aggravates *kapha*.
*Hāridraka* is a bird known as *aharitāla*.
The crane (*balākā*) is incompatible with the *vāruṇī* liquor; likewise, the crane is incompatible with boiled grain (*kulmāṣa*).

"Attached to a castor-wood post" (*eraṇḍasīsakāvasakta*) means attached to a castor-wood beam; for "castor-wood" (*sīsaka*) refers to the wood used for making a frame, and that very thing is the turmeric-colored meat (*hāridrakamāṃsa*).
*Matsyanistālana* refers to that in which fish are fried or cooked; alternatively, *nistālana* means fat (*vasā*). Jatūkarṇa also states: "Long peppers (*pippalī*) prepared with fish-fat.
Furthermore, the combination of *kākamācī* and honey is a contradiction in terms of medicinal compatibility (*saṃyogaviruddha*).
*Bhāsa* is a domestic cock.
In order to include those [factors] that were not mentioned and are contradictory [to the previous categories], he says: "Whatever it may be," and so forth;
it is called *āhāra* (nutriment) because it is taken in, and this includes medicine as well.
"Having caused the morbid humors (doṣa) to flow out" means that after producing the humors in their excited state, one does not eliminate them;
by this, he excludes emetic and purgative substances, for those indeed eliminate the humors after causing them to flow out.
Furthermore, as for the passage beginning with "place, time, fire," etc., which some read, that is clearly [an interpolation];
[the term] *ṣāṇḍhya* means eunuchism or lack of virility.

The defect of lineage (*santānadoṣa*), such as giving birth to stillborn children and so forth, is a statement of general contraindication that is overridden by specific instructions. Therefore, the drinking of garlic with milk is not in every case contradictory. As it is said: "One should prepare four *palas* of pure, dried garlic in eight times its quantity of milk and water; one should have the patient drink the remaining milk" (*Cikitsāsthāna*, chapter 5). Likewise, this should be inferred from formulations such as "the fresh juice of radish with milk," and others.

Alternatively, there is no contradiction here because of the combination of multiple substances; for it is only the combination with a substance that is inherently contradictory that constitutes a contradiction. As for the mention of "unripening" and so forth regarding honey when it is combined with hot emetics—even though it is combined with substances such as *madanaphala*—this is stated for the purpose of showing that honey remains non-contradictory [only] in the absence of those factors; whereas, even when honey is combined with other substances, its contradictory nature is demonstrated if it is associated with heat, because honey is a derivative of poison (*viṣa*), and poison is incompatible with heat.

However, from the scriptural statement that "the combination [of garlic and so forth] is forbidden only when not mixed with other substances," it is inferred that [this applies to] those things which are antagonistic to them, such as the six flavors (ṣāḍhya) and the like.
"Of those antagonistic to them" refers to those things that take away the six flavors and so forth.

"By such [means]" refers to those things contrary to diseases produced by incompatible food; "cultivation" (*abhisaṃskāra*) means the nourishment of the body through constant application, or alternatively, "by such [means]" refers to the employment of elixirs (*rasāyana*).
And this should be understood as the treatment for preventing future afflictions (104–106).

Regarding the statement in the *Saṅgraha* that "the enumeration of substances is based on tastes," and the subsequent passage beginning with "and their classification," the underlying sense is that the enumeration of tastes is, in ultimate reality, simply the enumeration of substances, because tastes themselves possess no qualities (*nirguṇatvāt*).

The reason for the enumeration of tastes is stated by [the verse beginning] “because of the suitability of the tastes therein”; the classification of the case-endings is by [the verse beginning] “therein, sweet...”;
the indication of substances is by [the verse beginning] “cold in its potency...”; and the exception regarding substances is by [the verse beginning] “certain [substances] are sweet...”.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Ātreya and Bhadrakāpya," in the *Annapānacatuṣka* (Section on Food and Drink) within the *Sūtrasthāna* of the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of Caraka composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 27 (27 of 120)] Now,

this chapter on the rules for food and drink (*annapānavidhi*) is expounded for the purpose of describing the specific qualities and actions of useful substances, which were previously mentioned only in general terms according to their qualities and actions, but have not been described individually for each specific substance;
here, the suffix *cha* that arose [after the word *prāya*] is elided (*luk*).

In this context, among foods, the solid (khādya) is to be understood as included by virtue of the commonality of solidity, and among drinks, the lickable (lehya) is included by virtue of the commonality of fluidity; thus, "the regimen of food and drink" (annapānavidhi) is prescribed and explained through its association with specific qualities and actions. Indeed, the description of the qualities and actions of substances is itself the regimen of food and drink, because it is only after knowing that [regimen] that food and drink are prescribed.
He asks: what does that food and drink do? He says: "Desirable" (*iṣṭa*), and so forth.
"Desirable" means both what is intended and what is beneficial. Alternatively, "desirable" means pleasant, whereas "beneficial" is obtained by the very term "prescribed by rule" (*vidhi-vihita*).
The rule will be stated in the *Rasavimāna* [chapter] as: "This is the prescription for diet" (*tadetad āhāravidhānam*).

1) That which is expressed by such passages as these, as well as the procedure stated in the *Indriyopakramaṇīya* chapter beginning with "one whose hands are not adorned with jewels" (Sūtra 8)— that which is prescribed by such a rule is "prescribed by rule" (*vidhivihitam*).
In this context, there is no perception of sound among the [qualities of] color and so forth in food and drink, because for the most part sound is absent therein.
Among color and the other [qualities], whichever is first perceived in food and drink is mentioned first.
Taste (*rasa*), however, although it is perceived after touch (*sparśa*), is placed before touch in order to demonstrate its preeminence.

Although the term "of living beings" (*prāṇinām*) alone would have sufficed, the explicit statement "of those designated as living beings" (*prāṇisañjñakānām*) is for the purpose of excluding stationary living beings. For trees and the like are called "living beings" in the treatise because they are taught to follow the nature of plant-sentient beings (*vanaspatisattva*); yet in common worldly usage, they are not designated as "living beings," but rather only mobile creatures are so called.

And although in this context the human being alone is the subject under discussion, the description of food is given generally as the cause of life for all living beings in order to demonstrate that food produces life even in creatures other than humans;

it is called "life" (*prāṇa*) because it is the cause of life. For example, [it is said] "clarified butter is longevity. Then, he asks: "In what way, then, do they call it 'life'? and replies: "Because its result is perceived directly."

The meaning is that it is observed through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) persist for those who take food according to the prescribed rule, whereas the vital breaths do not remain for those who abstain from food. Here, the word *pratyakṣa* refers to a clear means of valid cognition (*sphuṭapramāṇa*). Since the fact that the vital breaths have food as their effect is indeed to be understood through inference, [the author] states the reason for the vital breaths having food as their effect with the words beginning "for they have that as their fuel" (*tadindhanā hi*).

Since the maintenance of the internal fire depends on food and drink, and the maintenance of the fire is the cause of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), the implication is that food is the vital breaths themselves. For it has been said: "Strength, health, longevity, and the vital breaths are established in the fire.

Alternatively, while the fact that food and drink are the cause of the vital breaths was stated previously, here—by the words "for they are its fuel" and so forth—their role as the cause of the fire is described; and by the phrase "it invigorates the *sattva*," it means it provides strength to the mind.
The array of elements, the collection of elements;
the contrary is that which is practiced without rule.

We shall teach in its entirety—that is, in its fullness—the method by which food and drink are prescribed, consisting of substances, qualities, and actions, as well as the forms of the constituent parts of the body and so forth.

Although in this context he will not specify each individual substance by means of its qualities and actions, for he will say: "This has been stated as a portion of food and drink that is generally used," nevertheless, by the instruction on the mobile body parts and so forth, as well as by the description of the qualities and actions of the substances such as the earthy ones mentioned in the previous chapter, the prescription of those [substances] is also effectively stated; therefore it was said: "in its entirety. For he will say: "Just as there is no medicinal herb whatsoever, and just as there is the speech of those born in various regions..."

"However, that substance which might remain unmentioned here should be stated as such," and likewise, "the limbs of the body [are mentioned]," and so forth. Alternatively, the word *vidhi* (method/way) refers to the modes of eating, drinking, licking, and chewing; by this, all things such as what is eaten and so on are to be expressed in their entirety, whereas the substances that serve as their causes—such as red rice (*raktaśāli*) and others—are mentioned only partially. Therefore, he will state: "This is said to be a portion of food and drink. And since food and drink are to be discussed, having first described the general qualities of the substance most commonly used, he will teach its qualities through a summary of its groups (*varga*).

Water is mentioned first because it is employed both for food and drink; thus it serves as the illustration. Alternatively, "tatsvabhāva" means that which has that nature; therefore, the meaning is "because of its nature of moistening.
Even though [it is said] "water is for the refreshing [drugs], water is for the astringent [drugs]" (Sūtra...).
26) Although this has been stated, it is nevertheless repeated here in order to designate the previously unstated action of moistening (*kledana*).

Here, whatever action is mentioned regarding water, salt, and so forth, should be understood as their primary action among other actions. However, in the context of the "foremost" (*agrya*), one should understand the excellence of the substance that acts as the agent of that action:
"Alkali causes the cooking fire to cook. In this sense, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), meaning "by means of that, he causes [it] to cook."

In cases such as *snehayati*, however, the suffix *ṇic* is applied according to the rule "he does that" (*tat karoti*) or "he describes that" (*tad ācaṣṭe*). Thus, [the phrase] means that the *rasa* (nutritive essence), namely *māṃsarasa* (flesh-essence), joins together the separated skin, flesh, and other tissues.

It "pleases" means it nourishes those who are emaciated, but it does not cause excessive bulk. Therefore, through its flesh-building action of nourishment, it does not produce a state identical to that [excessive bulk], but rather causes the accumulation of flaccid flesh and so forth. As stated by Hārīta: "Wine causes flaccidity because of the abundance of blood and fat"; likewise, it is said in this very [text]: "Wine is for the nourishment of the emaciated."

“*Avadhamayati*” means it scrapes, because verbal roots have multiple meanings; for there is a saying: “*lekhanaḥ śītarasikaḥ*” (the scraper is fond of cold). Likewise, it is stated by Hārīta: “*śīdhu avadhamayati vāyvagniprabodhanāt*” (śīdhu scrapes [the channels] by awakening the wind and fire).

“*Ācinoti doṣān*” (it collects the *doṣas*)—this is the ellipsis; for there is a statement in another treatise: “*vātapittakaphāṃstasmādācinoti ca phāṇitam*” (therefore, *phāṇita* collects wind, bile, and phlegm).
*Piṇyāka* is sesame paste; however, the author of the *Nighaṇṭu* says: *piṇyāka* is green *śigru*.

It causes exhaustion and brings about the depletion of vitality. It produces feces containing abundant internal waste; for although it will later be stated that "black gram (māṣa) is high in waste," this is nevertheless a description of the qualities of *sūpa* (soup), which is a preparation of black gram, and thus there is no tautology. Furthermore, the properties of the raw material do not necessarily follow those of its derivative; for instance, a cooked ball (*piṇḍikā*) made from roasted barley flour (*saktu*) is indeed heavy. Therefore, this statement is made here to demonstrate the increase in waste even in the case of a preparation of black gram.
The property of alkaline substances being digestive (pācana) has been stated as a quality; however, here, their quality of destroying vision and semen is mentioned separately as a defect.
The term "mostly pitta-increasing" (*prāyaḥ pittalam*) is stated specifically [to distinguish it] from other salts and pungents, for which acidity is pitta-increasing;
thus, elsewhere too, the word "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*) should be understood as having a specific meaning. Alternatively, the word "mostly" may be connected with "acidity" (*amlena*).

In this context, *pitta* is mentioned first because it is produced by sour [tastes], since the predominance of the *doṣas* is not fixed. For it has been stated: “They are not separate from *pitta*, *kapha*, and *anila* (Sūtra 19),” as well as “those with balanced *pitta*, *anila*, and *kapha* (Sūtra 7). Alternatively, *pitta* is the heat (*ūṣman*) which is the fire; and that is primary here in the digestion of food and drink. As it is said: “That food which nourishes the body tissues, *ojas*, strength, complexion, and so forth...”
"In that regard, fire is the cause, for from uncooked food, the *rasa* and other [nutrients] do not arise" (Ci.

15). Therefore, here at the outset, only that which generates *pitta*—the cause of the digestive fire—is mentioned. And since that which generates *pitta* must be discussed first, the sweet (*madhura*) taste, although predominant in *rasa*, is not mentioned at the beginning.
By reading the word "madhunaḥ" as a separate term, he demonstrates that fresh honey does not produce *kapha*.

And here, the description of the six tastes is indeed by means of these three alone, because even the unmentioned salty, bitter, and astringent tastes are included by way of their post-digestive transformation (*pāka*); for salt is generally sweet after digestion, while bitter and astringent become pungent through digestion.
As for the passage beginning with "generally all that is bitter," that belongs to the work of Hārīta and has been written here by someone through oversight.
The "group-collection" (vargasangraha) refers to the collection of food substances such as awned grains (*śūkadhānya*) and others.
In the section beginning with "taste and potency" (*rasavīrya*), "specific action" (*prabhāva*) is mentioned separately because its scope is limited;

furthermore, the designation of taste and the other qualities should be understood according to their respective applicability. Consequently, it will not be the case that every substance is described as possessing all tastes and so forth.

Here, awned cereals (*śūkadhānya*) are mentioned first because they are the primary type of food; "awned cereals" refers to grains that possess awns. Furthermore, the names of substances here are well-known in various regions; therefore, other commentators likewise lack the capacity to know these names. Consequently, the names should generally be learned from those of other regions, though we shall record those that are current in Gauḍa as well as some that are well-known in other lands.
*Kalama* is well-known by its own name in the *vedāgrahāra* (gift lands);
*śakunāhṛta* is known as *vakra* in Śrāvastī;
and *raktaśāli* is indeed well-known [by that name].
Mahāśāli is well-known in Magadha;
here, *śāli* refers to winter grain (*haimantika*), while *ṣaṣṭika* and others are summer grains (*graiṣmika*), and *vrīhi* is autumn grain (*śārada*). This is the established classification.
Although red *śāli* and other varieties have a sweet post-digestive effect (*madhurapākitva*), their constipating nature (*baddhavarcastva*) is due solely to their specific potency (*prabhāva*).

"Mahān tasyānu" means following that [mahāśāli rice], namely following the red śāli (raktaśāli); therefore, the qualities of the red śāli are slightly less than those of the mahāśāli. In the same way, this should also be stated for "following that, the kalama," where "that" refers to the mahāśāli.
"Those subsequent to that" refers to the śakunāhṛta and so forth; the meaning is that they possess progressively fewer qualities.

Regarding the phrase "by means of qualities and non-qualities": the qualities of cultivated grains such as red rice (*raktaśāli*) include their ability to destroy thirst and remove the three impurities (*trimala*), and so forth. Barley (*yavaka*) and other grains imitate these by means of "non-qualities"—that is, defects that are the opposites of those qualities. Consequently, barley and the like produce thirst and the three impurities; thus, in this context, the word "quality" (*guṇa*) is used in the sense of praise.
It should be understood that "aguru" (not heavy) results from the elision of the vowel 'a' before "ṣaṣṭika-guṇa"; for in the chapter on "Measures of Food" (Sūtra 5),
the *ṣaṣṭika* rice is described as light (*laghu*),
and since [the *gaura-ṣaṣṭika*] follows it, its qualities differ only slightly from those of the *ṣaṣṭika*.
Varaka, koddālaka, and so forth are specific varieties of the sixty-day rice (*ṣaṣṭika*); some call varaka and others "inferior grains" (*kudhānya*),
while *vrīhi* is the designation for autumn-harvested grain,
of which *pāṭala* is a specific variety.

It is also recited in another tantra: “The *pāṭala* is indeed characterized by the three *doṣas*. In the *Suśruta*, however, the word *pāṭala* should be understood as referring to a specific type of grain distinct from this [flower]; therefore, there is no contradiction here with the description of its qualities.
Verses 13–15 concern specific types of inferior grains (*kudhānya*), such as *koradūṣa* and others.

*Koradūṣa* is *kodrava*. While *koradūṣa* alone destroys *kapha* and *pitta*, as for the statement made in the *Nidāna-sthāna* regarding *raktapitta*—"When a person eats foods consisting mostly of *yavaka*, *koddālaka*, and *koradūṣa*" (Ni.

2)—and so forth, which indicates that *koradūṣa* produces *pitta*, this should be understood as applying to it when combined with *niṣpāva*, sour gruel (*kāñjika*), and the like, due to the power of such association.
*Śyāmāka* and other such specific types of grass-grains (*tṛṇadhānya*) are also included.

Hasti-śyāmāka is a specific variety of *śyāmāka*; *nīvāra* is *uḍikā*; *gavedhuka* is *ghuluñca*, which is of two kinds—village and wild—the *praśātikā* being the *uḍikā* growing on dry land with red awns; *ambhaḥ-śyāmāka* is the water-born *oḍikā*, known in the world as *‘ḍe’*; *priyaṅgu* is well-known as *‘kāṅganī’*; *mukunda* is *‘vākasatṛṇa’*; *varuka* is the seed of hemp (*śaṇa*); *varaka* is the seed of *śyāma*; *śivi* is called *‘siddhaktāka’* in Tīrabhukti; and *jūrṇāhva* is known as *‘jonāra’*.

Even though barley (*yava*) is heavy, it possesses an abundance of *vāta* due to its dryness (*rūkṣatva*). Alternatively, since barley is described as light (*laghu*) in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*, it should be understood here also as not being heavy. It is strengthening (*balya*) because it cleanses the channels (*srotas*), or by its specific potency (*prabhāva*).

Furthermore, although its quality of subduing *pitta* is not explicitly stated—given its cold, sweet, and astringent nature—it is indeed obtained [by inference]; therefore, in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*, it is called a "subduer of *kapha* and *pitta*" (*kaphapittahantā*). (Su.)
Thus, what was stated [in Sūtra 46] is established.

Indeed, due to the consumption of wheat, which possesses qualities such as being sweet, cold, and unctuous, it acts as a producer of *śleṣman* (phlegm); for this very reason, it is stated in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā* that "it produces *śleṣman*" (*Suśruta Sūtrasthāna* 46).

As for the statement that in spring, when *kapha* predominates, one should "eat barley and wheat" (*yavagodhūmabhojanaḥ*, Sūtra 6), this is intended with respect to old wheat; and it has already been stated in this very chapter, in the passage beginning with "generally sweet and *śleṣmala*," that old wheat does not produce *kapha*. Furthermore, *nandīmukhī* and *yavikā* are varieties of wheat, as is *madhūlī*.
Thus, here the word "iti" has the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*).

While one should have said "it is completed" (*samāptaḥ*), by using the form "it is being completed" (*samāpyate*), he indicates this: because it consists of many substances, this group (*gaṇa*) is not yet finished; rather, it is completed by some means or other through the description of well-known qualities.
This same principle should be explained in other cases as well, such as "the sixth section is completed" (*ṣaṣṭho vargaḥ samāpyate*) and so forth.

Although the category of *śamīdhānya* (pulse grains) ought to be mentioned by way of its generic nature as grain (*dhānyatvena*), the mung bean (*mudga*) is specifically defined here because of its preeminence.
*Sūpya* refers to pulse grain suitable for making soup; among those, it is the best, hence "the best of pulse grains" (*sūpyottama*).

Regarding the quality of *māṣa* as being aphrodisiac (*vṛṣya*) and so forth: since its capacity to alleviate *vāta* is already established by its possession of qualities such as being unctuous, hot, and sweet, its explicit mention again is for the purpose of demonstrating that it specifically destroys *vāta*. Other similar cases should be explained in this same manner. By the statement "it promotes virility (*puṃstva*), [increases] semen (*śukra*), and acts quickly," the author shows that *māṣa* possesses aphrodisiacity characterized by the induction of seminal flow; for even the induction of seminal flow is indeed expressed by the term "aphrodisiac" (*vṛṣya*). As the saying goes: "One thing induces the flow of semen, while another increases the quantity of semen."
"Whatever increases the flow [of semen] is said to be a threefold aphrodisiac (*vṛṣya*). Thus, one should understand that complete aphrodisiac potency resides in the *māṣa*.

In the description of the qualities of the *rājamāṣa*, the phrase "it is sweet like the *māṣa*" means it is as sweet as the *māṣa*. Alternatively, there is a variant reading such as "it is dry," and so forth, which describes the qualities of the *kulattha* beginning with "hot," and so on. The *kulattha* is of four types—white, black, variegated, and red—and is also of two kinds according to whether it is cultivated or wild. For this very reason, it is stated in another treatise: "The wild *kulattha* is like that [cultivated one], but it specifically cures eye diseases."
*Maṣṭaka* is known as *amoṭha*;
*caṇaka* is well-known;
*khaṇḍikā* is the three-seeded pea (*tripuṭa-kalāya*); and *hareṇu* is the round pea (*vartula-kalāya*).

Regarding the statement that *kalāya* is wind-increasing (*vātala*), although the specific qualities of the *tripuṭa-kalāya* have not been explicitly stated, they should nevertheless be understood as being those of the black sesame seed (*kṛṣṇatila*), which is the primary type. For it is said in the Suśruta Saṃhitā: "Among all sesame seeds, the black is the best, the white is middling, and others are inferior" (Su.
"Various kinds of *śimbī* [pulses]" means the different varieties of black, yellow, red, and white *kuśimbī*.
Some read "the *śimbī* is dry," and so forth; furthermore, the division is: *āḍhakī*, *tuvarī*, and *vātālā*.
The quality of the seeds of avalguja and aiḍagaja is that they remove phlegm and wind.
Niṣpāva, valla, kākāṇḍa, and śūkaraśimbi [are types of legumes]. Umā is atasī; in the reading where it is "ūrṇā," it refers to the wool of that very plant.
Regarding the section on *śamī* grains (*śamīdhānyavarga*), here *śamī* refers to the pod; the grains contained within it are meant.
From verses 23–34, following the legumes (*sūpya*), the section on meat (*māṃsavarga*) is designated because of the predominance of meat as a condiment (*vyañjana*).

*Khara* is a donkey; *aśvatara* is a mule, which is born from a donkey and a mare; *dvīpin* is a spotted tiger; *ṛkṣa* is a bear; *vṛka* is a wolf, a beast that resembles a dog and is an enemy of livestock; *tarkṣu* is a species of tiger known as the "taraccha"; *babhru* is an excessively hairy dog found on the slopes of mountains, though some call it a large mongoose;
*lopāka* is a small jackal with a large tail.
The *śyena* is a well-known bird;
the dog is a vomit-eater;
and the *cāsa* is known as the "golden crow."
The *śaśaghnī* is known as the *apāñji*; the *bhāsa* is a bird with the color of ashes and a crest; the *kuliṅga* belongs to the group of raptors; and the *kālacaṭaka* is the black sparrow.
The *kākulīmṛga* is known as the *māluyāsarpa*; it has four varieties, beginning with the white one.
The *kūrcikā*, *saṅkuca*, *cillaṭa*, *ciyāra*,
*śallaka*— known as the *śalaka*— and the *mahāśakalī*; the *gaṇḍaka* is a species of *godhā*.

The plantain tree is known as *kadalīhaṭṭa*; the porcupine is known as *sejjaka*; and those that dwell on the ground or in holes are called *bhūmiśaya* (ground-dwellers) or *bileśaya* (hole-dwellers).
The *sṛmara* is the great boar;
the *camara* is the yak.
The rhinoceros, the gaṇḍaka, the gavaya, the gavākāra, the nyaṅku, the nyaṅkuśa, and the hariṇa.
The ruru deer, the many-horned antelope, the hare, the porpoise, and the crocodile with a cow's snout.
The *timiṅgila* is a great oceanic fish;
the *śukti* is a creature that is the source of pearls; the *ūdra* is a water-fox (*jalabiḍāla*); the *kumbhīra* is one possessing a pot-like snout; and the *culukī* is known as the "śuśu.
Although these would have been included by the general mention of "fish" (*matsya*), they are mentioned again for the sake of specific technical usage.
The term *haṃsa* (swan) includes all four types, beginning with the *rājahaṃsa*.
The *krauñca* is known as ‘koñca’; the *baka* has white wings, as does the *balākā*.
The *kāraṇḍava* has a crow-like beak;
the *plava* is well-known by its own name; the *prasevagala* is the *śarāri*, which is called "śarālī" in common parlance.
The water-crow,
the water-raven, the kādamba, the kalahamsa, the kākatuṇḍaka, and the white kāraṇḍava.
The *utkrośa* is known as the *kurala*;
the *puṇḍarīkākṣa*, *puṇḍara*, and *megharāva* are the *meghanāda*. Others claim that *megharāva* is the *cātaka*, but that is not so, because the *cātaka* does not frequent the water.
Ambukukkuṭī (water-hen), jalakukkuṭī (water-hen),
ārā— known by its own name—
and nandīmukhī (leaf-eater).
The *sārasa* is well known;
the *raktaśīrṣaka* is a variety of *sārasa* with a red head.
"Water-dwellers" (*ambucāriṇaḥ*) means those who float upon the water.
The *pṛṣata* is a spotted deer;
the *śarabha* is like a camel in size, possessing large horns and four legs positioned on its back, well known in Kashmir.
Rāma is the great deer (mahāmṛga) in the Himalayas;
Śvadaṃṣṭra and Caturdaṃṣṭra are well-known in Kārtikapura;
Mṛgamātṛkā is a small species of deer with a broad belly.
The *kuraṅga* is a species of deer;
the *gokarṇa* is a specific type of ox-faced deer;
the *hariṇa* is copper-colored; and the *eṇa* is the black antelope (*kṛṣṇasāra*).
The *ṛṣya*, *nīlāṇḍa*, *hariṇa*, *cāruṣka*, and others are indeed varieties of the *hariṇa*; however,
the *śaśa* (hare) is listed among the burrow-dwellers (*bileśaya*) in the *Suśruta*, for the purpose of indicating its close proximity [to those species].
The *lāva* is well known;
the *vartīra* is a species of *kapiñjala*.

The *kapiñjala* (grey partridge), the *gauratittiri* (grey partridge), the *vārtīka* (a type of sparrow), the *upacakra* (a type of pheasant that moves in flocks), and a variety of *cakora* (Greek partridge).
The *kukkuṭabha* is well known; *raktavartmaka* is an epithet of the *kukkuṭabha*, by which the large *kukkuṭabha* is understood.
The *vartaka* is known as *vaṭṭahī*;

the *vartikā* is of a smaller size and is a different species altogether, though some call the female *vartaka* a *vartikā*. Its inclusion here, despite the difference in gender, is for the purpose of prohibiting [the eating of] a specific light variety; otherwise, because it is feminine, the *vartikā* would be lighter than the *vartikā*.
The *barhin* is the peacock;
the *śārapada* has the luster of Indra;
the *mallakaṅka* is the *gonarda*, known as the *aghoḍākaṅka*.
The *krakara* is well-known;
the classification of birds into two groups, such as the *lāva* and others, and the *vartikā* and others, is for the purpose of describing the distinctions among their qualities.
The *śatapatra* is the woodcock; the *kāṣṭhakukkuṭaka* is the wild cock; the *bhṛṅgarāja* is well known as having the color of a bee; and the *koyaṣṭi* is known as the *koḍā*.
The *jīvañjīvaka* (the "living-together" bird), the *viṣadarśanamṛtyu* (which dies at the sight of poison),

the *atyūha*, and the *ḍāhuka*— or rather, the reading is *dātyūha*— which is well known as the *laṭṭā* or *pheñcāka*, having a red lower part of the tail; the *laṭūṣaka* is also a variety of that same species.
The *ḍiṇḍimānaka* has a loud sound like that of a drum;
the *kuliṅga* is shaped like a wild sparrow with a yellow head; the *kalaviṅka* is known in the world as the "vāai" [sparrow]; and the *grāmyacaṭaka* is the domestic sparrow.
The *caṭaka*, however, is the temple sparrow (*devakulacaṭaka*), which is very small in size.
Those [birds] which have not been mentioned here and are not well-known should be understood from those who know them and from people from other regions.
He states the definition through the etymological explanation of the term *prasaha* and so forth:
"by force" (*prasahya*) means by means of violence (*haṭhāt*).

Regarding the phrase "due to their resorting to marshy places" (*ānūpānūpasaṃśrayāt*): because the rule concerning what was previously established is not always mandatory (*anityatva*), the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) in the word *ānūpāḥ* is considered established (*siddha*); thus, the *saṃhitā* should be understood accordingly.
Regarding the phrase "because they move in water" (*jalecaryāt*), one should understand that this refers merely to moving in water for those such as swans (*haṃsa*) who dwell in water.

He says "those that move in dry land" (*jāṅgalacāriṇaḥ*) because, if only "land-born" (*sthalajā*) were said, there would be the possibility of including elephants and other such creatures born on land.

In the phrase "having scattered" (*vikīrya*), the word "they eat" (*bhakṣayanti*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis; likewise in the case of "having pierced" (*pratudya*), which means having struck [the victim] in many ways.

The *prasahas* are of two kinds: meat-eaters such as tigers, hawks, and the like, and non-meat-eaters such as cattle and the like. Therefore, he states the distinction regarding the meat-eaters with the words "of the *prasahas*" and so forth, which indicates that due to their aged nature, they cause chronic persistence of hemorrhoids and other diseases.
In the term *pratudas*, as well as in the term *jāṅgala*, the word "and" (*ca*) is indicated by elision.
The word division is "kaphānuge" (followed by phlegm).
"Because of the similarity of the bodily constituents (*śarīradhātu-sāmānyāt*)" means because it is similar to human flesh.
By this, it is stated that although goat meat is endowed with cold, heavy, and unctuous qualities, it does not produce *kapha* due to its similarity to the bodily constituents.
It should be understood that sheep meat, being sweet and cold, alleviates *pitta*; for this very reason, it is also stated in the *Śaradvidhi*: "The urabhra and śarabha... (Sūtra).
6) Thus, in the *Nidāna* section on *raktapitta* (Ni.

2), it should be understood that by the passage beginning with "boar, buffalo," etc., it is specifically the meat of sheep (*āvika*) combined with other substances that acts as the cause of *raktapitta*.
"In the womb" means among the eightfold classes [of beings] starting with the *prasaha*;

"due to having mixed spheres of activity" means that because they sometimes frequent marshy lands (*anūpa*), sometimes frequent arid lands (*dhanva*), and sometimes frequent both, goats and sheep have an "uncertain womb" (*aniścita-yoni*)—this is the meaning here.
In this context, "uncertain" (*aniścita*) is an adjective qualifying the womb; or alternatively, it refers to the goat and the sheep themselves as being uncertain.

[Objection: If this is so, then the partridge (*tittiri*) should also not be listed among the *viṣkira* birds, since it frequents both arid (*dhanva*) and marshy (*anūpa*) regions. [Response: This is not so. Because the specific species of partridge frequents arid and marshy regions as a rule, a restriction regarding its qualities can be established. However, no such rule exists for goats (*aja*) and sheep (*avi*), because some goats and sheep roam only in arid lands, some only in marshy lands, and others in both. Therefore, a distinction of origin (*yonibheda*) based on a restrictive rule cannot be made for these two. 61–62.
"Of some"— namely, the peacocks and others to be mentioned later—
"due to the excellence of their qualities," meaning because they possess distinguished qualities.
The heaviness and unctuousness of the peacock are already obtained by its being listed in the *vartakādi* group; that it is mentioned again is for the sake of specifying particular qualities.
This should be understood as the method of explanation whenever a quality already established by its inclusion in a group is stated once more.
The cock is the "foot-weaponed" (*caraṇāyudha*).
By stating the reason "due to frequenting arid and marshy lands," it should be understood that the partridge (*tittiri*) which frequents such lands possesses the aforementioned qualities;

likewise, other animals such as cows and others that frequent arid and marshy lands also possess qualities similar to those of the partridge. However, the partridge is mentioned specifically because it is the primary example, or else it should be understood that while frequenting arid and marshy lands is the cause for the partridge possessing these qualities, this does not apply to others like cows who do not inhabit such regions.

Some indeed read [the text] as "kapotā gṛhavāsinaḥ" (doves that dwell in houses), "pārāvatāḥ" (pigeons), and "caṭakā madhurāḥ" (sparrows are sweet), and so forth; however, in the opinion of those who do not read [these], the aphrodisiac quality of the sparrow—which is obtained through its general qualities as a "pratud" (pecking) bird—is acquired solely from aphrodisiac formulations such as: "Having attained satisfaction from the meat of sparrows, he who drinks milk afterwards... (Ci. 2).
However, because the many qualities of peacocks and other such birds exceed those qualities mentioned in the collective list, they have been treated in a separate reading.

Although the nourishing nature of meat is already established by the statement "Meat is the foremost among nourishing substances" (Sūtra 25), the subsequent declaration that "there is nothing else for the nourishment of the body" and so forth should be understood as serving both to introduce the specific context and to reinforce that very point.
63–87 – Vegetables are also taught immediately following [the grains] as being condiments.
Śuṣā is kāsamarda;
śaṭī is well-known by its own name;
vāstuka is ṭaṅkavāstuka.
"Neither excessively hot nor cold in potency" means that it possesses neither an intensity of heat nor an intensity of cold.
As for what is stated in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*: "The bitter *kākamācī* pacifies wind because of its hot potency" (*Su.

40) Thus it has been stated according to the opinion of Vīryavādin; for this very reason, even in the *Suśruta*, regarding substance and quality, it is recited exactly thus: "neither too hot nor too cold" (*Suśruta Sūtrasthāna* 46).
Rājakṣavaka is dugdhikā;
kālaśāka is known as ‘kāliyā’, and it is called kālākhyam, which is another name for kālaśāka itself; others, however, read it as ‘kālāyam’, while maṇḍūkaparṇī is known as maṇimaṇī.
Kucelā, akarṇaviddhakā, abhedā, vanatiktaka, pathyasundara,
avalguja, and vālgujī.
Śakulādanī, kaṭurohiṇī,
śārṅgeṣṭā, kākatiktā, kaṭhillaka, and punarnavā.
Nāḍī, nāḍīca,
kalāya, vartulakalāya, tilaparṇikā, and hulahulikā.
Gojihvā, dārvīpatrikā, kulaka, and kāravellaka; some, however, say that *kulaka* is a variety of *paṭola*,
while *karkaśa* is a small variety of *karkoṭaka*.
Leguminous vegetables such as *māṣaparṇī* and others.
Phañjī, brāhmaṇayaṣṭikā, cillī, gauḍavāstuka,
kutumbaka, and droṇapuṣpikā.
Ālukas include piṇḍāluka and others;
karbudāra is the golden *kāñcana*;
*suvarcalā* is *sūryabhaktikā*, though some call it *phappuka*.
Pattūra, śāliñca, cuccuparṇikā, nāḍīca-bheda, kumārajīva, and jīvaśāka.
Loṭṭāka, loṭṭāmāriṣa, nālikā, gonāḍīca, āsurī, rājikā, or maṇḍaka.
Vṛkadhūmaka is *bhūmiśirīṣa*;
lakṣmaṇā is known by its own name;
nalinī is the lotus stalk (*padmamṛṇāla*); and in the reading *nīlinī*, it refers to *buhvā*.
Barley greens, field-grown vegetables, pumpkin, *sarpacchatra*,
and *avalguja*— the latter being a variety of *avalguja*.
Yātuka, śuklā, śālaparṇī,
śālakalyāṇī, a variety of śāliñca, triparṇī, and haṃsapādikā.
Pīluparṇī, moraṭaka,
gaṇḍīra, śamaṭha, bilvaparṇī, and bilvārjaka.
Bhaṇḍī is known by its own name;
parvaṇī, parvaśāka, parvapuṣpī, and kukkuṭī [are synonyms].
The *pañcāṅgula*, *citra-aṇḍa*, *ervāruka*, *rājakarkaṭī*,

and *kūṣmāṇḍaka* are mentioned in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā* according to their different stages of ripeness, such as immature (*bāla*) and so forth; this too is not contradictory, because in that text it is stated that the immature and middle stages remove *pitta* and increase *kapha*, which here should be understood to apply to cases where *pitta* is predominant or where *kapha* is predominant in a *sannipāta* (combined) disorder.
98–113 Regarding *keluṭa*, there is the statement of Hārīta: "The *keluṭa* is a sweet branch; its tuber is sweet and cooling.
Some call the *kadamba* by the name *kadambikā*, while others refer to a small *kadamba* as such.
The *nadīmāṣaka* is known as *udīmānaka*;
it is the *ainduka*, the *nikṣāra*, the *tālapralamba*, and the *tālāṅkura*.
By the word *śasya* (grain), the marrow of the head is understood here;
*taruṭa* is the root of the *kahlāra* lotus;
*krauñcādana* is *dhiñculikā*.
By the word *kaśeruka*, both *ciñcoḍaka* and *rājakaśeruka* are included;
*aṅkāloḍya* is the bulbous root of the small blue lotus (*hrasvotpalakanda*);
and *muñjātaka* is the tuber found in the northern regions (*auttarāpathikakanda*).
The *amlikā* has very small branches and generally grows in places such as Kāmarūpa;
the *sarpacchatra* is a mushroom shaped like a snake's hood,
while other species of mushrooms are to be known as abundant, growing from dried cow dung, straw, and the like.

The phrase "based on leaves, tubers, and fruits" is stated by way of predominance; therefore, it should be understood that the vegetable group (*śākavarga*) also includes things based on flowers and so forth.
Since some fruits are used in the same manner as vegetables, he now describes the fruit group (*phalavarga*).
The grape (*mṛdvīkā*) is designated as *agra* because of its superior qualities;
the *phalgu* fruit of the *udumbara* tree is to be understood as both fruit and flower, due to its qualities being similar to those of the *madhūka*.

In this context, *parūṣaka* should be understood as the sweet *parūṣaka*; the *Candrikā* commentary states that *āmrāta*—known as ‘*āmaḍā*’—is similar to the mango fruit. This [fruit] is of two kinds: sweet and sour; here, only the qualities of the sweet variety are described, since the sour variety will be discussed later.
Regarding the phrase "the fruits of the palmyra" (*tālaśasyāni*), it refers to the fruits of the palmyra tree, just as in the expression "the fruits of the *harītakī*" (Ci.).

1) Here, "fruit" (phala) refers specifically to that which is praiseworthy (*śasya*), namely those that are perfected or ripe (*siddhāni pakvāni*); by this, the ripe *tāla* fruit is included, as well as the *bhavya* and *karmaraṅga* fruits; some, however, say it refers merely to the fruit that has formed its rind.
Āruka is well-known in Kārtikeyapura;
*karkandhū* is the jujube of the jackal (*śṛgālabadarī*). By reading *karkandhū* and *nikuca* as distinct items, he demonstrates that those two always produce *pitta* and *śleṣman*.
As for *parūṣaka* and the others, which exist in two forms—sweet and sour—only those *parūṣaka* fruits and so forth that are sour produce *pitta* and *śleṣman*.
Regarding the pigeon (*pārāvata*), which is well known for its ability to assume any form at will:
it should be understood that here, whatever is sweet is cold, and whatever is sour is hot.

Thus, although the potency (*vīrya*) is already obtained through the very description of the taste (*rasa*), the potency is stated again because the coldness of the sour *āmalaka* fruit is observed; this is how it should be understood.
*Ṭaṅka* is well-known in Kashmir;
*siddha* means "ripened" due to the influence of time.
The description of the qualities of *kapittha*, *bilva*, and *āmra* according to their different stages is because they are to be employed in all those stages.
The *badara* is of medium size; it is indeed sweet.
The *gāṅgeruka* is the fruit of the *nāgabalā*.
The *karīra* is a tree of the desert.
Todana is a type of *dhanvana*; *rājādana* is a milky fruit suitable for use as a relish (*avadanśa*). Having consumed the fruit of the *lavalī*, one develops a relish for other substances.
Nīpa is the kadamba tree;
śatāhvaka-phala is known as ‘seha’; and pīlu is that which comes from the northern region.
Tṛṇaśūnya, ketakī fruit,
prācīnāmalaka, pānīyāmalaka, tinduka, and kendu.

Regarding the qualities of the pomegranate (*dāḍima*), it is said that it is "not antagonistic to *kapha* and *pitta*. This means that the sour pomegranate is not antagonistic to *pitta*, while the sweet variety is not antagonistic to *kapha*; thus, its capacity to alleviate all three *doṣas* (*tridoṣaharatva*) is established. As stated in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā*: "It should be known to be of two kinds—sweet and sour.
The sweet variety destroys the three *doṣas*, while the sour variety removes *vāta* and *kapha*" (*Su.Sū.*).
46) Thus:
*vṛkṣāmla*, great *ārdraka*, *amlikā*, and *tintiḍī*.

The "remainder" refers to the skin and flesh; otherwise, it is heavy. Alternatively, it possesses qualities opposite to those of keśara as stated in the passage beginning with "in cases of colic and loss of appetite";
the *vātāma* and others are from the northern regions, while this *priyāla* is well-known in Magadha.
*Dantaśaṭha* is *jambīra*; some say it refers to *amloṭa*, but here the sour *āmrātaka* is to be understood, whereas previously the sweet *āmrātaka* was mentioned.
*Karamarda* is of two kinds: that grown in villages and that grown in forests.
Airāvata is the *amlātaka*; or is it the *nāgaraṅga*?

Or is it the eggplant (*vārtāka*) that bears fruit in the Deccan and is known as *goṣṭhavārtāka*, the properties of which are described here? Or rather, are these the properties of the eggplant used when unripe and bearing fruit?
*Ākṣikī* is a creeper; its fruit is *ākṣika*.
Anupākī is known as "anuyā," and it is equal to fire because it produces sparks and other such effects. 125–165.

Even for green vegetables such as ginger (*ārdraka*) and others, because they are consumed before and after the fruit—without undergoing cooking by fire—the description of the greens follows that of the fruits. However, the greens are mentioned after the fruits because they do not provide satiety.
The qualification "ginger" (*ārdraka*) is intended to exclude dried ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), the properties of which will be discussed in the section on substances used in food preparation.
*Jambīra* is a variety of *parṇāsa*; the *jambīra* fruit is fragrant.

The statement that young radish (*bāla*) removes the [three] *doṣas* refers to its state when it is young and its flavor is unmanifest; for there is a saying in another treatise: "As long as radishes are newly sprouted and possess unmanifest flavors, they are light, digestive stimulants, and indeed removers of *pitta*, *vāta*, and *kapha*."

"Old" (*vṛddha*) refers to that very same [root] when it has fully matured; and with reference to this very stage of being a "root" (*mūlaka*), it has been stated: "Among tubers, the root is the most excessively unwholesome" (Sūtra 25).
As for the statement "it removes wind when prepared with unctuous substances," this applies generally to both the young and the old [root].

Since the fact that dried radish destroys phlegm and wind is already established by the upcoming passage, "These [are] dried [substances] that destroy phlegm and wind," its mention again is for the sake of indicating excellence.
As for *pūtigandhahā*, it means that *arjaka*— also known as *śvetaparṇāsa*— destroys the foul odor of the body as well as the foul odor of meat used as a condiment (*vyañjana*).

*Śigru* is the *viṭapa-śobhāñjana*; *śāleya* is the root of *cāṇakya*, well-known in Marwar, or alternatively it is the *misteya* well-known in Pāṭaka, for there is a saying: "They call the root of *cāṇakya* by the name *śāleya* in *misteya*. *Mṛṣṭaka* is *rājikā*; *gaṇḍīra* is of two kinds, red and white. Of these, that which is red is listed among the pungent (*kaṭu*) vegetables, while that which is white and grows in water is listed among the greens (*śāka*); thus, one [type] is not listed in both groups. *Jalapippalī* is like a long pepper (*pippalī*) found in water.

*Śṛṅgaverī* is *gojihvikā*, or alternatively, *śṛṅgaverī* is that which has the appearance of fresh ginger (*ārdraka*). As it is said: "It is called *śṛṅgaverī* because its shape is like that of ginger (*śṛṅgavera*); and they call *tumburu* because its shape is like that of *kustumburu*. *Bhūstṛṇa* is *gandhatṛṇa*.
Kharāhvā is black cumin (kṛṣṇajīraka);
ajagandhā is wild yavānī; and sumukha is a variety of parṇāsa.

And this is the quality of coriander and the other [herbs] when they are fresh; however, for the dried ones, he will describe their qualities in the section on food ingredients beginning with "kāravī, kuñcikā," and so forth.
The *gṛñjanaka* is simply a type of onion with small stalks and leaves.
These are the items mentioned in the section on the green vegetables (*haritavarga*).

Although the qualities of dried substances such as *śuṇṭhī* and others have already been stated by the verse beginning with "śuṣkāṇi," they are mentioned again for the purpose of describing their specific additional qualities; since these will appear in the section on combinations of foods, there is no redundancy.

(Verses 166–177) Having discussed food, drink must now be discussed. Within that category, although water is the primary type of drink, the author sets it aside and first speaks of wine (*madya*), because it brings joy and other effects to people and is the foremost among beverages.
"By nature" means by its own inherent character (*svabhāva*).

And although when wine is being drunk, a manifest sour taste is not perceived, nevertheless, because it performs the functions of a sour substance—such as causing the teeth to tingle and salivation—it is indeed called sour.
For there is this statement: "We shall teach those things that are sweet and have a sweet potency as being simply sweet, and likewise for the others. (Vi.)

8) Thus, by that [principle], the sour potency (*amlaprabhāva*) of wine consists precisely in its sour taste (*amlarasa*); for this very reason it has been said: "Wine stands at the very top of all sour substances" (Ci.
"From the ripening" (*vipākataḥ*) is the suffix *tasi* used in the sense of the third case;
"surā" refers to liquor from which the scum has not been removed.
*Madirā* is the scum (*maṇḍa*) of *surā*;
*jagala* is *surā* prepared from boiled rice and fermenting agent (*kiṇvaka*);
*ariṣṭa* is that produced from a decoction of medicinal herbs, honey, and so forth, such as the *dantī-abhayā-ariṣṭa* and others which will be described later.
*Śārkara* is a fermented liquor (*āsava*) based on sugar;
it is a decoction made from boiled sugarcane juice,
whereas *śītarasika* is made from cold sugarcane juice.
Gauḍa is a spirituous liquor (surāsava) based on molasses, in which the function of water is performed by the wine itself;
madhvāsava is that made from madhūka flowers.
The definition of *maireya* is as follows: "One should know that *maireya* is the blending of both *āsava* and *surā* in a single vessel; it is based on both.
Thus, *dhātakī-phalāsava* is [an example] distilled from *dhātakī* flowers.

*Mādhvīka* is that which has honey as its primary ingredient, as will be described in the passage beginning with "it is appetizing and digestive"; similarly, an *āsava* made from a mixture of grape juice (*mṛdvīkā*) and sugarcane juice should be understood [as *mṛdvīkāsavā*].
*Madhu* refers to an *āsava* where honey is the primary ingredient.
*Surā* along with its *maṇḍa* (sediment) should be known as that which is made from barley and rice.
The word *viṣṭabhya* is a disjunctive term (*viccheda*).
*Madhūlaka* is a variety of wheat; the liquor made from it is *madhūlaka*. Others, however, say it is *medaka*.
[The phrase] beginning with "stimulating" (*dīpana*) describes the qualities of *sauvīra* and *tuṣodaka*.
"Amlakāñjika" refers to *kāñjika* (fermented rice water) that possesses sour qualities.
Now, he describes the qualities of water, which is primarily used for drinking, beginning with the words "jalaṃ" and so forth.
"All" refers to water— whether it be that which is described by Suśruta as being of the nature of rain,

dew, or frost— which is of a single type, possessing the qualities stated in the passage beginning with "Water is indeed auspicious" (Sūtra 26), as well as the qualities to be mentioned later, such as "cold and pure."
"Aindram" means that which is impelled by Indra through the power of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
Although it is of a single nature, he states the cause of its differentiation: "That falling," and so forth.

It falls toward a location consisting of the form of elements situated in space, and toward a time consisting of the forms of cold, heat, and so on; likewise, having fallen, it depends upon a specific location on the earth and time in the same manner—the ellipsis being "in relation to qualities and defects. (196)
He states this very connection of place and time: "From the sun," and so forth.

By the mention of the moon (*soma*), it should be understood that the earth is also included because of its lunar nature—referring both to the earth in the form of dust situated in the sky and to that which takes the form of poisons from spiders and the like accompanying the clouds. Alternatively, by the mention of air (*vāyu*) itself, the inclusion of the earth being carried by the wind is "touched upon" (the word "is [included]" is to be supplied).

"By those following time" means by those dependent upon time. By this it is shown that it is precisely the specific relationship with the moon and other factors produced by time that creates a distinction in the water; therefore, time is not ineffective.
He states the connection between the fallen water and place and time: "cold, hot," and so forth.
"According to proximity" means that at whatever time and on whichever earth certain qualities such as coldness and the like are predominant, the water becomes touched by those [qualities].

By this, it is shown that the distinction between *gāṅga* (river water) and *sāmudra* (sea water) established in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā* is based solely on the connection with specific qualities and defects of divine water.

Therefore, that which is tainted by poison and the like is called *sāmudra* because its qualities are similar to sea water; whereas that which is free from dust, poison, and so forth is called *gāṅga* because of its corresponding qualities—thus it was stated in the *Suśruta*.

In the month of Āśvina, however, divine water never comes into contact with dust, poison, or similar contaminants; even if such contact were to occur due to the power of time, it does not defile the water in that manner. Therefore, it is stated in the Suśruta Saṃhitā: "That oceanic water should not be drunk except during the month of Āśvayuja" (Su.Sū.

In this regard, according to the statement of Hārīta, atmospheric water is indeed to be taken even during the months of Kārttika and Āgrahāyaṇa; for he says: "Since the autumn has begun and the northwest wind blows in the winter, one should take that water in earthen jars.

Therefore, the statement "except from Āśvayuja" is intended to show that water is to be accepted starting from Āśvayuja, and not merely to indicate that it is to be accepted only in the month of Āśvina.

Others, however, say that the *paramāntarīkṣa* water should be collected specifically during the month of Āśvina; for there is the statement of Jatūkarṇa: "During the rainy season, serpents, insects, and spiders move through the sky along with the clouds; therefore, the water in the sky is unfit for drinking due to being tainted by their poison until the rising of Agastya."
He describes the natural quality of divine water [with the words] beginning with "cold" and ending with "auspicious," meaning it brings about well-being.
"Delicious," by virtue of being pleasing to the palate.
He states the cause for the specific qualities that will be described, beginning with "fallen" (*bhraṣṭam*) and so forth:
"it depends on the vessel" means that, depending upon its connection with a particular vessel such as a river and so forth, it comes to possess specific qualities.

Although this was already stated previously by the phrase "it depends on place and time," it is repeated here in order to demonstrate that, in terms of temporal dependence, a specific place is a particularly potent cause for specific qualities.
Some, however, recite the passage beginning with "In white, there is astringency," but that is not very well known.
[The following] states specific qualities in specific substrates, beginning with "rivers" and so forth.

Those [rivers] whose water is broken, agitated, and struck by stones are described as such. By this, it is stated that only those rivers in the Himalayas originating from the upper plateaus (*adhityakā*) are wholesome, and not those originating from the lower foothills (*upatyakā*), because the qualities such as being broken by stones and so forth exist only in those originating from the upper plateaus. Therefore, there is no contradiction with what is stated in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā*: "Those originating from the Himalayas produce heart disease and other ailments" (Sūtra-sthāna 45), for that statement refers to those originating from the foothills.

As for what was stated there, that "those originating from the Malaya mountains produce worms" (Suśruta Sūtra 45), that refers to rivers carrying stones and gravel; since in this context [the waters of] rivers carrying stones and gravel are compared to nectar, there is no contradiction.

As for the statement that those originating from the Pāriyātra mountains cause diseases such as headaches, that refers to the waters of rivers flowing from the caves of the Pāriyātra range; however, in the Suśruta Saṃhitā, it is stated with reference to the waters of lakes and rivers originating from the Pāriyātra mountains: "Those originating from the Pāriyātra are wholesome" (Su.Sū.

This has been stated by Viśvāmitra: “Water born of a lake and water born of a cave—water from a river that originates from a lake promotes strength and health, whereas that born of a cave is considered to be full of defects.

Because of the use of the term "generally" (*prāyas*), Ganges water remains wholesome even when it flows toward the eastern ocean; or rather, Ganges water is wholesome precisely because it originates from the Himalayas, which possess the aforementioned characteristics.
The mountains such as Pāriyātra are well-known by their own names.

They are called *varṣājalavahāḥ* because they carry water during the rainy season (*varṣāsu*), as it was stated in the section on the primary [elements]: "Of waters, the rain is non-conducting" (*varṣānādeyam udakānām*, Sūtra).
25) Thus, since this [water] is here described as unwholesome (*apathya*), there is no tautology in providing the reasoning for its nature.

Regarding the phrase "in springs and so forth," the word "water" (*jala*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Ponds (*vāpī*) and the like may exist in marshy regions (*anūpa*), in arid lands (*dhanvan*), and on mountains such as the Himalayas; therefore, their qualities must be specified according to the very qualities of the water of those marshy regions and so forth. Furthermore, the qualities of water from rivers flowing westward, water from rivers flowing eastward, water from marshy regions, water from arid lands, and water from mountains have already been stated; by that means, the extension (*atideśa*) of those qualities to ponds and the like should be understood.

And it has been stated by Hārīta: "In marshy regions (anūpadeśa), water that is heavy increases phlegm; the opposite of this is considered primary, being light and belonging to the arid (jāṅgala) region.

Furthermore, in the Suśruta-saṃhitā, the specific qualities of water from ponds and other sources are described separately; it should be understood that those qualities—such as salinity found in well-water and the like—are not mentioned here for fear of excessive length, as they are directly observable.

A *vāpī* is a long pond with steps constructed from bricks and other materials; a *kūpa* is a well, which is well known; a *taḍāga* is a reservoir whose water comes from a slope, which arises from the damming of water flowing down from a high place; others, however, call a *puṣkarīṇī* a *taḍāga*; an *utsa* is a place where water rises up from below; a *saras* is a divine excavation not produced by human effort, such as the Pampā lake and others; a *prasravaṇa* is a spring or waterfall.

Others, however, read "in pools, streams, water [falls], and so forth. In that context, a *hrada* is a deep reservoir of water located within a river; a *dhārā*, on the other hand, is water falling in the form of a stream from a mountain and so on; by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), fields, springs, and the like are included—the meaning being that which is moist and covered with leaves and such; and "in the abode of Varuṇa" refers to the ocean.
"Stale, smelling of raw flesh,
and thoroughly determined"— this is from the description of the qualities of all water [verses 213–216].
Following water, milk is described because of its commonality with life-sustaining substances (*jīvanīya*). Curd and other products are also mentioned because they are derived from milk.

"Clear" (*prasanna*) means free from defects; being free from defects is stated as a quality (*guṇa*) by virtue of its excellence. Alternatively, since qualities are innumerable, clarity should be understood as a quality even though it is not explicitly listed among "heavy" (*guru*) and the others. Thus, "possessing such qualities" refers to the ten qualities beginning with sweet (*svādu*).

Regarding the phrase "due to similarity" (*sāmānyāt*), this means because of their commonality. Some say that in terms of its oily quality (*sneha*), buffalo milk is inferior to cow's milk, yet it is superior to it in heaviness and coldness; however, that is not correct, for it is directly perceived that the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) produced from buffalo milk is indeed superior. Likewise, it is stated in the *Jatūkarṇa*: "Buffalo [milk] is heavy, cold, more unctuous, extremely strengthening, and foremost among nourishing agents. It is also stated in the *Suśruta*: "[Buffalo milk is] more unctuous than cow's milk" (Sūtra).

45) Thus; therefore, the reading is *snehānyūnam* (not deficient in unctuousness); by this, the meaning is "exceeding in unctuousness. Alternatively, *snehānyūnam* means "full of unctuousness. The fact that camel’s milk and the like possess saltiness and so forth should be understood as being due to their having a sweet secondary taste (*anurasa*). Sweet taste, however, is indeed predominant; for it is stated in the *Dīrghañjīvitīya* chapter, "For the most part, [it is] sweet" (Sūtra 1), but it is not exclusively sweet in every respect.
Regarding "single-hoofed" (aikaśapha), some say it refers to the mare; however, others maintain that by the word "all" (sarva), this quality of milk also applies to the asses, horses, and camels.

As for its being "hot," this is relative to other types of milk; therefore, its general quality of coldness as previously stated remains non-contradictory. For instance, even though pungent (kaṭu) taste is heavier than the best light bitter (tikta) taste, it is still called "light" when compared to sweet (madhura) and the rest. Similarly, although the milk of a mare is "hot," it is still considered "cold" when compared to urine, honey, and so forth. This same logic should be applied to its being described as "dry" (rūkṣa).

Although elephant’s milk and similar substances are not mentioned in the treatises regarding their practical applications, they should nevertheless be employed here and there once one has understood their stated qualities.
(217–224) He states the qualities of curd: "It is rochana," and so forth.

Here, although it is called "rocanam" (appetizing), the mention of "arucāv" (in cases of anorexia) is because it removes the disease of anorexia; its quality as "rocanam" (appetizing), however, is stated in the sense that at the time of its administration, it produces an appetite for other substances.

"Bṛṃhaṇam" (nutritive/tonic) means it nourishes one who is emaciated by disease and so forth; and regarding "kārśye" (emaciation), it should be understood that it is recommended even for natural emaciation. Therefore, there is no redundancy. It is beneficial in all four types of pīnasa (chronic rhinitis) due to its specific potency; alternatively, because it is a digestive agent for pīnasa, it is beneficial in every case.

Furthermore, whatever appears here to be inconsistent when considering the properties of curd—such as its being aphrodisiac, cooling, and wholesome—that must be understood as resulting from its specific *prabhāva* (potency).

Likewise, the fact that its quality of subduing *vāta* is stated again, even though it could already be inferred from other qualities such as acidity, heat, and unctuousness, is for the sake of emphasizing its excellence; this should be understood because one observes deviations from the rule where substances possessing acidity and so forth do not act as subduers of *vāta*. Examples of such deviations are to be sought among things like under-fermented curd (*mandaka*) and poorly prepared wine.

This same principle should be applied, as far as possible, when describing the qualities of all foods and drinks; however, fearing excessive prolixity in the text, we do not elaborate on every single item here.

By stating "generally," [the author] indicates that while something may be censured at one time, it can be beneficial at another time due to factors such as the season (e.g., autumn) or the individual's constitution (*prakṛti*).

When the milk has turned into *maṇḍaka* (curd-whey) but has not yet reached the state of thickness, that *maṇḍaka* is "wind-destroying" (*vātaghna*). However, when it has abandoned the stage of *maṇḍaka* and become thick, being sweet and slightly sour, then it becomes especially wind-destroying; this is the meaning.
As for the previously mentioned qualities of curd, they should be understood as applying to well-formed curd that is clearly sour.
The analysis of the compound is *śukralaḥ saraḥ*;

*sara* refers to the cream on top of curd, and *śukrala* means that which increases the flow and quantity of semen. For this very reason, regarding the qualities of *sara*, it is stated in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*: "It is aphrodisiac (*vṛṣya*) and increases semen" (Su.Sū.).
45) Thus, the employment of these two words is made;
"maṇḍa" means curd-cream (*dadhimanda*) or whey, according to the context.
By the verse beginning with "śopha," the qualities of buttermilk are described;
"mūtragraha" refers to urinary retention, dysuria, and so forth; and "gara" here refers to artificial poison.

Regarding "saṅgrāhī" and so forth, these are the qualities of butter (*navanīta*). "Freshly extracted" means newly drawn out; by the expression "freshly extracted," it is indicated that the aforementioned qualities of butter are most excellent only when it is brand new, whereas for old butter, these qualities do not possess such strength.
230. He describes the quality of ghee that has come through the process of production, beginning with "memory" and so forth;
"possessing a thousand potencies" means having abundant power.

How is it that it possesses "a thousandfold potency"? He says: "according to rule" (*vidhivat*). This means "endowed with the prescribed method. The "method" (*vidhi*) consists of both the processing (*saṃskāra*) and the combination (*saṃyoga*) with various substances used by those performing specific rites. For this very reason, it is said: "No other unctuous substance follows [the same] processing as such" (*Ni.

1*); likewise in another treatise: "Ghee is a vehicle for medicinal formulations" (*yogavāhi*). Therefore, it should be understood that because of its thousandfold potency, it performs a thousandfold of actions.

As for the fact that the commentators on the Suśruta read "remover of the three doṣas" (*tridoṣāpakarṣaṇam*) among the qualities of ghee mentioned by Suśruta, it should be understood that this is due to its removing *kapha* through processing (*saṃskāra*).

Regarding the phrase beginning with "madā" (intoxication), "digested" (*jīrṇa*) means having passed ten years; for there is a statement: "That which is ten years old is 'ancient' (*purāṇa*), and beyond that, 'very ancient' (*prapurāṇa*)."
To the extent that the degree of aging increases, to that same extent the excellence of its qualities should be understood;

for it is said in the Hārīta-saṃhitā: "In whatever measure it reaches old age, in that same measure it becomes possessed of qualities. This [verse] extends by analogy the qualities of ghee not explicitly mentioned: "ghees," and so forth.

The connection is that "clarified butter" (*sarpīṃṣi*) refers to its own [specific types]; therefore, one should specify "goat's clarified butter" (*ajā-sarpiḥ*) just as one specifies "goat's milk" (*ajā-kṣīra*).
This same principle should be stated for the remaining two [types of clarified butter] as well.

And by this logic, the clarified butter of elephants and so forth should also be understood, though it is not mentioned explicitly because there is no common usage for terms such as "elephant's clarified butter."
*Pīyūṣa* is the milk of a woman who has recently given birth.
That very substance, as long as it has not yet reached a state of complete clarity, is called *moraṭa*;
it is a congealed portion of milk from which the liquid part has vanished, which people call *kṣīrasāmi*.

It possesses the qualities of a solid mass of buttermilk (*takrapinda*) and is clear; a *takrapinda* is simply the thickened portion of buttermilk-cream (*takrakūrcikā*) from which the liquid has drained away.

In the phrase "of the *gorasas*," it should be understood that the word "etc. (*ādi*) is elided; by this, the milk of buffaloes and so forth are also included. Alternatively, the mention of *gorasa* is made because of its predominance. By the term *gorasa*, all products derived from cow's milk—such as milk, curd, and buttermilk—are intended; for in common usage, the designation *gorasa* applies to all of these. [Verses 234–236] This group, characterized primarily by sweetness, is called the class of sugarcane derivatives.
"Of what has been eaten" means of that which has been crushed by the teeth;
"mechanical" means crushed by a machine.
Its burning sensation (*vidāha*) generally occurs because it is crushed by a machine when it is joined with skin-fibers (*tvag-granthi*), as well as due to its remaining for a period of time.

For there is a statement: "Due to the conjunction with the root, bark, and knots, the juice within the cane is scorched. And it is said in the Hārīta-saṃhitā: "Because it is pervasive and delicate, the juice, when pressed by the machine, becomes intensely scorched within the body upon contact with wind and sun due to its subtlety.
Here, the term "because of pervasiveness" refers to its being like a stalk of sugarcane possessed of bark and other parts.

As for what is said—that the statement regarding the blood-pitta-alleviating property of mechanically extracted juice (*yāntrika*) contradicts its being caustic (*vidāhin*), as in: "Blood-pitta subsides from drinking honey-water and sugarcane juice" (Ci. A. 4)—that is not so. For in that context, only the non-caustic juice squeezed by the teeth is intended to be taken; or else, even in the case of mechanical extraction, it should be used after discarding the caustic quality resulting from contact with the skin and other parts, as well as its prolonged duration. The statement "mechanically extracted juice is caustic" should be understood as referring to a general rule (*prāyovāda*).
Others, however, fearing this fault, explain [the term] as "it burns" meaning "it ripens quickly.
Because it causes the production of many worms and such, treacle (*guḍa*) is said to produce many worms and such.

Likewise, in the phrase "the juice remaining with a fourth part, a third part, or half," the elision of the word *ca* (and) should be understood. By this, it should be known that small treacle (*kṣudraguḍa*) is heavier than juice remaining with a fourth part, and likewise, that which remains with a fourth part is heavier than that remaining with a third part, and so forth.
Small treacle is called black treacle (*asitaguḍa*).

And because it has become fibrous, the molasses (*phāṇita*) becomes "washed" (*dhauta*), meaning it has few impurities; by the removal of impurities, it becomes "washed" and thus possesses little impurity, which implies that there are few worms and the like within it. "From that" means from the washed molasses (*dhautaguḍa*).
Matsyaṇḍikā is that which, through cooking within the midst of *khaṇḍa*, becomes thickened and resembles fish-eggs (*matsya-aṇḍa*);
it is pure, and "most" (*param*) means it is increasingly pure in each successive stage.
"The coolness likewise becomes [greater]" means that the *khaṇḍa* of *matsyaṇḍikā* is cooler, and sugar (*śarkarā*) is even cooler than that. This is the meaning.
The mention of "guḍa" (molasses) and "śarkarā" (sugar) is for the purpose of distinguishing them from "yāsa-śarkarā" and "madhu-śarkarā";
"yāsa-śarkarā" is sugar prepared from a decoction of *durālabhā*,
whereas "madhu-śarkarā" takes the form of sugar within honeycombs.
238–242. In connection with honey-sugar (madhuśarkarā), there is a description of honey:
the bees are tawny (piṅgalāḥ); that which is produced from them is *mākṣika*.
*Bhramara* is well known [as honey from bees]; *kṣaudra* is that produced by small flies;
*piṅgalā* are large flies, [also called] *puttikā*; that which is produced by them is *pauttika*.

Furthermore, the other four types of honey mentioned by Suśruta, such as *chatrā* and so forth, should be understood as possessing the same general qualities as honey. Alternatively, some do not mention them here because they are not recommended; they recite the verse beginning with "mākṣikaṃ tailavarṇaṃ syāt" (beeswax-colored honey may be like oil) using the expression "uṣṇārtamathavā" (or for one afflicted by heat), which indicates that while hot honey might cause harm, it does not do so to the same extent for one who is already suffering from heat.

He states the reason for that very point: "because of its association with poison" (*saviṣānvayāt*). "Poisonous" refers to various flowers, or alternatively, to bees and the like themselves; "association" (*anvaya*) means the source of origin. That which has such [poisonous things] as its source is "associated with poison" (*saviṣānvaya*) honey. By this, there is an association of the honey specifically with the property of being opposed to heat (*uṣṇa-virodhitva*), which is inherent in the poison, but not with the state of being poisonous (*saviṣatva*) itself. If that were the case, then even hot [substances] would be lethal. Alternatively, the word "or" (*atha vā*) is connected with the phrase "because of its association with poison"; thus, the meaning becomes that honey is opposed to heat due to its association with poison, and also due to other factors, namely coolness (*śaitya*) and delicacy (*saukumārya*).

For it is said in the *Hārīta*: “Honey, which consists of the essence of the juices of various kinds of flowers, is incompatible with all hot substances due to its coldness and its delicacy. It is also stated in the *Suśruta*: “Because of that same delicacy and likewise because of its coldness” (*Suśruta Sūtrasthāna*).
45) Regarding the phrase beginning with "thus," etc., he states the reason for honey being beneficial in small quantities: "heavy," etc.
The sense is that because it is heavy, honey causes indigestion (āmadoṣa), whereas when it is dry, astringent, and cold, it produces a great calamity of vāta.
He describes the great danger of honey in undigested matter (āmamadhv): "Not from this," and so forth.

Regarding the contradiction with therapeutic measures in the case of honey in *āma*: for example, warm food is wholesome in *āma*, yet that is contradictory in the case of honey; whereas that which is beneficial for honey is cold, and that is contradictory in the case of *āma*.
