247–248 He explains that honey possesses the quality of being a "conveyor" (*yogavāhin*) through the verse beginning with *nānā*:
since that honey is produced from flowers possessing various tastes, potencies (*vīrya*), and so forth, it therefore possesses unmanifested manifold powers.

Furthermore, the meaning is that it performs the action of whichever substance it is joined with—whether it be a Vamanīya (emetic), Āsthāpanīya (non-unctuous enema), Vṛṣya (aphrodisiac), or a substance that produces some other effect—because its own potency is awakened by the similar substance.
The word "ca" (and) here serves to aggregate another reason; therefore, it should be understood as "and because of its specific power (prabhāva).

Consequently, even though milk and wine may arise from various medicinal herbs, they are not *yogavāhin* (carriers of the combined action) due to their specific power. Likewise, substances such as bitumen (*śilājatu*) and oils, which do not consist of various [herbal] components, are nevertheless *yogavāhin*.

Even though honey possesses the quality of being easily assimilable (*yogavāhitva*), it is not employed for oleation (*snehana*) in cases of *vāta*, because it is endowed with qualities such as dryness (*rūkṣa*).

Although honey consists of various substances, it manifests specifically through its dry and astringent (*kaṣāya*) properties; this is to be understood from the fact that honey-bees generally frequent flowers in which the qualities of dryness and astringency predominate.
By this principle, the objection that honey should possess all qualities simply because it is composed of various substances is refuted.

In the *Suśruta-saṃhitā* as well, the quality of being "conducive to medicinal application" (*yogavāhitva*) regarding honey is stated by the passage beginning with "And that is manifold" (*tacca nānā*, Su.Sū.A.

45). The phrase "consisting mostly of sugarcane products" (*ikṣuvikṛtiprāya*) means that sugarcane products are its primary component; therefore, the mention of *yāsa-śarkarā* (sugar from *yāsa*) and so forth here is not contradictory—this is the intended meaning.

Now, the section on prepared foods (*kṛtānnavarga*) is described in order to state the qualities of prepared foods such as *peyā* (gruel) and others, which have been produced from the groups of awned grains (*śūkadhānya*) and so forth as far as possible.
Furthermore, some of these qualities of *peyā* and the rest arise from processing (*saṃskāra*) and combination (*saṃyoga*), while others should be understood as innate (*prākṛta*).

Nor should it be argued that because [the qualities] of rice gruel (*peyā*) and so forth are sublated by the qualities of the [base grains] themselves, such as coarse grains (*śūkadhānya*), the qualities of the latter need not be stated separately; for rice gruel and the like, being dependent upon the qualities of their raw material (*prakṛti*), bring about their own specific qualities. Therefore, one should understand that whatever quality is attributed to a prepared food (*kṛtānna*) becomes powerful if that same quality exists in its raw material, such as red *śāli* rice; however, if the quality of the raw material is contrary to it, then the quality of the prepared food will be diminished.
In this context, that which is beneficial for both the healthy and the sick is stated first; *peyā* is a gruel (*yavāgū*) with much liquid, while *vilepī* is a gruel with thin liquid.

Although the sequence of foods beginning with *peyā* should be discussed starting from solid food (*anna*), the description of the qualities of *maṇḍa* is given first because it is produced prior to solid food.

It should be understood that since it stimulates the digestive fire (*agni*) through its carminative and light properties, it sustains the life-force (*prāṇa*) of those who have undergone fasting or similar treatments.
"Well-prepared" (*susaṃskṛta*) means well-prepared with coriander, long pepper, and other such ingredients.

"Remover of impurities for those who are pure" (*śuddhānāṃ malāpaha*) refers to its capacity to remove the defects that cause coating in the digestive tract (*koṣṭha*), even in those who are properly purified. As it is said: "For those who are pure" (*śuddhānām*) means for those who are slightly purified. Therefore, it is logical that it is called a "remover of impurities" because it removes the remaining connection to defects through slight purification. Furthermore, in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā* (Sūtrasthāna 46), the phrase "for those not purified" (*aviśuddhānām*) regarding parched-rice gruel (*lājamaṇḍa*) should be understood as "for those slightly purified" by the elision of the vowel 'a' (*akārapraśleṣāt*).

That is not correct; even when [the *kapha* and *pitta*] are slightly purified, *peyā* is indeed prohibited. For there is this statement: "When *kapha* and *pitta* are slightly purified, or in those who drink wine, or in those with *vāta* and *pitta*, the sequence beginning with *tarpaṇa* should be performed; for *peyā* would cause obstruction (*abhiṣyanda*) in them" (Sūtrasthāna, A. 6, verses 250–256).

"Svinna" means prepared with grains and rice that have been well-steamed, or alternatively, having become soft through being thoroughly steamed, it is "heated" by its own natural warmth and not by further heating; for there is a saying: "One should avoid food that has become hard and cold, even if it is heated again."
Rice made from fried grains is "fried-rice" (*bhṛṣṭataṇḍula*);
rice made from unfried grains is "unwashed-rice" (*adhauta*).

Here, although the heaviness of rice that is the opposite of that which is characterized by qualities such as being well-washed is established by implication through the statement of the lightness of the latter, it is stated again for the sake of clarity.

Regarding the term "santarpaṇas" (nutritive/pleasing foods), it should be understood that even at present, these are simply rice dishes prepared with combinations of meat and other ingredients that provide strength; furthermore,

it should be understood that even rice combined with dry vegetables and mung beans possesses such qualities as strength-giving power through the greatness of their combination, as well as through processing with ghee and other substances, because this is how they are practiced in worldly usage.
Barley flour sprinkled with warm water, slightly steamed, and made into a cake is called *kulmāṣa*.
"Those whose food is steamed" refers to those such as the *haṇḍarikas*, who have merely undergone the process of steaming.

By stating "according to the substance," [the author] shows that here there is no emergence of a different quality through the suppression of the qualities of the original material, as occurs in the case of parched grain (*lāja*) and the like. (260–261)

The definition of *akṛta-yūṣa* (unprepared broth): "All that is without fat and salt, and excluding pungent spices, is to be known as *akṛta*; that which is prepared with salt, fat, and pungent spices is *kṛta*. (Suśruta Saṃhitā, Sūtrasthāna)
46) "Lean" (*tanu*) means not dense due to having very little flesh; "refined" (*sāṃskārika*) means dense because it has been processed with much flesh, fat, and so forth.
Although parched grain flour (*saktu*) is dry, it is designated as aggravating *vāta* because even buttermilk (*takra*), though dry, is observed to alleviate *vāta*.
By the word "drunk" (*pīta*), he indicates a prohibition against using the flour in a solid mass (*piṇḍa*). "They satisfy" means they produce satiety.
"Sadyobala" (immediately strengthening) means they provide strength at that very moment, like aphrodisiacs (*vājīkaraṇa*); by this, it is also implied that they may diminish strength in the long run.
(263–264) *Yāvaka-vāṭya* is a gruel made of barley; *vāṭya* is boiled rice made from parched barley.
Dhānās are parched barley grains;
virūḍhadhānās are sprouted barley grains;
and śaṣkulyas are made from rice flour mixed with sesame seeds and fried in oil.
*Madhukroḍas* are those whose interior is like honey that has become thickened by cooking, and which contain *piṇḍakas*;

thus, *madhukroḍas* are indeed balls (*piṇḍas*) of ground sugar. Nala, however, says: "Having kneaded the powder of wheat flour with molasses until it is soft-cooked, one should form round balls, dip them in ghee, and cook them until they are baked and possess filaments."

"A wise man should prepare *pūpalikā* cakes scented with *saugandhika*; that same preparation, when combined with sugar and *saṃyāva*, filled with white *āmrātaka*, and wrapped with the rind of *mātuluṅga*, is called *madhuśīrṣaka*."
The *madhuśīrṣaka* is indeed the *madhukroḍa*;
*pūpa*, *piṣṭikā*,
and *pūpalikā* are known as *cāpaḍikā*.
*Palala* is sesame flour;
*veśavāra* is defined in the culinary treatises (*sūdaśāstra*) as: "Meat that is boneless, well-boiled, and then ground again on a stone slab."
"Pippalī, śuṇṭhī, marica, jaggery, and ghee should be cooked together thoroughly; this is known as veśavāra.
"Kṣīrapūpa" refers to cakes in which milk is the predominant ingredient.
In expressions such as *saguḍāḥ* ("with jaggery"), the term *sakṣīrāḥ* ("with milk") denotes merely the connection with milk, not that milk is the primary constituent; thus, there is no tautology.
As for *sasnehāḥ* ("with oil/fat"), this is because the fat is added even while [the mixture] is still in the state of flour-dough (*piṣṭāvasthā*).
He states that even for substances described as heavy, lightness occurs through processing such as contact with fire; thus he says, "From processing, lightness," and so forth.

Having understood this, one should prescribe [the treatment]. That is to say, having understood both the quality of processing and the quality of the primary nature (prakṛti), one should prescribe the appropriate quality.
"Pṛthukas" are flattened barley grains; others, however, say they are those known as "sampiṣṭa," famous in the land of Gāndhāra,
which are fresh and unroasted.
"Preparations of pulses" refers to derivatives of mung beans, black gram, and so forth.
Those that are soft-cooked, which require only a slight application of fire,
are called "overcooked" (vyatikrāntapāka) because they undergo decay after a long time.
To extend the rules regarding the qualities of foods not previously mentioned, he says: "In the combination of substances," and so forth.
Regarding the measure of substances individually: when preparing a food mixture, one should determine the quantity of each among the combined substances;
then, according to its own nature (*yathāsvam*), one should specify that substance whose heaviness or lightness is most pronounced.

The definition of *rasālā*: “*Rasālā*, also known as *śikhariṇī*, is curd that has been well-churned with sugar, fresh ginger, and *nāgara* (dry ginger), along with the four aromatic spices (*caturjātaka*) and cumin.”
In the context of *rasālā*, he describes the qualities of curd with jaggery, beginning with "snehanaṃ" (277–278).
Since drinks (*pānaka*) are also a variety of prepared foods (*kṛtānna*), he describes their qualities, beginning with "drākṣā" (etc.).
The connection is that "pānaka" refers to a preparation derived from sugarcane.

Regarding *rāgaṣāḍava*, some say: "Boiled [sugarcane juice] mixed with jaggery, fresh mango fruit, oil, and ginger—this is to be known as *rāgaṣāḍava*. Alternatively: "[It is made] with sugar, *rucaka* salt, sea salt, *vṛkṣāmla*, and *parūṣaka*..."
A *rāga* is prepared with the juice of *jambū* fruits combined with black mustard (*rājikā*).
As for *ṣāḍava*, it is made from sweet and sour ingredients.
Furthermore, *āmra-leha* and *āmalaka-leha* are made by thickening the separate decoctions of mango and emblic myrobalan with sugar.
He speaks [the verse] beginning with "buddhvā" etc., for the purpose of extending the qualities of the previously mentioned *pānaka* (beverage);
its explanation is like that of [the verse] beginning with "asya dravyasaṃyoga" etc. (279–283).

The definition of *śukta* is as follows: "That which consists of curd and so forth, kept for three nights in a clean vessel along with jaggery, honey, and sour gruel, within a heap of grain—that is called *śukra*, that is called *cukra*.
Thus, *āsutam* refers to radishes, pumpkin gourds, and the like, which have been placed within such *śukta*.
*Śiṇḍākī* is well known by its own name in Tīrabhukti;
*āsuta* is another type of fermented liquor (*sandhāna*);
and *kālāmla* is sour due to having been kept for a long time, not because of the addition of sour substances.
Having described food consisting of prepared items— such as *maṇḍapeya* and others produced by means of cooking—
in verses 284–285,
he now speaks of the substances associated with that [food].

Since ghee has already been mentioned there, he speaks specifically of oil because of its primary role in flavoring food, beginning with "kaṣāya" and so forth. This refers to "from combination and from processing" (*saṃyoga-saṃskārāt*); processing (*saṃskāra*) is the cooking of the oil with medicinal drugs, while combination (*saṃyoga*) is to be understood as occurring during administration (*avacāraṇā*), namely in battle (*saṅkhye*).
Regarding the purpose of specifying the qualities of oils not explicitly mentioned, he says "of fruits" and so forth.
The term "fruits" is illustrative; by it, the pith-oils (*sārasneha*) mentioned in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā* should also be understood.
"According to the fruit" means that the affection for [the food] is of the same quality as the fruit itself.

(286–294) "According to the being" means that for a living being such as one from a marshy region who is hot-natured, [the food] is hot; whereas for a living being such as one from a dry land who is cool-natured, it is cool.

In general, however, the fact that fat and marrow are neither hot nor cold has already been explained in the chapter on unctuousness (Sneha-adhyāya) by the passage beginning with "due to subtlety" (saukṣmyāt),
which describes the qualities of sauvarcala salt.
By the phrase "due to its pungency," etc., the quality of *biḍa* salt is indicated;
*audbhida* is rock salt (*utkārikā-lavaṇa*),
while *kālalavaṇa* is simply *sauvarcala* salt that is odorless.
That which exists near the southern ocean is *sāmudra*; *karakaca* is born from sand, produced in the eastern ocean.
Since alkalis also possess the nature of salt, he describes their alkaline qualities with the verse beginning with "hṛt" and so forth;
the entire quality of barley-alkali (yavakṣāra) applies to all alkalis, such as svarjikākṣāra, ṭaṅkaṇakṣāra, and others.
Kāravī is black cumin (*kṛṣṇajīraka*);
kuñcikā is large cumin (*sthūlajīraka*).
Ajājī is cumin (jīraka).

[Verse 307] He states that there are other things besides the aforementioned oils and so forth which, by acting as flavorings for food, become associated with food— beginning with the words "āhāra" and so forth.

"Bhakti" means a portion or a specific measure; alternatively, "bhakti" means desire. Therefore, because human desires are unrestricted, it is implied that even what has been mentioned may not generally be suitable for food, while conversely, even what has not been mentioned may become suitable for food through association with substances such as juices, oils, or grinding.
Now, in order to state the qualities of the awned cereals (*śūkadhānya*) and others that have not been previously mentioned, he says: "The awned cereal," and so forth.

"One year passed" means that it is praised [to store grain] for one year having passed; this is due to its lightness. However, the rule regarding new grain in the winter season is an exception, because it arrives quickly; what is sown becomes ready soon. Therefore, among all grains, the *ṣaṣṭika* (sixty-day rice) is the lightest, for they ripen in sixty nights.

And in this explanation, because the winter *śāli* rice is of shorter duration than the autumnal *vrīhi*, it would follow that [the latter] possesses lightness; therefore, it must be stated that lightness is caused by rapid digestion within the same species,
or else, that which "comes quickly" means that once eaten, it is digested swiftly— namely, that which is properly roasted or slightly roasted.
*Sūpyam* means suitable for soup, such as mung beans, black gram, and so forth (309–310).
*Mṛtam* means dead, that is, deceased on its own.
By the term "fatty" (*medura*), even that which is "emaciated" (*kṛśa*) is to be understood as included, provided it has been nourished by unsuitable conditions—
such as an animal from a marshy region (*ānūpa*) that has grown fat in an arid region (*dhanva*).
"Beasts of prey" refers to tigers and the like; alternatively, "beast of prey" may mean a snake. "Pierced by poisoned [weapons]" means struck by a weapon smeared with poison.

The qualities of meat broth—beginning with "satisfying" and ending with "the pacification of all diseases"—the word "all" here signifies a great many. By this, the prohibition of meat in cases such as insanity (*unmāda*) does not become contradictory; for it is stated regarding insanity: "He who has abstained from meat and wine... (Ci.)... 9) "And so forth,
according to each [case]" means that one should employ such a taste as has been prescribed for whichever specific disease.
"Prepared without oil" means prepared without fat;
"unripe" means uncooked; and this should be understood as excluding *bilva* and similar fruits;
"grown in an unsuitable place" means produced in an inappropriate locality.

The meaning is that there is no fault [in consuming] things produced out of season (*anārtava*)—such as green ginger, onions, and so forth—even if they are prepared without fat (*niḥsneha*) and not strained (*aparisruta*), provided they are "prepared" (*kṛta*); this is the established conclusion (*viniścaya*). Furthermore, the description of the qualities and defects of liquors has already been made in the passage beginning with "generally fresh" (*prāyaśo'bhinavam*); likewise for water, in the passage beginning with "slimy and infested with worms" (*picchilaṃ krimilam*). However, regarding the categories of food consisting of milk products and cooked grains, the implication is that if the qualities of the agent who prepares them are contrary to what was stated, the resulting qualities should be inferred as being the opposite.
Now he states what specific after-drink (anupāna) should be taken by those for whom it is required—beginning with "yad" and so forth.

"By the qualities of food" (āhāraguṇaiḥ) refers to qualities such as coldness, unctuousness, sweetness, and so on. "Opposite" (viparīta) means that which possesses opposite qualities should be consumed as the after-drink.

And thus, just as sweet milk would be an incompatible after-drink for sour curd, or fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*) for milk-rice (*pāyasa*), he says: "That which is not antagonistic to the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).

In this way, when milk is drunk as an after-drink with sour [substances], it is rejected because of its incompatibility, due to its antagonism toward the *dhātus*; likewise, other incompatible things should also be understood.
This has been indicated in the *Yajjaḥpuruṣīya* chapter (Sūtra-sthāna).

25) Regarding "that which is to be drunk" and "that which is not to be drunk," because they possess innate qualities and defects, he describes the after-drink (*anupāna*) according to the distinction of defects— such as being unctuous, hot, and so forth— in relation to the food consumed in that manner.
"Anuśastam" means that the after-drink (anupāna) is recommended.
[Verses 319–324] He states the qualities of after-drinks, beginning with "atha," etc.
Paryāpti means satisfaction (tṛpti).
Verses 325–326 state those for whom a post-prandial drink (anupāna) should not be taken: "Not for those with diseases of the upper body," and so forth.
By the phrase "situated in the throat and chest," it is shown that the upward-moving wind (*ūrdhvāṅgamāruta*) and others remain precisely in the throat and chest and do not go downward.

By the phrase "having destroyed the oil born of food," it means that having overcome the oily substance produced from food, it leads further to morbidity; that is to say, it produces the morbidity characterized by *vāta*.
The meaning is that water, due to its extreme coldness, overcomes that pacification of *vāta* which ought to be effected by the oil of food.
By this, that which is said—that the moistening by water is logical because of its inherent viscidity—is not so.

Furthermore, as for those who say: "Since there is a rule stating that *hana* means 'to injure' or 'to go,' the phrase 'having destroyed the unctuousness' (*snehaṃ hatvā*) means 'having gone toward the unctuousness' (*snehaṃ gatvā*)," that too is not correct. For it is logical that the upward-moving wind (*ūrdhvāṅgamāruta*) and others should destroy [the condition] due to being associated with unctuousness, rather than [the wind] performing the act of destruction itself.
Alternatively, *sneha* refers to the essence (*sāra*), as in: "The body [is destroyed] from the depletion of its unctuousness" (*dehaḥ snehaparikṣayāt*). (Cikitsā-sthāna)

8) This means "due to the exhaustion of the body's essence" (*sāra*). Furthermore, the destruction of that essence occurs through the digestive fire (*pāka*) because the water, having taken up the moisture of the food, remains in the throat.
(Verses 327–328) He states the explanation for the mention of a specific portion of the substances of food and drink, beginning with "annapāna... and so forth.

"Food and drink consist of a single part that is generally used" means that which is used most frequently. By this, he demonstrates that there is little fault in specifically mentioning those things that are used predominantly, while not specifically mentioning those that are generally not used. Furthermore, to address why even that which involves minor faults is not mentioned, he says: "The substances," and so forth.

"To describe the substances in their entirety" means to indicate them completely. "By names" means that even by means of their names, it is not possible for "anyone"—this being the ellipsis—to do so. The word "hi" (for) has the sense of "because. The meaning is this: since no one is able to state all substances even by name alone due to their extreme multitude, what need is there to mention the description of the qualities of every single food and drink substance by specifically identifying each one? Alternatively, the construction may be: "It is not possible for anyone to describe them by name in their entirety," meaning that they cannot be described according to their qualities.
Now, as for how the qualities of food and drink not mentioned here should be specified, he says: "In the same manner," and so forth.

In whatever manner it was stated in the previous chapter that "there is no substance which is not a medicine" (Sūtra 26), in that same manner, a substance not mentioned here must be described; the word "by its qualities" (*guṇataḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

For in the preceding chapter, substances were described according to their specific actions—such as being heavy or coarse—by way of their divisions into earthy and so forth, through the passage beginning with "Therein, substances [are characterized by] heaviness, coarseness" (Sūtra 26). Therefore, the meaning is that a substance not explicitly mentioned there should be identified as earthy and so forth by means of those very qualities such as heaviness and coarseness, and designated as the performer of the aforementioned actions, such as accumulation.

Regarding how the heaviness, hardness, and other qualities of a substance whose specific constituent matter has not been specified are to be known, he says: "Just as the speech of those born in a region. This means that those born in a region (deśajāḥ) are people from that particular land; their speech regarding those [substances]—such as their heaviness and hardness—is how they are to be known. Alternatively, just as those born in a region employ the conventional usage for a particular substance, saying "this is sweet," "this is sour," and so forth, one should explain that the cause of the perceived sweetness, sourness, and so on, belongs to the earth and other elements. Thus, it should be stated by means of the collection of qualities such as heaviness belonging to the earth and others, and by the action described in terms of taste. 329–330.
He states another cause for knowing the qualities of food and drink that have not been mentioned: "The term *cara*," and so forth.

That which is moved (*caryate*) is *cara*, meaning a location; however, in a general sense, it is taken to mean both what is to be eaten (*bhakṣya*) and action (*kriyā*), which is activity (*vyāpāra*).
The standard of measure (*pramāṇa*) is found here in this context concerning the qualities of food and drink (331).
He explains *cara* (dietary regimen): "The preparation of food," and so forth. *Bhakṣyasaṃvidhiḥ* means the consumption of food.

In that context, by the phrase "from marshy, aquatic, aerial, desert, and so forth," *cara* in the form of movement is expressed; and by the expression "the preparation of food," *cara* in the form of the food itself is expressed.
Regarding this very point, he provides an illustration beginning with "jalaja" (aquatic).

Here, by virtue of being aquatic (*jalaja*) or marsh-born (*anūpaja*), movement is observed either in water or in marshy ground. Indeed, those born in water and such environments generally do not remain elsewhere. However, as for those born elsewhere who nevertheless remain in other places—such as the crow (*kāka*) and the *madgu* bird—he says "and those that frequent water and marshes" (*jalānūpacarāśca ye*) in order to include them.

By this general rule, "being a water-frequenting creature" (*jalacara*) is understood here primarily from the fact of dwelling in water; likewise, "marsh-frequenting" (*anūpacara*) and so forth should be understood accordingly.
He states the quality produced by the form of the food to be consumed, beginning with "heavy foods" (*gurubhakṣyāḥ*).

In the phrase "those that move in the desert" (*dhanvacāriṇaḥ*), the word *ca* (and) should be understood as having been omitted. By this, even though not explicitly stated, the lightness of those that move in the sky, such as hawks (*śyena*) and others, is to be understood in comparison to other animals of their own species, because the sky is light.

As for those who say that there is no mention [of lightness] for sky-dwellers because there is no fixed rule regarding heaviness and lightness for them—that is incorrect; for if that were the case, the mention of the sky in the verse "movable [animals] are of the marsh, water, sky, desert, and so forth" would be purposeless, since the sky would then have no functional role.

"One should know that [the testicles] are heavier than flesh" means that one should know the testicles and so forth to be heavier than the flesh of the thighs and other parts, which have been established as heavy;

"according to their respective [parts]" (*yathāsvam*) means that this heaviness and so forth applies only to the thighs and other parts of a single body, and not in comparison to the bodies of others.
"Middle" refers to the marrow within the bone (*antarādhi*); "bone" refers to the flesh situated upon the bone.

Others, however, say that "middle" refers to the marrow located within the bone; but that is not very elegant, because [the meaning] is already obtained simply by the statement regarding the increasing weight of each successive constituent element (*dhātu*).

Regarding the phrase "by nature" (*svabhāvāt*), this is an illustration of action by way of inherent disposition (*prakṛtyā*); "to the lazy" (*alasebhyaḥ*) and so forth; "to the lazy" means to those of little activity (*alpakriyebhyaḥ*).

"Viśiṣyante" means they become distinguished (*viśiṣṭāḥ*), that is to say, they become lighter (336–337). That by which cows and other animals are characterized (*liṅgyante*) or known is the "characteristic" (*liṅga*), namely, the genus (*jāti*). Therefore, "in the commonality of characteristics" means "in the commonality of genera. This should be understood with reference to quadrupeds; among birds, the opposite is the case. As Hārīta says: "Among quadrupeds the female is light; among birds the male is light. Regarding this, it is also stated: "Among quadrupeds the females [are light]; among birds the male is light."

Regarding men, they state that the cause of excessive heaviness is the abundance of the initiating *śukra* (semen); however, we consider that nature (*svabhāva*) is the cause there, as it is an exception (*apavāda*), because the opposite is observed among birds.
"With its opposite" means one should understand that even light things may possess heaviness due to their conditioning (*saṃskāra*).
He explains that very lightness and heaviness produced by processing (*saṃskāra*) with the words beginning "of rice" (*vrīheḥ*).
The meaning is that even though rice is heavy, parched rice grains (*lāja*) are light due to processing;
and although flour (*saktu*) is light, prepared balls (*siddhapiṇḍikā*) are heavy. Prepared balls (*siddhapiṇḍikā*) are balls cooked by fire.
Regarding "taking little" (*alpādāna*) and so forth:

when there is lightness (*lāghava*) in taking only a small amount or a mere fraction of heavy substances, that lightness is the measure (*mātrā*), not the substance itself, because of the heaviness of the latter.
Thus, in the chapter on "Eating in Moderation" (Sūtra 5), it was stated that for light substances, the degree of heaviness is determined by the quantity consumed;
we have also explained this in detail in that very place. However, because it is relevant to the present context and is highly significant, it is stated once again.

The meaning is that substances depend upon quantity; thus, when they possess the appropriate quantity, they are digested easily. Furthermore, quantity depends upon the digestive fire (*agni*); therefore, depending on the variation of the fire for each individual and each day, the quantity may be large or small. The point is that no fixed quantity exists.
Why, then, is the measure [of food] employed in dependence upon fire? He says: "Strength," and so forth.
The meaning is that by means of the measure applied in dependence on fire, strength and the other qualities arise because fire is not destroyed.
"Established in fire" means dependent on fire; just as subjects are dependent on a king.
"Prāṇas" refers to the vital breaths (*vāyu*); or alternatively, the ten *prāṇas*, such as the *śaṅkha* and others, which have the breaths as their support.
"Fuel" (*indhana*) means wood; it is fuel because it is like fuel. Or else, fuel is said to be that which is combustible by fire; otherwise, it is "non-fuel" (*anindhana*).
Showing that this consideration of relative weight (guru-lāghava) performed by Caraka and others applies generally to those with weak digestive fire (alpāgni), he says "heavy" and so forth.
Here too, due to weakness, even by slow-digesting foods and the like, only a dullness of the digestive fire (vahnimāndya) is to be observed.
"Those whose food is coarse" (kharāhārāḥ) means those accustomed to hard food;
even with a large abdomen, he demonstrates a great digestive fire (mahāgnitva) due to the obstruction of fat (medas).

By the statement "it is not necessarily to be considered," he shows that even for those with a blazing digestive fire (*dīptāgni*), there certainly exists a consideration of relative weight and lightness (*gurulāghava*) regarding even small amounts [of food],
because even for those with a blazing digestive fire and the like, heavy substances indeed bring about a counteraction to the fire, since they are by nature opposed to fire.

"Like one who has established the sacred fires" (*āhitāgni*) means one who has established the fire according to his suitability (*sātmyena*). Alternatively, "like one who has established the sacred fires" (*āhitāgnir-iva*) refers to one who has established the fire. Just as such a person offers oblations in the morning and evening, so too does this person offer wholesome foods into the internal fire in the morning and evening, and he mutters the Veda—that is, he repeats the mantra beginning with the *praṇava*.

Regarding the phrase "he gives": when a man practices giving according to his ability, diseases do not afflict him in pursuit of the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) or welfare (*kalyāṇa*), even in the future—that is, even in other births. In this life, diseases do not arise because he eats wholesome food; in other births as well, they do not arise solely due to the power of the merit acquired through the recitation of the *Brahma-mantra* and the practice of giving.

For this very reason, he says: "due to internal absence" (*antarādṛte*); *antarāt* means from a cause, and *ṛte* means without. The sense is that because of the absence of unwholesome food, unrighteousness, and causes of disease, ailments do not arise.
He further states that even a lifespan of one hundred years results from wholesome diet, beginning with the words "thirty-six," etc. (verses 345–347).
By so many nights, exactly one hundred years pass for him who has conquered his self and mastered his senses—
he who is esteemed and honored.
To the question, "For what purpose should this be examined regarding the preparation of food and drink? he says: "The vital breaths," and so forth;
"runs toward" means he desires them.

*Pratibhā*, *prajñā*, *medhā*, and *dhī* endowed with retention (*dhāraṇāvatī*) constitute worldly knowledge (*laukika*), which exists among those who do not investigate (*aparīkṣaka*). For it is only the non-investigators who engage solely with the present; the investigators, however, concern themselves only with that which benefits future births.
Regarding the phrase "the action which [is performed] in the state of subsistence": while this is the subject to be established, "action" refers to agriculture and so forth;
"in the state of attaining heaven" refers to the journey to heaven;
and "Vedic" refers to sacrifices and the like.
"Apavarga" refers to liberation (mokṣa);
these [cases] are locative cases of occasion (nimitta-saptamī).
And as for what was said: "In the scripture on liberation (mokṣa-śāstra), there is truthful celibacy (satya-brahmacarya) and so forth."
"Food is established [as the foundation]"— since for one who is without food there is no maintenance of the body and consequently no undertaking of any activity,
and because food is the cause everywhere, one must therefore pay heed to it.
Regarding the qualities of food and drink in the section on "attraction" (*saṅgraha*), those described by the phrase "desirable color" and so forth are called "supreme" (*sāgrya*).
This refers to [the statement] "water moistens" and so forth; for water and the other elements are supreme—that is, the best—at the tasks of moistening and so on.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Rules for Food and Drink," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the section on Food and Drink (*Annapānacatuṣka*).
[Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 28 (28 of 120)] In the preceding chapter it was stated that "food is life" (Sū. 27).
To explain the manner in which food becomes the cause of life, the chapter titled "The Various Kinds of Food and Drink" (Vividhāśitapītīya) is now set forth.
This designation as well,
beginning with "of various kinds" (vividham), is intended for the sake of the meaning.
By the word "various" (*vividham*), he shows the internal subdivisions of what is eaten and so forth; among those things eaten and so forth, whichever is most commonly used has been mentioned first.
The expression "beneficial to a person" (*jantor hitam*) is used because that which is not beneficial lacks the capacity to produce strength, complexion, and other such qualities.
[The term] *antaragnisandhukṣitabala* refers to one whose strength is kindled by the internal fire, the digestive heat (*jāṭharo vahniḥ*).

"By its own heat" means by whichever heat belongs to each respective substance—such as earth and so forth—that has consumed the food, whether it be of an earthly, fiery, or other nature; for it is said: "The five heats—earthy, watery, fiery, airy, and ethereal—digest their respective five qualities of food, beginning with the earthen. (Cikitsā-sthāna 15)

Regarding the phrase "properly metabolized" (*samyagvipacyamānam*): whether it be food that has been eaten or otherwise, when that which has been eaten and so forth is properly metabolized by its own respective heat—that is, by the heat of blood and other elements in the form of the *dhātu-agni* (tissue-fire)—and having attained the state of nutritional essence (*rasatva*), it then enters the tissues such as blood; at that time, it is metabolized by the very heat of the blood and other tissues. Thus, the connection is as follows: while being metabolized in this way, the food and so forth provides nourishment, invigorates, and increases the body through accumulation and other processes.
To the question of what kind of body [is meant], he says: "in due time" (*kālavat*), and so forth.

Just as time is not stationary due to its constant movement, so too is that body in which the maturation (*pāka*) of all the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) is non-stationary and uninterrupted. By this, he demonstrates that it is logical for a body—whose constituents are constantly being depleted by the digestion of its own internal fire (*svāgni*)—to undergo processes such as nourishment through food and drink; for if the body were not subject to depletion through digestion, then what would be the purpose of food and drink when nourishment and the like are already established spontaneously? This is the intended meaning.

Alternatively, "like time" (*kālavad*) is a qualifier for "that which has been eaten" (*aśitādi*); thus, the meaning is that it is the eating and so forth performed at the aforementioned time. This is because eating at the wrong time does not produce accumulation and the like. Similarly, "the digestion of all the *dhātus* being unstable" is also a qualifier for "that which has been eaten" and so forth; thus, it refers to that eating and so forth by which the digestion within all the *dhātus* is unstable. By this, he demonstrates that when the essence (*rasa*) of what has been eaten and so forth is obstructed in any *dhātu*, the process of digestion ceases, and consequently, no accumulation or the like occurs.

Furthermore, this explanation is not very satisfactory; since this meaning is already obtained by the qualification of the body itself through the words "unimpaired" (*anupahata*) and so forth, the further qualification of the body is redundant.

"Unimpaired," and so forth: this refers to one whose channels for the heat (*ūṣman*), wind (*māruta*), and currents of all the *dhātus* are unimpaired. For when even a single digestive fire (*pācakāgni*) that matures the *dhātus* is impaired, or when the *vyāna* wind—which nourishes the *dhātus* and carries the nutrient essence—is impaired in some way, or when the channel carrying the nutrient essence that nourishes the *dhātus* is impaired, then food and other such items do not cause growth or accumulation because they fail to increase the *dhātus*; such is the meaning.

"Kevalam" means the entire body; or alternatively, "kevalam" means free from unwholesome factors (*adharma*), for when the body is joined with unwholesome factors, food and other nutrients become fruitless. Now, one might ask: since the bodily constituents (*dhātus*) that remain in their natural state undergo increase and so forth by themselves, what is the purpose of food and the like? To this he says: "The constituents... and so forth. Those whose nourishment consists of the constituents are called *dhātvāhārāḥ*. The meaning is that the constituents—such as *rasa* (nutritive fluid) and the rest—are constantly being depleted; only when they are replenished by the nourishment derived from food and the like do they maintain health, and not otherwise.
He explains that which is the nutriment of the elements, beginning with the words "Therein," etc.;
"therein" refers to the ingested food and so forth.
The grammatical connection is that "chyle and waste are produced.
That which is called "nutritional essence" (*āhāraprasāda*) is so designated; "essence" (*prasāda*) means the refined substance, while "waste" (*kiṭṭa*) is the non-essential portion.

"From the *kiṭṭa*" means from the waste portion (*kiṭṭāṃśa*); by this it is meant that from food, the waste portion becomes urine and feces as well as flatus (*vāyu*), and from the nutrient essence (*rasa*) while being digested, the impurity (*mala*) is phlegm (*kapha*). Such details are to be followed as they will be explained in the chapter on the *grahaṇī*; for it will state: "The waste of food is feces and urine; of the nutrient essence (*rasa*), however, it is phlegm; of blood, bile (*pitta*); of flesh, the impurity of the channels (*khamaḷa*); of fat, sweat is the waste; of bone, the waste is hair and body hair; of marrow, it is oiliness (*sneha*); and of the skin, it is the excretion of the eyes. (Ci.)
15) By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), eye-secretion (*akṣisneha*) and so forth are to be understood.

And although wind (*vāta*) is perceived even from fasting (*anaśana*), it nevertheless certainly arises from the impure portion (*malāṃśa*) of dry food, fecal matter (*kiṭṭa*), and the like; thus, the production of wind from fecal matter is indeed logical. Nor is there a fixed rule that [wind] arises only from impurity, since wind and other humors are present even due to physical exercise (*vyāyāma*), immersion in water (*avagāha*), and so forth.
He states that the generative organ (*liṅga*) is nourished by rasa in the passage beginning with "puṣyanti tu," etc.;
the "five material elements of the sense organs" refers to earth and the other [elements], which are the causes of the olfactory and other sense organs.
The phrase "designated as the clarity of the elements" (dhātuprasādasañjñakāni) shows that the sense-faculties are initiated by the extreme purity of the elements themselves.
"Body-binding" (śarīrabandha) refers to the sinews, vessels, and so forth; by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (ādi), menstrual blood, breast milk, and the like are also included.

Regarding the nourishment of blood and the other tissues from the essence of food (*āhārarasa*), some say: "The essence transforms into the form of blood, and blood into the form of muscle; in this way, muscle and the subsequent elements also transform into the form of each successive tissue.
On this point as well, some say: "Just as milk becomes curd in its entirety, so too the entire essence becomes blood; likewise, blood and the others also become the form of muscle and the rest."

Others, however, say that the nourishment of the tissues (dhātus) by the nutrient essence (rasa) follows the analogy of water from a field-channel. In this process, the rasa produced from food reaches the tissue-form rasa and increases it by a certain portion; another mass of rasa, having reached that site, becomes like blood because it possesses the smell, color, and qualities of blood, and nourishes the blood-form tissue by a portion equal to blood, while the remaining portion goes to the muscle tissue (māṃsa), where the same arrangement as for blood applies; and the same holds true for fat (medas) and the subsequent tissues.

For this very reason, this treatise is considered to have its primary meaning [in this context]; as it is said: "From rasa comes blood, from that flesh, from flesh fat, from that bone, from bone marrow, from that semen, and from semen the embryo is produced from the essence" (Ci.).

15) Thus it is said; likewise, it is also stated in the *Hārīta*: “The rasa, circulating within seven days, resembling in color respectively the white pigeon, the green, the turmeric, the lotus, the *kiṃśuka* flower, and liquid lac, undergoes a change of color through its daily revolution and, due to the influence of the heat of bile (*pitta*), attains the state of blood. Likewise, it is also stated in the *Suśruta*: “That aqueous rasa indeed remains in each constituent element (*dhātu*) for three thousand and fifteen *kalās*; thus, in one month, the rasa becomes semen (*śukra*). (Su.Sū. 14)

Others, however, say: according to the maxim of the pigeons in a threshing floor, this nutrient essence (*annarasa*), having entered the respective channels of the tissues (*dhātu*), nourishes the *rasa* and the other elements. Yet, that portion of the *rasa* which nourishes a particular tissue does not even come into contact with another tissue. The channels (*srotas*) that nourish the *rasa* and so forth become progressively narrower and longer as they proceed further on. Therefore, the portion of *rasa* that nourishes *rasa* nourishes the *rasa* itself because it travels through the *rasa*-channels. Similarly, after the time of nourishing *rasa*, the portion of *rasa* that nourishes blood (*rakta*) nourishes the blood because it travels through the blood-nourishing channels. Likewise, after the time of nourishing blood, the portion of *rasa* that nourishes muscle (*māṃsa*) nourishes the muscle because it travels through distant and subtle channels. This should be understood to apply similarly to the nourishment of fat (*medas*) and the other tissues.

Therefore, the meaning of the passage beginning with "From rasa [comes] blood, from that flesh" is as follows: blood is produced at a time subsequent to the period of the nourishment of rasa; likewise, flesh is produced at a time subsequent to the period of the nourishment of blood, and so forth.
In this same manner, the statements of Suśruta and Hārīta are also to be explained.

Furthermore, as for what will be stated regarding rājayakṣman—"Blood, because its path is obstructed, does not reach the flesh and other tissues"—that refers to the blood circulating within the heart (*hṛdayacāriśoṇita*), and not to the nourishing blood (*poṣakaśoṇita*).

Furthermore, according to the theory of transformation (*pariṇāma-pakṣa*), semen would only arise after a very long time through the gradual process of aphrodisiacs (*vṛṣya*) assuming the form of blood and so forth; however, substances such as milk and others are observed to be aphrodisiacs immediately. On the other hand, according to the "crow-on-the-threshing-floor" theory (*khalekapota-pakṣa*), it is logical that the nutrient essence (*rasa*) produced by an aphrodisiac, through its specific potency (*prabhāva*), quickly becomes connected with the semen and thereby nourishes it. Likewise, if there is a corruption of the nutrient essence (*rasa-duṣṭi*), then according to the theory of transformation, there would be a corruption of all subsequent elements—blood and the rest—born from it, because they are produced from a corrupted cause.

In the case of the "crow on the threshing floor" analogy, however, only that portion of the nutrient (*rasa*) which nourishes a particular tissue (*dhātu*) becomes vitiated, and not all [tissues], because the other [tissues] have non-vitiated causes. Likewise, when there is an increase in fat (*medas*), the bone (*asthi*) should also increase due to its being a frequent cause [of fat]; yet, in those with abundant fat, a depletion of the other tissues is observed. Furthermore, there is this statement: "In one who is obese, only the fat increases, and not so the other tissues" (Sūtra-sthāna 21). Such are the objections against the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*).

Among these positions, the theory of the transformation of the entire self (*sarvātmapariṇāmavāda*) is indeed contradictory, because if the entire self were transformed, death would occur from the body's loss of vitality after only three or four fasts, and during a month-long fast, the body would consist of nothing but semen. As for the analogy of the irrigation channel in a field (*kedārīkulyānyāya*), it possesses equal force with the analogy of the pigeons in the threshing floor (*khalekapotanyāya*); for regarding the aphrodisiac power mentioned, even in the case of the irrigation channel, the aphrodisiac will quickly reach the blood and other tissues through its very potency and produce semen, just as it does through its potency in the case of the pigeons in the threshing floor.

As for the claim that when rasa is vitiated, blood (śoṇita) is also vitiated—that is not so, because the portion of rasa that nourishes the blood as a constituent element (dhātu) remains undamaged; thus, this is the same as the previous case.

For even in this view, not every rasa becomes blood in the form of a bodily constituent (dhātu); rather, only a certain portion that resembles blood does so. The remainder, however, is called "blood" because it resides in the location of blood and possesses some similarity to blood in terms of color and other qualities. By this same logic, the increase of bone following the increase of fat is also refuted, since bone is not nourished by fat, but rather by the rasa located in the site of the fat which mimics the nature of fat.

Thus, because these two positions are equally respected by the great multitude and follow identical logic, we do not declare even one of them to be certain; for the strength or weakness of a position does not depend on the power of one's intellect. Since there is no contradiction in practice here, we shall desist.

Now, by stating that "the tissues such as *rasa* are nourished from the *rasa* of food," you imply that the production of the *rasa* of the [nutritive] tissue (*dhātu-rasa*) from the *rasa* of food is admitted as a distinct process. Therefore, why has it not been stated what its location is or what its measure is? It is replied: its variations of increase and decrease are not of such a nature, because there is no fixed measure for its increase and decrease. As for its location, it is indeed within the vessels (*dhamanī*), which serve as the nourishing food-*rasa*. Furthermore, it is not apprehended in a separate region apart from the *rasa* and other tissues, because it is already included by the very apprehension of *rasa* and the rest, since it exists in the form of their cause.

In this context, although *ojas* consists of the essence of the seven tissues (*dhātu*), and is thus already included by the mention of "tissues" itself, it is nevertheless listed separately because it performs the function of sustaining life. As for those who maintain that *ojas* is produced from semen (*śukra*), they would have *ojas* as an eighth tissue; regarding this view, the author will provide an extension [of the definition] and state: "That which is the supreme radiance (*tejas*) of the tissues beginning with *rasa* and ending with *śukra*, that indeed is *ojas*" (Su.Sū.A. 15). He concludes the section on how the tissues and wastes follow their natural constitution once they have been nourished as explained: "All these," and so forth.

It has been stated that even those substances known as waste products (*mala*), such as sweat, urine, and so forth, become *dhātus* because they maintain the body when they remain within their own proper measure. This is expressed by the phrase "the *dhātus* are called waste products" (*dhātavo malākhyāḥ*).

The construction is as follows: "according to age and body" (*yathāvayaḥśarīram*) means that they nourish the *dhātus* in whatever measure is appropriate for a particular age, such as childhood, and likewise in whatever measure is appropriate for a particular body, whether it be naturally long, short, thin, or stout.
Thus, in the passage beginning with "in this way," the phrase "remaining in their own measure" (*svapramāṇāvasthitāḥ*) means neither exceeding nor falling short.

"Of the substratum" means of the body; "properly ripened," they subsequently reach the entire substratum by means of the vessels— that is to say, the whole body— due to the equilibrium of the constituent elements (dhātus), meaning due to the balance of the *rasa* and so forth, as well as the balance of sweat, urine, and so on, and so forth.
By the phrase "by way of signs" (*nimittataḥ*), he refutes the notions of decrease and increase in the form of fatal omens (*ariṣṭa*) within the signless state.

By the phrase "through increase and decrease rooted in food," he refers respectively to those caused by excessive and deficient food intake. The meaning of this is that the nutrient essence (*rasa*), through the increase and decrease produced by specific types of food, brings about equilibrium.

Although the equilibrium of the constituent elements (*dhātu-sāmya*) is established as being synonymous with health, when he says "for the sake of health," he thereby excludes equilibrium resulting from either the depletion or the excessive growth of the natural constituents, precisely because such equilibrium is itself a cause of disease.

"And the waste products (*kiṭṭa*) of the impurities are exactly like this": just as the nutrient essence (*rasa*), so too the waste product brings about the equilibrium of the impurities for the sake of health through the aforementioned sequence of processing the essence. He states another treatment for increased impurities, beginning with "svamāna" (their own measure):

their "evacuation" (*utsarga*) means external discharge in the form of purification, which is prescribed in the scriptures; or, they are called "evacuators" (*utsargin*) because they carry out evacuation.
He states another treatment for chronic impurities (malas) with the verse beginning "cold and hot" (*śītoṣṇa*), etc.

"Paryaya" means reversal (*viparyaya*); thus, it means by means of qualities opposite to cold and hot. Consequently, the therapeutic regimen (*upacāra*) consists of heat for an impurity arising from cold, and likewise cold for one arising from heat.
Furthermore, the word "etc. (*ādi*) is used here elliptically; by this, qualities opposite to oily (*snigdha*), dry (*rūkṣa*), and so forth are also included.

Alternatively, it should be understood that "qualities" (guṇas) refer to secondary qualities (paryāya-guṇas) such as pairs of opposites (dvandva-guṇas)—namely, unctuousness (snigdha), dryness (rūkṣa), softness (mṛdu), sharpness (tīkṣṇa), and so forth—and that these are to be administered according to their suitability.

By this, it is stated that there is a threefold therapeutic approach for increased morbid humors (vṛddha-mala): avoidance of the cause (nidāna-varjana), purification (śodhana), and pacification (śamana). Among these, avoidance of the cause should be understood as the abandonment of food that increases the morbid humor and the consumption of food that diminishes the humor; purification is expressed by the term "evacuative" (utsargin); and pacification is explained by the passage beginning with "cold and hot" (śītoṣṇa). 4.

"Ayanamukhāni" means both "courses" (*ayana*) and "entrances" (*mukha*). Here, "courses" (*ayana*) are the paths by which things come (*āyanti*); "entrances" (*mukha*), however, are those through which they enter. By this it is stated that whatever is the course for the impurities and the *dhātus*, that alone is the entrance for their entry; thus, there is no entry by one path and movement by another. Alternatively, for the *rasas* and so forth, the "mouths of the channels" (*srotomukha*) are both the entrances and the courses. Or rather, "courses" (*ayana*) mean movements, and "entrances" (*mukha*) mean paths; therefore, "ayanamukhāni" means the paths of movement.

And those channels, filled with impurities and clarity, nourish the *dhātus* according to their respective [requirements]. "According to its own" means that whatever is to be nourished by a particular [channel], it fills that very thing; "according to division" (*yathāvibhāgena*) means it fills it with the very same measure as the division or quantity of that *dhatu*. The meaning is that they nourish only such quantities, neither more nor less.

Furthermore, this is the function of those [channels] situated in their natural state (*prakṛtistha*); however, it should be understood that for those in a state of transformation (*vikṛta*), there is indeed the production of *dhātus* that are either deficient or excessive.
And it is stated elsewhere: “The constituent element nourishes itself by means of its own respective channel” (Ci.
He concludes with the words beginning with “evam” (thus), etc.
He explains how there can be the arising of two contradictory states—the body and the disease that afflicts it—from such things as food and drink: "Beneficial and non-beneficial," etc.

A specific type of beneficial food and drink produces a specific wholesome result, whereas a specific type of non-beneficial food and drink produces a specific unwholesome result; thus, the meaning is that a contradictory effect does not arise from a cause of a single uniform nature.

For it is observed, O Blessed One, in such passages as "those who employ [the treatment] exactly as prescribed and designated," that there are both those afflicted by disease and those free from disease; this is the connection.
"Consisting of specific [qualities]" means arising from specific [causes].
"Caused by that" means caused by unwholesome food;
"not only" means not merely [those factors];
"the natures of disease" means the causes of disease.
"Of those who consume unwholesome food," and so forth;

"due to a cause" means due to another factor that acts as an obstacle. And that cause should be understood as being contrary to the text to be stated later, beginning with "for that very same unwholesome [food]," etc.;
"immediately" means at that very time.

By this, he shows that unwholesome [regimen] generally possesses the capacity to produce a disorder after a lapse of time in relation to the generation of disease; otherwise, the word "immediately" (sadyaḥ) would be redundant, because if it were not a producer of doshas even at a later time, it could not be called "morbid" (doṣavat).
"Morbid" (doṣavat) refers to that which generates disease, namely, improper conduct (apacāra), which is the consumption of unwholesome food.
He states the reason for what was said: "Not," and so forth.
"Possessing equal defects" means they produce equal defects;
that is to say, they possess resistance to disease, opposition to the strength of the disease, and the capacity to obstruct the manifestation of the disease.
He explains that very point—the similarity of defects and so forth—by saying "that very [thing]" and so on.

Although, in this context, the causes that act as obstacles to unwholesome food ought to be stated because they are the subject at hand, nevertheless, for the sake of consistency in reasoning (*samānanyāyatayā*), those factors that increase the potency of unwholesome food are now discussed.

In this context, "due to the association with place and so forth" means due to association with a compatible place and other factors. For example: rice is unwholesome because it produces *pitta*, yet it becomes even more unwholesome through association with a marshy (*anūpa*) region, whereas in an arid (*dhanva*) region its power is diminished. Likewise, through association with the compatible autumn season it becomes strong, while in winter it is weak. Regarding combination (*saṃyoga*): for instance, that same rice is strong when combined with curd and molasses, but weak when combined with honey and the like. Regarding potency (*vīrya*): that very same substance is strong when made hot, but weak when cold. Furthermore, it is powerful when used in an excessive dose, but weak when used in a deficient dose. These and other such principles are to be followed accordingly.
He states the equality of strength among the *doṣas*: "That very same *doṣa*," and so forth.

"Having a combined origin" (*saṃsṛṣṭayoni*) means that which has many origins (causes) joined together; alternatively, "having a combined origin" means having a corresponding *dūṣya* (vitiated tissue). For example, when *pitta* reaches blood as its *dūṣya*, it becomes difficult to treat and acts rapidly.

An example of contradictory treatment (*viruddhopakrama*) is as follows: Pitta is the initiator of urinary disorders (*prameha*); for it is stated: "All types of *pittameha* are palliative (*yāpya*), because their treatment is contradictory" (Ni. A. 4). Here, the contradiction in treatment consists in this: that which removes pitta, such as sweet substances (*madhurādi*), is contrary to the fat (*medas*)—the primary vitiated element (*dūṣya*) in *prameha*; whereas that which is beneficial for fat, such as pungent substances (*kaṭvādi*), is contrary to pitta. Furthermore, "deep-seated" (*gambhīra*) means having reached the marrow and other internal tissues (*dhātu*); for it is stated: "Superficial (*uttāna*) resides in the skin and flesh, while deep (*gambhīra*) resides within [the deeper tissues]" (Ci. A. 39).
"Long-standing" means that because it has established a deep root through its persistence in the body for a long time, it is difficult to cure.

"Arising from the seats of the vital breaths" refers to that which relies upon the ten seats of the vital breaths— such as the *śaṅkha* and others— to be mentioned in the subsequent chapter (*Sūtra-sthāna*, Chapter 29),
and thus it is a "marmopaghātī," meaning it causes injury to the *marma*s other than those seats of the vital breaths, such as the *kṣipra*, *tala*, and *hṛdaya*.

Since it is already established that [this disease] arises from specific vital points (*marman*) and seats of life (*prāṇāyatana*) by virtue of its very nature as a destroyer of vital points, the mention of those [seats] again is for the purpose of demonstrating specifically their extreme severity.
"Most severe" (*kaṣṭatama*) means being the cause of much suffering and being incurable;
"most rapidly acting" (*kṣiprakāritama*) means being the most swift in producing pathological changes.

By the use of the word "and" (ca), he indicates that due to the small number of causes such as combined origins (*saṃsṛṣṭayoni*), there are distinctions such as being difficult to cure (*kaṣṭa*), more difficult (*kaṣṭatara*), acting quickly (*kṣiprakārin*), or acting even more quickly (*kṣiprakāritara*); it should be understood that when all the aforementioned causes converge, the disease becomes most difficult to cure and acts most rapidly. Furthermore, the degree of difficulty and so forth should be understood according to what is appropriate. A disorder whose treatment is contradictory (*viruddhopakrama*) is indeed difficult to cure but does not act rapidly. He now describes bodies that are incapable of withstanding disease, beginning with the words "And the bodies... (*śarīrāṇi ca*).

Those bodies whose flesh and other tissues are "unfixed" (aniviṣṭāni) are loose; alternatively, "unfixed" means irregularly accumulated or excessively increased. The underlying sense is that a body nourished by unwholesome things inevitably becomes permeated by many morbid humors (doṣas).
"Opposed" (viparītāni) refers to those characterized by the absence of excessive stoutness and so forth.

"Vyādhisahāni" means those which obstruct the production of disease; and this has been presented with reference to the body as an illustration of the opposite case regarding the capacity to withstand disease. Therefore, it should also be understood that the aforementioned opposites of unwholesome diet and strength, as well as the opposites of the strength of the *doṣas*, do not immediately cause disease. Concluding this very point by summarizing the specific characteristics of unwholesome food, the *doṣas*, and the body according to their respective degrees of weakness or strength as causes of mild and other types of diseases, he says: "And from these... and so forth.

The specific characteristics (viśeṣas) are as previously stated and their opposites. In this regard, due to the specific characteristics opposite to those stated, [humors] become mild and slow-acting; however, due to the specific characteristics such as unwholesome diet (apathya) as stated, they should be understood to become severe and quick-acting. In this context, he says "ta eva" etc., in order to demonstrate the diseases that arise when Vāta and the others are aggravated in specific locations such as the Rasa-dhātu and so forth.

In that context, regarding the passage beginning with "tatra rasa... and "prakupitānāṃ doṣāṇām," it is stated without restriction that Vāyu, Pitta, or Kapha—either individually or in combination—when aggravated in the Rasa (nutrient fluid), produce lack of appetite (*aśraddhā*) and other symptoms. Although there is a distinction among the Doshas, because the substratum (the Rasa) here is non-distinct, lack of appetite and the other symptoms arise solely through the influence of that substratum; however, despite the difference between the Doshas, the specific signs of Vāta and the others appear within those very symptoms such as lack of appetite.

Alternatively, it should be understood that wind (vāta) and other factors, acting as the substrata for the tastes according to their respective capacities, produce lack of faith (aśraddhā) and so forth; for heaviness cannot properly occur when the taste is vitiated by wind. However, this [explanation] is not very elegant; therefore, the former position alone is superior. As for the distinction: in the case of lack of faith (aśraddhā), there is indeed the swallowing of food once it has entered the mouth, though there is no desire [to eat]; whereas in the case of aversion (aruci), one does not swallow what has entered the mouth at all.
Distaste of the mouth is a change from the habitual taste of the mouth;
lack of appreciation for flavors is the failure to perceive flavors;
exhaustion is the collapse of the limbs.

Since the occurrence of diseases such as *dadru* is already established by the very mention of *kuṣṭha* among those arising from the vitiation of blood (*raktapradoṣaja*), the repetition of that statement is for the purpose of demonstrating their specific manifestation.
Tilakālakas are marks shaped like sesame seeds; an aśramaṇḍala is a circular red mark.
By the word *kīla*, hemorrhoids (*arśas*) are meant here.

The "condemned" premonitory symptoms of *prameha* refer to conditions such as the mattedness of the hair and so forth, precisely because they are condemned; however, this does not include the bad taste or sweetness of the mouth,

nor indeed the eight condemned factors mentioned in the chapter on the "Condemned" (*Ninditīya*), such as the decline of life-span occurring in those who are excessively obese, since their condemnation is due to their association with that condemned state of extreme obesity.

Thus, in the former explanation, the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "those which and" (*yāni ca*) serves as a restrictive particle (*niyama*), whereas in the latter explanation, it serves as a cumulative particle (*samuccaya*);
by the term "bone and tooth" (*adhyasthi-danta*), both "above the bone" (*adhyasthi*) and "above the tooth" (*adhidanta*) are included.
"Śūla" (piercing pain) should be understood as bone-pain alone;
"rug" (ache) and so forth are to be known as resulting from defects of the marrow.
"Aruṃṣi" means wounds.
"Impotence" (*klaibya*) refers to the non-erection of the penis (*dhvaja-anucchraya*), as well as the inability to engage in sexual intercourse even when the penis is erect (*aharṣaṇa*).

Regarding the statement, "For corrupted semen (*duṣṭa-śukra*) always afflicts a man along with his offspring and his wife," here "affliction of offspring" occurs by producing offspring who are diseased or impotent, while "affliction of the wife" occurs by producing miscarriages and the like.
In the passage beginning with "upaghāta," etc., *upaghāta* means destruction, whereas *upatāpa* refers to some degree of impairment.
In the phrase "from the joints" (*kaṇḍārābhyaḥ*), the ablative case is used in the sense of the locative;
*khallī* is the crushing of the hands and feet,
while *granthi* is simply a knot in the tendons and so forth.
In the passage beginning with "21.

*malānityādi*," it should be understood according to the context that there is "separation, drying, and vitiation. Among these, "separation" (*bheda*) refers to feces; "drying" (*śoṣa*), however, occurs specifically in all the impurities (*mala*); and "vitiation" (*pradūṣaṇa*) is the impairment of their natural color and other qualities through the presence of abnormal color and so forth.

Furthermore, "excessive retention" (*saṅga*) means non-discharge, while "excessive discharge" (*atyutsarga*) means excessive discharge. "Retention" (*saṅga*) is indeed non-occurrence [of discharge], whereas "excessive discharge" (*atyutsarga*) is excessive occurrence.

Showing the defects produced by improper food, he instructs on what ought to be done: "Various... and so forth; the word "stated" is to be supplied [at the end of the verse] as the physician's remedy.

Although it was stated that there are "five procedures" (*pañcakarmāṇi*), the specific mention of "enemas" (*bastayaḥ*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the particular benefit of enemas prepared with bitter substances.

The term "purification" (*śuddhiḥ*) refers to success through emesis and other such measures; its application in certain cases, such as diarrhea and disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī*), has already been mentioned.

Now, since the *rasa* (nutrient fluid) and other elements constitute the peripheral branches (*śākhā*), [the author] explains how the *doṣas* residing in the visceral cavity (*koṣṭha*) move toward the branches: "Through physical exercise," and so forth. Therein, due to the agitation caused by physical exercise, the impurities (*mala*) leave the visceral cavity and go to the branches. Due to the sharpness of the heat of the digestive fire (*ūṣman*), the *doṣas* are liquefied and go to the branches. Through the non-administration of wholesome things, the consumption of unwholesome things, or excessive indulgence, the *doṣa* increases excessively; like an overflowing flood of water, having inundated its own site, it moves to another location—this is logical.

"Because of the swiftness of the wind" means that due to the mobility of the *vāyu*, it moves when propelled by the wind; and the propulsion of one *vāyu* by another *vāyu* is indeed logical. Otherwise, the plural form "malās" would be incorrect. Now, as for what those located in the branches do, he says: "Situated there," etc.;
"they sometimes linger" means that they occasionally cause a delay in the manifestation of the disease.

To the question "Why do they linger?", he says: those defects which were not provoked—that is, those that were weak due to their smallness—become aggravated when provoked by another cause; likewise, those same [defects] become aggravated in a non-conducive place (*anādeśe*), meaning in a place that is unsuitable, and in a non-conducive time (*akāle*), meaning at a time that is unsuitable.
He provides the reason for this very point with the words beginning with "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*).

Since those doshas that require more [time] to await their causes are weak, they depend on factors such as movement (īraṇa); by this it is implied that those which require less time to await their causes do not depend on movement because of their strength, and for this very reason it was said "sometimes" (kadācit).
Now, he states the cause for the doshas' movement from the peripheral branches (śākhā) to the visceral cavity (koṣṭha): "By increase," and so forth.
"Due to oozing" means due to liquefaction; and that which has liquefied moves downward into the visceral cavity precisely because of its fluidity.
"Due to digestion" means that the digested *doṣa* moves to the lower part of the visceral cavity by virtue of being unbound.
"Due to the cleansing of the openings of the channels" means due to the removal of obstructions.
"Due to the suppression of the wind": because of the suppressor's suppression of the wind, it returns to its natural location, the abdominal cavity (33).
Now, he provides a brief aphorism for the remedy against all diseases, beginning with "of those not yet born," and so forth.

If it is asked, "Is it not the case that the entire treatise (*tantra*) prescribes what has been observed [as the path]?"—and if the activity of all living beings is for the sake of happiness, then why does anyone engage in a wrong path? To this he replies with the words beginning "jñāna" (knowledge), etc.:

the meaning is that those who lack discernment engage [in such paths] simply because they think, "This is a means to happiness," due to ignorance alone, and not because they perceive its nature as a producer of suffering.

"Only that which is beneficial" means only that which is pure in its future consequences; "even if it causes pain now, it is only pleasant" means it causes pleasure at present but is contrary to the future.
Worldly people who lack discernment praise the discerning person—beginning with the words "it has been heard," and so forth—because they take refuge in the discerning person;

thus, they come to reside in the discerning person. Alternatively, the deities of the intellect and other faculties take refuge in the discerning person, as it is said: "The deities of knowledge entered [the body]" (Sūtra).
1) "Thus,
rooted in that" means rooted in rajas and tamas.
He explains how diseases rooted in *rajas* and *tamas* arise in one who lacks discernment: "From intellectual error," and so forth.
The meaning is that the pursuit of unwholesome objects and the like produces disease.

Regarding the phrase "in pleasures of the moment" (*tadātvasukheṣu*), the author uses the expression "in those perceived as pleasure" (*sukhasañjñeṣu*) to demonstrate that, although they are pleasant for the time being, such unwholesome things are in reality not even temporary pleasure, because they produce suffering as their consequence. This is as stated in the passage: "Health is what is designated as 'pleasure'" (Sūtra, Chapter 9).
"Known" refers to the investigator (parīkṣaka).
"Not from passion," and so forth.

Even though one knows [something] to be harmful, a certain wicked person engages in it out of passion alone; and another engages in it through ignorance—that is, by failing to recognize its harmful nature—due to the conviction that it is beneficial. Both of these [types of engagement] are prohibited.
(41) To explain how food should be examined, he says: "Of food," and so forth.

In the section on the rules for diet (*āhāra-vidhi*), eight specific factors—beginning with *prakṛti*, *karaṇa*, and *saṃyoga*—are to be explained in the *Rasavimāna* chapter (Vi. A. 1) as being designated as "causes" (*hetu*). To the question of where they are designated as causes, he says: "In the production of the auspicious and inauspicious," and so forth.
It should be understood that these factors, beginning with *prakṛti*, when auspicious produce what is auspicious, and when inauspicious produce what is inauspicious. (42)

One might object: "Even when following a wholesome regimen is being practiced, diseases may still arise due to the force of powerful past unrighteousness (*adharma*); so what is the use of this adherence to a wholesome regimen? To this he says: "Things to be avoided," and so forth. "Having attained freedom from debt" means having reached a state of being free from debt. By this, he demonstrates that through the avoidance of things to be avoided, a person becomes one who is without fault in his human effort (*puruṣakāra*). However, as for a disease that has arrived by fate (*daiva*), virtuous people do not reproach the one who follows a wholesome regimen in that regard. He states this very point with the words beginning "But that which... and so forth.
"It is impossible to avoid" means that it is produced by powerful karma;
"one should not grieve" means that human effort is of no avail against a disease born of destiny (daiva) which is inevitable.
The phrase "the subject matter of the compendium" (*saṅgrahe vastu*) refers to the body;

by means of the passage beginning with "in terms of tolerance and intolerance" (*sahatve cāsahatve ca*) and ending with "the bodies that are excessively large... [and] conversely, those that are tolerant of disease," this section makes known the contents of verses 45–48.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Various Things Eaten and Drunk," in the *Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya* commentary on the intent of Caraka, known as the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta; [this concludes] the section on food and drink within the *Sūtrasthāna*.
[Now begins Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 29 (29 of 120)]

Now, as the two remaining chapters are to be discussed, this chapter is called the "Ten Seats of the Vital Breath" (*daśaprāṇāyatanīya*) because the term "seat of the vital breath" (*prāṇāyatana*) was mentioned in the previous chapter in the phrase "arising from the seat of the vital breath. Alternatively, this "Ten Seats of the Vital Breath" is a summary of the *Sūtrasthāna*, whereas the subsequent chapter is a summary of the entire treatise (*sarvatantrasaṅgraha*); thus it is stated later.
This designation also refers to the meaning rather than merely imitating the word:
they are like "seats" (*āyatana*) because when they are afflicted, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is afflicted, and when they perish, the vital breath perishes—this is the meaning.

The vital breath (*prāṇa*), known as life and consisting of the conjunction of the body, the sense organs, the living being, and the self, does not have the conch-shell and so forth as its primary seats, because it has the entire body and its constituents as its locus.
The "three vital points" (*marmatraya*) are the heart, the bladder, and the head.
The word "those" refers to the conch-shell and other [instruments].

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the intellect (*buddhi*); the self (*ātman*) is the cause of consciousness, because it is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of consciousness. Alternatively, by the word "consciousness" the self is meant, while by the word "cause" the cause that generates diseases—the etiological factor (*nidāna*)—as well as the cause that pacifies them—the therapeutic agent (*bheṣaja*)—is expressed. And by the word "disease" (*āmaya*), the symptom (*liṅga*) is meant.

By this, it is meant that one who knows the internal factors such as the sense organs, as well as the external factors such as causes, signs, and medicines—this much constitutes this treatise: namely, the internal sense organs, as well as the causes, signs, and medicines, which are described in the *Mahācatuṣpāda* as the "Life-Sustainers" (*prāṇābhisara*).

Since all medical treatment depends upon the physician, [the author] demonstrates the summary of the meaning of the Sūtrasthāna through his skill in showing which kind of physician is to be accepted and which is not to be accepted— beginning with the words "of two kinds," etc.—
meaning those who are the bringers of diseases (abhisara) for illnesses.
"Knowledge of practice" means knowing what is to be done at that time;
"knowledge of the production of the body" refers to how the body arises from the union of semen and blood and so forth;
