and "knowledge of primordial matter and its transformations" is that which will be explained in the *Śārīrasthāna* according to the Sāṅkhya system.

Regarding the threefold aphorism of Ayurveda— namely, "knowledge of causes, signs, and medicines" (Sūtra 1)— the summary of the contents of the Sūtrasthāna, from this point up to the end of the section on the definition of the treatise's scope, should be followed in their proper sequence.

Regarding "that which includes the summary and the exposition": the summary is provided in the *Dīrghañjīvitīya* [chapter] by means of the passage beginning with "The general and the particular" (Sūtra 1), and the exposition is provided by the passage beginning with "The general brings about unity" (Sūtra 1).

Regarding "the search for the three [types of objects]": this refers to the ninefold [search] associated with the three types of seeking, beginning with the sūtra statement, “movements are the limbs of the body” (Sūtra 27).

Regarding "the course of nutriment" (*āhāragati*), this refers to the definition of the summary of the treatise (*tantra*) as stated in the passage beginning with "various kinds of food eaten and drunk" (Sūtra 28). In that context, the summary of the treatise is: "eight locations" (Sūtra...).

30) By such statements as these, [the author]—having already explained the definition of the treatise (*tantra*) through the etymological analysis of "life-span" (*āyus*) and "knowledge" (*veda*) which he will describe later—speaks here of skill in place, meaning, and knowledge, and further says "of the treatise," etc.:

retention (*dhāraṇa*) is the recollection at a later time of what has been grasped; discernment (*vijñāna*) is knowledge by way of the meaning; application (*prayoga*) is the application of medical treatment; action (*karman*) is the performance of treatment in its various forms; effect (*kārya*) is the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*); time (*kāla*) is the time for action; the agent (*kartṛ*) here is the physician; and the instrument (*karaṇa*) is the medicine.
"Śāstrayuktiḥ" means the application of the treatise; the genitive case in "yuktijñānasya" (of the knowledge of reasoning) is used in the sense of the instrument due to its skillful employment,
as in "ātmanaḥ" and so forth.

The connection of the text should be understood as follows: they are "skilled" (kuśalāḥ) because, by means of their own qualities of ethical conduct (*śīlaguṇa*) acting as instruments, they have accomplished a mind of loving-kindness (*maitra*) toward all living beings—regarding them like mothers, fathers, and kinsmen—and because they are non-deceptive.
A "practitioner in the guise of a physician" (*bhiṣakchadmacara*) is one who has assumed the dress of a physician for the purpose of deception.
One who acts in a counterfeit manner or otherwise, being a doer of harm, is called so in the world due to the negligence of kings; for those quack physicians ought to be punished by the king.
"Viśikhā" refers to a carriage road, or alternatively, the path of action (*karmamārga*).
"And in his hearing" means in a place suitable for the sick person to hear;
"gone to the end" refers to one who is about to die; "pretext" is a disguise.

"Like the unwholesome" means: just as those who are unwholesome describe their own skillfulness while being mutually contradictory; "like the undeliberate" means: being of loud voice, they are known as "consumed."
I ask about the *anuyoga* (8–9);
a bird-cage is the binding of birds.
*Śruta* (hearing) refers to listening to the treatise; *dṛṣṭa* (seeing) refers to observing clinical procedures;
*kriyā* (action) refers to the knowledge of medical treatment; *jñāna* (knowledge) is that which is produced by the treatise, whereas *śruta* is merely the act of hearing.
With the words "To them, let there be eternal homage," he praises the one who rescues life (Prāṇābhisara).

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Ten Abodes of Life" (*Daśaprāṇāyatanīya*), in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Section on General Principles (*Sūtrasthāna*).
29. [Sūtrasthāna,
Chapter 30 (30 of 120)] Alternatively, having explained the Sūtrasthāna by way of elimination, the Daśamahāmūlīya chapter is now spoken in order to state the compendium of the treatise.
Here, while the rule *adhikṛtya kṛte granthe* (Pāṇini 4.3.87) is being carried over, [the sūtra] *adhyāyānuvākayor luk ca* (Pāṇini 4.3.69) applies.
By [Pāṇini 7.1.29], *ccha* is substituted [for *ch*].
"In the *artha*" means in the heart; "having great roots" refers to those vessels whose root is the great heart; "well-attached" means they are supported by it.

He states synonyms for that heart: "great," and so forth. These designations—such as "Great" (*mahat*) and "Meaning" (*artha*)—are established in medical practice, but are not found everywhere in other treatises.

Regarding the greatness of the heart and its status as the primary object of pursuit (*artha*), he states its preeminence (*abhyarhitatva*) because of its being most worthy of honor: "having six limbs," and so forth. That which has six limbs—namely, the two arms, the two shanks, the head, and the trunk—is the "six-limbed body" (*ṣaḍaṅga-aṅga*).

Furthermore, since "limb" (*aṅga*) must be stated as being something distinct from the six limbs—either as a collective whole or as a composite entity—the qualification "of the six limbs" is intended to demonstrate that even those six limbs are themselves supported by the heart. Alternatively, it serves to preclude the sense of "limb" as a mere physical part.

As for consciousness (*vijñāna*), although it is already understood as a quality of the self from the statement "and the self with its qualities," it is mentioned separately again because of its preeminence among the qualities of the self; for there is the scriptural passage: "Bliss, in its entirety, and consciousness are established in the organ of evacuation."
The sense faculties are the five beginning with the eye; the five objects are sound and so forth;
by the phrase "along with their qualities" (saguṇa), the inclusion of pleasure and the other [feeling-tones] is intended.

"Cetaḥ" (consciousness), "manaḥ" (mind), "cintyam" (the object of thought), and "manoviṣayaḥ" (the domain of the mind)—these, along with the sixfold consciousness and so forth, are each recited individually as things to be adopted. Therefore, it should not be raised here that the inclusion of any one of them is redundant because its meaning is already obtained [by implication]; for a meaning obtained by implication is secondary because it is not explicitly stated.
3–4 Now, one might raise this objection: how can these six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and so forth have the heart as their locus? For it will be stated that "the heart is two finger-breadths [in size]" (VI.

8), and yet a limb is something large that rests upon the six limbs; the sense organs also reside in their own respective loci such as the eyes; objects rest upon external substances; the Self is pervasive and indeed without a locus; its quality, consciousness (*vijñāna*), rests in the Self alone; the mind (*manas*) is also without a locus, being situated within the Self; and the object of thought, such as that which is to be meditated upon, is not in the heart. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The foundation," and so forth.

The "establishment" (pratiṣṭhā) of these entities— the six limbs and so forth— is their abiding without contradiction to their functions; this is intended as the "heart," with the word "cause" (kāraṇa) understood as the remainder of the sense.
Regarding this very point, he provides an illustration beginning with "of the rafters" (*gopānasīnām*), and so forth.
"Rafters" (*gopānasyaḥ*) are the wooden beams that support the roof-covering of a house;
"ridge-poles" (*āgārakarṇikā*) are the wooden ties for the roof-covering located in the middle of the house's roof, which in common parlance are called "āḍakas."

"By those who contemplate the meaning" means by those who contemplate the heart (*hṛdaya*). By this, it is shown that the dependence of the six ancillaries (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and so forth upon the heart is not by way of a relationship between container and contained (*ādhārādheyabhāva*), but rather by way of following its positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*).

"Dependence upon the heart" means that when the heart remains in its natural state, the states of the six ancillaries and so forth remain in their natural state; and when the heart is afflicted, they are afflicted—this is the meaning.

And although it might be possible to assert, through a forced construction, that the self (*ātman*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the mind (*manas*) reside in the heart due to a relationship of container and contained (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*), nevertheless, because [the self] is all-pervasive, such a state of being container and contained should not be accepted.

This is not so; for here the "self" intended is the transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*) as the locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*). And it is established by experience that this very being perceives pleasure, pain, and so forth only in the region of the heart; therefore, the self is as if residing in the heart.

Likewise, the mind also generally abides in the heart alone; for when the mind has ceased its activity, it abides in the heart, and likewise, during meditation and yoga, the mind remains situated in the heart.
As for what was said—"when the mind is steady and established in the Self" (Śā. 1)—that "establishment in the Self" of the mind is indeed its establishment in the heart.

In this way, knowledge, pleasure, and pain are perceived as residing solely in the heart; for it is through excessive reflection or through the onset of suffering that the heart alone is afflicted, and no other limb. Let it be so. Having explained this relationship of locus and occupant (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*), which is not overly restrictive, he states that when the heart itself is impaired, there is an impairment of the six limbs and so forth: "From its impairment," and so on.
"Of that" means of the heart;
"affliction" (upaghāta) refers to some slight injury,
whereas "from breaking" (bhedāt) refers to a great affliction.
And death is the destruction of the entire foundation of all things, such as the six limbs and so forth, as previously described; this is the intended meaning.
To explain how this occurs, he says: "That by which... and so forth.

*Sparśavijñāna* means that by which touch (*sparśa*) is cognized, or that which cognizes touch; its specific qualification is "the sustainer" (*dhārī*). The sustainer, however, is the conjunction of the body, the senses, the vital principle (*sattva*), and the self (*ātman*). As it has been stated: "The conjunction of the body, the senses, the vital principle, and the self is the sustainer, [which is] life" (Sūtra 1). By this, that conjunction of the body and so forth which, through the sense of touch, cognizes all objects of knowledge—and which is called the "sustainer" because it sustains the body—is situated in the heart.
Therefore, it is logical that fainting results from the impairment of that [contact], and death results from its destruction, characterized by the non-continuation of consciousness.

For contact is of two kinds: sensory and mental; without these two types of contact, no cognition whatsoever occurs. As it has been said: "That which is sensory contact and that which is mental contact—these two are the instigators of the experiences of pleasure and pain" (Śārīra-sthāna).
1) Thus, we shall demonstrate the mental and physical contact according to their respective locations.

However, according to the etymological interpretation (*nirukti*) that "contact is that which is cognized," the word *sparśa* (contact) is intended here in a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) to mean the object being touched; by this, all objects of knowledge are included. It is that very object which the sense organs reach before they manifest the object through contact, as it has been said: "One who does not grasp [the object] is not touched, nor does one who is untouched perceive sensations" (*Śārīrasthāna*).

1) Thus, although the conjunction of the body, the sense organs, the vital breath (*sattva*), and the self exists even in other regions of the body, it is nevertheless not the primary factor in the maintenance of the body or in the production of cognition, because both the maintenance of the body and cognition are observed even when that [other-region] is impaired. However, the conjunction located in the heart is the primary factor, because the tactile cognition and the maintenance of the body conform to its presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Therefore, it is well said: "That is dependent upon that. Regarding the heart's state of being highly esteemed (*abhyarhitatva*), he states another property: "That belongs to the Supreme," and so forth.

By this, he demonstrates the two kinds of *ojas* belonging to the supreme [being]: the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*). Among these, the lower is the quantity measured by a handful (*añjali*), as it has been stated: "The measure of *ojas* associated with *kapha* (*ślaiṣmika*) is exactly that much" (Śārīra Sthāna 7). However, the higher is of small dimension, with reference to which it was said: "That which is pure, slightly reddish-yellow, and resides in the heart" (Sūtra Sthāna).

17) Thus it is said in another tantra: "The eight drops of *ojas*, which reside in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), are supported by the heart. Furthermore, the qualification "of the higher" (*parasya*) becomes meaningful only when there is both a higher and a lower *ojas*; it would not be so if *ojas* were of a single nature, for in that case, the channels alone would be the location of the *ojas* measured at half-an-añjali, residing within the heart.

Likewise, in *prameha*, only half an *añjali* of *ojas* is depleted, not eight drops; for even with the depletion of a mere fraction [of eight drops], death occurs. In *prameha*, however, one continues to live even when there is a depletion of *ojas*. Furthermore, the symptoms of the depletion of *ojas* should be understood as occurring specifically upon the depletion of half an *añjali* of *ojas*. Although the term *ojas* also applies to *rasa*, as it is said: "And *rasa* is reckoned as *ojas*" (*Nidāna* 4), and likewise: "That which becomes impure is mostly converted into *ojas*" (*Cikitsāsthāna*).
8) Thus it is said; nevertheless, here "ojas" (vital essence) is designated as the quintessence of all the *dhātus* (tissues).

Regarding this *ojas*, some say it is a form of *upadhātu* (secondary tissue). For a *dhātu* exists by virtue of its capacity for supporting (*dhāraṇa*) and nourishing (*poṣaṇa*), whereas *ojas*, although it supports the body, does not nourish it; therefore, some do not consider *ojas* to be the eighth *dhātu*.
Others, however, say that *ojas* is a specific form of semen (*śukra-viśeṣa*), yet that [semen] does not delight the mind.

However, those who maintain that *ojas* is the collection of the essence (*sāra*) of all the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) hold the view that, because it consists of the essences of *rasa* and the other constituents, *ojas* is non-different from *rasa* and the rest, and thus should not be designated as a separate *dhātu* or even as a secondary constituent (*upadhātu*). Their statement is as follows: “Just as honey is collected by bees from fruits and flowers, so too is *ojas* gathered from the bodies of men by means of the [bodily] qualities” (Sūtra 17). Here, “from the bodies” (*śarīrebhyaḥ*) refers to the *dhātus*, and “by means of the qualities” (*guṇaiḥ*) refers to the essential portions (*sārabhāga*).

Regarding the phrase "the collection of consciousness therein": therein, in the heart, the self performs the gathering of consciousness that has spread toward its own objects. By means of that, having restrained the mind that had spread out within the heart, one becomes a knower of yoga; this is what is meant by "the self. Furthermore, since yoga is to be adopted as a means for liberation, the heart alone is its location; therefore, the heart is most venerable. Because the heart possesses such qualities, it is called "great" (*mahat*) and likewise "the object" (*artha*) by physicians. 6–7.
Now he establishes that the vessels (dhamanīs) have their great root [in the heart]: "By that," and so forth.
"By that" means by the great heart; the word "connected" (yuktāḥ) is to be supplied as the ellipsis;
they are "pierced through" (vidhamyante), meaning they spread out.
Now, explaining the great fruitfulness of the vessels (*dhamanī*) that has been mentioned, he says: "By which *ojas*, etc.
By the phrase "by which *ojas*," both types of *ojas*—the general and the specific—are to be understood.
They cause to turn, they live; and regarding "they cause to turn," the causative suffix *ṇic* belongs to the *curādi* class.
"Satisfied" means gratified.

That which is the essence at the beginning of the embryo—that essence which exists at the mere moment of the conjunction of semen and blood when presided over by the living principle (*jīva*)—in that [essence] it also abides.

"That which is called 'rasa' from *garbharasa*"—meaning from the *garbharasa* in the form of the *kalala*, which results from the transformation of the union of semen and blood; "rasa" meaning that which has become the essence (*sāra*).

As it is evolving, it enters the heart. The phrase "which previously" means that at the very moment the heart is being formed, it presides over the heart as soon as its characteristics become manifest. This is the meaning.

By this, it is stated that *ojas* persists even during the three stages of fetal development: first, in the form of the essence of semen and blood (*śukra-śoṇita-sāra*); then, in the stage of the embryo (*kalala*), in the form of the essence of nutrient-fluid (*rasa-sāra*); and finally, upon the formation of limbs, it exists as endowed with its own specific characteristics. Thus, the greatness of *ojas* is described by its pervasion of all stages, for death occurs through its destruction even when other bodily constituents (*dhātu*) have not yet failed.
It is called "the sustainer" (*dhārī*) because it is primary among those things connected to the maintenance of life.

"Body-essence-oil" (*śarīrarasasneha*) means the essence of the essences of the body; both the word *rasa* and the word *sneha* denote "essence. Therefore, the meaning is that it is the essence even of the bodily fluids (*rasa*), namely the tissues (*dhātu*).
This is stated by way of another method as a description of its many esteemed functions, for the purpose of making known the preeminence of *ojas*.
"Having *ojas* as their fruit" (*tatphalāḥ*) means having *ojas* as their result, that is to say, they are the carriers of *ojas* (*ojovahāḥ*).

By this, it is stated that because they possess the aforementioned qualities, their vigor (*ojas*) is great; and because the fruits [of these qualities] seem to ripen through the carrying of this [vigor], the vessels (*dhamanīs*) are called "great-fruited" (*mahāphalā*).

He states a second etymological derivation: "or they bear fruit in many ways. This means that those ten vessels situated in the heart "bear fruit" in many ways—that is, in numerous modes—they come into being. By this, it is stated that while existing as ten forms at the root in the heart, they become of great number in the body due to the differentiation of their branches.
He states the etymological derivation of the term *dhamanī* and so forth: "from *dhmāna*" and so on; the meaning is "from filling (*pūraṇa*) with external [substances] such as rasa."
"Because of flowing" means because the very thing to be nourished, such as the nutrient fluid (rasa), flows— that is, moves— away from its place to another location. 12
Now he states the reason for protecting the mind residing within the heart: "That great [place]," and so forth.
"That great" refers to the heart, which is the locus of the six limbs and other parts;
"those with great roots" refers to the vessels (dhamanīs) that carry the vital essence (ojas).
And that is vigor (*ojas*), by which vigor and so forth the aforementioned quality is expressed;
tranquility (*praśama*) is peace;
knowledge (*jñāna*) is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).

By way of introducing the subject to be practiced, he also mentions the supreme practices such as the strengthening of the vital breath (*prāṇavardhana*) and non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), beginning with the words "Now, indeed" (*atha khalu*).
The term "one" (*ekam*) means "only one," implying that there is no second [practice] that is more supreme.

Regarding the phrase "of the paths" (*ayanānām*), although food increases the vital breath (*prāṇa*), non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) alone is superior; for since dharma is produced through non-violence, that which is accomplished by it becomes unshakable. Although meat is primarily nourishing, it nevertheless nourishes the body alone; knowledge (*vidyā*), however, excels as it nourishes both body and mind.

In connection with the hearing of Āyurveda, he states the section defining both *āyus* (life) and *āyurveda* (the science of life) by means of their etymological explanations (*nirukti*), beginning with the words "tatra" and so forth;
he himself will explain this phrase by phrase later on.
"Ārṣa" refers to a treatise or scripture composed by a seer (ṛṣi),
being recited according to tradition— that is, being recited according to the sequence of the textual reading.

The example (*udāharaṇa*) is the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*). The application (*upanaya*) is the restatement of the probative property (*sādhanadharma*), which has been established by the thesis (*siddhānta*), with respect to the subject (*sādhya*), such as: "And so, this [subject] possesses smoke. The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the statement of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) as established by the reason (*hetu*), such as: "Therefore, it possesses fire. Regarding the phrase "of those fixed in the system" (*tantraniyatānām*), it means "of those contained within the system"; it is stated by means of "elucidations" (*vibhāvana*), that is, by means of explanations (*vyākhyāna*); the word "stated" (*ukta*) is used here in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve ktaḥ*).

An example of this is as follows: in the passage, “That bodily movement which is intended for stability and increases strength” (Sūtra 7), only the phrase “the movement which is desired” (*iṣṭā yā ceṣṭā*) is stated; by this, the analysis of the second word *ceṣṭā*—which is difficult [to interpret]—is effectively accomplished. 16–19.
Now, since those who know Āyurveda must be determined by means of questions alone, he states the questions beginning with "tatra cet" (if there...), the remainder being:
"Which Veda do they teach?"—namely, "Āyurveda.

In the Atharvaveda, *bhakti* means service; by this, it is stated that the Atharvaveda possesses the nature of Āyurveda because it is to be served by physicians. He states the reason for the non-difference between Āyurveda and the Atharvaveda with the words "For the Veda... and so forth;
by this, it is stated that because they share a single purpose, Āyurveda is indeed a single part of the Atharvaveda.
He says—"and having taught the Veda," and so forth—in order to show that after the sequence of questions has established the Veda, it is life itself that must be established.

"Continuity of consciousness" (*cetanānuvṛtti*) refers to the stream of sentience; this should be understood as lasting from conception until death, because beyond that there is no continuity of consciousness. The sense is that its non-continuation is due precisely to its not being perceived directly [after death].

Nor should it be said that there is an interruption of consciousness for one who is fast asleep; for even in that state, because we observe the retrospective recognition at a later time—“I slept happily”—subtle cognition certainly exists.

Although in the *Dīrghajīvitīya* [chapter] it was stated that life (*āyus*) is the conjunction of the body and so forth, nevertheless, because it is the effect of that [conjunction], the persistence of consciousness here is called "life" by intending to express the non-difference between cause and effect.
The terms *anubandha* and *dhārī* were explained in the first chapter.
What is the reason for [it being called] Āyurveda? The answer to this is: "It reveals (vedayati) or makes known (bodhayati) that life-span (āyuḥ)," and so forth.

However, those meanings such as "acquisition" (*lābha*) and others that are explained here in other treatises (*tantrāntara*) are not directly produced by that [etymology], and thus they are not mentioned here in their specific definitions (*svalakṣaṇataḥ*). He himself will provide examples later, starting with the words "longevity" (*āyuṣya*) and "non-longevity" (*anāyuṣya*). Since "longevity" (*āyus*) should be expressed by the word *āyus* because it is the cause of life, the etymological derivation "Āyurveda" is figurative (*gauṇī*) in the view that it means "the knowledge of longevity and non-longevity. For this very reason, the word "also" (*api*) is used here: "Therefore, it is also called Āyurveda."

Furthermore, even that which is known as *anāyuṣya* (non-life-prolonging) becomes a cause of life when it is not practiced as something to be avoided; therefore, although it is *anāyuṣya*, it is denoted by the word "life" (*āyuḥ*) because it serves as a cause of life—there is no fault here.
This is established in this very context by the passage beginning with: "In that regard, life is the persistence of consciousness," and so forth.

In that context, by the words "bodily" (*śārīra*) and so forth, [the author] expresses happiness and longevity as the result of human effort (*pauruṣa*). The word "strength" (*bala*) refers to superior action (*karma*) through the faculties of knowledge (*jñāna*), discernment (*vijñāna*), and the senses (*indriya*); and the word "collection" (*samudaya*) is connected with the objects of the senses (*indriyārtha*). Alternatively, the word "collection" (*samudaya*) is connected with all [the factors] beginning with knowledge; or rather, it should be construed with all [the factors] beginning with knowledge as "the collection of strength" (*balasamudaya*), where "the collection of strength" means the gathering together of strength.
He whose supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) is supreme—that is, excessive—is "one of supreme power" (*paramarddhi*).
He whose all undertakings are prosperous—that is, accomplished and brought to completion—is likewise [described].
The connection is with the phrase "of beings who desire his welfare" (*hitaiṣiṇo bhūtānām*).
"Devoted to that" means devoted to the inner self (*adhyātma*); "the inner self" refers to the true nature of the self and so forth, as well as this world and the next.

By "characteristics of morbid transformation" (*vikṛtilakṣaṇaiḥ*) is meant characteristics that have the form of a morbid change. Their further qualification is "without cause" (*animittaiḥ*), which means they are *ariṣṭas* (signs of approaching death). For a morbid change in objects or the sense organs that occurs without a [discernible] cause is indeed an *ariṣṭa*.
In this regard, a morbid change in the object (*artha-vikṛti*) is, for example: "He whose breath smells like various flowers day and night," and so forth (Iṃ.
2); a morbid change in the sense organ (*indriya-vikṛti*) is, for example: "And he who sees things that are invisible," and so forth (Iṃ. 2).

4) And so forth; an alteration of the mind (*manovikṛti*) is as follows: "One should predict death for one who, being exhausted, seeks delight with those very same objects through which he formerly experienced supreme pleasure" (*Indriyasthāna* 8). An alteration of the intellect (*buddhivikṛti*) is as follows: "Intellect and strength are without cause," and so forth. An alteration of movement (*ceṣṭāvikṛti*) is as follows: "He who runs about with his shoulders drooping, as if dragging his feet," and so forth (*Indriyasthāna* 12).
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), attendants, deformities, and so forth are to be understood.
Furthermore, in this context of fatal signs (*riṣṭa*), the statement regarding the duration from a moment up to a year is because death resulting from a fatal sign does not occur after that year;
therefore, anything contrary to this is invalid. Thus, the meaning is that in the section on fatal signs, a lifespan free from fatal signs is not a certain measure.
Furthermore, he speaks of the knowledge of the measure of lifespan, beginning with "the nature of the body" (*dehaprakṛti*), and so forth.

"Body, nature, and characteristics" refers to *dehaprakṛtilakṣaṇa*. Regarding that, the measure of lifespan with respect to the body is as follows, starting from "endowed with all essential constituents" (*sarvaiḥ sārair upetāḥ*) up to "they become long-lived" (*cirajīvinaś ca bhavanti*). (Vi.)
8) Thus; by way of nature (*prakṛti*), as it is said: “Those with a predominance of phlegm (*śleṣman*) are strong, wealthy, learned, vigorous, peaceful, and long-lived” (Vi.
8); by way of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), as it is said: “In this regard, these are the characteristics of the long-lived princes” (Śā.
8), and so forth.

Alternatively, the innate characteristic of the body (*dehasya sahajalakṣaṇa*) refers to the characteristic of the body's fundamental nature (*dehaprakṛtilakṣaṇa*); all of that, including the characteristics of its essential nature (*sāraprakṛti*) and so forth, is to be understood [as such].
The three reasons for this are stated as "because it is beginningless" (*anāditvāt*) and so on. (Verses 25–26)
The explanation of the first [point] begins with "na hi" and so forth.

Here, what is to be established is the permanence of medical practice (*vyavahāra-nityatva*) within Āyurveda, and that pertains to the *Āyurveda* as the meaning (*artha-rūpa*), not to the *Āyurveda* as the verbal expression (*śabda-rūpa*). Alternatively, the permanence of the *Āyurveda*—which expresses the meaning of the eternally current medical practice—is established through its connection to a traditional lineage (*pāramparya-yoga*).
In this regard, first, there is the permanence of "life" (*āyus*), which is the subject matter expounded by the *Āyurveda*.

For it is not the case that the continuum of life (*āyuḥ-santāna*) has never existed; rather, by the principle of successive continua, life always exists because there is no interruption of living beings endowed with life. The construction is as follows: "the continuum of cognition (*buddhi-santāna*) likewise has never not existed. By this, the perception of that [object] through its continuum is also eternal, just like the eternal life.
By the statement "and the lifespan is to be known as eternal," the eternity of the knowers of Āyurveda is expressed.
Through this, the eternity of Āyurveda is established because the object of knowledge (vedya), the means of knowing (vedana), and the knower (veditr) are beginningless.

Furthermore, the subject matter of Āyurveda is not merely the nature of life itself; rather, it is life as affected by disease and so forth. To this effect, he says: "And [it is] beginningless," and so on.
Regarding "pleasure and pain": health is pleasure, and disease is pain. "Characterized by the cause of substantiality" means having the characteristics of a cause for treatment.

Since the cause of disease has already been stated by means of the term "substance" (*dravya*), the word "cause" (*hetu*) here refers to the cause of pacification. Some, however, read it as “*sahetulakṣaṇam*”; even there, by the word "cause," both the producer and the pacifier of the disease-cause must be expressed. Alternatively, it should be understood that the medicine is the cause of happiness and the etiology (*nidāna*) is the cause of suffering, while the "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) pertains to both disease and health. By this it is meant that suffering is never something not to be abandoned, yet that which is to be abandoned cannot be abandoned without a means; and the means is indeed Ayurveda, which is to be adopted for the sake of removing all suffering. Therefore, the sense is that Ayurveda, in the form of instruction on the means for pacifying suffering, is beginningless.
In this way, it should be understood that happiness, which is to be eternally pursued, is beginningless, as is its means, Ayurveda.
To explain how pleasure and pain are beginningless, he says: "due to the connection of one after another"; the meaning is "through the continuum" (*saṃtāna*).
He states the second reason—that it possesses a characteristic established by its own nature—beginning with "and thus," and so forth.

"Eṣa" (this) refers to life-span, intellect, the knower, pleasure, pain, and the summary of objects; that is, the summary of the subject matter. By this, he shows that life-span and the rest are what are to be expounded by Āyurveda.
Furthermore, "this life-span and so forth is the definition of Āyurveda here" means that it is analyzed—that is, it is known.

Āyurveda is defined by its subject matter, namely life-span (*āyus*) and so forth; for the statement—"the beneficial and the harmful, happiness and suffering" (Suśruta Sūtra 1)—is the definition of Āyurveda.

By this, the fact that the definition of Āyurveda, which consists of the objects such as life-span and the rest, is established by its own nature through its beginninglessness, as previously stated, is explained.
"Established by its own nature" (svabhāvasaṃsiddha) is intended to mean established at all times through the principle of continuity;
thus he explains the third reason, "because the nature of things is eternal": "heavy," and so forth.
For substances such as heavy, light, smooth, rough, cold, hot, and so on, there occurs an increase and decrease respectively according to their general and particular [qualities].
He explains that very point previously stated with the passage beginning with "by the heavy" and ending with "so it is for the others.

Regarding the phrase "so it is for the others," it should be understood as follows: through the practice of light [qualities], there is an increase of the light and a decrease of the heavy, and so forth.

"This" refers to such a manner. "The nature of existence (*bhāvasvabhāva*) is eternal" means that this nature of existence, characterized by increase and decrease through generalities and particulars, never becomes otherwise.
Not only is this intrinsic nature (*bhāvasvabhāva*) eternal, but so too is another; thus he says: "And the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)," and so forth.
Regarding how the specific characteristic of earth and the other elements—such as solidity and fluidity—is eternal, he says: "But they exist," and so forth.

Since substances (*dravya*) exist at all times and qualities (*guṇa*) are eternally present—by the use of "and" (*ca*), it is implied that substances are also non-eternal therein; for instance, substances such as space (*ākāśa*) are eternal, while effects such as earth are non-eternal. Likewise, qualities such as the dimension of space are eternal, whereas qualities of effects such as taste (*rasa*) are non-eternal. Furthermore, even though they are non-eternal, they persist at all times through the principle of a continuous succession of similar moments (*sajātīyāparāparasamtāna*). Thus, the sense is that it is logical for even non-eternal things to possess the eternity of their continuum (*santānanityatva*).

In this context, it should be understood that by means of the reason—the permanence of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities—it is stated that because the intrinsic nature of an entity which produces disease, as well as that which pacifies disease, is permanent, Āyurveda, which teaches that [nature], is also permanent. Now, one might ask: "Since the origin of Āyurveda is heard of here and there, how can it be permanent? To this he says: "For [there is] no... and so forth; "arising after not having existed" (*abhūtvotpatti*) means the arising of what was previously non-existent.

"Except through realization and instruction" means that wherever the origin of Āyurveda is described, it occurs there either through realization or through instruction. Origin through realization is, for example, the origin of Āyurveda from Brahmā; origin through instruction is, for example, the production of Āyurveda in the mortal world by Bharadvāja through the instruction of Indra, and so forth.
These two are "realization and instruction."

Now, regarding the reason stated as "because its characteristic is established by its own nature" (*svabhāvasaṃsiddhalakṣaṇatvāt*), one might argue that a characteristic can be both inherent (*svābhāvika*) and impermanent, just as the shape of a conch-like neck and so forth is inherent to a jar yet does not prove the jar's permanence. To this, he says: "And inherent," etc.
"Uncreated" (*akṛtaka*) means not made by us or others;

as was stated here [in the first chapter], in the *Dīrghañjīvitīya* section: "Beneficial and non-beneficial, pleasure and pain" (*hitāhitaṃ sukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ*), beginning with the passage: "By way of their own characteristics, by way of pleasure and pain," and so forth.

1) With the words beginning "Just as heat belongs to fire," etc., he provides an example here for the very point of being uncreated (*akṛtaka*). The intended meaning is that because the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is uncreated and thus eternal in its conventional usage (*vyavahāra-nityatva*), the Ayurveda which explains it is likewise eternal in its conventional usage.

Not only is the intrinsic characteristic (*svābhāvika-lakṣaṇa*) uncreated, but even the permanence of the intrinsic nature of entities (*bhāvasvabhāvanityatva*) is not created by anyone, such as Īśvara or others. Thus he says: "And even the permanence of the intrinsic nature of entities... By the word "and" (*ca*), he draws in [the term] "uncreated. He demonstrates that very permanence of the intrinsic nature of entities with the words "as has been stated," and so forth. The meaning is that even the intrinsic nature of entities—which brings about increase and decrease produced by universals and particulars—is not created by anyone; therefore, Ayurveda is also eternal.
Now, the answer to the question beginning with "And what are they? is as follows: "Of that," etc.; the medical treatment of the internal fire of the body is *kāyacikitsā* (internal medicine).

Śālākya is the primary branch [of medicine] concerning the piercing of cataracts and the application of probes; *gara* is poison that becomes active after a lapse of time; *vairodhika* is that which is incompatible due to its combination;
and *bhūtavidyā* is the knowledge for the purpose of discerning and pacifying malevolent spirits such as *rākṣasas*.
The term *kaumārabhṛtya* refers to that which is performed for the nourishment of a youth;
it is so called because it was established by the *rājanyas* (members of the royal class) for the purpose of protection, since protecting is the duty of a *kṣatriya*.
"He contemplates" means he reflects with the mind;
"he experiences" means he makes it known to another;
"he conforms" means he carries it out through the body in accordance with that [contemplation].

"Protection" means the protection of oneself and others, namely those dependent on one such as servants and so forth; "the very acquisition of the learned" means fame arising from being accepted by the learned.
Regarding "of desired things," this refers to women and so forth.
[The author] states the method of inquiry for the purpose of examining the physician, beginning with the words "Now," and so on.

Regarding the passage beginning with "tatra" and ending with "svalakṣaṇaiḥ": [the term] *āyurveda* means that which describes life (*āyus*), and so forth; by this, the meaning is that [it describes life] in the form of what is beneficial, what is harmful, and life itself.
"By means of the sections" (prakaraṇaiḥ) refers to the divisions of Āyurveda;
there are ten sections, which are ten categories, and these are the ten [topics] beginning with the body (śarīra).

In this context, the body (*śarīra*) consists of the collection of transformations of the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) and is of many types due to the distinctions of its parts and so forth. Sustenance (*vṛtti*) is food (*āhāra*), distinguished by categories such as what is eaten and what is drunk. The cause (*hetu*), however, is characterized by unwholesome contact with the senses and their objects, intellectual error (*prajñāparādha*), and the effects of time (*pariṇāma*), which are the causes of disease. Disease (*vyādhi*) takes the form of the imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). Treatment (*karma*) is medical therapy (*cikitsā*). The effect (*kārya*) is health (*ārogya*). Time (*kāla*) refers to the seasons and so forth, as well as the timing of actions. The agent (*kartṛ*) is the physician (*bhiṣaj*). The instrument (*karaṇa*) is the medicine (*bheṣaja*). The method (*vidhi*) is the procedure (*vidhāna*) or preparation (*upakalpanā*); it should be understood as being dependent on time, disease, and substance, as for example: "For one who practices drinking warm water during the winter, life is not diminished" (Sūtra).

6) and so forth; here, however, the unwholesome site (*deśa*) is included by the mention of the cause (*hetu*), whereas the wholesome site should be understood as being included by the mention of the instrument (*karaṇa*).

Furthermore, the many distinctions regarding the functioning of the body and so forth should be understood by an intelligent person through the entire treatise alone—that is, by means of the complete [work].

Regarding "of this tantra" (tantrasyāsya) and so forth: the word "location" (sthāna) is to be understood as the ellipsis for both "of the sense organs" (indriyāṇām) and "of the treatments" (cikitsitānām).
The thirty-three [chapters] consist of the Sūtrasthāna and the Cikitsita; the Śārīrasthāna is designated as "the basis" (āśraya), for the body is indeed called the basis.

Regarding the term *saviṃśam*: from the word *viṃśati*, the suffix *ḍa* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). Since this suffix *ḍa* is one that denotes the same meaning as its base, the usage *caturviṃśādhikam* (exceeding twenty-four) is established in the Laliteśvara [Tantra]. For the statement indeed says: "The three hundred worlds are to be known as exceeding twenty-four.
In the same way, the term *saviṃśam* (twenty plus) in the Suśruta [Saṃhitā] (Sūtrasthāna, chapter 1) should also be explained accordingly.
The designations such as "long-lived" (dīrghāyu) and so forth should be understood as indicating only a part [of the whole], in accordance with the requirements of the verse;
in the passage beginning with "the meanings of breath and body," the word "body" (deha) denotes *ojas*.

In the phrase "the head is auspicious" (*śiraḥ śubham*), the word *śiras* means "like a head"; in such cases as "the meaning of the verse is the head" (*ślokārthaḥ śiraḥ*), it signifies "a summary. By the inclusion of the word "and" (*ca*) [in the definition], the suturing and other procedures mentioned by Suśruta are also included. Thus: "Because of its threading (*sūtraṇa*), because of its indication (*sūcana*), and because of its retention of the continuous flow of meanings (*arthasantati*), it is designated as the Sūtrasthāna" (Suśruta).
By this, it is also understood that these [senses] have measurement as their purpose, meaning they have cognition as their purpose.

Regarding the phrase "of the sense organs" (*indriyāṇām*), this refers to two sets of four: one is the fourfold section on rejuvenation (*rasāyana*) and the other is the fourfold section on aphrodisiacs (*vājīkaraṇa*). Thus, it is entirely appropriate that this constitutes a chapter (*adhyāya*) consisting of four parts (*catuṣpāda*);
furthermore, the treatise (*tantra*) is completed within these [sections], meaning that when these are finished, the treatise is completed.

The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "the meaning of the chapter" (*adhyāyārthaḥ*) is placed out of its logical order; by it, it is indicated that the summary of the meaning of the chapter is made at the end of the chapter, and likewise the summary of the meaning of the section (*sthāna*) is made at the end of the section. Although the meaning of the section is not explicitly stated in the *Śārīra-sthāna*, it should nevertheless be understood through the etymological derivation of the word *śārīra* or from other medical treatises (*tantra*), as follows: "Because the entire body is considered in its divine and human perfections along with all its constituent states, therefore this section is called *Śārīra*. (Śārīra-sthāna)
8) Thus,

regarding the phrase "the question according to the rule" [in verse 36–68], the term "according to the rule" (*vidhinā*) refers to a statement that is free from defects such as contradictions between earlier and later parts.

"Because of *tantraṇa*" means because of the sustaining of the body; alternatively, it means because of the preservation of Āyurveda, or "by the establishment of the purpose," meaning by the persistence of the primary purpose. These are names based on both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*); therefore, one should not allege an over-extension of the term (*atiprasaṅga*).
"Adhikṛtya" means having made the subject (adhikārin) the point of reference.
"Artha" refers to the purpose, such as long life and so forth.

"Adhyāya-nāma-sañjñā" means the designation of the name of the chapter, which is the designation consisting of the form of the chapter. And this "designation" (sañjñā) is said to be a term based on both etymological derivation and conventional usage (yoga-ruḍhā). Alternatively, there is the reading "adhyāyo nāma"; in that case, the word "nāma" signifies manifestation, and thus the meaning is "the heading" (adhikāra).

The word *artha* here has a different sense; therefore, it constitutes the designation of the chapter (*adhyāya*). Furthermore, that [designation] should be understood as being formed through the instrumentals *adhikaraṇa*, *karaṇa*, or *karman*:
an *adhyāya* is so called because "in this one studies" (*asminn adhīyate*), or "by means of this one studies" (*anenādhīyate*), or "this is studied" (*adhīyate*).
He states the designation "to be refuted" for the eight questions mentioned: "They exist," and so forth;
it is well known in the world that *pāllavikas*—specific, localized birds that suddenly fly up—produce agitation in the mind.
"The eightfold" refers to the aforementioned eight questions concerning the higher and the lower, the superior and the inferior; therein,
"the strength of those who know the scriptures" means that only those who know the scriptures understand these eight questions, not those who are mere superficial observers.
*Prakṛti* means inherent nature (*svabhāva*).

A "tawny one" (*babhru*) is a certain woolly animal; just as such an animal, upon approaching a ram and seeing its own wool as if it were [the enemy's], suffers a breaking of its limbs, so too the ignorant person, having encountered [an opponent], is shattered—this is the meaning. Alternatively, just as a tawny one—a large mongoose—situated in the midst of a heap of wool perceives nothing at all, so too the unintelligent person [perceives nothing] amidst the chatter of the debate between the proponent and the opponent.

*Kuṇḍabhedin* is one whose caste has been lost; he is someone who, having been questioned about his own [caste] and having determined his own birth, speaks as if he were of pure birth. Likewise, even one lacking intelligence might engage in dispute during conversation and, having entered into debate, carry on discourse with others of improper conduct.
Those with very limited foundations and very little learning—
one should not tolerate them, nor should one neglect them.
He states the result of prohibiting consultation with ignorant physicians, beginning with the words "another [who is] toward beings," and so forth.
"Devoted" means intent upon that.
(75–81) He states the fruit of an ignorant physician, beginning with "asatpakṣa... and so forth.

Those for whom the means of proof (*sādhana*) consists of fallacious positions (*asatpakṣa*) and so forth are "those [who employ such means]"; a fallacious position (*asatpakṣa*) is a position established through a non-scriptural standpoint (*anāgamapakṣa*). These include: (1) *akṣaṇi*, which is the statement by one who has been questioned regarding the meaning of a question, "There is no time to speak now"; (2) *arti*, which is the speaking by one who has been questioned regarding the meaning of a question after manifesting a headache or similar ailment; (3) *dambha*, which is the demonstration of one's own excellence for self-interest by means of books, medical instruments, and so forth; (4) *pāruṣya*, which is harsh speech such as refusing to speak even with difficulty; and (5) *anāpta*, which refers to those who are not experts in their own treatise (*svatantra*) due to a lack of knowledge thereof.
Those who boast of themselves and those who revile others (verses 82–83);
"based on two" means based on the mind and the body.
"Complete" (*samagram*) refers to physical and mental happiness in the form of health and so forth.

"Pure in consciousness" (*vijñāne vimalaḥ*) means in pure knowledge; or alternatively, "pure in consciousness" means in liberation (*mokṣa*), for in liberation happiness is both clear and complete because it is unmixed with suffering. Or else, this scripture is that from which the excellent state arises, according to the Bhaṭṭa school of thought.
"Thus, of noble meaning" means expressing what is for the benefit of both worlds;
"of those whose vision is lost" refers to those whose sight has perished. 84–85.

The designation for these [virtues] is according to how they were established by the passage beginning with "By that great root, [they become] great-rooted," and so forth, ending with "the six foremost [virtues] conclude with restraint. Furthermore, those [virtues] such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and the rest, which were mentioned in the section on the foremost [virtues] within the *Puruṣīya* chapter, have been stated here again because they relate to the subject of the inner self (*adhyātma*), whereas those previously mentioned pertained to the section on the foremost diseases. For it was said there: "Enough of these morbid transformations," and so forth.

The group of seven questions begins with, “What is life? Why is it called Āyurveda? and so forth; the group of eight questions begins with, “The treatise (tantra) and the meaning of the treatise,” and so forth.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled “The Ten Great Roots,” in the Sūtrasthāna of the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.

Thus ends the first section, the Sūtrasthāna, in the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of Caraka, composed by the venerable Cakrapāṇidatta, the four-faced one (Caturānana) among the exponents of Caraka. 1.30.
[Nidānasthāna] [Nidānasthāna, Chapter 1 (31 of 120)]:

Following the Sūtrasthāna, which states the causes and signs in brief, the Nidānasthāna is now described, which states the causes and signs in detail; for medical treatment preceded by knowledge of the causes and signs is truly effective.

Since whatever is to be stated as a mere aphorism of treatment (*cikitsāsūtra*) is already included within the section on therapeutic suitability (*upaśaya*), or alternatively, because even the statement of causes and symptoms serves the purpose of treatment, only the aphorisms of treatment are stated here; and furthermore, since fever (*jvara*) is the primary among bodily disorders (*śārīravikāra*), its etiology (*nidāna*) is stated first.

Just as fever is the principal [disorder], so too will he state later in this very same section: "Fever indeed... is the foremost of all diseases and is powerful" (Ci. A. 3), and so forth. Likewise, he will state in the section on therapeutics (*cikitsita*): "It afflicts the body, the senses, and the mind; it is the progenitor of all diseases and is powerful," and so forth.

As for what will be stated—“In ancient times, there was the origin of *gulma*” (Ni.a.8)—there, the word "ancient" (*purā*) refers to the initial manifestation of *gulma*, and not to a prior existence of fever; for it is said that following the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the origin of *gulma* occurred among living beings seized by fever through their fleeing in all directions and so forth.
Here, "etiology" (*nidāna*) is spoken of as the cause; and this is generally stated here as both that which generates the disease and that which makes the disease known.

Among these, the etiology that generates the disease is the "cause" (*hetu*), while the etiology that makes the disease known consists of the "causes" (*kāraṇa*) in the form of the etiology, prodromal symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*), clinical signs (*rūpa*), therapeutic suitability (*upaśaya*), and pathogenesis (*samprāpti*).
In this context, the *nidāna* (etiology) constitutes both the cause (*hetu*) and the producer (*janaka*), as well as that which makes the disease known.

For this very reason, after first stating the cause with the words "Now, here indeed" (*iha khalu*) and so forth, the cause is stated once more through the passage beginning with "its perception is the etiology" (*tasyopalabdhir nidānam*). Thus, the etiology of fever is called *jvaranidāna*.
Alternatively, the word *nidāna* refers exclusively to the productive cause (*janakakāraṇa*); the chapter composed concerning that productive cause of fever as its *nidāna* is the "Nidāna of Fever.
By this, there is the inclusion of the premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*) and other factors that serve as causes for cognition, as well as the aphorisms on treatment (*cikitsāsūtra*).

Thus, while the etiology of fever (*jvara*) is to be discussed, [the author], being intent on first stating the etiology common to all diseases—since the specific depends upon the general—and considering that it is appropriate to state the characteristics of a disease once it has arisen, speaks of the very cause of its origin through synonyms for the sake of conventional usage and for the sake of definition, beginning with "In this world, indeed... and so forth.

The word *iha* means "in this context," referring to the present treatise (*prakaraṇa*) which sets forth the causes (*kāraṇa*). By using the term "cause" (*hetu*) and so forth, he shows that these words do not have different meanings within this specific context; however, he demonstrates that in other contexts, the words *hetu* and so on do indeed carry different meanings. For example, as he will state: "The cause is because of being uncreated" (*heturakṛtakatvāt*, Vi. A. 8); likewise, "there would be only ten bases" (*daśaivāyatanāni syuḥ*, Sū. A. 29); and in such passages as "the agent, the thinker, the feeler, the knower" (*kartā, mantā, veditā, boddhā*, Śā. A. 4). Similarly, the word *pratyaya* may refer to the *laṭ* and other verbal suffixes, while *utthāna* may refer to rising or emerging.

The extensive enumeration of synonyms such as "cause" (*hetu*) and so forth in the treatise is for the purpose of conventional usage. Furthermore, since words such as "cause" can apply to other meanings, their application is restricted to the [specific] cause itself through their grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with other synonyms. Thus, that single object to which those words refer is distinguished from other objects such as "reason" (*hetu*) and so forth. Therefore, the mention of synonyms serves to define the specific characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
This same principle should be explained in the case of other synonyms, such as those for "disease" (*vyādhi*) and so on.

In this context, eight causes are mentioned because the number eight is auspicious, and also because it follows from the enumeration of the eight types of diseases, fevers, and so forth. Therefore, other synonyms for cause—such as *yoni*, *mūla*, *mukha*, and *prakṛti*—should also be understood, though they are not mentioned here for fear of making the treatise too voluminous. Similarly, although other synonyms for disease have not been stated, one should follow the same logic for fear of excessive length. He states the divisions of the cause: "That is threefold," and so on.

This [topic] regarding the unwholesome contact of the senses with their objects and so forth has been explained in detail in the chapters on Longevity (*Dīrghañjīvitīya*) and the Three Pursuits (*Tisraiṣaṇīya*); therefore, it is not elaborated upon here.

Although the number three is already established by the very mention of the list, the explicit statement "threefold" is intended to demonstrate that even the extensive variety of unwholesome sensory contacts does not transcend this triad. Furthermore, it is intended to show that each of these is itself threefold, based on the distinctions of deficient application (*ayoga*), excessive application (*atiyoga*), and improper application (*mithyāyoga*).
Moreover, although this triad of causes has already been mentioned, its restatement here due to the requirements of the context does not incur the fault of redundancy.

Furthermore, this threefold nature of unwholesome contact between the senses and their objects serves as the regulator with respect to the primary cause; therefore, one should not raise the objection that there is no inclusion of proximate causes such as diseases mentioned in passages like, "From the heat of fever, *raktapitta* is provoked" (Ni.

A. 8). Alternatively, even in cases such as fever which serve as the cause for *raktapitta* and other conditions, unwholesome contact between the senses and their objects is itself the primary cause; thus, in the case of effects such as *raktapitta* resulting from fever, the very cause of the fever becomes the primary cause.

By stating at the outset here that "the improper and excessive union of time, intellect, senses, and objects" (Sūtra 1.1)—thereby deviating from the previously mentioned order—he demonstrates the primary importance of all these factors in causing disease; for let there be no restriction of primacy based on a one-sided enumeration.

Although intellectual error (*prajñāparādha*) is primary by virtue of being the root cause, nevertheless, because it is the proximate cause, even the contact of the sense organs with unwholesome objects (*asātmyendriyārthasaṃyoga*) is primary, since it serves as the cause for even intense improper application of sound and so forth, even when that occurs unintentionally.

Although time (*kāla*) is primary due to its inevitability, it is nonetheless not primary because it is dependent upon the sense organs and their objects; for excessive application of time and the like generally arise from the excessive application of cold and other qualities of the sense objects.

He states that the cause-effect relationship occurs when the causality of a cause exists toward its effect; thus he speaks of the disease as the "effect of the cause. Regarding the phrase "therefore, they are of three types" and so forth, there is no correspondence here according to numerical order (*yathāsaṅkhya*), because even from a single-type cause, the three types of diseases can arise.
Furthermore, the mention of "three types" here is intended to demonstrate that even though diseases are infinite, they do not transcend the categories of being fiery (*āgneya*) and so on.
Those [fevers] belonging to fire are caused by bile (*pittaja*), those belonging to the moon are caused by phlegm (*kaphaja*), and those belonging to wind are caused by wind (*vātaja*).

Although it would be more appropriate to mention the *vāyavya* first because of its predominance, nevertheless, since bile is predominant in this fever, they are designated as "belonging to fire" (*āgneya*).

By the compound *āgneyasaumyavāyavyāḥ*, he demonstrates that even from each individual unwholesome contact between the senses and their objects, the three types of diseases arise; for if the compound were not used, one might suspect a correspondence based on the order of enumeration.
He states that diseases arise from other causes as well, beginning with the words "and others are of two kinds," etc.

By separating the mention of the *rājasa* and *tāmasa* [causes] here in this treatise—which is currently engaged in the section on physical diseases—he demonstrates that they need not be elaborated upon here, as they do not fall within its scope. Furthermore, the mention of the *rājasa* and *tāmasa* [causes] is intended to avoid the deficiency of not having fully described the etiology of diseases in this context.

Furthermore, exogenous diseases arising from trauma and similar causes are included within the very categories of *āgneya* (fiery) and so forth; for even in those cases, there is indeed an unmanifest aggravation of the *doṣas*. Alternatively, "others" (*apare*) means secondary, since "para" is said to mean "superior"; and the reason for their being secondary has already been stated.

Having shown the classification of diseases as *āgneya* and so forth, [the author] states the synonyms for the sake of common usage and for the purpose of definition: "In that regard, disease," and so on.

Here too, since words such as *ātaṅka* and others—which are synonyms for fear (*bhaya*)—are excluded from having meanings other than [disease], it should be understood that they characterize disease (*vyādhi*).
For by the word *ātaṅka*, fear is also expressed; and by the word *vikāra*, even the sixteen transformations (*vikāra*), such as the sense organs and so forth, are expressed.
Thus, through the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of words such as *vyādhi*, the properties of disease are to be characterized.

For instance: it is called *vyādhi* because it brings about various kinds of suffering (*duḥkha*); it is called *āmaya* because it generally arises from an imbalance (*āma*); it is called *ātaṅka* because, being joined with pain, it makes life difficult—indeed, there is a saying: "Ātaṅka [refers] to a life of hardship"; by the word *yakṣma*, he shows that these disorders are possessed of many diseases, like royal consumption (*rājayakṣman*); by the word *jvara*, he shows that they cause distress to both body and mind; by the word *vikāra*, he shows that the disease effects a change in the state of the body and mind; and by the word *roga*, he shows its quality of causing affliction (*rujā*).

Now, having stated the cause that generates disease and likewise having described the disease produced by that cause, he explains the means for knowing that disease, beginning with the words "tasya" (of that), etc.

For indeed, when a disease is not recognized, medical treatment does not proceed; therefore, it is appropriate to state the fivefold diagnosis (*nidāna-pañcaka*) as the general means for knowing disease.

He explains the *nidāna* (etiology): "In that regard," and so forth, as stated previously, from the words "Now here" up to "and transformation. The proximate cause of diseases is *vāta* and the other doshas; the remote cause is the improper application of objects and so forth. Furthermore, the remote cause of *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disease) is the heat of fever and so forth. Moreover, the general remote cause of diseases has been stated, such as: "Even in the past, there was no arising of disease without unrighteousness (*adharma*)" (Vi. A. 3), and so forth. All of this is to be understood by the term "cause" (*kāraṇa*).

In this context, it is understood that diseases, being the result of unrighteous action (*adharma*), are curable through medical treatments such as those relying on divine intervention, expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*), offerings (*bali*), and auspicious ceremonies (*maṅgala*). Furthermore, because fever arises from the wrath of Rudra, its great power and its fiery nature (*āgneyatva*) are understood; for anger is indeed fiery, and therefore fever, being composed of that, is also fiery.

Thus says the authoritative text: "There is no heat without bile (*pitta*), and there is no fever without heat; therefore, one should avoid things antagonistic to bile especially when bile is predominant" (Vāgbhaṭa, Cikitsāsthāna 1).

Through the knowledge that a disease is produced by wind (vāta) and other factors, it is inferred that it is curable by medicines contrary to those factors, and likewise, a future connection with other latent (anudbhūta) modifications of wind and so forth is postulated.
Furthermore, by observing the consumption of unwholesome, dry, and similar causes, a future disease arising from them is deduced.
When doubt arises during the examination of a disease, that specific disease whose causes are observed to be present is identified. Such is the examination of disease by means of its causes.

Because the premonitory signs (pūrvarūpa) and so forth follow immediately after the causal factors (nidāna), they are described immediately after the causal factors; therefore, he states the definition of the premonitory sign, beginning with "premonitory" (pūrva) and so on—
meaning prior to its arising, i.e., before its production.

By this [definition], that which is the characteristic of a disease yet to arise prior to its manifestation is the *pūrvarūpa* (premonitory symptom). However, although the indulgence in causes (*nidāna*) makes known a future disease, it is not designated by the term *pūrvarūpa*; for while it is indeed included under the category of "causes" (*nidāna*), it is not denoted by the word "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*).
As it has been stated elsewhere: "The humors, provoked and residing in their respective locations, provide foreknowledge of the disease to come."
"The signs that the humors produce are called the premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa).

Nor should it be asked how there can be a characteristic sign for a disease that has not yet arisen and does not yet exist; for just as future rain is inferred from clouds, so too the rising of Kṛttikā is inferred upon seeing the rising of Rohiṇī.

And that premonitory symptom (*pūrvarūpa*) is of two kinds: one is the unmanifest form of the disease yet to arise, as it has been stated: "Its unmanifest characteristic is known as the premonitory symptom" (*Ci. A. 11*), and likewise: "The sign is unmanifest because of the subtlety of diseases, according to their respective nature" (*Vā.

Thus [is the first type]; the second, however, is produced from the state of the fusion of the *doṣas* and the *dūṣyas*, and is indeed distinct from the unmanifest *liṅga*. For example: aversion to children, horripilation, and so forth, during fever (*jvara*). This is not a *pūrvarūpa* that necessarily becomes manifest during the stage of the fever itself, but rather occurs only in the period preceding the fever. Furthermore, where it does become manifest, that [fever] is considered incurable. Therefore, with reference precisely to such a *pūrvarūpa*, he will state in the section on fatal signs (*ariṣṭa*): "All the *pūrvarūpas* mentioned for fever, when occurring in excessive measure..."
"That which they enter, death enters him, preceded by fever" (I.A. 5); likewise: "If the premonitory symptoms of any other disease enter a man in this manner, his death is certain" (I.A. 5).

For if this statement were intended to refer to the unmanifest characteristics of the premonitory stage (*pūrvarūpa*), then all fevers would be incurable; because in the state of the premonitory stage the symptoms are unmanifest, yet once the fever has arisen, they all become manifest everywhere. Therefore, this statement is intended only with reference to those specific premonitory symptoms that are restricted to the premonitory stage; and this "unmanifestness" of the symptoms consists precisely in their indistinctness due to their slight intensity.

However, that premonitory symptom (*pūrvarūpa*) which is restricted to the state of the convergence of the *doṣas* and the *dūṣyas* indicates the mere presence of disease, but it does not indicate the specific *doṣa*. And with reference to this type of premonitory symptom, it was also stated by Vāgbhaṭa: "The premonitory symptom is that by which a disease about to arise is characterized, without being influenced by a specific *doṣa*" (Vāgbhaṭa).

Regarding the statement "ni.a.1)," that which is the unmanifest sign (*avyaktaliṅga*)—the premonitory form (*pūrvarūpa*)—indicates the specific nature of the morbidity (*doṣa*) of the disease. As stated by Hārīta: "Thus is the premonitory form of the eight types of fevers in general; specifically, however, that characterized by frequent yawning and body aches, and causing distress in the heart, is born from Vāta," and so forth. Likewise, it is also stated in the Suśruta-saṃhitā: "In general, [it is the same], but specifically, excessive yawning arises from Samīraṇa (Vāta)."

"From *pitta* there is a burning sensation in the eyes, and from *kapha* there is a lack of desire for food" (Su.U.A. 39). This should be understood as the premonitory stage (*pūrvarūpa*), which is indeed a sign of an impending fever that is unmanifest due to its subtlety. For when the fever is manifest—whether born of *vāta* or other doshas—yawning and other such symptoms occur far more intensely than the premonitory signs. Thus, regarding this twofold nature of the premonitory stage: where a specific premonitory symptom exists, it is mentioned directly; where no specific one exists, he will state merely the general signs. Therefore, it should be understood therein that the premonitory stage consists precisely of these unmanifest signs.
He states the definition: "Prādurbhūta" and so forth.

The nature of a disease that has arisen is its *liṅga* (sign). That which makes known a disease—distinguished by specific qualifiers such as being caused by *vāta* and so on, or being *āmaja* (undigested) or *pakva* (digested)—as distinct from etiology (*nidāna*), therapeutic suitability (*upaśaya*), and pathogenesis (*samprāpti*), is the *liṅga*.

By this [definition], the specific symptom determined by the disease is included—just as fever has heat, so too does diarrhea have excessive evacuation, and so forth; likewise, the symptoms produced by Vāta and other humors, such as the irregular onset and remission of Vāta-type fever, are included; similarly, the characteristics of undigested (āma), ripening (pakva), and chronic (jīrṇa) fevers, which indicate specific stages of the disease, are included; and likewise, complications (upadrava) are indeed symptoms because they indicate the state of a disease that has reached incurability, whereas a fatal sign (riṣṭa) is specifically the prodromal stage of death.

Although the etiological factors (*nidāna*) and so forth may also lead to the removal of a disease once it has arisen, they are not referred to here by the term "sign" (*liṅga*), because their specific characteristics have not been described separately.
For the sake of conventional usage and for the purpose of defining its characteristics, he states the synonyms for *liṅga*, beginning with "In that context, *liṅga*... and so on.

In this context, "non-different from the meaning" (*anarthāntaram*) refers to the definition of a *liṅga* (sign) as its denoted object (*abhidheya*). However, in other contexts, even when there is a difference in meaning, the terms *liṅga* and so forth are used; for example: 1. In the passage, "The strong man should offer the *liṅga*" (*Ci. A. 2*), the term refers to the penis (*śepha*). 2. Similarly, in "The configuration (*saṃsthāna*) and form (*ākṛti*) should be known as either symmetrical (*suṣamā*) or asymmetrical (*viṣamā*)" (*I. A. 7*); 3. Likewise, in "Possessing characteristics (*lakṣaṇavat*) and possessing examples (*udāharaṇavat*)" (*Vi. A. 8*); 4. Similarly, in "One should prepare side dishes with oil and ghee"; 5. And likewise, in "That which is the continuity of form (*rūpa*) and of the vital essence (*sattva*)" (*Śā. A. 2*), and so forth.

Now, one might object: "Just as it was said here, 'in this sense' (*asminnarthe*), so too should it be stated as 'in this sense' when denoting the synonyms for cause (*hetu*) and the onset (*samprāpti*) of disease. To this we reply: No. First, regarding the denotation of the synonyms for cause, that meaning is already expressed by the very phrase "here indeed" (*iha khalu*). Furthermore, in the narration of the synonyms for onset, the meaning of the term "in this sense" is obtained precisely through the word "of the disease" (*vyādheḥ*). Moreover, among the synonyms for the disease itself (*gada*), no distinct difference in meaning is generally observed; therefore, the phrase "in this sense" was not employed there.

And this is the intention of the Teacher: wherever he perceives that a word has another meaning, only there does he employ the phrase "in this sense. For example, in the passage, "Furthermore, regarding the humors combined together, the distinction between their parts and sub-parts is the 'alternative' (*vikalpa*) in this sense," the word *vikalpa* indeed occurs elsewhere as well, such as in "of those conceptualized by other alternatives" (Vi. A. 1), and likewise in "there is no alternative for those [diseases] that cannot be cured" (Sū. A. 10), and so forth.

Now, one might ask: why are synonyms not provided for *pūrvarūpa* (prodromal symptoms) and *upaśaya* (therapeutic suitability)? We reply: as for *pūrvarūpa*, its synonyms are exactly the same as those of *rūpa* (manifest signs); for indeed, the very terms beginning with *rūpa*, when joined with the word "prior" (*pūrva*), become synonyms of *pūrvarūpa*. However, *upaśaya* is treatment (*cikitsā*); since its synonyms must be stated within the specific section on *cikitsita* (therapeutics), they are not repeated here. He states *upaśaya*: "Upaśaya," and so forth.
*Upaśaya* means *upaśayana*, which signifies a continuous association with comfort (*sukhānubandha*).

It is [determined] by the cause, by the disease, and by both the cause and the disease; thus, they are "contrary to the cause and the disease" (*hetuvyādhiviparīta*). Of those medicines, diets, and regimens, as well as of those medicines, foods, and regimens that produce effects contrary to the cause and the disease: "continuous association with comfort" means a sequence consisting of comfort, and the meaning is that this sequence is a cause of comfort. Furthermore, this *upaśaya* serves as a means of knowledge regarding a disease whose signs are hidden.

As it has been stated: "One should examine a disease with hidden signs through the methods of *upaśaya* and *anupaśaya*" (Viśeṣa-sthāna 4); and it is said in the Triśothīya chapter: "That which subsides through oil, heat, and massage is of the Vāta type" (Sūtrasthāna 18).

In this context, that very same thing is described as producing an opposite effect—that which, though appearing at first glance to be non-opposite, produces the characteristic of subsidence for the opposite [disease].

Examples are written here: Medicine contrary to the cause (*hetuviparīta-auṣadha*): for example, hot medicine such as *śuṇṭhī* in a fever born of cold and *kapha*. Food contrary to the cause (*hetuviparīta-anna*): for example, rice with meat broth (*rasaudana*) in a fever born of exertion and wind. Conduct contrary to the cause (*hetuviparīta-vihāra*): for example, staying awake at night in one who has woken from daytime sleep due to *kapha*. Medicine contrary to the disease (*vyādhiviparīta-auṣadha*): for example, astringent drugs like *pāṭhā* in diarrhea (*atīsāra*). Food contrary to the disease (*vyādhiviparīta-anna*): for example, astringent food such as lentils (*masūra*) in diarrhea. Conduct contrary to the disease (*vyādhiviparīta-vihāra*): for example, inducing straining (*pravāhaṇa*) in upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*). Medicine contrary to both cause and disease (*hetuvyādhiviparīta-auṣadha*): for example, *daśamūla*, which removes both wind and swelling, in a swelling caused by wind. Food contrary to both cause and disease (*hetuvyādhiviparīta-anna*): for example, a fever-curing gruel that is hot in a fever arising from cold. Conduct contrary to both cause and disease (*hetuvyādhiviparīta-vihāra*): for example, dryness (contrary to *tandrā*) and staying awake at night (contrary to daytime sleep) in *tandrā* born of unctuousness and daytime sleep. Medicine that produces an effect contrary to the cause (*hetuviparītārthakāri-auṣadha*): for example, a warm poultice (*upanāha*) that increases *pitta* in a ripening swelling dominated by *pitta*. Food that produces an effect contrary to the cause (*hetuviparītārthakāri-anna*): for example, burning food in a ripening swelling dominated by *pitta*. Conduct that produces an effect contrary to the cause (*hetuviparītārthakāri-vihāra*): for example, frightening (*santrāsana*) in wind-induced insanity (*vātonmāda*). Medicine that produces an effect contrary to the disease (*vyādhiviparītārthakāri-auṣadha*): for example, *madanaphala* and others that induce vomiting in vomiting (*chardi*). Food that produces an effect contrary to the disease (*vyādhiviparītārthakāri-anna*): for example, milk that causes purgation in diarrhea. For it is said: "In one with many morbid humors (*doṣa*), a stimulated digestive fire, and remaining vitality, [the medicine] does not stay [in the body]."
"If the diarrhea is caused by pitta, one should purge it with milk. (Cikitsā-sthāna)

a.19) Thus it is said: conduct that produces an effect contrary to both the cause and the disease is, for example, inducing purging for the purpose of emesis when emesis is the required treatment. A medicine that produces an effect contrary to both the cause and the disease is, for example, an ointment of *aguru* and other substances applied to a burn caused by fire; for heat appears appropriate both to the cause, fire, and to the disease, burning. Food that produces an effect contrary to both the cause and the disease is, for example, intoxicating liquor in a case of alcoholism (*madātyaya*) arising from the consumption of liquor; [for here] liquor produces intoxication. Conduct that produces an effect contrary to both the cause and the disease is, for example, physical exercise such as swimming across water when there is a "confused wind" (*sammūḍhavāta*) produced by physical exertion; this appears appropriate both to the cause, physical exercise, and to the disease, confused wind.

But surely, just as there is *upaśaya* (therapeutic suitability), there is also *anupaśaya* (non-suitability) which serves to examine the disease; and it is said: "One should examine a disease with hidden symptoms through *upaśaya* and *anupaśaya*" (Videha, Sūtra 4).
Likewise, it is stated by Vāgbhaṭa: "The opposite of *upaśaya* is *anupaśaya*; for that is known as *asātmya* (unwholesome)" (Vāgbhaṭa, Nidāna).
