a.1) Thus [it is said]. It is true that [the cause] exists, but because it is already included by the very mention of the *nidāna* (etiological factors), it is not stated separately; likewise, the absence of palliation (*anupaśaya*) occurs precisely through the service of those same causes.

Although the manifestation of symptoms follows immediately after the pathogenesis (*samprāpti*), nevertheless, because the determination of the disease has little utility for understanding the pathogenesis itself, he states the pathogenesis last—beginning with "pathogenesis," and so forth.

*Jāti* means birth (*janma*). The meaning denoted by the terms *samprāpti*, *āgati*, and *jāti* is what is meant by the "onset" (*samprāpti*) of a disease. Regarding this, some authorities state that the onset is merely the birth of the disease, produced by the operation of the final cause. Although this onset does not inform one of the disease in the same way as the etiology (*nidāna*) and other factors do, they nevertheless describe it as the means of perceiving the disease because it serves as the characteristic of a disease that has not yet arisen. Thus, by virtue of its logical consistency (*upapatti*), they explain its capacity to bring about the recognition of the disease.

Others do not accept this, because if that were so, no specific distinction regarding the disease would be understood through *samprāpti* (the process of manifestation), nor is there a rule that a disease is perceived only when it has already arisen; for even before it has arisen, a disease is recognized as being imminent by means of its causes (*nidāna*) and premonitory signs (*pūrvarūpa*). Therefore, what is denoted here by the term *samprāpti* is the arising of the disease characterized by the specific activity of the morbid humors (*doṣa*) that produce it; for this very reason, it is called "arrival" (*āgati*) as a synonym.
For *āgati* (arrival) is the progression of the causative factor of origin up to the point of producing the disease;
and this *samprāpti* (pathogenesis) indeed makes known the specific nature of the disease.

For example, regarding fever (*jvara*), the *samprāpti* that is described—beginning with "When that [dosha], having become aggravated, enters the stomach (*āmāśaya*)" and ending with "then it brings about fever"—makes known the properties of fever such as its corrupting of the stomach, its injuring of the digestive fire (*agni*), and its corrupting of the rasa.

Nor should it be said that this property—such as the affliction of the stomach (āmāśaya) and so forth—is a quality of the *doṣas*, and therefore, since the qualities of the causes are already included by the inclusion of the etiological factors (*nidāna*), [this should not be stated separately]; for although this is indeed a quality of the cause, it is described separately under the term *samprāpti* (pathogenesis) in order to convey its specific nature as the functional activity of the *doṣas* that produces the disease. Just as the *pūrvarūpa* (prodromal symptoms) is mentioned separately because it specifically indicates a future disease despite there being no difference in their status as signs (*liṅga*), for this very reason Vāgbhaṭa also stated the definition of *samprāpti* in this same way: "In whatever manner the *doṣa* becomes vitiated and in whatever manner it spreads..."
"This is the manifestation of disease; it is its acquisition, birth, and arrival" (Vāgbhaṭa’s Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya, Nidānasthāna,
verse 1).

Since the specific manifestation of *samprāpti* (pathogenesis) differs for each individual disease, and since there is no need to mention it for every single disease, such differentiation need not be stated here. However, whatever specific *samprāpti* is applicable will indeed be described by the author himself in the passage beginning with, "When that [dosha], having become aggravated, enters the stomach (*āmāśaya*)... Therefore, in order to avoid the fault of deficiency due to not describing all types of *samprāpti*, he states the general classifications of *samprāpti* common to all diseases, beginning with: "That [is] number," and so forth.

The meaning is that this *samprāpti* (pathogenesis) is differentiated by number and other factors; thus, when the disease is differentiated by number and so forth, the *samprāpti* becomes differentiated. This is because there is no undifferentiated arising of differentiated entities; rather, it is indeed differentiated. Furthermore, although the *samprāpti* is indeed distinct for each specific manifestation of a disease (*vyakti*), nevertheless, that differentiation of *samprāpti* is not mentioned here because it serves no purpose. For, in cases such as various manifestations of fever where the number, predominance, and types [of causes] are identical, and where the etiology (*nidāna*), signs (*liṅga*), and treatment (*cikitsita*) are uniform, there is no purpose in establishing a distinction. However, in cases like fever where the number and other factors differ, there exists a difference in etiology, signs, and treatment; therefore, it is entirely appropriate to state the differentiation of *samprāpti*, which is the generator of those differences in number and other factors.
12(1) He illustrates the classification by number: "Number, first of all," and so forth.

Although there is indeed a difference in number even when diseases are distinguished by differences such as predominance (*prādhānya*), nevertheless, here it is precisely that number established in the treatise and propounded in the *Aṣṭodarīya* and other chapters which is intended by the word "number."

For this very reason, after stating that there are eight types of fever, *raktapitta*—which follows in sequence as "blood-bile" (*śoṇitapitta*) is twofold—was not explicitly mentioned; for the twofold nature of *raktapitta* pertains to the distinction in its modes of manifestation (*vidhibheda*) rather than its numerical count, since it was already expressed by the term "twofold blood-bile" itself through the word "mode. Furthermore, in the passage beginning with "preeminence," the phrase "by degrees" (*taratamābhyām*) refers to the two increases denoted by the words "degree" (*tara*) and "super-degree" (*tamasa*).
He distinguishes the scope of the two terms *tara* and *tama* with the words beginning "of two," and so forth:

"in the case of two, *tara*" means that when two faults have increased, the suffix *tara* is employed—as in "increased more" (*vṛddhatara*). Likewise, "in the case of three, *tama*" means that when three faults have increased, the suffix *tama* is employed—as in "increased most" (*vṛddhatama*).

Thus, when a disorder is initiated by two doṣas (*dvandva*), the manifestation (*samprāpti*) differs according to the predominance of one of the two doṣas, as indicated by the word "more" (*tara*); likewise, when a disorder is initiated by three doṣas (*tridoṣa*), the manifestation differs due to the predominance of whichever single doṣa is indicated by the word "most" (*tama*). This is what has been stated. (12) He now states the rule regarding the classification of manifestations that follows in sequence, beginning with: "The rule [concerning] diseases is twofold, distinguished as endogenous (*nija*) and exogenous (*āgantu*)," and so forth.

"Method" (*vidhi*) means that which is performed by a method; thus, the "method" is that from which the various classifications such as the two-fold nature and so forth arise. Furthermore, "method" means a mode or a classification. By the phrase "through the distinction of curable, incurable, mild, and severe," it is meant: through the distinction of mild and severe as they pertain to the categories of curable and incurable. Consequently, there is a fourfold classification: (1) mildly curable, which is easily curable; (2) severely curable, such as *rohiṇī*, *valaya*, and so forth, which is curable with difficulty; (3) mildly incurable, which is palliable (*yāpya*); and (4) severely incurable, which is untreatable (*pratyākhyeya*).

Although there are indeed distinctions in the treatment of diseases based on factors such as number and predominance, nevertheless, because these distinctions of number and so forth are already grasped by their own specific designations according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), this term "treatment" (*vidhi*) should be applied to those types of diseases not already encompassed by [those] categories of number and so forth.
(12) He states the alternative (*vikalpa*) that follows in sequence, beginning with "of those combined," and so forth.

The term *samavetānām* means "of all [the doshas] combined. By this, there is the inclusion of doshas that have combined either singly or in pairs. *Aṃśāṃśabala* refers to the strength corresponding to each respective portion (*aṃśa*) of those doshas. The *vikalpa* of that—consisting of its increase or decrease—is called *aṃśāṃśabalavikalpa*. Such a variation in the strength of the portions of the doshas is what is termed "variation" (*vikalpa*) in this context, namely in this specific section.

However, in other contexts, the word *vikalpa* denotes mere differentiation; for example, in passages such as, "But there is no variation regarding those [diseases] that are incurable" (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 10). This is the intended meaning.

In this regard, the variation of the constituent parts (*aṃśāṃśa*) of the *doṣas* is as follows: even when *vāta* is aggravated, sometimes the cold part (*śītāṃśa*) of *vāta* is predominant, sometimes the light part (*laghvaṃśa*), sometimes the dry part (*rūkṣāṃśa*), and sometimes both the light and dry parts, and so forth. In the same way, the variation of the constituent parts for *pitta* and *kapha* should also be illustrated. Furthermore, this variation in the strength of the constituent parts of the *doṣas* arises from the differences in causes that give rise to qualities such as coldness and the like. (12, 5) He states the specific time of their strength, beginning with the word "strength" (*bala*).
The time of strength is "balakāla"; its specific divisions, such as spring and the forenoon, are the "balakālaviśeṣa" (specific times of strength).

The seasons (*ṛtu*), days and nights (*ahorātra*), and times for food (*āhāra*) constitute the "seasons, days and nights, and times for food. Their differentiation is their specific rule (*vidhi*). Within that, the specifically determined particular time of strength is "regulated by the rules of the seasons, days and nights, and times for food. In this regard, an example of a particular time of strength regulated by the season is spring for phlegm-fever (*śleṣmajvara*). An example regulated by the day and night is the forenoon and evening for phlegm-fever. An example regulated by the time for food is the period immediately after eating for phlegm-fever. Other such cases should be inferred in this manner.

Some, however, describe "vidhi" as karma performed in the past; even in that case, the specific strength and timing determined by that karma must be understood as occurring precisely at the time when the karma is ripening.

Although during these times of strength and timing there is no manifestation of the disease in the form of its previously non-existent appearance, nevertheless, it should be understood that within the continuum of the disease, a distinct "samprāpti" (pathogenesis) occurs at the moment of the disease's arising.
Furthermore, this *samprāpti*, which generates a powerful disease through the attainment of a specific time, makes the particularity of the disease clearly evident.

Since the fever's origin in *kapha* is inferred by the attainment of its strength in the forenoon, and its origin in *pitta* by the attainment of its strength at midday, and so forth—and since it is here that the specific variations of *samprāpti* (pathogenesis) based on number and other factors are stated, rather than the variations of the *nidāna* (etiology) and other factors; for the variations of *nidāna* and so forth are utilized only according to the distinctions to be described for each individual disease—since the etiology of fever is not the same as that of hemoptysis (*raktapitta*); and those specific features of the premonitory signs (*pūrvarūpa*) and so forth that belong to fever do not belong to hemoptysis and the like, but are indeed of a different nature.

Furthermore, that differentiation of etiology and the other factors is employed for the purpose of indicating the specific types of diseases and should therefore be discussed only in the context of describing those specific diseases.

However, as for the differentiation of the pathogenesis (*samprāpti*) by way of number and so forth, since it is of a uniform nature across all diseases, it does not serve as a differentiator of specific conditions; thus, it is explained here in the general section on the etiology of all diseases. As for the specific variations of etiology and the other factors, they are not elaborated upon here because they are distinct for each individual disease.

For this very reason, since "onset" (*samprāpti*) has already been mentioned in this same chapter by way of a general statement, the author sets aside onset and makes a specific promise regarding the etiology and other factors: "We shall now explain its specific etiology (*nidāna*), premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*), clinical signs (*liṅga*), and therapeutic suitability (*upaśaya*).

(12) Since these factors—etiology and the rest—are useful for the examination of disease according to the logic already stated, the application is that the physician should examine diseases by means of their causes and so forth.

Nor should it be argued: "If one is capable of diagnosing a disease through even a single one among the causes and so forth, then what is the purpose of mentioning all five? For as many means of knowledge as there are for diseases, all of them must indeed be demonstrated.

In that regard, for one who has forgotten the etiology (*nidāna*), the disease is examined by means of the premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*) and so forth; likewise, where the premonitory symptoms and other signs have been forgotten or are doubtful, examination occurs through therapeutic suitability (*upaśaya*). Thus, even when there is doubt as to whether a fever is born of *kapha*, its onset occurring in the forenoon or immediately after eating leads to the conclusion that it is born of *kapha*; such applications of the method should be followed accordingly.

Likewise, the determination of a general sign (*liṅgasāmānya*) by means of the premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*) has also been stated; as it was said: "One should not call that condition 'prameha' if a person voids urine that is turmeric-colored or bloody even without the premonitory symptoms of prameha, for that is indeed the provocation of blood and bile" (Ci. A. 6). Furthermore, even when a disease is determined by its signs, incurability is stated on account of the premonitory symptoms, as follows: "All the premonitory symptoms of fever mentioned [in the chapter on fever] occurring in excessive measure..."
"Death, preceded by fever, enters him whom [the disease] enters" (I.A.5).

Therefore, the pentad beginning with the etiology (nidāna) must indeed be explained. Now, from the statement that "disease is to be examined by means of its signs," it follows that the disease is distinct from its signs. However, in that case, no disease is perceived as something separate from the collection of its signs; for fever consists of irregular onset and discharge along with heat, and consumption (yakṣmā) is simply the combination of the eleven forms such as catarrh (pratiśyāya), cough (kāsa), and so forth.

This is not so; for if there were no morbidities (*vyādhi*) distinct from those established in the treatise as diagnostic signs (*liṅga*), it would be logically untenable for them to function as signs. For the text states: "Fever alone is said to have its roots in irregular onset" (Ni. A. 8).
Furthermore, in this context, a "morbid change" (*vikāra*) is denoted by terms such as "fever" and refers to a specific combination of the *doṣas* and the *dūṣyas*.

Since fever consists of a specific state of the *doṣas* and *dūṣyas*, it is indeed a different entity from symptoms like anorexia, which are themselves specific imbalances of the *doṣas* and *dūṣyas*.

Nor should it be argued that fever is simply a specific combination of the imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu-vaiṣamya*) characterized by symptoms such as feverishness, loss of appetite, and body ache, and that there is no need to postulate a fever distinct from those, since the relationship between the sign and the signified can exist through the distinction between a collection and its components; for even so, one must state that the fever-form aggregate—which follows the imbalance of the constituents such as loss of appetite and body ache—is indeed distinct [from them]. For the body, as an aggregate, is not something other than its constituent parts, such as the calves, arms, head, and trunk.

It has already been refuted previously that disease is nothing but suffering; therefore, it should not be argued that because disease is of the nature of suffering, it cannot possess the status of a whole (*avayavin*).

However, symptoms (*liṅga*) are diseases by their very nature, yet they become symptoms in relation to the disease to be diagnosed. As it has been said: "In that moment, those diseases are considered symptoms, not names [of diseases]. (Ni. A. 8)

And the relationship between the sign (*liṅga*) and that which possesses the sign (*liṅgin*) arises by virtue of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), as he will state: “Fever is considered the single sign of those [diseases] whose roots are irregular onset; and fever alone is defined by those [diseases] whose roots are irregular onset” (Ni. A. 8).
And we shall explain its meaning as it occurs in the section on the etiology of epilepsy;
therefore, the meaning is that the fivefold set beginning with etiology (nidāna) is well-established in making diseases known.
In the phrase "iti" and so forth, "iti" indicates completion;
"of the Nidānasthāna" means of the entire section on the causes of diseases;

and although the expression "summary of the meaning" (*arthasaṅgraha*) already implies a concise statement of the subject matter, the author uses the specific term "enumerated" (*uddiṣṭa*) to show that this is a concise statement even of the summary itself.

The construction is as follows: "That" refers to the brief mention of the general etiology; therefore, explaining further than this mere mention of the etiology, we shall provide a detailed exposition.

By this, he shows that here the meaning of the word "vistara" (detailed) refers to an elaborate explanation in contrast to the extremely concise statement. Consequently, the subsequent detailed discussion of the etiology and other factors becomes logically consistent.
With the words "Therein" (*tatra*) and so forth, he promises to explain the eightfold diseases beginning with fever in the Section on Etiology (*Nidānasthāna*).
By the phrase "first of all" (*prathamata eva tāvat*), he indicates that the treatments for hemorrhoids (*arśas*) and other conditions will be discussed later.
By the word "initial" (*ādya*), he shows that those [fevers] which arose at the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice are what are being described here first.

Although *rājayakṣmā* (consumption) arose as a distinct disease—since it is stated: "Furthermore, from excessive sexual indulgence, there arises *yakṣmā* of the King of Stars" (*Nirukta* 1.8)—nevertheless, it is mentioned here because of its preeminence.

Moreover, although it would have been appropriate to mention *yakṣmā* separately after enumerating the diseases beginning with epilepsy (*apasmāra*), which arose from the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, it is mentioned at the end, following the mention of wasting (*śoṣa*), because insanity (*unmāda*) and epilepsy are considered adventitious (*āgantuka*).

By the phrase "arising from greed and malice," [the author] demonstrates that fever and other diseases—which will be described in the section on the destruction of the population by the statement, "Even before this, no disease arose except through unrighteousness" (Vi. A. 3)—are produced by greed and malice. By this, it is stated that fever and the rest are born of unrighteousness (*adharma*).

This is done according to the sequence beginning with the etiology (*nidāna*), meaning by means of the general description of diseases consisting of etiology, premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*), clinical signs (*rūpa*), favorable factors (*upaśaya*), and pathogenesis (*samprāpti*).

And this sequence is sometimes set aside for the sake of a specific purpose; as in this very case of fever (*jvara*), where the *rūpa* (symptoms) are described first, whereas the *pūrvarūpa* (prodromal symptoms) ought to have been described first.

The reason for this deviation from the sequence here is that the *rūpas* must be described for each individual fever, whereas the *prāgrūpas* need not be described for each individual fever. Therefore, having described everything common to all fevers, the general *prāgrūpa* should be stated.
Likewise, the connection is: "We shall explain the treatment merely by way of summarizing the aphorisms."
The purpose of stating the treatment in the *Nidāna* has already been explained.

By using the term "sūtra" and then employing the term "saṅgraha" (compendium), he shows that even the *Sūtra-sthāna* is presented here in a condensed form. Likewise, nothing regarding the *Cikitsā-sūtra* needs to be stated here—for instance, fasting, barley-gruel, and so forth—because by the very fact that these are mentioned in the *Cikitsita* sections, their subsequent timing is already established. Furthermore, the explicit mention of "subsequent time" (*uttarakāla*) indicates that even within the *Cikitsita-sthāna*, the exposition of etiology (*nidāna*) and other factors occurs only after the description of fevers and other diseases has been completed, specifically for those disorders that have already manifested.
"Yathopacitam" means those various morbidities (vikāras) such as swelling, hemorrhoids, and so forth that have accumulated;
alternatively, there is the reading "yathācitam," in which case the meaning should be understood as "according to their predominance.

Furthermore, the statement of the etiology (nidāna) and other factors of diseases in the section on therapeutics (cikitsita) is intended with the view that when the subject matter is understood without the intervention of etiology and the like, the treatment is correctly understood.

For this very reason, he will later state the etiology and other factors for fevers and so forth once more; however, the presentation of the etiology and other factors for fevers and so forth here has been done by creating a separate section due to the vastness of the subject matter.
By making this division of sections, he demonstrates that in Āyurveda, just as with therapeutics, etiology also possesses primacy as something that must be known.

Regarding the phrase "here indeed," when the etiology of the eightfold diseases is to be stated, by the use of the term "of the bodily [diseases]," he demonstrates that fever does not hold primacy with respect to mental diseases such as desire, anger, and so forth.
He states the classification of fever (*jvara*), which is to be defined, according to its causes, beginning with the words "Now," and so forth.

By the statement "this cause [applies] to humans" (*manuṣyāṇām*)—referring to wind (*vāta*) and the other doshas—he shows that this eightfold nature of fever does not necessarily follow for cows, elephants, birds, and the like. For instance, in the case of elephants and others, fevers such as *pākala* and so on are taught, which are not of eight types.

Although one should have said "of the exogenous" (*āgantoh*), the statement "from the eighth" (*aṣṭamāt*) is intended to demonstrate the unity of the exogenous [fever] even when there is a difference in its four causes, such as trauma (*abhighāta*).

For the exogenous [fever], although produced by different causes, is indeed of a single form, since every exogenous [fever] necessarily arises preceded by pain (*vyathā*). As for the distinction that must be stated therein—such as "the wind [is provoked] by desire, grief, or fear" (Ci. A. 3)—the point is that this is caused specifically by Vāta and the other [doshas].
In the passage beginning with "of that" (*tasya*), the word "of that" refers to fever (*jvara*).
The term "specificities" (*viśeṣān*) is connected individually with each [category], such as etiology (*nidāna*) and so forth.

Furthermore, these specificities of etiology and the rest should be understood here according to their applicability, both in relation to other diseases such as *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disease) and the like, and in relation to one another among fevers caused by *vāta* and the other doshas.

Therefore, the specific nature of the premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*) here should be understood in relation to the premonitory symptoms of *raktapitta* and other such diseases, since no specific premonitory symptoms are explicitly mentioned here.

Furthermore, the absence of a specific mention of therapeutic suitability (*upaśaya*) is obtained simply from the mention of specific etiological factors (*nidāna*), because he will later describe therapeutic suitability as being the opposite of the etiology.
Moreover, the "specific" premonitory symptom mentioned here should be understood as consisting of the very nature of unmanifest signs.

However, there is no formal proposition regarding *samprāpti* (pathogenesis) here because it will be discussed later, as its various types have already been described in the section on all diseases (*sarvaroga*), and because, like etiology (*nidāna*) and other factors, it is not primary for the cognition of disease. Furthermore, the specific variations of *samprāpti* that must be stated are entirely common to all diseases; their differentiation is caused solely by the variations of the humors such as *vāta*, and the variation of *vāta* and the others is itself nothing but a variation of the etiological factors.

Others, however, say: "He will not mention *samprāpti* (pathogenesis) at all; rather, what he will state starting with 'When that [wind] is provoked' is merely an exposition of the qualities of vāta and so forth, which constitute the form of the etiology (*nidāna*), and thus it is included within the etiology itself.
This refers to the passage beginning with "dry" (*rūkṣa*).
Regarding the provocation of *vāta*, the quality of dryness (*rūkṣa*) is mentioned first because it is predominant; for the quality of dryness is the primary one among the qualities of *vāta*.

Although non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*) is said to alleviate *vāta*—as per the statement: "Indeed, among all therapeutic measures, non-unctuous and unctuous enemas are the foremost for disorders of *vāta*" (Sūtra Sthāna 20)—nevertheless, there is no fault here, because the excessive use of non-unctuous enema is specifically stated to be a cause of *vāta*.
For the text says: "From unctuous therapy comes nausea and loss of digestive fire; from non-unctuous enema comes fear of *pavana* (vāta)" (Śārīra Sthāna 4).
The established conclusion is that both *nirūha* and *anuvāsana* enemas are indeed appropriate when administered with the correct dosage, as they alleviate common types of *vāta*.
With the words beginning "sa yadā," [the author] describes the pathogenesis (*samprāpti*).

By the very use of the word "when" (*yadā*), it is shown that even though the wind (*vāyu*) may be thus provoked, it produces fever only when it possesses the state of having reached the stomach (*āmāśaya*) and so forth, and not at any other time.
By the phrase "having entered the stomach," [the author] demonstrates that the humor (*doṣa*) which causes fever is a corrupter of the stomach;
for this very reason, they universally prescribe fasting (*laṅghana*) in all fevers for the purpose of purifying the stomach.

Although the mixing with the heat (*ūṣman*) is indeed obtained simply by entering the stomach (*āmāśaya*), since the stomach itself is the seat of fire—as stated in the verse, "The space between the navel and the breasts is known as the stomach of a living being" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 2)—nevertheless, because the seat of fire is only one part of the stomach, even upon entering the stomach, a specific affliction of the seat of fire in the form of *grahaṇī* is not necessarily obtained. For this very reason, it is said: "having become mixed with the heat."

If it were stated simply as "that which is called *rasa*," there would be the over-extension [of the term] to the taste of food (*āhārarasa*), such as sweet taste and so forth; therefore, it is said: "the element born from the transformation of food" (*āhārapariṇāmadhātu*). An element produced from the transformation of food is the "element born from the transformation of food";

and since this state of being the element born from the transformation of food exists even in blood and the other [tissues] through a succession [of transformations], he says "the first" (*ādyam*); that is to say, the initial one.

When it should have been said "rasam" (the taste), by using the term "rasanāmānam" (named taste), he negates the designation "rasa" for blood and other substances through the mere etymological derivation that "it tastes, therefore it is rasa," and instead causes one to grasp that specific thing in which the designation "rasa" is conventionally established. Similarly, in other instances as well, when a word is perceived here as having an additional meaning, it is intended solely for clarity; for a treatise (*tantra*) is properly composed with clear meaning only when it is beneficial to the intellects of the three types of students. Thus, [the word] "anu" means "in the aforementioned sequence," and "ava" means "having gone."
"Having covered," meaning having enclosed; "from the place of cooking," meaning from the location of the digestive fire;
"heat," meaning the digestive fire itself.

Regarding the term "outside" (*bahiḥ*), although it is understood from the very statement "he should expel the heat" that this refers to [the heat] from the site of digestion (*paktisthāna*)—since it is distinct from the body outside that site—the explicit mention of "from the site of digestion" shows that the expulsion is of the entire fire from that site. Here, by designating the digestive fire with the word "heat" (*ūṣman*), he demonstrates that the digestive fire is of the nature of heat; he thereby negates the existence of *pitta* as a substance possessing flames similar to external fire.
For this very reason, the impairment of the digestive fire (*agnimāndya*) is indicated in the context of fever due to the expulsion of the fire.

In this context, the *vāyu* (wind), due to its excessive increase, becomes a suppressor of *vahni* (fire); therefore, it does not cause the kindling of the fire. For where the *vāyu* acts merely as an impeller, there it causes the increase of the fire; for example, the *vāyu* moving within the digestive tract (*koṣṭha*) of a person with abundant fat (*medasvin*) becomes a promoter of the fire. He states the symptoms [of this condition], beginning with "tadyathā viṣama... and so forth.

The word *tat* (that) refers in a general sense to the forms of the feminine, masculine, and neuter genders that are about to be described; for when referring to all genders, the pronoun *tat* is appropriate, as in the example *yathā* (as).

"Ārambha" means onset, and "visarga" means remission; he for whom these two are irregular is one whose onset and remission are irregular (*viṣamārambhavisargī*). This irregularity consists in [the pain] sometimes seizing the head, sometimes the back, sometimes the calves, and so forth; likewise, remission also occurs sometimes at the tip of the head, and so on. Alternatively, irregularity is simply the instability of the time of the fever's onset and remission;
this is the irregularity of the heat (*ūṣmaṇo vaiṣamyam*), such that in some part of the body the heat is great, while in another it is mild, and so forth.
The terms "intense," "mild," and "unstable" mean that the onset of fever as intense or mild is not restricted to a specific time;
all of this is consistent with the instability of *vāyu*.

Furthermore, the statement that *vāyu* performs its powerful functions at the end of digestion, at the end of the day, and so forth, should also be understood as being based on general tendencies (*prāyikatvena*).

Otherwise, this very irregularity regarding onset and so forth would not exist if the provocation of vāta were restricted solely to specific times such as the end of digestion and to specific body parts such as the calves. Therefore, the provocation of vāta should be understood as generally occurring in specific body parts that are seats of vāta, such as the calves, and at specific times such as the end of digestion;
it is with reference to this general time for vāta-provocation that he says: "at the end of digestion," and so forth.

"At the end of the heat" means that during the rainy season, there is the onset of fevers such as *satataka* (quotidian) and others characterized by a state of liberation [from the heat], whereas for those that are constantly persistent, there is an excessive increase.
Furthermore, considering that the roughness and reddishness are perceived most clearly specifically in the nails and so forth, the nails and other parts are mentioned here.

Although the mention of "skin" (*tvak*) would have included the face, the separate mention of the "face" is for the purpose of showing that roughness and other qualities are particularly evident on the skin of the face.

The state of being "klṛptī" is non-functioning (*apravṛtti*); and that, by virtue of its suitability, should be understood as applying specifically to urine and feces, while [the term] has already been mentioned in relation to the nails and so forth. Alternatively, *klṛptībhāva* means division or bursting; and that occurs in the nails and so forth. Furthermore, some pains are mobile and some are immobile due to their constant persistence, thus they are called "mobile and immobile" (*calācalāḥ*). Or else, "excessively mobile" (*atyarthaṃ calāḥ*) refers to the *piṇḍikās*, which are the fleshy masses below the kneecaps in the middle of the shanks.

*Bhagna* is that which is broken with some portion remaining; *chinna* is that which is severed; *rugṇa* is that which is crushed; *mṛdita* is that which is flattened on the side; *avapāṭita* is that which is torn up in one part; *avanunna* is that which is pushed forward. The meaning of these terms, such as *bhagna* and the rest, is understood from common worldly usage (*lokata eva*), since these words are well-known among ordinary people and are thus employed in various treatises. Regarding the jaw (*hanu*), there is no established technical definition; therefore, its non-performance of its own function is called "tastelessness of the mouth" (*āsyavairasya*), which means a lack of perception of taste.

*Annarasakhedaḥ* (distress regarding the taste of food) means distress or despondency toward the taste of food; the meaning is a lack of desire for all tastes. *Aruci* (loss of appetite), however, should be understood as the refusal to swallow food once it has entered the mouth, which will be described later. *Uṣṇābhiprāyatā* (a disposition toward heat) means a fondness for warmth.

By the very statement that there is "non-alleviation" (*anupaśaya*) for those factors mentioned under the heading of etiology (*nidāna*), the opposite—alleviation (*upaśaya*)—is already implied by the sense of the matter; nevertheless, it is stated explicitly for the sake of clarity. Alternatively, it is stated because the implication (*arthāpatti*) is not invariably certain (*anaikāntika*). For example, while daytime sleep is prohibited in the case of a new fever (*navajvara*), by implication one might assume that daytime sleep is permitted in an old fever (*purāṇajvara*); however, since daytime sleep is not actually prescribed there either, they say that the implication is not invariably certain.

By the inclusion of the word "stated" (*ukta*) in the phrase "of those stated as causes" (*nidānoktānām*), it is shown that only that which has been explicitly declared as a cause (*nidāna*) is indicated as being non-beneficial (*anupaśayitva*); it does not refer to that which merely appears to be a cause at first glance. Therefore, even though alcohol (*madya*) and the like are perceived as causes in conditions such as alcoholism (*madātyaya*), they are in fact beneficial (*upaśayitva*).
With the words beginning with "hot" (*uṣṇa*), etc., he describes fever caused by *pitta* (*pittajvara*): "It is as follows," and so forth.
This should be explained as before.

By the statement "because of its liquidity, it injures the fire," [the author] demonstrates that even though pitta is hot, its quality of liquidity—which is contrary to the nature of fire—renders it a destroyer of the digestive fire.
For he will state in the chapter on the *grahaṇī*: "Flooding [it], it destroys the fire, just as hot water destroys fire" (Ci. A. 15).

By the statement "having expelled [the fever] outward, one should squeeze [the body]," it is shown that in *pittajvara*, unlike in *vātajvara*, there is no sudden administration of fire (cauterization), but rather it should be done gradually and in small increments.

This connects with the preceding section beginning with "simultaneously" (*yugapadeva*) and ending with the subsequent section beginning with "not unevenly" (*na vaiṣamyeṇa*) and concluding with "increase" (*viśeṣeṇa*). It indicates that the onset or the increase [of the fever] does not occur through irregularity, but rather occurs simultaneously.
The phrase "the manifestation of abscesses is the body" constitutes the division [of the text] (verses 22–24).
With the words beginning with "unctuous" (*snigdha*), he describes phlegm-fever (*śleṣmajvara*).
The passage beginning with "sa yadā" and so forth should be explained in the same manner as for fever caused by *kapha*.

Now, one might object: since the seat of *śleṣman* (phlegm) is the stomach (*āmāśaya*), why is there the statement "having entered the stomach"? It is not so; the chest (*uraḥ*) is also a primary seat of *śleṣman*. Therefore, [the author] demonstrates that even the *śleṣman* located in the chest enters the stomach.

Where pitta exists solely as a function of the *āmāśaya*, the phrase "having entered the *āmāśaya*" is not used; instead, it says "having emitted heat from the *āmāśaya*. This is because pitta is already situated within the *āmāśaya*; it is logical that, being located in one part of the *āmāśaya*, it moves from its own site to the seat of fire (*vahni-sthāna*), which is a specific portion of the *āmāśaya* known as the *grahaṇī*.

(25-26) The word "simultaneously" (*yugapat*) means at one and the same time; it shows that in a fever caused by *kapha*, there is either an arrival or an increase occurring all at once through the pervasion of the entire body.
In another tantra, *śītapiḍakā* is called *śvetapiḍakā*.

Since the status of these as symptoms of *kapha*-fever is already established by the mere statement, "These are its symptoms," for what purpose is the further statement, "The symptoms of *śleṣman*-fever occur"? We reply: by the word "its" (*tasya*), there might be a reference to its own [general] morbidity alone; therefore, this repetition is for the sake of ensuring that the symptoms are not understood merely as symptoms of the morbidity. Alternatively, by the previous proposition, the initial delimitation of the symptoms was stated, while by the subsequent statement, "the symptoms of *śleṣman*-fever occur," the final delimitation is expressed. In the same way, the redundancy in other cases, such as *vāta*-fever and the premonitory signs (*pūrvarūpa*), should be avoided.
By the verse beginning with "viṣamāśanāt" (from irregular eating), etc., he describes the dual and combined (sānnipātika) fevers.

Although fasting does not produce pitta and kapha, it nevertheless produces all three doṣas because it causes a dulling of the digestive fire (agnimāndya). Alternatively, among these factors such as irregular eating, the causality of dual doṣas and the causality of all three doṣas should be inferred according to their respective suitability; therefore, fasting should be understood as producing vāta and pitta. As for the statement that fasting removes pitta, that is due to the depletion of the liquid portion of pitta.
For there is this statement: "The two liquid tissues, *kapha* and *pitta*, can endure great fasting.
This refers to the transformation of food; that is, from the sudden and unmethodical practice of such dietary transformation.

Just as the scent of an unwholesome substance causes harm when it enters the interior of the nose, so it is not with unwholesome forms and other [sensory objects]. For these do not necessarily enter the body; therefore, unwholesome forms and the like are not mentioned here.

"According to the cause" (*yathānidānam*) means that when the causes of two [humors] are indulged, then there is a dual combination (*dvandva*); when the causes of three are indulged, then all three *doṣas* arise. Even in the case of a dual combination, when the causes of *vāta* and *pitta* are indulged, then there is a dual combination in the form of *vāta* and *pitta*; the meaning is that in this way, others also become aggravated.

Although this is already understood by the phrase "all three *doṣas*," the explicit mention of "simultaneously" (*yugapat*) is for the purpose of negating gradual aggravation; the meaning is that they reach the state of aggravation all at once, not sequentially. 28

In passages such as "of the symptoms of fever" (jvaraliṅgānām), there is a specific combination [of symptoms], whether it be the symptoms of vāta and pitta, or the symptoms of vāta and śleṣman, or the symptoms of pitta and śleṣman, or any one of them; thus, [it refers to] vātapittajvara and so forth.
He speaks of exogenous fever (āgantujvara), beginning with the words "abhighāta" and so forth.

*Abhighāta* (trauma) refers to injury by clubs and the like; *abhiṣaṅga* (affliction) refers to obsession by desire and the like; *abhicāra* (sorcery) refers to the performance of *Atharva*-mantras and such that cause fever; and *abhiśāpa* (curse) refers to the pronouncing of a curse by a preceptor, a perfected being (*siddha*), or others. These four types of causes are mentioned here as the primary ones. By this, other causes of exogenous fever (*āgantuja-jvara*)—such as the smell of medicinal herbs, possession by spirits (*bhūta-abhiṣaṅga*), and the gaze of malevolent planets (*duṣṭa-graha-nirīkṣaṇa*)—should also be understood. Alternatively, by the term *abhighāta*, which denotes physical striking of the body, unwholesome smells and similar factors are to be included; whereas by *abhiṣaṅga*, possession by spirits (*bhūta-abhiṣaṅga*) and so forth are meant.

"Preceded by pain" (*vyathāpūrvam*) indicates that in an exogenous (*āgantuka*) fever, pain occurs first, and subsequently the symptoms produced by the involvement of the *doṣas* appear. Alternatively, by the statement "preceded by pain," they say that in exogenous fever, pain itself is the prodromal sign (*pūrvarūpa*);

however, the actual manifestation (*rūpa*) should be understood initially as the specific nature of the fever's own burning heat, devoid of the specific characteristics of vāta-fever and so forth. But when there is subsequent involvement of the *doṣas*, the signs of the respective *doṣas* occur exactly as will be described hereafter.

By the expression "the eighth," having negated the fourfold nature that would otherwise result from its association with the four causes such as trauma (abhighāta) and so forth, he demonstrates that these four are of a single type due to their uniform connection with being preceded by pain (vyathā). For if there were a fourfold classification, the exogenous (āgantu) [fever] would not be the eighth, as there could also be ninth and so on; furthermore, "for a short time" means for a brief duration—some say three days, others say seven days—for it is observed that in the case of exogenous fever, the symptoms of the doshas appear after seven days.
In that regard, he explains the specific connection with the doshas for each particular exogenous [fever] beginning with the words "tatrābhighāta" and so forth:
"by vāta and pitta. This means that in some cases it is caused by vāta, in some by pitta, and in some by both vāta and pitta;
for it is said: "Vāyu arises from desire, grief, and fear; pitta from anger; and all three impurities [arise from these]."
"Due to possession by spirits, those who share the characteristics of spirits become provoked" (Cikitsāsthāna,

chapter 3). Although it is stated that there is provocation of all three doṣas in the case of possession by spirits, nevertheless, on the strength of this very statement, vāta and pitta alone hold predominance therein.

He states the distinction between the exogenous (*āgantu*) and the endogenous (*nijā*) [fever] with the words "sa" and so forth. The specific diagnostic signs (*viśeṣaliṅgatā*) of the exogenous type have been explained in the preceding commentary on its etiology (*vyathāpūrvaka-vyākhyāna*). The specific causes of its origin (*samutthānaviśeṣa*), such as trauma (*abhighāta*) and the like, have also been mentioned. Furthermore, the specific treatment (*upakramaviśeṣa*) is stated here by the very statement, "it is treated with common therapeutic measures" (*sādhāraṇena karmaṇā copacaryate*); by "common" is meant that which relies on both divine power (*daiva*) and rational means (*yukti*). For reliance on divine power (*daivavyapāśraya*) consists of offerings, auspicious rites, oblations (*bali-maṅgala-homa*), and so forth, while reliance on rational means (*yuktivyapāśraya*) consists of light food, fasting (*apatarpaṇa*), gruel (*yavāgū*), decoctions (*kaṣāya-pāna*), and the like.

"Nature has been described" means that the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of fevers caused by wind (*vāta*) and the other humors is also described as being conditioned by etiological factors (*nidāna*) and so forth.
The connection is that [fever] is of two kinds due to the distinction between endogenous (*nija*) and exogenous (*āgantu*).

Regarding the statement "one's own [fever] is of two kinds," etc., the twofold nature is due to the distinction between the intentions of cold and heat (arising from being produced by combined or uncombined factors); it is threefold due to the distinction of the three *doṣas*; and it is fourfold due to the distinction of each being produced by *vāta* and the other *doṣas*. Within that fourfold classification, dual (*dvandva*) fevers are excluded, because they resemble the individual fevers caused by *vāta* and the others; however, the fever caused by all three *doṣas* (*tridoṣaja*) is mentioned separately because it is either incurable or difficult to cure.

With the words "tasyemāni" (these belong to it) and so forth, he describes the premonitory symptoms common to all fevers. Some authorities state that these premonitory symptoms apply to exogenous fever as well; others, however, maintain that these belong only to endogenous fevers, whereas for the exogenous type, pain alone constitutes the premonitory symptom.
Here too, as before, there is a distinction between the lack of desire for food and anorexia.

Weakness (*daurbalya*) should be understood as the loss of physical strength and the loss of mental strength characterized by a lack of vitality (*alpaprāṇatā*); alternatively, weakness refers to the wasting away of muscle tissue (*māṃsāpacaya*).

Procrastination (*dīrghasūtratā*), meaning performing tasks with excessive delay, and the prodromal symptoms of fever (*jvarapūrvarūpāṇi*) occur; the phrase "prior to the heat" (*prāksantāpāt*) means that these prodromal symptoms appear before the heat that constitutes the actual form of the fever.

Furthermore, by the statement "they persistently follow the suffering of heat," he shows that even when fever is fully manifest, certain prodromal symptoms such as a bad taste in the mouth and loss of appetite (aruci) may still occur. However, one should not describe the persistence of such prodromal symptoms as a fatal sign (riṣṭa); for it has been stated that a fatal sign consists in the excessive persistence of *all* the prodromal symptoms.
Indeed, the authoritative text says: "All the prodromal symptoms mentioned regarding fever, when occurring in excess..."

"Death, preceded by fever, enters him whom [these symptoms] enter. Alternatively, this verse has a different meaning altogether, which we shall explain in the section on the sense organs (*indriya*). Furthermore, the status of anorexia and other symptoms as "prodromal signs" (*pūrvarūpa*) is not undermined by their occurring in manifest fever, because anorexia and the rest constitute "signs" (*liṅga*) when accompanied by other specific symptoms, whereas they are "prodromal signs" when devoid of those other symptoms.

Regarding the phrase "the symptoms of fever for each [type] individually," the word *liṅga* (symptom) refers here to the etiology (*nidāna*), premonitory signs (*pūrvarūpa*), and so forth, both in detail and in summary. In detail, these are those described for fevers caused by Vāta and the other [doshas]; in summary, they are those arising from combinations (*saṃsarga*) and the aggregate (*sannipāta*). The intention is that what has been stated here in summary should be elaborated upon in the section on therapeutics (*cikitsita*).
Now, in order to demonstrate the great power of fever (*jvara*), he describes its mode of origin, beginning with the words "Fever, however...

By the phrase "originating from the wrath of Maheśvara," he refers to the origin of fever that will be described in the section on the treatment of fever (*jvaracikitsita*) in the passage beginning, "In the second age, Śarva was established in a vow of non-wrath" (Ci. A. 3). Furthermore, by characterizing it as arising from wrath, he demonstrates that even though fever is produced by *kapha* (phlegm), it possesses a fiery (*āgneya*) nature; for wrath is of the nature of fire, and therefore fever, being composed of that, is likewise so. For this very reason it has been said: "There is no heat without bile (*pitta*), and there is no fever without heat."

"Therefore, one should avoid substances antagonistic to pitta when pitta is predominant" (Vāgbhaṭa, Cikitsāsthāna 1). Furthermore, the fact that fever originates from the wrath of Rudra does not contradict its arising from greed, malice, and harmful conduct; for it is shown that fever itself, though born from the wrath of Rudra, manifested among humans in ancient times through the acquisition of sinful behavior characterized by greed and malice, and that for all living beings, fever alone is the destroyer of life at the time of death.

Regarding the phrase "causing affliction to the body, senses, and mind," the specific definition of "affliction" for each should be understood from the section on the treatment of fever (*jvaracikitsita*), starting with: "Distraction, restlessness, and exhaustion are the characteristics of mental affliction" (*Ci.

A. 3*). The word "it" (*iti*) indicates the cause; therefore, because it is characterized by such things as arising from the wrath of the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*) as previously stated, [it is called *tāpa*].

"Like a sovereign of all diseases" means he is the lord of all maladies. By various names—such as *pākala* among elephants, *kherika* among cattle, *indrajāla* among fish, and *bhrāmaraka* among birds—all living beings are born with fever and die with fever. Why, then, is this fever, which consists of torment, not perceived at their birth or death? To this he says: "He is great delusion (*mahāmoha*). The meaning is that at birth and death, the fever takes the form of great delusion, rather than being of the nature of physical torment.
For this very reason it has been said: "The influence of fever is greatest at birth and at death" (Ci.
A. 3). By the words "by that," etc., he describes its nature as great delusion (*mahāmoha*) at birth;
"prāgdaihikam" refers to what was performed in a previous life.

[Objection: Is it not the case that recollection of the pre-mortem state is logical due to the persistence of the pure mind (*śuddhasattva*)? For there is a statement: "When one is joined with that very same pure mind, then one remembers even that which transcends [one's current] birth" (Śārīrasthāna 3). [Response: No, because that [statement] is an exception (*apavāda*) regarding the persistence of the pure mind; setting that aside, elsewhere it should be understood that fever causes the forgetting of the pre-mortem state. He describes the state of great delusion (*mahāmoha*) at the time of death: "Of all living beings," and so forth.
The meaning is that fever itself is indeed the very form of great delusion (*mahāmoha*); therefore, the sense is that all those who are dying enter into great delusion.
Now, he states the aphorism on treatment which was previously indicated: "In that regard," and so forth.

Although fasting (*laṅghana*) will be prescribed for fevers and other conditions in the section on therapeutics, nevertheless, the provision here for occasional light meals is not contradictory, because even light eating possesses the quality of producing lightness (*lāghava*), which is the very essence of fasting. Alternatively, one should understand that light eating is intended for those fevers caused by Vāta and others where fasting is not to be performed; furthermore, depletion (*apatarpaṇa*) is indeed fasting itself.

Now, as to why even in a fever caused by Vāta, a light meal—which is Vāta-provoking—or depletion should be administered, he says: "Because it arises from the stomach" (*āmāśayasamutthatvāt*), and so forth.
The meaning is that even *vāta*, due to its connection with the stomach (*āmāśaya*), should be slightly restricted in terms of dieting, depending on its location;
for there is this saying: "One should indeed conquer the [affliction] first by not contradicting its location. (36)

Regarding the phrase "prepared with its own specific medicinal herbs," one might ask: how is it that ghee prepared with substances that pacify vāta and other doshas in vāta-type fevers and so forth should be used in all cases? To this he says: "For ghee, due to its unctuousness... and so on; and "due to processing [to remove] kapha" means through processing with pungent, bitter, and other substances that alleviate kapha.

Although, by the statement "prepared with its own specific medicine," ghee processed with Vata-alleviating substances is prescribed even for Vata, nevertheless, in the case of Vata, ghee is indeed Vata-alleviating because of its unctuousness (*sneha*), which is the opposite of dryness (*rūkṣa*); in Pitta as well, it is so because of its coldness (*śaitya*), which is the opposite of heat (*uṣṇa*); but in Kapha, since ghee possesses qualities such as unctuousness and coldness that are identical [to those of Kapha], there is no inherent contradictory quality; rather, it shows that through processing (*saṃskāra*), it is indeed beneficial.
The phrase "and the heat" refers to the heat produced by the influence of fever (*jvara*), and not to the heat of Pitta, because the latter is already included by the mention of Pitta itself.
By this removal of the fever's heat through clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*), its antagonism toward the disease of fever is demonstrated.

Here, after stating that clarified butter pacifies *vāta*, and while the pacification of *pitta* ought to have been stated next, the pacification of *kapha* is mentioned instead; this is because the quality of coldness, which is the cause for pacifying *pitta*, shares common properties with the remaining qualities to be described as the antagonists of the disease in the form of heat. However, if the pacification of *pitta* were stated here in the middle, then after subsequently mentioning "kapha" due to processing (*saṃskāra*), one would have had to say "heat" due to coldness.

However, in those recensions of the verse where the counteraction of disease by ghee is not mentioned separately, the sequence "it pacifies vāta through its unctuousness" and so forth has correctly placed pitta immediately after vāta. Therefore, because it is the counteragent to both the *doṣas* and the diseases, the statement "in chronic fevers" (*jīrṇajvareṣu*) prohibits its use in the presence of undigested matter (*āmaja-jvara*); for in the state of *āma*, ghee is contraindicated due to its similarity of qualities.
"Peace" (śāntim) means "the pacification of distress";
having intended this and accepted it with such an understanding, [one gives] ghee in the case of chronic fever—"gives"—is the ellipsis.

Now, one might ask: in this verse, which describes the qualities of clarified butter (sarpiḥ), why is the subduing of the heat that constitutes the disease not mentioned? We reply: because the heat of fever is not distinct from the heat of bile (pitta), it is already achieved simply by the pacification of the bile.

Now, if this is so, should the *ūṣman* (heat) not be recited separately in the prose version (*gadyapāṭha*)? We reply: whatever bodily *ūṣman* exists is indeed of the nature of *pitta*, since it is stated: "There is no heat without *pitta*" (Vāgbhaṭa, Cikitsāsthāna, Chapter 1), and likewise: "From *pitta*, through the heat of that heat, digestion arises in human beings" (Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 17). However, this *ūṣman* is never identical with *pitta* even when they are in equilibrium, as in the case of *kaphaja-jvara*; nor does it become weak when *pitta* is in excess, as in the case of *pittāgnimāndya*. Thus, *ūṣman* is both distinct from and non-distinct from *pitta*. Taking their distinction into account, the fever-heat (*jvaroṣman*) is recited separately in the prose version; however, in the verse version (*ślokapāṭha*), it is not recited separately because of the intention to express their non-difference.

In fever, however, the heat of the *pitta* increases through the influence of the fever; and that influence should be understood as belonging to the fever itself—which consists of a specific combination of the *doṣas* and the *dūṣyas*—and likewise to the specific living being described in such passages as "Fever has three feet and three heads. Now, one might ask: how does ghee (*sarpiṣ*) destroy *pitta*, given that while coldness—the opposite of *pitta*—is present in ghee, so too is unctuousness (*sneha*), which is similar to *pitta*?

This is not so, because in the definition of *pitta* ("It is unctuous," Sūtra 1), the word "with" (*sa-*) is used in the sense of "slight" (*īṣad-artha*) to indicate only a small amount of unctuousness; whereas heat is the predominant quality in *pitta*.

Although bile (*pitta*) is originated by water, nevertheless, having overcome its coldness, the heat produced by fire becomes predominant therein; likewise, the moisture produced by water in bile is overcome by the dryness of fire, but the liquidity produced by water is not overcome by fire, for it is observed that in water contacted by fire there is liquidity, a slight degree of moisture, and heat.

Or rather, what is the use of this illustration of heated water? This production of beings is caused solely by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Therefore, even though substances are composed of the five elements, only certain qualities manifest, and not all of them; for example, as stated in the *Sūtrasthāna*, rice possesses sweetness produced by water, but not heaviness. Furthermore, although bile is generally unctuous (*sasneha*), it may occasionally become dry due to an excess of the fire element, as in chronic fever (*jīrṇajvara*); therefore, there is no fault in the fact that unctuous and cold clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) is beneficial in that condition.

Therefore, it is stated in the Cikitsā-sthāna: "Dry heat causes fever" (Ci. A. 3), and so forth. Nor should it be argued: "If even the innate unctuousness of pitta disappears, then why does the dryness of vāta not likewise disappear? For the qualities [of substances] are indeed diverse—some are non-rejectable and some are rejectable. Among these, those that are not always observed, such as the coldness of vāta and the unctuousness of pitta, are precisely the ones that are rejectable; others are not, because they are observed to be exactly so. Thus, "possessing equal qualities" means possessing equal qualities in every respect.

One might object: "If phlegm is destroyed through processing (*saṃskāra*), then phlegm is destroyed by the processing itself; what then is the function of the ghee? To this he says, "Nothing else," and so forth.
"Nothing else" refers to substances such as oil;
"it follows the processing" means that it performs the function of the substance used for the processing.

By this, he demonstrates the following: when ghee is processed with a specific substance and in a specific measure, and if oil or other fats were processed in that same manner elsewhere, then ghee alone—compared to other fats—performs the function of the processing substance more specifically. This is the superior potency of ghee; therefore, for the conquest of *kapha* through processing, ghee alone should be used. This point has been explained in detail in the chapter on oleation (Snehādhyāya), verses 37–40.

One might ask: "Since the passage beginning with 'Indeed, [oil] pacifies vāta through unctuousness' was already stated in prose, for what purpose is it stated again in verse? To this he says: "That which was stated in prose," and so forth. The phrase "for the sake of its manifestation and determination" (*tadvyaktivyavasāyārtham*) means that "its manifestation" (*tadvyakti*) is the manifestation—that is, the clarity—of the meaning stated in prose; and "determination" (*vyavasāya*) means firm resolve or grasping. Since the statement is made again in verse for the purpose of clarifying the previously stated meaning, the sense is that because it possesses a different purpose, there is no fault of redundancy (*punarukti*).
It is a matter established by common worldly experience that expressing [a teaching] in verse (*śloka*) makes it easier to grasp than when expressed in prose (*gadya*).
In this context, the mention of "prose" is illustrative; therefore, it should be understood that what is expressed in verse may also be stated in verse—as in the *Āragvadhīya* chapter.

Likewise, it should be understood that what is expressed in prose may also be stated in prose—as in the passage where, after explaining the causes and so forth at length, it is said: "Thus, unwholesome contact between the senses and their objects, intellectual error (*prajñāparādha*), and the effects of time (*pariṇāma*)" (Sūtra-sthāna 11), and so on.

Thus, although it has been stated in verse, it is also stated in prose; for example, after stating in the first chapter [of the Sūtrasthāna] with the verse beginning, “Just as it was proclaimed by Brahmā” (Sūtra 1.1), it is stated elsewhere in that same chapter: “The two Aśvins gave me this Āyurveda” (Cikitsā 1.4).

Here, it should be understood that the expression in verse is intended for ease of comprehension; alternatively, it may be for the purpose of clarifying the specific details, as is appropriate in each case.

Therefore, it should be understood that the detailed exposition is for the purpose of clarifying the meaning, while the concise exposition is for the purpose of determination; thus, through the detailed and concise expositions, respectively, clarification and determination are achieved.
In this regard, the clarification of the meaning through detailed exposition is indeed manifest, whereas the concise exposition allows for easy comprehension in comparison to the detailed one.

In the *Saṅgraha*, although the synonyms for causes were stated previously and thereafter the threefold nature of causes, nevertheless, in accordance with metrical requirements (*chanda*), they are stated here in reverse order.
"Name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) refers to synonyms established through etymological derivation (*yogarūḍha*);
"the fivefold disease" refers to the divisions beginning with that of Agni.

Regarding the reading *‘gadaparyāyanāmāni’*: the mention of synonyms for the [specific] symptoms (*liṅga*) is included because all the meanings contained within the text beginning with “the perception of that” (*tasyopalabdhiḥ*) have already been grasped by the very term “the fivefold seizure of disease” (*vyādhipañcavidhagraha*). However, in the reading *‘gadalakṣaṇaparyāyān’*, there is no prior objection at all; furthermore, this reading is not very well-known.

As for the causes of fever, the remote cause is dryness (*rūkṣa*) and so forth, while the proximate cause is wind (*vāta*) and so forth; likewise, the remote cause is the wrath of Rudra, whereas the proximate cause is dryness and so forth.

Although the premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*) were mentioned after the specific symptoms (*rūpa*), they have nevertheless been placed first here for the sake of metrical convenience. Alternatively, the premonitory symptoms have been placed first by the author to indicate that the unmanifested characteristics of fevers arising from Vāta and other doshas constitute the premonitory stage of those specific fevers; for indeed, the unmanifested signs of Vāta and other fevers are the premonitory symptoms.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Fever" (*jvaranidāna*), in the *Nidānasthāna* of the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
1 [Nidānasthāna, Chapter 2 (32 of 120)]:
Because the onset of *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders) occurs due to the heat of fever at its initial manifestation, the diagnosis of *raktapitta* is stated immediately after that of fever.

By the passage beginning with "pittaṃ yathābhūtam" (bile as it truly is), [the author] shows that bile itself is called *raktapitta* (blood-bile) by virtue of its specific state, and not that *raktapitta* is a combination of blood and bile. By the passage beginning with "yadā jantuḥ" (when a person...), the etiology is stated.

*Yavaka* is a specific variety of rice; *uddāla* is wild *kodrava* (Paspalum scrobiculatum); and although *koradūṣa* is said to alleviate *pitta* in food and drink, it should nevertheless be understood that when combined with *niṣpāva* and other such substances, its nature as a cause of *raktapitta* arises through the power of the combination (*saṃyoga-mahiman*). Similarly, this should be understood regarding milk and other items mentioned here as causes of *raktapitta*.
*Dadhimaṇḍa* is whey; *udaśvit* is buttermilk mixed with half water; *kaṭvara* is waterless buttermilk, or alternatively, sour buttermilk;
*madhuśigru* is a small variety of *śobhāñjanaka* (Moringa oleifera).
*Khaḍayūṣa* is known as *rāgakarpūra*;
*sumukha* and others ending with *phaṇijjhaka* are varieties of *parṇāsa*.
"With *upadaṃśa*" means that after eating radishes and so forth, one eats food such as barley-gruel (*yāvaka*).
*Madhūlaka* is a specific variety of wheat; *śukta* is a specific type of fermented condiment;
*piṣṭānna-uttarabhūyiṣṭham* refers to that [meal] in which flour-based food constitutes the majority of the subsequent meal.
"Ativelam" means again and again; "rauhiṇīkam" refers to the *rohiṇī* vegetable;
"śauktikaiḥ" refers to *badarī* fruits.
The word "raw" (āmam) is connected with what follows;
it means that [the pitta] exceeds its own measure and increases.

By the phrase "that very [portion]" (yadeva), he demonstrates that even when pitta is thus aggravated, only that portion which possesses the aforementioned pathogenesis (samprāpti) vitiates the blood, and no other.

"Weighted by the flow of blood" means weighted by the increased flow of blood; "swollen" means, that is to say, dilated; "it would obstruct" refers to [the vessels] being filled with increased blood—this is the ellipsis. However, in the reading where the word "attains" (*pratipadyate*) is used, "blood" (*śoṇitam*) is the ellipsis, meaning that it attains the blood.
This [term] is a qualifier for "those originating from the liver and spleen"—namely, "those carrying blood."
The letter *ca* is used for emphasis;
as he will state in the treatment of *raktapitta*: "It exists presiding over both the spleen and the liver, for the blood-carrying channels are their very roots in embodied beings" (Ci. A. 4).
Thus, when pitta is a corrupter of blood, it receives the designation "raktapitta" (blood-bile); regarding this, he says: "From association," and so forth;
"from association" means from connection with the blood.

"Because it conforms to the smell and color of blood" means that it possesses a smell and color similar to blood. By this, three etymological explanations are shown: first, "Raktapitta is bile (pitta) associated with blood (rakta)"; second, "Pitta [acting] upon blood as the corrupted substrate (dūṣya)"; and third, "Raktapitta is bile that resembles blood. And it is said in the Cikitsā-sthāna: "But that [is called Raktapitta] due to association, corruption, and the similarity of its smell and color."
"Because blood is accompanied by pitta, it is called *raktapitta* by the wise" (Cikitsāsthāna, chapter 4).

This indeed is the general definition of *raktapitta*: that it conforms to the smell and color of blood. However, its specific definitions must be understood here according to the distinctions of upward flow (*ūrdhva*) and so forth, based on its association with *kapha* and other doshas. Furthermore, in the section on treatment (*cikitsita*), the author will describe its characteristics starting with "thick and pale" (Ci. A. 4).
The premonitory symptoms of vomiting include a loathsome appearance due to discoloration and foul odor,
eruptions (piḍakolikā), impurities of the eyes, bodily pain, and aching of the limbs.
He describes the specific signs known as complications (upadrava), which indicate the incurability of a disease and its underlying nature— beginning with the words "The complications,
however," and so forth. By this, it is shown that because a complication functions as a sign (liṅga), it is not distinct from the fivefold etiology (nidāna-pañcaka).

In the case of *raktapitta*, these complications (*upadrava*) are stated to be "certain" because they generally occur; however, in the case of fever (*jvara*), complications are not necessarily present, and for that reason they are not mentioned there. In the same way, the description of complications in *gulma* and other diseases should also be understood as referring to what generally occurs.
By listing "hoarseness of voice" (*svarabheda*) separately, [the author] indicates that hoarseness is also generally present.

In order to demonstrate the specific characteristics such as being curable (*sādhya*) and so forth, as well as the connection with phlegm (*kapha*) produced by the specific channels, he states the [two] paths, beginning with "the two paths" and so on.

By the statement "in a body with abundant phlegm, due to association with phlegm," he shows that in upward-moving *raktapitta*, there is a connection with phlegm even when that phlegm is produced by other causes.

As for the fact that phlegm is produced by the etiological factors of *raktapitta*, that is not necessarily the case; for this very reason, it is said: "Unctuous-warm and warm-dry are the causes of *raktapitta*."
In passages such as "the answer regarding downward movement is generally... (*Ci. A. 4*), [the author] employed the word *prāyaḥ* (generally);
in the same way, it should be explained here in the phrase "but when there is much wind" (*bahuvāte tu*).
From the "openings" (*khebhyaḥ*) means from the apertures (*randhrebhyaḥ*).
"Because it is to be treated with purgation"—this he will explain himself in the verse [8–9].
He states the prior origin [of the disease] in order to establish that *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorder) is also of fiery (*āgneya*) nature: "Blood... and so forth.

Anger (*kopayukta*) is indignation (*amarṣa*), and indignation is dogmatic insistence (*abhiniveśa*); furthermore, the distinction between anger and indignation is stated elsewhere, as follows: "Indignation, agitation, nakedness, threats, charging, heat, and wrath" (Ci. A. 9).
[The phrase] "by means of satiation" refers to that which moves downward, while "by means of depletion" refers to that which moves upward.
"Contact" (*saṃsparśana*) refers to pearls and other such items that are touched.
[The author] analyzes the suitability for purgation (*virecana*) in one who has ascended upward, beginning with the words "purgation," and so forth.

In upward-moving *raktapitta* (hemoptysis), *pitta* is the primary factor and *kapha* is the secondary associate (*anubandha*); thus, the disease known as *raktapitta* must be conquered. In that regard, for the purpose of conquering *pitta*, purgation (*virecana*) is the supreme medicine, based on the statement: "Purgation [is the best] among those things that remove *pitta*" (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 25). This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, regarding the *kapha* which is present there as the nature of the associate, for the purpose of conquering that, it is not inferior or low, but rather middling; for the authoritative text states: "The laxative (*sraṃsana*) should remove either *pitta* alone or *kapha-pitta* when located in the seat of *pitta* (the stomach)" (Cikitsā Sthāna, Chapter 3).

"And it is appropriate in that case" means that in the case of upward-moving *raktapitta*, that purgative is appropriate because it acts by removing [the humor] along its own path (*pratimārgaharaṇa*);

by this, its antagonism to the disease is expressed, since it primarily pacifies *pitta*, which is the principal cause of the disease, as well as *kapha* when moderately provoked, due to being a moderate medicine; and because it removes [the humor] along its own path, purgation is an excellent medicine for upward-moving [blood].

Regarding the phrase "and sweet [substance] is indeed medicine" (*madhuraṃ caiva bheṣajam*), the word *eva* here has the sense of *api* (also/even). Thus, the meaning is that bitter and astringent substances are certainly medicine because they are antagonistic to pitta and kapha, respectively; furthermore, even a sweet substance becomes medicine when kapha has been conquered through fasting (*laṅghana*) and other such measures. (12–14) He explains the unsuitability of emesis for downward-moving [doshas] with the words beginning "for emesis... (*vamanaṃ hi...*).

Emesis is not the best treatment for removing *pitta* that is the root of *raktapitta*; for emesis removes *pitta* accompanied by *kapha*, and it is not primarily applied when *pitta* is the main factor, being inferior in pacifying it. Furthermore, emesis is secondary in the removal of *vāta*, and because emesis is unsuitable for removing *vāta*, it leads to improper administration (*ayoga*). Thus, although that emesis might lead to proper administration (*yoga*) by way of removing [the humor] along its own path, it leads to improper administration due to the unsuitability of *pitta* and *vāta* according to the principle already stated.

The construction is that astringent (kaṣāya) and bitter (tikta) tastes lead to improper application (ayoga), because astringent and bitter tastes are antagonistic to vāta; thus, only the single sweet (madhura) taste remains as the medicine for downward-moving (adhoga) raktapitta. By this, its status as having few medicinal options is established;
the point is that sour, salty, and pungent tastes have no applicability at all in raktapitta, as they are contrary to pitta.

Regarding the phrase "from what was stated previously," he explains the unsuitability for emesis and purgation by noting both their lack of appropriateness for those therapies and their non-medicinal nature; the statement beginning with "for not...
uses the general term "purification" (saṃśodhana) to indicate the exclusion of both enemas and head-purgations as well.

That which is a purgative for the lower part provokes the blood-bile (raktapitta) of the lower part, and that which is an emetic for the upper part provokes the blood-bile of the upper part; therefore, there is no purification (śodhana) for blood-bile that flows through both pathways.

Now, he states that purification must indeed be appropriate [to the specific condition], just as an emetic is used for phlegm-induced vomiting, even in the case of blood-bile: "And according to the pathway," etc.
The meaning is that, due to the specific nature of the disease of blood-bile, the medicine must act by removing it along its own respective pathway, and nothing else.
Now, lest there be a purificatory medicine (saṃśodhana) in this case, [the author] says that there may be a palliative medicine (saṃśamana): "In this very way," and so forth.

The meaning is that because it follows both pathways and is associated with both Vāta and Kapha, just as there is no purificatory treatment that is appropriate, likewise there is also no palliative treatment, because there is no single remedy that simultaneously pacifies both Vāta and Kapha; "it does not exist at all" means that not even a trace of it exists.
This very point clarifies the absence of a medicine for pacification: "In combined [humors]," and so forth.

"In combined" should be understood as in cases of *sannipāta* (the simultaneous derangement of all three humors). "All-conquering" (*sarvajit*) means that which conquers the *pitta* which is the root of the *vāta* and *kapha* that have become secondary complications (*anubandha*). The sense is this: for sweetness produces *kapha*, while bitterness and astringency produce *vāta*, and the remaining tastes produce only *pitta*.
Alternatively, it should be construed as follows: "In this very way, without medicine, there is no pacification of *raktapitta*.

Regarding the phrase "having a threefold future outcome" (*trividhodarka*), it means having a threefold result for the future; and that consists of the forms of being curable (*sādhya*), manageable (*yāpya*), or incurable (*pratyākhyeya*).
In the introduction to the section on incurability, he states the causes for the onset of incurability that are common to other diseases as well, beginning with "ebhyas tu" (but from these), etc.;
"due to the absence of requisites" means due to the absence of medicinal drugs.
"Due to wickedness" (*daurātmyāt*) means because the patient lacks self-control (*anātmavattva*).

Regarding the term "due to non-treatment" (*akarmataḥ*), the negative particle (*nañ*) is used here in the sense of censure, as in the word "sonless" (*aputra*); thus, "due to non-treatment" means due to improper medical treatment.
