Alternatively, by the statement "some [diseases arise] from non-treatment, i.e., from unrighteousness (*adharma*) which generates incurable diseases," he demonstrates that not all [conditions], such as *tilālaka* and *maśaka*, necessarily become incurable simply through lack of treatment, since even those may be cured despite the absence of treatment.
Demonstrating that blood-bile (raktapitta) caused by the defects of servants and the like is incurable, he says: "In that case," and so forth.
"In that case" refers to blood-bile; "one [type] is incurable" means that it would be solely incurable.

"Because of the progression through the curable and the palliable" means because of proceeding by way of both the curable (*sādhya*) and the palliable (*yāpya*) paths, that is, by following both paths. Alternatively, "the progression (*parikrama*) of the curable and the palliable" refers to the progression through the curable and the palliable; therein, the progression of the curable is the movement along the path of the curable, and likewise, the progression of the palliable is the movement along the path of the incurable (*asādhya*).

Furthermore, this progression along the path is indeed incurable, whether through the abandonment or non-abandonment of the path. First, regarding non-abandonment, incurability exists precisely because both paths are present. Regarding abandonment, incurability has already been stated; for it will be said in the Cikitsita section: "If one should move from one path to another, that blood is incurable" (Ci. A. 4).
Alternatively, the phrase "from the progression of the curable and the palliable" means from the progression of a curable [disease] into a palliable state.
He states the symptomatic incurability even of *raktapitta* that moves upward, beginning with "of *raktapitta*" and so forth.
These colors, such as black and others, arise from connection with the deep-seated tissues (*dhātu*); therefore, its incurability is indeed logical.

Regarding the phrase "and the dyeing of cloth": it should be understood that even though the cloth has been washed, it still takes on color, and the stain does not depart by washing alone; otherwise, the statement "all [stains] become dye for the cloth" would be meaningless. Alternatively, there is the reading *arañjanam* (non-dyeing). Thus, the transformation of dyed cloth—whereby the dyeing agent fails to dye—is the corruption;
because of its connection with another verbal root (*pū*), it means "extremely putrid" and thus "foul-smelling."
"Accompanied by all calamities" means that the visible objects such as jars and cloths, as well as the sky (ākāśa), are possessed of the aforementioned calamities such as weakness and so forth.
"Red" means red in color;

although even space is considered visible according to the Mīmāṃsaka school, nevertheless, it is generally in space itself that redness is perceived in cases of incurable *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disease), and thus it is not redundant.
By the statement "with effort," he shows that even now, maintenance does not occur without effort.
The summary begins with "the cause," and so forth.
The phrase "the manifestation of the name" refers to [the condition] arising from contact with blood and so forth;
by the word "not," neither [is it] "incurability. By this, "manageable" (yāpya) is also included, for "manageable" is a sub-division of "incurable.
The description of causes such as the suitability of purgation here encompasses the state of being caused.
One from whom delusion and other such afflictions have departed and vanished is thus described.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Raktapitta" (Hemorrhagic Disorders), in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka Saṃhitā* composed by the venerable Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Section on Diagnosis (*Nidānasthāna*).
2 [Nidānasthāna, Chapter 3 (33 of 120):
Since the gulma arose following the hemorrhagic fever (*raktapitta*) at the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, this is the etiology of gulma following *raktapitta*.

In this context, the mention of "five" indicates that there are additional types of *gulma* beyond those [explicitly named] in the treatment section; for it will be stated later: "One should designate three other *gulmas* with mixed symptoms for the purpose of formulating the medicine" (Ci.
A. 5). *Nicaya* means *sannipāta* (the combination of all three *doṣas*); a *gulma* caused by that is a *nicaya-gulma*.
Since dual (*dvandvaja*) *gulmas* are treated here simply by combining the respective treatments for the *vāta*-type and other *gulmas*, they are not mentioned separately.

A *gulma* arising from the combination of all three doshas (*sannipāta-gulma*) cannot be cured by the combined therapeutic measures for *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha* gulmas, due to the power of their conjunction. Therefore, because it possesses an additional quality of incurability, the *nicaya-gulma* (the "accumulated" gulma) is mentioned separately.

To demonstrate this very incurability in this particular *gulma*, the term *nicaya* was used instead of *sannipāta*, even though the word *sannipāta* also applies to curable conditions such as fevers. For this *nicaya* is indeed of an extremely incurable nature.

In the passage beginning with "samutthāna" (etiology), pain (*vedanā*) which is included within the symptoms (*liṅga*) is mentioned separately in order to show that, among disorders such as abdominal tumors (*gulma*) where pain is the predominant manifestation, the specific diagnosis is generally determined by the pain itself. It should be understood that the reason the pathogenesis (*samprāpti*) is not discussed here is precisely because it does not serve to distinguish the specific types of *gulma*; for the knowledge of *gulma* is the subject at hand here. The general pathogenesis, however, differentiated by its various divisions such as number and so forth, has already been stated in the section on the etiology of all diseases. This is the intended meaning.

Although the onset (*samprāpti*) occurring at a different time from childhood does indeed indicate specific features such as its being caused by *vāta* and so forth, it is nevertheless not given weight because it is minor and because it is already subsumed under the symptoms (*liṅga*).

For the onset of *vāta* and the other [humors] at times such as the end of the day or the end of digestion is recited in various places precisely within the midst of the symptoms themselves; therefore, that [onset] is well-established by the very inclusion of the symptoms.

Although the premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa) that specifically indicate gulma caused by vāta and the other [doshas] have not been explicitly mentioned separately, nevertheless, the specific premonitory symptoms in the form of the unmanifested particular signs (*viśeṣaliṅgāvyaktatā*) have indeed been stated through the very description of those specific signs. Therefore, it is entirely logical to include the premonitory symptoms among the etiology (*nidāna*) and other factors that specifically indicate vāta-gulma and the rest. Alternatively, even though the specific premonitory symptoms are mentioned here in a general sense relative to other diseases such as *raktapitta*, they should be understood as being specific [to gulma].

Because of the statement "especially for one of vāta constitution," it is shown that even for those of pitta constitution and others who practice as prescribed, vāta-gulma may arise; however, it occurs "excessively" for one of vāta constitution.
This is indicated by the phrase "or especially cold," which means "extremely cold";
the word "atimātram" (excessively) is the appropriate reading.

The phrase "or there is a desire for excessive sexual intercourse, physical exercise, and so forth" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]; by the mention of a desire for sexual intercourse and the like, one indicates the actual practice of such acts.

The term "become hardened due to dryness" (*raukṣyāt kaṭhinībhūtam*) is a qualification of the great channel (*mahāsrotas*); and that hardness of the visceral cavity (*koṣṭha*) is logically established both by the dryness of the aggravated *vāyu* and by the dryness caused by the aforementioned fever, emaciation, and other factors.

"Having pervaded" (*āplutya*) means having filled; it is stated elsewhere regarding the *koṣṭha* itself: "Whose body here is entirely pervaded by the vital air" (*āplutaṃ māruteneha śarīraṃ yasya kevalam*). (Haṭhayogapradīpikā 1.35)
10) Thus; "āplutam" means pervaded.

However, when the reading is "raukṣyāt kaṭhinībhūtaḥ," then it is an adjective qualifying the wind (*vāta*); the hardness of the wind is to be understood as its extreme density due to intense provocation.
"Piṇḍitaḥ" means coiled or circularized.
The word "nābhyām" (in the navel) is the division [of the compound];

and by the second occurrence of the word "piṇḍitaḥ" (massed), the massing of the region of the *gulma* itself is expressed through the protrusion of flesh and so forth. However, there is no tautology, because the first word "piṇḍitaḥ" refers to the massing of the *vāyu* (wind).
The word "anekavidhān" (of many kinds) is the division [of the compound].
"Various kinds of knots"— meaning those differentiated by distinctions such as being long, round, or thick—
are called "gulmas" because they are massed together; by this, he shows that the designation "gulma" is based on their similarity to the clusters of creepers and the like,
and that it "swells," meaning it expands.
"Experiencing extensive or minute sensations in an indeterminate manner" means that at times there is extensive sensation and at times minute sensation, occurring without fixed regularity.
Regarding this, he states the reason: "because of the mobility of the wind.

*Āyāma* is expansion; *harṣa* is horripilation; *pralaya* is destruction; and *udaya* is birth. The meaning is that the birth and destruction of throbbing and other such phenomena occur in manifold ways.
In this case as well, it should be understood that mobility alone is the cause of the wind; for instance,

the phrase "his hairs stand on end" refers specifically to the manifestation of sensation, whereas in cases such as throbbing and the like, joy occurs even without sensation— this is how it should be known.

"In the stomach (āmāśaya) affected by dryness" means that it has been made dry by causes that produce dryness; alternatively, the construction should be understood as "for one who is practicing emesis while the stomach is affected by dryness."

By the statement that [the gulma] "is formed in a portion of the stomach (āmāśaya)," it is shown that the bladder (vasti) is not the location for pitta-gulma or kapha-gulma; for the text says: "The area between the navel and the breasts is known as the stomach of a living being" (Vi. A. 2). However, the bladder is indeed a location for vāta-gulma; for this very reason, it is referred to there in general terms as the "large intestine" (mahāsrotas), and by the inclusion of the term "large intestine," the bladder is also included. Likewise, in the case of vāta-gulma alone, the phrase "in the heart or the bladder" and so forth is used;
furthermore, specific pitta-related pains such as burning and piercing have been explained repeatedly.
The burning sensation (*davathu*) is what is commonly called "dhak-dhak" in the world.
Regarding the phrase "in one suffering from a phlegm-tumor (*śleṣmagulma*)," it means "one who has no appetite"; alternatively, there is a reading: "one who is excessively satiated."

Although *rājayakṣmā* (consumption) arises from all three *doṣas*, it should nevertheless be understood that it is produced by the very same three *doṣas* generated through the power of the disease itself, specifically in the case of *kaphagulma*.
[This is so] because of the contradiction in treatment (*vipratiṣiddhopakrama*), meaning that the treatments for *vāta* and the other *doṣas* are mutually opposed.
In this context, the presence of contradictory treatments should be understood as resulting from a discordant combination of the *vikṛti* (transformed) doshas;

therefore, even if there is a contradiction in treatment—such as measures opposed to vāta and the others—in cases like fever caused by all three doshas (*tridoṣaja*) which is curable, it does not render the condition incurable.

Since the statement "only for a woman" regarding blood-tumors (*śoṇitagulma*) already implies that it does not occur in a man, the further mention of "not for a man" is for the sake of clarity. The womb (*garbhakoṣṭha*) is the chamber for the fetus; in that fetal chamber, the specific condition consisting of the non-discharge of the menstrual flow (*ārtava*), which is the cause of the blood-tumor, occurs only in a woman. Therefore, a blood-tumor of this nature—produced by the obstruction of the menstrual flow—does not occur in a man;

however, a tumor produced by a general vitiation of the blood (*sāmānyaśoṇitaduṣṭi*) can indeed occur in a man as well. For instance, as he will state later: "When Vata has been mostly conquered, Kapha, Pitta, and even the blood [may increase]."

"If he becomes angry while the medical treatment is being performed," and so forth; likewise, it is stated [in the Sūtrasthāna] that "gulma, upakuśa, visarpa," and other such conditions are "diseases born of blood. Regarding the three causes for the suppression of natural urges (*vegavidhāraṇa*), the first is dependence (*pāratantrya*). Because of this very dependence, women suppress their urges due to lack of self-reliance (*avaiśāradya*) and ignorance (*ajñāna*); thus, because of this ignorance, they suppress their urges, whereby a great disease arises.
"By way of figurative usage" means that it refers to the metaphorical designation of the husband and so forth;
"the opening of the womb" should be understood as the entrance to the uterus,
and "milk in the breasts" should be understood solely from the influence of the disease.
The influence of the disease characterized by the obstruction of the menses (*ārtava*) is that it produces breast milk (*stanya*), as this has been observed;

therefore, the statement—“For in a woman who is pregnant, the nutrient essence (*rasa*) is transformed into three things: for the nourishment of her own body, for breast milk, and for the growth of the fetus” (Śārīra Sthāna, A. 6)—and the consequent claim that “the fetus itself becomes breast milk,” must be understood as refuted.
Here, by the term *dohada*, one should understand the woman’s connection with various mental states and cravings, which is designated as *dohada*.
As stated by Kṣārapāṇi: "A woman may have pregnancy-longings (*dohada*) or she may be one suffering from a blood-tumor (*śoṇitagulma*).

However, what is intended here is not the "two-heartedness" (*dvaihṛdya*) caused by [the fetus], for that arises from the connection between the heart of the embryo and the heart of the mother. For there is this statement: "His heart is born of the mother; it becomes connected to the mother's heart by means of the circulating channels that carry the nutrient essence (*rasa*). Therefore, through those [channels], an attachment to those [objects] arises for them both" (Śārīra-sthāna 4). Furthermore, in a blood-tumor there is no consciousness; therefore, such a "two-hearted" longing does not exist here.

Due to that delusion regarding the embryo, she experiences whatever longing (*dohada*) characterized by a desire to consume certain things and so forth, even in the absence of any actual connection with poison—just as the symptoms of poison arise from the "poison of fear" (*śaṅkā-viṣa*). For it is said: "Those afflicted by the poison of fear manifest the symptoms of poison. *Āṭālatvam* means expansion; and through the dilation of the birth canal, the expansion of the line of hair (*romarājī*) is also logically accounted for, just like the skin and hair being stretched.
"It throbs entirely" means not by only one part; for a fetus throbs even by a single part, therefore this definition serves to exclude the possibility that it is a fetus.

Now, as for what was stated regarding *raktagulma*—"having signs identical to those of pregnancy" (*samagarbhaliṅga*)—and likewise, "it should be treated after the tenth month has passed" (Ci.A.5); that [objection] is untenable, because there indeed exists a pulsation of the massified [blood] that is distinct from [normal] pregnancy. Furthermore, "novelty" (*navatva*) was stated as a cause for easy curability; so how can it be said here that treatment should be undertaken after the lapse of time? We reply: the statement "having signs identical to those of pregnancy" was made with the intention of referring to signs similar to those of an advanced pregnancy. Alternatively, "having signs identical to those of pregnancy" means that it possesses the signs of a normal pregnancy lasting up to ten months; by this, he shows that the symptoms of morbid conditions such as *suptanāgodara* and the like do not occur here.

The fact that [the fetus] is treatable in the tenth month should be understood here as being due to the power of the disease; the influence of the disease is such that it becomes treatable only when it has become laxified during the tenth month itself. Furthermore, dependence on time caused by the power of a disease is observed in such [injunctions] as: "In fever, gruels, decoctions, clarified butter, milk, and purgatives should be administered every six days," and so forth.

As for the claim that the requirement of a tenth month for a blood-tumor (*raktagulma*)—intended to dispel the suspicion of pregnancy because its symptoms are identical to those of a fetus—is incorrect; for even before the tenth month, a blood-tumor can be diagnosed by means of a pulsating mass, and furthermore, because the persistence of a fetus is observed even beyond the tenth month, the suspicion of pregnancy does not necessarily vanish. Indeed, he will state later regarding the persistence of the fetus beyond the tenth month: "Beyond this [tenth month], the persistence is abnormal" (Śārīra Sthāna, Chapter 4). With the words "tadyathā" and so forth, he describes the premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*).
"Unreasonably" means by the power of the disease itself, even in the absence of causes such as vomiting or belching;
"constipation" refers to the excessive retention of feces.
However, even regarding gulmas produced by pitta and the other doshas, [the author] states the predominance of vāta as established by its pathogenesis: "In all [types]," etc.;
"by the common [method]" means by that which is antagonistic to both combined doshas;
and "whatever else" refers to that which pacifies even a single dosha in a state of combination.

"Not contradictory" means it is not contradictory to the severe complications (*upadrava*). "Having distinguished" means having distinguished between the heavy and the light; the sense is that even when pacifying a single *doṣa*, one must perform that very same treatment which results in the pacification of the severe complication.
He says this very thing in the passage beginning with "gurūn" and so forth.

Since all *gulma* disorders have *vāta* as their root, and since no specific treatment independent of *vāta* is found, he states that the treatment for *vāta* itself must be performed with haste: "tvaramāṇas tu" and so forth;
the word "being performed" (*kriyamāṇe*) is to be supplied [in the context of] "urgent action" (*ātyayike karmaṇi*).
"Even a small amount" is a qualification of the action (karma). In the summary, "and a portion of actions" refers to the medical treatments.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Gulma," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of Caraka, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Section on Diagnosis (*Nidānasthāna*).

[Nidānasthāna, Chapter 4 (34 of 120)] Following the occurrence of gulma during Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the description of *prameha* follows because of the subsequent arising of urinary disorders. For it is stated: “From the consumption of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), there arose meha and kuṣṭha” (Ni. A. 8).

Thus, he demonstrates that the three doṣas are the cause in all types of *meha*, as they are provoked by the same etiological factors; and that the designations such as *ślaiṣmika* (phlegmatic) and so forth are used because of the predominance of one particular doṣa.

It is also stated in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*: "All types of *meha* arise from all three *doṣas*" (*Niścaya-sthāna*, chapter 6). Here, "disorders" (*vikāra*) refers to those that take the form of complications (*upadrava*) of *prameha*; alternatively, it may include any other conditions whatsoever that are born of the three *doṣas*.
In this context, the specific characteristics of the causes (*nidāna*) and so forth—such as their mutual interdependence and other qualities to be explained later—are to be understood.

"The state of the obstruction of disorders" (*vighātabhāva*) refers to the prevention of their arising; "the absence of the obstruction of disorders" refers to the production of disorders. Thus, "the state of the obstruction of disorders and its absence" refers to these two conditions. The "specific distinctions" (*prativiśeṣa*) regarding those two are the "specific distinctions of the state and absence of the obstruction of disorders."

In that regard, the specific types of impairment (*vighāta*) of the transformation (*vikāra*) are: the non-production of transformation, its production after a long time, the production of a minute transformation, or the production of a transformation lacking all characteristic marks—all of which will be explained hereafter.
The specific types of non-impairment (*vighātābhāva*), however, will be explained later as the opposites of the aforementioned non-production of transformation and so forth.
He explains the meaning of the preceding argumentative passage with the words beginning "yadā" (when...).
They do not bind one another; rather, they become mutually antagonistic, for "binding" (anubandha) is intended to mean being favorable.
In that context, it is precisely the primary cause (*nidāna*) that binds the *doṣa*; by virtue of a great degree of similarity, it vitiates the *doṣa* without opposition.
As for the *doṣa*'s binding of the *dūṣya*: it vitiates the *dūṣya*—which is the cause of disease—without opposition, due to its association with qualities such as commonality (*sāmānya-guṇa*).

Likewise, the "concomitance with the defect" (*doṣānubandhitva*) of the corruptible (*dūṣya*) is its remaining favorable toward the corruption by way of being lax [in resistance] or possessing similar qualities; similarly, this very thing constitutes the "concomitance with the cause" (*nidānānubandhitva*) of the defect—that the cause possesses qualities similar to those that produce the defect, for through such similarity the defect becomes favorable toward the production of disease by the cause. Furthermore, it should be understood that the absence of such concomitance occurs through the reversal of these examples.

The persistence of the defects (doṣas) from the etiological factor (nidāna) should be understood as occurring through the production of some degree of morbidity due to the association with qualities that are either similar or dissimilar. If there were a total absence of morbidity or if the etiological factor were indifferent toward the production of morbidity, it would not truly be an "etiological factor" (nidāna), for that which produces [disease] is called a nidāna.

Alternatively, the phrase "due to the prolongation of time" (kālaprakarṣāt) is to be construed with "they persist" (anubadhnanti); thus, when the etiological factors and so forth become mutually concordant through the prolongation of time, it should be understood that the disorders manifest after a long duration.
It should be understood that when [the factors] do not bind to one another, then the manifestation of the morbid transformation (*vikāra*) does not occur.

Furthermore, the binding of the etiological factor (*nidāna*) with the *doṣa* occurs due to the prolongation of time, when the cause, having been interrupted, is pursued again; or else, after a long time, the cause is encountered in a form possessing similar qualities (*samānaguṇatā*), and so forth—this is to be inferred. Alternatively, "they bind" refers to cases where the etiological factor is weak; when it is slight, it produces a slight *doṣa*, and a slight *doṣa* vitiates only a slight *dūṣya* (tissue to be vitiated), and so forth—this is how it should be known.

And when those that are weaker follow [the primary disease], then the disorders become slight, or they possess not all the symptoms as described; this is how it should be applied. "Slight" means of small degree, and "possessing not all the symptoms as described" means that not all the symptoms occur in the manner in which they were stated.

Thus, these specific variations regarding the presence or absence of the impairment of disorders caused by the particularity of the non-association of etiological factors and so forth have been explained.

Now, he describes the specific absence of impairment in disorders produced by the mutual association of the etiological factors (nidāna) and so forth: "In the case of reversal, they are contrary. Here, "reversal" refers to the association of the etiological factors and so on, as well as their rapid association and their association in a state of high intensity. "Contrary" refers to the disorders that arise—specifically those arising rapidly and those being great, possessing all the aforementioned symptoms respectively; this is how it should be understood. He concludes with the words beginning with "iti" (thus).

And although this section is common to all morbid transformations (*vikāra*), it is presented here in the context of the etiology of *prameha* (urinary disorders) to demonstrate that *prameha* arises specifically from causes such as the etiological factors (*nidāna*) which are mutually interdependent.

Now, regarding the present subject— the *kaphaja* and other types of *prameha*— the author states the specific characteristics of the mutually interdependent causes and so forth, beginning with the words "In that regard" (*tatra*).

Here, *kapha* alone is mentioned first because it is the primary cause of many types of *prameha*; "excessively" (*ativelam*) means repeatedly, as in the case of specific grains such as *hāyanaka* and others.
Hareṇu is the round pea;
kṛśarā is food prepared from sesame, rice, and māṣa beans;
mṛjā is cleansing with fragrant unguents.

"All that is a specific cause" means that such a cause alone is the reason for the phlegm (*śleṣman*) which produces urinary disorders (*prameha*). "Phlegm with much fluidity is a specific morbidity" means that only phlegm with abundant fluidity generates *meha*, not that which has little fluidity.
"Unbound" means not aggregated;
however, in this context, multiplicity and density should be understood according to their respective applicability.
Therefore, in fat, muscle, and both the adipose and marrow tissues, there is a dual nature; whereas in the remaining [tissues], there is a plurality, as they are reckoned as *ojas*.

Indeed, he will state later in the treatment of urinary disorders (*prameha-cikitsita*) that they consist of the very form of *ojas*: "Marrow, plasma, *ojas*, and flesh are the corrupted elements" (Ci. A. 5).
The word *iti* refers back to the many [conditions] such as discordant humors (*baddha-bheda*) and so forth; alternatively, the reading *asaṅkhyātāḥ* (innumerable) is easy to understand.
In the case of *sannipāta*, it means a confluence or meeting.
"It becomes provoked" means it becomes ready to produce *prameha*. From what does it become ready to produce *prameha*? He says: "Because of its prior excessive abundance";
"prior" means at the very time of its production.
The meaning is: because *kapha* has become both abundant and oriented toward the production of *prameha*.

For, by the etiology of *prameha*, this *kapha* is indeed produced as being directed toward the production of *prameha* and in great quantity; therefore, due to its abundance and its possession of the power to produce *prameha*, it is logical that it becomes provoked (*prakupyati*).
"Visṛptim" means spreading or diffusion.

"Because of the predominance of common qualities between the qualities of fat (*medas*) and the qualities [of *kapha*]"—the meaning of this and what follows is that there is a great degree of similarity between the qualities of fat, such as sweetness, unctuousness, and heaviness, and the qualities of *kapha*, such as heaviness and coldness. The underlying principle is that "like indeed mingles with like.

By the statement "because of being deranged" (*vikṛtatvāt*), he demonstrates that the connection of fat with *kapha* in its natural state (*prakṛta*) does not cause the vitiation of fat; rather, it is only with *kapha* in its deranged state (*vikṛta*) that such occurs.

"Because of being increased by excessive magnitude" means because of being increased through the possession of an exceeding measure; here, "increase" does not refer merely to an excess of qualities (*guṇa*), but rather to an accumulation of constituent parts (*avayava*). "Pustules containing putrid flesh" refers to *pūtimāṃsapiḍakās*.

This should be understood here as meaning that, due to the corruption of the flesh (*māṃsa-pradoṣa*), they possess the capacity to generate various types [of pustules] such as *śarāvikā* and others, because they have deviated from their natural state (*aprakṛtibhūtatva*).
Therefore, the statement "because it has become non-natural" (aprakṛtabhūtatvāt) is not redundant, as it serves a specific purpose.

[The phrase] "having reached and being obstructed" means that it remains after having moved [into the channels], because it has become a modification (vikṛti) of its natural state (prakṛti). This is because it is modified by all the qualities (guṇas) that constitute its natural state. Since all the qualities of phlegm (śleṣman) have become disordered (vikṛta), it becomes stable due to the intensity of its provocation; however, the meaning is that through excessive intensity, it becomes incurable.

Alternatively, phlegm (śleṣman) may be in its natural state when the vitiated substrate (dūṣya) is similar [to itself], such as fat (medas), muscle-fat (vasā), and so forth; and it may be in a state of morbid transformation when the substrate is dissimilar, such as blood (śoṇita) and so forth. Thus, the meaning is "due to being both similar and dissimilar. Consequently, by reaching a similar substrate, the strength (balitva) of the phlegm arises; and by reaching a dissimilar substrate, there occurs a contradiction in treatment (viruddhopakramatva). Therefore, it should be understood that stability or incurability (asādhyatā) is logically appropriate. 8
Now, he explains how there are ten types of *kapha-meha* due to their association with the qualities of *kapha*: "In the body," and so forth.

Here, "disequilibrium" (*vaiṣamya*) should be understood as being caused specifically by increase (*vṛddhi*), because disequilibrium in the form of decrease (*kṣaya*) does not produce this type of disease.

Within that very disequilibrium, decrease and increase are to be understood through states such as "increased" or "more increased. Therefore, the meaning is that even in those [types of] *śukra-meha* and others which are said to arise from the increase of qualities such as whiteness, the other qualities of *śleṣman* (phlegm) are also present in the form of disequilibrium consisting of decrease and increase.
Alternatively, it shows that when there is an imbalance, an increase occurs in two, three, or four qualities at various times;
thus, decrease and increase should be understood as resulting from the rise or fall in the number of these qualities.

Here, the ten types of *prameha* do not arise simply from the association with ten specific qualities such as "whiteness" and so on according to their respective numbers; rather, they arise from the association with these qualities both individually and collectively. For this very reason, he says: "by whichever quality—whether single or multiple," and so forth.

By the term "thick clarity" (*sāndraprasāda*), only a single quality is to be counted; however, the designation "thick urine" (*sāndrameha*) should be understood as arising from one specific part of that quality of thick clarity.
In passages such as "it receives the same name," it should be construed as meaning that it acquires either that same name or a specific secondary name.

That which has a name identical to its quality is called "named after that" (*tatsamākhya*). For example, in the cases of *śītameha*, *śuklameha*, and *sāndrameha*, the urinary disorders (*mehas*) are designated precisely by the names of their qualities such as "cold" (*śīta*) and so forth. However, in other cases such as *udakameha* and the like, the name is not identical to the designation of a quality like "white" (*śveta*) and so on. Rather, because they arise through a connection with qualities—due to the phlegm (*śleṣman*) possessing qualities similar to water and other substances—the name "water-diabetes" (*udakameha*) is secondary (*gauṇa*). Thus, the name "water-diabetes" becomes secondary due to the connection with the qualities of phlegm such as clarity, whiteness, and coldness; this same principle should be followed in other instances as well.

However, water and the others mentioned here are included as being endowed with those respective qualities of *kapha* for the purpose of defining the characteristics of the combination of *kapha*-qualities; they are taken up for the sake of establishing specific designations and for the sake of specialized knowledge—that is to say, they serve to demonstrate their mutually distinct characteristics. 9–11.

"Like water" means resembling the color and other qualities of water; but why is it said to be "like the juice of the stalk of sugarcane (*ikṣuvālikā*) and like the juice of the cane-sugarcane (*kāṇḍekṣu*)"? Is it not because *ikṣuvālikā* and *kāṇḍekṣu* are different things? It is not so; both are mentioned for the purpose of demonstrating that the juice of *ikṣuvālikā* and the juice of *kāṇḍekṣu* are of one and the same nature. Alternatively, by mentioning both, he shows that urinary disorder (*meha*) may be like the juice of *kāṇḍekṣu* and likewise like the juice of *ikṣuvālikā*.
"It is consolidated" means it becomes thickened;

"mūrtān" refers to the humors (*doṣas*) that are solid or hard. The plural number is used because it denotes a genus (*jāti*), for although there is only one humor here, it is *kapha* (phlegm) in abundance.
"Bound by threads" means long like a thread;
"like saliva" means having the form of saliva on all sides.
The statement beginning with "and [it occurs] at every urination due to the provocation of phlegm" is for the sake of easy comprehension.

And it should not be argued here: "Just as the ten qualities of phlegm (*śleṣman*) produce the ten types of urinary disorders (*prameha*), why do they not produce others as well through different combinations of qualities? For this is the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of things: one may only postulate what is observed, not what is unobserved. Indeed, it is an established fact that even when there is an abundance of the combination of the elements (*bhūta-saṃsarga*), an abundance of taste (*rasa*) does not necessarily follow. (Verse 12.23 begins with) "hot" (*uṣṇa*), etc., [describing] the etiology of pitta-type urinary disorders.
"Six [types] arise more quickly" means in comparison to the *śleṣmaprameha* (kapha-type urinary disorders); for pitta acts more rapidly than *śleṣman*, and thus its more rapid production is logical.
"As before, they become associated" means they are associated with decrease and increase [of the humors], as explained previously (verses 24–26).

"Because its site is a location where the *doṣa* and *medas* are combined (*saṃsṛṣṭa*)"—that is to say, because the site of the *doṣa*, namely *pitta*, and the *medas* are closely associated (*sannikṛṣṭa*). For the site of *pitta* is the stomach (*āmāśaya*), and likewise the site of *medas* is the omentum (*vapāvahana*), which is also but a part of the stomach. Therefore, due to the proximity of the sites of the *doṣa* and the *dūṣya* (the tissue to be vitiated), the vitiation is constant; the sense is that because of this constant proximity, it is difficult to overcome. Alternatively, [it may mean] "one whose site consists of *medas* in which the *doṣa* is combined"—this is the reason for the contradictory nature of the treatment.
Therefore, because the site in the form of fat (*medas*) is connected with the humor (*doṣa*) in the form of bile (*pitta*), there is a contradiction in treatment:

for that which is wholesome for bile—such as sweet and cold things—is unwholesome for fat; and that which is wholesome for fat—such as pungent things—is unwholesome for bile. By the word "and" (*ca*), he shows that it is palliable (*yāpya*) due to the influence of the disease itself.
27–35. "Dry" (rūkṣa) and so forth constitute the etiology of vātamēha.
It draws [the vāta] into the urinary bladder; being situated in the urinary bladder, it draws it [out], meaning it leads it specifically into the urinary bladder.
Lasīkā is the watery portion between the flesh and the skin;
for it will be stated in the *Śārīra-sthāna*: "That water which is between the flesh and the skin receives the name *lasīkā*" (*Śā. A.* 7), and so forth.
It is called an "anubandha" because it is continuous and uninterrupted.
It causes it to flow, meaning it causes it to fall;

or rather, due to its dryness (raukṣya), the Vāyu, by means of its astringent quality, transforms even the sweet *ojas* into something associated with an astringent taste. Then, by its power, the Vāyu carries this *ojas*, now joined with an astringent flavor, into the urinary bladder (*mūtrāśaya*) because of its dryness. Having cut through the urinary bladder due to its dryness and having made it parched, the Vāyu leads the *ojas* away. Furthermore, by its own greatness, the Vāyu makes the *ojas* astringent; for indeed, Vāta when increased produces an astringent taste through its inherent power. (36-37)
"Because it is a matter of great urgency" means that it causes the depletion of the essential elements (*dhātu*) such as marrow and so forth.
Furthermore, "contrary treatment" should be understood as follows: for example, that which is wholesome for *vāta*, such as unctuous substances (*snigdha*), is unwholesome for *medas*, and so on.
"Three" means "all three";
by this, he shows that this very same premonitory symptom is common to all types of prameha.
The phrase "occurring as a consequence of that" means they arise due to the persistent association with *prameha*.
(48–49) He now describes the kind of person in whom *prameha* generally occurs, beginning with the word "greedy" (*gṛdhnu*).

By such statements as "the tree that is the nest of birds [destroys] the greedy and covetous one" and "death [comes] in the form of prameha," it is shown that when prameha arises in one who possesses diminished enthusiasm and other such traits, it becomes indeed incurable.
"Various other activities" means those which bring about the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātus).
By the phrase "of the specific diseases" in the summary (saṅgraha), he includes the textual passage beginning with "In this [treatise], indeed... and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the distinctions between curable and incurable," here the term "incurable" includes those types born of *pitta* that are palliable (53–55).

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Prameha," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka Saṃhitā*, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Section on Diagnosis (*Nidānasthāna*).
4 [Nidānasthāna, Chapter 5 (35 of 120)]: Following the discussion on prameha, and prior to the onset of kuṣṭha, the etiology of kuṣṭha is now described.
For there is this statement: "From the consumption of sacrificial oblations [arise] meha and kuṣṭha" (Nirukta A.
8). Thus, there are seven substances: three doṣas and four dūṣyas.

"Nature" (*prakṛti*) means "cause"; it is an adjective qualifying the seven substances. Alternatively, there is the reading "having undergone transformation" (*vikṛtimāpannāni*), or perhaps the reading "having undergone transformation from their nature" (*prakṛtivikṛtimāpannāni*); in that case, the meaning is "having undergone transformation by way of their nature, which is the cause of leprosy."

By this, it is shown that when a morbid transformation of the *vāta* and other humors occurs apart from the specific causes that generate leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), then leprosy does not arise, but rather an erysipelas (*visarpa*) arises; for regarding erysipelas, it is stated [in Cikitsāsthāna 21]: "In the manifestation of erysipelas, blood, lymph, skin, flesh, the [three] corrupted tissues (*dūṣya*), and the three impurities (*doṣa*)—all these indeed become provoked"; thus, it is said that these seven [factors] in their morbid state are the cause.

Although there is a similarity between *kuṣṭha* and *visarpa* regarding the [afflicted] *doṣas* and *dūṣyas*, nevertheless, *visarpa* arises from a *doṣa* characterized by a tendency to spread (*visarpaṇaśīla*) and dominated by blood (*raktapradhāna*), whereas *kuṣṭha* arises otherwise; thus occurs the differentiation of these diseases.
For this very reason, it is said: "Because it spreads in various ways (*vividhaṃ sarpati*), it is designated as *visarpa*" (Cikitsāsthāna, Chapter 21).

Likewise, it should be understood that blood is predominant in visarpa, because intense pain arises solely due to the vitiation of specific blood, and because the primary importance of blood-treatment is taught [in this condition]. For there is this statement: "On one side are all those [therapies], and on the other side is bloodletting" (Cikitsā-sthāna, Chapter 21).

Others, however, say: in visarpa (erysipelas), there is not necessarily an affliction of the seven [dosas and] dhatus; rather, the affliction of the seven is shown there by way of possibility. In kuṣṭha (leprosy), however, there is invariably an affliction of the seven in every case. Regarding how the dosas that initiate kuṣṭha become aggravated and how the dhatus are affected, he says: "tadyathā" and so forth. "Prakopaṇavikṛtāḥ" means those transformed by the aggravating factors of the etiology of kuṣṭha; otherwise, the mention of "aggravating factors" would be meaningless, because without aggravation there is no transformation that produces disease.

By the phrase "altered by the affliction of the *doṣas*," he demonstrates that the alteration of the *dhātus* occurs solely from the affliction of the *doṣas*; the meaning is that the *dhātus* do not become vitiated in the absence of the *doṣas*.

Alternatively, having set aside the notion that the alteration of the *dhātus*—the causes of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*)—consists merely of their decrease or increase, he establishes that their vitiation consists in their association with the *doṣas*.
[This refers to] the seven-elementary body (*saptadhātuka*), which is a confluence of the seven elements.
"Thus transformed" means having undergone modification according to the sequence described;
"from birth" refers to the cause;
"originating from this" means having this as their cause.
"Manifesting" (*abhinirvartamānāni*) means spreading everywhere;
"only" (*kevalam*) means entirely, including even that which is beyond the four corrupted elements (*dūṣya*).

By this, he demonstrates that at the time of its first arising, there is a rule regarding the corruption of the four elements in leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), whereas once it has arisen, there is also the corruption of bones, veins, and so forth.

In that regard, Suśruta has stated that leprosy first takes refuge in the skin and subsequently spreads to the successive bodily constituents (*dhātus*) in the following passage: "Thus, once leprosy has arisen in the skin, through the lapse of time, it gradually pervades the constituents" (Su.Ni.A.
5). This [view] is not at all contradictory here as well.
In all types of *kuṣṭha*, first a specific abnormality occurs specifically in the skin; subsequently, due to the passage of time, a specific corruption arises in the blood and other elements.

Here, the corruption of the four *dhātus* is mentioned with reference to the general corruption involved in the production of *kuṣṭha*, whereas their specific corruption occurs sequentially. Furthermore, the specific corruption here is to be explained by the statement: "They afflict the body exclusively."

For this very reason, in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*, with the intention of describing specific types of corruption, the characteristics of particular corruptions are stated in passages such as: "Itching and suppuration indeed occur in leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) when it is localized in the blood" (*Su.Ni.A.* 5).

However, the general corruption of the four elements mentioned here does not possess those specific characteristics; rather, it should be understood merely as the cause for the arising of leprosy. Therefore, there is no contradiction.
Now, he explains how all types of *kuṣṭha*, despite being produced by the three *doṣas*, receive designations such as "vātika" and so forth: "And not even a little," etc.

The phrase "of those with similar constitutions" (*samānaprakṛtīnām*) refers to those whose seven causes—*vāta* and the rest—are equal and devoid of internal variations. For if there were no internal differences among the causes, the effect would likewise be of a single uniform nature.
The meaning of the sentence is that a specific variation in sensation occurs in *kuṣṭha* through the differentiation of the portions of the *doṣas* and their respective locations.

"Portion-by-portion differentiation of the *doṣas*" (*doṣāṃśāṃśavikalpa*) refers to the variation with respect to each individual portion of the *doṣas*; for instance, in some cases the Vāta becomes aggravated by its own dry (*rūkṣa*) portion, while in others it is so by its cold (*śaitya*) portion, and so forth. Likewise, a specific variation in sensation arises through the differentiation of the *doṣas*, the *dūṣyas* (vitiated tissues), and the locations. For it is said: "In that regard, among the locations beginning with rasa, whichever diseases arise in whichever location of the aggravated *doṣas," and so on (Sūtra-sthāna 28).

Although the location (*sthāna*) here is fixed as being of four types corresponding to the four kinds of corrupted tissues (*dūṣya*), nevertheless, this classification of locations for the humor (*doṣa*) within the corrupted tissue should be understood as being determined by its pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth. Among these: the distinction of sensation (*vedanā-viśeṣa*) is exemplified by "the *kāpāla* [type] is characterized by excessive pricking" (*Ci. A. 7*), and so on; the distinction of color (*varṇa-viśeṣa*) is exemplified by "that which has the color of a *kākaṇantikā* [berry]" (*Ci. A. 7*), and so on; the distinction of shape (*saṃsthāna-viśeṣa*) is exemplified by "that which has the shape of a deer's tongue" (*Ci. A. 7*), and so on; the distinction of efficacy (*prabhāva-viśeṣa*) refers to curability, incurability, and so forth; and the distinction of name (*nāma-viśeṣa*) refers to *kāpāla*, and so on.

Since, even when the cause is the same, there exists a distinction in sensations and so forth—such as the various types of *kuṣṭha*—due to the division of the relative strength and location of the portions of the *doṣas*, one should apply the description "of seven kinds" and so on. Here, "of seven kinds" refers to the distinctions of the major *kuṣṭhas* that will be explained in this very context; "of eighteen kinds" refers to the distinctions that will be explained in the section on treatment; and "innumerable" refers to the further subdivisions of sensations and so forth. To explain why these variations are indeed innumerable, he says: "For the *doṣas*... and so on.

"By conceptualizations" (*vikalpanaiḥ*) means by various distinct conceptualizations, such as the conceptualization of parts and wholes; "being conceptualized" (*vikalpyamānāḥ*) means being differentiated; they "conceptualize" (*vikalpayanti*) means they differentiate. The sense is that due to the difference in the causes—the specific doshas—there also arises a manifold variety of diseases as effects.

This differentiation caused by the difference in doshas is not applied here to an incurable disease; thus he says "elsewhere," etc. Here, "incurable" (*asādhya*) is intended to mean that which must be rejected [as treatment]; for indeed, the differentiation of the "manageable" (*yāpya*) type of incurable disease is certainly made for the purpose of palliation.

He thinks as follows: although a distinction based on the difference in humors (*doṣa*) exists even regarding diseases that are incurable, it is not made here because such a distinction does not prompt the application of specific treatments due to their being untreatable; however, it is appropriate to make such a distinction for the sake of specific treatments regarding curable diseases. Thus, demonstrating with reasons the abandonment of the previously mentioned classification, he proposes the statement of the sevenfold [classification] with the words "Of these," etc.: the enumeration of disorders according to all their variations is the "enumeration of variations of disorders" (*vikalpavikārasaṅkhyāna*).
"An over-extension" (atiprasaṅga) means the consequence of the fault of excessive verbal designation.

Now, an objection may be raised: if the eleven minor types of *kuṣṭha* (skin diseases) to be described later are included within the seven major types, then there would be two categories—namely, the sevenfold and the eighteenfold—just as fevers are classified as single-fold, double-fold, and so on, for in all such classifications, everything is included within them. However, the minor *kuṣṭhas* are not included within these seven major *kuṣṭhas*. Furthermore, if the minor *kuṣṭhas* were not included here, how could the Teacher be satisfied by merely mentioning seven *kuṣṭhas* in this section on etiology (*nidāna*)? It is said in reply: Here, by the mention of the seven types of *kuṣṭha*, the description of those arising from a single humor (*doṣa*), from two humors, and from three humors is accomplished through statements such as "when Vāta is predominant, Kāpāla-kuṣṭha occurs. There is no other category for the minor *kuṣṭhas* beyond these three types. Therefore, among the minor *kuṣṭhas*, whichever one is produced by a particular humor should be understood as being included here by virtue of possessing the characteristics of that specific humor already mentioned. However, it should be known that in the case of minor *kuṣṭhas*, the symptoms of the humors described for the major *kuṣṭhas* are present only in a mild degree.

In this context, its inclusion among the minor types of leprosy (*kṣudrakuṣṭha*) should be explained in accordance with the text to be stated later in the section on treatment: "The single type of leprosy called *carma*, as well as *kiṭibha* accompanied by *vipādikā*, and *alasa* leprosy, are generally known to be of the nature of Vāta and Kapha" (Ci.A.7).

The designations for the types of *kuṣṭha*, such as *kāpāla* and so forth, should be understood as being applied based on their resemblance to skulls (*kapāla*) and the like, and as established by technical usage in the treatises (*śāstra*). Indeed, there is no etymological derivation (*anvaya*) for the designation *sidhma*; therefore, the designation *sidhma* is established solely through technical usage in the treatises.

Thus, when the *prakṛti* (the primary form) is subject to optionality (*vikalpyamānā*), the number of options (*vikalpa-saṅkhyā*) refers to the number of distinct forms resulting from the differentiation of the causes that produce *kuṣṭha*.

And here, the non-mention of minor skin diseases (kṣudrakuṣṭha) should be understood as being because they are already included within the major skin diseases (mahākuṣṭha) according to the logic previously stated.
*Śītoṣṇavyatyāsa* means the reversal of cold and heat.

"Non-sequential" (*anānupūrvyā*) means by abandoning the stated order; the abandonment of order includes, for example, suddenly resorting to cold after consuming heat, or the reverse, as well as resorting to cold or heat at an unaccustomed time. Likewise, it should be understood that this applies even to the reversal of satiating and depleting foods when they are consumed non-sequentially.
*Cilicima* is a variety of *rohit* fish shown by the author of the treatise in the chapter on Ātreya and Bhadrakāpya.

"Having reached a site" means having attained a location such as the skin and so forth that is conducive to the production of *kuṣṭha*; alternatively, "site" means having reached the specific part of the body where the *kuṣṭha* is to be produced.
By the expression "remaining settled," he demonstrates that it is only the stable (*sthira*) *doṣas* that produce *kuṣṭha*, and not those characterized by mobility (*saraṇaśīla*). 6
The premonitory symptoms include the absence of perspiration and so forth; its specific power consists of horripilation and a tingling sensation.
"Udvṛttabahistanūni" means those whose external bodies have been tossed up;
"suptavat suptāni" means they are as if asleep, which signifies that they have no perception of touch whatsoever;
"kapālaḥ" refers to a fragment of a pot or similar vessel.
Those for whom the movements and so forth are attached and long-lasting are "thus" [described].
Regarding the characteristics of the *ṛṣyajihva* [type of leprosy], "externally" refers to the extent of the *kuṣṭha* [leprosy], while "internally" refers to the deformed middle;
*ṛṣya* is a specific kind of deer.

In the phrase "petals of the white lotus" (*puṇḍarīkapalāśa*), the word *tanu* in the expression "outer layers whose bodies have fallen apart" refers to a region or part; thus, the meaning is "those whose peripheral regions have fallen away. Regarding *sidhma-kuṣṭha*, authorities state that it is indeed distinct from *sidhma-puṣpikā*, as defined by its specific characteristics. Furthermore, with reference to *sidhma-puṣpikā*, *sidhma-kuṣṭha* is listed among the minor skin diseases (*kṣudra-kuṣṭha*) in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*.

Although *dadru* (ringworm) is listed among the major *kuṣṭhas* in the *Suśruta*, it is classified here among the minor *kuṣṭhas* because it does not penetrate into the successive bodily tissues (*dhātus*) and because it is devoid of extreme pain. In the *Suśruta*, however, it is listed among the major *kuṣṭhas* due to its intense association with them.

Since the meaning [of the term] is already established by the phrase "possessing the symptoms of all *kuṣṭhas," the further statement, "by the most wicked one, there is the manifestation of the symptoms of all *kuṣṭhas," indicates that whatever is the most wicked symptom of *kuṣṭha*, that alone occurs in *kākaṇaka* and nothing else;
thus, the word "most wicked" (*pāpīyasā*) refers to that which causes extreme pain.

By repeating the phrase "or rather, more sinful" (*kiṃvā pāpīyasa*) and so forth, [the author] demonstrates that because all the symptoms of *kuṣṭha* originate from sin in the case of *kākaṇaka*, it is incurable and causes extreme suffering.
By the word "sometimes" (*kadācit*), he indicates an alternative view to be discussed later regarding its being treatable with medical therapy.
"Or due to improper conduct" means that even when leprosy has arisen, it continues to spread because of the persistence of its causes; "becoming moist" means being filled [with humors].
Furthermore, the *doṣas*, while causing corruption,
seize— that is, consume— the very tender (*taruṇa*), meaning delicate, parts such as the skin and the bones of the nose.
"For a short time" refers to the period of an incurable disease;
"as if dead" means having reached the very brink of death.
Regarding the phrase "he perceives," the ellipsis is "death, which has as its fruit the neglect of curable diseases.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Kuṣṭha," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Section on Diagnosis (*Nidānasthāna*).
5 [Nidānasthāna, Chapter 6 (36 of 120)]: Following the connection established in the diagnosis of fever, the diagnosis of rājayakṣman (consumption) is now stated.

Regarding the phrase "two bases" (*āyatanāni*), although the number is already established by the very mention of "thousands" and so forth as the causes, the repetition of the word "four" is for the purpose of demonstrating that they belong to a single category, even though there are internal differences among the thousands and so forth based on distinctions such as strength or composition.
Striking with the feet and rubbing with the feet;
"excessively far" means very distant.
"Uraḥkṣatam upaplavate" means it spreads or pervades;
"uraḥstham" means situated in the chest by its very nature;
"urasyāḥ" refers to those [afflictions] located in the chest, such as heart-palpitations, colic, and so forth.

Because the chest is in close proximity to the stomach (āmāśaya), the production of disease by a thief residing in the stomach is effectively established and maintained through strength; thus, the body is called "that which is properly supported by strength" (balasamādhāna). And since the person (puruṣa) has the body as his root, the meaning is that he is a "person through conjunction" (saṃyogapuruṣa).
"Samājam" means an assembly;
"uccāvacaiḥ" means high and low.
"Going toward [the enemy]" means out of fear, and so forth; this should be understood according to the appropriate context, such as being near a king.

"Those which bring about security through application" (yogakṣemakarāḥ) refers to those things that provide safety by means of yoga; in this context, these include the non-suppression of urine, feces, and so on.

By the use of the word "especially" (*viśeṣeṇa*), he shows that one should apply effort specifically toward the bodily [faculties] in consideration of the mind's acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*). The word "of oneself" (*ātmanaḥ*) is intended to show the superiority of attending to the acquisition and preservation of one's own body over that of another's body. Now, as to how the acquisition and preservation of one's own body is superior to the acquisition and preservation of the mind, or likewise to the acquisition and preservation of another's body, he says: "The body," and so forth.

Since the body is the root cause for this person in regard to all human goals that are to be accomplished, one should therefore especially attend to the welfare (*yogakṣema*) of one's own body first, and only afterwards to the welfare of the bodies and minds of others;
the sense is that if one's own body is impaired, assistance to others as well as pure spiritual reflection become disturbed— this is the underlying idea.
Alternatively, "yogas" are the applications for the excellence of the body's strength, complexion, and so forth, while "kṣemas" are the preventions of future afflictions.
Now, if it is thus that even regarding internal states the body is the root, then is the person (*puruṣa*) not merely secondary? No, he says: "The person has the body as his root.
This means that even in the production of the body, the experiencer—the self (*ātman*) who experiences pleasure and pain—is the root cause, assisted by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
Furthermore, this word *mūla* (root) has the abstract state (*bhāva*) as its primary meaning; therefore, the masculine designation “that self whose root is the body” (*śarīramūlaḥ*) is appropriate.
“The non-existence of everything” means the non-existence of the fourfold aims of life, beginning with dharma.

The meaning is that "rasa residing in the heart" refers to that which has the nature of a *dhātu* (tissue/fluid) and is nourished by the essence of food (*annarasa*). Others, however, state that "rasa residing in the heart" refers to *ojas*, according to the definition to be taught later in the text beginning with "the joints become lax.

Now, among the causes of wasting (*kṣaya*) that produce emaciation (*śoṣa*), [the author] states that the primary cause of wasting is the depletion of semen (*śukrakṣaya*) with the words "when," and so forth.
"Of one whose resolve is excessively aroused" means of one who has raised the banner [of sexual desire] with great effort;
"of one who is striving" means of one who is engaging in sexual intercourse (*vyavāya*).
"Characterized by signs following the wind" (vātānusṛtaliṅga) means endowed with the signs of wind—that is, endowed with the signs of vitiated wind.
The construction is: the body, acting as the object, is entered by debility, acting as the agent.

"Vaśika" means empty; the meaning is that it is depleted due to the loss of semen and blood. This is a qualifying attribute containing a reason; by this, the meaning is: because the body is depleted, [the wind] creeps along it.
"Supreme attainment of the fruit" means the excellence of the perfection of the result of nourishment (*āhāra-phala-saṃpatti*).
"The supreme abode" means the most excellent essence. Furthermore, the superiority of the *śukra* (semen) is due to its nature as an extreme state of clarity (*ati-prasāda*).

It should be understood that among the causes of wasting (*kṣaya*) which bring about emaciation, this summary refers specifically to the wasting of *śukra* alone because of its predominance, not because of the absence of other causes for emaciation.
The depletion of blood and other elements caused by the consumption of dry food and drink is also stated to be a cause of *rājayakṣman* (consumption).
The factors such as *prakṛti* (nature) and *karaṇa* (instrumental causes) are to be explained in detail in the *Rasavimāna*.

And here, by the term *upaśaya*, it is precisely that consumer who is to be discussed in the *Rasavimāna* that is intended, because it is stated there: "Furthermore, the consumer is he who takes in that food; depending on him, suitability (*sātmya*) exists" (Vi. A. 1).
For by this, it is stated that through the examination of the consumer, suitability itself is examined.
"Ayanamukhāni" means gateways to movement; "ayanaṃ gatiḥ parivārya" means having surrounded the path of movement,
and thus, for all those who are exceedingly emaciated and weak, their excrement must be protected— this is the construction of the sentence.
And he will state this very same point: "The emaciated person abandons his limbs due to excessive loosening of the feces;

for one afflicted by the depletion of all bodily constituents (*dhātu*), strength indeed consists of the strength of the stool" (*Cikitsā-sthāna*, chapter 8). This is said in connection with cough (*kāsa*); that is to say, in relation to cough.

In the phrase "because it is most painful" (kaṣṭatamatvāt), the word *ca* ("and") should be understood as having been elided; by that, two reasons are to be known: because it is most painful, and because the moon arose earlier [than the sun].
When it is due to its being most painful, then the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) should be understood as "king-like consumption is *rājayakṣmā*."

By the phrase "of the king of stars" (*uḍurājasya*), [the text] demonstrates that Soma possesses the designation "king" (*rājan*); consequently, the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) occurs as "the consumption (*yakṣmā*) of the king is *rājayakṣmā*.

Regarding the prodromal symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*), conditions such as rhinitis (*pratiśyāya*) and others generally arise from the production of a prodroma associated with *kapha*. Even when *vāyu* is the primary [dosha] in the production of *śoṣa* (wasting), it should be understood that this occurs due to contact with phlegm (*śleṣman*) located in the chest. Furthermore, because *kapha* here generally becomes aggravated by virtue of its own location (*sthāna-mahiman*), they describe *śoṣa* as having symptoms dominated by *kapha* and call it a disease of *śleṣman* (*śleṣmaroga*).
"In those who are faultless" is a qualification of the vessels and so forth;

"the state of being loathsome to behold" refers to the hands due to their prior condition such as inspection, and to the body due to its discoloration, foul odor, and so on, by virtue of [the practitioner's] power.
A *nigama* is a specific type of town with many inhabitants; a *janapada* is a district, a province, or a region.

The "climbing onto the bodies" of lizards and other such creatures, as well as "riding camels or donkeys" in a dream, should be understood here according to the restriction of direction (*diṅniyama*); by that [restriction], no ill omen (*riṣṭa*) occurs. However, as for what he will say—“He who goes toward the southern direction on dogs, camels, or even donkeys,” and so forth—that should be known as an ill omen because of the restriction to the southern direction.

Where a dream-form constitutes a premonitory sign (*pūrvarūpa*), as in cases such as *rājayakṣman* or insanity, it is so described; however, in cases such as fever, it is not mentioned because it is absent.

As for that which will be stated in the section on fatal signs (*riṣṭa*) regarding the dream-form premonitory signs of fever and other diseases—beginning with "One drinks liquor together with ghosts" (I.5)—that is indeed a fatal sign (*riṣṭa*).
By the statement "there are eleven forms," it is shown that these eleven forms alone occur in the complete form of rājayakṣman.

Furthermore, those eleven forms such as cough, dyspnea, and so forth, which have been explained by way of illustration, are not intended to be restrictive; therefore, the four distinct sets of eleven forms to be described later in the section on treatment are not contradictory.

Even though his strength is not yet exhausted, the term "strong" (*balavān*) is used for the purpose of demonstrating that he is endowed with innate strength (*sahaja-bala*); the point is that one who possesses innate strength remains as if his strength were unexhausted even when his [current] strength is diminished.

Regarding the phrase "because of the endurance of the strength of disease and medicine": since he is strong, he endures both the force of the disease and the force of the medicine; therefore, the meaning is that he is not overcome by them.
"Only with slight symptoms" (*alpaliṅga eva*) means that he is as easily curable as if he had only slight symptoms.

15. "One should know [the disease] as having many signs (*bahuliṅga*) and as having manifested fatal signs (*jātāriṣṭa*). This means that one should know it as incurable (*asādhya*) like one with many signs, and likewise as fatal (*māraka*) like one where fatal signs have manifested. Now, an objection: there is no death without fatal signs (*ariṣṭa*), for the scripture says: "And there is no such thing as death which is not preceded by fatal signs" (Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya, Sūtrasthāna 2). Therefore, how can one who has not manifested fatal signs be known here as being like one who has manifested them, in terms of imminent death? To this, he says: "For in an instant," and so forth.

For a fatal sign (riṣṭa) occurs in an incurable condition, and incurability indeed exists when there is a depletion of strength and muscle tissue; therefore, the meaning is that a fatal sign must necessarily manifest. Now, regarding the question of whether a fatal sign that has not yet arisen will simply not occur by avoiding its causes, he says: "And the manifestation of a fatal sign occurs without a cause.
For a fatal sign does not depend on any other observed cause; rather, it arises precisely without a cause.

One should not feel reassured by the thought that "by avoiding these causes, no fatal sign (*ariṣṭa*) will arise"; for a fatal sign may occur even without such a cause, and therefore, as long as a fatal sign has not actually manifested, one must not feel reassured.

This concludes the sixth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Wasting Diseases" (*śoṣanidāna*), in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Section on Diagnosis (*nidānasthāna*).
6 [Nidānasthāna, Chapter 7 (37 of 120)]:
Having described the exogenous form of consumption (*śoṣa*), he now speaks of insanity (*unmāda*), which arose immediately after the leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) at Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
For the statement is: "Of those with insanity and epilepsy caused by fear, terror, and grief" (Ni. A. 8).
"Of beings afflicted" means those whose minds are impaired by rajas and tamas.
"Of those whose defects have been eradicated" means those whose increased and deluded defects have been removed.

"Defiled by impurities" (*samalavikṛtopahitāni*) means mixed with or combined with impure things, unwholesome substances, or incompatible foods. Alternatively, "defiled by impurities" means [food] presented or offered by attendants who are impure—such as those afflicted with leprosy or physical deformities—and thus "defiled by impurities and distortions."

"By means of a method of consumption associated with disharmony" (*vaiṣamyayuktenopayogavidhinā*): this refers to the method of consuming food, such as its nature (*prakṛti*) and preparation (*karaṇa*), which is to be described; it is by that [method] being associated with disharmony (*vaiṣamya*). Disharmony is to be understood as the unwholesome state of the [food's] nature and so forth, caused by factors such as heaviness of nature (*prakṛtigurutva*).

"Tantra" refers to the body; the application (*prayoga*) spoken of in the *Sadvṛtta* is for the purpose of protecting it. By the term "bodily activity" (*śarīraceṣṭā*), actions such as walking are included; thus there is no redundancy, as the word *tantra* here applies to the body—as it is said: "When the *tantras* and machines have been broken, for those about to enter into ultimate darkness... (*i.a.12*).
"Of those agitated by the onset of disease" means those who have lost their natural state through the power of illness;
"of those with impaired minds" is connected with [the afflictions] such as desire and so forth;
"again and again" (bhūyaḥ) means repeatedly.
Having approached [the patient] and pervaded [him],
he states the individual characteristics of insanity (unmāda), beginning with "Furthermore, insanity... and so forth.
The term "delusion" (*vibhrama*) is connected with each [of the faculties] beginning with the mind (*manas*).

Here, due to delusion of the mind, one does not contemplate objects that ought to be contemplated, yet contemplates those that ought not to be contemplated; for it is said: "The object of the mind is that which is to be contemplated" (*Sūtra*, A. 8).

However, due to delusion of the intellect (*buddhi*), one perceives the permanent as impermanent, and the pleasant as unpleasant; for it is said: "That which is an improper attachment to the permanent and the impermanent, and to the pleasant and the unpleasant..."
"That should be known as a derangement of the intellect, for when the intellect is balanced, it sees correctly" (Śālistamba Sūtra 1).

Here, *saṃjñā* refers to cognition (*jñāna*); due to its derangement, one does not perceive the burning caused by fire and so forth. Alternatively, *saṃjñā* is cognition characterized by the verbalization of names;
however, due to a derangement of memory (*smṛti*), one either does not remember at all or remembers incorrectly.
Devotion is desire; and due to its perversion, that which was previously a desire becomes a lack of desire,
as when one who was free from anger becomes angry through a perversion of character,
or one who acted appropriately becomes improperly behaved through a perversion of conduct.

Conduct (*ācāra*) is behavior produced by training in the scriptures; through its confusion, one practices impurity and so forth "in the wrong place," that is, in an improper domain. By this, it should be understood that one applies meditation (*dhyāna*) to an object where there is no need for meditation, and applies delusion (*moha*) to an object where there is no need for delusion, and so forth.
"Insanity of mind" means a state of a wandering or deranged mind.

"Arditatva" (afflictedness) refers to the affliction of the upper body and the production of the physical symptoms of the disease; that is, the manifestation of the form of the disease known as *ardita* (facial paralysis), by which one produces such effects as the twisting of half the face and so forth.

Alternatively, the phrase "of the disease," mentioned first, is connected with the word "of that" (*tasya*); thus, the construction is: "the aforementioned premonitory symptoms of that insanity, which consists of delusions of the intellect and so forth, [and] the withdrawal of the eyes"—meaning the departure of the visual faculty.

By the statement "immediately thereafter," it is shown that insanity (unmāda) occurs very quickly after the prodromal symptoms (pūrvarūpa); the meaning is that other diseases, even when the prodromal symptoms have appeared, manifest only after a long time, whereas this is not the case for insanity. "Specific knowledge of the types of insanity" means the diagnostic signs of insanity caused by Vāta and the other doshas. "Parisaraṇa" means wandering or roaming.
The *śamyā* is played with the right hand, while the *tāla* is played with the left hand; as Viśākhin stated: "The *śamyā* is played with the right hand, the *tāla* with the left hand;
that which is played with both hands is called *sannipāta*.
*Asāmnā* means loudly.

"By improper vehicles" means by vehicles other than those such as elephants. "Disrespect toward what is obtained" means the failure to utilize and the disregard for food and articles that have been acquired. It is not merely disrespect, but also intense envy; the meaning is that having obtained food, one does not wish to give any to anyone. Regarding "non-concordance with wind": *upaśaya* refers to the cause of relief, such as unctuous substances (*sneha*) which are concordant with wind (*vāta*); its opposite is dryness (*rūkṣa*) and so forth. By that [opposite], there is "non-concordance," meaning discomfort.
By the word "and" (ca), the fact that [the condition] is alleviated by unctuous substances and the like that are concordant with vāta is also included.
"Impatience" (amarṣa) and so forth are the symptoms of pitta-type insanity; "agitation" (saṃrambha) refers to violent or boisterous behavior.
"Sveṣām" means of one's own [relatives];
"in the case of the symptoms of phlegmatic insanity," "rahaḥ" means in a secluded place.

"Confinement" refers to confinement by means of the *tamas* grahas and so forth, performed according to the prescribed method; that is to say, according to the method to be explained in detail in the section on the treatment of insanity (unmāda).
Furthermore, in the passage beginning with "some others," the phrase "the cause of that" (*tasya nimittam*) should be repeated and connected both with the preceding and the following [clauses].

In this context, by stating that "intellectual error alone (*prajñāparādha*) is the cause of that," one does not deny that [suffering] is produced by past unwholesome karma; for even past karma is indeed born of intellectual error.

Alternatively, by the statement "intellectual error alone is the cause of that," it is shown that for that unwholesome karma as well, intellectual error is the very cause. By this, it is expressed that what is born of karma is included within intellectual error.
"Slain by themselves" means slain by their own unwholesome karma;
"striking down" means causing them to enter [into that state].
Regarding the phrase "of one who has been placed at the front": this refers to one established as being subject to formal accusation;

his "cruel intention" consists in a delight in harming others, and through the "scorching of his vital energy" (*ojas*), he is deprived of the strength and other qualities that are the effects of *ojas*.
"Setting forth" means impelling;
in the phrase "showing," the word "themselves" (ātmānam) is to be supplied as the object.
The term *atyātma* is connected with each [of the qualities] such as strength (*bala*) and so forth.
*Atyātma* means "exceeding the self" (*ātmānam atiricya*); thus, the meaning is that there is an endowment with strength and other qualities that are disproportionate to one's self.
The junctions of the lunar phases— the new moon and the full moon—
are "naked," meaning they are without clothing.

Furthermore, the mention of the crossroads at the beginning of the passage starting with "at night" (*niśi*) is for the purpose of demonstrating that one may go to a crossroads even with another person at night; whereas the statement beginning with "of a single person" (*ekasya*) refers to going to a crossroads alone even during the day,
which they describe as a transgression of the dharma-exposition— that is, the proclamation of dharma in an improper manner (14).
"Delight," "play," "veneration," and "worship"—

one should know [the state] by means of the specific characteristics of the conduct of the intoxicated; for indeed, one should recognize that which is intoxicated as being characterized by the specific modes of conduct of the intoxicated, such as those aimed at violence and so forth.

For in that state, one who is possessed by a spirit seeking to cause harm practices acts such as entering fire in accordance with its injurious intent; one possessed by a spirit seeking pleasure engages in play for the sake of sport; and one seized by a spirit seeking worship performs acts of worship. In this context, by the term "gods" (*deva*) and so forth, one should understand the attendants of the gods and those possessing the same nature as the gods; however, the gods themselves do not enter human beings. For it is said in the *Suśruta*: "They do not cohabit with humans, nor do they ever enter into humans."

"Those who say 'they enter you' out of delusion are to be excluded from the domain of *bhūtavidyā* (the science of spirits)," and so forth; for since one seized by a spirit seeking to cause harm is incurable, [the author] states the characteristics mentioned in general terms for the sake of identifying such a person, specifying them individually as if seizing them by the horn.
In the passage beginning with "of those two" (tayor), "going" refers to traveling to sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and other such places.
Regarding the phrase "those two," it refers to the resident and the guest.
"Sometimes they bind each other" means not always,
because of the conjunction of the aforementioned causes; "therein" refers to the conjunction of innate and adventitious causes.

Regarding "incurable association" (*asādhyasaṃyoga*): when, in the case of insanity born of the three *doṣas*, there is an affliction by a deity or similar being seeking to cause harm, then an association of two incurable factors occurs.
