However, an "association of the curable and the incurable" (*sādhyāsādhyasaṃyoga*) should be understood as follows: it occurs in insanity born of a single *doṣa* due to the addition of an insanity seeking to cause harm, and likewise in an insanity seeking pleasure due to the addition of an affliction from insanity born of the three *doṣas*, and so forth.

Since the curability of an "association of the curable" is established by its very nature as curable, the further statement "it is curable" is intended to prevent the suspicion of incurability that might arise from the presence of another disorder, on account of the increased severity of the condition.
"Only the conjunction of the means" (sādhanasaṃyogam eva) means the union of the innate and adventitious means.

Now, in order to avoid [the misconception that] gods and others are the cause of insanity, he shows that even in the case of insanity caused by gods and others, the very same action (karma) is the cause, beginning with "not indeed," etc.

By the statement "they follow [him]," it is shown that gods and others, impelled solely by his own evil deeds, take possession of one who performs unwholesome actions. For if gods and others were to act thus independently of karma, they would drive everyone insane; such is the implication.
The phrase "that affliction is not caused by that" means that this insanity is not produced by gods and the like.

Now, [the author] explains how this [possession], even though produced by the entry of gods and others, is not "made by gods and others": "For there is no state of having already accomplished what was to be done" (*na hyasti kṛtakṛtyatā*). This means that when madness is caused by unwholesome karma, there is no further agency on the part of gods and others; for what has already been done is not done again, and the point is that gods and others are themselves entirely dependent upon karma.
Alternatively, the reading is: "For there is no state of having accomplished what was to be done for him" (*na hyasya kṛtakṛtyatā*).

In this regard, it is by the very performance of past karma that a person becomes "driven mad" (*unmādita*)—that is, one who is to be acted upon (*kṛtya*) or made a victim; otherwise, possession by gods and others would occur indiscriminately for everyone alike. Therefore, only he by whom karma producing the fruit of madness has been performed is approached by the gods and others, who themselves are dependent on karma. With this intention, [the author] says: "For there is no 'having done what was to be done' for him"—meaning that for one who has not performed sinful karma, there is no state of being approachable by gods and others. Since the gods and others here are dependent on karma, they are not to be blamed.
19–20 And he says that one should not fear gods and the like: "From transgression of wisdom," etc.;
"one should not revile" means one should not reproach.

In the passage beginning with "the self" (ātmānam), the meaning of the sentence is that the self alone, by performing auspicious and inauspicious actions, becomes the cause of happiness and suffering respectively.
"One should not tremble" means one should not fear gods and the like, thinking, "These [beings] might seize even one who performs auspicious deeds.
"Apaciti" means honor or worship.
Regarding the passage beginning with "And those," etc.: "those" refers to the honoring of the gods and the cultivation of what is beneficial;
"and hostility toward them" means that hostility toward those [beings] such as the gods arises from inauspicious karmas. All of this is dependent upon the self (*ātman*).
By this, he demonstrates that both the avoidance of the causes of insanity and the cultivation of their opposites are indeed under the control of the self.

21–24. Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Insanity" (*unmādanidāna*), in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā*, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Section on Diagnosis (*nidānasthāna*).
[Nidānasthāna, Chapter 8 (38 of 120)] Following the discussion on insanity (unmāda), the etiology of epilepsy (apasmāra) is now stated, because epilepsy arises prior to the onset of insanity.

The statement "four" is intended to establish that there are four types of epilepsy (apasmāra), even when associated with exogenous factors; for epilepsy is not produced by an exogenous factor acting independently, as is the case with insanity (unmāda). In the phrase "of those whose humors (doṣa) are agitated, discordant, and excessive," agitation indicates that they have strayed from their proper course, while discordance shows that they occasionally produce the paroxysms of epilepsy.
The passage beginning with *samala* and so forth is similar to the explanation of insanity (*unmāda*).

Regarding the phrase *atyupakṣayād vā*, the meaning is "due to the body being excessively emaciated. This is because in the section on the etiology of insanity (*unmādanidāna*), in the text beginning with *samalavikṛta* and so forth, it is stated: "of those whose bodies are excessively emaciated" (*atyupakṣīṇadehānām*) [Caraka Saṃhitā, Nidāna Sthāna 7].

By the term "the most excellent abode" (*śreṣṭhatamāyatanam*), he demonstrates that while other parts of the body are also locations for the inner self (*antarātman*), the heart (*hṛdaya*) is the most excellent, precisely because it is there that the specific basis for consciousness (*cetanā*) is established.
The construction is as follows: "having approached" means having pervaded;
"they remain above" means they remain above the heart, and "having approached" refers to the seats of the sense organs;
the reading "paryavatiṣṭhante" (they settle around) is quite clear.
"Situated there" means they are situated in a state of dissolution within the heart and the seats of the senses;

and when those dissolved [elements], impelled by desire and the like, again specifically fill the heart and the seats of the senses, then one suffers from epilepsy—that is, one becomes possessed by the force of epilepsy—such is the meaning of the sentence.
He states the individual characteristics of epilepsy (*apasmāra*): "Furthermore, epilepsy... and so forth.
"From the convergence" (*samplavāt*) means from the transformation [of the humors].
"Characterized by loathsome movements" (*bībhatsaceṣṭam*) refers to that in which there are movements such as vomiting foam and convulsions of the limbs, which are loathsome in nature.

"Occasional entry into darkness" means an intermittent entry into darkness; it is called "entry into darkness" because of its similarity to ignorance (*ajñāna*), for one who is possessed by the force of epilepsy (*apasmāra*) perceives nothing at all, as if entering into darkness.
"Hearing what is not sound" means hearing that which does not exist as sound.
"Āṭopa" means that a specific gurgling sound produced by wind (vāta) is heard; this is the meaning of verses 6–7.
Regarding the passage beginning with "In that case, this... and so forth:
The meaning is that specific consciousness (viśeṣavijñāna) is the symptom of epilepsy caused by wind (vātāpasmāra);
"regaining consciousness in an instant" shows that in wind-induced epilepsy, there is a rapid awakening;
"with a distended neck" means with a neck that is filled and stiffened.
"Having a pierced head" means having a crooked head;
it should be understood that this refers to the perception of an unstable and flickering form at the time of falling, for once fallen, one is simply not conscious at all.
In the same way, the perception of form in other cases is also to be understood.
In the *Suśruta-saṃhitā* as well, the perception of forms at the very moment of falling is described: "He who says, 'A deformed black being is chasing after me;

therefore my consciousness shall perish,' that is epilepsy of a vātika nature" (*Su.U.A.* 61), and so forth. Although in the specific characteristics of paittika epilepsy it is stated that "one regains consciousness in an instant," nevertheless, a greater duration of time should be understood here in comparison to the vātika type; for indeed, vāyu acts more swiftly even than pitta.
"Ugra" means like a harmful [creature]; "bhairava," however, refers to places such as cremation grounds that cause fear even though they are not harmful; "ādīpta" means blazing or aflame;
and "cirād apasmarantam" means one who possesses the force of epilepsy after a long period of time.

In the phrase "it indeed exists" (*bhavatyeva*), the particle *eva* serves to exclude absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*). For example, in the statement "the lotus is indeed blue," the word *eva* indicates precisely this exclusion of absolute non-connection.
By this, it is shown that in every case of epilepsy there is a connection with the elements (*bhūta*), and that epilepsy is never independent or purely elemental in nature.

Regarding the phrase "at a later time" (*uttarakālam*), although a detailed exposition need not be stated even in the treatment of epilepsy (*apasmāra*), nevertheless, because the procedure for insanity (*unmāda*) is extended by analogy to that case, it is understood that the elaboration is exactly as described for insanity; thus it is said here: "We shall teach that at a later time. For it has been stated: "If a physician perceives that the sequela of [epilepsy] is adventitious (*āgantuka*) and its form exceeds the symptoms of the [doshas], he should administer the treatment for adventitious insanity" (Ci. A. 10).

The phrase "by the aforementioned signs" (yathoktaliṅgaiḥ) uses the instrumental case in place of the ablative; thus, it means that there is an excess of signs, or a state of being distinct from the signs, compared to the aforementioned signs of epilepsy. This means that [the signs] are not in accordance with the signs of the *doṣas*, but rather dissimilar to them. The word "some" (*kiñcit*) implies not all, but only a small portion of signs that differ from the signs of the *doṣas* occurs when an exogenous factor (*āgantuka*) is associated [with the endogenous factors]. By this, he demonstrates that an exogenous epilepsy does not occur independently; for if the exogenous factor were indeed independent, then the exogenous signs would not be merely slight, but rather total.
With the words beginning "beneficial" (hitāni), he states the aphorism on therapeutics;
the construction is: "and those which are pacifying are beneficial."
He explains the origin of the diseases already mentioned, beginning with the words "In that [time]," and so forth.

Although fever (*jvara*) was indeed the first to arise there, it is described later because it arose as a distinct manifestation of Rudra’s wrath; whereas *gulma* and the other ailments, occurring in the period immediately following the destruction of the sacrifice, are mentioned first because they were produced by the same causal complex (*ekasāmagrījātatvena*). The point is that the very first arising of fever has already been stated in the "Etiology of Fever" (*Jvaranidāna*).
"Purā" means at the beginning of creation;
"born from the forehead" (lalāṭaprabhava) means born from the fire of wrath arising from the forehead;
"anvaya" means a continuous sequence.
"Common" (*sādhāraṇa*) refers to treatments such as emesis that counteract the *doṣas*, as well as offerings and auspicious rites that counteract divine influences.
He states the fruit of knowing all diseases as described in the Section on Etiology (*Nidānasthāna*), beginning with the words "all," and so forth.

"And he does not fall into delusion" means that even though the etiology, location, and so forth have not been explicitly stated, and even though the object of knowledge is subtle, he does not fall into delusion because [these factors] have been observed frequently; rather, the meaning is that even those [details] are inferred.
Regarding the word "entirely" (*akhilena*): as much as the eightfold group of diseases was promised according to their etiology and location, all of that has been stated in its entirety.

Therefore, there is no deficiency [in this work], because the diagnosis (nidāna) that is to be discussed in the Section on Therapeutics (cikitsāsthāna) has already been mentioned here; and as for the fact that the diagnosis of fever and other diseases must be stated again, the intention is that it is merely an elaboration (prapañca) of this very same subject.
Now, from the section on etiology (nidāna), he says "nidānārtha... and so forth, in order to state that some diseases can also act as causes for other diseases.

The meaning of "nidānārthakara" is as follows: the purpose (artha) or function of an etiological factor (nidāna) is the production of disease; that which performs this [purpose] is "nidānārthakara," meaning that which generates disease.

While it should have been said "the form of the etiology" (*nidānarūpa*), by saying instead "that which performs the function of the etiology" (*nidānārthakara*), he demonstrates that even when a disease is being produced, the cause is precisely that which generates the fundamental disease; thus, he shows that the etiology is the intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) within the disease produced by the disease, whose function is to generate the fundamental disease.

Therefore, even in a disease born of another disease, the three causes—namely unwholesome contact of the sense organs with their objects and so forth—which constitute the root, remain the cause; thus, one should not argue that this leads to the occurrence of a fourth distinct cause, nor should such an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) be asserted. For it should be understood that the very causes of fever, such as excessive heat and so on, having produced the fever, also generate hemorrhagic fever (raktapitta) when their power is augmented by other factors. Likewise, abdominal tumors (gulma) also arise from hemorrhoids (arśas) themselves.

"From cough, wasting arises" means that from cough, the depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu-kṣaya*) arises; and that depletion of the constituents is observed to be the cause of the disease known as consumption (*śoṣa*). This is the construction [of the verse]. (16–19) Now, one might object: "In cases where the cause of a disease is itself a disease, is the disease acting as the cause not merely secondary? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Those [diseases] first," and so forth.

—Those [factors] such as fever (jvara) and the like, being merely diseases prior to the production of blood-bile (raktapitta) and so forth, are themselves primary by virtue of causing affliction (rujā); subsequently, they act as causes, meaning they become the producers of blood-bile and the like. Now, even in this case, having produced blood-bile and so forth, do fever and the like remain in the form of disease like their causes, or not? To this he says: "ubhaya... and so forth.

"Producing both purposes" means they produce the causal purpose, which consists of the generation of blood-bile (*raktapitta*) and so forth, as well as the pathological purpose, characterized by affliction; the meaning is that they do not cease merely after producing another disease.
He states another classification: "likewise, those that perform a single purpose" (*ekārthakāriṇaḥ*), meaning they perform the purpose of a single cause alone.
He explains these same two positions in reverse order, beginning with "Someone [thinks]... and so forth.

In this context, that which, having produced the purpose of the cause (hetvartha), namely the generation of disease, subsides, is "that which accomplishes a single purpose" (ekārthakārī). However, that which, having produced the purpose of the cause by generating another disease, persists itself as well, is "that which accomplishes both purposes" (ubhayārthakārī). When, even after initiating a cough, it persists itself, then the coryza (pratiśyāya) acts as a disease in its own right through its capacity to cause pain, and acts as the cause by way of generating the cough; but when, after producing the cough, it subsides of its own accord, then, because it has ceased at the time of the cough, it should be understood as accomplishing only the purpose of the cause.
Regarding the mixing and confluence of diseases, he asks from what cause such a thing occurs and says "due to improper application," and so forth.

As for the impurity of application: for example, if a constipating treatment is administered during diarrhea, it suppresses the [original] humor (*doṣa*) and thereby produces pain, abdominal distension, flatulence, and so on.
He states another reason: "because of mutual occurrence"; the meaning is "because they are of the nature of being causes for one another.
For catarrh is indeed the cause of cough by its very own nature, and that [cough] is [the cause] of consumption (rājayakṣman), and so forth.
He explains the impurity of the application (*prayoga-apariśuddhi*) with the words "the application," and so forth;

"one should not provoke" means one should not produce another disease. Furthermore, the mutual occurrence [of diseases]—such as how blood-bile (*rakta-pitta*) is provoked by the feverish heat—is already stated [elsewhere], and thus it is not explained again here.
23. From the section on causes, he states another property of the cause: "The cause is one," and so forth. He provides examples for these four positions: "In fever," and so forth.
Although dryness (*rūkṣa*) is a cause for many [diseases], it should nevertheless be understood that, depending on factors such as place and time, it may sometimes be the cause of fever alone.
Regarding the phrase "by means of dryness and so forth" (*rūkṣādibhiḥ*), this refers to dryness, heat, saltiness, and the like.
Regarding the phrase "fever and so forth" (*jvarādyāḥ*), this refers to fever, hemorrhagic disease (*raktapitta*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and others.

He states that the *liṅga* (logical mark) also has fourfold types, just like the *hetu* (reason), beginning with the words "the *liṅga*" and so forth. The connection is as follows: "one *liṅga* is characterized in the same way."

"Of those whose roots are irregular onset" means of those characterized by irregular onset as their primary feature; the meaning is "of those whose symptoms of fever, such as irregularity of onset and discharge, and irregularity of the *ūṣman* (thermal element), have been previously described.

Indeed, having observed the single [symptom] of fever—which consists of heat—one infers that its other characteristics, such as irregular onset and discharge, have occurred, will occur, or are currently present;
thus, it is understood that "fever alone is defined. This is the meaning.
"By these signs," and so forth;
by these [signs] such as irregular onset and cessation, fevers and other conditions "are present"—this is the ellipsis.
Indeed, irregular onset and the others are observed, as the case may be, in vāta-fever, as well as in vāta-type asthma or vāta-type hiccup.
27–29 He states that this fourfold classification applies to medical treatment as well— beginning with "one," etc.— 20–32.

In the context of explaining medical treatment (*cikitsā*), [the author] describes the different types of curable conditions, which are the objects of medical intervention, as well as the different types of incurable conditions, which are the objects where medical intervention ceases—beginning with the words "sukha" and so forth.

"Sukhopāya" means a means that is easily obtained, such as a physician and other resources; alternatively, it means being "easily remedied," in the sense that it is cured with only a small amount of effort. "Yāti nāśeṣatām" means it does not cease entirely [from its nature].
"Incurable in the highest degree" means incurable to a greater extent than palliable;
its further explanation is "to be rejected," referring to medical treatments or therapies.

Regarding the phrase "a change in state" (*bhāvāntaram*): that which is easily curable (*sukhasādhya*) becomes difficult to cure (*kṛcchrasādhya*), the difficult-to-cure becomes palliable (*yāpya*), and the palliable becomes incurable (*pratyākhyeya*).
In the context of describing the ease with which a disease may be cured (verses 33–35), he states the other stages such as "increase" (*vṛddhi*) and so forth: "In increase," etc. (*vṛddhītyādi*).

The construction of the sentence is as follows: one should observe not only the states of increase, maintenance, and decrease of diseases, but also those of the bodily fire (*agni*), strength (*bala*), and the mind (*cetas*).
He states the purpose of knowing these states of disease with the words beginning "the state of disease" (*vyādhyavasthā*):
"the fourfold welfare" (*catuḥśreya*) refers to medical treatment (*cikitsita*) which brings about the fourfold welfare; "attains" (*prapadyate*) means that one understands it.
Having described the various types of diseases (36–37), he now states the types of *doṣas* relevant for treatment—beginning with "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*) and so forth.

Since the *doṣas* that have moved laterally (*tiryaggatāḥ*) follow a deviant path, they cannot be properly or quickly joined with medicine; therefore, it is logical that they cause suffering for a long time.

By the phrase "knowing the strength of the body and the digestive fire" (dehāgnibalavid), it is indicated that a treatment administered with haste and excessive medicinal application when the disorder has reached the channels (tiryaggata) destroys both the body and the digestive fire.
The term "by applications" (prayogaiḥ) refers to applications of small doses over a long period of time.

"Or easily" (sukhaṃ vā) means that one should eliminate [the disorder] in a manner that is comfortable and proximate; that is, by means of purification such as emesis (vamana) and so forth, which is suitable for removal when the disorder is located in the stomach (āmāśaya) or other nearby sites. By this, one should eliminate it.

Now, he states that the diseases which were mentioned as symptoms in the section on etiology (nidāna) may also exist as independent diseases— beginning with the words "for the sake of knowledge" and so forth—
in the summary (saṅgraha), which is the compendium of the etiology of diseases and other topics.

The meaning is that those diseases which exist in the Section on Etiology (Nidānasthāna) for the purpose of knowledge—specifically for the purpose of knowing fever and other primary diseases—are themselves to be designated as diseases, even when they arise independently as indigestion, anorexia, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "but at that time they are signs" (*tadātve tu liṅgāni*): when anorexia and other such symptoms arise as dependent on fever and so forth, then, due to that dependence, they are merely signs (*liṅga*) and not diseases (*āmaya*). For the established principle of Āyurveda is that a disease is independent and must be pacified by its own specific treatment; whereas anorexia and other symptoms that take the form of signs of fever are to be pacified precisely by the treatment of the fever itself—this is the intended meaning. (40) Now, he describes the full scope of the cause (*hetu*) under discussion in the section on diagnosis, beginning with "disease" (*vikāra*), etc.
"Modification is disequilibrium,
while equilibrium is primordial nature;
by the word 'all,' he includes both the physical and the spiritual."
"Subject to the power of causes" means having an origin dependent upon causes.

By this it is meant that one who desires health, beauty, and a natural constitution should cultivate the causes of equilibrium (*sāmya-hetu*), and likewise, one who desires to avoid diseases characterized by pathological change (*vikāra*) should avoid the causes of such change (*vikāra-hetu*). Nor should it be argued that this statement—"In the absence of the cause, [the effect] does not persist"—is false, because we observe the persistence of swelling even after the cause of that swelling, such as curd and the like, has ceased. For even when the curd and so forth have ceased, the continuum of the *doṣas* produced by the curd and so forth continues there, acting as the generator of the swelling and other symptoms.

It should be understood that the summary of the contents of the chapter on epilepsy (apasmāra) has been stated up to the point ending with "in the compendium, only the sūtra [is included], not the treatment" (*saṅgrahe sūtramātraṃ cikitsitāt*);
however, by means of the passage beginning with "of fever and so forth" (*jvarādīnām*), he provides a summary of the contents as taught in the Section on Etiology (*nidānasthāna*).

Although the incurability of fever has not been explicitly stated in the etiology of fever, nevertheless, the word "of the eight" should be understood according to the maxim of "those with umbrellas are walking" (*chatriṇo gacchanti*). Alternatively, it should be construed as "the causes, symptoms, and alleviations of the eight. Incurability should be understood according to its applicability, both collectively and individually; thus, it is said "separately and one by one."

Therefore, the general causes and so forth common to all diseases have been stated in the sections on etiology (*nidāna-sthāna*) and elsewhere; likewise, the causes, symptoms, and alleviations of each individual fever and other diseases have been stated in their respective chapters. Here, by the mention of "symptoms" (*liṅga*), the inclusion of "premonitory symptoms" (*pūrvaliṅga*) is intended; and by the mention of "alleviation" (*upaśānti*), the inclusion of "therapeutic suitability" (*upaśaya*) is intended. As for "pathogenesis" (*samprāpti*), its non-inclusion here should be explained as being because it has already been described for each specific disease.

The synonyms for "cause" (*hetu*) are to be understood as those stated in the first chapter, beginning with "cause, sign" (*nimitta*, Ni.ma.1); likewise, the synonyms for "disease" (*vyādhi*) and the synonyms for "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) are also to be known as those mentioned in the first chapter. Regarding "onset" (*samprāpti*), the statement of its name—"onset, birth, arrival" (*samprāptir jātir āgatiḥ*, Ni.ma.1)—is primarily intended to define its characteristics, and thus it has not been included here; alternatively, it is already included within the summary of the section beginning with "the causes. Furthermore, the summary of the contents of the chapter on epilepsy (*apasmāra*) has not been presented separately, because it has already been accomplished by the immediately preceding summary of the sections.

In this context, the phrase "the causes" and so forth refers to the inclusion of all causes of disease and other factors; in this view, the term "separately" is connected with "of fevers and the like," while the term "individually" is connected with "causes, symptoms, homologous therapy, and pacification.
Furthermore, by the use of the word "in summary," it indicates that the diagnosis (nidāna) is intended to be expanded upon in the section on therapeutics (cikitsita).

Some here derive the word *nidāna* from the analysis: "that by which the pentad beginning with the cause (*hetu*) is indicated (*nidyate*) and bound (*nibadhyate*) is the *nidāna*"; they further state that by the word *nidāna*, the rope used for tethering cows at the time of milking is meant, and the term *nidāna* has indeed already been explained in the context of the diagnosis of fever (jvara-nidāna).

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Apasmāra," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of Caraka, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta. [Section on Specific Determination (*Vimānasthāna*)]

[Vimānasthāna, Chapter 1 (39 of 120)] In the *Nidāna* section, for the sake of medical treatment, there is a requirement to know the specific characteristics of the *doṣas*, medicinal substances, and so forth, based on the five factors such as the known causes; therefore, he speaks of the *Vimānasthāna*, which makes known the specific characteristics of the *doṣas*, medicinal substances, and so forth to be described hereafter.
Furthermore, because of the primacy of the *doṣas* and medicinal substances therein, he first speaks of the *Rasavimāna*, which makes known their specific characteristics.
And he will demonstrate this connection of the sections himself:

that by which [the nature of things] is specifically measured or known—such as defects, medicines, and so forth—is called *vimāna*; the meaning is the specific excellence of the power and other qualities of the defects, medicines, and so on. That section where such a *vimāna* resides as its subject matter is the *Vimānasthāna*.
The chapter composed concerning the *rasavimāna* (the measurement of tastes) is the *Rasavimāna*.
With the words "iha khalu" and so forth, he states the connection with the subject matter.

By including the distinctions of etiology (*samprāpti*), number, predominance, and so on, he demonstrates that by teaching etiology alone, all aspects of etiology—through its various divisions such as number and the rest—are effectively explained.

However, there is no such distinction among the *nimitta* (causes) and so forth that would require them to be described in detail with few words, such that they too should be mentioned here; therefore, they are stated only in general terms.
Understanding that one "enters" [the path] by means of these, defects (*doṣa*) and the rest have been explained in detail in the *Sūtrasthāna* itself.
"Māna" refers to specific qualities such as power and so forth;
he states the cause for knowing this in the passage beginning with "doṣādi," and "kriyāyāḥ" refers to medical treatment (cikitsā).
He makes a formal promise to state the subject matter of the third chapter, beginning with the words "tatrādau" (therein, at the outset), etc.

Although, in the passage beginning with "doṣabheṣaja" (the humors and the medicine), the humor (*doṣa*) was placed first because the medicine is dependent upon the humor, nevertheless, here—because the medicine in the form of tastes (*rasa*) and substances (*dravya*) acts to pacify the disease expected [by the physician], and because the humor is also a cause of those very tastes and substances—the tastes and substances indicated by the word "medicine" are treated first; subsequently, however, the morbidities (*vikāra*) along with the humors are taken up by the inclusion of the term "humor."
*Prabhāva* means an eminent state or power (*śakti*). In this context, it should be understood as both inconceivable and conceivable;

for, by the passage beginning with "In that regard, among those of manifold tastes," he will describe the *prabhāva* of substances and their transformations through the medium of taste and the medium of the *doṣas*, even though it is [partly] inconceivable.
The term *yāpayanti* means they maintain [the body] in a state of equilibrium.
In this context, the word "mithyā" (false/erroneous) refers to ayoga (non-application), atiyoga (excessive application), and mithyāyoga (perverse application).
The term "doṣas" (humors) refers to the bodily humors.
The word "punaḥ" (again) excludes mental defects.
It describes the action of unmixed tastes, beginning with the words "tatra" and so forth.

By this instruction on the action of tastes (*rasakarmopadeśa*), it is stated that even the *doṣas* are produced by their respective tastes and likewise pacified by those same tastes. Regarding the statement "pungent, bitter, and astringent [tastes] generate *vāta*," it should be understood that this applies when no opposing factor (*paripanthin*) is present. Therefore, there is no fault in the fact that bitter substances such as *arka*, *aguru*, and *guḍūcī* do not generate *vāta*; for in those cases, a hot potency (*uṣṇavīryatā*) exists as an opposing factor, and thus they do not generate *vāta*. This principle should be followed accordingly.

By the word "this" (enam), he shows that the sweet and other tastes specifically pacify that very wind which arises from pungent things and so forth, because they are entirely contrary to its nature; for when wind arises from waking and so forth, sleep and the like—which are the opposites of waking and so forth—are specifically wholesome.
In this way, he demonstrates the intended meaning of the words "this" (enam) and "this one" (enat) regarding bile and phlegm as well.
Now, by what reasoning do tastes (rasas) generate or pacify the humors (doṣas)? To this he says, "taste-humor," and so forth.
Regarding the term "in the combination" (sannipāte), it refers to the internal conjunction within the body;

the word "but" (tu) indicates a distinction. By this, he demonstrates that those [tastes] which possess contrary qualities specifically pacify [the humors], in comparison to those in which contrary qualities predominate.

Regarding how the qualities of tastes arise through their application, that has been stated in the aphorism beginning with, "The qualities and non-qualities are not mentioned as being dependent [on the substances]" (Sūtra 26), meaning they are those which are practiced repeatedly rather than those used only once.

Now, why is the multiplicity of combinations between tastes and *doṣas* set aside, and only the sixfold nature of tastes and the threefold nature of *doṣas* mentioned? To this, he says: "This very [point]," and so forth.
"Vyavasthā" (the systematic arrangement) refers to the detailed expansion and summary of the combinations of *rasas* and *doṣas*;
the phrase "mutually uncombined" (*paraspareṇāsaṃsṛṣṭānām*) is also to be construed with the word "of the *doṣas*" (*doṣāṇām*). 7
He states the reason for not describing the elaboration (*prapañca*) of the combinations of tastes and humors (*rasa-doṣa-saṃsarga*) with the words beginning "saṃsarga" and so forth:
because the expansion of the varieties of combinations is incalculable, therefore [the number] six and three are mentioned;

this is because the divisions of conceptualization (*vikalpa-bheda*) are incalculable. The "division of the conceptualization of combination" (*saṃsarga-vikalpasya bhedaḥ*) refers to its dissimilar modes (*vijātīya-prakāra*); because those are incalculable.

By this, the following is refuted: the argument that just as the sixfold nature of tastes is stated by designating them as "sweet" and so forth based on their connection with general properties like sweetness despite internal differences in individual instances, so too, by grouping mixtures of sweet, sour, sweet-salty, and so on under their general categories despite internal differences, a fixed number of sixty-three varieties will be established. This is because even within the mixture of sweet, sour, and so forth, there arises an incalculable variety created by distinctions such as "sweeter," "sweetest," and so on, which belong to a different genus [of taste].
For there is this statement: "The tastes indeed exceed that number by degrees of intensity" (Sūtra-sthāna, chapter 26).
Now, how then is the potency of combined tastes and doshas to be known? To this he says: "In that regard, indeed," and so forth.

In this context, while describing the potency (*prabhāva*) of a substance that possesses multiple tastes and multiple morbid humors (*doṣa*) through the combination of the individual potencies of its tastes and humors, he likewise describes the potency of the combinations of tastes and humors. This is because, since the potencies of the taste-combinations and humor-combinations here depend upon the substance and the morbidity, they are spoken of as being the potencies of the substance and the morbidity themselves.

By this principle, it should be understood that even though not explicitly stated, the potency of a single-tasted substance and a single-morbidity morbidity is indeed already expressed by the description of the potencies of uncombined tastes and humors.

"Having observed each one individually" means that by means of the individual powers of taste and so forth, one observes the combined power of a substance that possesses multiple tastes and causes a disorder involving multiple *doṣas*.

Furthermore, he states that this determination of the power of substances and disorders is not made through the gateway of the powers of taste and *doṣas* in every case, saying: "But certainly not in all cases."
Right here he states the reason with the passage beginning with "nahi" and ending with "adhyavasātum śakyam":

"of those combined in a modification and combined unequally" means of those combined in a modification (*vikṛti-samavetānām*) as well as those combined unequally (*viṣama-samavetānām*); thus, "combined in a modification and combined unequally" refers to tastes and humors (*rasa-doṣa*) that are combined (*samavetānām*) when they are joined together.

In this regard, the combination of tastes in a modified state (*vikṛtisamavāya*) is as follows: in the case of *taṇḍulīyaka*, which is sweet. For sweetness by its very nature produces unctuousness, aphrodisiac effects, and so forth; however, in *taṇḍulīyaka*, because it is combined in a modified state, it does not produce those effects. As for the astringent, pungent, bitter, and sweet [tastes] combined in sesame (*tila*), if these tastes were combined in equal proportions, then the sesame would also remove *pitta* and *kapha*, or perhaps remove all three *doṣas*; yet this [sesame] actually increases *pitta* and *kapha*. Therefore, in this case, the disparity is inferred from the fact that the tastes sometimes act as agents and sometimes do not.

The three reasons beginning with "of those consisting of various elements" (nānātmakānām) serve only to indicate *vikṛti-samavāya* (heterogeneous combination) and *viṣama-samavāya* (unequal combination).
Therefore, by means of "consisting of various elements" and so forth, there occur *vikṛti-samavāya* and *viṣama-samavāya*.

The phrase "of those consisting of various elements" refers to those produced by causes of diverse forms. Thus, the meaning is that by the very force of the difference in causes, a heterogeneous or unequal mixture of tastes and humors (*rasa-doṣa*) occurs.
Alternatively, "of diverse natures" means of diverse means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
and thus, this state of having diverse means of valid cognition is the cause for the unequal conjunction.
Furthermore, "of those mutually impaired" means of those whose qualities have been neutralized by one another.

Although there is generally no mutual impairment of the qualities among the *doṣas*, it should be understood that such occurs occasionally due to the influence of unseen factors (*adṛṣṭa*). However, in the case of the *rasas*, impairment of one by another certainly occurs through various preparations (*kalpanā*) and differentiators (*bhedaka*). In this context, the differentiators of a *rasa* are its fresh juice (*svarasa*), paste (*kalka*), and so forth. For indeed, even for a single substance, different qualities arise through specific preparations;
whereas for a *doṣa*, the differentiators are simply other affected tissues (*dūṣya*) due to their association with different qualities.

Regarding what was stated: "That very same aggravated *doṣa*, due to the particularity of its origin and having moved to another location, produces many disorders" (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 18)—in this interpretation, the separate mention of the unequal combination (*viṣama-samavāya*) of the *rasas* and *doṣas* caused by their increase or decrease is not tenable; for even in an unequal combination, the qualities of the predominant *rasa* and *doṣa* remain predominant, while those of the subordinate ones remain subordinate. Thus, by means of inference from the power of the individual components, it is possible to infer the power of the whole.

Now, it might be argued that in a heterogeneous mixture (*viṣamamelaka*), neither the qualities of the *rasa* nor those of the *doṣa* remain superior or inferior as they were before, but rather a different set of qualities arises altogether. Alas, in that case, this combination is indeed a transformation (*vikṛta*), because its effect is dissimilar to its causes.

Thus, having observed this objection, it is explained otherwise: the blending (*melaka*) of both *rasas* (tastes) and *doṣas* (humors) is of two kinds—concordant with their nature (*prakṛtyanuguṇa*) and discordant with their nature (*prakṛtyananuguṇa*). Among these, that blending which occurs without suppressing the natural qualities (*prākṛtaguṇa*) of the combined elements is termed "natural homogeneous combination" (*prakṛtisamasamavāya*). However, that which occurs by suppressing the natural qualities is designated as "unnatural heterogeneous combination" (*vikṛtiviṣamasamavāya*). The meaning is: a combination that is "heterogeneous" (*viṣama*)—that is, discordant with nature—due to a "modification" (*vikṛti*) acting as the cause, is called "unnatural heterogeneous combination."

In this very context, the three reasons— namely, "because of having various natures" (*nānātmakatva*) and so forth— should be applied exactly as they have been explained regarding the combination of modified and unequal elements (*vikṛtiviṣamasamavāya*).

As for those who treat the combination of modified and unequal elements as entirely separate— doing so because it is difficult to infer the qualities of unequal constituent parts due to the vast elaboration of the gradations of inequality in that case— they too designate it solely by the power of the modification of substances (*dravyavikāra*).
Now, how then is there knowledge of the power of transformation, discordant combination, and [the origin]? He says: "In that which is thus joined," and so forth.

"In that which is thus joined" refers to the origin (*samudaya*); [this means] that the reality of the power of the origin is the reality of the power of the combination of transformation and discordant union (*melaka*).

The meaning is this: when honey and clarified butter are held in equal proportions in the substance called *sūryāvarta*, its intoxicating quality does not arise from the sequence of qualities inherent in the combined honey and butter, nor does the tendency of the *sūryāvarta* to increase with the rising of the sun arise from the influence of the humors (*doṣa*) such as wind (*vāta*). Rather, it is produced solely by the power of their conjunction.

Furthermore, regarding the two-fold movement of the combination of humors and *rasa*, he [the author] described *sannipāta*—which consists of a balanced equilibrium of the constituent natures—as being defined by the very combination of the symptoms of the humors in the section on the etiology of fever.

Regarding what was stated: "One should recognize a dual-type fever or a combined (sānnipātika) fever as resulting from the combination of the characteristics described separately for each" (Nidāna Sthāna, Chapter 1), the symptoms of that fever caused by the three doṣas when they are combined in a state of morbid transformation (vikṛti) and inequality have been described in the section on treatment (Cikitsā Sthāna, Chapter 3) starting with: "At one moment burning heat, at another moment cold," and so forth. Indeed, the occurrence of dark-red urticaria (koṭha) and other such signs mentioned there are not found anywhere in fevers caused by vāta and the other doṣas individually.

Thus, regarding taste as well, where sweetness is naturally and inherently present in the āmrātaka fruit, there it is stated simply that "the āmrātaka is sweet. By this, its quality of alleviating vāta and pitta—which follows from the general property of sweetness—is indeed obtained.

Furthermore, in the case of the vārtāka, although pungency and bitterness lead to the production of vāta due to a morbid and discordant combination, the Teacher has stated, "vārtāka destroys vāta" (Sūtra-sthāna, chapter 27).
In such cases, one should follow the various examples set forth in the scripture.

However, it should be understood that when [the author] speaks of the substance and its qualities— characterized as modifications— even though they have already been established through the medium of tastes, defects, and qualities produced by the combination of similar natural constituents (*prakṛti-samasamavāya*), it is for the sake of excellence and clarity.
He concludes with the words "Therefore," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the reality" (*tattvam*): this refers to the reality of the potencies of taste (*rasa*) and so forth.

As for the previous promise to explain the potencies of taste and the rest, made in the statement, "First, we shall teach the potencies of tastes, substances, doshas, and morbid transformations," that purpose would be fulfilled simply by describing the potency of substances through inference from the potency of tastes, and likewise by describing the potency of morbid transformations through the potency of the *doshas*.

In this context, however, since there is no inference of the specific power of a substance or its transformation based on the inference of the power of taste or the *doṣas*—because a substance or its transformation consists of a complex combination of heterogeneous factors—it is proposed here to describe the true nature of the powers of taste and the other factors individually; thus, there is no tautology.

Furthermore, the powers of potency (*vīrya*) and post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*) regarding substances should be subsumed either under the power of the substance itself or under the power of its taste.

In this context, those potencies (*vīrya*) and post-digestive effects (*vipāka*) that are concordant with the tastes (*rasa*) are included within the taste itself. However, those potencies and post-digestive effects that are contrary to the potencies and post-digestive effects described according to the sequence of tastes should be understood as belonging to the specific substance (*dravyaprabhāva*).

The meaning is that we shall explain them separately; that is, the true nature of the potencies of taste and so forth will be explained individually throughout the entire treatise. The detailed exposition of the potencies of taste and so forth must be stated throughout the whole treatise.
Showing that this alone is the concise statement, he says: "In that regard, this," and so forth.
"This" means that which was stated by the passage beginning with "The flavors are six" and ending with "we shall teach the reality.
"It becomes taught" means it has been explained in brief.
Others, however, read: "In that regard, this is declared to be the influence of taste (rasaprabhāva).

According to this view, it should be understood that even the influence of substances, defects, and morbid humors (doṣavikāra) which is mentioned here is also [declared] by way of taste; therefore, since it is the elaboration of taste alone that has been stated, he concludes the description of that [taste] alone, and not of substances and the rest.

Furthermore, in the passage beginning with "the influence of substances" (dravyaprabhāva), because the influence of substances was previously stated in a general sense, the meaning is that we shall now describe the influence of specific substances such as oil (taila) and others by way of individual specification (śṛṅgagrāhikayā).
"For the purpose of pacification" means having pacification as their objective;
"practiced constantly" means being employed without interruption.

"Having contrary qualities" (*viruddhaguṇa*) means having qualities opposite to those of oil. Regarding "in the encounter of contrary qualities" (*viruddhaguṇasannipāte*), it refers to the meeting of two things with contrary qualities. Now, one might ask: "In the midst of two things with contrary qualities, the lesser is surely overcome by the greater; how then does oil overcome *vāta*? For it is not logical that oil possesses a greater degree [of power] relative to *vāta*. To this he says: "When practiced constantly" (*satatamabhyasyamānam*).
For oil becomes superior to wind through constant application; thus, the meaning is that it conquers wind.
"Clarified butter is exactly the same" means that clarified butter also, when practiced constantly, [conquers wind].
"Non-sweet" means the opposite of sweet due to its dryness, lightness, non-aphrodisiac nature, and so forth; it means having a pungent taste (*kaṭu-rasa*).

In this context, by the term *prabhāva* (potency), the general power of a substance (*dravya-śakti*) is meant, not its inconceivable power (*acintya-śakti*). Therefore, even from qualities such as oiliness and heat found in substances like sesame oil, the pacification of *vāta* and other humors occurs solely through the potency of the substance.

Furthermore, although the sweet taste (*madhura-rasa*) of clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) is operative in the pacification of *pitta*, the pacification of *pitta* by means of its sweetness, coolness, and mildness is indeed the specific action of the clarified butter itself; thus, it must be described as the potency of the substance.
However, when the action of a substance is considered through the medium of its taste, then the designation "potency of taste" (*rasa-prabhāva*) is used.

In this same way, the application [of the principle] should be stated regarding astringent aftertastes and honey. However, others say: the capacity of oils and the like to pacify Vata and other humors is called an inconceivable power (*acintya-prabhāva*). In that regard, the capacity of oil to pacify Vata is called an inconceivable power. And in the combination of oil and Vata—which possess contradictory qualities—it is the oil alone that conquers the Vata, and not the Vata that conquers the oil; thus is the inconceivable power of the oil. Likewise, the power of clarified butter (*sarpis*) and honey to remove Pitta and Kapha should be understood as arising from their [inconceivable] power.

Others, however, do not accept this, because by the phrase "oil and other substances being practiced constantly," it is stated that only an increase [in their potency] is the cause for conquering Vāta and the other doshas; likewise, by the passage beginning with "and whatever other substance," the inconceivable power of substances is set aside, and it is stated that the reversal of qualities through general practice alone is the cause for conquering Vāta and the others. (14) Having described the substance to be practiced as an illustration of its power, he speaks of those not to be practiced, beginning with "Now," etc.

Because of the statement "superior to others," it is shown that other substances of this kind, such as *citraka* and *bhallātaka*, should not be used in excess; however, substances like *pippalī* should be avoided even more strictly than others when used in excess.

The description of the qualities of *pippalī*—beginning with "being pungent yet having a sweet post-digestive effect" (*kaṭukāḥ satyo madhuravipākāḥ*)—is intended to demonstrate how, when used without habitual practice, they alleviate the *doṣas* by counteracting them. Likewise, it is intended to demonstrate the capacity to produce the defects mentioned in the text, such as "due to being heavy and moistening, they excite the *śleṣman*," when used in excessive habituation.

The phrase "bheṣajābhimatāśca sadyaḥ" (and considered as medicines immediately) is to be analyzed as follows: the word "sadyaḥ" (immediately) refers to when there is no repeated practice; thus, they produce auspicious results immediately. However, through the application of excessive practice, they become producers of inauspicious results.
This very point—the nature of performing wholesome or unwholesome actions—is demonstrated by the verse beginning with "āpātabhadrā" and so forth.

The phrase "due to the excellence of the application" (*prayogasamasādguṇyāt*) means that because the application is excellent; the sense is that when the application of *pippalī* and other such substances is balanced—both in terms of duration and quantity—they possess excellent qualities.
Those [substances] for which there is an accumulation of defects due to excessive use are called "doṣasañcayānubandhāḥ."
He explains this very state of being followed by an accumulation of defects with the words beginning "constantly" (*satatam*).

In the context of describing the properties of *pippalī*, he states another quality with the words beginning "but they are carriers of the formulation" (*yogavāhinyaḥ*): because they act as carriers of formulations, even though *pippalī* is pungent, it is employed in aphrodisiac preparations; likewise, in formulations for curing fever, abdominal tumors, skin diseases, and so forth, *pippalī* destroys the fever and other ailments.
And this prohibition of excessive use of *pippalī* should be understood as setting aside the exception;

therefore, the administration of *pippalī* as a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*), as well as the administration of *pippalī* in increasing doses (*pippalī-vardhamāna*) for conditions such as abdominal tumors (*gulma*), does not entail any contradiction.
For it is inferred from the words of the Sage that in the aforementioned context, *pippalī*s are indeed free from defects when used according to the prescribed method.

Others, however, maintain that the excessive use of long pepper (pippalī) and other such substances is prohibited when used as seasonings for food, but not when used independently; this should be understood to mean "constantly employed" both by way of being in excess and by way of constant application. 16
"Cutting the heart" means being possessed of the sensation of the heart being cut to pieces.
"Exhaustion" (glāni) refers to the wasting away of the flesh or the loss of vitality.
Salt does not only cause injury to the body through excessive consumption; rather, it also causes injury to the earth itself. Thus he says: "Those here... and so forth.
"Saline" (*ūṣara*) means those places where salt is predominant.

Regarding the statement "one should not consume salt excessively," this means one should not consume salt in excess quantity constantly; however, as a seasoning for food substances, even a small amount may certainly be used habitually.
He states the defects even for those in regions other than Bāhlīka and so forth who consume excessive salt: "Those who... and so on.

By this, it is inferred that even in other regions, the defects such as flaccidity (śaithilya) and the like in those accustomed to excessive salt are caused solely by the overuse of salt, and not by the inherent nature of the region.

"Of them" refers to those for whom excessively alkaline and salty substances are habitual; "due to that habituation" means due to the habituation to excessive alkali and excessive salt; "gradually" means by the gradual process of abandoning habitual practices as described in the section on the non-suppression of natural urges (*anega-dhāraṇīya*).
And here, by the term "sātmya" (habituation), "local habituation" (aukasātmya) is intended;
regarding the two positions—that it may be slightly harmful or entirely harmless—the determination is that extreme habituation is slightly harmful, while the other is harmless.
"Sātmya" means "habitual suitability" (*okasātmya*);
[the word *oka* means] "from habituation" (*abhyāsāt*).
"The meaning of *upaśaya*" means that which is denoted by the term *upaśaya*.
Regarding the phrase "that": *okasātmya* (habitual suitability) is threefold according to the divisions of superior, inferior, and middling;
however, it is sevenfold, consisting of six types based on each individual taste and one type resulting from the consumption of combined tastes; thus, it is sevenfold.
By the word "mixed" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*), those [foods] beginning with two tastes and ending with six tastes are included.
The phrase "standing between superior, inferior, and middling" refers to those beginning with two tastes and ending with five tastes;
it characterizes a person by means of the inferior and the middling.
"Excellent" means one should prepare a diet that is suitable for all tastes; "should practice" is the meaning,
and "gradually" refers to the aforementioned sequence of practice.

It is said that even when all tastes have been proven suitable, food must still be prepared only with ingredients that possess an excellent constitution and other such qualities; thus he says, "all tastes," etc.
The phrase "having thoroughly considered" means having deliberated upon what is beneficial and what is harmful;
by the words "only that which is beneficial," the meaning is that one should adhere to—that is, consume—only that which is beneficial according to one's constitution and other factors.

"Āhāravidhi" means the rule, type, or regulation regarding food; its "viśeṣa" (distinction) refers to its wholesomeness and unwholesomeness. The "āyatanas" (bases) of that [distinction] are its causes;
thus, "āhāravidhiviśeṣāyatanas" means that the wholesomeness and unwholesomeness of the types of food are caused by factors such as one's constitution (*prakṛti*). This is the meaning.
Those for whom the user is the eighth are "those with the user as the eighth" (upayoktr-aṣṭamāni).
Having thus stated [the categories] beginning with the primary cause (prakṛti), he analyzes them with the words "In that regard," and so forth.
"Innate" means not produced by conditioning factors (*saṃskāra*) and so forth.

Regarding "in the case of black gram and mung bean": by nature there is heaviness in black gram and lightness in mung bean; likewise, there is heaviness in the boar and lightness in the antelope. (22.1)

While it would have been sufficient to say "of substances" (*dravyāṇām*), by specifying "of those possessing their own inherent nature" (*svābhāvikānām*), he demonstrates that at the time of production, there is the imposition of its own qualities by the generative factors, whereas *saṃskāra* (processing/refinement) is the imparting of a different quality to that which has already been produced, such as by means of water and so forth.

And this is performed precisely by the suppression of the natural qualities; for example, by contact with water, fire, and cleansing, the heaviness residing in rice grains is destroyed and lightness is produced in the cooked grain, as it is said: "Rice that is well-washed, drained, steamed, and heated is light" (Sūtra-sthāna 27).
Likewise, even for light substances such as red rice (*raktaśāli*), lightness increases through contact with fire and the like;
and the acquisition of qualities occurs through churning, as in: "Curd that causes swelling becomes a destroyer of swelling when churned, despite being oily.
Regarding location (*deśa*), it is as in: "One should place [it] beneath a heap of ashes" (Ci. A. 1, pāda 1), and so forth.

The infusion of qualities through *vāsana* is as follows: water acquires a sweet fragrance by being infused with the scent of blue lotuses and the like; and through cultivation (*bhāvanā*) performed with one's own essence and so forth, there occurs an enhancement of the quality of even a stable substance such as *āmalaka*, according to the duration of time—as in: "One should drink the juice produced after a fortnight" (Cikitsāsthāna, chapter 15), and so on.

As in the case of a vessel—for example, in the passage beginning, “One should smear an iron bowl with the paste of the three fruits” (Ci.A.1, Pā.3)—the inclusion of the word “etcetera” (ādi) implies grinding, consecration, and so forth. Now, one might ask: how can an inherent quality (*svābhāvika-guṇa*) be destroyed by a quality produced through processing (*saṃskārādheya-guṇa*), given that it has been stated that “inherent nature is beyond remedy” (*svabhāvo niṣpratikriyaḥ*)? For if inherent heaviness were remedied by processing, then how could it be said that “inherent nature is beyond remedy”? We reply: the statement “inherent nature is beyond remedy” means that the inherent nature of things cannot be altered at the time of their production; it does not mean otherwise.

Therefore, the heaviness of beans and other substances, which is bound to their genus (*jāti*), cannot be altered even by that genus; however, its transformation through *saṃskāra* (processing) is indeed admitted, as it is observed in experience.
On the other hand, certain qualities of substances are not altered even by processing and the like, such as the heat of fire, the mobility of air, and the viscidity of oil;
for these are qualities that persist as long as the substance itself exists (*yāvaddravyabhāvin*).
However, qualities such as weight (*gaurava*) and so forth do not persist for the entire duration of the substance, since they are observed to disappear even in the case of old grain and the like;
for it has been said: "A quality undergoes destruction either through the destruction of the substance or through the imposition of another quality."

But where, by means of a refinement (*saṃskāra*), another substance characterized as boiled rice (*vrīhi-lāja*) is produced, there the production of a different quality is indeed perfectly appropriate.
(22.2) He states [the nature of] conjunction (*saṃyoga*): "Conjunction, however," and so forth.
"He initiates a specific quality" means that he initiates an unseen effect (*adṛṣṭa*) in a portion of the substance being conjoined;

"which not each individually" means that specific quality which substances, when not conjoined one by one, do not initiate. For honey and ghee are individually non-lethal, yet when combined they become lethal; and the conjunction of milk with fish and so forth causes leprosy and other ailments.

In this context, "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) is intended specifically as the meeting of substances that are currently perceived; therefore, although conjunction exists even in the case of mental states (*bhāvanā*) and so forth, they are not included under the category of conjunction because mental states and substances are not perceived there as primary entities.
(22) A heap (*rāśi*) is the measure (*pramāṇa*).

"For the sake of determining the results of proper and improper measure" means that it explains all the [astrological] influences (*graha*) regarding the auspicious result of food and medicine taken in the proper measure, and the inauspicious result of what is taken in an improper measure—whether deficient or excessive—as it was stated: "For the sake of knowing that, there is the 'heap' (*rāśi*) designation for both the appropriate measure and the inappropriate measure. This is what is elucidated in the passage beginning with "Therein," and so forth.
The phrase "of all" explains the measurement and inclusion of mixed items such as rice, meat, and soup as a single lump. Regarding the phrase "furthermore, inclusion," and so forth:

"one by one" refers to the measurement of individual components—such as a *kuḍava* of rice, a *pala* of soup, and two *palas* of meat—and based on these component measurements, the measurement of the aggregate is established.

In the case of *sarvagraha* (taking all), there is no restriction regarding the quantity for each individual part. Therefore, *sarvagraha* refers to the determination of the full measure of food by means of any food whatsoever, where the measure for each [part] is unrestricted.
He demonstrates this very point through the etymology of the word, beginning with "for of everything" (*sarvasya hi*), etc.;
"from all" (*sarvataḥ*) means from each individual part.
22(4) He analyzes the place— by the mention of "place" and so forth, he shows the location of the food substance as well as that of the eater.
"He explains" means that [the text] serves as the cause for the knowledge of qualities produced by the origin and distribution of a substance.
In this regard, regarding origin: that which is born in the Himalayas possesses excellent qualities, while that born in the desert is light, and so forth.

Regarding distribution: lightness is perceived in creatures that consume light food and those that roam in arid lands and perform many activities; conversely, heaviness is perceived in their opposites.

Furthermore, suitability (*sātmya*) characterized by qualities opposite to those of a region is adopted according to that region's specific suitability; for example, hot and dry qualities in marshy (*ānūpa*) regions, and cold and unctuous qualities in arid (*dhanvana*) regions. As for suitability regarding one's habitat (*okasātmya*), it is included within the category of suitability of the user. (22, 5) "Constant" (*nityaga*) refers to the form of day and night and so forth.
"State-dependent" (*āvasthika*) means characterized by specific states such as illness, childhood, and so forth.

"Dependent on modification" (*vikāram apekṣate*) means that, for the purpose of regulating diet, one must take into account modifications of phlegm (*śleṣma*) caused by childhood and other factors, as well as fevers and the like.
"Seasonal suitability" (*ṛtusātmya*) refers to that which depends on the season; thus, it is "dependent on seasonal suitability."

22(6) The rule regarding the proper use [of food]—namely, that "food should be consumed in this manner and not in that manner"—is stated primarily with reference to the signs of digestion (*jīrṇa-lakṣaṇa*). Therefore, in this context, it also necessarily depends on rules of usage such as "not speaking, not laughing, neither too fast nor too slow. However, since eating when there is indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) results in the great fault characterized by the provocation of the three *doṣas*, this very case has been cited as an example.

22(7) That which is dependent on habituation (*sātmya*) is so because it depends upon the experiencing person (*bhoktṛ-puruṣa*); for, through repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), something becomes habituated as either wholesome or unwholesome for a particular individual.

Regarding the passage beginning with "of these" (*eṣām*), it should be understood that specific qualities resulting in auspicious fruits and those resulting in inauspicious fruits are mutually supportive.

In this context, qualities such as lightness (*lāghava*) and so forth are auspicious by nature (*prakṛtyā*), while heaviness (*gurutva*) and so forth are inauspicious by nature. Furthermore, specific qualities produced through the instruments of action (*karaṇa*) and other factors are auspicious when prescribed by the scriptures, but inauspicious when prohibited.
Unwholesomeness regarding place (*deśāsātmya*)—such as a substance originating from a condemned region—and the like, results only in inauspicious effects.

Similarly, unwholesomeness regarding time (*kālāsātmya*), such as eating during indigestion (*ajīrṇa-bhojana*), results in inauspicious effects. Likewise, unwholesomeness regarding occasion (*okāsātmya*) should be understood as inauspicious and resulting in inauspicious effects. Conversely, however, that which results in auspicious effects may arise from delusion (*moha*), meaning from ignorance (*ajñāna*); or from negligence (*pramāda*), meaning even knowing [the truth], acting out of passion (*rāga*).
"Pleasant" means pleasant only for the immediate moment;

this is the explanation of "harmful": "having an unpleasant result"—"unpleasant" means consisting of suffering, and "result" (udarka) means the fruit occurring at a later time; that which possesses such a result is so described.
"Or something else" refers to medicinal substances, the monastic dwelling, and so forth;
"therein," and so on, means "this," which is what will be explained hereafter.

The "prescription for diet" (*āhāravidhi*) refers to that which is prescribed by means of the qualities about to be described, such as being warm, unctuous, and so forth; this is the "formulation of the dietary rules.

By the phrase "and for certain patients," it demonstrates the opposite rule—for instance, that for those with *rakta-pitta* (blood-bile disorders) only cold is beneficial, while for those with *kapha* diseases only dryness is wholesome.
The construction is: "for certain individuals who are eating, this formulation of dietary rules becomes most beneficial."

"By its very nature" means by its own inherent character (*svabhāva*). It is stated that [this regimen] is "the most beneficial. Therefore, that which is beneficial by nature may occasionally become harmful upon encountering a particular person; because such cases are merely occasional, they are disregarded. Thus, the intention is that we shall describe this as "the most beneficial" because it is the general rule. In the passage beginning with "hot," the word "properly" (*samyak*) is to be understood as a separate term. 24
"Of that" refers to food endowed with qualities such as heat;
"its excellence" means its possession of praiseworthy qualities;
"he diminishes" means he causes it to lose its integrity by breaking up its composite structure.
25(1-2) *Mātrāvat* contains the suffix *matup* in the sense of praise; thus, it means "possessing a praiseworthy measure.
*Apīḍayat* means that, by not being excessive in measure, [the food], remaining in its own place, does not provoke the *vāta* and other humors through the non-affliction of their locations.
"It circulates around the rectum" means that, having been transformed, it issues forth in conformity [with its function];
[this refers to] the heat, which is fire. (25.3)
"Of the previous" means produced on another day;
"untransformed" means not properly processed;
"by the food-essence" means by the sweet and other tastes resulting from the transformation of food, or alternatively, by the essence born of food.
"When the *doṣas* are situated in their own locations," and so forth, is the definition of digested food (25).
"Born from foods of antagonistic potencies" refers to leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), blindness, erysipelas (*visarpa*), and other conditions mentioned in the chapter on Ātreya and Bhadrakāpya.

"By means of things that cause mental distress"—this refers to desire and so forth, which will be explained in the *Trividhakukṣīya* (Vi.a.2) as mental afflictions (*cittopatāpakara*) or mental disturbances (*cittavikāra*).
The construction is as follows: "by enjoying all desired requisites, one does not incur mental distress"; for mental distress arises from the consumption of undesirable food and the like.
25(6) Excessive exaltation, going astray, despondency, and despair.

Non-abiding means that, due to its presence in the heart, there is no entry into the stomach; thus, the perception of defects such as hair and the like present in the food, as well as the perception of excellence such as sweetness and so forth, is not certain—it is perceived at times and not at others. Consequently, through the non-perception of defects, one consumes that which is indeed defective, and through the non-perception of excellence, there is an absence of delight.
25(7) And "it digests unevenly" means that due to eating at long intervals, there is an imbalance in the connection with the digestive fire; this is the intended sense.
The faults that arise from eating too quickly— namely, excessive salivation and so forth—

are not present here; by the word "iti" in the phrase "not present," which demonstrates the prescription for what is wholesome and unwholesome, he shows that the fruit of discernment is the practice of what is wholesome.
By the word "of oneself" (ātmanaḥ), he shows that the assimilation of [the qualities] to oneself is known by the self alone for each individual, and not through the instruction of the treatise.
He praises the knowledge of the power of tastes and so forth as stated in chapter 25, beginning with "the tastes... (rasān...).
"He is our physician" means he is highly esteemed by us.

(26) Although the doshas and their morbid transformations (vikāras) should have been explained in detail regarding their specific potencies in the chapter on the three types of stomach (Viśeṣa-viṣaya, A. 2), they are nevertheless stated here in brief; therefore, what is stated in the Saṅgraha—that the potencies of the doshas and their transformations have also been explained—is correct.

And because the enumeration of the three substances beginning with oil (taila) is understood as being included within the "influence of substances" (dravyaprabhāva), they are not listed separately in the summary.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Specific Determination of Tastes" (rasavimāna), in the Vimānasthāna of the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by the venerable Cakrapāṇidatta.
1 [Vimānasthāna, Chapter 2 (40 of 120)]:

In the *Rasavimāna*, the aggregate (*rāśi*) has been described; now, in order to demonstrate the detailed exposition of the results—both those resulting from proper and improper measures—and the detailed exposition of the disorders arising from the humors (*doṣa*), the *Trividhakukṣīya* is being expounded.
"Threefold" means of three kinds;
"the portion of space" means the part consisting of the space within the cavity.
"Of food" means for the sake of food;
therefore, two occasions for food must be stated, while one is for the *doṣas*. Thus, the threefold [classification] to be described is stated.

For the establishment of the occasion for the *doṣas* is said to be "for the sake of food" because it assists the food; indeed, it must be stated that if the occasion for the *doṣas* is not established, the food is corrupted by the *doṣas*.

Alternatively, the meaning is that one should set aside a portion of space for food in the stomach, consisting of the *āmāśaya* (receptacle of undigested food), in three parts according to the division to be described later.
Regarding how the portion of the stomach should be prepared, he says "tadyathā" (as follows) and so on;
"of solid foods" refers to those that are chewed and eaten (*āśya-khādya*), and "of liquids" refers to those that are licked and drunk (*lehya-peya*).

In this context, the word *aṃśa* (portion) does not refer to an equal division, but rather to a proportionate division as appropriate; therefore, it should be understood that for solid substances (*mūrta*), there is a large portion. Although wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*) have distinct locations, nevertheless, with respect to the portions of solid food and so forth, they come together in a certain location. Thus, by superimposing unity upon them, they are treated here as "one. Now, one might object: even when food is divided according to the portions of the stomach, defects arising from substances that are inherently heavy or otherwise corrupted are still observed. To this he says: "Not born of the quantity of food" (*nāmātrāhārajam*). The meaning is that what is caused by inherent nature (*prakṛti*) and other such factors certainly does occur.
He elucidates that very point with the words "na ca" and so forth;
"sauṣṭhavam" means excellence, which is to say, auspiciousness.
"Because the fruits are divided" means because the fruits are distinct;
"by way of the division of the portions of the womb" refers to [the statement] beginning with "one portion of space for material things," and so forth.
"Uddiṣṭam" means that which has been stated in brief.

From the statement "in the evening and in the morning," it should be understood that if there is easy digestion after eating in the evening, or if there is easy digestion after eating in the morning, and if there is likewise a comfortable continuity during standing, sitting, and other activities, then one should know that the meal was taken in the proper measure (mātrāvat).

"Shattering the essence" (*sāravidhamana*) refers to the shattering of the *tvak-sāra* (bark-essence) and other substances as will be explained in the chapter on "Victory over Disease through Physicians" (*rogabhiṣagjitīya*, Vi. A.
8), regarding the transformation of food; here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*), meaning "by means of satiety.
"Satisfaction with liquids" (*dravaiḥ tṛptim*) means "excessive satisfaction," as indicated by the qualification of the word "again" (*bhūyas*).
By the statement "located in the stomach," it is shown that the provocation occurs only of the *samāna* wind—the companion of the digestive fire—and not of that located in the large intestine;
the meaning is that they reside in one part of the abdomen, supported by food, together with the vitiated food.

While it must be stated that *āmapradoṣa* (the disorder of undigested matter) arises from eating in excess, [the author] now states another cause from which *āmapradoṣa* occurs: "And indeed," and so forth.

Mental affliction caused by desire (*kāma*) and other such factors corrupts food through its very power; likewise, even impure food, when recognized as such, becomes a corrupter of the *āma* because it afflicts the mind.
The corruption of undigested (āma) and uncooked food is *āmapradoṣa*.

It is called *āmapradoṣa* because it vitiates the undigested itself; here, the suffix *ac* is used in the sense of both object and agent, meaning that it becomes corrupted. Alternatively, it should be understood as follows: while remaining undigested and uncooked, it vitiates the body through contact with corrupted humors (*doṣas*).

In the passage beginning with "of two types," it should be understood that *daṇḍālasaka* and *āmaviṣa* are included within *alasaka* itself; for in those two conditions as well, the *doṣas* become stagnant (*alasībhūta*) precisely because they fail to move.

Furthermore, in the section beginning with "we shall describe *alasaka*," the specific cause that generally brings about the condition is stated, whereas it should be understood that the general cause—excessive food intake—has already been mentioned.

Because of the statement regarding the activity of two *doṣas*—that it is "afflicted by wind (*anila*) and its path is obstructed by phlegm (*śleṣman*)"—the predominance of wind and phlegm in *alasaka* is declared. However, it should be understood that bile (*pitta*), established by general statements, certainly exists as a subordinate factor, evidenced by symptoms such as thirst, intoxication, and vertigo. Regarding the phrase "vitiated *āma* with an unobstructed path," here "unripe" refers to undigested food or food-essence; "unripe" (*āma*) means entirely undigested.

Regarding the phrase "one who habitually consumes incompatible food, eats before the previous meal is digested, or eats while suffering from indigestion": this refers to *viruddhāśana* (incompatible eating), *adhyaśana* (eating before the previous meal is digested), and *ajīrṇāśana* (eating while there is indigestion). *Ajīrṇāśana* is the consumption of undigested (*apakva*) matter. Since the act of eating while indigestion is present is already covered by the term *adhyaśana*, the term *āmadoṣa* (the disorder of undigested matter) in the passage "they call *āmaviṣa* the disorder of undigested matter" is intended to mean a morbid state whose symptoms resemble those of poison (*viṣa*). For this very reason, it is stated that [it is so called] because its symptoms resemble poison and because its treatment is contradictory. That which is administered as warm in relation to *āma* is contradictory to poison, and that which is administered as cold in relation to poison is contradictory to *āma*.
And its similarity to poison arises from the influence of a specific non-productive cause, just as the state of being poison occurs in a mixture of honey and ghee.
"Varti" refers to a medicinal wick (phalavarti).
"Successive order" (ānupūrvī) means the sequence beginning with rice gruel (peyā) and so forth.
