"Digestion of food" (jīrṇāhāra) indicates that the state of digestion applies specifically to cases of *visūcikā* and *alasaka*.

Furthermore, the symptoms such as the channels being smeared by the humors (*doṣas*), the stomach being sluggish, and heaviness of the abdomen should also be understood as characteristics that qualify the specific individual.

However, by again issuing a prohibition against eating when food is undigested (*ajīrṇāśana*), [the author] demonstrates the great danger of administering medicine with the intention of pacifying indigestion when done out of negligence, as will be stated in the passage beginning with "for the digestive fire is weakened by the humors" (*doṣadurbalo hyagniḥ*). By the phrase "of those who have undergone fasting" (*kṛtāpatarpaṇānām*), he indicates the exhaustion of the state of undigested matter (*āmatā*) in the humors; for when fasting is properly performed, there is no persistence of undigested matter (*āmānubandha*). Consequently, in cases such as colic or fever that have been established as *visūcikā* or *alasaka* and are initiated by humors free from undigested matter (*nirāma-doṣa*), one should employ treatments that are contrary to the acute affliction (*ātaṅka*) but specifically remedial for colic and fever free from undigested matter.

"According to its own [nature]" (*yathāsvam*) means that whatever is contrary to a particular affliction, such as colic (*śūla*), should be applied in that case. Furthermore, by the term "contrary to the affliction," one should understand that which produces an effect for that purpose.

For this very reason, it is logically consistent with the subsequent statement, "or that which produces an effect for that purpose," when describing the medicines for all disorders; otherwise, how could that which was not mentioned here—namely, that which produces an effect for that purpose—be stated there when it is not the subject at hand?

By the passage beginning with "vimuktām apradoṣasya" (for one who is free from disease and free from vitiation), the prescription for massage and other treatments is intended for the purpose of pacifying defects such as extreme debility caused by illness. To include procedures not explicitly mentioned, he says: "anyaśca" (and another), etc.

The connection is as follows: "another" refers to the medicinal path described here as beneficial for the disorder of undigested matter (*āmapradoṣa*), which—unlike the disorders of the *grahaṇī* and diarrhea to be discussed later—does not cause the depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).

Furthermore, in order to demonstrate the dimensions of the stomach (*āmāśaya*), he states the subsequent text following the question to the Guru, beginning with "That which has been eaten," and so forth.
"Residing in all" means residing in the entire body.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Specific Determination of the Three Parts of the Stomach," in the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka Saṃhitā composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Vimānasthāna.
2 [Vimānasthāna, Chapter 3 (41 of 120)]:

The cause that generates disease in living beings is of two kinds—the common (*sādhāraṇa*) and the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*). Having explained the uncommon causes—which are restricted to each individual and produce *vāta* and the other *doṣas* through diet and so forth—the chapter on the "Destruction of Communities" (*janapadoddhvaṃsanīya*) is now set forth to explain the common causes of disease, which consist of wind, water, location, and time, and affect many people alike.
A "country-circle" (*janapadamandala*) is a circle characterized by the settlement of a country; "in the field of Pañcāla" is its specific designation.

By the expression "inhabited by the best of the twice-born," he shows that even in a region frequented by great people, the destruction of the country may occur due to the power of unrighteousness, as will be described hereafter.
"In the last [month] of the summer season" refers to the month of Jyeṣṭha;
"wandering through the forest" means wandering again and again after having already wandered through the forest.

"Those born of seasonal transformations" (*ṛtuvaikārikāḥ*) means those produced by the changes of the seasons. Furthermore, "seasonal transformation" is an illustrative term; therefore, it should be understood that [the phrase] refers to those produced by the changes of water, location, and wind. For the author will later describe the corruption (*vikṛti*) of the earth and other elements as well. Alternatively, "those born of seasonal transformations" refers to things that do not conform to the season. By this, it is stated that the corruption of the constellations and so forth consists precisely in their failing to exhibit the characteristics appropriate to the season. For instance, during the summer, the constellations are normally clear; if they appear shrouded in frost during the summer, then they should be understood as being corrupted.

By the inclusion of the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "earth also," water and air are likewise implied. Therefore, it is stated that earth is indeed the primary cause of medicinal plants, yet it will not produce their tastes and other qualities; and water and air also will not produce the tastes and other qualities of medicinal plants.
The term "will produce" (*pratividhāsyati*) means "will generate."

The plural form in "uddharadhvam" (extract [it]! is intended for Agniveśa, who is accompanied by many disciples; however, since Agniveśa alone is the principal figure, he is addressed with the term "Agniveśa" as well as the term "saumya" (gentle one). The plural is used with the intention that the extraction of the medicine must indeed be performed by many;

for when addressing the principal person regarding an action to be accomplished by a group, the plural is employed—as in "O general, fight!"—though others take the word "saumya" to be an adjective qualifying the medicine.

The meaning is: those who desire us, and those physicians who desire us; and those whom we desire to be treated by this [medicine]. Those who desire a physician are curable because they are dear to the physician; for it is said that those who hate the physician are incurable. And those whom physicians accept are indeed curable diseases, for physicians do not accept incurable ones.
By this, the meaning is that others as well, whose diseases are curable by medicine, will utilize the juices and other components of these medicinal herbs.

If it is explained that "those who have come to us, and those whom we have followed for the sake of some purpose, will utilize [these]," then Ātreya’s status as an authoritative person (*āpta*) due to his freedom from partiality (*pakṣarāgitva*) would not be possible; moreover, his freedom from passion (*nīrāgatva*) has been stated in the passage: "He is a refuge like a father to all living beings" (Cikitsāsthāna, chapter 5).

Furthermore, the expression "they have been extracted" (*uddhṛtāni*) should be understood as a usage where what is not yet real is treated as if it were real (*abhūte bhūtavat*), just as people say "it is done" regarding something that is only about to be done; for it is not possible to extract the medicinal plants at the very moment of speaking.

"By one [cause]" means that because those with dissimilar constitutions (*prakṛti*) and so forth lack a common cause, it is impossible for their diseases to be identical in form; such is the meaning of the question.
"Having the same gender" means having an identical gender;
"unseasonably," as in "according to the season," means not conforming to the season.
"Devoid of its qualities" means lacking the qualities of water such as the capacity to quench the thirst for life;
"whose color, smell, taste, and touch have become altered from their natural state" refers to that region where the natural color and so forth have changed;
"the cemetery bird" is the vulture.
"Like something never seen before" (*apūrvavat*): even that which is familiar appears as if it were something new because it is perceived as being ruined.

That place where the qualities of virtue, truth, and shame have been abandoned and destroyed by people is described thus. In such a place, those who possess virtue and the like abandon their virtue and so forth; yet for those who do not practice virtue and the like at all due to ignorance, virtue and the like are already lost.
For just as a region seized by *guhyakas* becomes filled with the sound of lamentation, so too is that place.
With the words "7-8.
Deficiency," etc., he explains which among the vitiated *vāta* and other humors has which predominance and by what cause;

[he states] that because they are difficult to avoid by their very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*), water is naturally more difficult to avoid than wind, land is more difficult to avoid than water, and time is more difficult to avoid than land.

For wind, being corrupted by residing in a windless place, can be avoided, whereas water cannot be avoided in the same way; indeed, water must necessarily be used for the maintenance of the body. Even if water were to be abandoned with great effort, a location is even more difficult to avoid than water, because it is impossible to remain without it. If a location is abandoned by traveling to another country, time is entirely impossible to abandon; thus, among all these, time is the most important. Regarding the reading "garīyaḥ param," the construction is as follows: one should know that whatever comes after [another] is more important than that.

He states the opposite case regarding lightness— beginning with "in wind, etc."— meaning that because the avoidance of wind and so forth is easily accomplished through the method already described, the remedy is easy to apply.

The meaning is that for those [beings] there is no commonality of death—that is, they do not share the same destiny that produces death—and there is no commonality of actions (*karma*)—that is, they do not possess the same life-terminating *karman*. For some, having acted together in a previous birth by performing deeds such as burning a village, become subject to simultaneous death through the power of that *karman*. Alternatively, even if the life-terminating *karman* was performed individually, it may ripen at the same time for some; they too become subject to simultaneous death.

In this context, by the phrase "not due to the commonality of death," he shows that some cases are incurable precisely because fatal signs (*ariṣṭa*) have already arisen. By the phrase "not due to the commonality of karma," he shows that some cases are incurable even when fatal signs have not yet appeared, owing to the power of determinative fatal karma (*niyatamāraka-karma*). Alternatively, by "not due to the commonality of death," the commonality of the fatal disease is expressed; and by "not due to the commonality of karma," the karma that produces the fatal disease is expressed as previously extracted—that is, those [karmas] seized prior to the onset of the calamity.
"Protection" (*gupti*) refers to defense through mantras and other means.
By the word "indeterminate" (aniyata), he shows that death which has been initiated by weak karma can indeed be countered in this way. "Whence the root? means "what is its root? (kim-mūlam).
"Unrighteousness (*adharma*) is its root" indicates unrighteousness pertaining to this life;
or "its root" means that the root of that [disturbance] of wind and so forth is either past karma or present unrighteousness.
Thus he states that either unrighteousness of this life or unrighteousness performed in another birth is the cause of the disturbance of wind and so forth.

It should be understood that by the words "When [he] points out," etc., he will state only that unrighteousness (*adharma*) pertaining to this life as the cause; this is for the purpose of establishing the clear meaning of the established doctrine through direct perception, and not because unrighteousness committed in another birth is not a cause.
"Of those two" refers to the two types of unrighteousness—those pertaining to this life and those belonging to another birth.
"Source" (*yoni*) means the cause.
"Due to the defect of what is touched and what is consumed" means because of the corruption of both that which is touched, such as water and so forth, and all that is consumed;

this should be understood primarily. By this, the defect of corrupted wind and odor should also be understood, for even unwholesome odors are mentioned among the defects of corrupted wind (Sūtra 19–20).
"Even of that which originates from weapons" means of that which originates from weapons and brings death to many people.
"For the sake of harming oneself, one's kin, and others" means that, for the most part, there occurs harm to oneself, to one's own kin, and to others.
He states that even the extermination of Rākṣasas and others occurs only because people have acted unrighteously—beginning with the words "rakṣogaṇa" and so forth.
"Or another transgression" means a cause of unrighteousness other than the aforementioned causes of unrighteousness, such as impurity and the like.
"Even before" means instantly; the meaning is that they are reduced to ashes as if cursed by the destruction of many lineages of men.
The construction is that because a certain causal condition is perceived, others who are "uncertain"—meaning uncollected—also go to ashes.
"Uncollected" (aniyata) means not gathered together.
The meaning is that through the curse of specific individuals, only those [specific people] are reduced to ashes, not all people. Furthermore,
he states that in the initial manifestation of diseases, unrighteousness (*adharma*) alone is the cause, beginning with the words "And even previously," and so forth.
Sacrifice is the deity of sacrifice; the ritual is the Veda that ordains sacrifice; the ordinance is the sacrificial act;
speed is velocity;
and possession is the sense of "mine-ness."
Those whose lifespan is immeasurable due to its extreme length are called *amitāyuṣaḥ*.
For in the Satya-yuga, the lifespan is four hundred years; as was stated by the Blessed Vyāsa: "In the Kṛta age, men have all their goals accomplished and live for four hundred years."
"For the sake of prosperous lords" means that at the end of the Kṛtayuga,
as the Tretā age comes to an end, it is shown that there is a gradual diminution of the qualities of food and lifestyle by one-quarter in each successive stage.

Furthermore, the dwelling of those who follow what is unrighteous becomes deficient in quality; therefore, it does not provide proper support for the body—that is, it fails to sustain the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) which are maintained through equilibrium.

"When a hundred years are complete" means when the hundredth part of a year is completed; "wherever a measure is intended" means in whichever age (yuga) a particular measure is intended, when its hundredth part is completed, one year undergoes diminution. By this, it should be understood that when the Kali age has a lifespan of one hundred years, as the hundredth part passes away, ninety-nine becomes the maximum lifespan, and so forth.
"Depends upon reasoning" (yuktim apekṣate) means that it depends upon the conjunction of destiny and human effort, whether [the lifespan] is fixed or unfixed.
"Strength and weakness" (balābala) refers to strength and lack of strength; therein, strength is to be understood as the fixity of lifespan, while weakness is its non-fixity.

Although the karma from previous lives has passed away due to its instability, nevertheless, because the *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) produced by it still exists, that karma indeed serves as a cause here in this life through that medium.
Furthermore, human effort (*puruṣakāra*) refers generally to actions performed in this very life;

therein, rites such as offerings and auspicious ceremonies function by generating *adṛṣṭa*, and likewise, medicines and the like function by way of transforming the bodily constituents such as plasma and blood.
"Of the two noble ones" means of those who are excellent by virtue of being praised.

"Of long life" means [longer] than even a hundred years through the use of elixirs (*rasāyana*) and so forth; "of happiness" means by virtue of being free from disease; "of fixed" means fixed for the current age (*yuga*), the meaning being that in the Kali age it is measured at one hundred years; here, even that which is less than a hundred years and not fixed is referred to by the word "fixed. Therefore, it is logical that its arising from destiny (*daiva*) and human effort (*puruṣakāra*) is not possible there [in the case of the fixed lifespan]; nevertheless, because it arises from unfavorable destiny and human effort, it is correct to say that it is produced by destiny and human effort. Furthermore, only those whose lifespan is unfixed (*aniyatāyuṣ*) are eligible for elixirs, because an elixir is of no avail for one whose lifespan is fixed. And it is logical that the lifespan produced by elixirs and the like is unfixed, and because it is auspicious, it is produced by auspicious destiny and human effort.

Alternatively, the construction is: "being long, it is the cause of a fixed lifespan. By this, a hundred years fixed for a particular age, as well as that which is longer and unfixed, is produced solely by great karma. However, its state of happiness is produced by great human effort (*puruṣakāra*) through the non-affliction of disease; and by means of elixirs (*rasāyana*), the obstruction of diseases such as old age is effected. The point is that even a lifespan obtainable through an elixir is indeed determined by powerful karma. [This applies] to the opposite case: that which is unfixed due to its length, and likewise unhappy due to being accompanied by disease.
The meaning is that "the other" refers to the application (*yukti*) of the two inferior factors, destiny (*daiva*) and human effort (*puruṣakāra*).

The meaning is that for the intermediate [factor], there is the application of the two intermediate karmas—namely, those of indefinite duration in terms of being long or short, and likewise indefinite in terms of being pleasant or unpleasant—regarding lifespan.
The meaning of "cause" (*kāraṇa*) is the logical justification (*upapatti*) for the mutual sublation of destiny and human effort.
Regarding the passage beginning with "daivam" (fate):

the weak life-producing *daiva* (destiny) is obstructed by a powerful *māraka* (fatal factor) through the consumption of unwholesome food and other such acts, which produce the contrary effect of death. By a particularly powerful [factor], the other *karma* known as *dṛṣṭa* (visible human effort) is obstructed, that is, overcome.
Because one observes this visible defeat caused by *daiva*, some believe that all life is determined solely by *daiva*; thus he says, "having seen," and so forth.

If lifespan were determined solely by visible causes, then death would not occur for those who have been properly treated with medicines; however, since death occurs due to the power of *karma* even when medical treatment is present, we conclude—based on the observed efficacy—that even in cases where it is thought that medical treatment has restored life, it is actually *karma* alone that is the cause of survival. Thus, by demonstrating that both destiny (*daiva*) and human effort (*puruṣakāra*) are subject to sublation, he rejects the position that lifespan is absolutely fixed—beginning with the words "karma," etc.
Nowhere does karma fail to come to fruition; as it is said: "Karma is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of eons;
whatever karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious, has been performed must necessarily be experienced."

"Sometimes it is not fixed as to time," meaning, for example, that this "karma leading to death" is not fixed to occur at a specific time such as twenty-five years; therefore, at whatever time it encounters what is called human effort (*puruṣakāra*)—that is, conditions conducive to visible action—at that time it kills, its strength augmented by the proximity of auxiliary causes. However, when it does not encounter visible [conditions] such as the consumption of unwholesome things, it does not kill then; it is "awakened" by conditions, meaning it is intensified by visible causes.

However, those who say: "Some karma is fixed by time (*kāla-niyata*), meaning that when it is to ripen at a certain time, it ripens precisely at that time; whereas karma fixed by ripening (*vipāka-niyata*) means that this karma certainly ripens, but it is not the case that it does not ripen; but karma fixed by both time and ripening is such that this karma ripens at this very time and only then; and because of this fixation by both time and ripening, it is called 'powerful' (*balavat*); and this alone is what cannot be subverted by direct perception"—in their view, it should be understood that even weak karma is exhausted without being experienced through means such as expiation (*prāyaścitta*). However, in the opposite case, one would have to say that some karma is fixed by the time of its ripening (*vipākakāla-niyata*); for from the statement "fixed by the time of some [ripening]" (*kiñcit-kāla-niyata*), it follows that it is indeed fixed by time.
Hereafter, he concludes the response with the words "Therefore," and so forth.
The phrase "because both are observed" refers to the observation that destiny is obstructed by human effort, and likewise, human effort is obstructed by destiny.

"Adherence to one extreme" means that life-span is necessarily fixed, or that all life-span is necessarily unfixed; this is the meaning. "Illustration" (*nidarśana*) means a logical argument (*yukti*), so called because by it the intended position (*pakṣa*) is established as the probandum (*sādhya*).
"In this case" refers to the position of the non-exclusive middle (*anaikāntika*).

By this section beginning with "yadi," it is shown that the cultivation of visible causes that produce longevity, as well as the non-cultivation of causes that obstruct longevity, are established without dispute among all authoritative persons.

Furthermore, if lifespan were fixed, then all such [cultivation and non-cultivation] would be ineffective; however, since lifespan is not fixed, they are effective. Therefore, the intended meaning is that even lifespan is not fixed.

Furthermore, for one who asserts that the unseen (adṛṣṭa) alone is the cause everywhere and that the seen is entirely ineffective, it is evident that even the seen—such as the *trivṛt* medicine—is indeed the performer of purgation and other effects. However, the causality of the unseen must be postulated only because the effect cannot otherwise be accounted for by the seen. Thus, the meaning is that the causality of the unseen is rooted in the seen cause. Moreover, the elimination of the seen cause cannot even be imagined, as evidenced by sacrifices (*iṣṭayaḥ*, *yajñāḥ*) and serpents (*uragāḥ*) which are exceedingly prone to crawling (*sarīsṛpa-uragāḥ*).
Or they might employ it as medicine—this is the remainder of the sense.

Those who say that [the *cakṣuṣas*] are supreme because of their extreme freedom from delusion and their incomparable lifespan, and who engage in combat, die by the sword; but those who do not engage in combat generally do not die by the sword.

The construction is that there is a disparity in lifespan due to the presence or absence of remedial measures, as expressed in the phrase "nor is it equal," etc. In this context, a "painted jar" (*citraghaṭa*) is established as being like one that has been painted; for it endures for a long time because it lacks the causes of impairment such as carrying water. A "well-jar" (*udapānaghaṭa*), however, perishes quickly due to its contact with water and from falling while being carried.
Furthermore, [the former] is rooted in beneficial treatment (*hitopacāra*). It is also rooted in beneficial treatment.
The correct application is gradual; this is the connection [of the verse]:
the maintenance of all excessive applications and the avoidance of all excessive applications.

Regarding the passage beginning with "this being so" (*evaṃ sati*): first, for that which is fixed by time, there is no untimely death precisely because death does not occur before its time. However, as for that which is not fixed by time, since it is itself indeterminate, how can there be either timely or untimely death? For when the lifespan is indeterminate, there is no fixed time limit; yet, death occurring prior to a fixed time is called "untimely death. This is the meaning of the question. (37)
"At the proper time" means at whatever duration of time the exhaustion of the sense-faculty (akṣa), which is free from transgression, occurs; that very [time] is the meaning.
"Precisely through the exhaustion of its own measure" means through the exhaustion of the measure consisting of hundreds of years and so forth, corresponding to the respective age (yuga).
"From the wrong path" means by traveling by no means other than the non-path.
"From the loosening of the peg" means from the release of the wedge;
"from the secondary member" means from the taking up of the lubricant;
"from overturning" means from the shifting around.
"Mithyopacaritān" means those treated improperly; "asamyakcikitsitān" means those treated incorrectly; "akālamṛtyūn" means untimely deaths; "akālamṛtyukarān" means those that cause untimely death.

Now, fearing that because of the mention of "false treatment" (*mithyopacāra*), hot water might also constitute a false treatment in the case of a fever of fiery nature (*āgneya-jvara*), he says: "But why," and so forth.

The meaning is that even though the bodily constituent (*dhātu*) to be treated with cold is pitta, which is of a hot nature, water is nevertheless given to all those afflicted by fever; therefore, it is water itself that he asks about here.
39. In one whose pitta has been depleted; 40. in one whose pitta has increased.

It is not only in the case of fever that treatment with heat or cold is applied according to the distinction of whether it arises from cold or heat; rather, this applies to every disease. Thus he says: "By cold," and so forth.
Those who are physicians and possess knowledge are called *bhiṣagvidaḥ* (learned physicians).

Not only is treatment for those [diseases] arising from cold and heat performed by reversing their causes, but even for those arising from under-nutrition (*apatarpaṇa*) and so forth, it is done by means of that which is contrary to the cause. Thus he says "in this way" and so on. By means of under-nutrition and over-nutrition (*santarpaṇa*), the entirety of medical treatment is encompassed; for there is no other method of treatment apart from under-nutrition and over-nutrition. Since all therapeutic procedures are thus merely varieties of over-nutrition and under-nutrition, he states the specific types of under-nutrition for the sake of specialized knowledge, beginning with "under-nutrition" and so on.

By the statement "lightening and digestive therapy" (*laṅghanapācanam*), it is shown that wherever digestive therapy is performed, lightening therapy must necessarily also be performed in a small measure; for if nourishing therapy (*bṛṃhaṇa*) were performed at the time of digestion, then because nourishing therapy is antagonistic to the digestive fire (*agni*), the process of digestion would not occur. In the phrase "as if by sprinklings," the word "as if" (*iva*) should be understood as "as if with water that is not too abundant. The phrase "or other [therapies]" refers to lightening therapies and so forth, as well as nourishing therapies and so forth.
"The remedy for what is said is beyond reproach" means that because one who lacks wealth possesses no resources, medical treatment cannot be performed.

One who considers himself a physician, due to his wicked pride, does not follow the instructions of a true physician; for one who takes intense delight in unrighteousness, unrighteousness arises even in the attempt at treatment, and the medical care fails because it is obstructed by unrighteousness—
this applies to one who possesses the signs of imminent death, that is, one endowed with fatal prognostic marks (*ariṣṭa*).
"By the more evil one" means by that which is a cause of evil, by that which generates evil, namely, infamy;
"or in the future" means at a later time.
Some read the passage beginning with "that which has little water and trees" (verse 46–48) here as the definition of regions such as the *jāṅgala*;
in the *Saṅgraha*, these are classified as "prodromal symptoms" (*pūrvarūpa*), referring to the portents involving the stars and other phenomena.

[The humors] possess their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as well as the characteristics of their respective transformations (*vikṛtilakṣaṇa*); that characteristic has been explained therein [in the previous verses] by such statements as "the wind is of this kind," and so forth.
Furthermore, it has been stated that medicine attains success when administered according to what is appropriate; thus, by the justification for giving warm water, everything is summarized.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Determination of the Causes of Epidemics," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Chapter 4 of the Vimānasthāna (42 of 120)]

In the chapter on the "Destruction of the Country," all diseases have been mentioned without distinction. To explain how their specific characteristics are to be understood, the section titled "Knowledge of the Threefold Specifics of Diseases" (Roga-viśeṣa-vijñānīya) is now set forth.

That by which the specifics of diseases—as will be described—become known is "knowledge of disease-specifics" (roga-viśeṣa-vijñāna); it consists of the three means of valid cognition (pramāṇa): instruction (upadeśa), direct perception (pratyakṣa), and inference (anumāna).
In this context, however, reasoning (*yukti*) is not treated separately precisely because it is included within inference (*anumāna*);

furthermore, these three means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) exist in the examination [of disease] sometimes combined, sometimes as two, and sometimes as one; for instance, in cases such as a deficiency of digestive fire (*vahni-māndya*), direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) does not necessarily operate.

In the *Tisraiṣaṇīya*, the definitions of inference (*anumāna*) and the other means of knowledge were stated first. Now, here, because the subject matter has been introduced, the definitions of authoritative instruction (*āptopadeśa*) and so forth are being set forth by the passage beginning with "In that regard, what is called instruction... For a topic belonging to the context remains incomplete if it is not explained. Regarding the phrase "those who lack inquiry" (*avitarkāḥ*) and so on: "inquiry" (*vitarka*) refers to a state of "how might this be?"—that is to say, uncertain knowledge. "Memory" (*smṛti*) is the cognition of recollection. "Division" (*vibhāga*) means a partial portion. Those who, through the opposite of these [uncertainty, memory, and division], know entities through certainty, direct experience, and in their entirety, are "those who know without inquiry, memory, or division."
However, one who possesses discursive thought (*vitarka*) and so forth is not authoritative (*āpta*), because he lacks knowledge of all the specific details of the matter to be explained.

Furthermore, although recollective cognition (*smṛtijñāna*) is indeed rooted in a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), nevertheless, since the object that is the focus of recollective cognition does not necessarily exist at the present moment, it is not itself a valid means of knowledge—this is the intended meaning. Alternatively, "recollection" refers to knowledge derived from the treatises on memory (*smṛtiśāstra*) and mathematical knowledge (*gaṇitajñāna*); and these two types of knowledge, because they do not directly reveal the object and because there is the possibility of their being false due to difficulty in comprehension, are not valid means of knowledge and thus should not be accepted.

Now, [the author] says—“those who perceive [reality] free from attachment and affliction”—to show that even those possessing right knowledge might speak otherwise due to the influence of passion and so forth.
Those whose nature it is to see with freedom from attachment (*niṣprīti*) and freedom from affliction (*nirupatāpa*) are "those who perceive [reality] free from attachment and affliction.
By this, it is stated that one who perceives things as they truly are is faultless and thus an authoritative person (*āpta*).

Such reliability belongs to someone like Brahmā or others in all matters; however, it should be understood that for a worldly person, instruction is authoritative only regarding those specific subjects concerning which he has no doubt or error.
It is not necessarily determined to be authoritative as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because of being tainted by passion and other defects.

This refers to one who is both "tainted and untainted" (*duṣṭāduṣṭa*); thus, a father is indeed a reliable authority (*āpta*) for his son because he is untainted [in that regard], even though he may be tainted otherwise—or rather, [the term] refers to one who is tainted, such as a deceiver.

By the phrase "perceived by oneself through the senses and the mind," he includes external perception (*bāhya-pratyakṣa*), which refers to that form and so forth which is apprehended directly by the self through the sense organs such as the eyes without any mediation. And by the phrase "by the mind," he includes mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), which refers to that pleasure and so forth which is experienced by the mind without mediation.
Here, *tarka* (reasoning) means indirect knowledge (*apratyakṣa-jñāna*);
*yukti* (logical connection) means a relationship of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). Therefore, inference (*anumāna*) is indirect knowledge produced from that inseparable concomitance.

"By the aggregate of knowledge" (*jñānasamudāyena*) means the aggregate of valid cognitions (*pramāṇasaṅghāta*). By that aggregate, there is a determination (*adhyavasāna*) consisting of the certainty: "This is indeed such-and-such a disease. Regarding the phrase "but in the threefold," and so forth:
"Knowledge" (*jñāna*) is that by which something is known; it is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

First, the instruction of a reliable authority (*āpta-upadeśa*) makes one aware of the disease. Then, one ascertains the disease taught by the authority through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) by examining the signs and so forth as they have been described. Furthermore, regarding a disease not taught in the scriptures, one does not perceive the disease through either direct perception or inference, just like an unlearned physician. Thus he says: "For what indeed is not taught," and so forth.

He thinks as follows: "The specific varieties of diseases are indeed difficult to master; they cannot be understood without instruction. Those who have mastered the medical treatises (*vaidyaka-śāstra*) are indeed able to explain these specific diseases. Therefore, one determines a disease by perceiving through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) those specific causes and other characteristics of diseases that have been explained through traditional scripture (*āgama*). One who lacks such instruction, even while perceiving those specific causes and so forth, does not ascertain the specific nature of the disease—just as one untrained in the examination of gems (*ratna-parīkṣā*), though seeing the distinctions among gems, does not determine the specific quality of a gem. This is the intended meaning.
The phrase "of those possessing knowledge" refers to those who possess the instructions of a reliable authority (*āpta*).

By the expression "or threefold," he demonstrates that at the time of diagnosing a disease, the instruction of a reliable authority is also operative; for instance, in determining the softness of the *grahaṇī*, the occurrence of dreams, and so forth, as well as in determining the location of a condition that is difficult to perceive, and likewise in examining whether the internal organ (*koṣṭha*) is soft or hard—the instruction of a reliable authority in the form of the patient's own words is also operative.
With the words beginning with "therein" (tatra), he states that which is to be understood through the instruction of a reliable authority:
the provocation of vāyu has dryness and so forth as its cause;
the source (yoni) consists of vāta and the other [doshas].
The self (ātman) is the essential nature (svabhāva); for example, the harshness of Rohiṇī, or the fact that renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is easily undertaken.
The substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) consists of the body, its limbs, and the mind;
this is the activity directed toward treatment, such as the activity for the purpose of fasting and digestive remedies in the case of fever.
And cessation is for the purpose of remediation; for example, it should be understood as the cessation of daytime sleep, bathing, and so forth during a recent fever.
And the phrase "the bursting of the finger-joints" is the connection [to be made].
"Others too" refers to cough, hiccup, and so forth;
by the phrase "and whatever others," signs such as radiance and the like are included.

By the crawling away of lice, one infers a distaste for the body, for lice indeed crawl away from a body that has become unpalatable; likewise, by the non-crawling away of lice and the like, the body may be inferred to be endowed with its natural essence (*rasa*).

"Dhāri-lohitam" means the blood of a living being. It should be understood that the blood which is "dhāri"—meaning it is not affected by the vitiation of *pitta* and thus does not have an abnormal taste—is what dogs and other animals consume; the point is that they do not eat blood that is afflicted by *pitta*, such as *raktapitta*.

In this context, having provided the instruction regarding sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, the author first shows form (*rūpa*), which is perceived by the eye immediately after sound, thereby indicating that there is no fixed rule regarding the sequence for the examination of sound and the other sense objects.

By the phrase "furthermore, to be known through inference," he indicates that while certain factors such as digestive fire (*agni*) and strength (*bala*), which will be described as accessible through inference, may also be understood through the instruction of a physician, the mind (*manas*) is established by its non-deviation from objects. That is to say, when there is a connection between the sense organs and their respective objects, the fact that one perceives sound at one time and taste at another, rather than perceiving all objects simultaneously, leads to the inference that there exists a mind which, immediately following a cause, apprehends the objects of the senses.

"Knowledge [is inferred] by means of purposeful activity (*vyavasāya*)," where *vyavasāya* means engagement (*pravṛtti*), such as the engagement for the purpose of drinking when water is to be drunk. By that, it is inferred that "knowledge of water has arisen in him," for otherwise, how could he engage in purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), which is the effect of knowledge?
"By attachment to passion (*rajas*)" means that its cause, passion (*rajas*), is inferred from attachment to women and the like;
"malice" (*abhidroha*) is engagement for the purpose of harming others.
Dejection consists of weeping and the like;
joy (*āmoda*) is the performance of festivals such as dancing, singing, and instrumental music;

contentment (*toṣa*) is the clarity of the face, eyes, and so forth. By this it is stated that while *prīti* is merely contentment, *harṣa* (joy) is a specific form of affection that causes an overflow of the mind.
Fortitude is the absence of dejection in the mind even in adversity;
vigor is the non-retrogression of the mind in undertakings of difficult tasks through exertion, that is, through the commencement of action.
"Stability" is the state of having a firm mind;
"without error" means without delusion, [referring to] faith and aspiration.
"By intention" means by request;
"by grasping" means by the retention of the text and so forth;
"memory" refers to the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) that produces memory; for it is through recollection that its cause, the mental impression, is inferred.
"Hri" means shame;
"apatrapā" means the outward manifestation of shame;
and "śīla" means the innate aversion toward attachment to objects.

"By means of cultivation" (*anuśīlanena*) means through constant practice (*santataśīlana*). One infers that a person has a certain character (*śīla*) based on the fact that they constantly pursue a particular object.
"By means of prohibition" (*pratiṣedhena*) means by way of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).

"A pretext" (*upadhi*) refers to a disguise (*chadma*), meaning that which is maintained (*dhīyate*) by approaching [something falsely]. "By means of connection" (*anubandhena*) means by means of a subsequent result. For it is known from a subsequent result—such as the killing of a brother—that this Candragupta is one who acts under the guise of madness.
By "in accordance with what is to be prescribed" (vidheyatayā), it means that through the application of the prescribed regimen,
the four factors beginning with age and ending with the onset of disease are understood respectively according to the specific distinctions of time and so forth.

In this regard, age—such as childhood and so forth—is known through specific time, such as sixteen years and so on; whereas inclination or desire is known through place, for instance: "This person is from the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa), therefore his desire for wheat, beans, and the like is inferred"; and because something is agreeable to him, it is known that this is his constitutional suitability (sātmya); and the onset of disease is known through specific sensations, for example: "Because this person possesses the sensation of burning heat, therefore the onset of the disease of fever has occurred in him"—thus it should be understood.

By the qualification "with hidden signs" (*gūḍhaliṅga*), he demonstrates that when a disease with manifest signs has been determined by its symptoms alone, further examination through therapeutic suitability (*upashaya*) and unsuitability (*anupashaya*) need not be performed.
By the phrase "by a specific transgression," he means that a great transgression results in many morbid humors (*doṣa*), while a slight one results in few.
"With a focus on well-being" (*kalyāṇābhiniveśena*) refers to the practice of the path leading to the highest good; for this [well-being] occurs only for those whose prosperity is imminent.
"Sattva" refers to the predominance of the quality of *sattva*.
"Without modification" means in the absence of modifications such as passion (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*).

By the phrase "only by questioning," [the author] shows that although the softness of the *grahaṇī* and so forth can indeed be known through inference, nevertheless, because inference involves great mental exertion, one should know the softness of the *grahaṇī* and other qualities simply by the patient's inquiry, which takes the form of a comfortable consultation.

The intention [of the author] is that "desire for food and so forth" refers to the longing for such things; however, by the term "the disliked and the desired," one includes those who are hated, those who are loved, servants, and so on.
By the phrase "as far as possible" (*yathāsambhavam*), he shows that in every case to be examined, not all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are necessarily applicable.

Now, regarding the passage beginning with "atha" (*then*): after the individual examination of objects such as words and so forth, one should subsequently determine the reality (*tattva*)—that is, the true nature of the disease—as well as its treatment, which is characterized by what must be done. The meaning is that one should form a determination or certainty (*adhyavasāya*) regarding that reality which has been stated and that treatment which has been prescribed.
"Immediately thereafter" (*anantaram*) means that which is not separated by an interval.
He states the result of the determination of the specific nature of the task with the words beginning "the task" (*kārya*):
"the undertaking" (*pratipatti*) is the performance of actions according to their appropriateness.
"Not deluded" means not deluded in one's practice;
"knowledge" refers to the scripture, and the "intellect of knowledge" is the understanding produced by that [scripture];
"enters" means he penetrates [the truth] through that intellect.

Regarding "the inner self" (*antarātmānam*), in the medical context, it refers to the interior of the body. Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Specific Determination of the Threefold Distinction of Diseases," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Section on Specific Determinations (*Vimānasthāna*).
4 [Vimānasthāna, Chapter 5 (43 of 120)]:

Having described examination in the preceding chapter, the Vimāna of the channels is now stated in order to explain the body— which is the object of that examination— by means of the classification of channels into those that are vitiated and those that are not.
"Possessing form" means possessing the dimension of a non-pervasive substance; for "form" is said to be the dimension of a non-pervasive substance.
"Particulars" refers to specific entities that possess origination.
Regarding this, he states the reason: "all," and so forth;
"are produced" means by way of a continuous stream (*santāna*), as in the phrase "streams," and so forth.
The word "khalu" (indeed) indicates the reason:

because they undergo transformation—meaning that by discarding their preceding forms such as taste (*rasa*) and so forth, they attain subsequent forms such as blood (*rakta*) and so forth—the channels do not carry stable elements; rather, according to the statement "for the purpose of movement," they carry [substances] by transporting them to another location.

He thinks thus: the increase of blood must be effected by the nutrient essence (*rasa*) that has been mixed with blood as it undergoes transformation into the form of blood; and this mixing of the nutrient essence located in another place with the blood does not occur without the channel known as a *srotas* serving as the path of movement.

This is the intended meaning: for the channels (*srota*) of the elements, such as blood and the rest, generally undergo transformation into portions that nourish the subsequent elements; and that nourishment of the subsequent elements does not occur without a channel. Now, whatever principle applies to blood applies to every bodily constituent. Furthermore, the nourishment of one element by another channel is impossible, because all things to be nourished occupy different locations; for there is no irrigation of two trees in separate locations by means of a single, undivided channel.
Although the mind (*manas*) need not be nourished because it is eternal, it nevertheless possesses channels for the purpose of reaching the locations of the sense organs;
moreover, he will state that for the mind and other supersensory faculties, the entire body constitutes the form of these channels.

As for the humors (*doṣas*), since they move throughout the whole body, all channels will be described as their pathways even without specifically naming the gross channels. However, upon closer investigation, there are indeed principal vessels (*dhamanis*) for the wind (*vāta*) and the others as well; as stated in the *Suśruta*: "Of those [channels], ten carry the wind," and so forth.
Furthermore, unlike in the Caraka and Suśruta [Samhitās], a distinction between *dhamanīs*, *sirās*, and *srotas* is not intended here;
the phrase "due to their omnipresence" (*sarvagatatvāt*) means that the *srotas* pervade all parts of the body.
The phrase "because it is the essence of everything" is connected with what follows.

Whether it be unwholesome food that aggravates the *doṣas* or wholesome food that pacifies the *doṣas*, it moves through every part of the body existing in the form of the *doṣas* as well as in the form of medicine. Therefore, channels (*srotas*) exist everywhere; thus, the prima facie argument is that the person (*puruṣa*) consists of channels.
He refutes this with the words beginning with "but not," and so forth.

For that which has channels—meaning those by which they are constructed—and that which they carry—meaning the fluids (rasa) and so forth that they transport—and that which they bring forth—meaning that which they nourish—and wherein they reside—meaning where they are connected to the flesh and other tissues—all that is distinct from the vessels (dhamanīs). Therefore, the meaning is that the person (puruṣa) is not merely of the nature of the channels (srotas).
Regarding the phrase "and from the knowledge of their provocation" (prakopavijñānataśca), the construction is: we shall explain how the provocation of the channels (srotasām) is recognized.
"For the sake of knowing the unspoken meaning" means for the sake of knowing the unspoken stream (*srotas*);
"for those possessing knowledge" means for those capable of knowing the unspoken meaning;
for indeed, by this indicative mark, those possessing knowledge infer even that which has not been explicitly stated as a stream.
"And for the sake of the understanding of those who lack knowledge" means for the sake of the knowledge of those with dull intellects regarding what has been stated;

"likewise" means that by the phrase "the body possesses consciousness," he excludes the non-conscious parts such as hair and nails from the movement of the *sattva* and other constituents, for [he holds that] the defects (*doṣas*) move even there.
"Having become the path" means having become the way;
"having become the foundation" means having the nature of a locus.
"Of those carrying the *prāṇa*" means of those carrying the wind designated as *prāṇa*.
This refers to a specific channel for the particular wind called *prāṇa*; however, there is no contradiction in the fact that, generally speaking, all the vessels (*dhamanī*) carry wind.
"Root" means the site of origin.
It should be understood as an alternative between "excessively released" or "excessively bound," since excessive release and excessive binding cannot coexist in one place;
furthermore, there is an alternative between "in small amounts" or "frequently," and the *kloman* is the seat of thirst located in the heart.

Regarding *vapāvahana*: *vapā* refers to the fatty tissue located in the abdomen, which people call "oil-wicks" (*tailavartikā*). However, in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā*, it is stated: "The kidneys and the waist are the root of those [channels] that carry fat" (*Su. Śā. A.*). Since this matter is accessible only to those who perceive objects beyond the senses, the intellects of people like us are not capable of fathoming it.
Furthermore, bone itself exists in a liquid state as it is carried by the channels; therefore, it is said that these are the "channels carrying bone."

Although in the section on various foods and drinks (*vividhāśitapītīya*) the characteristics of the vitiation of *rasa* and the other tissues have been described, and not those of the channels (*srotas*) carrying *rasa* and the rest, nevertheless, because the vitiation of the vessels (*dhamanī*) carrying *rasa* and the others occurs simultaneously with the vitiation of *rasa* and the rest, it is stated that "the cognitions of the channels carrying *rasa* and the others have been explained. As for those who assert that the vitiation of the vessels carrying *rasa* and the others is non-different from the vitiation of *rasa* and the others themselves—in their view, the separate mention of the vitiation of the vessels would be untenable; likewise, the vitiation of the bodily elements (*dhātu*) which he will describe through the vitiation of the vessels in the passage beginning with "By their provocation, those situated in their own locations... and so forth, would also be untenable.

Since the corruption of the vessels (*dhamanī*) necessarily results from the corruption of what lies outside them, the corruption of the vessels is described here by means of the very symptoms of the corruption of the tissues (*dhātu*). However, the specific symptoms of vessel-corruption distinct from the corruption of the blood and other tissues will be explained right here with the words "excessive flow" (*atipravṛtti*), and so forth.

The symptoms such as lack of perspiration (*asvedana*) belong to the corruption of the sweat-carrying vessels and are also present in the premonitory signs of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*); therefore, where other premonitory signs of leprosy are observed, one should determine that it is indeed a premonitory stage of leprosy, whereas when only these [specific] symptoms arise, it is a corruption of the sweat-carrying vessels.

Although no direct purpose for knowing the roots of the *dhamanīs* (vessels) is explicitly stated here, it should nevertheless be understood that, just as trees suffer great damage from injury to their roots, so too do the *dhamanīs* suffer great injury from damage to their roots; for this very reason, the characteristics of a wound at the root of the channels (*srotas*) are described in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā*.
To facilitate clinical usage, he states the synonyms for the channels, beginning with "the channels," etc.

"Covered and uncovered" is a single designation. Among these, those that are covered at the top but uncovered at the root—some call these synonyms for the root of the vessels (*dhamanī*); others, however, say these too are synonyms for the vessels, on the grounds that the vessels themselves indeed serve as locations for the *rasa* and other elements;
thus, "located in the locations" means located in the internal receptacles (*āśaya*).
The phrase "and those moving along the path" refers to those traveling through the *dhamanīs*.

With the words "and the channels," etc., [the author] explains the meaning previously stated in the passage beginning with "and of others": the meaning is that when the channels (*srotas*) and the tissues (*dhātu*) are afflicted, they vitiate the proximate channels and other tissues by transferring their own morbidities (*doṣa*).

Regarding the phrase "due to the inherent nature of the *doṣas*": this corrupting quality belongs to the *doṣas* themselves, and not to the other *dhātus*. Therefore, corruption of a *dhātu* (*dhātudoṣa*) should be understood as being caused solely by the *doṣas* residing within that *dhātu*. He now states the causes for the corruption of the channels (*srotas*) in their respective order, beginning with "from depletion" (*kṣayāt*), and so forth.
In the phrase "by means of dreadful [deeds]," the word "actions" (karmabhiḥ) is to be supplied as the ellipsis;
this connects with what was stated previously, "and for those who serve their gurus.
The term *medyānām* means "of those who are fat."

"From approaching [the womb] at an improper time" means approaching during a period that does not cause arousal; likewise, "from approaching an unsuitable womb" means from the suppression of the semen-urge;
and in the case of "urinated," etc., it should be understood as the consumption of water and so forth by one who possesses the urge to urinate.
With the passage beginning "And food" (āhāraśca), etc., he describes the general corruption of all the channels;
by the phrase "equal to the qualities of the *doṣas*," he demonstrates its quality of excessively increasing the *doṣas*.
It should be understood that when the *doṣas* are diminished, they do not cause further morbidity in others, but rather become exhausted of their own characteristic signs and so forth.

The phrase "impaired by the *dhātus*" means having a nature that is antagonistic to the *dhātus*, and not merely possessing qualities contrary to those of the *dhātus*; for, as stated, daytime sleep, fatty foods, and the like, though possessing qualities identical to *medas*, are said to be corrupters of *medas*.
With the words "excessive flow" (*atipravṛtti*) and so forth, he describes the general characteristics of the defects of the channels (*srotoduṣṭi*).

Here, "excessive flow" is to be understood as the excessive discharge of rasa and other [tissues] that are carried by the channels. Likewise, "adhesion" (*saṅga*) refers to the same [tissues], while "movement in the wrong path" (*vimārgagamana*) refers, for example, to the movement of waste matter (*mala*) into the urinary tract and so forth.
"Having the same color as their own elements" means having a color equal to that of the external elements; "pratāna" refers to the proliferation of creepers.

With the words beginning "prāṇodaka" (breath and water), he describes the medical treatment: it should be understood that for the channels carrying breath, the treatment is for dyspnea; for those carrying water, it is for the alleviation of thirst; and for those carrying food, it is for disorders of undigested matter (āma).
For the three [channels] carrying urine and so forth as well, three treatments—beginning with *mūtrakṛcchrikyā*—should be known respectively (26–28).

In the summary (*saṅgraha*), the "general sign of corruption" (*duṣṭilakṣaṇa*) means the sign of corruption not specified by [the individual doshas] such as Vata; the meaning is that the signs of corruption of the channels have not been stated here according to the distinctions of the doshas like Vata. Furthermore, corruption has not been described here in detail due to the fear of prolixity; therefore, corruption is to be determined by the predominance of the specific symptoms of Vata and the other doshas.
"At the beginning, the determination" means that at the start of the chapter, there is the determination regarding the doctrine that the person consists of vessels (*dhamanī*) and so forth.
With the words "merely," etc., [the author] states the worthiness of adopting the knowledge of the body as presented here through the distinctions of the vessels and other parts mentioned herein (vv.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Specific Determination of the Channels" (*srotovimāna*), in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Vimānasthāna, Chapter 6 (44 of 120)]

Having described diseases in the preceding chapter according to the distinctions of their channels, forms, and underlying substrates, this chapter on the "Classification of the Multitude of Diseases" (rogānīka-vimāna) is now stated in order to describe diseases according to the distinctions of their clinical manifestations and other such factors.
Here, "multitude of diseases" (rogānīka) refers to a collection of diseases.
Regarding the phrase "by the distinction of strength": here, "mild" (*mṛdu*) should be understood as having little strength, whereas "severe" (*dāruṇa*) should be known as having great strength.
A severe [disease] kills precisely because of its power after only a short lapse of time, as it has been said: "Indeed, there exist such diseases which, though considered severe, are curable."
"Those which would kill if not treated, or again through improper treatment" (Sūtra 18).

By the phrase "arising from the stomach," all diseases born of *kapha* and *pitta* that have the stomach as their locus are included; by the inclusion of "arising from the large intestine," all those born of *vāta* are included. Thus, there is an encompassing of all disorders. "Being twofold" means that [disease] exists in two ways.
"By means of another cause of differentiation" means by another causal factor that differentiates;
or alternatively, "even when being joined together" should be understood as being unified by another property that produces a single cognition.
"Due to the commonality of suffering" means that all diseases, by virtue of their common nature as the agents of suffering which pervades all illnesses, become uniform in form.
"Multiplicity as well" means that multiplicity arises not only from the aforementioned distinctions in power and so forth;
"countability" is stated in the *Aṣṭodarīya* chapter in passages such as, "In this compendium, there are forty-eight bases of diseases" (*Sūtra-sthāna*, A.
19); "innumerability" is stated in the *Mahārogādhyāya* and likewise in the *Triśophīya*: "For these very [diseases], when further divided, become innumerable."
This has been stated by [the verse]: "By means of pain, color, origin, location, shape, and name" (Sūtra-sthāna 18).

Now, one might object: "Are not these two properties—countability and uncountability—contradictory? Likewise, are not unity and multiplicity contradictory? Therefore, how can two properties known to be contradictory coexist in a single disease? To this, he says: "And not," and so forth.

"In the case of those whose limits are numerable" (*saṅkhyeyāgreṣu*) means in the case of those whose measure of diseases is numerable; the word *agra* here functions in the sense of "measure. For example, as it is said: "The limit of the divisions (*bhedāgram*) of each one is innumerable," which means the measure consisting of the number of divisions. "In the case of those belonging to other types of divisions" (*bhedaprakṛtyantarīyeṣu*) means in the case of those arising from other causes of division; "contradictory discourse" (*vigītiḥ*) refers to a statement, such as: "It is both one and many," and so forth—this is contradictory discourse.

The word "ataḥ" (hence) means because of the aforementioned contradiction (*vigīti*); thus, no thesis (*pratijñā*) is faulty. The construction is as follows: it might be argued that what has been stated here would take the form of a transition to a nature that is both one and many.

Having shown the absence of fault in the case of contradiction, he says "na cāvigītiḥ" and so forth, demonstrating that a fault does indeed exist even in the absence of contradiction when it is produced by another cause of differentiation.

For if, after stating "one group of diseases due to the commonality of pain," one were to then state "one group of diseases due to the difference in their potencies"—thereby making a declaration of unity that is not contradictory—such a statement would indeed be contradictory. The point is that unity among diseases is not established by a difference in potency; rather, there is only duality. He states the reason why there is no fault in such a contradictory statement: "The divider... and so forth. The divider is the person, and the object to be divided is the disease. He divides it in one way as a duality and so on, and in another way as a unity; having previously divided it in one manner, he then divides it otherwise.
He explains the meaning of this with the passage beginning "by means of another division of the nature [of things]," etc.:

"in many ways" refers to two types of masses of diseases (*rogānīka*), as well as ten masses of diseases, and so forth; yet, the prior enumeration of divisions does not invalidate the measure of those divisions.

He thinks as follows: If unity is stated with the intention of referring to the connection with a particular attribute, and multiplicity is also stated with the same intention of referring to that very same connection with attributes, then there is a contradiction; for it is not logically possible for that very same thing to be both one and many. However, when multiplicity is stated with the intention of referring to the connection with different attributes, then there is no contradiction; because at the time of denoting multiplicity, it is precisely many attributes of diseases that are intended. Therefore, the unity of diseases refers to the scope of a single attribute, while their multiplicity refers to the scope of multiple attributes; thus, there is no contradiction.

[Objection: Surely, where there is a non-common cause of differentiation, the aforementioned logic may hold that the distinction is properly established because it is produced by another cause. But where ten groups of diseases (*rogānīka*) are mentioned due to a twofold nature based on their power (*prabhāva*) and so forth, how can one first state a twofoldness based on the number two—saying "there are two groups of diseases"—and then again state the number ten through the same division of twoness and so on? For this word "two" is common as a cause for both the twoness and the tens of diseases. To this he says: "Even though it is the same," meaning: even though they appear to be identical at first glance because they are denoted by the same word.

The meaning is that another subsequent usage must be expected for the subject under discussion; that is, for the sake of resolving the contradiction, one must rely on a subsequent usage that follows after the subject—which was already expressed by a synonymous term—has been manifested as distinct [from others].

By this, he demonstrates the following: although the word *dvi* (two) is common to both "the power of a disease" (*roga-prabhāva*) and "the strength of a disease" (*roga-bala*), nevertheless, in one case it refers to the two-fold nature of power (*prabhāva*) by depending on the subsequent application of the term "due to a difference in power" (*prabhāva-bhedāt*), and likewise, the word *dvi* refers to the two-fold nature of strength (*bala*) by depending on the subsequent application of the term "due to a difference in strength" (*bala-bhedāt*).

Thus, the sense is that even the state of being ten (*daśatva*) as well as the state of being two (*dvitva*) is logically established for that which is differentiated by various words denoting different meanings through such applications of the word *dvi*.
To illustrate the point that multiple meanings can be expressed by a single word, he says "santi hi" and so forth;
"other meanings" refers to those meanings not denoted by synonymous terms.
To provide an example for this, he says "samāno hi" and so forth.

The word *roga* (disease) is identical in its application to both *doṣas* (humors) and *vyādhis* (manifest diseases), as it denotes both equally. Therefore, because of this commonality between *roga* and *doṣa*, all the terms to be mentioned hereafter—such as *rogātaṅka*, *yakṣma*, and so forth—which share the same referent, are included.
Regarding the phrase "in the remaining [categories]," such as *hetu* (cause) and others, "possessing distinction" means possessing a distinction in their mode of expression.

In that regard, although the defects (*doṣa*) and the morbid alterations (*vikāra*) are identical in being denotable by the term "disease," there exists a discrepancy (*vigīti*) regarding their being countable or uncountable; yet, with the intention that this is not a fault, he says "tatra" and so forth.

One should understand that, with the intention that many morbid alterations arise from each individual defect, the defects are not excessively numerous when considered in relation to the morbid alterations.

"Yathācitram" means "according to the arrangement. Therefore, we shall explain only those modifications (*vikāra*) which the former teachers have declared to be the most important; we shall not explain all of them, because that would be impossible.

Alternatively, there is the reading "yathocitam" (as appropriate). And by the phrase "without remainder" (*anavaśeṣeṇa*), he demonstrates that the defects (*doṣa*), being not excessively numerous, can indeed be stated without remainder.
In this context, since the mental afflictions (*mānasa-doṣa*) and their transformations (*vikāra*) require extensive explanation, they are discussed later [in verses 5–6].
Now, one might ask: "How can immeasurable transformations arise from a limited cause in the form of the *doṣas*? To this, he says: "But when provoked... and so forth.

For that very same humor (doṣa), when vitiated by a specific cause and having entered another location, produces many different disorders due to its association with distinct potencies; this is indeed logical.
And it has been said: "That very same humor, when provoked by a specific etiological factor and having moved to another site, produces many disorders" (Sūtra-sthāna 18).
He describes the mutual association of physical and mental disorders with the words "And those disorders," etc.

By the term "persisting" (anuvartamāna), the meaning is this: whenever fevers and the like, or desire and the like, persist for a long time due to their intensity, they generally become chronic (anubadhnanti); however, when they remain for only a short duration, they generally do not become chronic.
Alternatively, "following one another" means mutually increasing their strength;

and here, by the word "mutually," one should understand the connection of bodily factors with bodily factors, mental factors with mental factors, bodily factors with mental factors, and mental factors with bodily factors.
Having shown the connection with morbid transformations (*vikāra*), he states the connection with the humors (*doṣa*): "But it is fixed," and so forth.
He states the connection with bodily humors: "Bodily," and so forth.
By the phrase "of those having a single substratum," he shows that the association of the *doṣas* occurs through their proximity within a single body.

He explains the reason—"because they possess similar qualities"—with the words beginning "for the *doṣas*... where "by afflictions" (*dūṣaṇaiḥ*) means "by causes. Generally, the causes for the bodily *doṣas*, such as *vāta* and the others, are indeed the same. For example, sour, salty, and pungent tastes produce *pitta*; therein, the sour taste produces *pitta* along with *kapha*, the salty taste produces *kapha* along with *pitta*, and the pungent taste produces *pitta* along with *vāta*.

Likewise, although spring produces phlegm (*śleṣman*), it also causes wind (*vāta*) and bile (*pitta*) by way of its depleting nature; similarly, even in the rainy season, the bile that has been accumulated becomes aggravated in autumn and is aggravated specifically while following phlegm; likewise, summer, by means of its dryness, brings about an accumulation of wind, and by means of its heat, it also slightly brings about an accumulation of bile—this is how it should be understood.

(10) To demonstrate this very sequence of the association of the *doṣas* through the distinction between the primary affliction (*anubandhya*) and the secondary affliction (*anubandha*), he states the definition of the primary and secondary afflictions, beginning with "In that regard" (*tatra*).

The distinction between the primary affliction (*anubandhya*) and the secondary affliction (*anubandha*) is the "distinction between the primary and secondary afflictions," which is characterized in the text by the passage beginning with "independent" (*svatantra*). This very term "independent" is further explained by the passage beginning with "distinctive gender" (*vyaktaliṅga*) and ending with "arising and subsiding as previously described. This means that [the disease] arises from its own causes and is to be pacified by its own specific treatment alone.

Alternatively, by the term "independent" (*svatantra*), its predominance (*prādhānya*) in producing its own morbid transformation (*vikāra*) is expressed; for an independent humor (*doṣa*) produces transformations at the time of its own provocation, whereas a dependent humor produces a transformation only at the time of the provocation of the independent one, being impelled by the predominant humor.

By the phrase "having characteristics contrary to that," it is understood that the secondary factor (*anubandha*) has unmanifest signs (*avyaktaliṅga*), is provoked by its own cause, and is to be pacified by the treatment of another [primary] factor; for a secondary factor, due to its weakness, does not make its signs manifest. Likewise, when produced by another cause that is somewhat favorable, it is pacified by the treatment of that other factor which is likewise somewhat favorable—for example, in autumn, *kapha* is produced by a *pitta*-inducing cause such as the sour digestion of water and so forth, and it is pacified by the very treatment for *pitta*, such as bitter ghee and the like, which is also favorable to *kapha*.
The construction is as follows: "Or rather, when two things have attained the characteristic of being concomitant (anubandhya), they are called a 'conjunction' (saṃsarga).
Furthermore, this term *anubandhya* refers to a fault (*doṣa*) characterized by manifest gender and other such properties;

therefore, even in a *sannipāta* (complex) that follows what is not primary, the designation "concomitant" (*anubandha*) indeed occurs, even in the absence of a [separate] concomitant, because it is established by the specific nature of the conjunction consisting of the concomitant (*anubandhya*) and the concomitant (*anubandha*).
"Produced by designations" (*sañjñāprakṛta*) means produced by the designations such as "complication," "associated condition," "conjunction," "combination," "fever," "diarrhea," and so forth.

"An array of various specific types" (*nānāprakṛtiviśeṣavyūha*) means a collection of diseases and humors (*doṣas*) in the form of fever, diarrhea, etc., produced by the specific causes already mentioned. By the word "by physicians" (*bhiṣajām*), he shows that these designations, such as "complication" and so on, are established by convention among physicians alone.

Having described the different types of defects and morbidities, he states the classification of *agni* (fire), which is the primary cause for the maintenance of the body, beginning with the words "In the fires," etc.

By the general term "in the bodily [fires]," he includes all the fires present throughout the entire body. However, in the detailed explanation, the fourfold classification mentioned—beginning with "The sharp fire is capable of enduring all types of improper conduct"—is intended to indicate that the sharpness of the skin-fire and so forth is rooted precisely in the sharpness of the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*).
For there is this statement: "They are rooted in that [fire], for their increase and decrease consist of its increase and decrease" (Ci. A. 15).

Although a balanced (*sama*) digestive fire is logically the first to be mentioned as being the most commendable, nevertheless, it is mentioned here first in order to demonstrate the preeminence of the sharp (*tīkṣṇa*) fire over the balanced one. For the preeminence of the balanced fire is firmly established by its very state of being free from morbid change (*nirvikāra*), whereas the preeminence of the sharp fire lies in its capacity to withstand all types of dietary indiscretions (*apacāra*).
The meaning of "dull" (*manda*) is that which does not tolerate even a slight indiscretion, as its characteristics are the opposite of those [of the sharp fire].

Regarding the phrase "characterized by normal and abnormal signs": sometimes one does not undergo transformation even due to irregular conduct, while at other times one does undergo transformation when the *vāta*, *pitta*, and *śleṣman* are in equilibrium.
Even though this was stated, the term "abiding in their natural state" (*prakṛtisthānām*) was added for the purpose of excluding those whose *vāta*, *pitta*, and *śleṣman* have become increased;

furthermore, the phrase "of those with balanced *vāta*, *pitta*, and *śleṣman*" was employed to eliminate the ambiguity of the word *prakṛti*, which has multiple meanings such as "cause" and so forth.
By the statement "when the seat of fire is overcome by vāta," it is shown that even for those dominated by vāta, imbalance occurs precisely when the seat of fire is impaired by vāta;
this should be explained in the same way for the cases beginning with "overcome by pitta" and so forth.

"Because of the consumption of irregular food"—the meaning is that this person does not consume food as if it were weighed on a scale by Tulādhāra; therefore, one or another of the *doṣas*, such as *vāta* and the rest, necessarily becomes deranged.

By the phrase "one whose *vāta*, *pitta*, and *śleṣman* are in equilibrium," etc., he shows that health indeed exists among people, as established by medical practice. The point is that just as a state of equilibrium is desired for the *doṣas*—in which the inequality of their parts, minutes, and so forth is abandoned and they do not manifest as pathological changes even if the balance is not perfect—that very same kind of equilibrium exists in *prakṛti* (the primordial constitution) as well.
Others, however, do not even consider this discrepancy, because it does not produce a diagnosable disease;
"doṣaprakṛti" means a constitution conditioned by vitiated doṣas.
When a *doṣa* has increased, the yogin should apply practices that are contrary to that *doṣa*—

that is, practices contrary to *vāta*, *pitta*, or *śleṣman*. However, when the fire [of digestion] has reached equilibrium (*samatā*), one should perform the application of practice equally for all [constitutions, such as those dominated by *vāta*], according to the appropriate method.

In this manner—that is, by this method—there are also applications of activities and medicines for the [increase of] vāta and the other doshas. However, those who say "in this manner" means "by the fourfold method thus described," explain it as follows: it indicates that for those of balanced constitution (samaprakṛti), balanced physical activities such as exercise and the like, as well as medicine prescribed according to the seasonal regimen (ṛtucarya) that induces emesis and so forth, are indicated by this. (14) "The other two doshas are not likewise" means even when there is the consumption of their respective causes; otherwise, by the consumption of things that aggravate vāta, there would be no increase at all of pitta and kapha.

It should be understood that although practices such as inducing terror (*vitrāsana*) produce *vāta*, they are nevertheless prescribed for the purpose of destroying insanity (*unmāda*) caused by *vāta*.
For, after describing terror-inducing treatments as medicine for insanity, it is stated: "By that, his mind, which was deranged in every way, attains tranquility" (Ci.
A. 9). The phrase "for all purposes" means they are to be employed through drinking, massage, enemas, and so forth.

"Bastiniyama" means the practice of the prescribed rules regarding enemas (*basti*); alternatively, by the term "bastiniyama," he indicates that the regulation of the number of enemas—consisting of the specific actions, times, and formulations to be described in the *Siddhisthāna*—must be observed, for he will say: "Thirty enema formulations are considered for clinical procedures, half that time [for administration], and then the application" (Siddhi Sthāna, Chapter 1).
"Sukhaśīlatā" refers to the state of being constantly accustomed to comfort.
"By those [methods] as stated" means by those described in the chapter on major diseases;
