"and the removal of the *doṣas* from below" means by means of purgation (*virecana*).
"Agryacandana" refers to white sandalwood; "hastānām" means of bundles [of sticks].

Regarding the statement "mostly dry" (*rūkṣaprāyāṇi*) instead of simply saying "dry" (*rūkṣāṇi*), which is what would be appropriate for the purpose of conquering phlegm (*śleṣman*), he thereby demonstrates that food which is excessively dry should not be consumed, because such food is conducive to *vāta* and fails to nourish the bodily tissues (*dhātu*). For it is said in the *Rasavimāna*: "One should eat unctuous food; for unctuous food tastes pleasant when eaten, and it stimulates the digestive fire in the stomach" (Vi. A. 1), and so forth. "Fasting" (*laṅghana*) includes jumping, wandering about, moving in circles like a coil, and total abstinence from food—all of these constitute the various forms of fasting.
As it has been stated: "Purification is of four kinds: thirst, wind, sunlight, and digestive treatments; fasting and physical exercise constitute *laṅghana*" (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 22).
For here, the word "fasting" (*upavāsa*) is used in the sense of *laṅghana*.

"For the sake of happiness" means for the sake of future happiness; for when phlegm (śleṣman) is diminished through the cessation of [excessive] happiness, the characteristic of happiness arises, which is the absence of disorders caused by phlegm.
By means of the knowledge of the chapter as it has been described, he praises [the physician] who is cognizant of all diseases, beginning with the words "all," and so forth.
He who protects and guards the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) is the Lord of Breath (*prāṇapati*).
He who digests [the food] in the aggregate is the digestive fire (*jaraṇa-vahni*); reflection upon that [fire] has been undertaken in the passage beginning with "In the fires," and so forth.
"Medicines that restore the natural state," verses 20–22.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Classification of Groups of Diseases," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Section on Specific Determinations (*Vimānasthāna*).
6 [Vimānasthāna, Chapter 7 (45 of 120)]:

Having established the nature of disease in the preceding chapter, the "Chapter on the Characteristics of the Diseased" is now declared in order to establish the classification of the diseased person for the purpose of medical treatment, and as an incidental discussion, to establish the nature of parasites (*krimi*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "dvau" (two): one who has developed a disease is "vyādhitaḥ" (afflicted); those whose form is like that of such a person are "vyādhitarūpau" (having the appearance of the afflicted). This means they resemble someone suffering from disease.
By this term "vyādhitarūpau," it should be understood that they resemble those who possess either severe or mild diseases.

For when a severe illness appears as a mild illness due to factors such as the strength of one's constitution (*sattva*), that person is not actually afflicted by a mild illness; rather, he is indeed afflicted by a severe illness, yet because of his severe illness, he is perceived as having a mild illness by one who lacks far-sighted vision. This should be explained in the same way for other cases, such as "one who is afflicted by a mild illness" and so forth, due to the presence of error (*viparyāsa*). The term *adhamatvāt* means "due to inferiority" (*avaratvāt*).

"By the eye alone" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for the means of other cognitions; by this, it should be understood that [it refers to] even touch and so forth, provided they do not apprehend specific qualities. "Determining the form as 'form'" means forming a definitive ascertainment (niścaya).
"They disagree regarding what is heavy and what is light" means they do not correctly understand heaviness and lightness.
Regarding this very point of contradictory apprehension, he states the reason, beginning with "for not," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "by means of a portion of knowledge," he states the result of a misconception through partial knowledge with the words beginning "those who are misinformed.

*Upakrama-yukti* is the application of a therapeutic procedure in accordance with the nature of the disorder; those who possess contradictory understandings regarding its knowledge are the ones referred to as being "misinformed."
He explains this very point with the words "te yadā" and so forth:
"they attain" means they perceive;
"they utter" means they indeed provoke [the poison] further, but because of their own weak strength, they do not carry it away—this is the meaning.
"Atinirhṛtya" means having extracted by means of excessive practice (*atiyoga*).
"Of knowledge" (*jñānasya*) refers to the means of attaining knowledge (*jñānasādhana*).
"According to possibility" (*yathāsambhavam*) means that by whichever means of knowledge are available in a particular place, one should [proceed] with those in that place.
Existence and so forth are not to be examined anywhere at all, such as in [the context of] heaviness and lightness.
To facilitate easy comprehension, he expresses this very point in verse: "sattva... and so forth.
"In the form of a disease" (vyādhirūpam) means "in the form of the course of a disease" (vyādher gatirūpam).
However, the reading "vyādhitarūpam" is more straightforward.

"Children" refers to those of little knowledge; "by excessive application" means by improper application. By this, both excessive application (atiyoga) and false application (mithyāyoga) are included.

Now, following the discussion on the difficulty of discerning the severity or mildness of a disease, he begins a section that also elucidates the difficult-to-know parasites—starting with the words "thus, one who is diseased," etc.
The phrase "the possibility of the foremost number" means the possibility of the measure of numbers; for the word *agra* denotes quantity.

The cause of the manifestation of the disease consists in the strength or weakness of the *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* constituents; the resulting confusion regarding that cause is "confusion concerning the cause of the disease's manifestation. In that regard:
Knowledge that is partial in its cause is fallible and thus defective;
correct practice is right practice.
"Previously indicated" means that in the *Aṣṭodarīya* [chapter], they were mentioned merely by name;
by the phrase "except for those born with [the body]," he shows that the worms born with the body (*śarīrasahaja*) are non-transformative (*avaikārika*) and exceed even twenty in number.
"By the primary natures" means by the causes; "born of impurity" means born of external impurity.

Some say that *pipīlikā* (ant) and *likṣā* (nit) are designations for types of worms; these should be understood as established through usage in their own treatises and as well-known in other regions.
"Power" (*prabhāva*) means that which is accomplished by one's own capacity.
Itching, horripilation, and so forth are to be understood as occurring only at the site of the ulcer.
*Paramānna* is milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
*Saṅkīrṇabhojana* is food consisting of side dishes (*vyañjana*) and the like mixed with loathsome substances, impurities, and so forth.
*Bradhna* is a creeper-like skin.
"Yadantaram" means at which time; "tadantaram" refers to that very same time.
"Ūrṇāṃśusaṅkāśāḥ" means resembling the fibers of a sheep's wool.
They say "paryāsata" means they cast [it] away; or else, it means they sit around the anus excessively, again and again.

"Extraction" refers to the hands and so forth; "purifications" refers to the removal of the primary cause in the form of phlegm and other humors—this is the meaning of "destruction of the primary cause.
"By means of instruments" means by means of tools such as forceps and the like.
The construction is: "that [should be]," "there would be an obstacle," and "the non-cultivation of those factors mentioned in the introduction. This is a restatement of the commentary;
its explanation begins with the words, "As it has been said," and so forth.
"Of those of such a nature" means of those similar to the etiology of worms born from phlegm and feces;
"by way of their characteristics" means in brief; for a summary is the defining characteristic that grasps the details.
"For the purpose of reaching the storehouse" means for the sake of going to the storehouse by abandoning one's own country out of greed for things such as milk and molasses.
"On that very day" means within a single day; and this performance of extensive work in just one day is to be understood as resulting from the power of the disease.

Furthermore, this completion of everything in a single day should only be undertaken if the person possesses a full complement of physical strength and other such qualities; otherwise it should not be done. This is stated in the passage beginning with "if he should be capable of being brought [to the storehouse]," and so forth.
Madhuśigru (the sweet drumstick tree) and śobhāñjana (the black nightshade);
here, the proportions of the decoction ingredients, water, and so forth, should be determined according to the standard rules for preparing decoctions (kvātha-paribhāṣā).
The meaning is "mostly consumed" or "mostly exhausted. Regarding the phrase "when the medicinal herbs have lost their potency," this refers to when the potency has transferred into the water.

By this definition of the successful completion of a decoction (*kaṣāya*), he demonstrates the procedure that one must use exactly as much water and perform exactly as much cooking as is required for the herbs to become devoid of their potency; it is not necessarily the case that this applies everywhere according to the general technical rule (*paribhāṣā*).
"Thoroughly purified" means filtered through a cloth;
the dosage for the decoction and so forth in the bladder should be understood from what will be stated in the section on successful treatment (*siddhi*);
*alarka* is *mandāra*.
In the third enclosure on the west,
"having combined" means having mixed together.
"By means of *śaikharika* decoction" means by means of *viḍaṅga* decoction; for, according to medical convention, *viḍaṅga* decoction is called *śaikharika* decoction.
"Successively following the *vilepī*" means having performed the sequence beginning with the *yavāgū* and so forth.
"With the grains of *apāmārga* and so forth" means as described in the *Apāmārgataṇḍulīya* [chapter];
*mūlakaparṇī* is *śobhāñjana*.
Regarding the term *upakuḍya*, it means "having caused to cook"; the verbal root *kuḍ* is listed [in the lexicons] in the sense of "to burn.

In this very context, the group of five beginning with *pippalī* (the *pippalyādi-pañcavarga*) is included, as well as the *pañcakola* mentioned in the sequence beginning with *peyā*, along with *sahacara* and *jhiṇṭikā*.
"Madhuvilulitān" means stirred with honey (madhunā āloḍitān).
Regarding "supari" and so forth, the meaning is: having meditated in such a way that they become well-meditated upon (suparibhāvitāni).
"Anuguptam" means that it is made so as not to be accessible to wind and other elements, and is protected;
"bradhnaḥ" refers to the anus, but here it refers to the lower part of the jar.
"Having wrapped the body" means having enveloped it; "the raft" refers to the covering, which is prepared with the oil of *bhallātaka*.
"From the second" means from the pot situated below (verses 23–24);
"having winnowed" means having removed the impurities such as clay and other debris.
"Having purified" means having washed until the defects have departed;
here, "the departure of the defects of the sesame seeds" should be understood as the removal of the impurities adhering to the sesame husks. "Having plucked out" means having dehusked them.
"Having fixed it" means having placed it;
"having grasped it with both hands" means having held it repeatedly with the hands attached to it.
Uddālaka is *bahuvāra*;
[the two fruits] are the size of a *bilva* fruit, measuring one *pala* each;
*paryoga* is a cauldron.

"According to their respective [requirements]" (*yathāsvam*) means that the perfection of color and other qualities occurs in proportion to whatever substance is used for processing the oil; "it comes about" (*saṃvartate*) means it becomes like the wick (*varti*). "In small measure" (*alpamātram*) means that the medicinal drug, excluding the substances for the non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*) and the downward-moving purgative (*anuloma-haraṇa*), should be prepared in a small quantity.
He states that these same three—evacuative therapy (*apakarṣaṇa*) and so forth—are expressed by different terms in the context of other diseases, beginning with "this very [therapy]," etc.

Here, *saṃśodhana* (purification) is *apaharaṇa* (removal), *saṃśamana* (pacification) is *vighāta* (destruction), while the avoidance of causes (*nidānavarjana*) is identical even in terms of terminology.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Classification of the Forms of Disease," in the Vimānasthāna of the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka-saṃhitā composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.

[Vimānasthāna, Chapter 8 (46 of 120)] In the preceding chapter, the erroneous cognition regarding the signs of disease was described; that arises from defects of the intellect. Therefore, in order to explain the study, teaching, and discussion of that science—which are the causes for the production of pure intellect—the *rogabhiṣagjitīya* [chapter] is now set forth.
The chapter composed concerning the conquest of disease by means of the physician’s treatment is called *rogabhiṣagjitīya*.

Its role as the healer of disease is to be understood from the description of the means for right knowledge utilized in healing— such as the injunctions for study and so forth— as well as the instruments and causes thereof. Here, regarding the injunctions for study and other duties that must be performed, the author, demonstrating what kind of scripture is to be studied, points out the person who seeks Ayurveda by saying "the wise one," and so forth.

An action (*kārya*) is that which ought to be performed; its "gravity" (*gaurava*) consists in its being accomplished through great effort, while its "lightness" (*lāghava*) consists in its being accomplished through little effort—this is the gravity and lightness of the action.
The "fruit of the action" (*kāryaphala*) is the fruit of the undertaking; this is the immediate, desired result, whereas the "consequence" (*anubandha*) is the future fruit of that very same action.
"Place and time" means place and time that are appropriate for the task to be performed;
having understood all this, if one wishes to become a physician through the observation of reasoning—that is, the observation of logical justification—then one should first examine the scripture.

He thinks as follows: one who, regarding the task characterized by the study of Āyurveda, considers it a burden relative to his own capacity, does not proceed; likewise, one who has no desire for the fruits of Āyurveda such as health and so forth; likewise, one who resides in a region where the knowledge of Āyurveda is not to be adopted; and one whose body has reached the stage of old age—who, due to the very inability to reach the end of the study of Āyurveda, does not wish to become a physician because he perceives the aforementioned impossibility—we do not even instruct these individuals in the examination of the Āyurvedic treatise. However, one who possesses qualities contrary to those mentioned and who desires to become a physician through the adoption of the study of Āyurveda should examine the scripture.

"Various" means innumerable, very great, and renowned, and practiced by wise men (*dhīrapuruṣa*); or alternatively, the analysis of the compound is "practiced by those who are very renowned and wise men. "Honored by trustworthy persons" means approved as appropriate by many kinds of trustworthy people.
Disciples are of three kinds: those with superior, middling, and inferior intelligence.

Regarding that which ought to be stated as "free from repetition," if one recites it with a fault, yet does so because it is necessitated by the context (*adhikaraṇavaśaprāpta*), then that statement is not a fault of repetition.
For there is this saying: "By virtue of the context, due to the attainment of qualities or faults from a difficult point, and through the connection of the meaning..."
"For the purpose of praise, for the sake of removing doubt from the minds of disciples, and for the sake of their further advancement;

and because [the meaning] is only slightly obscured even regarding the qualifiers, that which is redundant in the Tantra is not desired by the authors of the Tantra— having discerned this, the commentary is composed."
"Having its own support" means having an excellent subject matter;
"not fallen" means having non-vulgar words;
"having unstrained words" means having words that are not difficult to pronounce, or alternatively, words whose meanings are well-known.
"Named Puṣkala" means a statement that correctly conveys the meaning;
"having a sequentially arrived meaning" means having a meaning obtained through the proper order; and "having a coherent meaning" means having a meaning that has been established.
The section on "unconfused" (*asaṅkula*) means a section that is not mixed up.

"Possessing characteristics" (*lakṣaṇavat*) means like the exposition of the specific common properties known as the primary subject matter, causes, signs, and medicines in Āyurveda; alternatively, it means like the characteristics of an excellent treatise, or "possessing examples" (*udāharaṇavat*) means like an illustration.
Since the scripture must be studied after examination, he describes the examination of that teacher from whom the scripture is to be studied, beginning with the word "tataḥ" (therefore) and so forth;
"dakṣam" means one who is not of dull intellect.

"Provided with requisites" means that since there is no practice of medicine for a teacher who lacks such requisites, the observation of the [medical] action does not occur. "One whose knowledge is unrefined" means one for whom there is no knowledge refined by the study of other treatises; however, one who knows Āyurveda and is further refined by other sciences is all the more worthy of acceptance. "Seasonal" means occurring at the appropriate time.
By showing many examples such as fire and others, [the author] demonstrates that in whatever manner one serves fire and the like, in that very same manner one serves the Guru;
this refers to "firmness," meaning the stability in grasping the scriptures.
"Of the designation" means of the designation of the treatise,
in the power of expression, that is, in the capacity for proclaiming the meaning. 5

In this context, "firmness in the treatise" and so forth refers to conversing with those who know that [treatise], which means engaging in discussion with students of that science; "healthy" means free from disease.
"Having made the opportunity" (*kṛtakṣaṇa*) means having set aside time for study by dedicating oneself exclusively to that task;
the construction is: "having risen in the morning," or "having risen at dawn" (*upavyūṣam*).
The term *upavyūṣam* refers to when a small portion of the night remains.
"Preceded by men" means led by those whose minds are one-pointed.

"For the sake of avoiding one's own faults and for the purpose of measuring the faults of others" means for the purpose of avoiding the faults of one's own study and for the purpose of measuring—that is, for the purpose of knowing—the faults of the study of others; "pramāṇa" (means of knowledge) is that by which something is measured, and here merely knowledge is intended.

Having correctly understood the reality of the meaning, one who studies after such understanding becomes free from defects in study; and through the correct knowledge of study, one recognizes the defective study of others—this is the conclusion of the previously stated injunction regarding study.
Study performed according to the prescribed rule becomes well-mastered.

The avoidance of times forbidden for Vedic study—due to the attainment of visible or invisible [impediments]—is indeed prohibited here as well; thus, it is not mentioned specifically. (6–7) Here, among the qualities of a disciple, such traits as having straight eyes, mouth, and bridge of the nose are to be accepted as innate characteristics; one who possesses contrary characteristics is indeed dull-witted.
"Conduct according to that science" means the practice of those who know Āyurveda;
"restrained" means disciplined and not arrogant; "not haughty" means free from egoism.

By the word *anurāga*, devotion to study is expressed; and by the phrase "one who is devoted" (*anurakta*), devotion toward the teacher is expressed. Having shown proficiency (*dākṣya*), he says "not indolent" (*analasa*); even when a task has been undertaken through proficiency, he says "not indolent" regarding that which must be accomplished with great effort.
"One who carries out instructions" (*anuśiṣṭipratikara*) means one who obeys commands.
Tiṣya is the Puṣya constellation; Aśvayuṅ is Aśvinī.

Regarding the statement "when the moon is auspicious" among the aforementioned constellations, since the moon becomes auspicious [during these], study should be undertaken only when the moon has risen.

"At an auspicious moment" means at a favorable moment; the moments (muhūrtas) include Śiva-bhujaṅga and others. "Muṇḍa" means one who has had his head shaved. "Gandha-yukta-hasta" means a hand endowed with fragrance, specifically a hand with five fingers [anointed] with perfume.
By the word *hiraṇya*, unworked gold is understood; by the word *hema*, worked gold is meant.
The *paridhis*—staffs of *pālāśa* wood and other species measuring one cubit (*hasta*)—are to be placed on the four sides of the sacrificial fire-pit (*homakuṇḍa*).

Furthermore, from the statement of the sages, it is inferred that in this context, the mere presence of the acquired object itself is what bestows the fruit [of the rite] (therefore, even desirable perfumes and such brought by others need not be displayed).
Here, a *kiṣku* is the measure of a cubit;
"well-donned" means well-wrapped.

The intention is that the teacher (adhyāpaka), having placed [the materials] upon the fire and reciting the mantra "svāhā" to Brahmā and the others, should offer the oblation; this is the construction of the sentence: "the teacher, while reciting the mantra, should first offer the oblation into the fire."
Therefore, the oblation (homa) should be performed with the Rigvedic verses beginning with "To Brahman, Svāhā! and others that invoke blessings;
and the disciple should touch him from behind—meaning that the disciple should also offer oblations immediately after the teacher has done so.
"You must become [so];

you must reflect; you must act for the sake of healing, beginning with cows and Brahmins—that is, first the welfare of cows and Brahmins must be prayed for, and thereafter that of other living beings."
The word division is "upaviśatā ca. *Śuṇḍā* means a tavern; one who frequents such a place is *śauṇḍa*. However, one who does not frequent it is *aśauṇḍa*.
It is "pure" (*śukla*) as it were, because of its faultlessness; this statement is made for that reason.
The connection is that "one must be diligent.
"One who is hated by the king" means *rājadviṣṭaḥ*; however, he who hates the king is *rājadveṣī*.
"The practice of conduct" means *ācāropacāraḥ*.
The construction is: "or [the means] for those things that are not directly perceptible should not be undertaken.
Alternatively, "activities" (*pravṛttayaḥ*) refers to worldly affairs (*vārtāḥ*);
in this context, it is connected with the phrase "should not be described."

"Of another"—meaning a patient's son, father, or others; "elsewhere," that is, regarding a neutral person, speaking of the decline of life is indeed conducive to fame, yet one must not boast or engage in self-praise even from a trustworthy person (*āpta*). Here, a "trustworthy person" is said to be one whose speech is truthful; elsewhere too, he will state that truth alone is trustworthy. The meaning is that one should speak only what is appropriate for the occasion.
"And certainly not," and so forth;
because even Āyurveda cannot be fully mastered, one should therefore exert effort for the sake of knowing Āyurveda.
Regarding this difficult-to-traverse Āyurveda,
he says "And this," etc., for the purpose of enjoining virtuous conduct not previously mentioned:
"And this" refers to that which is to be practiced as stated in the text beginning with "Then, in the presence of the fire," and so forth.
"And thus, 'excellence of conduct' (vṛttasauṣṭhava) means virtuous behavior similar to what has been described;
'worldly' (laukya) means approved by the world.
The word 'iti' is used for emphasis; therefore, whatever speech of an enemy is endowed with qualities such as being beneficial (dhanya) and so forth, that alone should be followed and heard."
"By those [means] as stated" refers to other treatises (*śāstrāntara*); for in this treatise, the fruit of study is not explicitly stated anywhere.

"Exultation" (*saṃharṣa*) means rivalry; it is called "that which produces application and exultation toward knowledge" because it brings about both application and exultation for the sake of knowledge.

"Confidence" (*vaiśāradya*) means skill in overcoming the speech of others; and this arises from practice in the assembly as "increased resolve," that is, firm conviction. Now, how might there also be the state of having heard some secret matter? To this he says: "speaking in summary."
"By way of a summary" means by way of an extraction of the essence (*sāra*).
[Objection: "If it is secret because it is the essence, then why does this seeker of victory (*vijigīṣu*) speak of it? To this he says: "Out of exultation.
The sense is that even a secret matter may be stated for the sake of victory through the spirit of rivalry (*spardhā*).
Discourse based on a hidden intention (*sandhāya-sambhāṣā*) is called "non-agreement" (*asaṃvāda*) in the *Naya*;
however, discourse involving dispute (*vigṛhya-sambhāṣā*) should be understood as consisting of *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*.

With the words beginning with "therein" (tatra), he explains the procedure for conversation based on intentional meaning (*sandhāya-saṃbhāṣā*); "one should speak confidently" means one should say that one should speak without fear of the points of defeat (*nigraha*) mentioned in the contexts of frivolous talk (*jalpa*) and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*).

And having refuted him, one should not rejoice. Regarding the formal debate (*anuloma-sambhāṣā*) consisting of the statement of reasons, those points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) which are possible—namely, those that obstruct the truth such as fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), contradictory tenets (*apasiddhānta*), deficiency (*nyūna*), and redundancy (*adhika*)—having refuted [the opponent] by means of these, one should still not rejoice. However, the points of defeat mentioned in the context of *jalpa* (quibble) are certainly not to be accepted here;
for "unknown" means unknown to the opponent.

And "one should conciliate properly" is the connection [of the phrase]; by this, he instructs that one must not employ quibbles (*chala*) or futile rejoinders (*jāti*) here, and that one should be attentive therein—one should apply careful attention to proper conciliation.

Regarding the phrase "by another," while in ordinary debate anyone unqualified may participate, in this context the qualified person authorized is either a teacher (*guru*) or a fellow student (*brahmacārī*). For it is stated in the *Nyāya* [Sūtra]: "One should approach that [teacher] with students, teachers, and fellow students who desire the highest good and are free from malice" (Nyāya-darśana).

In the phrase "in conversation" (sambhāṣāyām), the term "conversation" is an illustration for any discourse that has commenced; by this, it should be understood to include both *jalpa* (disputation) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil).
The phrase "the difference between the higher and the lower" (*parāvarāntaram*) means the distinction in intellectual brilliance (*pratibhā*) and other qualities between the opponent and oneself.

"Another type of debate" (*jalpāntaram*) means a specific kind of debate characterized by such qualifiers as "conventional" (*sāmayika*) or "pertaining to all matters" (*sarvārtha*). (Verse 18) "By the deposition of qualities" (*guṇavinikṣepataḥ*) means that one is superior because of possessing superior qualities relative to the measure of qualities [of the opponent]; "inferior" (*pratyavara*) means having inferior qualities; and "equal" (*sama*) means having equal qualities in relation to the proponent (*vādin*).
The phrase "not at all completely" means that here, even by way of lineage, conduct, dharma, and so forth, the *pravara* (ancestral lineage) and the like are not intended.

Regarding the expression "an assembly of fools," it is called "foolish" because it is like a fool in some particular task; however, if it were foolish in every respect, no one would speak to it nor would anyone [speak] from it—thus, the meaning is "not even by one who is base."
When one intends to mock the opponent, the respondent, it should be said that the argument is "twisted" (*āviddha*) or "crooked" (*vakra*).
The connection is that [the speaker] ascertains the assembly by means of its gestures (*ākāraiḥ*).
Regarding the word "difficult" (*kaṣṭa*), it is not stated because its meaning is not well-known;

rather, it must be said that "it is not stated by you. For the foolish assembly simply does not know the meaning of the word "difficult"; thus, the sense is that the pointlessness of the word "difficult" is easily established once one has reached the assembly.
Likewise, if he utters a cry of distress (*kaṣṭa*), he should be addressed thus: "Your vow has failed.
Having attended upon his teacher for a full year of study, he should be told: "Study again;
this much is sufficient," with the implication that it is enough to cause him to despond.
"Parikṣepikam" refers to the word "pratikṣepika" (one who rejects);

the meaning is that one should not again apply a reason of rejection to a position that has already been once defeated—that is, a rejected thesis should not be joined with a further reason for its rejection.

With the words "kathañcit" and so forth, he states the opinion of certain teachers regarding formal debate (*vigṛhya-sambhāṣā*) with a superior; with the words "natveva" and so forth, he states his own view.
"The strength of excellence" (sādguṇya-bala) refers to the presence of good qualities; likewise, "the strength of defects" (doṣa-bala) refers to the presence of faults.
One should consider this "strength of excellence and defects" to be superior, meaning that in whatever subject of debate one perceives the opponent to be superior.

In that regard, one's opponent's argument must be refuted before them in such a way that no inconsistency (*ayoga*) is revealed or made manifest in the assembly. Regarding an undesirable subject, the cessation of the debate must be conducted in such a way that no one at all realizes that one is unable to speak on that matter.
The construction is: "in that very place" means one should restrain the one who has proceeded toward the inferior position.

By the phrase "with a long recitation of the aphorisms" (*sūtrapāṭha*), it is meant that one who is deficient in learning (*śrutahīna*) is unable to produce a long recitation of the aphorisms due to lack of familiarity.
"Devoid of discernment" means one who does not understand the meaning.

"By a word of manifold meanings" means by a word that expresses multiple referents; "of a single kind" means by a word of a single type. For it is observed that one devoid of intuition (*pratibhā*) cannot determine the manifold meaning, namely, with what intention this word was employed by this speaker.
One devoid of the power of speech is unable to speak again after having interrupted a sentence half-uttered.
"Unconfident" means one who has not seen an assembly; for one who has not seen an assembly, being excessively ashamed due to a lack of self-confidence, does not accomplish anything at all.

Thus, the word "evam" (thus) connects to what is stated in the text beginning with "tadyathā śrutahīnam" (just as one deficient in learning), meaning that one should act in such a manner when the debate has commenced. This is the syntactical division.
To address what one should do when the debate has not yet commenced, he says: "Even beforehand," and so forth.
"Becoming the path" means that through repeated practice it has become like a path; the sense is that it has been cultivated.

"Extremely difficult for another" means it is as difficult as a fortress because it is unknown to the opponent; that [fortress] should first be presented by the assembly (*pariṣad*) with which one has made an agreement.
He states an alternative position with the words "or else the position," and so forth.

One should conduct the debate in such a way that the position (*pakṣa*) of the opponent, the adversary, becomes utterly and excessively averted in the assembly. This means that if the opponent's position is "there is no world beyond" or "there is no fruit of karma," then because this position is inherently hateful, whatever proof for one's own position is stated will be accepted by the assembly as well.
Thus, it is said "in the *upasaṃhitā*"—meaning in a situation joined with a stratagem (*sandhi*)—one should remain silent; such is the construction [of the meaning].

For an assembly that has been won over will carry out everything exactly as it was presented behind their backs when they were not present; therefore, enough with this excessive talk that diminishes his greatness—this is the intended meaning.
(25) He states the definition of the boundaries of debate: "In that regard, this... and so forth.

In this context, by the word *vāda* (debate), one merely refers to the statement of a thesis and its counter-thesis after having engaged in formal dispute (*vigṛhya*). However, debate as practiced through conciliatory conversation (*sandhāya-sambhāṣā*) is said to be for one who desires to know the truth.

Now, in order to provide knowledge of the path of debate, the author, demonstrating the categories such as substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and so forth which are to be understood in debate, says: "These," and so on.

The "path of debate for physicians" (bhiṣagvādamārga) refers to the method of discourse among physicians; since terms such as "debate" (vāda) and so forth will be explained by the Teacher himself later on, they are not explained here in this discussion of technical definitions.

With the words beginning "In that regard" (*tatra*), the definition of debate (*vāda*) is given; here, by the term *vāda*, formal debate (*vigṛhya-vāda*) is intended, whereas discussion for the sake of seeking truth (*tattva-bubhutsu-vāda*) is already expressed by the term "consultative conversation" (*sandhāya-sambhāṣā*).
By the phrase "preceded by the treatises" (*śāstra-pūrvaka*), it implicitly excludes debates concerning worldly matters (*artha*) and quarrelsome disputes (*kala-ha-vāda*).

In that debate, because it takes the form of contentious discussion (*vigṛhya-sambhāṣā*), the employment of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is obtained for those engaged in the desire for victory, specifically for the two who rely on a position—that is, for those who seek to establish their respective theses (*pakṣa*). Therefore, even in the case of cavil (*vitaṇḍā*), the respondent indeed possesses a position characterized by the refutation of the opponent's thesis; the distinction, however, is that he does not establish his own doctrine. The example of "of one [person]" and so forth refers to the case of disputational talk (*jalpa*).
By the phrase "merely stating the faults in the opponent's position," it is shown that the sophist (*vaitaṇḍika*) does not state a proof for his own position;
this was previously stated in the *Dīrghañjīvitīya*.
It establishes the proven matter for the sake of another; thus it is "establishment" (*sthāpanā*).
And that establishes the probandum for the other by means of the four [members], beginning with the reason (*hetu*).

A thesis (*pratijñā*) also constitutes a proof (*sthāpanā*) for another, since inference consists of exactly five members; however, because that [thesis] is already obtained here as the very thing to be established, it is not cited here as a "proof.

The first term, *pratiṣṭhāpanāpada*, indicates that "counter-proof" (*pratiṣṭhāpanā*) has now reached its proper occasion; the second term, "that which is called counter-proof," is for the purpose of demonstrating the definition that is about to be stated with the words "of that very [proof]," and so forth.

In this way, the purpose of the repetition in "establishment" (*sthāpanā*) and so forth must also be stated. He explains the meaning of the word *prati* contained in the term *pratiṣṭhāpanā*: "the establishment of a contrary meaning. The meaning is that this prefix *prati* signifies a contrary sense.
And this *pratiṣṭhāpanā* is the refutation of the reason known as *prakaraṇasama* (the "neutralized" reason) within the science of logic (*ānvīkṣikī*).

Although a "reason" (*hetu*) is the statement of a mark (*liṅga*) that is inseparably connected [with the probandum], nevertheless, it should be understood that here the term "reason" refers specifically to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as perception, which apprehend that mark, because they serve as the basis for the aforementioned reason. Otherwise, the mention of perception and so forth would be redundant;
for [the phrase] "the cause of apprehension" refers to the cause of apprehending the pervading probandum (*sādhya*).
"That is the reality" means that it is its characteristic mark (liṅga).

By the phrase "the equality of the intellects of the ignorant and the learned," it is meant that whatever matter is established without dispute for both common people and scholars serves as an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), but not something established by scholars alone.
The point is that even a *dṛṣṭānta* (example) well-known in the world does not attain the status of an example until it has been established for the person being instructed.

Now, he says that something becomes an example because it is accepted as having a similarity to the *sādhya* (the thing to be proven) based merely on a commonality of understanding: "that which describes what is to be described"; the meaning is, that which proves the *sādhya*.
Furthermore, an example is that in which the relationship between the *sādhya* and the *sādhana* (the means of proof) is well-established; the point is that it proves the *sādhya*.

Fire and the others have been cited as examples because they are well-known in the world; therefore, he shows that for these too, there is an illustration of the probandum and the probans—just as with the sun and so forth—in certain compounds, such as "this is like this.
(34) [This refers to] the subsequent passage beginning with "uttaram," etc.

By the word "uttara" (rejoinder) here, a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*)—that is, a semblance of a rejoinder—is intended; for the author will demonstrate in the section on rejoinders that it is merely an opposition based on a similarity that does not prove the point, and as it is stated in the *Nyāya*: "A futile rejoinder (*jāti*) is an opposition by means of similarity or dissimilarity" (*Nyāyadarśana*).
(1/2/18). This is for the purpose of illustrating examples of similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*);

therefore, the futile rejoinders (*jātyuttara*) mentioned in the *Nyāya*—such as the "equalization by addition" (*utkarṣasama*), the "equalization by subtraction" (*apakarṣasama*), and so forth—which were not explicitly stated here, should also be understood from this very context.
"Having the same nature as the cause" (*hetusadharmāṇaḥ*) means being similar to the cause.
Cold is [the effect]; the tactile sensations associated with frost, coldness, and cold winds possess the same nature as the causes of cold—this is how the connection is to be understood.

Therefore, those tactile sensations of cold which belong to the causes such as frost also exist in that which is "cold-like" (*śītaka*); thus there is a commonality between the cause and its transformation.
"Another might say" means the opponent would say;

"in burning, heating, scorching, and boiling"—the word "without alteration" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the phrase]; "dissimilarity of the reason" (hetuvaidharmya) means dissimilarity with the reason.

The meaning of the sentence is as follows: "contacts such as snow" refers to contacts produced by snow and the like; they are "dissimilar" to heat when there is a bodily transformation such as a burning sensation.
Thus, when a counter-argument is made that establishes parity with the reason (*hetu*) through the reversal of the stated dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), then a "reversal" (*viparyaya*) occurs.
In this way, both examples constitute a complete counter-argument along with their respective reversals. This is the sense.

The explanation of the statement "having examined it in many ways and established it through reasons, it is settled" is "conclusion" (*nirṇaya*). It is called a conclusion because it is concluded (*nirṇīyate*).

Furthermore, this definition of a tenet (*siddhānta*) does not apply to the tenet by mere admission (*abhyupagama-siddhānta*); therefore, in that case, the status of being a tenet should be understood as existing only by way of mental determination (*buddhi-vyavasthitatvena*).
He analyzes the *siddhānta* with the words "sa" and so forth.

Regarding the *pratitantrasiddhānta*, although the doctrines that there are six tastes and that there are eight tastes are mutually contradictory, they should be understood as *siddhāntas* by virtue of the power of establishing them through their own respective reasoning.
In the phrase "in which" and so forth, the word "adhikaraṇe" (locative case) is used when the expressed subject (*abhidheya*) is primary.
"Even others" means even those not explicitly mentioned;
"consequential" (*ānubandhika*) means that which follows along, i.e., that which persists even in another birth.

"Liberated" (*mukta*) refers to one for whom liberation is imminent. One who is liberated in every respect does not perform action because of being bodiless; or rather, he does not specifically perform consequential action.
The phrase beginning with "siddhāḥ" (the perfected ones), and so forth.

If there were no fruit of action here in this world, then even one desiring liberation would still perform action; for it is because he is agitated by [the prospect of] results that he does not perform such action. Furthermore, if liberation did not exist, then the statement "one is liberated" would be impossible. Likewise, if the person (puruṣa) did not exist, then whose bondage would there be, or whose liberation? And if there were no other birth, then the fact that action follows one into another birth would be untenable. By stating "not liberated" and so forth, the very force of the context establishes and accepts as the final doctrine (siddhānta) the existence of the fruits of action and the rest.
The explanation of the term "unestablished" (*asiddha*) is "unexamined," and so forth. Here,
by the word "sound" (*śabda*), a phoneme (*varṇa*) that reveals meaning through the power of convention (*saṅketa*) is intended.

The term *āptopadeśa* (authoritative instruction) is twofold: that composed by the supreme authority such as Brahmā and others, and likewise that composed by worldly authorities (*laukikāpta*). That which is composed by the supreme authority is subsumed under the term *aitihya* (tradition); however, that composed by worldly authorities should be understood as a specific form of verbal testimony (*śabda*) established through the method of truth, namely the "enumeration of phonemes" (*varṇasamāmnāya*), which means a collection of phonemes.

Although there is no simultaneous coexistence of phonemes here for them to be collected, nevertheless, their "collection" should be understood as being formed by being represented within a single recollection, or else by the ascent of the experience of the final phoneme accompanied by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by each preceding experience.
"Perceived object" (*dṛṣṭārtha*) refers to an object capable of being apprehended by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
"By three causes" refers to [the causes] beginning with intellectual error (*prajñāparādha*).
"Six therapeutic measures" refers to jumping (*laṅghana*) and so forth, as described in the chapter on *laṅghana* and *bṛṃhaṇa*.
The fact that the meaning of these statements is seen right here constitutes their "perceptible purpose" (*dṛṣṭārthatva*);
the opposite of truth is to be understood as [the claim] that "the instructions of Āyurveda do not exist," and so forth.
"By oneself" means by the mind; thus, mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) such as pleasure and so forth is included.
By the phrase "by the senses," external perception is grasped.

"Is perceived by oneself" means it is directly perceived. By this, he demonstrates that even when the operation of the senses is present, inferential cognition is not perception because it lacks directness (*asākṣātkāritva*).
"Reasoning (tarka) depends upon logic" is the definition of inference (*anumāna*), which has been explained specifically in the chapter on the knowledge of various diseases.
He provides an example of inference with the words beginning, "By the power of digestion [one infers] fire," and so forth.
He states that the extraordinary instruction of a trustworthy person is expressed by the term *aitihya* (tradition), saying: "The Vedas and so forth.

In the passage beginning with "by means of another" (*yadanyena*), "by another" refers to that which is well-known (*prasiddha*), while "of another" refers to that which is not well-known (*aprasiddha*).

This is said with reference to similarity (*sādṛśya*), meaning that similarity—being the object to be established—is the basis for the relationship between the name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*). However, when the *upamāna* is to be explained according to the system of Bhaṭṭa, it should be construed as "with reference to similarity as the object to be established"; for them, the purpose of *upamāna* is the cognition of similarity.

In the Nyāya system, the fruit of analogy is the cognition of the relationship between the name and the named, and this arises from the first explanation; for it is stated therein: "Analogy is the means of establishing that which is to be established through similarity with something well-known" (Nyāyadarśana 1.1.6).

Regarding the phrase "by means of a *daṇḍa*, [one understands] the *daṇḍaka*": through a well-known *daṇḍa*, one hears from an authoritative source the similarity (*sādharmya*) of the unknown *daṇḍaka*; then, upon seeing a modification, one understands—just as in the case of a potter’s staff—that "this is the modification designated as *daṇḍaka*. Alternatively, according to the view of Bhaṭṭa, one understands the well-known similarity residing in the *daṇḍa* as being connected with the modification called the unknown *daṇḍaka*. This should be understood in the same way for other examples as well.

"By an archer" means by one who releases arrows; just as an archer does not miss when the target is not too distant, so too [should one act] with a physician who bestows health and accomplishes the cure of the patient through the qualities of a physician.

By the phrase "in matters that are doubtful due to the characteristics of doubt," he shows the subject matter suitable for doubt; and by this, [he refers to] the Nyāya-sūtra statement: "Because of the occurrence of common or multiple properties" (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.19).
From such statements as (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.23), he shows the object of doubt;

the definition of doubt should be understood as "non-determination" (*aniścaya*). Non-determination is a cognition that reflects upon contradictory attributes belonging to alternative sides, such as: "Is it a post or a person?"
With the words "For it is seen," etc., he states the causal complex for the arising of doubt:

when it is observed that those endowed with the characteristics of longevity do not act [prematurely] yet perish quickly, while others who do act [prematurely] live for a long time, the cognition arises that untimely death exists;
and in the opposite case, the cognition arises that untimely death does not exist.
"For which purpose" means for whatever reason; "should overcome" means he should kill.
*Savyabhicāra* means 'inconclusive' (*anaikāntika*);
or alternatively, it means 'not so,' i.e., it would not be [the case]."

Furthermore, in this context, an inconclusive medicine (*anaikāntika-auṣadha*)—whether by virtue of being appropriate or inappropriate—generates doubt alone; therefore, one should not suspect that [the medicine] is identical to doubt, as will be examined right here in this section on investigation regarding the inconclusive at a later time, or as stated in the section on elixirs (*rasāyana*): "That medicine is of two kinds," and so forth. (Ci. A. 1, Pāda 1).
"Attainment of meaning" (arthaprāpti) means presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).

Because of the expression "stated here," it is specifically presumptive testimony based on what is heard (śrutārthāpatti) that is intended; however, presumptive testimony based on what is seen (dṛṣṭārthāpatti) should also be understood by way of this same general category.

The meaning is this: this *arthāpatti* (presumption) is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it can be accounted for otherwise; therefore, it is not listed among the categories of valid means of knowledge. However, that which is free from defects is indeed included within inference (*anumāna*). The intention is as follows: regarding one who would not be cured even by fasting, the statement "this is not curable by nourishment" would not be a case of an "inefficacious qualification" (*asamartha-viśeṣaṇa*), and thus there is no *arthāpatti*. For if [the patient] were incurable in both ways, one would have to say simply "incurable.
This should be understood to apply to other examples as well.

*Sambhava* means that from which something arises or exists; for the cause (*kāraṇa*) has been described as the unmanifest (*avyakta*) source of its own effect. Since, according to the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), the effect is already inherent in the cause, the embryo exists within the six elements (*ṣaddhātu*), and likewise, disease exists even when it is not yet manifest. It is stated according to the Sāṅkhya view that this [disease] becomes manifest at a later time.
Furthermore, as for the example of possibility mentioned elsewhere— such as "A *droṇa* is possible in a *khārī*" and so forth— this present example is also similar to that.
[The author] states another point to be questioned, beginning with "In general," etc.
50. Regarding "that which is not to be questioned" (*ananuyojya*): this should be understood as being the opposite of the two examples of things to be questioned (*anuyojya*) as previously stated.
He states the inquiry: "Now" (atha) and so forth.

By the word "question" (praśna), the complete question as stated in the aforementioned treatise is understood; for example, right here [in the text], from "If there, a physician should ask another physician," and so on, everything that has been said should be known as the complete [question]. And in this very context, even a single part of the question should be understood.
52–53 He illustrates the defects of speech with the words "atha" and so forth.

By the phrase "in this matter," he shows that even those things subsumed under the categories of *chala* (quibble), *hetvābhāsa* (fallacious reason), and so on, are to be regarded as defects of speech. For *chala* and the others are indeed defects of speech; however, they are not mentioned here because they have been treated separately elsewhere. Likewise, the *asiddha* (unestablished) and other fallacies mentioned in other treatises are indicated by these terms as defects of speech.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Or else" (*yadvā*), when the reasons for the eternity of the *puruṣa* have been stated—namely, "because it is beginningless," "because it is uncreated," and "because it is changeless"—if one promises to state all those reasons but then mentions only one, it should be understood that this constitutes the fault of deficiency (*nyūna*), because the stated matter is deficient in its content. When a reason is to be stated, it is proper to state only one, since even a single reason is capable of proving the probandum (*sādhya*). Therefore, it should be understood that in such a case, stating many reasons is indeed a fault, as it constitutes redundancy (*adhika*).
The term "under discussion" (*prakṛta*) refers to that which has been proposed as the subject to be proven.

By stating that the *Nītiśāstra* of Bṛhaspati and Uśanas is "unconnected in its meaning," he shows that even if the treatises of Bṛhaspati and others should happen to be mentioned incidentally in the course of discussing the pursuit of wealth, they are not excessive when spoken of in a brief manner, as they serve to assist Āyurveda.
"Because of the fault of redundancy" means because of a faulty redundancy;

and as to how it is faulty, it has already been stated that it is "like the five groups," meaning like the collection of groups beginning with *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṅa*, and so on; for in that case, the intended meaning does not manifest.

The term *arthavat* means that while [the words] are well-known as individual word-forms possessing meaning, they do not convey a meaning when not joined with one another because they lack the form of a sentence; for words such as "wheel" (*cakra*) and so forth do not express the meaning of a sentence without an action—this is the sense.
An example contradictory [to the intended point] is one that contradicts the illustration, such as: "Just as cold water is a heater, so too is fever."

An example of that which contradicts established doctrine (*siddhāntaviruddha*) is as follows: a physician says, "The medicine does not cure the disease. In the *Āyurveda*, however, the established doctrine is precisely that medicine consists of four components (*catuṣpāda*); thus, the designation "four-component" should be understood as being established by convention (*samayakṛta*). Similarly, among ritualists, the designation "to be immolated" (*ālabhya*) is established by convention. In such cases, if one asserts something contrary to one's own convention, it becomes "contrary to convention" (*samayaviruddha*).
"Not to be questioned" means not fit for questioning.
"Chala" and so forth mean "fraudulent"; that which is engaged in deception appears as if it possessed meaning, and thus it is called an "appearance of meaning" (arthābhāsa).
He explains this very point with the words "meaningless," and so forth;
the meaning is that it is a mere verbal entity because it is devoid of correct meaning.
For *chala* (quibble) is indeed postulated for the purpose of undermining the opponent's statement by imagining a different meaning than the intended one.
As it is stated in the *Nyāya* [Sūtra]: "Quibble (*chala*) is the subversion of a statement by means of a fabricated alternative interpretation of its meaning" (Nyāya Sūtra 1.2.10).
In this context, the *upacāra-chala* (quibble regarding metaphorical usage) mentioned in the Nyāya system is possible only within the scope of the *vāk-chala* (quibble regarding speech).

For when an object is expressed by a general term, the *vāk-chala* consists in imagining a different meaning than that intended by the speaker. Thus, even in the case of the statement "The platforms cry out" (*mañcāḥ krośanti*), the word "platform" (*mañca*) is primary when it refers to the platform itself; however, when the word "platform" is used metaphorically for the persons situated on the platform, the objection—"How can insentient platforms cry out?"—falls squarely within the *vāk-chala*. This is the intended meaning. The passage beginning with "This is not a new system," etc., is clear.

The definition of *sāmānyacchala* (quibble regarding the general) has not been stated here; in that regard, the definition as stated in the *Nyāya* [sūtras] should be understood: "Quibble regarding the general (*sāmānyacchala*) is the imagining of an impossible meaning through the application of an overly general sense to a possible meaning" (*Nyāyadarśana* 1.2.13).

"Good is for the sake of the pacification of the good"—taking it thus that "the pacification of the good is brought about by the good," the quibbler (chalavādī) formulates the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). Because he objects based on the generality of existence (*sattvasāmānya*) which was not intended [by the original speaker], this constitutes a "quibble regarding the general" (*sāmānyacchala*).
"Non-reason" (*ahetu*) means that it is a non-probative reason (*asādhakahetu*). 56.

By the etymological derivation that "that which is treated as the subject to be established" (*prakriyate*) is "the topic" (*prakaraṇa*), the term *prakaraṇa* refers to the thesis (*pakṣa*). That which is similar to this is "similar to the topic" (*prakaraṇasama*).
Regarding the proposition that "the self is distinct from the body and is eternal," both the distinctness from the body and the eternality of the self are the properties to be established (*sādhya*).
Therefore, the phrase "by that which possesses contrary properties" (*vidharmiṇā*) means by that which is eternal and possesses properties contrary to the non-eternal body.

By the phrase "that very same position," he demonstrates that the distinctness of the self from the body is not established. For if there were permanence [of the self], its distinctness from the body would also be established; however, in the Cārvāka position, the body itself is both conscious and impermanent, so for them, both [distinctness and permanence] are yet to be proven. And that which is yet to be proven cannot serve as a means of proof, because it is unestablished—this is the intended meaning.

The statement "this person speaks a portion of Āyurveda" is a cause for doubt, because it indicates that one might be either a physician or a non-physician. The point is that the mention of a single portion occurs even without having studied the entire treatise, simply by hearing it from somewhere.
Thus, it does not qualify the cause for the removal of doubt; the meaning is that it does not demonstrate a specific cause for the resolution of doubt.
And this is "not a reason": the aforementioned reason is not a valid reason for the elimination of doubt.
The "equal to the subject" (*varṇyasama*) fallacy occurs when the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is equal [to the thesis] by virtue of being unestablished (*asiddha*). [For instance:

"Sound is the subject (*varṇya*); because it possesses intangibility (*asparśatva*), sound is also to be proven (*sādhya*) as impermanent. And that which is yet to be proven cannot serve as an example, because there is no distinction between the two as subjects—meaning that in both cases, namely the subject and the example, there is no distinction insofar as the subject (the thing to be proven) remains something that must itself be proven.
That which ought to be stated first is stated later— just as when the conclusion (*nigamana*) is stated first and the proposition (*pratijñā*) is stated afterwards—
one is known to have incurred a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), and thus is subject to defeat.

By the statement "the declaration of a fault in the reason," both the *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed) and the *asiddha* (unestablished), though not explicitly mentioned here, are to be understood as included; however, for the sake of illustration,
those that appear like reasons have been called "pseudo-reasons" (*hetvābhāsa*) because they resemble reasons.
By the passage beginning with "Just as [the self] is eternal," he removes the defect in the reason stated as being "equal to the point at issue" (*prakaraṇasama*);
"eternal" means always.

The signs of life, such as reconnection [of consciousness] and memory, are no longer perceived due to its departure; by this, since consciousness and so forth are absent in a dead body, another cause for them is inferred. Because the dead body does not perceive due to the departure of that [cause], the distinctness of the self (*ātman*) from the body is established. Furthermore, because it is distinct from the body, its eternity—established previously as being of a nature different from the body—is also proven; thus he says: "And it is eternal" (vv. 60–61).

The acceptance of what is desired and undesired is as follows: when one is told, "You are a thief," instead of avoiding one's own fault, one says, "You too are a thief. This statement indeed admits one's own undesired state of being a thief while simultaneously admitting the other's desired state of being a thief; such a statement is called "admission of the opponent's position" (*matānujñā*) in the context of logic.
A *nigrahasthāna* is a ground for defeat, meaning a cause of defeat; it is called a "ground of defeat" (*nigrahasthāna*) because it occurs in an assembly possessed of discernment.

By the phrase "in an assembly possessed of discernment," it is meant that if the assembly understands the meaning of what has been stated three times, yet the opponent does not understand it, then that constitutes a ground of defeat for the latter.

He states that others as well, which have already been mentioned, are points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), beginning with "the questioning of what is not to be questioned" and so forth. Furthermore, those [defeats] mentioned in the *Nyāya* [system], such as "lack of ingenuity" (*apratibhā*) and the rest, should be included here by the intelligent. However, because they do not provide a similar kind of assistance in the science of life (*āyurveda*), this detailed exposition has not been elaborated upon even in this context. For those who know the *Nyāya*, this is easy to understand even if not explicitly stated; yet for those who do not know it, even a slight elaboration is insufficient for their understanding—so enough with further elaboration.

Now, those who study Āyurveda must conduct their discourse (*vāda*) exactly as described in this Āyurveda; for it is only such a discourse that is intended here, as it generates correct knowledge. Thus he says: "Discourse," etc. Furthermore, he asks: for what purpose do these subjects of discourse exist? To which he replies: "For here," etc.
In all these cases, the word "exist" (*santi*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis;
or one should say they are "non-pervasive"—this is how it connects with what precedes.
Those for whom debate (*vāda*) is like a body or a conflict (*vigraha*) are called *vādavigrahas*; these are varieties of *jalpa* (contentious discourse) and varieties of *vitaṇḍā* (cavil).
He explains how discourse becomes a cause for medical treatment by virtue of being produced by one of praiseworthy intelligence, with the words beginning "all," etc.:
the meaning is that it is not only the accomplishment of medical treatment that unimpaired intelligence brings about, but rather the accomplishment of all undertakings.

Now, in the context of describing the rules for discourse on the sciences that serve as causes for increasing the intellect, he promises to describe those sections which also state the causes and other factors useful for Āyurveda, as they too increase the intellect—beginning with the words "these" (imāni), etc.
"Preceded by knowledge" (jñānapūrvakam) means preceded by the knowledge of objects suitable for the tasks to be performed;
he states those [factors] by saying "for having known," etc., meaning those things by knowing which, when a task is performed, it becomes successful.
"Manifesting" means occurring directly;
"having a desired result and consequence" refers to that which has a desired immediate fruit (*tādātvika-phala*) and a subsequent future fruit (*āyaty-aphala*).
He explains the [factors] beginning with the cause (*kāraṇa*) by means of the passage starting with "therein" (*tatra*), etc.
The word "which" (*yat*) is neuter because it refers back to the cause;
"he acts" (*karoti*) means he acts independently.
Therefore, by this term "cause" (*kāraṇa*), that which is an independent cause characterized as an agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed.
He explains the instrument (*karaṇa*) with the words beginning "the instrument, moreover," and so forth.
"For the sake of an accessory" means for the agent who is striving— that is,

making an effort— with a view toward the accomplishment of the task, [the accessory] being present as a cooperative factor and functioning toward the production of that effect which is to be accomplished.

By this [it is meant]: that which impels other causes toward the effect is here called the "agent" (*kartṛ*) by the term "cause" (*kāraṇa*); whereas that which is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) in an operation dependent upon the agent is the "instrument" (*karaṇa*).

And agency belongs primarily to that alone which, being endowed with intellect and effort, impels the other causes; as for the designation of agency applied to the insentient, it is figurative (*bhākta*), intended to express its independence.

The "source of the effect" (*kāryayoni*) refers to the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), which is the source of the effect. This means that whatever source, being of the nature of a cause, undergoes modification—that is, attains another form and thereby becomes the effect—is the source of the effect. In this regard, clay is the source of the effect for a jar; for it is the clay itself that, by attaining a different state, becomes the jar.
71 "With a view toward actualization" means having stabilized the thought that [this] is what must be done;

In this context, by the term "result of the action" (*kāryaphala*), one should understand the immediate result of the action, such as a potter obtaining the price for making a jar. However, the "consequence" (*anubandha*) is the future result, such as the expenditure of that jar's price on the maintenance of one's family and so forth. It is called *anubandha* because it follows after and attends upon the agent at a later time.
"Whether auspicious or inauspicious" means that for an auspicious effect, [the cause] is auspicious, and for an inauspicious one, it is inauspicious.
"Place is the locus" means the place, which serves as the substratum, is either conducive or non-conducive to the effect.
"Transformation" (pariṇāma) refers to time (kāla) in the form of the seasons, years, and so forth, which undergoes transformation;
by this, he excludes eternally moving time, because that [eternal time], being common to all things, is not something to be depended upon for the production of an effect.
Furthermore, words such as "activity" (pravṛtti) and "effort" (ceṣṭā) are synonyms; indeed, [the latter] is the definition [of the former].
He states the means (*upāya*): "The means, moreover," and so forth.
"Excellence" (*sauṣṭhava*) means the state of being excellent (*suṣṭhutva*), which is the suitability of the agent and other factors for the effect.

"Appropriate application" (*abhividhāna*) means the correct positioning of the cause and other factors in accordance with the effect; for example, the heating and application of a cotton swab for a medicinal substance that acts as a head-purgative, or, for instance, the positioning of the threads and other causes of cloth in a manner suitable for the production of cloth.

And one should understand that this excellence, which consists of the means (*upāya*), as well as the inclusion (*abhividhāna*), pertains to causes and so forth that are devoid of the triad beginning with the effect (*kārya*). Thus he says "the effect," etc.
He states another essential characteristic of the means: "Because it brings about the effects, it is called the means (*upāya*).
The meaning is that in the absence of the means, causes and so forth do not produce the effect.

Now, he explains how the status of being a means (*upāyatva*) is not possible in relation to the effect (*kārya*) and so forth: "Once [the effect] is done," and so on. For a means is that which brings about an effect; once the effect has been produced, there is no further purpose for a means, since what has already been done is not done again. Therefore, we do not accept that the status of being a means, even when residing in the effect, functions toward the production of the effect once more. If it is argued that the nature of being a means will exist while the effect is as yet unproduced, he says: "And it does not exist at that time"; the word "effect" is to be supplied. At that time—prior to the production of the effect—the effect itself does not exist; therefore, even at that time, the status of being a means does not belong to the effect.

And when the status of being a means (upāyatva) exists only in what is to be accomplished (*kārya*)—since it does not exist at a time subsequent to the means—then the two factors connected to the fruit (*phala*), namely the arising [of the result] and its subsequent maintenance, also have no purpose as a means. Thus he says: "And after that which has been performed," etc.
(verse 78). He concludes with: "This," etc.

79. Having just stated these ten causes, [the author] now begins the section beginning with "tatra cet" in order to demonstrate them through the analogy of a physician and so forth employed by a medical practitioner; therein, the phrase "abhiṣag vā" means "some physician."
"How many kinds are there of that which is to be examined? means: of how many types is that which is to be scrutinized? [The answer is:
"The conjunction characterized by engagement and withdrawal. This refers to the meeting of two characteristics—one conducive to engagement and one conducive to withdrawal—in a single locus.
"What is the final conclusion? means: what arises from the *niṣṭhā*, which is certainty (*niścaya*); that which results from it is the *naiṣṭhika*. The meaning is: what is to be done with certainty?
80. "If he should wish to delude" means if, by engaging in contentious conversation, he should wish to delude;
"in such a manner" means in many ways.
A difference consisting of a positive form is a "positive difference" (*vidhibheda*). Its "different nature" (*prakṛtyantara*) means another cause;

"the limit of difference" (*bhedāgra*) means the measure of difference (*bhedaparimāṇa*). And here, the measure of difference is to be understood precisely as the determination of the number of differences, [as indicated by the word] "being declared" (*ākhyāyamāna*), which is the grammatical split (*cheda*).

In response to the expectation of why one asks this again, he says: "Not now," and so forth. The meaning of the sentence is: "If I were to explain the matter you desire to hear in a manner other than [what you intend], I would not fulfill your wish; therefore, you yourself should first ask by specifying [the point].

However, when the reading is *na vedānīṃ pūrayeyam*, then it should be construed as: "If I were to explain it later (*vedānīm*), I would not fulfill your wish. Alternatively, *na* is to be connected with what precedes it.

By which specific methodological distinction (*vidhibheda-prakṛtyantara*) do you intend it to be expressed, or by which specific methodological distinction do you not intend it to be expressed? This is how it should be applied.
As for the phrase "now" (*idānīm*) and so forth, however, this statement is made as before in response to a doubt;
the sense is that the questioner becomes confused when asked about these specific particulars.
The construction is as follows: "If I were to explain otherwise than what you desire to hear regarding the matter to be examined [81],
then, having reflected upon that"— meaning, having reflected upon those words— whatever is appropriate [should be done].

As it was stated regarding the rule for responding, one should speak the reply after considering what was said in this very chapter concerning the rules for contentious discourse (*vigṛhya-saṃbhāṣā*).
He states another alternative: "If, however, he should speak correctly," and so forth; that is, if he should speak during a conciliatory discourse (*sandhāya-saṃbhāṣā*).

"It is obtained" (*prāptam*) means it is appropriate (*ucitam*); for at the appropriate time for speaking, one must indeed speak. "It is truly obtained" (*āptameva*) means it is exactly according to the facts (*yathārtham*).
He states that very same answer, which is according to the facts, regarding the previous questions in their proper sequence, beginning with "Of two kinds," and so forth.
"Of those possessing knowledge" refers to those who possess knowledge produced by the scriptures in the form of authoritative instruction (*āptopadeśa*).
In another interpretation, he states the threefold nature of examination: "This indeed," and so forth;
and this twofold or threefold nature of examination has been explained specifically in the chapter on the "Knowledge of the Specifics of the Three Types of Diseases."

83. "The physician and others are involved in the process," thus it is said. Having cited the physician and others as examples of those employed [in the treatment], [the text states] "disequilibrium of the elements" (*dhātuvaiṣamya*); that is, the elements have reached a state of imbalance. For it is the elements themselves, by abandoning their diseased state and attaining a state of equilibrium, that—acting as the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of what is called health—attain the status of being the source of the effect.
"Attainment of happiness" refers to the attainment of health;
for it is said: "Health is that which is designated as happiness" (Sūtra-sthāna 9).

Furthermore, although longevity—which is of the nature of a consequential result—resides here in the patient and not in the physician, nevertheless, because it is desired by the physician, it should be understood as residing in the physician alone.
Therefore, what was stated—that one intends toward the agent as characterized by the consequence—is appropriate;

for here the agent is the physician, and thus even the lifespan residing in the patient is to be understood as the fruit belonging to the physician alone, since it is dependent upon him. "Pratikarma" refers to medical treatment.

Regarding the passage beginning with "ihāpyasya" (here too, of this), he shows that here as well, the excellence and the thorough application of the causes and so forth— distinct from the connection to the fruit of the effect— are the means (*upāya*) according to the logic already stated. 84
What is the specific characteristic to be examined, and how is it to be examined? To provide answers to these two questions, he says "of that," and so forth.

The meaning of "whatever specific characteristic" is that whatever specific quality the causes and other factors possess—such as having observed efficacy (*dṛṣṭakarmatva*)—is their distinction from similar things like fellow physicians and patients, as well as from dissimilar things like medicines and the like.
As for the example of "how it is to be examined," it should be understood as that which will be stated in the text beginning with "Am I [capable] for him? and so on.
"He heals" means he treats "in every way," that is, by means of [determining] what is beneficial or harmful, pleasure or pain, and so forth; thus,
this physician as the cause is not to be examined by another, but rather it shows that one should examine oneself by oneself.

Now, as to how one should examine oneself, he says "among those possessing qualities" (*guṇiṣu*), and so forth; the meaning is that one should examine oneself by way of connection with qualities (*guṇa*).
In the phrase "by way of qualities" (*guṇataḥ*), the ablative case is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*).
*Kaccit* is used to express a wish;
*pratipatti* is the prompt performance of what must be done when a calamity has arisen.

By the phrase "especially [distinguished] from the means and so forth," he demonstrates that whatever serves as an instrument (*upakaraṇa*) for the agent, other than the source of the effect, the activity, the place, the time, and the means, is the *karaṇa* (instrument).

For in common worldly usage, the source of the effect is spoken of separately from the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama karaṇa*) because it functions as the object to be modified (*vikārya-karman*). Furthermore, activity and means do not receive the designation of *karaṇa*, as they possess the nature of the agent, the instrument, and so on. Place and time, moreover, are not the most effective instruments. Therefore, by the aforementioned distinction, that which serves as the agent's instrument—other than the means and so forth—is the *karaṇa*.

In this context, regarding the two-fold division of reliance on divine power (*daivavyapāśraya*) and reliance on rational means (*yuktivyapāśraya*), it should be understood that the subjugation of the mind (*sattvāvajaya*) is also included within the category of medicine (*bheṣaja*). For the subjugation of the mind, acting through the visible door, is included within reliance on rational means, whereas acting through the invisible door falls under reliance on divine power. Therefore, it is stated in the exposition of reliance on rational means: "And activities whose fruits are visible"—by the word "activities" (*ceṣṭā*), mental activities characterized by the subjugation of the mind are also intended.
He again states the twofold division of medicinal substances by another method: "Due to the difference in parts," and so forth.
"Part" (*aṅga*) means the body, that is to say, its own form (*svarūpa*); thus, the meaning is "due to the difference in its own form.
[The two types are] those that have become substance (*dravyabhūta*), i.e., having the nature of substance (*dravyarūpa*), and likewise those that do not have the nature of substance (*adravyarūpa*).
"Overwhelmed by skillful means" (upāyābhipluta) means pervaded by skillful means; that is to say, grasped by the apprehension of skillful means.

He thinks as follows: fear and the like are formless states (*amūrta-bhāva*) and do not directly become the causes of health. Rather, they act upon the bodily humors (*vāta*, etc. situated within the body, producing them in a state of equilibrium (*samatva*), whereby health arises. For formless things cannot be the inherent causes (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) for the production of the material constituents (*mūrta-dhātu*) of the body. Medicine (*bheṣaja*), however, being a substance (*dravya*), is indeed the inherent cause in the production of a balanced body; therefore, it is correct that a substance is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) toward health.
