Since formless things such as fear do not possess this status of being the most effective means like medicine does, it is logical that their role as a means occurs only when the equilibrium of the humors is produced by a substance.

Thus, by means of subtle intellect, fear and the like function as *upāya* (means), whereas by means of gross intellect, they also function as *bhaiṣajya* (medicine). On this basis, the Master’s intended usage of the term "medicine" (*bhaiṣajya*) with respect to fear and the like is inferred from the inclusion of fear and so forth—which are not physical substances—among the two types of medicine.

He states: "And the aforementioned means for success," indicating that it is not only non-substantial medicine that is pervaded by *upāya*, but other factors such as attendants and the like are also included within the grasp of the term *upāya*.

The aforementioned means of success, such as attendants and so forth, though not explicitly mentioned here among the ten types of things to be examined, are nonetheless included within these very means; that is to say, they are "overflowing with" (abhipluta) the means.
Alternatively, "overflowing with the means" (upāyābhiplutam) means "mixed with the means.

In that context, regarding the immaterial medicine for fear and other [mental afflictions], the aforementioned means consist of excellence in the causes and so forth, and the proper administration [of treatment]; thus, they are understood to be included within the category of non-substantial (adravyabhūta) medicine.
By this, he demonstrates that the term "medicine" (bheṣaja) is applied even to things that are not substances, such as fear and so forth, as well as to those denoted by the word "means" (upāya).

However, those who read the text as "upāyāntābhiplutam" claim that space and time themselves are the non-substantial medicine; they further assert that by the word "substance" (dravya), a substance fit for application—such as decoctions or medicinal pastes—is meant. But this [interpretation] is not very convincing.

The meaning is that it was endowed with this aforementioned means—expressed by the words “of such a nature” and so forth—and likewise with the aforementioned probandum—expressed by the words “of a person of such a kind” and so forth.
(87) Its characteristic is the specific form of the individual [patient] resulting from the imbalance of the bodily constituents (dhātu). This is the meaning.
"Of the nature of transformation" means of the defect which is the cause of transformation;
"in all aspects" means by all auspicious marks.
89. "The attainment of happiness" means the attainment of the happiness that is one's own quality. 90.
"Conjunction with the vital breaths" (prāṇaiḥ saha saṃyogaḥ) means union with the wind characterized as the vital breath;
thus, because the word "prāṇa" has a different meaning from "life-span" (āyus), there is an identity between the indicated object (lakṣya) and the characteristic (lakṣaṇa).

He states the location as it follows in sequence: "The location," and so forth. Here, by the word *ātura* (the afflicted), both those who are currently manifesting illness and those who are healthy (*svastha*)—who must be maintained in a healthy state—are included; for even the healthy person is examined for the purpose of applying the regimen for maintaining health.

The word *pari* has the sense of "specificity" (*viśeṣa*). Therefore, the thorough knowledge of the patient (*āturaparijñāna*) is the knowledge of the patient through all the specific characteristics pertaining to their location;

likewise, in the case of the thorough knowledge of the medicine (*bhaiṣajyaparijñāna*), thorough knowledge should be understood as the knowledge of the specific characteristics pertaining to its location.
The term *saṃvṛddha* means "increased" (*vardhita*).

"Such suitability" (*sātmyam*) means suitability to one's own environment (*okasātmyam*). By the phrase "this is beneficial," he speaks of a suitability characterized by qualities opposite to those of the location;
this is the analysis of the term "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*). The construction is: "by the inclusion of the word 'mostly,' one should not examine [the matter] with absolute certainty."
By the word "mostly" (*prāyas*), he shows that the inference of food and so forth from the location is not certain, but rather occurs mostly (*prāyobhāvī*).
Regarding the phrase "in the [subsequent] kalpas":

although the examination of the ground should have been stated in the very first kalpa, the plural number is used because its meaning is extended (*atideśa*) to the intermediate kalpas as well; this is for the purpose of showing that even the substances to be mentioned in the subsequent kalpas are to be taken from the same location as previously described.
Having described the location in the form of the earth, he states the location in the form of the patient— beginning with "The patient, indeed," and so forth.
"The site of action" means the substratum for the restoration of equilibrium among the bodily constituents (dhātus) that must be performed.

The measure of strength and the measure of the doshas is "baladoṣapramāṇam. This [measure] will be explained later in the text beginning with "Therefore, one should examine the patient" (*tasmād āturaṃ parīkṣeta*).
Now, for what purpose should the examination of the measure of strength and the doshas be performed? To this he says: "doṣapramāṇa... and so forth.

The dosage of medicine is determined in relation to the degree of the *doṣas*; since it is by that very [dosage] that the successful accomplishment of the objective occurs, the meaning of this section is that an examination of the body’s strength (*bala*) must be performed.

Regarding the phrase "in relation to the specific measure of strength": if the body is strong, then the dosage of the great medicine is determined in relation to the measure of the *doṣas*, but in the opposite case, it is not.
He explains this very point through its reverse: "sahasā" and so forth.

It has been stated that for one who is weak and diseased, medicine administered by an unexamining physician becomes excessive; however, it is not said that medicine administered by an examining physician would likewise be fatal. By the implication of the term "in one who is weak" (*alpabale*), it is understood that [the medicine] should not cause despondency or produce exhaustion of body and mind.

This demonstrates that for those [remedies] whose weight according to the characteristics of their potency increases progressively, if a great fault exists in a weak [disease], and although that [fault] might be curable by a vast amount of medicine, nevertheless, out of fear of immediate complications, one should not suddenly administer a large quantity of medicine; rather, one should increase the quantity of medicine in accordance with the strength gained through progressive practice.
The term "without confusion" (*avibhramaiḥ*) indicates that they are free from adverse effects even at the time of digestion.
"By those that are not urgent" means those that do not cause great calamity.
He says "especially," etc., to indicate that the aforementioned medicinal qualities should be applied particularly to women;
by the word "heart" (hṛdaya), one should understand the mind (manas) residing within the heart.
It is gentle, superficial, shallow, and feeble, easily overcome by even slight afflictions; by this, their weakness of mind is expressed,
for they require support from others and do not steady themselves by the power of their own inner strength.
With the words beginning with "tathā" (thus), he describes the fault of using medicine in a very small quantity.

By the statement "when overcome by a powerful disease," it is meant that whatever disease is powerful in a strong person is indeed incurable even with a large amount of medicine; however, that which is of little strength even in a strong person is curable with only a small amount of medicine. Having stated the reasons for examination, he explains how the body is to be examined, beginning with the words "tasmāt" (therefore).
Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of grasping the specific measure of strength," both bodily strength and the strength of the *doṣas* are grasped in a general sense;

by means of this, knowledge of the body arises from its morbid transformation (*vikṛti*), which serves as the cause for knowing the strength of the *doṣas*. This very point will be explained later with the words, "of *prakṛti* and the others, excluding *vikṛti*," and so forth.

Alternatively, what is meant by "strength" (*bala*)? It refers specifically to bodily strength (*śarīrabala*). In this context, it is stated generally because bodily strength is understood even through the strength of morbid transformation (*vikṛtibala*); however, since the measure of the humors (*doṣapramāṇa*) is generally known through morbid transformation in what follows, it is stated that "the threefold nature of the strength of the humors is inferred from the threefold nature of the strength of morbid transformation. (94) "Natural constitution" (*prakṛti*) means inherent disposition (*svabhāva*).
"These" refers to semen and so forth.

Here, whatever state the *doṣa* (humor) is in within the semen or the blood, such becomes the *prakṛti* (constitution) in the embryo. Likewise, at the time of the union of semen and blood during the fertile period (*ṛtu*), whichever *doṣa* is predominant initiates the *prakṛti*. Similarly, there is the *doṣa* residing in the uterus (*garbhāśaya*). Furthermore, the mother’s diet and lifestyle at that time, which possess the nature of producing a particular *doṣa*, result in that same *prakṛti* in the body of the embryo. Among these causes that initiate the *prakṛti*, whichever one is most powerful and is augmented by other factors, that alone becomes the initiator of the *prakṛti*.

Furthermore, since time (*kāla*) and other factors merely transform semen and blood into the primary constituents (*prakṛti*), it is shown in another treatise that the production of the *prakṛti* occurs solely through the defects residing in the semen and blood. This process begins at the initial union of the embryo (*garbha*).

It should be understood here that when the *doṣas* are equal or increased, the birth of an embryo does not even occur; thus, a *prakṛti* characterized by a morbid state of the three *doṣas* is not mentioned.
The nature and transformation [of the elements] have been explained in the Sūtrasthāna itself;
softness is produced by water.
"White-limbed" means they are white precisely because of their softness.
The word "not hurried" is to be connected individually with each [quality] beginning with "commencement.
Their gait is substantial; they do not stumble. Their gait is steady; they traverse the earth with every step. Their gait is composed; by virtue of being composed, their movement is not fickle.
He whose face is radiant with a gracious look is thus; whatever wealth and other qualities arise as his natural form should be understood as resulting from the power of that nature.
Furthermore, *daṇḍaśūkāḥ* are those whose nature is to bite again and again; they are "voracious eaters" (*prabhūtāśana*) because of their habit of eating much;
and they are so called because they possess a foul odor (*pūtigandha*) in their armpits and other parts of the body due to eating excessively.
97. *Pratata* means extended; *prasṛta* means spread out;
*sanna* means degraded; *hīna* means inferior; *sakta* means attached; *baddha* means bound; and *jarjara* is like the sound of a broken vessel.
"Always possessing the sound of joints" means they have sounds produced by the cracking of their joints.

"Endowed with all qualities" means they possess the praiseworthy qualities mentioned regarding all [bodily] constituents (*prakṛti*); as it is said in the *Vāgbhaṭa*: "One whose constituents (*dhātu*) are balanced is the best among all [women]. (Vā.Sū.A.1)
Furthermore, if one were not possessed of praiseworthy qualities, then there would be no state of excellence;
it should be understood that when defects remain in a state of equilibrium, by the very power of that equilibrium, they render the qualities supreme rather than the defects.
"Equilibrium occurs" means that there is a state of mutual equality of qualities;
and "the strength of the causes and signs is great" means that the causes (*hetu*) and signs (*liṅga*) are both powerful and numerous.
"Due to some commonality with one or another" means that when there exists some similarity between the *doṣas* and so forth [and the patient].
In the passage beginning with "101.
By way of essence (*sāra*) and so forth," the word *sāra* refers to the most refined element (*dhātu*),
while "with its radiance" (*saprabha*) means the skin together with its luster.
The word *tvaksārāṇām* is to be analyzed as a compound (meaning "of those whose essence is the bark").
Now, he asks what this "essence" (*sāratā*) does, and says: "That essence," and so forth.
In other instances as well, "that essence," and so forth, should be explained in the same manner.
"Śrīmat" means endowed with beauty; "aratni" refers to the elbow;
"śikharadaśanāḥ" means those with beautiful teeth.
Those for whom enjoyment consists of what is dear to women are "those fond of pleasure";
those who fight with valor in battle are "warriors valiant in combat";
and "established in themselves" means they are not dependent on others.

"Having offspring of equal qualities and extensive [lineage]" means having produced children who resemble themselves; the word "mostly" (prāyas) excludes the middling ones by way of a restrictive rule, as they possess only a small degree of excellence.
"By means of excellent core-essences" (madhyaiḥ sāraviśeṣaiḥ) means by those endowed with the qualities of essence that are possible therein;
"because of being accumulated" (upacitatvāt) means because of being massive;
"because of having a large body" (mahāśarīratvāt) means because of having a body of extreme proportions.
"Like ants carrying a burden": just as very small ants carry a great burden because their bodies are substantial, so too [do these beings], meaning they have small and slender bodies.
(102–115) "Conjunction" (*saṃhati*) means the state of being densely compacted.

With the words "by means of measurement" (pramāṇataḥ) and so forth, he states the excellent measurement of the limbs: the two feet are respectively four finger-breadths in height, six in width, and fourteen in length.
The shank is said to be that which is below the knee; its circumference is called the *parikṣepa* or *pariṇāha*.
The knee (*jānu*) is the joint between the shank and the thigh.

The measurement of circumference that is mentioned refers to the middle portion; therefore, in cases where the shanks and other parts have unequal circumferences, this [measurement] should be understood as referring to the middle portion.
The height of the waist has not been stated, because, being the junction between the upper and lower torso, it lacks a separate measurement of height.
[The term] *prabāhu* refers to the region from the shoulder down to the elbow.
The *prapāṇi* is four finger-breadths below the *kaphoṇi*;
the *trika* is from the bone of the anus up to the upper limit of the pelvic bone;
and the chin, the lips, the ears, the middle of the eyes, the nose, and the forehead are each four finger-breadths apart.
The head is six finger-breadths in height; this should be understood as being above the neck, following from the back.
"Only" means that from the soles of the feet up to the top of the head, it measures eighty-four finger-breadths; thus, the body measures three and a half cubits according to one's own hand-span.

And here, as for the body that exceeds eighty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) by the height of each individual limb, this is due to the inclusion of those parts which have entered into the length of other parts; therefore, one should not calculate eighty-four finger-breadths by measuring the length of each limb individually, but rather the body as a whole.

In that regard, there are four finger-breadths for the foot, eighteen for the shank, four for the knee, eighteen for the thighs, eighteen for the back, four for the neck, and six for the head; thus, eighty-four finger-breadths are accounted for.
Any contradiction with Suśruta regarding this matter should be resolved by the difference in the measurement of the finger-breadth (*aṅgulimāna*);
for there, a man's height is stated to be one hundred and twenty finger-breadths,
and thus, in that context, the measure of the finger-breadth itself must be understood as smaller.

"Equal in length and breadth" means possessing the length and breadth of the individual limbs as previously described. Alternatively, it means that if the body's breadth is equal to the eighty-four finger-breadths of its length—measured by the span of the two outstretched arms—then it is "equal in length and breadth";
this should be understood as referring to a body of such specified proportions.
"Deficient" means having deficient proportions.
Regarding the term "adhike" (in excess), it refers to an excessive measure (117).

In the phrase "and by way of suitability" (*sātmyataśca*), it should be understood that the word *sātmya* denotes "habitual suitability" (*okasātmya*), because [other forms of suitability], such as "natural suitability" (*prakṛtisātmya*) and so forth, have already been examined through the very examination of the medicine and other factors.
"Having few means" (*alpasādhanā*) means having few medicines; the sense is that for those accustomed to a single taste, the five tastes are unwholesome because they are incompatible (*asātmya*).
(118) "A mechanical device" (*tantraka*) refers to both that which impels and that which supports.

The meaning is that those who have been instructed in the essentials (*sāra*) should be known as the very best of beings (*pravarasattva*), because of the excellence of their qualities as beings (*sattvaguṇavaiśeṣya*).
The meaning is that, because the transformations of sensation (*vedanāvikāra*) have been steadied by the quality of being (*sattvaguṇa*), they appear as if free from pain.

"Having placed another in oneself" means that, having seen another capable of enduring sensation, one endures sensation thinking, "If this person is capable of enduring sensation, then I too shall be capable of enduring sensation."

Because of the statement "by the power of digestion," one who eats much and transforms it is here called "possessed of the power of food" (*āhāra-śaktimān*); however, this does not refer to that which is grasped by the actual transformation of the substance (*vastu-gata-pariṇati*).
Action (*karman*) refers to the bearing of burdens and so forth; the capacity for that is "action-capacity" (*karmaśakti*).
(121) He states the nature of age (*vayas*) with the verse beginning "In time," etc.
"Dependent on a specific measure of time" means that it arises through connection with a specific measure of time.

By the statement "according to the distinction of gross [stages]," he shows that age can also be greater due to the distinctions between stages such as childhood and further childhood. There are two kinds of children: one whose constituent elements (*dhātu*) are immature until the sixteenth year, and likewise one whose constituent elements are still developing until the thirtieth year.
He states the distinction between these two types of children based on their suitability for treatment, beginning with "tatra" (therein), and so forth.

For a child sixteen years of age is described in the treatise as such because he is treated with small doses of mild medicine and so on; beyond that age, even though he is still a child, he is not treated in that same manner with small doses of medicine and so forth, but rather gradually, not all at once. This demonstrates that after sixty years of age, there is a decline in the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) and other factors.
Regarding the phrase "in this time," which refers to the Kali age, he explains how the three stages of life are to be divided for those who live more than a hundred years: "Of them," and so forth.

Here, the ten subjects beginning with *prakṛti* (nature) are to be examined, as stated in the verse beginning with "the essence of nature and its transformations. In this context, by the phrase "excluding the transformations (*vikṛti*)," the exclusion of *vikṛti* is effected.

By means of the specific strengths of the *prakṛti*, *sāra*, and so forth—which are differentiated by the distinctions of superior, inferior, and middling regarding the constitution (*prakṛti*) and other factors—the measure of lifespan is determined in its superior, inferior, and middling forms. Having perceived this superiority, inferiority, and so on, one should divide the three stages of life accordingly. By this, for one whose constitutional strength (*prakṛtibala*) is supreme—whether of the phlegmatic constitution (*śleṣmaprakṛti*) or of a balanced constitution (*samaprakṛti*)—the lifespan is long; however, when the constitutional strength is deficient, the lifespan is short. The same should be understood regarding the *sāra* and the other factors. Thus, one who is endowed with the highest strength in all respects, such as age, constitution, and so forth, lives beyond a hundred years.

Therefore, if a lifespan of one hundred and twenty years is observed for him, then—by inference from the previously mentioned divisions of age—he is a child until thirty-six years, middle-aged until seventy-two years, and old thereafter; however, for one whose lifespan is determined to be eighty years due to being of moderate constitution and so forth, he is a child until twenty-five years, middle-aged until fifty, and old thereafter—thus the divisions are to be made accordingly.

Life span is not to be determined solely by means of [the signs of] *prakṛti* and so forth, but it must also be stated in the *Śārīra-sthāna* by means of the characteristics of life (*āyurlakṣaṇa*) which are connected to the body. Thus he says: "and by the characteristics of life.
The meaning is that even by means of the characteristics of life, age is to be determined and the divisions of age, such as childhood and so on, are to be established.

Furthermore, this division of childhood and so forth is to be made for those whose lifespan is slightly less than or more than one hundred years; however, for those whose measure of maximum lifespan is twenty years and so on, there is no such classification of age by inference, for they die while still having not reached the middle stage of life.
He concludes the examination of the strength of the body as described through the divisions of *prakṛti* (constitution) and so forth with the words "evam" and so on.
As for the strength of the *doṣas*, he states how it is to be examined through the examination of the form and location of the body with the words "vikṛtibala" and so on.

Having declared the examination of the body for the purpose of examining the strength of the body and the strength of the humors (doṣas), [the author] again refers back to the examination of the body for the purpose of knowing the measure of lifespan, beginning with the words "of lifespan" and so forth;
"in the sense organs" (indriyeṣu) means in the chapters on the sense organs (indriyasthāna).

In this regard, a diminished lifespan is to be known through abnormalities of the sense organs, such as changes in complexion that constitute signs of impending death (*ariṣṭa*); furthermore, longevity and shortness of life are to be known from the characteristics associated with birth, as described in the *Jātisūtrīya* and *Śārīra* sections.
(124) Having completed the examination of place (*deśa*), he states the examination of time (*kāla*) with the words beginning "Time," etc.

The year is to be understood as twofold by the division of the two solstices (*ayana*); threefold by the division of cold, heat, and rain; sixfold by the division of seasons (*ṛtu*); twelvefold by the division of months; twenty-fourfold by the division of fortnights (*pakṣa*); and manifold by means of the watches of the day (*prahara*) and so forth.

"The task to be accomplished according to each respective [division]" means that the task to be performed must be accomplished in accordance with the specific divisions to be known, such as the solstices and so on.
"Ordinary" (*sādhāraṇa*) means characterized by neither excessive cold, heat, nor rain.
He divides the rainy season (*prāvṛṣ*): "The rainy season," and so forth.
By the term "the first rain," Āṣāḍha and Śrāvaṇa are meant.
Taking this two-month division of the seasons as the beginning, the remaining pairs of months—such as the monsoon (*varṣā*) and so on—should be understood in their proper sequence.

And this sequence of seasons is not for the purpose of the production of the *rasas* and so forth, but rather to demonstrate that it pertains solely to the process of purifying the body; thus it was stated, "with reference to purification. He will state this very same sequence in the *Siddhi* [section] as follows: "The rains (*prāvṛṭ*), Śukra, and Nabhas are to be known [as the first three]; then again, Śarad, Ūrja, and Sahas; and Tapasya and Madhu—these constitute spring (*vasanta*) with respect to purification" (Siddhi-sthāna, Chapter 6). In this sequence of seasons, the cold season (*śiśira*) is absent.

However, some say: "On the southern bank of the Gaṅgā, there is much rain; therefore, the sequence beginning with the rainy season (*prāvṛṭ*) occurs there. On the northern bank of the Gaṅgā, there is much cold; therefore, the winter (*hemanta*) and cool seasons (*śiśira*) occur there. For it was said by Kāśyapa: 'The rain-cloud rains more on the southern side of the Gaṅgā, and by that water, the two seasons known as *prāvṛṭ* and *varṣā* are designated for them.
On the northern bank of the Gaṅgā, which is thick with snow and water...'"
"Furthermore, because it is cold for them, their seasons are Hemanta and Śiśira"—

this is not correct; for here, due to the statement "with reference to purification (saṃśodhana)," if this distinction were caused by the region, then he would have mentioned that very distinguishing factor, rather than purification.
Therefore, by that distinction of place mentioned by Kāśyapa, the sequence beginning with the rainy season (*prāvṛṭ*) is not intended here;

and since bodies and medicinal herbs are non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*), they do not differentiate [the treatment] through qualities produced artificially in the body, nor do they cause distinctions in the increase or decrease of the potency of the medicine—this is the meaning.

And when bodies and medicinal herbs are conceptual (*vikalpaka*)—that is, when emetics and so forth must necessarily be performed due to an emergency—then they do differentiate the medicine by the application of artificial qualities as will be described, and likewise they differentiate the body.
He explains how there is the state of being most painful during the winter season and so forth: "In that regard, 'winter' and so on";
"bound by defects" means excessively bound by defects.
"Of those two" refers to the aforementioned body and its medicine.

"The conjunction of water and the wind following the cloud"—from that [conjunction], there are "heavy activities"; the meaning is that just as the activity of a teacher is not conducive to happiness, so too is this [activity] of his. Alternatively, "heavy activities" means activities requiring many countermeasures.

"Arising from heavy [doshas]" (gurusamutthānāni) means that bodies afflicted by purification therapies (saṃśodhana) attain their natural state (prakṛti) only with great effort and over a long period of time.
Regarding the phrase "at the ends of the seasons" (varṣānteṣu), this refers to the winter, summer, and rainy seasons;
furthermore, he states "if not," etc., to show that purification may be administered even during winter and other such times in cases of urgent illness (ātyayika-vyādhi).

"Having conceptualized" means having fashioned something endowed with few qualities by superimposing artificial qualities—such as, for example, constructing a warm dwelling and so forth for the purpose of counteracting the cold when it is cold. And it is said elsewhere: "Having provided a remedy for the cold when it is cold, and a warding off of heat when it is hot, one should perform the treatment that has been reached and not let the time for action pass. (Su.Sū.A. 35)

Having shown the remedy regarding the season (*ṛtu*), he now states the remedy regarding the medicine (*bheṣaja*): "The medicine," and so forth. Regarding the variation of combination (*saṃyoga-vikalpa*): for example, mixing *trivṛtā* with warm cow urine when it is cold. Regarding the variation of dosage (*pramāṇa-vikalpa*): for example, administering an excessive dose of *trivṛtā* for the purpose of counteracting non-efficacy (*ayoga*), and so on. Furthermore, the variation of dosage should be performed in such a way that there is no violation of life-force (*prāṇa*); likewise, the variation of combination should be performed in such a way that there is no blending of medicines with contradictory potencies (*viruddha-vīrya*). Demonstrating this, he says: "having made [the medicine] equal in dosage and potency."
He states the time for [administering] the signs of the patient's condition, beginning with "In the stages of the patient," etc.
An example therein is as follows: there is no time for decoctions (*kaṣāya*) in acute fever (*navajvara*), but there is a time for decoctions when the fever has passed six days, and so forth.
"Attainment of the application of medicine" means the successful accomplishment of what is to be achieved through the application of medicine.
(128) Having stated the time, he now describes the activity that follows in sequence, beginning with "The activity, however," and so forth.
Regarding the treatment for each specific condition (pratikarma-cikitsā),
section 129 states the supplementary method: "The method," and so forth.
By the phrase "endowment with the aforementioned qualities," excellence is expressed;
however, by the words "in this way" and so forth, he speaks of the correct and complete performance.
Regarding the question "What is the purpose of investigation?", the answer begins with "But as for investigation," and so forth;
[the author] analyzes the meaning of the word *pratipatti* (comprehension) starting with "That which," and so forth.
"Pratipattavyaḥ" means that [the teaching] is to be applied through practice (anuṣṭhāna).

Regarding the question, "Where does the engagement in vomiting and so forth occur, and where does its cessation occur?", he provides the answer by means of an extended application (atideśa), beginning with the words "yatra tu," etc.
Regarding the question, "In the conjunction characterized by engagement and withdrawal, what is the final goal?", the answer begins with "engagement," etc.;
"one should determine" (adhyavasyet) means one should form a firm resolve (adhyavasāya).
Regarding the phrase "in one of the two cases" (*anyataraniṣṭhāyām*), this refers to the determination of one of the two alternatives.

Once the relative gravity or lightness of a condition has been understood here, the decision regarding the treatment of the more serious case is known even if it is not explicitly stated. Therefore, the author of the treatise did not directly state, "One should apply oneself to the definitive treatment of a serious disease.

Instead, he expresses this very point through a different turn of phrase that implies the treatment of a serious disease by means of [describing] the management of a minor disease, beginning with the words "For there exist... (*santi hi...*) and so forth.

"One should determine correctly" means that one should set aside the general rule (*utsarga*), which is light [in application], and proceed by determining according to the exception (*apavāda*), which is weighty; for, by the statement "a powerful affliction," etc., he will describe the treatment for the strong while setting aside that for the weak.
Now, the answer to the question, "Which medicinal substances enter into formulation in emesis and the other therapies? begins with the words "Those which... and so forth.
Śārṅgeṣṭā is *guñjā*; somavalka is *khadira*; suṣavī is *kāravellaka*;
dvīpī is *kaṇṭakārī* (though if the reading is *dvīpiśatru*, it should be understood as *śatāvarī*);
vidula is *vetasa*; śatapuṣpā is *ghaṇṭāravā*; and sadāpuṣpā is *raktārka*.
Kālaṅkṛta is kāsamarda; poṭagala is hoggala; sumanā is jātī; saumanasyāyanī is the bud of the jātī or the calyx of the jātī;
śālmalika is rohitaka or small-leafed śālmali; bhadraparṇī is bhādālī; elāparṇī is rāsnā; uddāla is bahuvāra; gopī is sārivā.
The action of making *varti* refers to the preparation of long, wick-like medicinal foods (*bhakṣya*).
Here, the separate grouping of the "Āragvadha" and "Madhu" categories has been made primarily to demonstrate their common properties through their distinct recitation.
*Kalpanā* means *kalpa*, which signifies application (*prayoga*).

Regarding the phrase "at a later time": in the context of the *kalpa* (section 135), *viklipti* refers to conjunction with another substance, while *aviklipti* refers to simple application alone; therefore, by the term "by those that are *viklipta* and *aviklipta*," the meaning is "by those that are conjoined and un-conjoined."
Kṣīriṇī is dugdhikā; klītaka is yaṣṭīmadhu;
masūravidalā is śyāmalatā;
however, the first [type], śyāmā, which has black roots, is said to be identical to trivṛt.
"Most kalpas" means those with many applications and those generally to be employed;
since a teaching that is neither too concise nor too extensive is desired, it is intended that the treatise be explained with a degree of brevity and detail that is neither excessive.

The meaning is that the author and the listener both desire not only the knowledge of the specific [substances], but also the knowledge of that which was not explicitly stated through a presentation that is neither too concise nor too detailed, provided it occurs by way of general principles.

Therefore, "precisely from the perspective of *rasa*" means that with *rasa* as the primary focus, there is instruction on the substances that serve as the substratum of *rasa* in a manner that is neither too brief nor too prolix.
"Those" refers to the substances suitable for use in non-unctuous enemas (*āsthāpana*).

And here, although the instruction is given by way of the tastes (*rasa*), since the combinations of tastes are exceedingly numerous, they would become as innumerable as the description of all individual substances; therefore, showing that the instruction regarding the substances used for *āsthāpana* (non-unctuous enemas) must be made by means of the six tastes alone, he says "rasa... and so forth.
The phrase "for the purpose of illustration" (*udāharaṇārtham*) means for the purpose of illustrating the substance which serves as the substratum for the sweet and other tastes.
"Having distributed [them] among the tastes" (*raseṣvanuvibhajya*) means having taught a portion of the substances as being the substrata within the tastes, such as the sweet and others.
"By means of each individual taste" (*rasaikaikaśyena*) does not mean for the purpose of defining the names through the combination of tastes.

Rather, it means that the groups of six *āsthāpana* (non-unctuous enemas) will be explained as collections of substances suitable for *āsthāpana*, for the purpose of defining the names of those explicitly mentioned—such as *jīvaka* and others—and for the purpose of defining by way of analogy those unmentioned substances belonging to the same category, such as those that are sweet and so forth. Alternatively, "for the purpose of the name and definition" (*nāmalakṣaṇārtham*) means for the sake of knowing the names:
*āsthāpana* is that substance, such as *jīvaka* and others, by which one is stabilized (*āsthāpyate*); *skandha* means a collection.

"Having classified according to taste" means having designated them by way of their being sweet and so forth. (137) Furthermore, this enumeration of groups of substances (*dravyagaṇa*) by means of sweet and other tastes is not intended by us in the same manner as it is described by others—as referring only to a substance that possesses a single taste such as sweet; rather, we maintain that wherever other tastes may be present, if the sweet and so forth are predominant, or where a substance produces effects such as sweetness through its post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*) and potency (*prabhāva*), that too must be included by us within the group of sweet and so forth. Demonstrating this, he says: "As for that which... and so on.
"Of a single taste" means of a pure, single taste;
"mostly sweet" means possessing an excellent sweet flavor;

likewise, "the others" refers to sour and so forth—those that are mostly sour and have a sour post-digestive effect (pāka)—we shall teach by treating them as simply sour. He shows that the same applies to salty and other tastes through the phrase "likewise the others."
The heroes [use] Jālandhara, Śāka, Aśanaparṇī, and Aparājitā.
Madhuparṇī, vikaṅkata, chatrā, kokilākṣa,
aticchatrā, and aruṇakokilākṣa.
Mahāśrāvaṇī, Alambuṣā, Śuklā, Śarkarā,
Kṣīraśuklā, and Bṛhacchṛṅgāṭikā.
Kṣudrasahā, kumārī,
ṛṣyagandhā, ṛṣyajāṅgalaka, balābheda, moraṭa, or mūrvā.
Saṃharṣā, bandāka, madhukaparṇī, madhukabheda,
madhūlikā, and markaṭahastatṛṇa.
Rājādana is known as veñculikī;
kaśeru is ciñcoḍaka,
and rājakaśeru is a variety of kaśeru.
Śītapākī, śītalā, odanapākī, nīlajhiṇṭī,
ṛṣyaproktā, and the varieties of balā.
Dvāradā, śākataru,
bhāradvājī, vanakārpāsī, vanatrapuṣī, bṛhatphalā, and goḍumbā.
*Abhīrupatrī* is a variety of *śatāvarī*; *kuliṅgākṣī* is *peṭikā*. According to the reading *kuliṅgā*, it is *uccaṭā*, *kṣīravallī*, or *kṣīralatā*.
*Kapola-pallī* is known as *kavaḍaveṇḍuā*;
*kapotavallī*, *sūkṣmailā*, *somavallī*, and *somalatā* [are synonyms].
Gopavallī is Anantamūla; Madhuvallī is a variety of Yaṣṭīmadhu.
In the category of sour [fruits], there are *nandītaka*, *karparanandī*, *śītaka*, and *amlaloṭa*; *airāvata* is the orange (*nāgaraṅga*).
They say that *amlikā*, which is prevalent in Kāmarūpa and has a bulbous root (*kanda-pradhānā*), is simply a variety of *amlikā*.
Regarding the phrase "solidified by liquids" (*dravaiḥ sthirāṇi*), it means they have become firm through immersion in liquid.
*Kūpya* and other varieties of salt are well-known in other regions; therefore, they should be understood from those belonging to other regions.
*Romaka* is that which originates from the Rūmā river.
Tejasvinī and tejovatī are synonyms for kilima (Pinus deodara), also known as devadāru.
In the group of bitter [plants], *karkaśa* is a variety of *paṭola*.

In the group of astringents (kaṣāya-varga): *aśvakarṇa* is *priyāla-śāla*; *paripelava* is *kaivartamustaka*; *jiṅginī* is well-known by its own name; *mācīka* is *devadāru*; *ajakarṇa* is a variety of *śāla*; *kumbhī* is known as *kumbhīka*, or alternatively as *haṭha*; *mṛṇāla* is the stalk of the lotus; *tālakharjūrataruṇāni* means the sprouts of the *tāla* and *kharjūra* trees. Furthermore, regarding those substances that are listed in two sections [of this treatise], they should be understood as being applicable in both places because they possess the qualities of both categories. 144.

"Sārvayaugikān" means those that are appropriate (yaugika) for all diseases treatable by non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana), such as vāta disorders, fever, abdominal tumors (gulma), and so forth, provided there is a connection with the doshas as previously described.
He explains this very point with the words "sarvaśo hi," etc.;
"sarvaśaḥ" means either by the entire group, by half a group, or according to what is available.

Now, regarding the statement that all groups [of drugs] are suitable for all diseases treatable by non-unctuous enemas (*āsthāpana*), [the author clarifies]: in the case of a fever caused by *pitta*, an enema prepared with the pungent group (*kaṭuvarga*) increases the fever because it generates *pitta*. Therefore, this suitability of all groups was not stated with reference to every specific disorder; rather, it refers generally to their benefit for all diseases treatable by *āsthāpana*. However, he says "yeṣām... etc., demonstrating that in specific disorders, one must strictly prohibit the use of any group that is unsuitable or provocative for that particular condition—referring here to those various disorders of *vāta* and so forth mentioned previously.

In this context, the sweet group (*madhuraskandha*) is not mentioned for the purpose of pacifying *kapha*, and therefore it increases *kapha*. This should be understood to apply to the sour and other groups as well.

Alternatively, by the phrase "suitable for all [therapeutic] applications" (*sārvayaugika*), it is stated that the groups previously mentioned act as remedies for all diseases curable by *āsthāpana* (non-unctuous enema) through their combined or individual application, rather than each one individually. However, by the verse beginning with "of those which... (*yeṣām*), it is stated that each group specifically overcomes those diseases which have not been explicitly mentioned as curable by them.

Now, demonstrating the addition of homologous elements and the removal of non-homologous ones by considering diseases and other factors within the groups already mentioned, and with regard to their etiological suitability (*yaugikatva*), he says "from them," etc.

By the word "the wise one" (*buddhimān*), he shows that the addition and removal must be performed by one who possesses intelligence, and not by one of small intellect who is incapable of performing *ūha* (inference) and *apoha* (exclusion).
It should be understood that one group may be combined with one group or with many groups.

"Taking reasoning as the authority" means taking deliberation (*ūha*) as the authority, [thinking] "this here is etymological (*yaugika*), this is non-etymological (*ayaugika*). "Practicing" refers to alms-based food such as rice and so forth placed in a bowl. Now, one might ask: how can a person of dull intellect fail to follow what has been stated? For it is said that the wise understand the non-etymological [usage] through deliberation; in that very context, how could one of dull intellect, by employing it [incorrectly], not bring about misfortune? To this he says: "For as it has been stated," and so forth.

By the phrase "because it does not cause excessive great [difficulty]," he shows that for one of dull intellect who practices as prescribed, no great calamity occurs without [the application of] reasoning (*ūha*).

For whatever rule is stated in the treatise is generally etymologically applicable (*yaugika*) therein; even where it is non-etymological due to differences in the body and so forth, the meaning is that it remains etymologically applicable to a small degree.
By the phrase "because the example is not too brief," the meaning is that the rule stated as an example in the treatise is not overly concise.

By this it is meant that if there were only a few examples of the means for treating diseases, then much would have to be inferred; in that case, a person of dull intellect—due to a lack of direct knowledge regarding the scope of the examples and because of their own inability to infer them—would not be capable of performing the therapeutic action characterized by the pacification of disease. Since, however, the examples are numerous, it is logical that one accomplishes the aforementioned diseases as curable through those very examples in the form of clinical applications.

Furthermore, these two methods of addition (*āvāpa*) and subtraction (*uddhāra*) should generally be understood to apply only to substances mentioned within a group (*gaṇa*), as stated in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*: "Even a substance mentioned in a group may be unsuitable for a particular disease."
"One should extract that [ingredient] and add what one considers to be specifically synergistic" (Suśruta Cikitsāsthāna 1).

Regarding those substances such as Agastya-harītakī and others which perform their function through the power of combination (*saṃyoga-mahiman*), neither addition (*āvāpa*) nor extraction (*uddhāra*) should be performed for them.
With this very point in mind, it is stated in the Suśruta: "This is because it is established by traditional scripture (*āgama*) and because the result is observed accordingly."
"It should be employed like a mantra and must never be subjected to critical analysis" (Suśruta Cikitsāsthāna,
Chapter 1). Following this, he states the substances for the oil enema (anuvāsana), which comes next in the sequence, beginning with the words "ataḥ param" (henceforth, etc.).
"Oil here" (*tailam*) means that which has become oil, such as mustard oil and the like;

this is because of the predominance of "oil" [in general], meaning that among vegetable fats, sesame oil alone is predominant. By this, whatever procedure applies to oil should be understood to apply to mustard oil and the others. However, the inclusion of mustard oil and the others under the term "oil" (*taila*) here is for the purpose of proclaiming the predominance of the fat derived from sesame; indeed, the inclusion of mustard oil and the others by the word "oil" does occur.
As it is stated in the Suśruta-saṃhitā: "Because of its production and because it possesses those qualities, the nature of oil (*tailatva*) exists in others as well" (Su.Sū.A.
15). By means of elimination (*pariśeṣya*), he states the head-purgatives (*śirovirecana*) beginning with the words "head-purgative," etc.

By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and fruits" (*phalāni ca*), he indicates the use of other parts of that aforementioned substance; thus, there is also the use of the bark of *śigru*, which will be mentioned later. In this same way, examples may be cited elsewhere as well.
*Sumukha* and others are varieties of *parṇāsa*; *tarkārī* is *jayantī*.

Gaṇḍīrapuṣpī, śamaṭha, vayasthā, brāhmī, varāṅga, and guḍatvak are known as "suitable for the senses" (indriyopaśayanī). By this term, those substances such as salts and others which do not impair the senses are to be employed in head-purgation (śirovirecana); likewise, other substances—namely those that are sweet, sour, or astringent—which are also suitable for head-purgation [are to be used].

151. Regarding "the examination of the characteristics, teachers, and disciples in the compendium" (*saṅgraha-lakṣaṇācārya-śiṣyāṇām*): this refers to the examination of the treatise (*śāstra*), the teacher, and the disciple. For "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is said to be the treatise, and [it refers to] that which is the cause; thus, the meaning is that which is the cause for the examination of the treatise and so forth. This includes the cause for the examination of the treatise, such as: "A treatise of such a nature is like the stainless sun," and so on.

The reason for examining the teacher is stated in the passage beginning with "For such is the teacher," while the reason for examining the student is stated in the passage beginning with "For one who teaches what is to be taught is a teacher.
That which is to be studied is the subject matter (*adhyeya*); the rule concerning that is precisely the rule of study (*adhyayanavidhi*).

"This collection of topics has been stated" means that the collection of subjects to be explained—consisting of the examination of the characteristics, the teacher, and the disciple, and so forth—has been stated.
"With beautiful meaning" means it has been stated in such a way that its meaning is lovely due to qualities such as its logical coherence. This is the sense.
The conjunction of words within a sentence is *śabdasandhi*.
By the phrase "of the defects (*doṣa*) and so forth," he provides a summary of the contents of the Vimānasthāna.
The term *hetumat* means that it possesses logical justification (*upapatti*), that is to say, it is established by the measurement of the defects and so forth.

"Niruktāni" means those spoken by way of etymological derivation (*nirukti*); and "vimānāni" refers to those by which faults (*doṣa*) and so forth are specifically measured (*mīyante*) or known. 155–157.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Determination of Disease and the Physician," in the Vimānasthāna of the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka Saṃhitā composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta. [End of the Śārīrasthāna]

[Śārīrasthāna, Chapter 1 (47 of 120)] In the Section on Diagnosis (Nidānasthāna), the causes and other factors have been understood; likewise, in the Section on Specific Determination (Vimānasthāna), the measures of tastes, humors (doṣas), and so forth have been established. Consequently, the body (śarīra), which serves as the substratum for the medical treatment to be performed, must now be known. Since medical treatment dependent upon the knowledge of the body cannot be effective unless the body is understood in its entirety and in all its specific details, the Section on the Body (Śārīrasthāna) is expounded in order to demonstrate the body through its specific characteristics such as its cause, origin, maintenance, growth, and so forth.

In this context as well, the chapter titled "Katidhāpuruṣīya" (On the Various Types of Persons) is designated as the primary section because it establishes the distinctions among persons who employ medical treatment— the cause for liberation through the absolute cessation of suffering.
The term "katidhā" means "of how many kinds."

By the term *puruṣa*, the object denoted by the word *puruṣa* is expressed without distinction; for, according to such passages as “the elements beginning with ether, with consciousness as the sixth,” as well as “the twenty-four-fold division,” it is the *karmapuruṣa* (the embodied soul) who possesses a body that is meant; likewise, by the statement “the single element of consciousness is also known by the name *puruṣa*,” it is the self (*ātman*) devoid of a body that is to be expressed as the meaning of the word *puruṣa*, since the element (*dhātu*) is so called because it sustains (*dharaṇa*) the person (*puruṣa*). Therefore, “by the difference of the elements” means by the difference in the objects sustained by the person.

By the qualification "O wise one" (*dhīman*), he shows that only one who is truly wise is capable of explaining this extremely subtle matter about the distinctions between persons and so forth which is about to be described.

[The question] "Why is the *puruṣa* the cause? means: for what reason is the *puruṣa* the primary, enduring cause in *saṃsāra*? [The word] *prabhava* means the cause, in the sense that "from this [cause] things originate."
"In wombs" means in births;
"all" refers even to those who have gone to other men;
"the knower of the field" (kṣetrajña) is the self (ātman).
The entire field (kṣetra), excluding the Unmanifest, which will be described starting with "is to be known" and so forth—

[the meaning is that] in the absence of the field, since there would be no knowledge of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the state of being the Knower of the Field would not be possible. This is the intended sense.
"Acting as a witness" means being like a witness;
"a particularity produced by feeling" means a specific state such as joy generated by feelings in the form of cognition regarding a son and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of the three," among the three forms of suffering—past, future, and present—which one does he treat?

In the passage beginning with "the past," the word *kim* (what) is to be supplied; thus it should be construed as: "Does one treat what is past? Or what is present? Or what is yet to come? As for the statement that "there is no [fixed] place," this means that due to momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), there is no duration of the sensations in a state suitable for the application of treatment.

Although the cause and the substratum of sensations have already been explained in the *Dīrghajīvitīya*, nevertheless, here, by virtue of the context and the desire for a specific understanding, these questions are asked again in a more detailed manner.
Since these points concerning the questions are to be elaborated by the Teacher in the subsequent section of the treatise, they need not be explained here.
(3-15) "The ether and so forth," etc.

The elements beginning with space (*khādayaḥ*) are those to be mentioned later as "space, air, fire, water, and earth"; in the phrase "with consciousness as the sixth" (*cetanāṣaṣṭhāḥ*), the word "consciousness" (*cetanā*) refers to the self (*ātman*) which is the substratum of consciousness and possesses the mind (*samanaska*); by the inclusion of the elements beginning with space, the sense organs composed of those elements are also encompassed;

and this is the *puruṣa* (person) accepted in the Vaiśeṣika system and the subject matter of the medical science (*cikitsāśāstra*); this very same [puruṣa] is defined as "the person is the aggregate of the five great elements and the embodied being" (*pañcamahābhūtaśarīrisamavāyaḥ puruṣaḥ*).
(Suśruta Sūtrasthāna)

By this, he shows that even Suśruta stated [this] using the expression "it is remembered," indicating that this person denoted by the word *puruṣa* was intended by the ancient teachers as well, and is not merely our own invention.

He speaks of that Self which is called by the word *puruṣa* according to the etymological derivation "he who sleeps (*śete*) in the city (*puri*), i.e., the body"— beginning with the words "consciousness" (*cetana*), etc.

In this context, by using the term "designated as *puruṣa*" (*puruṣasañjñaka*) instead of simply "person" (*puruṣa*), he demonstrates that the *puruṣa* intended here in medical treatment is not the conscious element (*cetanādhātu*) itself, but rather that it is designated by the word *puruṣa* here as well, in accordance with the usage of other treatises. However, the *puruṣa* who is the actual subject of medical treatment consists of the six elements (*ṣaddhātuka*); for this very reason, the term "designated" (*sañjñita*) was not employed there [in the definition of the six elements].

And although this term "person" (*puruṣa*) applies even to cows and other beings as a collection of the six elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*), it nevertheless applies specifically and primarily to the human being alone; therefore, the word "person" is not overly well-known in the case of cows and the like.

Furthermore, he describes the person, who consists of the six elements, according to the divisions of the Sāṅkhya system as being twenty-fourfold, beginning with the words "Furthermore... and so forth.
He analyzes the group of twenty-four itself, beginning with "the mind" and so forth:

although this Puruṣa is said by the Sāṅkhyas to consist of twenty-five principles—as it is stated [in Sāṅkhya Kārikā 3]: "Root-prakṛti is not a transformation; the seven, beginning with Mahat, are both prakṛti and transformations;

the sixteenfold set is only a transformation; the Puruṣa is neither prakṛti nor a transformation"—nevertheless, here [in this system], having subsumed the Puruṣa—who is distinct from prakṛti and indifferent—into the unmanifest prakṛti itself on account of the common characteristic of being unmanifest (avyaktatva), he includes him by the very term 'unmanifest' (avyakta). Therefore, the statement that "the Puruṣa consists of twenty-four" is not contradictory.
For it would serve no further purpose here to explain the distinctions of the subtle *udāsīna* (the indifferent self); thus, it is not done.
"The ten organs" refers to the five organs of action and the five organs of cognition.

"Consisting of eight elements" means having the form of the pentad beginning with ether (*ākāśa*), intellect (*buddhi*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*), and ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*). For he will say: "Ether and the other [elements], intellect, the unmanifest, and likewise ego-consciousness as the eighth."
Here, in this [chapter] of twenty-four [verses], he speaks—beginning with "the definition" (*lakṣaṇam*)—in order to define the mind (*manas*), which was mentioned first.
He explains how the absence of cognition (*jñāna*) and the presence of cognition serve as indicators of the mind, saying "when existing," and so forth.

"Due to the withdrawal of the mind" means because of its non-connection with a sense organ; "due to its presence" means because of the connection of the mind with a sense organ. Thus he thinks: when sense objects are simultaneously in contact with the sense organs, it is observed that cognition arises with respect to some sense object and does not arise with respect to others. Therefore, this presence and absence of cognition indicates another cause of cognition; and that other cause is the mind (*manas*).

Furthermore, as for that cause, the mind (*manas*), if it is accepted as being all-pervasive (*vibhu*) like the self (*ātman*) and thus simultaneously reaching all the sense organs, or if it is accepted as being multiple in number like the sense organs themselves, then—given the simultaneous connection of the sense organs with their objects—there would necessarily be five cognitions at once, either by means of a single all-pervading mind or by means of multiple minds due to the simultaneous presiding over the organs. Yet, simultaneous cognitions do not occur. Therefore, from the mark (*liṅga*) of the non-arising of simultaneous cognitions, it is established that the mind is atomic (*aṇu*) and singular. Thus he says: "Atomicity," etc. (vv. 18–19).
Having described the qualities of the mind, he states the objects of the mind, beginning with "the thinkable" (*cintya*):
that which is thought by the mind as something to be done or not to be done; that which is investigated through reasoning and non-reasoning; that which is deliberated upon.
That which is to be inferred (*ūhya*) is that which is inferred through the possibility [of its occurrence], such as "this will be so";
that which is to be meditated upon (*dhyeya*) is the object of the knowledge of cultivation (*bhāvanājñāna*);
and that which is to be conceptualized (*saṅkalpya*) is the object of determination by way of its possession of qualities or its possession of defects.
By the phrase "whatever it may be," objects not previously mentioned, such as pleasure and so forth, are included.

"Cognizable by the mind" means graspable by the mind independently of the [external] senses. And these mental objects are indeed of the nature of sound and the other [sensory qualities]; therefore, there is no excess over the number twenty-four by postulating a sixth object.

Pleasure and the like, however, which are distinct from sound and other [objects], are to be grasped as objects of the mind (*manas*) precisely through the apprehension of specific cognitions (*buddhi*).
Having thus described the object of the mind, he states its function: "The seizing of the senses," and so forth.

The seizing of the senses—that is, the presiding over the senses—is the function of the mind; likewise, self-restraint is the function of the mind. For the mind, when it has strayed toward undesirable objects, is restrained by the mind itself. As some say: "And the mind, being endowed with another quality (*guṇa*), restrains it from other objects."
As it has been said: "The mind, being inclined toward sense objects, cannot be restrained from harmful matters due to the loss of firmness (*dhṛti*); for firmness consists in self-restraint.
Therefore, by means of firmness as the instrumental cause, [the mind] restrains itself; thus, there is no contradiction regarding an action upon itself.
He states another function of the mind (*manas*): "speculation (*ūha*) and deliberation (*vicāra*).
Here, speculation is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) cognition consisting of mere observation, while deliberation is the conceptualization of things as being either to be rejected or accepted.

For the Sāṅkhyas consider there to be four causes of conceptualization: among these, the external is the form of the sense organs, while the internal consists of the triad of mind (*manas*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and intellect (*buddhi*).

In this context, the sense organs "perceive," which means they apprehend [objects] through non-conceptual cognition; the mind, however, "conceives," which means it conceives of things in terms of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted; the ego-sense "identifies," which means it thinks, "This is mine, I am authorized here"; the intellect "determines," which means it makes a definitive judgment such as, "I shall abandon this faulty thing and I shall accept this virtuous one. As for deliberation (*ūha*), although it is an activity of the external senses such as the eyes, it is nevertheless described as an activity of the mind because the mind serves as its governing basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

For there is this statement: "Since the intellect (*buddhi*), together with the internal organs, perceives every object, therefore the threefold organ is the gatekeeper, while the remaining ones are the gates" (Sāṃkhya Kārikā 36).
35) Thus,
"thereafter the intellect (buddhi) functions" means that following deliberation (ūha) and investigation (vicāra), the intellect performs determination (adhyavasāya). Furthermore,

although the operation of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra)— namely, self-conceit (abhimana)— is not explicitly mentioned here, it should be understood as being indicated by the very operation of the intellect.

The intellect (*buddhi*), forming the determination—“I shall abandon this” or “I shall take up this”—occurs only with respect to an object that is identified by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). Therefore, the operation of the ego-sense is also grasped through the very operation of the intellect;

for the offering of the operations of all the instruments (*karaṇa*) takes place within the intellect, as it has been said: “These specific qualities (*guṇaviśeṣa*), which are like lamps and distinct from one another...”
"Having illuminated the entire object of the person, they deliver it to the intellect" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 36).
This very point— that the intellect is preceded by deliberation (*ūha*)— is explained in the passage beginning with "by means of the sense organ," and so forth.
"It is grasped" means it is grasped by mere conceptualization;
"by way of qualities" means as something to be accepted,
and "by way of defects" means as something to be rejected.
He elucidates the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the intellect (*buddhi*) with the words "is born," and so forth.
"In that object" means in the object constructed by the mind;
"consisting of certainty" means having a stable nature, which is to say, having the form of determination (*adhyavasāya*).

"Exerts himself" (vyavasyati) means he performs the practice; that is to say, he becomes intent upon it. It means that he carries out what has been determined by the intellect, whether for the purpose of speaking or acting.

By the phrase "preceded by the intellect" (buddhipūrvakam), he shows that only such an undertaking as is preceded by the intellect is of this nature, and not the undertaking of one who is insane or otherwise deranged.

Having designated the mind (*manas*), he now designates the sense organs (*indriya*). Among those, because of their preeminence, he first speaks of the cognitive organs (*buddhīndriya*). Regarding the phrase "each one by one" and so forth: among the elements beginning with ether (*khādi*), the five sense organs, such as the eye and the rest, are joined with each of the elements in turn as an additional constituent. By the expression "each one by one additional," it is indicated that all five are composed of the five elements (*pāñcabhautika*), yet it suggests that fire (*tejas*) is predominant in the eye, and so on. They are said to be "inferred from their functions" (*karmānumeya*), meaning they are inferred from their effects (*kārya*); the effect being the cognition of the eye and the other senses.
He shows that those from which cognition proceeds are the five sense organs of cognition.

Although in the Sāṅkhya system the sense organs are derived from the *ahaṅkāra*—as it is said: "The group of eleven, characterized by *sattva*, proceeds from the *vaikṛta-ahaṅkāra*" (Sāṅkhyakārikā 25)—nevertheless, due to differences in philosophical opinion, the elemental nature (*bhautikatva*) of the sense organs should be understood; or rather, this elemental nature of the sense organs should be understood as figurative (*aupacārika*). The basis for this figurative usage is that whichever sense organ perceives a particular element in its predominance, it is said to be "abounding in" that element. For example, the eye perceives fire (*tejas*), and therefore it is said to be "fiery" (*taijasa*), and so forth. (24) Now, he describes the organs of action (*karmendriya*), beginning with "the two hands," etc.
The hands and feet are each a single sense organ because they perform the same function; the anus and the generative organ are also each one.
Regarding speech, he states its distinction for the purposes of acquisition and rejection, beginning with "And speech," and so forth.

"Light is like light," because, by being the agent of dharma, it causes both worlds to shine; in contrast to this is "darkness," which consists of untruth (25–26). Now, following the order of the enumeration, since the meanings are to be explained, he first speaks of the elements themselves as comprised within the eightfold material nature (*prakṛti*), because they are dependent on others due to their being qualities of the five elements as grasped by the inclusion of *prakṛti*—beginning with the words "the great elements" (*mahābhūtāni*).
Sound and the other qualities should be understood as the natural attributes of ether and the other elements respectively;
however, that excellence of quality which is to be described arises precisely from the connection with the elements that have entered [into them].
Thus, because the four elements enter into earth, it possesses five qualities; in the same way, water and the others should be understood to possess four qualities and so forth.
Having described the inherent quality (*naisargika-guṇa*), he describes the quality produced by the entry of other elements, beginning with "Of these" (*teṣām*):
"The preceding one has a single quality" (*ekaguṇaḥ pūrvaḥ*) means that the preceding element, being of the nature of space (*kha-rūpa*), possesses the single quality of sound (*śabda*).

The masculine gender of the elements beginning with space (*ākāśa*) is due to their being conceived as having the nature of verbal roots (*dhātu*); for it has been said: "Space and the others, with consciousness as the sixth, are the elements (*dhātavaḥ*).
Furthermore, as there is a progression [in the order] of the elements, so too is there a progressive increase in qualities (*guṇa*), corresponding respectively to each.

Now, even by this much, the specific rule regarding which quality resides in which element—such as whether it possesses one quality or two—is not definitively known. To address this, he says: "In the preceding," and so forth.

Among the elements beginning with ether (*kha*), the preceding quality (*guṇa*) occurs in sequence according to their respective order. It is not only the preceding [element] that exists, but also the quality of that preceding one;

thus, in ether (*kha*), the preceding quality of sound (*śabda*) exists. In air (*vāyu*), however, touch (*sparśa*) is the quality obtained by sequence and becomes the "preceding," while the "quality of the preceding" is sound; thus, it possesses two qualities. This should be understood similarly for fire and the others as well.

Since there is no other quality subsequent to smell, it is not "prior"; nevertheless, in the text "smell and its qualities," the priority of smell must be understood in relation to the phrase "its qualities. Alternatively, the term "prior" is used according to the maxim of "those with umbrellas are walking," whereby even though smell is not actually prior, it is to be understood as occurring first in the sequence on earth. (28) He states the unique characteristic of the elements, beginning with "hardness," etc.

Non-resistance means non-obstruction, which is to say the state of being intangible (*asparśatva*); for that which possesses tangibility obstructs movement, whereas space does not, because it lacks tangibility. All of this—such as hardness and so forth—is the domain of the tactile faculty (*sparśanendriya*), and is thus cognizable by the tactile faculty.
How is all this known by the tactile faculty? He says: "tactile," etc., [ending with] "along with its opposite. "Its opposite" means the absence of touch.

Whatever sense faculty perceives a certain object, it also perceives the absence of that [object]. Therefore, it is logical that even the intangibility (*asparśatva*) of space is perceptible by the tactile faculty.

In the Sāṅkhya system, liquidity and mobility are merely the quality of touch belonging to the gross elemental air (*vāyu*), because they are perceivable by the sense of touch. Indeed, whatever is grasped by the sense of touch is nothing but a transformation of the gross elemental air. These elements, beginning with space (*ākāśa*), should be understood as subtle in the form of *tanmātras*; however, the gross elements such as space are mentioned therein as modifications (*vikāra*) within the category of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), while the subtle forms are called *tanmātras*.
For there is this statement: "The subtle elements (*tanmātras*) are the non-specific (*aviśeṣa*); from those five [subtle elements] arise the five gross elements (*bhūtas*).

These are known as the specific (*viśeṣa*), being calm, terrible, and delusive" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 38). Therefore, here too, space and the other elements denoted by the term *tanmātra* should be understood as subtle.
He states the further characteristics of the subtle elements residing within the body: "the qualities," and so forth.
"Qualities" refers to sound and the rest;
"of the possessors of qualities" refers to the subtle-form elements.

The meaning of the sentence is that by the inclusion of the word "evam" (thus), sound and the other [objects] are also manifested as the characteristics of the subtle elements (*bhūta*) residing within the body.
31 He states the objects: "the objects," and so forth.

However, those things denoted by the word *artha* (objects), such as sound and the rest, should be understood as being merely gross forms of space (*khādirūpa*). This is because one holds the view that sound is a transformation of space, touch is a transformation of air, and so forth.

Thus, when space and the other elements are referred to here through the mention of sound and the rest, it is entirely logical that sound and the others are simply transformations of space and the other elements.
By this, it should be understood that whatever is perceivable by the ear is all space and sound, and whatever is perceived by touch is all air and touch, and so on.

Now, in order to demonstrate the intellect (*buddhi*) as it is included among the group of primary constituents (*prakṛti*), he describes its specific forms of knowledge through the distinctions of that intellect’s functions, beginning with the words "That which... and so forth.

The phrase "relying upon whichever sense organ" means relying upon the channel of whichever sense organ; the cognitions, which are specific functions of the principle of intellect known by the term "the Great One" (*mahat*), arise through the channel of the sense organs. It is precisely because they are produced by those sense organs that they are designated according to those organs—by such designations as "visual cognition" (*cakṣurbuddhi*), "auditory cognition" (*śrotrabuddhi*), and so on.

The intellect (*buddhi*) that has objects such as the thinkable (*cintya*) and so forth as its domain is designated by the mind (*manas*); the meaning is that it is referred to as "mind-intellect" (*manobuddhi*).

Having established that there are six types of intellects based on the distinction between the senses and the mind, he states the multiplicity of intellects with the words "due to differentiation," and so forth.

Because of the difference between the effect—the sense-object—and [the senses], many intellects arise, being differentiated through their connection to those. The "effect" refers to the various distinctions of pleasure and pain; for, due to that manifold effect consisting of pleasure and pain, the causal knowledge (*jñāna*) also becomes manifold.
Now he states the means for knowing all external objects: "The self," and so forth;
"the unmanifest" (avyakta);
"each one" (ekaika) means individually.
He provides an illustration for the fact that cognition (*buddhi*) is produced by the conjunction of multiple factors, beginning with the words "the fingers" (*aṅguli*), etc.

By means of this illustration, he mentions two types of sound: one is the sound produced by the fingers and the palm of the thumb; this refers to the sound of the palm arising from the contact of the middle finger, which is constrained by the thumb, with the palm. The other is the sound of the lute (*vīṇā*) produced by the nails on the strings; this is one [type of] lute-sound. Others, however, describe the lute-sound as being produced from the fingers and so forth as a single [instance].

By this, he shows that just as sound does not arise when there is a deficiency in even one of its causes, such as the fingers and so forth, so too cognition (*buddhi*) does not arise when there is a deficiency in even one of its causes, such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth (vv.

32–34). Furthermore, by the very mention of the functions of cognition—that is, the various forms of knowledge—the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is also implied; for this cognition, which is associated with the self and other factors, takes the form "I see" and so on, being entirely dependent upon the ego-sense. Thus, since both cognition and the ego-sense have been mentioned, he speaks of the remaining unmanifest (*avyakta*) by way of its effects, beginning with the word "cognition" (*buddhi*).
"Supreme" (*param*) means the unmanifest (*avyakta*).

It is called "the bearer of yoga" (*yogadhara*) because it maintains the union (*yoga*) or conjunction of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the other [evolutes]. For the unmanifest, which is of the nature of *prakṛti*, being impelled by the purpose of the *puruṣa*, produces the conjunction of the intellect and so forth that accomplishes experience.
Having thus explained the group of twenty-four principles, he concludes with the words "the group of twenty-four," and so on.

Alternatively, having first mentioned the organs of action, the passage beginning with "the great elements" (*mahābhūtāni*) and so forth refers to the objects themselves by describing the ether and other elements as their substrates; whereas the passage beginning with "whatever sense-organ it relies upon" refers to the distinct modifications of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti-bheda*) that are clearly perceived. However, the intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and the unmanifest (*avyakta*)—which are subtle—are not explicitly mentioned here. All of these are subsequently referred to by the word "supreme" (*para*) in the passage beginning with "of the sense-organs, the mind, and the objects. Therefore, by the phrase "the supreme sustainer of yoga," both the root nature (*mūla-prakṛti*) and the seven principles that are both nature and modification (*prakṛti-vikṛti*), beginning with the Great One (*mahat*), are denoted; thus, there is a collection consisting of twenty-four principles.
And the state of being "other" (paratva) in relation to the modifications (vikāra) is indeed appropriate for the primal causes (prakṛti).
Now, he states the cause of the transmigratory existence of the Puruṣa of such a nature, as well as the cause of liberation, beginning with the words "rajaḥ" and so forth.
This "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) is the union consisting of the twenty-four principles;
by those two— namely, *rajas* and *tamas*—

through the increase of *sattva* acting as the cause, there occurs the cessation of *rajas* and *tamas*, whereby the conjunction in the form of the *puruṣa* ceases, meaning liberation (*mokṣa*) comes about.

When *sattva* has increased, by generating pure knowledge and thereby conquering *rajas* and *tamas*— which are the causes of transmigratory existence— it brings about liberation through the discriminative knowledge of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. (36) Furthermore, demonstrating the fruits of action and so forth in the *puruṣa* consisting of the twenty-four [principles], he shows the absence of the fruits of action and so forth in the *puruṣa* who is free from defects, beginning with the words "In this," etc.
"Result is here" means that in the person who is the aforementioned aggregate,
there is action; "action" refers to the unseen (adṛṣṭa), and "result" refers to the unseen result (adṛṣṭaphala).

Although the notions of "mine-ness" (*mamatā*), "I-ness" (*svatā*), and knowledge (*jñāna*) belong only to the indifferent [Puruṣa], who is distinct from the twenty-four principles, nevertheless, through identification with that [Puruṣa], even Prakṛti attains consciousness and becomes conscious itself; thus the statement "knowledge is here" is justified—indeed, as it is said: "Therefore, due to that conjunction, the insentient *liṅga* appears as if it were sentient" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 20).
(Thus, according to Kārikā 20:
"Dissolution and emergence" refer to life and death.

"Tradition" (pāramparya) refers to the succession of bodies and medical treatment; however, that which pertains to the ultimate goal—the absolute medical treatment for suffering and the means to liberation—is what must be understood.
By the phrase "whatever [is to be known]," this includes the entirety of all that is knowable, even that which has not been explicitly mentioned.
37–38. The answer to the question "Why is the Puruṣa the cause? begins with "Light, darkness," etc.; here, *bhās* means intuitive insight (*pratibhā*).
In this context, "man" refers to the self intended as the subject, while "darkness" and "delusion" refer to the body as their substratum.

Movement occurs from the pursuit of a purpose; likewise, coming [into being] also has the Puruṣa as its cause. Therefore, the meaning is that the Puruṣa is the cause in the case of light, darkness, truth, and so forth.
He states this very fact—that the Self is the cause of light and the rest—in the passage beginning with "na cet" (if not).

He thinks as follows: light and darkness are produced by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*); and since merit and demerit cannot exist without a substratum, they cannot exist in the absence of a self (*ātman*). Likewise, truth is to be adopted because it generates merit, while falsehood is to be rejected because it generates demerit; yet this capacity to generate merit and demerit does not exist if a permanent self is absent. Consequently, even the distinction between truth and falsehood is non-existent, as it serves no purpose. The same should be said regarding auspicious and inauspicious actions.
