Furthermore, there can be no agent who links causes together, because of the absence of a self that performs such linking. Similarly, there can be no cognizer who links prior and subsequent states. Moreover, the body, which is the locus of the self’s experience, cannot exist without a self. In this way, the self's causality with respect to pleasure and so forth should also be inferred. Knowledge—namely, the knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures—is such that the scriptures themselves were composed by a self that links [experiences] together.

"Knowledge would not be possible in these [objects]" means that without a self as the knower, knowledge could not arise in objects such as sound and so forth, because of the absence of a knowing self. "And there would be no purpose for them" means that since objects like sound exist for the sake of the self, in the absence of a self, there would be no purpose for the arising of those objects; and due to the absence of a purpose, their production would not occur. For in all cases, merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) residing in the self are the producers of all objects for the sake of the person's experience; when there is no experiencer, even the object of experience cannot come to be, due to the absence of its cause.
(Verses 39–42)
Regarding the non-arising of the body without a self, he provides two examples because of the weight of the subject matter: "made by a lump of clay, a staff," and so forth.
This means it is made by elements acting in combination through their instruments, independent of a self.

It is "devoid of reason and scripture" (*yuktyāgamabahiṣkṛta*), meaning it lacks both inference in the form of reasoning and authoritative tradition. Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not mentioned here, as it is generally unsuitable for establishing the existence of a self.
"By all means of valid cognition" (sarvaiḥ pramāṇaiḥ) refers to perception and so forth;
"from which" (yebhyaḥ) is in the ablative case (pañcamī), intended to express the source (apādāna) even though it functions as the instrument (karaṇa).

"Āgamas" are indeed means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because they cause one to come (*āgamayanti*) [to the truth] and awaken [the mind]; others, however, claim that "āgamas" are simply the treatises (*śāstra*) by virtue of being both [means of valid cognition and scriptures].
(45) He now sets forth the view of the proponents of non-self (*nirātmavādin*): "Not those," and so forth.

Regarding this body, what are those entities such as earth, water, and so forth that are designated by the word "those" (te)? They do not exist [in the sense that] they are not the same as those previously experienced, nor do they experience [now]; this is the meaning.
If they are not those, then how is there recognition (*abhijñāna*) of them as "those"? He says: "But others similar to them," meaning similar to the previous ones;
"arisen through succession" means established in a continuous stream of similarity.
"Due to similarity" means because they possess a similar form; "their collection" means the assemblage of those things which are subject to momentary destruction.
"Without a lord" means devoid of a permanent self.
"Called a sentient being" means "called a living creature"; some, namely the Buddhists, hold this view.

For the Buddhists maintain that the body is merely a collection of momentary cognitions and so forth, devoid of a self (*anātman*); and they maintain that even though these cognitions and so forth are momentary, there is a continuity (*pratisandhāna*) due to the cause-and-effect relationship among them within a single stream of results.
46–47 He refutes this with the words "of them," and so forth:

for those who maintain the doctrine of a continuum of consciousness (*jñānasantāna*), it would follow that others consume the fruit— such as food— of an act like cooking rice performed by someone else.

And this is inconsistent, because it is reasonable for one to engage in activity out of hope for a future result, thinking "I shall enjoy the fruit"; however, no one engages in activity while perceiving the fruit as something to be enjoyed by another. Even a cook or the like who acts for the sake of another does so only with the desire to achieve his own self-interest through that service to others—this is the point. (48) Having refuted the opponent's view, he states his own position with the words beginning with "karaṇa" (the instrument), etc.
The meaning is that while the body, which is the instrument of action, is seen to undergo transformation and thus become different at various times,
the self is the agent and is not subject to destruction. Regarding this very point, he provides an illustration, beginning with "For the agent," and so forth.

Just as a craftsman skilled in many arts performs the carving of wood or the forging of metal using tools such as a flute-shaped chisel, a pair of pincers, and a mechanical press, so too does the Self; this is the meaning.
(Verse 49) Now, let it be granted that the existence of this Self is stable; but what becomes of the elements that constitute the body? To this, he says: "In a twinkling," and so forth.
"Of entities" means of entities such as the body and so forth;
"passing away" means destruction. The meaning is that the destruction of the body, being cooked by its own internal fire, occurs even more swiftly than the blink of an eye.
And the meaning of "there is no further existence for these broken entities" is that there is no returning again.

By this, it is stated that the body by which an action was performed does not obtain its fruit. Now, [the opponent] might say, "Let it be so; what of it? To this, he says: "The performed," and so forth. An action such as a sacrifice (*yāga*) performed does not pass over to another in the form of its fruit. This being the case, even Yajñadatta and others would become partakers of happiness through the auspicious action performed by Devadatta. Therefore, the intended meaning is that there exists a performer of action and enjoyer of its fruit who is distinct from the body that perishes in every moment.
"Action and enjoyment" refers to [the involvement] of living beings— that is, of sentient creatures— in action and in the enjoyment of its fruit. 50–51.
He states another reason for the existence of the self: "Egoity," and so forth.

The meaning is that these [qualities], beginning with egoity, exist only in a permanent supreme self (*paramātman*), because they are attributes of an entity that persists through prior and subsequent times.
"Apart from the body" means without the body; the sense is that egoity arises when there exists a cause distinct from the body.
The answer to the question “What is the origin of the person? is as follows: “Origin,” and so forth;
“origin” means the cause.
"Known as a heap" (*rāśi*) means having the nature of an aggregate of the six elements, or having the form of the twenty-four heaps;
it is born from karma produced by delusion, desire, and hatred—that is, born from delusion, desire, and hatred.

For indeed, from delusion toward entities, desire and hatred arise; from those, activity (*pravṛtti*) arises; from activity, merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*); and these two produce a body for the sake of experience.
53. The answer to the question “Is the ignorant one [the same as] the knowing one? is: “The Self,” etc.;
here, the instruments are the mind, the intellect, and the sense organs.
The construction is: "knowledge does not function.
Now, if this self is indeed a knower, why is it that knowledge does not occur for it at all times? To this he says: "Even though seeing," and so forth.
"Even though seeing" means even though possessing eyes.
The term "tattva" (reality) is a qualification of "darśana" (perception);
thus, the meaning is that even if a perception occurs in a tarnished mirror or in water, it does not possess the nature of reality because it apprehends things incorrectly.

The mention of "in the mind" (*cetasi*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); by this, it should be understood that [the condition applies] when the eyes and other sense organs are also impaired.

Since the topic of instruments (*karaṇa*) has been introduced, he now states what constitutes the instrument of the self with respect to cognition (*jñāna*), action (*karman*), and feeling (*vedanā*): "The instruments," and so forth;
[the phrase] "born of conjunction" (*saṃyogaja*) is to be construed with action, feeling, and intellect (*buddhi*).
"One does not enjoy the fruit" is how it should be construed;
"one" refers to one who is without instruments (karaṇa),
[yet] he exists through association, meaning he arises from the collection of instruments.
"Without that [cause], there is no conjunction" (56–57).
Right here, he states the justification for all effects being produced by a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), beginning with "For not one... and so forth.

The meaning is that a single entity, being of the nature of a cause, does not exist in the production of an effect when devoid of other auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*). Thus, first of all, a single cause does not exist in the effect; and he says, "nor does it exist without a cause," meaning that an entity characterized by the property of arising does not exist—that is, it does not come into being—without a cause. Therefore, it is stated that the effect, produced from a self endowed with the instruments of action, does not arise from the self alone in its capacity as a cause.
Now, if an entity does not exist without a cause, then does the absence of corporeal entities also depend upon a cause or not? To this he says: "Because of its swift motion," and so forth.
Because it is characterized by the nature of swift motion, an absence does not transcend that nature; the meaning is that it does not abandon the nature of swift motion.
Therefore, absence occurs entirely without a cause, whereas an entity possesses a cause.
For it has been said: "The cause for the arising of entities exists, but there is no cause for their cessation" (Sūtrālaṃkāra 16).
Alternatively, the meaning of the text is that because of its rapid movement and instability, non-existence does not proceed toward the destruction of the self as a distinct state.

The answer to the question “Is that eternal or non-eternal? is as follows: “Beginningless,” and so forth. The meaning is: the Puruṣa, which is beginningless, unmanifest in form, and denoted by the word *ātman*, is the opposite—that is, the Puruṣa who is a heap possessing a beginning.
In this very context, he also cites the consensus of other treatises regarding the eternity of the beginningless: "The existent," and so forth.

By the term "existent" (sat), which refers to that which is of the nature of a positive entity (bhāva) accessible through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) across the three types of time, it is shown that the non-eternality of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)—despite its lack of a cause—is not a case of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), since it is nonetheless of the nature of a non-entity (*abhāva*).
Regarding the phrase "otherwise it is produced by a cause," here too it should be construed as being of the nature of an existent entity (*bhāvarūpa*);
by this, the non-perishability of even that destruction which is produced by a cause is avoided.
To the question "What is that permanence?", he says: "That very [nature]," and so forth.
That permanence does not arise from any entity characterized by the property of origination; for that which is eternal does not arise from anything whatsoever.

Furthermore, because the Self is independent of all states of being, it exists eternally even prior to all states; and such a Self, being eternal and unmanifest, is to be known as inconceivable— this is the qualification of the Unmanifest.

The unmanifest (*avyakta*) is the root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), while the manifest (*vyakta*) is otherwise; thus, any effect of nature, such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth, is impermanent. Space (*ākāśa*) also is indeed impermanent, as it is of the nature of a transformation (*vikāra*). But the indifferent Spirit (*puruṣa*), being eternal, is indicated by the very term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*); this has already been stated.
Now, he states synonyms that pervade other attributes of the unmanifest, beginning with "the unmanifest," and so on.
Furthermore, he states the meaning of the manifest and unmanifest by way of another method, beginning with "it will be explained," and so forth.
"The other pair" refers to the pair of the manifest and unmanifest produced by another method;
"to be grasped by the mark" means to be grasped by inference.

By the term "beyond the senses" (atīndriya), that which is ungraspable by the senses and is not perceived by any sign such as sound or the like is not what is meant by the "unmanifest" (avyakta); rather, it is precisely that which is eternally inferable, such as the mind (manas) and the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra).
The answer to the question "What is primordial nature (prakṛti)? What are the transformations (vikāra)? is given by the words "the ether and so forth," etc.
The subtle elements (khādīni) are the subtle forms of the gross elements, denoted by the term *tanmātra*;
the intellect (*buddhi*) is denoted by the term *mahat*;
and the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is the root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*).
Ego (ahaṅkāra) is a modification of the intellect (buddhi); it is threefold: the "origin of elements" (bhūtādi), the "fiery" (taijasa), and the "transformative" (vaikārika).
Here, the "origin of elements" refers to the material cause of all beings, both stationary and moving;

in this context, the Unmanifest (avyakta) alone is the ultimate material cause, yet the intellect and the others—though they are modifications of their own causes—are also described here as "material causes" insofar as they serve as the material basis for their own effects.

Regarding what was stated—“Root nature is not a transformation; the seven, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), are both nature and transformation” (Sāṃkhyakārikā 3)—he speaks of the transformations, saying "the transformations," and so forth.
The word *eva* is placed out of its natural order for the sake of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*); thus, the sixteen are indeed only transformations and are not, ultimately, natures (*prakṛti*).
The sense organs of the intellect are the "intellectual organs" (buddhīndriyāṇi).

The five objects are the gross elements, such as ether and the rest, appearing in the form of sound and so forth. For in this philosophical system, there is indeed no ultimate difference between a quality and that which possesses the quality.

He now divides this very aggregate of nature (prakṛti) and its modifications (vikāra) according to the distinction between the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña)—beginning with "Thus," etc.
The phrase "excluding the unmanifest" means excluding that which is indifferent to nature; for nature indeed possesses consciousness through the consciousness of the indifferent Puruṣa.

Now, he explains how the production of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the other faculties occurs at the beginning of creation following the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*): "It is born," and so forth.

The meaning is that one thinks "I" by means of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) produced from the intellect; thus, one conceives "I" through the intellect. "The [elements] beginning with space" refers to the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) in the form of space and the rest, as well as the eleven sense organs.

For the statement—“From *prakṛti* arises the Great One (*mahat*); from that, the ego (*ahaṅkāra*); from that, the group of sixteen” (Sāṃkhya Kārikā 22)—is according to the sequence, meaning by the order in which they arise from the ego. In this regard, from the modified (*vaikṛta*) or *sāttvika* ego, assisted by the *taijasa*, the eleven organs arise; whereas from the elemental (*bhūtādi*) or *tāmasa* ego, assisted by the *taijasa*, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) arise, as it has been said: “The group of eleven, characterized by *sattva*, proceeds from the modified (*vaikṛta*) ego.”
"From *bhūtādi* comes the subtle element (*tanmātra*), which is *tāmasa*; from *taijasa*, both [arise]" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 25).

Regarding the word "thence" (*tataḥ*), it means that immediately after the effects of the *ahaṃkāra*, through the connection with the gross elements produced from the subtle elements (*tanmātras*), he was born with all his limbs complete; thus he was born in the initial creation (*ādisarga*).

Having thus shown the creation of the intellect (*mahat*) and the rest from primordial nature (*prakṛti*) at the beginning of creation, he describes the dissolution of the intellect and the other faculties into primordial nature— which exists in an unmanifest form— during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), starting with the words "the person" (*puruṣa*).
The phrase "by means of desired states" (*iṣṭair bhāvaiḥ*) refers to the intellect and so forth, which are desired for the sake of the experience of the person (*puruṣa*).
Others, however, claim that attachment to such states occurs at birth and the dissociation from the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties occurs at death;
but that is not so, because the intellect and the rest persist through both birth and death.
For it has been said: "The self has never before been separated from those [faculties], which are beyond the senses and of an extremely subtle nature."
"Neither by the senses, nor by the mind and intellect, nor even by the defects of the transformations of the ego. (Śāstradīpikā 2)

Likewise, it is stated elsewhere: “The *liṅga*—arisen previously, unattached, determinate, consisting of [the principles] from the Great One (*mahat*) down to the subtle elements (*sūkṣma*), devoid of experience, and perfumed by dispositions (*bhāva*)—migrates. (Sāṃkhyakārikā 40)

40) Therefore, dissolution into *prakṛti* occurs only at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), and likewise, the creation of the *mahat* and other principles from *prakṛti* occurs only at the beginning of creation (*ādisarga*).
To elaborate upon this very process of the manifestation and dissolution of *prakṛti*, he says: "From the unmanifest," and so forth.

"From the unmanifest" means from *prakṛti*; "to the state of manifestation" means it attains the form of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) and ending with the gross elements (*mahābhūta*); "from the manifest" means from the state consisting of the phenomenal world of the gross elements, it again attains and goes back to the state of the unmanifest. For at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), the gross elements dissolve into the subtle elements (*tanmātra*); likewise, the subtle elements and the sense organs dissolve into the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*); the ego-principle dissolves into the intellect (*buddhi*), and the intellect dissolves into *prakṛti*. This sequence of dissolution also occurs in the case of liberation (*mokṣa*).
However, in that state, primordial nature (*prakṛti*) does not again initiate creation toward that person;
as to why this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) occurs, he says "passion" (*rajas*), etc.,
meaning "possessed" (*āviṣṭaḥ*), i.e., joined with.
"It revolves like a wheel" means it is joined again and again with dissolution and creation;
"the pair" refers to the couple consisting of *rajas* and *tamas*; "intent on egoism" means they are intent on false knowledge such as "this is mine" arising from egoism (*ahaṅkāra*).

Arising and dissolution are birth and death, or alternatively, they are the creation and the reabsorption [of the world]; however, for those who are free from passion and hatred and devoid of egoism, neither arising nor dissolution occurs. (67–69)
The answer to the question, "What is the mark (liṅga) of the Puruṣa? is as follows: "Inhalation and exhalation," and so forth.
"Inhalation and exhalation" refers to the out-breath and the in-breath.
By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (ādi) in the phrase "winking and so forth," specific types of glancing, such as opening the eyes and others, are understood.
"The movement of the mind" refers to the mind's journey to places such as Pāṭaliputra;

likewise, the transition between other sense organs is also solely that of the mind— for instance, it should be understood that the impulse by which the mind, having abandoned the eye, presides over the sense of touch, as well as its subsequent retention, belong to the mind alone.
"Movement to another place in a dream"—this is the analysis [of the compound].
"Grasping the state of being five" means the cognition of death.
"Cognition by the left" means the cognition by the left eye that "this very same jar seen by the right eye is this one"; such is the meaning.

Volition is mere cognition, whereas intellect (*buddhi*) is the knowledge of deliberation and exclusion (*ūhāpoha*); now, how do these lead one to understand the self? To this he says: "Because," and so forth.

Regarding the term "living": although the state of being composed of the five elements (*pañcatva*) does not occur in one who is living—since such a state belongs only to the dead, as it involves a separation from the self that transcends the five elements—nevertheless, the observation of this "fivefoldness" in a dead body serves as a mark (*liṅga*) for the living body by way of contrast, namely through the absence of such fivefoldness in the living. It should be understood that the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), downward breath (*apāna*), and so forth, cited in this very context, do not belong to the mere elements alone, because they are not observed in soulless things such as bricks or dead bodies.
Nor can the mind alone be the Self as something distinct from the elements, because it too, being of the nature of an instrument, must have an agent to impel it and so forth.

Nor can the sense organs be accepted as the Self, for if that were the case, the sense organs would not be capable of synthesizing an object perceived by another sense organ—just as Devadatta cannot synthesize an object perceived by Yajñadatta. Yet there is indeed such synthesis of objects perceived by different senses, as in the instance: "I touch the fragrant sandalwood."
Therefore, it should be understood that the Self exists as something distinct from the mind and the senses;

for although by the word "intellect" (buddhi) consciousness, resolve, memory, and ego-sense are indeed included as modes of the intellect, they are nevertheless mentioned separately because they signify distinct objects.

For instance: volition (cetanā), as a quality, indicates the self through its nature as a non-material attribute distinct from insentient elements such as earth; sustenance (dhṛti), being of the nature of restraint, indicates the self as a controller; intellect (buddhi), moreover, indicates the self as the single cause of both reasoning (ūha) and exclusion (apoha); and memory (smṛti) indicates the self as a stable entity that remembers objects previously experienced—such points should be followed accordingly.
Regarding the absence of vital breaths and so forth in the body when there is no presiding self, he says "the body," etc.: just as an empty house is devoid of an inhabitant, so too is a dead body.

The body consists of six elements; when the sixth element, the self (*ātman*), has departed, the body remains composed of the five gross elements (*pañcabhūta*). Therefore, it is said that [the body] has "gone to the state of the five" (*pañcatva*).
(Verses 70–74) In response to the question, "How can there be action for that which is inactive? the text says: "It is insentient," and so forth.
"The other is the volitional agent" means that the supreme self is the volitional agent, but it is not directly the possessor of action. [Objection:
If this is so, how can there be action belonging to it? [Response: He says "of the one joined," etc.;
the meaning is that the action belongs to the mind alone when presided over by the self, yet it is called the "action of the self" by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

He establishes this very point with the words beginning "one who possesses consciousness" (cetanāvān), etc. For the mind, presided over by a conscious self (ātman), engages in activities; however, the mind not presided over by consciousness does not engage in activities. Therefore, it is appropriate to designate that which performs an action as the "possessor of action," but not the insentient mind. The meaning of the sentence is that, because its activity is dependent on another, even though it is in reality possessed of action, it is not called an "agent" (kartṛ) in the ultimate sense; the word "is not called" implies the word "agent. (75–76)
Now he addresses the objection that even in the state of independence, one might fall into undesirable wombs: "As by his own... and so forth.

In all wombs—whether human, bovine, elephantine, insect, or otherwise—he governs by means of his vital breaths (*prāṇaiḥ*), that is, he joins himself with vital breaths. By himself alone, aided by merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), this self leads itself through all wombs; it does not go impelled by another. For there is no other person who is its instigator, due to the non-existence of a Lord (*īśvara*); or, even if a Lord exists, because He too is dependent upon karma.

And this very thing constitutes his independence regarding the entering into undesirable wombs: namely, independence in performing unrighteousness (*adharma*), which is the cause for entering undesirable wombs. For even though he does not desire it, he is led by his own karma initiated through the performance of unrighteousness, and thus the entering into an undesirable womb occurs. And his independence is as previously stated. [In response to the question: "If he is self-controlled (*vaśī*), why is he overcome by states that are unpleasant?"—the answer begins with "self-controlled," etc. (verse 77).

"Vaśī" means one whose activity is under his own control (whether toward the desirable or the undesirable). Thus, being self-controlled, he performs those actions—whether auspicious or inauspicious—due to attachment to immediate results, having performed which he attains union with a result, whether auspicious or inauspicious, through the power of that action.
By this, his mastery (*vaśitva*) over the action to be performed is shown, whereas the fruit of the performed action occurs even against his will. Therefore, he has no mastery over that [result].
He states another result of mastery: "Being self-controlled, he concentrates the mind."

Being self-controlled (*vaśī*), he turns back the mind from undesirable objects; for if he were not self-controlled, he would not be able to turn back the mind. He states another action that indicates self-control: "Being self-controlled, he casts everything aside.
This means that being self-controlled, he who has set out for the sake of liberation abandons every undertaking, whether it bears auspicious or inauspicious fruit.

In this context, one who is independent (*svatantra*) is said to have an activity impelled by another, such as God (*īśvara*). One who possesses mastery (*vaśin*), however, acts even by himself according to his own will; he does not act merely through an activity impelled by another regarding what is desired or undesired. Thus is the distinction between independence and mastery. (78) He provides the answer to the question, "Since [the Lord] is omnipresent, why does he not perceive all sensations? with the verse beginning with *dehī* and so forth.

The construction is as follows: although it is "all-pervading" (*sarvagata*), even while being all-pervading, it "experiences sensations"—that is, sensations in the form of pleasure and pain—only within the body endowed with the sense of touch (*saṃsparśana-indriya*); it does not experience those situated in all substrates.

The meaning of the sentence is that because the self, though all-pervading, experiences sensation only in its own body which possesses the sense of touch, it therefore does not experience all sensations situated in all substrates;
"situated in all substrates" means those located in the bodies of others.
Furthermore, in another body, although the self exists, it does not perceive pleasure and pain because of the absence of sense organs acquired through its own karma;

while it should have been stated that this occurs "in one's own respective bodies," the author uses the term "at the organ of touch" (saṃsparśanendriye) to show that even within one's own body, the self perceives nothing where the organ of touch is absent, such as in the hair or nails.

In order to provide an answer to the question, “Why does the omnipresent one not see? and so forth, he proceeds to establish the omnipresence of the self by first establishing that very omnipresence through the attainment of the causal qualities that prove omnipresence—beginning with the words “Omnipresence,” etc. “Omnipresence” means the possession of an all-pervading dimension;
“for this very reason” means because of the aforementioned all-pervasiveness.
To clarify this very point, he states directly: "Because... and so forth.

Since all-pervasiveness (*sarvagatatva*) belongs even to things such as space (*ākāśa*), which possess a magnitude that is perceived everywhere, the word "great" (*mahān*) is used to exclude those. Consequently, the result is that an omnipresent substance (*vibhu*) is defined as a substance possessing a great magnitude that is perceived everywhere.
Having thus established omnipresence, he says "of the mind," etc., demonstrating that knowledge obstructed by walls and the like does not occur invariably.
"Samādhi" means concentration;
by this, he shows that through the power of samādhi, yogis perceive even that which is concealed.
Regarding those who do not perceive what is concealed, he states the logical justification for that as well, beginning with "nitya... and so forth.
One should understand that even though the Self has entered all wombs, it remains situated in a single womb through the mind which follows its connection; this is how the construction should be made.

By that mind—which follows the body and its actions and is connected to the Self by means of the karma that brings about the body—even though the Self is not concealed by walls and such, because the mind, which is the instrument for perceiving it, is restricted to a single body, one does not see it when it is obstructed; this is what is meant.

The answer to the question beginning with “Is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) or the Field (kṣetra) the first? is as follows: by the words “the first” and so forth, [it is meant that] there is no designation such as “this is the first of the Field and the Knower of the Field,” because the lineage of the Field—consisting of the twenty-three principles beginning with the Great One (mahat), excluding the Unmanifest (avyakta)—is indeed beginningless due to its continuous succession. This is the meaning.

Objection: If the succession of fields (*kṣetra-paramparā*) is also beginningless, then, like the self (*ātman*), its destruction would not occur; for that which is beginningless is eternal, as is seen in the case of the self. We reply: Even though it is beginningless, that which is beginningless by its very nature is not destroyed, such as the self. However, that which has the property of being subject to destruction, such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, is indeed destroyed. Furthermore, in the ultimate sense, the continuum (*santāna*) does not exist as something distinct from the members of the continuum (*santānin*); if it were [distinct], it might be beginningless. Therefore, the beginninglessness of the continuum is merely figurative.
Furthermore, regarding the cessation of such a continuum of cognition and so forth, the scripture that establishes liberation must be understood as the very authority [for this].
As for the question, "And of what is this the witness?", the answer is: "The Knower," and so on.

In the world, one who knows, who possesses knowledge, is called a witness (*sākṣin*), but not one who lacks knowledge, such as a stone or the like. Therefore, the meaning of the statement for all [the elements], beginning with ether (*kha*), is that it is called a "witness" by virtue of its being a knower, even though there may be no other agent.
"All phenomena" means all elemental properties that are fit for vision;
"attested by oneself" means perceived by the self.

The answer to the question beginning with “How could there be [change] for the immutable? is as follows: “Not one,” and so forth. The meaning of the statement is that for the immutable Supreme Self (paramātman), there is no distinction whatsoever produced by cognition; however, where there is a distinction produced by cognition, that is of the nature of an aggregate (rāśi) and is indeed distinct from the Supreme Self. The Self that presides over the elements is the "Self of the elements" (bhūtātman). This Self of the elements is not perceived as a single entity distinct from the elements through the aforementioned characteristics such as the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
To the question "Why is it not perceived? he says: "The particular," and so forth.

This refers to the single [self] devoid of the elements. Since no particularity of the self, such as sensation and so on, is perceived at all, the meaning is that non-perception itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in this case.
The person consisting of the conjunction [of the elements] is composed of twenty-four [principles].

[Objection: Even so, the elemental self (*bhūtātman*) included within the twenty-four [principles] must also possess a specific quality produced by sensation (*vedanā*), because the property of a whole belongs only to its constituent parts—just as the weight of a heap of beans arises from the weight of each individual bean. To this he says: "Sensation," and so forth.
Sensation consists of pleasure and pain;

wherever it is fixed and established—that is, in that very aggregate of intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest—the specific qualities such as dejection and joy produced by that sensation are also fixed. The point is that these reside only in that aggregate of intellect and the rest, and not in the self (*ātman*).

The self (*ātman*), which is indeed devoid of pleasure and pain, becomes possessed of pleasure, pain, and so forth through its connection with that which resides in the intellect (*buddhi*)— namely, pleasure, pain, and so on, which consist of the transformation of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*).
(Verses 84–85) Alternatively, he provides the answer to the question beginning with "Now, for one who is suffering" (*athavā ārtasya*) and so forth, starting with "He treats" (*cikitsati*) and so on.
The meaning of the sentence is that treatment for past sensations is not primary; rather, it is spoken of by way of conventional usage well-known in the world.
Thus, "treatment according to each action" refers to medical treatment expressed through words commonly known in the world.
Regarding the term "basis" (*āśraya*), by stating "in the body" and "premonitory signs" (*pūrvarūpa*) and so forth, he establishes the treatment of future sensations;
for although premonitory signs belong only to diseases that are yet to come, nevertheless, by the word "future," he excludes those signs which occur even when a disease has already manifested.

For it has been said: "Even before the onset of distress, moreover, they follow him who is afflicted by distress" (Nirukta 1.1); by this, the presence of premonitory symptoms even during the stage of manifest disease is indicated.

Thus, having explained the medical treatment for past and future feelings, he states the ultimate view while also demonstrating the treatment for the present: "By way of succession," and so forth; "succession" (pāramparyānubandha) means a continuous connection by way of a stream (santāna).
"Of sufferings" means of diseases;
"by the application of the causes of happiness" means by the practice of medical treatment which has health as its cause;
"happiness" means health.

He thinks as follows: when medical treatment, which is a cause of happiness, is practiced, then suffering does not arise because of the absence of the practice of causes of suffering; and the suffering already arisen, in the form of disease, perishes by itself due to its momentary nature (*kṣaṇabhaṅgitva*). Because of the presence of the causes of happiness, happiness in the form of health arises. Therefore, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that through medical treatment, future suffering is ceased by way of obstructing its causes, and happiness is produced.
He states this very point in the words beginning with "not equal" (*na samā*).

The meaning is that both the balanced (*sama*) and the imbalanced (*viṣama*) states do not transition into a state of imbalance or a state of balance because their inherent nature is momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgitva*).
Thus, they are "similar to their causes": they are balanced due to a balanced cause, and likewise, they are imbalanced due to an imbalanced cause;
this has indeed been explained in detail in the chapter on *Cikitsāprābhṛta*.
In the context of medical treatment, he describes the treatment that removes all suffering and has liberation as its fruit, beginning with the words "But the treatment...

"Finality" (niṣṭhā) means the absolute release from suffering, which is the nature of liberation. "Aimed at that finality" (naiṣṭhikī) means without attachment (upadhā); the meaning is that activity devoid of craving results in the fruit of liberation.
86–94. "The other cause" refers to the root cause;
the body, which is the substratum of suffering, exists precisely in the form of suffering.

For one who proceeds with thirst for enjoyments (*bhogatṛṣṇā*) takes up merit and demerit (*dharmādharmān*) which produce a body of suffering; but by the renunciation of all substrates (*sarvopadhātyāga*), one does not proceed anywhere out of passion or aversion. Not proceeding, one does not take up merit and demerit; thus there is the cessation of future merit and demerit. As for the merit and demerit already taken up, their exhaustion occurs through experience alone for one who is devoid of passion and aversion. Therefore, the sense is that through the complete exhaustion of karma, there is an absence of the body of suffering. Regarding this very point—that thirst is the cause of suffering—he states an illustration beginning with "the silkworm" (*koṣakāra*).
The silkworm, a well-known insect by its own name,
is "always afflicted" (sadātura), meaning it is perpetually seized by the suffering of saṃsāra;
"due to non-undertaking" means due to the absence of undertaking actions preceded by passion and hatred.

"Because of non-union" means because of the absence of union with a body, brought about by the destruction of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) through the emptiness of [renewed] undertaking; and the sense is that in the absence of a body, suffering—which is without a substratum and lacks a cause—does not exist.
(Verses 95–97) He provides the answer to the question "What is the cause of sensations? with the verse beginning "Intellect, fortitude," and so forth.
And this point, being stated as it arises from the context, does not entail redundancy; for wisdom, fortitude, and mindfulness are varieties of *prajñā*,
and these are described here as distinct types of *prajñā* in order to facilitate the student's understanding, having been explained otherwise [previously].

"Samprāpti refers to the arrival of time and of actions. Thus, the arrival of time (*kāla-samprāpti*) as well as the arrival of actions (*karma-samprāpti*)—meaning the conjunction with actions that are currently ripening—is intended here by the term "arrival of time.

By this inclusion of the arrival of time, those [diseases] manifested by time are included, though they are not necessarily produced by time alone. For he will later describe even those that are natural (*svābhāvika*), as well as tertian fevers (*tṛtīyaka*) and others produced by unwholesome contact of the senses with their objects, as being "born of time" (*kāla-ja*).

However, those born of karma—which are indeed produced by intellectual error (*prajñāparādha*)—are mentioned separately here specifically as "born of karma" for the sake of the student's understanding; furthermore, because they are manifested by time, those born of karma should be included among the conditions arising from the arrival of time (*kālasamprāpti*).
And just as there is an inclusion of intellectual error within those born of karma, so it was stated in the very first chapter.
Moreover, the Teacher himself stated in the *Unmādanidāna* (The Etiology of Insanity): "When a disease arises from intellectual error, it is [considered] born of karma for the self" (Ni.).

7) And so forth; likewise, in the *Janapadoddhvaṃsanīya* chapter, it is further stated in the *Vimāna* section: “Whatever deficiency arises in the wind and other elements, its root is unrighteousness (*adharma*), or its root is improper action (*asatkarma*) performed in the past; the source of these two is precisely the error of intellect (*prajñāparādha*).
Therefore, by the statement “here [diseases] arise from time and karma,” diseases produced by time are not being spoken of, but rather those manifested by time.
He explains the failure of intellect (*dhīvibhraṃśa*) with the words beginning "viṣama" and so forth:

"A distorted adherence" (*viṣamābhiniveśaḥ*) is a determination (*adhyavasāna*) of things as they are not, such as [perceiving] the permanent as impermanent; likewise, whatever cognition takes the beneficial to be harmful, or the harmful to be beneficial—that is the failure of intellect.

Now, as to why this is called "confusion of the intellect" (*buddhivibhraṃśa*), he says: "For the intellect sees equally. Since the appropriate intellect sees things equally, according to reality (*yathābhūtam*), therefore the perception of inequality is indeed a confusion of the intellect; such is the meaning. (Verse 99) He speaks of the confusion of fortitude (*dhṛtibhraṃśa*) with the words beginning "objects," etc.

The meaning is as follows: since *dhṛti* (fortitude) is by nature restrictive (*niyamātmikā*), it is intended to restrain—that is, to turn back—the mind that is inclined toward objects and attached to them; for *dhṛti* turns back the mind from engagement in what should not be done by its very essence. Therefore, the sense is that *dhṛti* which is unable to effect the restraint of the mind falls away from its own function.
100 He analyzes the loss of mindfulness (*smṛtibhraṃśa*): the construction is that it refers to one whose mindfulness regarding the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) has fallen away.
For that which is to be remembered resides in memory; thus, the recollection of an object accepted as being worthy of remembrance is the characteristic of excellent memory.

In this regard, the meaning is that the non-recollection of the knowledge of reality—which is accepted by the learned as an object worthy of remembrance—occurs due to a lapse in memory (smṛtyaparādha).

Thus, demonstrating that action produced by the three types of impairment—beginning with the impairment of the intellect—is itself an intellectual error (*prajñāparādha*), he says "by [impaired] intellect," and so forth.

By the word "all defects" (*sarvadoṣa*), wind and the other humors, as well as *rajas* and *tamas*, are included. "Transgression of the time for action" means the passing of the proper time for medical treatment.
"False undertaking" refers to improper application, excessive application, and perverse application;

furthermore, although [offenses] are already included by the transgression of disciplined conduct (*vinayācāra*), that which is specifically mentioned as "assaulting those worthy of honor" and so forth is for the purpose of demonstrating its particular provocation and as an illustrative example.
"By those of afflicted karma" means by those who have fallen [from their vows].
"Defiled" means censured.
(102–108) He states the definition of the transgression of wisdom in brief, beginning with "by the intellect," and so forth.
"Inappropriate" (*viṣama*) means improper. Erroneous cognition (*viṣamavijñāna*) is, by its very nature, a transgression of wisdom (*prajñāparādha*).
Furthermore, erroneous engagement (*viṣamapravartana*) is designated by the term "transgression of wisdom" because it is the effect of such a transgression.

For that [engagement] is within the range of the mind; thus, the meaning is that both that erroneous engagement and erroneous cognition fall within the range of the mind, as they are objects of the wisdom that is the mind's activity.

The "unequal engagement" [of speech and body] is stated metaphorically because it is produced by the objects of the mind; for from a cognition of dissimilar mental objects, an unequal engagement of speech and body also occurs. (109) He states the arrival of diseases at their specific time: "nirdiṣṭa... and so forth.

Regarding the "Summary of Diseases" (*vyādhisaṅgraha*), it is stated in the chapter on "The Head" (*kiyantaḥśirasīya*): "The accumulation, provocation, and pacification of pitta and the other [humors] occur respectively, one by one, during the six seasons beginning with the arrival of the clouds" (*Sūtra* 17);
this is so both by this statement and by way of illustration.
Therefore, it should be applied that the onset of diseases, as well as the accumulation, provocation, and pacification of *pitta* and the other humors, were previously described.

He states another example beginning with "wrongly" (*mithyā*) and so on; in the passage beginning with "digested" (*jīrṇa*), "time" refers to the period characterized by the three stages of food such as digestion, while "non-time" for food is characterized by stages such as indigestion (*ajīrṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "the three watches of the night when [food] is digested or indigested," it should be understood that these are three parts consisting of the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch of the night, rather than the *yāma* being a *prahara* (a three-hour period).
Furthermore, in other contexts as well, the term *triyāmā* (three-watch) for the night is used in the science of grammar (*abhidhāna-śāstra*) by dividing the night into three *yāmas*.

"At those times" refers to periods such as when food has been digested; it should be understood that wind-born diseases occur when digestion is complete, during the afternoon, or at the end of the night; phlegm-born diseases occur immediately after eating, during the forenoon, or in the early part of the night; and bile-born diseases are fixed to occur when digestion is incomplete, at midday, or at midnight; furthermore, when there is no desire for food due to the symptoms of indigestion, all three doshas become aggravated by eating.

Alternatively, the analysis of the compound may be ‘the times of food that has been digested, is being digested, and has been fully digested’ (*jīrṇa-bhukta-prajīrṇa-anna-kālā*); by this, the times of food associated with the states of digestion and so forth should be understood as before. Likewise, the construction is ‘and whatever is the stability of time’ (*kāla-sthitiś ca yā*). By the term ‘stability of time,’ the threefold division of age such as childhood and so forth is expressed;
it should be understood that in childhood, diseases of the phlegm (*śleṣman*) increase, in youth, those of the bile (*pitta*), and in old age, those of the wind (*vāta*).
Showing that even irregular fevers (*viṣamajvara*) are considered timely (*kāla-ja*) by virtue of occurring only at specific times, he says: "The quotidian (*anyedyuṣka*), etc.
[and] the *dvyahagrāhī* (occurring every two days), which is the reverse of the quartan (*caturthaka-viparyaya*).
For he will say: "Another irregular fever is indeed the *caturthaka-viparyaya*."

Regarding the statement, "It causes fever at midday and releases [the patient] at the beginning and end [of the day]," he explains how they manifest specifically at their own times: "For the arrival of their strength occurs at their [respective] time."
Because they become powerful at the very time [of their manifestation] that has been described, the meaning is that, having become strong precisely then, they manifest themselves.
(113) He states the sequence of treatment for these: "And these... and so forth.
By the phrase "and others," he indicates other [diseases] such as swelling (śotha) and leprosy (kuṣṭha), which manifest upon reaching specific stages of time.

Since even those factors that are innate (*svābhāvika*) are manifested through the transformation of time, he says "of time," etc., in order to include them here within the category of time-born (*kāla-ja*). "Born from the causes of old age and death" (*jarāmṛtyu-nimittaja*) means born from the causes consisting of old age and death. Here, by the word "death" (*mṛtyu*), one should understand the death at the end of the lifespan corresponding to the particular *yuga*. Alternatively, "born from the causes of old age and death" means born from whatever is the cause of old age and death. And the cause of old age and death for living beings consists of both the nature of the elements that produce the common body and *adṛṣṭa* (unseen karma). Now, he asks: what is the treatment for those that are innate? He says: "nature," etc.

"Incurable" means that it cannot be remedied by common treatments, excluding *rasāyana* therapy; however, it can indeed be remedied by *rasāyana*. Therefore, there is no contradiction with such statements as, "By its use, Cyavana, though very old, became young again" (*Cikitsā-sthāna*, Chapter 1, Section 1), which refer to the application of *rasāyana*. Alternatively, natural conditions such as old age are said to be incurable because they inevitably recur even after the excellence produced by *rasāyana* has passed.
Now, demonstrating that even a disease produced by the acquisition of karma is manifested through a specific time, he says: "nirdiṣṭam" and so forth.
The meaning is that karma becomes the cause [of disease] when it is joined with time, characterized as being in the process of ripening (*pacyamānatā*).
He states the rule regarding the connection between an action and its fruit, beginning with "na hi" and so forth.
By the qualification "mahat" (great), he shows that some small action, whose fruit is to be suppressed by expiation, does not indeed yield its fruit.
He states the incurability of those diseases born of karma with the words "kriyāghnā" and so forth;
"tatkṣayāt" means from the exhaustion of karma; and the exhaustion of karma occurs primarily only through the experience of the fruits of that karma.
He explains the unwholesome contact with sense objects that has come down through tradition: "excessively intense," etc.;
"not in every way" means because the word "intense" is not heard in all cases;
"of tangible things" refers to those mentioned in the treatise as being tangible, such as oil massage, rubbing, and so forth.

The construction is as follows: it refers to the contact with the poisons of spirits (*bhūta*), worms, and *śāca* and so forth; likewise, it includes the contact with oiliness, cold, or heat that occurs at an improper time.

In this context, contact with oiliness at an improper time is, for example, the application of anointing oil when digestion is incomplete and phlegm is increasing; similarly, contact with cold during the cold season, or contact with heat during the hot season, should be understood as occurring at an improper time.
The connection is as follows: "Because of non-perception in every respect" means because luminous and subtle objects are not perceived at all;
"extremely close" means adjacent to the eyes;
and "because of the perception of dark-colored forms, vision perishes. Thus is the construction.
That is false application (*mithyāyoga*), consisting of the perception of things such as the two-faced Bhairava;
furthermore, the perception of what is extremely subtle should be known as false application itself.
The connection is that "the taking of unwholesome food" [occurs] by means of factors such as place and suitability (*okasātmya*).
Due to the discordance of habitat, suitability, and so forth—excluding the defects of the zodiac signs (*rāśi*)—the seven defects beginning with *prakṛti* (nature) are to be understood;
"threefold" refers to the forms of deficient application (*ayoga*), excessive application (*atiyoga*), and improper application (*mithyāyoga*).

He demonstrates the meaning of "unwholesome" (asātmya) with the words beginning "asātmyam": that which, when combined with the body, does not attain its own state—that is, its unaltered form—is unwholesome. By this, it is meant that whatever, when consumed, causes damage to the natural constitution is unwholesome.

127. Thus, demonstrating that a disease arising from unwholesome objects is "sensory" (*aindriyaka*) by virtue of having the sense organs as its gateway, he says: "Mithyā," etc.; here, "improper application" (*ayoga*) should be understood as the inferior mode of practice (*hīnayoga*).
"Aindriyaka" means that which has the sense-faculties as its gateway (verse 128).

He concludes the explanation of the cause of sensation in the form of suffering, which was discussed in the context of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), with the words "of sensations," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of those that are not pacified," which refers to sufferings, he then asks:
what is the cause of a sensation that has the nature of pleasure? He replies with the words beginning "pleasure" (*sukha*), etc.;
"proper conjunction" (*samayoga*) means the correct conjunction of time, the intellect, the sense faculties, and their objects.
The phrase "extremely difficult to obtain" refers to the fact that the proper conjunction of time and other factors is extremely rare because it is free from non-conjunction and the like;

for generally, among time and the other factors, a person is connected with at least one form of non-conjunction or the like. Consequently, people remain in a state of constant affliction, and the designation of being "healthy" is applied to men only by disregarding minor ailments—this is the intended meaning.

Now, in order to demonstrate the worthiness of adopting right yoga (*samyagyoga*) and the necessity of abandoning non-yoga (*ayoga*) and so forth, he speaks—showing that yoga itself is the fourfold cause—beginning with "Not the senses," and so on.

[Objection: But how can the senses and their objects, which are perceived as the causes of pleasure and pain, be considered non-causes? [Reply: He says "They exist," and so on. Furthermore, "yoga does not exist" means that there is no connection between the senses and their objects.
The word-break is "na sukham" (not pleasure).

The meaning is that when there is an absence of contact between the sense organ and its object, [pleasure] is not a cause; however, when contact exists, it is a cause. Thus, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), contact alone is determined to be the cause.
Furthermore, this contact is stated explicitly with reference to the sense organ and the object; by implication, it should also be understood to apply to wisdom (*prajñā*) and time (*kāla*).

Having treated these—the sense-faculties and their objects—as not to be accepted, this [verse] establishes the causality of the fourfold yoga for the purpose of demonstrating which among the yogas are to be abandoned and which are to be adopted. (vv.

130–131) But from the perspective of ultimate truth, it is shown that it is precisely the self, the sense-faculties, the mind, the intellect, the objects, and the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), when so configured, that are the causes of pleasure and pain; thus he says: "Not the self," and so forth.
The sphere of experience consists of the sense objects, the senses,
and karma (the unseen force); therein, pleasure and pain do not arise in a clod of earth or similar things in the absence of a self.
The fact that the sense organs, their objects, and so forth are causes of pleasure and pain is quite evident;
likewise, virtuous karma is a cause of pleasure and non-virtuous karma is a cause of suffering.
If the self and other such factors alone were the cause, then for what purpose are the improper and excessive application of time and so forth mentioned here? To this, he says: "Just as... and so on.
Whatever is to be understood regarding pleasure and pain, and how it is to be understood according to the requirements of the task at hand—that is stated exactly as it is, and not otherwise.

Therefore, pleasure and pain as they are perceived here—being produced by the contact of sense organs with objects that are either wholesome (*sātmya*) or unwholesome (*asātmya*)—are what are relevant for medical treatment (*cikitsā*). Pleasure and pain are not defined here as being produced by the self (*ātman*) and so forth; for although the self and other such factors are recognized as causes of suffering, they are not presented here as things to be abandoned. Rather, the point is that only the contact of sense organs with unwholesome objects and the like, which are causes of suffering, are to be relinquished, while the contact of sense organs with wholesome objects and the like, which are causes of pleasure, are to be adopted.
Now, in order to explain the yoga that pervades all causes and to demonstrate tactile sensation—both sensory and mental—he says: "By touch," and so forth.

By the phrase "contact with the sense-organ of touch" (*sparśanendriya-saṃsparśa*), he demonstrates the connection of the sense-organs with their objects as effected by the sense-organ of touch. Even the eyes and other organs perceive an object only when it has been touched. For if the eye, ear, or nose were to grasp an object without touching it at all, then they would also grasp what is distant; yet they do not so grasp it. Therefore, the sense-organs apprehend an object only after having touched it. However, there certainly exists a subtle mental contact (*mānasa-sparśa*) with an object such as that which is being thought about, by means of which the mind thinks of only a certain thing and not everything. Thus, the established position is that the mind grasps only that which is touched by the mind.
He explains the sequence of the arising of pleasure and pain: "Desire," and so forth;
craving arises in the form of desire for pleasure, and craving arises in the form of aversion toward pain.

The meaning of the sentence is this: this craving, once arisen, produces pleasure and pain by depending on the fact that its objects of engagement and withdrawal are the causes of pleasure and pain—engaging one toward desired objects and withdrawing one from those that are loathed.
As it has been said, showing that craving is the cause of pleasure and pain, he says: "For it grasps," and so forth;

"those things termed the bases of feeling" refers to those such as time and the like, which are stated to be the causes of feeling because they are associated with [the conditions of] conjunction and so on.
Now, if craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the cause of pleasure and pain, then what is the use of another cause, namely the sense-object (*indriyārtha*)? To this he says: "It is touched," and so forth.

"Without grasping" (*anupādāna*) means that when the cause of contact (*sparśa*)—which consists of the form of a non-existent object—is absent, there can be no contact with an object in the absence of that object.

Now, let us grant that there is no contact with an object; what follows from that? He says: "One who is not touched does not experience sensation" (*vedanā*). The meaning is that one devoid of contact with an object does not experience pleasure or pain precisely because they have not arisen.
He provides the answer to the question, "What is the basis of the sensations? with the words beginning "of the sensations," etc.
By the phrase "the body together with the sense-faculties" (*sendriya*), he excludes the body devoid of sense-faculties, such as hair, nails, and so forth.

He explains that very point for the sake of clarity with the words beginning "hair" (*keśa*), etc., or alternatively: even the sense-faculties (*indriya*) are mentioned separately by the term "sense-faculty" as the basis of sensation (*vedanā*) in order to demonstrate their predominance.
It should be understood that sensation resides in the body and the sense-faculties because it is perceived as having them as its support.
The liquid is urine;
the qualities are sound and so forth residing in the body; for these, such as hair and the like, are not the substrata of sensation—this is indeed established by direct experience as the proof.

As for the sensation pertaining to urine and feces, which is to be mentioned in the context of *grahaṇī* (malabsorption), urinary obstruction (*mūtrakṛcchra*), and so forth, that should be understood as belonging specifically to those regions of the body that serve as the receptacles for urine and feces.
The answer to the question, "Where do all these sensations reside? and so forth, is: "In the *yoga*," and so on.
Yoga is that which will be described in the text beginning with "from non-undertaking" (Anārambhāt); liberation is the absolute cessation of the body and so forth,
such that there is no further rebirth.

By this, he indicates that sensation which had ceased in yoga arises again; thus, [the Lord] is the "promoter of liberation" (*mokṣapravartaka*), meaning He is the cause of liberation—or rather, there is the reading “*yogamokṣau nivartakau*” (Yoga and liberation are the two that cause cessation). In that case, although the fact that Yoga and Liberation cause the cessation of sensation was already stated in the half-verse beginning with “*yoge mokṣe ca*,” nevertheless, since Yoga and Liberation are here seen to function as the agents (*kartṛ*) with respect to the cessation of sensation, there is no tautology.
How yoga becomes the means for turning back sensation—that yoga is stated as follows: "The self," and so forth.
"Because of non-commencement" means because of not commencing with the mind for the purpose of grasping sense objects.

"When the mind is established in the Self" means when it has withdrawn from sense objects and is steady— meaning immobile— being fixed solely in the knowledge of the Self; "both of those" refers to pleasure and pain.
Regarding yoga, he states the attainment of other yogic qualities, beginning with "mastery" (*vaśitva*).
Mastery refers to the eightfold power of sovereignty (*aiśvaryabala*) that will be described hereafter.
By the phrase "of one together with the body," he demonstrates that mastery occurs precisely along with the physical body.
138–139 "Possession" (āveśa) and so forth: possession is the entry into another's body (parapurapraveśa).
"Knowledge of the mind" refers to the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*);
"acting upon objects according to one's will" means performing actions regarding objects according to one's desire;
and "vision" is the perception of that which transcends the senses (*atīndriyadarśana*).
The ear is the hearing of that which transcends the senses;
memory is the recollection of the reality of all phenomena;
and radiance is superhuman radiance.
"Non-perception according to one's will" means that whenever he desires it, even though [the object] is indeed suitable for perception, it is not seen; and whenever he desires it, then it is seen.

Or else, "possession of the mind" (*āveśaścetasaḥ*) refers to the entry into another's mind. "Knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to the knowledge of all things, past, future, and so forth. The rest is as before.
"Sovereign power" (*aiśvara*) means that which is produced by the sovereignty made possible through the power of yoga.
"From the stabilization of the pure being" means from the correct placement of the mind—free from *rajas* and *tamas*—upon the Self (140–141).
Now, how does liberation occur, and what is it? To this he says: "Liberation," and so forth.
"Due to the destruction of powerful karma" means due to the exhaustion of that karma whose fruit must necessarily be experienced;
"by all associations" means by all things connected to the self, such as the body, intellect, and ego-sense;
thus, because there is no further connection with the body and so forth, it is called "non-rebirth" (apunarbhava).
From the context, he states the means to liberation: "Of the virtuous," and so forth;
"supreme fortitude" refers to the extraordinary restraint of the mind.
The non-commencement of actions means the non-performance of the means for future merit and demerit;
the exhaustion of performed actions means the exhaustion through the enjoyment of the fruits of actions performed in previous births;
and renunciation is the desire to depart from saṃsāra.

"Non-egoism" (anahaṅkāra) is the avoidance of such cognitions as "this is mine" or "I am doing this. "Union" (saṃyoga) refers to the concentration of the mind and intellect upon the Self during the union of the Self with the body and so forth; that is, the fixing of the mind and intellect upon the Self.
"All this" refers to what was stated previously, beginning with "the non-commencement of actions.

"Mindfulness of reality" (*tattvasmṛti*) is the recollection of things such as the self exactly as they are. And that [mindfulness] consists of the form of recollection such as: "The self is not something to be benefited by the body and so forth, and these bodies and so forth are distinct from the self.
Now, he explains how memory (*smṛti*) is the cause for the removal of suffering: "Having remembered," and so forth.
"Intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to the form restricted to each individual self.

For, by remembering the nature of the self and other [entities] as first apprehended from the teacher's word—established as mutually distinct and existing without mutual benefit—one does not engage in any activity whatsoever. And not engaging [in activity], one is not joined with suffering born of such engagement; this is the meaning.
147. Now, following the introduction of mindfulness (*smṛti*), he states the causes of mindfulness: "They will be explained," and so forth.
The apprehension of a sign (*nimitta*) is the knowledge of the cause; for having seen the cause, one remembers the effect.
The apprehension of form is the apprehension of the specific configuration;
for example, having seen a gavaya in the forest, one remembers a cow because of their similarity, or just as, having seen a man who resembles one's father, one remembers the father.

"By way of contrast": memory also occurs due to extreme dissimilarity; for example, having seen someone who is extremely ugly, one remembers their opposite, who is extremely handsome. "By way of connection with a mental object": through the application of the mind, one whose mind is directed toward remembering a particular object remembers that object to be remembered.
"By way of repetition": one remembers a familiar object solely by the power of habituation.

"From the yoga of knowledge" means from the yoga of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*); for one who has produced the knowledge of reality remembers everything by its very power. Thus, even a meaning that was heard but forgotten is remembered again upon hearing a portion of it once more.
Having stated the cause of memory, he describes the nature of memory with the words beginning "seen," and so forth.

"Seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) is characterized by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); "heard" (*śruta*), however, is understood through scripture (*āgama*). By this, there is an inclusion of all previously experienced [objects] in certain cases.
Regarding the reading “*smaraṇaṃ smṛtir ucyate*,” even there, there is no difference in meaning.
Having thus established mindfulness in a general sense, he says "this," etc., demonstrating that the mindfulness of reality (tattvasmṛti) is the means for achieving liberation:
"the single path" means the supreme way;

it should be understood as being [traversed] by those who are liberated while living (jīvanmukta), because for those who are completely liberated, there is an absence of a body and therefore an absence of any [need for] instruction.

"The power of the recollection of reality" (*tattvasmṛtibala*) means the power whose nature is the recollection of reality; or alternatively, it is the power consisting of the recollection of reality upon that path which is the means to liberation. By means of this "power of the recollection of reality," they have gone—meaning they have gone to liberation—and have not returned; they have attained release and do not come back again.
150–151 Now, briefly demonstrating ignorance as the cause of saṃsāra and right knowledge as the cause of liberation, he says "all," and so forth:
"All is possessed of a cause" means that everything which arises, such as the intellect (*buddhi*), the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), the body, and so on.
"It is suffering" means it is precisely the cause of suffering;
"it is not-self" means that, in ultimate reality, everything possessing causes is distinct from the self;
and "it is not made by the self" means it is not created by a self that is indifferent [to it].
In this context, regarding the intellect, the body, and so forth— which possess causes—
the sense of "mine" (*svatā*) takes the form of "this intellect is mine," and so on. Now, he explains for how long this arises through delusion by saying "as long as," and so forth.
Truthful intellect is right knowledge; by means of that truthful intellect, one realizes:

"I am not this intellect and so forth, but rather I am entirely distinct from them; likewise, this intellect and so forth do not belong to me, but are the manifestation of *prakṛti*. Having understood this...
The knower, possessing the direct realization of reality, transcends everything; that is, he abandons everything, beginning with the intellect (buddhi). 152–153.
Regarding "final renunciation" (*caramasaṃnyāsa*), this refers to the renunciation of all subsequent actions.

For indeed, at the outset, by the word of the Guru, renunciation of ritual action (*kriyā-saṃnyāsa*) was already performed as a means to liberation; however, it was not performed out of detachment born from one's own direct experience. When that total renunciation is performed through knowledge arisen from practice—which has directly perceived the true nature of reality—then all sensations, cognitions, and so forth, along with their roots, cease upon the cessation of the body.
The phrase "along with their roots" means together with their causes; and the causes are the intellect (*buddhi*) and the other faculties.

Perception (*sañjñā*) is non-conceptual apprehension (*ālocana*); knowledge (*jñāna*) is conceptual (*savikalpaka*); and consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the determination by the intellect (*buddhyavasāya*). Alternatively, perception is knowledge accompanied by the mention of a name, while consciousness is knowledge derived from the scriptures or knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*); for even this [latter] ceases once it has produced liberation, due to the absence of its cause. (154)
The answer to the question beginning with "Omniscient" (sarvavit) is as follows: "Beyond this," and so forth.

By the phrase "having become Brahman," he is shown to be devoid of the primary elements and the like; and by the statement "whose mark does not exist," it is demonstrated that because the liberated self lacks the bodily signs such as inhalation and exhalation, there is indeed no indicative mark [of his existence].
It does not perish and it does not undergo change; thus it is "imperishable" (*akṣara*).
It is "without characteristics" (*alakṣaṇa*) because its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) does not exist.
By this very [term], he demonstrates that this liberation is unknowable to other persons, beginning with the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*), and so forth.

The meaning is that in this matter, the mind conforms only to those who know Brahman, and not to the ignorant who are seized by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth; the summary is clear.
Saṅgrahaḥ vyaktaḥ.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Anatomy of the Human Being in Its Various Aspects" (*Katidhāpuruṣīya Śārīra*), in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka Saṃhitā* composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Section on Anatomy (*Śārīrasthāna*).
[Śārīrasthāna, Chapter 2 (48 of 120):

In the preceding chapter, the primordial creation of the body pertaining to the self (*ādhyātmika*), which is useful for the ultimate treatment consisting of liberation (*naiṣṭhikamokṣa*), was described; now, in order to declare the creation beginning with conception (*garbha*), the one of incomparable lineage (*atulyagotrīya*) is being addressed.

"Of one of unequal lineage" (*atulyagotrasya*) means of a man who is not of the same lineage [as his wife]; for sexual intercourse with those of the same lineage constitutes unrighteousness (*adharma*), as it is prohibited in the *Dharmaśāstras*.
"At the end of the flow of menses" (*rajaḥkṣayānte*) means at the conclusion of the onset of menstruation; by the word "end," he prohibits [intercourse] during the three days of the onset of menses.

"Secretly emitted" (*raho-visṛṣṭam*) means emitted in a secluded place; he shows by the word "secretly" that the emission of semen occurs properly only in seclusion because of the absence of inhibiting shame.
By the phrase "of one who has engaged in sexual union," he demonstrates the proper application of sexual intercourse and prohibits perverse acts such as inverted coitus.
The fact that [the seed] has four parts and six origins is made clear in the subsequent text itself.

Furthermore, this passage is presented as a question from a disciple and should be understood as intended merely to provide the teacher’s authoritative opinion for a disciple who lacks wisdom. Therefore, it should not be said: "How could a disciple who knows the subtle distinction of the four parts and so forth of the seed not know that which is designated by the term *śukra* (semen)?
The answer to the question is as follows: "Pure" (*śukra*) and so forth means that it is deposited or superimposed.

Although one could have simply said "like the quarters consisting of air and so forth," by adding the word "quality" (*guṇa*), he shows that only those elements such as air that possess excellent qualities are the originators of pure semen.

By the designation of "parts" (*pāda*) regarding the wind and other elements that originate the semen (*śukra*), [the author] shows that all of them equally originate the semen. Although space (*ākāśa*) exists within the semen which consists of the five elements, nevertheless it does not depart from the male body and go to the womb; rather, only the four elements that possess motion go there. Space, however, is all-pervading and becomes connected with the semen once it has reached that place. Therefore, because space lacks motion, it is not mentioned here in the context of discussing the movement [of the constituents] as being part of the semen.

Furthermore, in other contexts concerning the departure of the elements (*bhūta*), space (*ākāśa*) is indeed excluded, as in: "Accompanied by the four extremely subtle elements, [the self] possessing the speed of mind departs from the body.
And since semen (*śukra*) becomes pure only when produced from food consisting of the six tastes, it is said: "From the six tastes," and so forth.
As for the statement that sweet [taste] generates semen while sour and other tastes destroy it, this should be understood as occurring due to excessive consumption.
There is one question: "How is a complete body produced? A second question: "How is it produced at the proper time? And a third question: "How is it produced with ease?"

"How is it that even though she is 'with offspring'— meaning she is not barren— she conceives a fetus only after a long time? This is the answer to the five questions, beginning with "semen" (*śukra*).

The word "sampat" (perfection) is connected with each of the factors beginning with semen (*śukra*): perfection consists in the non-defilement of the semen, the blood, and the receptacle; for the self (*ātman*), which presides over the union of semen and blood, perfection consists in being endowed with auspicious living-karma (*jīvakarman*); for time (*kāla*), however, perfection consists in its not being excessively sharp and so forth;
and "attentive care" (*upacāra*) refers to the care provided for the pregnant woman.
Regarding "time," as it was stated in the ninth or tenth month: "Time, moreover, begins from the ninth month up to the tenth" (Śālistamba Sūtra).
4) "Happy" means not seized by any disease;
"blissful" means without affliction.

"From union at an improper time" means from sexual union with a man after the period of the menses has passed. The period of the menses lasts for sixteen nights, as stated by Hārīta: "Sixteen days are the period of the menses";
however, in the Suśruta, the period of the menses is said to be twelve nights.

The answer to the question, "Having come into being, by what does the embryo perish? is as follows: beginning with the words "blood" (*asṛk*) and so forth, he states that when there is an obstruction of blood caused by *pavana*—that is, by vitiated wind (*duṣṭavāta*)—there arises the delusion of being pregnant; this is expressed in the passage beginning with "the form of the embryo" (*garbhasya rūpam*).
The meaning is that blood, increasing within the womb, displays certain signs of pregnancy through its own power;
"only blood" means it is merely blood and not yet designated as a fetus— that is, it does not yet have the form of a mass or other such structures characteristic of a fetus.
He states the reason for the extraction of the fetus by the *bhūtas* in the passage beginning with "ojośanānām" and so forth. Those who consume the *ojas* (vital essence) are called *ojośanas*.
If they were to extract the fetus even though it has not yet become food, then they would extract the *ojas* which is the mother's very sustenance, as it has found its opportunity [to be consumed].
"Having obtained the opportunity" means having attained the cause for approaching a pregnant woman;
"a maiden," etc., refers to the eightfold set of questions.

The first [question] is: "Why is a daughter born separately? The second is: "Or why is a son born separately? The third is: "Why are both daughter and son born together? The fourth is: "Why are two sons born together? The fifth is: "Why are two daughters born together? The sixth is: "Why are many children born? The seventh is: "How does a woman give birth after a very long time? The eighth is: "In the case of twins, how is it that only one attains growth? 11. The answer begins with "By the blood," and so forth.
The term "by the excess" (*adhikena*) should be construed with both the blood (*rakta*) and the semen (*śukra*).
"Made twofold" (*dvividhīkṛtena*) means divided into two parts (*dvikhaṇḍīkṛtena*);
