that seed in which one part is greater according to its own nature is meant by "by that seed. By this it is stated that if, in the two parts, the blood is excessive in one and the semen in the other—such being the division—then a daughter and a son are born.
The phrase "as many times as he divides" means that he brings about a large number, such as four, five, and so forth;
the connection is that the wind has arrived at or entered the semen and the menses.
The phrase "according to the division" means that daughters and sons are produced according to the respective division of the semen and blood, depending on the predominance of one's own seed.
Those things whose nature is karma and which have karma as their cause—
due to being subject to karma and lacking self-mastery—
the acquisition of food by the fetus occurs through the acquisition of food by the pregnant woman, as in the case of "food" and so forth.

He states that the unequal division of the portions of semen and blood, which occurs in both gross and subtle forms, arises solely through the power of the karma of the embryo being born—namely, "because it has karma as its essence" (12–16).
[This follows] the eightfold series of questions beginning with "Why? and so forth.
The male group and the female group are together called the "male-female groups.
"From the seed" means from the semen and blood.
"From a scorched seed" means from the seed-portion that produces a scorched seed.

"Possessing the marks of female and male" means being endowed with marks common to women and men, such as the nose, eyes, and so forth; however, those marks which are unique to women and men—such as the genitals, the penis, breasts, and beard—do not occur in this [embryo]. Since unique marks are produced by an increase in either the semen or the blood, and here, because it is initiated by semen and blood in equal proportion, there is no increase of one over the other, the specific marks such as the genitals and the penis do not come into existence.

One who possesses semen that exists in two ways—by being capable of producing both femininity and masculinity—is called *dviretas*. Alternatively, one who possesses the marks (*liṅgin*) of both female and male is called *strīpuṃsaliṅgī*; that is, one who is endowed with the marks of woman and man, namely the sexual organ and the phallus. However, in this case, the breasts, beard, and so forth, which occur at a later time, do not appear.

According to this view, it is said that through the impairment of the seed (*bījopatāpa*), the obstruction is placed upon the development of the breasts and other features occurring at a later time, but there is no obstruction to the production of the sexual organ and the phallus; for these arise solely by the power of karma.

Alternatively, why are the genitals and the phallus so powerful that they manifest even at the time of conception? However, the breasts and other organs develop at a later time and are therefore weak; because the affliction of the seed is weak, it does not cause harm to the powerful genitals and phallus, but only to the weak organs such as the breasts. It should be understood that when the semen and blood are in equal proportions, the affliction of the seed occurs solely through the power of their union. He explains the wind-related organ with the words beginning "the seat of semen" (śukrāśaya).
The "semen-receptacle" (*śukrāśaya*) is the site of semen (*śukrasthāna*).
"The state of being wind-semen" (*pavanendriyatvam*) means that wind is of the nature of semen;

for semen is called the "organ" (*indriya*), and this alone is the "semen-nature" of wind here: namely, its proceeding at the time of sexual union (*vyavāya*) with a form resembling semen. For it is indeed the wind itself that moves forth at the time of sexual union.
The passage beginning with "at the opening of the seminal receptacle" (*śukrāśayadvāre*) is an explanation of the "conveyor by processing" (*saṃskāravāha*).

Regarding the phrase "by the unlocking of the gate" (*dvāravighaṭṭanena*), this refers to the impairment of the gate through medical processing such as enemas (*basti*) or aphrodisiacs (*vājīkaraṇa*); he whose semen flows when the gate is undamaged is one who is a "conveyor by processing."

In this context, those described by Suśruta as *āsekyas*, *saugandhikas*, and *kumbhīkas* should be included within the category of those who require refinement (*saṃskāra*), because these too discharge semen only through specific forms of refinement. As it is stated therein: "Due to the extremely low potency of his parents, a man becomes an *āsekyas*;
he obtains an erection without doubt only after consuming semen.
He who is born from a putrid womb is known as a *saugandhika*."

"He who, having smelled the scent of the female genitals, gains strength in his own anus, and who, due to a lack of celibacy, behaves toward women like a man— he is to be known as a *kumbhīka*. (Suśruta Saṃhitā)
Thus, regarding men, women, and eunuchs, it says "slowly," and so forth. (Śā. 2)
Those two whose seed was slow-moving and scanty were thus "weak," meaning naturally devoid of strength;
they were "joyless," meaning lacking in enthusiasm.
Regarding the two types of *klība* (impotent), these are of defective seed (*duṣṭabīja*).

It should be understood that here, a woman possessing the aforementioned qualities is the cause for a female eunuch (*strīṣaṇḍa*), whereas a man possessing the aforementioned qualities is the cause for a male eunuch (*puruṣaṣaṇḍa*).
However, these two should be known as being entirely without seed (*abīja*). As it is stated in the *Suśruta*: "One who has no semen at all is a *ṣaṇḍaka*. (*Suśruta Sūtrasthāna*)
(Śā.

2) Thus, "due to opposition to the mother's sexual intercourse" means that at the time of intercourse, the mother's lack of desire for intercourse or an improper positioning of the limbs constitutes opposition to intercourse; by this, he whose semen does not necessarily enter the womb is called *vakrī* (one who is crooked).
The construction is: "And by the weakness of the seed, the father's [semen] may become crooked.

Here, *daurbalya* is the action (*karman*) of one who is weak; its state is *daurbalyatā*. By that, the meaning is: "by the weak efficacy of the father's seed. Having seen another man engaged in sexual intercourse, his penis becomes erect and he becomes capable of intercourse; such a person is one whose pleasure consists of envy (*īrṣyārati*).
As it is stated in the Suśruta-saṃhitā: "He who engages in sexual intercourse upon seeing others doing so should be known as an *īrṣyaka* (one driven by envy). (Su.
Śā.)
2) By the phrase "consisting of karma" (*karmātmakānām*), he shows that these various types of impotence generally arise solely through the power of past karma (verses 18–21).
The five questions beginning with "of the embryo" refer to one who has just followed [the path], that is, one who has just been grasped;
[the answer begins with] "the cause," and so forth.
What is that cause, by which cause the offspring—the embryo—attains sameness of form, that is, similarity?
This is the fifth question.
The "taking of the seed" refers to the non-emission of the semen once it has been discharged into the womb.
"Movement with the left side as predominant" means she moves with her left limbs foremost.
"One who has dreams and so forth like a woman" means she possesses dreams, drinking, eating, habits, and movements characteristic of a woman.

She by whom the fetus has been taken up or held with the left side is "savyāttagarbha"; alternatively, there is the reading "savyāṅgagarbhā," meaning she whose fetus is in the left limb, and not "vṛttagarbha" (one with a rounded fetus), but rather "dīrghagarbhā" (one with a long fetus).
She from whose left breast excellent milk flows is "savyapradugdhā."
The third nature, however, characterized by mixed gender signs, is to be known through the movements of both the left and right limbs; thus, it is the neuter (*napuṃsaka*).
By the passage beginning with "in the production of the embryo," he states the cause for its lack of uniformity.
At the time of conception, when the seed is taken, the mind goes toward whichever being—that is, whichever living creature—the person contemplates with their mind.

It should be understood that this mental contemplation at the time of conception produces an offspring resembling that which is being contemplated, solely by its power (*prabhāva*). Alternatively, it may be that the seed itself is rendered, at that very moment, possessed of the capacity to initiate an embryo similar to the being being thought of. Indeed, a specific power in producing particular beings is observed even in mental states; for example: intention (*saṅkalpa*) causes the emission of semen, and likewise, upon the non-attainment of a desired object, a deformity occurs in the fetus through the mere thought of it; furthermore, envy, fear, and so forth act as causes for the depletion of vitality (*ojas*) and semen, and so on.

And seeing this very same cause for similarity, it must be stated again as follows: having begun with "Whatever woman should desire a son of such-and-such a kind," [the text continues] "she should mentally traverse those various regions" (Śāntiparvan,
Chapter 8).
Having stated that reflection upon living beings (*jantvanudhyāna*) is a cause of similarity, he states another cause of similarity with the words beginning "of the embryo" (*garbhasya*).
He explains that there are four elements by excluding the undifferentiated space (*ākāśa*), saying "the fourfold elements," and so forth, beginning with "the mother."

Those derived from the mother are those pertaining to the blood; those derived from the father are those pertaining to the semen. Those born of nutriment, however, arise from the essence produced by the mother's food after the union of semen and blood. Those born of the self (ātma-ja) should be understood as being subject to the power of karma bound to the self:
it should be known that through auspicious karma they produce a similar form, whereas through inauspicious karma they produce a dissimilar form.
As for those subtle elements within the self which take the form of the *ātivāhika* body, they are not to be considered here, as they are common to all and serve as causes of non-specific similarity.
Regarding that, he asks what the cause is for the fourfold similarity and of what nature it is, and says: "Of those," and so forth.

By the word "particularity" (*viśeṣāt*), he shows that while all things indeed serve as causes of similarity, those which are powerful produce a greater degree of similarity due to their particularity.

In this context, since it is understood that only those [tissues] born from food (*āhāraja*) possess the quality of being causes of similarity by virtue of depending upon prior karma, the term "born from food" was not explicitly included [in the definition]. Therefore, it should be understood that those born from food are subsumed within those born from karma (*karmaja*). However, it should be understood that the phrase "born from food" used previously merely indicated their existence.

Alternatively, while the [tissues] born from the mother and so forth produce results similar to the mother and so forth, those born from food do not produce results similar to the food; therefore, they are not mentioned here.

For indeed, in the subsequent chapter, [the qualities] such as the connection with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth must be explained by the passage beginning, "Those which are born from the *rasa* of this [body]" (*Śārīrasthāna*, Adhyāya 3). Since these cannot exist here in the form of similarity, [the author], having stated the cause for similarity to the body, states the cause for similarity to the mind: "The *sattva*," and so forth.

*Anūka* refers to the immediately preceding species of body from a previous life. Thus, "according to the *anūka*" means that one who comes without interruption from the body of a god becomes one whose *sattva* is divine; one who comes from the body of an animal becomes one whose *sattva* is that of an animal, and so on.

By the word "also" (api), he indicates both connection with action (*karman*) and connection with genus (*jāti*); thus, by the power of action, a being becomes *rājasa*, *tāmasa*, or *sāttvika*, and likewise it conforms to its genus, such as that of humans and so forth.

From the words beginning with "Why? up to "or with impaired senses," there is one question; therein, the explanation of the term "distorted" (*vikṛtām*) is given by the words beginning with "deficient" (*hīna*).
The second [question] is: "By whom is the body, the sun, and so forth, always pursued? This is the third [question].

As for those who claim that by the word *vikṛtām* (deformed) they mean one of ugly form, and by the phrase *hīnādhikāṅgīm* (having deficient or extra limbs) they mean one whose form is deficient in limbs and so forth—distinct from the ugly—then in their view there would be a discrepancy in the questions; furthermore, the number of questions stated at the end of the chapter would be exceeded.
One's own action is *ātmakarma*; the womb is the *garbhāśaya*; a defect is *vaiguṇya*;
stone-masses are fragments of rock; and velocities belong to the three [elements], such as wood and so forth.
The answer to the second question begins with "by the elements" (*bhūtaiḥ*) and so forth; by the term "extremely subtle" (*susūkṣmaiḥ*), he demonstrates their supersensuous nature (*atīndriyatva*).
Space is not mentioned here as a factor in the action of moving to another body because it is inactive;
"mind-swift" (*manojava*) means that one goes with the speed of the mind.

By this, it is shown that although there is no movement to another body for the all-pervading self, nevertheless, its movement—consisting solely of the movement of the mind accompanied by the elements—is expressed by the word "movement."
"From the body" means from the dying body;
"the body" refers to the body being produced;
"because it consists of karma" means because it is dependent upon karma.
By this it is meant that he goes to that very body composed of the elements, which is led by his karma—consisting of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)—for the sake of experience.
Now, as he departs, why is he not perceived? To answer this, the author says "But not... and so forth.
The meaning is that for that self (*ātman*) joined with the subtle transport-body (*ātivāhika-śarīra*), there is no visible form, because its form is exceedingly subtle.
Now, he asks why everyone does not see him as he goes, and answers: "Except for divine vision.
By "divine vision," he means the eye of yoga; thus he shows that only yogins perceive him.
He then states other attributes of this very self, which is endowed with the subtle body (*ativāhika-śarīra*), beginning with: "He is all-pervading," and so forth.
"Sarvaśarīrabhṛt" means one who is capable of sustaining all bodies;

"Viśvakarmā" means one who is able to perform all actions; and "Viśvarūpa" means one who, by the power of karma, assumes universal forms through the nature of bodies such as those of humans, animals, and so forth.
"Ever-yoked" (*nityayuk*) means it is constantly joined with the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth;
"with latent tendencies" (*sānuśaya*) means it exists together with the underlying propensities (*anuśaya*) such as passion (*rāga*).
In order to explain the four elements that constitute the subtle transport body (*ātivāhika-śarīra*), he states the elements that are possible within the body, beginning with "rasa" and so forth.

These elements, although already mentioned in the context of the discussion on similarity (*sārūpya*), are stated again here by virtue of the present topic and for the purpose of establishing the nature of the unmentioned forms such as semen and blood;

they are said to be "resting in the self" (*ātmani saṃśritāni*), meaning they are bound within the self in the form of the subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*) through the agency of the self's karma. Likewise, the self is "situated" in those elements for the sake of performing functions such as entering another body.

The destination resulting from the transition to another body and so forth is said to belong only to the self as it is situated within those elements, not to the all-pervading [self], because that [all-pervading self] is omnipresent; this is the meaning. "Born of mother and father" refers to the female and male reproductive fluids respectively; "born of mother and father" means they are merged with the self, being eternally connected to the self.
He states another property of those elements that have merged into the self: "That is the nature of a seed," and so forth.

That continuum of elements which has merged into the self possesses the nature of a seed (*bījadharmā*), meaning its very essence is that of a seed; for a seed produces a sprout similar to itself. Therefore, this continuum of elements merged into the self also becomes one possessing the nature of a seed (*bījadharmā*) by producing a similar body-form through conjunction with other elements.
Alternatively, there is the reading *sā bījadharmiṇī*; in that case, the word "that continuum of elements" (*bhūtasantatiḥ*) must be supplied [as the subject].
The construction is as follows: "when the self (ātman)—that is, when the self conjoined with the mind—goes or moves, it goes to other bodies.
And the movement of the self is indeed the movement of the mind.

Or there is the reading *parāparāṇi*; in that case, it should be construed as follows: "higher" (*parāṇi*) refers to superior bodies such as those of the gods, and "lower" (*aparāṇi*) refers to inferior bodies such as those of worms. Now, one might ask: why must this fourfold aggregate of elements—which is not directly perceived, yet is endowed with the activity of the mind and possesses the nature of a seed—be accepted? For why not simply accept that this directly perceived body, composed of the six elements, has semen and blood as its cause? To this he says: "Because of form," and so forth. That which is formed (*rūpyate*) is "form" (*rūpa*), namely, the physical body composed of the elements.
Therefore, it is well-known from scripture that a material body arises from an immaterial body;
thus, the meaning of the sentence is that from the subtle body (*ātivāhika-śarīra*)—which consists of the Sāṅkhya system according to scripture alone—the manifest body (*vyakta-śarīra*) is produced.

Although semen and blood are the causes, nevertheless, it is only when they reach the subtle body composed of subtle elements (*ativāhika-sūkṣma-bhūta-rūpa-śarīra*) that they produce a body, and not at any other time. If semen and blood were to produce an embryo independently of the subtle body, then they would produce it even in the absence of the presiding soul; however, they do not so produce it. Therefore, the birth of the embryo occurs from the semen and blood combined with the subtle elements residing within the self, which serve as the seed.

And he says—starting with "karma"—that this causal factor for the body, which consists of the elements residing within the self, arises as something equal to that which is born from the parents, solely through the power of karma.

The phrase "of those whose nature is karma" means "of those whose cause is karma. Alternatively, since it is well known that a cloth possessing color arises from threads possessing color, the subtle body (ativāhika-śarīra) must be similar to the body it is to produce; for an effect is indeed similar to its cause. Therefore, the intended meaning is that the existence of the subtle elements (sūkṣma-bhūta) residing within the self as attributes of the self is established.

Now, as for the question of how the mind—which is divided into the *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* types—becomes differentiated in various individuals, he says: "The mind [is] from the mind"—meaning that whatever kind of mind one had in the immediately preceding birth, such a very same mind arises here in this birth.
And it has been said elsewhere: "Whatever was practiced birth after birth—be it charity, study, or austerity..."
"By that very same practice, that very same thing is practiced again.
Here too, in the context of the arising of the mind, the phrase "of those whose nature is karma" should be supplied;
thus, it is solely by the power of karma that the differentiation of the mind occurs.

If this were so, one might object that since the subtle elements residing within the self are of a single nature, all living beings ought to possess bodies of a single form; to this he says, "They come into being," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: although the cause—the nature of the subtle elements—is undifferentiated, the *ākṛti* (form), which is the configuration (*saṃsthāna*), and *rajas* and *tamas*, which are divided into various degrees such as more or less intense, as well as *karman* (action), which is likewise manifoldly differentiated, serve as the causes of differentiation.
The answer to the question “By what is the self always bound? begins with the words “by those beyond the senses” (*atīndriyaiḥ*), etc.;
“by them” (*taiḥ*) refers to those previously described as having the nature of seeds (*bījadharmitva*).
Are the defects merely the transformations of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*), or are *rajas* and *tamas* themselves the defects?
Furthermore, he states that this connection with the subtle elements and so forth belongs to the mind alone—beginning with the words "Rajas" and so on:
by means of *rajas* and *tamas*, which act as causes, the mind becomes bound to all the elements and the rest.
He states the reason for this very point: "From knowledge," and so forth.

"From knowledge" means from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). The meaning is that without the knowledge of reality, the mind remains possessed of all defects, whereas through the knowledge of reality, it becomes free from defects.
To the question, "What happens when the mind is possessed of defects? he says: "Gait," and so forth.

"Gati" (movement) is the transition to another body; "pravṛtti" (activity) is engagement in actions of merit and demerit. The meaning of the sentence is that the mind, by virtue of its being possessed of defects, becomes the cause of saṃsāra.
He states another cause for movement and activity: "and powerful karma," etc.
"Powerful" means having a fixed ripening (*niyatavipāka*); or there is the reading "fruitful" (*phalavat*), which has the same meaning.
The fruit of determinate karma arises solely through the power of that karma;

and regarding what is further stated here in the questions and answers by the phrase "of the movement toward the realms of rebirth" and so forth, that should be understood as being due to the force of the context itself.
"From where do diseases arise? is the first question; "What is their pacification? is the second; "What is the cause of joy? is the third.
"What is the cause of sorrow? is the fourth;
"How can the transformations arising from the body and the *sattva* not recur once they have been stilled? is the fifth.
In this way, the thirty-six questions to be stated in the summary are completed.
Faults such as those of wisdom and so forth are stated again by virtue of the context;
"at the time of transformation" means at the time of the transformation of time.

Forty [actions] are righteous (dharmya), which are the means for accomplishing dharma; because they perform dharma, which is a cause of joy, they become causes of joy. Conversely, actions other than those are unrighteous (adharmya).
"By the non-occurrence of those two" means through the cessation of the continuum of body and mind;
for in liberation, both body and mind cease, and consequently, the continuum of disease ceases in every respect.

[Objection: Is it not the case that whatever undergoes cessation must have a beginning? Therefore, does the continuum of the body and mind have a beginning, such that its cessation is said to be the cause for the actual cessation of disease? To this, he says: "Of form," and so forth. "Form" refers to the body;

for the body is called by the word "form" (rūpa) because it is that which is manifested (rūpyamāṇatvena), as it was stated in the scriptures: "For from form arises form. It is not [merely] stated [in common parlance]. Thus it is said in the Āgamas.
To the question "Why was it not stated?", he says: "For that does not exist"; the meaning is that it was not stated precisely because of its non-existence.
Now, if the continuum of body and mind is beginningless, how can there be its cessation? To this he says: "Of those two," and so forth.
"Of those two" refers to the body and the sentient being as they continue in succession.
"By the two supreme ones" means by the two best [qualities];

however, how fortitude (*dhṛti*) and the others are the cause of liberation has been explained in the *Katidhāpuruṣīya* chapter. Furthermore, how the beginningless continuum of the body is destroyed has also been stated in that very same place.
He states another way in which the treatment of physical and mental diseases is practiced in the treatise, beginning with the word "satī" (being):
by the term "āśraya" (substratum), both the body and the mind are understood.

By the phrase "previously, from diseases," he shows that even when morbid forms have not yet arisen, there is a constant application of remedies; by "constant future treatment" and "always having the senses conquered," he demonstrates the avoidance of the causes of disease—namely, intellectual error (*prajñāparādha*), unwholesome habits (*asātmya*), and sensory objects (*indriyārtha*); and by "constancy in remedial action," he demonstrates the treatment of defects caused by time (*kāla*) which cannot otherwise be avoided.

"Appropriate to that time" means that which is necessarily ripening at that specific time by way of producing disease; by this, he shows that powerful destiny (*daiva*) inevitably bestows disease. (43) From the context, he speaks of the action known as destiny, and following upon that, he also mentions human effort (*puruṣakāra*): "Destiny," and so forth.

Therefore, because it is being stated here by virtue of the context, there is no tautology with the previously mentioned characteristics of the formal act for one who is to be expelled from the country;
"in another birth" refers to a future life, while "here" refers to this present life.
"Causes of manifestation" refers to the causes for the manifestation of disease;

"unequal" refers to destiny (*daiva*) in the form of unrighteousness (*adharma*) and human effort (*puruṣakāra*) that generates disease; whereas "equal" refers to destiny in the form of righteousness (*dharma*) and human effort that counteracts disease.

The masculine designation "it" (*saḥ*) should be understood as referring to *karman* (in the masculine gender) by way of its nature as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), since it is through this that human effort (*puruṣakāra*) is reflected upon.

Others, however, explain that by the phrase "the cause of engagement" (*pravṛttihetuḥ*) it means the cause of the engagement in saṃsāra, and by the phrase "the cause of cessation" (*nivṛttihetuḥ*) it means the cause of liberation (*mokṣa*).
Now, as to how the avoidance of diseases caused by the defects of time and conduct should be performed through specific treatments, he says: "Haimantika," and so forth;
"vasante" means in Caitra; "abhrakāle" means in Śrāvaṇa.
Regarding the phrase "at the end of the rainy season" (*ghanātyaye*), which refers to the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,

the statement beginning with "in the first month of spring" (*mādhavaprathame māsi*) from Sūtra-sthāna 7 should be understood as applying, by way of *pravāhana* (purgation), according to what is appropriate through emesis and other such measures.
He states another reason for the absence of disease, beginning with "nara" (man):
"sama" means one who possesses an even mind toward all living beings.
The phrase "connected with happiness" (*sukhānubandha*) should be applied both mentally and verbally by changing its gender;
thus, it refers to wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind that have happiness as their subsequent fruit.
"Sattva" refers to the mind that is to be disciplined and brought under one's own control.
"Clear intellect" means not a turbid intellect;
here, "intellect" (buddhi) is intended to possess the capacity for reasoning and refutation,
whereas "mind" (mati) refers to memory, reflection, and so forth.
Knowledge is the knowledge of reality; the rest is easy to understand.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Embryology of Unequal Lineages," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Śārīrasthāna, Chapter 3 (49 of 120)]

In the preceding chapter, semen and ovum were mentioned as causes of conception; however, the complete cause of conception was not fully stated. Therefore, in order to explain the complete cause of conception, the *khuḍḍikā-garbhāvakrānti* (the minor discourse on the descent of the embryo) is now described.
The term *khuḍḍikā* means "minor" or "small," and *garbhāvakrānti* refers to the descent of the embryo—that is, its union or, in other words, its origination.
Regarding the passage beginning with "of the man" (puruṣasya) and so forth:

the term "of the man" is already implied by the phrase "whose semen is unimpaired" (anupahata-retasaḥ), since it has been stated that only the semen of a man produces the embryo. Therefore, by the word "man," the text intends to include specifically that individual whose constituent elements (dhātus) are complete, who is denoted by the term "man," and who is distinct from a child.
The word "of a woman," though already implied by the sense, specifies that the woman must be one who possesses youth; "conjunction" refers to sexual intercourse;
"the time of the season" (*ṛtukāla*) is the recommended period following the appearance of menses; by this, he prohibits the first three days of that period.
For, by the statement beginning with "Approaching a woman during her menses is the foremost of misfortunes" (Sūtra 25), intercourse for three days is forbidden during the fertile period (*ṛtu*);
and the appearance of the menstrual flow (*ārtava*) is referred to by the word *ṛtu* because of its similarity to the characteristics of the seasons beginning with autumn.

Just as seeds sown during the proper season sprout, so too the seed in the form of semen is sown during the season known as the appearance of menses; thus there is a similarity to the [proper] season. However, such a union alone is not the sole cause of conception; rather, it occurs when there is the presiding presence of the *jīva* (individual soul). To this effect, he says "when," etc., meaning: when there is a union between a man with unvitiated semen and a woman with an unvitiated womb and other such factors, [conception occurs]. Thus it is "properly joined."

Although this matter was already established by the passage beginning with "this [is] for the man," it is restated here for the purpose of prescribing additional qualities that will be described in the subsequent text beginning with "the union of semen and blood. Therefore, there is no redundancy.

Alternatively, while the passage beginning with "for the man" previously stated that the semen must be unimpaired prior to coitus, the phrase "and when it is so prepared" indicates that even at the time of coitus, the semen, the womb, and other factors must remain undamaged;
for during the act of coitus, the corruption of semen through envy or other emotions is possible.
By the phrase "the union of semen and blood," meaning the meeting of semen and blood,
he excludes as a cause of the embryo that union occurring outside the womb;
by the word "jīva," he refers to the self as the element of consciousness.

Now, since the self (*ātman*) is all-pervasive, how does it enter [the womb]? To this he says: "Through association with a sentient being," and so forth; the meaning is "through the movement of the mind.
As it has been said: "The activities of that omnipresent one who is joined with the mind are pointed out" (Śāstrālaṃkāra 1).

The meaning is this: although the self (*ātman*), due to its all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*), does not go anywhere because it is omnipresent, nevertheless, wherever the mind (*manas*) goes by the power of karma, the self is also said to have gone there, because consciousness is perceived precisely there.

Now, he explains how the embryo thus produced grows and how it is born: "by means of proper treatments" (*samyag-upacāraiḥ*); that is to say, by means of diet and lifestyle conducive to the welfare of the embryo.
"At the proper time" (*prāpta-kāla*) means when the time for delivery has arrived; the time of delivery refers to the ninth and tenth months.

"Of a fully developed body" means one whose body has all its limbs well-nourished; the word "sampat" (perfection) is connected with each [term] beginning with strength (*bala*); "from the collection" means from their perfect integration.

By the word "eṣām" (of these), he refers back to the semen, ovum, soul (*jīva*), *sattva*, suitability (*sātmya*), nutrient fluid (*rasa*), and proper regimen mentioned in the preceding text beginning with "of the person.
Demonstrating that the embryo arises from this very collection by explaining each of the causes of the embryo—beginning with the mother and so forth—he says: "born of the mother," etc.

In the phrase "born of suitability" (*sātmyaja*), the term "suitability" (*sātmya*) refers to form and other qualities distinct from the nutrient fluid, as well as conduct (*ācāra*) which is considered suitable.
That which is congenial to one's constitution (*sātmya-rasa*) is already included by the term "born of [one's own] essence" (*rasaja*);
as for "spontaneous" (*aupapāduka*), this refers to that which brings about the connection of the self with another body,
and this has indeed been explained previously.

In this context, although the father alone is mentioned first by the phrase "of a man whose semen is unimpaired," nevertheless, the mother is mentioned first in the statement "and this [embryo] is born of the mother" in order to demonstrate the predominance of the mother regarding the embryo. For the mother is the primary cause in the embryo, such that from the moment of insemination until delivery, the embryo conforms to the qualities and defects of the mother alone. However, the father is mentioned first because he possesses independence in sexual intercourse and because he is the primary skeletal cause for maintaining the body.

In order to establish the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by refuting the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the author] raises objections against the causes such as the mother and so forth through the mouth of Bharadvāja: with the words "no" and so on, there is a general rebuttal of what was stated by Ātreya;

with the words "for what reason," he asks for the reason why this statement of Ātreya is contradictory; and with the words "it is not the mother" and so on, Bharadvāja asserts that the causes such as the mother and others are not actually causes.

4 (1) By the words "If indeed," etc., [the author] states the reason for the fact that the mother and others are not the cause; or alternatively, Bharadvāja has asserted that the mother and others are not the cause, and in that regard, the question for the reason is "What is the cause?", whereupon the statement of the reason begins with "For the mother," and so forth.
And this is its meaning: that parents and so forth are not perceived by direct observation as the cause of the embryo; therefore, parents and so forth are not the cause of the embryo.

Furthermore, with the words "if indeed," etc., he demonstrates that there is also a contradiction with logical reasoning (*upapatti*) in the case of parents being the cause. Thus, there is no tautology;
"sexual intercourse" (*maithunadharma*) means copulation (*vyavāya*).
The construction is: "those desiring sons shall beget only sons, and those desiring daughters shall beget only daughters.
It does not mean that women and men, while engaging in sexual intercourse, would lament or not lament over the fact that "some [of these] are women.

Since the embryo is dependent upon the mother and father, whenever they desire offspring, they should become possessed of offspring simply by engaging in sexual intercourse at that very time. Consequently, because all [would have] offspring, no one would lament; this is the meaning.

4 (2) It refutes the notion that the embryo is produced from a self— “and not a self,” and so forth; the meaning is that [the self] does not produce itself in the form of humans, elephants, horses, and so on.
"Because of existence" (sattvāt) means that since the self (*ātman*) which is to be produced already exists, and that which already exists is not produced; this is the meaning.

"Because of non-existence" (asattvāt) means that in the position where the self, which is the cause, has not yet arisen, its status as a cause is untenable due to its non-existence; this is the meaning.
Regarding this very point, he states another refutation, beginning with "let it remain," etc.
"In various wombs and births,
or even more than that" means that it is superior even to what is endowed with the aforementioned qualities, being equal to the supreme prosperity of Śakra and others.
And that "both" refers to both having offspring and being childless;
"in both cases" means among those who consume what is wholesome and those who consume what is unwholesome.
The meaning of "he who does not consume *rasa*" is as follows: if *rasa* were the cause of conception, then since all women and men partake of it, everyone would consequently have offspring.
Alternatively, if the statement "conception is born of *rasa*" is interpreted to mean "excellent *rasa*," he states the refutation of that view as well, beginning with "excellent...
(verse 4).
Regarding the statement, “And there exists a spontaneously born being (*aupapāduka-sattva*),” he refutes it with the words “na khalv api,” etc.
“Paurvadehika” means experienced in a previous body;

“unknown” (*avidita*) or “unseen” (*adṛṣṭa*) means that even in this life, what was experienced in a previous body would not be unknown or unseen. “Known” (*vidita*) is that which is apprehended by a means of valid cognition other than direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); “seen” (*dṛṣṭa*) is that which is apprehended by direct perception. By contrast, the opposite of these two should be understood as “unknown” and “unseen.”
"And he does not remember anything at all" means that he does not remember what was experienced in a previous birth.

He thinks as follows: "Whatever the mind experiences in a previous body continues here in this life as well; likewise, whatever was experienced by it in another birth should be remembered here in this life in the same way—for example, just as Devadatta remembers what was experienced in childhood during his youth—and yet he does not remember it in that manner. Therefore, there is not one single being across previous and subsequent births. With the words "Therefore," etc., he demonstrates again by way of conclusion the point already refuted by the critique.
He refutes the opinion of Bharadvāja by means of the words of Ātreya, beginning with "No," and so forth;
by the statement "from the combined [elements]," he negates the status of the mother and others as causes of the embryo when they exist individually and independently of other causes.

Therefore, even when the causes of conception such as the mother and so forth are present, it is entirely logical that conception does not occur due to the absence of other necessary factors for conception, such as the descent of the soul (jīva).
Furthermore, the idea that a factor which produces only a portion of an effect produced by a causal complex is not a cause at all is untenable;

for if that were the case, then even threads—which are causes of a cloth—would cease to be causes whenever other auxiliary causes are absent, simply because they would not produce the cloth [in isolation]. This is the intended meaning.
This very fact— that the embryo is produced from the mother and others— consists in its not being produced apart from the mother and so forth.
He states that the mother’s causality is precisely of this kind, beginning with the words, "And this embryo is born of the mother," and so on.

Having demonstrated the mother's causality in the production of the embryo, he states her causality regarding birth from a womb (jarāyuja) with the words "na ca janma" and so forth. *Jarāyu* means the placenta (*amarā*), enveloped by which humans and other beings are born. Because they are born enveloped by the placenta, humans and others are called "womb-born" (*jarāyuja*). Furthermore, birth occurs even without a mother for those born from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*), such as mosquitoes and the like, and for those born from sprouts (*udbhijja*), such as frogs and the like.

Although the mother is indeed a cause for the birth of egg-born beings (*aṇḍaja*), nevertheless, since the womb-born human is intended here in this context, the term "of the womb-born" (*jarāyuja*) is used, setting aside the egg-born. Alternatively, it may be that in the case of the birth of a womb-born being—which consists in its manifestation—the mother is a cause as long as that manifestation occurs; this is not the case for the egg-born. In the latter instance, such as with a tortoise and the like, the mother is a cause merely for the production of the egg, but not for the birth in the form of manifestation.

As for the statement that will be made, "There is no birth of womb-born beings without a father," that is intended to demonstrate the necessity of a father for the production of womb-born beings; the point is that egg-born beings, such as fish and others, come into existence even without a father simply by reaching their specific season of conception.

Regarding the explanation of the term *mātṛjāni*: the construction is as follows—"those which arise from his mother" means those which arise from the mother of the developing embryo; "arising from what has come from the mother" means they are produced from the blood (*śoṇita*) derived from the mother; these, such as the skin and so forth, are the "mother-born" (*mātṛja*) parts, which we shall explain in detail.

In the same way, the passage beginning with "yāni tu" and so forth should be explained in other instances as well. Furthermore, the fact that the skin and other tissues are derived from the mother is to be understood solely through scriptural authority (*āgama*). The receptacle for feces is the *pakvāśaya* (the large intestine).
The upper and lower portions of the anus— the upper and lower parts of the rectum—
are called the "flesh-remover" (*vapāvahana*), also known as the "oil-wick" (*tailavartikā*).
By the separate reading "śukram" (semen), he demonstrates the desirability of semen as the essence of all the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).
With the words beginning "ātmaja" (self-born), he explains its nature as being born of the self.

By the phrase "the inner self is called," he distinguishes the self that is the cause of the embryo from the self denoted by the word "self" as existing within the collection of the six elements; "they declare" means that the elders speak of it in the scriptures using terms such as "eternal" and so forth;
"unshakeable" means imperturbable.
The meaning is that he produces himself as an embryo; thus, it refers to the self consisting of the six elements (*ṣaḍdhātuka*) which is the very nature of the embryo.
He states that the term "self" applies to the embryo by saying, "for the designation 'self' [is applied] to the embryo.
By the word "his," he refers back to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

Since birth is not possible for this [Self] because it is beginningless, the position that "this one, though already born, produces an unborn embryo" is untenable; thus it should be connected. Now, if being born he does not produce [the embryo], how then does he produce it? He says: "For this one is unborn"; the meaning is that he is eternal.
Because of that eternity, like space, the inner Self (antarātman), though not born, produces itself in the form of the embryo.
Therefore, because it exists eternally as the nature of the inner self (*antarātman*), that which is unborn is said to be "born" during the state of being in the womb;
thus, both the states of being unborn and being born are predicated of the Self.

To demonstrate this very birth and non-birth of the Self, he shows the states of being born and unborn even within the embryo itself for the sake of an illustration, beginning with the words "And that very... and so forth.
"Placed in front" (*puraskṛtā*) means that which will exist beforehand;

just as the state of old age in a child is produced though it has not yet arisen, so too the expression "the unborn produces itself by itself" is merely a justification for the use of words, to be understood according to the difference in intended meaning (*vivakṣābheda*).

By this justification of "being born" (*jātatva*) based on a distinction of states within the self, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) posed by the author of the text—namely, "Does that which is already born produce, or does that which is unborn [produce]?"—is refuted as being merely a justification for the use of words.
In the ultimate sense, however, the Self is indeed unborn by virtue of its eternity; it brings about the state of the unborn Self in the form of the embryo and so forth.
Therefore, the position remains established that there is no causality for what is non-existent, nor is there the state of being produced for what is already existent.
By the words "for [what] exists," etc., he demonstrates the Sāṅkhya view, which maintains the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*).
Or rather, he shows that there is no distinction based on age, for the very transition to another state is itself "birth"; the phrase "in each respective state" is the division [of the sentence],
and "fatherhood" means being designated as a father.
Regarding what was said—that if the self produces itself, it should produce it endowed with qualities such as mastery—the response to that is stated: "Certainly not," and so forth;
this should be construed as meaning that among all entities, including the embryo, there is no power to act according to one's will on the part of the mother and others.
And here, although it is the self (*ātman*) alone that is the subject under discussion, nevertheless, because the resolution is the same, the mother and father are also included.

Just as the objection—that since the self has the power to act according to its will, there would be the undesirable consequence of it entering any womb at will—is resolved, so too is the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) that "since the parents also have the power to act according to their will, they might produce only sons" or the like, refuted.
Now, he asks: why is it that the self and others do not have the power to act according to their will in some cases? To this he says: "Furthermore," and so forth.

"Not everything" means that in this regard, the mother and father are independent when they engage in sexual intercourse as the cause of conception and practice habits such as the consumption of compatible tastes; however, regarding the entry of the living being (*jīva*) into the womb and so forth, they are dependent on others, being subject to *karma*. Likewise, the self (*ātman*) is independent in the consciousness of the embryo and in the performance of actions caused by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*); but in going to desired or undesired wombs and other states produced by *karma*, it is entirely dependent on merit and demerit. Therefore, regarding matters dependent on *karma*, there is no power of arbitrary action for the mother and the others.
Showing that even the mother and others act according to their own will in certain instances, he says: "And in some cases, of these," and so forth.

"Instrument" (*karaṇa*) means an accessory (*upakaraṇa*), that is to say, the means of accomplishment. "Sattva" is the mind (*manas*). Those things of which "sattva" and the rest are primary are "sattva-ādi," namely the mind, the sense organs, semen, blood, and so forth.
"According to one's strength" means according to one's karma; here, the word "strength" (bala) refers to the unseen force (adṛṣṭa).

By this it is understood that where the mother and others possess the capacity to engage in intercourse with a desired womb and so forth at the father's wish, and where the karma is favorable, then the act of approaching a desired womb occurs in relation to the intended son and others. For example: if there is a man possessing pure and abundant semen, and a woman endowed with qualities such as having a pure womb, and if the karma for producing a son is strong in both of them, then, engaging in sexual union with the intention of producing a son, they give birth to the desired son. Likewise, when the Self (Ātman) is endowed with qualities such as purity of being (sattva) and possesses auspicious karma, and at that time contemplates a desired womb, it then accomplishes its own approach to that desired womb; such examples of acting according to one's will are to be understood.

The phrase "otherwise than this" means that when there is an incapacity for the production of beings and so forth, or when destiny (*daiva*) is deficient, a reversal occurs; thus, there is no acting according to one's own will.

Alternatively, in certain cases such as sexual intercourse, these [agents], such as the father and others, possess self-mastery. Why, then, do they not possess self-mastery even in the initiation of the living being (*jīva*) and so forth? To this he says: "And in some cases, of these," and so on.

The meaning is that because a particular instrument, such as the mother and so forth, is capable only of a specific effect and not of everything, the embryo does not possess autonomy over all its constituent states.

Furthermore, even in those cases where these factors—the mother and others—act with autonomy, they act only when endowed with their respective instruments; thus he says, "wherein [the qualities] such as *sattva*," etc., and "according to their strength" (*yathābalam*), meaning according to their capacity.

And by this, he demonstrates that the mother and others are capable of acting according to their will regarding those specific qualities of the embryo for which they possess the power—namely, the perfection of the instruments [of action] such as *sattva* and so forth—but they are not capable of acting according to their will regarding an impossible object, nor are those whose instruments are impaired capable of doing so.

The meaning of the phrase "otherwise, there is the reverse" has been explained further on. Now, one might object: "If this self does not produce such an embryo because of defects in the instruments such as *sattva*, then alas, this self is not a cause at all! For whatever is a cause necessarily produces its effect. To this, he says: "Nor... and so forth.

It is not the case that the self does not become the cause for the production of an embryo simply because it fails to produce one due to defects in the instruments [of action]; rather, it certainly remains the cause. This is the view: even though a potter does not produce a jar due to the absence of clay and other materials, he still remains the cause of the jar because he possesses the capacity to generate a jar. Likewise, the self, although not producing such an embryo due to defects in the instruments, remains the cause precisely because it is repeatedly observed to possess the power to generate it.

Likewise, the possibility of approaching a desired womb has also been raised; demonstrating that this occurs in some cases by virtue of the self being the cause, he says, "And it is observed," and so forth.

A "desired womb" with respect to a person is a womb dependent upon the self. Similarly, sovereignty and other qualities are observed to be dependent upon the self, as stated in the *Katidhāpuruṣīya* chapter: "The entry of the mind [is] knowledge," and so on.
He states another reason for the self being the cause: "For there is no other," and so forth.

For (*hi*) because there is no creator of pleasure and pain other than the self, but rather the self alone is the creator of the body, the senses, and the actions that are the means to pleasure and pain; therefore, the meaning is that the self is the cause of the embryo, which is the substratum of pleasure, pain, and so on.

Now, [the opponent asks]: why do the elements themselves, having acquired consciousness through the power of conjunction, not become the causes of pleasure and so forth? To this he says: "Nor from anything else," and so forth.
"From another" means arising from a heterogeneous [cause];

that is, while being produced, an effect arises from a cause that is indeed similar [to itself], whereby the sprout of a hemp plant does not arise from a coconut seed. "From what is not a seed" means [that the sprout] which is intended to be an effect does not arise from what is not its seed.
By this, it is shown that the consciousness of the embryo does not arise from the insentient elements, but rather from the conscious element, the self (ātman) itself.
Having thus established that the embryo is born of the self, he states the specific qualities of those born of the self, beginning with "yāni" and so forth.

In this context, regarding the impelling and sustaining of the very senses— such as when one enters the wombs of various gods or animals produced by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)— the self alone is said to be the fundamental cause, as it is the generator of that merit and demerit. However, in cases such as the impelling of the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and in-breath (*apāna*) through the instrument of the mind (*manas*), the self itself is the immediate cause.

By the passage beginning with "born of suitability" (*sātmyajaśca*), he explains the state of being born of suitability; by showing that unwholesome conduct (*asātmyasevā*) is injurious to the embryo, he strengthens the position that wholesome conduct is a cause for the embryo. By demonstrating that even among those who practice unwholesome conduct there is the possibility of procreation, he refutes the prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "those who practice unwholesome conduct would be entirely childless. Furthermore, by the subsequent text beginning with "but for those who practice wholesome conduct," he addresses the claim that "for those who practice wholesome conduct, offspring will certainly arise."
Regarding the phrase "of those who have come together," this refers to those who have engaged in sexual intercourse;

here, both tone (*svara*) and complexion (*varṇa*) are described as being born of suitability (*sātmyaja*) and likewise born of oneself (*ātmaja*). Therefore, it should be understood that both are the causes in this case.
The phrase "even the maintenance of life" means that even the mother, who is the cause of conceiving the fetus, must maintain her own life-force (*prāṇa*).
Furthermore, by the passage beginning with "nor when used improperly," he demonstrates that the consumption of unwholesome tastes (*asātmya-rasa*) causes injury to the fetus.

As for the birth of offspring from those who consume unwholesome tastes, that follows the same logic as the birth of offspring from those who indulge in what is unwholesome; therefore, it is not demonstrated here again.
By the statement "the totality is also a cause here," he shows that for those who do not consume food improperly, dharma and other factors are the causes for the production of offspring;
[this includes] manifestation (*abhinirvṛtti*), the clarity of major and minor limbs,
the continuity of life-force (*prāṇānubandha*), the continuity of strength (*balānubandha*), nourishment (*puṣṭi*), and growth (*upacaya*).
"Vṛddhi," however, means increase in length;

"utsāha" (enthusiasm) and "bala" (strength) are words used in the sense of a specific mode. By this, he shows that other qualities such as color and so forth are likewise born from rasa in this same manner.
In this way, the word "iti" (thus) should be explained in the preceding cases as well.

However, when the word "iti" signifies completion, then it should be understood that the manifestation of those qualities born of *rajas* is complete; by this, even unmanifested qualities such as color and so forth are obtained through *rajas*.
With the words beginning with "it exists," he resolves the objection raised regarding the spontaneous birth (*aupapāduka*) of the mind.

Here, the word "also" (*api*) functions as a restrictive particle. Furthermore, the statement beginning with "that which connects the living being with the body" serves as the very proof for the mind's spontaneous birth, because these aforementioned attributes cannot be established apart from the mind.

It is called *spṛk* because it constantly touches the self (*ātman*); *śarīra* refers to the subtle body (*ātivāhika-śarīra*). By means of that subtle body acting as the cause, it connects the individual soul (*jīva*) with its own nature—that is to say, with the body which is the locus of experience.

The existence of the subtle body is established by the statement: "Accompanied by the four extremely subtle elements, [the soul], moving with the speed of thought, goes from one body to another" (Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka 2).

Alternatively, the construction is as follows: that which the living self (*jīva*) connects with the mind by means of a "touching body"—that is, a body possessing the quality of touch—is the spontaneously born (*upapāduka*).

He thinks thus: if the mind were here accepted as being connected to the self through its connection with the body, then, because the self is all-pervading (*vyāpaka*), there would have to be perception everywhere; yet it does not occur. Therefore, only where the mind is bound to a body possessing touch is it that one experiences pleasure and so forth.
By the qualification "having touched," he demonstrates the non-perception of the self, since the mind does not go to the urine, nails, hair, and so forth of the body.
"Preceded by departure" means being directed toward going to another body; "devotion" (bhakti) here means desire (icchā).
"By whom" means by a mind that has abandoned [the Self] as inferior;
"by which" refers to a mind that is predominantly *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, or *tāmasa*—this is the intended meaning.

"In the second birth" (*dvitīyāyām ājātau*) means in the second life; the sense is that whatever kind of mind one had in a previous birth, for the most part, that very same kind arises in another birth.
However, some read "tena na dvitīyāyām" and so forth;
even there, the meaning is that for the most part, in the second birth, a connection with an equal mind does not occur, though occasionally it does.

Showing that the aforementioned statement—"nothing pertaining to his previous body would remain unknown to him"—implies that such knowledge of his previous life does indeed occur in certain cases, he says: "But when," and so forth.
"By the pure" means by the quality of his own purified *sattva*; "of him alone" is connected with the word "whose" (*yasya*) which will be mentioned later.

For the mind, overwhelmed by *tamas* arising during the pressure of the womb, does not remember what occurred in a previous birth. However, he whose *sattva* has arisen and is not overcome by *tamas* certainly remembers what was experienced in a past birth—this is the sense.
"Having placed [it] foremost" means having determined it as the cause.

Furthermore, although this collection of mental factors (*manodharma*) was already mentioned in the section on the "approach of the sense organs" (*indriyopakramaṇīya*), it is stated here again due to the requirements of the context; thus, it does not incur the fault of redundancy.

Although it has not been explicitly stated that *sattva* directly produces the embryo, nevertheless, by the very fact that *sattva* is "born from [the parents]" (*upapāduka*) with respect to the embryo, one should understand that the production of the embryo by *sattva* is thereby asserted.

Therefore, the statement beginning with "those which are indeed born of the *sattva* of this embryo" is entirely appropriate as an explanation of the existence of *sattva*-born qualities within the embryo.

Furthermore, the description of the cause of the embryo as being of a "spontaneously arisen" (*upapāduka*) nature is intended to demonstrate that the cause of the embryo is the property of the mind (*manas*), which consists in the transition from one body to another, rather than anything else.
The phrase "of various kinds" (*nānāvidhāni*) refers to those [qualities] which are distinguished by various modes of activity (*vṛtti*) belonging to the *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* types.

By the statement "these exist in a single person," it is shown that there is only one person who at one time becomes characterized by *sattva* in the performance of dharma, at another time becomes characterized by *rajas* in the contemplation of desire, and at yet another time becomes filled with *tamas* in delusion; it does not mean they exist simultaneously. Thus, qualities such as *sāttvika* and the rest do not occur at one and the same time, but rather occur in succession. Now, if all these *sāttvika* and other qualities belong to the very same person, how is it that designations such as "this person is *sāttvika*" occur? To this he says: "But one... and so forth.

"By way of predominant tendency" means that he whose mental states (*vṛtti*) are for the most part *sāttvika* is called *sāttvika*, while he whose mental states are for the most part *rājasa* is called *rājasa*, and so forth. This very point was stated previously: "The *sattva* that constantly follows a person is designated as being of that very nature, because of its predominance and persistence" (Sūtra 8).

Having thus established through the analysis of causes such as the mother that the embryo arises from a combination [of factors], he says "In this way, this... and so forth, in order to strengthen that point with an illustration.
A *kūṭāgāra* is a circular-shaped house prepared for sudation (*jentāka-sveda*); others, however, say that a *kūṭāgāra* is a mobile house made of cloth and other materials.

In this context, although all factors—mother and the others—acting together constitute the cause for the embryo, nevertheless, when the causality of *sātmya* (habituation) and *rasa* (taste/nutrition) alone is established by excluding the mother, father, self, and *sattva*, the statement "the aggregate (*samudāya*) is also a cause here" is intended as follows: Just as the four factors beginning with the mother are necessarily causes for the embryo, such is not the case for *sātmya* or *rasa*. Since the embryo arises from the very conjunction of semen, blood, *sattva*, and the self (*ātman*), there is no necessary requirement for *sātmya* and *rasa* at the moment of the embryo's formation. It is only after the formation of the embryo that nourishment and growth are produced by *sātmya* and *rasa*; therefore, by demonstrating that an aggregate is required for *sātmya* and *rasa*, it was stated in that very place, "the aggregate is also a cause here. However, while the mother and other factors do depend on one another as an aggregate, they do not necessarily depend on the aggregate of *sātmya* and *rasa* at the initial formation of the embryo; thus, their dependence on an aggregate was not mentioned again in that regard.
By this passage, "from the collection of these entities," that which is the mutual dependence of the four factors beginning with the mother is indeed stated.

Furthermore, regarding the fact that suitability (*sātmya*) and taste (*rasa*) are also causes for the embryo without distinction, as stated by the words "this [embryo] is born of suitability" and "this [embryo] is born of taste," it should be understood that these function as causes after the union of the embryo; likewise, the parents are also causes through an indirect lineage, by virtue of being the cause for producing pure semen and ovum.
Furthermore, Bhāradvāja asks:
"How is this joined? and so forth; the meaning is, by what sequence does it meet?
"One is born with a human body" means that within the human class, for what reason is one born specifically with a human body?

Regarding the statement that [the self] consists of a collection, that is incorrect. The point here is that by asserting that a *jāti* (universal) distinct from the *mātrā*s and so forth is the cause, and that such a *jāti*—in the form of "human" and so on—is the powerful cause, it is not tenable for [the self] to originate from the aforementioned collection of *mātrā*s and the like.
He states another refutation: "And if," etc.; "jaḍaḥ" means dull-witted; "minminaḥ" means having a nasalized and indistinct voice.
Regarding the phrase "having a form similar to their father," the word "father" (pitṛ) here should be understood as referring to both mother and father.

The underlying intention is that if human beings possess forms resembling their causes, then those born from causes such as insentient matter (*jaḍa*) would likewise possess forms resembling their causes—that is, they would be insentient and so forth.
The reason for providing numerous examples such as insentient matter here is to demonstrate the firmness of the position by establishing it through a wealth of illustrations.
Having established the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), he anticipates the following resolution: "Now, in this case," and so forth.
By the phrase "by his own [self]," it is meant by that which has been acquired through the self's own karma.

Since the sense faculties (*indriya*) are said to be born from the self and not produced by human parents, the sense faculties of the parents are not the cause for [the child's] faculties; therefore, the sense faculties of this [child] do not become similar to those of the parents—this is the intended meaning.
The phrase "by their own" is to be connected with the ears and other sense organs.
In the expression "born from the dull-witted and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) denotes a category; by this, those who are hunchbacked, leprous, and the like are included.

For the body that serves as the substratum for hunchbackedness, leprosy, and so on, is not born of the self, but rather is born of the mother and father. Consequently, the fact that one born hunchbacked or otherwise is impaired precisely through the occurrence of hunchbackedness and so forth remains exactly as stated.

He refutes the proposed resolution of the doubt with the words "atrāpi" and so forth, stating that there would be a defect in the proposition (*pratijñādoṣa*). This refers to the proposition of the Self's nature as a knower in the passage beginning with "The Self is a knower" (Śā.
1), as well as [the proposition] "But the supreme Self is changeless" (Sū.).
The sense is that there would be a flaw in the proposition of immutability established by [the verse beginning with] "ityādi.

By the phrase "asatsvajña" (one who is ignorant of himself), the asserted quality of being a knower (*jñatva*) is contradicted because of occasional ignorance; furthermore, since the self's status as a knower would depend on the senses, it would be contingent upon another and thus not real—this is the sense.
With the words "yatra" and so forth, he establishes the presence of modification (*savikāratva*).
The sense is that by the abandonment of consciousness, the primordial nature (prakṛti) undergoes modification through its transformation into unconsciousness;
thus, "savikāra" means "possessing modification," which should be understood as resulting from the elision of the possessive suffix -matup.
He states another objection regarding the soul's consciousness being dependent upon the senses, beginning with "yadi ca" and so forth.
"Because of ignorance, there would be no cause": the meaning is that due to ignorance, [the self] would not be the cause for the impelling of the body and so forth, which are preceded by knowledge.

"And because of being without a cause, it is not the self": the meaning is that since it would not be the cause for the impelling of the body and so forth—which are accomplished through intelligence—there must exist something distinct from the five insentient elements, designated as "consciousness," which is denoted by the word "self.
"It is a mere matter of words": this statement—that "the self sees form with its own eye," and so on—is a mere sound devoid of referential reality.
Ātreya provides the resolution: "Previously," and so forth;
this is the answer to the question, "How is this [self] joined?"
"Sattva" means the cause of the union of semen and ovum;
"of beings" (bhūtānām) means of living creatures.

"Yoni" means birth or species. Even when the word *yoni* denotes a cause, those born from a womb and so forth are still called "womb-born" (*jarāyuja*) and so on, because the term for the cause is figuratively applied to the effect.
"Form" (ākṛti) means configuration; its specific varieties are indeed mutually dissimilar forms, such as those of humans, elephants, horses, and so forth.
Having shown the distinction of the sources of birth (yoni-bheda), he explains how there is a conformity to the source [of birth] by saying "therein," etc.;
the entities that produce the embryo are semen and the like.
Regarding the phrase "in figures made of beeswax" (*madhūcchiṣṭavigraheṣu*): this refers to figures in the form of dolls fashioned from clay using beeswax.
The term "human image" (*manuṣyabimba*) refers to a doll in human form made of beeswax.

The illustration of "many substances such as gold" (*kanakādibahudravyodāharaṇa*) is for the purpose of showing the commonality (*sādharmya*): just as many substances like gold, when placed within a beeswax mold of a human doll, produce a human shape, so too do many elements such as semen, when fallen into a human womb, act as the makers of a human body.

Although it is true that [the embryo] consists of a composite whole and is thus produced from a collection [of causes], nevertheless, by the power of its primary cause (yonirūpakāraṇa), it becomes similar to its own source (svayoni) and not similar to another source. Furthermore, the nature of the cause does not admit of such questioning;

therefore, even the composite of semen and so forth constitutes the cause, and the mother and father specifically serve as the cause for the embryo's belonging to the same species—thus there is no inconsistency. This is because, as indicated by the phrase "because of being of that source" (tadyonitvāt), the human parents specifically function as the cause for the human being.
"Seed" refers to semen and blood;
the seed-portion (*bījabhāga*) is that part of the seed which brings about the formation of the limbs and minor members.
The meaning is that there is also a twofold occurrence here: they may have forms similar to their fathers, or they may not. "Born of oneself" (*ātmaja*) means born from karma bound to the self.

As for the statement that destiny (*daiva*) is the cause of existence and non-existence, the meaning is that when the sense organs are present, auspicious destiny is the cause that generates the sense organs, and when the sense organs are absent, inauspicious destiny is the cause.
He summarizes [the argument] with the words "Therefore," and so forth.

He thinks as follows: The human seed consists of a collection of parts that are themselves seeds; it generates a person whose form is a collection of parts similar to itself. Furthermore, the sense organs are the instruments of experience, dependent upon the karma bound to the self. Therefore, even if the father is afflicted with leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), provided the seed is not corrupted and produces skin and other tissues free from leprosy, then skin and other tissues that are free from leprosy and similar [to those of the parents] will be produced from the unafflicted seeds of the skin and so forth. However, when, due to the extreme advancement of leprosy in the parents, the seed itself becomes corrupted by the morbidity (*doṣa*) that causes leprosy, then from the corrupted seed-parts of the skin and so forth, skin that is itself corrupted by leprosy is produced.

As it has been said: "When a child is born to a husband and wife who both suffer from an abundance of leprosy and whose blood and semen are corrupted, that offspring should also be known as leprous" (Sūtra-sthāna, Nidāna-sthāna).

5) Thus, even in the case of one afflicted by leprosy (*kuṣṭhin*), if by the power of causes a defect that produces leprosy exists in the seed, then the offspring of the leper will likewise be leprous. Furthermore, regarding blindness and other forms of sensory impairment, misfortune alone is the cause; and that [misfortune] is necessarily present even in the case of blind offspring. Therefore, when an inauspicious factor that impairs vision exists in the case of a blind offspring, then, by the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit (*kākatālīyanyāya*), one born blind is seen to be blind [due to that specific cause].
The same should be explained in the case of the hunchbacked and others, as well as the insentient and others.
Regarding the objection raised concerning the possibility of ignorance in the Self, he says: "And not," and so forth.
The meaning of the proposition is that the self is always possessed of knowledge, both when the sense organs exist and when they do not;

for in the phrase "never indeed non-existent," the word "indeed" (*hi*) indicates the reason. Therefore, since the self is always accompanied by the mind (*manas*), even in the absence of external sense organs, because of its connection with the internal organ—the mind—this self is eternally possessed of knowledge, having the mind as its instrument. This is the meaning.

However, that cognition which pertains to external objects arises from a specific state of the sentient being's sensory faculties; therefore, when the senses exist, there occurs a specific cognition produced by the senses. But as for the knowledge of the Self (*ātman*) produced solely by the mind, that indeed exists at all times. Therefore, since the knowledge of the Self—which is eternally present and produced merely by the proximity of the mind—exists always, its power to generate cognition is not obstructed; with this intention, he says: "No," and so forth.

The knowers of the inner self (adhyātmavid) maintain that this [cognition] which pertains to the senses and involves the enjoyment of objects occurs at certain times and does not occur at other times due to the absence of the senses. Furthermore, even regarding external cognition, this Self possesses the very power to generate knowledge; however, due to the absence of instruments, it does not at times engage in the cognition of effects—that is, the cognition of external objects which generates the activity toward those effects. By the word "by means of" (bhāvaiḥ) in this context, the word "by which" (yaiḥ) is to be supplied as an ellipsis, thereby indicating that there is objectless cognition of the Self when the senses are absent.
It proceeds, that is, it arises;
regarding this very point, he states an illustration: "even though knowing," and so forth.
"Even though knowing" means even though knowing how to fashion a jar.
Because of the absence of soft earth (mṛdu-mṛttikā).
He states another means of proving the self’s nature as a knower: "Listen," and so forth. *Adhyātmam* means with reference to the self;
*ātmajñānabalam* is the power of the knowledge of the self.
"Having withdrawn" means having turned the mind away from sense objects; "having withdrawn" also means having restrained the mind from objects other than the Self;
and "fickle" refers to its nature.
"In one's own knowledge" means in the knowledge of the self (*ātmajñāna*).

Because one becomes omniscient by examining all states of being through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) alone, even without the sense organs, therefore the self, though devoid of sense organs, has the nature of consciousness. (20–21)
Furthermore, he provides another worldly example of the existence of knowledge in one who lacks sense faculties, beginning with "Take [it]," etc.;
"one who has entered a dream" means one who has reached the state of perceiving a dream.
He states the distinction between the knowledge of the self (*ātmajñāna*) and the knowledge of objects (*viṣayajñāna*): "Not [without] the self," and so forth.
Without the eternal knowledge of the self, no knowledge born of an object proceeds—that is, it does not arise without the assistance of instruments such as the senses.
Furthermore, the knowledge of the self is indeed eternal; as stated in the Sāṃkhya system by the passage beginning with "The power of consciousness is unchanging" and ending with "of the self."

He states the proof for this: "For a single entity does not exist"—that is, an entity characterized by the property of arising (*utpatti-dharma*) does not exist as a single thing while being devoid of a cause; it does not exist, meaning it does not arise. Likewise, even though an entity may be produced from causes, if it were causeless—that is, without an agent—it would not exist, meaning it would not arise. Rather, it is only when clay, the potter's wheel, and so forth are presided over by an agent, the potter, that they function. Therefore, the implication is that object-cognitions (*viṣaya-jñāna*) are likewise produced by the sense organs, the mind, the objects, and the agent, which is the self (*ātman*).
22–24 He concludes: "Therefore," and so forth.

Here, since the fact that the self possesses modifications—which was raised by the contingency of the self being either a knower or a non-knower—is already refuted by the very proof of the self's eternal consciousness, it has not been refuted separately.

By the word "Bharadvāja" here, the teacher of Ātreya is not meant; rather, it refers to someone else belonging to the Bharadvāja lineage. Therefore, it is entirely appropriate that his resolution of doubts was performed by Ātreya.
In the *Saṅgraha*, the word "cause" (*hetu*) is connected with the stages beginning from conception up to birth.

The negation of the thesis (pratijñāpratiṣedha) is to be understood as that performed by Bharadvāja, and its proof (sādhana) is that which belongs to Ātreya; this is expressed by the phrase "the clear determination of the self" (viśadaścātmanirṇayaḥ). The word "that" (tat) is neuter because it refers generally to the mother and so forth.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Minor Treatise on the Descent of the Embryo," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka Saṃhitā*, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Section on Anatomy (*Śārīrasthāna*).
[Śārīrasthāna, Chapter 4 (50 of 120):
Because it is an elaboration of the minor entry into the womb, the major entry into the womb is described immediately after [the former].
