"From which" (*yataḥ*) means from which cause;
"of which modification" (*yadvikāraḥ*) means consisting of which (*yanmaya*);
"by which sequence" (*yayā-anupūrvyā*) means by which order (*yenānukrameṇa*).
"Not perishing in its entirety" means not undergoing death. As for those various constituents—

such as those derived from the mother, those derived from the father, and so forth, including skin, blood, and the rest— from whichever sources such as the mother they arise, having separately analyzed those maternal and other constituent parts in the previous chapter (the first), the resulting sense of the sentence is that those [parts] derived from the mother and so forth are not mentioned here.
Although this matter has already been stated in the preceding chapter by such passages as "And this [embryo] is born of the mother" (Śā.

3), it is nevertheless repeated here in accordance with the purification of the sequence of questions; for in this way, the questioning becomes elegant in its proper order: first the cause, then the embryo in the form of the effect, and finally the characteristics of the embryo as the subject to be described.

As for that which was stated [in the *Śārīrasthāna*] beginning with "the union of semen and blood located within the womb" and ending with "the embryo is produced" (*Śā. A.* 3), the specific meaning denoted by the term "embryo" (*garbha*) was not explicitly defined there, yet it is required [for clarity]. Therefore, the definition of the meaning denoted by the designation "embryo" provided here is certainly not redundant.
In the phrase "when [the semen and blood] have entered the abdomen" (*kukṣigate*), this refers to their being located in a specific part of the abdomen, namely the womb (*garbhāśaya*).

"In the union" (*saṃyoge*) means in a proper union (*samyagyoge*). By this, the conjunction of the living soul (*jīva*) with its subtle body (*ativāhika-śarīra*) is encompassed; it does not refer to that conjunction of the self (*ātman*)—which, being all-pervading, cannot be the cause of the birth of an embryo—that was mentioned previously.
And although such a conjunction occurs only within the womb, nevertheless, the term "entered into the womb" was employed in order to establish the proven point for the disciple;
[this is followed by] the passage beginning with "But the embryo," and so forth.

Even though the elements such as earth and so forth are the initiators of the formation of the embryo, the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) is placed first, in accordance with the elements that will be mentioned later;
for he will say: "He first takes up the intermediate space from among the other qualities," and so forth.

"The substrate of consciousness" means the nature of the self's locus of experience; for by the word "consciousness" (*cetanā*), the self is denoted. Alternatively, the word "element" (*bhūta*) is used in the sense of similarity; thus, the body is like a substrate for the self, but in reality, there is no substrate for the self apart from its being the locus of experience, for the self is inherently without support.

"By this reasoning" means that by this method of conjunction consisting of the modifications of the primary elements (*bhūta*), the body becomes a composite of the modifications of the five great elements; by another reasoning, as stated in the *Katidhāpuruṣīya* chapter, it consists of twenty-four constituents; likewise, by considering its form as being born of the mother and so forth, it means that it becomes a composite of the mother and other factors.

Nor is there any contradiction among these positions; for even when designated as "born of the mother" and so forth, their nature as modifications of the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) remains entirely uncontradicted, such that those born of the mother and the rest are indeed merely modifications of the great elements. For it has been said: "One should know that there are sixteen elements in the body, consisting of the essence of food (*rasa*), and those produced from the mother and father" (Śārīra-sthāna 2).

Furthermore, even though [the body] consists of twenty-four principles (*tattvas*), it is precisely its nature as being composed of the five great elements that is elaborated therein in the passage beginning with "He... and so on.
"Of this" refers to the embryo;
"gone" means having ceased.

By the statement "in the old [semen]" (*purāṇe*)— meaning accumulated through the passing of the fertile period— and "situated in the new," he shows that even in the case of new semen, if it is not situated [within the womb], it lacks the capacity to cause conception.

By the phrase "one who has bathed after purification" (*śuddhasnātām*), he shows that only a woman who has bathed after purification is to be approached for intercourse, and not one who has not bathed, because she is impure.
A woman (*strī*) is so called because the embryo (*garbha*) coagulates (*styāyati*) within her; by this [definition], he excludes the barren woman.
In the word *ṛtumatīm*, the suffix *matup* is used in the sense of praise.
By the phrase "together with her" (*tayā saha*), it means "with that woman."
"By one who has become thus" means by one joined with such a season.

"Joy" (harṣa) is a particular kind of affection; "impelled by that" (tenodīritaḥ) means urged or driven by it—this is the essential meaning. Alternatively, "the supreme" (para) refers to that which arises at the subsequent time, for semen indeed arises as the supreme among all bodily constituents (dhātu).

Regarding the phrase "the self as the bodily element": that which has the form of the bodily element is the semen-element; thus, it arises from limb after limb and is manifested [therein]. Therefore, semen is not produced from the limbs, but rather that which already exists in the form of semen is manifested.
For there is this statement: "Semen is present throughout the body" (Cikitsā-sthāna,
Chapter 2, Verse pāda).

4) "By one who has become joyous" means by one who has attained a state consisting of joy (*harṣamayatā*); and by the phrase "urged forth and presided over," he shows that at the time of urging and likewise at the time of emission, the presiding of the self (*ātman*) as consisting of joy is the cause for the semen (*śukra*) reaching the womb (*garbhāśaya*). If, at the time of the flow of semen, the man were devoid of joy, then there would not be a proper flow of semen; likewise, due to the obstruction of the impulse (*vega*), the element in the form of the seed—the semen—would not reach the womb.
"Abhisaṃsarga" means perfect merging (samyaṅmūrcchanam).

"Sattvakaraṇaḥ" refers to one whose instrument (karaṇa) is the mind (manas), which is of the nature of *sattva*. Since the Self (*ātman*) is actionless (*niṣkriyatvena*), whatever action it performs through the active mind, that action—though performed by the mind—is nevertheless attributed to the conscious Self alone, as the mind itself is insentient (*acetana*).
For the statement—“Since the self possesses volition, it is therefore designated as the agent” (Śā.

1)—is intended for the purpose of grasping the qualities; here, by the word *guṇa* (quality), the elements possessing those qualities are expressed through the metaphorical identification of quality and the possessor of quality (*guṇaguṇinor abhedopacārāt*).
Alternatively, [one might ask]: "The *guṇas* are subordinate (*apradhāna*) and the Self (*ātman*) is the primary (*pradhāna*), yet the elements (*bhūta*) distinct from them are also *guṇas*;

for what reason does the Self grasp the elements which are subordinate in nature? In response to this doubt, he states the synonyms that demonstrate the primacy of the Self, beginning with "He indeed... and ending with "...does not perish" (*akṣara*).
It is called *akṣara* because it does not decay (*na kṣarati*).
"Endowed with qualities" means possessing the qualities of the elements;
"grasps the elements" is the meaning of *grahaṇa*.
By these synonyms, it is shown that the self, which is the subject denoted by the word, is well-known as a substratum (*āśrayatva*) because it is assisted by other categories of entities.
"Earlier" means first, prior to the other qualities such as air and so forth;
here, regarding the sequence of grasping the elements within the womb, he provides an illustration beginning with "just as," and so on.
"At the end of dissolution" means at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*); "at its passing" means at the beginning of creation.
"Desirous of creating" means wishing to create; "beings" refers to ether and the other elements.
Regarding the "appropriation by a being" (*sattvopādāna*), this refers to the agency of the mind (*manaḥkaraṇa*).

For at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), because all modifications dissolve back into their primal nature (*prakṛti*), only *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* remain in a state of supreme unmanifestness (*paramavyaktarūpa*). Subsequently, at the commencement of creation, the manifold world (*prapañca*) beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) arises from *prakṛti* in due order. Among these, space (*ākāśa*) arises first, followed by air (*vāyu*) and the other elements in their manifest forms; such is the established doctrine of the Sāṅkhya.
Furthermore, the fact that space is produced should be understood according to the Sāṅkhya system itself.

"Even in the taking of a body" means even in the taking of the nature of the embryo, it "appropriates," that is, it takes for itself the space contained within the semen and blood by virtue of its own spatial nature.

Regarding "the qualities become more manifest": compared to space, which possesses a single quality, air—possessing the qualities of sound and touch—is more manifest; compared to that, fire—possessing the qualities of sound, touch, and form—is more manifest, and so forth.
And this sequence for seizing the spirits (bhūtagrahaṇakrama) is established by scripture alone; no such reasoning as that is found here which is truly heart-warming.
And showing that this seizing of the spirits occurs in a very short time, he says "all," and so forth.
"Defiled by all the elements" means defiled by the state of having all the elements unmanifested;

and by the word "element" (*dhātu*), the primary constituents (*bhūta*) are meant—or else the seeds of the elements such as the vital fluids (*rasa*); thus, "become like phlegm" (*kheṭabhūta*) means resembling phlegm (*śleṣman*).

The explanation of the phrase "avyaktavigraha" (having an unmanifest body) is "sadasadbhūtāṅgāvayava" (possessing limbs and members that are both existent and non-existent); the meaning is that its major and minor limbs are both manifest and unmanifest. They are "existent" because they exist in the form of seeds, and "non-existent" because they are in an unmanifest state.

Alternatively, the construction may be: "sadasadbhūtāṅgāvayavo ghanaḥ sampadyate" (it becomes a solid mass with limbs and members that are both existent and non-existent), where "ghana" means hard or solid.
The *piṇḍa* is shaped like a knot;
the *peśī* is elongated, shaped like a strip of flesh;
and the *arbuda* is round and elevated.
The nine or ten limbs are the head and so forth, and their constituent parts are the sub-limbs (*aṅgāvayava*).
By the statement "simultaneously," [it is meant that] "the head of the child is produced first" (Śā. [Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā]).

6) By the phrase "ityādi" (and so forth), he refutes the various views of certain schools that will be discussed hereafter; for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the completion of all parts occurs simultaneously.
The phrase "some" (*kecit*) implies not all;

for while sound and the other [objects] will hereafter be described as modifications of the elements (*bhūta-vikāra*), they are not all mentioned here. Rather, by the statement "only some," such as the skin (*tvak*) and so forth, it is indicated that those [qualities] born of the mother (*mātṛja*) and others—which were previously mentioned in the passage beginning with "the skin and blood" (*Śārīrasthāna* 3)—need not be stated explicitly here. Instead, those qualities residing in the skin, such as form (*mūrti*), unctuousness (*sneha*), and softness (*mārdava*), when described as being produced from the elements, serve as designations for the skin itself.
In this way, by the description of the modifications of the elements (bhūta-vikāra) residing in blood and so forth, the description of blood and the other constituents is to be understood;
for skin and the others, which will be described later, are likewise merely aggregates of elemental modifications.
The designation of skin and the rest as "born of the mother" and so forth is intended to demonstrate their dependence upon the primary elements (tanmātra) and the rest.

Furthermore, the mention here of the bodily constituents (*dhātus*) as being produced from the primary elements (*bhūtas*) is for the purpose of knowing how their increase or decrease is generated, through the prohibition or application of those primary elements that serve as their causes. Specifically, whichever constituent is derived from a particular primary element, that constituent increases when supplied with a substance dominated by that same primary element, and it decreases when supplied with a substance of the opposite nature.

Although lightness (*lāghava*) is recited among the qualities of air—as in "rough, cold, and light" (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 1)—it should nevertheless be understood as being present in an even greater degree in space (*ākāśa*); for this reason, it is listed here among the modifications of space. Indeed, because space is exceedingly subtle, it is lighter than even air.

Furthermore, [space is characterized by] discernment (*viveka*), separation (*viccheda*), the structural arrangement of the elements (*dhātu-vyūhana*), the formation of the elements (*dhātu-racanā*), and the transport of the elements (*dhātu-vahana*).
That by which one sees is the "vision," namely the visual faculty;
"form" (mūrti) refers to solidity.

Knowing that this body consists of transformations of the five elements is the cause even for liberation, which is the supreme desire; thus, demonstrating its similarity to the world, he says: "In this way, this [body]," and so forth.
"In this way" means by virtue of consisting of transformations of the five elements, it is equal to the world; thus, it is "world-like."

Furthermore, regarding the statement here that the body consists of modifications of the elements (*bhūtavikāramayatva*), similarity between the world and the person (*lokapuruṣa*) has been stated with reference to that very fact of consisting of elemental modifications. As for the internal similarity between the world and the person which was to be explained in the "Investigation of the Person" (*puruṣavicaya*), even though it was not explicitly stated here, it should be understood as being indicated by the specific mention beginning with "as many as... (*yāvanto hi*).

By this, it should be understood that however many specific internal states there are—whether they belong to the inner self such as the intellect (*sattva*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and so forth, or whether they are elemental such as form (*mūrti*), moisture (*kleda*), and so forth—all those residing in the person are identical to those in the world.
And this similarity between the world and the Puruṣa will become manifest in the "Investigation of the Puruṣa" (Puruṣavicaya).
Showing that this exposition of the similarity between the world and the Puruṣa is useful only for those seeking liberation (mumukṣu), he says: "But the wise [think] thus," and so forth.
"The wise" means those possessing correct knowledge; that is to say, those engaged in liberation.
And he will himself state in the "Investigation of the Person" (Puruṣavicaya) that the description of the similarity between the world and the person is solely for the sake of liberation.
He concludes the development of the limbs, beginning with the sense organs, which occurs during the third month—the subject at hand—with the words: "In this way, of him," and so forth.

"Simultaneously" means at one and the same time. The designation "simultaneously" is intended to demonstrate that the development of the sense organs (*indriya*) occurs at the same time as the formation of all the limbs.
Anticipating the question of whether teeth and so forth also appear in the third month, he says "elsewhere," etc.;
"secondary characteristics" (*vyañjana*) refers to the beard, breasts, and so on.
The manifestation (*vyaktībhāvaḥ*) refers to the appearance of semen and blood;
"likewise joined" means that the limbs, such as the teeth, and the faculties such as the intellect, arise as things produced after birth.

This is the nature (*prakṛtiḥ*): the sense organs and the constituent parts of the body arise simultaneously, whereas the teeth and so forth appear only after some time even for one who has been born—this is the meaning of the human nature (*manuṣyasvabhāva*).
"Otherwise" means that sometimes teeth are born already present, and so forth; such is the transformation (*vikṛti*) of a human being.
Now, why are teeth and other such things, which arise from the womb and so on, called "transformations"? To this he says: "They exist," etc.; the word "indeed" (*khalu*) indicates the reason.

"Permanent" refers to those things that persist as long as the body exists, such as the hands and feet; "impermanent" refers to those that do not persist as long as the body exists, such as the teeth.

By this, the meaning is that it is logical for the teeth and other such things—which are impermanent by nature—to undergo transformation (*vikṛti*) because they arise [only] from the womb and so forth, whereas permanence [belongs to the former].
Now, among these permanent and impermanent things, he states which ones bear the gender of female and so on, beginning with the words "of that" (*tasya*).
"They remain" means they persist as long as the body exists.

By this [statement], those very eternal entities such as the generative organ (*upastha*) and so forth assume either the feminine or masculine gender; therein, the eternal entity in the form of the generative organ is the feminine gender, the penis is the masculine gender, and the mere cavity devoid of the shape of the generative organ becomes the neuter gender.

Alternatively, the meaning of the sentence is this: whether it be the female characteristic such as the breasts, or the male characteristic such as the beard, or the neuter form which possesses the appearance common to both female and male and arises after birth—even these are simply those same eternal entities, such as the chest or the cheeks, that assume them under the influence of time.

For indeed, it is the chest itself, when endowed with the seed for the production of breasts, that later becomes possessed of breasts in a woman; likewise, it is the cheek itself, when endowed with the seed for a beard, that becomes possessed of a beard.

Nor is it necessarily the case that because the seed of the breasts, beard, and so forth exists within the body, why then do the breasts and other such features not emerge from the very moment of conception? For this is the power of the seed: that it produces its effect only at its own proper time, just as a seed of rice or the like, even when fallen upon the earth, generates a sprout only when the appropriate season arrives. Furthermore, nature does not deserve reproach for the fact that "only when the limbs and members are fully formed do they bear the characteristics of female and so forth. In the case of the reading beginning with these words, the meaning is quite explicit.

Now, he asks: "From where does the distinction between female and so forth arise when the causes, such as the semen (*śukra*) and other factors, are identical? He replies: "The Vaiśeṣikas" means those who are distinguished, that is to say, mutually distinct; "relying on the *pradhāna*" means relying on the self (*ātman*).

"Resorting to qualities" (*guṇasaṃśrayāḥ*) means resorting to the elements (*bhūta*) present in the semen and the ovum (*śukraśoṇita*); here, by the word "quality" (*guṇa*), the elements are intended, as indicated by the suffix *-tasi* used in the locative sense (*yataḥ*). Therefore, whichever specific state (*vaiśeṣika bhāva*) becomes predominant by the power of destiny (*daiva*), from that state the production of one of the two types of embryo—either female or male—occurs. If the female-producing states, such as those causing impotence (*klaibya*) and so forth, are more numerous, then a female is born; in the opposite case, a male is born—this is the meaning. In this regard, he describes the female-producing states, beginning with "tadyathā" (as follows).

Lack of firmness (*avaiśāradya*) is delusion (*moha*), which is laxity or a lack of dense conjunction, such as the looseness of a cloth woven from sparse strands of strong hemp. Softness (*mārdava*), however, is the inherent softness of the parts even when there is dense conjunction, such as the suppleness of a cloth woven from continuous threads of silk. From weakness (*klaibya*) up to instability, these qualities reside primarily in the substrate (*pradhāna*); the remainder reside in the attributes (*guṇa*).
By the phrase "thus joined," he indicates the womb, the seed, the portions, and so forth;
it should be understood that these qualities, such as downward gravity and the rest, occur only when the seed is predominant in *rajas*.
Therefore, [it is said]: "By blood, a girl [is produced] when it is in excess" (*Śārīra*).
2) Thus, what was stated is not inconsistent with this;
the meaning is that the contrary qualities, such as lack of timidity (*aklaibya*) and so forth,
are the constituent parts of both sides— that is, the components that constitute the functions of both female and male.
Regarding the statement "they produce the neuter," this neuter designation is intended with reference to the unmanifested qualities (*avyakta-guṇa*).

Thus, the initial phrase "they produce the neuter" is employed with the intention of referring to the mass of unmanifested qualities. Subsequently, when the expectation arises as to "what are they?", the designation is understood to be in the masculine gender—"the parts belonging to both [sexes]"—due to the inclusion of specific particulars.

"They remain" means they are produced; "feelings" refers to the perception of pleasure and pain; "attain persistence" means they attain continuity; the meaning of the sentence is that at the very moment the sense-faculties arise, one becomes a knower of pleasure and pain.

"Therefore" means because of the connection with pleasure and pain; it vibrates and moves for the sake of producing pleasure and avoiding pain, and likewise desires the causes of pleasure experienced in other births—this is the meaning. The elders, who are advanced in knowledge, declare that the mother's heart, being joined with the longing for that [embryo], is "two-hearted" (*dvaihṛdayyam*).
Because of the state of having two hearts, it is "two-heartedness"; the mother's heart becomes a pair of hearts together with the embryo's heart.

Now, one might ask: how is the heart of the fetus connected with the heart of the mother? To this he says: "born from the mother" (*mātṛja*). This means it is born from the cause that is the mother. By means of the "rasa-carrying channels"—that is, by the rasa-carrying channels connected to the mother's heart and the navel of the fetus for the purpose of nourishing the fetus—whatever the fetus desires, through that desire, the desire reaches the heart via the rasa-carrying channels, and thus the mother also becomes possessed of that same desire. In this way, by the mother's desire, the fetus also becomes possessed of desire.
"Of those two" refers to the mother and the embryo;
"devotion" means desire;
"by them" refers to the channels that carry the vital fluids (rasa).
"It vibrates" means that it moves from the mother's heart to the embryo's heart, and from the embryo's heart back to the mother's heart.

Regarding the destruction or deformity of the embryo: destruction occurs through a great frustration of desire, whereas deformity occurs through a slight one. Alternatively, the mother’s desire may be preceded by the desire of the embryo; through the frustration of that [desire], the embryo is destroyed. For when that desire is frustrated, it directly destroys the most delicate embryo due to the provocation of *vāta* (wind) because of its direct connection to the embryo. However, when the mother’s desire is frustrated, it generates a disturbance of *vāta* in the mother, which produces deformity in the embryo as well—since they share the same state of well-being (*yogakṣema*)—by causing even a slight deformity.
This very point is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "For they share the same state of well-being," and so forth.

*Yoga* is the acquisition of the means for happiness, and *kṣema* is the avoidance of misfortune; by the statement that "these two, yoga and kṣema, are equal to those of the mother in respect to certain matters," he shows that there are cases where yoga and kṣema are not identical.
By this, he demonstrates that the mother's afflictions, such as hunger and so forth, do not necessarily bring about a distortion in the fetus, nor does the fetus [necessarily affect] the mother.
Because of the specific statement "especially for a pregnant woman," even a woman who is not pregnant should be treated with what is pleasant and beneficial during her fertile period,
as it is said: "Her companions should constantly attend to her with what is pleasant and beneficial" (Śārīra 8), and so forth.
The means of providing care (*upacāra-sādhana*) refers to the performance of appropriate care for the fetus thus conceived, as well as for the *dvaihṛdayya* (the "two-hearted" state of the mother).

Regarding that, the regimen for one who has conceived is as follows: "If she has conceived, she should drink unadulterated milk at the proper times" (Śārīrasthāna 8), and so forth. Furthermore, he will describe here the regimen for the "two hearts.
"Knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to the knowledge of both the embryo and the two hearts;
the phrase "specifically the desire for sour things" (*amlakāmatā viśeṣeṇa*) is the [grammatical] division.
"Faith and desire regarding high and low things" means among things that are elevated or depressed; the meaning is regarding things that have been prepared as food and those that have not,
[and] there is slight swelling in the feet.

It should be understood that these characteristics—swelling of the abdomen, distension, and so forth—occur by their very nature in the fetus; however, when associated with the third month, they also become the signs of *dvaihṛdayya* (the dual-hearted state).
Terrible activities such as sexual intercourse and the like;
protection from gods and the followers of Rākṣasas is "protection from gods and the followers of Rākṣasas" (*devatārakṣoanucaraparirakṣaṇam*);
[the section beginning with] "that which," and so forth.
Furthermore, whatever else women declare as things not to be indulged in during pregnancy should also be avoided;
for women say, "A pregnant woman should not look into a well, nor should she go to the other side of a river," and so forth.
The meaning is that even the words of elderly women are rooted in traditional authority (*āgama*), though they have not been shown here for fear of making the book too voluminous.
*Prārthanā* is the entreaty for a desired object; its intensity consists precisely in being produced by a powerful desire.
It is "conjoined with the beneficial" (*hitopahita*), meaning it is joined with what is beneficial, or rather, it is beneficial by way of conceptualization (*kalpanā*).
The removal of prayer is its bursting; for that purpose, prayer itself passes away only through the attainment of what was prayed for.
Regarding the fault in the frustration of prayer, he says: "Prayer," and so forth.
The firm maintenance of a prayer is "prārthanā-sandhāraṇa";

this occurs even when one receives what was prayed for only in small measure. Or, when one receives what is beneficial according to the prescribed method, the desire—whether slight, complete, or partially fulfilled—is thwarted;
and such frustration of desire, like fear and other such factors that disturb the mind, provokes the wind-humor (*vāta*).
By the phrase "of one who is undergoing [the process]," he shows that because the embryo is extremely tender, it cannot withstand even the slightest agitation of the *vāta*;
however, the conceptualization of deformity or destruction should be understood as being caused by the intensity or mildness of the provocation of the *vāta*.

Having explained the specific characteristics of the embryo as they arise in the context of the sequential account of the third month, he now describes the sequence for the fourth month as it follows in order, beginning with "In the fourth," and so forth.
"Stability" refers to density;
therefore, it is logical that a pregnant woman, being overcome by the dense and heavy embryo, becomes one whose limbs are weighted down.
By the phrase "exceeding others," he shows that even during other months there is a gradual increase of flesh and so forth,
by which the embryo is nourished through its physical state; thus, it is entirely logical that the pregnant woman diminishes as a result of this.
Since the essence of food (*āhārarasa*) is exhausted merely by nourishing the embryo, flesh, and so forth, it does not properly nourish the mother’s own flesh and other tissues.

"Accumulation of strength and complexion" (*balavarṇopacaya*) refers to the increase of strength and complexion; alternatively, "accumulation" (*upacaya*) means the nourishment of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).
"By all constituents" means by flesh, blood, and so forth;
the embryo is nourished by all of them simultaneously in the seventh month, whereas in the preceding months it is not nourished by all of them simultaneously—this is the distinction.
"In all ways" means by all forms produced from flesh, blood, and so forth;
"most exhausted" means most debased.

"From the eighth [month] onwards," and so forth; "by means of the nutrient-carrying channels" means that by means of the nutrient-carrying channels connected to the mother's heart and the umbilical cord of the fetus, they take up *ojas* from one another: the fetus takes up the *ojas* of the mother, and the mother takes up the *ojas* of the fetus.
He states the reason for the non-abiding of the *ojas*: "because the embryo is incomplete.
Since the embryo is incomplete, the *ojas* does not remain stable within the embryo because its substratum (*āśraya*) has not yet been fully formed.

Regarding the statement that "the mother's *ojas* (vital essence) enters the embryo," this means that the embryo's own *ojas*, being connected to the mother, is designated as the "mother's *ojas*. If, however, the meaning were that the mother's *ojas* itself enters the embryo, then the reason given—"because of the incompleteness of the embryo"—would be inconsistent, for it would be illogical for the *ojas* residing in the mother's complete body to depart [to the embryo]. Furthermore, just as the birth of the embryo while its *ojas* remains in the mother causes the death of the embryo, so too, if the mother's *ojas* were to reside in the embryo, then the birth of the embryo would result in the death of the mother as well. This is not desired, since it is stated here that "in both cases, it is the embryo alone that dies," by the words: "then the birth of the embryo becomes fatal."

In the *Jatūkarṇa* as well, the eighth month is shown to lead specifically to the destruction of the embryo, as it is stated: "In the eighth month, the vital essence (*ojas*) of the woman and the embryo mutually take hold of one another; therefore, at that time, birth leads only to the destruction of the embryo.
Others, however, explain: "Even though the mother's *ojas* enters the embryo, it results in the death of the embryo alone due to the force of past karma (*adṛṣṭa*), and not of the mother."

The commentators on the Suśruta, however, explain: "In the eighth month, because the fetus belongs to the domain of Nirṛti, even though the instability of the *ojas* is equal [for both], only the fetus is destroyed and not the mother. This should be understood as follows: because of the connection with the *ojas* of the fetus, the pregnant woman becomes repeatedly filled with joy (*harṣa*), whereas due to the departure of that *ojas*, she becomes repeatedly exhausted (*glāna*). Likewise, the term "fetus" implies that the fetus, like the pregnant woman, is repeatedly filled with joy and repeatedly becomes exhausted.
The word "therefore" (tasmāt) directly states the previously mentioned cause for fetal death;
"due to the instability of the *ojas*" has already been explained.
He now states another specific characteristic of the eighth month, beginning with the words "and that very... (*taṃ caiva* etc.).
"And that very matter" refers to the matter consisting of the miscarriage of the fetus;
"not to be counted" means it should not be explained to the pregnant woman by way of enumeration.

For if the pregnant woman were to hear about the eighth month—which is being enumerated—as something that causes the destruction of the fetus at birth, she would become afraid; and from that fear, there might be a miscarriage due to the agitation of the bodily winds (vāta). This is the intended meaning.
Regarding the phrase "in that [time]," the statement "from the eighth month up to the tenth" is intended to refer to the most commendable period for birth.

In the *Suśruta*, the designation of the period for a successful delivery as lasting up to twelve months should be understood as follows: since the eleventh and twelfth months, involving only slight defects, are placed within the category of "no defect" due to their minor nature.
He concludes the response given with the words beginning "evam" (thus), etc.
The answer to the question, "And what is the cause of its growth? is as follows: "Of the mother and so forth.

By the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), the father, self-habituation (*ātmasātmya*), tastes (*rasa*), and temperament (*sattva*) are understood—these being those mentioned in the passage beginning with "This [body] is born of the mother" (*mātṛjaśca yaṃ*, Śārīrasthāna, chapter 4).
The excellence (*sauṣṭhava*) of conduct (*vṛtta*), which consists of the proper behavior of the mother, is "excellence of conduct" (*vṛttasauṣṭhava*);
the term "from the mother" (*mātṛtaḥ*) is connected both with this excellence of conduct as well as with "moistening" (*upasneha*) and "perspiration" (*upasveda*).
Furthermore, the excellence of the suitability of the nutritional essence (*rasasātmyasauṣṭhava*) is indeed obtained through the perfection of the [mother's] diet and other factors.

*Upasneha* (moistening) is the connection with the natural exudation (*niṣyanda*) of the elements; *upasveda* (fomentation) is the heating of the embryo by the heat of the body. Indeed, *upasveda* is the cause of the growth of the embryo, just as the fomentation of the egg of oviparous creatures is seen to cause growth through the transformation of time. As the duration of time increases, so does the embryo grow.
He states another cause for growth: "and because of the perfection of its own nature."
The meaning is that the embryo becomes prone to growth by its very nature produced by karma;
for the embryonic body, being commenced by karma which brings about a body characterized by experience, is commenced with a nature inherently disposed toward growth, and therefore it indeed grows.
The answer to the question, “From what does its non-arising occur? is as follows: “Due to the mother,” and so forth.

This means having as its cause the impairment [of the parents]. In this context, the mother’s impairment refers to defects such as those of the blood or the womb (garbhāśaya), while the father’s impairment refers to defects of the semen; this is how it should be understood. 28

The answer to the question beginning with "yataśca jāyamānaḥ" (from what being born... is as follows: those factors designated as causes of growth, such as those mentioned in the passage beginning with "the excellence of the factors that produce the embryo, namely the mother and so forth," or alternatively, when there is a total reversal due to the morbidity of the mother and others, then the embryo meets its destruction; however, when there is only a slight reversal due to the presence of minor morbidity, then it should be understood that the newborn perishes shortly after birth.
29. To show the answer to the remaining question, he says: "Since, however," and so forth.

Here, in the phrase "not perishing" (*avināśyan*), "perishing" (*vināśa*) is intended to mean "transformation" (*vikṛti*); for the word "perishing" is also seen to be used in the sense of transformation, as in the designation "this man is ruined" (*vinaṣṭaḥ*) when he has been transformed by bad character. And this being the case, since the word "perishing" is observed even when there is transformation in only one part [of a thing], the qualification "in its entirety" (*kārtsnyena*) is appropriate.

The phrase "when the provocation of the *doṣas* has already been achieved through the consumption of provocative factors, yet one continues to consume other things said to provoke the *doṣas*" is intended to show that the provocation of the *doṣas* becomes powerful through the consumption of their own specific causes. For even through the consumption of extrinsic causes, a provocation of the *doṣas* occurs in the form of a secondary association (*anubandha*) when it is only slight in measure; for example, bile (*pitta*) being produced by sour substances is produced as accompanied by phlegm (*śleṣman*).
By the statement "they do not corrupt [the embryo] in their entirety," it is shown that if they were corrupted in their entirety, conception itself would not occur.
The term "born of the mother" (*mātṛja*) refers to the skin, blood, and so forth.

The term *anyatama* is a singular used in the sense of a class (*jātāvekavacana*); therein, even a single component is *anyatama*, and likewise, multiple components are expressed by the word *anyatama*.
For this very reason, the explanation of *anyatama* as "either one or many" is logically consistent.
Otherwise, since only a single constituent part would be grasped by any one of the terms, the explanation "many" (aneka) would be inconsistent.
To the question, "How then does the modification of one or of many come about? he says: "Of which," and so forth;
"in the seed" means in the entire productive seed.

Or, regarding the phrase "in the seed-part" (*bījabhāge*), he speaks specifically by way of pointing out [the defect]— as if grasping it by the horn— to describe this very transformation as occurring in a portion of the seed-component; thus he says "when," etc.,
and "in the blood" (*śoṇite*) refers to the menstrual blood (*ārtava*).

The "uterine seed-portion" (*garbhāśayabījabhāga*) refers to that portion which generates the uterus; alternatively, it refers to the portion that generates both the uterus and the seed in the form of menstrual blood (*ārtava*). Furthermore, once the uterine and menstrual portions have fallen among the maternal constituents, they are produced solely from blood. Consequently, the corruption of the seed-portion other than the menstrual blood is logically established. And although the manifestation of menstrual blood occurs after the twelfth year, nevertheless, the actual production of the menstrual blood takes place precisely during the period of gestation.

Since the manifestation of menstrual blood (*ārtava*), facial hair, and so forth occurs in healthy individuals only at the proper time, it follows that a corruption (*pradoṣa*) of the seed which initiates the menstrual flow must have occurred during the period of gestation.
By the prefix *pra-* in the word *pradoṣa*, he demonstrates an intensity of corruption capable of producing the effect of extreme sterility (*prakṛṣṭavandhyatā*).
Thus, through the impairment of both the uterus and the menstrual blood, the woman's sterility becomes manifest.
The phrase "a portion of the seed-element of the uterus" should also be explained as before.
Here, by the word "portion," a part of both the uterus and the menstrual blood (*ārtava*) is meant.

Regarding the term "one who gives birth to putrid offspring" (*pūtiprajā*), it refers to one whose child dies at birth; others, however, say it refers to one whose limbs and minor parts are moist with putrefaction.
"Of the female-producing portions of the bodily seeds" means of those seed-portions that generate the indicators of femininity, such as the breasts, the pubic region, and the line of hair;
"not a woman" means one who does not possess the complete characteristics of a woman;
"vārtā by name" refers to the designation "vārtā" assigned according to the conventions of the treatise.

"Strīvyāpad" (disease caused by a woman) refers to a disorder produced by the defects of the *ārtava* (menstrual blood) due to a woman; in this same way, they describe "puruṣavyāpad" (disease caused by a man), and here too, "puruṣavyāpad" is to be explained accordingly.

Regarding the term *bīje* (in the seed): it refers to the portion that produces the seed in the form of semen (*śukra*). By the phrase "then [the woman is] barren" (*vandhyā*), he speaks of one who is barren with respect to the male. Here too, the explanation of *pradoṣa* and the explanation of *pūtiprajā* are as before.
"Apuruṣa" means one who does not possess the characteristics of a [normal] male;
even the designation "grass-doll" (tṛṇaputrikā) is established by the conventions of the treatises.
They say that while there may indeed be a desire for sexual intercourse between a "story-teller" (vārtā) and a grass-doll, there is no capacity for actual sexual intercourse.

Thus, for the purpose of extending [the principle of] modification to the parts born of suitability (*sātmya*), rasa, and *sattva*—just as there is modification of certain parts born of the mother and father—he says "by this" and so forth:
however, due to the impairment of suitability (*sātmya-vibhrama*), one is deprived of any one of the qualities born of suitability, such as health, freedom from lethargy, and so on.
In this same manner, the [effects] of *rasa* (taste) and *sattva* (mental essence) are also to be inferred.

(32) Since this embryo is said to be born of the self (*ātman*), why is its own morbid transformation (*vikṛti*) not stated here as the cause of the embryo's morbid transformation? To this, he says: "It is free from modification," and so forth.
By the word "supreme" (*para*), he distinguishes the Self from the aggregate of the mind, body, and so forth.
By the phrase "without distinction in all beings," he means that although this Supreme Self exists within all beings, It is exactly the same everywhere.

As for the specific experiences of pleasure, pain, and so on that are perceived therein, they are perceived due to the differences in the specific bodies and specific minds which serve as the causes for those particular experiences of pleasure, pain, and so on. This very point has been stated in the passage beginning with "But [the difference] of the body and the being... and so forth.
It has already been demonstrated that pleasure and the like are not modifications of the Supreme Self, but are indeed attributes of the intellect (*buddhi*).

Furthermore, those [births] which were shown by the passage beginning with "In those various wombs, there is birth" (*Śā. 3*) as being born from the Self in the womb—those too are not modifications of the Supreme Self; rather, they are produced solely by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which arise from modifications of the mind (*manas*) consisting of transformations in the form of the predominance of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

Therefore, the meaning is that those [modifications] which were described as being born from the self (*ātman*) in the subtle contemplation are in fact born from *sattva*; consequently, even here, a modification of a part of the self should be understood as a modification of a part of *sattva*.

By the passage beginning with “But of the body and the sentient being,” the body and the mind are stated to be the causes even for modifications in the form of suffering. In that very context, he states those defects by which the body and the mind, when joined with those two types of defects, become the cause of suffering—namely, the verse beginning with “Therein, three,” etc., meaning that a modification arises in the form of physical and mental diseases. (34)

Now, with the words "due to the distinction between body and being," he explains those very distinctions between body and being that were indicated: "Therein," and so forth, up to "fourfold"— namely, the womb-born (*jarāyuja*), egg-born (*aṇḍaja*), sprout-born (*udbhijja*), and sweat-born (*saṃsvedaja*)—
as will be explained later in the *Khuḍḍikā*.
"Because it possesses a virtuous portion" means because it possesses a portion of pure form.

For the mind consists of three portions: the virtuous portion, the portion of anger, and the portion of delusion. Among these, the portion of anger and the portion of delusion are defective, as they are causes of unrighteousness (*adharma*).
"Bhedāgram" means the measure of differentiation.

"Taratamayogāt" (due to the connection of degrees) refers to the connection with various grades of mental differentiation, such as being more pure or most pure. "Śarīraviśeṣāḥ" are the specific distinctions of the body, such as the differences between childhood, youth, old age, and so forth. "Yoniviśeṣāḥ," however, are the specific distinctions of genus, such as the different species of humans, animals, and so on; or alternatively, the specific distinctions of the body caused by human, animal, and other genera are the "śarīrayoniviśeṣāḥ. From these [distinctions arise the variations].

Now, he explains how the differentiation of the mind occurs following the dissolution of the body: "And because of their mutual conformity. He analyzes this very point with the words "For the body also...

and so forth. The body conforms to the *sattva* (psychic quality): if it is pure *sattva*, then it becomes the body of a deity and so on; likewise, the *sattva* conforms to the body. For example, it should be understood that in the body of an animal it is *tāmasa* (of the nature of darkness), in the body of a human it is *rājasa* (of the nature of passion), and in the body of a deity it is *sāttvika* (of the nature of goodness), and so forth.
Or rather, "due to mutual conformity" means due to the mutual conformity of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

In this view, although the conformity of the mind to the body is separated by the textual passage beginning with "for the body also conforms to *sattva*," it is explained here because it is difficult to understand; thus it should be interpreted accordingly.
"The varieties of *sattva*" refers to the varieties of the mind.
By way of an *anūka*— that is, by way of an indication of similarity—
he is "one who shares," meaning one whose nature is to correctly distribute the fruits [of merit].
One who observes the vow (*vrata*) of offering the guest-offering (*arghya*) and so forth to a guest as is appropriate is called *atithivrata*.

A "line" (*lekhā*) refers to the boundary of what ought to be done and what ought not to be done; one whose conduct (*vṛtta*) is established within that is *lekhāsthavṛtta*—meaning one who does not transgress the boundaries of what must be done and what must not be done.
"Unassailable" (*asamprahārya*) means incapable of being restrained.
"One who attains sovereignty" (*aiśvaryalambhī*) means one who obtains power.
"One whose anger and favor are directed toward the appropriate occasion" (*sthānakopaprasādaḥ*) refers to one for whom wrath and grace are applied to the proper place.
"Happy dwelling" (*sukhavihāra*) means sporting in happiness.
Ullāpa means praise or hymn;
vihāra means play or sport, or alternatively, "strīvihāra" means sporting together with women;
"gāndharva" refers to the nature of music.

The same should be understood regarding the passage beginning with "the Brahma [state]" and so forth. And thus, by means of words such as "Brahma" which denote *sattva* and which are referred back by the word "thus" (*evam*), the description of the sevenfold division of *sattva* becomes logically established for that which is "pure," meaning that in which the quality of *sattva* predominates.

Now, as to how these [states] beginning with Brahma are indeed varieties of pure *sattva* alone, he says: "Because they are portions of auspiciousness" and "because of union with that," meaning because of the correct union (*samyagyoga*) of *sattva* which consists of an auspicious portion.
"Aupadhika" means one who acts with deceit;
"ananukrośa" means merciless;
"strīrahaskāmaḥ" means one who desires to stay in private with a woman.
Regarding the terms "fierce when angry" and "timid when not angry": one is fierce when anger is present, and timid when anger is absent.
By the word *gocara*, the movement within a range or object is indicated; thus, *santrastagocaram* means moving within a terrifying range or object.
A *preta* is indeed distinct from a *piśāca*, as its conduct is as described; therefore, the *sattva* that is a *preta* is mentioned separately.
"Having the nature of movement" means having the nature of proceeding;
the factors of enlightenment (buddhyaṅga), such as investigation, reflection, mindfulness, and so forth, have been explained.

In order to facilitate easy recollection, he states the divisions of *sattva* by categorizing them according to distinctions such as the "pure" (*śuddha*) and so forth—beginning with the words "of the pure" (*śuddhasya*) and ending with "by emulating the *sattva* of trees" (*vanaspatisattvānukāreṇa*). This portion of the text, which constitutes a single section of the divisions, has been explained; it should be connected with this [present passage], as there is no other action [to be performed].

And since these varieties of *sattva* generally occur among humans, it is with this in mind that they alone have been mentioned for the sake of illustration. By the words beginning with "How indeed" (*kathaṃ nāma*), he shows that even though they were not explicitly mentioned, other varieties of *sattva*—such as those imitating Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, tigers, and so forth—must certainly be understood. The meaning of the sentence is: "In what way, indeed, might the conduct of all living beings toward humans be in accordance with their respective *sattva*? For this purpose, these varieties of *sattva* have been explained by way of illustration.

He concludes the meaning as explained according to his promise with the words "kevala" and so forth: "Kevala" means the entire summary, referring to the author's own text beginning with "Since this embryo... and so on.
"According to the enumeration" means without deviating from the order of the enumeration;
"efficacy" means the purpose;
"conformity with meditative concentration" means the performance.
"Vighāta" means the avoidance of those things that cause harm, namely, those things that cause harm to the embryo. 41.

Now, among these, he explains which are the auspicious factors of the embryo that should be practiced during gestation, and which are the inauspicious ones that should be avoided: "The cause," and so forth.
"The cause" refers to the meaning indicated in the text: "from which the embryo arises.
"The self" refers to the self in the form of the embryo, which is the meaning indicated in the text: "that in which the designation 'embryo' occurs."
"From this the embryo is produced, thus it is the *prakṛti* (primary cause)"—this is the meaning indicated by the text "and that which is the modification of the embryo.
"And growth in the womb in due order"—this is the meaning indicated by the text "by which sequence the embryo is brought forth in the womb.
"The cause of its growth"—this is the meaning indicated by the passage beginning with "and that which is the cause of its growth."
By the phrase "the cause for non-birth," the meaning indicated by "from which its non-birth occurs" is grasped;

by the phrase "the cause for destruction," the meaning stated by "and from which, being born in the womb, it meets destruction" is grasped; and by the phrase "the cause for modification and departure," there is a summary of the meaning expressed by "and from which [it departs] in its entirety," and so forth.
Those [verses] spoken as causing miscarriage are called "garbhavighātoktāḥ" (42–45).

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Great Chapter on the Descent of the Embryo" (Mahatī Garbhāvakrānti Śārīra), in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka Saṃhitā* composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Section on Anatomy (*Śārīrasthāna*).

4 [Śārīrasthāna, Chapter 5 (51 of 120)] It was stated in the preceding chapter: "As many as there are entities in the world, so many are there in the person" (Śā. A. 4). This, however, was not elaborated upon because it involves much that must be said; therefore, for the purpose of providing that detailed exposition, he speaks of the investigation of the person (puruṣavicaya).

The investigation of the person (*puruṣa*) by way of counting them according to their commonality with the world is "investigation of the person" (*puruṣavicaya*); the chapter composed concerning that is the "Investigation of the Person.
[It is] measured, meaning equal.

He analyzes the very fact of its being commensurate with the world, beginning with the words "As many as... and so forth. The construction is: "being explained by the Blessed One through his intellect. The parts of the world consist of trees, grass, animals, and so on; likewise, the parts of the person consist of sinews, tendons, vessels, and so on, and these are innumerable. Therefore, it is impossible to describe them in their entirety. Consequently, the meaning of the sentence is that whichever gross parts of the world and the person exist, those are mentioned for the purpose of demonstrating the commonality [between them].
The explanation of Brahmā: by the words "the unmanifest" (avyakta) [in verse 3.4] and "of that" (tasya) etc., he demonstrates the six elements within the person (puruṣa).
In this world, "form" (mūrti) is solidity; the six elements are indeed manifest, yet they have not been further analyzed.
"Brāhmī" is the manifestation (vibhūti) of the specific Self who is the creator of the universe.
Prajāpati, named Dakṣa, is "ādāna," meaning grasping or taking up; the Sun (Āditya) also takes up [light], and thus there is a similarity between them as "ādāna.
Furthermore, in this context, the fact that the mind and the other organs possess the nature of Prajāpati and so forth is to be understood as already established by scripture (āgama).
All sense-objects are indeed the Viśvedevas;
thus, the period following the dissolution (pralaya) is the beginning of creation.
By the phrase "of those not mentioned," it is understood that Mati is Bṛhaspati, Kāma is the Gandharva, and so forth; such [assignments] are to be inferred as general rules.
"Anapavādam" means that which is not contradicted;
"what, then, is its purpose? means that in Ayurveda, there is some purpose in stating this equilibrium.
In the construction of the phrase "true cognition arises," it should be understood that the word "what is its purpose? (*kiñcāsyāḥ prayojanam*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
And as to how the similarity with the Cosmic Person (*lokapuruṣa*) becomes the generator of true cognition, he says: "For [he sees] the entire world," and so forth;
"seeing within himself" means seeing it as non-different from the Self (*ātman*).

By the word "self" (ātman), the person consisting of the aggregate of the six elements is meant here. Therefore, whatever in the world produces pleasure or pain is of the very nature of the self. Consequently, even that pleasure which is produced by the external world is indeed produced by the self; it is associated with constant suffering, is to be abandoned, and likewise, suffering is naturally to be abandoned. Seeing this, one becomes free from attachment and aversion and possesses the knowledge of truth—this is the intended meaning. Now, what is the purpose of this knowledge of truth? To this he says: "Karma," and so forth.

The meaning of the sentence is that even when there is knowledge of the similarity between the world and the Person, the purpose of the knowledge of truth is the practice for liberation (*apavarga*). In this context, the phrase "because it consists of action" means because it is dependent on action;
the reasons and so forth will be explained later.

The meaning is as follows: this Self, being subject to *karma* and joined with causes and so forth, proceeds [into transmigration]. When that *karma* ceases through the activity of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), it no longer occurs due to the absence of its cause. Furthermore, once produced, *karma* is destroyed by the knowledge of reality for one who is no longer attached, and by the experience of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Thus, through the absolute exhaustion of *karma*, liberation (*mokṣa*)—which consists in the absolute absence of the fruits of *karma*—comes to be.

The phrase "dependent on conjunction" means that it exists in the form of the Person (*puruṣa*) within the confluence of the six elements. In this context, by the word "world" (*loka*), it is the Person himself who is meant—derived from the sense of "being perceived"—and not the world in the form of the universe.
For this reason, those factors such as the causes (hetu) and so forth which are spoken of in the world as being under the sway of karma, are possible only in the case of the Person (puruṣa);
by the word "all," he includes all living beings.
Having indicated the pentad beginning with the cause, he analyzes it: "Its cause," and so forth;
"its root" means the cause of that departure of the life-force (*jīva*), as well as the cause of all calamities—that is, of all sufferings.
Activity is rooted in attachment and aversion;
"cessation" means non-activity.
The word "repose" (uparama) is connected with both the phrase "by that [knowledge]" and the phrase "and of all afflictions."

Therefore, the cessation of sufferings and of death is indeed produced by cessation (*nivṛtti*); and because it is produced by cessation, the cessation itself is expressed by the word "cessation" through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), based on the metaphorical identification of cause and effect—just as it should be understood that "activity is suffering" and likewise "cessation is happiness. He states the nature of the knowledge of truth: "That which is knowledge," and so forth.
The word "iti" refers back to what precedes.
Demonstrating that this knowledge of truth (*satyajñāna*) is the cause for the knowledge of the common nature of the world and the person (*lokapuruṣasāmānyajñāna*), he says: "Of that," and so forth.

He asks for the cause and the means of both *pravṛtti*, which is of the nature of *saṃsāra*, and likewise *nivṛtti*, which is of the nature of liberation—beginning with "What is the root? and so forth. The answer begins with "Delusion" (*moha*) and so forth:

"The root is delusion, desire, aversion, and action. This means that from delusion—which consists of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*)—arise desire and aversion; from these two arise action in the form of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*); and that [action] is the root of *saṃsāra*.
How are these [afflictions], such as delusion (*moha*) and so forth, the cause of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*)? To this he says: "For born from that," and so on.
Here, one should understand that delusion and the others act as causes for ego-grasping (*ahaṅkāra*) and the rest, according to their respective suitability.
Furthermore, the eight [factors] beginning with ego-grasping are to be understood as those which will be explained below.
"Having pervaded" (avatatya) means having encompassed;

"it does not transcend existence" (na sattām ativartate) means it does not transcend its station within saṃsāra. Here, he explains the aforementioned *ahaṅkāra* with the words beginning "tatra evam," and so forth.
Egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) is the knowledge that "I am superior," being endowed with [qualities] beginning with birth and ending with power.
As for the phrase "that which... and so forth, it is the explanation of attachment; doubt (*saṃśaya*) is the cognition as to whether the fruits of action and so forth exist or not.

He speaks of "overflowing" (*abhisamplava*) with the words beginning with "all," and so forth. "Overflowing" refers to the overflowing [of the notion] of a self into what is not-self as desired by oneself; the meaning is that it is the cognition of a self due to the non-self being the domain of the self.

"In all states" means in all bodily states; the knowledge that [the body], which consists of the aggregate of the six elements, is indeed nothing other than this [self]—that is what is to be understood here as "overflowing. However, the knowledge that the Supreme Self is non-different from all states is indeed right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*).
In this way, even in the thought "I am the creator" or "I am established by my own nature," it should be understood that the object of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is indeed the body.

Furthermore, in the thought "I am a collection of specific body, senses, and intellect," one should understand that the conceit of being conscious—based on the locus of the ego-sense within the insentient body and so forth—is contradictory.
By the words "mine" (*mama*) and so on, he describes "clinging" (*abhyavapāta*); clinging is, in the ultimate sense, the sense of ownership (*mamatā*) toward that which is not one's own.

By the words "kārya" and so forth, he expresses *vipratyaya*—that is, a perverse attachment or knowledge that is contrary [to reality]. For example: regarding what ought to be done (*kārya*), one thinks it ought not to be done (*akārya*), and regarding what ought not to be done, one thinks it ought to be done, and so on.
By the words "jñājñayoḥ" and so forth, he states their lack of distinction.

The distinction between these two is that non-discrimination (*aviśeṣa*) is the non-perception of distinctions, whereas misconception (*vipratyaya*) is the apprehension of distinctions in a contrary manner.
By the words "sprinkling" and so forth, he states what are not means;
"not means" means that although they may exist as other means, they are not means for liberation, which is the supreme human goal.

Regarding the three daily ablutions at the three junctions of the day (*triṣavaṇa-trisaṃdhyasnāna*), [the author] now states in brief—beginning with the words "In this way" (*evam*) and so forth—the nature of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) and the rest as the cause of physical and mental suffering, which is a constant attachment to the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). This is preceded by the designation of [these factors] as intellect (*dhī*), fortitude (*dhṛti*), and memory (*smṛti*), since they are the root of the impairment of intellect, fortitude, and memory. He shows that just as a tree of residence (*nivāsavṛkṣa*) is the constant refuge for birds, so too one who is joined with egoism and the rest becomes the abode of disease.
"Being whirled about" means being led again and again into other bodies;
"he does not transcend activity" means he does not abandon *saṃsāra*.
Thus, having shown that activity has its root in karma born of delusion and desire, [the author] states that activity itself has karma as its cause: "And that is the root of evil."

Even worldly activity (*pravṛtti*) is the root of evil (*agha*), which consists of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*); and here, both merit and demerit are designated by the word "evil" because they are, without distinction, causes of the suffering of *saṃsāra*.
Now, in order to state the means for cessation (*nivṛtti*), [the author] first speaks of cessation itself through synonyms that establish its desirability, beginning with the words "cessation," etc.
The indeclinable ‘ut’ has the sense of ‘liberation’ (mokṣa); thus, the meaning is that [these] are the means of rising toward liberation.

The phrase “seeing the defects of the world” is a qualifying attribute containing a reason; by this, the Teacher—the instructor of this treatise on liberation—shows that [the person concerned] is one who has become dispassionate through constantly observing the world as overwhelmed by suffering.
Therefore, by means of firm resolve, one should maintain steadfastness through the awakening of the enemy; the meaning is that not even the slightest hesitation should be felt therein.
The actions as described must be performed—this is the ellipsis.
"One should look upon [others] as upon oneself" means that just as one has the notion of being incapable of being harmed regarding oneself, so too should it be maintained toward all living beings.
"Non-conceptualization" means non-contemplation.

"A loincloth for the purpose of covering" means for the purpose of wrapping around the waist; or alternatively, "a needle-case for the purpose of a loincloth and for the purpose of covering," meaning a container for holding needles.
"A bowl for the purpose of wandering for alms" means a begging bowl;
by the phrase "for the purpose of sustaining life," it is shown that one should take only as much food as is necessary for the maintenance of life, and not out of attachment.
In the same way, in the case of "for the purpose of removing fatigue" and so forth, the fact that these serve only such limited purposes should be explained.
The yogapaṭṭa is a physical bond;
"dwelling without a home" means not living in a house. By this, it is shown that one should not remain even in the forest having made a house for oneself.
One must exercise restraint over attachment to the objects of the senses, such as sound and so forth, as well as over aversion, which takes the form of affliction toward them.

The meaning is that one should always remain mindful of the fact that "action is preceded by mindfulness," such as asking, "Who am I? and "For what purpose is this undertaking of renouncing passion and so forth being begun?

"Honor" (*satkāra*) means worship. When honor or praise occurs, one should remain without elation; likewise, when there is censure or humiliation, one should remain without aversion. This should be understood as "endurance of honor and the like. Furthermore, "lack of agitation amidst hunger and other conditions" means the capacity to endure hunger and so forth.
Non-dwelling and non-association;
the eight [defilements] beginning with egoism (ahaṅkāra) have been mentioned right here as being designated as "obstacles" (upasarga), because they are to be contemplated as causes of harm.

"Observing the commonality between the world and the Person regarding creation and so forth" means that just as the commonality between the world and the Person from the very beginning of creation has been stated right here, so too is there this observation.
"Fear of the lapse of the time for action" means that one must maintain fear of the passing of the time for performing those duties conducive to liberation.

"Restraint of the senses in the mind" means that the senses, having withdrawn from external objects, must be fixed solely upon the mind; for the mind, having turned away from objects such as those of thought, restraint must be exercised toward the Supreme Self for the sake of self-knowledge; and the construction is "restraint of the self in the self.
By this, the self also—having been turned away from the objects of the senses and so forth—must be restrained within the self.
"The enumeration of the parts of the body according to the division of the elements" refers to the knowledge of the body in its form as essence (*rasa*), waste (*mala*), sinews (*snāyu*), and so on.

For the body, when contemplated in its form as consisting of lymph, impurities, sinews, and so forth, becomes a cause for dispassion (vairāgya); as it is said: "Women are leather bags filled with marrow, bones, dust, spleen, liver, feces, and also sinews and veins. By this contemplation of dispassion, [the author] shows through the term "that which has a cause" that everything other than the eternal self is impermanent.
"‘Suffering’ refers to the cause of suffering;

‘not-self’ refers to that which is distinct from the self and devoid of anything belonging to a self, [to be understood] in the context of the renunciation of everything and the cessation of all activity."
"Impure" (*avimalam*) is an adverbial modifier;
"seizer" (*grahaḥ*) refers to Rāhu.
Since there are exactly five faculties that obscure the consciousness of a being, it is said that for the sun as well, there are exactly five obscuring factors, such as the planets and so forth.
"It blazes" means it shines by generating the knowledge of the absolute Self;
"it is confined within the Self" means it has withdrawn from the senses and is fixed within the Self.
"In a covered opening" (saṃvṛtāyane) should be understood as "in oneself," meaning in one's own person whose sensory apertures (indriya-rūpa-cchidra) are closed.
"Lamp-receptacle" (dīpāśayaḥ) refers to a lamp-holder or a house.

Having described the pure being (*śuddhasattva*), he now describes, through various appropriate forms, the true intellect (*buddhi*) produced from it—which is to be intensely cultivated as a means to liberation—beginning with the words "pure," and so forth.
"Great delusion" (*mahāmoha*) is beginningless false knowledge;
"free from longing" (*niḥspṛha*) means devoid of the desire to acquire or the desire to discard.
"Yoga" refers to the supreme union of the mind—withdrawn from sense objects—with the Self alone;
"Sāṅkhya" is the knowledge of the principles (tattva), and one who exists by means of that is a Sāṅkhya. He does not worship a cause, meaning he does not resort to the causes of pleasure and pain.
"He does not take anything as an object" means he does not form any attachment anywhere; "he renounces" means he becomes indifferent toward everything;
"Brahman" refers to liberation.

Although terms such as *vidyāsiddhi* (attainment of knowledge) are well-known even in the context of specific types of cognition, they should nevertheless be understood here—due to the context—to refer exclusively to the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).

Regarding the phrase "the Self expanded in the world" (*loke vitatamātmānam*), it refers to the Self in its form as the world; likewise, one perceives the world within the Self, in the form of the union of the body and the Self—the word "established" (*vyavasthitam*) being understood as the ellipsis.

Regarding the term "one who sees the high and the low" (*parāvaradṛśaḥ*): "the high" refers to the Self (*ātman*), and "the low" refers to those things distinct from the Self, such as worldly activity (*pravṛtti*) and so forth. By the phrase "of him who sees the high and the low, [knowledge is the cause]," he sets aside a peace that is rooted in delusion and unstable.

Now, he explains why the one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) does not come into contact with merit and demerit, which are the causes of pleasure and pain—beginning with the words "of the one who sees" (*paśyataḥ*).
"Of the one who sees" means of one who merely observes, but not of one who is attached nor of one who is averse.

"Of the one who has become Brahman" (*brahmabhūtasya*) should be explained as meaning "of the one liberated while living who is similar to Brahman"; for in one who is completely liberated, even knowledge no longer exists, and therefore the term "of the one who sees" would not apply.
"Conjunction" (saṃyoga) refers to the relationship between dharma and adharma. Now, he states the definition of the liberated self (muktātman) with the words beginning with "not" (na), etc.
"Of the self" refers to the liberated self (*muktātman*).

"Due to the absence of instruments" means due to the absence of instruments such as the mind (*manas*) and so forth. For it has been stated: "The instruments are the mind, the intellect (*buddhi*), and the organs of perception and action" (Śāstradīpikā 1.1). Furthermore, because of the absence of the mind and the other instruments, the absence of the body is also established by implication. Since everything is absent, there is no characteristic whatsoever in the self; moreover, by its very nature, the self is indeed beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). Therefore, the meaning is that the self is not perceived because it lacks the fitness for perception, and its indicative marks (*liṅga*) are likewise not perceived precisely because they are absent.
With the words beginning "free from evil" (vipāpam), he states synonyms that reveal the true nature of liberation.

Regarding the phrase "having known which" (yajjñātvā), the meaning is "having attained knowledge"; alternatively, it should be understood that because knowledge is self-luminous, knowledge itself becomes the object of knowledge (jñeyam).

By the phrase "the stabilization of pure being (*śuddhasattva*) within the compendium," the meaning stated in the passage beginning with "by these, [the mind] is not stainless" and ending with "as in the case of the lamp and its receptacle" is summarized.
Furthermore, by the words "of pure being," etc., true cognition (*satyā buddhi*) is described.
The term *naiṣṭhikī* is an adjective qualifying *satyābuddhi* (truthful intellect) alone; *naiṣṭhikī* means that which accomplishes liberation (*mokṣa*). *Niṣṭhā* is liberation.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Anatomy of the Investigation of the Person," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Section on Anatomy (*Śārīrasthāna*).
5 [Śārīrasthāna, Chapter 6 (52 of 120)]:

Having described the investigation of the person (*puruṣavicaya*), which is beneficial to the person as it is useful for liberation, he now speaks of the investigation of the body (*śarīravicaya*), which is beneficial to the body as it is useful for the treatment being explained.
"Analysis of the body" (*vicaya*) means the knowledge [obtained] through the detailed classification of the body;
it is for the sake of benefiting the body, that is, for the sake of the body's health. Now, he explains how knowledge of the body is beneficial to the body, saying: "For having known," and so forth.

The meaning of the sentence is this: only after knowing the essential nature (*tattva*) of the body—which consists of blood and other constituents—is there produced the knowledge that "this [substance], because its qualities are dissimilar to this increased constituent, is beneficial as it causes its decrease," and conversely, that [the opposite] is harmful due to the aforementioned reversal; this knowledge does not arise in the absence of knowledge regarding the essential nature of the body to be benefited.
First, he states the essential nature of the body as a whole with the words beginning "In that regard" (*tatra*).

By the word *cetanā* (consciousness), the self (*ātman*) is meant as the cause of cognition, and the word *bhūta* (element) is used in the sense of a comparison. Therefore, because consciousness—which belongs to the self—is perceived only in the body, it follows that the body is the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the self. However, in the ultimate sense, consciousness has the self as its support, and the self is itself without any support. Alternatively, [the term] "having consciousness as its locus" means having the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) as its locus; the modifications of these five elements, such as taste and so forth, are the constituents that initiate the body. The collection or combination of these is that which has the self as its essential nature (*svarūpa*), and thus it is described as such.
By the term "aggregate" (*samudāya*), only the elements (*dhātu*) that constitute the aggregate are meant; therefore, there is no possibility of mere conjunction being considered the body.

Alternatively, even if "aggregate" were taken to mean conjunction itself, the body—being a substance consisting of a collection of modifications of the five great elements, which has as its cause an aggregate whose self is [that conjunction]—is called *samayogavāhi*, meaning it functions in a state of health through a balanced and appropriate union of the elements.

When, however, there is an unequal combination of the elements due to their deficiency or excess, he says "when indeed," etc., demonstrating that it is then a state of improper union (*asamayogavāhin*).
By a slight imbalance, which produces merely illness, one experiences suffering; but by a great imbalance, which produces incurable disease, the body reaches destruction, that is, death.
Then, what is this imbalance? He says: "the onset of imbalance," etc.

"Attaining imbalance" (*vaiṣamyagamanam*) means reaching a state of disequilibrium; the meaning is that imbalance itself is occasional. For if one were to say simply "imbalance," then the student might also grasp that natural imbalance of the *dhātus* which exists as a constant state of deficiency or excess. Therefore, by the inclusion of the word "attaining" (*gamana*), it excludes innate imbalance and demonstrates that imbalance arises only occasionally in relation to their own normal proportions. Furthermore, in this context, "the attainment of increase and decrease" should be understood as referring to both individual and collective imbalance.

He states the specific distinctions regarding increase and decrease itself as "in part" (*akārtsnyena*) and "by nature" (*prakṛtyā*). "In part" means by way of a single portion; "by nature" means by way of the entire intrinsic essence.
By this, the increase and decrease of the *rasas* and so forth occur through their partiality, while their increase and decrease are also understood to occur in their entirety.
Others, however, connect the term "in part" with the phrase "it undergoes affliction or destruction."

Therefore, even when the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) fall into a state of imbalance, the destruction of the afflictions (*kleśa*) does not necessarily occur; for by the phrase "not in its entirety," the deviation from the destruction of afflictions has been stated. And this is observed: just as the destruction of afflictions does not occur despite an increase in semen through the application of aphrodisiacs, so too, in the case of a child whose constituents are increasing, only an increase in excellence (*guṇa*) is seen.

And that is not very satisfactory, because even for a child whose bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are increasing, the constituents remain established at their natural measure (*prākṛtamāna*) appropriate to his age; therefore, they are not called "increased" (*vṛddha*) merely by being at their natural measure.
