the *kuḍyakīṭa* is known as the "kavaḍigaṇā"; or perhaps the *jyeṣṭhī* is the *kuḍyakīṭa*.
In this same practice, Jatūkarṇa also reads "bhittimatsyaḥ"; by the term *bhittimatsya*, a small fish (*matsyaka*) or a tiny fish known in the West as *jyeṣṭhī* is meant.

Having placed it upon the *dehalī*—the lower wooden threshold of the house door—the word "head" (*śiraḥ*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Alternatively, it should be understood that one places oneself directly upon the threshold.
As stated in the *Jatūkarṇa*: "Seated upon the threshold" (19).

Now, that which prevents the occurrence of conditions harmful to the fetus currently situated within the womb, and which causes its continued maintenance, is called *garbhasthāpana* (the stabilization of the embryo); this is explained by the passage beginning with "From this point forward," and so on.
Aindrī, gorakṣakarkaṭī,
śatavīryā, sahasravīryā, the two types of dūrvā, amoghā, and pāṭalā.
Avyathā, guḍūcī, ariṣṭā, kaṭurohiṇī,
vāṭyapuṣpī, and pītabalā.
The priyaṅgu plant is beloved by Viṣvaksena.

(20) Even for a child who has only recently been born, there is the designation "in the womb" (*garbha*); therefore, even though death can occur outside the womb, the qualification "inside the womb" (*antaḥ-kukṣeḥ*) is appropriate.

One who habitually lies on her back, or lies in an exposed, uncovered place, or likewise wanders about at night, becomes accessible to *rakṣas* and other malevolent spirits. Consequently, it is logical that a fetus overcome by such spirits becomes insane.
*Kali* is verbal quarreling, while *kalaha* is physical fighting;
*straiṇa* is being under the control of women,
characterized by coveting with the mind and having a disposition toward malice.

The *krathana* [fever] is characterized by the suppression of breath occurring suddenly in one who is deceitful and practices guile; one who possesses this condition is also called *krathana*. Furthermore, in this context, she should be understood as one who, having abandoned the milk prescribed for pregnant women, consumes other sweet substances; however, because milk is specifically prescribed, its excellence is established.

In this context, after describing the defects resulting from the excessive use of all six tastes, the fact that he specifically mentions the distinct defects of liquor and other substances should be understood as being for the purpose of explaining the specific morbidity caused by the particular power (*prabhāva*) of those substances. Furthermore, whatever disorders are observed here in the fetus due to the consumption of certain things, provided they arise from appropriate causes, are indeed produced by those very factors;

for example: through excessive sleep one becomes drowsy, through the consumption of sweets one becomes diabetic (*mehī*), and through sourness one becomes afflicted with hemoptysis (*raktapitta*) and so forth.

However, those transformations of the fetus that are seen to be inconsistent with their causes—such as the occurrence of gravel or stones due to the consumption of monitor lizard meat and so forth—should also be understood as resulting solely from the specific potency of substances.

Although the mother’s indulgence in unwholesome things even prior to conception may produce a disorder in the embryo by way of corrupting the menses (*ārtava*), and likewise the man’s indulgence in unwholesome things may produce a defect in the embryo by way of corrupting the semen (*śukra*)—which would have been stated right here in the passage beginning with "But those born of the father" (*pitṛjās tu*)—nevertheless, because for a woman who has already conceived, such specific transgressions cause a defect in the embryo without any interval, it is said: "Indulging in this or that, she who is pregnant... (*tattadāsevamānā antarvatnī*).

"Explained by the mother's improper conduct" means that just as fetal diseases arise in accordance with the mother's improper conduct, so too do diseases arise in accordance with the father's improper conduct prior to sexual intercourse due to the corruption of the semen.
By the phrase "especially the woman," it is shown that the man should also avoid [improper conduct].
"Virtuous conduct" (sādhvācārā) refers to one whose character is marked by auspicious behavior.
"By mild emetics and so forth" means by emetics and other therapies prepared with mild substances and in small doses; or alternatively,

"by those that serve the same purpose," such as spitting which serves the purpose of emesis, or the medicinal suppository (*phalavarti*) which serves the purpose of purgation— by such means the treatment should be administered.
Restraining [the urges] means suppressing natural impulses;
bad food refers to contemptible food;
and "śiśira" means cold.
Regarding the statement "one should cause [the woman] to wear gossamer cloths (*celāni*) prepared with *yaṣṭīmadhuka*-clarified butter," the word "vagina" (*yoni*) is to be supplied as the object;
and from the phrase "and for this very reason," it follows that [the treatment involves] the sprouts of the *nyagrodha* and other such trees.

Alternatively, in the reading "akṣīrasarpiṣaḥ," *kṣīrasarpiḥ* means ghee produced from milk. Regarding the phrase "from the connection with *āma*," the meaning is "from the cause that generates *āma*."

"Because of the contradiction in treatment": for in the case of miscarriage (garbhasrāva), stabilization (stambhana) must be performed, and that [treatment] is cold, mild, and sweet; yet this is contradictory because it generates *āma* (undigested matter). Thus, there is a contradiction in the treatment, or else [the condition] is something other than what is defined as *ārtava*.
Although it was stated "even though some [say]," nevertheless, since there is no prohibition, this is also the opinion of the Teacher.

Regarding the phrase "specific treatment" (cikitsitaviśeṣam) in verses 25–26, by the word *viśeṣa* (specific), one should understand a specific treatment in comparison to other treatments for fetal diseases. Alternatively, a distinct treatment must be stated here for *upaviṣṭaka* and *nāgodara*. Or else, it refers to the specific state described in the passage beginning with "whose fetus is dormant and does not throb," etc.; with reference to that, it is said: "specific treatment. This may refer to a *bhautika* remedy—beneficial against elemental afflictions—such as *vacā*, *guggulu*, and so forth; or it should be understood as the *mahāpaiśācika* ghee which is about to be described.
"In times of famine" (*subhikṣāyām*) means in times of great hunger;

"one should not consider it treatable by unctuous enema" (*na cānuvāsanasādhyaṃ manyeta*) means that because the upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*) is characterized by dryness (*sāmatvāt*), it is not curable by unctuous enema; "the pacification of its disorder" (*tadvikārapraśamanam*) means the pacification of *udāvarta*.
He describes the *nirūha* enema for the pacification of that *udāvarta*: "In that regard," and so forth;
*parivyādha* is a variety of reed (*vetasa*);
"having caused the essence to emerge" means having prepared a decoction.
The quantity of the decoction and other ingredients should be determined by the very same rules governing the dosage of a *nirūha* enema;
"with the face downward" means with the head bent low.
"Like something within a stone" means like something within a rock; "āvī" refers to the labor pains at the time of childbirth.

By the use of the word "some" (*eke*) and by the absence of an explicit prohibition, he shows that the three [factors], such as the act of inducing miscarriage, do not constitute a complete means for the removal of a dead fetus.

By the phrase "merely the time for the drying up of the moisture of the humors and elements" (*doṣadhātukledaviśoṣaṇamātraṃ kālam*), he shows that the aforementioned sequence has as its limit the drying up of the moisture of the humors and elements.

He describes the monthly activity of the embryo: "From the [previous] month onwards," and so forth, ending with "that is not so, according to the venerable Ātreya. The meaning is that because the major and minor limbs are produced all at once in the third month, the hair is also born at that very time and grows gradually; it is not [born] in the seventh month. Now, if so, why does itching occur specifically in the seventh month? He says: "Due to the pressure of the fetus," and so forth; *kikkisa* refers to the tearing of the skin.
The breasts, the belly, and the space between the breasts and the belly—
these are the "exclusions" (*parihāra*) for the [root] *kaṇḍū* (to itch), according to the remainder of the rule.
The condition of *paiṅgalya* (tawny-eyedness) consists of having yellowish-brown eyes;

and although this is caused by *pitta*, as stated in the *Śālākya*: "When *pitta* is excessively vitiated, there occurs yellowness of the eyes," nevertheless, it should be understood that in this case, during the eighth month of gestation, *paiṅgalya* arises specifically through the influence of the mother's consumption of milk and barley-gruel (*kṣīrayavāgū*).

The point is that one must indeed administer the milk and barley-gruel because *paiṅgalya* is a minor defect, easily remediable at a later time, and because great benefits are obtained from its use. Thus, the consumption of milk and barley-gruel must certainly be performed.
And for this very reason, it is stated that another woman who has conceived from oil prepared with sweet medicinal herbs will give birth to a son;

this is mentioned in terms of excellence, and by that it should be understood that she may also give birth to a daughter. Therefore, it is explained that through the monthly rite, the birth of a son alone is not the sole result.
Where a pregnant woman has given birth and where she remains—that is called a lying-in chamber (*sūtikāgāra*).
The connection [of the sentence] is that one should have the house constructed from wood such as *bilva* and other similar materials.
*Vāraṇa* means *punnāga*; *varuṇa* means clothing or a garment, as well as a covering or a bedspread; *apidhāna* means a door-panel;

*vāstuvidyāhṛdaya* is the essence of the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyātattva*). Because of its connection with that [science], the house is "such" (i.e., a place for fire and so forth). The meaning is that the house should be constructed according to the layout of the places for fire and so forth, as determined by an expert in architecture (*vāstuvit*).
"Seasonal comfort" (ṛtusukha) refers to the comfort derived from depending on the current season (vartamānartu).

First, the utility of items such as clarified butter and oil, which are to be kept in the house, must indeed be stated; however, for those things which are too numerous to be mentioned individually, their utility should be inferred in this same manner.
*Kilima* is *devadāru*;
*kaṇa* is known as *kuṇḍaka*; *kaṇikā*, however, refers to the larger fragments of rice than *kuṇḍaka*;
and that by which rice is pounded is the *musala*.

*Kuṇḍamusale* means short pestles; alternatively, there is the reading *caṇḍamusale*, in which case it means heavy pestles. Although the taking up of a pestle is prohibited, nevertheless, since it must be stated that the pestle is to be placed at the door later on, the mention of the pestle is appropriate.
*Sūcīpippalakau* refers to a needle-shaped weapon, or rather, the *sūcīpippalaka* is that upon which the needle is placed.
One should consider a couch or a bedstead to be fit; that is, one should consider it suitable.

"Having performed the *śānti*," that is, having performed the *śānti-homa* (the propitiatory oblation), "and the *nāndīmukha* fruits"—that is, fruits suitable for the *nāndīmukha-śrāddha*; or alternatively, *nāndī* refers to the drum (*muraja*), and thus "fruits with the shape of its mouth," such as dates and the like;
"the *puṇyāha* sound" is an auspicious sound.
Moving clockwise, following after the cow and the Brahmin,
one should speak words that express the intended meaning of the instruction in a manner that is easy to grasp.
"Yawn! means "stretch your limbs";
"having found an opening" means "having encountered a cause.
"Thoroughly shaken" (*sunirdhūtam*) is an adverbial modifier;
"one should strike" (*ākoṭayet*) means one should press;
"a braid made by children" (*bālakṛtā veṇī*) is a *bālaveṇī*.

*Balvajayūṣaḥ* is a decoction (*kvātha*) of *balvaja*; *maṇḍūkapippalī* refers to *maṇḍūkaparṇī*. Alternatively, *maṇḍūkā* may mean *maṇḍūkaparṇī* and *pippalī* simply means *pippalī* itself; the meaning is that their *sampāka*, or decoction, is used.
By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), the drinking of *sūkṣmailā* and other such substances is prescribed along with the *balvajayūṣa* and the rest.
A donkey, a bull, and a fierce ox— by these very means, such as *balvaja* grass and the like,
the internal and external passages become obstructed; that is, the excrement and other waste products, which by nature tend to move outward, become stuck within the interior regions.

The alternative between "with cold water" or "with warm water" should be understood according to the difference in seasons; that is to say, with cold water during the summer season, and with warm water during the winter season.
"Afflicted by afflictions" means struck by the sufferings such as being crushed by the mechanism of the womb.

A *kṛṣṇakapālikā* is a reed made from black potsherds, reeds, *nalas*, *muñjas*, bamboo, and so forth; a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) made from that is a "black-potsherd winnowing basket. With it, they should "winnow," which means they should fan [the body]. Now, for how long should that fanning continue? He says: "until the return of the vital breaths.
The taking up of water is for the purpose of cleansing the urinary passage.
The "upadhāna" is a covering; here, having made a mark of eight finger-breadths— meaning having made a sign at the eight-finger-breadth point— with either a finger or a cotton wad.
An *ardhadhāra* is a specific type of blade with a curved edge;
one should release that [blade]— the vein remaining after it has been cut—
into the throat, meaning one should tie the thread fastened to the tip of the vein around the boy's neck.

44. He states the fault in the improper construction of the *nāḍī*: "Asamyak," etc. *Āyāma* is length; *vyāyāma* is breadth. *Āyāmavyāyāmottuṇḍitā* means protruding in both length and breadth—that is, possessing both length and thickness. *Piṇḍalikā* means circular. *Vināmikā* is swollen at the ends and depressed in the middle. *Vijṛmbhikā*, however, is that which increases again and again.

"Having carefully considered the relative gravity or lightness [of the humors]" means that among the bile which causes the ripening in the channels (*nāḍī-pāka*) and the wind which produces the fourfold disorders such as *āyāma*, *vyāyāma*, *uttaṇḍita*, and so forth, whichever humor is more severe should be treated with urgency.
(45) "The rite for one just born" refers to the *jātakarma* prescribed in the Vedas.

"According to tradition" means according to the scriptures; "by this very rite" means that one should cause [the child] to drink even breast milk that has been consecrated with mantras—this is the meaning.

Regarding the division of the *ghoṣaka* [mantra] for the *ādāna*, he states how long the *taṇḍulabali-homa* should be performed: "until the naming ceremony" (*ānāmakarmaṇaḥ*), which means for ten days; for the naming ceremony will take place on the tenth day.
Jatūkarṇa also states: "An offering of rice and oblations [should be performed] twice a day for ten days.
By the phrase "of those designated as 'demon-slayers' (*rakṣoghna*)," he includes substances such as guggulu and others.
Regarding the expression "on the northern threshold" (*uttaradehalī*), it means above the door; however, others say that the *dehalī* is the wooden beam at the bottom of the door.
Having described the birth-rites (*jātakarman*) for the boy, he states what is to be done for the woman who has given birth (*sūtikā*): "But the woman who has given birth... and so forth.
By the word "hungry" (*bubhukṣitām*), it is meant that when she becomes hungry after a certain period of time, then the drinking of unctuous substances (*sneha-pāna*) should be administered.

"With the supreme power" means she should drink the unctuous substance (sneha) characterized by the highest capacity; one must supply the phrase: "she should drink that quantity of unctuous substance by which no opposition to strength occurs. "Having considered her habituation" (sātmyībhāva) means that among ghee and other substances, whichever is suitable for her should be given to her.
"Clear" (acchena) means pure.

The term "at both times" (*ubhayataḥkālam*) is to be construed with the phrase "one should sprinkle with warm water. He specifies those two times: beginning with the word "before" (*prāk*), etc., it means that the sprinkling following the intake of oil (*sneha-pāna*) should be performed in the forenoon; likewise, once the oil has been digested, gruel (*yavāgū*) should be administered to the one who has been sprinkled.

However, this practice [of the previous section] is not applicable in a non-Aranya (jāṅgala) region because living beings there have a predominance of kapha; rather, it should be understood as the practice for a jāṅgala country.

(48) To demonstrate how a disease arising from improper treatment of a woman in childbirth becomes difficult to cure or incurable, and thereby to show that the procedure must be performed with careful attention according to the stated sequence, he says: "tasyās tu... and so forth.

She is one whose *dhātus* (tissues) have all been diminished and loosened by the growth of the fetus and the nourishment of other elements; this departure of the fetus is the cause of such emptiness of the body. Furthermore, he states that the causes are specifically the pain of straining (*pravāhaṇa*), discharge of moisture, and the flow of blood—beginning with the words "straining" and so forth—as previously described through the drinking of oleaginous substances (*sneha*) and other treatments.

By this, he demonstrates that performing the procedure according to the aforementioned method is itself the supreme medicine for the disease of puerperal fever (*sūtikā-vyādhi*), which is difficult to cure, insofar as it constitutes the avoidance of its causes; however,
the medicine prescribed for once the disease has arisen is generally not successful, and thus it has not been mentioned here—
[the medicine] which is elemental (*bhautika*) and removes the [malignant] spirits (*bhūta-hara*).

"Appropriate" (ucitā) means that whichever deity is always appropriate for a person as an object of worship, having worshipped that [deity], [he should offer oblations] to the "crested ones" (śikhinaḥ), that is, to the fires; or alternatively, to the "crested ones," meaning those possessing a crest or topknot, namely, to the unshaven Brahmins.

"Connected with the deity of the lunar mansion" means that one should give the name of whichever deity belongs to the lunar mansion in which the boy was born, according to the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*). Alternatively, there is the reading: "One should cause two names to be made: the one connected with the lunar mansion (*nākṣatrika*) and the intentional (*ābhiprāyika*).
In this case as well, the *nākṣatrika* has already been explained; regarding the intentional names, there are qualifiers such as "containing a sonant," and so forth.
The gutturals (*ghoṣāḥ*) are *gh, j, b, d, bh*; the semivowels (*antasthāḥ*) are *y, r, l, v*; and the sibilants (*ūṣmāṇaḥ*) are *ś, ṣ, s, h*.

Regarding "name-ritual" (*nāmakarma*): it refers to rituals such as the fire-oblation (*homa*) performed at the time of the naming ceremony; or alternatively, the ritual that is the name itself is the "name-ritual."
The term *sthira* means firm or not loose.
Regarding the phrase "the head slightly exceeding [the standard] measure," this should be understood according to the principle of general rule and exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*).

Therefore, one should understand that although the statement previously made—"the head is six fingers in height and thirty-two fingers in circumference"—and what was said following that, from "therein [reside] longevity and strength" up to "when the body possesses the [proper] measure; however, the opposite occurs when it is deficient or excessive" (Vi. A. 8), applies as a general rule, a slight excess in the measure of the head constitutes an exception (*apavāda*) to that very statement and is nonetheless highly praiseworthy.

In this same way, the phrase "the hands and feet are greatly developed" (*mahadupacita-pāṇipāda*) should also be explained accordingly. By the word "conformable" (*anurūpa*), he demonstrates that the head is proportionate to the body, showing that the head does not exceed the proportions already described; for a head that is excessively large is disproportionate to the body, and such a thing is indeed inauspicious. "Possessing upward marks" (*ūrdhvavyañjana*) means being endowed with the characteristic of three upward lines; for Jatūkarṇa has stated that the forehead should have three lines.
"Low and increased" means not having risen, increasing in succession,
and being unjoined; "at a great distance" means having clearly manifest divisions of parts, such as the distinct divisions of black, white, and so forth.

Those two whose limbs, beginning with the feet, are beautiful, and whose outer corners of the eyes (*apāṅga*) are likewise beautiful, are "those with beautiful limbs and outer corners" (*svaṅgāpāṅga*).
Here, although the outer corners are already included by the mention of "limbs," they are mentioned again specifically to demonstrate the excellence of the beauty of those outer corners.
"Covering the face" (*āsya-pracchādana*) means capable of concealing the face; that is, they serve as veils for the mouth.

And it should be understood that the spinal column is "hidden" (gūḍha); "not falling away" (asampātinī) means well-protruded, or alternatively, "unobservable," meaning naturally endowed [with its proper form], that is, conforming to the body.
"Eṇīpade" means resembling the legs of a female deer;
"endowed with natural proportions" means neither too many nor too few [joints].
"Of equal caste" means of the same lineage;
by the phrase "situated in youth," he excludes both the child and the aged, since their bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are respectively incomplete or decayed;
"modest" means disciplined.
"Of similar appearance" means one whose limbs are not deformed;
"without deficiency" means one who is not lacking any organs; "of the same country and caste" means born in the same region.

The term *anantyāvasāyinīm* refers to a Śūdra woman, for it is with respect to a Śūdra that a woman of the same caste (such as a Cāṇḍāla woman) might otherwise be considered permissible, and she is here prohibited; whereas for Brāhmaṇas and the other castes, such women are already excluded by virtue of being of a different caste. Alternatively, the word *anantyāvasāyinīm* may also include fallen Brāhmaṇa women and others among Brāhmaṇas and the rest. The phrase *yuktapippalakau* refers to high nipples.
"Water goes away" (*udakaṃ vyeti*) means that the water specifically goes forth or pervades;
it is also stated in the *Jatūkarṇa*: "Milk that spreads in water is excellent."
He describes the characteristics of milk vitiated by Vāta and the other doshas, beginning with "śyāva" (dark-brown) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "having a saline aftertaste" (*lavaṇānurasam*), it should be understood as resulting from the power of the combination of the dosha and the dūṣya (vitiated tissue) when the milk is vitiated by Kapha; for it is by this that a saline taste occurs in milk vitiated by Kapha. Furthermore, through the association of these individual characteristics, the vitiation by two or all three doshas (*dvandva-sannipāta*) should also be inferred.
He states the treatment, beginning with "of these" and so forth:

"having observed each specific characteristic" (*prativiśeṣam abhisamīkṣya*) means having carefully examined the specific features of vāta and the others, such as their location in the *koṣṭha* (viscera) or their intensity, in accordance with what is suitable for purification.

By the phrase "according to its own [nature]" (*yathāsvam*), he demonstrates the respective purificatory measures: emesis for *śleṣman*, purgation for *pitta*, and non-unctuous and unctuous enemas for *vāyu*.

By the phrase "according to the [state of the] *doṣa*s," he shows that when a *doṣa* is greatly increased, purification (*saṃśodhana*) should be administered in excessive measure, whereas when it is slight, it should be in small measure;
this is to be applied by the term "dividing" (*vibhajya*).

By the phrase "according to their own [nature]," the meaning is that when the reading is "the specific constitution" (*prakṛtiviśeṣam*), one must also consider the specific constitution of the nurse (*dhātrī*) and determine the distinction between the abundance or scarcity of emetics and other treatments.
The specific regimen should be administered accordingly; thus, the dietary prescription should be made to counteract the specific increase of the doshas.
By the use of the plural "kaṣāyāṇām" (of the decoctions), the decoctions of the individual and combined [herbs] from the list beginning with pāṭhā are intended.
And the milky plants, such as *dugdhikā*, *kalambikā*, and others that exhibit visible milk,
as well as *amoghā* and so forth, have just been explained immediately above.
"Avyathā" refers to *guḍūcī* (58).
"With well-washed pillows" means with well-rinsed upper coverings.

"Clean and dry" means that they should be used only when they are not only washed but also free from stains and the like, and are dry; for even if well-washed, they might still be damp, and likewise, even if washed, they might remain impure if they have been permeated by strong dyes, stains, and so forth; therefore it is said, "clean and dry.
(59–60) *Vayaḥsthā* is *brāhmī*; *golomī* is white *dūrvā* grass; *jaṭilā* is *māṃsī*.
"Jewels" (maṇayaḥ) refers to pearls and other gems; the construction is that the tips of the horns of rhinoceroses and so forth, as mentioned in the Atharvaveda, should also be worn.
For it is stated in the *Jatūkarṇa*: “One should preserve the tips of the right horns of living ruru deer, rhinoceroses, and so forth.
Furthermore, Jīvaka and Ṛṣabha are mentioned in the context of establishing progeny, and the ten medicinal herbs beginning with Aindrī are mentioned in that same place.

In the passage beginning with "prakṛti" (nature), *prakṛti* refers to the humors such as wind (*vāta*), while *nimitta* (cause) refers to external factors such as dryness that act as the cause for the humors.

In the passage beginning with "sarvaviśeṣa" (all specificities), by the word *ātura* (the afflicted), the disease—which is the cause of affliction—is understood; however, by the word *āśraya* (substratum), the body is meant.
He who brings about well-being (*śaṃ*) is Śaṅkara.

In the passage beginning with "place, time," etc., the word *ātman* refers to the body; therefore, one should practice the regimen for health (*svasthavṛtta*) by engaging in food, conduct, and so forth that are contrary to whatever qualities—such as coldness—belong to that particular place, time, and body.

This is also stated elsewhere in the *Svasthavṛtta*: "The proper application consists in the performance of food and activities that are contrary to the qualities of place, time, and so forth" (Śārīra-sthāna, Chapter 6).
He states another aspect of the regimen for those in good health: "In due order," and so forth.

This means one who consumes [food] starting from milk, then milk-rice, then rice alone, and even within that rice, whatever is wholesome for children—such as sweet substances—and who does so according to the sequence described in the chapter on the restraint of natural urges (*Navegāndhāraṇīya*), and according to the sequence taught in the chapter on the regimen for the healthy (*Svasthavṛtta*), beginning with: "A wise man should gradually withdraw from unwholesome things to which he is accustomed" (*Sūtra-sthāna*, Chapter 7). This is the meaning.
Likewise, even regarding the habitual use of other substances, the same explanation applies to the child;
he states the result of practicing the regimen for health (svasthavṛtta) as follows: "tathā" and so forth.
'The fulfillment of the blessings for sons' means that it brings about results corresponding to the prayers for sons; this is a summary verse of the chapter's subject matter."
The term "jña" (wise) is used as a qualification of the man because of his predominance;
therefore, by the man's obtaining of a son, the woman's obtaining of a son is also obtained by implication.
Furthermore, he is called "anasūyakaḥ" (free from envy), meaning he does not harbor resentment such as, "How might I have a son? when a son is obtained who is suitable to her.
Some recite a verse that demonstrates the etymological derivation of the term *śārīrasthāna*: "The body," and so forth;
and its meaning is indeed explicit.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Anatomy of the Rules for Procreation," in the Section on Anatomy of the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of Caraka, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta. [Section on the Sense Organs]

[Indriyasthāna, Chapter 1 (55 of 120): Having established the body as the basis for treatment in the Section on Anatomy (*Śārīrasthāna*), treatment must now be discussed. Furthermore, that treatment should be described only for curable diseases, not for incurable ones, as it has been said: "A physician who attempts to treat an incurable disease will certainly suffer loss of wealth, knowledge, and fame, as well as reproach and a lack of patients" (*Sūtrasthāna* 10). Since the recognition of incurability cannot occur without the recognition of fatal signs (*riṣṭa*), the Section on Vital Signs (*Indriyasthāna*), which elucidates those signs, is taught prior to the Section on Therapeutics (*Cikitsāsthāna*).

By the word *indra*, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is meant; the sign (*liṅga*) residing within that is the sense organ (*indriya*) known as *riṣṭa*. As stated in grammar: "The sense organ (*indriya*) is the sign of Indra" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 5.2.93), and so forth. The location of that sense organ is the "sense-organ-location" (*indriyasthāna*). Although the general sense-organ-location should be discussed there, because it most clearly indicates the *riṣṭas*, this specific sense organ pertaining to complexion and voice (*varṇasvara-indriya*) is mentioned here; for those *riṣṭas* which are to be described here are the most manifest among all other *riṣṭas* due to being perceivable by the eyes and other senses.

The chapter concerning complexion and voice is titled *Varṇasvarīya* because it is composed with reference to complexion (*varṇa*) and voice (*svara*). The chapter that sets forth the signs of impending death (*ariṣṭa*) pertaining to the sense organs (*indriya*) is titled *Indriya*; we shall explain that.
In the same manner, elsewhere as well, such terms as *puṣpitaka* and so forth should be understood as adjectives qualifying the sense organs.
He states the entire subject matter to be established in the section on the sense organs (indriyasthāna), beginning with "here" (iha) and so forth;
here, in this section on the sense organs,
the word "khalu" serves as a rhetorical ornament for the sentence.

And here, although it would have been more appropriate to discuss the sense organs first—since they are the perceivers of objects such as color and so forth—nevertheless, because those organs are beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*), the omens residing in them are unmanifest. Therefore, only the manifest colors and other qualities, which serve as the substrata for manifest omens, are discussed first.
Furthermore, among the colors and other qualities, they are mentioned in their respective order according to the degree of their manifestness.

Although sounds such as "megha" (cloud) are more manifest than individual phonemes (*varṇa*), nevertheless, it is specifically a particular sound produced by the palate and other articulatory organs—denoted here by the term *svara* (vowel/intonation)—that is intended as the locus of the omen (*riṣṭa*). Furthermore, that sound is indeed less manifest than the phoneme.

By using the non-compound form (*asamāsa*) in the phrase "here [and] so forth," he shows that each element, beginning with the phoneme, individually serves as the locus of the omen; for were there a compound, one might suspect that only the aggregate as a whole would need to be examined as the locus of the omen.

By the word "color" (*varṇa*), those qualities associated with color that are perceptible by the eye—such as roughness (*raukṣya*) and so forth—are also included. For this very reason, in the very context of discussing color, it will be stated: "By the mention of color, pallor (*glāni*), exhilaration (*harṣa*), roughness (*raukṣya*), and oiliness (*sneha*) are explained.

Furthermore, by the mention of tone (*svara*) and so forth, the absence of tone and so forth is also included; thus, the absence of sounds such as those from finger-joints and the absence of odors are also encompassed as fatal signs (*riṣṭa*).
And by the mention of touch (*sparśa*), the inclusion of hardness and other qualities perceived through touch is secured.

Sattva is the mind (*manas*). An illustration of a modification of *sattva* is as follows: "The *sattva* experiences longing, and the heart is also entered by fear" (*Iṅgita-jñāna*, 12), and so forth.
Devotion (*bhakti*), desire (*icchā*), character (*śīla*), and innate disposition (*sahaja-vṛtta*) [are also such modifications].
Conduct (*ācāra*) refers to behavior resulting from training in the scriptures.

Although qualities such as devotion (*bhakti*) and the like are already included under the category of *sattva* because they are modifications of *sattva—as it has been stated: "Devotion, character, purity, aversion, memory, delusion, renunciation, lack of envy, fear, anger, lassitude, enthusiasm, sharpness, mildness, profundity, and instability—these and others are modifications of *sattva*" (Śārīrasthāna 3)—nevertheless, devotion and the rest are treated separately here because they serve as distinct bases for fatal signs (*ariṣṭa*).

"Tandrā" refers to sleepiness due to the weakness of sleep; by the word "tandrā," sleep itself is meant. In this context, the fatal sign (*ariṣṭa*) has been stated as: "Sleep becomes constant, or it does not occur at all" (Iṃ.A. 11). "Ārambha" means the onset of a fatal disease. As it has been said: "He whose swelling located in the abdomen spreads to the hands and feet" (Iṃ.A. 9), and so forth. Regarding heaviness (*gaurava*), the fatal sign is as follows: "Spittle, feces, and semen sink in water" (Iṃ.A. 9), and so forth.
Regarding lightness as a fatal sign (*riṣṭa*): lightness of the heavy parts of the body should be understood as a fatal sign.

As an example of a fatal sign regarding qualities (*guṇa-riṣṭa*), it is said: "The qualities of the regions of the body—cold, hot, soft, and hard—are perceived in their opposites when they appear in other locations" (Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya, Indriya-sthāna 12).

An omen regarding food (*āhārariṣṭa*) is as follows: "One who consumes food well-prepared by a physician... (Indu, Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya 12), and so forth. An omen regarding the transformation of food (*āhārapariṇāmariṣṭa*) is as follows: "The patient who, being weak, eats excessively without having eaten before, and has little urine and feces... (Indu, Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya 7).

*Upāya* means the approach [of a disease], which signifies the meeting with illness; as it is said: "Sudden feverish heat, thirst, fainting, loss of strength, and the loosening of the joints" (I.A.8).
*Apāya* is the departure of illness; as it is said: "The man whom the disease suddenly releases while he is weak," and so forth (I.A.9).
"Disease" (*vyādhi*) refers specifically to fatal signs (*ariṣṭa*), as in: "A hard, well-rounded *vātāṣṭhīlā* (a stone-like tumor caused by wind) remains in the heart" (*Indriya-sthāna*, chapter 10).

"Shadow" (*chāyā*) consists of five types related to the elements; "reflection" (*praticchāyā*), however, is the shadow of the body. By means of reflection, even the pupils of the eyes (*netrakumārikā*) should be understood as having the form of a reflection.
Furthermore, this classification of shadows and so forth should be demonstrated in the chapter on the sense organs (*pannarūpīya-indriya*).

Regarding the fatal signs (*ariṣṭa*) pertaining to the state of being in a patient's family, it is said: "A physician, upon merely entering the house of those about to die, sees vessels filled with fire, broken [utensils], and empty houses" (*Indu's Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā*, 12), and so forth. Regarding the fatal signs pertaining to the medicine itself, as stated in the *Bheṣajasaṃvṛtti*: "The medicine which the physician prepares for the sake of a particular patient..."

"Though striving, he cannot [recover]; his life is difficult to sustain" (I.A.12). Thus, the application of medicine that corresponds to the modification of the disease is "the application of medicinal modification. In this regard, the fatal sign (*riṣṭa*) is as follows: "If a medicine that has been identified many times, proven effective, and administered according to the rules fails to succeed for someone, there is no cure for him" (I.A.12).
The remaining examples of misfortune (riṣṭa), however, are clear; thus, at the conclusion [of this section],
perception (pratyakṣa) is treated first here, because all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are preceded by perception.

Although complexion and other signs described as characteristics of lifespan are also examined when there is a desire to know the measure of long life, they must nevertheless be examined here in this section on fatal signs (riṣṭa) solely for the purpose of knowing the remaining measure of one's lifespan; therefore it is said: "by one desiring to know the remainder of the measure.
[This refers to] fatal signs that do not depend on the person himself, but rather depend on messengers and other external factors.
"And by reasoning" (yuktitaḥ) means by inference (anumānataḥ). This is because reasoning is capable of determining whether there is an ill omen (riṣṭa) here;
for perception grasps only the physical form of the messenger and so forth, whereas an ill omen is known from the very arrival of the messenger and others.

However, regarding the perception of an ill omen residing in the complexion and other features of a person, perception itself is engaged through its respective specificities in grasping those various particular ill omens; thinking this, it is prohibited in this context.

Inference, however, which has been established as a means of valid knowledge (*ṛṣṭa*), operates in the investigation of properties such as being without a cause (*animittatva*); likewise, in all cases, it operates toward the knowledge of the modifications (*vikṛti*) based on the primordial nature (*puruṣa-āśraya*) by way of being the cause for knowing the modifications through their nature, since the knowledge of the modifications is dependent upon the knowledge of the nature; yet the examination of the nature and the modifications is to be understood here precisely through well-known means of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, as authorized in this context.

He analyzes *prakṛti* (inherent nature) with the words "In that regard," and so forth: 1. That which pertains to a genus (*jāti*), such as purity in the Brāhmaṇa caste; 2. That which pertains to a family (*kula*), such as a certain family being characterized by pure conduct; 3. That which follows from a region (*deśa*), such as those dwelling within the *Antarvedi* [the land between the Ganges and Yamunā] being pure; 4. That which follows from time (*kāla*), such as purity in the Kṛta Yuga; 5. That which follows from age (*vayas*), such as impurity in childhood; 6. That which is restricted to each individual (*pratyātmaniyatā*), such as a certain person being pure by nature. These and others should be cited as examples.
Furthermore, as for the question of how there can be a nature determined by birth and so forth, he states the reason: "birth, family," and so on;
"those various specific states" refers to purity, impurity, and the like.

In order to analyze the morbid transformation (vikṛti) pertaining to the section on fatal signs (riṣṭa), he states all the various types of morbid transformations, beginning with "vikṛti" and so forth.
The term "hetubhūtāni" means those that resemble the causes.

Therefore, it is destiny alone that is the cause for the occurrence of transformations—such as the attainment of sovereignty, wealth, death, or imprisonment—in a body endowed with the marks described in the *Sāmudrika* (physiognomy), such as nail-marks, lotuses, and so forth. The marks, however, are merely indicators caused by destiny; for this very reason, it is said "from destiny" (*daivāt*). Furthermore, "destiny" is defined as past karma (*prāktana-karma*); since it is this that produces the transformation, the term "from destiny" should be applied here as well. Thus, it is solely by the power of destiny that the marks possess the agency to produce transformations in the form of sovereignty, wealth, death, imprisonment, and the like.
By the phrase "at such and such a time," he demonstrates the necessity of transformation at the time when the maturation of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is indicated by its characteristic marks.

Furthermore, since sovereignty and the like—which are indicated by their characteristics—occur for a person only occasionally and are therefore not inherent to him, they are designated by the term "transformation" (*vikṛti*).

As it was stated in the *Nidāna* [sections]: the meaning is that the morbid transformation (*vikṛti*) consisting of the provocation of wind (*vāta*) and so forth through the consumption of dry substances and the like is what is described in the *Nidāna*.
(7) "Corresponding to the cause" (*nimittānurūpa*) means similar to the cause.
He clarifies that very point with the words "imitating the purpose of the cause" (*nimittārthānukāriṇī*).
That which imitates the purpose of the cause—whether that purpose consists in the production of an effect or the cognition of an effect—is what "imitates the purpose of the cause.
For the bodily transformation known as *riṣṭa* is the cause for either death itself or for the cognition thereof.
He further states a distinction regarding the transformation corresponding to the signs, beginning with the words "tām" (that [death]), etc.

The term "animittām" (without a cause) means that its cause is not perceived at that time (*tadātve*), but it does not mean that it is entirely without a cause (*ahetukī*); for he will immediately state the qualification "caused by the exhaustion of the life-span" (*āyuṣaḥ kṣayanimittām*). Indeed, no cause such as dryness or the like connected to the body is perceived in the case of a fatal sign (*riṣṭa*).

Alternatively, that cause which consists of the exhaustion of the life-span (āyuḥkṣaya) is not perceived by others even though it exists; rather, it is inferred solely from the *riṣṭas* (signs of death). Therefore, "having an unmanifest cause" should be understood here as being "causeless.
In this context, the mere fact of having reached the end of one's lifespan is the proper cause that pervades all *riṣṭas* residing in a person.
As he will state: "Having transcended the path of medical treatment, they reside solely within the body."

"Whatever defects produce signs, those they declare to be *ariṣṭa*" (Indu on Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya 11). This should be understood as referring specifically to *ariṣṭas* residing in the person, since it does not encompass *ariṣṭas* occurring in messengers and the like.
"Of the knowledge of the measure of life" means of the knowledge of the measure of the remainder of life.
"Exceedingly" (*bhūyaḥ*) means to a great degree.

By that [cause], she becomes one whose life-span is exceedingly diminished—meaning, produced by the imminent exhaustion of her life-span—and thus one characterized by the effects of exhausted longevity, resembling a *preta* (hungry ghost); as will be stated in the text beginning with: "Impurities arise on the teeth, and the form of a *preta* is manifested" (Iṃ.A. 12).
For they say that this [change] which occurs within the lifespan is for the purpose of [foretelling] knowledge [of death];

however, that other [change], which does not correspond to the signs of a *preta* and is based on color, indicates that death is imminent. Therefore, the meaning is that it is not the effect of a lifespan that is excessively diminished.

Thus, having described the specific effect characterized by death—which is a specific change corresponding to the [specific] cause—by means of the passage beginning with "furthermore" (*bhūyaśca*) and ending with "the wise" (*dhīrāḥ*), he again states another property of the [change] that is without a [specific] cause in general, starting with "that which [he] has taken as the subject" (*yāmadhikṛtya*).
By the qualification "depending upon a person," he shows that misfortunes (*riṣṭa*) not dependent on a person—such as those involving messengers and so forth—are not necessarily without cause;

for those misfortunes which occur in the context of messengers and the like are determined to be misfortunes based solely on scripture (*āgama*), even though their causes are visible, just as it is said:
"Whether with disheveled hair, or naked, or weeping, or impure..."
"Upon seeing a physician who has arrived as a messenger, one should predict death" (Indu, Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya 12).

In this regard, a reason is indeed evident from the statement regarding the physician having disheveled hair; likewise, there is certainly a reason for the messenger's arrival, such as being dispatched by the patient. Therefore, the lack of a [specific] cause refers only to that which pertains to the patient.

Others, however, explain it as follows: when such a meeting with a physician or a messenger—which is known to be something to be avoided—occurs by chance, then, being caused by fate (*daiva*), it becomes a fatal sign (*riṣṭa*). Therefore, this "causelessness" (*animittatā*) pervades all fatal signs. Furthermore, they interpret the passage beginning with "Moreover" (*bhūyaśca*) as teaching a transformation corresponding to the signs of a deceased person for the purpose of knowing that [the end] has entered within the remaining lifespan; likewise, they explain that those [signs] residing in the person will be taught extensively, whereas those not residing in the person will be taught with very little text.
This is the summary; the meaning is that this is the summary of the subject matter concerning the sense faculties (*indriya*).

Since the knowledge of the transformation (*vikṛti*) is inseparable from the knowledge of the original nature (*prakṛti*), he first states the descriptions of the original natures, beginning with "black" (*kṛṣṇa*), and so forth.

It should be understood that "pure" means fair; and here, generally speaking, those colors which exist by nature are called *prakṛtivarṇa* (natural colors), while those which generally exist through modification are called *vikṛtivarṇa* (modified colors).

By this it should be known that even natural colors may sometimes become modified colors, and likewise, even modified colors may sometimes become natural colors by virtue of being produced from birth onwards.
He states [the following] for the purpose of extending the description of the colors of the unmentioned *prakṛtis*: "And those which... and so forth.

[The words] "having approached" (*upetya*) mean "observing" (*īkṣamāṇa*); "not mentioned" (*anūkta*) means "by way of similarity. And the construction is that one should know those being indicated by the word "color" (*varṇa*), such as "dark" (*śyāma*) and so on.
"By those who know that" means by those who know the distinctions of the letters and their names.
With the words "blue," etc., he states the modified (*vikṛti*) letters, [insofar as they] arise from modification.
Here, by the expression "others" (aparān), the castes born from the mixture of modified colors (varṇa-saṅkara) are to be understood.
He states another modified color with the words beginning "prāk" and so forth; "previously modified" (prāgvikṛtān) means having become otherwise than their previous color.

To this, he says: "those that arise having not previously existed. For instance, when one who was dark-complexioned (śyāma) attains a fair complexion (gaura-varṇatva) through the use of elixirs (rasāyana), and then, having abandoned those elixirs, becomes dark-complexioned again due to the force of time—even for him, the emergence of the dark complexion as a transformation from his previous fair complexion would constitute a fatal sign (ariṣṭa). Therefore, this objection does not apply. In this case, it is simply the previously existing complexion that reappears; thus, it is not a fatal sign.
The phrase "demarcated by boundaries" (maryādā-vibhaktau) means established with equal limits according to the division of before and after, that is to say, by way of the front and back parts.
Regarding the phrase "by way of internal and external division," here the internal *varṇa* (phoneme) is to be understood as being situated within the mouth, nose, ears, and auditory canals;
"elsewhere" refers to other intermediate locations such as the hands, feet, and so forth.

"By means of the distinction of color" means that just as there is an ill omen (*riṣṭa*) through the differentiation of color, so too there is one through the differentiation of exhaustion and the like.
Here, "increase" (*harṣa*) should be understood as physical growth, because mental joy would be irrelevant in this context of visual perception.

In the passage beginning with "tathā," the word "eva" (indeed) indicates that for moles and the like, as well as for [other] marks, birth on the left, right, or other parts of the body constitutes a fatal sign (*riṣṭa*), just as it does for [the primary] letters.
In the passage beginning with "nakha," there is no fatal sign provided that there is no loss of strength and so forth.
By the words "and whatever else" (*yac cetyādi*), he summarizes the portents regarding complexion (*varṇariṣṭa*) not previously mentioned.
The phrase "never before seen" (*abhūtapūrva*) is intended to exclude the manifestation of a complexion produced by the previously explained elixirs (*rasāyana*).
By the phrase "it arises suddenly," he demonstrates the rapid nature of the *riṣṭas*.
The term "without cause" (*animitta*) refers to the very meaning previously stated.
The word "constantly" (*śaśvat*) is a description of the inherent nature of one who is declining; through the arising of a *riṣṭa*, the state of decline occurs constantly and inevitably.
He speaks of the tone that has come down through tradition, beginning with "in the tone" and so forth;
*jarjara* is a specific type of musical instrument.

The phrase beginning with "yāṃśca" and so forth is to be explained as before: *eḍaka* means a sheep, or alternatively, a wild goat; *kala* means subtle; *grasta* means entirely indistinct in pronunciation; *kṣāma* means harsh; *dīna* means a tone uttered with distress; *anukīrṇa* means uttered repeatedly one after another. 14
The *prakṛtivaikārikas* are so called because they are modifications (*vaikārika*) that have become otherwise from their original nature (*prakṛti*).
Regarding "the multiplicity of vowels," this means that at one time there is the vowel *e* (from *ai*), and at another time the vowel *o* (from *au*), and so forth;
thus, the oneness of a single vowel appears as if it were manifold.
The term "signless" (*animitta*) is connected with everything [in the preceding verses].
This very same meaning, which was stated in prose, is now expressed in verse for the sake of clarity and ease of comprehension, beginning with the words "of whom... (*yasya*).

In the passage beginning with "tilakāḥ," although he uses the dual number in "oṣṭhau" (the two lips) after mentioning "mukhe" (on the face)—meaning on half the face—he uses the word "ubhau" (both), thereby showing that the [marks] pervade the entire lip. Furthermore, although he has already stated "mumūrṣuḥ" (one about to die), he uses the term "gatāyuṣam" (whose life-span is gone); by this, he shows that one who possesses fatal signs (*riṣṭa*) is both "about to die" and "one whose life-span is gone. However, one who has not yet developed fatal signs may be "about to die" even if his life-span is not yet gone, due to the absence of remedial measures.
"Arising from death" means for the purpose of knowing the causes of death (17–26).

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Chapter on Complexion and Voice," in the *Indriyasthāna* of the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā*, composed by the venerable Cakrapāṇidatta.

1 [Indriyasthāna, Chapter 2 (56 of 120)] Immediately following the discussion of complexion and voice, since odor (*gandha*) is now the subject under consideration and has been specifically mentioned, the *Puṣpitaka*— which establishes the desired [outcomes] based upon it— is stated, beginning with "Just as a flower" (*puṣpaṃ yathā*), etc.

Although the subject matter of this section ought to have been discussed in the very first chapter—since it pertains to all the sense organs alike—it is nevertheless treated here because, following the analogy of a flower, it concerns the *ariṣṭa* (signs of death) which has the flower as its substrate. Since the flower is the topic at hand, this section is also spoken of here as a discourse that explains the properties of the flower related to that context, beginning with the words "Just as the flower... and so forth. In this context, the flower should be understood as one whose connection to its fruit is unfailing; for this very reason, the author demonstrates the mutual variability between the flower and the fruit by means of the passage beginning with "Even so, however... (1.3).

Because it is difficult for a student to understand the distinction between an ill omen (*riṣṭa*) and death through the analogy of flowers and fruits— fearing that the student might also grasp at the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding flowers and fruits— the author says "even so" (*apyevam*), etc., in order to refute that [misconception]. [The phrase] "connected with the fruit" (*phalenānubandhī*) refers to cases such as the flower of the *vetasa* tree, where the flower does not precede [the fruit], and the fruit of the *aśvattha* tree and others.
The term "of one who is born" refers to one for whom [the signs] are complete; for if an *ariṣṭa* has arisen only slightly and is incomplete, death is not necessarily certain.

Others, however, explain [the phrase] as "of one who is born and destined [to die]. For fatal signs (*riṣṭa*) are of two kinds: certain (*niyata*) and uncertain (*aniyata*). Among these, the certain is described by Ātreya Punarvasu as: "Ātreya Punarvasu declared him to be already dead" (Iṃ.A.7), and so forth. The uncertain is, for example: "Ātreya considers his life to have reached a state of doubt" (Iṃ.A.9), and "having fallen into doubt, even a healthy person may somehow be released from it" (Iṃ.A.5). Likewise, with reference specifically to uncertain fatal signs, it is stated in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*: "Death is indeed certain when there is a fatal sign, according to those stainless Brahmins... (Su.Sū.30.21).
"Or it may be warded off by those devoted to elixirs, austerities, and recitations" (Su.Sū.A.).
Others do not accept this [interpretation], because the Teacher has demonstrated with great effort the invariable concomitance between *riṣṭa* and death;

thus, the statement "when doubt has arisen" was spoken by the Teacher in a different manner as a means of establishing death. We shall explain the Teacher’s meaning regarding *riṣṭa* in that very passage itself.

As for the fact that a fatal sign (*riṣṭa*) may be subverted by elixirs (*rasāyana*) and the like, that is indeed admitted; for elixirs, the grace of Maheśvara, and so forth, are capable of even overstepping the boundaries of the entire world. Therefore, having observed such exceptions, this treatise is composed here. For instance, Maheśvara restored Kāma to life after he had been reduced to ashes, and by means of his ascetic power (*tapas*), Rāma brought back to life the son of a Brahmin who had already died; these and other such cases are to be followed as precedents.

Others, however, describe death preceded by *riṣṭa* (ominous signs) as occurring only at the time of natural death (*kālamṛtyu*), and they say: "If an *riṣṭa* occurs during untimely death (*akālamṛtyu*), then that *riṣṭa* which bestows death through changes in complexion and so forth would be fruitless; for while death occurs even when one performs the appropriate [remedial] actions during natural death, it does not occur during untimely death. In that case, if the appropriate action is performed once the *riṣṭa* has arisen, death ought not to happen; therefore, *riṣṭa* pertains only to natural death.
This is not correct, because it is stated as a rule that *riṣṭa* exists without distinction in both timely and untimely deaths.

Regarding untimely death, when a disease arises from improper conduct (*apacāra*) once one has transgressed the path of medical treatment, at that very moment the ultimate fatal sign (*riṣṭa*) appears; therefore it is said: "Fatal signs manifest in an instant.

For one who does not accept this [principle], there would never be an incurability of a disease caused by improper conduct for a person of fixed lifespan; because, just as defects born of improper conduct become generators of incurable diseases due to excessive negligence, so too do they become generators of fatal signs preceding death.

Showing that any cognition of death through ill omens (*ariṣṭa*) that occurs in a case where there is no deviation [from life] is erroneous, he says: "False," and so forth. "Resembling an ill omen" means similar to an ill omen;

"perceived as false" means known as being an ill omen. This cognition of an ill omen regarding what is not an ill omen is born from an error of judgment (*prajñāparādha*). Likewise, even a real ill omen may be unconnected to a fatal disease due to its subtle form; this too is a false cognition born from an error of judgment.

Therefore, the knowledge that death does not occur even when an *riṣṭa* (ominous sign) is present is erroneous; likewise, the knowledge that death occurs in some cases even without an *riṣṭa* is erroneous.
Consequently, the meaning of the statement is that the concomitance between death and the *riṣṭa* is established as invariable.

"Jñāna" (knowledge) is that by which death is known; "jñānasambodhana" is the correct awakening to that [knowledge]. Regarding the phrase "by those preceding death": those who are endowed with the scent of *riṣṭa* (ominous signs), just as trees and the like become fragrant when they are in flower, are called "puṣpita" (flowering); one should [avoid] those who are thus flowering.
The construction is: "with many kinds of signs, [he saw] many [trees] in bloom.

Although it was already stated "of the forest," the fact that he specifies "possessing various trees and creepers" (nānādrumalatāvataḥ) indicates that he intends for us to understand a forest consisting of diverse species; for a forest might otherwise consist of trees of a single species, such as a "campaka grove" or an "aśoka grove. Furthermore, diversity could exist even among flowers of a single species due to differences in their stages of development, such as buds and so forth; therefore, the qualification "possessing various trees and creepers" is well-chosen.
One should connect [the phrase] "they say that he has blossomed" with the aforementioned signs of death and odors;
"within a year" means within the span of one year;
and "thus" means day and night.

By the phrase "in brief" (*samāsena*) and so forth, it is meant that even through association with inauspicious odors such as corpses—which are distinct from flowers—one is said to be "flowering" (*puṣpita*); the word "is defined" (*paribhāṣyate*) is to be supplied.

By "in brief," meaning by way of a synthesis, one should understand the reversal of the specific distinctions between those who have bathed and those who have not bathed (as mentioned in the passage beginning with *āpluta*), as well as the reversal of auspicious and inauspicious odors.
Furthermore, wherever the designation "flowering" occurs, in each of those instances, the life span lasts until the end of the year, according to the previous statement.
With the words "tadyathā" (namely) and so forth, he speaks of pure and impure substances.
"Dead" refers to dead animals such as cows and the like, excluding humans; "corpses," however, refers specifically to human bodies.

By the phrase "of various origins," he indicates the scents of incense sticks and other items made from diverse substances. By the phrase "of various natures," however, natural scents derived from various substances are meant.

"By this inference" means for the purpose of extension (*atideśa*), according to the portents (*ariṣṭa*) described in the passage beginning with "those who have bathed and those who have not bathed," for the sake of knowing what has not been explicitly stated;
"born from a non-womb" (*viyoni*) means without a cause (*nirhetuka*).
The stable emotion (sthāyin) is "far-off" (vidūra).
"Vairasyam" means the state of having an unpleasant taste.
"Katham" is used in the sense of an objection; by that, the meaning is "not in any way.
"Avāpnuyāt" means one would come to know [it].
"Exceedingly flavorful" means having an extremely delicious taste;
"of one whose mouth is ripened by time" means of one whose time [of death] is complete;
"in every way" means in all limbs.

Since the term "one who has flowered" (*puṣpita*) is used generally in the summary verse (*saṅgrahaśloka*), its "flowering" is intended to apply even to fatal signs related to the *rasas* (tissues/flavors). Consequently, it follows that death occurs within one year even in the case of a fatal sign related to the *rasas*.

Thus ends the second chapter, named "The Flowering Chapter on the Vital Signs" (*puṣpitakam indriyam*), in the *Indriyasthāna* of the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of Caraka, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Indriyasthāna, Chapter 3 (57 of 120)]

Because the undesirable signs (*ariṣṭa*) follow upon the objects of the senses, and by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the sense organ that expresses the undesirable signs pertaining to touch is called the "palpable sense" (*parimarśanīyendriya*). Demonstrating this very connection between chapters, he says: "In color and voice," etc.

Although one should have said "by touch" (*sparśena*), by using the phrase "by the predominance of touch" (*sparśaprādhānyena*), he shows that even those undesirable signs perceivable by the eye, such as redness and so forth, which are not grasped by touch, must be mentioned here within the examination of touch because they arrive there by way of the general flow (*ogha*).
"By one who is in his natural state" means neither too hot nor too cold;
"only" means entirely.
When it is not appropriate for one to personally touch the wife of a guru or others, he states what should be done in such a case: "or one should have another touch her."

Regarding the phrase "the non-existence of that which exists," it should be understood here as referring to the existence of the *vṛṣṇa* (muscle fibers) and so forth; for even when there is injury (*riṣṭa*) to the gross constituent parts, their absence [in function] is observed.
*Sraṃsa* is slight displacement; *bhraṃśa*, however, is falling far downward; *dhāvana* is movement to the sides;
and *vītībhāva* is extreme attenuation.
"Lakṣaṇam" means the characteristic of death; "in brief" (samāsena) is the grammatical division [of the compound].
The backbone is the spinal column;
"separately" means one by one;
the *maṇika* is the joint of the forearm.
I believe that when the two vessels located at the sides of the throat are scattered—
that is, covered with impurities— the lengthening and shortening of the breath can be perceived by touching the tip of the nose with the hand.
The whiteness of the teeth and so forth, although perceptible by the eye, is mentioned here in the context of the properties of the teeth which are to be examined by touch.
The general statement "the eyes are devoid of their natural state and possessed of abnormality" is explained as follows: "excessively protruding," and so forth;
"excessively protruding" means excessively bulging out.
"Excessively crooked, excessively curved,
and excessively uneven"— this refers to one [eye] being closed and the other being open; thus,
they function excessively in the act of closing and opening, which is why they are called "excessively active in closing and opening."

"Those with perverted vision" means those with the vision of a keyūra (a type of snake); or alternatively, "those with perverted vision" refers to those who perceive things incorrectly, those with inferior vision, those who do not see far, or those whose vision is lost—characterized like a blind mongoose or a blind pigeon—as the text states: "A blind mongoose sees white forms during the day."

"A pigeon-blind person sees forms as black during the day. Here, "alāta" refers to a heated coal; since this occurs in the context of describing omens (*ariṣṭa*) pertaining to the eyes, the color of the firebrand (*alāta-varṇatva*) and so forth—which are not actually grasped by touch—are mentioned in relation to the eyes.

In this context, it has been stated that the veins following the abdomen are perceivable by touch; in connection with that, the colors of the veins perceivable by sight have also been described [in the passage] beginning with "one should incise" (*āyacchet*) and "one should burst open" (*sphoṭayet*). However, since touch is indeed operative in the examination of fatal signs (*ariṣṭa*) located on the nails and fingers, that fatal sign has also been mentioned here.
These are said to be "touchable" because they are the majority; likewise, the phrase "touching these" is also stated because they are the majority.
In the reading "of the knowledge of life-span" (*āyurjñānasya*), the genitive case is used to express a relationship.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Diagnostic Chapter on Palpation," in the *Ayurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of Caraka’s work, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Indriyasthāna, Chapter 4 (58 of 120):
In accordance with the sequence of the enumeration, the *indriyānīka* is stated for the purpose of describing the fatal signs (*ariṣṭa*) pertaining to the range of the senses;
*indriyānīka* means a multitude or collection of the senses, and it is so called because it is composed concerning that [collection].
1–2. Vision is the eye; the five sense organs, such as the eye and so forth, are those beginning with vision.
He states that the examination of these sense organs is not by means of direct perception (pratyakṣa), beginning with the words "addhā hi" and so forth.
He adds [this] as a truth: because the sense faculties are beyond the senses, their examination occurs only through inference; this is the remainder [of the thought].
"From those that are healthy" means from the sense organs remaining in their natural state; "arisen" is the understood remainder.
"Dependent on the senses" means produced by the external senses.

"Without a cause" means in the absence of external causes that produce distorted cognition. Furthermore, the removal of defects that produce cognition based on the functioning of the senses is accomplished precisely by the qualification "from those that are healthy."
The phrase "arising of the unwholesome" refers to the cause of death.
The word *punaḥ* is used for emphasis, as in the example: “Furthermore, there are three defects” (*Viṣṇu Purāṇa*, Aṃśa 1).
Alternatively, the word *bhūyaḥ* has the sense of "again and again," or the word *bhūyaḥ* may have the sense of "great"; therefore, the words *punaḥ* and *bhūyaḥ* have distinct meanings.
"5–6 *ghanībhūtam* means having become solid; alternatively, the word *bhūta* may have the sense of 'become' (as in *kṛtārtha*), as in the expression *upadhānībhūtam*,
and the particle *iva* is used for comparison."
Others, however, say that it has become solidified and attained the form of earth;
they consider the earth to be of the nature of emptiness, like space,
and describe it as "viparītam," meaning known in a perverted manner.

By the word "both," it is intended that the perception of earth and space as contrary [to their true nature] occurs simultaneously, not individually; and this is the power of the omen (*ariṣṭa*) in that such a form of omen arises. Thus, among the aforementioned omens, the occurrence of each in its respective manner is to be understood through its own inherent power. And although these omens are already obtained by implication from the section defining the general omens of the sense organs, they are stated here specifically by name because they generally occur together.
Regarding the term "vision" (*darśana*),
by the phrase "having the sky as its range," he excludes the vision of the forms of deities situated on the earth.
By this, the connection is that the perceptual cognition of the wind, which has the form "this is wind," does not appear as a portent (*ariṣṭa*). 8.
Regarding the term "sthite" (when situated), it refers to when [the signs] are stable,
moving, or flowing;
and in those cases where no specific time limit for death is stated among these omens (*riṣṭa*), one year is the boundary, because death is not mentioned to occur beyond that point.
The meaning is that because of the plural forms such as "pretān" (ghosts), the sight of only a single ghost or similar being does not constitute an ill omen.
"Abiding in its natural color" means that, being free from discoloration, transformation, and so forth caused by poisonous food, it remains established in its own red-brown color;
thus it reaches the seventh night, and by that, death occurs on the eighth day.
Regarding the phrase "non-existent rays" (*marīcīnasataḥ*), in this context the word *marīci* refers to the light of the clouds.

It is a qualifier of the rays—meaning "of lightning even without a cloud"—and thus only those streaks that are always perceived in connection with clouds should be understood, not other types of lightning; for those [latter] are perceived from afar by healthy observers even without the sight of clouds.
By the word "pure," he shows that [the fire] is not obscured by clouds;
and by the phrase "at night," he shows that the sight of the fire lacking luster during the day is not an ill omen (*ariṣṭa*).
"Viliṅgān" means those whose innate marks have disappeared;

by that, when there is a reversal of the marks such as complexion and so forth, distinct from their natural state, "bhāvān" refers to the vital breaths (prāṇas). Alternatively, "bhāvān" refers to the five great elements in the form of the body.
"Variegated" means having diverse forms;
"discolored" means having conflicting colors;
"having reached an incorrect number" means being endowed with a perverted count.

"Signless" (*vinimittāni*) means devoid of signs; the meaning is that the perception of forms associated with the predicted [rebirth] and so forth, apart from the causal factors such as the act of prediction itself, constitutes a portent (*ariṣṭa*).
"Forms" (*rūpāṇi*) refers to substances possessing form.
With the words "of that which is soundless" (*aśabdasya*) and so forth, he describes an omen concerning the ear:
"flame-sound" (*jvālāśabda*) refers to a sound like that of a flame. That [sound].
By the words "by the reverse," etc., the omen regarding the sense of smell (*ghrāṇāriṣṭa*) is stated;
[the phrase] "or one should not know them at all" means that one does not perceive smells whatsoever, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
"In reality" means by its own nature.
The term "mouth-sourness" (*mukhapāka*) is an indicator for defects of the tongue; by this, the perception of flavors as they are not [due to] the tongue being corrupted by *pitta* is excluded.
"Ripe" means having reached the full span of its life (verse 22).
"Otherness than that" refers to perceiving coldness in what is hot, roughness in what is smooth, and so forth.
Now he describes the prodromal signs (ariṣṭa) pertaining to all the sense organs in general—beginning with "antareṇa" and so forth;
"antareṇa" means "without" (vinā).

The qualification of "yoga" is "according to rule" (*vidhipūrvakam*); by this it is stated that only yoga performed according to the prescribed rules has the capacity for super-sensory knowledge (*atīndriyajñāna*).
"Excessive" (*adhika*) means beyond the range of the senses of people such as ourselves.
"Fivefoldness" (*pañcatvam*) means death.

"Vision" (*dṛṣṭi*) means perception (*upalabdhi*); by that vision, the power of vision is figuratively expressed. Therefore, "without vision" means without perception. Consequently, he who would see with his senses things that cannot be perceived by the senses without the perceiving power of the senses—he does not live. Furthermore, by the phrase "not born of defects," he excludes the apprehension of objects impossible for the senses as being due to the nature of the defects themselves.

Just as an eye pressed by a finger perceives two nearby objects that are not within its sensory range due to a disorder of the wind (*vāta*), so too should it be understood that a tongue impaired by bile (*pitta*) does not perceive molasses as sweet, and so forth.
(Verses 24–25) "Healthy" (*svastha*) means those whose sense organs and minds are unimpaired.
Regarding the phrase "by distortions of wisdom" (*prajñā-viparyāsaiḥ*): this refers to a distortion of wisdom produced by the residual influence (*śeṣībhūta*) of past karma.
The term "non-existent" (*asat*) means that which is not as it truly is (*ayathābhūtam*).
By the word "repeatedly" (*bahuśas*), it is indicated that seeing [the object] only once does not constitute a fatal omen (*ariṣṭa*).

It should be understood that here, the cognition of the sense faculties (*indriyavijñāna*), the cognition of signs of impending death located in the sense faculties (*indriyagatariṣṭavijñāna*), and the cognition of life (*jīvitajñāna*) occur when there is a cognition of the sense faculties devoid of such signs of death (*riṣṭaśūnyendriyajñāna*).
Thus ends the fourth chapter, named "The Array of the Senses," in the Indriyasthāna of the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the purport of Caraka, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Indriyasthāna, Chapter 5 (59 of 120):

Having described the fatal signs (*ariṣṭa*) pertaining to the sense organs (*indriya*), it is now appropriate to describe the fatal signs of those previously mentioned, such as the mental disposition (*sattva*) and others. However, because those [latter] require little to be said, they are set aside; instead, the fatal signs of the premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*), which require extensive explanation, are addressed here in the section on premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpīya*). As for the mention of *sattva* and the others at the beginning of the first chapter, it should be understood that this occurred in the context of their being means of cognition (*buddhisādhana*) alongside the sense organs.

Although disease (*vyādhi*) has much to be said about it and was even aphorized at the beginning of the *Śārīrasthāna*, nevertheless, because disease is preceded by its premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*), the determination of premonitory symptoms is presented here first. In the aphorism, however, by mentioning "disease" later, he demonstrates the primacy of the premonitory symptoms—which are to be understood prior to the disease—over the disease itself.
(1–2) "Distinct and non-distinct" means common and uncommon [symptoms].

In this context, from the words "the premonitory symptoms" (*pūrvarūpāṇi*) up to "his death is certain" (*tasyāpi maraṇaṃ dhruvam*), the common premonitory symptoms (*ariṣṭa*) of all diseases have been stated. However, from the words "but the partial premonitory symptoms" (*pūrvarūpaikadeśāṃstu*) onwards, the specific premonitory symptoms (*ariṣṭa*) distinct for each individual disease are stated. Others, however, say that these are both distinct and non-distinct, and thus both mentioned and unmentioned. Among these, the premonitory symptoms of fever and other diseases have been stated; but the phrase "by dogs, camels, donkeys," etc., refers to a premonitory symptom not previously mentioned. The word "all" (*sarvāṇi*) means collectively.
"Excessively" (*atimātrayā*) means by way of being extremely intense;
"preceded by fever" (*jvarapuraḥsara*) means occurring immediately after fever;
and by the phrase "by this method" (*anena kalpena*), he shows that all [the aforementioned factors] are present in excess.
"Three to five diseases follow" means they are necessarily joined by a subsequent disease;
"death is followed by which" means death is followed by those diseases.

By this, the following result is obtained: those diseases with which the premonitory symptoms have a fixed association are necessarily fatal; this is the meaning. Furthermore, in the *Śoṣanidāna*, it is stated: "Traveling by camel, boar, or donkey" (Ni. A. 6), and so forth; therefore, that fatal sign (*ariṣṭa*) is specifically characterized by traveling toward the southern direction.
"From near" means from close proximity;
"having obtained blood" means having obtained *raktapitta* (blood-bile), he sinks, that is, he dies.
*Āṭopa* is a rumbling sound in the abdomen caused by the wandering of wind;
*graha* means that by which something is grasped, i.e., a symptom (*liṅga*).
"Touched" means touched by weapons, grass, and so forth.

Although the symptoms beginning with "one whose limbs are bathed and anointed" were already stated in the *Puṣpitaka* chapter as "even for one who is bathed and anointed" (*api-snātānuliptasya*, *Indriya-sthāna* 2), they are nevertheless repeated here for the purpose of demonstrating death by means of *prameha*.

In that context, when other premonitory signs of *prameha* occur and this specific characteristic is present, then death occurs due to *prameha*; however, when the premonitory signs of *prameha* are not present, then death should be understood to result from some other disease.

"Udardita" means afflicted with urticaria (udarda); alternatively, "udarditam ūrdhvavātārditam" means afflicted by upward-moving wind (ūrdhvavāta), and "āvidhya" means having turned [the patient] head-downward.
"Such as that" refers to the form of cakes and fried pastries (24–25).
"The sequel of these" refers to the disease occurring at a time subsequent to the premonitory symptoms.
