And their fruit is either death (verse 26) or even great affliction; here, it should be understood that for those who are healthy, it leads to great affliction, whereas for those who are ill, it leads precisely to death. For this reason, in the subsequent conclusion beginning with "Thus these are dreadful dreams," he will make the very same distinction as stated.
"Vayāṃsi" means birds;
the connection is that he is surrounded by vultures and others ending with crows.
"Saṃsajjati" means he becomes joined [with them].

Alternatively, there is the reading *pramuhyati*; in that case, "he becomes bewildered" should be construed with the passage beginning with "on the ground," meaning that being stuck in a narrow space such as a bamboo thicket, he cannot find a way out and even falls down onto the ground covered with dust (*pāṃśūpadhānāyām*).
Alternatively, the phrase "on the ground" and so forth should be construed with the word "falls";
"upānat" means a foot-protector (shoe),
and "raktapuṣpa" is an epithet of the forest.
"Confined by the darkness of the cave" means having the nature of the darkness within a cave, which causes distress;
"digvāsāḥ" means being naked; "by a vehicle yoked with monkeys"—this is the ellipsis.

"Only some are liberated"—this [statement] regarding those who are healthy does not constitute the fatal sign (*riṣṭa*) nature of dreams. Therefore, they say that among the healthy, these dreams do not possess the status of a fatal sign because of their deviation from death, as they are not absolute.
(27–40) He explains how this dream-vision occurs, beginning with "of the channels carrying the mind" (*manovahānām*), etc.

Although the channels carrying the mind (*manovahāni srotāṃsi*) have not been mentioned separately, nevertheless, because the mind is described as "that which consists solely of consciousness and serves as the vehicle for the body" (Vi. A. 5), all the channels of the entire body are included. Specifically, however, because the mind is located in the heart, the ten vessels (*dhamanyaḥ*) situated there are designated as "mind-carrying.
The phrase "by three" means even by the three [doṣas] collectively; therefore, their filling by the doṣas individually should also be understood.
The term "not excessively numb" (*nātiprasupta*) means not overcome by excessive sleep.
"By the lord of the senses" means by that which impels the senses (41-42).
Having stated that dreams possess both fruitfulness and fruitlessness, he describes the various types of dreams in order to demonstrate that: "That which is seen," and so forth.
"Seen" refers to that which is experienced by the eye;
"known" refers to that which is perceived by the remaining sense organs;
and "imagined" refers to that which is conceptualized by the mind.
"Prārthita" means that which has been made the object of a request;
"bhāvika" means indicative of future auspicious or inauspicious results;
and "doṣaja" means produced by the aggravated humors (doṣas) such as wind (vāta) and the rest.
Having previously described the fivefold dream beginning with "seen" (dṛṣṭa) and ending with "imagined" (kalpita), which are fruitless,
he now states another type of fruitless dream, beginning with "daytime sleep" (divāsvapna).

One should know that every dream seen during the day, as well as one seen at night that is either excessively long or excessively short, is fruitless because it lacks result; by process of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), those [dreams] that are natural (*bhāvika*) or caused by a disorder (*doṣajanya*) are fruitful. Among these, the natural dream—by way of being auspicious or inauspicious—bestows auspicious or inauspicious results; whereas that which is caused by a disorder is fruitful because it indicates a result in the form of a disease produced by the provocation of that disorder.

In this chapter, only those [conditions] for whom specific omens (ariṣṭa) occur in the form of dreams have been mentioned. Therefore, one should not ask why the dreams of those with chronic diarrhea (grahaṇī) and other such conditions are not mentioned; it should be understood that they are not described precisely because specific omens do not occur in them. Some recite the passage beginning with "He who is seen in the first watch... here; its meaning is quite clear.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Prodromal Symptoms," in the Indriyasthāna of the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka-saṃhitā, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta. 44–47.

[Indriyasthāna, Chapter 6 (60 of 120)] Now, following the chapter on premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpīya*), for the purpose of describing the fatal signs (*ariṣṭa*) based on impending diseases, the "Chapter on the Body" (*katamāniśarīrīya*) is being stated:
concerning which bodies was it composed? What is the "body-related" (*katamāniśarīrīya*) [chapter]?
"The question" (*praśnam*) refers to the subject matter of the inquiry;
"the upper chest" (*ura ūrdhvam*) means the upper portion of the chest.

They say that because there is a commonality with *riṣṭa*—which indicates death—in its capacity as an indicator of death, diseases that are incurable and taught in this chapter are also designated as *ariṣṭa*.
Even if these very incurable diseases are indeed *riṣṭa* by nature as premonitory signs of death, there is no contradiction;
therefore, based on the context of *ariṣṭa*, we maintain that the diseases described in this chapter possess the very nature of *ariṣṭa*.

"Deep-seated" (*gambhīrajā*) means arising in deep locations such as the navel and so forth, but it does not mean that the hemorrhage itself is deep; for since that [deep hemorrhage] has already been stated to be incurable by its very nature, the qualification "and blood is discharged" would be redundant.
Indeed, by the term "afflicted" (*vyādhita*), he indicates that the patient is seized by a disease other than constipation (*ānāha*) or diarrhea (*atisāra*).

Although *ānāha* (obstipation) and *atisāra* (diarrhea) are established as diseases, the term "two diseases" (*rogau*) is used here specifically to demonstrate their nature as agents of suffering (*rujā-kartṛtva*). Furthermore, even though life is unattainable [in such cases], it is stated that it is "difficult to obtain" (*durlabham*); just as that which is entirely unobtainable is called "difficult to obtain. Others, however, maintain that by the expression "difficult to obtain," a prognostic sign of death (*riṣṭa*) that is not yet fixed is indicated. They explain this similarly in passages such as: "Ātreya considers his life to have reached a state of uncertainty" (I.A. 9).
The uncertainty regarding the prognosis and the lack of internal consistency have already been stated by us in the *Puṣpitaka* [chapter],
and we shall explain the meaning of the verse beginning with "Ātreya considers his life to have reached a state of doubt" in the chapter on the signs of death (*yasyaśyāvanimittīya*).
"Bound urine" (mūtraṃ grathitam) should be understood as having become thickened.

By the statement "he distresses the circle of kinsmen," it is meant that his illness persists for a long time; consequently, the kinsmen, out of hope, undergo suffering for the sake of its remedy. Yet, he simply dies and cannot be cured.
"Piṇḍike" refers to the two masses of flesh on the calves.
"Released from the chest" (*uroyu(mu)kta*) means inferred as originating from the chest;
"characterized by difficulty" (*kaṣṭābhilakṣita*) means known for being difficult to treat.

Or perhaps the reading is *koṣṭhābhilakṣitā*; that clearly refers to a *ḍambarī*, one who looks with fixed eyes. Or else, *ḍambarī* means "possessing agitation," and thus he is one whose breath is agitated (*kupitocchvāsaḥ*), meaning he is angry.

"The vital breaths (prāṇas) reside in the chest" means that the winds (vāyus), having become aggravated, move within the chest. If, however, "vital breaths" here refers to life itself, then they reside in the chest [only as long as one lives]; once [the breaths] leave the chest, the person is indeed dead. Therefore, considering that at such a time the physician's failure to treat arises from knowing the incurability through fatal signs (ariṣṭa) and the consequent abandonment of the patient, they say that "vital breaths" here refers to the winds. We, however, say: like the fatal signs of immediate death, this must be an indicator of imminent death. 20.
"They contract their limbs" means they throw them about.
"Of contradictory origins" (*viruddhayoni*) refers to those possessing mutually contradictory properties.

Even though those of contradictory origins may have non-contradictory treatments due to being minor or having only a single point of corruption, it is therefore stated: "of contradictory treatments" (*viruddhopakrama*).
"Health declines" means that here, the loss of health should be understood as occurring through the increase of diseases other than those already mentioned.

"One's nature (*prakṛti*) declines" means that one's innate character (*svabhāva*), such as good conduct and so forth, is diminished; or alternatively, that the constitutional type (*prakṛti*) bound to birth, such as the phlegmatic temperament (*śleṣmaprakṛti*) and so forth, is lost.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Which Constituent Elements of the Body," in the Indriyasthāna of the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka Saṃhitā, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Indriyasthāna, Chapter 7 (61 of 120)]

Immediately after the description of the forms of disease (*vyādhi-rūpa*), pain (*vedanā*) and complications (*upadrava*) were indicated; since these have already been described as signs of impending death (*ariṣṭa*) in the preceding chapter by such passages as "colic, flatulence, and intestinal gurgling" (I.A.5) and elsewhere as "constipation and diarrhea" (I.A.6), the chapter titled *Pannarūpīya* is now spoken to explain the signs of impending death in the form of *chāyā* and *praticchāyā*, which follows in the sequence.
It is called *Pannarūpīya* because it was composed concerning the *pannarūpa*.
"Pannarūpā" means one whose form has perished;

"kumārikā" refers to a young girl who has gone into the sight of another man, or rather, one who has gone into the sight of a sick person, as stated by Hārīta: "The non-seeing of the eyes when they do not blink is called 'naṣṭakumārikā'."
"Consisting of a reflection" (*praticchāyāmayīm*) means having the form of a reflection.
Elsewhere as well, he speaks of a transformation of the shadow, beginning with "moonlight" (*jyotsnā*), and so forth.

The meaning is that "distorted in its limbs" (*aṅgeṣu vikṛtā*) refers to the reflected image (*praticchāyā*) appearing distorted within the head, arms, shanks, and so forth, which serve as the substratum for the reflection.
By this, a reflection distorted in one or all of the limbs is included.
Others, however, explain it by changing the case ending to "of the limbs" (*aṅgānām*); in that case, the meaning is indeed straightforward.
He describes these very same varieties of shadow-transformations, beginning with "chinnā" (severed) and so forth; "ākula" means having an indeterminate reflection.

Although it has already been stated in the section on *ariṣṭas* (signs of approaching death) that whatever occurs without a cause is indeed an *ariṣṭa*, nevertheless, for the sake of clarity, it is further stated [in verses 5–6]: "If they are not born from a visible cause (*lakṣya-nimitta-jāḥ*)."
Now, demonstrating the nature of *chāyā* (complexion) in general, he describes the fatal signs (*ariṣṭa*) based on *chāyā*, beginning with the words "by configuration," and so forth.
This is a common aphorism for both *chāyā* and *praticchāyā* (reflection).

Among them, the description of the essential nature of the reflection is given by means of its configuration and its dimensions; likewise, the description of the essential nature of the complexion is given by means of its color and its luster.

In this context, a shadow (*chāyā*) that is similar in shape and size is to be understood as a reflected image (*praticchāyā*); whereas that which is characterized by color and radiance, being the locus of color and radiance, is to be known here as the fivefold shadow that will be described below. Since there is an obligatory connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative *tat*, the word "that" (*sā*) must be supplied [as the subject].

Thus, the construction is as follows: that shadow which exists in the form of a reflected image, defined by its shape and so forth, undergoes transformation—that is, becomes otherwise—belongs to a *preta* alone.
He explains the very configuration (*saṃsthāna*) and dimension (*pramāṇa*), which serve as the causes for the reflected image, starting with the words "configuration," etc.;
[it means] shape (*ākṛti*) or form (*ākāra*).
The term *pratītyādi* is an explanation of *praticchāyā*; however, the passage beginning with “*chāyā varṇaprabhāśrayā*” will be an explanation of *chāyā* itself.

In the phrase *pratipramāṇasaṃsthāna*, the prefix *prati* denotes similarity (*sādṛśye*). Thus, that shadow which appears in water and so forth—resembling [the object] in its dimensions (*pramāṇa*) and resembling it in its configuration (*saṃsthāna*)—is, by virtue of that similarity in dimensions and configuration, called a *praticchāyā*.
The fivefold shadow, however, is based upon color and radiance; the meaning is that it is perceived as concomitant with color and radiance.
With the words "of earth and so forth," he analyzes shadow.
"Radiant" means possessing a blazing luster.

"Wind-born" (vāyavī) is censured; it generally leads to misfortune for one whose [nature] is wind-born from birth onwards, and such a person also becomes a partaker of abundant afflictions—thus he says, "wind-born," and so forth.
"For destruction" means that [the wind] which arises suddenly leads to destruction; however, it should be understood that the innate (*sahajā*) aerial [wind] leads to the afflictions (10–13).

Now, the differentiation of colors has been stated by way of their being the substratum for the shadow (*chāyā*); therein, the differentiation of colors and their fatal signs (*ariṣṭa*) were already explained in the first chapter. But he now states the differentiation and the fatal signs of the radiance (*prabhā*)—beginning with "it may be fiery," and so forth.

Although *prabhā* (luster) was not explicitly mentioned in the summary of the first chapter, it should be understood that while the various colors were described therein as being the substrata of *chāyā* (complexion), and those color variations along with their omens were briefly stated in the first chapter, *prabhā* is also indicated there by virtue of its being the substratum of *chāyā*.

Regarding the phrase "arising of the inauspicious" (*aśubhodayā*), it should be understood that when they arise suddenly, they portend death; however, when they arise naturally, they are of the nature of great suffering and constitute the "arising of the inauspicious.
Because light (*prabhā*) and shadow (*chāyā*) are difficult to distinguish, he states the defining characteristic that differentiates them: "It takes on the color," and so forth.
A color that is overtaken by shadow (*chāyākrānta*) is not perceived correctly;
rather, the shadow is perceived as being close at hand, just as a shadow depicted in a painting is perceived only when it is very near.
"Luster" (bhās) shines forth most intensely; the meaning is that, for example, the radiance (prabhā) of gems, pearls, and the like is perceived from a distance.
"Specific qualities" (viśeṣāḥ) refers to the specific auspicious or inauspicious forms of shadows and radiances; they "indicate" means they cause one to understand [the nature of the object].
"At the proper time" means at the time of maturation (16–17).
"With eyes like those of a jaundiced person" refers to having yellowed eyes, as if one were suffering from jaundice.
"Boastful" means intent on disparaging others; "intermingled" means mutually connected, or else produced by intermingled defects;
"proceeding in reverse and direct order" means moving along the downward path and the upward path.
The word *vyāpannā* is to be construed with *grahaṇī*; or rather, the reading is *vyāpannagrahaṇī*, meaning "one whose *grahaṇī* is corrupted.
By the phrase "he does not live for even half a month," it is indicated that death occurs even after the lapse of half a month, yet there is no deviation from this certainty of death (verses 18–20).
"Than what was previously eaten" means that he eats much more than the amount of food he used to eat on previous days;
"desired" means having a desired flavor; "endowed with qualities" means wholesome.
The term "loose" (śithilam) is connected with what precedes; by that, it means he cries out and sighs as if relaxed, drawing the breath inward;
"disturbed" (vyāviddham) means crooked.
"With the tip pointing upward" means with the face turned upward; "in the trembling of the *ārataka*" means in an unremitting trembling.

"Utsikta" means internally retracted; "viparyāsa" refers to the penis being excessively protruded and the testicles being excessively withdrawn, occurring through "vikṛti," that is, deviating from their natural state. Therefore, a naturally protruded penis and so forth are not *riṣṭa* (fatal signs); rather, only that which occurs occasionally without a [natural] cause is indeed *riṣṭa*.

"Accumulated" (*nicita*) means "wasted away" (*kṣīṇa*), because the prefix *ni-* has the sense of negation. Thus, the flesh becomes wasted away such that it is seen adhering only to the skin and bones; or alternatively, "accumulated" (*nicita*) may mean "grown thick" (*upacita*), in the sense that the flesh is seen [only] on the skin and bones, meaning that nothing remains but the skin and bones.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Signs of Death," in the *Indriyasthāna* of the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā*, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Indriyasthāna, Chapter 8 (62 of 120)]

After the two chapters concerning the collection of stated and unstated portents (*ariṣṭa*) have been declared, the chapter on "Head-Down" (*avākśirasīya*) is now being expounded because it shares the common characteristic of describing portents related to shadows.
"Head-down" means having the feet upwards.

Although this matter concerning the shadow (chāyā) should have been discussed in its own section, it is mentioned here among the "swift-killers" (śīghramāraka) for the purpose of demonstrating their rapid lethality.
For it must be explained that these fatal signs (ariṣṭa) cause death within three days and so forth;
they do not occur simultaneously, nor do they coincide with one another.
"Unprecedented" means not co-nascent;
"uncreated" means not produced by effort.

Although this [sign] was already stated as an *ariṣṭa* by the passage beginning with "his hair and body hair" (*Caraka Saṃhitā*, Indriyasthāna 3.10) through the phrase "having pulled [them] forcibly," it is nevertheless mentioned here again for the purpose of explaining the subject of the patient who is not in a healthy state.
Furthermore, there is a distinction: in that [previous] case, by the word "would fall out" (*pralucyeran*), the non-pulling out of the hairs was indicated, whereas it is not so here.
"Glāyati" means it undergoes weakness;
"aśūnaḥ" means that, in the ultimate sense, it is not diminished.
"Opened" means gone out; "closed" means entered;
"sound-hearers" refers to the ears.
"Having transformed" means without their innate nature; that is to say, without a cause. "White as bone" means those who are white like bone.
"Spreading" means it has gone outside;
"having exhaled" means having drawn the breath inward; "he casts it off" means he expels it; "repeatedly" means he repeatedly turns his face away.
"Without the Sāman" is said loudly;
"the openings" refers to the channels of the nose, ears, and eyes.
"Of the weary one" means of one who is wasting away;
"his own burden" refers to the upper body;
"the back" refers to the lower part of the body.
"At the time of dawn" means at daybreak; "lepajvara" is a phlegm-fever accompanied by slight coldness;
"with difficulty" means not quickly releasing [the fever]; [he] tosses his head from the wrists upward to the elbows.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Head-Turning [Prognostic] Signs," in the Indriyasthāna of the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the purport of the Caraka-saṃhitā, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta. 8.21–27.
[Indriyasthāna, Chapter 9 (63 of 120):
That which is described as having a dark-brown (śyāva) cause is also said to indicate unmentioned fatal signs;
by the word "śyāva," one should understand the fatal signs mentioned in the text beginning with "yasya śyāve" through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).
Therefore, that chapter which was composed concerning the ill omen (*riṣṭa*) characterized by the appearance of a dark horse is titled "Yasyaśyāvanimittīya" (1–2),
and it is complete and well-expounded.

The hands, feet, and other limbs at the end of the body "shine" (rājante), meaning they appear beautiful or possess splendor; or rather, a patient who has wind (vāta) as their disease is one suffering from "wind-disease" (vātavyādhi).

"Those" refers to those afflicted by the wasting of strength and flesh; "one whose abdominal distension has been removed by purgation" is so described; "by improper means" means in an unsuitable manner.
"3-13 *Apasvaram* means with a distorted voice, speaking in such a manner.
To the question of what he was saying, it says: 'of his own death'; the meaning is that he was saying, 'I shall die, I shall die.'"

Regarding the passage beginning with "the listener," and so forth: immediately after the [description of] fatal signs (ariṣṭa), in the verse starting with "Ātreya, having reached a state of doubt," he states that Ātreya has a doubt concerning death here because the fatal signs are not yet fixed.

That is not the case, for the teacher has stated with great effort that *riṣṭa* is invariably concomitant with death, and this has been demonstrated by us as well. Furthermore, Ātreya, whose doubts have been dispelled, possesses no doubt himself; rather, for the sake of instructing his disciples, this teacher displays a doubt and likewise provides a resolution. For example, in such passages as, "Having seen a prameha that is sweet, slimy, and honey-like, there may be various considerations" (Ci. A. 6), he first shows the doubt and then demonstrates the resolution. Similarly here too, when a weak person is suddenly freed from disease, there is a doubt: "Is this a *riṣṭa*, or is it simply the subsiding of the disease due to complete nourishment? In the event of it being a *riṣṭa*, death would follow; therefore, with the words "If, however... (*atha cet*), he begins the examination. And in that examination, if no specific improvement is observed through meat broth, the determination of *riṣṭa* occurs. Thus, this text is well-ordered.
"Durlabham" means unattainable (14–17).
In the passage beginning with "niṣṭhyūta," the combination of various types of syllables constitutes a distinction from the previously mentioned omens.
"It sinks" means it submerges.
Although *śaṅkhaka* was mentioned in the Sūtrasthāna in the passage beginning with "He whose bile... (Sū. A. 18), it is also described here as a fatal sign (*riṣṭa*) because it indicates death.

The "consciousnesses" are to be understood as the characteristics consisting of the distortions of the eyes and other senses; they are called "characteristics" because all of them are characterized. They are observed among various persons, but not all of them enter into every human being; that is, they do not all enter into a single person.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Signs of Impending Death Based on the Appearance of Darkness," in the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the purport of the Caraka Saṃhitā, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.

[Indriyasthāna, Chapter 10 (64 of 120)] Having described the fatal signs (*ariṣṭa*) that indicate death after an interval, the author now speaks of those who are destined for immediate death (*sadyomaraṇīya*), in order to explain the fatal signs (*riṣṭa*) that indicate imminent death.
Regarding the word "immediate" (*sadyas*), some maintain it refers to seven nights, while others maintain it refers to three nights.
"1-2 They endure (titikṣate); they indeed endure, because the vital breaths (prāṇas), being dear, are themselves unfit to be killed;
'the two piṇḍikas' refers to the two calves."
"Between the anus and the navel" means in the middle of the anus and the navel;
"having seized the heart" means having reached the heart through its own modification;
"the head of the bladder" means the upper portion of the bladder.
"Cut" (*pracchinna*) means as if cut; it is so called because it is associated with the sensation of the act of cutting.
"Sunk" (*āpluta*) means pervaded.
"Swollen" (*śothita*) means possessed of swelling.
*Parikartikā* is a sensation having the form of cutting;
*ghurghuraka* is the sound "ghur-ghur," which arises from breath obstructed by phlegm,
and the mouth becomes like fine powder due to its whiteness.

"Siprāyante" refers to the river Siprā; they "siprāyante" because they behave like it due to the excessive manifestation of perspiration. Alternatively, "siprāyante" means they become relaxed (*śithilībhavanti*), since verbal roots have multiple meanings.
"He perceives his life" means that by the absence of the aforementioned fatal signs (*riṣṭa*), he perceives life, and by the presence of fatal signs, he perceives death.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Signs of Immediate Death," in the Indriyasthāna of the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka Saṃhitā, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.

[Indriyasthāna, Chapter 11 (65 of 120)] Having described the fatal signs (*ariṣṭa*) determined by immediate time, the "Little Light" (*aṇujyotis*) is now stated, which describes fatal signs determined by specific periods of time; and here, *aṇujyotis* is employed as a technical term, setting aside its literal meaning of "disease."
*Jyotiḥ* refers to the light, the radiance residing within the entire body; *aṇujyotiḥ* is a weak digestive fire (*mandāgni*).
*Anekāgraḥ* means one whose mind is distracted or agitated. By the term *durmanāḥ*, mental weakness is expressed; therefore, there is no tautology.
"Samāntaram" means in the middle of the assembly;
"bali" refers to food offered according to the prescribed rite to the crows.
The term *mahattama* refers to the darkness (*tamas*) in the form of death.
"Having transformed" means without a well-known cause such as wealth and so forth—that is, without a specific instrumental cause.

[This implies] without the signs indicative of wealth and so forth connected to the body; for it is precisely by virtue of signs connected to the body that at some time wealth and so forth, or their depletion, occurs. And because that has signs as its instrumental cause, it was stated in the very first chapter that this is a *ariṣṭa* (fatal sign).
"Accumulation" refers to the accumulation [of fat] in the body itself;
therefore, "decline" refers to the absence of beauty and so forth.
"Devotion" (*bhakti*) means "desire";
"without cause" (*ahetukam*) is an adverbial modifier.

Since the number six is already obtained from the very mention of the things to be numbered, the word "six" (*ṣaḍ*) is used again to show that the term "misfortune" (*ariṣṭa*) refers to the cessation of all six [defects] taken together.
"Net" means having the form of a net;
"with faces curved like the moon" means with faces curved like the crescent moon.

Although [the conditions for] misfortune have been stated in such passages as “semen, etc., and excrement” (Īśvarasaṃhitā 9), nevertheless, because of the concise statement here, it should be understood that the immersion of semen and the other substances *only when they are combined* becomes fatal when there is hatred toward one's own kinsmen.
The word "both" indicates the simultaneous withering of the hands and other limbs;
"resembling coral beads" means they appear like beads made of coral;
"of one surrounded by the noose of Time" refers to one who will die soon.
The construction is: "he takes food like one who is healthy"; the meaning is that, being weak, he consumes food excessively as if he were healthy.
12–17 "In the vicinity," etc.
Placing his hand near his eyes and looking at it, he searches for and longs after it; he smiles and becomes amazed, and his gaze is directed upward and unblinking;
thus, he searches for and longs after that which is non-existent and not present, such as a bed or a seat.
"Laughing when one should not laugh" means laughing in a situation where laughter is inappropriate; "daśanacchadau" refers to the lips.
The word "cold" (śīta) is connected with the end of the phrase "with sighs" (ucchvāsāntaiḥ);
by the maxim of "the cow and the bull," it refers to one's own kin (svajana).
"Of the *khādins*" means of the elements (*dhātus*) that perform the function of eating; or alternatively, it refers to the ears and other [senses] that perform the function of eating.
Non-application (*ayoga*) is the failure to grasp appropriate objects; excessive application (*atiyoga*) is the grasping of non-existent objects.
Like a garment, the body is like a house to the self; whether it exists or not, the meaning is that in every respect it does not exist [as the self].

Regarding the terms *samavartin* and so forth, these belong to Yama; however, others explain that by the word *samavartin*, they mean "timely death" (*kālamṛtyu*), and by the word *ca* ("and"), they include the grasp of all portents (*ariṣṭa*) both mentioned and yet to be mentioned. Thus, they describe that every single portent occurs subsequent to timely death. Furthermore, he states—beginning with the words "In these cases"—that there would be hatred [toward the patient], the progression of disease, and even the administration of medicine would be fruitless.
"The medicine is counteracted" means that even a medicine properly prepared is rendered ineffective.
"One should not eat their food" is generally because that food is impure;
the same should be understood regarding the prohibition of their water.
25–26. The four feet, such as the physician and the others,
are endowed with the qualities of the practitioner, namely the sixteen qualities beginning with "purity of learning" (*śrute paryavadātatvam*, Sūtra-sthāna, chapter 9).
He explains why physicians and others do not cure the diseases of those whose life-span has expired: "Without substance (dravya), there is no arising of excellence (guṇodaya).
Without substance—that is, without the cause—there is no arising of excellence characterized by health;
and in this case, regarding the production of health, the cause is the fact that the life-span has not expired, and that [life-span] does not exist. This is the intended meaning.
27. The fruit of knowledge regarding lifespan is the giving of medicine when one's lifespan still remains.
He states the definition of fatal signs (riṣṭa): "those that have transcended the path of treatment," and so forth.
"Transcended" means gone beyond;

this is not a definition of fatal signs pertaining to messengers and the like, but rather a definition of fatal signs pertaining to the body. Therefore, one should not allege that the definition is under-inclusive (avyāpti).

As for the definition that pervades all types of fatal signs (*ariṣṭa*), namely "the sign of that which has entered into the lifespan," this has already been stated by the very term *indriya*; thus, it was explained in the first chapter itself during the commentary on the term *indriya*.

One might object: "Has it not been stated that *riṣṭa* (fatal signs) are causeless, whereas here it is said that *riṣṭas* are produced by the *doṣas*? How is there no contradiction? No, for "causelessness" was stated with reference to the non-perception of a cause. Thus, what is being asserted here is that those various *riṣṭas* are produced by *doṣas* provoked by the power of imminent death, even in the absence of the attainment of causes such as dryness (*rūkṣa*) and so forth. Therefore, since there exists the presence of perceptible manifest causes here as well, there is no contradiction. 29

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Minute Light" (*Aṇujyotīya Indriya*), in the *Indriyasthāna* of the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of Caraka, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Indriyasthāna, Chapter 12 (66 of 120)]
By process of elimination, this is said to be powdered cow dung (1–2).
"Powdered" is the term being qualified by "moist."
The phrase "as if rubbing" (*nikaṣann iva*) means as if grinding;

by the word "wearing away" (*vikṛtya*), he prohibits the natural rubbing of the feet and so forth. Since the moisture of the remaining limbs is already established by the previous statement that "the chest first withers," the subsequent mention of "all limbs being moist" specifically demonstrates the moisture of the other limbs.

The phrase "prepared for the sake of whom" (*yamuddiśya*) means food known to have been prepared repeatedly for that person's benefit; this refers to an ill omen (*ariṣṭa*) concerning a patient. Therefore, there is no tautology with the ill omens concerning healthy persons described in the passage beginning with "and desired, endowed with good qualities" (*iṣṭaṃ ca guṇasampannaṃ*, *Indriyasthāna* 7).
"Aprayate" means "impure";
"supte" means "asleep."
"Not [when] the master" means not when he is distressed by sending messengers;

for although messengers desire the welfare of the sick person and do not intend to kill him, and messengers do not kill by their very nature with the intent to kill, nevertheless, because they come impelled by fate in such a way that the destruction of the sick person occurs, they act as if they intended to kill and as if they were killing. Therefore, in this context, the word "as if" (*iva*) should be understood as being omitted.
The connection is that [the physician] thinks of inauspicious things;
the construction is that he even speaks of the dead, the burnt, and the ruined.

Regarding the location (deśa) having qualities in common with the disorder: for example, in the case of *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders), a location near fire. Regarding the time (kāla) having qualities in common with the disorder: for example, in the case of *raktapitta*, midday, and so forth—this is how it should be understood.
"Three" refers specifically to the number three; such messengers are inauspicious, as are eunuchs, hermaphrodites,
those with bodily defects, and those with severed noses and the like.
"Ugrakarmā" refers to one engaged in improper acts such as killing.
In the phrase "palāla" and so forth, messengers who touch straw, wood, and the like [are indicated].
"Upon seeing them first" means upon seeing the physician first; the construction is that those touching straw, chaff, and so forth announce the patient's state of being about to die.
The connection is that one should not follow anyone whom one sees wearing the very ornaments of a *preta*; "speaking of those" refers to those who speak of schisms and the like;
and "intense" means that which causes agitation to the sense faculties.
"Contact" (*sparśa*) is extensive, such as contact that is intense, fierce, and so forth;
"prior to that" (*tatpūrvam*) means before the messenger's speech;
"the statement on all sides" (*abhito vākyam*) refers to the statement regarding all times and beings.
"Vyāhṛtam" (spoken) refers to the description of the state of the patient.
"Portentous" refers to an omen indicating an impending death;
"sneezing" is a sneeze; "shouted" is a cry uttered in terror.
Prohibition is of the form "do not go";
misfortune refers to the tearing and so forth of garments and other items;
one who is "misfortunate" (*vyasanin*) is one who is maimed or one who is prone to quarreling.
"Full" refers to full water-jars and the like;
"defilement" refers to the scattering of ashes and dust;
and "obstructing the path" refers to the crossing of the way by cats and other such creatures.
Cruel beasts and birds, such as jackals, vultures, and the like;
the direction in which the sun is situated is said to be "blazing," or alternatively, the southern direction is called blazing;
a bed refers to a couch and so forth, while a seat refers to a stool and so forth.
"Viśikhāni" means broken; alternatively, there is the reading "vaśikāni," in which case it means empty.
"Household people" refers to those established in domestic life.

By the expression "like a deceased person," he prohibits friends from performing acts such as lying down [in mourning] out of malice or for the sake of inauspiciousness—acts that non-friends might perform toward a deceased person—just as such acts are performed for one who has died. Thus, he forbids treating them like a *preta*.
The light is fire; if it goes out while there is fuel and no wind, then there is misfortune for the vessels—such as bowls, pots, and so forth. (32–39)
Now, in order to clarify the *riṣṭa* (fatal signs) described in the twelfth chapter—which is difficult to comprehend—the author says "by twelve," etc., for the sake of a summary.

By stating that it is "resorted to by another synonym" (*paryāyāntaram āśritam*), he indicates that it is proclaimed under a different name so that the meaning may be understood; for when there is doubt or false cognition regarding a previously mentioned term due to its having multiple meanings and so forth, the meaning becomes clear through its expression by another word.
"Of those who are oppressed" means of those who have risen up;
"of those wishing to depart" means of those preparing to go abroad.

By the phrase "a desirable dwelling" (*kāntaṃ vāsaḥ*), he shows that for all living beings, in all conditions, the body is indeed desirable. Furthermore, although this "desirable dwelling"—which takes the form of the body or life—is being abandoned by its own karma through sheer force, it is here designated independently, either by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) or due to the elision of the word [denoting agency], as in the expressions "those wishing to abandon" (*jihāsatām*) or "those wishing to endure" (*titikṣatām*). The *tantra* is the body; its *yantra* (mechanism) consists of the veins, ligaments, and so forth, and thus it is called the *tantryantra*.
"Darkness is the end" means that the darkness consisting of death [destroys] "forms here," such as the affliction of the vital breaths;
"it becomes barren" means it becomes one that takes to wrong paths.
"Evils" refers to diseases produced by sin and unrighteous actions; "and shadows go toward deformity" is the ellipsis, meaning that each shadow individually undergoes deformation.
"Smoke arises on the head" refers to the context at hand: in the absence of the emission of vapor, a thick smoke-like substance forms upon the head.

And regarding "the one called Dāruṇa" and "Cūrṇaka"— the latter being the Cūrṇaka described in the passage beginning with "whose [complexion] resembles powdered cow dung"— the phrase "of that same kind in other locations" means that in other parts of the body, the *snehas* and so forth exist in their opposite state, as indicated by the plural number.
They come into being— that is, they arise and are established—
as various natures, meaning that they possess mutually contradictory intrinsic natures.
The application of specific treatments is the application of therapeutics (*cikitsāpravṛtti*);
"accidental" (*autpātika*) means occurring spontaneously. Its qualification is "ominous" (*ariṣṭa*); thus, the result is that "the accidental [sign] indicates a fatal sign (*riṣṭa*).
He now explains how a known fatal sign (*riṣṭa*) remains unmanifest: "For death," and so forth;
it should be construed as "harmful to the patient," and the connection is "it would cause suffering for another."

62–64: "Alas! If death is to occur for the afflicted person, it is not stated; [one might ask] why then should health, which is also possible, not be stated? To this he says: "From signs," and so forth.
Those which announce death are called "death-indicating"; those contrary to them indicate health.
"Having come" (*āgantv iti*) refers to things occurring at a later time;

"by portentous phenomena" (*autpātikair bhāvair iti*) means by phenomena that have arisen unexpectedly for the purpose of indicating auspiciousness. Generally, that which arises unexpectedly as an indicator of the auspicious or inauspicious is called "portentous" (*autpātika*).
The construction [of the verse] is that health should be declared as something adventitious (*āgantuka*), ending with the phrase "characterized by the attainment of wealth."
With the words "the characteristic of a pure abode," "one's own conduct," and so forth, he speaks;
by the term "amuṇḍa," one who has shaved his head except for the top-knot is intended.
"Equal to the afflicted in birth and so forth" means equal in birth, dress, and conduct to the one who is ill.
"In [times] free from planetary seizures" (*agraheṣu*) means at times not presided over by cruel planets situated in inauspicious positions.

"In non-cruel constellations, those that are not fierce, and the fixed ones" (*dhruveṣu*): "cruel" (*dāruṇa*) refers to those that are sharp (*tīkṣṇa*). As Varāhamihira said: "Mūla, Śiva, Śakra, and Bhujagādhipa are sharp" (*Bṛhat-saṃhitā*, A. 18); here, Śiva is Ārdrā, Śakra is Jyeṣṭhā, and Bhujagādhipa is Āśleṣā.
And there are fierce [nakṣatras] mentioned by Varāhamihira, as follows: "The fierce ones are Pūrva-bharaṇī and Pitrya" (Bṛhat-saṃhitā, Adhyāya 98).
In that context, by the word *pūrva* [is meant] Pūrvaphālgunī, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and Pūrvabhādrapadā; and *Pitrya* is Maghā.
Excluding the constellations such as Dāruṇa mentioned by Varāha, messengers arriving under other constellations are auspicious.
The term "empty" (riktā) is a qualification for the fourth day and so forth; it refers to the fourth, ninth, and fourteenth lunar days.
Likewise, by the qualification "empty" (*riktā*), which indicates the fruitlessness of the fourth and subsequent lunar days, their unsuitability for undertaking ritual actions is taught.
That which possesses auspicious, portentous, or accidental characteristics is called "one with auspicious-portentous-characteristics" (*śastautpātikalakṣaṇa*).
With the words "curd, unbroken rice," and so forth, Suradhvaja (the Indra-banner) describes auspicious sights on roads and other places.

Regarding the phrase "maidens, boys, and *vardhamāna*s": maidens and boys who have been placed upon a scale-pan are the "increasing ones" (*vardhamānānām*); the compound is like that of "Puruṣottama. Others, however, say that *vardhamāna*s are shallow bowls; these should be understood as being adorned with ointments and the like.
"One animal" means an excellent animal; the connection is "of a full cart by men";
and the construction is "of a mare and of a woman with her calf."
The *jīvañjīvaka* bird, well-known by its own name, and the *cātaka* bird, which speaks pleasantly. 71–79.
When there is application (*yojanā*), there is accomplishment; "accomplishment through application" (*yojanāsiddhi*) is the emergence from confinement, the crossing over of narrow straits.
And "the crushing of enemies"— this is to be understood as the end [of the section on dreams] (verses 80–86).
The conjunction of the quality of *sattva* with its characteristics is "conjunction with the characteristics of *sattva*."
"And not despondency" means not disparaging oneself;
this concludes the summary of the first chapter, beginning with the words "It has been said."

The signs of death and recovery for messengers and others have been stated here separately. The sign of death based on logic (*yukti*) is clearly as stated in the passage beginning with: “The physician who prepares medicine for a patient [and finds it ineffective]...”.
The sign of death based on success (*siddhi*) is as stated in the passage beginning with: “That which was understood... and so forth.
The characteristics of health, based on reasoning and based on attainment, are as stated in the text: "The non-attainment of the desired, and [the attainment] with ease" (89).

With the words "iti" and so forth, he concludes by demonstrating that the collection of objects of knowledge taught in the *Indriyasthāna* must necessarily be understood due to their great fruitfulness.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Cow-Dung Powder," in the Indriyasthāna of the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka Saṃhitā composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Section on Therapeutics] [Therapeutics Section, Chapter 1 (67 of 120)] [Chapter 1, Part 1]

Since medical treatment that brings about virtue, wealth, and fame must be performed for one whose longevity has been determined by the absence of the characteristics mentioned in the previous section, the section describing medical treatment is stated immediately thereafter.
Although the means of rejuvenation (*rasāyana*) and aphrodisiacs (*vājīkaraṇa*) are also forms of medical treatment, the author will explain this later;
however, even there, because rejuvenation and aphrodisiacs yield great results, they are mentioned at the beginning, prior to the treatment of fever and other diseases.

Furthermore, among those two [branches], Rasāyana alone is described first because it yields great results by being the cause of longevity lasting thousands of years and other benefits; even within that, the chapter on Abhayāmalakīya is mentioned at the outset as it sets forth the essential aphorisms for the Cikitsāsthāna (the Section on Therapeutics).

Therein, at the beginning, he states the synonyms of "medicine" (*bheṣaja*), which is the subject matter of this section, for the sake of conventional usage, starting with the words "Cikitsitam," etc.
And thus, at the outset, he provides an enumeration of synonyms for the primary subject matter, such as the statement of synonyms for "cause" (*hetu*) and so forth in the *Nidāna* [chapter].

This enumeration of synonyms applies primarily to the four-legged medicine (*catuṣpāda-bheṣaja*), as it has been said: "Physicians declare that medicine consists of four legs and sixteen parts" (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 10).

However, because they constitute limbs of such medicine, the status of being "medicine" should be understood as applied to medicines consisting of stationary and mobile substances through internal conventional usage.
The term *prāyaścitta* is a designation for medicine; for, like a *prāyaścitta*, medicine removes the disease caused by unrighteous action (*adharma*).
He explains the twofold nature [of *ūrja*] with the words "of one who is healthy" (*svasthasya*), etc.
"Something" (*kiñcit*) means not everything.

Because it removes natural diseases such as old age for a person conventionally designated as "healthy," and because it removes unwholesome bodily states—such as lack of exhilaration, excessive expenditure, depletion, and non-increase of semen—it bestows a wholesome state; thus, it is "nutritive" (*ūrjakara*) for one who is healthy.

By the qualification "the remover of disease for the afflicted," although the state of being a specific type of afflicted person— namely one afflicted by fever and so forth— is already understood from the expression "remover of disease" itself, the fact that he uses the word "of the afflicted" (ārta-sya) shows that this excludes the non-distressing pain caused by natural aging and the like, and instead indicates one who is tormented by unnatural diseases such as fever.
In connection with the discussion of medicine (*bheṣaja*), he states the two types of non-medicine (*abheṣaja*)—beginning with the words "non-medicine" and so forth.
Here, "affliction" (*bādhana*) refers to that which causes affliction only in the immediate moment, such as a small amount of unwholesome food;
whereas "affliction with consequences" (*sānubādhana*) refers to that which produces chronic disorders such as leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) and the like.
The two types of medicine mentioned are now classified: "of one who is healthy," and so forth;
the division is as follows: "that [medicine] is aphrodisiac (*vṛṣya*) and that is generally an elixir (*rasāyana*)."

That which is generally aphrodisiac (*vṛṣya*), as well as that which is generally a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*), and that which for the most part removes disease in the afflicted (*ārta*), is called a strengthener for the healthy (*svasthorjaskara*). As for the second type, which removes disease in the afflicted, it generally consists of fever-alleviating remedies, rejuvenatives, and aphrodisiacs. For example, the ghee, jaggery preparations, and so forth mentioned under the treatment of chest-wounds and emaciation (*kṣatakṣīṇa*) are both rejuvenatives and aphrodisiacs; likewise, the "King of Formulas" (*yogarāja*) mentioned under the treatment of anemia (*pāṇḍuroga*) is stated to be a rejuvenative; similarly, the *Agastyaharītakī* mentioned in the section on cough (*kāsa*) is stated to be a rejuvenative—such instances should be followed accordingly.
Furthermore, the capacity of those substances described as *rasāyana* to alleviate fever and other diseases is quite evident here;

however, in the *rasāyana* treatises, others maintain that what merely cures a specific disease is not *rasāyana*, but rather, because it possesses the common characteristic of producing longevity through the strengthening of the body's integration, it is designated as *rasāyana* by way of metaphorical usage when it cures diseases.

Now, if that which promotes vigor for the healthy also removes disease, and that which removes disease also promotes vigor for the healthy, then what is the purpose of the term "kiñcit" (something/specific) used to indicate the classification of medicinal actions? We reply: it is established that [a substance] generally promotes vigor for the healthy and removes disease; however, it is not here asserted that everything which removes disease for the afflicted promotes vigor for the healthy. Thus, even in the case of *pāṭhā*, *saptaparṇa*, and others, although they are said to remove disease for the afflicted due to their capacity to be proven as effective, the fact that they are also *rasāyana* and *vājīkaraṇa* is merely indicated as a small portion [of their function]; this constitutes their performing the purpose of both the healthy and the afflicted.
He explains the intended meaning of the word "mostly" (*prāyas*):
"mostly," etc., means for the sake of a specific purpose; that is to say, for the sake of abundance.
He describes the action of the elixir (rasāyana) with the words beginning "dīrgham" and so forth;
the magnificence of the three qualities, beginning with splendor (prabhā), is to be applied here.
"Perfection of speech" (vāksiddhi) means that whatever is spoken necessarily comes to pass.
He explains how prostration and being honored by the world are brought about by this elixir: "By the acquisition [of wealth]," and so forth;
by the mention of "taste" and the rest, mindfulness and other qualities are also included.
7–8 He describes the purpose of aphrodisiac therapy (*vājīkaraṇa*): "offspring" (*apatya*) and so forth.

"Offspring lineage" (*apatyasantāna*) means the succession of progeny; thus, it means "that which produces sons and grandsons. The meaning is that a son born from semen produced by aphrodisiac therapy becomes capable of fathering sons himself.

And "extreme dearness" here arises from being one who practices sexual intercourse continuously due to having accumulated *śukra* (semen); as it has been said: "Kings desire even a deformed warrior as a servant, just as women desire a husband who is devoted to sexual intercourse, though he be foolish and impudent.
"Is accumulated" (*upacīyate*) means that it attains nourishment (*puṣṭi*).
A shrine (*caitya*) or a temple of a deity is that which produces offspring, being fruitful and as if inexhaustible.
He is worthy of worship (*arcya*), meaning he is to be adored (*arcanīya*);
"infinitude" (*ānantya*) refers, as it were, to infinitude—that is, the state of having a long continuity.

Regarding the term "cikitsita" (therapeutics): surely, *rasāyana* and *vājīkaraṇa* are also included within the therapeutics for fever and other diseases; why then is it stated specifically that "it will be explained in the section on therapeutics"? He replies with the words "for the purpose of therapeutics," and so forth.
This is true; the meaning is that *rasāyana* and *vājīkaraṇa* are also denoted by the word "therapeutics" because they remove diseases such as fever.

Now, since they remove disease and because they are to be discussed in the context of therapeutics, [the author] asks where the Rasāyana and Vājīkaraṇa [sections] should be stated; he says: "Rasāyana," etc.
"Vidhi" means the method or the prescription known as Rasāyana;
"agre" means immediately following.
The phrase "vājīkaraṇaṃ ca agre abhidhāsyate" (and aphrodisiacs will be explained first) is the remainder [of the sentence].
He now explains that which was previously mentioned as "non-medicine" (abheṣaja), beginning with the words "abheṣajam" and so forth.

That which is contrary [to the natural state], producing disease and failing to fulfill its purpose, is called *kuṭīprāveśika* (the "entering-the-hut" [type of practice]) because it is performed by entering a hut.
That which is constructed even by exposure to wind and sun is called *vātātapika*;

it has three inner chambers (*trigarbhā*), meaning that within the first house there is a second, and so on, such that it has three inner spaces (*garbha*) or recesses. Thus, "three-chambered" (*trigarbhām*) means having three internal courtyards;
"with small windows" (*sūkṣmalocanām*) means having few lattice-windows.
"In the bright fortnight" means that in which physicians and others are prepared;
"honored by lunar day and asterism" means honored through the conjunction with an auspicious lunar day and asterism.
"Having performed the shaving" means having had one's hair cut;
"mental defects" refers to desire, anger, and so forth;
"by means of purifications" refers to emetics, purgatives, non-unctuous enemas, and head-purgatives.
"Happy" means free from disease.

"Having regained strength" means having had the impurities removed by purification (*saṃśodhana*) and having regained strength again through the sequence of dietary rehabilitation (*saṃsarjana*) and so forth.

Although all forms of purification are intended here because of the use of the plural *saṃśodhanaiḥ*, nevertheless, because they are particularly suitable for this *rasāyana*, only the administration of *harītakī* and other such drugs is mentioned. Others, however, say that the supreme purification should be performed by the administration of *harītakī* and others alone; the plural *saṃśodhanaiḥ* further indicates that one should employ the administration of *harītakī* and others until purification is achieved.
"Barley-food" (yāvaka) refers to food made of barley;
the three alternatives beginning with "three nights" pertain respectively to inferior, middling, and superior purification.

Although there are other substances prescribed for rejuvenation (*rasāyana*) that grant a lifespan of a thousand years, nevertheless, only *harītakī* and *āmalaka* are mentioned at the beginning of this chapter by virtue of their qualities and actions, because they alone possess both characteristics: the removal of disease and the promotion of longevity. Furthermore, although it was stated [in Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 25] that "the *āmalaka* is the foremost among those that maintain youth," nevertheless, *harītakī* is mentioned first because it excels in the removal of disease.

The production of the five tastes and so forth in the *harītakī* group [of drugs] is caused by the power of a specific arrangement of the elements (*bhūta-sanniveśa-viśeṣa*) through the force of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*). Therefore, logical arguments do not apply here to the *śivā*, which brings about auspiciousness because it is endowed with praiseworthy qualities and pacifies all diseases through its combinations, processing, and so forth.

Although it has already been stated that [this medicine] removes all diseases, the specific mention of its power to destroy skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*) and so forth is intended to demonstrate its particular efficacy against those conditions. Furthermore, even though it acts as a purgative, its ability to cure diarrhea and *grahaṇī* should be understood as resulting from its capacity to eliminate obstructed morbid humors (*vibaddhadoṣa*). As it has been said: "One who suffers from diarrhea—whether in small quantities or with obstruction and colic—should be purged with lukewarm pastes of *abhayā* and *pippalī*."

Although its quality of bestowing memory (*smṛti*) has already been stated, the subsequent mention of its removal of confusion of memory and intellect (*smṛtibuddhipramoha*) is for the purpose of demonstrating a specific power in that regard.
By the phrase "the opposite of vigor" (*vīryasya tu viparyaya*), the cold potency (*śītavīryatva*) of the *āmalaka* is expressed.
The term "crops" (*śasyāni*) refers to fruits that are devoid of seeds.

Although it has been stated that "the Himavat is the ground of medicinal herbs" (Sūtra-sthāna, chapter 25), nevertheless, in order to demonstrate that for the purpose of *rasāyana* only those medicines originating from the Himavat should be taken, the phrase beginning with "of medicinal herbs" (*auṣadhīnām*) and so forth is mentioned.
"From time to time" (*kāle kāle*) means at the time of the ripening of the fruit.

"According to the prescribed method" means that just as the administration of medicine must be preceded by auspicious rites and the worship of deities, so too must it necessarily be performed in the case of *rasāyana*.
By the term "remedies" (*agadāni*), he demonstrates that the fruit [of this practice] is free from defects such as those caused by wind or fire.

In the passage beginning with "of the five," ten *pala* portions are to be taken of each individual substance; for it is stated in the *Jatūkarṇa*: "Thus there are five groups of the five roots (*pañcamūla*); of these, ten *pala* are taken from each substance.
"A thousand *harītakī*s" means a thousand *harītakī* fruits. "The two *śūrpaparṇī*s" refers to *mudgaparṇī* and *māṣaparṇī*.
The heroes, having prepared the Jālandhara herb and the Kūrcana plant— which is the means for causing emaciation— by means of a grindstone, a son-of-stone pestle, and so forth, [they] cast them in.
Plava, kaivartamustaka, kanaka, nāgakeśara, tvak, and guḍatvak.
"Audumbara" means made of copper;
"sneha-ardha" means half [the amount] of ghee and oil; this is one meal, not to be taken in the afternoon.

"By the method of steaming flour" (piṣṭasvedanavidhinā) means that just as flour is steamed when placed upon grass or similar materials set over a vessel filled with water, so too should that [substance] be steamed;
"soaked in its own juice" (svarasaparipīta) means impregnated with its own juice.
Medicinal herbs such as *brahmasuvarcalā* and others will be described in the section on the origin of Āyurveda;
*yuvati* is *navamālikā*, and "eighth part" (*aṣṭamo bhāgaḥ*) means one-eighth.
"Having the form of small jaggery" means having the form of molasses (*phāṇita*);
"increasing by half a *karṣa*" means one should increase it starting from half a *karṣa*;
"by the prescribed method" refers to the method of entering the small hut (*kuṭīprāveśika*).
"Those qualities as described" refers to those recited in the scriptural accounts of the fruits of prior practice.

"Possessing the essence of the earth-supporters" (dharaṇīdharasāra) is like the compound *uṣṭramukha* ("camel-faced"); by that, "earth-supporters" means mountains, and their "essence" is iron—thus, the meaning is "having an essence like that.
"Non-poisonous" (*aviṣam*) means not subject to transformation by poison.
The four *parṇīs* are *śālaparṇī*, *pṛśniparṇī*, *mudgaparṇī*, and *māṣaparṇī*;
*tāmalakī* is the wild *āmalakī*.
*Kākanāsā* is *nāsāphala*; others call it *kākatuṇḍaka*.
Here, the loss of flavor in substances occurs when they have been kept in water for one-fourth their weight;
"seedless" means stripped of its stones.

Because of the compound designation "of oil and ghee" (*tailasarpiṣoḥ*), twelve *palas* are for both together, not separately; as for *matsyaṇḍikā*, which is a mass of sugar-candy, it is not contradictory that even though honey and ghee are equal [in quantity], they are combined with other substances here in the measure of six *palas* each.
Kukūlaka is a fire of dried cow dung;
"of the akulakas" means those without bones.

The specific measure for the substances and so forth has not been stated here; therefore, the primary substance, the powder (cūrṇa), should be equal in measure to the curd and other ingredients combined, or else each ingredient, such as the curd and others, should be equal in measure to the powder.

The statement that one "should eat" (bhakṣayet) sesame paste (palala)—which is sesame powder—is appropriate even in the case of a linctus (lehya), because it merely signifies a small amount of consumption.

"Not eating food" means not consuming any other kind of food whatsoever; "at its end" refers to the time of relinquishing that practice, which is a qualification of the specific sequence beginning with gruel (*yavāgū*). Thus, the meaning is that when the reintroduction of solid food (*anna-saṃsarjana*) must be performed at the conclusion of the practice, the establishment of the previously stated rule—that it be done according to the sequence of gruel and so forth—is reiterated here.
The option "with broth or with milk" is based on consideration of the strength of the digestive fire (agni-bala).
Here, in the case of the *harītakī* group and so forth, *kṣīraśuklā* refers to *kṣīravidārī*.
In this case, there is one part of the decoction of harītakī and so forth, eight parts of milk, and one part of ghee;
[the total measure is] a *kumbha*, which is two *droṇas*.
For it is said: "A *sūrpa* should be known as double a *droṇa*, and likewise a *kumbha*."
Amṛtavallī, guḍūcī, somavalka, and viṭkhadira.

Milk-ghee is ghee produced from milk; there is a fourth part of iron powder, because this iron powder constitutes a fourth part, for this very reason Jatūkarṇa has stated in this formulation that it is "combined with a quarter-part of iron powder.

It is the nectar of the immortals (*amarāṇām amṛtam*), removing old age and other ailments, and the ambrosia of the serpents (*nāgānām sudhā*), which removes old age and death; thus both are mentioned as an illustration.
Brahman is liberation;
and here, the fact that the elixir (*rasāyana*) is a means to liberation is stated by virtue of its making the practitioner one whose mental essence (*sattva*) is purified.
By the words beginning with "abhaya," he shows the number of previously mentioned applications for the purpose of dispelling doubt;
in this way, the formulation of numbers elsewhere should also be understood at the end.

Thus ends the first quarter on Rasāyana, titled "The Chapter on Abhayā and Āmalakī," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka-saṃhitā, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Adhyāya 1, Pāda 2]

In the previous chapter, the *āmalaka* rejuvenation therapies (*rasāyana*) were described; since there are also *āmalaka* rejuvenation therapies here, the following is called the "Prāṇakāmīya" (Chapter on those Desiring Vitality), as it was composed with reference to the term "one desiring vitality" (*prāṇakāma*).
The quality of removing sleep belongs to the *rasāyana* by way of removing abnormal sleep; alternatively, one becomes perpetually awake and free from sleep like a deity.

The definition of *tandrā* (drowsiness) in another treatise is as follows: "One should diagnose *tandrā* in that person for whom these symptoms—non-perception of sensory objects, heaviness, yawning, and exhaustion—occur as if they were afflicted by sleep" (Suśruta Saṃhitā, Śārīrasthāna 4).
"Abaddhamāṃsa" (unbound flesh) means not dense flesh; it produces excellence such as radiance (*prabhā*) and so forth, thus [the compound] is "prabhā-varṇa-svara-uttama-kara.
This kind of lack of fixed word order (*pūrvanipātāniyama*) exists in the *Caraka* without restriction; it should be understood as falling under the list beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka*.
With the words beginning "anena hi" (for by this), he praises the elixirs (*rasāyana*) that are about to be described, in order to encourage their application.
Indicating those things to be avoided during the practice of elixirs—such as the food of the village—as defects, he says: "all," etc.
Here, *tila* refers to the sesame seed in its whole form, while *palala* refers to sesame paste (sesame flour).
"For this reason" means that because of causes such as coarse food and so forth, semen does not flow; the meaning is that semen is not produced.

The meaning of "cooked a hundred times each" (*ekaikaśaḥ śatapākam*) is that the preparation for each individual cooking must be performed separately; by this method, there comes to be three hundred cookings.
Furthermore, in this case, whatever remains after being consumed by the paste, the ointment, and so forth, that alone is to be taken, on the strength of the scriptural injunction.

In vessels made of gold and other materials, there is a gradation of excellence as previously described; otherwise, if they were equal in quality, then since clay vessels are easily obtained, the gold vessel—which is far more difficult to obtain—would not deserve to be taught according to the aforementioned rule.
Thus, by the rule for entering the hut (*kuṭī-prāveśika*), "the essence of the mountain" refers to iron.
"Four to six young *palāśa* trees" means a young *palāśa*; by this, the avoidance of saplings and old trees is indicated.
"Abounding in alkaline water" shows that it should be performed in such a way that the alkaline water remains on the surface of the ground.
The meaning is that this [attainment] is also logical, because of the scriptural statement regarding the fruit of the previous yoga: "A fourth part, a quarter, is equal to the former.
"At the end of the rains" means at the conclusion of the rainy season.

"As far as the blessing" (*āśīḥ*) refers to the declaration of the fruit [of the rite]; by this, he demonstrates the performance of the ritual procedure described in the passage beginning with "at the end of that year."
"By the preceding" means that it is the same as the preceding yoga up to the point of hearing the fruit of the preceding yoga; this is the meaning.
"In a desert" means in a wilderness region; "plowing with a plowshare and so forth" refers to cultivation;
"not overgrown" means not covered by a large tree standing nearby.
In the month of Māgha it is Tapasī; in Phālguna it is Tapasyā; in Caitra it is Calā; and in Vaiśākha it is Sumuhūrta. In the month of Indra (Jyeṣṭha) it is Muhūrta.
"Only sour" refers to a quantity of one *pala*.

Furthermore, the ten [herbs] ending with *punarnavā*— namely, "Amṛtā, Abhayā, Dhātrī, Śreyasī, Śvetā, Atirasā, Maṇḍūkaparṇī, Sthirā, and Punarnavā" (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 4)— are all mentioned as being for the maintenance of youth (*vayaḥsthāpana*) in the chapter on the six hundred purgatives (*ṣaḍvirecanaśatāśritīya*).
It is explained that they are like *nāgabalā*; thus, their application is also like that of *nāgabalā*.
The preparation of *bala* and the others should be done using their fresh juices (*svarasa*) alone, and their use for meals and so forth should be understood to be like that of *nāgabalā*.
Regarding the alternative method when fresh juices (svarasa) are unavailable, he says "of the juices," etc.
Jyeṣṭha is Śuci; Śukra is Āṣāḍha; Saha is Āgrahāyaṇa; and Sahasya is Pauṣa.

Furthermore, this *bhallātaka* should not be used immediately upon being extracted from the sprouts of barley and so forth after having been kept for four months; rather, it should be used only at the prescribed time when endowed with cooling qualities (*śītaguṇa*),
by internally anointing the mouth with clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) to avoid burning of the mouth,
and not beyond this— meaning there is no application of *bhallātaka* after the thirtieth day.

Regarding the statement "the application of *bhallātaka* culminates at one thousand": by means of the cumulative total of the *bhallātaka* fruits consumed, one must cease the practice precisely when the number reaches one thousand. Furthermore, the abandonment of the practice may indeed occur even before reaching one thousand, depending on factors such as one's physical constitution (*prakṛti*). Moreover, the completion of the count of one thousand here does not occur through a sequence of increasing or decreasing by one; rather, the application should be performed up to thirty times by repeating the cycle. Having acted in such a way that the completion of the count of one thousand occurs through the practice of the *bhallātaka* regimen, one should then discontinue it.

Others, however, seeing a contradiction between this [text] and the *Bhallātaka-prayoga* ending at one hundred mentioned in the *Arśaścikitsita* of Suśruta, propose that the Suśruta application should also be interpreted differently so as to consist of only thirty measures. That interpretation is not very consistent;

furthermore, while two thousand uses are prescribed there, here the application extends up to one thousand. Therefore, that application concerns a different type of disease, whereas this one concerns *rasāyana*.

That is *piṣṭasvedana* (steaming of flour), wherein the flour is steamed while remaining in its place; the vessel used as a cover over it should be understood here as having perforations, otherwise the oil dripping from the heat of the *bhallātaka* fruits situated above would not reach below.
"Bhallātaka oil" refers to the oil of *bhallātaka* obtained by the method described immediately preceding.

The ten formulations beginning with *bhallātaka-sarpi* (ghee processed with *bhallātaka*) should be understood here as involving both the processing (*saṃskāra*) and the combination (*saṃyoga*) of ghee and other substances with *bhallātaka*, according to their respective suitability.

As stated in the *Jatūkarṇa*: “Clarified butter, milk, honey, jaggery, broth, oil, *palala* (sesame paste), roasted barley flour (*saktu*), salt, and *tarpaṇa* (refreshing drinks), prepared in combination with *bhallātaka*.

Thus, clarified butter, milk, broth, and oil are processed with *bhallātaka* according to the proper method; honey, *palala*, roasted barley flour, and *tarpaṇa* are combined with *bhallātaka*; as for jaggery and salt, there is either processing or combination—with the option of processing, one should take an amount of *bhallātaka* equal to the salt, burnt by internal smoke (*antardhūma*).
Others, however, explain that all substances such as ghee and the rest are to be processed with *bhallātaka*;
in this context, the application of roasted grain flour (*saktu*) is distinguished by its specific action, such as its dryness and its tendency to increase *ūrdhva-gati* (upward movement).
"Equal to fire" means by virtue of causing burning and eruptions;
"having gathered" means having produced [them].

In the section on the maintenance of life (*pādānusaṅgraha*), thirty-seven applications have been described; among these, eighteen applications consist of the eight beginning with *bala* and the ten ending with *navā*, while the others are explicitly stated and clear. Thus ends the second quarter of the Rasāyana chapter in the Cikitsāsthāna, titled "The Desire for Vitality" (*prāṇakāmīya*), within the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā*, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
2 [Adhyāya 1,

Pāda 3] Following the section on *āmalaka* as a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*), the section concerning what is gathered by hand (*karapracitīya*) is now stated, due to the similarity in their nature as rejuvenatives.
The phrase "gathered by hand" (karapracitānām) precludes the taking of what has fallen of its own accord;
this is inferred from the scriptural tradition that one has the authority to take only those fruits gathered in the manner prescribed by the statement "in the month of Māgha or Phālguna."
In this context, "its own juice" refers specifically to that of the *āmalaka* fruit due to the governing topic;
"vegetable" refers to a tree with large leaves;
and "of those cut" means of those that have been severed.

In this context, it is inferred from the words of the sages that the excellence of power (*śakti*) arises precisely through the restriction of implements such as cow-dung fire and so forth, as it has been said:
"The sages alone know the fruit born of the application of yoga.
In the same way, the restriction of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is to be explained elsewhere as well.
Regarding the phrase "of the black antelope skin" (kṛṣṇājina), it refers to the skin of the black antelope (kṛṣṇasāra).

Now, demonstrating that an elixir (rasāyana) yields great fruit only when it is conjoined with austerity (tapas), celibacy (brahmacarya), meditation (dhyāna), and so forth, he says: "By austerity," and so on.
"By life joined with time" means by life joined with indefinite time; however, it has already been stated that for one whose lifespan is fixed in time, elixir (*rasāyana*) is not fruitful.
Thus, [the text] says "they remain," meaning those who live for a long time.
By contrast, he states the fruitlessness of elixir in the absence of austerity (*tapas*) and so forth, beginning with "for not... and so on.

Even though the restraint of the senses has already been obtained through the state of being a *brahmacārin*, the connection with the term "one who restrains the senses" (*yatendriya*) is for the purpose of demonstrating an excellence in that restraint.
The fact that the months beginning with Pauṣa constitute the end of the year should be understood as the completion of the year starting from the day of the vow.
At the end of the word "phālgunīm," the word "having reached" (*prāpya*) is to be supplied as a supplement.
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule "he shall not climb a tree" (Sūtra 8), by means of the statement here, "having climbed a tree.
"Reciting the Brahman" means reciting the syllable *oṃ*.
"Until the arrival of nectar" means up to the point when nectar arrives;
"sauhityam eṣām" (their satisfaction) uses the genitive case in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*);
"vāgrūpiṇī" refers to the deity who presides over that [speech].
Regarding "alkali" (*kṣāra*), it refers to alkaline water that has been strained;
regarding "salt" (*lāvaṇa*), it refers to the alkali of *jyotiṣmatī*.
"One should accomplish" means one should quench [the metal].

Since the inclusion of gold and silver within the category of "metals" (*lauha*) is already established by the word "of metals," their separate mention again is for the purpose of showing special regard for them;
it should be understood that their status as great wealth arises precisely from the power of the *rasāyana*.
*Matsyākhyaka* is known in the world as *mācchu*; others, however, say that *matsyākhyaka* is a variety of *aindrī*.
*Triyavakān* means having the measure of three *yavas*.
"Abounding in ghee" is an adjective qualifying the food;
"kṛtyā" means malevolent sorcery.
The four formulations beginning with *maṇḍūkaparṇī* (30–31),
as well as the one beginning with "five" (pañca) and so forth, indicate by the deviation from the stated number that *pippalī* may also be employed even when its specific quantity is not mentioned.

Although it has been stated that "one should not excessively consume these three substances: long pepper (pippalī), alkali (kṣāra), and salt" (Vi. A. 1), nevertheless, the habitual use of long peppers combined with other substances here is not contradictory. Alternatively, according to the principle of general rule and exception (utsargāpavāda), that prohibition should be understood as applying to long pepper except in the context of the aforementioned Rasāyana therapy. Kiṃśuka is Palāśa. (32–35)
Regarding the *pippalīvardhamāna* (the increasing dose of long pepper), he says "by gradual increase," and so forth.

The day on which ten long peppers (*pippalī*) are increased is called a "ten-long-pepper day" (*daśapaippalika*); the meaning is that ten long peppers should be increased every day. Consequently, through the sequence of increase and decrease over nineteen days, the total of one thousand is completed in just one [cycle].
Regarding the reading "cūrṇīkṛtā" (ground), there is also the variant reading "śītīkṛtā" (cooled).

Demonstrating that the regimen of increasing by one *pippalī* per day (*pippalī-vardhamāna-krama*) is superior, he describes two other methods of increase—namely, the middling and the inferior—beginning with the words "ten," etc., up to "six are proclaimed. This [middling method] was taught by the former masters as an increase of six [per day].

Because there is a pause at three *pippalīs* at the end of this sequence, the increase occurs only by means of groups of three *pippalīs*; thus, when one has reached ten *pippalīs*, there are exactly ten at the conclusion.

In the passage beginning with "ending with digestion" (jaraṇānta), the phrase "with honey and ghee" (madhusarpirbhyām) is joined with "abhayā, bibhītaka, and āmalaka," while "with madhuka" (madhukena) and so forth constitute one distinct formulation.

"By all metals," and so forth, is another [reading]. When "by metals" is stated, gold might be understood; therefore, the word "by gold" is used to exclude the possibility that what is commonly known as a metal would not be included.

To demonstrate the elixir (rasāyana) of *śilājatu*, he first describes the qualities of this highly esteemed substance, beginning with "not sour" (*anamlam*) and so forth. Regarding the word "excellent" (*varāt*), although in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā* six types of *śilājatu* are mentioned in general— adding those derived from tin and lead— in this section on elixirs, only the four types specifically authorized here are discussed.
He describes the method for the saturation (*bhāvanā*) of *śilājatu*: "inserted" (*prakṣipta*), etc.
"Inserted and then extracted" (*prakṣiptoddhṛta*) means that which has been removed immediately after being inserted.
Regarding the phrase "along with metals," this refers to the application of *śilājatu* in equal proportions to the metals when no specific rule for the parts is given.

The expression "seven times seven days" means a regimen that extends over seven periods of seven days each; this same principle should be understood to apply to the phrase "three, one, and seven" as well. (51–54)

"Along with the procedure" means that the procedure for *śilājatu* (bitumen), together with its ritual application, is to be explained in due order by the passage beginning with "In cases of *vāta* and *pitta*," and so forth.

By the word "hemādi" (gold and so forth), the rock that serves as the source of gold and other minerals is intended here; for bitumen does not flow directly from gold and such substances themselves, but rather as something soft, smooth, clear, and transparent.
