As for the statement that in the case of silver-derived [bitumen] there is a pungent taste but a sweet post-digestive effect—which appears contradictory—it is to be understood according to the maxim of the general rule and its exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*).

However, there is no room for the potency (*vīrya*) of copper-derived [bitumen] to be hot, nor for that of the three cold substances to possess excessive heat or cold potency. Therefore, by the phrase "neither excessively hot nor cold" used in the description of its general qualities, the intensity of both hot and cold potencies is negated; by this, its state of being neither hot nor cold (*anuṣṇāśītatva*) is established. Consequently, it is understood that although the potency of bitumen (*śilājatu*) is described as either cold or hot, it does not become powerful.

(55–61) Regarding the plural number in the expression "in the applications of bitumen," it should be understood as having in mind the various methods of application, such as mixing (*āloḍana*) and so forth.

Regarding the administration of *śilājatu*, although heavy foods (*guru*) are generally prohibited, milk and other such substances may be used at all times due to specific injunctions, as long as the beneficial qualities of the *rasāyana* persist;

however, some authorities state that one must avoid *kulattha* beans for as long as one lives, as it is stated in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā*: "One who has been treated with this [śilājatu] should avoid pigeons and *kulattha* beans" (*Su.Ci.A.* 13).
He praises the application of *śilājatu* with the verse beginning "There is no... (62–66).

Thus ends the third quarter on Rasāyana, titled "The Hand-Gathered," in the chapter on Rasāyana within the Cikitsāsthāna of the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā*, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta.
3 [Adhyāya 1, Pāda 4]:
The section on elixirs (rasāyana) called "The Origin of Āyurveda" is now stated by way of remainder.
Because the "origin of Āyurveda" exists in this [treatise], it is called *Āyurvedasamutthānīya* by means of the possessive suffix *cha*.
The sages’ state of being *śālīna* (restrained) and *yāyāvara* (wandering) results from their adoption of specific modes of action.
Those who are employed because they possess excellence are called *sāmpannikas*;
"not too feeble" means not excessively diseased;
"activity" refers to the performance of duties (*itikartavyatā*).
The account of the cycle of Indra is for the purpose of praise; and this praise is because it reveals the longevity of Indra.
"Asukhānubandham" means that which binds (anubadhnāti) unhappiness (asukham) in the form of disease; thus, it is "asukhānubandham."
"Root" means the cause.

"How was the favor toward living beings accomplished? means that by staying in the village and revealing the means for health, dharma, and so forth as taught in Āyurveda, the favor toward living beings was indeed accomplished;
this word [“favor”] is to be construed with both instances of the word "time."
The analysis [of the compound] is *prajāpataye brahma* (the Veda for Prajāpati);
the construction is "having perceived that the lifespan of living beings is short and so forth.
Because it is short, the word "of life" (*āyuṣaḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder.

In this short lifespan, there is an accumulation of even small amounts of austerity and so forth; thus, the word "tat" (that) is used, and the word "prati" is connected individually with "maitrī" (friendliness) and the others,
while the word "atha" introduces the subject matter.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: "Therefore, with regard to [qualities] such as loving-kindness and compassion, it is fitting that one should listen to that which Brahmā gave to Prajāpati.

"Born in a suitable region" (*viṣayābhijā*) means born in a land appropriate for their own [medicinal] merit; for in an unmeritorious land, even divine herbs do not grow, or if they do grow, they become devoid of potency—this is the intended meaning (verses 8–10).
Now, he explains how *brahmasuvarcalā* and other such herbs possess mild potency, beginning with the words "But those which... (*yāstu*).

In the passage beginning with "balyānām" (11–12), *joṅgaka* refers to *aguru*; *dvāradā* is the *śākataru* tree, or alternatively, the *kapikacchu*.
Śrīparṇī, gāmbhārī, and palāśa-alkali; "palāśa-alkali-water" means water [prepared] with palāśa-alkali; "in a very clean place" means in a thoroughly purified location.

Once purity of mind has been attained through self-restraint (*prayatātmatā*), the mention of it again is for the purpose of showing that self-restraint is the most esteemed among other mental qualities.

At present, the accomplishment of elixirs (*rasāyana*) and other such treatments is dependent upon physicians; therefore, he begins the praise of the physician with the verse beginning "He who... and so forth.

39–51 He states the grounds for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the terms *vaidya* and *dvija*: "by knowledge," and so forth.

By this it is stated that one becomes a physician (*vaidya*) through connection with knowledge (*vidyā*), and likewise, one becomes twice-born (*dvija*) by birth characterized by the completion of Vedic study.

The alternative between "Brahmanic" (*brāhma*) or "Rishi-like" (*ārṣa*) arises from the intention of a particular type of physician; the distinction is that the *brāhma* method pertains to that which aims at definitive treatment, whereas the *ārṣa* method pertains to the other, which benefits the world.
(Verses 52–54) "Having heard" (*saṃśrutya*) means having made a formal promise (*pratijñāya*).
"Medical treatment itself is the merchandise to be sold," thus [it is called] "medical-merchandise.

By the phrase "having abandoned that," etc., medical treatment performed for the sake of dharma is equal to a heap of gold due to its great fruit; however, other [treatment] is like something worthless, equal to a heap of dust, leading to "the abode of Vaivasvata," which is the house of Yama.

Regarding the phrase "the elixir of jewels in the compendium" (*saṅgrahe ratnarasāyanam*), the construction is as follows: that which the Lord of the Immortals (*amareśvara*) proclaimed to the celibate students (*brahmacāriṇaḥ*)—namely, the elixirs (*rasāyana*) composed of gold and other precious gems, as well as the methods for divine medicinal herbs (*divyauṣadhi*) and so forth, as revealed in the *Āyurvedasamutthāna*—that has been fully elucidated here.

Section 1] Since the commonality of promoting vigor (*ojas*) exists in both, the treatment for virilization (*vājīkaraṇa*) should be discussed following the treatment for rejuvenation (*rasāyana*). Furthermore, within that *vājīkaraṇa*, because it contains a section demonstrating the inclination toward its practice, the "Chapter on the Arrows and Roots" (*saṃyogaśaramūlīya*) is stated first.
That which has a connection (*saṃyoga*) with the roots of *śara* grass is called *saṃyogaśaramūlīya*.
That by which one who is not virile (*avājī*) is made excessively capable in sexual intercourse (*maithuna*) like a stallion (*vājī*) is *vājīkaraṇa*.
For it has been said: "Like a horse of exceeding strength, by which one goes to a woman unimpeded," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "one should seek," [the author] indicates that since *rasāyana* yields great fruit, a man should subsequently seek *vājīkaraṇa*, which yields lesser fruit in comparison.
By the word "man" (*puruṣa*), which denotes a young man, he excludes both children and the elderly, whose sexual intercourse is prohibited.
For it has been said: "A very young man, whose bodily constituents are not yet fully developed, by approaching women would suffer suddenly, like a shallow pond with little water when dried up,
or like old, parched wood that has been gnawed by insects and is decayed."
"Like an old man approaching women, he would quickly waste away upon contact.

By the word "constantly" (*nityam*), it is shown that the aphrodisiac is not to be used only once like an elixir (*rasāyana*), but rather should be employed at all times like food. By the word "self-possessed" (*ātmavān*), it prohibits the practice of aphrodisiacs by those of evil character; for such a person, having increased their bodily constituents through the use of aphrodisiacs, might even engage in sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached.
He explains how dharma and the other qualities depend exclusively upon the aphrodisiac (vṛṣya) in the passage beginning with "of the son" and so forth.
"Āyatana" means cause;
these qualities refer to dharma and the rest. The meaning is that a son produced through the application of an aphrodisiac brings about dharma and the other virtues for his father.

In this context, sexual intercourse during the fertile period (*ṛtukāla*) is primarily intended through the practice of *vājīkaraṇa* (aphrodisiac therapy) with proper method; therefore, there is no contradiction with the statement regarding celibacy (*brahmacarya*) made in the passage beginning with "the three supports" (*tisraiṣaṇīye traya upastambhāḥ*, Sūtra-sthāna 11), as that [teaching on celibacy] does not prohibit sexual intercourse performed according to the rules during the fertile period.
He describes the preeminent form of aphrodisiac (*vājīkaraṇa*) among all aphrodisiacs, beginning with the word "vājī":
"The field" (*kṣetra*) is like a [fertile] field, because it is there that the seed in the form of semen (*śukra*) germinates.
"Objects" (*artha*) refers to sound and so forth; these are well known as the lower lip-fluid, the song of the *kalaviṅka* bird, beautiful forms, and other qualities residing in women.

Regarding "dharma and wealth [are found] in women": *dharma* is so stated because of such instructions as "one should practice dharma together with one's wife"; likewise, *artha* (wealth) is so called because a devoted housewife performs the protection of wealth and other such tasks;
thus, the meaning is that when there is union with a woman—that is, with *lakṣmī* (fortune)—there arises an abundance of riches, which is to say that *lakṣmī* is established in women.
*Vaśyā* means dependent or submissive.
"Trained" means she has been instructed in the sixty-four arts (kalās), such as singing, instrumental music, and dancing, as described in the treatises on erotics (kāmaśāstra).
Showing that even apart from [the usual] form and so forth, a certain woman may become aphrodisiac for someone due to the power of karma, he says: "In various ways," and so on;
"by the conjunction of fate" means by the power of prior karma;
"they increase" means they bring about the state of being aphrodisiac.
*Hāva* is a particular manifestation of amorous gesture (*śṛṅgāraceṣṭā*) by women directed toward a man.
As stated by Bharata: "The supreme sages have said that *hāva* and the rest are produced from those [emotions] which are the surges of *sattva*, and that *sattva* is of a manifest nature."
"By fate" means by past karma;
"by action" means by present actions such as the practice of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*);

The term "having become a snare" refers to its being the cause of bondage for the mind and the senses.
By the statement, “For men have diverse dispositions,” he shows that women are not beloved by all men equally due to their possession of qualities such as beauty and the like. (8–15)

Now, demonstrating the desirability of a son who is to be achieved through the application of aphrodisiacs (*vṛṣya*), he says: "without shadow," and so forth; "single-stemmed" means having a single nature.

because it possesses the characteristic of being a mere semblance (pūlī).
By the expression "a bundle of grass in the shape of a man," he demonstrates the absence of purposeful human activity (*puruṣārtha-kriyā*).
And by the phrase "and sensual pleasures," he shows that the result—other than the procreation of a son—is not particularly praiseworthy;
for sensual pleasures pertain only to this world, and unlike a son, they do not benefit both worlds.

They are called "pleasures of enjoyment" because they produce pleasure in the enjoyment of sexual intercourse; alternatively, they are called "pleasures of enjoyment" because they are pleasant for one who enjoys them.

Regarding the passage beginning with "haṃsa" and so forth: although the applications of the *haṃsa*, *barhi*, and *dakṣa* [mantras] are distinct, nevertheless, from the perspective of their application, they constitute a single application.
Thus, as stated in the summary, fifteen applications are completed through the single application of the *haṃsa*, *barhi*, and *dakṣa*.
Showing that aphrodisiac formulations (*vṛṣyayoga*) should be administered only by those whose bodies are purified, he says: "In the channels," and so forth;

"In the afflicted" (kliṣṭe) means "withered. Regarding the summary [verse], "of whom and which": the meaning is "for whom and whichever aphrodisiac."

[Adhyāya 2, Pāda 2] Following the discussion on the term *vṛṣyapāda*, the word *āsiktakṣīrika* is mentioned as a specific instance of a compound-final element (*padānta*) due to its particular relationship [to the preceding member]. [The derivation is as follows:

because there exists in it the word *āsiktakṣīra* (one in which milk has been poured), it is called *āsiktakṣīrī*; here, the suffix *ka* is added in its own sense (*svārthika*). Alternatively, it may be formed as *āsiktakṣīrika* by means of the suffix *ḍhak*, following the pattern of technical (*vaiśeṣika*) terminology.
"Āsiktakṣīra" means increased by sprinkling with milk, as stated by Jatūkarṇa: "Sixty-day rice (ṣaṣṭika) that has been cooked and increased by sprinkling with milk," and so forth.
"Pure sixty-day rice" (*śuddhaṣaṣṭika*) refers here to white sixty-day rice.

In this context, the juices of *balā* and the other ingredients are to be taken in equal measures. Alternatively, since the word "measure" (*mātrā*) implies a small quantity, it may mean that the juices of *balā* and the others are to be used in small amounts. Regarding the quantity of the powder to be added, he says: "by which the juice becomes thick"; one should take that amount of powder by which the juice attains thickness.
The "abundance" (*prabhūtatva*) of honey and sugar should be understood as that amount by which there is an extreme sweetness.

Furthermore, by the very power of the application (*prayoga*), even in a formulation containing honey, contact with fire during the process of roasting does not bring about any contradiction. For instance, in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*, in the *Triphalā-ayas-kṛti* preparation, there is indeed a connection between honey and fire.
The term *ātmaja* means "born from joy" (*harṣa-bhūta-ātmaja*), that is to say, semen (*śukra*).

Although it has been stated that "the semen of a cockerel is [to be taken]," nevertheless, because it is impossible to obtain the semen of a sparrow and so forth, their eggs, which possess similar qualities, are also included here.
*Vartikā* refers to edible items in the form of wicks;
*dhānā* refers to edible items in the form of parched grains. Because they consist of similar substances, these various forms of edibles constitute a single *yoga*.
10–17 *Ajaḍā* is *śūkaśimbī*.
Ghee should be prepared with the pastes (kalkas) beginning with *jīvaka* and ending with *vidārī*, along with milk and water (verses 21–23).

Regarding the phrase "by means of skillful method" (*yuktyā*), the addition of black pepper and other ingredients should be performed in such a way that the pungency and other qualities do not become excessive.

its definition as *rasālā* is: "Rasālā, also known as *śikhariṇī*, consists of curd that is well-whipped (*sughṛṣṭa*) along with sugar, the four spices (*cāturjātaka*), cumin, jaggery, ginger, and long pepper."
"Resembling a digit of the moon" means exceedingly white.
In this context, "suitable" means capable of being employed as an aphrodisiac (vṛṣya);

The connection with the *māṣarṇa* and so forth is also as before. 1-2.
By the term "gṛṣṭi," he indicates one that has calved once;
by "four-teat" (catuḥstanī), he shows one whose four teats are fully developed; and by "rohiṇī," he indicates one of red color.

It should be understood from the statement that "the state of having upward-pointing horns belongs only to one who has pure and abundant milk" [that this applies to such a cow]. "Eating sugarcane" means those who eat stalks of sugarcane; "eating arjuna" means those who eat the leaves of the *arjuna* tree.
There are three alternatives: [the milk] may be from sugarcane, or from *arjuna*, or from *māṣaparṇa* plants;
there are two preparations, either boiled or unboiled;
and the third is that it is combined with sugar, honey, and clarified butter.

Regarding its application, Jātūkarṇa states: "Her milk, combined with sugar and honey, or alone, whether boiled or unboiled"—this should be applied separately according to each of the five permutations; thus, there are five formulations with the five groups [of drugs].
One should avoid" means one should avoid the paste of *medā* and so forth;
"an elder" should be understood as someone younger than seventy years of age.
Although the cessation of semen is mentioned in the case of *saptatika*, it should nevertheless be understood that [erection] still occurs due to the influence of aphrodisiacs (vṛṣya).

Regarding "of gold" (*jātarūpasya*), this refers to gold; it should be understood from the statement that the circular form of the gold's appearance here serves to assist in the application of aphrodisiacs through its specific power.
"Of that very one" refers to the cow carrying the māṣa-parṇa leaves; "a *prakuñca*" is a *pala*.

Regarding the phrase "milked with a stream of milk" (*kṣīradhārāvadohitā*): after the paste of *pippalī*, one should perform the milking with a stream of milk; and the milk should be milked until the *pippalī* fruits become fit for drinking.
Regarding the phrase "of the fruits," etc.
The term "of fruits" (*phalānām*) is connected individually with each of the three [terms] beginning with "of the vitalizing" (*jīvanīyānām*).
"Of the vitalizing" refers to the ten [substances] beginning with *jīvaka* and *ṛṣabha*, as mentioned in the group of six decoction-classes (*ṣaṭka-kāṣāya-varga*).
"Of the unctuous" (*snigdhānām*) refers to the ten [substances] beginning with *mṛdvīkā*, which are adjuncts to oleation (*snehopagā*), as mentioned in the group of seven decoction-classes.
Likewise, "of those that produce relish" refers to the ten pleasant fruits such as mangoes mentioned in the group of four types of *kaṣāya*;
"of these," meaning of the fruits beginning with the *jīvanīya* group, one *kuḍava* should be taken once they have been ground into powder. The rest is clear in meaning.

For this very application is recited in the *Jatūkarṇa*: "One *kuḍava* each of grapes, dates, black gram, *jaḍā*, wheat, rice, and ghee; two *kuḍavas* each of sesame and mung beans, having powdered them," and so forth (verses 15–17).

In the case of the *śatāvarī-ghṛta* and others, since sugar and other ingredients to be added are not explicitly specified, the quantity of one-quarter part (*pādikatva*) relative to the ghee is established by the maxim of what is observed elsewhere (i.e., the standard proportion of one-fourth for additives), [implying that the ghee itself constitutes one *prastha*].
19. These fifteen applications, beginning with "one *karṣa*," are concluded here.

The section beginning with "frequented by intoxicated bees" and ending with "and houses," although not explicitly stated according to the seasonal divisions due to its general applicability, should be understood as pertaining specifically to summer. Likewise, the section ending with "of clouds" pertains to the rainy season; that ending with "fragrant" pertains to autumn; and the arrangement ending with "beloved" should be understood as applying to both the winter and the cool seasons.
[In these nights] "saṅkoca" refers to saffron, and "saṅkoca-aguru" refers to agallochum; those nights in which women find pleasure in anointing themselves with these are described as such. (26–28)
The prescription of the text beginning with "sukhā" (pleasant), however, was intended for springtime; yet it is not contradictory in other seasons either.

By this it is meant that even though strength is produced by satiety, joy does not arise because the body and mind have been impaired by wasting and other conditions; and due to the absence of joy, the capacity for sexual intercourse does not occur.
Now, regarding how semen is produced in the body, how it is situated, and how it is discharged, he says: "Rasa... and so forth.
By means of the three examples beginning with sugarcane, he shows, respectively, persons whose semen is discharged with no effort, with little effort, and with great effort.
The term "in contact" (saṃsparśana) refers to that which possesses contact; by this, he shows that since contact does not pervade [the entire body], semen is also not present in hair and so forth.
The union of man and woman is their mingling.

*Ceṣṭā* is the act of sexual intercourse; *saṅkalpa* is the longing for a woman; *pīḍana* is the mutual friction between the man and the woman. In this process, the union of the man and the woman is the primary cause, while *ceṣṭā* and the others are its auxiliary factors.
By means of the analogy of a wet cloth, he demonstrates that the emission of semen occurs without injury to the substratum.
He further states another cause for the flow of semen, beginning with "from joy" (*harṣāt*), and so forth.
Joy (*harṣa*) is the desire preceded by conceptualization that causes the arousal of semen, the increase of anger, the raising of the sexual organ, and so forth;
thirst (*tarṣa*) is the longing for a woman;
and fickleness (*saratva*) is instability.

The state of following along (*anupravaṇabhāvaḥ*) means that, while possessing minuteness (*aṇutve*), it has the inherent nature of exiting outward due to the swiftness of the wind; the meaning is that this is because the wind that impels the semen has a tendency toward rushing forward (*abhidravaṇaśīlatvāt*).

And although these are indeed causes, they are not counted within the collective totality of the causes previously set forth—primarily the union of man and woman and so forth—because of their relative insignificance.
"Wandering" means moving through various species such as humans, animals, and so forth;
"of Viśvarūpa" refers to the Self, for it is said in the section on the Self: "He is Viśvakarman and he is Viśvarūpa" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.15).
"Material form" (*rūpadravya*) refers to the prior cause of form;
by this it is stated that semen is the cause for the manifestation of the unmanifest self (*ātman*) in the production of a manifest body.
And since semen is mentioned here as being relevant to the present context, it should be understood that menstrual blood (*ārtava*) is also the material form of the self.
46–49 He describes the excellent qualities of semen, beginning with "bahalam" (thick), etc. 50.

He states the etymological derivation of the term *vājīkaraṇa*: "by which," and so forth. "One would go excessively" means one would go again and again. Alternatively, there is the reading *vyajyate*; even in that case, it means that by frequent intercourse with women, one's virility (*puṃstva*) is manifested.
Even with the reading *vyajyāt*, the meaning is the same; this should be carefully considered by the learned.

By this etymological derivation (*nirukti*), all three types of aphrodisiacs (*vṛṣya*) are encompassed: namely, those that increase semen such as black gram (*māṣa*) and others; those that cause its discharge such as sexual intent (*saṅkalpa*) and others; and those that both cause discharge and increase it such as milk and others, as stated elsewhere: "Some cause the discharge of semen, some increase the semen, and some cause both discharge and increase; thus, the aphrodisiac is said to be threefold."
For this [substance], being of three kinds, again and again produces potency in sexual intercourse and the capacity for repeated intercourse;
such is the cause, and so forth.
The summary is clear (verses 52–53).

Thus ends the fourth section on aphrodisiacs (*vājīkaraṇapāda*), titled "The Man Whose Strength Has Been Restored," in the *Vājīkaraṇa* chapter of the *Cikitsāsthāna*, within the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of Caraka composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta.
Thus ends the second chapter on aphrodisiacs (vājīkaraṇa).
[Cikitsāsthāna, Chapter 3 (69 of 120)] Having described the treatment that promotes vigor for those in good health, the treatment that eradicates disease must now be discussed.
Since fever is the foremost among all diseases, its treatment is stated first.

And as to how fever holds such preeminence, the author will state this very point in the chapter that sets forth the treatment of fever; it is called "Jvaracikitsita" (The Treatment of Fever), because of the metaphorical identification of the name with the subject matter. This same principle should be understood to apply to the subsequent chapters as well.

Regarding the term *vijvara*: the word *vijvara* indicates being free from disease (*nīroga*). This is because, in this context, the word *jvara* is intended to signify disease in general—as in the passage, "Fever (*jvara*), disorder (*vikāra*), and disease (*roga*)..."—and thus, by means of freedom from disease, the author here expresses that the teacher is the locus for the inquiry into the pacification of diseases.
Regarding "jvarasaṃdeham" (doubt concerning fever), this refers to doubt concerning characteristics of fever not mentioned in the etiology of fever;
by the words "viviktaḥ" and so forth, he shows that the teachers should be questioned in this manner.

The phrase "tormenting the body, senses, and mind," and so forth, is a qualifying description containing a reason for the preeminence of fever (*jvara*). Some diseases, such as tumors (*arbuda*), torment only the body; some, such as dogmatic adherence to untruth (*atattvābhiniveśa*), torment only the mind; and others, such as ophthalmia (*timira*), torment only the senses. This [fever], however, torments all three; for it will be said: "No being whatsoever that is entered by fever is not tormented."
In this context, the heating of the body is described by "fever" (*santāpa*) and so forth, while the heating of the mind and senses will be explained by "mental agitation" (*vaicittya*) and so forth.

It is called the "foremost of all bodily diseases" because it is the foremost among all diseases of the body. As for mental diseases, they exist even prior to fever and other ailments; furthermore, its status as the "foremost" is due to its power to produce a vast multitude of disorders, even at the beginning of the *Satya-yuga*.

And its predominance is due to its connection with qualities such as causing affliction to the body and mind; it belongs to the "rival of living beings," meaning the enemy of living beings by way of being their slayer;
and it is "certain," meaning inevitable.
At the onset of dissolution, at death, and at birth, fever in the form of darkness (tamas) is to be known here;
for it will be said: "The power of fever is most intense at the beginning of birth and at the end."
The *prakṛti* and other factors, which are to be explained throughout the entire chapter, shall be commented upon as the occasion arises.

The term *balakālātmalakṣaṇam* is a *dvandva* compound meaning "strength, time, and the characteristics of the self. The phrase "in detail and according to the distinctions of rules" (*vyāsato vidhibhedācca*) means by way of an elaborate exposition based on the differences in the rules.

The word *yataḥ* [in the first instance] means from those things such as sexual intercourse (*vyavāya*) etc., from which he is to be protected; the second *yataḥ* means for what reason he is to be protected.

By the phrase "for the sake of the welfare of the world" (*jagaddhitārtham*), Agniveśa demonstrates his own compassion—a quality among the virtues of a disciple that is worthy of being adopted—by showing that upon hearing this, he will undertake the practice of medicine for the benefit of the world.
The section beginning with "In the chapter on fever" (jvarādhikāre) and so forth is the descriptive text [4–10],
starting with "Fever is a disorder" (jvaro vikāraḥ) and so forth.

Some say that although the synonyms were already indicated by the preceding questions, they are stated here nonetheless because of the context of the section, and thus there is no fault of redundancy. Alternatively, this is a statement of synonyms for fever (*jvara*) itself, which is the subject under discussion.

And although terms such as *vikāra* (disorder) and so forth generally denote "disease" (*roga*), nevertheless, due to the context, they refer here specifically to the particular disease that is fever—just as in the instruction "one should feed a Brāhmaṇa," the word "Brāhmaṇa," though general, refers specifically to the invited Brāhmaṇa because of the context of the meal.

And in that explanation, the exposition consisting of synonyms and designations for fever and so forth is stated by the passage beginning with "Fever is a morbid change" (*jvaro vikāraḥ*); thus, there is no suspicion of tautology. The word *nāma* signifies manifestation; therefore, the meaning is that a single object—characterized as fever or characterized as disease—is expressed by means of synonyms. Synonyms (*paryāya*) are words of different classes that denote the same object. Alternatively, the phrase "by synonyms of names" (*nāmaparyāyaiḥ*) means by synonyms in the form of names; that is, by synonyms as they are used in common parlance.
For a synonym may exist even when it is not being employed, as for example, the two synonyms *nityaga* and *anubandha* were mentioned in relation to *āyus*.

Here, by the word *prakṛti*, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is meant; likewise, that from which this effect arises is called its cause. In that context, he states the *prakṛti* in the form of the proximate cause with the words "of that," and so forth.
"Uddiṣṭā" (indicated) means stated in brief.
He states the reason why the *doṣas* constitute the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) of fever: "dehinam" and so forth.
The sense is that because no *doṣa* ever deviates from it, it is established that fever has the *doṣas* as its fundamental nature.
By the word *dehin*, the person (*puruṣa*) possessing a body is intended, not the Self alone, because the latter is changeless.

By the expression “he closely attends to,” he demonstrates the possession (*āveśa*) by fever in the form of a specific being; furthermore, the physical form of fever must indeed be described independently, as stated in such passages as: “Fever has three feet and three heads.
He describes the nature of fever (*jvara*) according to its essential form: "Kṣaya," and so forth.

It is called *kṣaya* (decay) because it is the cause of the decay of the body; *tamas* (darkness) because it produces delusion (*moha*); *pāpmā* (evil) because it is brought about by sin; and *mṛtyu* (death) because it is the cause of death—it is *jvara* itself that is spoken of here.

Furthermore, in this context, the plural forms in the phrases "they have been described" (*uktāḥ*) and "consisting of *Yama*" (*yamātmakāḥ*) should be understood as intended to express the distinction between the various attributes, such as being the cause of decay and so on, even though they refer to the single entity that is *jvara*.

"Consisting of Yama" (*yamātmakāḥ*) means having the nature of Yama. For just as Yama is a bringer of death, so too are these [fevers] bringers of death; therefore, the meaning is that they "consist of Yama. Alternatively, there is the reading *yamātmajāḥ* ("sons of Yama"); here too, by virtue of being the sons of Yama, their performing actions identical to those of the father is expressed. Furthermore, Kṣaya and the others are well-known by their own names as distinct from fever, yet they are mentioned here because of the context of describing fever as consisting of Yama.
In this commentary, by the word "death" (mṛtyu), a fatal omen (riṣṭa) indicative of death is meant; for it is not death itself that acts as the cause of death.
He states the reason for its being of the nature of Yama: "Because of the conviction of the five elements (pañcatva) for beings afflicted by their own karma.

By this, the meaning is that just as Yama is the cause of the dissolution (pañcatva) of living beings who are afflicted by their own actions, so too do consumption (kṣaya) and the other [fatal signs] kill those who are afflicted by their prior karma.
Alternatively, there is the reading ‘pañcatvapratyayāḥ’, yet even so, that same meaning is to be understood.
He states the established progression that has come down through tradition, beginning with "The progression, however," and so forth.
"Progression" refers to the initial manifestation.

By the phrase "due to grasping" (*parigrahāt*), he causes one to recall the onset of fevers and other diseases mentioned in the section on the destruction of the countryside, starting with: "But when the Kṛta Yuga declines" (*Viṣṇu Purāṇa*, Aṃśa 3).

Likewise, the onset of fever from the wrath of Rudra, beginning with Dāruṇa and others, was previously indicated in the *Nidāna* [section]; the meaning is that it was stated briefly in the *Nidāna* by the passage: "Fever indeed originates from the wrath of Maheśvara" (*Ni.a.* 1).
By the word "previously," he shows that the first onset is that originating from the wrath of Rudra, while the second onset is that originating from possession (*parigraha*).

Since the state of being born from grasping has been explained in detail and the state of being born from Rudra’s wrath has been stated in brief, he now elucidates specifically that birth from Rudra’s wrath: "In the second [age], indeed," and so forth.
That which is practiced without anger is the vow of non-anger (*akrodhavratam*).
Those who consume obstacles to austerity (*tapovighnāśanāḥ*) are those who subsist upon obstacles to austerity (*tapovighnopajīvinaḥ*).
"Dhruvam" means that which must necessarily be given;
"satranāśanam" means the destruction of sacrifice;
"śaive" means that which brings about auspiciousness.
Regarding the phrase "in other instances of improper conduct" (*apacārāntareṣu*), which refers to the practice of the causes of fever (*jvara-nidāna*):

since even in this *satya-yuga* there exists the fever consisting of delusion (*moha*) regarding birth and death, it is not illogical for that same fever to occur in the second *yuga* as well, given the occurrence of birth and death.
Therefore, the construction should be understood as follows: "He who was established at the beginning and at the end of birth shall now exist in these other instances of improper conduct."
Or rather, it should be understood that in the Satya Yuga, the fever in the form of delusion regarding birth and death did not exist at all for men free from blemish.

Furthermore, even though Śiva’s essential nature is auspicious, his discharge of the fever that afflicts living beings must be understood as having occurred only after observing the suffering that living beings inevitably experience due to the influence of their own unrighteousness (adharma).
By the words beginning with "santāpa" (feverish heat), he describes its *prabhāva* (specific potency);
and *prabhāva* is defined as an unconditioned power (*anaupādhikā śakti*). Therefore, the designation *prabhāva* is applied to feverish heat and the other symptoms.

Since this is the *prabhāva* of the disease, consequently, even in a fever caused by *vāta* and *śleṣman*, the heat takes on a non-warm (*anuṣṇa*) form; likewise, the fact that at birth and at death there is a state of great darkness is the *prabhāva* of fever—this is the meaning.

With the words "And the primordial nature," etc., he provides a summary of the section; by the statement "Thus its primordial nature has been declared," however, a summary of the introduction is made; and at the end of the chapter, he will provide a summary of the chapter's meaning.
Furthermore, this repeated making of summaries should be understood as being done for the purpose of stabilizing the student's intellect, because it is the method of the Tantras.
By the words beginning with "nidāna," he states the causes;

"the eight causes" refers to the three factors such as dryness (rūkṣa) and so forth, which are described as the agents of the vāta and other doshas that initiate fever. Furthermore, by the passage beginning with "from the combination of the aforementioned causes" (Ni. A. 1), the causes of the dual combinations (dvandva) and the aggregate of all three (sannipāta) are stated. Likewise, the cause of exogenous (āgantuka) fever is explicitly stated there in direct speech.

Others, however, maintain that the terms "causes" (*kāraṇa*) and "nature" (*prakṛti*) refer respectively to the wind (*vāta*) and other humors when they have reached the state of pathogenesis (*samprāpti*) as initiators of fever—thus including those causes mentioned in the passage beginning with "Indeed, fever arises from eight causes" (Ni. A. 1)—and to the humors themselves when they exist as seeds (*bīja*) in immediate connection [with the disease]; whereas they assert that factors such as dryness (*rūkṣa*) are merely causes for the aggravation (*prakopa*) of the humors and are not themselves causes of fever.

In that case, there would be no inclusion here of factors such as dryness (*rūkṣa*) which are causes of fever; however, dryness and the like certainly possess causality with respect to fever by way of the intermediate operation (*vyāpāra*) of provoking the *doṣas*. Just as a sacrifice possesses the agency of producing heaven, the cause of diseases is twofold: the remote, such as dryness and the like, and the proximate, namely the *doṣas*.

Since the status of being "prior" (*pūrvatva*) is already established by the word "in the *Nidāna*," the phrase "previously mentioned" (*pūrvoktāni*) is used here for the purpose of excluding other etiologies of fever that have not been discussed.

27–29. Although the premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*) have also been mentioned in the *Nidāna* [section], nevertheless, in accordance with the context here, those which generally manifest are recited— beginning with "laziness" (*ālasya*), and so forth.
The word *kevalam* means "entirely"; by this, the external sense organs (*bāhyendriya*) are also included.
By this [statement], it is said that both the body and the mind are necessarily afflicted by fever.

"Time of strength" (*balakāla*) refers to the time characterized by the increase of strength, or the time characterized by the onset of fever; and that has been described in the *Nidāna-sthāna* in such passages as: "The onset of fever or its increase occurs at the end of the day, at the end of the heat, or at the end of digestion" (*Ni. A. 1*).
By the passage beginning with "The individual symptom of fever," etc., he states the definition of the self;
"the symptom of the self" refers to a non-deviating characteristic.

In this context, by the word *santāpa* (feverish distress), suffering in general is intended to be expressed; however, because it is specified as a modification of the body, it refers specifically to the characteristic of heat (*tāpa*). In the mind, as well as in the sense organs which are comprised of the qualities of the body, it should be understood as consisting of despondency and so forth, as described in the passage beginning with "despondency" (*vaicittya*).

The distinction here is that while in the case of the influence of *jvara* (fever) it is stated to be a distress whose effects are inconceivable, in this instance it is characterized by its invariable concomitance with *jvara*. Others, however, maintain that distress accompanied by symptoms such as anorexia constitutes the specific influence (*prabhāva*), whereas distress devoid of anorexia and the like constitutes the essential nature (*ātma-lakṣaṇa*) of the fever itself.
He states the reason for the fact that suffering has the characteristic of being experienced individually: "By fever," and so forth.
By the word *bhūta*, all living beings are meant;

therefore, when fever enters a living being, there is no human or other creature who is not tormented, but rather everyone is indeed tormented. Thus, because it is invariably concomitant with fever, the point is that it is logically established that its very nature is that of fever.

In this view, it should be understood that even in fevers such as those designated by the terms *kūṭapākala* and so forth, which affect elephants and other animals, there occurs an internal sensation of burning heat.

Alternatively, do bodily heat and mental distress here constitute the signs of fever either combined or alternatively? They cannot be alternative signs; for if that were the case, one would have to say that in some fevers there is only bodily heat, while in others there is only mental distress. Consequently, because these two vary independently, they cannot be non-deviant (invariable) signs. Therefore, it must be said that only when bodily and mental distress are combined do they constitute the definition of fever. This being established, he explains why bodily and mental distress occur in all fevers with the words beginning "by fever" (jvareṇa).

When a spirit enters by means of fever, neither the body nor the mind remains untouched; rather, they are indeed afflicted. Therefore, the meaning is that affliction of both body and mind is logically established in all fevers.

And in this view, regarding the demonstration of the distinction between physical and mental fever, that which must be stated—namely, that physical fever has the body alone as its locus and mental fever has the mind alone as its locus, as expressed in the passage beginning "Physical fever first arises in the body"—is intended with reference to a subtle moment of time. At that subtle moment, although the fever is indeed a burner of both, because it is produced immediately [after the initial moment], it is considered a burner of both body and mind in consideration of the property of burning both that arises subsequently. This is just as, in the definition of substance, a substance produced in the first moment is said to be without qualities, whereas a substance produced in the subsequent moment is said to possess qualities.
With the words "of two kinds" and so forth, he states the division of the methods;
these divisions will become clear in the *Vivaraṇa*.
"Saumya" (lunar) means having Soma as its presiding deity because it is produced from a cool cause; "Āgneya" (fiery) also has Agni as its presiding deity because it is produced from a hot cause.

Regarding the statement "furthermore, fever is seen to be of five types," the fivefold classification does not encompass all fevers, because the author will later state: "Fever is generally seen to be of five types when caused by *sannipāta*.

Consequently, fevers consisting solely of *vāta* and the other individual *doṣas* are not included within the categories of *santata* and so forth. Likewise, a temporal regulation must be stated for the *santata* types and others; therefore, those which lack such temporal regularity are indeed distinct from the *santata* group. Thus, the meaning of the sentence is that those fevers which arise according to the relative strength or weakness of the *doṣas* and time are precisely of these five types.

"According to the strength or weakness of the humors and the time" means according to the strength or weakness of the time caused by the humors. Regarding the strength or weakness of the time: in the case of *santata* (continuous) fever, because it is predominant, the strong time of seven days and so forth is determined by the powerful humor; however, in *satataka* (quasi-continuous) fever, the time of the fever is weak due to a humor of inferior strength relative to the *santata* period, for it pervades only two times during the day and night. Likewise, this very time of *satataka* fever is stronger than the weaker time of *anyedyuṣka* (tertian) fever. In this manner, the time of *anyedyuṣka* and other fevers should also be explained.

Alternatively, "doṣakāla" means the time of the humors (doṣas), the time of their aggravation, or the time of fever; the meaning is "by virtue of the strength or weakness," that is, by the intensity or lack of intensity of that [time].
And the rules regarding the intensity or lack of intensity of time have already been explained.
Others, however, say: "doṣa" and "kāla" together form the compound "doṣakālau"; [the phrase refers to] "by virtue of the strength or weakness of those two."

In that regard, [fever] becomes continuous (*santata*) due to the strength of the *doṣas* and the strength of time (*kāla*). As it has been stated: "For when the *doṣa* is equal to the time, the affected tissues (*dūṣya*), and the constitution (*prakṛti*), it is indeed continuous," and so forth; thus, the strength and weakness of the *doṣa* and the time have been explained in the commentary (*vivaraṇa*). Likewise, the weakness of the *doṣa* occurs in cases such as the *satataka* (quotidian) fever due to its being counteracted (*sapratyanīkatayā*); similarly, in the *satataka* and other types, the weakness of the time occurs upon the subsiding of the fever's intensity (*jvaravega*). In this view, all fevers would be encompassed by the strength and weakness of the *doṣa* and the time, and consequently, the restriction to five specific fevers—beginning with the *santata*—would be difficult to establish.
Others, however, explain [the text] by means of a transposed statement, taking it as "due to the strength or weakness of the defects" (*doṣabalābalakālāt*).
This is an ungrammatical explanation;

for by the compound designation "third-and-fourth" (*tṛtīyakacaturthakau*), he demonstrates that the third and fourth possess common characteristics such as being adventitious (*āgantuka*) or having a secondary suffix (*anubandha*).

Regarding the question, "the form of [fever] that is separate and distinct," the answer following in sequence is as follows: because of the statement "beginning with the bodily" (*śārīra*) and so forth, it should be understood that after the initial [occurrence], bodily fever also occurs in the mind, and likewise, mental fever occurs in the body immediately after its arising in the mind.

And thus, although all fevers have both the body and the mind as their substrata, nevertheless, that fever which is first initiated by a powerful bodily humor (*doṣa*) must be treated specifically with the therapy for that humor; likewise, a mental fever must be treated specifically with the therapy for the mental humor. To demonstrate this distinction between the bodily and the mental, the presentation of their differences is appropriate. Now, while the characteristic of burning heat (*santāpa*) is manifest in bodily fever, one might ask: how can there be burning heat in mental fever, such that it becomes its characteristic? To this he says: "distraction of mind" (*vaicittya*), and so forth.
The meaning is that states such as *vaicitya* (mental confusion) are expressed by the term "mental affliction" (*mānasasantāpa*), because the word *tāpa* (affliction) denotes *pīḍā* (suffering).

In connection with the discussion on mental affliction, they explain the "affliction of the senses" mentioned regarding fever in the passage "afflicting the body, the senses, and the mind," starting with the words "of the senses, etc.
*Vaikṛtya* means a deviation from one's natural state (*svabhāvānyathātva*), and this is to be inferred from the non-perception of objects and other such symptoms.
Explanation of the divisions of *saumya* (somatic) and *āgneya* (bilious) according to the method of reverse-order exposition— beginning with "consisting of wind and bile," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "consisting of wind and bile" (*vātāpittātmaka*), this means having wind and bile as its cause. In this context, that which is produced solely by wind, as well as that produced solely by phlegm, desires heat due to its gentle nature resulting from its cold intrinsic quality; likewise, that which consists of wind and phlegm is also observed [to desire heat]. Similarly, it is evident that even that consisting solely of bile has a desire for non-heat due to its fiery nature. Therefore, now, concerning one who consists of wind and bile—[a state] produced by cold wind and hot bile—their fiery nature being difficult to establish, they say: "one consisting of wind and bile [desires] cold."

This being the established rule, if it is observed that in a fever caused by *vāta* and *pitta*, the *vāyu* acts in a contrary manner through the power of its association, then one might suspect: "Does *vāyu* also produce a contrary effect when associated with *kapha*? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In [a fever] consisting of *vāta* and *kapha*, [the patient] desires heat. The meaning is that [the *vāyu*], being of the nature of *vāta* and *kapha*, specifically desires heat.

The "mixed characteristic" (*vyāmiśralakṣaṇa*) refers to fevers other than those characterized by the previously mentioned mixed defects—namely, those of *kapha-pitta* and *sānnipātika* (tridiscordance). This fever, due to the desire for both heat and cold, is indeed distinct from the two lunar and fiery constellations (*rāśi*). Just as a "three-fingered" length is distinct from two fingers, so too should one consider this in the case of the mixture of physical and mental [factors].
As for the statement "the fever desires," it should be understood as a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the desire of the person afflicted by fever onto the fever itself.

Regarding fever caused by *vāta* and *pitta*, the author states that *vāyu* is a "conveyor" (*yogavāhin*) in order to explain how it brings about the desire for cold: "It is a conveyor," and so forth.
"Yogavāha" means that which carries the quality from yoga;
"param" means excessively;
"saṃyogāt" means due to contact with both heat and cold.
"Performing both purposes" means, according to the respective order, performing the purpose of heat and cold;
he analyzes this very point with the words "causing burning," and so forth.

Although one should have said "by bile" (*pittena*), by using the word "by fire" (*tejasā*), he indicates for the sake of illustration a meaning well-known in the world: that wind, when joined with external heat such as sunlight, causes burning.

It should be understood that while the cold-producing nature of wind is established by its very quality of coldness, it occurs specifically through its association with substances such as soma, kapha, and water.
With the passage beginning "Internal burning" (39–41), there is an exposition on internal and external morbid impulses;
with the section beginning "Natural" (prākṛta), there is an exposition on natural and unnatural [diseases].

In this context, the *doṣa* aggravated by the nature of the season (*kāla-svabhāva*) is called the "natural" (*prakṛti*). A fever arising from such a *doṣa* is called "natural" (*prākṛta*), as he will state: "The natural fever is specified with reference to the season and the constitution. If this were the case, a fever caused by *vāta*, which is the constitutional *doṣa* of the rainy season, would also be considered natural; therefore, to preclude that, he says: "But that which arises in spring and autumn is easily curable."
The word "tu" (but) is used for emphasis;

therefore, the meaning is that only that which is easily curable, arising in spring and autumn, and being of natural origin (*prākṛta*), is here designated by the term "natural. However, that which occurs during the rainy season and is caused by Vāta is not easily curable; thus, it is not called "natural," for the conventional usage of the designations "natural" (*prākṛta*) and "modified" (*vaikṛta*) serves the purpose of indicating, respectively, what is easily curable and what is difficult to cure. If even a Vāta-born disease that is difficult to cure were considered "natural," then what would be the use of the designation "natural"?

Since the natural (*prākṛta*) [seasons] are only those arising in spring and autumn, he will provide an elaborate exposition of those two alone through the passage beginning with "hot" (*uṣṇam*), and not that of the *vātika* [season].
Regarding this point, Jatūkarṇa states: "The Saumya and Āgneya [seasons] desire heat and cold; digestion occurs on the thirteenth day;
the natural [seasons] are spring and autumn, while elsewhere they are modified (*vaikṛta*)."
Although that which arises in spring was mentioned first, nevertheless, by means of an inverse explanation starting with "hot," he indicates that which arises in autumn:
it should be understood that the hot *pitta* accumulated during the rainy season becomes aggravated in autumn by the rising heat;
and "in the cold" refers to the winter.
Regarding the commentary beginning with "in the rainy season" (*varṣāsu*) which follows the statement beginning with "hot" (*uṣṇam*), one might object:

if all medicinal herbs possess an acidic transformation (*amlavipākitva*) during the rainy season, then there would be a lack of consistency regarding the specific transformation attributed to each individual substance, since that [specific] transformation is seen to become acidic due to the influence of time.

Do not say so. Just as a substance that is sweet due to its final stage of ripening may become sour through a particular state of cooking—as stated in the passage beginning, "But when it is being cooked and becomes overcooked, it turns sour" (Ci. A. 15)—so too here, by the power of time, there will be a state of sour post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*). In the same way, the fact that medicinal herbs have a sweet post-digestive transformation during the winter should be explained accordingly. Others, however, maintain that the sourness of the post-digestive transformation of herbs in the rainy season is caused by burning (*vidāha*) due to the dullness of the digestive fire (*vahni-māndya*), as it is said: "In the rainy season, food burns... (Ci. A. 15).
"For at that time, almost all food is indeed burnt [digested] by him.
Even so, they have not stated that there is a sweet digestion during the winter; therefore, it is solely by the power of the season that another type of digestion occurs in medicinal herbs.
Because of the rapid action of bile (*pitta*), it quickly produces this effect.
Regarding "anubala" (supporting force), it refers to *kapha* acting as a secondary associate (*anubandha*).
Thus, he describes the suitability of fasting (*laṅghana*) for fever: "By its very nature," and so forth.

By "by the nature of the time of elimination" (*visargasya prakṛtyā*), he means that through the natural state of the season—characterized by qualities such as *saumya* (cooling)—there is no danger from fasting.

The period of *visarga* (the rainy season) is indeed mild and moist; men are strong during that time, and therefore a fever arising therein—by virtue of its origin in the *āmāśaya* (stomach)—is fit for fasting and must certainly be treated with fasting.
Alternatively, there is the reading "prakṛtyaiva visargācca" (and by nature and from the *visarga*).

In that case, "by nature" refers to the cause of the fever, namely the *kapha* and *pitta* constitutions which are the reasons for fasting, as well as "from the *visarga*" referring to the season; thus, there is no fear regarding fasting.
For it has been said: "The two liquid tissues, *kapha* and *pitta*, can withstand great fasting.

Thus, it is entirely logical that the *kapha* accumulated during the *hemanta* season becomes aggravated in the spring (*vasanta*). This is because, according to the sequence of the accumulation and so forth of the *doṣas*, there is no distinct cold season (*śiśira*);

rather, within the period of *ādāna*, its *vāta* and *pitta* also follow along. Consequently, the fever arising from *kapha* in spring is accompanied by *vāta* and *pitta* as its secondary accompaniment (*anubandha*).

In that regard, during the spring and so forth, vāta and pitta are weak; in the middle [season], they are moderate; but at the end, they become powerful. Likewise, in autumn, kapha becomes [powerful].
Showing that medical treatment should be administered after understanding these specific distinctions, he says: "At the beginning," and so forth.
The construction is: having understood the strength or weakness of the *doṣas* at the beginning, middle, and end of the fever during autumn and spring. (47)

The definition that "the natural fever (prākṛta-jvara) is indicated with reference to the nature of time" means that the term "nature of time" refers to the dosha associated with the inherent character of time; "with reference to" means having identified it as the cause.

One might object: "In that case, a fever caused by the wind (vāta) which is the natural state (prakṛti) of the rainy season would also be 'natural' (prākṛta). To this he says: "Generally, that born of wind is difficult [to cure]. A fever born of wind, even if it corresponds to the natural state of the season, is difficult to treat because its therapeutic measures are contradictory.

Since for a fever arising from the stomach (āmāśaya), fasting and similar measures are wholesome, yet these are unwholesome for the wind, it is difficult due to this contradiction of treatment; therefore, the vātika fever is not considered "natural. The point is that even among those fevers that are "natural," only that which is easily curable is designated as "natural."

Thus, first of all, every fever arising from Vāta is considered morbid (*vaikṛta*); likewise, showing that fevers born of Kapha and Pitta occurring outside the seasons of spring and autumn are also indeed morbid, he says: "In other times, it is morbid"; the remainder [of the sentence] is "whether born of Kapha or Pitta. Now, he states the cause of this morbid fever with the words beginning "The causes," and so forth.

Others, however, say: although the wind-born [fever] during the rainy season is also natural (*prākṛta*), it is difficult to treat; whereas that which arises in spring and autumn is natural and easily curable—this is the distinction. And so it was stated by Vāgbhaṭa: "The wind-born [fever] is natural" (Vāgbhaṭa, Niścala commentary, Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya, Cikitsāsthāna 2).
Thus ends [the section]. 48–49.
With the words "In those with strength," etc., the description of fevers that are easily curable is provided.

Although the complications (*upadrava*) of fever are not explicitly listed here, nevertheless, diseases characterized by the general definition of a complication should be understood as such in this context. As it has been said: "A complication (*upadrava*), indeed, is a disease that arises after the primary disease, resides in the same location as the disease, and is itself a disease—whether gross or subtle—which occurs subsequent to the disease; thus it is designated as a complication" (Cikitsāsthāna, Chapter 21). And in another treatise it is stated: "Hiccups, dyspnea, cough, thirst, vomiting, diarrhea, fainting, body aches, anorexia, and difficult defecation—these ten complications afflict fever."

50. [Objection: Surely, by many and powerful causes, the disease will necessarily possess many symptoms; so what is the purpose of the term "bahulakṣaṇaḥ" (possessing many symptoms)? [Response: It is said: Due to specific factors such as the digestive fire (*agni*) and strength (*bala*) of the person, even the aforementioned defects that act as causes of disease do not produce a disease with many symptoms. Furthermore, due to the absence of a specific mode of manifestation (*samprāpti*), the state of having many symptoms does not occur.
As it has been stated: "Whether one, two, three, or even many [symptoms] appear in the body, this is due to the association with the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) and other factors."
"But when provoked, the winds and other humors manifest their transformations"—
the word "immediately" (*śīghram*) means at the very moment they arise.
"—or within seven days," and so forth:

a vāta-dominant [fever] characterized by delirium, vertigo, and dyspnea, being acute, kills within seven days; a pitta-type [fever] with these same qualities kills within ten days; and likewise, a kapha-born [fever] with these same qualities kills within twelve days. They explain this as being due to the fact that vāta, pitta, and kapha respectively produce their pathological effects most rapidly, very rapidly, and rapidly.
The word "or" (*vā*) signifies an alternative; by it, killing is indicated as occurring either before or after seven days and so forth.
Others, however, explain that [the poison] kills with delirium after seven days, with confusion after ten days, and with labored breathing after twelve days.

It has a profound internal impulse; or rather, it abides in a deep realm (*gambhīradhātustha*), being long-lasting (*dairgharātrika*) and persisting for a long time; or else, it is called "long-lasting" because it makes the night—that is, death—long.
52. With the words beginning "by the streams" (srotobhiḥ), he states the distinctions such as the continuous (santata) and so forth.
"Gurus" refers to the elders;
"for ten days," etc., means that it persists for a period of ten days and so forth, becoming extremely difficult to endure— the word "becomes" being understood as the ellipsis.
"Quickly" (*śīghram*) refers here to periods such as ten days and so forth, which are designated by the word "quickly" in comparison to much longer intervals.

Furthermore, the alternative durations of ten days and so on should be understood according to the sequence of the continuous fever (*santata-jvara*) being initiated by a predominance of bile (*pitta*), phlegm (*kapha*), wind (*anila*), or a combination of all three (*sannipāta*).
As it is stated elsewhere: "Due to the increase of bile, phlegm, and wind, [the fevers cease] after ten days, twelve days, seven days, and [ten days respectively]."
"It either kills or quickly releases [the patient] due to the digestion of the bodily tissues (dhātu) and wastes (mala) arising from the three doṣas";
likewise: "In ten, twelve, or seven days, the fever—predominant in pitta, śleṣman, or anila—having scorched the bodily tissues and wastes with its heat, either kills or releases [the patient]."
The conceptualization regarding killing and liberation must also be stated in terms of the impurity and purity of the *rasas* (tastes/flavors) and so forth.
Why is it that this [affliction] is so difficult to endure, acts so swiftly, and is continuous? To this he says: "Time," and so forth.

"Time" (*kāla*) refers to the rainy season and so on; "the corruptible" (*dūṣya*) refers to the *rasas* and so on; and "nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to the bodily constitution, such as the *śleṣman* (phlegm) constitution and so forth.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the "similarity to time" (kālāditulyatā) of a *doṣa* occurs only occasionally—as for example, when the season is spring, the constitution (*prakṛti*) is characterized by phlegm (*śleṣman*), the bodily humor (*dūṣya*) is fat (*medas*), and the *doṣa* is phlegm; and likewise, one should understand that bile (*pitta*) [predominates] in autumn? However, for the other cases such as the three *doṣas* together, similarity to time and so forth is difficult to attain. Therefore, how can there be a continuous (*santata*) fever caused by that [similarity]? Furthermore, since a continuous fever has twelve substrates, it must be said to arise from all three *doṣas*. [Response: It is said: Even after stating "similar," the author uses the term "without opposition" (*niṣpratyanīka*). By doing so, he clarifies that "similarity to time and so forth" means precisely being in accordance with time and the other factors.

Furthermore, even when factors such as time (*kāla*) and the rest are discordant, if they are seized by a powerful *doṣa*, they lack the capacity to produce an opposing effect and thus become merely concordant. For example, even if minor kings are hostile to the heart of a powerful king, they remain merely compliant.

Moreover, in our view, a continuous fever (*santata*) is indeed initiated by all three *doṣas*; and in that case, it is entirely possible for time and the other factors to be equal with respect to any one of those *doṣas*.

In this regard, some read the passage beginning with “*yathā dhātūn*,” etc., immediately after “*tasmājjñeyaḥ suduḥsahaḥ*”; and having read up to “*prāyaḥ prāgapatarpaṇaiḥ*,” they then read the characteristics of the *satataka* (quotidian) fever and others starting with “*raktadhātvāśrayaḥ*.

Others, however, read “*suduḥsahaḥ*” and then read the characteristics of the *satata* and *anyedyuṣka* fevers; thereafter, they read the section beginning with “*yathā dhātūn*,” and subsequently, according to the opinion of another teacher, they read the characteristics of the three types of fever beginning with *anyedyuṣka*.

In that regard, according to the sequence of the first chapter, by the passage beginning with "as the elements" (*yathā dhātūn*), they describe the sequence of the arising and so forth of the continuous [stream];
here, "elements" (*dhātūn*) refers to the seven elements beginning with taste (*rasa*),
and specifically, by the mention of "vitiation of taste," the vitiation of taste is to be understood.
"In what manner" (*yathā*) means by which mode, such as heaviness, rigidity, and so forth;
"simultaneously" (*yugapat*) means at one and the same time;
and "necessarily" (*niyamāt*) means that all [the elements] beginning with the *dhātu*s, as well as all the *doṣa*s, follow along together.

"By purity," and so forth, refers to that which is continuous: when all the *rasas* (tissues/flavors) and other constituents are entirely purified, then [the disease] subsides within seven days or so; when all the *rasas* and others are entirely unpurified, then it kills—this is the meaning. Now, as to what the procedure is when there is only slight purification, he says: "But when," and so forth.

"They are not purified" means that all of them are not exceedingly pure; the meaning is that they remain possessed of residual defects. "Or they are not purified in every respect" means that among the [twelve] constituents such as *rasa* (nutritive fluid) and the rest, some are purified while others remain unpurified.
The twelve are: the seven tissues (*dhātu*), the three humors (*doṣa*), urine, and feces.
In this context, the purification of the humors (*doṣas*) should be understood as their return to their natural state (*prakṛti*).
As for the claim that the continuum (*santati*) is initiated by a single humor based on its twelvefold substratum, that must be known as already refuted.
"Emission" (*visarga*) means abandonment.

He describes the nature of the *visarga* as "having unmanifest characteristics" (*avyaktalakṣaṇam*); that is, the *visarga* is that whose characteristic is unmanifest. By this, he shows that even then the fever is indeed still latent, but its symptoms do not become manifest. Subsequently, it persists for a long time starting from the thirteenth day, and therefore it is rightly said that its subsidence becomes difficult to achieve.

By these characteristics—such as being based on the twelve factors like the *dhātus* and so forth, and pervading for ten days and so on—the *santata* fever is indeed distinct from the fevers caused by *vāta* and the others, which occur with no fixed duration and persist intermittently for two, three, or more days.

As for what is stated in another treatise: "Likewise, there is another type called *santata*, which arises from slight and weak causes, involves one or two *doṣas*, and is characterized by mild secondary symptoms (*upadrava*)."

This is stated in the passage beginning with "atulyadūṣyaprakṛtiḥ" and so forth; that [the subject] is indeed different from this [body] is established by the use of the word "anya" (other/different) even in other tantras, and thus there is no contradiction.

He explains the *satataka* (intermittent fever): by the mention of "having the blood constituent as its substrate" (*raktadhātvāśraya*) and so forth, he shows that because of the inclusion of "occasional" (*prayoga*), the *satataka* also takes as its substrate constituents other than blood, such as flesh and so on.
Regarding "with an adversary" (*sapratyanīka*), among [the factors] such as time and so forth, it means having one or another as an adversary.
"Consisting of increase and decrease according to time" means that in a time suitable for increase or decrease, there is increase or decrease;

thus, fever occurs at a time concordant with the *doṣa*, and its decrease occurs at a time other than that which is concordant with the *doṣa*. Although strength may be acquired from any one among time, constitution (*prakṛti*), or the affected tissue (*dūṣya*), it should be understood that the rule of being manifested by time is due to the power of the *doṣa*s' pathogenesis (*saṃprāpti*).
Regarding verses 61–62, "medovahā" (fat-carrying): the vitiation of fat (*medoduṣṭi*) should be understood as resulting precisely from the obstruction of the fat-carrying channels (*medovahā-nāḍī*).

For it has been stated: "Due to the obstruction of those channels, the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), both those residing in their own sites and those moving along their paths, undergo provocation" (Viśeṣa-sthāna, chapter 5).

Some recite the passage beginning with "following the channels of the flesh" (*māṃsasrotāṃsy anusṛtaḥ*) as the description of the tertian and quartan fevers; here too, the corruption of the bodily constituents (*dhātu-dūṣi*) is to be understood through the corruption of the channels (*srotas*).

As for those who do not recite the text that establishes the specific corrupted constituents (*dūṣya*) for the tertian and quartan fevers, their inclusion of the corrupted constituents is based on the authority of other medical treatises (*tantrāntara*).
By the very designations "tertian" (tṛtīyaka) and "quartan" (caturthaka), it should be understood that these fevers manifest on the third and fourth days respectively.
Verses 63–67 provide an illustration regarding the cessation and recurrence of fevers, beginning with the words "adhiśete" and so forth.
"Adhiśete" means "he remains presiding over";
"dhātuṃ" refers to the bodily constituents such as blood, which are listed among those that are constantly subject to corruption;
"kāle" means at its own proper time.

If the *doṣa* produces fever at its own [specific] time, then why does it not do so during the days of rest for tertian (*tṛtīyaka*) and quartan (*caturthaka*) fevers, even though those times—such as the forenoon—are favorable to the *doṣa*? To this he says: "It [requires] increase," and so forth. It is not only time that is required, but the *doṣa* also requires an increase (*vṛddhi*) in order to produce the tertian and other types of fever. And that increase occurs in three days for the tertian fever, and in four days for the quartan fever; such is the meaning.

The depletion of the antagonist—such as time, constitution (*prakṛti*), and so forth—which is opposed to the [increased] *doṣa*, occurs; the meaning is that when the depletion of the antagonist takes place due to that increase of the *doṣa*, then it causes fever (*jvarayati*).

(68–69) Now, regarding continuous fever (*satataka*) and the others, he explains how the increased *doṣa* generates the paroxysm of fever and how its subsidence occurs, beginning with the words "having done" (*kṛtvā*).

In the *satataka* (quotidian) fever and others, the *doṣas*, having manifested their force, become depleted of strength; being thus depleted, they remain situated in their respective locations such as the blood (*rakta*) and so forth. Then, having increased again at their own time, those very same *doṣas* cause fever.
Regarding the specific excess of *doṣas*, he describes the manifestation of *tṛtīyaka* (tertian) and *caturthaka* (quartan) fevers with the verse beginning "kaphapittāt" and so forth.

"Abhipṛṣṭham" means from the back (*pṛṣṭhāt*), meaning "one who seizes from the back"; or alternatively, the ablative case in "from the back" (*pṭṛṣṭhāt*) is used with the elision of a verbal suffix (*lyablope*), thus meaning "having taken hold of the back.

"First by the two calves" (*jaṅghābhyām pūrvam*) means it causes pain first in the two calves. In this case, one should understand that the quartan fever caused by *pitta* is not primary (*svapradhāna*); rather, it occurs as a secondary accompaniment (*anubandha*), like *pitta*-type *gṛdhrasī*, because it is not explicitly mentioned [as a primary type]. As for what was stated in the *Hārīta-saṃhitā* regarding its being born of *pitta*, that refers to its being born of *pitta* as a secondary accompaniment, since it does not act independently (*pṛthakprabhāva-kartṛtva*); for independent power (*prabhāva*) is not contradictory to the acceptance of the quartan fever [as a distinct entity].

71-72 Now, demonstrating that a fever which fevers during the middle of the day and releases [the patient] at the beginning and the end is indeed included within the category of *caturthaka-viparyaya* (the reverse quartan), he says: "viṣama... and so forth;
"trividho dhātuḥ" refers to the three humors (*dhātus*), namely vāta and the others.
"Residing in two elements" means it has reached the bones and marrow;
this was stated generally as being "like an irregular fever" (*viṣamajvara*), yet it should be understood here that it is specifically an irregular fever of the quartan type (*caturthaka*).
On this point, another treatise states: "When it has reached both the bones and the marrow, there is the reversal of the quartan fever."
“It causes fever for two days after three days, and indeed releases [the patient] at the beginning and at the end.

(73) Regarding the five types of combined fevers associated with the *caturthaka-viparyaya* (the reversal of quartan fever), he states their common characteristic, beginning with the word “prāyaśaḥ” (mostly).

By the inclusion of the word "mostly" (*prāyaśas*), [the author] indicates that quotidian fevers (*satataka*) and others may also be produced by combinations of two or more doshas. Now, if these are indeed initiated by *sannipāta* (the combination of all three doshas), then how is it that the fourth-day fever (*caturthaka*) is described as being of the phlegmatic (*ślaiṣmika*) type and so forth? To this he says: "But whichever [dosha] is most predominant in the *sannipāta*," and so on. For, according to the passage beginning with "An external factor (*āgantuka*) is generally a secondary association (*anubandha*) in irregular fevers (*viṣamajvara*)," it should be stated that there is an association with a spirit (*bhūta*). Furthermore, Jatūkarṇa, after mentioning the reversals of the third-day and fourth-day fevers, states: "Even though irregular fevers arise from all three doshas, they receive their names based on the predominant dosha."

All five of these fevers are considered by some to be irregular fevers (*viṣamajvara*). For instance, irregularity arises from having an uneven onset, intensity, and duration; as it is stated elsewhere: "An irregular fever is characterized by an uneven commencement, action, time, and persistence" (Vāgbhaṭa, *Nidāna-sthāna*, chapter 2).

In the case of *santata* (continuous fever), however, there is a disparity in timing because it ceases for twelve days and recurs on the thirteenth day; therefore, others consider that too to be irregular (*viṣama*). Yet others, setting aside *santata*, maintain that only the four types beginning with *satataka* are irregular fevers; for in *santata*, such a disparity in timing does not exist. And it has been stated by Kharanāda: "The five fevers previously mentioned by me, beginning with *santata*, are to be known as irregular fevers, excluding the four starting with *santata*."

Others, however, maintain that only the tertian and quartan fevers are irregular (*viṣama*), because irregular fevers arise after a long time. As Dāruvāha said: "In the extremely subtle and even subtler channels, and in those that are very distant, the *doṣa* moves slowly and in small amounts through the pathways of blood and so forth; thus it either does not enter the body at all, or it enters only partially and for the most part remains behind."
They say: "Therefore, this sequence is observed as the fever in which the heat has been interrupted.

Now, just as *santata* (continuous) fever itself takes on forms such as *satataka* (quotidian), so too do *satataka* and the others take on forms such as *santata*; he states this in the verse beginning with *ṛtvahorātra*.

The phrase "due to strength and weakness" (*balābalāt*) is connected with everything ending in "mind" (*manaḥ*). Strength and weakness constitute "strength-and-weakness"; by virtue of the object—that is, by virtue of karma—the fever attains its respective time as described for the continuous (*satata*) and other types of fever, through the strength of the season (*ṛtu*) and so forth, as well as through the weakness of the season and so forth.

In that regard, a *satataka* (daily) fever caused by a predominance of *vāta* arising in the rainy season (*varṣākāla*) becomes a *anyedyuṣka* (tertian) or other type upon reaching the opposing season of autumn (*śarad*), due to the relative strength or weakness of the day and night.

Regarding the attainment of specific times based on the strength or weakness of days and nights: for example, a quartan (*cāturthika*) fever born of *vāta* during the middle days and nights of spring becomes strong upon reaching the dry final days and nights of spring and turns into a tertian (*tṛtīyaka*) or other type; likewise, a daily (*satataka*) fever born of *śleṣman* on those very aforementioned days becomes a tertian or other type on the remaining days which are antagonistic to *śleṣman*.

The transformation of fever resulting from the service of corrupted causes due to the relative strength or weakness of the *doṣas* is indeed logical through the power of the mind (*manas*). One suffering from a continuous fever (*santata-jvara*) becomes one afflicted by a quotidian fever (*anyedyuṣka-jvara*) and so forth through the cessation of mental [disturbances] and similar means. Conversely, due to mental weakness caused by fear and other factors, one suffering from a quartan fever (*caturthaka-jvara*) and so forth becomes one afflicted by a tertian fever (*tṛtīyaka-jvara*) and so forth.

It should be understood that when there is a transformation of fever through the power of karma (*karman*), by means of auspicious karma (*śubha-karman*) and the transformation of painful fever, whatever [fever] is pleasant arises; however, by means of sinful karma (*pāpa-karman*), a painful fever arises.
75–83. Now, regarding the description of the eightfold types of fever (*jvara*), he states what is to be said: "By causes," and so forth.
Since even the causes serve as forms of manifestation (*ākṛti*) by way of indicating the specific type of fever, it is entirely appropriate that the statement of the causes was also made.
