"Previously" refers to what was taught in brief in the section on etiology (*nidāna*); that is, regarding those exogenous (*āgantu*) disorders arising from two or three *doṣas* which were mentioned there in summary, hear now their detailed characteristics here. However, those fevers such as *vāta-jvara* and others produced by a single *doṣa* have already been explained at length in that very place, and thus need not be stated again here.
"Vertigo" (*bhrama*) is that by which one perceives oneself as if situated on a moving wheel; alternatively, *bhrama* means delusion (*bhrānti*).
"Coldness," "cold state," and "stiffness" refer to being as if wrapped in a garment;
"fever of moderate intensity" refers to a fever that is not excessively intense.
"Sweat-stopping" (svedastambha) means the non-emission of sweat.

Regarding the phrase "after [the symptoms of] sannipāta fever," some commentators explain that the word *ūrdhva* (after/above) signifies "additional"; thus, the meaning is: "I shall describe those symptoms of the fever produced by a modified (*vikṛti*) and discordant (*viṣama*) combination of the humors, which are additional to the symptoms of the sannipāta fever produced by a natural (*prakṛti*) and balanced (*sama*) combination. They argue that if things such as "tearful, turbid, and sunken eyes" were to be mentioned here, they would not be present merely through the conjunction of the symptoms described for the individual fevers of Vāta and the others; rather, they occur in a fever produced by a modified and discordant combination due to the power of that specific conjunction.

We, however, say this: if by the word "subsequent" (ūrdhva) here it were intended to denote the definition of fever produced by a morbid and discordant combination (vikṛti-viṣama-samavāya), then the symptoms that arise from the conjunction of the individual doshas' characteristics—such as "burning at one moment and coldness at another"—would not be mentioned here. Rather, those symptoms which generally manifest here are described as being produced both by a morbid and discordant combination and by a natural and concordant combination (prakṛti-sama-samavāya). Therefore, the meaning of the word "subsequently" (ūrdhvam) is "after this" (ataḥ pareṇa).
"Nirbhugna" means extremely crooked; "paridagdha" means burnt, being black in color and rough to the touch like a cow's tongue.
Lassitude of the limbs is the state of having limbs that lack strength; spitting is the slight disgorging from the mouth of blood or bile;
and rolling of the head is the turning of the eyes here and there.
The emaciation of the limbs is continuous and uninterrupted due to being filled with the *doṣas*.
Regarding the *koṭha* (urticaria), Bhālukīya states: "Resembling the bite of a *varaṭī* (gadfly), it is itchy, red, and arises from blood, phlegm, and bile."
"Those who know [the truth] call momentary arising and perishing 'koṭha'";
muteness is the state of speaking slowly or the absence of speech.
He states the characteristics of the incurability and the difficulty of curing *sannipāta* with the words beginning "doṣa," etc.;
here, the word *doṣa* refers to the morbid humors (*mala*) when accompanied by the prefix *vibaddha*.
"In one whose digestive fire is extinguished" (*naṣṭāgnau*) means that, in comparison to other fevers, the digestive fire has been extinguished to a greater degree.
"One in whom all symptoms are complete" (*sarvasampūrṇalakṣaṇaḥ*) refers to one who possesses all the symptoms in their entirety and in a powerful state.
By designating this condition as "incurable" or "difficult to cure," it is shown that it does not constitute a case that is easily curable (*sukhasādhya*).
As it has been said: "The *sannipāta* [disorder] is the most difficult among diseases to treat," and likewise by Bhāluki: "One who treats *sannipāta* must fight against death itself.
(Sūtra-sthāna 25, verse 109)
Regarding the phrase "in the Nidāna," etc.:

in the *Nidāna* [section], specifically the *Jvara-nidāna*, it was previously stated by the passage beginning with "there, of the aforementioned symptoms" (*tatra yathoktānāṃ liṅgānām*, Ni. A. 1); since it is being stated again because it pertains to the current context, there is no redundancy.

By that [fever], its own specific characteristics were stated; thus, by that fever in the form of *dvandva* (dual combination), the characteristics of *dvandva* are stated, and likewise, by that in the form of *sannipāta* (combined morbidity), the characteristics of *sannipāta* are stated—this is the meaning.
Analyzing the fourfold adventitious [nature], he says: "The adventitious," and so forth.

The *kaśā* is known as the "arrow," and the *muṣṭi* is known as the "nail. When struck or severely injured, it generally causes blood to become excessively vitiated; the meaning is that while it excessively vitiates the blood, it vitiates the flesh and other tissues only slightly.

Although it was stated in the *Nidāna* [section] that "there, by the wind produced from trauma (*abhighāta*), which is based upon vitiated blood" (Ni.A.1), nevertheless, the distinction here is that the direct vitiation of the blood is indicated, as well as the slight vitiation of the muscle (*māṃsa*) and other tissues.

Regarding the specific association of the *doṣas* in fevers born of affliction (*abhiṣaṅga-jvara*), he says "kāmādi" and so forth. Now, in the *Nidāna-sthāna* it was stated: "Furthermore, that born of affliction is associated with *vāta* and *pitta*" (Ni. A. 1). Why, then, is it said here that the fever born of affliction by spirits (*bhūta-abhiṣaṅga*) is associated with all three *doṣas*? It is not so; what was stated there—"it is associated with *vāta* and *pitta*"—was said with reference to that which generally arises from afflictions such as desire (*kāma*). For among those [afflictions] beginning with desire, in some cases *vāta* and in others *pitta* is involved; thus, the association with *vāta* and *pitta* should be understood accordingly.

Regarding the phrase "characterized by the common features of spirits" (*bhūtasāmānyalakṣaṇā*): the eight [entities] beginning with the gods are called "spirits" (*bhūta*) in the context of insanity (*unmāda*). Among them, the symptoms that belong to a spirit acting as the agent of possession are identical here to the symptoms of the humors (*doṣa*) in the fever caused by spirits (*bhūtajvara*).

On this point, the Kashmiris recite the passage beginning with "From contact with the wind from poisonous trees" (*viṣavṛkṣānilasparśāt*), which describes the poison-born fever (*viṣajvara*); however, even for those who do not recite it, the poison-born fever is included within the category of fever born of affliction (*abhiṣaṅgaja*), since the fever arising from the smell of poison or medicine is also subsumed under affliction.
Others, however, cast poison-born [fever] into the category of that born from the humors (*doṣaja*), on the grounds that it is produced by bile caused by poison;
*abhicāra* refers to rites such as the recitation of *Atharva*-mantras and oblations for the purpose of harming others;
*abhiśāpa* is simply the act of cursing.
The *siddhas* are those perfected through mantras, medicinal herbs, asceticism, tranquility, and so forth.
Regarding this, the Kashmiris recite the passage beginning with "It has been said concerning the fever of combined humors" (*sannipātajvarasyoktam*), but that [text] is not very well known.
He states the property that distinguishes the adventitious from the innate: "Those [are] prior," and so forth;
"pure" means free from innate defects.

"By their own" means by the characteristics of their own [specific] doshas. "Distinguished by specific causes and remedies" means that they possess causes and remedies distinct from those of endogenous fever; therein, the specific cause is injury and so forth, and the remedy consists of affusion, mantras, and the like.
With the words "combined" (*saṃsṛṣṭā*) and so forth, he states at the end the pathogenesis (*samprāpti*) common to all fevers;
for the pathogenesis of all fevers is indeed their very manifestation (*ākṛti*), and therefore its mention here does not contradict the sūtra.

Alternatively, since the characteristics of *sāma* fever have reached their turn to be discussed, the "mode of arrival" (*samprāpti*) is now stated in order to demonstrate the rationale for the emergence of these characteristics of *sāma* fever, such as anorexia and so forth;
"combined" (*saṃsṛṣṭāḥ*) means existing in pairs,
and "congregated" (*sannipatitāḥ*) means all three having come together.
"Digestion" refers to the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni) by virtue of being the cause of digestion;
"from its location" refers to the *grahaṇī*, for the *grahaṇī* is indeed the seat of the digestive fire;
"by its own" means by the heat of the [bodily] humors (*doṣa*); "by that" means by the heat of the digestive fire.
Regarding "of the bodily heat" (*dehoṣmaṇaḥ*): this refers to the natural heat (*prākṛtoṣman*) that pervades the entire body.

Although wind (*vāta*) and phlegm (*śleṣman*) do not possess heat in the same way as bile (*pitta*), nevertheless, because they are composed of the primary elements (*bhūta*), they do possess heat, and it is this that is to be understood here. For it must be stated in the chapter on the *grahaṇī*: "The five heats—earthy, watery, fiery, airy, and ethereal—exist together with the ether. (Ci. A. 15)

Alternatively, by the word "tena" (by that), he indicates the heat (*ūṣman*) of the humors (*doṣa*) produced by the power of the supernatural form (*divyarūpa*) presiding over the fever; or else, he demonstrates the heat of the *pitta* acquired through the general pathogenesis (*samprāpti*) of fever, for *pitta* is necessarily present in every case of fever. As it has been said: "There is no heat without *pitta*, and there is no fever without heat" (Vāgbhaṭa, Cikitsāsthāna, Chapter 1).
The term "kevalam" (only/merely) refers to the whole [of the preceding].
In the phrase "the man does not obtain perspiration," the word "generally" (prāyaḥ) should be supplied, because perspiration is also mentioned in certain cases of fever;
"man" (nā) refers to a person.
"Without emission" means constantly attached.
"Of the humors" refers to the non-activation and non-discharge of the humors associated with impurities;
"destruction of hunger" means the absence of appetite.
There is no indigestion, nor is there undigested feces;
there is no exhaustion, nor is there emaciation of the flesh.
By the passage beginning with "hunger and emaciation," [the author] describes the characteristics of a fever free from *āma*.

In this context, hunger and the other symptoms, arising from the digestion (*pāka*) of the *doṣas*, constitute the characteristics of a fever initiated by *doṣas* free from *āma*, even without the passage of eight days.

Aṣṭāha, however, declares that when hunger and other such symptoms are absent, even if there is no digestion (*pāka*) of the *doṣas*, the fever—meaning the disease—is free from *āma* and thus fit for the administration of medicine. For this very reason, the statement, "One should have him drink either a digestive (*pācana*) or a pacifying (*śamanīya*) decoction," presents two alternatives: when, during the eight-day period, the signs of the digestion of the *doṣas* such as hunger and so forth do not arise, then a digestive medicine should be given for the sake of digesting the *doṣas*; but if the onset of hunger and the rest has occurred, then a pacifying medicine should be given, since the fever is in every respect free from *āma*.
Teaching this very state of being entirely devoid of relish, Kharanāda stated: "The mere absence of fever for seven days is not the sole characteristic of a fever free from relish;
for in a *sannipāta* fever, the humors (*malas*) may take a long time to ripen, and symptoms such as emaciation occur even after the seven-day period has passed."

"Therefore, having observed these two [symptoms], one should diagnose the fever as being free of *āma*. Thus, Suśruta established that the state of being free from *āma* (*nirāmatā*) occurs before eight days, based on the observation of hunger and other signs produced by the digestion of the *doṣas*, while demonstrating the administration of medicine prior to the eighth day, as it is said: "Medicine may even be administered before [the eighth day] once the *doṣa* has been digested" (Su.U.A. 39).

Therefore, the eighteen [defilements], beginning with hunger, should be understood as the characteristics [of the states of existence], both individually and collectively, according to the logic already explained.

Although medicine (*auṣadha*) was mentioned first by the phrase "medicine and the sequence of treatment" (*sauṣadhaṃ ca kriyākramam*), nevertheless, because it serves as a qualifier for the sequence of treatment, it is secondary; thus, setting aside the medicine, he describes the sequence of treatment starting with "in acute fever" (*navajvare*).
The sequence (*krama*) of treatment—that is, the method of medical therapy—is such that, therein, the prohibition of what is unwholesome comes first.
By the word "food" (*anna*),

Hārīta refers specifically to heavy food (*gurvanna*), for he has stated: "In the case of a new fever (*navajvara*), sexual intercourse and other such acts individually provoke the *doṣas*, and the consumption of heavy food also causes constipation (*viṣṭambha*) and provokes the *doṣas*."
The plural number in "astringent decoctions" (*kaṣāyān*) is used because it refers to the genus; therefore, the meaning is that one should avoid astringent [substances].
For it has been stated here by Jatūkarṇa: "In acute fever, one should avoid astringent taste, heavy food, hot food, unctuous food, bathing, and massage.

Regarding the passage beginning with "in fever" (*jvare*), the term *laṅghana* here intends fasting (*anaśana*). Although ten types of *laṅghana* were described in the chapter on lightening and nourishing therapies (*laṅghanabṛṃhaṇīya*) starting from "purification is of four kinds" (*sūtra* 22), nevertheless, because they are applied here according to specific conditions, the restriction that it is *laṅghana* alone should be understood as an inclusive determination (*samuccīyamānāvadhāraṇa*), excluding the scope of exceptions. For example, as in: "He himself begot two sons, Nara and Nārāyaṇa alone."
In that state, emesis also occurs, as will be described later.

As for what was stated in the chapter on lightening and nourishing therapies (*laṅghanabṛṃhaṇīya*)—where fever is listed among phlegm-pitta disorders such as fever and vomiting, and it is said: "The wise physician should generally treat those [disorders] first with digestive remedies" (*Sūtra-sthāna* 22)—there he means that digestion should be performed at the beginning of the administration of medicine, not necessarily at the very onset of the fever; therefore, the mention of lightening therapy (*laṅghana*) at the outset here is not contradictory.

Regarding what was stated by Hārīta, "One should first administer emesis for the purpose of purifying pitta and śleṣman," that is to be understood as applying to the state to be described later, beginning with the words "those in whom kapha predominates. By the word *kṣaya*, one should understand either fever caused by the depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu-kṣaya*) or the fever of *rājayakṣman*; by the word *anila*, there is the inclusion of *nirāma-anila* (vitiated wind without associated toxins); or alternatively, by the compound *kṣaya-anila*, there is the inclusion of wind aggravated by the depletion of the bodily constituents, as it has been said: "The provocation of vāyu occurs due to the depletion of the constituents and by the obstruction of its pathways" (Ci. A. 28).

However, when the *vāyu* becomes aggravated due to an obstruction of the channels (*mārgāvaraṇa*), it generally becomes associated with *āma* because of its obstructive nature (*āvarakadharmitā*). In that case, fasting (*laṅghana*) must indeed be performed in the proper measure, as it has been said: "Even when *vāta* is associated with *āma*, one should certainly perform fasting by means of skillful application for the sake of digesting the *āma*, but not in the same manner as in the case of *kapha*."

Even after describing fevers caused by wind (*anilajvara*), the mention of fevers caused by desire and so forth (*kāmādijvara*) is for the purpose of demonstrating that these latter fevers are not to be treated with fasting (*alaṅghana*), even though they may later become associated with wind; for even at the outset, when there is no connection with wind, they remain unfit for fasting.
He states the result of fasting (laṅghana) with the words beginning "by fasting" (*laṅghanena*), etc.

"Without contradicting the vital breaths" (*prāṇāvirodhinā*) means without contradicting strength; here, "contradiction" is spoken of in terms of causing excessive depletion. Since health belongs only to one who possesses strength, health is said to have strength as its basis.
By the word "yat" (which), he refers back to health.

Demonstrating that the prescribed fasting (*laṅghana*) acts as a digestive (*pācana*), he mentions other digestive measures such as sudation (*sveda*) and so forth, beginning with the words "Fasting," etc.
Here, "time" refers to eight days;

the bitter taste (*tikta-rasa*) is to be understood here as a flavoring agent for gruels, drinks, and the like, for the independent administration of medicinal drugs is strictly prohibited during the acute stage (*taruṇa*).
For it has been said: "Medicine for one with the disorder of undigested matter (āmadoṣa) further inflames the fever.

Although this refers to "undigested humors," the fact that he specifies "in the case of acute fever" indicates that after eight days, when the fever is no longer acute and the humors remain undigested, the primary treatment authorized is the drinking of decoctions (kaṣāya) as a digestive (pācana) measure, rather than fasting (laṅghana) and other such methods.
Regarding the statement that water should be given specifically during certain conditions such as the time of fasting (laṅghana), he says "to one who is thirsty," and so forth;
this applies to fever caused by vāta, fever caused by kapha, and fever caused by both vāta and kapha.
In fevers arising from alcohol or from phlegm (kapha) and other humors, cold water is also to be understood as appropriate;
"boiled with bitter [herbs]" refers to being boiled with musta and others as will be mentioned later;
and "both" refers to both hot water and cold water boiled with bitter herbs.

Although water is not specifically mentioned here for fevers caused by the three *doṣas* (*tridoṣa*) or by *kapha* and *pitta*, nevertheless, because of the authority of what was stated generally in the *Vimānasthāna*—beginning with, "Why indeed do they give warm water to those suffering from fever? (*Vi. A.* 3)—warm water alone should be given. However, in the case of a *vāta-paittika* fever that causes excessive burning and so forth, cool water should be given; this too has been indicated in the *Vimāna* itself by the passage beginning with, "When *pitta* is excessively increased" (*Vi.

The six-fold formulation beginning with *mustā* is for the preparation of a medicinal drink (*pānīya*). Here, *śuṇṭhī* and *atiktā* are prescribed because they alleviate fever caused by the corruption of the stomach (*āmāśaya*). Regarding the instruction "one should give water that has been boiled and cooled," this refers to the purification of water (*jala-saṃskāra*); it does not involve the preparation of a decoction (*kvātha*) according to the general rules for decoctions. Rather, it follows the specific rules for the purification of water. Although these specific rules are not explicitly stated in independent treatises, they are established by the practice of the elders and are indeed authoritative.

And that [is stated] as follows: "When the six-fold [decoction] and other preparations are used with water that has been boiled and cooled, one should prepare the medicinal substance in the measure of one *karṣa* from one *prastha* of water;
it should be administered when half-boiled for drinking or in the preparation of gruel (*peyā*) and the like. The meaning of this technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) is indeed clear.
Without distinction, regarding acute and chronic fever, he states that emesis is to be administered according to the specific stage of the disease: "Those in whom *kapha* predominates," and so forth.
Those for whom *kapha* is predominant are "those with *kapha* as the primary factor.

The term "agitated" (*utkliṣṭān*) means those that are intent on moving outward due to nausea and other symptoms; by the phrase "situated in the stomach" (*āmāśayasthitān*), it shows that they have left the entire body and reached the stomach.

By the phrase "those which cause fever," he shows that one should eliminate such fever-inducing *doṣas* in a case of acute fever (*navajvara*) by means of emetics, and not otherwise; by the word "at the proper time" (*kāle*), he indicates this should be done in the aforementioned state;

and by the plural form "by emetics" (*vamanaib*), he demonstrates the application of many formulations of emetic substances according to the requirements of the patient's constitution and other factors.
By the phrase "of those who should not be vomited," he prohibits emesis for those such as pregnant women and others unfit for it;

furthermore, in this case, since the morbid humor (doṣa) has already become agitated on its own, oleation and sudation—which serve to agitate the humor—are either not performed at all or are performed only in small measure.
He states the fault in emesis when it occurs apart from the prescribed stages, beginning with "anupasthita" and so forth;
"pervading the entire body" means they have followed into the subtle vessels, the skin, and other parts.
They are called *sāmā* because they are solidified (*styāna*) and motionless (*apracala*) by virtue of being *sāman*.
They are "established in the elements" (*dhātustha*), meaning they are situated in a state of ultimate penetration into the elements;
thus, they are "not easily removed" (*asunirhara*). Alternatively, they are "not easily removed" because they extract the vital breaths (*asu*).

Here, with the words "the purposes of fruits," etc., he provides an illustration: just as the natural juices of raw fruits become dangerous when extracted, so too are the aforementioned defects; "sātyayā" means accompanied by calamity (savyāpadaḥ). 147–148.
He states what should be done after emesis and fasting: "Vamitam," etc.
Regarding "emeticated" (*vamita*) and "fasted" (*laṅghita*), depending on the condition, sometimes one has been emeticated, sometimes fasted, and sometimes both emeticated and fasted.
For when, after emesis, proper purification has not yet occurred, then even lightening therapy (laṅghana) is performed on that day at the appropriate time.

"At the time fit for the administration of food" means with gruels prepared with the respective medicinal drugs—whatever medicine, such as long pepper (pippalī) or ginger (nāgara), is to be prescribed for a specific case in a particular gruel—with those prepared [gruels]; or alternatively, whatever digestive medicine is to be prescribed for a particular fever, [the gruel is] prepared with that.
For it is stated in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*: “At the time of eating, a beneficial *peyā* prepared with appropriate digestive agents [should be given]” (*Su.U.A.* 39).
The phrase “preceded by *maṇḍa*” means those in which *maṇḍa* is the primary component;
in that case, one should first drink the *maṇḍa*, and thereafter the thin portion of the *peyā* should be administered.

"Until the fever becomes mild" means until the intensity of the fever ceases due to the digestion (*pāka*) of the *doṣas*. Even in the absence of the fever becoming mild, this six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) may begin either from the day of starting the liquid diet (*peyā*) or from the day the fever arose; we shall examine these two positions later in the passage beginning with "when six days have passed for one who has had fever. In the phrase "for the purpose of inducing perspiration" (*svedanāya*), the word "occur" (*bhavanti*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

Having described the suitability of *yavāgū* (gruel) for fever, he states the cases where a fever patient is not a fit subject for it: "Except... and so forth. The phrase "except that arising from liquor" indicates a prohibition regarding fever caused by liquor.

Likewise, in the disease of *madātyaya* (alcoholism), as well as any fever born of other causes; likewise in the summer season; likewise in a fever where *pitta* and *kapha* predominate; and likewise in a fever of one who has upward hemorrhaging (*ūrdhva-rakta-pitta*)—in all these cases, *peyā* (thin gruel) should not be administered.
In this context, although fever arising from conditions such as alcoholism (madātyaya) is generally fit for gruel, it is considered unfit for gruel [in these cases];
by the phrase "when pitta and kapha are predominant," it is taught that gruel should not be administered when there is an excessive manifestation of pitta and kapha.
Consequently, gruel should be administered in fevers born of kapha and in fevers born of pitta where the doshas have not yet fully manifested.

For it is said in another treatise: "Even when phlegm is diminished by the sequence of fasting and other treatments, gruels (yavāgu) are indeed recommended; likewise, this same procedure applies even in cases of bile.
And similarly in this very work: "Or else, one with a bile disorder should drink [the preparation] cold, mixed with honey."
By the phrase "lājapeyām," [the author] will also prescribe gruel (yavāgū) for pitta.

As for what was stated by Hārīta— "Just as rain upon a heap of dust excessively moistens the mud, so too, when phlegm (śleṣman) is greatly increased, gruel increases the phlegm"— that should be understood as referring to a case of excessively increased kapha.
Others, however, maintain that gruel is prohibited for those individuals in whom *pitta* and *kapha* are combined and predominant;

yet, if the reading is "and when *kapha* and *pitta* move upward" (*ūrdhvage kaphapitte ca*), then the meaning is that even for one suffering from a *vāta*-fever, when *kapha* and *pitta* move upward and are expelled by themselves through vomiting, then too gruel should not be administered. In the *Suśruta*, however, it says: "For one overwhelmed by *kapha* and *pitta*, and likewise for one with upward-moving blood and *pitta*..."
It has been stated: "For one who is habitually addicted to liquor, gruel is not beneficial" (Su.U.Tantra 39). Therefore, the reading "in upward-moving rakta-pitta" is appropriate.

Although by the statement, "In upward-moving [hemorrhage], nourishment first" (Ci. A. 4), *tarpaṇa* is indeed prescribed for upward-moving *raktapitta*—thereby setting aside *yavāgū*—nevertheless, this prescription of the sequence beginning with *tarpaṇa* applies also to the fever of one suffering from upward-moving *raktapitta*.
*Tarpaṇa* consists of parched grain (*saktu*) saturated with water;
it removes fever, as do fruits such as grapes, pomegranates, and others.
For the statement says: "A refreshing drink (tarpaṇa) made with grapes, pomegranates, dates, priyāla, and parūṣaka should be prepared for those requiring refreshment; it destroys fever. (155)
One for whom the *tarpaṇa* has been digested is called "one whose *tarpaṇa* is digested.
The alternative options between mung bean soup and the broth of wild game should be understood as depending on the patient's suitability (*sātmya*) and their strength (*bala*).

For a weak person generally has a weak digestive fire; therefore, mung bean soup should be given to such a person because of its lightness, whereas for another, the meat broth of wild animals (jāṅgala) is appropriate.
Now he speaks regarding the subject of drinking decoctions (kaṣāya): "pācana" and so forth;
"pācana" means the digestion of undigested morbid humors (āmadoṣa), and "śamanīya" means the pacification of digested morbid humors.

And these two alternatives should be understood, according to their suitability and in their respective order, as referring to cases where the *doṣas* are immature (*āma*) and where the *doṣas* are matured (*pakva*).

"When six days have passed" means starting from the onset of the fever, once six days have elapsed. Therefore, the meaning of the statement is that on the seventh day, the patient should be given light food in proper quantity and form, and on the eighth day, one should administer a decoction (*kaṣāya*) to the fever patient.

In this way, the application of either a digestive (*pācana*) or a pacifying (*śamanīya*) treatment becomes appropriate within the previously established rule of eight days for the elimination of *āma*.

Now, an objection may be raised: regarding the administration of *peyā* (gruel), it is stated that "the wise [physician] should continue for six days or until the fever becomes mild. Consequently, the six-day period would be occupied by the *peyā* alone. Furthermore, fasting (*laṅghana*) was previously prescribed at the onset of fever; and although its duration was not specified there, it should be performed for as long as it takes to achieve the results of fasting described in the text beginning with "when [the doshas] have been reduced by fasting. However, Hārīta has also indicated a specific time, as follows: "One should administer fasting to those who require it in accordance with the nature of the doshas."

“[One should administer] for three nights, one night, or six nights in the case of fever. By this, since the period of fasting for fever lasts [one day], and likewise [the period of light diet] lasts for six days, there occurs an exceeding of eight days starting from the day the fever began. Therefore, let the digestive or pacifying decoction (kaṣāya) be administered on the eighth day counting from the day the fever began; thus, the intention is that after the six-day period of using thin gruel (peyā) has passed, one should cause the patient to drink a digestive or pacifying decoction. Likewise: “In fever, thin gruels, decoctions, milk, ghee, and purgatives [are indicated].”

By the passage, "Every sixth day, [the decoction] should be administered, having observed the relative strength and weakness of the *doṣas*" (Ci. A. 30), it is stated that the six-day period for decoctions (*kaṣāya*) follows the six-day period for the administration of gruel (*peyā*); however, this does not mean it follows the six days from the onset of fever. Here we say: by the statement, "Or the wise physician [should administer it] for six days until the fever becomes mild," the administration of gruel is prescribed for a period of six days starting from the day the fever arises. For gruel is primarily employed in cases of fever for the purpose of digesting the *doṣas*, as it has been said: "Fasting, sudation, time, gruels (*yavāgū*), and bitter tastes..."

Regarding the statement, "Digestives [are used] for undigested humors in acute fever," it is taught that the humors are to be treated with fasting and other digestive measures specifically within the first eight days; beyond the eighth day, digestion is said to be achieved by decoctions alone.

In that regard, for a Vata-fever where fasting is not indicated, the liquid gruel (*peyā*) should be administered starting from the first day and continued for six days. Even when the fever has been treated with fasting for one, two, or three days, the *peyā* should be employed for five, four, or three days respectively, beginning from the onset of the fever and continuing until the end of the sixth day.

However, where even the humors (*doṣas*) are in a state of equilibrium, or in cases of *sannipāta* fever, fasting (*laṅghana*) alone is administered for six nights or according to a sequence of six nights and so forth; in such specific prescriptions, this general rule of six nights for gruel (*peyā*) does not apply. Furthermore, when excessive fasting is employed, gruel is not taken for the purpose of digesting the humors, but rather to kindle the digestive fire (*agni*) that has been depleted by extensive fasting; once the digestive fire has been rekindled, the administration of medicinal decoctions (*auṣadha-pāna*) follows.

In passages such as “In fever, gruels and decoctions” (Ci. A. 30), the term *peyā* (gruel) serves as an indicator for all therapeutic measures that share its function, such as fasting (*laṅghana*) and so forth. Consequently, where gruels are prohibited—as in fevers arising from alcohol and similar conditions—the six-day period should be understood as applying even to the sequence beginning with *tarpaṇa* (satiating drinks).

Thus, since the general rule is that fasting, digestive treatments (*pācana*), and the like must be administered during the first six days, it is stated that "gruel is to be given for six days. To this effect, a statement is also cited in the Suśruta-saṃhitā: "When the morbid humor (*doṣa*) is not digested by means of fasting, water, and gruels, then [one should treat it] with those things that eliminate bad taste in the mouth, thirst, and loss of appetite..."

Having stated, "One should treat [the patient] with decoctions that are digestive, pleasing to the heart, and fever-alleviating" (Su.U.Tantra. A. 39), the rule regarding the timing for drinking these decoctions is declared: "Some maintain that the medicine should be administered after seven nights," and so forth.

Consequently, since there is no prohibition against administering medicine after the six treatments beginning with fasting (*laṅghana*) have been completed, Suśruta’s statement implies approval for giving medicine after seven nights.

Likewise, in the Caraka Saṃhitā, fasting and other measures are prescribed for acute fever (*taruṇajvara*) by the passage beginning "Fasting, sudation... and so on; furthermore, the state of being acute (*taruṇatā*) lasts for exactly seven days.
As it is stated in the *Puṣkalāvata*: “The wise say that fever is ‘acute’ (*taruṇa*) for up to seven nights, ‘intermediate’ (*madhya*) for twelve nights, and beyond that, ‘chronic’ (*purāṇa*).

Thus, for an acute fever occurring after seven days, fasting, gruel, and so forth are generally not prescribed even by Caraka; likewise, Hārīta, after describing fasting, warm water, drinking water boiled with *mustā* and other herbs, and gruel, stated: “One should employ this regimen for six nights; on the seventh day...”

"One should drink decoctional formulations that destroy fever, properly prepared. Likewise, Kharanāda also says: "Therefore, whether the patient has fasted or not, or has undergone emesis, one should first treat the fever in one afflicted by it, because of its suitability [to the patient's condition]."

Having described the sequence beginning with *tarpaṇa* (satiating drinks) and so forth, starting with "with gruels according to the [specific] *doṣa*," it is stated: "Thus has been declared the six-night regimen for curing acute fever (*navajvara*);
thereafter, digestive (*pācanīya*) or pacifying (*śamana*) treatments are beneficial for the fever."

Furthermore, regarding this prescription for the administration of decoctions (*kaṣāya*) on the seventh day found in another treatise (*tantrāntara*), it should be understood that there is no contradiction, as it is not far removed from the administration of decoctions prescribed for the eighth day due to their proximity. Therefore, starting from the onset of fever, when six days have passed and the patient has been fed light food, the administration of decoctions occurs; likewise, the regimen of gruel (*yavāgū*) continues for up to six days. Thus, statements such as "In fever, gruels and decoctions [are used]" (Ci. A. 30) are general rules (*utsarga-vidhi*); consequently, it is entirely logical that these may be set aside in certain instances. 160—

Now, by means of the general term "decoction" (kaṣāya), he describes the fault in administering a decoction—which is prohibited during acute fever and causes great harm—during acute fever, beginning with the words "they become stiffened" (stabhyante):
"stiffened" means they become characterized by immobility;
"they do not undergo digestion" means they do not digest easily even after a long time.
"Because of its constipating nature" means because its intrinsic nature is to cause constipation;
for it has been said: "Astringent [taste] is constipating and cold" (Sūtra-sthāna 26).
This point is also stated by Hārīta: "They do not praise astringent [taste] for people suffering from acute fever."
"When the humors are agitated by the astringent, they are very difficult to conquer."

Previously, in the chapter on the "Six Hundred Purgatives" (*Ṣaḍvirecanaśatāśritīya*), the term *kaṣāya* was used even for the five types of pharmaceutical preparations such as fresh juice (*svarasa*) and others. Therefore, if here the term *kaṣāya* were used in its general sense to exclude all preparations like fresh juice made from sweet and other tastes, then it would follow that those very fluids are excluded from the list of the six-fold water (*ṣaḍaṅgapānīya*)—which must necessarily be included within the five-fold pharmaceutical preparations—as well as from the liquids used for preparing gruels (*yavāgū*). Since the administration of the six-fold water and the liquids for gruels must be included within these five-fold preparations (because the application of medicine is subsumed under the five-fold pharmaceutical preparations), he says "but not... (*na tu...*) and so forth, so that there may be no exclusion of *kaṣāya* as a category encompassing all pharmaceutical preparations.

The phrase "not with reference to a preparation" (na tu kalpam uddiśya) refers to the specific preparations consisting of fresh juice (svarasa), paste (kalka), decoction (śṛta), cold infusion (śīta), and powder (phāṇṭa). The meaning is that what is prohibited is a "decoction-decoction" (kaṣāyakaṣāya)—that is, a decoction prepared from substances such as āmalaka and others in the form of fresh juice and so forth.

Furthermore, by this prohibition of fresh juice and other forms made from astringent (kaṣāya) tastes, there is no implication that fresh juice and other forms made from sweet (madhura) and other tastes may be used in acute fever (taruṇajvara); for medicinal substances such as fresh juice that are excessively heavy (atiguru) are not prescribed in acute fever.

By that prohibition of "decoctions" (*kaṣāya*) as a general category, there is established no contradiction with the prescribed decoction prepared from bitter substances using the six-fold method (*ṣaḍaṅga-kalpanā*) and so forth; however, this does not constitute a prescription for un-prescribed fresh juices (*svarasa*) and the like.

For regarding heavy medicinal substances such as fresh juices, there is a prohibition in the case of acute fever: "For medicine given to one whose doshas are undigested (*āmadoṣa*) further inflames the fever" (Suśruta Uttaratantra, Chapter 39).

Others, however, say: Since the drinking of decoctions (*kaṣāya*) is prescribed for the seventh day after the sixth night in the *Svatantre* [the independent treatise] with the words "digestive and pacifying" and so forth, one perceives a contradiction therein—namely, that on the seventh day the fever is still in its acute stage (*taruṇa*), and the drinking of decoctions is prohibited during an acute fever. To demonstrate that there is no prohibition on the seventh day for a decoction made from substances such as sweet ones (*madhura*), whereas there is a prohibition on the seventh day for a decoction made from astringent substances (*kaṣāya*), the phrase "but not with reference to the pharmaceutical preparation" (*na tu kalpanām uddiśya*) and so forth was composed. Consequently, the meaning of the sentence is this: there is a total prohibition of all decoctions during the six days of fever and so forth, but when the seventh day arrives, there is a prohibition solely of the decoction made from astringent substances while the fever is still acute.
He states the means for preparing the meal following the gruel: "with soups," and so forth.

If there is a predominance of *kapha* and a strong digestive fire (*agni*), then [the diet] should be with soups (*yūṣa*); however, if there is a predominance of *vāta* or weakness [of the body], it should be with meat broths (*rasa*). This is the established rule. Furthermore, the various preparations of sour substances (*amla-vikalpa*) should be understood in consideration of the patient's suitability (*sātmya*) and the state of the digestive fire; for it will be said: "For one with weak digestion who is accustomed to sour things, one should prepare that [diet] even with sour ingredients."

In this case, a sour remedy such as pomegranate and other fruits that destroy fever should be prepared; "light" refers to both light in dosage and light by nature, such as red śāli rice and similar grains.
Regarding what should generally be done after ten days, he says "ataḥ" (from this) and so forth.

"When phlegm is diminished" means even when phlegm is diminished; if phlegm as a morbid humor (*doṣa*) is entirely absent, then ghee should be administered in a fever where vāta and pitta are predominant—this is the meaning.

Regarding the phrase "when fully matured" (*paripakveṣu*), although it would suffice to say simply "when completely ripened" (*sarvathā pakveṣu*), the inclusion of the term "excessive drinking" (*adhikapāna*) prohibits the use of ghee at this time through methods such as unctuous enemas (*anuvāsana*) or massages (*abhyaṅga*).
For indeed, unctuous enemas and massages are to be prescribed for a later stage.

This state, characterized by the predominance of *kapha*, *vāta*, and *pitta* in diminished strength, generally becomes manifest in all fevers after ten days due to the power of time alone. For instance, just as there is an increase in *vāta* in an elderly person, or the presence of undigested *doṣas* (*sāma*) in a recent fever, so too does there arise a predominance of *kapha* because the fever originates in the stomach (*āmāśaya*). However, after ten days, *kapha* is depleted through fasting and other measures, while *vāta* and *pitta* increase due to the parching of the bodily tissues by the heat of the fever and its drying effects.
As for the rule that gruel, decoctions, ghee, milk, and purgatives are to be administered every six days, that is general;
therefore, after ten days, if a specific condition arises during the second six-day period, the administration of ghee is not contradictory.
He states the exception to the aforementioned rule regarding the drinking of ghee: "nirdaśāham," etc.;
that for which ten days have passed is "nirdaśāha."

"Unleaped over" (*alaṅghitam*) means that the characteristic of having been leaped over has not yet arisen; it should be understood that this stage occurs because the fever was initiated by a predominance of *sāma* (undigested) doshas and due to improper treatment. One should treat that [fever] which is dominated by *kapha* and is "unleaped over" with decoctions (*kaṣāya*) until lightness [of the body] is achieved—this is the division of the text.

The meaning is that even when lightness has been achieved, if the predominance of *kapha* and the state of not having undergone fasting (*alaṅghitatā*) do not depart, then the administration of ghee alone must be continued.

Regarding the question of why meat broth—which is contrary to *kapha*—should be given as food during a fever beyond ten days even when *kapha* is predominant and the patient has not fasted, he says: "Strength indeed... and so forth.
The meaning is that eating with meat broth is strength-promoting.
With the words beginning with "burning," he describes the stage of milk.

Regarding the phrase "knowing the defects of constipation and those of discharge," here "constipated defect" (*baddhadoṣatva*) refers to the state of not being discharged at all, whereas "discharged defect" (*pracyutadoṣatva*) refers to being discharged only slightly.

In that regard, just as milk acts as a promoter for constipated [stools], so too it is beneficial for discharged [stools] by promoting their discharge despite obstructions; for this very reason, among the qualities of milk, it is stated: "wholesome when the feces are knotted" and likewise "wholesome in diarrhea" (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 1).
Alternatively, if the fault lies with the calf, cow’s milk should be given because it flows; but if it has fallen away, goat’s milk should be given because it is held back.

"If the fever does not reach subsidence through these treatments, then one should pacify it with purgatives"—by this statement, he shows that purgation is to be employed only when other treatments have failed, due to its being attended by many complications.

By the use of the plural "purgatives" (*virecanaiḥ*), both emesis and purgation are included; as it has been said: "Both [emesis and purgation] receive the name 'purgation' (*virecana*) because they purge the morbid humors and impurities" (Ka. A. 1). Likewise, in the detailed exposition of purgative formulations, he will describe only the formulations for both emesis and purgation.
Having described the purification for one not emaciated by fever, he now states the purification for one emaciated by fever, beginning with "of one emaciated by fever" and so forth;
"with milk" means by the drinking of milk.

Milk, by virtue of its laxative nature, becomes a remover of the *doṣas*; and since this laxative quality is designated as purgation (*virecana*), milk is mentioned here as being suitable for purgation.

Since the qualities of milk have already been obtained through the previously mentioned context, [the author] states the remaining quality regarding *nirūha* (non-unctuous enema), beginning with "In the *nirūha*," and so forth.
He states the scope of purgation (virecana) and non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) according to the distinction of the *doṣas* and the distinction of their locations, beginning with "pitta," etc.

The indications for emesis according to the differentiation of the *doṣas* and the differentiation of the locations have already been stated by the passage beginning with "those in whom *kapha* predominates" (*kaphapradhānān*), and thus are not repeated here. However, the distinction is as follows: the previously mentioned emesis prescribed for specific stages should be understood as applicable when the *doṣas* are spontaneously aggravated, whereas this emesis prescribed for chronic fever (*jīrṇajvara*) must be performed after aggravating the *doṣas* through oleation (*sneha*) and sudation (*sveda*).
Furthermore, the phrase "evacuation (*sraṃsana*) into the seat of *pitta*, specifically the lower part of the seat of *āmāśaya*" is the correct grammatical division.
He states the scope for non-unctuous enema (anuvāsana): "Fever," and so forth.
Even though antiquity is already established by the context, the word "purāṇe" expresses an extreme degree of antiquity.
With the words "gaurava" (heaviness) and so forth, he describes the subject of head-purgation (*śirovirecana*);
the phrase "of the head" is to be construed with both the preceding and the following [terms].
"Obstruction of the sense organs" (*indriyāṇāṃ vibandhaḥ*) refers to their dullness (*jāḍya*) in functioning toward their respective objects.
Having described internal cleansing, he speaks of external cleansing, beginning with the words "and massages" (abhyaṅgān) and so forth.
In this context, "pradeha" refers generally to an application that may be either thick or thin.

However, those who follow the opinion of Suśruta and accept a thick, drying *pradeha*, would imply that for the alleviation of burning sensations (*dāha*), a thick application should be used; yet, according to our view, it must be made thin. For it has been stated: "Even a thick paste of sandalwood, if ground too finely, causes a burning sensation," and so forth. (Ci. A. 30)

Having distinguished [fevers] as caused by cold and heat, one should differentiate between those intended for heat and those intended for cold, and apply treatments accordingly—cold-caused and heat-caused respectively. For it will be said: "One should administer massages, plasters, and affusions, distinguishing between the two types of fever according to the patient's desire and whether they are cold or hot. This quality of coldness or heat should be understood through the inherent power of the substances and through their processing.

"Remaining as skin alone" means that, through the departure of other bodily elements (*dhātu*), they are produced by defects residing in the skin alone; and those fevers for which an external material substance (*bhūtarūpa*) serves as the causal concomitant (*anvaya-kāraṇa*) are pacified by means of fumigation and other such treatments.
He states the latter half of the answer to the question concerning the sequence of medicines, beginning with "yeṣām" (of those who...).

Some read: “Red rice (*raktaśāli*) and others are recommended, along with *ṣaṣṭika* rice”; here, by the word “rice” (*śālayaḥ*), grains such as *yavaka* and the like are excluded. Others, however, read: “Red rice and others are recommended when old (*purāṇāḥ*”). Although it has already been stated that “awned grain (*śūkadhānya*) and leguminous grain (*śamīdhānya*) are praised when they have stood for a year” (Sūtra-sthāna 27), nevertheless, the word “old” (*purāṇāḥ*) is used to prohibit the consumption of non-old grain due to negligence.
There are ten types of gruels (yavāgū) beginning with *lājapeyā*.

Regarding these, Haricandra maintains that the first one is for the alleviation of *śleṣman* (phlegm). Alternatively, there may be eleven gruels: one consisting of *lājapeyā* which is easily digested, and a second prepared with long pepper (*pippalī*) and ginger (*nāgara*), followed by the remaining nine in the same manner.

The construction is: "one should drink [the decoction] with ginger and fermented gruel (sṛṣṭaviṭ). Alternatively, one suffering from pitta disorders should drink it cold and mixed with honey; this is because ginger, due to its sweet post-digestive effect (pāka) and its digestive properties (pācana), is employed in the treatment of pitta.
Here, the Vidārīgandhādi group refers to the *hrasvapañcamūla* (the small pentad of roots).
By the phrase "with barley" (*sayavām*), one should drink [the decoction] prepared with sixty grains of rice;

and by the passage beginning with "with *bilva*" (*sabilvām*) and ending with "boiled with *dhāvanī*," a single gruel (*yavāgū*) is prescribed for *parikartikā*, which is a pain shaped like a cutting instrument.
Kalaśī, siṃhapucchī, dhāvanī, and kaṇṭakārī;

and in this matter, regarding the proportions of water, rice, and other ingredients for preparing gruels (yavāgū), the practices of experienced physicians are honored and should be accepted as authoritative.

In this *Agniveśasaṃhitā*, it is taught: "Having boiled one *añjali* of powdered decoction ingredients in one *āḍhaka* of water until one-quarter remains, one should then prepare gruel (*yavāgū*) with that;
[adding] half a *karṣa* of long pepper (*kaṇā*) and ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), or one *pala* of any paste-like substance."
"Having prepared [the paste], one should cook another [type of gruel] with a prastha of water according to the proper method.
The word "another" refers to that which is distinct from the gruel previously mentioned as being prepared by means of a decoction; it means a gruel prepared by means of a paste (*kalka*).

Thus, the technical rule for preparing a gruel using one *pala* of paste in that context is indeed accepted here as well, since the preparation of the gruel is taught here using one *pala* of medicinal paste. For instance, the preparation of the *jīvantī*-gruel and others is stated to be accomplished with eight substances, each measuring the size of a *kola*.

As for what was stated there regarding "combined with *vṛkṣāmla*" and so forth, the addition of *vṛkṣāmla* is for the sake of acidity alone, and not necessarily in the measure of eight *māṣakas*. Alternatively, even if that too were measured at eight *māṣakas*, nevertheless, because the difference is not great, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) prescribing the preparation of one *pala* of paste is indeed accepted by the instruction to prepare a paste exceeding eight *māṣakas*. For it has been said: "With *jīvantī*, *ajājī*, *śaṭī*, *puṣkarāhva*, *kāravī*, *dīpyaka*, and the pulp of *bilva*, together with *yāvaśūka*, in the measure of a *badara* fruit, combined with *vṛkṣāmla* and fried in ghee and oil..."

"Gruel prepared according to that same method with the five spices (*pañcakola*) is beneficial for hemorrhoids, diarrhea, wind disorders, abdominal tumors, edema, heart disease, and weak digestion; it is identical to the former. (Ci. A. 12). Therefore, because this statement regarding the measure and signs of gruel is observed, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) prescribing a paste of one *pala* for the preparation of gruel is indeed accepted. Likewise, another rule associated with it, which indicates the quantity of half a *karṣa* for *kaṇā* and *śuṇṭhī*, is also accepted. However, regarding the quantity of substances for gruels prepared with decoctions and the like, this venerable rule of the elders is respected: "Whatever is used as a six-part (*ṣaḍaṅga*) preparation and so forth in waters that have been boiled and then cooled..."

“Then one should prepare a substance weighing one *karṣa* in one *prastha* of water; when it is half-boiled, it should be administered for drinking or in the preparation of gruels (*peyā*) and so forth.
By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), soups (*yūṣa*), meat broths (*rasa*), and the like are included here.

The determination of the procedure for the technical rule beginning with "one handful of crushed decoction-substances" (kvāthyadravyāñjaliṃ kṣuṇṇam), as well as for other unstated rules, and the investigation into the measurement of rice, water, and so forth required for preparing all types of gruel (yavāgū), have been thoroughly examined in the chapter on *Apāmārgataṇḍulīya* (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 4); that [section] should be followed.
The passage beginning with "mudgān" is a collection of substances for making soups (yūṣa) that are free from fever;
the method of preparing the soup is like the preparation of gruel (yavāgū).
"Mudga" is well-known by its own name.
188 - *Kulaka* is the *kāravellaka*.
Pāpacelika, pāṭhā-vegetable, kaṭhillaka, and red punarnavā. 189
The francolin partridge, the grey partridge, the antelope, and the black antelope.
The *upacakraka* is the *cakora*;
the *kālapuccha* is a particular kind of deer;
and the *hariṇa* is copper-colored.
The *pṛṣata* is a spotted deer.
Regarding the preparation of broth (*rasa*), the *Sūdaśāstra* states: "One should divide twelve *palas* of meat for a thick broth; six *palas* for a thin one; and one *pala* for a very clear broth."
Where, however, there is the preparation of the *rasa* with other substances, there the preparation should be explained as being like that of *yavāgū*.

By the phrase "knowing the variation of dosage," he shows that birds such as quails (*lāva*) should be given in such a quantity and with such a processing-based variation that they are neither heavy nor hot; thus, they do not cause an increase in fever due to heaviness or due to heat, which would otherwise suppress the digestive fire (*agni*).

— Some say that the verse beginning with "gharmāmbu," "uṣṇāmbu," and "gharmāmbvādi" is not of human authorship (anārṣa); that is not so. Since the suitability of warm water and wine as post-drinks (anupāna) had not been previously mentioned, this [verse] is included to establish that rule. Thus it is said in another treatise: "In fever, one should drink warm water; however, one who is habituated to wine should drink wine."
"For him, having observed the strength of the humors, wine is prescribed by means of reasoning.

By the words "heavy," "hot," and so forth, heavy, hot, and other such [qualities] are prohibited. Although the prohibition of astringent (kaṣāya) substances was previously stated in a general sense, it is repeated here both because of the context of the prohibition regarding food and because of the prohibition of those that are extremely unwholesome.
"Pākyam" means boiled (śṛtam).
Regarding the cold decoction (*śītakaṣāya*): a substance that has been crushed is placed in hot water and left overnight.

Here is the technical definition of the cold decoction: "The decoction which emerges from a substance that has been pounded and left in heated water overnight is designated as 'cold' (*śīta*)" (Sūtra-sthāna 4).

In this case as well, although the specific measure for the medicinal substance and the water is not stated, nevertheless, the medicinal substance should be taken in a quantity equal to the substance to be boiled (the *kvāthya-dravya*); as for the water, it should be taken in such a measure that when boiled, the resulting decoction (*kvātha*) is of a drinkable consistency, for there is no reduction in the amount of water here. Alternatively, water should be given according to the general rule: "For cold infusions (*śīta*) and hot infusions (*phāṇṭa*), one *pala* of medicine is soaked in six or four *palas* of water; for what is called a decoction (*rasa*), two *palas* [of medicine].

A cold infusion (*śītakaṣāya*) should be administered in cases where the doshas are very weak or when one is overcome by burning sensations (*dāha*), because of its mild potency and its cooling quality.

The third formulation consists of *parpaṭaka* together with *durālabhā*; the fourth is the *kirātatiktādi* group for weak digestion involving *pitta* and *kapha*, and the *pāṭhādi* group for *vāta* and *kapha* in cases of *pitta*.
And when there is a *bhelaka* (a medicinal powder) with *kirātatikta* and other ingredients, the group of seven beginning with *pāṭhā* is used for *kaphapitta* based on the authority of Jatūkarṇa;
for it is stated therein: "Bhūnimba, ghana, guḍūcī, śuṇṭhī, udīcya, uśīra, and pāṭhā.
Since the measure of the substances and so forth has not been specified here regarding the preparation of the decoction, the determination of the measure follows from general principle (*nyāya*).

In this context, although the specific procedure for preparing a decoction (*kvātha*) has not been explicitly stated here, nevertheless, the procedure for making a decoction that was taught in the *Vyādhitarūpīya* chapter—beginning with "having cut those parts to be excised into pieces, and having broken down those containing fat into small fragments, one should wash them and sprinkle them with water," and so forth, ending with "when the medicinal substances have lost their juice, one should remove the pot and [use] the strained decoction" (Vi. A. 7)—is to be understood as the procedure for preparing all decoctions.

For although the quantity of the substance to be boiled, the quantity of liquid, and the quantity of the decoction to be retained are not explicitly stated there, it is nevertheless understood that one should add as much of the substance to as much water as will result in the medicine losing its juice when cooked; likewise, it is understood that the decoction should be retained at that point where the medicinal drugs have lost their juice. And this loss of juice in the drugs is observed to occur precisely upon the depletion of three parts of the liquid; therefore, in the absence of a specific statement, a quarter-remnant (one-fourth remaining) must be made for all decoctions.
The addition of water for the purpose of decoction, however, depends upon the quantity of the medicinal substance.

In that process, when a soft substance is boiled with water four times its weight, a hard substance eight times its weight, and an even harder substance sixteen times its weight, it becomes "devoid of essence" (*gatarasa*) when one-fourth remains. This rule is applied when preparing large decoctions using fats and other such ingredients. However, where the substance to be boiled is small, the less of it there is, the more water is added even to a soft and small substance, because a small amount of water would not suffice to render the substance devoid of its essence.

Therefore, starting from one *karṣa* up to one *pala*, sixteen times the amount of water is given even for a mild decoction; however, from one *pala* upwards up to one *kuḍava*, eight times the amount of water is given. Thus, although the measure of the remaining water for substances whose proportions were not specifically prescribed has been stated by the Teacher through his mention of "loss of flavor," had he instead stated a fixed measure for the substances and so forth, then that distinct measure which depends upon the substance, as well as upon the oil or other base to be prepared and the specific material to be boiled, would not have been included.
And definitions from other independent [treatises] that express this same meaning are recorded here:

Kṛṣṇātreya states regarding the decoction to be drunk, "One should take one *pala* of the substance to be boiled and reduce it to one-fourth (*pādaśeṣita*), leaving half a *prastha*"; elsewhere it is also said, "For one *pala* of the substance to be boiled, sixteen-fold water is prescribed"; likewise, "From one *karṣa* up to one *pala*, one should add sixteen-fold water."

"Then, from one *kuḍava* onwards, the water should be eightfold. And in the *Suśruta*, regarding the technical rules for decoctions of fats and so forth: "Having poured in fourfold, eightfold, or sixteenfold water, one should boil it until a quarter remains and then remove it from the heat" (*Su.Ci.A.* 31). Due to such variations in the readings, the traditions of providing fourfold, eightfold, or sixteenfold water are heard; these are to be understood according to the difference in the hardness of the substances, as it has been said: "Fourfold water should be given for soft [substances], likewise eightfold for hard ones, and sixteenfold water should be given for those harder than hard."
In this way, the established rule regarding the terminology of other tantras must also be stated;

for it is heard in the Agniveśa: "Having added sixteen parts of water to the drug that is to be boiled after being crushed, it should be reduced to one-fourth; this is remembered as the procedure for decoction."

"The second [method] is declared to be with water four times [the quantity of the drug]. In this context, by the middle rule, eightfoldness of the water is also obtained. Therefore it has also been said: "Where the measure is not shown for the purpose of the medium cooking of substances, one should add water four times the amount of the medicine;
and the physician should have the decoction prepared until one-fourth remains."
In this manner, other technical definitions from other tantras should also be interpreted without contradiction.

Regarding this, some say: that preparation of decoction (*kaṣāya*) which is prescribed in the chapter on the "Form of Disease" (*Vyādhitarūpīya*) pertains specifically to the section on non-unctuous enemas (*nirūha*); such a method of preparing a decoction does not apply elsewhere. For example, in the case of *Balātaila*, the measurement stated in the passage beginning with, “Having boiled one hundred parts of *balā* and a quarter part of *guḍūcī* along with one-eighth part of *rāsnā* in one hundred *āḍhaka*s of water” (Ci. A. 28), does not apply to other decoctions, but is restricted to that specific instance alone.

It is not so; for even a rule prescribed for a specific subject matter is established as being equally applicable to other subjects as well, based on the consensus of the practice of experienced physicians, the corroboration of definitions in other treatises, and by observing that the treatment is similar despite differences in the specific medical system. For example, in the *Ikṣvākukalpa*, it is stated: "As long as [the substance] fallen into water remains fibrous and does not dissolve" (*Ka. A. 3*), and so forth; this definition of the cooking of a linctus (*leha-pāka-lakṣaṇa*), though mentioned in a specific context, becomes common to other contexts as well.

In this context, even the quantity of the liquid decoction to be drunk has not been specified, because it varies according to the individual, such as the person's constitution and so forth. Furthermore, it has been stated in general terms: "The determination of the dosage of medicine is indeed in accordance with the measure of the *doṣas*, and it depends on the specific measure of the patient's strength" (Viśeṣa-sthāna, Chapter 8). By this, it is meant that whatever amount of medicine is appropriate for a particular person in consideration of their strength, digestive fire (*agni*), and other factors, that much medicine should be given to them. And it has been said elsewhere: "There is no fixed rule for dosage; [it depends on] the *doṣa*, the digestive fire, strength, and age."

"One should administer the dose after having examined the disease, the substance, and the patient's constitution. In this regard, the dose intended for a person of medium build, which is neither too small nor too large, has already been indicated by the author of the treatise in such passages as: "Having boiled one *pala* of *vatsaka* seeds, one should drink the decoction" (Ci. A. 19), and likewise regarding *paṭola* and others: "One should drink one *pala* of these [drugs] ground together and boiled in water to remove the *doṣas*" (Ci. A. 20).

In the *Suśruta*, it is stated: "When [the patient] is in the middle stages of disease and so forth, one handful (*añjali*) of decoction is desired" (*Su.Sū.A.* 39). And when two *pala* of the substance to be boiled are reduced to a quarter, the result is indeed one handful (*añjali*) consisting of four *pala*.
Dāruka also said: "The lowest dose is declared to be two *pala*, the middle four *pala*, and the highest six *pala* for decoctions, fats, and medicinal herbs."

And it is stated elsewhere: "The dose for the best [individual] is one *pala*, for the middling [individual] three *akṣas*, and for the lowest [individual] half a *pala*; this applies to oils, decoctions, and medicinal herbs.
These technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*) concern matters that are not far removed from each other and are indeed employed according to the measure of strength, digestive fire, and so forth.

Another point is considered: regarding this water that has been described as having four qualities and so forth, should that [measure] be taken everywhere as doubled? For it has been stated: "This measure applies to dry substances; for liquids and moist substances, it is double. This is not so. Even though the preparation of thirty-two *pala*s of ghee from one *prastha* of liquid is established for substances such as *sunipaṇṇaka*, the author states here: "In this case, a *prastha* should be understood as thirty *pala*s plus two more" (*Ci. A. 14*). By doing so, he demonstrates that doubling of the measure occurs only from the *kuḍava* onwards in accordance with the technical conventions of other treatises, whereas for measures prior to the *kuḍava*, there is no doubling for liquids and moist substances.

Since the doubling [of the measure] was already obtained by the previous rule, the fact that thirty-two *pala* are again mentioned as the *prastha* indicates that when the previous rule deviates, there is doubling in certain cases.

Thus, the deviation from the meaning of that rule regarding *raktikā* and so forth is inferred from the authority of other treatises; and Ātreya says: "But for liquids, there is doubling starting from the *kuḍava* onwards, compared to the measure of the dry substance."

"Because fresh substances possess very little potency, it should be understood that elsewhere they are equal [in measure]. Likewise, it is stated in the *Jatūkarṇa*: "For fresh and liquid substances, the measures such as the *kuḍava* and so forth are doubled. It is also stated elsewhere: "In measures beginning with the *raktikā*, as long as one does not reach the *kuḍava*, the measure for dry and liquid-fresh substances is declared to be the same.
And thus, even in cases where a substance suitable for measurement by *kuḍava* and so forth is taken by mentioning its weight in *palas*, there is no doubling of the measure.

Therefore, in such passages as "one should cook one *droṇa* of oil with a decoction of a thousand *palas* of *rāsnā*" (*Cikitsā-sthāna*, chapter 28), the water taken by measure of *pala* is not necessarily double [the quantity of the solid drugs],

because in some cases where the measurement is prescribed by *pala*, other treatises show that when the intention is to use *kuḍava*s and so forth, the doubling applies even to liquids measured in *palas*.

Just as the formulation stated in the treatment for those emaciated by chest wounds—beginning with "in a decoction of eight palas of madhuka and one prastha of drākṣā" (Ci. A. 11)—is recited in the *Jatūkarṇa* with the text beginning "one prastha of drākṣā, half a decoction of madhuka," etc.; therefore, because the *Jatūkarṇa* mentions half a prastha of madhuka, the liquid becomes doubled; and based on that precedent, here too, although the decoction is prescribed with eight palas of madhuka, water should be given in a doubled amount, intended as two kuḍavas.
This same principle should be followed elsewhere as well.

Others, however, maintain that in the phrase "in a *kuḍava* and so forth," an *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi* compound is intended, meaning that there is no doubling [of the measure] in a *kuḍava*. Consequently, regarding the statement in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā*: "When preparing a *kuḍava* of oil, one *pala* of medicinal paste (*kalka*) should be ground" (*Sū.Ci.A.* 31), they argue that this implies one *pala* of medicine is used for four *pala*s of oil in a *kuḍava*; thus, the practice of administering eight *pala*s of paste for a *prastha* of oil becomes logically consistent. If, on the other hand, eight *pala*s of oil were taken by the term *kuḍava*, then the administration of four *pala*s of paste for a *prastha* would be inconsistent with established practice. This argument is not very sound; for in that very same context, it is stated that when preparing a *kuḍava* of oil, one *prastha* of the decoction substance (*kvāthyadravya*) should be prescribed. If four *pala*s of oil were taken by the term *kuḍava*, then for four *pala*s of oil, sixteen *pala*s of the decoction substance would have to be taken, yet such is not the practice. Indeed, sixteen *pala*s of the decoction substance are taken only when there are eight *pala*s of oil. Therefore, this does not prove that there is no doubling of the measure in a *kuḍava*.

Doubling is appropriate for a *kuḍava* measure; for instance, where one *kuḍava* of honey is prescribed in the *Agastyaharītakī*, it is read as "eight *palas* of honey" in another treatise (*tantrāntara*). Likewise, in another treatise: "Four *palas* of *trāyamāṇā* [are boiled] in ten *palas* of water until one remains."

"One should cook *kuḍava*s of ghee, milk, and *dhātrī* juice in a *kuḍava*"—thus it is heard. In that regard, if a *kuḍava* were four *palas*, then there would be a contradiction with the *trāyamāṇā*-ghee mentioned here. For it has been stated: "Four *palas* of *trāyamāṇā* should be cooked in ten times as much water," and so on, up to: "Having added eight *palas* each of the juice of *āmalaka*, milk, and ghee, one should cook them thoroughly" (Ci. A. 5). Likewise, it is stated elsewhere: "With eight *palas* each of fresh substances and liquid substances..."

"A *kuḍava* is declared to consist of four parts of dry substance"; therefore, doubling applies correctly to the *kuḍava*. However, regarding the doubling of moisture: for those substances that are prescribed for use in their dry state, there is a doubling when they are used in their moist state. But for those that are always used only in their moist state, there is no doubling—as it has been said: "Vāsā, kuṭaja, kūṣmāṇḍa, śatapatrī, and sahācara..."
"They should always be applied moist; for them, there should not be a doubling [of the quantity].

All of this has been stated in connection with the decoctions to be drunk; it should also be considered in the context of cooking medicated fats (*sneha-pāka*). In the cooking of medicated fats, however, a paste (*kalka*) amounting to one-quarter of the fat should be used; as he will state: "Where the proportions of water, fat, and medicinal drugs have not been specified..."
Regarding this, it is said: "From the medicinal substance there should be oil, and from the oil, four times as much water" (Ka. A. 12).
Thus, even though oil possesses the quality of liquidity, it is specifically fourfold [in quantity] and does not become eightfold merely because of its consistency with the paste (*kalka*).
It is stated elsewhere as well: "Water four times the quantity of the decoction ingredients becomes fourfold when reduced to one-fourth."

Regarding the statement, "The milk should be equal to the oil, while the paste (kalka) should be one-fourth the measure of the oil," although it is established by tradition that when the oil is exactly eight *palas*, the paste should be one *pala*, this is not practiced in common usage. For it is stated by Kṛṣṇātreya: "In the procedure for cooking medicated oils, wherever no specific measure is mentioned, one should cook one *kuḍava* of oil with one *pala* of paste."
Likewise, in the Suśruta-saṃhitā as well, one pala of paste (kalka) is prescribed for a kuḍava of oil;
this rule regarding the absence of paste should be established for an oil that is prepared with an extremely heavy expressed juice (svarasa), or for an oil prepared with flower-paste,
since it is observed that the quantity of the paste— whether small or large— depends on whether the substance possesses substantial essence (sāra) or lacks it.

As Vāgbhaṭa, repeating the statement of Śaunaka, said: "When the oil is being cooked, one should gradually add a fourth, sixth, or eighth part of the paste (kalka) using pure water, decoctions, or fresh juices (svarasa)"; likewise: "Because of the abundance of paste from *śaṇa*, *kovidāra*, *karbudāra*, and *śālmali*, they praise four *palas* of flower-paste."

In this context, since a paste of four *palas* relative to one *prastha* of oil constitutes exactly one-eighth part of the oil, the general rule—"the paste should be one-fourth of the oil"—is set aside by this specific statement in certain particular cases; let there be no contradiction here. Enough with excessive elaboration; in every way, the scripture must be accepted as authoritative only insofar as it conforms to practical usage (197–199).
Regarding "five [types] of fivefold fever," Kaliṅga and the others are to be understood as corresponding respectively to the continuous (*santata*) and other types;
however, others say that there are five specific medicinal formulations for each of the five [fevers].
Regarding the passage beginning with "vatsakāragvadham" and ending with "balām," some authorities describe three formulations, while others maintain that there is only one;
the phrase "niśi sthitam" (kept overnight) indicates that it is a cold infusion (*śītakaṣāya*).
In the passage beginning with "jāti," it refers to the sprouts of the *jāti* flower.

In the instruction "one should drink it with jaggery" (*saguḍaṃ pibet*), the jaggery is to be understood as being one-quarter of the quantity of the substance to be boiled, since it is an additive; this same principle regarding additives should be understood in other cases as well (207–209).

Here, because this section falls within the discussion on *kaṣāyas*, [the author] sets aside even the occasion for the treatment of *sannipāta* and recites two formulations—those beginning with *śaṭī* and those beginning with *bṛhatī*—which alleviate *sannipāta*, in the group of four medicinal preparations in the chapter on medicines (210–214). For the term "chapter" (*adhyāya*) indeed applies to a group of four as well, based on the etymology: "that in which meanings are studied."

However, regarding the mere application of yoga in that context, two great decoctions (mahākaṣāya) for curing fever and thirst are taught in the chapter on the six hundred purgatives (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 4). Since there are many decoctions made from each individual drug of those two, the use of the plural form "decoctions" (kaṣāyāḥ) is appropriate;
furthermore, gruels (yavāgū) are taught in the chapter on the grains of *apāmārga* (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 2).
Now, in order to describe the applications of clarified butter (sarpiḥ), he states the scope of its use: "Fever," and so forth.

By the word "emetics" (vamanaiḥ), he indicates here that the application of emetics—which are to be administered according to the specific stage [of the disease]—occurs during the six-day period involving clarified butter.
And by the mention of "lightening therapy" (laṅghana), treatments such as sudation (sveda) and others, which share the same duration as lightening therapy, are included.

By the statement "of one who is dry" (*rūkṣasya*), he shows that even when there is the administration of decoctions (*kaṣāya*) and so forth, ghee should not be given where dryness does not occur due to the persistence of dampness (*sāmatā*) or because of a predominance of phlegm (*kapha*).

Here, by the indication of the non-compounded term "with decoctions" (*kaṣāyaiḥ*) and so forth, he shows that the drinking of ghee should be performed by one who is dry, whether the administration of decoctions and so forth is done individually or collectively.
Now, one might ask: since ghee is prescribed after decoctions for all fevers without distinction, how is this [specific rule] justified? To this he says: "Dryness is fire," and so forth.

In this context, although the word *tejas* (fire/heat) applies to bile (*pitta*), digestive fire (*anala*), unctuousness (*sneha*), power (*śakti*), luster (*dyuti*), and the summer season (*grīṣma*), here the word *tejas* denotes heat (*ūṣman*). By this, it is stated that heat, which is dry by nature, is the cause of fever everywhere. That heat should be understood as threefold: that of the digestive fire (*agni*) dispersed in the stomach (*āmāśaya*), that arising from the body itself, and that which takes the form of fever produced by the influence of fever. As it has been said: "By its own heat and indeed by the bodily heat, it produces strength."
"They produce excessive heat within the body," and so forth.

And although this heat (*ūṣmā*) arises from bile (*pitta*) during subtle investigation—as it has been said: "Heat does not exist without bile, nor does fever exist without heat" (Vāgbhaṭa, Cikitsāsthāna 1)—and although bile is described as "unctuous, hot, and sharp" (Sūtrasthāna 10) and so forth, nevertheless, due to the influence of its state (*avasthā*), bile becomes free from *āma* and devoid of unctuousness (*niḥsneha*). Furthermore, the unctuous quality of bile is caused by association with fluidity and is not innate; therefore, the departure of unctuousness in bile is indeed expected in that particular state.
