Consequently, the heat of bile that is devoid of unctuousness becomes specifically dry (*rūkṣa*).

Furthermore, this stage of the disease arises from the very influence of the disease itself during the state of chronicity (*jīrṇāvasthā*), just as in the case of alcoholism (*madātyaya*), where there is a predominance of *vāta* and *pitta* at its conclusion. As it has been stated [by Caraka]: "Alcoholism generally culminates in *pitta* and *māruta*" (Ci.

A. 24). Kṣārapāṇi also said: "When the bodily tissues (*dhātu*) have been dried up by the heat of fever, the powerful *māruta* may produce a sequelae of fever or one of the irregular fevers (*viṣamajvara*)" and so forth.

In that context, when the feverish person has been parched by dry heat due to the association with the time of fever, the *dhātu* (constituent) which is *anila* (vāyu/wind) becomes the persistent factor (*anubandha*); and since that is "to be destroyed by unctuousness" (*snehavadhya*), it means it is to be overcome by the unctuous qualities produced by ghee (*sarpiḥ*). The word "and" (*ca*) implies that the dry heat which causes the fever is also to be overcome by the unctuousness produced by ghee. By the qualification "constituent" (*dhātu*), the nature of *vāyu* as being characterized by retention (*dhāraṇātmakatā*) is expressed; and this indicates that the provocation of *vāyu*, which is of the nature of retention, leads to great calamity. Furthermore, the term *anubala* refers to that whose strength (*bala*) comes after (*anu-paścāt*).

Therefore, in all fevers, when the portion of *kapha* has been diminished over a period of twelve days by means of decoctions and other treatments, the heat of the fever increases; and due to that drying (*virūkṣaṇa*), the *vāyu* also increases.

In this regard, since it is well known that ghee is prescribed for the heat of the fever—which possesses the quality of *pitta*—because of its cooling nature, it is not explicitly mentioned here. However, by its oily (*sneha*) component alone, ghee pacifies both the *pitta*-heat that causes the fever—which is dry in nature—and the *vāyu*, through its unctuousness; this is what is expressed by the verse beginning with "dry [is] fire" (*rūkṣaṃ teja*).
Others, however, understand by the word *tejas* (fire/heat) here specifically *pitta* (bile).

For *pitta* is of two kinds: that which is with fluid (*sadrava*) and that which is without fluid (*nirdrava*). That which is with fluid is oily (*sasneha*), whereas that which is without fluid—having its moist portion diminished through fasting and other means—is dry (*rūkṣa*); it is this latter type that is grasped here by the expression "dry fire" (*rūkṣaṃ tejaḥ*).

Others, however, interpret the phrase "the humor that has an accompanying factor" (*anubala*) as referring to *kapha* by way of its etymological suffix (*anubandha*). Thus, the meaning is that when *kapha* is the accompanying factor, *pitta* becomes dry and *vāta* becomes unresponsive to oleation (*sneha*). By the word "oleation" (*sneha*), clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) is intended due to the context; and clarified butter conquers *kapha* through specific processing (*saṃskāra*). As it is said: "Clarified butter possesses qualities equal to [those of] the doshas, yet through processing it overcomes *kapha*" (Ni. A. 1). Furthermore, by the passage beginning "Henceforth, when *kapha* is diminished," the administration of clarified butter is sanctioned for all three doshas. Therefore, in this case as well, it is established that these same three doshas are the objects for the application of clarified butter according to the aforementioned explanation.
In our own previous commentary, however, this is the natural intent;

others, however, read "tejas in a dry [person] causes fever," where "in a dry [person]" should be understood as one whose body has been made dry by astringent decoctions and the like, while the remainder is as before.
Furthermore, this reading is not to be rejected, as it has been explained by previous commentators such as Bhāsadatta, Svāmidāsa, Āṣāḍhavarmā, Brahmadeva, and others;
Kharanāda also maintains this same reading, for it is stated there: "From the drinking of decoctions, from emesis, from fasting, and from light food..."

"For those who have been treated with drying therapies, when fever is about to be released, the drinking of ghee is expected if the body has an excess of dryness and heat," and so forth (verses 216–217).
Now he speaks of medicated ghees (*sarpirṇi*): "The decoctions," and so forth.

These aforementioned fever-alleviating decoctions, when combined with ghee and employed as the means for preparing ghee, are to be used; the meaning of the sentence is that one should prepare and employ ghees using the decoction substances exactly as described, within their respective domains. Others, however, maintain that by this statement, the application of the decoctions mixed with ghee is intended.

Regarding the passage beginning with "pippalyaḥ" (Pippalyādi), since no specific distinction is stated for the *pippalyādi* group in this ghee preparation, some authorities maintain that the ingredients serve as both a decoction (*kaṣāya*) and a paste (*kalka*), while others assert that they function solely as a paste.

As for a liquid preparation (*dravakārya*), since no specific liquid is mentioned, it must be made with water alone, according to the statement: "In all cases where a liquid is not specified even for a liquid preparation, water is traditionally prescribed" (Ka. A. 12). Now, in a case where a substance is mentioned as a paste (*kalka*) but no liquid is mentioned, water should be taken; for example: "In a paste of *tryūṣaṇa* and *triphalā* the size of a *bilva* fruit, along with one *pala* of jaggery..."

“Having cooked eight palas of ghee, one with weak digestive fire should drink the appropriate dose” (Ci.A. 15). However, where neither decoction nor paste is specified, both decoction and paste should be prepared, as it is stated in the Suśruta Saṃhitā: “In the absence of a specific instruction regarding paste or decoction, one should employ them from that [specified] group of drugs” (Su.Ci.A. 31).

Do not say so; for this technical definition stated by Suśruta pertains specifically to *gaṇas* (groups of drugs), based on the statement: "One should employ [the preparation] from that *gaṇa*. Furthermore, these [drugs] beginning with *pippalī* have not been mentioned as a *gaṇa*; moreover, the preparation of decoction (*kvātha*) and paste (*kalka*) occurs only where a *gaṇa* is explicitly mentioned as the substratum. As it has been stated elsewhere: "Where the mention of a *gaṇa* is made in connection with a substratum in the preparation of medicated fats..."

"In that very context, the paste (*kalka*) and the decoction (*niryūha*) are prescribed by those who know the science of oleation. Furthermore, if the general statement regarding the preparation of an oil from a substance implied both the paste and the decoction, then in the case of *Balā-taila* and others, one would not have specified the use of both paste and decoction in the passage: "One should cook the oil with an equal amount of milk along with the decoction and paste of *Balā*" (Ci. A. 29), because these would already have been obtained through the general rule of preparation. Therefore, for substances such as *pippalī*, one should provide only the paste itself and four times the amount of water; this should be understood to apply elsewhere as well.

In this context, since no specific measure for the ghee to be cooked is indicated, the clarified butter should be prepared in an indefinite quantity according to one's desire; however, it should be understood that where a measure such as a *prastha* is specified, the alleviation of the disease treatable by unctuous substances occurs with exactly that much.

For instance, regarding Vātavyādhi (winds-related diseases) which are to be treated with abundant fats, he will prescribe a very large dose of fat; in the Prapauṇḍarīka and other nasal formulations, he will prescribe a measure of one kuḍava of fat; and in the Tiktaka-ṣaṭpala and other formulations mentioned for Kuṣṭha, by prescribing a very small quantity for cooking, the Great Sage—who perceives the power of medicinal substances—teaches that the processed ghee performs its intended function.

In that regard, if for leprosy—which is a chronic disease—there is a need for repeated applications of the *ṣaṭpala* ointment, then ghee must be cooked again and again in the measure of six *palas*, according to the statement: "Whatever they do is the method" (*Sūtra-sthāna*, chapter 26). In the same way, the purpose for stating specific measures in the case of *Agastyaharītakī* and other formulations should be explained.
Therefore, the teacher’s mention or non-mention of a measure in any instance is not arbitrary.
Tāmalakī, known as ‘bhūmyāmalakī,’ subdues— that is, equalizes— halīmaka, which is a variety of jaundice.

Regarding verses 219–221, although the quantity of the decoction is not explicitly stated for the *vāsādyaghṛta*, nevertheless, the decoction should be taken as exactly double [the quantity of the fat]. In the cooking of fats (*sneha-pāka*), the liquid must indeed be four times the amount of the fat, according to the statement: "The water is four times the fat" (Ka. A. 12). Furthermore, the word "water" (*jala*) here is an indicator for any liquid in general. And in this context, although milk would be understood as double the decoction according to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating "there is a fourfoldness for both," they say that the explicit mention of doubling the milk is for the sake of clarity and for the benefit of students of three types of intellect.

In that regard, since the quantity of milk is not explicitly stated, based on the statement: "Water should be four times the decoction; when reduced to one-fourth, it should be four times the oil; milk should be equal to the oil; and the paste should be one-fourth of the oil," when another liquid (the decoction) is present, the milk must indeed be equal to the oil. Consequently, by taking three parts of the decoction and one part of milk, the rule of "fourfoldness" would apply to both together. Therefore, the explicit statement of doubling the milk must be made.

Others, however, maintain that by the technical rule "quadrupling occurs from both," quadrupling applies to each liquid individually; consequently, in this case, while there is quadrupling of the decoction, there is only doubling of the milk.

In that context, because of the statement—"quadrupling [occurs] even with one, quadrupling even with two, quadrupling even with three, and equality with four"—the quadrupling of the liquid is stated precisely through the expression of equality with the oil when all four are combined.

Therefore, by two or even by three [substances], the fourfold proportion (*cāturguṇya*) must be achieved such that the oil becomes fourfold; and this fourfold proportion occurs only when they are combined, not individually.

However, the technical definition of "liquid substances" being fourfold is set aside by a specific statement when five or more liquids are present, for the text says: "Where there are five or more liquid substances in the preparation of an oil..."
Regarding this, it is said: "In that case, they say there is a commonality of oil; however, [the liquid] below should be four times [the quantity].

(222–223) Furthermore, even in the case of decoctions and milks beginning with *bala*, one should understand that each is doubled in quantity, based on their association with the previously mentioned decoctions and milks.

Now he states the formulations for emesis and purgation indicated by the sequence, beginning with "to those suffering from fever" and ending with "to those with abundant *doṣas*"; by this last phrase, he indicates that purification is prohibited in cases where the *doṣas* are minimal.
"Time" (kāla) refers to the stage of fever when one is fit for the aforementioned emesis and purgation;
"method" (kalpa) refers to the section on procedures (kalpasthāna),

wherein [the preparation] combined with *madana* and *pippalī* is used for *kapha*, that combined with *kaliṅga* for *pitta-śleṣman*, and that combined with *madhuka* for cases characterized by burning sensations (*dāha*).
Water sweetened by the addition of honey is *kṣaudrāmbu*;
water rendered salty by the addition of rock salt (*saindhava*) is *lavaṇāmbu*, which is a purgative known as *praskandana*.
Having explained [the preparation] by adding [the ingredients],
he now describes the applications of milk as they appear in the sequence of the text from verses 227 to 233, beginning with "In cases of cough," and so forth.

In this context, since the quantities of the five roots (*pañcamūla*) and other substances, as well as milk and water, are not specified, the measurement is determined by the convention established through the practice of experienced physicians. As it is said: "Milk is eight times the quantity of the substance, and water is four times the quantity of the milk;

the cooking of milk should be performed until only the milk remains—this is the rule. Accordingly, having added half a *pala* of the substance, four *palas* of milk, and sixteen *palas* of water, the decoction should be cooked until only the milk remains; such is the system of measurement.
In the chapter on *māṣaparṇī* and others, it is stated: "Having boiled one karṣa each of medā, payasyā, jīvantī, vidārī,
kaṇṭakārikā, śvadaṃṣṭrā, kṣīrikā, māṣas, wheat, and *śāli* and *ṣaṣṭika* rice in half an āḍhaka of milk and water..."

"One should avoid the residue of milk" (Ci.A.2), and so forth—the measurement of substances such as milk mentioned therein is to be understood as applying specifically to that context, because this measurement is governed by technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*). For a measurement stated in one section indeed serves as the indicator of measurement in another section only if it conforms to the technical definition; however, a measurement that subverts another technical definition remains restricted to its own specific domain. As it is said: "One should prepare four *palas* of pure, dried garlic..."

"One should drink milk that remains after water eight times its quantity has been added" (Ci.A.5). In this way, any other statement regarding measurements that contradicts the technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*) found in another treatise should be understood as being restricted to that specific application.

Regarding "parikartikā," which refers to a cutting pain in the anus and so forth, and in cases such as "nāgara" (ginger), since honey is unfit for cooking, it should be understood that other substances are added at a later stage in quantities equal to the [original] measure.
The conceptual distinction between "hot" and "cold" is produced by specific desires; [it is designated as] "hot" when *vāta* is predominant, but "cold" when *pitta* is excessively strong.

(234–239) By the statement "fever-alleviating [substances]" in the procedure for *nirūha*, he demonstrates the preparation of both *nirūha* and *anuvāsana* enemas using substances that alleviate fever.

Regarding the statement "boiled in milk and half-water" in the *paṭolādya* non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*), it should be understood that the word "half" signifies an equal division; thus, an amount of water equal to the milk is to be taken.
Furthermore, the determination of the proportions for the decoction (*kvātha*), paste (*kalka*), oil (*sneha*), and so forth, must be understood exactly as it will be explained in the *Siddhisthāna*.
In the case of *guḍūcyādi*, the instruction "one should prepare the juice" means that one should make a decoction (*kvātha*).

It should be prepared with a small amount of salt and a small amount of honey mixed with ghee (240–249). In the *jīvantyādi* enema (*anuvāsana*) using the *yamaka* (double) formulation, the milk is equal in quantity to the oil, while the water is three times the oil; thus, the liquid should be four times the quantity of the oil.
In the phrase "oil cooked with madana fruits," the "unctuous substance" (sneha) mentioned immediately prior should be understood as the *yamaka-sneha* consisting specifically of ghee and oil;
this should likewise be understood in the case of the phrase "the unctuous substance is prepared.

By the words "as has been stated," and so forth, he refers to the substances for head-purgation (*śirovirecana*) mentioned in the Chapter on Medicines (*Bheṣajādhyāya*), specifically in the *Apāmārgataṇḍulīya* (Sūtra-sthāna, chapter 2); and by the phrase "the oil for nasal administration," he refers to *Aṇutaila*.
With the words "and massages" (abhyaṅgān) and so forth, [the author] speaks of external cleansing as it follows in sequence;
"according to desire" (yathābhilāṣam) means according to one's wish.

"Having distinguished between cold and heat" means having distinguished the fever arising from cold and the fever arising from heat; therein, for the fever arising from cold, warm massages and so forth are to be applied, and for the hot [fever], cooling ones. Here, by way of an inverse explanation, he mentions massages and other measures intended for the cold [fever] with the words beginning "sahasra... and so on.
The word *sahasra* has the sense of "extensive"; by it, the meaning is indicated that the clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) has been washed many times.
[Now], he speaks of the oil (*taila*) beginning with sandalwood (*candana*), starting with the words "atha" and so forth.
The word "atha" (now/thereupon) indicates the commencement of a topic;
likewise, oil that has been processed with substances such as sandalwood is also called "candanādya" (sandalwood-based).

Candana is red sandalwood; bhadraśrī is white sandalwood; kālānusārya is cooling; nalina is a variety of lotus; bisa is a fiber of lotus stalk; vetasa has fragrant roots; vānīra is a variety of it with non-fragrant roots; aśvakarṇa is a variety of śāla; ariṣṭa is the mountain nimba; syandana is the *nemivṛkṣa* tree; vātapotha is the *palāśa*; tiniśa is the *vañjula*; kadara is the *viṭkhadira*; kapītana is known as 'gandhamuṇḍa'; vaṭa is a non-sprouting fig tree; nyagrodha, however, is one that possesses sprouts; jyotiṣmatī is the *kāṅgaṇikā*; saṃvartaka is the *bibhītaka*; śataparvā is white dūrvā grass; śītakumbhikā is *kāṣṭhapāṭalā*; mahāśrāvaṇī is the large-fruited *alambuṣā*; śītapākī is *gaṇḍadūrvā*; odanapākī is blue *bheṇḍī*; kālā is *kākoli*; ṛṣyaproktā is *ṛddhi*; and tṛṇaśūnya is *ketakī*.
By the phrase "according to what is available," he shows that even by abandoning medicines that are difficult to obtain, one may prepare a decoction of sandalwood and so forth.

In this decoction where there is double the quantity of milk—referred to as "double-milked"—even though the specific measure for the paste (*kalka*) is not mentioned here, the paste is to be one-quarter of the oil, because of the statement: "The paste is one-quarter of the oil."

In this context, although oil is warm while ghee is cool, and coolness is recommended for the pacification of burning sensations, nevertheless, because oil follows subtle channels, possesses a pervasive quality (*vyavāyin*), and removes excessive *vāta* through its tactile contact, it is oil alone that is prescribed in the section on massage (*abhyaṅga*) using sandalwood and other ingredients, rather than ghee. Others, however, maintain that oil is mentioned here because it carries medicinal processing (*saṃskāra*) more effectively even than ghee.

Now, what is the purpose of assigning the name "candanādyam" (the candana-group and so forth)? If you argue that it is for the sake of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) in other sections [of the treatise], we say no. Even without the assignment of such names, conventional usage is observed through etymological designations (*yaugika-sañjñā*) in other sections, as in: "One should administer six *pala* of clarified butter" (*Ci. A. 5*), and likewise, "One should drink *vāsāghṛta*, *dādhika*, and *tryūṣaṇa*" (*Ci. A. 17*), and so on. Furthermore, even when a name has been assigned, its usage is not seen, as in: "This is known as *prāyogika* clarified butter, called *pārūṣaka*" (*Ci. A. 29*). Similarly, although names such as "six-part decoction" (*ṣaḍbhāgakaṣāya*) have been assigned, no usage is made of them in other sections.

Do not say this: although there is no such usage in the technical treatises (*śāstra*) under the designation *pārūṣaka* and so forth, nevertheless, for those who possess that knowledge—the physicians—there will be usage according to that designation. This is the purpose of establishing the designation.

Furthermore, at the time of stating the application of designations, even if they are not explicitly formulated, designations such as *ṣaṭpala* and others are indeed established through their functional efficacy (*yoga*).

Therefore, in some instances, there is usage of functional designations even in other contexts; and in other cases, a designation is applied at the very moment of usage based on its suitability or common medical convention (*vaidyaprasiddhi*). Thus, there is no fault whatsoever.
In this manner, it should be explained in other instances as well where a technical designation is employed.

By the statement "with finely ground [powders]," the author indicates that even a thick coating of finely ground paste acts as a caustic agent; as it has been said: "A thick coating of sandalwood, though finely ground, causes burning because it obstructs the heat residing in the skin; otherwise, [a coating] of agallochum produces cold. (Cikitsā-sthāna, Chapter 30).

Based on the statement that "one should touch objects with flavors of contact," it shows that one should not hold them for long; for if they were held for a long time, even those [moonbeams] would become hot.

In the phrase "the winds and the moonbeams are cool," the qualifier "cool" applies to the wind, but not to the moonbeams, because they are always cool. Alternatively, since even the moonbeams might become hot during the summer due to contact with heat, the word "cool" is used to exclude that possibility.

Subhūti said: “Blessed One, is it possible to apprehend that dharma which the Tathāgata has designated as ‘emptiness’? The Blessed One said:

In the *aguru* group [of fragrant substances], there are: *kṣemaka*, *coraka*, *rohiṣa* (known as *rāmakarpūra*), *śigru* (a variety of *śobhāñjana*), *mūlakaparṇī* (guggulu), *tilaparṇī* (known as *hulhula*), *pīluparṇī* (also called *moraṭā*; others say it is *mūrvā*), *gaṇḍīra* (a variety of *śamaṭha*, which is of two types—aquatic and terrestrial), *ātmajā* (known as *putrañjīvaka*), *ekaiṣikā* (also *ambaṣṭhā*), the *sumukha* and others (varieties of *parṇāsa*), *ruhā* (*vṛkṣaruhā*), *rohā* (*añjalikārikā*), *śītaparṇī* (*vṛkṣakalambukā*), *nākulī* (*cavikā*), *gandhanākulī* (a variety of *rāsnā*), and *adhyaṇḍā* (*śūkaśimbī*).

By the phrase "and others," he includes the hot substances mentioned in the *Rogabhiṣagjitīya* and other chapters, as well as those to be described later in the *Trivṛt-kalpa* regarding *sauvīra* and *tuṣodaka*. *Maireya* is a type of liquor made from *surā*; *medaka* is the dregs; *kaṭvara* is liquid curd mixed with fat;
and *pātra* refers to a measure of one *āḍhaka*.

In this context, liquid substances such as decoctions (kaṣāya) and the like should each be made equal in quantity to the oil; as it has been said: "Wherever there are five or more liquids in the preparation of an oil, they say those [liquids] should be equal in quantity to the oil. (267)

Since thirteen types [of sudation] have already been mentioned in the chapter on sudation (*svedādhyāya*), the repetition of "thirteen types" here is for the purpose of including all of them; alternatively, it is for the purpose of prohibiting additional forms of sudation by fire. Furthermore, although the *kuṭī* (enclosure) is included among the thirteen types of sudation, it is mentioned again because it is particularly beneficial; and that "bed" (*śayana*) is presented as an accessory to the *kuṭī*. The same applies to the "covering" (*ācchādana*).
And this bedding and clothing are beneficial here even when used separately; this is shown by their separate mention.
"Dense" means thick;
"sudorifics" refers to hot substances such as chicken, wine, horse gram (*kulattha*), and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "due to the application of the force of association" (*saṃsargabalayojanāt*), it is the very association of Vāta and Kapha mentioned immediately above—which produces fever characterized by a desire for warmth—that is understood here by the term "association. Therefore, the meaning is that in the case of an association of Vāta and Kapha, when Vāta is predominant, food and drink consisting mostly of heavy, warm, and unctuous substances should be administered; whereas when Kapha is predominant, light, warm, and dry substances should generally be employed.

Furthermore, this fever born of Vāta and Kapha is stated here specifically because, due to the mobile nature (*yogavāhitva*) of Vāyu, it becomes cold; by implication, one should know that fever arising solely from Kapha or solely from Vāta may also manifest with a desire for cold.
Now, setting aside the fasting (laṅghana) previously contraindicated for fevers born of Vāta and the other [doshas], he describes the specific treatment beginning with "vātaja" and so forth;
"by pacifying measures" (śamanaiḥ) refers to pacifying treatments such as the drinking of decoctions and medicated ghees.

Now, he describes fasting (*laṅghana*) as a general means of producing lightness for those diseases caused by *vāta* and others even in their specific states, as well as for those caused by *kapha* and others in their essential nature— beginning with the words "sāmā" and so forth.
By the term "sāmā," he declares that even a *vātika* disorder associated with *sāma* (undigested toxins) is subject to fasting.

For it is stated elsewhere: "Even in *vāta* associated with *āmadoṣa*, fasting (*laṅghana*) is prescribed. However, in the case of [diseases] born of *kapha*, fasting is recommended even when there is no *āma*.

By the term "born of *kapha* and *pitta*," it is indicated that fasting is required specifically for those born of *pitta* associated with *kapha*, and not merely for those born of *pitta* alone when free from *āma*; yet, for those born of *pitta* accompanied by *āma*, fasting is indeed recommended for the purpose of exhausting the *āma*.
As it has been stated elsewhere: "One should certainly perform fasting even when pitta is associated with ama, for the sake of digesting the ama";

and as it has also been said: "Kapha and pitta, when in their liquid state, can withstand great fasting"—this too refers to the presence of liquidity due to the association with ama; however, when the liquid portion of pitta is diminished, fasting must not be performed at all.

By the statement "as described in the chapter on lightening therapy" (laṅghanīya), one should understand the ten types of lightening therapies mentioned in that section, as well as those described in the chapters on lightening and nourishing therapies, excluding those contraindicated in specific conditions such as emesis and so forth, and excluding all forms of exercise that are strictly prohibited.

Previously, it was stated that "one should remove [the doshas] by means of emetics" in the case of fevers where the doshas are combined and phlegm (kapha) predominates; however, what is now stated regarding emetics and other therapies—beginning with "by emetics in those born from each individual dosha"—is not redundant.

He states the aphorism for the treatment of combined (saṃsarga) and aggregated (sannipāta) disorders: "In combined [disorders], by the more or less [intense] and equal [doshas]," and so forth. In a combined disorder where one dosha is predominant, [the others are treated] by those that are more predominant; and in an aggregated disorder initiated by doshas that have increased to a greater or greatest degree, [treatment is] strictly according to the doshas. Likewise, even in an aggregated disorder where two doshas are more predominant, those two doshas are to be understood by their intensity alone; and in a three-dosha disorder initiated by doshas that have increased, increased further, or increased most, the excessively increased doshas are to be understood by those [other doshas] that are equal [to them].

That which was stated as "the suffix *tama* is used when [comparative] among three" occurs when one is determined to be the most excellent among the three; however, when two out of the three are intended to be excellent, then that falls within the scope of "the suffix *tara* between two," and this should be understood as *samadoṣa* (equal-defect) and *sannipāta* (combination), where the association is initiated by defects of equal degree.

Regarding the phrase "dependent on the sequence of the humors" (*doṣakramāpekṣī*): by the term "dependent on the humors" (*doṣāpekṣī*), it is stated that one must take into account the various specificities—such as whether the humors are increased, more increased, or so forth—which are relevant for medical treatment; and by the term "dependent on the sequence" (*kramāpekṣī*), it is shown that there is a dependence on the sequence of treatments such as fasting (*laṅghana*) and so on, as described in the "Treatment for Fever" (*jvaritacikitsita*), using the aforementioned medicines ranging from fasting to collyrium (*añjana*).

Now, one might object: "Is treatment not impossible in a fever born of the three doṣas? For there is generally no substance that pacifies all three doṣas simultaneously; for that which is wholesome for vāta is unwholesome for śleṣman, and that which is wholesome for pitta is generally unwholesome for śleṣman. Indeed, for example, what is bitter and astringent removes kapha and pitta but produces vāta; and what is sweet removes vāta and pitta but produces kapha. As for substances like āmalaka which remove all three doṣas, they are few in number, restricted to specific diseases, and are not necessarily suitable for fever. Furthermore, this sannipāta is a most serious condition; therefore, how should its treatment be performed? To this, he says: "By aggravating [one], etc. (vardhanena, etc.).

In this context, the combination (*sannipāta*) is said to be of twenty-five types, as stated in the passage beginning: "There are six [types] with two [doṣas] predominant and one [doṣa] predominant, and six with [doṣas] being diminished, moderate, and so forth" (Sūtra-sthāna 17). Among these, according to our own school's view, the twelve diminished (*kṣīṇa*) combinations of *sannipāta* do not initiate fever; for when the *doṣas* are diminished, they produce only disorders consisting of the loss of their own specific symptoms, and are not capable of causing further conditions such as fever. However, regarding the remaining thirteen [combinations], since there is no substance that can simultaneously pacify all three *doṣas*, treatment is prescribed based on the most prominent *doṣa*, as there is no other alternative.

In this context, the phrase "by the aggravation of a single *doṣa*" means "even by the aggravation of a single *doṣa*. By the word "single" (*eka*), it is intended that the *doṣa* has increased by two or three degrees, but not further increased (*vṛddhatara*) nor excessively increased (*vṛddhatama*);
for if those two were excessively aggravated, their increase beyond measure would result only in great harm.

By the phrase "by increasing one [of the] doshas," it is meant by that which increases one dosha while simultaneously pacifying two doshas that have become more increased or most increased. For example, when kapha is increased and vāta and pitta are more increased, a sweet substance is used; for although that [sweet substance] increases the already diminished kapha, it removes the fever because it overcomes the two more increased doshas (vāta and pitta), being a powerful destroyer of the [dominant] doshas. Similarly, the application of sweet substances should be understood when kapha is increased and pitta is more increased.
Other examples should be understood in this manner.

Therefore, by the statement "by increasing [the one] that is deficient," the treatment for the three types of *sannipāta* (combined disorders) where two *doṣas* are aggravated is described; and by the statement "by reducing [the one] that is deficient," it is meant that even a medicine which increases two diminished [doṣas] should be administered if it brings about the reduction of a *doṣa* that is greatly increased, more increased, or most increased. For if the most increased [doṣa] is not countered, it kills instantly; and in its counteraction, the increase of the two diminished [doṣas] involves little risk, and thus it should be managed gradually—this is the intended meaning.
By this, the three types of *sannipāta* in which a single [dosha] is predominant have been treated.

Regarding this matter, another treatise states: "In a *sannipāta*, one should act according to the influence of the [dominant] *sannipāta*, whether it be the increase of a deficient single dosha or the overcoming of an increased one."

He states the treatment for the remaining combined disorders: "Or by the sequence of the seats of *kapha*. The word "or" (*vā*) expresses a restricted alternative. The "seat of *kapha*" (*kaphasthāna*) refers to the upper portion of the stomach (*āmāśaya*). "Sequence" (*ānupūrvī*) means order. Thus, "one should conquer by the sequence of the seat of *kapha*" means one should first conquer the seat of *kapha*. By mentioning the "seat," the *kapha* residing therein is also implied. However, the conquest of *kapha* itself is not explicitly stated, as the purpose is to demonstrate that the treatment must be directed toward its seat—the stomach—which has been vitiated by the doshas initiating the fever.
For it has been said: "Fever indeed arises from the stomach (āmāśaya)" (Vi. A. 3).

Thus, although the doshas are equal [in their involvement], they initiate fever because they specifically vitiate the stomach and thereby produce the disease; therefore, in the case of fever, treatment must first be directed toward the site [of the disease] in accordance with its location.
For, with regard to the dosha located in a particular site, the site itself is the primary object of treatment.
Regarding what was stated— "one should indeed conquer the site first"—

the "site of phlegm" (kaphasthāna) refers to the location of kapha; therein, the treatments such as fasting (laṅghana) and digestive stimulation (pācana), which were prescribed for fever, are to be administered first.

And although this treatment is common to all fevers, it is nevertheless stated here regarding balanced *sannipāta* for the purpose of precluding the application of fever-treatment preceded by stronger treatment for *vāta* in cases of *sannipāta*.

For in a *sannipāta* other than fever, it is the *vāta* itself that is treated first when balanced; as it has been said: "One should conquer *pitta* after *vāta*, and *kapha* after *pitta," and so forth.

When treatment is being administered according to the sequence of the seats of *kapha*, whichever *doṣa* becomes predominant, there the treatment should be performed according to the principle: "by increasing one *doṣa* or by diminishing that which is elevated.
This very point was stated by Bhela: "In a *sannipāta* fever, one should first eliminate the *āma* and *kapha*;
afterwards, when the *śleṣman* has been diminished, one should pacify *pitta* and *māruta*."

Others explain it as a *bahuvrīhi* compound—like the term "camel-faced" (*uṣṭramukha*)—with the elision of the final member, meaning "that which has its location in the seat of *kapha*, namely the stomach (*āmāśaya*)," referring thus to *pitta*. Consequently, the meaning is that one should conquer [the fever] by means of the sequence starting with *pitta*.
To support this sense, they cite the statement of Suśruta: "In fevers arising from the combination [of all three doṣas], one should pacify *pitta* first;
for it is indeed the most difficult to restrain among those afflicted by fever, especially so. (Su.Ci.A. 39)

In that case, for the sake of clarity, one should read Suśruta’s statement exactly as "in the sequence of pitta" (pittānupūrvyā); indeed, this should be understood with reference to the three doṣas having become fully aggravated (jīrṇa), whereas this treatment for the first-occurring sannipāta fever should be understood according to the sequence of the seats of kapha (kaphasthānānupūrvyā).

However, for those who form a *dvandva* compound of "kapha" and "sthāna," their view is that the conquest of both phlegm (*kapha*) and the seat of disease (*āmāśaya*), which is the location of fever, must first be achieved; and since this is indeed accomplished even by a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound through treatment directed toward the seat—the *āmāśaya*—in relation to the phlegm residing there, there is no contradiction in meaning.

Furthermore, although this treatment for *sannipāta*, consisting of increasing one humor and so forth, is not entirely pure—as it has been said: "A therapeutic application that pacifies one disease while provoking another..."—it is still employed.

"It is not pure; rather, that which does not provoke [the humors] but pacifies them is pure" (Nirvāṇa-aṣṭaka 8). Nevertheless, it should be understood that in the treatment of a *sannipāta* (combined disorder), when no other alternative is possible, this is practiced because it involves little harm and many benefits.

Others, however, derive [the term] from the root *vardh* meaning "to cut," thus establishing it as *vardhanena*; by the word *vardhana*, they mean a purifying treatment (*saṃśodhana*) that effects the cutting of the root [of the disease]. By the mention of "one" (*eka*), it is shown that the purification of the bladder and other channels for vāta and the other doshas should not be performed simultaneously, but rather one by one. By the phrase "by depletion of what has increased," palliative treatment (*saṃśamana*) is indicated regarding the subject of purification. The explanation of the remainder is as before. By this verse, the treatment for the thirteen types of fever arising from the combination of all three doshas (*sannipāta*) is stated.

Regarding the six types of *sannipāta* caused by the combination of diminished (*kṣīṇa*) and increased (*vṛddha*) doshas, the treatment for the fever should not consist merely of alleviating the increased state of two or even one of the doshas that initiate the fever; rather, in those cases, the restoration of their own respective normal measures (*svamāna*)—both for the diminished and the increased—is also necessary. However, the twelve-fold *sannipāta* characterized by diminished normal measures does not initiate fever at all.

In this context of the *sannipāta* (combined humors), having referred back to the swelling described in the *Triśothīya* chapter as arising from that [combination], he states the treatment, beginning with the words "sannipāta...

etc. By the phrase "only some are liberated," he demonstrates the severity of this condition. As it is said: "Indeed, there are such diseases considered severe yet curable, which would kill if left untreated or if managed improperly" (*Sūtrasthāna*, ch. 18). Alternatively, this [condition] is generally curable, though occasionally it may be difficult to cure.

Now, one might object: "In the *Triśothīya* [chapter], it was stated that 'at the end of a fever, a swelling arises for him that is difficult to conquer and leads to death' (*Sūtra*, ch. 18); this indicates its incurability. Yet here, it is said that 'some indeed are liberated. How is there no contradiction? Do not say so. Even there, the meaning is that it becomes difficult to conquer or leads to the end; therefore, there is no contradiction. (287–288)

Regarding the term *śākhānusārī* (branch-ascending), although it has been stated that "the branches are the bodily constituents such as blood" (*Sūtra-sthāna*, chapter 11), here specifically the fever that vitiates the blood is to be understood. This is because bloodletting is particularly effective when the *doṣa* is localized in the blood itself.

Furthermore, the site for bloodletting should be known as the middle of the arm; as it is said elsewhere: "If a fever does not subside through cold, hot, unctuous, or dry treatments, one should quickly bleed the veins in the arms in succession for that patient who has a branch-ascending fever."

By stating that one should employ [therapies] such as cold and heat, it is shown that when the entire sequence of treatment is applied according to the specific doshas involved, the persistence of fever generally occurs due specifically to the vitiation of blood (raktaduṣṭi).
He describes the treatment for fever associated with complications from other disorders, beginning with "visarpeṇa" (by erysipelas), etc.

Regarding the terms "kaphottara" and "pittottara," one should understand that they refer to the predominance of both kapha and pitta together, based on the grammatical rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining one of two similar terms). Alternatively, it may be understood as the predominance of kapha and pitta combined.
Therefore, ghee should indeed be administered when pitta does not move upwards.

In the passage beginning with "due to weakness" (*daurbalyāt*), by means of the mention of the "body," [the author] excludes the self (*ātman*) and so forth, and applies the term "constituent" (*dhātu*) specifically to chyle (*rasa*) and the others; for it is chyle and the rest that specifically sustain the body.
Bṛṃhaṇa means that which produces nourishment and growth.
He describes the treatment for the third-day and fourth-day fevers associated with *bhūtas* (spirits), beginning with the word "karma" (*karma* etc.).

"Common treatment" (*sādhāraṇa*) means that the treatment for both the *bhūta*-association and the [aggravated] *doṣa* is common; it consists of reliance on divine power (*daivavyapāśrayā*), such as strengthening therapies (*balya*), and reliance on rational methods (*yuktivyapāśrayā*), such as drinking decoctions appropriate to the *doṣas*.
By the term "irregular fever" (*viṣamajvara*), only the third-day and fourth-day fevers are intended; by "fourth-day fever," the "reverse fourth-day fever" (*caturthakaviparyaya*) is also included.
It should be understood that [this applies] to medicines with bitter and cold after-drinks;
"astringent and hot" means hot astringents (kaṣāya-uṣṇa).

"Having distinguished the humors and so forth" means that one should administer whatever is appropriate for a specific case after considering the humors (doṣa), time (kāla), location (deśa), constitution (prakṛti), and other factors; "six-pala" refers to the formulation to be described later in the section on abdominal tumors (gulma).

Nīlinī, nīlikā, or nīlabuhnā—this group beginning with nīlinī constitutes a purgative formulation that becomes effective through purging on the day the fever arrives due to its specific potency (*prabhāva*). A large dose (*mahatī mātrā*) is to be administered over a period of a full day and night; however, in other contexts, a "large dose" is said to consist of six *pala*s.

Elsewhere, beginning with "The one-day fever, the two-day fever, the third-day, and the fourth-day fevers," and ending with "They are to be treated before they arrive by one who knows the times of strength," the treatment described prior to the day of the paroxysm should be understood as distinct from the emesis and other therapies mentioned here.

However, it should be understood that emesis and the other therapies are performed here on the day of provocation because, when administered when the provoked *doṣa* has reached the gastrointestinal tract (*koṣṭha*), they effect a proper and immediate expulsion.
The construction is: "having drunk abundant food and wine, one should again undergo emesis"; likewise, the construction is: "having drunk wine with food, one should sleep on that very day.
*Yāpanā* refers to the enemas (bastis) containing *mustā* and other ingredients which will be described later;
*vṛṣadaṃśa* means a cat.
In the phrase "of the bull" (vṛṣasya), the word "dung" (śakṛt) is also to be connected;
"medyānām" means "of the fatty ones," or alternatively, "of the pure ones" (medhyānām).
In the term "vaivyāghrī," it is inferred from the statement that the masculine gender itself is the governing factor.
They say that a lion is indeed a tiger.

Since the root *añj* is listed in the sense of "manifesting" (*vyakti*) and "smearing" (*mrakṣaṇa*), it might follow that even mere smearing would be called *añjana*; therefore, he says "eye-salve" (*netrāñjana*).
This refers to mental derangement, namely insanity (*unmāda*) and epilepsy (*apasmāra*).
The word "dhāraṇāt" (from wearing) is the division [of the compound]; it is to be construed as "and from the use of medicines.

He describes the treatment based on divine recourse (daivavyapāśraya-cikitsā): "Soma," and so forth; "Soma" is that which is with Umā; "him along with his followers" means him accompanied by the group beginning with Nandin.
"Accompanied by the host of mothers" means together with the assembly of mothers;
"pure and restrained" refers to one who is purified;
"thousand-headed" refers to that which is proclaimed in the Veda, beginning with the verse "Thousand-headed," and so forth.
"By the Thousand Names," and so forth; that is, by the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) consisting of the Thousand Names spoken in the *Mahābhārata*.
With the words beginning with "śāpa" (curse), he describes the treatment for exogenous fever;
"naśyet" means that it subsides.
"Sānāha" refers specifically to fever caused by trauma (abhighātajvara).

Regarding "of those with chest wounds" (kṣatānām), the meaning is that for those with chest injuries, as well as for those with ulcers, the fever subsides through the treatment of the wound— that is, through the treatment of the chest injury and the treatment of the ulcer itself.

For this fever is of the nature of a complication (*upadrava*); the sense is that a complication is pacified only by the treatment of the primary disease. [The phrase] "by the pacification of the wind" is appropriate because in fevers such as those arising from desire (*kāma*), there is an association with *vāta*.
[The phrase] "with good words" means with excellent speech.
He states the medical treatment by means of the opposites of desire and so forth— beginning with "kāmāt" and so on (verses 317–322).

Since even a fever arising from the consideration of the timing of a fever's onset is produced by mental transgression, just like [fevers] caused by desire and so forth, he states its treatment beginning with "of fever," etc.
Having now stated the medicine, he provides the answer to the question beginning with "he releases" (*vimuñcati*), starting with "at the release from fever" (*jvarapramokṣe*) and so forth.
"He dissolves" (*līyate*) means he becomes delirious;
"with all his limbs hot" (*uṣṇasarvāṅgaḥ*) and "with all his limbs cold" (*śītasarvāṅgaḥ*) means that he becomes either one whose entire body is hot or one whose entire body is cold.
"Accompanied by a foul odor and sound" means both having a foul odor and being accompanied by sound;
it should be understood that these characteristics occur only in *sannipāta* fever and not elsewhere, precisely because they are not observed in other cases.
For this very reason, some read the passage beginning with "of one whose humors are bound and strong" right here.

These symptoms are produced at the time of liberation from fever even by a diminished *doṣa*, just as a great light is produced by a lamp that is about to go out. (324–328) Now follows the answer to the question regarding the characteristics of a subsided fever—beginning with "vigata... and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the natural being" (*prakṛtisattvena*), which refers to the innate being (*sahajasattva*):
this is the answer to the question, "For how long and from whatever source must one who remains afflicted by fever be protected?"— namely, "one who is feverish," and so forth.

By the statement, "In this way, the fever subsides and, once pacified, does not arise again," the answer to the question "From what [cause]"—which takes the form of an inquiry into the causes for avoiding [certain activities] after being freed from fever—is to be understood.

In the passage "sexual intercourse (vyavāya), excessive exertion (aticeṣṭā)," and so on, the repetition of the term "sexual intercourse" even after mentioning "exertion" indicates that sexual intercourse is absolutely prohibited. Others, however, say that this is merely a scribal error.
Even bathing, though it bestows vigor, brings back fever due to its inherent power; as it is said elsewhere: "Bathing quickly induces fever in a person who has just been freed from fever."
"Therefore, one who is free from fever should avoid bathing as if it were poison.

Immediately following this (verses 330–332), the Kashmiris recite the passage beginning with "But he whose strength has not yet arisen," and they also recite a corresponding interrogative text for this very passage in the *Prakṛtyādisūtra*.
333–343 He states [the following] for the purpose of including treatments both mentioned and not mentioned: "In that [condition]," and so forth.
He says "the king of diseases," etc., in order to urge effort toward the treatment of fever;
"in due order" is the summary verse for the contents of this chapter.
By the phrase "with the desire for the welfare of living beings," he shows that this medical treatment is for the benefit of all living beings.
Thus ends the third chapter, on the Treatment of Fever, in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka-saṃhitā, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
3 [Chapter 4 of Cikitsāsthāna (70 of 120)]:
Following the treatment of fever, the treatment of *raktapitta* is now described, because *raktapitta* arises from the heat of fever at its initial onset.
Pañcagaṅga is a specific region.
It should be stated what is "furthermore" (param), meaning the treatment that is distinct from the causes and symptoms of raktapitta already mentioned.

Although the causes and symptoms of *raktapitta* have already been explained in the *Nidāna*, they are nevertheless stated here again—briefly and according to the requirements of the context—for the purpose of providing the necessary background for treatment:
namely, heat and exposure to the sun.

The burning sensation of food (*annavidāha*) arises from consuming substances that are inherently burning (*svarūpavidāhin*). Likewise, it also occurs due to the vitiation of the food-carrying channels (*annavahasrotas*) by *pitta*, even when the food consumed is not burning in nature;

as it is stated elsewhere: "In one whose *pitta* resides in the food-carrying channel or in the digestive fire (*pakti*), even food that is not burning, or any other [food], becomes burned for him" (Suśruta Sūtrasthāna 46).
With the words "by those causes" (5–6) and so forth, he describes the attainment;
"it reaches the blood" means it goes to the blood.

Although blood naturally flows [to the site] according to the statement: "Bile, sweat, rasa, lymph, and blood, as well as the stomach (āmāśaya), are the seats of bile; among these, the stomach is specifically the seat of bile" (Sūtra-sthāna 20), nevertheless, in the pathogenesis (samprāpti) of raktapitta, one should understand that the movement of bile into the blood here occurs from its primary seat, which is the stomach; and this movement of bile into the blood occurs by virtue of the power of the pathogenesis itself.

Regarding the phrase "because of having that as its source" (*tadyonitvāt*): "having that as its source" is the reason, which should be understood as referring to the increase of *pitta* when it has reached the blood (*rakta*). Thus, the meaning is that since *pitta* has the blood as its source, it increases upon reaching the blood.
For it has been stated: "Pitta [arises] from the blood" (*asṛjaḥ pittaṃ*, Ci.A. 15). Therefore, it vitiates that [blood].

The term "liquid element" (*dravo dhātuḥ*) refers to the liquid portion of each respective tissue (*dhātu*). Regarding the phrase "from each tissue," it means that as the flesh and other tissues are heated, they exude—that is, they overflow—[fluid]. Thus, the construction [of the sentence] is as follows: joined with that liquid element which has flowed out from the tissues being heated by the heat of the *pitta*, [the *pitta* itself], becoming associated with *pitta*, undergoes further and even greater increase.
He states the definition and cause for the designation "raktapitta" (hemorrhagic fever/blood-bile): "Due to the conjunction," and so forth.

The meaning of the sentence is that because of the conjunction with blood, as well as due to the vitiation of blood, and because of the similarity between the smell and color of blood and bile, bile is called *raktapitta*.
He states the location of *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disease): "and the spleen," etc., continues [the verse];
it moves upward and downward; or there is the reading "it increases."
He explains why it resides specifically in the liver (*yakṛt*) and spleen (*plīhan*): "The channels," and so forth.

Since the primary location of even blood is indeed the liver and spleen, the implication is that the very same location belongs to *raktapitta*, which is produced through the combination of blood and other factors.
He describes the symptoms according to the specific association with those defects: "thick" and so forth.
That which has an appearance like a decoction (kaṣāya) is "decoction-like" (kaṣāyābha), meaning it is pale-red (pāṭala).
The color of black cloth or similar materials that have been polished with substances such as *sāra* and *gandhaka* is called *mecaka*.

Is it not said that *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disease) is bile alone? How then can it be of the phlegmatic (*ślaiṣmika*) type? It is explained as follows: In the general pathogenesis (*sāmānya-samprāpti*), bile alone is the producer of *raktapitta*, just as wind is in all abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and just as bile is the initiator in all fevers (*jvara*). When that very [bile] becomes associated with an aggravated phlegm (*kapha*) that produces its own specific characteristics, it then ceases to be designated by the bile reached through the general pathogenesis, and is instead designated by the phlegm itself—which produces specific characteristics such as thickness—as "phlegmatic *raktapitta*. Just as in a phlegmatic tumor (*gulma*), one disregards the wind arrived via the general pathogenesis and there is designation by phlegm alone; or as in a phlegmatic fever (*kaphajvara*), one disregards the cause common to all fevers and there is designation by phlegm alone, which produces specific characteristics; so too should it be explained for the windy (*vātika*) type of *raktapitta*.

However, that *raktapitta* which is produced by powerful *pitta* alone, devoid of *kapha* and *vāta*, possesses the characteristics of *paittika-raktapitta* and is therefore called *paittika-raktapitta*;

for the designation of the *doṣa* occurs precisely through its symptoms. Thus, whichever *raktapitta* possesses the symptoms produced by a particular *doṣa*, it is designated as being born from that specific *doṣa*.

In comparison with *raktapitta* caused by *kapha* and other doshas, in *paittika* (bile-type) *raktapitta*, the *pitta* is extremely dominant, because it manifests its own specific symptoms there and not elsewhere. This being the established rule, as for what is said—that there is no upward path for purely *paittika* *raktapitta* because it has been taught that *vāta-rakta* moves downward while that initiated by *kapha* moves upward—that too is incorrect. For even in the case of *paittika* [raktapitta], both upward and downward movement certainly occur. However, when the *paittika* type moves upward, it becomes associated with *kapha* due to the nature of that pathway; and when it moves downward, it becomes accompanied by *vāta* due to its connection with the seat of *vāta*.

Furthermore, a disorder (*doṣa*) that follows the connection with a [specific] channel (*mārga-sambandhānugata*) is not considered a secondary associate (*anubandha*) because it does not produce its own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, even in cases of *raktapitta* caused by *pitta*, such a disorder is not included in statements such as "a condition following a single *doṣa* is curable. This is because only a *doṣa* that is independent (*svatantra*), possesses manifest signs (*vyaktaliṅga*), and acts as a primary associate is a true associate; its opposite, however, is merely a secondary associate. Consequently, the designation of *raktapitta* as being caused by *vāta* and so forth is based on the *doṣa* acting as a primary associate that produces its own specific characteristics, and not on a *doṣa* that merely follows a channel connection and does not produce its own specific characteristics in the form of a secondary associate.

Others, however, say: "When, at a later time, there occurs a connection of the bile accumulated in another location with the blood, only then does the blood-bile disease (raktapitta) become of the bilious type.
Now he states the distinction between the curable and the incurable: "One [disease]," and so forth.

"Accompanied by a single dosha" means possessing the characteristics of the single dosha previously described; likewise, a disease with two doshas should be understood as possessing the characteristics of those two doshas, and the same applies to a disease with three doshas.

However, one should not count a condition as being caused by two or three *doṣas* by adding a defect associated with the pathways (*mārga*), for if that were the case, there would be no such thing as pure *rakta-pitta* at all. Furthermore, by taking a *doṣa* already present through its manifestation (*samprāpti*) and joining it with a *vāyu* or *kapha* following the pathways, everything would always result in being born of two *doṣas*; thus, the statement that "that which follows a single *doṣa* is curable" would be contradicted. Therefore, what has been stated [previously] alone is correct.
"Like a slow fire with a weak impulse" is a distinct sign of incurability, as is "one whose body is wasted by diseases," and so forth (verses 13–14).
To demonstrate the classification of curable and other conditions based on the course of the disease (*gati*), he states the different types of courses, beginning with "the course is upward," etc.
He states another type of course for the incurable with the words beginning "When, however, from all the openings...
and ending with "and that which by both... up to "...excessively black.

Here, by the phrase "by the two paths," he does not establish the simultaneous operation of the two paths; rather, they operate individually, because it was previously stated that one who proceeds by both paths is incurable.
"By the stench of a corpse" means by the odor of a dead body;
"it clings to the throat" means it does not pass out from the throat.

"By those as described" refers to those mentioned in the introduction (nidāna); for there, the complications (upadrava) beginning with debility and anorexia and ending with hoarseness of voice have been described.

It should be understood that [the disease] characterized by a turmeric-colored [sputum] and so forth does not succeed in a patient who is emaciated and coughing. By the phrase "associated with two doṣas," the curability [only through palliative means] is stated due to the presence of two doṣas acting as secondary complications (anubandha); whereas what was previously stated—that a disease born of two doṣas is palliable—was intended to refer to cases produced by two doṣas acting as primary causes (anubandhya). Thus, there is no redundancy.

"One should move from channel to channel" means that [the *vāyu*] abandons the upward-moving mouth and enters the nose, and so forth; this should be understood. However, when an upward-moving [wind] moves downward, it becomes palliable (*yāpya*) precisely because of its downward movement. An downward-moving [wind], on the other hand, is palliable by its very nature even without going to another channel. Therefore, the exchange between the upward and downward channels is not what is intended here.
(Verses 15–21) By the words "one channel," etc., the characteristics of the curable (*sādhya*) are stated.

Although the expression "single path" (*ekamārga*) is a general term, it refers specifically to the upward path (*ūrdhvamārga*), because even one who moves along the downward path (*adhogati*) is merely palliable (*yāpya*).
Regarding the phrase "at a pleasant time," this refers to the late autumn (*hemanta*) and early winter (*śiśira*).
Here, the distinctions between curable, incurable, and palliable conditions have been stated separately by way of the path (*mārga*), the humor (*doṣa*), and the symptoms (*lakṣaṇa*).

In that regard, when there is a combination of a curable (*sādhya*) and a palliable (*yāpya*) characteristic, it is indeed palliable; when there is a combination of a palliable and an incurable (*asādhya*) characteristic, it is indeed incurable. For example: that which is caused by a single *doṣa* and has descended downward is curable because it is caused by a single *doṣa*, yet it is palliable because it has descended downward; whereas that which is caused by all three *doṣas* and has descended downward is palliable due to its descending nature, but it is indeed incurable because it involves all three *doṣas*.

As it has been said: "The incurable does not become curable, but the curable may become incurable" (Ni. A. 8); and also: "The curable turn into palliable, and likewise the palliable into incurable" (Ni. A. 8). 22

Although [the qualities] such as "unctuous and hot" were already mentioned in the section on etiology (*nidāna*), they are stated here again for the purpose of demonstrating specific exceptions, since that was merely the general rule.

By the word "generally" (*prāyas*), he shows that sometimes even dry-hot [qualities] can be the cause of upward-moving [diseases], and likewise, unctuous-hot [qualities] can be the cause of downward-moving [diseases]. Thus, when there is no fixed rule regarding the etiology and the pathways, the five factors—including the pathways and so forth—that were listed in the passage beginning with "Having carefully examined the pathways, the association with the *doṣas*, and the etiology... [are now explained].

Although dry and hot [qualities] alone are the primary cause for downward movement, nevertheless, unctuous and hot [qualities] may occasionally be a cause, and phlegm produced by unctuousness may also move downward. This should be considered similarly regarding upward movement as well;
even in cases such as "upward-moving [vata] associated with phlegm," one should understand that there is deviation from the rule due to the connection with the word "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*).

By the word "aśnataḥ" (of one eating), he indicates [the condition] arising from over-satiation; "utkliṣṭam" means ready to manifest, because it is dependent on the defect of undigested matter (*āmadoṣa*).

Regarding the phrase "baladoṣavicāriṇā," as soon as one perceives a decrease in strength or a state where the humors are diminished, at that very moment a constipating (*stambhana*) treatment should be administered.
25–28 Now he states the complete set of reasons for fasting (laṅghana): "The two pathways," and so forth.

Among these, the upper pathway consists of pitta with undigested matter (sāma), as well as the humor (doṣa) kapha; and unctuous-hot etiological factors (nidāna) are the motivators for fasting. Conversely, the other factors, such as the [lower] pathway and so on, are the motivators for nourishment in the form of food.
"Tarpaṇa" means that which satiates, namely food; by this, both rice-gruel (*yavāgū*) and *tarpaṇa* (the liquid offering) are to be understood.
However, for those who take the word "tarpaṇa" to mean only the *saktu*-tarpaṇa (the flour-offering), the alternative of giving rice-gruel would not be included.
"Kevalam" (alone) means devoid of *hrībēra* and other such ingredients. Only water alone is to be given first to a person who hates medicinal substances;
by the word "first," [the author] precludes that which causes a loss of strength later on.

*Time* (*kāla*) refers to winter and so forth; *continuity* (*anubandha*) refers to the persistence of the *doṣas*; *nature* (*prakṛti*) is the inherent quality of substances, such as heaviness or lightness; and *preparation* (*kalpana*), meaning *kalpa*, signifies processing or refinement.

By this [verse], the meaning is that having understood the time and the continuity of the *doṣas*, one should administer nourishment or gruel using whatever substance is appropriate for the specific nature of the patient.
Water prepared with dates (*kharjūra*) and other such ingredients should be made according to the six-fold procedure (*ṣaḍaṅga-vidhāna*).
This water, though sweet, is suitable here for upward-moving *raktapitta* even when it is associated with *kapha*, because it is antagonistic to the disease of *raktapitta*.
With the words beginning with "śālī," he speaks of food:
*praśāntikā*, *priyaṅgu*, and *kaṅgu* generally grow in the midst of water.

In the *Nidāna*, it is stated that *koradūṣa* is a cause of *raktapitta* only when combined with soups of *niṣpāva*, *māṣa*, and so forth, due to the power of such association; however, here it is taught that *koradūṣa* alone, because of its astringent, sweet, and light qualities, indeed cures *raktapitta*.

Similarly, in the *Nidāna*, *gaṇḍīra* is described as a cause [of blood disorders] only when combined with wine, *sauvīraka*, and so forth; however, by itself, it is indeed beneficial. Alternatively, *gaṇḍīra* is of two kinds, distinguished as land-born and water-born: that which is listed in the section on greens (*haritavarga*) constitutes the [causal] *nidāna*, whereas the other—the water-born variety listed in the section on pot-herbs (*śākavarga*)—is to be understood here [as beneficial] in cases of *raktapitta* where *kapha* is predominant.

"Boiled like broth" (yūṣavad-vipācita) means that just as broth is boiled in water combined with sour substances such as pomegranate and the like, so too is this [preparation]; or alternatively, it means it is boiled in such a way that it is accompanied by broth.
"Raktākṣa" refers to the *cakoraka* bird;
"broth and vegetables" (yūṣa-śāka) is a compound meaning broth and leafy vegetables.
He speaks of food according to its state: "The rabbit," and so forth.

Here, the rabbit, because of its astringent nature, certainly removes blood-bile (raktapitta); furthermore, because it is prepared with vāstuka, which removes constipation, it also becomes a remover of constipation.

Thus, although partridges, peacocks, and the like remove wind due to their heat, they are nevertheless not beneficial in cases of *raktapitta* because of that same heat; consequently, for their treatment, substances such as the juice of the *udumbara* fruit, which alleviate *raktapitta*, are employed. This being so, it is understood that they destroy both wind and *raktapitta* through the power of combination itself, by means of the presentation of specific remedial substances.

Even a rabbit causes constipation when prepared with *vāstuka* greens; partridges and the like do not provoke *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders) when prepared with the juice of *udumbara* and other ingredients. Thus, there is no occurrence of contrary results, because the power of combination (*saṃyoga*) is inconceivable.
The application of the rabbit as a remedy is specifically for *vāstuka* juice, due to its association with other [corrective] substances.
For it has been said: "One should cook the rabbit in *vāstuka* juice for the purpose of treating constipation."

"Proven with the Vidārigandhādi [group]" refers to water boiled with the *pañcamūla* of the Śāliparṇyādi group (49–51). Now, he describes the manner of administering the drink, beginning with the words "Having known," etc.
The two *doṣas* are wind (*vāta*) and phlegm (*kapha*); however, bile (*pitta*) is only the leader and not the auxiliary.
"Until emission" means until cessation; the meaning is "as long as one desires.
He states another alternative: "or even slightly," meaning in small amounts.

In this case, if the digestive fire (*agni*) is strong and the body is large, then water should be given until the completion of the evacuation (*visarga*); however, in the opposite case, water is not very wholesome and should therefore be given only in small quantities.
(52) To avoid the causes of *raktapitta*, he says: "The etiology," and so forth.
53. By the words "it will be said," etc., the purificatory therapies are mentioned because they constitute the primary medicines.
By the phrase "one whose strength and flesh are undiminished," innate loss of strength is indicated; by the phrase "one who is strong," strength produced by time is indicated.

"At a time suitable for purification"—meaning a season that is neither too hot nor too cold—is an adverbial modifier of the action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), or alternatively, it is an adjective modifying *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disease).

By the passage beginning with "by purgation [one treats] the upper part," etc., [the author] prohibits downward evacuation (*anulomaharaṇa*) in cases of *raktapitta*. As it has been stated: "And evacuation according to the path [of the disease] is prescribed in *raktapitta*" (Ni.
A. 2). By the phrase "especially in *raktapitta*," it is indicated that elsewhere than in *raktapitta*, these [medicinal preparations], such as pastes (*kalka*), and so forth, may also be employed.

"Vamana" refers to a formulation that induces emesis; the dosage for *madana* fruit, such as one *karṣa* and so forth, depending on the humors (*doṣa*) and other factors, should be understood as it will be described in the section on pharmaceutical preparations (*kalpa*).
It should be known that the emetic action arises solely from the *madana* formulation when combined with sugar in water or likewise with sugarcane juice.
In the phrase "if there is downward movement" (*adhovahe*), the term "of one with pure bowels" (*śuddhakoṣṭhasya*) should also be applied.

By the statement "provided the wind is not strong" (*na cet syān māruto balī*), it indicates the procedure mentioned for fevers: that if the wind (*māruta*) is strong, then only meat-rice (*māṃsaudana*) should be given.
He states the scope for palliative treatment: "Strength, flesh," and so forth;
"by consumption" means by *rājayakṣmā*;
some say that the formulation beginning with "aṭarūṣaka, grapes," and so forth, removes jaundice (*kāmalā*).

In the case of "the decoction of *aṭarūṣaka*" and so forth, one should take one *karṣa* of the combined paste (*kalka*) of *priyaṅgu* and the other ingredients, and one *karṣa* of honey (*kṣaudra*), by virtue of the established technical rule (*paribhāṣā*).

As stated by Agniveśa: "One *karṣa* is the measure for powder, paste, and pills in all cases; for honey, ghee, and the like, as well as in decoctions and medicated oils, it is the same as for powders."

Others, however, say: "The weight of one *karṣa* for the powders (*cūrṇa*) and so forth applies to their independent administration; here, however, the decoction of *āṭarūṣaka* should be prepared according to the rules for decoctions, and the paste (*kalka*) should be prepared according to the rules for pastes.

Since each of the ingredients beginning with *priyaṅgu* would individually amount to one *karṣa*, there would be an excess of medicinal substance; therefore, it is appropriate that the total combined weight of one *karṣa* be administered here."
"By that same method" means combined with a decoction of *aṭarūṣaka* and honey.

In the passage beginning with "of *khadira*," because of the plural number in the word "flower-powders" (*puṣpacūrṇāni*), the qualification "curing *rakta-pitta*" should be understood as referring to the person [who consumes them]. "Of those born in the *dhanva* region" means of those from the *jāṅgala* (arid) lands.

In the passage beginning with *uśīra* (62–72), the term *pṛthak pṛthak* indicates distributive repetition (*vīpsā*); thus, it shows that each of the ingredients, beginning with *uśīra* and equal to *candana*, should be used individually. Consequently, there are eight formulations.

By the statement "together with sugar" (*saśarkarā*), it is indicated here that the sugar should be given in an equal proportion. For it is stated in the *Agniveśa*: "One *māṣaka* of asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), while the rock salt (*sindhūttha-lavaṇa*) and the others are each one *śāṇa*."
"Sugar, sugar-candy, jaggery, and alkali are equal; this is the method of preparation.
Wherever sugar is to be added, it should be given according to the principle of addition.
Furthermore, by the statement "Kirāta and the others are each joined with sandalwood," it is indicated that each individual substance is to be used in an amount equal to the sandalwood.
By the phrase "in that very manner," the presence of sugar and soaking in rice-wash water are expressed;
*kramuka* is *paṭṭikālodhra*,
and *dhanañjaya* is *arjuna*.
By the passage beginning with "latā priyaṅguḥ samaṅgā varāhakrāntā, ‘lajjāluḥ’ iti loke niśisthitā," [the author] states the pharmaceutical preparations (kalpanā) of kirātatikta and the other drugs.
By the term "niśāsthitā" (left overnight), a cold infusion (*śītakaṣāya*) is meant;

by "mṛditāḥ" (crushed), those made into a *phāṇṭa* are indicated. By the mention of "pulp" (*kalka*), the powder (*cūrṇa*) is also included, since in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā*, exactly six pharmaceutical preparations (*kalpa*) are taught according to different recensions: "Milk, juice, pulp, as well as decoction, cold infusion, and likewise *phāṇṭa*—these are indeed the six preparations of medicinal substances, and they are declared to be progressively lighter [in potency]" (*Su.Sū.A.* 44).

Others, however, maintain that even powder (*cūrṇa*) is included under the term *phāṇṭa*; yet, when that reading is authoritative in the *Suśruta* precisely because of the mention of *phāṇṭa*, then by the word "powder" a different preparation (*kalpāntara*) is intended.
But here, since *phāṇṭa* is explicitly mentioned, one should accept the *phāṇṭa* as it is recited by Kṛṣṇātreya and others.
As it has been said: "That essence which is extracted from [a substance] that has been crushed in hot water, kneaded, and strained, is proclaimed as *phāṇṭa* by those who know it"—
by this [definition], here the powder (*cūrṇa*) itself, being devoid of liquid, is referred to by the word *kalka*.
Now he states their application both individually and collectively, beginning with "ete" and so forth.
"In groups" (*gaṇaśaḥ*) means in the group beginning with *uśīra*, in the group beginning with *kirātatikta*, and in the group beginning with *tugā*.

Regarding this, it is stated that in each individual application, there should be an equal amount of sandalwood (*candana*); the elders explain that even when the application is made in groups, an equal portion of sandalwood must be given.
73–77. Regarding "balā-water": these are cold decoctions (śītakaṣāya), meaning they have been left overnight in cold water prepared with *balā*.
Water that remains together with lapis lazuli and other such substances is to be understood as "lapis lazuli water" and so forth;
in the context of the *uśīra* and other [herbs], "clarified decoction" (*prasāda*) refers to clear water that has been strained.
In the *priyaṅgvādi* group, *abhayā*, *uśīra*, and *samṛtprasāda*—where *mṛtprasāda* should also be added immediately thereafter; likewise in the application of *yaṣṭikā*.

Regarding the phrase "there [it] would be wind," this means that in that case, the application (prayoga)—that is, the practice—would involve a powerful wind. In the passage beginning with "sajīvakam" and so forth, it should be understood that the milk boiled with *sajīvaka* and *sarṣabhaka*, combined with ghee and sugar, is to be used; that is, it is to be known as something to be drunk.
Regarding the term *parṇinībhiḥ*, the *parṇinyas* consist of a group of four *parṇinīs*. 85.
"Vaṭa-śuṅgāḥ" refers to unopened fresh banyan shoots.
"Kaṣāya-yogān" means having drunk the paste (kalka) of *aṭarūṣaka* and other such ingredients prepared with milk;

"by these" refers to those that will be mentioned hereafter. Alternatively, clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) should be prepared using these very decoction-formulations (*kaṣāya-yoga*) according to their suitability.
Regarding "atisrave" (excessive flow), this refers to the excessive discharge of blood and bile;
since the procedure for *vāsā* itself is restated here as being performed while it is still fresh, there is no doubling of the dose.

Regarding the paste of *vāsā* flowers, some say that because the flower-paste becomes exceedingly abundant, one should add four *palas* of flower-paste to one *prastha* of ghee; however, by the statement "mixed with honey," it should be understood—based on the authority of other medical treatises—that the honey is one-quarter (*pādika*) of the ghee. For it is said: "The paste is traditionally held to be one-quarter of the fat; honey and sugar are like the paste. It is also stated in the *Agniveśa*: "The dosage of honey and ghee in [preparations with] fats and decoctions is as previously described."
"As before" means [the mixture] is one-quarter [of the total];
"with liquid honey" means it has been liquefied with one-quarter [measure] of honey.

For *trāyamāṇā* as well, ghee should be cooked in the same manner as previously described. Furthermore, by the statement "the leaves of *udumbara* and *paṭola* [are] destroyers of *pitta*-fever," all the remedies for *pitta*-fever mentioned in the section on general therapeutics (*sakalacikitsita*) are to be understood as removing *pitta*-fever. However, in the section on the treatment of fever (*jvaracikitsita*), the various ghees are stated to be for the purpose of curing chronic fever (*jīrṇajvara*), not specifically for curing *pitta*-fever. Others, however, maintain that those very ghees which cure chronic fever are also the ones that cure *pitta*-fever; yet, their status as being directed toward *pitta* is indicated by the commonality of their application to fever through the passage beginning with "the heat [of *pitta*] is dry" (*rūkṣaṃ teja*).

In other sections as well, one should employ the ghees (ghṛtas) that cure pitta-fever, which are taught throughout the entire section on therapeutics (*sakalacikitsita*), such as those beginning with "In ten parts of water, four *palas* of *trāyamāṇā* should be prepared" up to "gulma arising from pitta and blood, erysipelas (*visarpa*), and pitta-type fever" (Ci. A. 5), as well as those beginning with "*trāyantikā*" up to "in vātarakta, wasting due to injury (*kṣatakṣīṇa*), erysipelas, and pitta-type fever" (Ci.
