A. 29). By the phrase "oil-massages (*abhyaṅga*) and formulations," etc., he extends by analogy (*atideśa*) all those [remedies] stated to alleviate burning fever (*dāhajvara*) for the purpose of pacifying pitta-fever.
Regarding the phrase "in blood with bile" (*rudhire sapitte*), this refers to the application of alkali (*kṣāra*) that is properly administered in cases of *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disease).
Here, the word "properly" (*yuktyā*) signifies the correct dosage (*mātrā*). Thus, it is the application of alkali when it is joined with the appropriate measure.

Although alkali (kṣāra) is said to be sharp (tīkṣṇa), it is nevertheless administered in cases of raktapitta for the purpose of dissolving the phlegm (kapha) located in the throat, because its qualities are modified by being processed with lotus stalks and other ingredients. Due to its specific potency (prabhāva) in removing raktapitta, alkali made from lotus stalks and such materials indeed becomes a remover of raktapitta; this is why, setting aside substances that are inherently sharp, he specifically prescribes lotus stalks and the like for the purpose of preparing the alkali.

Now, one might object: "Surely the coldness of the blue lotus (*utpala*) and other such things departs when they are burned by fire; and it has been stated in the *Vārttika* by Kṣīrasvāmin: 'When scorched, it immediately abandons its lunar coldness for the most part,' for a quality is indeed seen to arise even in ashes. [Reply: This refers to the citron (*phalapūraka*), which is the "fruit-filler" (*bījapūraka*).
The five pentads of roots mentioned as *rasāyana* act in that same manner; thus, it imitates the previously mentioned ghee prepared with *śatāvarī* and other ingredients (verses 95–96).
He describes the treatment for bleeding from the nose (*ghrāṇapravṛtta-raktapitta*): "Decoction preparations" and so forth.
The decoction preparations mentioned in the passage beginning with "uśīra, kālīyaka," etc., are to be administered in cases of nasal hemorrhage.

An *avapīḍa* is that which is prepared by crushing a substance, squeezing it, and administering the resulting juice; this should be given once the morbid blood has been expelled. He states the fault in the opposite case: "In [the presence of] blood," and so forth.
"With sugar-water" means with water containing sugar;
having ground blue lotuses (*nīlotpala*) and other such ingredients into a paste, an *avapīḍa* (expressed juice) should be administered.
Regarding "priyāla oil" and so forth: the priyāla oil, ghee, or clarified butter from buffalo or goat should be prepared using milk as the liquid medium along with a paste of *madhuka*.

Regarding the phrase "preceded by mango stones" (*āmrāsthipūrvaiḥ*): it refers to those formulations stated in the medical texts, such as "nasal medication [consisting of] mango stone juice and *samaṅgā*," and so forth;
furthermore, *sārivā*, *kamala*, and *utpala* constitute the paste (*kalka*), while milk is to be understood as the liquid medium.
He mentions *bhadraśrī* and others for the purpose of external application (*pralepa*):
*vānīra* is a specific type of *uśīra*, namely the fragrant root;
*kālānusāryā* is *śītala*.
Up to the words "and all [the breezes] are cool," this concludes the prescription for the plastering.
Regarding the phrase "breezes from clusters of lotuses and water-lilies" (*padmotpalānāṃ ca kalāpavātā*), the meaning is "breezes produced by clusters of lotuses and water-lilies.
The summary of the chapter's subject matter through the verse beginning with "hetum" (110–111) is indeed explicit.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Raktapitta," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the *Carakatātparyaṭīkā*, known as the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
4 [Chapter 5 of Cikitsāsthāna (71 of 120)]:
Following the sequence established in the Nidāna section, he now speaks on the treatment of gulma after that of raktapitta.
By the passage beginning with "of all creatures," the praise of the Guru is [offered] because he generates Dharma and because he is thus worthy of faith for the subsequent text;
and because his knowledge is unimpeded regarding the past and the future, he is indeed the Lord—thus, he is the "Lord of the Past and Future."

Although it should be stated that all medical treatment is indeed "established" (siddha) because it is invariably effective in achieving its objective, nevertheless, the word *siddha* should be understood here in this context for the purpose of praise.

Although the causes and symptoms of *gulma* have already been described in the section on etiology (*nidāna*), they are stated again here due to the requirements of the present topic; furthermore, certain specific details not mentioned in the etiology are now being stated.

In the *Nidāna* (Etiology), the obstruction caused by the provocation and increase of *vāyu* through its specific causes was stated; here, by the phrase "or by excessive afflictions," that very same [obstruction] is expressed as being caused by those very factors—namely, feces, *kapha*, and *pitta*.
"Improper therapeutic measures" refers to emesis and the other five procedures (*pañcakarman*) performed incorrectly.
By the passage beginning with "kaphaṃ ca pittaṃ ca," he describes the pathogenesis (samprāpti);
and this is the pathogenesis for the four types [of gulma], excluding the blood-born (śoṇitaja) gulma.
In that context, regarding "kapha and pitta," sometimes it is pitta and sometimes it is kapha.

Among these, in a kaphaja [gulma], the independent kapha is increased; in a pittaja [gulma], the independent pitta is increased by its own causes; and in sannipāta, the pitta and kapha possess the aforementioned qualities. Having agitated [these], the vāyu produces the gulma. It should be understood that in a vātagulma, the independently aggravated vāyu produces the gulma by agitating the pitta and kapha which remain in their natural state.
Regarding "the paths," this refers to the upward, downward, and transverse paths.

Regarding the phrase "it does not go downward," the word *ca* (and) is here indicated by elision (*luptanirdiṣṭa*); therefore, it should be understood that [the wind] does not go upward nor does it go transversely.

Alternatively, since the downward movement of the wind from the stomach (*koṣṭha*) generally occurs, its prohibition is stated explicitly; however, the prohibition of its movement through other paths is obtained by the same principle (*samānanyāyatayā*).

As for the term "in the receptacle of digested food" (*pakvāśaye*), this refers specifically to the lower portions of the receptacle of bile (*pittāśaya*) and the receptacle of undigested food (*āmāśaya*).

It should be understood that "independent" (*svatantra*) refers to a Gulma caused by Vata, while "supported by another" (*parasaṃśraya*) refers to those located in the colon (*pakvāśaya*), the seat of Pitta, and the seat of Kapha— namely, the Kaphaja, Paittika, and the combined (*nicaya*) Gulmas— as these are supported by others. Furthermore, by the term "Gulma" (meaning "a massed cluster"), just as even the ignorant designate a dense growth of creepers or similar things as a "Gulma" because they exist as a compact mass, so too here the designation "Gulma" is applied because it exists as a compact mass.
"According to the humor" means according to whichever humor is predominant;
"name" refers to the designation, such as "this is born of wind" (vātaja) or "this is born of bile" (pittaja), and so forth. 6–7.
He states the locations of gulma: "In the bladder," and so forth.
There are five locations for gulma: in the bladder, the umbilicus, the heart, or the two sides.
Although there are only these five starting with the bladder, the explicit mention of "five" is intended to exclude any additional locations.
Since the *raudhira* (blood-born) *gulma* is also situated at the sides of the uterus (*garbhāśaya*), it occurs in the abdomen specifically at the sides;
however, others maintain that this fivefold location applies to those other than the *raudhira*, whereas for the *raudhira*, the specific location is the uterus itself.
Now he announces the separate exposition of the causes, signs, and treatments—beginning with the words "of that which consists of five," etc.—"consisting of five" means having five constituent forms;
"source" (*prabhava*) refers to that from which something originates, i.e., the cause; the causes are fivefold, consisting of *vāta*, *pitta*, *kapha*, and their combination (*sannipāta*).

"Staying in this" is *sthāna*, such as the bladder and so forth; "configuration" (*saṃsthāna*) is the shape; "affliction" (*rujā*) is pain; the "variation" (*vikalpa*) of these is their changeability from moment to moment.
"Causing a cold fever" (*śiśirajvara*)—meaning a fever characterized by cold—is to be connected with the preceding [verb].
That which, upon digestion, undergoes excessive provocation and does not subside, thus produces no comfort. 8–11.
By the verse beginning with "bitter and sour" (kaṭvamlādi), he describes the pitta-type gulma;
by the terms "undigested matter" (āma) and "trauma" (abhighāta), it should be understood that undigested matter and trauma are the generators of pitta;
and by the phrase "and corrupted blood" (rudhiraṃ ca duṣṭam), he demonstrates the birth of pitta—which has become waste (mala)—from corrupted blood.
12–13. By the passage beginning with "cold" (*śīta*), the causes and symptoms of *kapha*-gulma are described.

In this context, at the conclusion of the statement regarding the three causes, he describes the effect of the combination of the three *doṣas*: "But all [of these] are declared to belong to that which consists of an accumulation (*nicaya*)."
That which consists of an accumulation is the *sānnipātika* (combined) type;

and the *sānnipātika* is designated as such because it arises from a gulma formed by an accumulation [of humors], due to a discordant combination (*vikṛti-viṣama-samavāya*) and the power of their conjunction.
Having described the *autpādika* (primary) *nicaya-gulma*, he states the characteristics of the present *śleṣma-gulma* with the verse beginning "staimitya" (15).
Then, for the purpose of extending the causes and symptoms of the *dvidoṣaja-gulma* (gulma arising from two doṣas), he says "nimitta" and so forth.
By the phrase "the strength and weakness of the *doṣas*," [the author] indicates that two [doṣas] may be predominant as a pair;

and by "three," he refers to those arising from vāta-pitta, pitta-kapha, and vāta-śleṣman for the purpose of formulating medicine. By the phrase "because of the combination of equal proportions in their natural state," [it is meant that] since they do not produce effects distinct from themselves when existing individually, the Gulmas arising from pairs or all three are indeed established within each individual *doṣa*. Their mention is intended merely to demonstrate that they are to be treated by combining the treatments prescribed for each individual *doṣa*.

By this, there is no contradiction even with the number five mentioned in the *Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya*, because the distinction between dual (*dvandvika*) and cluster (*gulma*) types is not a determining factor for the count. However, in the case of *sannipāta-gulma*, since its symptoms and its specific influence—such as incurability—are indeed distinct from the symptoms of each individual doṣa, it is logical that it be enumerated separately.
It should be understood that in the case of fever (*jvara*) as well, the dual fevers (*dvandvaja-jvara*) are appropriately classified as such due to their possession of distinct symptoms.
With the words "accompanied by great pain" (*mahāruja*) and so forth, he describes the symptoms of *sannipāta*-originated [gulma].

Some, however, state that any gulma which possesses symptoms distinct from these, yet exhibits merely the combined characteristics of the individual doṣas as previously described, and which arises from the natural combination (*prakṛti-samavāya*) of the doṣas—that is indeed curable.
By the words beginning with "during the season" (ṛtau), he describes blood-tumor (śoṇitagulma);
by saying "during the season," he refers to the time of menstruation,
and by the word "woman" (striyam), he excludes virgins and the very elderly.
"Consolidated indeed" means that the fetus throbbs with its limbs;
"possessing signs identical to a [normal] fetus" means that signs such as the swelling of the breasts occur, which are the same as those of a [normal] pregnancy;
"only in the female state" indicates by this that the occurrence of a blood-tumor (*raktagulma*) in a male is excluded.

"Curable after the tenth month has passed" means that by its very nature, its treatment becomes easy only upon the lapse of the tenth month; if treated earlier, however, there may be excessive hemorrhaging or injury to the uterus and so forth.

As for what is said—that because its symptoms are identical to those of a pregnancy, it is diagnosed as a "blood-tumor" (rudhiragulma) only after the tenth month, and therefore treatment before then is not mentioned here—that is not correct, because even after the lapse of the tenth month, the continued presence of the fetus is observed.

For it has been said: "When [the embryo] may remain nourished even for many years" (Śārīrasthāna 2). Likewise, the state of being fully formed (*sampiṇḍitatva*) has been described as a characteristic contrary to the characteristics of the fetus; therefore, the determination of a blood-tumor (*śoṇitagulma*) certainly occurs even before the tenth month. Consequently, what was stated previously is indeed correct.
Regarding the phrase "after this" (*ata ūrdhvam*), it refers to the subsequent [section] because it designates the sequence of medical procedures.
Regarding the phrase "by means of unctuous substances," he describes the administration of oleation by means of all four types of unctuous substances—beginning with "food" and so forth.

By the use of the word "specifically," it is indicated that not every [substance] is used in every case; specifically, however, the drinking of unctuous substances is contraindicated when a gulma has arisen above the navel.

"Located in the receptacle of digested food" (pakvāśayagata) means that the enema (basti)— both the non-unctuous (nirūha) and the unctuous (anuvāsana)— is applied to the lower part connected to the receptacle of digested food;
"located in the abdomen" (jaṭharāśraya) refers to those situated at the navel and the sides of the navel.
The phrase "both" refers to both *nirūha* and oil enemas (*snehabasti*).

By stating that these are for "vāta-type abdominal tumors" (*vātagulma*), it indicates that what has been prescribed should also be performed for abdominal tumors where *vāta* is predominant; for it is said: "For those with abdominal tumors, the pacification of *vāta* [should be achieved] by means... (Ni. A. 3), and so forth.
"Protecting the *kapha* and *pitta*" means that oleation (*sneha*) should be administered in such a way that the *kapha* and *pitta* do not increase (20–26).
Regarding the treatment of increased *kapha*, *pitta*, and blood through the treatment of *vāta*, he says: "When *kapha* [is increased] in *vāta*, etc. (27).

Because of the statement "mostly conquered," one should administer Vāta therapy in such a way that Vāta becomes mostly conquered through the non-increase of Kapha and the other [doshas], just as one treats what is predominant.
This indicates that whatever dosha—such as Kapha—is predominant due to Vāta therapy, its treatment must be performed;
furthermore, even during that treatment, it must be done in such a way that there is no increase of Vāta. Thus he says: "At first," and so forth.
Although emesis is prohibited in cases of *gulma*, nevertheless, showing that emesis is an exception (*apavāda*) in certain conditions, he says: "In *vāta-gulma*," and so forth;
"phala-vartayaḥ" means fruit-enemas (*phala-varti*).
By the statement "with favorable [measures]," he prohibits strong purgation, as it aggravates vāta (29–31).

Bloodletting with a horn or similar instrument should be performed specifically at the site of the gulma, because the gulma has blood as its substrate; bloodletting by venesection of the arm should be understood as an alternative treatment when the gulma is not relieved by other therapies.
Furthermore, the state of being a seat for blood should be observed in the context of the discussion on the suppuration of *gulma* (32);
this should be applied when [the condition] arises through dry and hot [factors], as in the case of the *paittika* type.
Pitta increases precisely through dryness and heat;
therefore, Tailvaka ghee should be prescribed for abdominal disorders.
With the verse beginning "In the fever of thirst" (tṛṣṇājvare), he describes the treatment for the burning sensation in a gulma.
If bloodletting is performed, the gulmas, their roots severed, do not burn; "with their roots severed" means with the blood cut off.
He clarifies this very state of having the root severed with the words beginning "For blood... (raktaṃ hi).
The sourness and the burning sensation are absent; "it is not" means that due to bloodletting (avaseka), the blood is no longer present,
and because of the absence of that blood, the disease is also no longer present.
"With the humors removed" means with the humors removed by bloodletting; "withered" means one whose body is emaciated.
"The treatment" refers to the procedure consisting of bloodletting;
"he would be consumed by fire" means he would suppurate.

With the words "the guru is hard," and so forth, [the author] describes the characteristics of the unripe (*apakva*), the ripening (*pacyamāna*), and the ripe (*pakva*) stages of a *gulma*. "Having deep-seated flesh and being situated within" means it is deeply embedded in the flesh and located internally;
"firm" means elevated.
"40. One should apply a poultice": this means one should apply a plaster made from warm substances for the purpose of ripening [the swelling].
"Characterized by burning" means in cases such as burning sensations;
"elevated on the outside" means raised externally,
"well-elevated" meaning elevated with evenness, not with a distinction between low and high.
"Immediately after being pressed, elevated" means that when pressed, it rises;
"stiff" means round;
"asleep" means having dull pain.
"Of the Dhānvantarīyas" means of those who study the *Dhanvantari-tantra*, that is, of the surgeons (*śalyavid*);

"those who have practiced" (*kṛtayogya*) refers to those by whom proficiency has been achieved in surgical procedures (*śastrakarman*). Furthermore, the suppuration of a *gulma* is prohibited in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*: "Because it accumulates within itself like a bubble in water..."

"Because it flows internally, it does not reach suppuration" (Uttara-tantra 42). Nevertheless, here it is stated that suppuration occurs in a *gulma* that has occupied a site (*kṛta-vāstu-parigraha*), whereas that which has not occupied a site does not suppurate; this is also accepted here. As for that which is said to suppurate due to having occupied a site, its suppuration arises by virtue of being a *vidradhi* (abscess); thus, there is a discrepancy in terminology regarding the internal portion—that which is situated within the trunk (*koṣṭha*).
Although every type of *gulma* resides within the abdominal cavity (*koṣṭha*), that which does not bulge outward here is intended as being "situated therein" (*tatstha*).

When it is internal, there is swelling of the chest and abdomen (*hṛtkroḍa-śūnatā*); when it is external, there is protrusion toward the sides (*pārśva-nirgati*). This protrusion toward the sides is seen specifically in *gulma*.
However, some do not recite this verse.

By the word "ascends" (*vrajaty ūrdhvam*), that which resides within is intended. "One should wait with wholesome foods" means one should remain on a wholesome diet and not administer any medicine whatsoever.
"Protecting against complications" means protecting from complications such as fever and the like;
"with purification" refers specifically to the administration of ghee for cleansing;
"bitter" means prepared with bitter substances.
With the words beginning with "śītalaiḥ" (by means of cooling [remedies]), he describes the sequence of treatment following the management of *kaphagulma* (gulma caused by phlegm).
"Sakṣārakaṭukam" means prepared with alkaline and pungent substances;
"apasṛtam" means moved or displaced;
"dāśamūlikaiḥ" refers to enemas (basti) made from the ten roots, which are to be described in the *Bastisūtrīya* chapter (*Siddhānta Astāṅgahṛdaya*, Sūtra-sthāna 3).

"Deluded" (*mūḍhe*) means rendered unconscious (*sammūrcchite*), that is to say, "obstructed. Regarding the phrase "pills, powders, and decoctions," it should be stated that pills and so forth [are used] along with alkalis (*kṣāra*), fermented liquors (*ariṣṭa*), and thermal cautery (*agnikarma*). Among these, since alkalis have not been introduced here, they are explained in detail specifically within the *Śalyatantra* (Surgery); furthermore, alkalis are also to be discussed in this very chapter on the digestive tract (*grahaṇī*). Thermal cautery, moreover, is to be briefly mentioned in the section on abdominal tumors (*gulma*), because there is no detailed exposition in a section devoted to other topics.

Because alkali (kṣāra) carries a great risk, [the author] describes its intermittent administration preceded by the knowledge of the humors (doṣa) and other factors, beginning with the words "doṣa... and so forth.

In this regard, the humor (doṣa) compatible with alkali (kṣāra) is phlegm (kapha), the constitution (prakṛti) is of a phlegmatic nature, the abdominal tumor (gulma) is stable, and the season is either late winter (hemanta) or early spring (śiśira). When all such factors—humor and so forth—are compatible with alkali, one should administer it every other day after allowing an interval; however, when only some of these factors are compatible, one should allow an interval of two days or three days. Alternatively, the choice may vary according to the strength of the patient and the state of the humors.
"Skilled in the increase and reduction of bodily strength and the humors" means he is an expert in augmenting physical vigor and diminishing the *doṣas*.

By the phrase "one who eats meat, milk, and ghee," he demonstrates that the preservation of bodily strength must be achieved through the consumption of meat and other such foods, as well as the application of alkaline substances (*kṣāra*).
By the phrase "with arrows, iron, and so forth," he indicates cauterization with dry substances (*rūkṣadāha*);
and this cauterization must be performed specifically on the site of the abdominal tumor (*gulma*).

Since caustic application (*dāha*) and alkali (*kṣāra*) are under the jurisdiction of another [specialty], they are intended for the power of another; therefore, he describes their application specifically through that other specialty—beginning with "caustic" (*dāha*), etc.

Because the *Kṣāra-tantra* is not mentioned separately within the *Aṣṭāṅga*, the *Śalya-tantra* itself, which prescribes surgical instruments and the application of alkali, is called the *Kṣāra-tantra*.

Regarding "in the case of mixed defects" (vyāmiśradoṣe): it refers to that which arises from combination (saṃsargaja) and that which arises from the simultaneous derangement of all three humors (sannipātaja).
Now he states the perfected formulations (siddhayoga), beginning with "the perfected" and so forth.
The term "perfected" is a praise of the formulations about to be described, intended to encourage the student.
Since no other liquid is mentioned for the *tryūṣaṇa* and following recipes, milk alone is to be four times the quantity [of the medicinal ingredients].
"These very [substances]" refers to those mentioned in the verse beginning with "tryūṣaṇa" (the three pungents).
*Prasannā* is a specific type of wine;

it should be given in place of milk for the purpose of obtaining milk. In this same manner, the purpose of milk [substitutes] by means of *svarasa* (fresh juice) and so forth should also be explained.
In the *hiṅgvādi* [formula], there is a paste (*kalka*) of the *hiṅgvādi* group; curd is fourfold, because it is a liquid (69–70).

There is a paste of the *hapuṣādi* group; the five liquids, such as the juice of *kola*, are equal in quantity to the oil. Regarding this, it is said: "Wherever there are five or more liquids in the preparation of an oil..."

This is because of the statement, "In that case, [the liquids] are equal to the oil"; furthermore, even for pomegranate (*dāḍima*), only the juice itself should be taken due to its proximity to other tastes. For it is said by Viśvāmitra: "With *pṛthvīkā*, cumin, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *hapuṣā*, *jīraka*, rock salt, along with *cavya*, long pepper root, *vahni*, and *dīpyaka*—[these are added] to the juice of pomegranate and *kola* roots, as well as to curd and milk."
"This prepared ghee conquers gulma and is a supreme stimulator of the digestive fire.
(71–73) A *picu* is a *karṣa*; thus, "one and a half *picus*" means one and a half *karṣas*.
And here, although a greater quantity of ghee (*ghṛta*) would logically follow, it must be prepared [in a smaller amount] based on the scriptural injunction itself;

for those who know the principles of logic have said: "In whatever manner a specific instruction for substances is heard, that very [instruction] must be carried out therein, even in the absence of an explicit word, by virtue of established convention."

Furthermore, the statement "here again, ghee is prepared" is intended to exclude the application of the *pippalyādi* group as a linctus (*leha*) and to indicate the purpose of preparing the ghee (verses 74–75).
He now states that the medicinal substances mentioned for the ghee may also be used in powders (*cūrṇa*) and other forms: "of the ghees," and so forth.
Regarding "vartya" (to be made into a bolus), this refers to the fruit-boluses (*phalavarti*).
Having reduced the aforementioned substances to powder, he states the liquids for the purpose of an adjunct (*anupāna*): "kola," etc.
Since no specific rule for preparing a decoction (*kaṣāya*) is mentioned in this context, it should be understood that the decoction is prepared according to the general rule.
In the *hiṅgvādi* group, *ajamoda* and others are well-known;
there are two alkalis: those derived from *sarjikā* and *yavaśūka*.

"Before the meal" means prior to eating; or, by way of transformation, it refers to that which occurs frequently in close proximity to eating, namely for seven days, according to the statement, "for seven days there is cultivation by that.
"Capable of action" (kārmuka) means competent in action.
Regarding the phrase "of that which has been husked" (*luñcitasya*), it means that which has been freed from its chaff;
in this context, it should be understood that the application of medicinal herbs occurs solely through the power of the disease itself.
"Previously" means the castor oil mentioned in the preceding formulation;
"subsequently" means that one should have him drink the castor oil mentioned in the following formulation combined with milk—this is the meaning.

In the phrase "one should prepare" (*sādhayet*) and so forth, [the substance] should be pure, dried, dehusked, and full of potency. Regarding the statement "in milk and water eightfold," according to the rule "when no portion is specified, they are equal," there are four parts of milk (sixteen *palas*) and four parts of water; thus, combined, it is "eightfold. One should prepare this until only the milk remains. Since abdominal tumors (*gulma*) are treatable by many medicinal formulations, the quantity of sixteen *palas* of milk does not cause any fault.

Furthermore, although the simultaneous use of milk and meat-juice (*rasa*) is contradictory, nevertheless, due to the gravity of the disease and the word of the Great Sage, there is no dispute on this point.

In the passage beginning with "tailaṃ prasanna... (oil, clear...), because of its etymological derivation and in accordance with the agreement of Jatūkarṇa, it should be understood as castor oil (*airaṇḍataila*).
For it has been stated: "Castor oil, having been combined with sour gruel (*āranāla*), urine, and alkaline substances," and so forth.
In the term *pañcamūlī*, by the first interpretation, it should be understood as referring to the *pañcamūlī* consisting of *śālaparṇī* and the others;
*pippalīyūṣaḥ* is a soup in which long pepper (*pippalī*) is the primary ingredient.
By the phrase "due to the mixing of vessels and bedding" (98), he indicates that other types of sudation are unsuitable for gulma (abdominal tumors).
"They succeed quickly" means they conquer *gulma* rapidly;
he states the reason for this: "For oil is supreme in conquering *vāta*. Since oil conquers *vāta*, it therefore quickly conquers *vāta-gulma*, which is a disorder of *vāta*.

Others, however, interpret that oil which conquers *vāta* should be administered with *nīlinī* powder to one afflicted by impurities (*samala*), and likewise, the previously mentioned *tryūṣaṇa*-based ghee should be administered combined with *nīlinī* powder.

In the first explanation, however, the meaning of the phrase "only ghee" should be understood as follows: the previously mentioned *tryūṣaṇa*-ghee and other such preparations are to be given combined with *nīlinī* powder.

In recipes such as *nīlinī*, a paste (*kalka*) is not explicitly mentioned; yet, in the absence of a paste, there is no knowledge of how to perform the cooking (*pāka*), for it has been stated that cooking is of three types depending on whether it is mild (*mṛdu*) and so forth. Therefore, even when a paste is not specified, a paste must be added for the sake of knowing how to cook; and they say that this paste should be added using only the substances used for the decoction (*kvātha*), because of their suitability and proximity.

It is not so, because the potency of the means, such as clarified butter and other ingredients, is diverse. Regarding what has been stated, exactly what was stated should be understood, and nothing unstated should be imagined. Furthermore, there is no logical justification for such an imagination, since the cooking of an oil (*sneha*) indeed occurs even without the addition of a paste (*kalka*), provided it is with a liquid such as a decoction; for the knowledge of cooking an oil even without a paste has been explicitly taught. Therefore, one should act exactly as the Teacher has stated.

In this context, setting aside the general rule regarding the sequential administration of thin gruel (*peyā*) and so forth for one who has undergone purgation, the consumption of meat broth (*rasa-bhojana*) is prescribed due to its suitability for the specific application; as it is said: "For one who has been purged with *āvartakī* ghee, the diet consists of *kāñjika* and *kodrava* grain" (Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha, Cikitsāsthāna).
By the verse beginning with "kukkuṭa" and so forth, food and drink are prescribed for those suffering from abdominal enlargement (*gulma*).
Excessive satiety and excessive fasting are both prohibited, as they are causes for the destruction of the digestive fire (*agni*);
as it has been said: "The bodily fire is not kindled by fasting, nor by overeating," and so forth. (Ci. A. 15)
*Rohiṇī*, *kaṭukā*, and *kaṭurohiṇī* are each in the measure of one *karṣa*; thus, they are of the quantity of one *karṣa*.

Because of the statement "one pala each of paṭola and trivṛt," [the liquid] is eightfold—that is, eightfold relative to the ghee—and "equal to the ghee" means that four palas of ghee are specified here; therefore, eight palas in total consisting of the decoction and the ghee are to be drunk. Furthermore, the dose of eight palas is established precisely because this formulation is prescribed for gulma.
As it has been said: "For those suffering from abdominal tumors (gulma), those bitten by snakes, and those afflicted by erysipelas (visarpa), a specific dose is prescribed, specifically eight palas.

In the case of *trāyamāṇā* weighing four *palas*, ten times the amount of water— forty *palas*— should be added along with the medicinal pastes (*kalka*); that is, it should be understood as being joined with the pastes of *tāmalakī* and others, as well as the pastes of *kaṭurohiṇī* and others (verses 118–121).
Regarding "one-fourth part of ghee" (*ghṛtapāda*), this refers to the ghee being one-quarter of the combined quantities of *āmalaka* and sugarcane juice.

In the case of "one-fourth part of *pathyā*" (*pathyāpāda*), because the *harītakī* is heavy, it constitutes one-eighth part relative to the ghee. However, some, citing the statement, "And since the designation 'quarter' (*pāda*) means a fourth part, that is what it signifies" (*Kaumārabhṛtya-aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya* 1.12), maintain that in a *prastha* of ghee, it should be eight *palas*, which is indeed a fourth part.
In passages such as "drākṣāṃ madhūkam" (grapes and madhūka), because of the association with a *prastha* of the remaining decoction, the ghee and other ingredients are also measured by a *prastha*.

In passages such as "vṛṣaṃ samūlam" (vṛṣa with its roots), the decoction is prepared by adding eight times the amount of water and reducing it to one-eighth; this is the distinction from the *vāsāghṛta* mentioned in the treatment of *raktapitta*.
For in this case, according to the general rule of interpretation, water four times the quantity of *vṛṣa* is taken, and the decoction is reduced until one-fourth remains;
because this constitutes a distinct formulation, no extension (*atideśa*) of the *vāsā-ghṛta* mentioned for *rakta-pitta* has been made here.
By the phrase "with honey" (*sakṣaudram*), the honey is to be added in a quantity of one-quarter, following the principle of medicinal adjuncts (*prakṣepanyāya*).
"According to one's strength" means in such a way that there is no excessive administration of the purgative (virecana).
Kampillaka and guṇḍārocanikā [are used] with oil,
or with oil prepared from madhuka.

Regarding the passage beginning with "those which alleviate pitta-fever" (pittajvara-hara), although enemas (bastis) have not been explicitly mentioned here as being alleviators of pitta-fever, nevertheless, it is stated that "those which alleviate pitta-fever" refers to those very bitter enemas consisting of *paṭola* and other such drugs that were previously described; this is what is intended here.
Furthermore, those [enemas] which are to be described in the section on successful formulations (*siddhi*) as being alleviators of *pitta* should also be understood to apply here.
"When it has become loose" means that when the *gulma* has reached a state where the defect is removable by surgery due to the laxity of the disorder, one should place it at the mouth of a jar;
having secured it well with a jar-churning apparatus (*ghaṭamanthana-yantreṇa*), one should squeeze it or break it—this is the construction [of the sentence].
The removal of the intestines and heart [is performed] due to the fear of their bursting, etc.

Regarding the verse beginning with *savyoṣa*, the meaning is that ghee prepared with a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*) and the pastes (*kalka*) of the remaining ingredients, such as the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), overcomes *kapha*-type abdominal tumors (*gulma*).
The *ṣaṭpala* ghee prepared with *pippalī* and other ingredients should be cooked with an equal quantity of milk;
according to the rule "it should be prepared with four times the liquid," three parts of water are to be understood here.

In the case of the formula beginning with *trivṛtām* (147–148), fifteen *palas* are to be boiled. Four times that amount of water should be added—since the measurement is prescribed in *palas*, this results in sixty *palas* of water. Milk, by association, is also fifteen *palas*. Here, the fat (*sneha*) should be cooked with one-fourth the quantity of these two liquids combined; alternatively, according to the statement "milk equal to the fat," the fat should be made to have one-fourth liquid by using milk equal to the fat and fifteen *palas* of decoction, resulting in five *palas* of fat with one-fourth liquid.
However, according to Jatūkarṇa’s intention, when measuring fifteen palas of *trivṛt* and the other ingredients, one should add four *prasthas* of water by way of the *prastha* measure;

for he has stated this in general terms: "Castor oil and ghee boiled with equal parts of *trivṛt*, *dantī*, *triphalā*, and *daśamūla*, along with an equal amount of milk, [are used] in cases of upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*), colic, and so forth.
"Dviguṇam" means measuring two palas; for in that case, it is stated that one pala of ghee is to be drunk.
"Tailārdhakuḍavam" means four palas of oil.
"Like a linctus" (lehavad) means it should be cooked according to the characteristics of cooking a linctus.

Here, one *pala* of the combined four aromatics (*caturjātaka*) constitutes a "doṣa-prastha," which is thirteen and a half *palas*. For it has been stated by Bhoja: "In emesis, in purgation, and likewise in bloodletting..."
The meaning is that the wise say a *prastha* consists of thirteen and a half *palas*,
as specified in verses 154–160 in the section on the treatment of *grahaṇī* and hemorrhoids (*arśas*).
By the statement "but burning at the end," [the author] indicates that since burning cannot be established as a separate action, it must be performed precisely at the end.
With the verse beginning "accumulated" (sañcita), [the author] describes *gulma* as it reaches a state of incurability through its successive stages.
"Mahāvāstuparigraha" means encompassing a vast area of land (verses 169–171).
"Upon the lapse of the period of gestation" refers to the passing of the ten-month period of gestation.
"In a vessel of alkali" means two āḍhakas of alkaline water; "the dose" means the appropriate measure;
"palala" is sesame paste.
And the alkali here is specifically the ash of *palāśa*, because it is the subject under discussion;
"by those two" refers to the alkali and the milk of *sudhā*.
*Kaṭukamatsya* is the *śapharī* fish, that is, a dried fish.
Lactakas are pieces of cloth;
*kiṇva* is the fermenting agent for liquor;
and "alkali that removes blood and bile" refers to the alkali of blue lotus (*nīlotpala-kṣāra*).
The drinking of sour ghee— that is, ghee prepared with sour substances— after a meal, or alternatively, an enema (uttarabasti),
or the ghee known as Jīvanīya, should be prescribed for vātarakta.
"An oil enema (anuvāsana) prepared with bitter substances and bitter drugs" [verse 172–182].
With the words "Sneha," etc., he again provides a summary in brief.

By the phrase "and [the] yogas," those [remedies] which were already included individually under the treatment for vāta-gulma and the others, are further included here by means of this collective summary (saṅgraha).
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Gulma," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka-saṃhitā composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
5 [Cikitsāsthāna, Chapter 6 (72 of 120)]:
Following the sequence of connection as stated in the Nidāna [section], the treatment of urinary disorders (meha) is explained immediately after the treatment of abdominal tumors (gulma).
One from whom delusion and the like have departed is such [a person]; *anuśaya* is anger;
one from whom hope has departed is *nirāśaḥ*, that is, free from passion (*nīrāga*).
Although the causes, signs, and so forth have already been stated in the *Nidāna* [section], they are now mentioned in their entirety due to the requirements of the present context.

"Comfortable posture" (*āsyāsukha*) refers to a posture that produces pleasure and not one that produces pain; the same should be understood regarding the "pleasure of sleep. A painful dream or a painful posture caused by defects in the bed and such are not causes of *prameha*.
Products of molasses (*guḍavaikṛta*) are foods prepared with molasses (4).
The etiology of *meha* arising from *kapha* and other doshas is described by the passage beginning with "fat and flesh" (*medaśca māṃsaṃ ca*).

The types of *meha* arising from *kapha* are mentioned first because they are most prevalent and because they are curable when [the other doshas] are diminished—that is, when *kapha* and *pitta* are diminished. The plural number used for both [doshas] should be understood as referring to individual instances. The term "when diminished" (*kṣīṇeṣu*) is used in relation to increased *vāta*; thus, it shows that the *vāta* which subsequently increases after *kapha* or *pitta* have increased is not intended here as the cause of the four incurable types of *meha*. In that case, curability exists because treatment is prescribed: "The treatment previously described for the *vāta-mehas*, which was ordained for those in whom *vāta* is predominant..."
"For the wind (vāyu) becomes aggravated in those excessively emaciated by urinary disorders; there is no concern regarding incurable cases"—
thus he describes the general pathogenesis of all types of *meha* concerning the bodily elements (*dhātu*) known as marrow, semen, and lymph, beginning with the words "doṣo hi" and so forth.

"Because of similarity of action" means that because the humor (doṣa), namely phlegm (kapha), and the affected tissue (dūṣya), such as fat (medas) and so forth, are similar, the action of pungent, bitter, and other [tastes] is dissimilar;
"because of dissimilarity of action" means that the pacifying treatment (saṃśamana-cikitsā) for pitta, consisting of pungent and other [tastes], is dissimilar.

"Because they cause great calamity" means that they bring about a major disaster by depleting the profound elements such as the marrow, and because they act with rapidity; the word "and" (ca) combines with this the "irregular action" mentioned in the etiology of those [fevers] characterized by wind (vāta), according to their respective order—that is, sequentially.
By the words "kapha" and so forth, [the author] states the summary of the doshas and dushyas for all types of meha.

Regarding "rasa and ojas": although fat (medas) and other substances are mentioned here as dushyas, nevertheless, because fat, muscle tissue (māṃsa), and bodily moisture (śarīrakleda) are invariably involved, they are included; furthermore, even ojas is a dushya in madhumeha. Thus, "rasaujas" refers to both rasa and ojas.

Furthermore, marrow and the other tissues (*majjādayaḥ*) are not necessarily vitiated in all types of *meha*, or they may be only slightly vitiated. Alternatively, is it being stated by the passage beginning with "Kapha along with Pitta" (*kaphaḥ sapitta*) that all *mehas* are characterized by the involvement of all three *doṣas* as well as all the *dūṣyas*? As for fat (*medas*), muscle (*māṃsa*), and so forth, they are mentioned separately for the purpose of illustrating the excessive vitiation [of specific tissues]. For, in the *Kiyantaḥśirasiya* chapter, while describing *madhumeha* as denoting all types of *meha*, the provocation of the three *doṣas* was also stated;
as it says: "Of the wind (*maruta*), the bile (*pitta*), and the phlegm (*kapha*), repeatedly..."

It has been stated [in the *Sūtrasthāna*, chapter 17]: "Having assumed a form, it manifests; having reached its destruction, it is replenished again. Likewise, Suśruta also says: "Kapha, combined with vāta, pitta, and fat, produces urinary disorders (*meha*).

To refute the possibility of an excessive number of pramehas resulting from the infinite combinations of kapha and the other dosas—such as those where two or more are predominant—he states: "There are exactly twenty types of prameha."
With the ten [verses] beginning with "like water" (jalopama), he describes the ten types of prameha caused by the qualities of phlegm (śleṣman);
this should be clearly followed in the *Nidāna* [section].
By the phrase "thick and clear on top," he refers to *sāndraprasāda-meha*.
It should be understood that *majja-meha* [occurs] with marrow, *madhu-meha* with *ojas*, *vasā-meha* with fat (*vasā*), and *hasti-meha* with lymph (*lasikā*).
Regarding the remaining ones—namely those beginning with fat (*medas*) and excluding the tissues (*dhātu*) already mentioned such as chyle (*rasa*) and so forth.

"In those that have been diminished" means when they have been depleted; their depletion is brought about either by the very vāta that initiates the prameha, or by emaciation through fasting and other such means. (9–11) He states the characteristics of kaphaja and other types of prameha in brief, beginning with "the color," etc.
In that case, the kaphaja [type] has a white color, a sweet taste, a cold touch, and a raw (āma) smell;
these same characteristics should also be understood for pittameha.
Regarding vāyu, because it is extremely colorless, [the author] states the natural bodily color [of the patient]: "dark-red" (śyāvāruṇa), and so forth.

Although it has been stated that *vātika* *meha* is indeed incurable when the marrow and other tissues attain a quality similar to that of marrow-fluid (*majjala*) and so forth, nevertheless, by the repetition here of the term "incurable," [the author] demonstrates that only that which is abundant in form from the very moment of its onset possesses all the symptoms such as the dark-red (*śyāvāruṇa*) color and the rest; whereas that which becomes associated with these later on is curable. In that case, the similarity to marrow and other tissues does not necessarily occur. Furthermore, those cases which are associated with *vāta* at a later stage and possess the dark-red color and other such features are also incurable.

Likewise, those types arising from *kapha* and *pitta* are also indeed incurable when associated with the marrow (*majjā*) and other tissues. And it has been said: "Indeed, all cases of *prameha*, if left untreated over time, turn into *madhumeha*; at that stage, they truly become incurable" (Suśruta Saṃhitā, Nidāna-sthāna).
By the passage beginning with "svedo'ṅgagandha" (sweat and body odor), he describes the premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa).
"Paridurbalaḥ" means one who has lost strength.

"Of one who is emaciated" means of one who is depleted of flesh; "of one in whom the humors and strength are excessive" means of one in whom the humors (*doṣa*) and strength (*bala*) are predominant; "depletion" refers to the depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).
*Yavaudana* is rice cooked from crushed and dried barley, devoid of the scum (*maṇḍa*).
*Vāṭya* is that same preparation made from dehusked barley that has been split, but including the scum.
*Atasī* is well known; according to the opinion of those who read *tilātasī*, the *atasī* intended here is of the form of sesame (*tila*).
The grass-grains are *śyāmāka* and so forth;
the cakes are those made from barley flour.
*Dhānāḥ* refers to parched barley;
*veṇuyavāḥ* means bamboo seeds that have the shape of barley. (18–24)

Since purification (*saṃśodhana*) by definition includes emesis (*vamana*), its separate mention here as "emesis" (*ullekhana*) is for the purpose of emphasizing that it is the primary treatment for disorders arising from *kapha*. Others, however, state that "emesis" refers to fasting (*laṅghana*) in cases of *kapha*-type urinary disorders (*kaphameha*);

because *pitta*-type urinary disorders are palliable (*yāpya*), the word "conquer" (*jayanti*) is said to refer only to the palliation of those born of *pitta*. Alternatively, when the fat (*medas*) is excessively vitiated, *pitta*-type disorders are incurable; thus, the term "conquer" is appropriate for those [disorders] regarding which it must be said, "But they are curable if the fat is not excessively vitiated.
The two formulations beginning with *dārvī* that were mentioned are to be used in all types of *surāmeha*;

*devadāru*, *harītakī*, and the other ten [drugs] are to be applied respectively to the [ten] types of *kaphameha*. Alternatively, all of them may be used for all types of *kaphameha*. Furthermore, those [formulations] beginning with *uśīra* mentioned for *pittameha* are to be understood as applicable to all [types of *pittameha*].

Kaṭaṅkaṭerī and dāruharidrā are for drinking the *mantha*; "for drinking" means for the purpose of drinking the *mantha*, and "for food" means for the preparation of the food; likewise, oils prepared for the preparation of drinks are also accomplished by these very same decoctions.

"In those whose nature is dominated by vāta" refers specifically to cases of kapha and pitta-type meha (urinary disorders) where vāta is a secondary factor; this is because those mehas arising from a specific predominance of vāta are incurable and thus not to be treated.
"One suffering from kapha and pitta meha" means one who has kapha-type meha and one who has pitta-type meha.
"Made into a paste" (kalkīkṛtāni) refers specifically to kampillaka and the other ingredients made into a paste.
"Anubandha" means that which follows after.

Regarding "oil should be prepared with its own decoction for kapha": this means that for kapha and for conditions associated with kapha, oil should be prepared with the decoctions of kapha-alleviating drugs. Similarly, for pitta and for conditions associated with pitta, ghee prepared with the decoctions of pitta-alleviating drugs should be administered.

Since it was stated "with all [the drugs]," one might think that the preparation of the unctuous substance (sneha) could occur even with all [the drugs] used separately; therefore, he says "with all combined," meaning they are mixed together.
"Mixed" refers here to a combination of both oil and ghee.

"In the three characteristics" means when there is a combination of the characteristics of the three *doṣas*. The state of being born from the three *doṣas* (*tridoṣaja*)—produced by the relationship between the primary and secondary factors—should be understood as applying specifically to the urinary disorders (*meha*) born of *kapha* and *pitta*. Furthermore, it should be known that because all *mehas* are born from the three *doṣas*, they may occasionally manifest with the full emergence of the three *doṣas*. In the verse beginning with "lodhram," *kramuka* refers either to *paṭṭikālodhra* or to betel nut (*pūga*).

Regarding "indrasāhvām indravāruṇīm" (41–44), the meaning is that the decoction is prepared in exactly that same quantity of water by adding eight palas of *danti*, four palas of *bhallātaka*, and one karṣa each of the *lodhra* group of drugs. Thus, the decoction should be made.
"Kṣaudraṃ ca tāvat" (and honey likewise) means one-eighth part in relation to the decoction.

"Sārodakam" (water of heartwood) should be understood as water prepared according to the *ṣaḍaṅga* method using the heartwoods (*sāra*) of *khadira* and other such trees; in the same way, "kuśodaka" (water of *kuśa* grass) is to be understood.
"Madhūdaka" refers to water made sweet with honey;
"śūlyāni" means cooked on a spit (śūla).
In the phrase "mṛgadvijānām," because it is used in its etymological sense, it should be understood as referring to wild (jāṅgala) animals and birds.

"From application" means from practice (abhyāsa). Regarding the formulations for diseases arising from over-nutrition (santarpaṇa), those stated in the chapter on "Conditions Requiring Nourishment" (Santarpaṇīya-adhyāya), beginning with "Triphalā, Āragvadha, Pāṭhā... (Sūtra-sthāna, A. 23), [are to be used].

Regarding the statement "Uśīra should be used with sandalwood and so forth," by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (ādi), there would indeed be the inclusion of śaileya and other such substances.

Now, he states that, as a general rule, depletion (apatarpaṇa) is the treatment for disorders of phlegm (kapha), bile (pitta), and urinary disorders (prameha)—beginning with "moisture" (kleda) and so forth.

Although a disorder such as abdominal tumors (gulma) may arise from depletion, nevertheless, depletion must be performed in such a way that the manifestation of tumors and similar conditions does not occur; this is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "moisture and fat" (kledaśca medaśca).

Showing that those "oils and ghees which have been proven effective in previous treatments should be administered in cases of *meha* caused by *vāta*" (and so forth), he says—beginning with "those [which treat] *vāta-mehas*"—to demonstrate that they concern *meha* associated with *vāta*. As for how there can be a predominance of *vāta* even in those born of *kapha* and *pitta*, he says—beginning with "Vāyu... and so forth.
"Those that are incurable" (asādhyān) refers to [those] from the very moment of their onset (utpattitaḥ).

The definition of the meaning of the verse beginning with "by which causes" (yaiḥ hetubhiḥ) and so forth is accepted for all diseases; however, in this case, it is stated for the purpose of abandoning the pursuit of [remedial] causes, because *prameha* is characterized by its persistence over a long period of time.

Now, since the symptoms of *prameha* (urinary disorders) resemble those of *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic diseases), [the author] states the differentiating characteristics of *prameha* and *raktapitta* so that the treatment for *prameha* does not mistakenly apply to *raktapitta*: "of turmeric color," and so forth.
Regarding the passage beginning with "having seen," the phrase "when the *doṣas* have diminished" refers to when *kapha*, *medas*, and so forth have diminished.

Here, the status of being a *doṣa* (humor) is not intended for the *dūṣyas* (vitiated tissues) such as *medas*; nevertheless, the term *doṣa* should be understood here [for these tissues] due to their connection with the *doṣas*. Alternatively, "in the *doṣas*" refers to *kapha* and *pitta*; and the use of the plural for these two is because of the multiplicity of individual instances (*vyakti*).

The meaning is that if it were indeed caused by Vāta, then Kapha would not be increased due to the absence of its cause; however, if it is known through over-nutrition (*santarpaṇa*) that there is an increase in Kapha produced by such nourishment, then, because the etiological factors for Vāta are absent, it is determined that this is not born of Vāta but rather of Kapha—this is the intended sense. (55) Now, in order to demonstrate the curability, incurability, and manageability of the aforementioned and unmentioned types of Prameha, he says: "Those with premonitory symptoms," and so forth.

They are called *sapūrvarūpa* (accompanied by premonitory symptoms) because they exist together with the premonitory symptoms such as "perspiration" and "odor of the body. Among them, those *kapha*-type urinary disorders (*kaphameha*) which were stated to be curable become incurable when they coexist with premonitory symptoms. Those *pitta*-type urinary disorders (*pittameha*) which were stated to be palliable (*yāpya*) become untreatable (*pratyākhyeya*). Although it has been stated that all diseases are incurable even when in a curable stage due to the presence of premonitory symptoms, it has also been said: "The premonitory symptoms of any other disease [which afflict] a man..."

"By this method, his death is certain as well" (I.A.5). In that [previous] passage, it was stated that all diseases are incurable when accompanied by all their premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*); however, here, through a specific statement, it is understood that incurability occurs even when not all premonitory symptoms are present. Likewise, those diseases caused by *vāta* which follow the aforementioned sequence of etiology (*nidāna*) are incurable even if they lack premonitory symptoms, provided they follow that sequence.

By this [statement], those four types of urinary disorders (meha) born of vāta which arise through the connection with causes and so forth mentioned in the *nidāna* section are incurable. However, those born of kapha or pitta which are classified as vāta-born due to being accompanied by vāta are curable or manageable; for this very reason, the treatment for them is stated as: "Proven oils and ghees should indeed be administered in cases of urinary disorders caused by vāta. To demonstrate the exceptional rule—that a pitta-induced prameha may sometimes be curable due to the absence of premonitory symptoms—he reiterates the general rule that pitta-born [disorders] are manageable: "But those caused by pitta are manageable."
He describes the curable types of *paittika* (bile-related) disorders: "But those that are curable," and so forth.
"Not excessively vitiated" (*na praduṣṭam*) means not severely corrupted; the meaning is that *paittika* disorders occurring when the *medas* (fat tissue) is not vitiated are curable.

Alternatively, those *kapha-pitta* types of urinary disorders (*meha*) are indeed incurable when they are excessively vitiated; likewise, those *kapha-pitta* *mehas* which, due to the depletion of the bodily tissues (*dhātu*), become caused by *vāta*, are also incurable when accompanied by their premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*).

As for those who describe the *prameha* mentioned in the *Kiyantaḥśirasīya* chapter as being a premonitory stage (*pūrvarūpa*) distinct from the twenty types of *prameha*, they are refuted by the very restriction of number stating that "there are exactly twenty types of *meha*. (56) He now states another way in which *mehas* are incurable, beginning with the word "jāta": jāto mūtravikāreṣu yaḥ pramehī na sidhyati | yo vā kṛcchreṇa mandāgnirbahumūtro 'lpabubhukṣaḥ || 57 || One who has been born among those suffering from urinary disorders (*mūtravikāra*) and is afflicted by *prameha* does not recover; nor does one who, despite having suppressed [the disease], suffers from weak digestion, excessive urination, and little appetite. (57) The term "born" (*jāta*) refers to one who has been afflicted by *prameha* since birth. Alternatively, it may refer to one who has been afflicted by *prameha* since childhood. The phrase "does not recover" (*na sidhyati*) indicates incurability. Furthermore, even if the disease is suppressed through treatment, if the patient subsequently develops weak digestion, excessive urination, and a lack of appetite, such a person is also incurable. (58) He states yet another way in which *mehas* are incurable: yo vā pramehī madhumehinaṃ jātamātraṃ puruṣam abhibhavati, sa na sidhyati | yo vā kṛcchreṇa mandāgnirbahumūtro 'lpabubhukṣaḥ || 59 || Or, a *pramehī* who overcomes a person who has been born with *madhumeha* does not recover; or one who, despite having suppressed [the disease], suffers from weak digestion, excessive urination, and little appetite. (59) The term "born with" (*jātamātra*) refers to one who has been afflicted by *madhumeha* since birth. Alternatively, it may refer to one who has been afflicted by *madhumeha* since childhood. The phrase "overcomes" (*abhibhavati*) means that the disease manifests again after having been suppressed. The rest is as previously explained. (66) He states yet another way in which *mehas* are incurable: yo vā pramehī mad

A person with *prameha* who is born from a parent with *prameha* is also incurable. Regarding this, he states the reason: "Because of the defect of the seed" (*bījadoṣāt*). This means that because one is born with *prameha* from a seed (sperm/ovum) corrupted by the same doshas that initiate *prameha*, the term *madhumeha* here refers to *prameha* in general. If, however, *madhumeha* were defined as a neglected *vātika* type of *prameha*, then a person with *prameha* born from parents afflicted with other types of *prameha* would not necessarily be incurable.
Furthermore, it is logical that for one born with *madhumeha*, the state of having *madhumeha* itself [should be the cause], in accordance with its cause;
consequently, it is appropriate to say that one born from a person with *madhumeha*, or from one who has *madhumeha*, is incurable.

Therefore, although the offspring is referred to generally by the term *prameha*, it should be understood that in the case of the father—the cause—there exists a corresponding *prameha* denoted by the specific term *madhumeha*.

This term *meha* indeed applies generally to all types of urinary disorders (*meha*), because those pustules (*piḍaka*) which were mentioned in the *Kiyantaḥśirasiya* chapter in connection with *madhumeha* are here referred to by the phrase "the pustules of those suffering from *prameha*" as being related to *prameha* in general. Therefore, the word *madhumeha* applies both to *prameha* in general and to the specific variety known as *madhumeha*; just as the word *tṛṇa* (grass) applies to grass in general and to a specific type of grass. This point has been elaborated upon in the *Kiyantaḥśirasiya* chapter, and thus it is not further expanded upon here.
In the context of the incurability of hereditary *prameha*, he states the incurability of other types as well, beginning with the words "And those which...
Hereditary (*kulaja*) means arising from causes such as one's father or grandfather.

Although the incurability of hereditary *prameha* is already established by this general statement, the repetition of that term is for the purpose of demonstrating its persistence through successive generations.
For it has been stated: "Of those afflicted by prameha" (Sūtra, Chapter 25).
He now states the aphorism for the treatment of prameha-piḍakās (boils associated with prameha), beginning with "of those suffering from prameha," and so forth.

Regarding the section on diseases (*rogādhikāra*), in this context of the fourfold group of diseases, no detailed exposition has been provided because of the statement: "In other sections, there is no extensive discussion" (*anyādhikāreṣu na vistaroktiḥ*, Ci. a. 26), as this belongs to the section on surgical shafts (*śalyādhikāra*).

The summary beginning with "the cause" (hetu) and so forth is threefold: the physician's victory consists of purification (saṃśodhana), pacification (saṃśamana), and avoidance of the etiological factors (nidānavarjana);
these are the "first," meaning they are to be consumed.
The remainder is easy to understand.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, named "The Treatment of Prameha," in the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka-saṃhitā, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
6 [Chapter 7 of Cikitsāsthāna (73 of 120)]:

It has been stated that the onset of urinary disorders (meha) and skin diseases (kuṣṭha) results from the consumption of sacrificial oblations (haviṣ); therefore, following the treatment for urinary disorders, the treatment for skin diseases is now described.

Although the etiological factors (nidāna), causes (hetu), and so forth have already been mentioned, they are stated again for the purpose of demonstrating certain specificities as being instrumental to medical treatment;
"āśraya" means the substratum (ādhāra).

The word "and" (ca) in the phrase "and its pacification" (praśamanaṃ ca) includes the premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa) and the pathogenesis (samprāpti), which will be described later. Alternatively, the premonitory symptoms should be understood through the signs (liṅga), and the pathogenesis through the causes (hetu). Furthermore, there are other skin conditions such as moles (piplu) and freckles (vyanga) that destroy touch; therefore, listen specifically to the causes and other factors of those leprosy-like diseases (kuṣṭha) that destroy touch. Or, since leprosy is infinite, listen to the causes and so forth of those eighteen types specifically mentioned here that destroy touch—such is the interpretation.
For it has been stated: "Leprosy is of seven types, eighteen types, and even of incalculable types" (Nidāna-sthāna, Chapter 5).
Furthermore, in the *Ātreya-bhadrakāpyīya* chapter, those [foods] that are incompatible have been mentioned, such as: "One should not consume fish with milk," and so forth (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 26).

Regarding the passage beginning with "cold and hot," etc., it has been stated that cold, hot, and so forth should be utilized in their respective order; however, for those who utilize them in a manner contrary to that sequence, the result is the opposite. This should be understood to apply equally to fasting (laṅghana) and diet.
Furthermore, when one is afflicted by heat and other such conditions, it should be applied to those who consume cold water immediately and without rest.

Regarding the phrase "those who eat while suffering from indigestion" (*ajīrṇādhyaśinām*): *ajīrṇa* refers to undigested food, that is to say, food that has not been processed; *tadbhuñjānānām* means those who eat while that [food] remains; *adhyaśinām* means those who eat while the previous meal is still untransformed; and *pañcakarmāpacāriṇām* means those who act improperly during the performance of the five medical procedures (*pañcakarman*), namely, those who indulge in what is forbidden.

"Engaging in sexual intercourse when food is undigested"—that is, for those who indulge with women while food is undigested in the form of *vidagdha* (sour) or other types of indigestion—and "those who perform sinful deeds":
since the assault of Brahmins and others is already established by the very fact of performing sinful acts, this statement is made again to demonstrate a specific cause [for the resulting suffering].
He states the summary of the *doṣas* (humors) and *dūṣyas* (vitiated tissues) with the words beginning "Vātādayaḥ" (Vata and the others).

Although the triad of Vata and the others is already established, the explicit mention of "three" is for the purpose of showing that all three are involved in the vitiation (*dūṣi*) in all types of *kuṣṭha*.
The term "summary of substances" (*dravyasaṅgraha*) refers to the substance as the originating cause (*ārambhaka-kāraṇa*).

Although the group of seven is already implied by the term "sevenfold" (*saptaka*), the word "seven" is stated again everywhere for the purpose of establishing a fixed rule regarding the number seven.

Even though these same seven factors are the causes for the arising of *visarpa* (erysipelas), as it is said: "Blood, lymph, skin, flesh, the corrupted tissues (*dūṣya*), and the three impurities (*doṣa*)—these seven constituents (*dhātu*) are to be known as the origin of *visarpa*" (Ci. A. 21); nevertheless, the distinction is that *kuṣṭha* (leprosy/skin diseases) is produced by doshas that are chronic and stable, whereas *visarpa* is produced by those that are prone to spreading.

Others, however, say that visarpas also occur from vāta and the other [doshas] individually; as it has been stated: "There are three visarpas arising separately, one arising from all three, and three born from combinations of two" (Ci. A. 21). That is not so; for even though visarpas arise from all three doshas, they are designated as "arising from a single dosha" and so forth, just like kuṣṭhas arising from a single dosha. In that context, by the specific reading of the numbers "seven and eleven," it is made known that among the kuṣṭhas mentioned in the Nidāna section, seven are classified as major kuṣṭhas (mahākuṣṭha) and eleven as minor kuṣṭhas (kṣudrakuṣṭha). Thus, even though the minor kuṣṭhas were not explicitly described there, they are prescribed here for the purpose of treatment.
The connection is that "touching" and so forth are the premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*), or else "perspiration."
Absence of sweating and excessive sweating should be understood as being caused by the obstruction or non-obstruction, respectively, of the channels that carry sweat;
likewise, the rapid onset and the long duration of ulcers [are to be understood in the same manner].
*Kapāla* refers to a broken potsherd;
*viṣama* means difficult to treat;
and *lomapiñjara* means tawny with hair, that is, reddish-brown due to its bristles.
"Utsannamaṇḍala" means a raised circular area; "ṛṣya" refers to the blue antelope (hariṇa). "Ṛṣyajihvā-saṃsthāna" means having the shape of its tongue;
it generally occurs on the chest because of the predominance of phlegm (śleṣman), though the sense is that it may occasionally occur elsewhere as well.

Although it is already established that *kākaṇantikā* and *guñjā* possess the symptoms of the three *doṣas* by virtue of being types of *kuṣṭha*, their mention again is for the purpose of demonstrating that they exhibit particularly dominant symptoms of the three *doṣas*.
"Mahāvāstu" means a large site.
"Like a fish-scale" means resembling the skin of a fish.
"Kiṇakharasparśa" means that which has a rough touch like a scar; a "kiṇa" is the site of a wound.
Regarding the predominance of Vāta and other doshas in various types of Kuṣṭha for the purpose of treatment, he says "Vāta" and so forth;
in the case of Ṛṣyajihva and the others, the predominance of Vāta, Pitta, and so on should be understood according to their respective order.
Demonstrating that there is no contradiction among the various types of *kuṣṭha* regarding their being caused by a single *doṣa* and so forth, he says "all" and so on.

The meaning is as follows: the state of being produced by all three *doṣas* (*tridoṣaja*) is indeed established for all *kuṣṭhas*; however, the designation of them as being caused by a single *doṣa* and so forth is intended for the purpose of treatment, based on the desire to express the relative strength or weakness of the *doṣas*.
Regarding the phrase "of the secondary factor" (*anubandhasya*), which refers to that which is non-primary (31–32),

[the author] now states the mutual indicative relationship between the specific types of *kuṣṭha* arising from specific doshas, as well as the causes that produce *kuṣṭha*, in the passage beginning with "by the specific types of *kuṣṭha*" (*kuṣṭhaviśeṣaiḥ*).

"By specific types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha), the humors (doṣa) [are known]" means that by specific types of skin diseases such as kāpāla and others, the humors—wind (vāta) and so forth—are recognized. Likewise, "by specific types of humors, again, the skin diseases" means that once a skin disease is fully understood in terms of its humor—such as "this one has an excess of wind" or "this one is of the bile type (paittika)"—specific skin diseases are known through the knowledge of the specific humors; for example: "This skin disease is dominated by wind, therefore it is kāpāla"; "This one is maṇḍala because of the predominance of bile," and so forth.

Likewise, the cause of leprosy (kuṣṭha) that is not directly perceived is known through the specific aggravations of the humors (doṣa). For example, having observed that a case of leprosy is dominated by Vāta, one infers the causes such as the consumption of dry, incompatible foods, and so forth, which produce Vāta-dominant leprosy; and through these causes that generate specific humoral imbalances, the types of leprosy are identified: "Because this person has indulged in factors that produce Vāta-dominant leprosy, therefore he will develop Kāpāla leprosy, which is Vāta-dominant."

Showing how the mutual indication of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*) and the humors (*doṣa*) is established through their relationship as effect and cause, he says: "By those" (*taiḥ*). The meaning is that by those skin diseases, which are of the nature of effects, the cause—namely, the humor—is inferred; and the cause, in the form of the humor, makes known those specific skin diseases which are of the nature of effects. (33) To explain the knowledge of the humors present in skin diseases, he states the signs of Vata and the others, beginning with "dryness" (*raukṣya*).
Burning sensations and other symptoms are the signs of pitta (34–36).
To determine whether to proceed with or desist from treatment, he describes the curable and incurable types of kuṣṭha, beginning with "sarvaiḥ" and so forth.
37–38 He describes the treatment in due order, beginning with "In cases where Vāta is predominant" (vātottareṣu) and so forth.

The word "first" (agre) should be understood as referring to ghee and the other [medicines]; thus, the meaning is that in cases where Vāta is predominant and so on, ghee and the others should be administered first, and thereafter the treatment to be described later should be performed.

"Many times" means for many occasions; it should be purified again and again by removing [the impurities] little by little. For if a great amount of morbid humors (*doṣa*) were removed at once, there would be a loss of strength and a great calamity. Therefore, he says: "For when the humors are removed in excess," and so forth. The word "humors" (*doṣe*) is used in the singular to denote the class; by this, both phlegm (*kapha*) and bile (*pitta*) are included. Alternatively, by using the singular "humor" (*doṣa*), it is implied that even if only a single humor is removed in excess, it may destroy the wind (*vāyu*).
When the digestive tract is purified and the blood has been drained, the drinking of unctuous substances (sneha) is prescribed;
for the drinking of unctuous substances by one whose digestive tract is unpurified results in the aggravation of disease.
As it is said: "If a remnant of the doshas remains, the disease increases excessively."
However, when the dosha has been eliminated entirely through purification, there is no longer any state of having residual dosha.
With the verse beginning with "kuṭaja," etc., he describes the emetic substances.

A cold taste and a cold decoction are desired according to the degree of purgation; thus, the sequence of *peyā* and so forth should be administered threefold, twofold, or singlefold, depending on whether the purification is superior, moderate, or inferior. For it has been said: "A person purified by superior, moderate, or inferior cleansing should consume, in sequence, *peyā*, *vilepī*, unprocessed and processed soup, meat broth—three, two, or one—at each mealtime" (Siddhisthāna, Chapter 1).

Although non-unctuous enemas (*āsthāpana*) and unctuous enemas (*anuvāsana*) are prohibited in cases of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*) by the statement, "Those suffering from *kuṣṭha* should not be given non-unctuous enemas" (Sūtra-sthāna 2), nevertheless, they must indeed be administered when the condition is one that can be cured solely by these two types of enemas. As it has been said: "When there is a conflict between the indications for proceeding and those for desisting, one should determine the correct course of action after carefully weighing the relative gravity and lightness of the consequences. Therefore, he says: "In cases where Vāta is predominant," and so forth.

Although only one purgative smoke (vairecanika-dhūma) is mentioned in the Sūtrasthāna, nevertheless, because many smokes can be prepared from the substances mentioned therein—both individually and collectively—the plural number has been used here.
(Verses 43–49).
The term *nāḍī* refers specifically to the tube (*nāḍī*) as described in the chapter on sudation (sveda-adhyāya).
They say that *kūrca* is a specific type of surgical instrument;
*raktotkleśa* is the provocation of blood; *utkliṣṭam raktaṃ* is blood that has been stirred up; and *svinnotsannam* is [blood] that has become elevated due to being heated by perspiration.
The connection is that one should scratch [the skin] for the purpose of bringing forth blood;
those whose defects of blood have been removed are called "those whose defects of blood have been removed" (nirhṛtāsradoṣāḥ).
"Surgical instruments do not apply" means that because of the narrowness of the vessels and other structures, surgical instruments are not suitable;
"destructive of the sense of touch" means they take away the tactile faculty;
"as if asleep, deeply asleep" means they are insentient, in the sense that there is no perception of touch whatsoever.

Bitter medicated ghees, such as *tiktaṣaṭpala* and others, should be administered to those suffering from *pitta*-type skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), for they effect the removal of *kapha*, *pitta*, and blood, and so forth; this is how it should be applied.
58–59: Dārvī (dāruharidrā) and rasāñjana prepared with a decoction of dārvī.

Although jaggery and oil are mentioned as causes of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) when used without *abhayā* (harītakī), their administration together with harītakī becomes a destroyer of leprosy due to the power of their combination. "The root of *paṭola*" refers to the root of the *paṭola* plant; likewise, the root of *gavākṣī* is also taken in a measure of one *pala*.
The bark of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) is one *pala* each for each.

Although the individual portion of the three myrobalans in every case has been established by the twenty-eighth word mentioned in the *Kalyāṇaka-ghṛta*, nevertheless, he employs the word "separately" (*pṛthak*) again in order to illuminate that very same meaning; or rather, it shows that *trāyamāṇā* and *kaṭurohiṇī* have half a portion each separately, whereas for the three myrobalans, the inclusion of separate portions is already established by the context itself.

Six *śāṇas* each of *trāyamāṇā* and *kaṭurohiṇī*, and for *nāgara*, which completes half the portion of both, four *śāṇas* (two quarters of a *pala*) are required based on half a *pala*. Thus, with *trāyamāṇā*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, and *nāgara*, there is one *pala*; and with *paṭola*-root and the others, there are five *palas*. Combined, these total six *palas*. Therefore, having extracted one *pala* from these six *palas* of *paṭola* and the others, which have been pulverized—that is, crushed—one should drink it boiled in water. This should be administered for six days.
By its application for six days alone, its capacity to remove *kuṣṭha* (skin diseases) is generally inferred. Other tantras that provide corroboration for this explanation are cited as follows:
Agniveśa states—“One pala each of *paṭola* root, *triphalā*, and *viśālā*...”
"Half a *pala* each of *trāyamāṇā* and likewise *kaṭukarohiṇī*, and half a *karṣa* of *nāgara*— having added these, one should sprinkle six *palas* [of other ingredients] with this powder;
one should drink it lukewarm after boiling it in water, adding one *pala* of this powder for every *pala* [of the decoction]," and so forth.
Cakṣuṣyeṇa also said: "One pala each of paṭola root, triphalā, and viśālā, half a pala each of kaṭukā and trāyamāṇā, and one-quarter nāgara—
having boiled these in water until reduced to one-sixth, one should drink it to remove the bodily humors."

Others, however, explain it as follows: by the word *palāṃśa*, a *karṣa* is meant. Thus, there is one *karṣa* of *paṭola* root separately, likewise one *karṣa* of *gavākṣī* root, and likewise one *karṣa* of *kṛtavedhana* combined; and *trāyamāṇā*, when joined with a quarter-part (*pāda*) of *nāgara*, becomes half a *karṣa*; similarly, *kaṭurohiṇī*, when joined with a quarter-part of *nāgara*, becomes half a *karṣa*. Thus, these combined amount to one *pala*, which should be powdered, boiled in water, and drunk.

Furthermore, this is not very sound because it contradicts other tantras, because the portioning of the *triphalā* as a collective whole is not established by logic, and because it contradicts the statement of Jatūkarṇa, which begins: "One should drink one *pala* of powder made from one *pala* each of *paṭola* root, *triphalā*, *gavākṣī*, and *trivṛt*, along with two parts of *trāyantī* and *kaṭukā*, and a quarter-part of *nāgara*; once that is digested, one should eat rice with meat broth."
