Furthermore, the specific causes for the provocation of *vāta* and the other humors have not been stated individually, because they are already established as being common to [the etiology of] insanity (*unmāda*).

For it has been said: "Whatever is prescribed for the treatment of epilepsy should also be applied in the case of insanity, due to the similarity of the causes and the affected tissues" (Ci. A. 9). As for the specific cause of epilepsy that distinguishes it from insanity, that has already been stated [in the verse] beginning with "from unwholesome and impure food."
With the words beginning with "separately" (pṛthak), he describes the fourfold characteristics of epilepsy (apasmāra).

Regarding the phrase "perceiving yellow and blood-like forms": it refers to one who perceives yellow and red forms and is characterized by thirst and heat, and so forth; the compound means one who is both thirsty, hot, and a perceiver of a world pervaded by fire.
By the words beginning with "white," the phlegmatic (ślaiṣmika) type is described.

The phrase "with thrilled limbs and bristling hair after a long time" indicates that there will be a swift release from the wind (vāta) and bile (pitta) disorders; the underlying sense is that a wasting condition characterized by such symptoms is incurable even if it arises from only a single humor (doṣa).

In the passage beginning with "or after a fortnight" (*pakṣāt*), by indicating the time of the impulse (*vega*) out of its sequential order, it suggests that the impulse of epilepsy (*apasmāra*) occurs both after and before the stated time;
thus, "after some interval" (*kiñcid athāntaram*) means they produce the impulse after a certain lapse of time— that is, after a short interval (8–13).
With the words beginning with "by them" (tair), he describes the medical treatment (*cikitsā*).
"Awakening" (*prabodhana*) means performing its own function correctly by being free from defects.
In the phrase "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*) and so forth, the word *prāyaḥ* has the sense of "especially"; by this, other [treatments] are also indicated as occurring.
Regarding the phrase "of one who has been consoled," which means of one whose strength has been restored:
in the passage beginning with "cow dung" (*gośakṛt*), the word "cow" (*go*) should also be applied to curd and the other ingredients; by doing so, this *pañcagavya* becomes a small quantity.
In this context, although the equality of cow-dung juice and so forth is established by technical convention (*paribhāṣā*), it is stated explicitly for the sake of clarity.
Regarding the two *pañcamūla* groups mentioned in such passages as "the two *pañcamūlas*," the pair known as *daśamūla* (the ten roots) should be understood.
Nīlinī, nīlikā,
śampāka, āragvadha, phalgu, and kāṣṭhodumbarikā.
The two-pala quantity for each of the ten roots and so forth has already been explained; [in the case of] unmāda,
nicula, hijjala, śreyasī, and hastipippalī [are used].
The two *sārivās* are *śyāmalatā* and *anantamūlī*.
In the passage beginning with "brāhmī," the term "ancient" (*purāṇa*) is an adjective qualifying ghee; therefore, ancient ghee is what is to be prepared here.
Regarding the phrase "in the urine of the bull and the goat" (*vārṣe bāste*):

although it has been stated that the urine of women is recommended over that of men—based on the statement, "The urine of cows is sharp for women, but not so for men; for women possess a portion of *pitta*, whereas men are known to be of a *soma*-like nature"—nevertheless, because of the specific selection made here, the urine of only those of the masculine gender is appropriate for this medicinal application.
*Kaiṭarya*, *pārvata*, *nimba*, *vayaḥsthā*, and *guḍūcī* [are indicated].

Regarding the mention of "dual combinations" (*dvandva*) as *vāta-śleṣmātmake*, it should be understood as referring to those of the *vāta* type and the *śleṣma* type respectively. Others, however, maintain that the *apasmāra* arising from a dual combination (*dvandvaja*)—which, like *gulma*, was not explicitly mentioned but is produced by a natural equilibrium of the two humors—is indicated by the term "*vāta-śleṣmātmake*."
In the passage beginning with "25–27 tailaprastham," etc., it is understood that the paste (kalka) is measured in *pala*s, because milk alone is present in place of a liquid; thus,
"in a *kaṃsa*" means in an *āḍhaka*.
"In *kāśmarya*" means in the juice derived from *gambhārī*; "in the decoction" (*rase*) means in the boiled extract;
by the phrase "in that same manner," he indicates the declaration of the fruit resulting from the preceding formulation.

Similarly, by the phrase "a prastha of ghee is prepared," the word "quickly" mentioned in the preceding formulation is drawn in; thus, the result is that it becomes a swift remedy for *pitta*-type epilepsy (28–31).
Regarding the passage beginning with "anointing" (*abhyaṅga*), the oil should be cooked without any medicinal paste (*kalka*).

In the case of "cow-dung" (*gośakṛt*) and so forth, there is an ointment (*utsādana*) with cow dung, and by implication, a bath (*snāna*) with cow urine. In the case of "kaṭabhī" and so forth, one should take the bark of all four—*kaṭabhī* and the others—and prepare a decoction three times the quantity of the oil; the fourth [ingredient] is completed by a portion of urine equal in measure to the oil.
In the passage beginning with *palaṅkaṣā*, the term *pūtanākeśī* refers to *golomī*.
For instance, in the *Jatūkarṇa*, *golomī* is listed under the name *pūtanākeśī*.

As it is said: "With *vṛścikālī*, *pathyā*, *golomī*, *nākulī*, garlic, and *kuṣṭha*; with mustard, *jaṭilā*, *coraka*, asafoetida, *vacā*, *madhuka*, *citraka*, and *arka*; and with the flesh, excrement, and feathers of carnivorous birds, boiled in goat's urine—this [mixture] is for massage."
Atirasā, jalaja, yaṣṭīmadhu (34–36), citrā, and dantī.
Hiṅgu, śivāṭikā, and vaṃśapatrikā— [the term] *skandhāsthi* means the bone of the shoulder;
by grinding [these] under the asterism Puṣya, he teaches the refinement (*saṃskāra*) performed through conjunction with the lunar mansion.
In the passage beginning with "apetarākṣasīsvarasaḥ" (the juice of apetarākṣasī) and "jalaukaḥśakṛt" (leech dung), the phrase "tadvat" (likewise) refers to *utsādana* (rubbing/cleansing).

From the authoritative statement that "the urine of tawny cows possesses a specific potency," and because it is praised for lions and other animals as well, the word "urine" (mūtra) should be supplied here [in the verse].
In the passage beginning with "bhārgī," *nāgadantī* refers to *kāṣṭhapāṭalā*,
*śvetā*, *śvetāparājitā*, *śvetasyandā*,
*śvetāviṣāṇikā*, and *śatāvarī*.
In the verse beginning with "triphalā," *pītadru* refers to *devadāru*;
the "salts" (*lavaṇa*) refer to the five types starting with *saindhava*, or alternatively, all those mentioned in the section on salts should be taken according to availability (41–45).
In the passage beginning with "kāyasthām," the term "śāradān mudgān" refers to green mung beans, for they generally appear in the autumn;
"vartiḥ" refers to a collyrium stick for the eyes;
and "viṣapīte" means one who has drunk poison.

One who is as if dead due to immersion in water is called "water-dead" (*jalamṛta*); its characteristics are described as follows: "One should recognize a person who is water-dead by their anus, head, eyes, abdomen, and genitals being distended, and by their feet, hands, and face being cold.
[The term] *bāstamaiṣārṣabhaiḥ* refers to those derived from goats, sheep, and bulls.
"Extracted under Puṣya" means taken during the Puṣya lunar mansion;
"insect" refers to a scorpion and the like.
Now, regarding epilepsy (apasmāra), he describes the etiology, symptoms, and treatment by means of a verse beginning with "yasya" and so forth.

"Having a form exceeding the symptoms of the doshas" means that its form exceeds the symptoms of the doshas mentioned in the context of epilepsy and resembles that of exogenous (āgantu) insanity. Therefore, an exogenous symptom occurs within those born of the doshas, yet the state of being purely exogenous is not possible without the symptoms of the doshas. Consequently, there is no separate exogenous epilepsy; rather, that exogenous factor is a subsequent accompaniment (anubandha) of the dosha-born type. Thus, regarding what was stated [in Sūtra 19], "There are four types of epilepsy," it is simply that the exogenous factor sometimes serves as a secondary accompaniment.

By this, it is shown that in the case of *bhūtāpasmāra* (possession by spirits), it exists only as a secondary consequence (*anubandha*); it is not to be treated independently like *unmāda* (insanity).
It has been stated elsewhere as well: "Apasmāra is a great disease, and it arises solely from the [deranged] *doṣas*.

Others, however, such as Bhīmadanta and others, explain the text here for the purpose of indicating the characteristics and treatments of independent (*svatantra*) and exogenous (*āgantu*) apasmāras; thus, there is no restriction of number regarding only those apasmāras born of the *doṣas*.

In this region, the Saindhavas and Kāśmīras recite a treatise on the characteristics and treatment of adherence to what is not reality (atattvābhiniveśa), beginning with the words "O Blessed One" (bhagavan) and so forth; and the elders maintain that this is not of Vedic origin (anārṣa).
The five formulations beginning with oil and garlic demonstrate, by this, a treatment that proceeds slowly over a long period of time.
By the words "water, fire," and so forth, he shows that if an attack of apasmāra occurs in the presence of water and other such elements, then death itself ensues.
By the words "they bring about," and so forth, he describes the pathogenesis (samprāpti) in the Saṅgraha.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Epilepsy," in the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka Saṃhitā, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsāsthāna). 10.67–68.

[Cikitsāsthāna, Chapter 11 (77 of 120)] In the disease of epilepsy (apasmāra), chest injury (uraḥkṣata) also occurs due to falling from uneven heights or similar causes; consequently, one becomes emaciated from that injury (kṣatakṣīṇa). Therefore, following the treatment for epilepsy, the treatment for those emaciated by chest injury (kṣatakṣīṇacikitsita) is now described.

In this context, the disease that arises from a person who is emaciated by chest wounds (*kṣatakṣīṇa*), as well as from the depletion of semen and vital energy (*ojas*) caused by factors such as the aforementioned indulgence in women, is the primary condition. Although its characteristics will be described later with the words "the chest is afflicted with pain" (*uro virujyate*) and so forth, it is called "chest wound" (*uraḥkṣata*) through the metaphorical attribution of the effect to the cause. Furthermore, when the reading is *kṣīṇakṣata*, the word "emaciated" (*kṣīṇa*) refers to a person characterized by the depletion of semen and vital energy; thus, because a wound occurs in such an emaciated person, it is termed "wound-and-emaciation" (*kṣatakṣīṇa*).
Others, however, say that *kṣata* (injury) and *kṣaya* (wasting) together constitute *kṣatakṣaya*; by this, it is understood as two distinct diseases.

Likewise, he will describe the symptoms of *kṣata* (wound/trauma) and *kṣīṇa* (emaciation) through such statements as "chest pain, vomiting of blood," and so forth. In that case, the singular reference in phrases such as "its symptoms are unmanifest" and "curable when recent and in a strong person" would be untenable. Therefore, there is a twofold classification of symptoms for a single condition, *kṣatakṣīṇa*, based on its causes; or rather, this statement regarding the specific causes of the symptoms of *kṣata* and *dhātukṣaya* (loss of bodily constituents) should be understood as intended for the purpose of treating the disease during its premonitory stage (*pūrvarūpa*).
By the term "brahmarṣi" (brahmin seer), he precludes Ātreya’s status as a *devarṣi* (divine seer) or *rājarṣi* (royal seer);
"for the sake of medical treatment" (*cikitsārtham*) means for the sake of a remedy; "medical treatment" (*cikitsitam*) refers to the treatise that sets forth medical therapy.
Medical treatment occurs only when the disease has been identified through its etiology and other factors; therefore, he first describes the etiology of the injury: "By the bow," and so forth;
"of one who exerts" means of one whose body is being exerted.
"By those stronger than himself" means by those possessing greater strength relative to him;
"restraining" means warding off.
"Nirghāta" is a specific type of missile (*astra*), or alternatively, *nirghāta* is a specific kind of hurling of stones and other objects produced by exceeding strength.
"Of one who is struck by others" means of one who has been beaten;

"disease" refers to the disease known as *kṣatakṣaya* (wasting due to chest injury), whose characteristics will be described later. Others, however, maintain that by the word "disease" (*vyādhi*) they mean the injury itself, based on the statement: "The term 'disease' also applies to the *doṣas* and so forth.

Furthermore, one should not suspect this condition of being *rājayakṣmā* (consumption), because chest injury is produced solely by the three *doṣas* and has a distinct pathogenesis: "When a person's chest is injured by exertions beyond their strength..."

The statement beginning with, "Vāyu, aggravated, drives both doshas upward and courses through them" (Ci. A. 8), describes symptoms that are indeed distinct from those to be described later with the words, "the chest is afflicted with pain," and so forth;

for this very reason, the author will state the difference between these two here: "If this [condition] is neglected, it becomes a precursor to yakṣman (consumption). Furthermore, the connection is as follows: "In one who is excessively attached to women and who eats dry, scant, or measured food, a powerful disease arises."
Moderate eating is the practice of consuming a single taste; alternatively, it refers to eating at the wrong time.
(4–8) He describes the symptoms of chest injury and wasting with the verse beginning with "chest," etc.
"Bhidyate" means it is split;
"even from the destruction of fire" indicates here that even without the destruction of fire, a splitting of the feces occurs through the power of the disease.
Others, however, read: "viḍbhedo 'gnivadhastathā" (splitting of the feces and likewise the destruction of fire).

When corrupted and vitiated, it wastes away; thus, one becomes subject to the depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu-kṣaya*). One does not waste away solely due to physical injury, but also from the depletion of semen and vital energy (*śukra-ojas*) caused by excessive indulgence with women and other such factors, thereby becoming subject to the depletion of the remaining constituents (9–11).
He states the premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa), beginning with "unmanifest" (avyakta) and so forth.
"Unmanifest" means incomplete due to its smallness, according to the aforementioned definition.
The section beginning with "chest pain" (*urorug*) has been largely explained.

Regarding the phrase "cough is *vaiśeṣika*," it means it is distinct; that distinction is to be understood as stated by the words "discolored, dark-brown," and so forth. Alternatively, *vaiśeṣika* may be understood as "additional," occurring when [the vital essences] are depleted—that is, when semen and *ojas* are diminished.
Others, however, describe these two as the characteristics of two stages by means of the passage beginning with "chest pain" (uroruk) and so forth.
[Verses 12–13].
To facilitate the commencement of treatment, he states the classification of conditions as curable and so forth, beginning with "slight" (alpa) and so forth.

Regarding one who has been ill for a full year— that is, more than a year— he states the treatment to be performed for a specific known disease, beginning with the words "considering the chest," and so forth.
The construction is as follows: "Thinking there is an immediate wound in the chest, one should drink lac (lākṣā)";
"with sugar" means food accompanied by sugar;
one whose stool is broken should drink lac along with mustā, ativiṣā, and pāṭhā.

In this context, those who read "two-year-old calf" (*dvivatsakām*) intend for two portions of the *vatsaka* to be taken; or rather, is it that the word *dvivatsaka* itself refers to two *vatsakas*? For instance, in the ritual manual (*kalpa*), the *kuṭaja* is described as being of two types according to the distinction between male and female: "The male shall have large fruit, white flowers, and glossy leaves; the female shall be dark with reddish flowers, and likewise with small fruits and flowers" (Ka. A. 5). This is stated for the purpose of joining [the two], specifically for the purpose of joining the chest of the *kṣatra*.
By the word *madhūka* here, the *madhūka* flower is to be understood.
With the verse beginning "elāpatratvac" (15–20), he describes the *elādi-guṭikā*.
"By means of logic" (yuktyā) means that one should give as much honey as is required to form the pills.
*Dakṣa* is a domestic cock.

Regarding "goat and wild meat": this refers to a powder prepared from goat meat or from wild animals such as deer and the like; it is "prepared" (siddha) in the sense of being processed in the aforementioned manner.
The preparation of the powder must be performed by means of liquids such as grape juice through the application of fire.
For it is said in the *Jatūkarṇa*: “*Punarnavā*, red *śāli* rice, grapes, and sugar, powdered together and prepared with milk and ghee.
(25–26) Regarding the verse beginning with *madhūka*, the *taṇḍulīyaka* vegetable is prepared with milk and a paste of *madhūka* and *madhuka*.
When the wind is weak (*sabale*),
the flesh-eating beasts and birds (*kravyādāḥ*) [devour];
"born from milk" means [the fetus] was seized while still in the state of being milk.
In the formulation beginning with *yaṣṭyāhva* (liquorice), there is a fourfold quantity of the decoction, milk, and ghee.

In the formulation beginning with *vāṃśī* (bamboo manna) and *kośātakī*, the same applies—that is, it is beneficial for wounds. Here, some authorities state that the juice of *kola* and *lākṣā* should each be four times the amount of ghee, while the milk should be eight times the amount. Alternatively, they maintain that the juices of *kola* and *lākṣā* should be equal in measure to the milk. This principle is indicated in the chapter on epilepsy (*apasmāra*).
By the statement "two *nidigdhikās*," both the large and the small varieties are to be taken;
*payasyā* is *kṣīravidārī*.

Fruits such as vātāma, abhiṣuka, and other similar varieties from the northern regions that pacify vāta and pitta, as well as the juices of the dhātrī (myrobalan)—even though it is said: "In the preparation of an oily [medicated] substance, where there are five or more liquid ingredients... [the rule does not apply here].

By the statement, "In that regard, they say there is a commonality of oiliness," the fact of being measured by a *prastha* is established; nevertheless, this mention of the measure should be understood as intended solely to reinforce the meaning of this technical definition (*paribhāṣā*).

Here, the status of being half a *pala* applies to black pepper and the other ingredients when combined, because the enumeration is primarily concerned with the aggregate (*samāhāra*); however, the elders maintain that each individual ingredient is half a *pala*.
Sudhā (nectar) is the food of those on earth, whereas amṛta (ambrosia) is the food of the gods.

In the formula beginning with *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, having added three *prasthas* less a quarter (*pāda*) of water according to the quantity of the decoction ingredients, forty-four decoctions result when one-quarter remains;
and here the milk is four times the amount of the ghee—or alternatively, the milk is four times the amount of the decoction.
In the case of the formula beginning with *madhuka* (44–47) as well, following the method of decoction, there is half a *prastha* of the decoction;
since it is combined with an equal amount of parched grain flour (*saktu*), it is called *samasaktughṛta*.

By the verse beginning with "Ghṛtaṃ tu" (But ghee...), he demonstrates that those ghees which are suitable for linctuses due to their combination with sugar and other ingredients should be used as linctuses in cases of *pitta*, whereas those suitable for drinking because they are devoid of sugar and such additives should be used in cases of *vāta*. Alternatively, those ghees which are in a thickened state should be employed as linctuses for *pitta* during their use, while the very same ghees, having reached a liquefied state, should be employed in cases of *vāta*.
He states the distinct results of ghee linctuses and ghee drinks separately in the verse beginning with "Nirvāpayet" (One should quench...).
"Because of its smallness" means because it is small precisely by virtue of being a liquid (leha), since the liquid is stated to be measured at one karṣa.
"It steps upon" means it conquers, restrains, or strikes back; some read "it does not restrain."
Regarding the passage beginning with "kṣāma," "kṣāma" means one whose body is exhausted; "kṣīṇa" means weak; and "kṛśa" means one who has lost his flesh.
The quantity of *tvakṣīrī* and the other ingredients should be understood as that amount by which the ghee attains consistency.
By the phrase "equal parts of honey" (*samadhvaṃśān*), he indicates that the honey is equal in measure to the *tvakṣīrī* and the other substances.
The milky trees (kṣīrivṛkṣa), such as the banyan (vaṭa), the udumbara, the aśvattha, the plakṣa, and the kapītana.
And it is stated in the Śālākya: “The Udumbara, Vaṭa, Aśvattha, Madhūka, and Plakṣa—these five milky trees are proclaimed in this treatise.
[In this context,] "handfuls" (muṣṭi) refer to a measure of one pala.

In this case, when the thirteen *pala*s of *balā* and the other ingredients have been reduced by boiling in eight times their quantity of water until one-fourth remains, there are twenty-six *pala*s of decoction (*kvātha*). The milk should be double the amount of this decoction, and the juice of *vidārī* and the meat-broth of goat should be equal in measure to the decoction. Thus, one hundred and thirty *pala*s should be cooked here in one *āḍhaka* of ghee.

Others, however, state that according to the rule of adding sixteen times the quantity of water to the substance to be boiled, there are fifty-two *pala*s of decoction once prepared; they further maintain that the measurements of the milk and other ingredients should be increased accordingly.
However, in this case of thirteen *pala*s of decoction, water should be added in such a way that the decoction becomes equal in quantity to the ghee;
for in the preparation of ghee where four parts of liquid are used, the decoction indeed becomes equal in volume to the fat (sneha).

Twice the amount of this decoction of milk, along with an equal amount of *vidārī* juice and goat-meat broth, should be added; alternatively, two *āḍhaka*s of the combined *vidārī* and goat-meat broth may be given.

For it is said in the *Jatūkarṇa*: “Having boiled *vṛścīva*, the five roots (*pañcamūla*), *balā*, *vidārī*, and the sprouts of the *vaṭa* tree and others, one should cook one *āḍhaka* of ghee with two parts of milk and an equal amount of goat’s milk and *vidārī* juice, along with a paste of the *jīvanīya* group of drugs.”

For here the specific distinction is that the quantity of the substance to be boiled is indefinite; however, the decoction must be equal in volume to the oil. The *khaja* is a churning-stick (*manthānadaṇḍa*), ten fingers long or a cubit (*hasta*) in length, and it is wrapped in birch bark for the sake of increasing its efficacy.
In verses 56–61, regarding "tvakkṣīrī" and so forth: *śrāvaṇī* is *muṇḍitikā*; *vīrā* is the tuber of *vidārī*.
In the passage beginning with "drākṣām" (raisins), two *pala*s each of *yaṣṭyāhva* (liquorice) and *sauvarcala* salt are combined;
for *marica* (black pepper), the remainder is stated as "two *pala*s.

For it is said in the *Jatūkarṇa*: "Having boiled one *tulā* of sugar in three *āḍhaka*s of ghee, oil, and milk, one should boil ten *palika* portions of raisins (*drākṣā*), *vidārī*, *vṛścīva*, *śatāvarī*, *kṛṣṇā* (long pepper), ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), *balā*, and *dhātrī*, along with one *palika* portion each of *yaṣṭyāhva* and *rucaka* salt," and so forth.
The term "boiled" (*kvathita*) indicates that the powder should be added only when the milk has been completely reduced [to a solid consistency].

Regarding the passage beginning with "cow's milk" (*gokṣīra*), cow's milk is mentioned as the causal material and not for the purpose of cooking the ghee; for if that were the case, the boluses (*modaka*) would not be formed by the powder to be added.
The fourth [dose] is 70–77 *palas* when manifesting transformations, that is, when producing disorders such as colic and the like.
In the case of "sugar" and so forth, it should be understood that, according to the principle of adding ingredients, sugar and other substances are added to milk;
"filtered through cloth" means those [substances] fallen between layers of cloth;

and it should be known that the procedure prescribed for those with weak digestion (*mandāgni*) and for those suffering from consumption (*yakṣman*), as well as the method for those who have loose stools, is intended here as the rule to be followed.
78–84 *palikam* means a measure of one *pala*;
"Sixteen *palas* of pomegranate and sour *vṛkṣāmla*": by saying "twice, twice," it shows that each is double the previous two *palas*, meaning four *palas* each.
By the phrase "as before," he indicates that the result is identical to the previous formulation.

Regarding this, Jatūkarṇa states: "Two palas each of *dhānyaka*, *rūcaka*, *jīraka*, and *dīpyaka*; one pala of *śuṇṭhī*; and one *kuḍava* each of *kapittha*, *dāḍima*, and *vṛkṣāmla*," and so forth (verses 88–90).

In the passage beginning with "nāgabalā" and so on, the phrase "increased by half a *karṣa*" means increased by exactly half a *karṣa* at a time; [this preparation] should be drunk for one month, consisting solely of milk.
For it is stated in the *Jatūkarṇa*: "The root of *nāgabalā*, increased by half a *karṣa* at a time until it measures one *pala*, should be drunk for a month by one who subsists solely on milk.

(91–92) Furthermore, even that which is cool to the touch and brings about pacification may become burning (*vidāhin*) [if consumed in excess]; for that reason, it is described as "non-burning" (*avidāhin*).
93–94 Regarding the need for prompt treatment in one who is emaciated by chest wounds, he says "upekṣite" and so forth;
"tasya" refers to *yakṣman* (consumption).

In the summary [of the chapter], the general and specific forms of the symptoms arising from injury (kṣata) and those arising from wasting (kṣaya) have been established separately, such as "the chest is pierced" and so forth. 95–97.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Wasting Due to Chest Injury," in the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka Saṃhitā, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Chapter 12 of the Cikitsāsthāna (78 of 120)]

In the case of wasting due to injury (*kṣatakṣīṇa*), there is impairment of the vital points (*marmopaghāta*); in swelling (*śotha*) as well, impairment of the vital points is a cause. Because they share this common cause, the treatment for swelling is stated immediately after that for wasting due to injury. *Juṣṭam* means "practiced" or "resorted to."

"Prakopa" means that which causes provocation; thus, the meaning is "the cause. Alternatively, by the metaphorical treatment of cause and effect as non-different, the word *prakopa* refers to the cause of swelling (*śvayathu*). By the word "form" (*rūpa*), both the actual form and the premonitory signs (*pūrvarūpa*) are included. By "pacification" (*śamana*), medical treatment (*cikitsā*) is meant.

That Veda which has the purpose of medicine (*agada*)—that is, the purpose of health—is the *Agadaveda*. Because it is profound yet clear, it is like a river (*sindhu*); the meaning is that, like the Himalaya, the best of mountains, it is the source for its flow. Just as the Himalaya is the source of the Gaṅgā, so too Atri’s son is the originator of Āyurveda.

Regarding the word "tān" (those), it refers to anger and the others which the disciple questioned. In the phrase "of that which arises from a single limb and that which arises from the whole," the term *sarvaja* (arising from the whole) denotes that which arises from the entire body, while the term *ekāṅgaja* (arising from a single limb) denotes generally that which does not pervade the body. Therefore, although a threefold classification should be stated based on their dependence on parts of the whole body, a half-body, or a limb, one should understand that here the category of *ekāṅgaja* includes both those dependent on a half-body and those dependent on a limb.

Purification refers to cleansing procedures such as emesis; diseases refer to fever and the like; fasting refers to the absence of food or the consumption of unwholesome food. For those who are emaciated and weak due to these factors, the use of alkalis and similar substances is to be understood as the cause of endogenous swelling (*nijashvayathu*). Curd and other such items, however, are independent causes. Raw refers to that which is uncooked; "vitiated" refers to things that provoke the *doṣas*, such as newly drawn water and the like; and *gara* is poison produced by the combination of substances.

And regarding "purity of the body," even though the body is worthy of purification, the impurity of the body here refers specifically to injury to the vital points (*marman*) caused by internal defects (*doṣa*); however, injury to the vital points arising from external causes is indeed due to exogenous factors (*āgantu*),
such as difficult labor, premature miscarriage, and so forth.

"Of the therapeutic procedures" refers to emesis and the others; "improper management" means incorrect performance and incorrect application. With the words "external," etc., he states the cause of exogenous swelling.

"External" means not deep-seated; by this it is indicated that the skin does not become corrupted by the depth of the swelling. "Skin" (*tvac*) is a word ending in a consonant (*halanta*) used as the object of the action.
The corrupter [of the skin] is due to a specific type of trauma.

"By wood, stone, weapons, fire, poison, iron, and so forth" means having wood and the like as its cause. For the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) denotes the cause; thus, the meaning is "an injury caused by wood and such.
Furthermore, wood and the others mentioned here should be understood as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for teeth and other such things.

Alternatively, the word "and so forth" denotes a type or kind; therefore, since the injury produced by wood and the like is expressed by the term "wood and so forth," one should understand that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "injury" (*abhighāta*).
The analysis is: "the adventitious cause.

"Threefold" means that it is inherently threefold by virtue of being based on all three types of body parts (upper, middle, and lower); the word "and" (ca) implies that the exogenous type is also threefold according to the aforementioned divisions.
This concludes the description of the pathogenesis (samprāpti), beginning with the phrase "the external vessels," and so forth.
"External" means not deep;
by the word "veins" (sirā), there is a general inclusion of all channels (srotas).
"With its path obstructed" means its passage is blocked.

It is called *utsedhaliṅga* because it is characterized by swelling (*utsedha*) that is never absent [from the disease]. By the passage beginning with "situated in the chest" (*uraḥsthitaiḥ*), he describes the specific pathogenesis (*samprāpti*) of particular types of swellings.
"Upward" refers to the upper part of the body starting from the chest; "downward" refers to the lower part starting from the colon;
the location of the wind (vāyu) is the colon.
"Located in the middle" means situated between the chest and the colon (*pakvāśaya*).
"In some places" refers to locations such as the throat and palate.

"Named after that" should be applied everywhere, meaning named after terms such as "swelling of the throat" (*galaśotha*), or alternatively, named after terms such as "swelling above" (*ūrdhvaśotha*) and "swelling below" (*adhaḥśotha*).
With the words beginning with "heat" (ūṣma), he describes the premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa):
"davathu" refers to distress or affliction in the eyes and other sense organs.
The extension of the vessels refers to the spreading of the vessels (10).

Although all swellings (*śotha*) arise from the three *doṣas*, he explains how their designations as "vata-born" and so forth, as well as their treatments, become distinct: "All," etc. "Excessive signs of the *doṣa*" means the signs of whichever *doṣa* is predominant (*adhika*). By means of those excessive signs of the *doṣa*, they "attain that term"—that is, the designation of the predominant *doṣa*, such as "this is vata-born" and so on. Likewise, they attain the "physician's treatment" by means of the excessive signs of the *doṣa*; the meaning is that they attain a specific variation in treatment prescribed by the signs of the predominant *doṣa*.
10. With the words "with reverence," etc., he recites the general characteristic (sāmānyaliṅga).
By the words "moving" (*cala*) and so forth, he describes the symptoms of swelling caused by wind (*vātaja-śotha*).
"Thin-skinned" (*tanu-tvak*) means having sparse skin; "black" (*asita*) means dark.
Sleep is the lack of perception of touch; exhilaration (*harṣa*) is the sensation known as *jhaṇajhaṇikā*, or else it is the bristling of the hair (*romaharṣa*).
"It subsides without a cause" means that due to the mobile nature of wind (*vāyu*), it sometimes becomes latent even without a [specific] cause.
Some read "with a cause" (*nimittataḥ*); by that, what was stated [in Sūtra 1.18], "And that vātika [itch] may be destroyed by oiliness, heat, and massage," is precisely what is being said here.
"Rising up" (pronnamati) means that it rises immediately after being pressed;
by the words "soft" (mṛdu) and so forth, he describes the swelling caused by bile (pitta-śotha).
"It burns" means it is scorched;
"pain from touch" means it cannot endure contact.
With the words beginning with "guru," he describes phlegmatic swelling (*kapha-śotha*);
"accompanied by anorexia" means it is associated with the disease of anorexia;
and "difficult birth and subsidence" means its onset and disappearance occur over a long period.

The *rātribali* (night-aggravated) swelling is characterized by *kapha*. Because *kapha* increases during the night due to bodily moisture resulting from the obstruction of the channels (*srotas*) and due to a lack of physical activity, the swelling produced by it becomes powerful at that time. During the day, however, when the channels are open and the body is engaged in activity, *kapha* does not become strong, but rather *vāyu* does; therefore, a *vāta*-induced swelling becomes powerful during the day, while the *kapha*-induced swelling diminishes. (14) Now he describes the incurability [of the condition], beginning with the words "of the emaciated" (*kṛśasya*).

Regarding the phrase "preceded by vomiting," this refers to those symptoms stated in the *Triśothīya* chapter: "Vomiting, dyspnea, anorexia, thirst, fever, and diarrhea, as well as numbness, emaciation, and constant debility—this is the summary of the complications of swelling" (Sūtra-sthāna 18).

Furthermore, "followed by vital points (*marmānugata*) and marked by streaks (*rājimān*)" is a distinct characteristic, while "it exudes fluid (*parisravet*)" and so forth are distinct signs of incurability.
By the words beginning with "ahīna," the characteristics of that which is easily curable (sukhasādhya) are stated;
the characteristics of that which is difficult to cure (kṛcchrasādhya) should be understood as the non-completion of the characteristics of that which is easily curable.

Although the causes and symptoms of swelling (*śvayathu*) have already been described in the chapter on the three types of edema (*triśothīya*), they are stated here again in brief for the sake of the present context.
(16) He states the general therapeutic principle: "The etiology," and so forth.
The meaning is that one should treat [the patient] with methods such as fasting (*laṅghana*) by means of sequences contrary to the etiology (*nidāna*) and so forth.

By the phrase "knowing strength, the dosha, and time," the action contrary to the etiology and other factors is stated; it shows that having understood the strength, the *doṣa*—distinguished by its divisions such as undigested matter (*āma*) and so forth—and likewise the time in the form of the stage of the disease, whatever [treatment] is appropriate should be performed.
In the passage beginning with "etiology" (*nidāna*), the word *doṣa* refers to Vata and the others, and the word "season" (*ṛtu*) refers to time in its constant progression.
Because that very [term] expresses it as qualified by those [factors], the statement "knowing the doshas, the body, and the time" (*baladoṣakālavid*) is not redundant.

Others, however, say that by the first word *doṣa* the corrupted tissues (*dūṣyadhātu*) are included, while by the second the [specific] humors (*vātādi*) are included; in the first interpretation, it should be understood that by the word *doṣa* itself, the corrupted matter (*dūṣya*)—which is the substratum of the doshas—is also included. 16
"Āmaja" means produced by the defect of undigested matter (*āma*); and "immaturity" (*apakvatā*) generally occurs when the *doṣas* are first vitiated.
By "gradually" (*kramaiḥ*), one means by "therapeutic measures" (*upakramaiḥ*).
"Below" (*adhaḥ*) means arising from the lower part of the body; one should treat it with purgatives (*virecana*).
"By upward-moving [remedies]" means by emetics; "arising from the upper part" means arising from the upper portion;
"bitter ghee" means ghee prepared with bitter substances;
and "in the case of pitta and vāta" refers to the combination (dvandva) of vāta and pitta.

In this context, for one in whom fainting and other such symptoms have arisen— that is, for one afflicted by fainting, feverish thirst, and burning sensations who requires purification— the phrase "in one requiring purification while possessed of fainting" refers to one who must be cleansed using urine and similar substances, namely through formulations of buttermilk and *āsava* in equal parts with urine.

With the words beginning with "grāmya," [the author] speaks in order to demonstrate an absolute prohibition—despite the fact that [certain acts] are already prohibited by virtue of being causes of transgression—because they bring about great calamity.
"Gauḍam" means a product of molasses (*guḍa*); the suffix *aṇ* is used here in the sense of a derivative product (*vikāra*).
Dhānā refers to roasted barley that has sprouted;
vallūra is dried meat;
and samaśana is the eating of wholesome and unwholesome foods together in one meal.
Here, treating the disorder of *kapha* first, he describes the treatment for *kapha*-type swelling with the verse beginning "vyoṣam" (the three pungents).

Regarding the phrase "sāyorajaska," they maintain that only processed iron powder (*mṛtam ayorajaḥ*) is intended here, because even in the context of *rasāyana*, the instruction is to employ only processed iron powder.
Iron dust is not equal when measured; for iron is difficult to digest, therefore, when using iron, only a small amount of metal should be understood as the dose according to the proportions.
The paste of *harītakī* and the others should be drunk with lukewarm water, or all of them together with *punarnavā*; thus [ends the section on] *harītakī* and the others.

Since the procedure beginning with "having bathed" (*snātaśca*) and so forth is stated at the end for all three types [of fever] arising from wind (*vāta*) and the others, it should be understood as applicable to all the aforementioned applications.
In the formula beginning with *punarnavā*, one *prastha* of milk should be boiled until half remains due to its great volume, and then it should be drunk;
in the formula beginning with *mayūraka* as well, the milk and the quantity of the medicinal substances should be understood as stated in the preceding formulation.
The term "weighed in half-palas" (*palārdhikaiḥ*) means measured at two *karṣas* each.

And here, because the milk is more abundant than the medicinal drugs, some maintain that a small amount of milk should be administered as the means of preparation, according to the statement: "Whatever they do is the method" (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 26).
Pītadru is Devadāru;
ūṣaṇa is Marica.
"Abstaining from food and water" means that both food and water must be renounced.

In the passage beginning with "cow-related [products]" and ending with "the urine of cows," they likewise maintain the application of the phrases "for seven days or a month" and "abstaining from food and water.
In the term "with urine" (*samūtra*), it is connected to the meaning of consuming milk that is equivalent to urine.
Regarding the phrase "of *kūrcika* curd" (*kūrcikamastunaḥ*): the *mastu* (whey) that has been cooked in milk together with curd is *kūrcika-mastu*; the *mastu* of plain curd is ordinary *mastu*.
The term "in the air" (*vaihāyase*) refers to the intermediate space (*antarikṣe*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "kāśmarya" (29–31), the term "in the heat" refers to the hot season;
"twofold" means for two weeks, and it should be kept during the cold season.
The designation "one hundred and eight" should be understood as being formed by combining the seven hundred [substances] beginning with *kāśmarya*. Furthermore,
in the passage beginning with "the two *punarnavās*," each individual substance consists of two *palas*.
And because of the rule regarding a remainder of one *droṇa*, it should be understood that four *droṇas* of water are required;

this being so, when one-fourth remains, there will be one *droṇa* of decoction in a heap of barley—that is, in a pile of barley—having placed it in a jar smeared with honey and ghee, it should be kept for a month; or alternatively, having placed it in a fragrant vessel smeared with honey and ghee, one should cook it.
Regarding the "six abdominal enlargements" (ṣaṭjaṭhara), those caused by *chidrodaka* and *udara* are incurable by medicine and should be excluded (34–38).

In the passage beginning with "the three fruits" (*phalatrika*), one should add four times as much water to two *prasthas* of the *triphalā* and other ingredients; it should be understood that this results in a decoction (*kaṣāya*) reduced to one-quarter, as seen in other *āsavas*.
"Reduced to powder" means crushed for the purpose of making a decoction;

however, others give half a *droṇa* of water to the powder itself. Alternatively, the measure of the powder to be given may be one *kuḍava*, by which "twice the portion of honey" amounts to two *kuḍavas*.

In the *pippalyādi* powder, "arising from the three doṣas" should be understood as being produced by vāta and the others, either individually or combined; moreover, it is not logical here that a disorder arising from the three doṣas should be considered incurable.
(41–42) The four salts, excluding sea salt (*sāmudra*), are those mentioned in the *Dīrghañjīvitīya* chapter.
"Fine, dry powder" means that a subtle powder should be taken here;
furthermore, the quantity of water to be added should be four times the amount of the powder;
"thickened" means dense.
43–46. Regarding "fresh ginger" (*ārdraka-nāgara*): this refers to fresh ginger (*aśuṣka-nāgara*).

Furthermore, the increase by half a *pala* mentioned here is to be understood as applying to both the jaggery (*guḍa*) and the ginger; otherwise, if there were an increase of only the fresh ginger, then at the measure of five *palas*, the total would reach ten *palas* when combined with the jaggery, and due to such a large quantity, it would cause defects such as the suppression of the digestive fire (*agni-vadha*). Starting from half a *pala*, by increasing half a *pala* every day, the amount reaches five *palas* in ten days. From that point, the consumption of the five *palas* continues for one month.

In the passage beginning with "rasas tathaiva" (47–48), everything— including the increase by half a *pala* as in the preceding formula and the addition of jaggery— is understood by the phrase "tathaiva" (in the same manner). 49.

Since it is specified in the passage beginning with "of the two sets of five roots" (*dvipañcamūlasya*) that a *kaṃsa* [measure] results from the decoction, one should take ten roots (*daśamūla*) weighing sixty-four *palas*.
Others, however, read: "In a decoction of one *tulā* of the two sets of five roots, there is a *kaṃsa* of *abhayā* and a hundred [palas] of jaggery.

As for the *vyoṣa* and the three aromatics (*trisaugandhya*), since no specific measure is mentioned, their quantity should be understood according to the proportions of the powder (*cūrṇa*) prescribed in other electuaries (*leha*).

In the *Agastyaharītakī*, four *pala*s of *pippalī* powder are prescribed for one *tulā* of jaggery (*guḍa*); likewise, in the *Cyavanaprāśa*, two *pala*s of *pippalī* powder are prescribed for half a *tulā* of sugar candy (*matsyaṇḍikā*). Similarly, here too, four *pala*s of the pungent substance (*vyoṣa*) are [prescribed] for one hundred *pala*s of jaggery. Furthermore, in the *Cyavana* formula, one *pala* of the four aromatics (*cāturjātaka*) intended for fragrance is prescribed; according to that precedent, two *pala*s of the three aromatics (*trisaugandhya*) are [prescribed] here.

Since the word *kiñcit* (some/a little) denotes a small quantity, it should be understood here as half a *māna* of *yavaśūka* compared to the previously mentioned powder of *nāgara* and the other ingredients; however, some say that the word *kiñcit* is a synonym for one *karṣa*. Based on the authority of another treatise (*tantrāntara*) and in agreement with *Jatūkarṇa*, the measure for each of the three aromatics (*trisaugandhya*) is one *karṣa*, whereas the measure for each of the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*) and the alkali (*yavakṣāra*) is one *pala*, as it is said: "In a *kaṃsa* of the decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*), [add] a hundred *pathyā* fruits and jaggery..."

Then one should cook the *tulā* [of the herbs]; to this, one should add four *palas* each of the three pungents (*vyoṣa*) and the alkalis (*kṣāra*), one *karṣa* each of the three aromatics (*trisugandha*), and half a *prastha* of honey when it has cooled, and so forth.
(Verses 50–52)

In the case of *paṭolamūla* and similar recipes, three *palas* of the decoction ingredients should be boiled according to the rule of eightfold water (*aṣṭaguṇajala*). Then, when one-fourth remains, the resulting decoction measures six *palas*.
For it is said: "From one *karṣa* up to one *pala*, one should provide sixteen parts of water;
from that point until one *kuḍava*, the water should be eightfold."

Regarding the passage beginning with "sacitraka" (53–54), some read "bilvāt palaṃ"; according to that view, the *bilva* fruit is measured by a *pala*, while the remainder is measured by a *karṣa* (55–57).
"Dadhyāgatam" means that which has been transformed into the state of curd;
"with buttermilk" (takreṇa) refers to the buttermilk produced from churning the aforementioned curd.
In passages such as *jīvanti*, the phrase "with [berries] the size of jujubes" refers to those weighing two *śāṇas*;
in the passage beginning with *tenaiva vidhinā*, it should be understood that the substances are to be measured by the size of a jujube;
and in the passage beginning with *sakūrma*, the prescription of the tortoise should be understood as an exception (*apavāda*) even to the prohibition of fish and meat.
The *śallaka* is known as *śalalī*;
*suvarcikā* is *sūryāvarta*;
*gṛñjanaka* is similar to *rasonaka* (garlic); or alternatively, *gṛñjanaka* is *śobhāñjana*.
Regarding *vāyasī* and *kākamācī* (60–63),

in the passage beginning with "śaileya," they state that oil is prepared with well-ground [drugs], meaning the oil is prepared with well-ground *śaileya* and the others; likewise, they prescribe an external application (*pradeha*) using those same drugs when well ground.
He should be bathed with warm water heated by the sun and anointed with fragrant substances such as aguru and others (verses 64–67).
With the verse beginning "savetasā," he describes an ointment for the Pitta-type [fever].

Regarding "milk-exuding trees such as the *aśvattha* and others" and "cooked with oil": the fat (*sneha*) should be prepared by boiling it with the decoction and paste of *mañjiṣṭhā* and the other [ingredients] mentioned;
in the phrase "with sandalwood and so forth," *abhaya* and *uśīra* are included.
68–69 Sand, gravel,
and the bark of the *śigru* tree.
"Anulepana" refers to an ointment applied immediately after bathing; "upon those pustules" (tatpiḍakāsu) means upon pustules accompanied by burning sensations and other symptoms.
With the verse beginning with "rāsnā," [the author] describes rubbing and affusions for all types of swellings.
Vyāghranakha, nakhī, and mūṣikaparṇī— known as ‘putraśreṇī’— are [the same]. 70–73.
Regarding the passage beginning with "The swellings (śothas)," etc.:

the locations (sthāna) are the throat and so forth; the affected tissues (dūṣyas) are blood and the rest; the shape (ākṛti) is the form, such as length and so on; and although the differences in names have been explained in detail in the section on foreign bodies (śalya) and elsewhere, they are mentioned here briefly by way of examples such as "kaṇṭhaśālūka" and others. Thus, it should be understood that because of the extreme multiplicity caused by these differences in location and other factors, they are to be known by a great number.

In this context, the definition provided for "sughora" (the terrible) refers to that caused by the three *doṣas*; its name should be known as "śiraḥśotha" (swelling of the head), while in another treatise (*tantrāntara*) it is called "upaśīrṣaka.
The phrase "accompanied by ghurghurikā" means being joined with a sound in the form of "ghurghura" or with a corresponding type of pain.
"In the junction of the throat" means in the junction of the throat and the mouth;
"in the breaths" means in the channels that carry the breath.
In the *biḍālikā* [type of swelling], the three doṣas persist as the underlying cause;
it is called "valayīkṛtā" because it encircles the entire neck and thus takes the shape of a ring (*valaya*).
As stated in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā*: "They call that [swelling] *valaya*, which is in every way of irresistible potency and must be avoided. (Su. 26.10)
Thus, [in] Nya.
A.
And this [disease], although born from the three doṣas, should be known as being predominant in blood and pitta (raktapitta).
Although the upajihvikā was mentioned here in the chapter on the thirty swellings, it was not described there and has been mentioned here in connection with the adhijihvikā.
"Curable" (sādhya) is mentioned [in the verse], meaning that those free from chronic rhinitis (pīnasa) and other such conditions are considered curable.
The distinctions such as the classification of curable and incurable conditions are to be understood for all [diseases], including swellings of the head and so forth;
"sire" refers to venesection (sirāvyadha),
while the specific treatment is to be sought in the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
With the passage beginning "a portion of a limb" (79–80), he describes the *granthi*s;

"one who maintains his own nature" means one who, through wind (*vāta*), maintains the characteristics of wind, through bile (*pitta*), maintains the characteristics of bile, and through phlegm (*kapha*), maintains the characteristics of phlegm.
By the designation "knot" (granthi), he shows its knotted shape;
"throbbing" means vibrating;
it arises from fat and becomes painless.
"A large tumor arising from flesh occurs when [the area] has been purified"; this means that once the person has undergone purification (*kṛta-śodhana*),
one should cause it to dissolve (*vilayet*), that is, cause it to wither away (*vimlāpayet*).
"Along with its sheath" means having extracted it together with its sheath and then incinerated it, one should treat it like a wound.
Regarding the defects that arise when the glandular growth (granthi) is incompletely burnt or remains [unburnt], he says "adagdhe" and so forth;
"with their own medicines" refers to the medicines for erysipelas (visarpa).
With the words "one should avoid," etc., he describes the types of knots that are incurable (vv.
He states "of the knots and tumors," etc., for the purpose of extending the treatment prescribed for tumors (arbuda) to these as well.
In this context, "non-specific" (aviśeṣa) should be understood as being without distinction;

for in the Suśruta-saṃhitā, the characteristics of an arbuda (tumor) are also stated: "In some region of the body, the doṣas, having become concentrated and severely corrupting the flesh, produce a growth that is round, firm, with mild pain, large, deeply rooted, slow to increase, and non-suppurating."
Those learned in the scriptures declare that when they produce an excessively deep elevation of flesh, it is called arbuda. (Suśruta Saṃhitā, Nidāna-sthāna)

11) Thus; therefore, even though there is a slight difference [between the two], because there is no difference in the discharge and so forth, the specific treatment for a *granthi* (knot/tumor) is extended by analogy to the *arbuda* (cyst).
Regarding "in the space between the skin and the nail" (*carmanakhāntare*), it refers to the junction of the skin and the nail.
Here, *vidārikā* is said to arise from *kapha* and *vāta*. In the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*, *vidārikā* is described as "arising from all [doṣas] and possessing all characteristics" (*Su.Ni.A.* 13).
Therefore, it should be understood here as well that it is characterized by a predominance of *kapha* and *vāta* with a deficiency of *pitta*.
By the word "of these" (*teṣām*), he refers back to the diseases of *alajī*, *kṣata*, and *vidārikā*.
"Bloodletting" (visrāvaṇa) means the draining of blood;
"with a bolus" (piṇḍikayā) refers to fomentation with a medicinal bolus (piṇḍikāsveda).

The "sphoṭas" mentioned here as "kakṣoktasphoṭas" are long-lasting; they are indeed sphoṭas that pervade only the location occupied by the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), being designated by the term *kakṣā*. Thus, they are called "kakṣās."
"Scattered" (prakīrṇā) means of various types;
"in those" refers to those beginning with visarpa—namely, visphoṭaka, kakṣā, and masūrikā—as well as vidārikā mentioned immediately prior. (90–93)
In the passage beginning with "bradhna," the term "vṛṣaṇe" is used in the singular to denote the class; thus, both testicles are included.
Regarding the phrase "by their own signs," this means by the signs of wind (vāta) and so forth:

by the sign of wind, a *bradhna* caused by wind (*vātika*) is to be known; by the sign of bile (*pitta*), one caused by bile (*paittika*); and by the sign of phlegm (*kapha*), one born of phlegm (*kaphaja*). This is the meaning.

The intestine repeatedly protrudes from its place and enters the scrotum; this is the characteristic of *antravṛddhi* (intestinal hernia). That which is caused by urine is swollen and soft, while that produced by fat is oily and hard.

Thus, the sixfold *bradhna* has been described; however, in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*, a blood-born (*raktaja*) *bradhna* is also mentioned, which should be included here within the category of that born from *pitta*.
With the words "by purgation" (*virecana*) and so forth, he states the general therapeutic principle.

The specific treatment for those [types of scrotal swellings] born of *kapha* is now stated: one should incise, cleanse, and suture a suppurated *bradhna* (scrotal swelling), and treat it like a wound; this is the intended meaning.
(94–95) By the verse beginning with "worms and bone" (*krimyasthi*), he here briefly describes the five types of *bhagaṃdara* (fistula-in-ano) in general terms.
"Searching with a probe" refers to examining the path [of the foreign body];

"with a well-cooked alkaline thread for what has been severed" indicates the procedure for the alkaline thread (*kṣārasūtra*) as taught in the *Śalyatantra*. However, a detailed exposition has not been provided here because it belongs to another section [of the treatise]. "Well-cooked" means with an alkaline solution that has been properly processed.

The plural number in "in the shanks" (*jaṅghāsu*) is used with respect to individual instances. Alternatively, one should understand that the plural is employed because the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) has been elided after "shanks," as it is said:
"Some say it is also in the penis, lips, and nose," and so on.
For instance, Puṣkalāvata states: "It resides in the neck, the groin, the shanks, the lips, the feet, the ears, and the hands."
"One should know that elephantiasis (ślīpada) arises from the flesh and fat";
here "piṇḍī" refers to a mass of flesh, and "prapada" refers to the forepart of the foot.
In the passage beginning with "mandāḥ," the term *mandāḥ* refers to those who are slightly aged (*alpavṛddhāḥ*). The plural number (*bahuvacanam*) is used with respect to individual instances.
Those for whom *pitta* is predominant are called *pittaprabalāḥ*.

*Tanū-rakta-pākam* refers to that in which there is slight suppuration of the blood; for in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*, the term *apāka* is used to denote slight suppuration, as it says: "The swelling caused by pitta that is known as *jālagardabha* is to be understood as *apāka*" (*Su.Ni.A.*).
13) Thus,
"red-cooking" (raktapāka) refers to that which is appropriate for the ripening of blood, and not merely the color red.
To include the types of swelling not mentioned here, he says: "of such kinds," and so forth (verse 101).
He states the treatment for exogenous swelling: "mostly," and so forth.
The connection is "in swelling caused by poison" (102).
In the summary, the connection is "of the threefold [swelling] due to the distinction between the whole body, half the body, and individual limbs."
"Of two kinds" refers to the distinction between innate (*nija*) and exogenous (*āgantu*).

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Swelling" (*śothacikitsita*), in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by the venerable Cakrapāṇidatta.
12 [Chapter 13 of Cikitsāsthāna (79 of 120):
Since abdominal enlargement (*udara*) is a type of swelling (*śotha*), the treatment for abdominal enlargement is stated immediately after the treatment for swellings.
"Of those who know Āyurveda" means of those who know the science of medicine; "by sufferings" means by the causes of suffering.
Regarding the phrase "of them" (*teṣām*), it refers to abdominal enlargements (*udarāṇām*);
"site" (*āyatanam*) means the cause;

and as for their "number," although it was stated in the section on diseases that "there are eight types of abdominal enlargements" (*aṣṭāvudarāṇi*, Sūtra 19), nevertheless, because an excess of numbers is observed in the cases of *gulma* and *kuṣṭha*, the number is asked about here once again; or else, since it is relevant to the present context, the number is stated even though it has already been mentioned.

Here, "defect of the digestive fire" (*agnidoṣa*) refers specifically to weak digestion (*agnimāndya*); it is this very condition that is stated to be the cause of the three *doṣas* in the etiology of abdominal enlargement (*udara*), as in: "In the rainy season, when the strength of the digestive fire has diminished, the *vāta* and other [doshas] become aggravated" (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 6).
The "impurities" (*malāḥ*) refer to both *vāta* and the others, as well as feces and the rest.
By the word "malinais" (by impure things), it is meant by those factors that cause disorders, such as incompatible diet (*viruddhāhāra*) and so forth.

Although it has been stated that both sluggish digestion (*mandāgnitva*) and impure food (*malinānna*) individually produce the three *doṣas*, nevertheless, here a preeminence (*prakarṣa*) is observed due to their being the generators of both. For this very reason, for the sake of indicating this preeminence, he used the prefix "sam-" [in the term] "sañcaya.

Furthermore, by mentioning the further aggravation of the digestive fire (*agni-dūṣaṇa*) in the passage beginning with "prāṇa," he demonstrates that the already sluggish fire becomes even more excessively weakened by the *doṣas*.

The vitiation of the prāṇa and apāna breaths by the vāyu produced through the accumulation of the doṣas is indeed not contradictory; for even by vāyu, the vitiation of vāyu occurs within the space between the skin and the flesh— that is, in the middle of the skin and the flesh (9–11).

With the words "excessively hot," etc., he states the cause: "due to the confusion of karma" means due to the improper performance of emetics and other treatments, and "due to the lack of remedy for afflictions" means due to the failure to treat afflictions such as diseases of the spleen (*plīha*).

Arising from dryness (*raukṣya*) because it persists due to the absence of its remedy; "from undigested matter" (*āmāt*) means due to the persistence of *āma*; and by the phrase "for those performing sinful actions," he states that this [disease], which consists of great suffering, is produced by powerful unwholesome factors (*adharma*).
The phrase "especially for those with weak digestion" refers to those whose digestive fire is extremely impaired;
the description of the premonitory symptoms begins with "loss of appetite," and so forth.

Although for those who eat sweet foods, digestion occurs only after a long time compared to pungent foods and the like, nevertheless, by the word "after a long time" (*cirāt*) here, it is meant "exceedingly long"; furthermore, it should be understood that the phrase "if one does not know whether [the food] is digested or undigested" indicates its origin from *vāta*.
Regarding the reading "caused by dryness and upward movement" (*rūkṣodāvarta-hetukā*), there is also a variant reading: "caused by obstructed upward movement" (*baddhodāvarta-hetukā*).
Regarding the phrase "at the joint of the bladder" (*basti-saṃdhau*): where there is a connection between the body and another region together with the bladder, there a line (*rājī*)—
meaning a distinct vessel (*sirā*)— is stretched out, that is, extended.

With the words beginning with "ruddhvā" (having obstructed), [the author] describes the general pathogenesis (*samprāpti*) of the four types of abdominal enlargements (*udara*) caused by the *doṣas*. Some say: "The pathogenesis previously described applies to all types of *udara*. Others maintain: "There is no redundancy, because the obstruction of the sweat-carrying and water-carrying channels—whose nature was not mentioned in the previous pathogenesis—is specified here by the words 'having obstructed,' etc.

This distinction should be understood from the statement: "The root of the sweat-carrying channels is the fat (*medas*) and the hair follicles (*romakūpa*), while the root of the water-carrying channels is the palate (*tālu*) and the *kloma*" (Viśeṣasthāna, Chapter 5).
He states the general characteristics of those with abdominal enlargement (*udara*): "of the belly," and so forth.

Although weak digestive fire (*mandāgni*) is indeed a cause, nevertheless, this "weak digestive fire" should be understood here in the context of the diagnostic signs as "smoothness of the cheeks," meaning the smoothness of the temples.

Regarding the phrase "their *liṅga*," it should be understood that here the word *liṅga* includes both the etiology (*hetu*) and the pathogenesis (*samprāpti*) to be described later, as they too serve to indicate the disease. However, in this context, either the pathogenesis or the causes must be stated specifically; therefore, there is no tautology with the etiology and pathogenesis mentioned as general factors for all diseases [in the previous section].
By "emaciating factors" (*karśanaiḥ*) is meant causes of thinness such as fasting (*laṅghana*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "having expelled the phlegm from the path of the rectum" (*gudamārgāt kapham uddhūya*), this indicates that phlegm is not the primary factor here; thus, he shows that designating the abdominal enlargement (*udara*) by the name of "phlegm" (*kapha*) in this context is incorrect.

The increase and decrease are also irregular; "of the abdomen" is the ellipsis. It is covered and pervaded by dark lines and veins, sounding like an inflated leather bag—that is, like the sound of a skin filled with air.
23–25. With the words beginning with "bitter" (kaṭu), he describes pitta-type abdominal enlargement (pittodara).
Here too, wind (anila) and phlegm (kapha) are secondary, while bile (pitta) is the primary factor.
By the statement "it destroys the fire in the seat of the self," it means that after destroying the digestive fires of the bodily constituents (dhātus) located in other sites,
[the substance] becomes yellow— meaning it takes on the hue of turmeric—
and "is pained" means it suffers distress.
"It fumes" means it emits smoke as it were;
"it heats up" means it is burned by the fire situated right beside it; "it perspires" means it becomes moistened with heat.
"It becomes quickly suppurated" means that due to rapid suppuration, it leads to *jalodara* (ascites).
With the verse beginning "lack of exercise," etc., [the author] describes *kaphodara* (ascites caused by phlegm).
"Bahirantraga" means that which is located outside the intestines (29–31).
By the verse beginning with "durbalāgneḥ," he describes sannipātodara.

Regarding the phrase "given by women," it means that women generally give menstrual blood and the like out of ignorance for the sake of securing good fortune (*saubhāgya*). The mention of "women" is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇārtha*); therefore, the inclusion of menstrual blood and other substances given by others is certainly intended as well. Regarding the phrase "and poison by the dull-witted," this refers to *dūṣīviṣa* poisons, for *dūṣīviṣa* poisons themselves are indeed "dull" (*manda*). By the word "three" (*traya*), he indicates the independent inclusion of all three [humors], beginning with wind (*vāta*).
"And the colors of all [these] are the defects"—this is the connection.

Here, although the colors of the nails and so forth, as well as all various colors and streaks, are already included by the very mention of the "conjunction of all characteristics," they are nevertheless mentioned specifically for the purpose of showing that their appearance is inevitable.

Enlargement of the spleen (*plīhavṛddhi*) is of two kinds: it occurs either through the enlargement of [the spleen] that has been displaced due to agitation, or through the enlargement of [the spleen] that has not been displaced by means of the increase of blood. It is located on the left side; this is the description of the nature of the spleen. Regarding the phrase "blood [arises] from the *rasa* and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) denotes a category. By this, it is meant that through the increase of the cause, which is *rasa*, there is an increase of the effect, which is blood; likewise, the increase of blood also occurs from *māṃsa* and the others. Thus, the increase of blood is said to result from diet and lifestyle (*āhāra-vihāra*).

The first type of enlargement mentioned for one who has passed away should be understood as fourfold, according to the combination of *vāta* and the other [doshas]. By this, the five types of splenic disorders (*plīhadoṣa*) that were mentioned—including those arising from blood—are accounted for; for it is said: "The five types of splenic disorders are explained by the same [principles] as the abdominal tumors (*gulma*). (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 19). An *aṣṭhīlā* is a long, iron-like knot well known among blacksmiths.
The "flank" (kukṣi) refers to the lateral region;
the phrase "situated on the right side" is the specification of its location.

Having separately named the abdominal enlargement caused by the liver (yakṛd-udara), he includes it within the category of splenic enlargement (plīhodara) by means of the verse beginning with "tulya" and so forth.
With the words beginning "pakṣmabālaiḥ" (by the eyelashes), he describes *baddhagudodara* (intestinal obstruction with abdominal enlargement).
Regarding the term *baddhāyane*, it means in the obstructed passage (*baddhamārge*).

In the passage beginning with "by upward-moving [vātas]" (*udāvartaiḥ*) and so forth, the phrase "in the anus where the passage is obstructed" (*baddhāyane gude*) should also be understood as carrying over.

Due to the entanglement of the intestines or the twisting of the intestines—as indicated by the mention of "eyelashes and hair" (*pakṣmavālaiḥ*) and so forth—an obstruction of the anus is produced by multiple causes. Because it produces the single condition of "obstruction of the anus," it generates *baddhagudodara* (abdomen with obstructed anus) as a uniform entity. Therefore, one should not infer that there are five types of *baddhagudodara* simply because they are produced by five causes, such as the obstruction of the anus by eyelashes and the rest.
With the verse beginning "śarkara" (gravel), etc., he describes *kṣatodara* (perforated abdomen); the construction is that the entrails, struck by gravel and so forth, would burst.
The phrase "it undergoes digestion" means that it undergoes internal digestion and then moves outward;
thus, that very rasa (nutritive fluid), filling the intestines and the rectum, causes the abdomen to swell as it flows through the digestive tract of the intestines.

Because the liquid that initiates the abdominal swelling generally moves downward from below the navel, it results in *dakodara* (ascites); the meaning is that, compared to other types of abdominal enlargement, its progression is rapid.
Alternatively, there is the reading “of ascites and of the humors” (*udakodarasya doṣāṇāṃ ca*).
In that case, the construction is as follows: it shows the symptoms of ascites, and it shows the symptoms of the humors according to their respective strength;
"according to their strength" means that it shows the symptoms of whichever humor is the most powerful.
Verses 42–44 describe *jalodara* (ascites) characterized by its origin;
"kloma" refers to a specific part of the heart.
"It should increase" refers to what was stated regarding *kapha* and *vāta*;
it should be understood that these two increase water through the production of thirst, which leads to the consumption of water and so forth.
He states the distinction between the curable and incurable cases with the words "In that regard," etc.

"Attaining a state without water" means being in a condition where the defect in the form of water has not yet arisen; here, it should be understood that the liquidity of the humors (*doṣas*) occurs through maturation by their very nature. "Having its movement obstructed in the external channels" means being unable to go outside.
In this context, a slimy substance (*piccha*) arises as the precursor to the birth of water; therefore, he first describes the very characteristic of the arising of that slime.
The portion resembling *picchā* is *picchā*; others, however, say that *picchā* is like the scum of boiled rice (*bhaktamaṇḍa*).
It "creeps" (*sarpati*), meaning it moves, like a water-filled leather bag; it is the agitation of the flesh that has reached the state of being like the liquid *picchā*.
Tamaka is a specific type of dyspnea;
one should know it to be incurable by means of any treatment other than severe measures such as the administration of poison or the application of surgical instruments (45–49).
"Successively more difficult" means that as the designation of "further" (para) is applied, so too is the difficulty of treatment.
Regarding the specific distinctions among *baddhaguda*, *chidrodara*, and *dakodara*, he says "after a fortnight," etc.:

*baddhaguda* abdominal enlargement generally leads to destruction after a fortnight; however, by using the word "generally" (*prāyaḥ*), he indicates that occasionally it may not lead to death even after a fortnight.

The presence of fluid (jātodaka) and perforated intestines (chidrāntra) generally lead to destruction; however, by the use of the word "generally" (prāyaḥ), he indicates that perforated intestines with fluid and obstructed anus (baddhaguda) may occasionally be cured through the administration of poison, surgical instruments, or desired medical treatments.
With the verse beginning "swollen eyes" (śūnākṣam), he describes the incurability even of those cases previously stated to be curable.
"Kuṭilopastha" means having a curved vulva; "upaklinna" refers to one whose skin is moist and thin.

Although a decline of the digestive fire (agnikṣaya) occurs first in the abdomen, it should nevertheless be understood that among the symptoms of incurability, a decline of the digestive fire specifically manifests along with other distinct signs.
"By birth alone" means by the mere fact of arising.
(52–54) He describes the characteristics of non-arisen swelling (*ajāta-śotha*) and so forth: "without arisen swelling," etc.
"Not too heavy" means not burdened with an excessively heavy load; "having pressed upon the navel" means having caused the navel to stiffen;
"having produced the urge" means having produced the urge of feces and wind—that is to say, having discharged wind and feces.
"Perishes" means it becomes dissolved;
"harsh" means possessing force; "emits" means the wind moves forth.
With the passage beginning "vātodara" (wind-belly) and so forth, he describes the treatment;
"parimlāna" means emaciated,
and "tathā" (likewise) refers to by means of wrapping with a cloth.
Furthermore, he explains the appropriate treatment for purification in the stomach with the words beginning "doṣa" and so forth.

The phrase "due to the obstruction of the channels and pathways" (srotomārganirodhanāt) means "due to the obstruction of the openings of the channels" (srotomukhanirodhanāt). Here, the word "pathway" (mārga) signifies the "opening" (mukha);
and in the context of the phrase "having combined" (saṃsṛjya), it refers to having prepared [the patient] through the sequence of thin gruel and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "prior to excitation":
when excitation is observed, milk should generally be withdrawn after it has performed its function of generating strength;
alternatively, castor oil or sesame oil boiled with Vātaghna and other such drugs should be used as an unctuous enema (anuvāsana).
"By means of anuvasas" means by means of *anuvāsana* (oil enemas).
*Sātalā* is *carmakaṣā*.
A "milk enema" (kṣīrabasti) is an enema in which milk is the primary ingredient;
"when phlegm is present" means when pitta is associated with kapha; and regarding "with urine," the word "with milk" (payasā) is understood to carry over from the previous context.
When pitta is associated with vāta, purgation should be administered using bitter ghee (tikta-sarpiḥ) combined with substances such as trivṛt;
the construction of the sentence is that one should conquer pitta-udara by means of this sequential application beginning with the administration of milk.
Regarding the term "purified" (*viśuddha*) here, it should be understood as purified without the use of emetics (*vamana*), because emetics are contraindicated for the abdomen.

"Iron preparations combined with powders" (*cūrṇāyaskṛti*) refers to those described in such passages as: "Nine parts of fresh iron dust, that powder [mixed] with honey and ghee" (Ci. A. 16). Alternatively, the "powders" (*cūrṇa*) may refer to those to be mentioned right here, while the "iron preparations" (*ayaskṛti*) should be understood as the applications of metals described in the section on rejuvenation (*rasāyana*).

"All as described" means that all those [therapies] prescribed individually for wind (*vāta*) and the other [humors] must be applied in every case of *sannipāta*-type abdominal disease (*udare*). "But when it has arisen with complications" means that it has manifested together with its attendant complications.
He describes the treatment for *plīhodara* (enlargement of the spleen) with the verse beginning "udāvarta...

and so forth. Regarding "the doshas such as vāta and the rest in their respective order": one should observe vāta by symptoms such as upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), pain, and abdominal distension; pitta by burning sensations, delusion, thirst, and fever; and kapha by the remaining [symptoms]. Furthermore, having observed the vitiated blood through its specific characteristics, one should administer treatment. The characteristics of blood are those stated in the *Vidhiśoṇitīya* chapter; however, according to other treatises (*tantrāntara*), they should be understood as "burning sensation, thirst, bad taste in the mouth, heaviness of the limbs, and fainting," and so on.
Regarding "plīhī" (splenic disorders), in cases of *plīhodara* (enlarged spleen),

the phrase "according to the dominant *doṣa*" refers to the pacification of the aggravated *doṣa*. Although venesection in the left arm is mentioned as a general rule, based on the authority of Suśruta, it should be understood that venesection is to be performed on the vein known as the *kūrpara*.
"One should employ *pippalīs* (long peppers)" means one should employ the *pippalī-vardhamāna* (the increasing dose of long pepper) described in the section on *rasāyana*.

"The groups of alkalis (*kṣāra*) and fermented liquors (*ariṣṭa*)" refers to the collections of alkalis and fermented liquors that will be described later in the chapters on *grahaṇī* and hemorrhoids (*arśas*). Furthermore, he will describe the alkali here with the verse beginning with "viḍaṅga," and likewise the fermented liquor with the verse beginning with "rohitaka-latā.
"Twice the amount of *abhayā*" means two parts of *abhayā*.
One should press the *rohitaka* creeper— known as *rohitaka*,
consisting of small-sized pieces called *kāṇḍakas*— and,
having submerged them in a liquid, one should set it aside for the purpose of fermentation.

In the case of *rohitaka* and so forth, one should add eight times the amount of water to fifty-seven *palas* of the ingredients to be boiled; when reduced to one-fourth, the decoction measures fourteen *śarāvas* plus two *palas*.

The phrase "equal to all of those" means that five *palas* of *rohitaka* bark are used. Regarding the term "with the ground [substances]," it refers to the five spices (*pañcakola*) being ground; likewise, by changing the case ending, it should be understood as "with the ground bark of *rohitaka*."
