Regarding "cauterization" (agnikarma), they state that it is to be performed here as in the case of abdominal tumors (gulma); this is to be understood as applicable only to splenic enlargement (plīhodara) where vāta and kapha are predominant.
The phrase "combined with digestive stimulants" (dīpanīya-samāyutaiḥ) means prepared with the pippalyādi group of digestive stimulants.

Since it is established by general rule that a *nirūha* (non-unctuous enema) contains oil and salt, the specific phrase "with oil and salt" is intended to indicate the administration of these two in greater quantity here.

Furthermore, although the *āsthāpana* (non-unctuous enema) is prohibited for those with obstructed channels (*baddhaguda*), perforated channels (*chidrada*), or abdominal dropsy (*dakodarin*), nevertheless, in cases where the condition can be cured solely by it, both *nirūha* and *anuvāsana* (unctuous enema) are to be understood as applicable here.

Regarding the statement, "The *parisraṃsī* [type] consists of downward-moving [disorders], and the *chidrāntra* [type] is the abdomen of men," although incurability (*asādhyatva*) has been declared therein, nevertheless, because the word "mostly" (*prāyas*) was included there, a deviation from incurability is also indicated. Therefore, its treatment is stated here; furthermore, the treatment for *chidrōdara* caused by ant bites and so forth will be mentioned later, and likewise, by the statement "this powder destroys all types of *udara*," the treatment for all *udara* must be explained. Others, however, say that the claim of destroying all types of *udara* is not absolute.
By the phrase "except for sweat" (*ṛte svedāt*), he shows the prohibition of sweat within a perforated abdomen (*chidrodara*) due to its watery nature;
by the verse beginning with "thirst" (*tṛṣṇā*), he describes the perforated abdomen that must be rejected [as incurable].

With the passage beginning "removers of the defects of water" (*apāṃ doṣaharāṇi*), he describes the treatment for *dakodara* (ascites) characterized by its specific origin; the phrase "from water and so forth" (*udakādibhyaḥ*) refers to various types of water and other liquid substances.
"One should restrain" means one should cause [them] to turn back;
"gradually" means one should cause them to turn back in sequence.
Here, in order to state the treatment common to all types of abdominal enlargement (*udara*), he says, beginning with "all," etc.;
"to be eaten" (*bhojyāni*) means they are to be consumed again and again.
In the passage beginning with "mandāmle," the word *manda* signifies "slight" (*alpa*).
Regarding the phrase "yānayānam," it refers to traveling by means of horses and other such vehicles. (95–100)
"Sweet" means freshly churned; "sweet" means it has become sweet; "pellucid" means its oil has been removed.
"Kavoṣṇa" means slightly warm.
"Having boiled" means having cooked it in water; in the phrase "one should pour," the word "belly" (*udara*) is understood to carry over from the preceding context (107–110).
Regarding the term "dīpanīyāni," some read it as "snehanīyāni.

In the passage beginning with *pippalī*, regarding the reading “one should cook two *prasthas* of ghee with half-*palas* of alkali,” the word *dvi-* (two) is to be construed both with *prastha* and with *ardhapalikaiḥ*. By this, the term “twice” (*dviḥ*) applies to the *pippalī* and other ingredients, resulting in six *palas* (since twice half a *pala* is one *pala*). Furthermore, by construing the word *dvi-* with *prastha*, there are two *prasthas* of clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
However, in the Kashmirian tradition, it is read as: “One should cook two *prasthas* of ghee with one *pala* each of *pippalī* and alkali.”

Jatūkarṇa also says: "Half a prastha of ghee, together with half a tulā of the decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla), along with the five pungent spices (pañcakola) including the alkalis, and one āḍhaka of curd-whey, destroys abdominal diseases.
In the passage beginning with "caturguṇe" (fourfold), by the term "sakṣāram" (with alkali), it is stated that one *pala* of barley alkali (*yavakṣāra*) should also be given, just as with *citraka*;
for it is said elsewhere: "With two *palas* of fire-alkali (*agnikṣāra*), four parts urine, and one *prastha* of ghee.
'The seat of the *doṣas* has become lax' means that the *doṣas* have become lax because their bonds have been released by the unctuous substance (sneha).

In the verse beginning with "paṭola," by the phrase "six and so forth, one karṣa each," it is meant that each of the six items—starting with *paṭola* root and ending with *triphalā*—is one *karṣa*. For *kampillaka* and the others, there is a doubling, tripling, and quadrupling respectively.
The term "muṣṭi" refers to one *pala*.

One should drink milk boiled with *savyoṣa* (the three pungents) for six days. On the day of purgation (*virecana*), one of the following—*maṇḍa*, *peyā*, or *vilepī*—should be prepared according to the state of the digestive fire (*agni*). Thereafter, one should subsist on the aforementioned regimen of milk. Then, again on the seventh day, the powder of *paṭola* and other herbs should be drunk. This procedure should be repeated again and again.
Śaṅkhinī, śvetabhallātakī (?), and the juices of kola and karkandhū are to be understood [as the substitutes];
in the context of "yavānī" and so forth, upakuñcikā refers to black cumin (kṛṣṇajīraka).
*Ajamodā* is *ugragandhā*, and *kāravī* is *alpajīraka*; however, by the word *jīraka*, *mahājīraka* is meant.
There are three parts of *dantī* relative to the portion already taken; likewise, there is a doubling relative to the initial portion for both *trivṛt* and *viśālā*.
He states the cause for the designation "Nārāyaṇa" with the words "not this," and so forth;
by this it is meant that it is called "Nārāyaṇa" because it possesses the same characteristics as Nārāyaṇa. (124–132)
In the case of *hapuṣā* and so forth, "black salt" (*kālalavaṇa*) refers specifically to *biḍalavaṇa*; others, however, say it is a salt having the appearance of *sauvarcala*.
[The word] "is to be drunk" (*peyaḥ*) is connected with all [the ingredients], beginning with pomegranate.
The medicated ghees (ghṛta) described beginning with "one droṇa of milk" and so forth perform identical functions.
And in that context, regarding the first [recipe] where ghee is mentioned but no liquid is specified, the cooking is done with water, or else with the ghee extracted from the curd under discussion;

then, by the passage beginning with "in the same way" and ending with "with six palas," the second ghee is described; and by "in the same way," it refers specifically to the ghee produced by the previous method.
In the same way, they describe the meaning of the word *ghṛta* (clarified butter) in the subsequent verses (138–140).

Regarding the three types of food beginning with *peyā* (thin gruel), their role as post-prandial drinks (*annānupāna*) is prescribed for cases of *kapha*, *pitta*, and *vāta*; alternatively, a distinction in the choice of post-prandial drink should be determined in consideration of the individual's natural constitution and digestive fire (*prakṛti-agni*).
Regarding the phrase "boiled by the citizens" (*nāgarakaiḥ śṛtam*), this refers to the preparation of water according to the six-fold method (*ṣaḍaṅga-vidhi*).

On the second day, thin gruel (*peyā*) is to be drunk; on the third day, as stated in the phrase "then the soup of horse gram" (*yūṣaṃ kaulatthikaṃ tataḥ*), horse-gram water is used. For it has been said: "On the first day, horse-gram soup; on the following day, thin gruel; on the third day, horse-gram water. The term "dry person" (*rūkṣa*) is connected with the instruction to drink repeatedly; thus, it indicates that this unctuous purgative (*snehavirecana*) should be administered to one who is dry, and that one who is already unctuous (*snigdha*) is not eligible for it. However, in the case of a person who is unctuous, this very [purgative] should be given after being prepared with boiled water and other ingredients such as *nāgara*, depending on the individual's strength.

"Or having been fed again" (*bhūyo vā pratibhojita*) means that after being fed in measured amounts for additional days, one should drink [the medicine] repeatedly; this is how it should be construed.

"Destroying abdominal tumors" (*gulmaghna*) refers to what was stated in the chapter on abdominal tumors (*gulma-adhyāya*) regarding its quality of removing *gulma*; the *Miśraka* formulation is exactly as described in the *Gulma* chapter (verses 141–145).
In the case of *citrakā* and so forth, the word division is *māsaṃ yuktaḥ*;
likewise, in the case of *hastipippalī* and so forth, it is connected with *pibet kṣīreṇa*.
The milk, eight *palas* in measure, should be prepared with four times as much water along with *viḍaṅga* and the other ingredients.
In the passage beginning with "one should drink the decoction," *vyoṣa* and *kṣāra* are to be added;
in the passage beginning with "or meat," the previously mentioned ghee prepared with the milk of *sudhā* is to be understood;
and the phrase "not eating food" is to be applied to all three formulations beginning with "cow's urine."
"Subsisting on milk" means one should consume *śilājatu* together with milk;

by the phrase "according to the procedure for *śilājatu*," it is specifically the procedure for *śilājatu* mentioned immediately above that is intended, not the procedure mentioned in the section on *rasāyana*, because the latter is separated [from this context].
By the word *śṛṅgavera* (ginger) or *ārdraka*, it prohibits the juice produced from a decoction of dried ginger.
The caesura is: "One should administer *dūṣyodara*, *sānnipātikodara*, *saralā*, *trivṛt*, and *ariṣṭas*."

In preparations such as *pippalī-kṣāra*, the quantity of liquids like curd and so forth should be understood as that which is sufficient to turn the powder into a paste; this measure is called a *biḍālapadaka* or one *karṣa*.

In the case of "alkali of goat dung" (*ajakarīṣa-kṣāra*) and similar formulas, the goat-dung alkali should be washed twenty-one times with six times its weight of urine until the liquid alkali is obtained; this liquid should be taken until it becomes eight times the volume of the total powder mass by virtue of its fluidity.
In the passage beginning with "pārśva," the term *upastambham* contains the prefix *upa*, which signifies proximity.

Regarding *bilvakṣāreṇa*, it means with the alkali prepared from the burning of *bilva* fruit; one should administer oil processed with white [alkali], and the connection is that one should administer oil processed with the alkalis derived from sesame stalks.

Regarding "in phlegm" (kaphe) and so forth, the meaning is: when phlegm is obstructed by wind (vāta), when phlegm is obstructed by bile (pitta), or when wind is obstructed by both those—phlegm and bile.
"Combined with its own medicinal [remedies]" means combined with the medicines that remove the obstructing defects.
Regarding the phrase "well-purged" and so forth, it should be understood that flatulence in one who has been purged is a fatal sign (*ariṣṭa*).

Therefore, in this context, when the wind (*vāta*) has not been fully conquered, subsequent flatulence is not a fatal sign; hence, the instruction for its treatment is appropriate here. Alternatively, in cases where flatulence occurs again due to being supported by an obstruction (*upastambha*), it is a fatal sign; taking this into account, the term "with support" (*sopastambha*) was used here, meaning "with an obstruction" (*sāvaraṇa*).

By the expression "one who has passed the ritual action" (kriyātivṛtta), he indicates that the water has already been produced; for in that case, the ritual action is prohibited by such [rules] as "one whose water has not yet been produced."

By the phrase "in the case of the three doṣas" (tridoṣe), it should be understood that this refers specifically to the condition where ascites has already arisen (*jātodaka*). Even though the treatment for the three doṣas when ascites has not yet arisen (*ajātodaka*) has already been stated, and although such a state of the three doṣas could have been included by the very term "excessive action" (*ativṛtta*), the inclusion of the word "in the case of the three doṣas" is intended to demonstrate the treatment for the three doṣas even when ascites is present.
Furthermore, by means of obtaining the consent of kinsmen and others, there is a prohibition against the infamy resulting from the opposite course of action.
"Permitted" means authorized; the connection is that a physician, in the administration of poison and so forth, should employ that fruit upon which he would release the poison.
And here, "poison" is to be understood as specifically fang-poison.
For it is said: "In cases of intestinal obstruction, anal stricture, perforated intestines, and even ascites, the application of the very poison from fangs is indeed used for purification.
Thus, "steady" means not fickle.
"Līna" means having entered another element;
"because of its agitating nature" means because it causes agitation,
as is well known in the case of *kālaśāka* (black potherb).
Then, that which is prepared with its own juice and water is likewise called "its own juice" (*svarasa*); this refers to the fresh juice of *kālaśāka*.

"Four finger-breadths below the navel": having measured four finger-breadths on the left side of the abdomen such that it is below the navel, and having left a space of four finger-breadths from the center of the belly, an incision should be made in the left side of the abdomen below the navel.

Having opened the abdomen for those with a bound wound or a perforated abdomen, one should examine the intestines for the purpose of performing the appropriate treatment; thereafter, an incision in the abdomen, the clearing away of hair and other debris, and the extraction of any obstructed intestine must be performed.

In the case of perforated intestines (*chidrāntra*), however, one should have ants bite the openings of the intestinal perforations in the region of those holes; once it is known that the intestinal openings have been seized by the ants, the heads of the ants should be cut off.
Then, for both cases where the perforated intestines have been closed, the procedure for reinserting the protruded intestines as described by the *pratiyogas* (counter-measures) should be performed.
With the words "tathā" (thus) and so forth, he describes the procedure for one whose [wound] has healed.
"One should pierce" means at a distance of four finger-breadths from the navel.

"Beyond this" means after drinking unsalted *peyā* (thin gruel), one should subsist on milk for six months. Then, after those six months of subsisting solely on milk, one should drink *peyā* along with milk for three months. After that, for another three months, one should be fed milk along with [grains] such as *śyāmāka* and *koradūṣa*, as mentioned in the text; in this way, what was stated regarding "one year" is fulfilled.
"Of those whose limbs have been diminished by practice" means those whose bodies have been worn away through yogic disciplines (prayoga).
With the words "the cause," and so forth, he states the summary.
The summary of the chapter as stated [in the verses] from 195–196 should be followed.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Abdominal Enlargement" (*udaracikitsita*), in the *Cikitsāsthāna* of the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā*, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta.

[Chapter 14 of Cikitsāsthāna (80 of 120)] Because of the commonality of being born from the three *doṣas* and because they cause *baddhaguda-udara* (intestinal obstruction with abdominal distension), the treatment of hemorrhoids (*arśas*) is stated immediately following that.
1–2. "Seated," and so forth;
"having made the occasion" means having created the opportunity.
The construction is: "He asked what was appropriate and fitting, beginning with the causes of provocation (prakopa)," and the sense is that "what is appropriate" means "prepared for exposition.

Alternatively, *prakopa* refers to the cause of the arising of disease; for it will be stated here that by the word *prakopa*, the arising of disease is meant—as in: "The cause for the provocation of hemorrhoids (*arśas*) should be known as an excess of *pitta*. *Saṃsthāna* means shape or configuration; although *saṃsthāna* is indeed included within *liṅga* (signs), it is mentioned separately here because there is much more to be said regarding its detailed elaboration.
Having explained the two types of hemorrhoids with the words beginning "here" (iha), he speaks of the congenital ones with the words beginning "cause" (hetu): therein, the seed (bīja) and so forth;
here, the seed refers to semen and blood.

And that [semen], being afflicted by the seed that initiates the rectal folds (*gudavalī*), becomes the cause of the congenital hemorrhoids. This very affliction of the seed that initiates the body by the corrupted seed that initiates the rectal folds consists in the association of the non-corrupted [seed] with the corrupted.

Consequently, due to the defect in the seed of the rectal folds, the birth of hemorrhoids occurs specifically in the rectal folds; because the seed initiating the remaining parts is non-defective, it does not produce a disorder.

It is not the case that a corrupted seed fails to produce anything at all, because the seed has not been entirely destroyed. And it has been said: "For whichever part of the embryo the seed-portion is afflicted within the seed, a deformity arises in that very part" (Śārīrasthāna 4), and so forth.

Others, however, based on the reading *āhitāgni* and the lack of a fixed rule regarding the prior placement of words, maintain that the term *gudavalībījopataptam* means "that in which the seed of the anal folds is afflicted.
*Apacāra* refers to improper diet and lifestyle, which corrupts specific portions of the semen and blood.
Regarding "karma performed in a previous life": this refers to the karma from a prior birth that brings about congenital hemorrhoids (*sahajā-arśas*) in one being born.

It should be understood that when such karma is weak, it becomes a defiler of the seed (*bīja-dūṣaka*) in conjunction with the misconduct of the parents; however, when it is strong, it produces [the disease] even without such misconduct.
By the words "in the same way" (*tathā*) and so forth, he extends these two aforementioned causes to other congenital diseases as well.
With the words beginning with "tatra," he explains the meaning of the term *sahaja* and states what is denoted by the word *arśas*: "the hemorrhoids (*arśāṃsi*), etc.
refers to specific types of fleshy growths (*adhimāṃsa-vikārāḥ*).
"Separated by three parts" means having an interval of one-third part, which consists of one and a half finger-breadths (sārdhāṅgula) out of four and a half finger-breadths (ardhapañcāṅgula).
"The anal circle" refers to the muscular ring of the anus.

In this division, within the anus which measures four and a half finger-breadths (ardhapañcāṅgula), the portion grasped by the anal lip (gudauṣṭha) and measuring half a finger-breadth is the field or site (kṣetra); that is to say, the region where hemorrhoids (arśas) grow.

By the word "some" (kecit), it is indicated that in other treatises (tantrāntara), even excessive fleshy growths (adhimāṃsa) located in the birth canal and elsewhere are designated by the term "hemorrhoids."
"Adhiṣṭhāna" (the substratum) is the object to be refuted;
therein, by the words "those which are innate," etc., he speaks regarding the sign of configuration.
"Jaṭilāni" means having the appearance of sprouts of grass;
"doṣānubandhavarṇāni" means having colors corresponding to the [three] humors (doṣas).
The state of being undetermined (*aniyatattva*) should be understood as referring to the triad of pairs of contradictory qualities, such as being bound or liberated;
"at intervals" (*antarā-antare*) means sometimes, not always,
[referring to] one whose eructation is predominantly endowed with qualities such as being bound.
"Characterized by the practice of suffering" means having suffering as its cause. "Dhyāna" here refers to reeling.
Why, then, does this person afflicted with congenital hemorrhoids become seized by such a disease? To this he says: "Birth," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "ascending" (pratyārohan), it means moving upward;

here, in this sequence, an aggravation of the five types of *vāta* occurs, and in every respect the *vāyu* becomes disordered (*viguṇa*). Consequently, disorders of *vāta* generally arise everywhere, and due to the aggravation of *pitta* and *śleṣman*, their respective disorders also occur—this is indeed logical.
"Arśasam" means a person afflicted with hemorrhoids;
in the phrase "guru-śīta" and so forth, "pramitam" means small.

*Kṛśa* is that which comes from weak animals; *paramānna* is milk-rice (*pāyasa*); *piṇyāka* is sesame paste; *kilāṭa* is a lump of inspissated milk; *takrapiṇḍa* is the thickened portion derived from buttermilk; *visa* is thick lotus-fiber; *mṛṇāla* is thin lotus-fiber; *tarūṭa* is the core of a plantain tree; and *krauñcādana* is known as *ghen-culikā*.
"Confused food" (*saṅkīrṇa*) refers to food of a mixed nature, such as meat, rice, and so forth;

"transgressed wine" (*atikrāntamadya*) means spoiled wine; "non-intercourse" (*avyavāya*) and "excessive intercourse" (*adhivyavāya*)—the latter being understood here as irregular or excessive sexual conduct—are to be understood as such.
Because it flows out extensively and because it flows in an excessively long stream;
*ṭiṇṭikera* is the fruit of the *karīra* tree, and *dakṣa* is a cock.
By the statement, "Because they are generally dominated by vāta, pitta, and kapha," [the author] demonstrates that hemorrhoids (arśas) exhibit various forms due to all the doṣas.
To the question, "When the signs and other features of those arising from vāta and the others are similar, what determines their specific distinction? he says: "This is their distinction."

The word "this" (ayam) refers to the specific characteristic (*viśe�sha*)—consisting of the distinctions of signs and causes to be described hereafter—which serves to differentiate [fever] from those born of Vata and the other doshas. Although it would be more logical to state the cause first when describing a specific characteristic, nevertheless, because of the connection with the description of the signs in the form of physical appearance (*samsthāna*), or due to the method of reverse-order exposition, the sign itself is stated first by the words beginning with "dry and withered" (*shushka-mlāna*). Thereafter, he will state the cause by the words beginning with "astringent" (*kasāya*). In this same manner, the presentation of cause and sign for fevers born of Pitta and Kapha should also be understood as occurring in reverse order. Here, "measured eating" (*pramita-aśana*) means eating very little.
Although the touch of sunlight is hot, it generates wind due to its dryness; for it has been said: "Sunlight is pungent and dry," and so forth (Sūtra 11–13).
By the words "soft" and so on, he describes that which is born of bile (pitta).
"Loose, soft, delicate, non-rugged,
and discharging blood and yellow [fluid]": here, by the word "blood" (rakta), the red color is meant.
By the phrase "flowing with blood," the discharge of blood itself is expressed.
The first instance of "foul-smelling" (*visragandhi*) is an adjective qualifying the blood; the second instance of "foul-smelling" is an adjective qualifying feces and urine.

The first mention of "yellow" (*pīta*) is for the purpose of indicating that excrement can be greenish-yellow; the second, however, is for the purpose of indicating a yellow color along with a foul odor; the third, such as in the case of "yellow nails" (*pītanakha*), is for the purpose of demonstrating a purely yellow color.

In the passage beginning with "pungent and hot" (*kaṭūṣṇa*), the first word "hot" (*uṣṇa*) is for the purpose of teaching the hot tactile sensation (*uṣṇa-sparśa*), while the second word "hot" is for the purpose of demonstrating the hot potency (*uṣṇa-vīrya*).
Alternatively, the reading may be "pungent, sour, salty, and alkaline" (*kaṭv-amla-lavaṇa-kṣāra*).
Therein, with the words "those which... and so forth, he describes the phlegm-born [piles]; "of considerable size" means of large dimensions; "extremely numb" means utterly devoid of sensation.
"Long-term latent tendencies" (*dīrghakālānuśayī*) means those that persist for a long time (verses 17–19).

In the passage beginning with "the characteristics of the causes" (*hetulakṣaṇa*), by the word "prominent" (*ulbaṇa*), he shows that although even the third humor (*doṣa*) is indeed a producer of the dual-humor combination (*dvandvaja*), it is not prominent therein.

"Every cause" means every aforementioned cause; every cause, together with its innate characteristics (*sahaja-lakṣaṇa*), becomes the cause of the three *doṣas*. Therefore, because it is the cause of all [three] *doṣas*, the innate characteristics arise in the state of the three *doṣas*—this is the meaning.
"Obstruction" (*viṣṭambha*) means a lack of movement.
Āṭopa is a rumbling sound in the abdomen (guḍaguḍāśabda).
Verses 21–22 state that although hemorrhoids (arśas) are produced by all three doṣas, they are designated as being caused by a single doṣa and so forth— beginning with the words "arśāṃsi" and so on.

Although the expression "by those who have come together" (*sannipatitaiḥ*) implies a confluence of three, nevertheless the word "by three" (*tribhiḥ*) is used here to demonstrate that all three are to be associated [with the disease].

Regarding the phrase "due to a specific disorder" (*doṣaviśeṣāt*), this refers to the predominance of a specific form of wind (*vāta*) and so forth; "specificity" (*viśeṣa*) refers to distinctions such as "this is born of wind" (*vātaja*) or "this is born of bile" (*pittaja*).
"Fivefold self" means having the form of prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna.
With the words beginning with "haste," he explains the distinction between the curable and the incurable:
"pain in the limbs" refers to pain in all the limbs;
"because of the remainder of life" means provided that there is a remainder of life remaining.
The word *samanvita* is formed with the suffix *kta* in the sense of a state (*bhāve*); thus, it means "when there is an endowment with the four quarters.
With the words beginning with *tatra*, he explains the medical treatment.
*Kartana* means cutting;
*bhūritantra* refers to one by whom many treatises (*tantra*) have been studied.
This is the meaning of the section: surgical procedures must be performed only by one who is trained according to the prescribed rules.
"Re-growth" means re-arising; "of those that have healed" refers to those whose ulcers have closed (vv.

Regarding the statement "predominant with vāta and śleṣman," although a discharge caused by kapha has been mentioned there, it is nevertheless a slimy (picchā) accompaniment and not a flow of blood; therefore, this refers to dry hemorrhoids (*śuṣkārbuda*). A slimy discharge, however, occurs even when there is a combination of the causes for both dry and moist [hemorrhoids].

"With oil of *citraka*, *kṣāra*, and *bilva*" means with oil prepared from *citraka* and the other aforementioned ingredients; "with *kārṣṇagandhika*" means prepared from *śobhāñjana*. "Pulāka" refers to husked grain.
With *kharāhvā* (black cumin), *ajamodā* (caraway),
and *kuṣṭha-taila* (oil prepared with *kuṣṭha*), [one treats] *jatukā*, which is the leather-winged bat (*carmacāṭikā*).
Vṛṣadaṃśa (musk), biḍāla (cat),
and akṣatā (unbroken barley)—
these four incenses end with ghee as the base; and the fifth incense consists of hastimada (musth) and sarjarasa (resin).
Kiṇva is the seed of surā;
madana refers to the grain of the madana fruit; dantī and nikumbhā [are medicinal plants].
Amṛtāsaṅga, mayūratuttha, haritāla,
the fat of the vāsantaka, and the fat of the camel.
In expressions such as *kaṭukālābuḥ*, *tiktakālābuḥ*, and *jalaukobhiḥ*, it should be construed that one should cause the blood— which was not present [previously]— to flow;
*bilvapeśikā* means the pulp of the *bilva* fruit.
"Steeped in cow's urine" means it has been kept overnight in cow's urine.
Regarding "combined with *bhallātaka*," the powder of *bhallātaka* should constitute one-tenth of the amount of roasted barley flour (*saktu*).

For it has been said: "The powder, combined with nine parts of *tarpaṇa*, should be administered. Others, however, state that there should be a small amount of both the *tarpaṇa* and the *bhallātaka* powders, in equal proportions.
Regarding *takrāriṣṭa* in the treatment of *grahaṇī*: "Three *pala*s each of *yavānī*, *āmalaka*, *pathyā*, and *marīca*..."

"One should grind five *pala*-measures of salts together and ferment them in buttermilk (*takra*); when it has fermented, a person should drink that *takrāriṣṭa*" (Ci.A. 15). According to this description of *takrāriṣṭa*, the determination of the quantity of the powder for the buttermilk here is also established accordingly.

Furthermore, it is stated that by adding the powder of *hapuṣā* and other ingredients in accordance with this, it becomes mildly sour and pungent (*mandāmlakaṭuka*). "One should let it stand until it is mildly sour and pungent" refers to the characteristic of its having been produced; "manifestly sour and pungent" (*vyaktāmlakaṭuka*) means it is sour and pungent in a manifest way. However, the pungency here is not yet fully manifest, because the pungency does not become manifest during the process of fermentation (*sandhāna*).
Regarding "at three times for food": this refers to the beginning, middle, and end of the meal;
in cases of *vāta*, one should take *takra* with fat, while in cases of *kapha*, it should be without fat.

The administration of *takra* (buttermilk): In the forenoon, only *takra* should be drunk; for one whose digestive fire (*agni*) is extremely weak, *takra* alone should be consumed even in the evening—this is what is meant by the statement, "one should prescribe *takra* alone for one with an extremely weak bodily fire. When the fire has increased slightly, *takra* alone should be drunk in the morning, but in the evening, a linctus (*avalehikā*) made of parched grain flour (*lāja-saktu*) mixed with *takra* should be given. Thereafter, as the fire gradually increases, *takra-peyā* (gruel prepared with *takra*), *takraudana* (rice cooked with *takra*), and meals consisting of soups and other items prepared with *takra* should be given in the evening, while in the morning, *takra* alone is taken. This duration of using *takra*, beginning from seven days, should be understood.

On this point, Jatūkarṇa states: "The application of buttermilk in the morning, with gradual increase and decrease; when digested, rice with buttermilk mixed with rock salt; or, for one with extremely weak digestion, buttermilk alone.
[The phrase] "at once" means all at once;
"at the end of a month" means within a month, not exceeding it.

"Reduction is like increase" means that by the same sequence in which the buttermilk was increased, by that very sequence of dosage the buttermilk is reduced. Thus, when there is a decrease in the administration of buttermilk, no reduction should be made from the total quantity of food; the meaning is that whatever portion of the buttermilk has been reduced must be compensated for by another food. He asks, "Why is this the sequence for the administration of buttermilk? and answers with the words beginning with "capacity" (*śakti*).

The three types of *takra* (buttermilk) described by the verse beginning with "rough" (*rūkṣa*) should be understood as being indicated respectively for the *doṣas* of *kapha*, *pitta*, and *vāta*; for digestive fires that are very weak, moderately weak, and weak; and for strengths that are low, medium, and high.
Some read "also on the ground," etc., and state that there are one hundred diseases: twenty disorders of *śleṣman* (phlegm) and eighty disorders of *vāta*, making one hundred diseases in total.
76–88: *Bilva* (Aegle marmelos), *bālabilva* (young *bilva*), and *phalāmla* (sour fruits) such as pomegranate (*dāḍima*) and others; these are sour by virtue of their fruits.
"Endowed with grāhibhiḥ" means processed with the ten *grāhin* substances;
rice such as *raktaśāli* and so forth are described as food and drink.

In recipes such as "yavānī, nāgara," and so forth, the yavānī and other ingredients are to be taken in equal parts and drunk with buttermilk (takra); the salt should be added until the salty taste is clearly perceived. 96–102.
In recipes such as *pippalī-nāgara* and others, some authorities maintain that the ghee should remain uncooked;
however, in the case of the instruction "combined with jaggery and alkali," it should be understood that the jaggery and other ingredients are to be added once the ghee has been cooked.
In recipes such as *pippalī-pippalīmūla* and others, curd is the liquid medium, while the remaining ingredients constitute the paste (*kalka*).

In the case of *jāte dadhni* ("in curd from freshly made [milk]") and *sujāte nāgaram* ("in well-made [curd] with ginger"), and likewise in the case of ghee prepared with the fresh juice of *cāṅgerī*, the word "and" (*ca*) implies that the curd must also be four times the quantity [of the other liquid].

In recipes such as *pippalīm* ("with long pepper") where a large quantity of the solid substance is present, since no specific measure for the decoction is mentioned, it should be equal in weight to the fat (sneha). Therefore, even when the decoction substance is twelve *palas*, one should add three *prasthas* of water and reduce it until forty *palas* remain.
With the verse beginning with *gaṇḍīram*, he states the ingredients for the medicinal paste (*kalka*);
from verse 103 to 118, he states the vegetables that promote downward movement (*ānulomika*). He begins with the verse starting with *upodikām*.
Suvarcalā, sūryāvartā, ruhāpatra, udagraśāka,
mahāpatra, and śyonāka.
Fermenting agents such as curd, pomegranate, and so forth (119–126).
"Śārkara" means an *ariṣṭa* (fermented medicinal liquor) made from sugar, which will be described [in verses] 127–129.

Regarding the *pippalyādi* oil, some, based on the observation of other treatises (*tantrāntara*), state that water should also be four times the quantity [of the oil]; however, this is not correct, for we see that what is stated in those other treatises refers to a different formulation altogether.
(130–134) "With the *ānuvāsanika* [drugs]" means with the *pippalyādi* group mentioned for the purpose of preparing the *anuvāsana* oil.

The qualification "ending with *dāru*" is for the purpose of excluding the decoctions mentioned in the chapter on the six hundred purgatives (*Ṣaḍvirecanaśatāśritīya*) that are intended for the administration of non-unctuous enemas (*anuvāsana*); by this, only those [decoctions] stated up to *dāru* are included. "Consisting of the ten roots" (*dāśamūlika*) means combined with the decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*).
"By means of fruits and so forth" refers to the fruits of the *madana* tree and others suitable for non-unctuous enemas (*āsthāpana*).
By the verse beginning with "of *harītakī*s," the five *ariṣṭas*, such as *abhayāriṣṭa* and others, are described.

Regarding "of triphalā," it refers to three *palas* of the combined triphalā itself, because the indication here is primarily concerned with the measure. In the case of "harītakī" and so forth, by using the word "phala" (fruit), he intends to include the seedless *harītakī*; thus, there is half a *prastha* of *harītakī*. However, in the *Jatūkarṇa*, this formulation is recorded with double the quantity, as follows: "One *prastha* of *harītakī* fruit, twice as much of *āmalaka*, *kapittha*, *pāṭhā*, and *indrā* along with *citraka*, and two hundred [palas] of jaggery. *Kramuka* is *pūga* (betel nut); *paṭṭikā* is *lodhra*.
Regarding *surāhvā* (the plant called *surā*) and *gorakṣakarkaṭikā*:

although here the measure of substances such as *āmalaka* is two *āḍhakas*, and by the general rule (*sāmānyaparibhāṣā*) alone the addition of two *droṇas* of water and its reduction to one *droṇa* would be obtained, nevertheless, the explicit mention of "water and decoction" should be understood for the sake of clarity.

By the statement "two *āḍhakas* of grape juice" (*mṛdvīkā-dvyāḍhaka-rasa*), it is shown that having added two *droṇas* of water to two *āḍhakas* of grapes, the water should be boiled down until it remains equal in volume to the original [grapes]. Others, however, have provided the interpretation that the fresh juice and the liquid [extract] of the *drākṣā* are equal in quantity.

For it is stated in the *Jatūkarṇa*: “One *tulā* of *dhātrī*, one *kauḍavika* each of *pippalī*, *marica*, and *kṛmighna*; half a *pala* each of *indrāhva*, the two types of *sārivā*, *dāruniśā*, *suradāru*, *ghana*, and *kuṣṭha*; one *pala* each of *mañjiṣṭhā*, *pāṭhā*, *tilvaka*, *granthika*, *elavāluka*, *cavya*, *kramuka*, and *bilva*—these are to be boiled with fire; and two separate decoctions of the two types of *drākṣā*; two *tulās* of sugar; and two *kuḍavas* of honey,” and so forth.
Furthermore, here too, the general technical rules (*paribhāṣā*) are identical to those stated by Caraka for the preparation of powders (*cūrṇa*).
The essence of flower-nectar is honey (madhu).
Now, demonstrating the symptoms of hemorrhoids associated with vāta and kapha, and presenting the distinct treatment, he says: "The treatment," and so forth.
In this treatise, it should be understood that hemorrhoidal growths (arśāṃsi) arising from blood are characterized by disordered secretions and are exudative, just like those arising from bile;
this is inferred from the indication "the stool is dark-brown" (*viṭ śyāvam*), which suggests that the word *viṭ* exists even as a neuter noun.
Furthermore, the term "stained" (*malinam*) indicates that it is excessively corrupted.

It indicates that one who knows the specific characteristics of the causes and so forth should practice indifference toward the discharge; the sense is that when wind (vāta) is the secondary factor, oleation should be administered, whereas when phlegm (kapha) is the secondary factor, indifference or treatments such as fasting (laṅghana) should be performed.
*Sanāgara* (with ginger) means slightly pungent (*īṣannāgara*). That which is astringent for unctuous blood is "the astringent for unctuous blood" (*snigdhara ktasaṅgrahaṇaḥ*).
By the phrase "in that manner" (*tadvat*), he demonstrates both the result of the preceding formulation and the method of preparation.

Regarding the passage beginning with "bark of *kuṭaja*," one hundred *pala*s constitute a *tulā*; this is to be boiled with one *droṇa* of water, and the decoction should be taken when reduced to one-eighth.
This is also stated in another treatise: "One hundred *pala*s of *kuṭaja* bark [are added] to one *droṇa* of water, [and the decoction is taken] when reduced to one-eighth."

The water of Mahendra (rainwater) and atmospheric water are to be taken as "dārvīpralepana" (that which sticks to a ladle); it should be administered at that stage when it becomes sticky enough to adhere to a ladle.

Because blood-bile (*rakta-pitta*) affecting both parts is incurable, by the term "both parts" (*ubhaya-bhāga*), only that which moves purely upward and that which moves purely downward are intended. Furthermore, since the downward-moving type is palliable, the phrase "it should destroy [the disease] by merely palliating it" (*tad-yāpanam eva iha nihanyāt*) refers to its management through palliative means.
*Kadamla* means slightly sour.
By the term "bark of the fruit of *kuṭaja*," both *indrayava* (seeds) and *kuṭaja* bark are meant.
Regarding the phrase "sadāḍimarasam," clarified butter (sarpiḥ) prepared with this is intended [in verses 193–198].
With the verse beginning "gṛñjanaka," another formulation is presented; *gṛñjanaka* is a species of onion (*palāṇḍu*).
In cases such as "karbudāraḥ kāñcanabhedaḥ bhojanam," the word *bhojana* should be construed with *adyāt* (one should eat), as in "bhojanam adyāt.
A *dvikakuṭ* is a camel.
*Antarādhi* refers to the interior of the body; and that [substance] should be from a young goat, being first sweet and sour, and subsequently slightly sour, like churned curd-cream (*dadhisara*).
*Dadhisaramathita* means churned curd-cream.

"Navanītaghṛta" refers to fresh butter and ghee; others, however, say it refers to goat's butter and goat's ghee, since the goat is said to possess the quality of arresting hemorrhage (199–211). "Yavāsa" is *durālabhā*.

"By means of *śiśira* oil" means by means of oil prepared with cooling substances; "cool water" and so forth refers to that which is cool and pleasant to the touch; by this, it wards off excessive coldness. 212–221.

Now, regarding the case where bleeding cannot be stopped, the author describes nourishing therapy (*bṛṃhaṇa*) for the purpose of satiating the depleted tissues (*dhātu*), beginning with the words "by these" and so forth.
*Avapīḍaka-sarpis* is clarified butter that is drunk after a meal; alternatively, a large quantity of clarified butter is called *avapīḍaka*.
"That" refers to the person from whom blood is flowing.
222–223 He describes the picchābasti (mucilaginous enema), beginning with "yavāsa" and so forth;
*yavāsa* is *durālabhā*.
And here, the dosage for the paste (kalka) and other components should be understood as being like that for an enema (basti).
224–229. *Yavāgraja-kṣāra* is alkali derived from barley (*yavakṣāra*).
In this case, four times the amount of *cāṅgerī* juice should be taken, as no other liquid is mentioned [in proximity];
*Avākpuṣpī* is *adhaḥpuṣpī*.

In this context, although sixteen *pala*s of the substance to be boiled are prescribed, and although by general rule only four *prastha*s of water should be given— so that the remaining one-fourth portion would indeed be one *prastha*— nevertheless, this statement from Caraka is intended to indicate the general procedure for setting aside the decoction as a quarter-remnant when adding fourfold the amount of water.
Likewise, the statement, “Thirty *pala*s plus two more are to be known as a *prastha*,” should be understood as expressing a meaning established by technical convention (*paribhāṣā*).
For this very reason, even though the preparation involves solid substances (*dṛḍhabala*), there will be a mention of the "deficiency of fluidity" (*dravadvaiguṇya*).

When it would have been appropriate to specify "two *pala*s more" as a qualification of the thirty *pala*s, the use of the masculine singular form should be understood as intended to refer to a *prastha*.

By way of inversion— that is, through mutual exchange— there is the combination of sweet and sour, and cold and hot. (243) Regarding hemorrhoids (*arśas*), in order to state the protection of the digestive fire (*agni-rakṣā*), [the author] states the following— beginning with "three"— to indicate those other conditions where the protection of the digestive fire must be performed specifically.

When the digestive fire (*agni*) increases, there is emaciation; when the strength of the digestive fire increases, there is destruction—especially in these three cases. By this, he shows that the protection of the digestive fire must be practiced even in other circumstances as well.
With the verse beginning "yadvāyoḥ" (247–248), he states the essence of the previously mentioned treatment;
with the verse beginning "arśasāṃ dvividham" (249), there is a summary of the chapter's subject matter.

Although the mention of *ariṣṭas* would already include *śārkaras*, the separate mention of *śārkaras* is for the purpose of distinguishing them from those made with jaggery (*guḍa*) for practical usage; likewise, they have been treated separately for the purpose of specifying their respective after-drinks (249–255).

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Hemorrhoids," in the *Carakatātparyaṭīkā*, known as the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Section on Therapeutics (*Cikitsāsthāna*).
14 [Cikitsāsthāna, Chapter 15 (81 of 120)]:

Since the disorder of the digestive tract (grahaṇī-doṣa) is caused by hemorrhoids (arśas), the author speaks of the treatment of the digestive tract immediately following the treatment of hemorrhoids.

The "defect of the *grahaṇī*" (*grahaṇī-doṣa*) is the defect of the digestive fire (*agni-doṣa*) residing in the *grahaṇī*. Thus, by the metaphorical treatment of the locus and the occupant as non-different, the term "defect of the *grahaṇī*" also includes the defect of the digestive fire residing in the *grahaṇī*.

In this context, while the defect of the digestive fire specified for the *grahaṇī* is to be discussed, since the knowledge of morbid transformation (*vikṛti-jñāna*) follows immediately after the knowledge of the natural state (*prakṛti-jñāna*), he first describes the form of the digestive fire in its non-transformed state: "Life-span," and so forth.
Life-span is the persistence of consciousness; complexion is fair and so forth;
strength is power, inferable from physical exertion and the like.

Although the inclusion of complexion (*varṇa*) and other qualities is already obtained by the very term "health" (*svāsthya*), nevertheless, it is stated: "That which promotes vigor (*ojas*) for one who is healthy is aphrodisiac (*vṛṣya*) and is a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*)" (Cikitsā-sthāna, Chapter 1, Verse 1). Therefore, because the absence of disorder in complexion and the other qualities is not necessarily present in every healthy person, complexion and the rest have been mentioned separately. Enthusiasm (*utsāha*) is the determination to undertake even difficult tasks; nourishment (*upacaya*) is the growth of the body;
and *ojas* is that which resides in the heart and consists of the essence of all the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).
Tejas (fiery energy) is either the bodily heat or the semen; as it is stated in Śālākya: "The vision is said to consist of tejas, and semen is purely tejas;
therefore, one who depends on the strength of vision should practice the increase of tejas.
"Agnayaḥ" (fires) refers to the twelve fires: the five elemental fires and the seven tissue-fires (dhātu-agnis).

"Prāṇas" refers to all five vital airs characterized by prāṇa and apāna; or else, the single prāṇa air itself is always expressed by the word "prāṇāḥ" with a plural ending. Just as the singular feminine vidyādharī is also designated by the word "apsarasaḥ," [so too here]. [The phrase] "caused by the bodily fire" means they have as their cause the primary digestive fire (jāṭharāgni) which nourishes the body; [the phrase] "when that has subsided" means when it has perished.
"In balanced" means when it is equal;
"in altered" means when it is dull or uneven or sharp.

"Fire is the root of that" means that, due to its excellence and because of the rules of positive and negative concomitance, fire is the root—that is, the primary cause—of lifespan, complexion, and so forth.
It is "defined" (nirucyate) in the sense that it is stated with certainty.
Having stated the general cause [of fire], he says "that food which... and so forth, in order to demonstrate that fire is the direct cause.
Since external substances such as red ochre are also referred to by the word *dhātu*, the term "body" (*deha*) is used as a qualifier for *dhātu* in order to exclude them.

Furthermore, regarding how fire (*agni*) acts as the cause for the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) and so forth produced during day and night, he says: "from food" (*āhārāt*). By this, it is shown that [fire] produces the *rasa* and other constituents only in dependence upon food;
by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), blood (*rakta*) and the other constituents are encompassed.

Now, he explains how the digestion of food that has been obtained occurs by means of fire, and how the food being digested attains the state of the bodily tissues (*dhātu*) and so forth; beginning from its entry through the mouth, the function of food is described here as follows: "Food," and so on.
That whose function is the taking up and the bringing forth of food is so described; it "carries" (nayati) means it leads with fluids such as water and the like;
"with its mass broken apart" means having reached a state of looseness in its constituent parts.
"At the proper time" means at the time of hunger.
"Eaten in equal measure" means balanced according to one's constitution (*prakṛti*) and other factors.

By the *samāna* wind, he is said to be "stirred by the equal one," meaning he is kindled by the *samāna* situated beside the fire. And this *samāna*, because it is natural (*prākṛta*), serves to kindle the fire like the external wind and does not cause imbalance; however, when it is deranged (*vikṛta*), it produces imbalance. Thus, it is logically established that "by that wind, the fire becomes unbalanced."

And by this passage it is stated that these factors—fluidity and the rest—act as auxiliaries to the digestive fire (*pācaka*): "These are the factors that effect the transformation of food; namely: heat, wind, moisture, unctuousness, time, and proper application" (Śārīra Sthāna 6).
The term *udarya* means the digestive fire.
Some read "pavanodvaha" as an epithet for the fire.

Some read "samyak" as a qualifier for what has been eaten; in that case, by the word "samyak," moderation in quantity is expressed, while by the inclusion of "samyak," the excellence of the ingredients and so forth is expressed. The phrase "for the increase of life" means for the maintenance of the conjunction of the body, senses, mind, and self, and for their further growth.
The dative case in *rasamalāya* is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*).
The phrase *āśayastham* means "situated in the stomach" (*āmāśayastham*).
By the expression *adhaḥsthitaḥ*, he indicates that because fire has the inherent nature of flaming upwards, it possesses the capacity to digest food situated above it.
Regarding this point, he provides an illustration with the words "yathā" (just as) and so forth.
Having thus described the process of gross digestion, he now describes the intermediate process of atomic digestion with the words "annasya" (of food) and so forth.
The phrase "immediately after eating" (*bhuktamātrasya*) means right after one has finished eating.
The term "possessing the six tastes" (*ṣaḍrasasya*) is stated by way of praise; alternatively, it shows that even for that which possesses the six tastes, sweetness is first manifested.
The term "from the initial cooking" (*prapākataḥ*) means from the very first stage of cooking; the prefix *pra-* denotes the beginning of an action.

"Madhurādyaḥ" means that which is both sweet (*madhura*) and primary (*ādya*); alternatively, there is the reading "madhurāt prāk kapho bhāvāt," meaning that which has become froth-like (*phenabhūta*), that is, resembling froth and not dense.
"Param" means after the initial sweet transformation (*ādyamadhurapākānantaram*).
"Of the 'vidagdha'" means of that which is partially digested; "acid states" refers to the nature of produced acidity arising from the *āśaya*, that is, the stomach (*āmāśaya*).

This shows that for one who is passing away, as the lower part is being carried away by the wind, there is a connection with the seat of *pitta* due to the food being burnt (*vidagdha*); "clear" means thin, and it is said to be "aroused," whereby *pitta* is produced; and since *pitta* is sour, it is entirely logical that it is produced from the sour nature of the food.

Regarding the phrase "of that which has reached the receptacle of digested food" (*pakvāśaya*): this refers to [the waste] having gone to the *pakvāśaya* in the form of impurity (*mala*) and being dried up by the fire.
Although fire is capable of burning upwards, nevertheless, its being dried up by fire as it moves downwards is also logical for that which has reached the *pakvāśaya*.

Furthermore, because the activity of the fire is not fully effective during downward movement, the term "being cooked" (*pacyamānasya*) was omitted and replaced with "being dried up" (*śoṣyamāṇasya*).
Regarding the phrase "of that which is fully consolidated and matured": when [the food] has become fully consolidated in form and matured in the form of waste, the wind becomes pungent;
thus, pungency arises from the wind in the state of full consolidation. In this way, such is the maturation of the states of food consisting of the six tastes.

Now, one might object: "If it is stated here that the six tastes themselves act as producers of *kapha* and the other *doṣas* by virtue of their *avasthā-pāka* (transitional ripening), then this contradicts the statement regarding *vipāka* (ultimate digestion) such as: 'The post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*) of pungent, bitter, and astringent tastes is generally pungent' (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 26); for the latter is sublated by the former *avasthā-pāka*. This is not so. This *avasthā-pāka* does not sublate the *niṣṭhā-pāka* (final digestion), which is the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of the taste; rather, it performs its own specific action during its particular state. Consequently, the tastes and the rest perform their own actions, and the *avasthā-pāka* also performs its own action. For example, when food containing the six tastes—sweet, bitter, and so on—is consumed, the sweet taste performs its own action, and the bitter and others likewise perform their respective actions. However, there is this distinction: when the *avasthā-pāka* known as "sweet" is accompanied by tastes such as sweet that generate *śleṣman* (phlegm), then it produces a large quantity of phlegm; but when that *avasthā-pāka* is governed by contrary qualities such as pungency, then it produces only a small amount of *kapha*. The same should be said regarding an *avasthā-pāka* that generates *pitta*.

Regarding the three-fold post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*) described in the passage beginning with "of pungent, bitter, and astringent" (Sūtra-sthāna 26), it occurs at a different time than the *avasthā-pāka* (the transformation occurring during the state of digestion), which is simultaneous with the separation of the rasa and the waste products (*mala*). Thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, although this [post-digestive] transformation occurs at a different time, it either accords with or does not accord with the humors (*doṣa*) resulting from the *avasthā-pāka*; consequently, it brings about the increase or the diminution of those humors produced by the *avasthā-pāka*. Therefore, its mention in the treatise is indeed purposeful.

Although all food is digested during its state of digestion (*vidāha*), nevertheless, those foods which cause excessive burning are specifically called "burning" (*vidāhin*), because they possess the specific quality of being burners.

Others, however, say: "From food consisting of the six tastes, phlegm (*kapha*) and the other humors are not produced generally during the digestion of the state; rather, even from food of six tastes, in the first stage of digestion, this manifested sweet taste (*madhura-rasa*) generates phlegm. Likewise, bile (*pitta*) arises from the manifested sour taste (*amla-rasa*) during the state of burning; similarly, wind (*vāyu*) also arises during the state of pungency (*kaṭu*) of the food."

Others, however, say: it is not that the sweet and other tastes arise in food through contact with fire; rather, the sweet and other tastes exist by their very nature within the seats of *kapha* and the rest in human beings. These [tastes], having brought the food into their own nature, generate *kapha* and the others. For it is said in another treatise: "The sweet taste, situated in the stomach above the heart, increases *śleṣman* (phlegm), which increases the strength of the body."
In the middle of the navel and the heart, a sour taste is naturally established in human beings; from that, bile increases. Below the navel, however, there is indeed one pungent taste established.
"Generally, among those [digestive fires], the wind (anila) increases most in living beings;

therefore, the transformation (vipāka) of tastes is threefold—of this there is no doubt. However, upon examining the meaning of the passage beginning with "tatra" (therein), it is logical that the meaning of the text is exactly as stated [previously].

In other tantras, however, they describe sweet and sour tastes as residing in phlegm (śleṣman) and bile (pitta); we too accept those tastes that have reached phlegm and the like as being indeed conducive to digestion. As for the statement that it is only the portion of the food that generates phlegm which, through the process of transformation (avasthā-pāka), acts as the producer of phlegm—that is certainly accepted by us. Thus, we maintain that the portion of the food which generates phlegm, by virtue of its location, brings about the sweetness of that food and thereby specifically produces phlegm.

As for the claim that by this "intermediate digestion" (*avasthāpāka*) there is merely the stimulation of *kapha* and *pitta*, but not their increase—since increase occurs only at "final digestion" (*niṣṭhāpāka*)—that appears devoid of logical justification. Furthermore, we consider it more reasonable that from intermediate digestion there is an increase of *kapha* and *pitta*, whereas from final digestion they are produced in the form of waste matter (*mala*).
(9–11) Food is also digested by another process; he describes that as follows: "Food," etc.

"Food that is desired and provided"—here the word *hi* is used for emphasis. By the word "desired" (*iṣṭa*), both what is pleasant and what is beneficial are meant, not merely what is pleasant alone; for food that is merely pleasant but harmful does not maintain the stability of the body, nor does it provide satisfaction through smell and so forth. "Provided" (*upahita*) means "made available";
"by desired things" means by those things that are pleasant and beneficial, namely smell, taste, form, touch, and sound.

In this context, although it is precisely the quality of being beneficial (*hitatva*) that is primary for odors and so forth contained in food in nourishing the odors and so forth within the body, nevertheless, because the quality of being pleasant (*priyatva*) also provides immediate assistance to those odors and so forth contained in food, both "pleasantness" and "beneficiality" have been mentioned for the sake of inclusion.
Thus, it "delights the odors and so forth residing in the body," meaning it nourishes the odors and so forth supported by the body;
likewise, it "delights and satisfies"—that is to say, nourishes—the olfactory, visual, gustatory, tactile, and auditory faculties with desirable odors and so forth.
For in our system, the sense organs are also composed of the five elements, and they are decaying every moment.
He describes the function of the elemental fire with the verse beginning "bhauma" (earthly), etc.

The five types of heat, beginning with that of the earth (*bhauma*), which reside within substances such as the earthly and possess strength kindled by the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*), digest the internal substance and produce their respective qualities—earthly and so forth—which are non-different from the preceding qualities of earthiness, odor, and the rest. This very point was also stated in the *Sūtrasthāna* [of the Caraka Saṃhitā], beginning with: "The various things eaten, drunk, licked, and chewed, when beneficial to a living being, are properly digested by their own respective heats through the power kindled by the internal fire" (Sūtra 28).

Although earthly and other substances are cooked by the elemental fire (*bhūtāgni*), nevertheless, for earthly and other substances, this very "production" (*janana*) through cooking consists in their being endowed with specific qualities (*viśiṣṭaguṇayuktatva*). Therefore, with the intention that even when a substance is produced by that cooking, it is only the qualities that are produced, it is said that [the fires] "produce the qualities of the food consisting of earth and so forth.
By this, only the production of qualities is expressed by the word "fire," not the production of the substance.

Alternatively, based on the analysis of the compound as *āhārāś ca guṇāś ca* ("food and qualities"), the word "food" (*āhāra*) also includes the substance which serves as the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) of the food.
"Of the earthy and so forth" means of those consisting of earth, water, fire, air, and ether.

Among these, the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) digests all the nutrients, waste products, and transformations of food, whereas the elemental fires (*bhautikā agnayaḥ*) produce their respective qualities.
And it has been said: "Once the dissolution of the aggregate has first been effected by the digestive fire, afterwards the five elemental fires digest each their own substance."

This activity of the elemental fire (bhūtāgni) also exists within the tissues (dhātus), because the five elements are present even in the tissues; furthermore, the activity of the tissue-fire and the activity of the elemental fire therein should be understood as being described according to the sequence of the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni).
He describes the qualities of food digested by fire, beginning with "yathāsvam" (according to their respective nature), and so forth.

"According to their own nature" (*yathāsvam*) means that whatever belongs to a particular thing [belongs to it]. Substances and qualities of the same class nourish substances and qualities of the same class. Therefore, substances in the form of earthy and other types nourish those designated as the bodily elements (*dhātu*), humors (*doṣa*), and impurities (*mala*); whereas qualities such as digestion, stability, odor, unctuousness, heat, and heaviness nourish the body's odor, unctuousness, heat, heaviness, and so forth. He clarifies the meaning of the phrase "according to their own nature" and so on with the words beginning "earthy" (*pārthivā*).
The qualities of the material substances of food nourish only the earthly substances and qualities within the body.
In this context, by the term "qualities of the material substances of food," only the qualities inherent in the substance are meant;

however, the nourishment of the substance is achieved through the nourishment of its qualities, because it is impossible to effect the nourishment of the qualities without the nourishment of the substance.

Having shown the activity of the elemental fire (*bhūtāgni*), he speaks— beginning with "by seven," etc.— to show the activity of the constituent fire (*dhātvagni*): "the sustainers of the body" means those who specifically maintain the body.
"Of two kinds" means of two types of transformation (*pāka*).
He states those very two types as "like dross and essence" (*kiṭṭaprasādavat*); the meaning is that it consists of the form of dross and essence.

Although the transformation of semen (*śukra*) itself does not possess dross, nevertheless, because many [other substances] do possess dross, this designation as "of two kinds" should be understood according to the maxim: "those with umbrellas are walking."
The word "again" (*punar*) means after the digestion by the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*).
He describes the sequential production of the rasa and other elements resulting from that digestion, beginning with the words "rasāt" and so forth.

From *rasa* (nutritive essence) blood is produced from its refined portion (*prasāda*); from that blood, muscle is produced from its refined portion; from muscle, fat is produced from its refined portion, and so on, up to the embryo being produced from semen as its refined portion.

By the term "produced from the refined portion," it is meant that blood and the other tissues are generated from the refined fractions of *rasa* and the rest, whereas those generated from the waste fraction (*kiṭṭa*), such as phlegm (*kapha*) and others, will be described later.
However, because of its purity, the embryo is produced solely from the refined portion of semen, and not from anything generated by waste.
Some, however, claim that the beard is produced from the impurity of semen (*śukramala*); that is not correct, because it is not mentioned as such in the *Tantra*.

Furthermore, if the beard were indeed the impurity of semen, then women would also have beards due to possessing semen; yet women do possess semen, though it has been established previously that their semen does not initiate conception, and so forth.
Others, however, maintain that by the term "born from the refinement of the embryo" (*garbhaprasādaja*), they denote the vital essence (*ojas*) of the neuter.

In the phrase "born from faith" (*prasādaja*), the word *jāta* refers specifically to nourishment, not to the production of something previously non-existent; for blood and the other [constituents] are produced from the very beginning of the embryo and are subsequently nourished by the nutrient fluids (*rasa*) and so forth. Indeed, blood and the others are nourished starting from the stage of the embryo itself.

Regarding the production of the three humors (*dhātu*), commentators explain as follows: therein, the nutrient essence (*rasa*), being digested by its own fire, becomes blood (*rakta*); blood becomes muscle (*māṃsa*), and so forth. Thus, through the transformation of each preceding humor, each subsequent humor is produced; just as curd comes from milk, butter from curd, clarified butter (*ghṛta*) from butter, and the cream of clarified butter (*ghṛtamaṇḍa*) from clarified butter—this is one position.

Alternatively, the *rasa* itself first floods the blood; there, through its connection with the site of the blood, it acquires a resemblance to the blood and nourishes the blood with a portion equal to that of the blood. Then, having flooded the blood, it floods the flesh; there too, it performs the nourishment of the flesh and acquires a resemblance to the flesh. In this manner, the *rasa* itself floods and increases each successive tissue (*dhātu*). It is just as when water from a canal poured into a field irrigates the adjacent field and gradually floods other fields in succession.

Or rather, having arisen from the essence of food (*āhārarasa*), it satisfies the blood and other constituents through distinct channels with equal portions. In that process, the portion of the constituent (*dhātu*) that nourishes whichever tissue is proximate nourishes it quickly; however, for that constituent which is distant, nourishment occurs after a long time due to the distance of the path. Thus, the nourishment of the constituents occurs through distinct channels. This is just as when pigeons take flight on a threshing floor and travel toward different directions, each following its own respective path; depending on whether their destination is near or far, they arrive either quickly or after a long time. It is exactly like that.

Thus, according to the analogies of milk and curd (*kṣīradadhi-nyāya*), the irrigation channel in a field (*kedārīkulyā-nyāya*), and the pigeons in a threshing floor (*khalekapota-nyāya*), there are three ways in which the elements are nourished. Among these, here, upon careful consideration of the words and their meanings, either the analogy of the irrigation channel in a field or the analogy of milk and curd is appropriate; however, the analogy of the pigeons in a threshing floor is somewhat difficult to establish. For in that view, it would be difficult to explain the meaning that "blood arises from the refined essence of the *rasa*"; this has been explained in detail in the chapter on "The Two Kinds of Food and Drink" (*vividhāśitapītīya*), and the full elaboration should be sought there.

Objection: In the section on various foods and drinks (*vividhāśitapītīya*), nourishment from the essence of food and so forth has been described by such statements as, "They nourish you through the essence of food, [producing] plasma, blood," and so on (*Sūtra-sthāna*, chapter 28). In that context, two types of *rasa* are accepted; however, here only one *rasa* is said to nourish the blood. How is there no contradiction? Reply: It is not so. Even there, by the term "essence of food" (*āhārarasa*), the refined product (*prasāda*) born of food is designated; and that is indeed included within the category of *rasa*.

Since *rasa* is of two kinds—namely, the stable (*sthāyin*) and the nourishing (*poṣaka*)—therein, a distinction was stated with the intention of highlighting the difference between the nourishing portion of *rasa* and the *rasa* that is to be nourished (the tissues). Here, however, both the stable and nourishing portions of *rasa* are indicated as one; they are treated as a unity because there is no difference in their location or other such factors between the stable portion of *rasa* and the nourishing portion of *rasa*. Having established this, the body is said to consist of seven tissues (*saptadhātuka*), which has also been explained in detail in the chapter on "Various Foods and Drinks" (*vividhāśitapītīya*).
Having explained the nourishment of the primary elements (*dhātu*), he now describes the nourishment of the secondary elements (*upadhātu*):

"From *rasa* comes breast milk," and so forth. From *rasa* comes breast milk, which is produced from the pure essence (*prasāda*); likewise, blood known as *rajas* is also produced from *rasa* alone, arising from its pure essence portion. And it is stated in the *Suśruta*: "From *rasa* alone does the blood of a woman proceed, known as *rajas*" (*Suśruta Sūtrasthāna*, ch. 14). Furthermore, although this *rajas* is produced from *rasa*, it arises only after a long time due to its subtlety. As stated in the *Suśruta*: "In this way, *rasa* becomes semen in [one] month, and in women, it becomes the menstrual flow (*ārtava*)" (*Suśruta Sūtrasthāna*, ch. 14).

The *asrajas* are the *kaṇḍarās*, which are the thick tendons (*sthūla-snāyu*). Regarding the nourishment of the subtle tendons by fat (*medas*), it should be stated here that "fat gives rise to the tendons" (*medasaḥ snāyusambhavaḥ*). For in this context, the word *kaṇḍarā* refers to the thick tendon. However, in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*, the thick vessels (*sthūla-sirā*)—namely, breast milk and so forth—are called *upadhātus* (secondary constituents) because they nourish other tissues and thereby nourish the body. On the other hand, *rasa* and the others are called *dhātus* (tissues/constituents) because they sustain the body and nourish the other tissues. And it has been said in the *Bhoja*: "Vessels, tendons, *asrajas*, breast milk, and the skin are devoid of movement."

Regarding the statement, “And they arise from the *dhātus*; therefore, they are called *upadhātus*,” here too, by the phrase “they arise from the *dhātus*,” it is stated that while they certainly arise [from them], they do not produce [them] in turn;
however, semen (*śukra*) is indeed included within the *dhātus* because it generates vitality (*ojas*).

Ojas, however, is not enumerated here among the *dhātus* nor even among the *upadhātus*, because it is essentially the quintessence (*sāra*) of the seven *dhātus* and is therefore already included within them. For this very reason, its fire (*agni*) is also not mentioned separately.
(17) Having described the production of the pure portion (*prasādabhāga*), he speaks of the production of the impure portion (*malabhāga*) with the words beginning "kiṭṭam" and so forth.

Regarding "phlegm is the waste of rasa": when rasa is being digested, its waste product (kiṭṭa) becomes phlegm (kapha), and its refined essence (prasāda) becomes blood (rakta); in this same way, it should be understood for the impurities of blood and the other tissues. Regarding "the impurities of flesh are the orifices": these are the excretions of the ears, eyes, nose, mouth, and genitals. Regarding "sweat is the impurity of fat": although sweat has been described as a specific type of water, it nevertheless arises specifically as the impurity of fat; or rather, sweat may arise even from water, yet it exists as the impurity of fat, just as phlegm arises both from the digestion of its own stage [of transformation] and as the impurity of rasa.

The nails (*nakha*) should also be understood as bone-secretions (*asthimala*), based on the authority of Suśruta. For in that work, by the statement "nails and body hair" (*Su.Sū.A. 46*), the status of the nail as a bone-secretion is declared; and it is stated in the *Vividhāśitapītīya* chapter: "From waste products (*kiṭṭa*), hair, nails, and so forth, flourish" (*Sū.A. 28*). However, in the anatomical enumeration of bones, they are designated as bones themselves by the statement "twenty nails" (*Śā.A. 7*).

The meaning is that by the sequence thus described, the *prasāda* (pure essence) and the *kiṭṭa* (waste product) emerge in two ways. Now, he explains the mutual production of the *dhātus* (tissues), stating that nourishment is provided to the *rasa* (plasma) even by the blood that is to be nourished (*poṣya*), and likewise to the blood by the flesh, and so forth—beginning with the words "paraspara" (mutually).
The phrase "the succession of *dhātu*-moistures is mutually supported" means that they are sustained by one another through mutual moisture; that is to say, they are fully satiated.

Denying that substances such as aphrodisiacs (*vṛṣya*) produce semen and so forth through the sequential process of the transformation of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), he says: "Of aphrodisiacs," and so on.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), [the author] includes the breaking of obstructions (*balyabhedana*) and so forth.

The meaning is that the specific potency (*prabhāva*) of substances such as milk, which act as aphrodisiacs (*vṛṣya*) and the like, nourishes strength (*bala*) quickly; consequently, those substances—milk and the rest—their strength augmented by this potency, perform the functions of food, such as the production of semen, very rapidly, rather than following the aforementioned sequence of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). Alternatively, the meaning is that the potency of substances such as milk, which act as aphrodisiacs and the like, nourishes strength quickly—that is, the strength of the semen and other products they generate themselves. The particle *hi* is used for emphasis. Thus, through the potency of aphrodisiacs and the like, the production of semen and so forth occurs swiftly.
Now, he explains by how much time, as a general rule, the transformation of the elements (*dhātu-parivṛtti*) occurs, beginning with the words "by six," and so forth.

Some maintain that the transformation of the nutrient essence (*rasa*) into the form of semen (*śukra*) takes place over six days and nights. In that system, the nutrient essence produced [from food] becomes blood after one day and night; thus, excluding the day of its initial production, it attains the state of semen after six days. However, when the day of the nutrient essence's production is also included, it should be understood that the transformation into the state of semen occurs on the seventh day, once six days have elapsed.

For it is said by Parāśara: "The food of men becomes plasma on this very day; on the third day, it becomes blood; on the fourth, it also becomes flesh; on the fifth, fat; on the sixth, bone; and on the seventh, it reaches marrow."

They say that even this statement— "In the eighth [day], it necessarily attains the state of marrow and the state of semen for men"— must be explained as referring exclusively to the completion of the day of utilization;
furthermore, the transformation of the nutrient essence (*rasa-dhātu*) into the form of the blood essence (*rakta-dhātu*) is also accomplished specifically on the sixth day.
As it is stated in the *Suśruta*: “That aqueous rasa indeed remains in each tissue for thirty thousand and ten kalās; thus, in one month, the rasa becomes semen” (*Su.Sū.A.* 14).
By the words beginning with “some say,” he shows that both of these two positions [are held], and then states his own view starting with “by way of continuity” (*santatyā*).
When food has been consumed, there occurs a wheel-like rotation of the elements, such as the nutrient essence (*rasa*) and so forth; thus, the production of the elements proceeds without ceasing.

By means of the analogy of the wheel (*cakradṛṣṭānta*), however, he demonstrates the lack of fixedness regarding the time of transformation (*parivṛtti*). Just as a wheel employed for drawing water, when being turned by the exertion of arm strength, sometimes revolves very quickly and sometimes takes a long time due to the weakness of that strength; so too, the *dhātus* transform quickly when there is excellence of the digestive fire (*agni*) and other factors, but transform slowly when there is impairment of the digestive fire and other factors. Thus, even in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā*, in the passage: "Like sound, a flame, or a stream of water, [the *rasa*] moves through the body solely by way of subtle distinctions" (*Sūtrasthāna*, ch. 14), the transformation of *rasa* is indeed stated to occur over superior or inferior durations of time depending on the state of the digestive fire and other factors, using these three analogies.

For in that context, by means of the analogy of the continuity of water, it is stated that the transformation of the nutrient essence (*rasa*) into semen occurs over a long period, up to the limit of a month; by means of the analogy of the continuity of sound, however, the production of semen is said to occur neither too quickly nor too slowly; and by means of the analogy of the continuity of a flame, the production of semen is said to occur very quickly.

Likewise, it is stated elsewhere: "Some say [it becomes semen] after a day and night, others after six nights, and others say that food reaches the state of semen in a month through the process of digestion."

All of this should be understood as being grasped through the analogy of the wheel (cakradṛṣṭānta). Now, [the author] asks: who impels the nutrient essence (rasa), which nourishes the blood and other tissues (dhātu), so that the rasa flows here and there? To this he says: "By Vyāna," and so forth.

The element (*dhātu*) is of the nature of rasa (flavor/fluid); alternatively, that which "tastes" (*rasati*) is called *rasa*, referring to the fluid element (*dravadhātu*), by which blood and other fluids are also included. "Vikṣepocitakarmā" means one whose appropriate natural function is dispersal (*vikṣepa*). By means of that *vyāna* [vital air], "simultaneously" (*yugapat*) meaning at one time, "everywhere" (*sarvataḥ*) meaning throughout the entire body, "is dispersed" (*vikṣipyate*) meaning it is carried about; "unceasingly" (*ajasram*) meaning it is dispersed without rest, and "always" (*sadā*) meaning at all times.

Now, if there is such a dispersal of rasa everywhere, why is it that a locus for morbid changes (*vikāra*) in rasa and so forth is observed in only one specific part? To this he says: "being dispersed," and so forth.
"Due to a deficiency" means due to a deficiency in the channels (*srotas*);
"it adheres" means it remains;
