"it produces a disorder" means it produces a disorder residing in the *rasa*. For even *rasa* is involved as a substratum (*āśraya*) in the production of a disorder; therefore, its agency (*kartṛtva*) in this context is appropriate.
The phrase "like a rain-cloud in the sky" means that just as a cloud driven by a fierce wind pours down rain exactly where it becomes attached, so too does the *rasa* (humor).

Just as the *rasa* produces a disorder in one specific location, so too the *doṣas* produce disorders in specific locations; thus he says, "of the *doṣas*" and so forth. Suśruta also says: "For when the *doṣas* are provoked, they run about throughout the body..."
"Where there is attachment due to a deficiency in the elements, there disease arises" (Suśruta Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 24).
He concludes the discussion on the functions of the fires with the verse beginning "Thus, the elemental," and so forth.
There are five elemental fires, seven tissue-fires (*dhātu-agni*), and one fire that digests food.

Furthermore, whatever other internal fires exist within the secondary tissues (*upadhātu*) and waste products (*mala*), these too are included within the elemental fires themselves; alternatively, they are not mentioned because they are not primary and are of no significant function.
He states the preeminence of the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) among all fires with the words beginning "of food" (*annasya*).
He states the reason for its preeminence with the words beginning "rooted in that" (*tanmūlā*).
To provide the reason for its being the root, he offers a qualifying attribute containing the reason itself with the words beginning "with its increase" (*tadvṛddhi*).

Since the fires in this world increase with the increase of that digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) and diminish with its diminution, they are rooted in it; the meaning is that they follow its presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Furthermore, since this internal fire is the root everywhere, one should protect it—this is how the text should be construed. In the phrase "by those properly employed," it means by those [foods] utilized through the application of the rules for diet.

Regarding "the maintenance of life-force and strength": when the digestive fire (*agni*) that digests food and drink is maintained, the maintenance of life-force and strength occurs; by this, other highly desirable qualities such as complexion (*varṇa*) and so forth are also to be understood.
He states the fault in the opposite case with the words beginning "he who," etc.;
"born from disorders of the *grahaṇī*" means born from disorders localized in the *grahaṇī*.

By this [statement], the four disorders of the *grahaṇī* whose characteristics will be described hereafter are specifically designated by the term "diseases of the *grahaṇī*" (*grahaṇī-doṣa*). Likewise, diseases such as weak digestion (*agnimāndya*) and indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), which are dependent upon the *grahaṇī*, are also included.

Although weak digestion, indigestion, and so forth are indeed diseases of the *grahaṇī* by virtue of being dependent on it, nevertheless, in this context, only those four diseases that arise through the impairment of the function of the channel (*nāḍī*) that constitutes the *grahaṇī* are primarily denoted by the word "diseases of the *grahaṇī*."

For, by the statement beginning with "Below, however, whether cooked or uncooked," he will describe *grahaṇī* disease as being characterized by the general symptoms of *grahaṇī* disorders, arising through the suppression of the natural function of the *grahaṇī*;
and he will further describe the afflicted and non-afflicted states of the *grahaṇī*: "It retains undigested food and discharges the digested from the sides;
when afflicted, it repeatedly releases even what has been eaten raw."

Furthermore, this "diarrhea" (duṣṭi), characterized by the discharge of digested food, does not occur solely from defects of the digestive fire (agni-doṣa) or from the indigestion of undigested matter (āmājīrṇa).

By specifying this particular definition, it is stated here that the term *grahaṇī* refers specifically to the disease of the *grahaṇī* caused by defects residing in the *grahaṇī*. Defects of the digestive fire do not constitute the specific condition of *grahaṇī-gada*. Although there is a discharge of digested food in diarrhea (*atisāra*), nevertheless, because its pathogenesis (*samprāpti*) is distinct and its treatment differs, it is declared to be different from *grahaṇī-doṣa*.
This being established, he states the causes and other factors for the disorders of the *grahaṇī* in general—beginning with "from lack of food" (*abhojanāt*) and so forth.

By the word "time" (*kāla*), the time consisting of a year is meant. "Disturbance of place" (*deśavaiṣamya*) refers to regional calamity; and that has been explained in the chapter on the destruction of countries (*janapadoddhvaṃsana*).
By the word *ṛtu* (season), the season beginning with *śiśira* (winter) is intended;

through the irregularity of one season, the irregularity of all seasons is implied. Through the irregularity of the seasons, there is the specific distinction of the irregularity of two or one season, which results in "sourness," meaning acidity (*amlatā*).

"Having the nature of poison" (*viṣarūpatām*) means that it possesses the same character as poison, which causes many morbid transformations (*vikāra*). By this [term], all varieties of indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) are to be understood as being included, which are stated in another treatise: "Some maintain that indigestion consists of *āma*, *vidagdha*, and *viṣṭabdha*, produced respectively by *kapha*, *pitta*, and *vāyu*, while the fourth is due to the residue of *rasa*" (Suśruta Sūtrasthāna 46.42–44).
The phrase "of that" refers to the general symptoms of indigestion (*ajīrṇa*).
"Distension" (*viṣṭambha*) means remaining in a state of non-movement.
And that which is "terrible food-poison" (*annaviṣa*), when combined with bile (*pitta*) and so forth—by this [passage], he states the symptoms of indigestion corrupted by bile and the other *doṣas*.

And this is a definition based on the association with *pitta* and other [humors], because it is observed that indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), being confined solely to the digestive tract (*koṣṭha*), lacks the capacity to produce disorders such as consumption (*yakṣman*).

Furthermore, regarding "acid bile" (*amlapitta*), the definition stated in another treatise is: "Acid bile is *pitta* characterized by an excess of acidic qualities, [diagnosed] by indigestion, exhaustion, excessive moisture, bitter and sour eructations, and heaviness. [The verse continues: "With indigestion, exhaustion, excessive moisture, bitter and sour eructations, and heaviness..."

"One should diagnose *amlapitta* by means of burning sensations in the heart and throat, and loss of appetite. Although consumption (*yakṣman*) arises from all three *doṣas*, it is described here as being born of *kapha* because *kapha* predominates in the obstruction of the channels (*srotas*).
He describes the diseases resulting from food that remains as *rasa* through its association with the waste-element (*kiṭṭa-dhātu*), beginning with "urinary diseases" (*mūtra-roga*) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "arising from [improper] tastes and so forth," it should be understood that those symptoms such as loss of appetite (aruci) and others mentioned here arise from them.
(Verses 45–49). Having described the characteristics of indigestion (ajīrṇa), he now states the characteristics of the defects of the digestive fire (agnidoṣa): "Irregular" (viṣama), etc.
He states the function of the sharp fire: "The sharp," and so forth.
Here, by the phrase "with dull fuel," he demonstrates that even if [the fire] is sharp, if it possesses pure fuel, then there occurs the nourishment of the *dhātus*.
In connection with the discussion of fire (*agni*), he states the function of balanced fire (*samāgni*)—beginning with "properly" (*yukta*) and so forth. "Properly" means balanced;
the meaning is that by digesting food properly, it brings about the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).

By the word *sama* (equal), either the balanced *vāyu* that assists *agni* is understood, or else it refers to the equilibrium of the *dhātus* produced by the balanced *vāyu*; and by the word *yukta* (balanced), the equilibrium of *kapha* and *pitta* within *agni* is intended, since it is stated in the passage "the equal [agni] by the equals" (*Vāgbhaṭa Sūtrasthāna*, ch. 1) that the state of balanced *agni* occurs precisely through the balance of the *doṣas*.
He describes the activity of weak digestive fire (mandāgni): beginning with "durbala" (weak), etc.
Determining that the disorder of *grahaṇī* is the primary subject among the aforementioned disorders, he says "adhastu" (but below), etc.
In the phrase "cooked or raw," the word "or" (vā) is used in the sense of conjunction; thus, it implies that some is cooked and some is uncooked.

To the question "From where does he create both the cooked and the uncooked? he says: "For all food indeed is consumed by him"; thus, what is created becomes both cooked and uncooked, being released [as excrement].
Tamaka is indeed *tamas* (darkness).
Regarding the prodromal symptoms [sūtra 51–54], *vidāha* refers to a specific, intense burning sensation (*viśiṣṭo dāhaḥ*) of the food.
Now, for the sake of easy comprehension of the disorder of the *grahaṇī*, he describes the nature and the natural function of the *grahaṇī*—beginning with "the seat of fire" (*agnyadhiṣṭhāna*).
"The seat of fire" means the substratum of the digestive fire (*agni*).
He states the definition and cause for the designation "grahaṇī" (the receptor): "of food," and so forth.
"From grasping" means from holding; the meaning is that it holds the food above the navel.

Alternatively, when it is supported and strengthened by the power of the fire blazing upward from the navel, it holds the undigested food and releases the digested food to the side—that is, it releases the digested food to the left side. Since the grahaṇī and the rectum are located on the left side, it is logical that it releases the digested food on the left side.

"Supported" (*upastambhitā*) means assisted by fire through its function of heating (*pitta*); "strengthened" (*upabṛṃhitā*) means empowered by fire through its function of nourishment (*bṛṃhaṇa*). Alternatively, it may mean strengthened by way of support. In this latter view, [the author] states the commonality of support for the *grahaṇī*. Having described the natural (*prākṛta*) function of the *grahaṇī*, he describes its morbid (*vaikṛta*) function, beginning with "weak," etc.—meaning both having weak fire and being weak, or alternatively, having weak digestive power (*agni-bala*), she is called "one with weak digestive power."
"Corrupted" (*duṣṭā*) means corrupted by defects (*doṣa*).
"It discharges undigested matter" (*āmaṃ vimuñcati*) means it discharges food that is uncooked (*apakva*).

By the statement "it discharges either the pre-formed or the cooked," the form of the *vidagdha* (burnt) is actually referred to as "undigested" (*āma*); however, in this context, since it discharges undigested matter as a rule, there is no contradiction.
He states the distinct causes and other factors for the various types of *grahaṇī* arising from *vāta*, *pitta*, *kapha*, and their combination (*sannipāta*):
"From the three," meaning from *sannipāta*.
"Varieties of form" refers to those symptoms that will be described as the signs of *grahaṇī* disorder.
"Sour digestion" (*śuktapāka*) means the digestion of food being like sour gruel (*śukta*).
In the phrase "greed for all tastes," the genitive case is used in the sense of the locative (*saptamy-arthe ṣaṣṭhī*).
The phrase "when the food is digested" (*jīrṇe jīryati*) is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
The suspicion of being a *gulma* (abdominal tumor) or similar condition arises because it is accompanied by pain resembling that of a *gulma*.

Anticipating the objection that in *pittaja-grahaṇī* (bilious malabsorption syndrome), an increase of bile is logical since bile is identical to fire (*agni*), [the author] states—"it destroys the digestive fire while flooding it"—in order to show that bile, due to its liquid nature, actually extinguishes the fire. "Flooding" (*āplāvana*) means moistening with a liquid.
Regarding the use of even hot water for extinguishing fire due to its liquidity, he provides an illustration beginning with "water when heated," and so forth.

As for the verse beginning with "the weakness [of] the fire" (*daurbalyaṃ balahāniḥ yaścāgniḥ*), some claim it is unauthored (*anārṣa*), asserting that it is inconsistent to include the three types of fire-defects—distinct from the Vaiśeṣika *grahaṇī-doṣa*—within the category of *grahaṇī* diseases. However, we see no contradiction in this, as the phrase "and that too" (*taṃ cāpi*) serves as a general inclusion of natural conditions such as impaired digestion (*agnimāndya*) and others, provided they do not conflict with the general *grahaṇī-doṣa*; indeed, it has already been demonstrated that impaired digestion and the like are included within the general *grahaṇī-doṣa*.

"Excluding *sama*" means excluding the fire situated in the equilibrium of the *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. In the passage beginning with "residing in the *grahaṇī*," the term "defect" (*doṣa*) is used as a general designation, and thus it includes all three— vāta and the others.
"Endowed with the signs of the unripe" means accompanied by the symptoms of *āma*;
"one should extract" means one should vomit;
"of fruits" refers to *madana* fruits.
"Līna" means not agitated;
"situated in the receptacle of digested food" (pakvāśaya-stha) means having gone downward and reached the vicinity of the colon;
"to be drained" (srāvya) means to be purged by means of a laxative.
"With stimulants" means with purgative applications combined with stimulating substances.
"Pervading the body" refers to the *āma* (undigested matter) located within the body;

"in the rasa" means in the undigested *rasa*. Here, *āma* is intended specifically as the form of undigested *rasa*, because it is difficult for the *rasa* of food to pervade the entire body through its connection with [the bodily] *rasa* while still in an undigested state.

Fasting (laṅghana) and starvation (anaśana), as well as digestive treatments (pācana) such as gruels (yavāgū) and the like, are indicated when the āmāśaya has been purified; here, "purification" should be understood as occurring through purgation (virecana) and fasting according to what is appropriate.

"Combined with digestive stimulants" (dīpanīya-yuta) means prepared with the group of digestive stimulants (dīpanīya-gaṇa) mentioned in the chapter on the six hundred purgatives (Ṣadvirecanaśatāśritīya).
"Svinnābhyaktam" means both fomented (*svinna*) and anointed (*abhyakta*); "srastadoṣam" means that the morbid humors have been displaced by the non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*). 73–81.

In the passage beginning with "two *pañcamūla*s," the fresh juice of *suṣavī* occupies the place of water; the measure of one *droṇa* should be taken by combining this with the decoction of *āranāla* and other ingredients. By the phrase "having added the two alkalis according to the proper method" (*kṣārau dattvā ca yuktitaḥ*), the small quantity of the two alkalis is indicated; however, the two alkalis should be added separately in a quantity equal to that of whichever salt is to be used as an additive. Furthermore, by the term "according to the proper method" (*yuktitaḥ*), he indicates the appropriate time for adding the alkalis, and that appropriate time here is precisely the moment when the ghee is removed from the heat, as Jatūkarṇa states: "The ten roots, the five pungents, horse gram (*kulattha*), fragrant grass (*surabhi*), and barley..."
"One should prepare devadāru, sarala,
and hemp seeds with curd and sour gruel; when that has been cooked in one āḍhaka of ghee, one should add two palas each of the two alkalis and the seven salts."
Audbhida is salt from saline soil;
utkārikā-lavaṇa is salt from saline earth; romaka is salt produced in Rumā; pākya is salt produced by boiling.

Regarding "in the measure of a *bilva*" (82–86), this refers to a paste weighing one *pala*; however, according to the word of the Great Sage, exactly eight *palas* of clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) should be cooked here, because of its fruitfulness.
In the *pañcamūlādya* [formula], each of the thirteen liquids, beginning with *śukta*, is equal in quantity to the oil (*sneha*).

Regarding the phrase "with the juice of *bījapūraka*," some authorities maintain that the *pañcamūla* and other ingredients should also be used as a paste (*kalka*); alternatively, the meaning is that the previously prepared ghee should be drunk mixed with the juice of *bījapūraka*.

In the passage beginning with "oil" (*tailam*), oil processed with these *pañcamūla* and other ingredients should be applied for massage (*abhyaṅga*); likewise, the powder of these very same *pañcamūla* and other ingredients mentioned as the paste should be drunk with lukewarm water.

He speaks regarding the powder formulation: "In vāta," and so forth. This refers to *grahaṇī* disease covered by *vāta* and *śleṣman*, as well as *grahaṇī* disease with *āma*. Some say "in *āma*-contaminated feces"; they state that *āma* is of many kinds, as it is said: "Some declare *āma* to be the essence of food (*annarasa*), some as the accumulation of waste (*malasañcaya*), and some as the initial corruption of the *doṣas*."
Bhoja also said: "The first constituent of food which remains in the stomach and is not digested due to the weakness of the body's fire is designated as *āma*.
Īśvarasena also said: "In this way, even in the stomach, a large amount of food does not digest properly."
"that very food, as it is being accumulated, in time attains the state of *āma* (undigested matter)," and so forth;
therefore, here too, the determination of *āma* must be established based on the authority of that statement.
In order to provide knowledge regarding the diseases of *sāma*, *nirāma*, and *agrahaṇī*, he states the characteristics of *sāma* and *nirāma*: "it sinks," and so forth.
*Āma* refers to that which is dependent on *āma*; "due to heaviness" means due to the heaviness produced by *āma*.

"Ripe" (*pakva*) means free from *āma*. Regarding the statement, "Having previously examined whether it is *sāma* (with *āma*) or *nirāma* (without *āma*), one will administer [the treatment]," he states an exception (*apavāda*) for both the characteristics of *āma* and *pakva*: "Except in cases of excessive liquidity," and so forth. Because of excessive liquidity, even *āma* floats; however, that which is excessively compact, even if *pakva*, sinks due to its extreme density. Furthermore, because of the vitiation of coldness and *śleṣman*, and due to the heaviness induced by the association with *kapha*, even *pakva* matter sinks; it does not float precisely because of its heaviness.

[Objection: But since *sāma* has already been described by the passage beginning with "accompanied by obstruction, salivation, pain," etc., what is the purpose of this redundant definition of *sāmatā*? [Response: It is said: That was stated in the context of [predominance of] *vāta* and *kapha*, whereas this is stated for the sake of knowing *viḍāmatā* (fecal *sāmatā*); such is the distinction.

Regarding the phrase "having examined" and so forth, and the expression "one who is *nirāma* yet possesses *āmadoṣa*"—how can this be, given that *āmadoṣa* does not exist in the state of *nirāmatā*? [Response: No, because by the term *āmadoṣa* one who suffers from *grahaṇī-doṣa* is intended; [this is understood] by the other [term], namely, by the alleviation of *grahaṇī-doṣa*.

Regarding the passage beginning with "citraka" and ending with "lavaṇāni ca," some maintain that there are three salts, following the principle of the *kapiñjalādhikaraṇa*; however, that principle applies when the number is unspecified. In this case, since five salts are specifically mentioned in the *Dīrghañjīvitīya* chapter as being primary, and because five salts can be readily procured, exactly five salts are to be taken.
"Mustāntakalka" means the paste of the group beginning with *nāgara* as mentioned later; "arśogranthi" refers to the condition where feces are obstructed by hemorrhoids;
and up to the phrase "mixed with black pepper," the expression "having made into a powder, one should drink" is understood to follow.
The meaning is that when there is an excess of *sāma* (undigested toxins), one should add *ativiṣā* and other such substances to the powder consisting of *pippalīmūla* and the rest.
Regarding the phrase "with *surā* and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes *kāñjika*, *sauvīra*, and similar liquids.

Regarding the phrase "four parts of the four sours" (*caturṇāṃ prasthamamlānām*), some authorities state that the "four sours" mentioned first in the section on heart-tonics (*hṛdyavarga*) consist of *vṛkṣāmla*, *amlavetasa*, pomegranate (*dāḍima*), and jujube (*badara*). Others, however, maintain that it refers to the inclusion of wood-apple (*kapittha*), *cukrikā*, *vṛkṣāmla*, and pomegranate, as will be mentioned in the upcoming formula beginning with "cavyatvak. In another treatise, it is stated: "This is called the 'four sours' consisting of *vṛkṣāmla*, citron (*mātuluṅga*), sour jujube (*badara*), and *amlavetasa*; the 'five sours' includes the pomegranate as well."
"Three palas from the trikaṭu" means three palas from the combined [ingredients];
*rāga* is a specific type of sauce (*vyañjana*) prepared with substances such as wood-apple (*kapittha*).
In the passage beginning with "cavya," *śālmala* refers to the resin of the silk-cotton tree (*śālmalīveṣṭaka*),
and *śilodbhava* refers to that which is produced from stone (*śailaja*).
Cukrikā and cāṅgerī are known as soṣaṇa, which includes black pepper.
By the passage beginning with "takram" (buttermilk), the qualities of buttermilk are described:

because it is sweet in its post-digestive effect (*pāka*), it does not aggravate *pitta*. Although its sourness would normally lead to the aggravation of *pitta*, due to its sweet post-digestive effect, it does not aggravate *pitta*; yet, they say that it likewise does not pacify *pitta*.

"Sadyaska" means "not causing burning. Freshly churned *takra* (buttermilk) does not cause a burning sensation while in the state of being cooked; however, once it has stood for some time, it certainly becomes burning.

In the context of *yavānī* and other substances, the phrase "pressed into *takra*" (*tadāsutam*) means it has been infused into one *āḍhaka* measure of *takra*; thus, it has become [fermented] by having acquired a sour taste.
"By means of emesis" (vamana) should be understood with reference to pitta that has moved upward.

Regarding the phrase "and also with bitter ghees" (sarpirbhiś cāpi tiktakaiḥ), the plural number is used because it refers to the genus (*jāti*). Alternatively, the plural is appropriate as it refers to the two types of bitter ghee mentioned in the chapter on skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), as well as other ghees prepared with bitter substances.
Kuṭannaṭa, kaivartamustaka, ṣaḍgranthā, and vacā.
Āsphotā is known in the world as *asphuramallikā*;
kapītana is known as *gandhamuṇḍa*.
"In *nāgarādye sakṣaudram*" means mixed with honey (*madhu*);

"with *taṇḍulāmbu*" means with rice-washing water. Others, however, say that *taṇḍulāmbu* is sour liquid (fermented rice-water) that has stood for a long time, consisting of twice as much sour liquid as rice and an equal amount of rice.
By showing that this is honored by Kṛṣṇātreya, its status as a proven formulation (*siddhayoga*) is demonstrated. The elders maintain that Kṛṣṇātreya is indeed non-different from Punarvasu.

*Bhūnimbādya* (the *bhūnimba* group) combined with jaggery is *guḍayuta*; *guḍa-śītāmbu* (jaggery-cooled water) consists of cooled water mixed with jaggery; here, "jaggery" (*guḍa*) should be added merely to impart a jaggery-like color and sweetness.
In the verse beginning with "vacām," by the two terms *syonāka* and *kaṭvaṅga*, both types of *syonāka*—the large-podded and the small-podded—are included.
The phrase "desiring the pacification of that disease" means desiring the cessation of diseases such as the disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī-doṣa*) mentioned in the *Bhūnimbādi* group.

The phrase "by means of the *Bhūnimbādi*" means one should compound the *vacā* and other ingredients with the collection of substances mentioned in the *Bhūnimbādi* group in the prescribed proportions. Others, however, state that by the expression "by means of the *Bhūnimbādi*," the practice of consuming it with jaggery and cold water, as prescribed for the *Bhūnimbādi* group, is extended to this case as well.

Regarding "for the purpose of drinking" (*pānīyārthaṃ pānāya*): [it refers to] "by means of pungent, sour, alkaline, and sharp [substances]," meaning by means of the sharp substance (*paṭunā*) which possesses pungent qualities and so forth, acting as an exciter of the sense faculties (*indriyottejakena*).

In the case of *kapha-grahaṇī*, although buttermilk (*takra*) is appropriate because it is astringent (*kaṣāya*) and fresh, nevertheless, because it kindles the digestive fire (*agni-dīpana*), buttermilk that is sour (*amla*) alone is prescribed by the statement, "and one should drink it with sour [liquids].
Regarding the phrase "pure *sīdhu*," this refers to faultless *sīdhu*.
"Rendered half-decayed" means made to remain as half [of its original state] due to cooking;
"one should place it nearby as before" means one should store it in a jar smeared with *elā* and other substances.
"Two muṣṭis of dantī and citraka" means two palas of citraka and dantī combined;
"likewise" means it is placed in a large jar smeared with the elādi [powder].
In the context of "prāsthikam" and so forth, pippalī, jaggery (guḍa), bibhītaka, and marrow are each measured at one prastha;
"one who eats unctuous meat-broth" (snigdharasāśana) refers to one who consumes meat broth containing fat.
In the verse beginning with "nave" (163–167), the cinnamon, cardamom, and other ingredients are measured in karṣas;
"pippalī with its root" refers to both long pepper and long pepper root.
It should be understood that *bhallātakaghṛta* (ghee from marking-nut) is also prescribed for gulma (168–170).
Regarding *biḍa*, it refers to *kālotthalaṇa* (black salt); *biḍa* is *biḍalavaṇa*, while *kālalavaṇa* means *sauvarcalalavaṇa* (black salt).
"Broken into pieces" means made into fragment after fragment;
"when the liquid has been absorbed" means when the moisture has been drunk up;
"the palm of the hand" refers to one *karṣa*.
The sweetness of consumption here should be understood as being figurative (yaugika), by virtue of its capacity to eliminate the application of alkaline substances.
"In equal parts with cow's urine" means that the powder is mixed with an equal amount of cow's urine.
And its administration with ghee should be understood to be like the previous alkaline preparation (179–180).
In the case of "with buffalo urine" and so forth, the buffalo urine is equal in quantity to the powder, because it has been observed in the preceding application.

Regarding the passage beginning with "four *pala*s" (181–182), those who read, "Four *pala*s from the stem of *sudhā*, and the three salts of *triphalā*," state that these four *pala*s consist of the *triphalā* salts combined together;
or alternatively, they should be burnt in the juice of *vārtāku* until they become alkaline (*kṣārībhūta*), and then pills should be prepared again in the juice of *vārtāku*.
In the passage beginning with "triphalām" (183–187), *muṣkaka* refers to the *ghaṇṭāpāṭalaka*.
In the phrase "with ghee and oil," because of its association with curd (*dadhi*), three *kuḍava*s of ghee and oil together are intended.

Regarding the statement "the five purificatory procedures (pañcakarma) [are indicated] in the case of the three doṣas," although head-purgation (śirovirecana) may not be appropriate here, the term "five purificatory procedures" is used because most of the other procedures are indeed appropriate; alternatively, if diseases of the head and so forth are present, head-purgation should certainly be administered here as well.

"By inversion, one should perform that entire [treatment]" means that one should perform the aforementioned actions for Vāta and the other [doshas] by inverting them—that is, by alternating the treatment for each individual dosha—or alternatively, the combined actions should be performed simultaneously; furthermore, the combination of treatments occurs precisely through the combination of the substances for Vāta and the others.
With the verse beginning with "snehanam," etc., he summarizes the medicinal treatment for disorders of the *grahaṇī* (196–197).
Regarding the phrase "and the treatment according to the stages": listen to the treatment to be performed during specific stages of *grahaṇī* disorder.

If one applies only drying (*rūkṣa*) therapy when the patient is emaciated, there will be a loss of strength; if one applies only unctuous (*snigdha*) therapy, there will be an increase in *kapha* for one who already has much *kapha*. Therefore, with regard to both conditions, the meaning is that one should alternate between drying and unctuous treatments.
The phrase "combined with unctuous substances, salt, and sour [tastes]" means it is digestive-stimulant (*dīpana*).
"He kindles with fuel according to the rule" means that he has been ignited in accordance with the prescribed ritual procedure.
Ascertaining the fruit of the affection (sneha) both mentioned and unmentioned, he says: "Affection alone," and so forth;
"supreme" (param) means best.
He states the reason for affection being the best among those that kindle [the flame] with the words beginning with "not capable" (nālam), and so forth.
"It is not sufficient" means it is not capable;
"of that which is kindled by oil" means of that which is ignited by oil.
Here, by the word "oil," which denotes a general category, clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) alone is intended, because clarified butter is the subject under discussion here.

In passages such as "mandāgni" (weak digestive fire), the term "undigested" (*avipakva*) is an adjective qualifying feces (*purīṣa*). Therefore, by the word "undigested" in this context, the undigested state of the *rasa* (nutrient fluid) is not intended. Regarding the undigested *rasa*, the use of oleation (*sneha*) is prohibited in the passage: "Those afflicted by abdominal indigestion and poisoning... (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 13). Indeed, the administration of oleation toward undigested feces is strictly contradictory. Furthermore, even when oleation is processed with digestive (*dīpanīya*) drugs, its suitability for undigested feces arises precisely because the beneficial properties of the processing are not impaired. However, the oleous portion is employed as an auxiliary factor for the purpose of restoring the natural qualities of *vāta*. For this very reason, it is stated: "It is similar to that," and so forth.
"Serene" means being free from malice;
"having entered the path" means having attained the natural path;

and "because of moving nearby" means that when one possesses qualities such as serenity, being situated near the fire produces only strength for the fire and not discordance, because its inherent nature is to cause the fire to blaze—this is the meaning.
"Annāvagraha" means that for which there is no obstruction (avagraha) by food; the meaning is that it is not accompanied by food.
When the digestive fire is weak due to excessive unctuousness, powders, fermented liquors (ariṣṭa), and so forth should be administered. 201–205.

The meaning of the statement "when [the digestive fire] is impaired" is that when the digestive fire is sluggish due to specific accumulations in the rectum (*guda*), oils, wines, and fermented liquors (*āsava*) should be administered.
"One should follow the regimen for the doshas" means one should apply the medicinal treatment for the doshas that cause the impairment of the digestive fire.
One should drink ghee with gruels (*yavāgū*) in such a way as not to be oppressed by food; and "not oppressed by food" refers to ghee drunk during the middle meal.

Regarding the passage beginning with "dīrghakāla" (for a long time), "emaciated" (*kṣāma*) means devoid of effort; "wasted" (*kṣīṇa*) means weak; and "lean" (*kṛśa*) means having diminished muscle mass. Because there are two types of *prasaha* animals—those that eat meat and those that do not—the term "meat-eaters" (*māṃsāśinām*) is used as a qualification. By this, there is an exclusion of non-*prasaha* animals such as cattle and the like, which feed on grass. Now, one might object: "In the section on food and drink (*annapāna*), it was stated that *prasahas* are 'heavy, hot, unctuous, and sweet' (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 27); yet here, by saying they are 'light and sharp' (*laghutīkṣṇa*), etc., how can their lightness be asserted? This is not so. The construction is "one should feed [the patient] light [food]" (*bhojayed laghu*). Therefore, among the *prasahas*, one should feed light food here using the meat-juice (*rasa*) of those that are light.
By the words beginning with "sharp" (*tīkṣṇa*), the qualities of the *prasaha* (carnivorous) animals are stated.

Others, however, maintain that among the *prasahas*, those which are light are what are referred to here by the word "light. Likewise, others establish lightness in this context through processing (*saṃskāra*) by means of the addition of sour substances and so forth. By this, the qualities of the *prasahas*—such as sharpness, heat, and lightness—which are mentioned even in the treatment of pulmonary consumption (*rājayakṣma*), are indeed logical.
By the passage beginning with "not by fasting," etc., having excluded both non-eating and overeating, he states that the proper application of food generates the digestive fire;
by the term "non-eating" (abhojanena), both total fasting and insufficient eating are included.
The construction is: "either small, or covered by a lack of fuel, it does not blaze";
"fire with heartwood" (*sāradārvagni*) means fire that has heartwood as its support; "food with oil" (*snehavada-anna*) means food containing oil.

"Measured" means possessing the proper quantity (*mātrāvat*). Although diseases certainly arise even for one who eats wholesome and measured food due to factors such as the reversal of time, [the author] nevertheless shows that for those who eat wholesome and measured food, no disease born of diet occurs, by stating "he enjoys health for a long time"; the sense is that he does not suffer from a disease arising from food.

Regarding "by the non-inequality of the *dhātus*," one should strive for an increase of the digestive fire (*agni*) brought about by the equilibrium of the *dhātus*; by this, he prohibits that increase of the digestive fire which takes the form of excessive fire (*atyagni*), characterized by an aggravation of *pitta* resulting from the inequality of the *doṣas*.
With the words beginning with "samaiḥ," he speaks of the different types of fire for the purpose of maintaining the equilibrium of the digestive fire (*samāgni*).
By the phrase "in the middle" (*madhye*), meaning not too close [to the body],
and by the expression "designated as fire" (*agnisañjñita*), he negates any identity between the internal digestive fire— which exists in the form of heat (*ūṣma*)— and external fire.

Although it is stated generally as "by the *doṣas*," they should be understood—according to their respective suitability—as being dull, sharp, and irregular due to *kapha*, *pitta*, and *vāta* respectively.
"To be spoken" (*vācyam*) means that which is to be declared for the sake of counteraction; that is to say, the medical treatment (*cikitsita*).
The connection is that *pitta* is aggravated in the seat of fire (*pāvakasthāna*).

And because that *pitta* is accompanied by *māruta* (vata), it becomes a producer of excessive heat; thus, due to this difference in properties (*dharmabheda*), it should be understood as performing contradictory functions.

It should be understood that even though fire consists of bile and heat (*pittauṣman*), its capacity to diminish the localized bile and heat is entirely logical, because of the distinction between the producer and the produced.
By the phrase "those moving in still water," [the author] demonstrates the extreme heaviness of those who move in still water due to their lack of activity.
*Utkruñcas* are called the lumps of sesame, vata, and other substances ground on a stone and kneaded with warm water; others call them *utkārikās*.
In the phrase "thickened and combined with the three fats," the word *ghana* refers to curd (*dadhi*).
That which has milk-rice (*pāyasa*) as a subsequent meal during the treatment for removing *pitta* is called "having milk-rice as a subsequent meal" (*pāyasapratibhojana*).
"Fatty" (*medya*) means either fat (*medura*) or that which generates fat (*medojanaka*).
"Unwearied" means not hungry;
"calamity" means death— this is the sense—
and it should be construed as "he attains nourishment indeed."
Now he states the characteristics of balanced eating and so forth mentioned previously, beginning with "wholesome and unwholesome" (pathyāpathya), etc.

When wholesome and unwholesome food meet in one place—for example, red śāli rice and barley meal eaten together, whether in large or small quantities—likewise, eating before the previous meal has been digested or eating after the proper time has passed, this is called *viṣama-bhojana* (irregular eating). Eating again on the same day after having already eaten during the morning is *adhyasana* (overeating); in order to prohibit this, he says: "In the morning meal," and so forth.
"Eating" (āśana) means food (āśa), that is to say, eating.
Why does this not cause harm? He says: "By day," and so forth.

"Clarity" (sphuṭatva) means openness (vivṛtatva). Because the channels are open, the movement of the nutrient essence (rasa) remains unimpeded through their flow; consequently, the channels do not become moistened. Likewise, being dried by physical exercise and other such activities, the channels do not undergo moistening.
Physical exertion consists of walking and so forth; movement (*vihāra*) refers to activities such as stretching the limbs.
To the question of what occurs when the channels are not moistened, he says: "when they are not moistened," and so on;
"sprinkled" (*āsikta*) means poured in.
With the words "in the undigested," etc., he provides an illustration here;
"withered" means contracted,
and "in the unripe" refers to other [states].
He summarizes [the point] with the verse beginning "naiśeṣu" and so forth; the construction is that one should not eat anything else [at those times].

With the words "The internal fire" (*antaragni*) and so forth, he states the summary of the chapter; by the phrase "those fires," he refers to those mentioned in the passage beginning with "Terrestrial, aqueous, fiery... (*bhaumāpyāgneya...*), and by the phrase "and those which," he summarizes the meaning stated in the passage beginning with "the five qualities of food" (*pañcāhāraguṇān*).
The phrase "as many as they nourish" summarizes what was stated as "each according to its own [nature]," and so forth;
the phrase "those which ripen those [elements]" summarizes what was stated as "the seven are the sustainers of the body," and so forth;
and by reason of their rapid action, they are the "cause of rapid action."
The remainder is clear (verses 244–249).

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Grahani," in the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka Saṃhitā composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsāsthāna).

15 [Chapter 16 of Cikitsāsthāna (82 of 120)]: Since the administration of sharp and other such treatments during the treatment of *grahaṇī* disorder generates *pitta*, the treatment of *pāṇḍuroga*, which is primarily characterized by *pitta*, is described immediately following the treatment of *grahaṇī*.
Pāṇḍuroga is a disease characterized by the predominant color among the colors—such as green and others—that will be mentioned by Pāṇḍu.
For it is stated in the Suśruta Saṃhitā: “Because the state of pallor (*pāṇḍubhāva*) is indeed predominant in all of these, it is therefore called *pāṇḍuroga*” (Su.U.A. 44).

Furthermore, the treatment for jaundice (*kāmalā*), chlorosis (*halīmaka*), and so forth, must also be discussed here because they are merely varieties of *pāṇḍuroga*. Alternatively, by adopting the interpretation that "the treatment of *pāṇḍuroga* and other diseases is the 'treatment of *pāṇḍuroga*'," the treatment for jaundice and the rest is already implied.
Regarding *triśothīya*, although anemia (*pāṇḍuroga*) was stated to be of five types, here, by restating that [topic], he negates the number four mentioned by Suśruta.
For it is said in the Suśruta Saṃhitā: "Anemia is declared to be of four kinds [lit., half of eight], [arising] from the humors individually, collectively, and all together" (Su.U.A. 44).
For in that context, the [symptom] arising from eating clay is already included within the [category of] sannipātaja; thus,
by the words "the doshas," etc., he describes the pathogenesis (samprāpti).

Those in whom *pitta* is predominant are called *pittapradhāna*. The plural number is used with reference to the multiplicity of individual instances, not as an ultimate category, because heaviness (*gaurava*) is unsuitable for their functions. They state that heaviness in a patient suffering from jaundice (*pāṇḍuroga*) arises from the depletion of the bodily tissues (*dhātu*).

"Qualities of *ojas*" refers to those qualities of *ojas* which consists of the blood constituent (*raktadhātu*); alternatively, they should be understood as the ten qualities of *ojas* itself that have been described as being similar to milk.

Since the depletion of *sneha* is already understood through the depletion of *ojas*, the separate mention of the depletion of *sneha* is for the purpose of specifying a particular type of depletion—that is, the excessive vitiation of the *dūṣyas* by the *doṣas*.
Thus, "due to the vitiation of the *doṣas* and *dūṣyas*" means from their excessive corruption.

"Devoid of essence" (*niḥsāra*) means that the essence of the bodily constituents (*dhātu-sāra*) has departed; the meaning is that the person is bereft of the essences described in the passage beginning with "There are eight essences" (Vi. A. 8).

He is one whose sense organs are slack and whose sense organs are weak; for although that person [suffers from blood disorders], since blood and bile share a single origin, an increase in blood would normally be expected here due to the bile, nevertheless, there is a depletion of blood in this case because the bile consumes the nutrient fluids that nourish the blood and fails to produce the essential constituents that sustain it.

Although pitta is said here to produce color by virtue of its fiery nature—as it has been stated: "The fire element, being predominantly composed of the water and space elements, produces a bright white color" (Śārīra Sthāna, Chapter 8)—nevertheless, because it is subject to transformation (*vikṛta*), pitta here functions only as a producer of abnormal color.
By the verse beginning with "caustic" (*kṣāra*), he states the common cause.

*Niṣpāva* (flat beans) and *śimba* (legumes) cause disease when physical exercise, sexual intercourse, or improperly digested food are involved. "Imbalance of treatments and seasons" (*pratikarmartuvaiṣamya*) refers to the improper application of therapeutic measures such as emesis and so forth, as well as irregularity regarding the seasons.
"Ten vessels" refers specifically to the ten vessels situated in the heart;
"entirely" means completely.

In the reading "having vitiated the phlegm, wind, and blood," the corruption of the dispersed wind by bile is intended. However, when the reading is "phlegm, bile, and blood," then the corruption of the bile located in another site by the bile residing in the heart should be understood.
By the passage beginning with "samudīrṇam" (arisen), this attainment (*samprāpti*) is merely an elaboration of the previously mentioned general attainment.
With the words beginning with "tasya," he describes the premonitory symptoms;
some read "svedābādhaḥ" [instead of "svedāpāyaḥ"].
"When this has arisen" means when pāṇḍuroga has been produced;
"tinnitus and so forth" refers to the general symptoms. "Tinnitus" (karṇakṣveḍī) means having ringing in the ears;
by "aversion to food" (annadviḍ), the refusal to take food is expressed, while by "having a lack of relish" (arucimān), the inability to consume even desired food is expressed.
"An aversion to cold" means an aversion to chill; and this aversion to cold occurs even in this bile disease (pittaroga) due to the magnitude of the disorder.
Some describe the following distinction: "twisting of the calves" refers to pain in the calves caused by climbing and physical exertion.

"The specific characteristics of this will be stated" means that the specific causes and symptoms pertaining to the various types of anemia (pāṇḍuroga), such as its being born of vāta and so forth, will be explained.
With the verse beginning "By foods... (āhāraiḥ), he states the causes and signs of the vāta-born type.
General characteristics apply everywhere, whereas specific characteristics lead to the understanding of particularities;
by the words "of one with a bilious temperament" and so forth, he refers to the bilious type.

All cases of anemia (pāṇḍuroga) are born of pitta; nevertheless, this [specific type] is called "paittika" because it is produced specifically by a powerful pitta that is unmixed with other doṣas, just as paittika raktapitta is. For this very reason, in order to demonstrate the extreme predominance of pitta here, the term "of one who is pitta-prone" (pittalasya) is used to indicate that even the pitta-constitution (pittaprakṛti) serves as a cause; elsewhere, however, terms such as "of one who is vāta-prone" or "of one who is śleṣman-prone" are not employed. By the phrase "by those as described," namely "by sour [substances]" and so forth, the various types of blood (raktaprakārān) are indicated right here; by that, the strong vāta and other factors are also included.

Regarding the phrase "afflicted by thirst, fainting, and thirst" (*tṛṣṇāmūrcchāpipāsārta*), "thirst-fainting" (*tṛṣṇāmūrcchā*) refers to fainting caused by thirst; therefore, there is no redundancy with the word "thirst" (*pipāsā*). Others, however, say that "thirst" here means hunger; some read it as "of one overcome by thirst and fainting" (*tṛṣṇāmūrcchāparītasya*). With the words beginning "increased" (*vivṛddha*), he describes the type arising from phlegm (*kaphaja*).
As stated previously, having described the disorders of blood and so forth (verses 23–25), he explains the *sānnipātika* type with the verse beginning "sarvān na... and so on.
"Symptoms of the three doṣas" means being endowed with the combined symptoms of each individual doṣa.
With the words "earth," etc., [the author] describes that which arises from eating earth.

And here, even though there is a connection with the humors (doṣas), it is the *mṛd* (soil) alone that is designated [as the subject], not the humors; for it is the *mṛd* itself that acts as the agent of the different treatments and the different symptoms, as shown by the passage beginning "decoctions [cure] wind" (*kaṣāyā mārutam*), which demonstrates that the *mṛd* possesses the symptoms located in the *vāta* and other humors;
and [the term] "alkaline" (*ūṣarā*) refers to that which has a saline secondary taste (*kṣārānurasā*).
It should be understood that one should cause the consumed *rasa* and other elements to become parched (*virūkṣayet*).

By the phrase "only while uncooked" (*avipakvaiva*), it means that while remaining solely in its own natural state, it fills and obstructs the channels (*srotas*). Due to this obstruction of the channels, the strength of the *rasa* and other elements does not become proper;
by the statement "destruction of strength, complexion, and digestive fire," he demonstrates the loss of strength and the rest.
With the words "pāṇḍuroga" (anemia) and so forth, he describes the symptoms of the incurable [condition].
"Kharībhūtaḥ" means excessively dry.

By the words beginning with "at the proper time" (kāle), another definition of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is given; "with limbs smeared white and so forth" means that his limbs are coated with the color white.
By the words beginning with "one suffering from *pāṇḍu*," he describes *kāmalā*.

Because of the expression "one suffering from *pāṇḍu*," it is understood that a specific state such as *kāmalā* arises from a particular cause of *pāṇḍu* disease itself. For this very reason, Hārīta has also stated that *kāmalā* and other such conditions are indeed forms of *pāṇḍu* disease;
for the statement says: "By wind, by bile, by phlegm, and likewise by the three doṣas combined, and also upon the consumption of earth..."

"Kāmalā and Halīmaka—thus Pāṇḍuroga is indeed remembered as being of eight types. However, another type of Kāmalā mentioned by Suśruta is distinct: "For he who suddenly eats sour food at the end of an illness, or even unwholesome things, his *pitta* makes the face especially pale (*pāṇḍu*), along with the previously mentioned lethargy and loss of strength" (Su.U.).

By such statements as these, the specific cause of *kāmalā* has been stated; likewise in the *Vāgbhaṭa*: "This [disease] may occur even in one with a predominance of *pitta*, even apart from *pāṇḍuroga*" (*Vā.

Thus [it is said]. However, in this context, jaundice (kāmalā) may occur even in one suffering from anemia (pāṇḍuroga), or it may occur even without anemia, just as carbuncles associated with urinary disorders (prameha) occur both in those with urinary disorders and without them. Similarly, although jaundice is described in relation to those with anemia, it also occurs independently, residing in either the visceral tract (koṣṭha) or the peripheral tissues (śākhā), characterized by an abundance of bile and preceded by anemia. Some maintain that the type which resides solely in the peripheral tissues and involves little bile should be considered independent; for this very reason, the author will later in the remainder of the chapter state its etiology and symptoms separately, beginning with the words "dry and cold" (rūkṣa-śīta).

By the term *bahupitta* (excessive bile), he indicates that the bile residing in the peripheral tissues (*śākhā*) is minimal. He will later state that the consumption of sour, pungent, and sharp substances is for the purpose of bringing the bile residing in the peripheral tissues into the visceral cavity (*koṣṭha*).
The term *kharībhūtā* means having become hardened;

*kumbhakāmalā* is the specific name for jaundice located in the visceral cavity according to its distinct stage. *Kumbha* refers to the visceral cavity; jaundice localized there is called *kumbhakāmalā*.
In this [disease], swelling is also a symptom;
for it is stated in the Suśruta-saṃhitā: "Its specific variety is indeed called Kumbhasāhvā; there is great swelling and a breaking pain in the joints" (Su.U.).
a.
44) Thus [ends] 34–38.
With the words beginning with "tatra" (therein), he describes the treatment.

By the term "ūrdhvānulomikaiḥ" (those that move upwards and downwards), the inclusion of both emesis (*vamana*) and purgation (*virecana*)—which respectively move [the doshas] upwards and downwards—is stated; for even in the case of *pāṇḍu* disease, he will later prescribe purgation in the passage beginning with, "In kaphaja *pāṇḍu*, however, one should take *harītakī* soaked in cow's urine."
"By those two" refers to anemia (pāṇḍuroga) and jaundice (kāmalā).
In the reading "for one whose internal organs have been purified by those two," "by those two" refers to emesis and purgation.
Regarding the phrase "specific [medicine]" and so forth, the specific medicinal formulations to be described right here for jaundice and anemia should be understood.
Regarding the passage beginning with *dāḍima*, it is stated that the *aṣṭamikā* consists of two *karṣas*.
For it has been said: "Two *suvarṇas* shall be half a *pala*; likewise, a *śukti* is also an *aṣṭamikā*" (Kāvyālaṅkāra 12).

A decoction should be prepared with one hundred *pathyā* fruits; for this purpose, water should be added such that when reduced to one-fourth, it becomes four times the quantity of the ghee. Therefore, one *droṇa* measure of water should be used along with fifty stalks of *pathyā* and fifty seeds of *harītakī*. Others, however, say that "stalks of *pathyā*" refers to the powder of the *harītakī* fruit itself, specifically that which is devoid of its stone.

In the case of *dantī* and others, a decoction of four times the amount of ghee should be prepared; for, according to the observation of other treatises, the decoction here is indeed of the measure of one *prastha*.
For it is stated elsewhere: "In a *prastha* of decoction from one *kuḍava* of *nikumbha*, [ghee] should be added along with its paste."
“One should cook one *prastha* of clarified butter [with these]; it cures splenic enlargement, jaundice, and anemia.
In the verse beginning with “purāṇa,” water is used as the liquid since no other liquid is specified.
In the case of the paste (kalka) consisting of half a prastha of grapes (drākṣā),
as in the formula beginning with "haridrā" and others, since no other liquid is mentioned, milk alone is used in a fourfold quantity.
Two akṣas of the paste of *dārvī* cooked in one prastha of buffalo ghee is to be administered;
in the case of "in a decoction of five palas of *dārvī*" as well, following the previous rule for ghee, the decoction of five palas of *dārvī* must likewise be made double the quantity of the ghee.
The paste of *kālīyaka* is also, as before, in the measure of two *akṣas*;

"the former" refers to the former [type of] jaundice (*pāṇḍuroga*). A *prastha* of ghee prepared with the paste of *dārvī* and cow's urine is for the former; however, for the latter, known as *kāmalā*, the "latter" is that prepared with the decoction of *dārvī* and the paste of *kālīyaka*. The word "should be given" is to be supplied [to complete the sense].
"Kāśmarya" refers to the fruit of Gambhārī;
"boiled" means it has been added according to the procedure for a *phāṇṭa* decoction. By the phrase "having crushed an *añjali* of grapes," he clearly indicates a *phāṇṭa* decoction.
In the case of "dviśarkara" (two parts sugar) and so forth, the powder of *trivṛt* weighing half a *pala*, when combined with two parts sugar, becomes one and a half *palas* in measure.

Regarding the phrase "moistened with cow’s urine" (*gomūtraklinnayuktām*), it means one should drink it after it has been moistened—that is, turned into a paste—with cow’s urine and likewise mixed and stirred with cow’s urine.

Others, however, apply the interpretation that one should drink *harītakī* with the juice of *āragvadha*; others apply the interpretation that one should drink *bilva* leaves with the juice of sugarcane and other such substances, along with the three pungents (*trikaṭu*).
Another interpretation is that one should drink *āragvadha* together with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*) with the juice of *vidārī* and *āmalaka*.
Regarding the verse beginning with "viśālā," the elders state that for a substance measured at one *pala* according to the method of a *phāṇṭa* decoction, four *palas* of liquid should be used.

"Nine parts of iron rust" means that the iron rust is ninefold in comparison to one part [of the other ingredients]; thus, the iron rust is equal in measure to the combined powder of the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa) and so forth.
*Maṇḍūra* is old iron dross (*lohakiṭṭa*).
Regarding the phrase beginning with "triphalā" and so forth, "silver dross" (raupyamala) should be understood as that which is the impurity (kiṭṭa) of silver.

Regarding "of *mākṣika*": there are five parts each of *mākṣika-dhātu* (bitumen), *aśmajatu*, and the other three [minerals]; or alternatively, five parts of *aśmajatu* and likewise of *rūpyamala*. The term "*rūpyamala*" is an epithet for *śilājatu*; therefore, that *śilājatu* which is described as having the form of silver-stain (*rūpyamala*) in the passage beginning with "the silver one is pungent" (*Ci. A. 1, pāda 3*), that is what is taken here. (80–86)
"Developed," and so forth; [the substances] have been developed for ten days in double and triple [quantities].

"By juices" means by decoctions of *kuṭaja* and other such herbs; here, the saturation (*bhāvanā*) should be performed according to the very same procedure prescribed for *śilājatu*. Regarding the quantity of the herb to be boiled and the amount of water, another treatise states: "The medicinal substance to be boiled should be equal in weight to the *girija*, and it should be boiled in four times that amount of water."
"When the decoction has been reduced to one-fourth, strained, and made lukewarm, one should add the mountain-born [gypsum];

once it has reached a state of equal flavor, one should again add the dried substance to the liquid. Thus, in other procedures for impregnation (*bhāvanā*) as well, the substances to be boiled and the resulting decoction are to be understood accordingly;
"one *pala* from fruits and roots" refers to one *pala* combined.

"By logic, 'the three aromatics' (trigandhaka) means that the amount of the three aromatics by which a good fragrance is produced should be understood as the measure for the three aromatics. And the three aromatics are said to be cinnamon leaf, cinnamon bark, and cardamom, according to the statement: 'The three aromatics are declared to be equal parts of cinnamon bark, cardamom, and cinnamon leaf; that same [mixture] with nutmeg is declared to be the four aromatics (cāturjāta).
In this context, the word 'defect' (*doṣa*), such as 'putridity' and so forth, is to be connected with each [of the preceding terms]."
In the passage beginning with "dvipalāṃśām" (87–99), *drākṣā* refers to one *prastha* of grapes, and *dhātrīphalarasaḥ* refers to the fresh juice of *dhātrī* fruits.
Twenty-eight palas of the trikaṭu group and other ingredients, with maṇḍūra in double that amount, result in a total powder measuring eighty-four palas.

Because of the reading "pṛthak" (separately), the maṇḍūra powder itself should be cooked separately in cow's urine; when that has been prepared, the powder of tryūṣaṇa and the other ingredients should be added.
By the word "śuddha" (purified), he indicates the purification of the maṇḍūra through processes such as heating and quenching it in cow's urine.
However, some say that eight times the amount of cow's urine should be used starting from the raw maṇḍūra itself; this latter view appears to be the correct one.
Regarding the passage "sixteen palas from the seed" (102–104), some read it as "twice eight palas of seed" (*dvirbījakapalāny aṣṭau*); even there, the meaning remains the same.
Bījaka, asana, vyāghranakha, and the two types of nakhī— these,
having been kept for twenty nights during the two winter seasons (śiśira), [are used].
In the passage beginning with "dhātrī," the fresh juice of two thousand *dhātrī* fruits should be taken.
For those afflicted by jaundice (kāmalā), the juice of grapes and emblic myrobalan (mṛdvīkāmalakīrasa) is recommended for both drink and food; this is the meaning.
By the phrase "that which is to be conceptualized," he states the procedure for conceptualization, beginning with "in the vātika," and so forth.
With the words beginning "nipātayet," he describes the treatment for jaundice caused by earth-eating.
"Grassland" refers to *dūrvā* grass;
"of one who is attached" means one who does not turn away from eating earth.
"Cultivated" means refined by substances that destroy those defects.
The passage ending with "or even with *mūrvā*" is connected with what precedes it (verses 117–122).
He extends by analogy the specific treatment for the doshas mentioned in the section on anemia (pāṇḍuroga) to jaundice (mṛjjī) as well: "according to the dosha," etc.;
"this" refers to what was stated regarding anemia.
With the verse beginning "resembling sesame paste," etc., he describes the treatment for *kāmalā* (jaundice) localized in the peripheral tissues (*śākhā*), preceded by its symptoms.

Regarding the phrase "the path obstructed by phlegm" (*śleṣmaṇā ruddhamārgam*): it means that the *pitta* residing in the peripheral tissues, which causes *kāmalā*, has its path blocked by the phlegm located in the visceral cavity (*koṣṭha*); that is to say, its path toward the visceral cavity is prohibited.
This very point is explained in detail by the passage beginning with "rough" (rūkṣa) and so forth.

Regarding the term "white-stool" (śvetavarcas): due to the outward discharge of the bile residing in the digestive tract (koṣṭha), which colors the feces, the phlegm (śleṣman) increases and the stool becomes white;
this occurs gradually and is associated with the conclusion of the fever.
The connection is that [this occurs] when pitta is diminished and located in the peripheral tissues (śākhā).

With the verse beginning with *barhi* and so forth, [the author] describes a balanced treatment that alleviates *kapha* while increasing *pitta*, because the increase of the *doṣas* residing in the peripheral tissues (*śākhā*) is for the purpose of bringing them into the visceral cavity (*koṣṭha*). For it has been said: "By means of their increase, by moistening, by suppuration, by the cleansing of the openings of the channels, and by the suppression of the *vāyu*, the impurities (*malas*), leaving the peripheral tissues, move toward the visceral cavity" (Sūtra-sthāna 28).

As long as the impurity located in the path of the digestive tract (koṣṭha) is not colored by the bile from the point of its origin down to the feces, it is called "pitta-increasing" in the first stage, as previously stated.
"The procedure is for those with *kāmalika*" means that the treatment for impurities residing in the digestive tract (*koṣṭha*) should be performed.
With the words beginning with *yadā*, he describes *halīmaka*.
This very condition is called by the name *lāghavaka* and the name *alasa* in other tantras;
for it is stated in the *Suśruta*: "Accompanied by fever, body ache, vertigo, burning sensation, drowsiness, and emaciation, one is characterized by lightness and laziness."

"Some describe that [condition], which is yellowish-green or blue due to wind and bile, as *halīmaka*" (Suśruta Uttara-tantra 44). Furthermore, the loose stools mentioned therein are merely a stage of jaundice (*kāmalā*) and not a separate disease;
for it is stated in another treatise: "There is a burning sensation, loose stools, and swelling both externally and internally..."
"Pallor and redness of the eyes are considered the characteristics of a drink-addict.
With the verse beginning "guḍūcī" and so forth, he describes the treatment for *halīmaka*,

as well as the previously mentioned *drākṣāleha* (grape electuary), which was described in the text beginning with "two-pala portions of *tugākṣīrī*" and so on; furthermore, the *yāpanā-bastis* (sustaining enemas) are those explained in the *Siddhisthāna*.
The Kāsika and Abhayāleha preparations consist of Agastyaharītakī.
He states the summary with the words "of the fivefold Pāṇḍu," and that is indeed manifest.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Anemia," in the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of Caraka, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Chapter 17 of the Cikitsāsthāna (83 of 120)]
Because hiccup and dyspnea have pāṇḍuroga as their cause, they are mentioned immediately after pāṇḍuroga;
for it will be stated: "These two diseases proceed from pāṇḍuroga and indeed from poison.
Furthermore, because hiccup and dyspnea share the same causes and require the same treatment, they are both described in a single chapter.
"One who knows the reality of the meaning of both the Vedic and the worldly" means one who knows the reality of the purpose of the Vedas and the world;

"of two kinds" refers to the distinction between the general and the specific, or alternatively, the distinction between the mild and the harsh, and the distinction between one's own and what belongs to others.
The "three humors" (tridoṣa) refer to wind (vāta) and the others, whether individually or combined;
"three types of provocation" refers to those caused by unwholesome contact with sense objects, improper digestion, and intellectual error;
and "at will" (kāmam) signifies consent.
"Many" refers to conditions such as fever, śaṅkhaka, rohiṇī, and so forth; by the phrase "as well as asthma and hiccup," he demonstrates that hiccup and asthma are swift destroyers of life.
"At the end" means at the time of death.
"Arises" means that one of the two—hiccup or dyspnea—necessarily arises.

By the phrase "originating from the seat of pitta," he demonstrates that there is only a connection with the upper seats of pitta, and not its acting as an initiator in the same manner as vāta and kapha; by the term "seat of pitta," the *āmāśaya* (stomach) is intended.
"They are common" means that for the most part they require similar treatment;

like two venomous serpents (*āśīviṣa*), meaning two snakes whose very glance or breath is poisonous, even another disease kills when approached with false [treatment]. Thus, by the analogy of the venomous serpent here, he indicates the quality of being a swift killer when there is improper treatment.
"Separately" means individually in each of the fivefold groups of diseases, as stated in the chapter on the eight types of abdominal enlargements (*aṣṭodarīya*).

In this context, the section beginning with "rajasā" and ending with "pravartete gadāvimau" enumerates, for the most part, the group of factors that provoke *vāta*; the section beginning with "niṣpāva" and so forth describes the group of causes that provoke *kapha* as the cause of *hikkā* and *śvāsa*. By thus presenting these two distinct groups of causes—one generating *vāta* and the other generating *kapha*—the author demonstrates that *vāta* and *kapha* here exist independently by being provoked by their own respective causes, rather than existing in a state of secondary association (*anubandha*). [Verses 10–16] He explains the pathogenesis [of the disease] starting with "mārutaḥ prāṇavāhīni... and so forth.

This is the common pathogenesis (samprāpti) of both hiccup (hikkā) and dyspnea (śvāsa); he will describe the specific [pathogenesis] later with the words "obstructing the vital breath" (prāṇoparodha), which means "generally fatal to life" (prāyaḥ prāṇaharaṇāya). Regarding the phrase "five and five," it means there are five types of hiccups and five types of dyspneas.

17— The premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa) of hiccups, characterized by the grasping of specific signs, are described by [the verse beginning with] “In the throat and chest” (kaṇṭhorasoḥ), etc.; those of dyspnea (śvāsa) are described by [the verse beginning with] “Distension” (ānāhaḥ), etc.
"Vilomatva" means confusion or disorder.
From verse 18 to 20, [the author] describes the specific pathogenesis of hiccups beginning with "prāṇodaka... and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "whose flesh, strength, vitality, and luster are exhausted": here, *prāṇa* refers to the vital breath (*vāyu*) or energy (*utsāha*), while *tejas* refers to fire (*agni*).
One should apply the term "loudly" (*uccaiḥ*) to the phrase "having grasped the resonant [vowel]";
it makes [the mantra] twice-continuous, thrice-continuous, or possessed of many qualities. In that context, "twice-continuous" means it occurs twice in a single commencement.
"Having obstructed the heat" means the heat of the body;
"one whose delirium consists of faltering speech" refers to one whose prattle is characterized by stammering;
"having a great root" means having its root in the defects of the profound substratum.

Although "having a great sound" (*mahāśabdatva*) has already been expressed by the phrase "possessing a loud resonance" (*uccairghoṣavatī*), it is repeated here for the purpose of providing the specific designation "great hiccup" (*mahāhikkā*). Therefore, the designation is "great hiccup.
In that context, *hikkā* refers to that which "utters" (*kāyati*) the sound "hi," i.e., makes the sound "hi."
"Resounding deeply" means making a deep sound following the hiccup;
"contracting the limbs" is to be supplied [to complete the sense].
It is designated as "deep" (*gambhīrā*) because it arises from a deep location.
"Vyapetā" means "matured" (pariṇatā).

"At the end of the transformation of food" (āhārapariṇāmānte) means when the transformation of food has occurred. By this, it is shown that [the sensation] arises even during the digestion of food and becomes powerful at its conclusion; he indicates that state by the designation "vyapetā."
"Vināmin" means that which causes the body to bend;
"asantata" means not too long.
With the words beginning with "kṣudra," he describes minor hiccups (*kṣudrahikkā*).
"Kṣudravāta" means a small amount of wind (*alpavāta*); some say that "kṣudravāta" refers to the *udāna* wind.
The connection is that for one who is "exerting" (*āyasyataḥ*), meaning performing physical exertion, [the hiccups] become mild (*mārdavaṃ yāti*).

Since it ceases from the very same cause from which it previously arose, it is such that while it is being produced, its momentum is already ceasing; it does not persist in a continuous succession like a great hiccup (mahāhikkā). It ceases from the very same cause of its production, such as physical exertion (vyāyāma), because the subtle wind (vāta) that generates the hiccup is dispersed by such exertion, thereby breaking the pathogenesis (samprāpti). Because it is generated by a subtle wind, it is called "minor" (kṣudrā) hiccup.
With the words beginning with "sahasā," he describes that which is born of food (*annajā*).

Although this [fever] has been called "born of food," it is nonetheless produced solely by the humors (*doṣa*) and so forth; nevertheless, because food is stated to be its cause in the phrase "afflicted by drink and food," it receives the designation "born of food."
With the words beginning with "atītya" (38–41), he states the distinction between those who are curable and those who are incurable;
one for whom the humors (*doṣas*) have been excessively accumulated is described as such.

Regarding the phrase "of one emaciated by the cutting off of food" (*bhaktacchedakṛśasya*), this refers to a person who is weak from fasting and possesses the symptoms described in the passage beginning with "the hiccup among these five... That [hiccup] destroys life.

Furthermore, by the term *yamikā*, it should be understood that the minor (*kṣudrā*) and food-born (*annajā*) types, which were previously stated to be curable, become *yamikā* when they arise with a dual force (*yamalavega*). That which arises with the force mentioned previously is the *mahāhikkā*; it is incurable by its very nature, and thus the prescription of its incurability through the application of the symptoms beginning with "excessive... is redundant.

Likewise, the three types of hiccups beginning with *mahā-hikkā* are curable when their symptoms are incomplete; however, the two minor types (*kṣudrā* and *annajā*) are curable even when their symptoms are complete. The triad beginning with *mahā-hikkā* is incurable by its very nature. Others, however, say that even *mahā-hikkā* and the others can sometimes indeed be cured; in that regard, the statement "fatal" was spoken with the intention that they generally take away life. For instance, Jatūkarṇa states: "The first [type] is difficult to cure; *yamikā* takes away life immediately for those suffering from thirst and delusion; and *gambhīrā* [is fatal] when the [other] signs have departed."
"Unwasted" means one whose flesh is not wasted (42–44).
With the words "When," etc., he describes the onset of dyspnea.
"Channels" (srotāṃsi) refers, by virtue of the context, to the channels that carry breath and water;
"preceded by phlegm" means dominated by phlegm; "it moves in all directions" means it spreads everywhere.
With the words "being tossed upward" (*uddhūyamāna*) and so forth, he describes the characteristics of the great breath (*mahāśvāsa*):
"being tossed upward" means the wind being blown upwards.
"Highly" means long; "intoxicated bull" means a rutting ox;
"miserable" means like one who is wretched.

Or there is the reading “*dīnaṃ praśvasitam*”; for in that case, if the exhalation were feeble (*dīnatve*), what he will say later—that it is “perceived from afar”—would be untenable. With the words beginning with “long” (*dīrgham*), etc., he describes upward breathing (*ūrdhvaśvāsa*).
He breathes long, making the outward movement of the breath last for a long time, and does not draw it back downward; thus he does not lead the breath down,
like a "malicious wind" or a corrupted air.
He states the reason for the long-term upward expulsion and downward drawing back of the breath with the passage beginning "In *ūrdhvaśvāsa*," etc. (verses 49–51).
Then, with the passage beginning "But he who," etc., he describes the characteristics of *chinnaśvāsa*.
He breathes with interruptions; having sighed, he breathes again after a moment, or perhaps he does not breathe at all— he finds no breath,
for there is a pain like the severing of his vital organs.
"Obstruction of the bladder" means obstruction of urine;
"redness of one eye" here [is mentioned] due to the influence of the disease;
"severed" means having the joints and bonds loosened.
These three types of breathlessness (śvāsa) are incurable by their very nature (52–54).
With the verse beginning "pratilomam" and so forth, [the author] describes *tamaka-śvāsa*.

By the phrase "having provoked the phlegm," the author indicates that although phlegm was already mentioned as part of the general pathogenesis (*samprāpti*), it is stated here again to show its specific causality in this case.
"Gurgling" (*ghurghuruka*) refers to a gurgling sound in the throat;
"is completely obstructed" (*sannirudhyate*) means it becomes motionless.
And for that very [phlegm], the word “of phlegm” (śleṣmaṇaḥ) is to be supplied as the remainder; “seated” means sitting down;
“with eyes bulging” means with swollen eyes.
"And it is repeatedly blown upon" means it is blown upon moment by moment by the breath-wind (śvasana-vāyu).
(55–62) Showing that *tamaka* itself receives the designation *pratamaka* due to its connection with *pitta* and the occurrence of fever and other symptoms, he says: "In fever," and so forth.
With the words beginning "udāvarta," he describes the causes and symptoms of *pratamaka*;
indeed, *pratamaka* is the same as *santamaka*.
*Rajas* means dust; *kāyanirodha* is the suppression of natural urges. Alternatively, it refers to one whose body is moistened (*klinnakāya*) or aged, and *nirodha* is the suppression of urges.
"By *tamas*" means by darkness; or alternatively, by *tamas* as the *tamas* quality (*guṇa*).

Although it has been stated that *tamaka* increases due to cold, nevertheless, because *pratamaka* is associated with *pitta*, what was said—that "it is quickly pacified by cold things"—is thus justified. Alternatively, just as liquor is the pacifier for a disorder arising from liquor, so too should it be understood that even for that which arises from cold, there is pacification by cold things at that very moment.
Since *pratamaka* is merely a variety of *tamaka*, the established number of five types of dyspnea (*śvāsa*) is maintained.
With the words beginning with *rūkṣa*, he describes *kṣudraśvāsa* (minor dyspnea): that which has its origin (*udbhava*) from dryness (*rūkṣa*) and exertion (*āyāsa*) is *rūkṣāyāsodbhava*.
"Minor wind" (*kṣudravāta*) means slight wind; "not excessive" means it does not cause extreme suffering; "not painful" means it is not curable by painful means.

By the statement "and all [of them] have unmanifest characteristics," he establishes that the curability of the major dyspnea (*mahāśvāsa*) and other conditions mentioned as being to be cured exists only in a state distinct from that in which all their characteristics are manifest.
Life-threatening conditions such as *mahāśvāsa* (dyspnea) and others exhibiting complete symptoms should be rejected;
the use of the plural number in "curable" (*sādhya*) and "manageable" (*yāpya*) should be understood as referring to the multiplicity of sub-classifications within those categories.
Now, demonstrating how the treatment for hiccup (hikkā) and dyspnea (śvāsa) is the same even though they are distinct, he states the common treatment beginning with "kāraṇa" and so forth:
"kāraṇa" refers to external causes; "sthāna" refers to locations such as the navel; "mūla" refers to the doshas;
and "snigdhaiḥ" is an adjective qualifying "svedaiḥ" (by oleaginous sudations); others, however, read it as "snigdham" (oleaginous).
"Lavaṇataila" means salted oil.
Regarding the phrase "in the groves," it refers to the branches;
and in the phrase "of fish and so forth," the juice (rasa) or fresh extract of the fish and other such ingredients should be prepared with a paste (kalka).
Curd-whey (*dadhisara*) is curd with a high water content;

such food is prescribed for the purpose of increasing phlegm (*kapha*), which is conducive to emesis, for it has been said: "One who has a predominance of phlegm vomits without difficulty" (Sūtra-sthāna 1).
By the term "not antagonistic to wind" (vātāvirodhī), he prohibits dry food and sharp emetics; "one whose composition is corrupted" means one whose structural integrity is impaired. 70–76.
He describes smoking for the purpose of removing residual morbid humors (doṣas) remaining after emesis with the verse beginning "līna" and so forth.
By this, it is established that smoking should indeed be administered even without emesis when the morbid humor is slight; for in that case as well, the specific indications for smoking still exist.
Enough with the yellow orpiment (haritāla).
The smoking wick (dhūmavarti) for this [condition] should be prepared according to the procedure for smoking wicks described in the eighty [chapter].

In this context, they maintain that the measurement of the smoking pipe (dhūmapānanalikā) should be the same as that of the smoking pipe prescribed for curing cough, which will be described later; for hiccup (hikkā) and dyspnea (śvāsa) are also similar to cough.
Madhūcchiṣṭa is beeswax (sikthaka).

Furthermore, although not explicitly mentioned here, an opening should be made at the top of the hollowed-out coconut shell (*mallakasampuṭa*) for the purpose of inhaling and exhaling smoke; this applies to the *padmaka* and other vessels as well, following the description of the "coconut shell" and so forth.
The *vardhamāna* is an *eraṇḍa* (castor oil plant) vessel.
Loha, agaru,
and śallakī are known by their own names [77–80].
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "by cold and so forth," there is the inclusion of things that remove *pitta* (bile) and things that are slimy (*picchila*), and so on.
