With the words beginning with "vividham," he provides the answers to the questions in their respective order.
It is called *visarpa* because it spreads (*sarpati*) in various ways—downward, upward, and horizontally—and because it extends through eruptions, swellings, and so forth.
He explains the meaning of the term *parisarpa* with the passage beginning "or else, *parisarpa*," and so on.

"Paritaḥ" means "from all sides"; the word *pari* has the sense of "everywhere. Alternatively, by the word *parisarpaṇa*, mere crawling (*sarpaṇa*) is expressed, while the meaning of the word *pari* is explained by the word *sarvataḥ*; therefore, it is said: "because of crawling from all sides.
[The phrase] "sevenfold due to the defects" means that it becomes sevenfold according to the different types of defects.
By this, he shows that a distinction between curable and incurable [diseases] is also possible for this [treatment],
and by the passage beginning with "separately" (pṛthak), he demonstrates its sevenfold nature as specified.
With the words beginning with "blood" (*rakta*), he clarifies the sevenfold nature of the *dhātus*.

Although the presence of blood and other *doṣas* exists in *kuṣṭha*, nevertheless, *visarpas* are produced by *doṣas* characterized by spreading (*visarpaṇaśīla*), whereas *kuṣṭhas* arise from *doṣas* that act slowly; this and more should be followed as explained in detail in the *Kuṣṭha-cikitsita*.

Regarding the statement "the three *doṣas* are the impurities" (*malāḥ*), although the term *doṣa* itself already implies *vāta* and the others, the word "impurities" (*malāḥ*) is stated to demonstrate their quality of defiling the body through extreme corruption.

And it is said elsewhere: "Because they corrupt the body they are *doṣas*, because they cause impurity they are *malas*, and because they sustain [the body] they are *dhātus*; thus there are three: wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*kapha*). (15)
The answer to the question "By what causes does it arise? is as follows: "Salty, sour," and so forth.

Regarding the term "of hot things" (*uṣṇānām*), this refers to those with a hot potency (*uṣṇavīrya*). Although substances such as rock salt (*saindhava*) and *āmalaka* are salty, sour, and pungent, they are classified here as "hot" because their potency is hot.
Regarding the term "of green things" (*haritānām*), this refers to substances such as fresh ginger (*ārdraka*) and others listed in the category of green vegetables (*haritaśākavarga*).
*Kūrcikā* refers to curd-cream (*dadhi-kūrcikā*) and buttermilk-cream (*takra-kūrcikā*). *Kilāṭa* is a lump of spoiled milk. *Mandaka* refers to curd that has been produced slowly;
*śāṇḍākipūrva* refers to those who have previously prepared *śāṇḍākī* (fermented curd).

"Eating during indigestion" (*ajīrṇāśana*) means eating while one has indigestion, or alternatively, eating food that has not yet been digested (*apariṇata*). "Eating in between" (*adhyāśana*) refers to eating during the day before it has been properly processed (*avidagdha*).
[The term] *vyāmiśra* means mixed or combined.

He states [the symptoms] such as "residing in the branches" (*śākhāśritatva*) for the purpose of knowing the distinction between curable and incurable cases—beginning with "externally," etc., in increasing order.
The meaning is that one residing internally is more serious than one residing externally, and one residing in both is more serious than one residing internally.
"Internally" means within the body; "externally" means in the branches; it "creeps" (*sarpati*).

He describes the characteristics of *visarpa* (erysipelas) regarding the intermediate substratum (*antarāśraya*) and so forth: "Due to injury to the vital points" (*marmopaghātāt*), etc.; here, "vital point" (*marman*) refers to the heart.
"One should know [the disease] by its specific characteristics" refers to the characteristics of visarpa (erysipelas) that will be described hereafter (verses 26–27).
"Of whom all [characteristics]" refers to the characteristics of visarpa affecting both the internal substratum and the external substratum.
With the words "by dry and hot [substances]," etc., he states the characteristic of the individual causes.

In this context, it should be understood that Vāyu is independent when provoked by dry substances and the like, whereas it is dependent when provoked by the obstruction of the channels due to filling [the body with food].
Although heat (*uṣṇa*) does not directly generate wind (*vāta*), nevertheless, through its association with dryness (*rūkṣa*), heat produces wind;

it should be understood that the *pitta* produced here is that which has attained the state of being associated with heat through general acquisition (*sāmānyasamprāpti*). "Burning sensation" (*davathu*) refers to excessive heating of the eyes and other organs; and although burning sensation is generally of the nature of *pitta*, in this context it arises from the presence of *pitta* and blood (*rakta*) spreading according to the rule of *visarpa*.
With the words beginning with "pittam" (29–30), he describes the Pitta-type [visarpa].

Although the phrase "filling the vessels" is mentioned specifically in the context of the Pitta-type, nevertheless, according to the maxim that "a rule stated in one instance regarding similar matters should be applied elsewhere as well," it should be understood to apply to the other types of visarpa as well.
And this same procedure, because visarpas are dominated by pitta, has been described under the treatment of pitta disorders;
[it applies to] thirst for cold wind and cold water, in a place characterized by cold wind and water.
With the verse beginning "sweet and sour" (*svādvamla*), etc., he describes the type caused by *kapha*.
Although other causes of *śleṣman* (phlegm) are present, sweet and other tastes are specifically mentioned because these [tastes] are generally the generators of *visarpa* (erysipelas).
In this way, even when the causes that generate wind (vāta) and bile (pitta) have been stated, it should be described as follows:
the painful condition spreads rapidly through the limbs, yet it does not spread throughout the entire body;
it is cold and feels chilly.

"Upward" means from that time onward; or else, "in the upper body," because phlegm remains only in the upper part of the body. "Spread like a net" means as if spread with a net; "adherent" means persisting for a long time.
With the verse beginning "Vāta and pitta" (33–34), he describes the characteristics of agnivisarpa;
"mutually having gained strength" means that vāta and pitta have increased their respective potencies through one another.
"Having the appearance of extinguished embers" means black, like the embers of nirvāṇa;
"from its place" means from its upward position; "to move" means to go.
By the phrase "of this kind," the state of *agnivisarpa* to be described as curable by the passage beginning with "when the vital point (*marman*) is not impaired" (vv. 35–36) is established;
and by the passage beginning with "kapha-pitta... (v. 37), he describes *kardamavisarpa*.
The meaning is that it spreads to the stomach (āmāśaya) because *kardama* is produced by *kapha* and *pitta*, and both *kapha* and *pitta* reside in the stomach;
"alasaka" refers to a slow-spreading [disease] that affects only one part and does not pervade the entire body.
*Malinaḥ* means smeared with impurities; *maladigdhaḥ* means the same; *stimitavedanaḥ* means having dull pain, that is, mild pain; *gambhīrapākaḥ* means internal suppuration.
"Provides an interval" means it grants space;
because of its similarity to mud (*kardama*), it should be known by the name *kardama*.

One should recognize that as incurable when it is enveloped by the spreading of *kardama* and possesses all the aforementioned characteristics; one should know *kardama* to be untreatable. However, he will indeed describe the treatment for cases where the characteristics are incomplete.
With the words beginning with "sthira" (37–38), he describes *granthivisarpa* (granuloma-visarpa);
"duṣṭapravṛddhau" means that they have increased by way of mutually corrupting one another.

"Difficult to ripen and difficult to cure" means both that which is difficult to ripen and that which is difficult to cure. "Difficulty in ripening" should be understood as occurring after a long time due to the ripening process.
Regarding the phrase "of one with increased blood," this refers to one whose blood has increased;

it should be connected with the statement that [the humors] produce a glandular erysipelas (*granthivisarpa*) in the vessels, ligaments, flesh, and so forth. Therefore, the meaning is that they produce a glandular erysipelas, which serves as the substrate for glands characterized by intense pain and other such symptoms.

"Due to that affliction" means that because of the pain caused by that *granthivisarpa*, one transcends the scope of all medical treatments; the meaning is that it has passed beyond the domain of all therapeutic interventions.
Furthermore, by the word "sa" (that), the *granthivisarpa* as described here, specifically when accompanied by the aforementioned complications (*upadrava*), is being referred to.
And they say that this *granthivisarpa* is described under the name *apacī* in other treatises (39).

Because *visarpas* have many complications (*upadrava*), he explains the nature of these complications right here as a supplementary discussion, beginning with "The complication, however," and so forth.

The word *tu* (but/however) serves to exclude the primary disease (*mūlavyādhi*). Alternatively, the word *tu* indicates that [the secondary symptom] arises after the onset of the disease, meaning it arises during the middle stage of the disease; by this, the symptoms that arise simultaneously with the disease are excluded.

Furthermore, those symptoms which sometimes arise after the onset of the disease are not strictly "arising after the disease" because they generally arise together with the disease; therefore, they do not possess the status of a secondary complication (*upadrava*).
"Having the disease as its substratum" (*rogāśraya*) means that because it is produced by the provocation of the *doṣas* that initiate the disease, it shares the same causes as the disease itself.

By this, he excludes the status of being a complication (*upadrava*) for fevers and other conditions arising from their own specific causes after a goiter (*galagaṇḍa*) has developed, even though they occur subsequent to the primary disease.

By the phrase "the disease itself" (*roga eva*), he indicates that what is designated by the term "disease" separately from the root disorder is a complication; thereby, he distinguishes it from the state of the disease that arises subsequent to the primary disease.

Consequently, there is an exclusion of that state of swelling which takes the form of an ulcer, as well as an exclusion of all states of disease characterized by their specific symptoms; for a state of disease, being inevitable, is essentially identical in nature to the primary disease itself, whereas a complication (upadrava) is not necessarily present.

Although some diseases arising from the fault of great strength (*mahābala*) are produced only as accompanied by complications (*upadrava*), and there is no sense of "complication" for that which is co-arisen (*sahotpanna*), nevertheless, those ailments that arise in the form of complications are called "complications" there by way of their functional suitability (*yogyatā*), even though they are co-arisen.

In the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), however, those existing together are not characterized by the definition of a complication; rather, they arise therein as a mixture of diseases (*rogasaṅkara*).

Suśruta himself provides the definition of this characteristic of complications (*upadrava*): "In that regard, the so-called *aupasargika* [complication] is that disease which, arising at a later time, afflicts a disease that has previously arisen; it is designated as a complication precisely because it is rooted in that [primary disease]" (Su.Sū.A. 35). Thus he describes the type of complication. By the words "whether gross or subtle," he states the etymological derivation of the term "complication" (*upadrava*). By the phrase "it arises afterwards," he explains the designation "complication."

By this, the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) is established: it is called *upadrava* because it "approaches" (*upaiti*) in the vicinity of the emergence of the primary disease (*vyādhi*). Thus, it is subordinate to the disease; the meaning is that it is secondary (*apradhāna*) in relation to the root disease.
He states the reason for its being subordinate: "For the most part, its subsidence occurs upon the subsidence of the primary [disease]."

The meaning is that because the alleviation of a complication (*upadrava*) is dependent upon the alleviation of the primary disease (*mūlavyādhi*), the complication is not primary. By using the word "mostly" (*prāyas*), which implies occasional exceptions, it is stated that in some cases there is an independent treatment for the complication.
Explaining the fact that a complication must be treated promptly, he says: "But that... and so forth.

The ablative case in "vyādhiparikliṣṭaśarīratvāt" (because of the body being afflicted by disease) is used in the sense of separation (*digyoge*); thus, the meaning of the sentence is that [the secondary disorder] becomes more painful because it arises subsequently in one already afflicted by disease.
He concludes with "tasmāt" and so forth:
"one should treat it with haste" means one should treat it urgently; and it has already been stated that such treatment, by pacifying the primary disease, also becomes independent.
40. Now he describes the *sannipāta-visarpa* that has been introduced: "arising from all [the causes]," etc., meaning it arises from all causes.
"Pervading all *liṅgas*" means it possesses all the characteristics mentioned for [diseases] such as Vāta and the others.
"Following all the *dhātus*" demonstrates that it takes as its substratum not only the *dhātus* mentioned as the basis for *visarpa*, but also those not mentioned;

for indeed, in another treatise, it is stated that *masūrikā*, which is itself a form of *visarpa*, has its substratum in all the *dhātus*. Thus, by general rule, due to the excessive vitiation of the *doṣas*, the vitiation of the seven *dhātus* and other *dhātus* also occurs in cases of *visarpa*.
Regarding 'the vital points' (marman): this refers to the primary vital points such as the heart.
Regarding 'by means of common activities': this refers to activities that are identical for both types of initiating faults."
"Being practiced" (*abhyasyamānau*) means being constantly administered.

"Commenced with neglect" (*anādaropakrānta*) means commenced improperly. By this, it is distinguished from the previous case where there was no treatment at all, in which the state of being a killer was stated by the rule: "those who kill when [the disease] has not been treated" (*Sūtra* 18); here, however, the distinction is that it refers to improper treatment.
There, with the words "of those to be treated" and so forth, he describes the treatment;
*ullekhana* means emesis (*vamana*).
"Located in the seat of *kapha*" refers to the upper body;
"by virtue of being the seat of *pitta*" refers to the middle part of the body; and by the term "abode of *māruta*," the lower part of the body below the colon (*pakvāśaya*) is understood.

Regarding the phrase "bitter ghee is recommended for *vāta*-predominant [fevers] and for *pitta*-type [fevers] when the doshas are light," the word division is as follows: "when the doshas are light" applies to both the *vāta*-predominant and the *pitta*-type cases. Therefore, it should be construed as: "for the *pitta*-type [fever] when the doshas are light."
"Because it has many defects" means "because it has much bile," since bile is the subject under discussion;

"by that" refers to the non-purgative ghee (*avirecanaghṭa*). "For that is designated as its substrate" means that blood is stated to be the substratum (*āśraya*) of this erysipelas (*visarpa*); therefore, by means of bloodletting, through the destruction of the substratum, the destruction of the erysipelas occurs—this is the meaning.
"Vyāsataḥ" means in detail; "kaphapittaje" refers to [fevers] arising from phlegm and bile, whether they arise from phlegm and bile individually or combined.
50–53. The *kirātatiktādi* decoction compound is also prepared by that same method— that is, by the method for decoctions as described in the *mustādi* compound.
"Left overnight" means a cold decoction (*śītakaṣāya*);
and this procedure for a cold decoction is also to be applied in the case of *paṭola* and so forth.
"With split lentils" means with the split pieces of lentils (*masūra*); and here, *vidalā* does not refer to the plant *śyāmā*, because that word is feminine.

Regarding the passage beginning with "triphalārasa" (the juice of the three myrobalans) and so forth: ghee mixed in equal parts with the juice of the three myrobalans and other ingredients should be administered to one with a "heavy bowel" (*gurukoṣṭha*), meaning one with a hard or rough bowel (*krūrakoṣṭha*); others say that a "heavy bowel" refers to a bowel filled with morbid humors (*doṣa*).
Regarding the phrase "when the doṣa has further entered the gastrointestinal tract" (doṣe koṣṭhagate bhūyaḥ), the word *bhūyas* here signifies "mostly" or "generally.
He describes the treatment when the blood is vitiated by defects residing in the peripheral tissues (*śākhā*): "When the blood is vitiated in the *śākhā*s," and so forth.

Regarding the specific method for bloodletting when the blood is vitiated in the *śākhā*s according to the particular humor (*doṣa*), he says: "Accompanied by Vāta," and so forth. The detailed procedure for bloodletting is not stated here because it falls under another section; that should be understood from the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*.
"According to proximity" means that one should pierce the vein which is closest to the site of the disorder;
and venesection is common to all [therapies].
Regarding the fault in not extracting blood, he says: "Skin, flesh," and so forth.
"In the case of one who is thoroughly purified" means by means of purgation and bloodletting;
"from the very beginning" means at the very moment of birth.
"External" refers to ointments, sprinklings, and so forth;
"nyagrodha-pādas" are the aerial roots of the *vaṭa* tree; "kadalī-garbha" is the *kadalī* plant while it is still within its sheath.
*Kāleya* is known as *kāleyaka-kāṣṭha*;
*hema* is the powder of *nāgakeśara*;
and *vanya* is *kaivartamustaka*.
Śādvala grass, durvā grass, lotus stalk, uśīra root, vīrā, and vidārī tuber.
Hareṇu is the round pea;
white rice refers to unhusked white grains;
and dugdhikā is well known by its own name.
*Mṛṇāla*, *padmanālikā*, *vṛṣakarṇī*, *mūṣikaparṇikā*,
*kākāhvā*, and *kāṣṭhodumbarikā*.
The analysis of the compound is: *indrāṇī*, *nirguṇḍī*, and *balāghṛta*.
*Plakṣa* is the *parkaṭī* tree, which has small, long leaves.

Some maintain that by the phrase "other plasters," it is indicated that the previously mentioned plasters are also beneficial when associated with *kapha*. We, however, observe that the word "other" (*aparān*) is used in relation to the previously mentioned plasters; therefore, we conclude that those previously mentioned plasters have different indications and do not apply to *kapha*.
[The herbs are: *anantā*, *utpala*, *sārivā*, *kuraṇṭaka*, and *amlānaka*.
*Śleṣmātaka* is well known as *bahuvāraka*;
some say *indrāṇīśāka* is *matsyākṣaka*, while others say it is *nirguṇḍī*; and *gandhapriyaṅgu* is simply *priyaṅgu*.
The phrase "śevālam" and so forth represents a combination both distributive and collective;
thus, "all these" refers to the plasters (pradehas) prescribed for kapha.

Regarding the statement "in cases where vāta and pitta are predominant," although plasters are not explicitly prescribed for vāta-predominance, it should be understood that those prescribed for blood-bile (raktapitta) or for kapha—provided they are observed to be composed of vāta-alleviating substances after considering the properties of the ingredients—are the ones to be employed in such cases.
The cream of ghee (*ghṛtamaṇḍa*), the surface-scum of ghee (*ghṛtasantānikā*), and that which arises on top of ghee (*ghṛtoparibhavā*).

Regarding the five barks (*pañcavalka*), it is stated in another treatise: "When the barks of all [the following]—*nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, and *vetasa*—are combined together in one place, it is called the 'five barks'. Thus it is said.

Others, however, prescribe *gandhamuṇḍa* in place of *vetasa* here; one should employ the very substances mentioned for the external application (*pradeha*) also for the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*), the preparation of ghee, and the dusting of the wound (*vraṇāvacūrṇana*).

Regarding the verse beginning with *dārvī*, "this is the washing" means that a decoction for the purpose of washing should be prepared from these *dārvī* and other ingredients; likewise, the ghee should be prepared with these same ingredients, and a powder should be made for application as a paste (*pralepana*).

*Samprasādanāḥ* means those which effect normalization (*savarṇakarāḥ*); the meaning is that they should be applied when normalization is to be achieved. Alternatively, *samprasādanāḥ* refers to the clearing of blood-bile (*raktapitta-prasādanāḥ*). Therefore, this is the meaning: these applications for blood-bile that have been described as to be performed should be used by removing the previous application at every moment, neither after a long time nor over the previous application.

When the previous application has been removed while still in a non-dry state, numerous thick and thin applications should be made. Regarding the specific procedure for kapha-pastes, he says "they should be applied," and so forth; "removed after drying" means removed once it has become dry.
Having described the medicines from verses 98 to 107, he speaks of food and drink, beginning with "annapānāni" and so forth;
"jīrṇe" means when the food in the form of an electuary (*avalehikā*) has been digested.

In the passage beginning with "of wild animals" (*jāṅgalānām*), by the term "dry" (*rūkṣān*), one should understand that dryness arises from the absence of fats that modify the taste, and thus it refers to being made from meat that is drier than the extremely unctuous meat of fish and other such creatures. "Red, white, and large" refers to red *śāli* rice, white *śāli* rice, and large *śāli* rice; the white *śāli* is known as *puṇḍarīka-śāli* in Magadha. Regarding "barley, wheat," and so forth: for those to whom barley and wheat are habitual (*sātmya*), one should administer barley and wheat themselves.
Furthermore, for those to whom rice is neither suitable nor accustomed, barley and wheat alone should be given; because these two are contrary to *kapha* and are beneficial for *visarpa*.
For it has been said: "Everything sweet produces *kapha*, except for aged *śāli* rice, barley, and wheat" (Sūtra-sthāna, A. 27).
Regarding visarpa, he states the things to be avoided— beginning with "vidāhīni" (115)—
and then describes the treatment according to the specific doshas— beginning with "kuryāt" (116).
116–117 He describes the treatment for *granthi-visarpa* (glandular erysipelas) beginning with "raktapittottaram," etc.,
and he prescribes poultices (*upanāha*) beginning with "utkārikābhiḥ," etc.

The application of *upanāha* is warm and thick; it is prepared with "alkali made by boiling" (*pākyakṣāra*), which refers to alkali produced according to the method taught by Suśruta and others. Alternatively, there is a reading "combined with barley-alkali" (*yavakṣārayutena*).
In the phrase "with cow's urine" and so forth, "leaf" (*patram*) refers to the leaf of the castor-oil plant (*eraṇḍa*) or similar plants.
In the phrase "naktamālaḥ karañjaḥ bibhītakatvacām," the word "kalkena" (with a paste) should be supplied.
The sense is that the ointment described in the verse beginning with "dantī," which can even split stone, will certainly split a phlegmatic gland (kapha-granthi).
"By these" refers to those that will be mentioned below;
"girija" is bitumen (*śilājatu*); the application of *girija* should be understood as that described in the section on rejuvenation (*rasāyana*);
"musta-saktu" refers to the barley-flour preparations for leprosy mentioned in the verse beginning with "mustaṃ vyoṣa" (Ci. A. 7).
Bhallātaka flour is prescribed as a rejuvenative (rasāyana);
"of honey" refers to mineral honey (dhātumākṣika);
and "with the previously mentioned breakers of abdominal tumors" refers to the *vimārgājapa*, *adarśa*, and other such remedies.
"By iron, salt," and so forth, means by means of torments such as heated iron;
"by arrows or gold" means by an arrow or by gold that has been heated;
"by those who cook" means by means of cooking-masses.

Furthermore, although smoke and the other [therapies] have already been mentioned by the words "again" (*punaśca*) and so forth, they are here enjoined again with respect to the removal of the knots (*granthi*); therefore, there is no tautology here.
Having stated the treatment for knots (*granthicikitsita*), he says "ya eva... and so forth, extending that [treatment] by analogy to goiter (*galagaṇḍa*) and cervical adenitis (*gaṇḍamālā*).
By the mention of "galagaṇḍas" (goiters), "gaṇḍamālās" (scrofula) are also intended [to be included].
Regarding visarpa (erysipelas), he states the praise for bloodletting, beginning with "yāni" and so forth.

He asks, "Why is bloodletting alone the primary [treatment]? and answers with the verse beginning "visarpa na... and ending with "sādhāraṇam. This means that in the case of a vāta-kapha visarpa, the treatment that removes blood and pitta has not been omitted; rather, it has already been stated.
141–143. The summary beginning with "nirukta" refers to the definition of the secondary affliction (upadrava), that is, what the characteristics of a secondary affliction are like.
The meaning of "na ca" (nor) is that it is not something to be proven; [this is said] to one who desires to speak, that is, to one who wishes to ask. 144–146.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Treatment of Visarpa," in the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the essential meaning of the Caraka Saṃhitā, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Chapter 22 of the Cikitsāsthāna (88 of 120)]
Since thirst generally occurs as a complication in cases of *visarpa* (erysipelas), the treatment of thirst is described immediately after *visarpa*.
In the verse beginning with "jñāna," *jñāna* refers to the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), *praśama* means tranquility, and *tapas* refers to penances such as the *cāndrāyaṇa*.

*Cikitsita* is a treatise that prescribes medical treatment; furthermore, the exposition of diagnosis (*nidāna*) and so forth is solely for the sake of treatment, since treatment is preceded by the knowledge of diagnosis and the other factors.

By the statement "of the five," [the author] demonstrates that all five are subjects of treatment; the meaning is that none among them is incurable here like cough or dyspnea. Likewise, he indicates the inclusion of the two additional types of thirst mentioned by Suśruta within these very five;
for it is said in the Suśruta: "Three are traditionally known; the fourth arises from injury (*kṣataja*), and likewise that which arises from wasting (*kṣaya*) and from undigested matter (*āma*)."
"And there may be a seventh [type] born from the cause of food" (Suśruta Upaniṣad Adhyāya 48).
Thus, according to the etiology stated beginning with "from agitation" (*kṣobha*), one should infer, as appropriate, that *vāta* is the agent or that *vāta* and *pitta* are the agents.
The passage beginning with "pittānilau" describes the pathogenesis (*samprāpti*) of all types of thirst;

the phrase "saumyān dhātūn" means that [pitta and vāta] vitiate the watery elements— namely phlegm (*kapha*), rasa, and water— which possess qualities exceeding those of Soma, by means of drying them out.
The word *klomnaḥ* ends in the accusative plural;
by the word *dehe* (in the body), he demonstrates the physical nature (*śārīratva*) of these thirsts.

For that thirst which is mental has been described in such passages as: "Thirst, consisting of desire and aversion, proceeds from pleasure and pain" (Śārīrasthāna 1); however, this [thirst] is born of the body alone, being caused by the bodily *doṣas*. This is the intended meaning.

If one asks, "Since wind (vāta) and bile (pitta) are indeed the initiators even of natural thirst, why is that [natural thirst] not included here?"—do not say so. Having kept in mind that it is pacified simply by the intended drinking of appropriate liquids, and thus has no place here in this section concerning unnatural diseases, [the author] states the distinction between the wind and bile that cause natural thirst and the wind and bile that initiate the thirst to be described: "Drunk, drunk," and so forth.

The bile (*pitta*) and wind (*vāta*), which initiate the primary thirst, dry up the water as it is repeatedly drunk; therefore, due to this drying of the water, the person does not find relief. The sense is that by drinking water naturally, one attains tranquility.
He describes the production of thirst as a secondary complication (*upadrava*) with the words beginning "ghora" (terrible), etc.;
"become afflictions" (*upasargabhūtāḥ*) means they take the form of complications.
4–7 He states the premonitory signs (*pūrvarūpa*) of craving (*tṛṣṇā*):

in the very midst of the description of the premonitory signs, he states the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) that is invariably concomitant with cravings, beginning with "its own specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*).

"Svalakṣaṇa" means an unerring characteristic; for example, heat is the specific characteristic of fever, and swelling is that of edema. Now, he states the "prakṛta," which is the premonitory symptom (*prāgrūpa*): "the lightness and disappearance of the signs. This means that the lightness—meaning the slightness or even the absence of some—of the signs of thirst arising from vāta and other humors, which will be described hereafter, constitutes the premonitory symptom of the various types of thirst.

Therefore, in the stage of the premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*), some of the characteristics to be described hereafter do not occur at all, and those that do occur are indistinct due to their slightness.
As it has been said: "Its premonitory symptom is known as the unmanifest characteristic" (*Ci. A. 11*).

Alternatively, this "premonitory symptom" (prāgrūpa) is dryness of the mouth, and the "specific characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa) is the constant desire for water; these constitute the premonitory symptoms and specific characteristics of thirsts. Thus, dryness of the mouth and the desire for water exist as both the specific characteristics and the premonitory symptoms. However, in the state of the premonitory symptoms, dryness of the mouth and the desire for water should be understood as being mild. As for those who read, "The premonitory symptoms are dryness of the mouth, loss of voice, and constant desire for water," in their opinion, the specific characteristic of thirst would not have been stated.

And it is stated by Hārīta regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of thirst: "The specific characteristic of thirsts is always a desire for water. Alternatively, dryness of the mouth and loss of voice are the premonitory signs (*pūrvarūpa*), while the constant longing for water is the specific characteristic. Furthermore, the lightness of the symptoms means the departure or cessation of thirst as a disease; this very cessation of thirst is the attenuation of the symptoms to be described hereafter. For there is no total eradication of the characteristics of thirst, because these symptoms persist in a slight degree due to being seized by innate thirst.

Some, however, maintain that the lightness of the bodily signs and their rapid onset—this being the departure known as death—is the defining characteristic of the incurability of thirst; this [interpretation] is not very convincing.
He now describes the complications of all forms of thirst, beginning with "dryness of the mouth," and so forth.

Regarding the term "manifested" (*udbhūta*), some elders state that it refers to symptoms such as dryness of the mouth; however, according to their view, there would be no mention of thirst as a complication (*upadrava*). Yet, complications are included in the summary of this chapter. Therefore, the established distinction is that dryness of the mouth and other such symptoms are complications when they have increased excessively, whereas when they have merely increased [without being excessive], they are considered signs (*liṅga*).
With the words "the water element" and so forth, he describes the attainment and other states of the five [elements].
Regarding the phrase "situated in the body," it means existing within the body in the form of various tastes and so on;
it should be understood that when the water element is dry, it withers.
"Obstruction of the channels" refers to excessive injury.
With the words beginning with "pittam," he describes [the disease] born of pitta.

In the *Śārīra-sthāna*, regarding the enumeration of the bodily constituents (*śarīrasaṅkhyā*), Pitta is stated to be of the nature of water (*āpya*) by the passage: "That which is liquid, flowing, unctuous, slow, soft, and slimy—namely rasa, blood, fat, kapha, pitta, urine, sweat, and so forth—is of the nature of water; rasa and the sense of taste are also [of that nature]" (Śā. A. 7). Likewise, in that same section, its dual nature is stated by the passage: "That which is pitta, whatever heat there is, and whatever luster exists in the body—all that is of the nature of fire" (Śā. A. 7). Nevertheless, because its fiery form predominates, he states—"Pitta is considered to be of the nature of fire"—to show that Pitta is indeed predominantly fiery. Furthermore, even though Pitta possesses a dual nature, due to the predominance of its fiery component, among the various classifications of disorders as somya, āgneya, and vāyavya, those disorders arising from Pitta are invariably categorized as āgneya.
"He is indeed tormented" refers to the water-element being tormented;
in the reading "for it is tormented," it should be construed that it would produce bile itself.
When the water-element produces [fever], it does so only when tormented by bile; thus, bile alone is the agent.

By the words beginning with "thirst" (tṛṣṇā), he describes *āmajā* [diarrhea]. Here, by the term *āma*, through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), *kapha*—which has a treatment similar to that of *āma* and characteristics similar to those of *āma*—is also included.
By the etymological derivation of the term *tenāmaprabhavā* (arising from that undigested matter), even the *kaphaja* type mentioned by Suśruta is included here;
furthermore, by the phrase "that too is fiery" (*sāpy āgneyī*), it reinforces the previously established fact that all types of thirst are produced by *vāta* and *pitta*.

Moreover, although *vāta* was mentioned as a cause of thirst, it is not the primary factor here; rather, it is inferred from the lack of mention of *vāta* in this context that *pitta* alone is the predominant factor.

It is also stated elsewhere: "Vision, digestion, body heat, hunger, thirst, suppleness of the body, radiance, clarity, and intelligence—these are the functions of *pitta* arising from its non-disorder" (Sūtra-sthāna 18).

This means that [the aforementioned symptoms] arise because they are produced by *pitta* generated through the obstruction of *āma*; that is to say, they are produced by *pitta* increased due to the blockage of undigested matter (*āma*).
With the verse beginning "The body is born of rasa" (rasaja), he describes [the disease] arising from depletion (kṣayajā).

From the essence of food (āhārarasa), the essence of the bodily constituents (dhāturasa) which nourishes all the tissues is produced; and that rasa, being "born of water" (ambubhava)—meaning aqueous—nourishes the body.

"From its depletion" means from the depletion of *rasa* (plasma), one becomes thirsty. From the depletion of *rasa*, there occurs a depletion of water (*ambu*); by that depletion of water, the person becomes possessed of thirst in the form of a longing for drink—this is what is being shown as logical.

For it is stated in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā*: "A person whose *doṣas*, *dhātus*, and wastes are depleted, and whose strength is also depleted, desires that food and drink which increases their own source" (*Su.Sū.A.* 15). And here too it is said: "And from its depletion, one indeed becomes thirsty."
With the words "it becomes," etc., he describes that which arises from an *upasarga*;
by "from an *upasarga*" is meant from a complication such as fever, that is to say, in the form of a complication such as fever.
"Difficult" means difficult to treat.

Thus, five types of thirst have been described here, consisting of the complications (*upasarga*) of wind, bile, undigested matter (*āma*), water, and depletion, as previously outlined in the aphorisms.

Among these, the type arising from phlegm mentioned by Suśruta is subsumed under that arising from *āma*, the type arising from injury is subsumed under the complication-type, and the type arising from food should be included within the *āma*-type itself.
Now he states the characteristic of the incurability of craving (tṛṣṇā), beginning with "all these," etc.;
"accompanied by terrible afflictions" means possessing afflictive disturbances that cause suffering.

Now, demonstrating that other types of thirst are included within those already mentioned, and stating that even the aforementioned and yet-to-be-described thirsts are produced by *vāta*, *pitta*, and depletion (*kṣaya*), he says: "Not [without] fire," etc.
Furthermore, as to why thirst does not occur without fire and *vāta*, he says: "For those two," etc.

For those two, the fire and wind, being excessively increased and manifesting as pitta and vāta, are the causes for the drying up of the water element; therefore, the meaning is that thirst does not occur without fire and wind.
Thus, when there is a depletion of the water element caused by fire and wind, a person becomes thirsty by the very nature of things.

Having thus described the varieties of thirst born from the depletion of the water element caused by pitta and vāta, he states the varieties of thirst that should be included [within these]: "gurvanna... and so forth.
"By those that coalesce" means by those that attain a state of unity.

Here, the increased *vāta* is the cause of thirst during the process of digestion (*sammūrchana*); and as for the thirst that occurs at the time of burning (*vidāha*), there *pitta* is the cause of thirst. Including even that thirst born of liquor within this category, he says: "Sharp, hot," and so forth.
"In the sands" means "in the grains of sand"; this is a statement regarding their tranquility (*upaśama*), and "sharma" means happiness (*sukha*).
Including *śītamlāna* within [the category of] *jāta*, he says: "In the cold season," and so forth;
*śiśira* means cold.

"The heat is blocked" means that the heat, unable to exit through the pores of the skin due to the cold water, is obstructed and turned back; by this, it is stated that this [thirst] is also born of bile (*pitta*).
By the phrase "not suddenly," he shows that when one resorts to cold water after resting, such thirst does not occur.

Now, having described the obstruction caused by the depletion of *pitta* following the depletion of *vāyu* through the aforementioned sequence beginning with the coagulation of food (*anna-sammūrcchanādi*), [the author], demonstrating that all [types of thirst] indeed arise from the depletion of *vāyu* and *pitta*, says: "The symptom in all [types]... and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "arising from the depletion of *vāyu* and *pitta*" (*anila-kṣaya-pittaja*), the term "arising from depletion" (*kṣayaja*) specifically refers to arising from the depletion of the water-element (*ab-dhātu*).
Furthermore, he provides the reason for stating the treatment separately despite the general similarity of these thirsts, saying: "But now... and so forth.

"From separate tradition" (*pṛthagāgamāt*) means from separate causes, for "tradition" (*āgama*) is that from which [knowledge] comes, namely the cause. The meaning is: "I shall describe the difference in treatment due to the differences in causes such as wind (*vāta*) and so forth. Alternatively, it means: "I shall describe a separate treatment," because of the authority of the tradition of Āyurveda; since treatment is declared in the tradition according to the distinctions among thirsts (*tṛṣṇā*), I too shall describe a separate treatment.
With the words "from the abode of the waters" (*apāṃ kṣayāt*) and so forth, he describes the medical treatment.

Regarding what was stated— that [the fever] is "Aindra," meaning it belongs to the atmosphere (*āntarikṣa*), or possesses its qualities, or is something else— he says "moreover" (*kiñcit*) and so forth.
"Kiñcit" means slightly;

that which is tasted or relished due to having a slight astringent aftertaste is "tuvarānurasam. The intermediate space (*antarikṣa*)—that is, water—is indeed endowed with all unmanifest tastes, for it is said: "The unmanifest state of tastes occurs either in the primary element (*prakṛti*) or in a substance accompanied by a secondary taste" (Cikitsāsthāna, Sūtrasthāna 26).
By the word "aindravat" (like Indra's), it becomes connected with the earth while imitating the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*);
however, others say that by the word "tuvara" they mean "astringent," thus meaning it has a slight astringent aftertaste;
"tanu" means clear.

"Sugandhi" means free from unpleasant odors; for it is stated in the *Suśruta*: "Unpleasant odor is a defect of fragrance" (*Su.Sū.A.* 45). It is called "surasam" because it is tasted by the tongue without being disagreeable; it does not mean that the distinct and excellent taste itself is "surasam," for it is stated in the *Suśruta*: "A manifest [excessive] taste is a defect of flavor" (*Su.Sū.A.* 45). 25–26.

Regarding "with the five roots beginning with *śara*": this refers to the five roots beginning with *śara*, as stated in [Cikitsāsthāna, Chapter 1, Section 1]: "the roots of *śara*, *ikṣu*, *darbha*, *kāśa*, and *śāli*.
"A gruel of roasted barley for those with illness" (*āmayavānāṃ vāṭya*) refers to a preparation of slightly parched and crushed barley flour (*maṇḍa*).
"Muñjātaka" is well known in the Northern Region (*Uttarāpatha*).
"Well-prepared" means well-processed;
"by those" refers to grasses, the five roots, and so forth; "sweet" means having a sweet taste.
"With cold [substances]" means those possessing a cooling potency (*śītavīrya*).
"Born from that" refers to milk boiled with sweet (*madhura*) and other [herbs].
Mārdvīka is wine made from the juice of grapes;
a *gaṇḍūṣa* is a liquid that fills the mouth;
and the five acids are the acid of *kola*, the acid of *cikrikā*, the acid of *mātuluṅga*, and *amlavetasa*.
It should be understood from the statement, "The fourfold sour is thus declared, while the fivefold sour always includes pomegranate," that *dadhittha* refers to the *kapittha* (wood-apple).
The phrase "with white *āmalaka*s" means with *āmalaka*s that are of a pale color due to their being fresh.
A garment moistened with whey and the scum of curdled milk;
the rays of the moon;

With the verse beginning "vātaghna" (wind-destroying), etc., he describes the specific treatment for the various types of thirst; [the decoction] boiled with drugs that alleviate wasting-cough (kṣayakāsa) removes wasting-cough, while [the decoction] boiled with wind-destroying drugs alleviates upward-moving wind (ūrdhvavāta), which is dyspnea (śvāsa).

Regarding the statement "in thirst born of vāta and pitta," thirst arising from a combination of doshas (saṃsargajā tṛṣṇā), although not explicitly mentioned in the aphorism, is discussed here according to the same principle by which dual combinations of doshas were mentioned in the context of gulma.
In the case of *paitta* [fever], the word "thirst" (*tarṣe*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].

Regarding the phrase "a *prastha* of red rice" (*lohitaśāliprastha*) and so forth: four *palas* of the combined *lodhra* and other ingredients are used; according to the rule of addition, one-fourth part (*pādika*) of honey is added; and having added enough boiled and cooled clay (*pakvāmaloṣṭa*) for clarification (just sufficient for stirring), a *prastha* of red rice grains is kept overnight. That food (with the addition of just enough honey for drinking) is drunk from an earthen vessel—this is the method of procedure shown by the elders. "New potsherds" (*navakapāla*) refers to fragments of new bowls and the like.
"Āpākaśarkaram" means sugar prepared by means of cooking;
"amṛtavallī" is *guḍūcī*;
and "mṛdbhṛṣṭasaṃyutā" means combined with roasted earth.
"Another [remedy] with astringents" refers to a linctus containing astringents such as *āmalaka* and so forth;
"afflicted by thirst from excessive drinking" means one suffering from the torment of thirst caused by the overconsumption of liquor.

Regarding "obstruction of food," "interruption of food," and "the mouth made clear by *māgadhikā*": in this context, long pepper (*pippalī*) should be administered merely to produce clarity of the mouth.

Although ghee is prohibited in cases of dryness of the palate—according to [Sūtra-sthāna 13], which states, "those overcome by thirst and fainting, pregnant women, and those with dryness of the palate"—nevertheless, here, the drinking of ghee for one afflicted by powerful thirst is not contradictory, because of its specific therapeutic purpose.

Regarding the thirst that occurs when unctuous food has been eaten, although jaggery-water (*guḍāmbu*) is not beneficial because it possesses unctuous qualities—as it is said: "The drink is desired to be of qualities opposite to those of the food" (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 27)—nevertheless, due to its sweet taste, it allays thirst, or by virtue of its specific potency (*prabhāva*), it is employed.
Thus, the treatment for secondary thirst (*aupasargikī tṛṣṇā*), beginning with "thirst, fainting," and so forth, is described [in verses 47–56].
Regarding where cold or hot water should be given or avoided, he says: "In thirst," and so forth;
"in poison and bile" refers to poison (*viṣa*) and bile (*pitta*);
and "in *sannipāta*" refers to thirst arising from *sannipāta* fever.

"Water is not beneficial" means that even in diseases such as jaundice (pāṇḍu) and in cases of thirst, water is not beneficial; the phrase "if the thirst is unbearable" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Regarding these cases of unbearable thirst, he states the fault in taking water with the verse beginning with "pūrva... and so forth.

"Afflicted by a prior illness" means tormented by a disease that arose previously. "An affliction produced by that" refers to the thirst; the meaning is that drinking water for the sake of quenching that thirst becomes a means of comfort for the purpose of overcoming it—that is, for the purpose of conquering the thirst which causes great calamity.
This is a summary of the first chapter beginning with "The cause" (*hetu*).
Regarding the phrase "fire and wind," the remainder of the sentence is: "Fire and wind produce thirst accompanied by complications."

The complications, such as dryness of the mouth and others, have been mentioned previously [in verse 63]. Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Treatment of Thirst," in the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka Saṃhitā, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsāsthāna).

22 [Chapter 23 of Cikitsāsthāna (89 of 120)] Following the treatment for thirst (*tṛṣṇā*), the treatment for poison (*viṣa*) is now described, due to the commonality of their primary relief through cooling measures— beginning with "prāk" and so forth.
"Prior origination" means initial production; "source" means the substratum;
"signs" refers to the signs related to the body, as well as the signs pertaining to food and so forth.
In this regard, according to the maxim that "teachers do not speak unless asked," the question of the disciple must be inferred.

Furthermore, although poison (*viṣa*) is not explicitly mentioned in the section on diseases (*rogādhikāra*), it should nevertheless be understood as having been implicitly mentioned therein by virtue of its being the cause of the intoxication (*mada*) described as "poison-born" (*viṣaja*); therefore, the mention of poison here does not constitute a deviation from the established doctrine (*utsūtra*).
The statement regarding the prior origin of poison, beginning with "for the sake of immortality" (amṛtārtham), is intended to demonstrate its great power.
"Harikeśa" means one with tawny hair;
that person is called "poison" because of his consumption of poison. In this way, the etymological derivation of the word "poison" (viṣa) is explained.

"Therefore, it is of two kinds, arising from water and [the womb]. This means that it arises from water (*ambusambhava*) because it is produced from the ocean; and it is of two kinds because it was assigned two types of origins (*yoni*) by Brahmā. Furthermore, its quality of being "arising from water" logically accounts for its aggravation during the rainy season, as will be explained later. It should also be understood that because its origin is water, its pacification is achieved through water due to its inherent potency (*prabhāva*).

For it has been said by the Blessed One Vyāsa: "Fire arose from water, the Kṣatriya from the Brāhmaṇa, and iron from stone; therefore, fire that spreads everywhere is extinguished within its own source.
The phrase "eightfold speed" (*aṣṭavega*) refers to eightfold speed relative to human beings.
The tenfold [factors] and so forth to be described hereafter are the "approaches" (*upakrama*), which are the various methods for the application of medical treatment.
He states the reason for the specific aggravation of poison during the rainy season and its subsidence in autumn with the verse beginning "tad varṣāsu" and so forth.

Just as molasses, being of watery origin, becomes liquefied when formed into a lump during the rains, so too does poison spread when moistened and its potency becomes excited; for this very reason, those afflicted by *dūṣīviṣa* (latent or residual poison) become extremely distressed. The arrival of the rainy season is the cause for the increase of clouds, and the power of Agastya destroys that [increase].
Because poison is the subject matter of another section, [the author] briefly mentions the two types of sources—mobile and immobile—with the words "serpents" and so forth.

Although the qualities of poison were mentioned previously, nevertheless, since qualities depend upon that which possesses them (the qualified), the substances of poison—which are divided into the categories of immobile and mobile—are described first. In the initial enumeration, however, the qualities were mentioned first in order to demonstrate the predominance of the qualities in the production of the effects of poison.
The specific varieties of snakes and other creatures shall be described further on; therefore, they should be explained in that very place.
By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of scorpions and others mentioned in other treatises.

Here, even those without fangs are called "fanged" (*daṃṣṭrin*) because of the predominance of fanged snakes. Likewise, by the phrase "originating from fangs" (*daṃṣṭrottha*), since poison originating from fangs is the most predominant among all poisons, there is the inclusion of even those not originating from fangs, such as the poison of rats (*unduru*).

For it is stated elsewhere: "Sixteen substrates for mobile poison have been described: therein, [the poison is found in] the gaze, the fangs, the breath, the claws, the urine, the feces, the semen, the saliva, the menses, the mouth, the pincers (claws), the eructation, the anus, the bones, the bile, the bristles, and the corpse" (Suśruta Saṃhitā, Kalpasthāna, Chapter 3).
Likewise, it is stated elsewhere: "But the semen, urine, and feces that have fallen upon the body..."
"They say that *gara* is terrible.
(9-10) Regarding poison born of stationary beings (*sthāvaraja*), the term "root-born" (*mūlajāni*) is used because of the multiplicity and preeminence of those poisons produced from roots.

By this, poisons derived from leaves, flowers, and so forth are also included; as it is stated in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*: "Root, leaf, fruit, flower, bark, latex, heartwood, resin, minerals, and the bulb is recorded as the tenth" (*Suśruta Kalpasthāna*, chapter 2).
Here, however, because the bulb is a specific type of root, it is already included by the word "root" itself.
Regarding the application of these names, only the Śabaras, Kirātas, and others who possess that knowledge are the authority, for they explain them through the lineage of their teachers.
[Sūtras 11–13] He states the third type of poison, which is composed of both stationary and moving entities, beginning with "produced by the combination of poisons" (garasaṃyogaja), and so forth.
Those substances whose association has poison as its object are "poisonous associations" (*garasaṃyoga*); that which is produced from them is "born of poisonous association" (*garasaṃyogaja*).

That which is designated by the technical term "poison" (*gara*) in the medical treatise is called "that which bears the designation 'poison'" (*gara-sañjña*); and it is that which produces diseases of long duration without being fatal.
He states this very point with the words beginning "at another time" (*kālāntara*) and so forth.

In the *Suśruta Saṃhitā* as well, poison is described as being of only three types: "Poison is indeed of three kinds: that which is stationary (*sthāvara*), that which is mobile (*jaṅgama*), and also that which is artificial (*kṛtrima*)" (*Su.Ka.A.* 2).
As for the "corrosive poison" (*dūṣīviṣa*) which he will discuss later, we shall demonstrate how it is included within these three types.

Poison (*gara*) is of two kinds: that produced by the combination of non-poisonous substances, and likewise that produced by the combination of poisonous substances. Of these, the former is designated as *gara*, while the latter is established as "artificial" (*kṛtrima*). Having adopted this very classification, it is stated in the section on Rasāyana: "In the case of fang-poison, root-poison, *gara*-poison, and artificial poison" (Ci. A. 1, Pā.). Similarly, it is also stated by Vṛddhakāśyapa: "The third type of poison is said to be that which is born of combination (*saṃyogaja*)."
"Garā would be non-poisonous there, whereas that which is artificial is considered poisonous.

With the verse beginning with "sleep," [the author] states the symptoms of mobile poison (jaṅgamaviṣa) occurring during all its stages; and with the verse beginning with "fever," he states the symptoms of stationary poison (sthāvaraviṣa) occurring during all its stages.
In order to state the nature of mutual injury between the mobile and the immobile, he states the very reason for their mutual destructiveness, beginning with "the mobile," and so forth.
"Therefore" means because they follow mutually opposed paths;
by this, what he will say later—"for those bitten, there is the drinking of poison, and when poison is drunk, there is biting at the end"—becomes logically established.

[Objection: But does this not contradict the description in the *Ātreyabhadrakāpyīya* chapter (*Sūtra-sthāna*, A. 26), which states, "Poison is said to be an antidote to poison; therein, its specific potency (*prabhāva*) is the cause"? [Response: Not so. For if the potency of a substance were not the cause, then any upward-moving drug such as *madanaphala* would eliminate the venom of fangs, and any downward-moving drug such as *trivṛt* would destroy the root-poison; yet this is not observed. Therefore, it is the very nature of potency (*prabhāva*)—as a unique quality of the substance—that is the cause of these properties of moving downward or upward.
By the passage beginning with "thirst and delusion" (*tṛṇmoha*), he describes the characteristics of the eight stages of poison-velocity (*viṣavega*) in sequence.

In the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*, seven stages of velocity are declared to occur with the passing of each successive *kalā* (unit of time). Here, however, there are seven stages by the mere transgression of the *kalās*; but at the eighth, following the transgression of the seventh *kalā*, there occurs for the bitten person a lethal stage of velocity, which serves to cause the ingested poison to reach the heart and the site of the bite—thus there is no contradiction with the *Suśruta*.
"Arising from wind and so forth" means that, according to their respective suitability, they arise from one, two, or all three of the aggravated doṣas.
Here, the word "etc. (*ādi*) in "fainting and so forth" (*mūrchādyāḥ*) denotes a category.

Furthermore, even though not explicitly stated regarding the fourth and subsequent stages of the impulse (*vega*), the vitiated elements such as fat (*medas*) and others are to be inferred, based on the statement of Suśruta.

In the phrase "of blue and so forth" (*nīlādīnām*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) denotes the primary [color], whereby there occurs the perception of colors other than the primary blue; furthermore, the word "hic" is to be separated [as a particle] in the sixth verse.
And because this is an introduction to the stages of poison (*viṣavega*), he describes the stages of poison for quadrupeds and birds as well.

The purpose of describing these stages of the poison's onset (*viṣavega*) is as follows: even the flesh of one who has died from the onset of poison may be used for consumption—provided it is not the heart of one who ingested the poison, nor the bitten site of one who was stung—according to the prescribed rules mentioned above. However, through the knowledge of the stages of onset, the flesh of one whose final stage has not yet been reached must not be taken according to the stated injunctions; for the entire body of such a person afflicted by poison becomes like poison itself.
Furthermore, because their mental strength (*sattva*) is diminished, four-legged animals and the like suffer from a sluggish onset of the poison, leading to exhaustion and other such symptoms.
In the second [verse], [the qualities of] "empty" and so forth are stated; in the third [verse],
from verse 18 to 23,
he describes the qualities of poison, beginning with "light" and so forth.
He states the specific effect of each of the qualities, beginning with "from dryness" (*raukṣyāt*) and so forth;
"from lack of coldness" (*aśaityāt*) means from heat (*uṣṇatvāt*);
and "provoking the blood" (*asṛkprakopaṇam*) is due to its subtlety (*saukṣmyāt*), because the blood itself follows subtle channels.
The state of having an unmanifest taste (*avyaktarasa*) leads to the provocation of *kapha*, because the unmanifest taste and *kapha* share the same causal substance, which is water;

thus, it follows the tastes of food. Just as water, by virtue of its unmanifest taste, acts as a "carrier" (*yogavāhin*) in the perception of odor, so too does poison quickly follow the tastes of food. Consequently, the food is rapidly permeated by it.
It should be understood that, due to its "speed" (*śīghratva*), it spreads swiftly, and due to its "pervasive nature" (*vyavāyitva*), it pervades the entire body.
Pervasive nature (*vyavāyitva*) means having the habit of spreading everywhere, like oil fallen into water.

Because of its sharpness (*tīkṣṇatva*), it strikes the vital points (*marmaghna*); thus, one should understand that there is a contradiction between the vital points—which are gentle and soft—and that which is sharp.
"Because of its expansive nature" (*vikāsitvāt*) means because of its habit of causing injury (*hiṃsanaśīlatvāt*); for the root *kas*, preceded by the prefix *vi-*, has the meaning of injury.

"Because of lightness" means because of instability; and for that which is unstable, treatment is ineffective due to its lack of connection with medicine. "With unattached movement" refers to a condition where the movement among the *doṣas* is unattached and uninterrupted. Indeed, it is "clear" (*viśada*) because, being devoid of a slimy portion (*picchābhāga*), it does not adhere anywhere.

Furthermore, regarding the specific determination of qualities in performing contradictory actions, it should be understood that the very nature of poison as harmful (*aśivatva*) is the regulating factor; therefore, one should not suspect the depletion of *śleṣman* and so forth due to dryness (*raukṣya*) and other such qualities.

Regarding the state of "digestion" (pākitva) mentioned by Suśruta in the context of the qualities of poison, it is not discussed here because it is useless for poisons that act rapidly. For instance, poison does not require such a long duration of time that its digestion would become an unavoidable consideration;

furthermore, Suśruta has stated that the aggravation [of poison] at a later time pertains specifically to *dūṣīviṣa* (latent or chronic poison), and this point should likewise be considered here in the case of *dūṣīviṣa*.
Now, he describes the specific symptoms according to the particular location and the acquisition of a particular constitution—beginning with "of one of vāta constitution" and so forth.

Although poison and liquor aggravate all three doṣas, nevertheless, due to the acquisition of a specific location and constitution, they cause a greater aggravation of the doṣa that corresponds to them, while for the remaining two [doṣas], the aggravation is slight; this is the meaning.
"Of one of vāta constitution" means of one whose constitution is dominated by vāta.

Because of the statement, "In the site of Vāta, such as the colon (pakvāśaya) and so forth, the signs of Kapha and Pitta are slight," the signs of Vāta become predominant; these should be understood as those described in the passage beginning with "thirst and fainting" (tṛṇmūrchā). This same principle should be applied to the subsequent cases as well;
the phrase "likewise for Kapha and Vāta" means that [their signs] are slight. However, thirst and the other symptoms are the predominant signs, meaning they belong to Pitta.
In the passage beginning with "kapha," the word "ca" (and) implies "of one of kapha constitution";
this should be construed with the phrase "slightly [affected] by vāta and pitta.

He describes the characteristics of *dūṣīviṣa* (latent poison) with the words beginning "dūṣī" and so forth: *koṭha* is a swelling resembling the bite of a *varaṭī* (gadfly); *dūṣīviṣa* is a poison that becomes aggravated after a lapse of time.

And it is said elsewhere: "Because it repeatedly corrupts the bodily constituents (dhātus) by being corrupted through [exposure to] place, time, and so forth, as well as daytime sleep, it is therefore known as dūṣīviṣa.
Such a substance is generally indeed poison (gara), and likewise, it may be either stationary (sthāvara) or mobile (jaṅgama).

As stated in the Suśruta-saṃhitā: "Poison that has been digested, or destroyed by anti-poisonous drugs, or dried up by forest fires, wind, and sun, or naturally deprived of its potency, indeed attains the state of *dūṣīviṣa* (latent or chronic poison)" (Su.Ka.A.2).
Here too, the insects known as *dūṣīviṣas* should be understood as those whose venom has lost its potency.

Regarding what was stated by the passage beginning with "viṣamekaikam" and the passage beginning with "syādvātikasya," he says "sandūṣya" to express the excessive provocation of each individual humor; that is, having excessively corrupted [them].
He describes the collection of factors that cause death even when not explicitly stated, beginning with the words "it flows" (kṣarati):
the poison, once drunk, especially remains in the heart of the deceased;
and in the case of those bitten or pierced, the poison resides at the site of the bite or wound.
One who is pierced by a poisoned arrow may here become as if dead, while another, due to the vital air (*pavana*), becomes as if immortal;
as it is said in the *Kāśyapa*: "If a mortal should be as if dead, yet devoid of the signs of incurability..."
"He can be brought back to life, provided that protection of his heart has been performed.
To provide specific knowledge regarding this, he states the diagnostic signs beginning with "blue lips," and so forth.
"Daṇḍarājiḥ" means a line in the form of a staff (33–34).
"Mantra," etc. [refers to the following].

Mantras are mentioned first because they are the most excellent among those that remove poison, as it has been said: "Poison is quickly warded off by mantras consisting of vital energy, truth, sacred knowledge, and austerity when they are properly applied, in a way that medicinal drugs cannot" (Suśruta Kalpasthāna, Chapter 5).
There are two types of *ariṣṭa* (protective charms): the binding of poison by means of a mantra or by means of cords and the like.
The "application" (upadhāna) is for the purpose of transferring the poison; "bestowing medicine upon the head" (mastake bheṣajadāna);
"covering the heart" (hṛdayāvaraṇa) is the medicine that effects protection of the heart;
and "counter-poison" (prativiṣa) is the employment of another antidote against the poison.
The "Reviver of the Dead" is a medicine that brings back to life one who has died from poison, as if by nectar;
the remainder is clear and will become evident through the explanatory commentary (vivaraṇagrantha).
"Unreleased" means that the body has not been pervaded;
"having tied a *veṇikā*" means having tied a poison-holding cord.
By this general statement, the operation of the mantra regarding the omens (*ariṣṭa*) is also described, and the omen is said to be distinct from the mantra.

And it is said elsewhere: "An expert in mantras should bind even a *ariṣṭā* [serpent] with mantras; when bound by means of ropes and the like, it is considered a counteragent to poison" (*Suśruta Saṃhitā*, Kalpasthāna 5).
Regarding the word "should squeeze": by squeezing, one should extract the poison.
"Uddharet" means one should extract it after cutting;

"avoiding the vital points" (marmavarjyam) prohibits injury to the vital organs (marman); and filling the opening with barley powder or dust in a case where there is no wound is for the purpose of avoiding contact with poison.
He describes bloodletting as a therapeutic procedure by means of venesection and other methods.
By stating the transgression of the [standard] procedures, he prohibits the application of a fixed order and explains the rationale for bloodletting: "In the case of blood," etc.;
"nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to the inherent constitution of the bodily elements (*dhātu*) and so forth.
"By means of rubbing" (*pragharṣaṇaiḥ*) means even by means of rubbing; it refers to [treatment] through rubbing and so forth, as well as by means of rubbing.
Rubbing with leaves and other materials, and applying ointments (*pratisāraṇa*) by means of rubbing, has been described among the medical procedures (*upakrama*).
The word *gharṣaṇam* is the division [of the compound];
*viṣādhānam* means the spreading of poison;
*skandati* means it becomes stable.
If [the patient] has fainted, he should be fanned with the breezes of fans while remaining steady.
With the words "like a tree," etc., he explains the feasibility of removing poison through cutting and other means;
with "as a bridge," the meaning is "that which obstructs the flow";
in the second [verse], the word "in the current" (vege) is to be supplied as the remainder.
"In the beginning" means at the commencement of all [rituals];
"of that" refers to the heart.
"According to what is available" refers to the heart-protection (hṛdayāvaraṇa) among the applications to be described; it is the heart-protection obtained as required,
which will be explained as "the alkaline ointment" (kṣārāgada) in the context of "the third stage" (tṛtīye 'vege), which is the understood remainder.
*Kākāṇḍā* is a type of pod;
it, along with *rajanī* mixed with cow-bile, is to be used for eye-drops (*āścotana*) and other such treatments.
The word "at the end" means at the conclusion of all preliminary measures, during the seventh stage of the poison's intensity, a bite by a snake should be administered.
In the eighth stage [of poisoning], beginning with the words "śikhipitta" (the bile of a peacock) and so forth, he describes the *mṛtasañjīvana* (life-restoring) formulations.
The term *mṛta* means as if dead.
In the passage beginning with "by hanging" (*udbandha*), the word "having died" (*mṛte*) is connected with the three [causes] starting with hanging.

Regarding "smearing, fraud, food, and drink" (*lepa-upadhi-nasya-pānāni*): these are smearing and so forth, which should be understood as applicable to hanging and the others according to their suitability.
In the phrase "smearing, fraud," etc., "fraud" (*upadhi*) refers to that which is placed on the head in the shape of a crow's foot (*kākapada*) for the purpose of neutralizing poison.
In the passage beginning with "spṛkkā" (51–53), *kāṅkṣī* is *saurāṣṭrikā*, and *kuṣṭhaghna* is *khadira*.
Sāvaraka,
lodhra, kauntī, reṇukā, mayūraka, apāmārga, gandhaphalā, priyaṅgu, nākulī, and rāsnā.
By the word *dhāraṇa*, he speaks of maintaining [the body] within the physical frame; and this maintenance enters among the preliminary measures under the term "medicine.
A householder is one who dwells in a house (*gṛhe-avatiṣṭhan*);
a *kārmaṇa* is the employment of spells and the like for the purpose of harming others. A *mantra* is a spell of malevolent incantation (*abhicāra*).

"Regarding the faults of women" means the faults such as poison administered by women; "prior to the nectar" means before the emergence of the nectar (*amṛta*); by this, its equality with the nectar is demonstrated. 54–60.

In the passage beginning with "with mantras," *avamārjanam* refers to the cleansing of the poison by means of the mantras themselves in reverse order; this self-protection is for the purpose of preventing possession by spirits.
Regarding the word *jayet*, it means one should conquer the affliction residing in the [victim's] body.

Although sweating (sveda) is prohibited in the chapter on sudation (svedādhyāya), it is nevertheless prescribed for specific conditions by the statement beginning with "in the seat of vāta" (vātasthāne).

However, because its application is similar to the prescription of foods such as *peyā* and so forth, it is not mentioned among the twenty-four therapeutic measures (*upakrama*). Alternatively, by the word "fire" (*agni*), sweating is also included; and it must necessarily be understood that "when located in pitta" (*pittasthe*) refers to when it is situated in the seat of pitta.

In the passage beginning with "dūṣīviṣa," "sirā" refers to venesection; "pañcavidhaṃ karma" refers to the fivefold treatment beginning with emesis (vamana). Alternatively, "pañcavidhaṃ sirākarma" means the venesection of five specific vessels.
"Sthāna" refers to the wind (vāta) and other humors located in their respective sites;
"sthānasthasya" means that which is not contraindicated for the poison situated in those sites. The word "should perform" (kuryāt) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

One whose wind, characterized by inhalation and exhalation, is obstructed by the blockage of the channels; "by the signs of incurability" refers to the previously mentioned symptoms such as blue lips and so forth.
"Carmakaṣāya" refers to the decoction of *carmacāṭikā* or perhaps *saptalā*.
"Kākapada" is a wound shaped like a crow's foot.
In the passage beginning with "kaṭabhī," "kaṭuphalā" refers to the bitter gourd (*tiktālābu*), or alternatively, "kaṭu" refers to the three pungent spices (*trikaṭu*).

The six [substances] beginning with *jyotiṣmatī* are stated among the hundred purgatives; the head-purgatives [beginning] with *dārvī* [are as follows]: "alternately processed" means that having processed it with cow-bile, it is then processed with horse-bile, and likewise, having processed it with horse-bile, it is then processed with cow-bile.
With the verse beginning with *ṛṣabhaka*, the treatment for complications of poison, dyspnea (*śvāsa*), and so forth is described.
*Sitagiri* is white *aparājitā*; *kolamadhyam* is the pulp of the jujube fruit (*badara*).
"Bhujagapatiśiras" refers to the head of a two-headed serpent;
"vastrakṛmi" means a louse;
"palāśakṣāra" is alkali from the Palāśa tree; and "srutam" means it has been filtered according to the method of alkaline straining prescribed by Suśruta.
Lohitamṛd is red ochre;
surasamañjarī is a variety of parṇāsa. 77–104.

"Listen, therefore, to the separate instruction regarding the various kinds of poison and their respective remedies"—this means listen to the distinct explanation of the characteristics of the diverse poisons and the specific medicines for them.

"From women joined with enemies" means from women employed by foes; "from women" refers to those who, though they have offered forbidden food for the sake of securing good fortune, have nevertheless proceeded to do so out of ignorance.
Regarding the phrase "engaged in food and recreation": while partaking in food and recreation,
he says "servants" (referring to cooks and others) to state the means of examination— beginning with the words "excessively," and so forth.
If it has lost its luster and is devoid of beauty,
one should consider it as "to be eaten" (bhojya) [only after purification]; otherwise, one should cast that food into the fire.
In the passage beginning with "situated in the vessel" (*pātrastham*), the word "poisoned" (*saviṣam*) also carries over.

It should be understood that [the verse] "the cakorākṣī would become dispassionate" means that upon seeing poisoned food, the cakorākṣī becomes dispassionate; and furthermore, by the mere sight [of him], she would cause even crows to have feeble voices.
"In drinking" (*pāne*) refers to intoxicating liquor and the like;
"in the shade" (*chāyām*) means a reflection;
"smeared with salt" (*lavaṇākta*) is a qualification of the drink.
By the passage beginning with "mukhage" (located in the mouth), the characteristics of poison related to the mouth and other such areas are described;
"binduḥ" refers to a skin lesion in the shape of a drop.
By the passage beginning with "danta" (tooth), the characteristics of tooth-cleansing brushes and the like when vitiated by poison are to be understood from the context.
The brush for cleaning the teeth is a tuft for removing dental plaque; it would become worn out (*śīrṇa*) by foodstuffs,
that is, by edibles.
"By touchables" means by means of massages and the like;
"garland" refers to a garland tainted with poison;
the grammatical split is "it does not harm the nose."
"Vision" refers to the eye;
as for the phrase "what does it paralyze," and so forth, this is the effect of smoke alone.
"Maṇḍalī" means one who possesses a maṇḍala;
"bindulekhavicitrāṅgaḥ" refers to one whose limbs are variegated by drops (bindu) and lines (lekhā).
The detailed exposition of the *darvīkara* and other [classes of snakes] has not been provided here, as it pertains to another section [of the treatise].

Specifically, in passages such as [the description of] "roughness" and so forth, it should be understood that the poison of the *darvīkara* snakes is predominantly dry (*rūkṣa*), that of the *maṇḍalin* snakes is sour and hot (*amlōṣṇa*), and that of the *rājiman* snakes is sweet and cold (*svāduśīta*). Furthermore, although [all these poisons] provoke all three *doṣas*, one should understand that they specifically aggravate *vāta* and the others respectively. And although poison possesses unmanifest tastes (*avyaktarasa*), its designation here as having pungent (*kaṭuka*) and other tastes should be understood as referring to its secondary or latent tastes (*anurasa*). This is just as pungency is perceived in sunlight; likewise here as well. Alternatively, even within the state of unmanifest taste itself, a slight predominance of pungency and the like should be understood.
"Pṛthvarpita" refers to those whose fang-marks are deeply embedded (vv.

With the verse beginning "vṛttabhoga," etc., [the author] explains the classification of snakes into types such as *puruṣa* and so forth, for the purpose of knowing the severity of their venom and for the purpose of knowing the specific medical treatments required for each.
And although that distinction is not mentioned here, it should be understood from another tantra;
for instance: "In the case of Sāvitra [poison], it ripens at night; women with potent poison [act] thus at night, while men always [act] during the day.
Likewise: "When bitten by a female, the physician should provide excellent care, provided there is no [further] onset [of symptoms]."
"Mahākāya" means having a large body;
"klība" means a eunuch or neuter;
"gāḍhasampādita" means excessively deep or thoroughly accomplished.
The *ūrdhvaparivṛtta* is turned upward; the *udvṛtta* is twisted; the *pīḍita* causes excessive pain;
the *lambitārpita* is characterized by all the tips of the fangs being applied [to the wound].
He describes the intensity [of the venom] of the *darvīkara* and other snakes according to their age: "The young," and so forth;
that which is smeared with snake-venom is characterized by a bite-mark where the fangs have not penetrated deeply.
"Like venomous serpents" means that venomous serpents have poison in their gaze and their breath;
by [the passage] beginning with "the fangs of a snake," he explains the different types of fangs for the purpose of identifying the poison of the bite.

"Red and dark-brown for the lower and upper [fangs]" means that the lower right fang is red and the upper right fang is dark-brown. "With poison-portions increasing by one, two, three, and four respectively" means that in these [fangs], the portion of poison increases successively in the form of one, two, three, and four; this is the meaning of the sentence. "Of the same color" means having a color identical to their respective fangs.
"Bahūttaraviṣāḥ" means that they possess increasingly greater poisons; "bhṛśāḥ" means difficult to treat, and it should be understood that this difficulty of treatment also increases progressively.

Now, an objection may be raised: previously, a distinction in color was stated regarding the bite of the *darvīkara* and other snakes, whereas here a distinction in color is stated according to the difference in fangs; thus, since all colors would be applicable to every *darvīkara* and so forth, there would be a contradiction with the colors of the bites mentioned earlier. Furthermore, regarding this very point, Āṣāḍhavarmā has said: "The bite of the *darvīkara* and the *maṇḍalī* is black and yellow respectively by color," according to that definition, because the bites are indeed of many colors.
