To this it is replied: the coloration that resembles the fangs occurs when the poison remains only at the site of the bite; however, the coloration produced by the defects (doṣa) resulting from the scraping by the snake’s hood and so forth occurs when the poison has spread. Thus, there is no contradiction because of the difference in stages. And it is said in the *Parihāravārtika*: "These colors [occur] at the bite, but the similarity of color [occurs] when the poison has spread due to the defects.
He speaks to explain [the origin of] insects, beginning with "of snakes," and so forth.

The mention of these two—feces and urine—is for the purpose of etymologically defining the word *kīṭa* (insect); by this, it should be understood that other things as well—namely, snake semen, corpses, putrid matter, and eggs—are causes of insects.
For it is said in the *Suśruta*: "Insects arise from the semen, feces, urine, corpses, and putrid eggs of snakes."
"Kīṭas are traditionally said to be of three types, having the natures of air, fire, and water" (Suśruta Saṃhitā, Kalpasthāna 8).

Although in the Suśruta sixty-seven [types of] kīṭas, such as the *kumbhīnasa* and others, are set forth as aggravators of vāta, pitta, kapha, and sannipāta, they are nevertheless mentioned here according to their classification as *dūṣīviṣa* (chronic poisons) and *prāṇahara* (life-destroying poisons), with the intention of explaining their designations. In the same way, regarding spiders (*lūtā*) and other [venomous creatures], one should understand that the statement of their twofold nature is based on the distinction between their designations.
*Dūṣīviṣas* are those whose poison acts slowly (*cirakārin*), while *prāṇaharas* are those whose poison takes life instantaneously.
That which exists together with *ugragandhyāsṛj* is called *ugragandhyāsṛk*, meaning blood of pungent odor.
From the passage beginning with "in the middle of the bite" (*daṃśasya madhye*), etc., the characteristics of a bite by a *dūṣīviṣa* spider are described.

Elsewhere, eight spider-bites are said to be curable and eight others incurable, such as those caused by the *trimaṇḍala* and *sauvarṇika* spiders; regarding these, as well as [the bites of] mice, *kṛkaṇṭaka*, scorpions, *ucciṭiṅga*, frogs, fish, leeches, centipedes, mosquitoes, and flies, those seeking detailed elaboration should follow the extensive accounts in the works of Suśruta and others. However, the author of this treatise does not provide such elaboration here, as it falls outside the primary scope of this work. (144–146) The verse beginning with "ādaṃśāt" describes the symptoms of rat-poisoning (*ākhu-viṣa*).
The *kaṇabha* is a specific type of insect, as listed among insects in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*;
"inflicted by a single fang" means caused by a single fang alone.
Fishes, however, are said to have bile, bone, and lotus-like poison.

Six types of leeches—black, variegated, and so forth—are said to be venomous; they are known as *sandaṃśaviṣa* (pincer-venomous), while some call the house-lizard (*gṛhagodhikā*) by that name, others say it is the chameleon (*saraṭa*), and still others say it is the centipede (*śatapadī*). The *kāruṇḍā* is also mentioned.
Regarding the statement "the wound caused by a mosquito is incurable," they say that among the five types of mosquitoes, that which is produced in the mountains (*pārvatīya*) is incurable;
for it is stated in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*: "The mountain-born [mosquito], however, has symptoms identical to those of life-taking insects" (*Suśruta-kalpa-sthāna*, chapter 8).

Regarding the phrase "the *sthagikā* is unfriendly": among the six types of flies mentioned by *Suśruta* in the *Kāntāraka* and other sections, the fly named *sthagikā* is fatal to life. This is the meaning.
Now he describes the incurability of those bitten by snakes according to place, time, nature, and location—beginning with "in a cremation ground" (*śmaśāna*), etc.
A *caitya* is a large tree that serves as a refuge for the village deity.

"At the junctions of the fortnights" refers to the new moon and full moon days. "Heretics," such as the Kāpālikas and others, are defined by the phrase "with the poisons of their gaze, breath, and impure touch."
For it is said in another tantra: "The divine serpents are venomous snakes because they kill swiftly by means of their gaze, breath, and so forth.
He states the cause for the increase of poison: "fear" and so forth.

The constitution (*prakṛti*) and the season (*kāla*) are equal [in their influence] upon poison; for example, it should be understood that if one has a constitution of dominant *pitta* and the season is hot, [the poison increases].
Conversely, "it is small otherwise": when there is the opposite of fear and so forth, the poison becomes small.

In the passage beginning with "vārī," the term "vṛddhāḥ" (aged animals) should be understood as excluding the *goṇasa*; however, it was previously stated that for the *goṇasa*, the status of being a "poisonous aged animal" applies only upon reaching old age.

Regarding the statement "the poison residing in the entire body [arises] from anger," it should be specifically understood that although the poison resides throughout the whole body, it is particularly concentrated in the fangs—just as semen, though circulating through the entire body, is specifically localized in the testicles.

For the purpose of treatment, he describes the *ucchiṭiṅga* and other [poisons] according to the distinctions of the predominance of wind (*vāta*), poison, and so forth— beginning with the words "predominant wind" (*vātolbaṇa*) and continuing with "pain in the heart" (*hṛtpīḍā*) and so on— thereby stating the symptoms of the excessive wind and other humors present in the poison (verses 165–169).
He describes the treatment according to the divisions of wind (*vāta*) and so forth, beginning with "with sugar-candy" (*khaṇḍena*), etc.; *pulāka* refers to empty grain,
and "with thick substances" (*ghanaiḥ*) means specifically with thickened dust.
Regarding the passage beginning with "The dog [is characterized by] the three doṣas," etc., this describes the characteristics of poisonous dogs and the like.

It should be understood that wherever a dog’s three doṣas become provoked—whether by chance or through possession by the *alarka* spirit—the symptoms such as the head being tormented by poison and so forth will manifest in that very place.
Some, however, say that head-ache and other symptoms as described for the dog occur likewise when one is bitten by it;
the details of this are found in the *Suśruta* itself.
"Others also of this kind" means that others such as jackals, hyenas, and so forth, being of this same nature, cause difficult diseases of the head and other ailments.

For it is stated in the Suśruta-saṃhitā: "When the wind, vitiated by phlegm, resorts to the channels that carry consciousness and robs one of consciousness in [the case of] dogs, jackals, hyenas, bears, tigers, and so forth" (Su.Ka.A.7).

Thus, by means of general symptoms such as itching, pricking, and so on, the signs of the bite of poisonous insects and the like, as well as the signs of the bite of non-poisonous creatures, are described.
The *karṇikā* and the *māṃsakandī*—all these twenty-four [diseases] are to be treated with the aforementioned procedures.

The meaning is that the previously mentioned treatment, as well as the therapy to be described hereafter, must be performed according to the specific stage of the disease even within the previously stated regimen. When the reading is *pūrvoktāḥ* (previously mentioned), then this serves as an adjective for the word *upakramāḥ* (procedures).

In the case of one bitten on the upper part of the body, it should be understood that even when [the instruction says] "on the two feet," the application of flesh and blood to the wounded feet is for the purpose of transferring the poison;
"by those two" refers to sugar and honey; *nata* is *tagara*.
*Śelu* is *śleṣmātaka*;
this is connected with the following word "in the case of [the disease] having reached the flesh.
*Khadirāriṣṭa* refers to both *khadira* and *ariṣṭa*, or alternatively, it means an *ariṣṭa* (fermented liquor) made from *khadira*.
The analysis of the compound is *samadhuka-natam*.
The application (*pratisāraṇa*) beginning with *pippalī* and so forth is for the bite itself.
"White pepper" (*maricaṃ sitam*) refers to the seed of the *śobhāñjanaka* plant;
"and white" (*śvetā ca*) is an adjective qualifying *girikarṇikā*, by which the white *aparājitā* is understood—
though some say *girikarṇikā* refers to the *syandana*.
Pākala leprosy (kuṣṭha) 189–198.
"Muktā" means pearl;
"kṣīraśuklā vidārī" refers to the white lily-like tuber;
"karṇikāpatanam tayoh" means the removal of the callus (karṇikā) that forms at the site of the bite by the aforementioned insects and spiders. This is the meaning.
The deity Jālamālinī, Devatāḍaka,
Tiktekṣvāku, and Kaṭukālābū [are used] against the poison of the scorpion (vārścike).
The *duradura*, the frog, the *śvetabhaṇḍī*, the *aparājitā*,
the *vārścika*, and so forth— in the case of the poison of the *ucciṭiṅga* (scorpion), that same formulation which was prescribed for the *vārścika* should be employed.
In this manner, the formulation stated for the poison of the *kaṇabha* spider against a rat should also be administered (199–211).
[The ingredients are] *nākulī* and *rāsnā*.
*Guhā* is *pṛśniparṇī*; *atiguhā* is *śālaparṇī*;
*ajagandhā* is known as *phophāndha*; "by bile" means by cow's bile.
The *viśvambhara* and other such insects mentioned by Suśruta are provokers of phlegm (*śleṣman*).
The *akṣapīḍaka* is a variety of white or yellow *śimbī*.
*Vāyasī* is *kākamācī*.

The term "best" (*śreṣṭha*) expresses the superiority of the five-leaved *śirīṣa* in comparison to the three-leaved *śirīṣa* and others; the term "excellent" (*pravara*) states its excellence among other medicinal formulations for neutralizing poisons; thus, there is no tautology. Alternatively, "best" refers to that which is prepared from the best fruits of the *śirīṣa*. (Verses 212–218) Bipeds include forest-dwellers such as humans, monkeys, and so forth.
*Aśvakarṇa* is a variety of *sarja*.
(219–220) With the verse beginning "In thick darkness," etc., he describes the poison of doubt (*śaṅkā-viṣa*).
"By someone" means even by one who is not actually poisonous;

"due to the agitation caused by the suspicion of poison" means that the poison manifests precisely because of that very suspicion. Furthermore, this suspicion itself produces the poison through its own power, just as sulphur (*gandhaka*) alone, when purified, becomes *vaigandhika* (a potent medicinal substance).
*Koradūṣa*, *kodrava*, *kulaka*, and *kāravellaka*; others say these are varieties of *paṭola*.
"Annamiśritān" means mixed with food;
"garaścāsyopajāyate" means that a disease arises in him characterized by the symptoms to be described later, such as the striking of vital points (marmas) and so forth.
"One whose faculties are impaired" means one whose faculties are afflicted by disease.
In such passages as "one should ask," it is understood that the result of the inquiry is precisely the ascertainment of poison (*gara*);
having understood [this], meaning having understood the cause of the poison.
In the passage beginning with "sūkṣmam," the copper powder of immortality (amṛtatāmracūrṇa) should be administered in a dose of one *māṣa*; by means of this very *amṛta*, emesis occurs.
Regarding the term *hemapa*: he who drinks gold (*hema*) is a *hemapa*.
*Nāgadantī* is a variety of *dantī*.
*Phala* refers to *madanaphala* (emetic nut), and not the reading *palaiḥ*.
This formulation is recited in the *Jatukarṇa*: "One should administer buffalo ghee prepared with *nāgadantī*, *snuh* milk, and *phala*, boiled in cow's urine.
In the passage beginning with "śirīṣatvak" (the bark of the śirīṣa tree), *āsphotā* refers to another kind of jasmine (*mallikā*), known as *surabhī*, which is a variety of *parṇāsa*.
Bandhujīva, putrajīvaka, aśvakhuraka, syandana; or perhaps kokilākṣa? 242–249

Regarding the verse beginning with "chatrī" (the umbrella-bearer), some say that during the day he should go about with an umbrella, and at night with a *jharjhara* (a rattle-drum) in his hand; others, however, maintain that he should carry both at both times— wherein the word *chāyā* refers respectively to the umbrella and the *jharjhara*, which is known as a "khurkhuraka."
Regarding what should be done at the time of being bitten when one is terrified by those two, he says "as soon as bitten," and so forth;
and regarding the removal of poison through mere retention [of breath], he says "the thunderbolt," and so forth.
"Sāra" is a qualifier for *sarajū*;
"picuka" is a gem well-known in the northern regions;
"viṣamūṣikā" is a poison-gem.
*Karketana* is a ruby (*padmarāga*).
By the term *garamaṇi*, various gems are included.

"Excellent medicinal herbs" refers to those mentioned in other tantras, such as *akṣīvajāta*, *pippala*, *ajaruhā*, *kāyoṣī*, and so forth. And it is said: "The gem of the *pippala* tree that grows from an *akṣīva* [seed] removes all poisons," and so on.
"Thus, this collection of 'it is thus' and so forth" means that he would go to a state of being unbearable for poisons; the sense is that the poisons are not able to withstand him.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Treatment of Poisoning," in the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka Saṃhitā, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsāsthāna).
[Chapter 24 of Cikitsāsthāna (90 of 120):

Because of the commonality of producing delusion, and because it arises from qualities similar to those of poison, the treatment for intoxication (madātyaya) is stated immediately after the treatment for poisoning.

By means of the praise of wine beginning with "by the gods" (*suraiḥ*) and likewise by the censure to be stated later, [the author] demonstrates that wine being drunk according to the prescribed rule (*vidhi*) yields auspicious results, whereas drinking it contrary to the rule results in exceedingly censurable consequences.

By the phrase "which was formerly worshipped," he shows that first this very [wine] was worshipped by the gods alone, and subsequently, because of its connection with the *sura* (gods), it was designated as *surā*. The *Sautrāmaṇī* is a specific sacrifice included within the *Surā-havis* sacrifice; in that [sacrifice], the *surā* is offered.

"Established by those who perform rituals"—that is, established and brought to a state of stability by the performers of sacrifices through the *abhiṣavaṇa* (pressing) and other rites; she "bears the sacrifice," thus she is called *yajñauḥ*. By this it is also stated that other worldly sacrifices are likewise performed with *surā*. However, in the *sautrāmaṇī* oblation, she alone is declared to be the primary constituent part (*pradhānāṅga*). Regarding Indra, the scripture states: "Indra has fallen due to excessive soma-drinking. This means: "Indra, his strength exhausted, his vigor gone, and rendered powerless by the over-drunk soma, was indeed replenished and restored to his own inherent power. He is called *atipatita* because he fell (*patita*) due to excessive drinking (*atipāna*).

"Prakalpyāḥ" means they are to be pressed for the purpose of mixing—that is to say, they are fit for sacrifice (*yajñīyā*) for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice (*yajñasiddhaye*). In the ritual procedure (*yajñavidhi*), some items, such as the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), serve the purpose of the rite (*kratvartha*); others, such as clothing and the inner sanctum (*garbha*), serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*); and some, such as clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) and bricks (*iṣṭakā*), serve both the purpose of the sacrifice and the purpose of the person. Here, by the term "fit for sacrifice," liquor (*surā*) is said to be for the purpose of the person, like the inner sanctum and so forth; and by the phrase "for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice," its status as serving the purpose of the sacrifice is stated, like the sacrificial post and so forth. 3–5.
In the passage beginning with "yoni," the word *viśeṣa* (specific) is connected to each term individually:
*yoni* means cause; its specific types—grain, fruit, root, pith, flower, leaf, stalk, and bark, as well as sugar and honey—are those mentioned in the *Sūtrasthāna*.
Furthermore, *saṃskāra* (processing) refers to the application of various methods of processing.
The specific names are *surā*, *madhu*, *maireya*, and so forth;
by the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), the powers, qualities, and other attributes are included.
From that general nature characterized by intoxication—that is, from the essential form of liquor (*madya*)—which has intoxication as its defining characteristic.

In the passage beginning with "having become nectar" (amṛtaṃ bhūtvā), it is shown that the deity presiding over the liquor (surā) gratifies the gods and others in the form of nectar and so forth; this is indicated by the phrase "with blessings" (śreyobhiḥ), meaning with great auspicious things.

In passages such as "The splendor that is yours, O Āśvina," one should understand that the identity [of the deity] with splendor, vigor, and so forth belongs precisely to the presiding deity of the *surā*;
for splendor (*tejas*) is present in all deities, and likewise, the *sārasvata* strength is the power of the mantra.
In the passage "and [He who is] Soma in the Sautrāmaṇī," the nature of Soma is expressed by this; since it was previously stated that He is offered in the Sautrāmaṇī, there is no tautology.
In the verse beginning with "That which is joy" (prīti), it should be understood that He is designated as having the form of joy and so forth, because He is the cause of joy and the like.
Regarding the statement "one should drink according to the prescribed rule," he states that rule as follows: "Having performed the purification of the body" (śarīrakṛtasaṃskāraḥ) and so forth.

This means one who has performed external purification of the body through bathing, clothing, and the like, and internal purification—considering factors such as one's constitution—through unctuous and warm food and other means; such a person is "pure," meaning pure in mind.
"With fragrances unrestrained according to the seasons" means:
strewn with heaps of flowers that release their blossoms, providing the pleasures of all seasons and being prepared in accordance with the specific requirements of each season.
"Full of flavor" means beloved;
"established in their approval" refers to being established in the pleasure of one's own body,
as expressed by the word *sukṛtaiḥ* (by well-performed deeds) in its refined (*saṃskṛta*) form.
"Trained" means those who have practiced [such] services;
"betraying their scent" means rich in fragrance;
"those moving in the sky" refers to hawks and other such birds.
The group of *paurogava*s are those skilled in the science of cookery (*sūdaśāstra*).
"To the petitioners" refers to Baladeva, Caṇḍī, Yakṣas, and others who are petitioners; to them [11–20].

Having stated the general rule for administration, he now describes the method of drinking [medicinal soups] for those suffering from vāta and other disorders, beginning with the words "abhyaṅga" and so forth.
The term "māricakaiḥ" means prepared with black pepper;
"vasumatām" refers to those who possess wealth.

Those who will possess wealth and those whose riches are currently arising—according to their birth and according to the quality of their attendants—for those with a predominance of *kapha* and *pitta*, and so forth, one applies the method of "contrary logic" (*viparyaya-tantra-yukti*): for those with a predominance of *kapha*, [one prescribes] *mādhava*; for those with a predominance of *pitta*, however, *mārdvīka*. *Mārdvīka* is that made from *mṛdvīkā* grapes, while *mādhava* is that made from honey (*madhu*).

"Consisting of many substances" (bahudravya) means prepared from various kinds of substances; "possessing many qualities" (bahuguṇa) means possessing the numerous qualities such as lightness (laghu) and so forth that will be described extensively below.
"Bahukarma" means that which performs many functions such as writing, lighting lamps, and so forth.
"Madātmaka" means having intoxication as its inherent nature (*svabhāva*).

Because it has such a nature, one must consider that liquor in terms of both its qualities (*guṇa*) and its defects (*doṣa*); for, depending on a particular person, it may produce a quality due to suitability (*yaugikatva*), while for another it may produce a defect due to unsuitability. The sense is that, for example, it produces a quality in the first stage of intoxication, whereas it produces a defect in the second stage of intoxication.
"According to the rule" means by the method as previously described;
"at the proper time" means at that time which is suitable for a particular liquor but possesses contrary qualities;
"with wholesome foods" means with foods that are beneficial for that liquor.
"According to what it has acquired" means that even intoxicant which is unwholesome, when consumed through addiction— that is, in excess—
acts like poison because it produces delusion and other such states.

He explains how liquor intoxicates, beginning with the words "liquor" and so forth, by means of ten qualities such as lightness (*laghu*) and others. By agitating even all ten of the qualities of *ojas*—such as heaviness (*guru*) and the rest—and not merely two or three, it leads the mind to transformation; that is, it causes it to become deranged.
He explains by which quality the disturbance of the *ojas* (vital essence) occurs in alcohol: "Heaviness [destroys it] due to lightness," and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding "clarity (*prasāda*) from the cultivation of the impure" (*aśubhabhāvanā*), the quality called clarity is destroyed by rapid movement (*āśugatva*). Although rapid movement is not inherently contrary to clarity, nevertheless, alcohol itself, through its adverse nature, destroys the clarity of the *ojas*; it should be understood that in this process, the quality of rapid movement functions as the instrument of destruction.

Because of its pervasive nature (*vyavāyitva*), it possesses stability (*sthiratva*); here, "pervasive" means "all-pervading," and that stability destroys [the opposite quality] precisely because it is its contrary. Furthermore, this is the distinction between "swift-moving" (*āśugatva*) and "pervasive" (*vyavāyitva*): that which is swift moves quickly, whereas the pervasive, however, extends everywhere. "Expansive" (*vikāsitva*) means having the nature of expanding, which is to say, mobility (*saratva*); and that destroys smoothness (*ślakṣṇatā*) precisely because it is its contrary. "Dense" (*sāndratā*) means solidity (*ghanatā*).

Although these qualities, such as expansion (*vikāsitva*) and swift movement (*āśugatva*), are not enumerated among the twenty qualities, their status as qualities is nonetheless established because qualities are infinite in number. However, those that are enumerated therein should be understood as being the most manifest.
Demonstrating that injury to the substratum results in injury to what is supported, he says: "Sattva," and so forth.
*Sattva* has *ojas* as its substratum, and *ojas* is that which is to be benefited; just as a person is supported by a king.

"Rasavātādi," etc. The heart is the seat of the ten vessels that carry rasa, vāta, and so forth. Those very ten vessels carrying rasa which are said to have their basis in the heart are themselves the carriers of vāta and the other [doshas]. As it has been stated: "The channels of vāta, pitta, and śleṣman, which move throughout the entire body, serve as the pathways for all [substances]" (Vi. A. 5). However, although blood and the other [dhatus] also move throughout the entire body, the heart is specifically declared to be their seat: "The six limbs, the sense organs, the objects of the five senses, the mind, the intellect, the vital breaths, the channels, the seats of the vital breaths, the sense-perceptions, the elements, the excretions, the secretions, the nutrient fluids, the waste products, the diseases, the medicines, the tastes, the humors, the channels, the seats of the channels, the vessels, the seats of the vessels, the tissues, the seats of the tissues, the cavities, the seats of the cavities, the joints, the seats of the joints, the openings, the seats of the openings, the movements, the seats of movement, the strength, the seats of strength, the channels of the channels, the seats of the channels of the channels, the vessels of the vessels, the seats of the vessels of the vessels, the tissues of the tissues, the seats of the tissues of the tissues, the cavities of the cavities, the seats of the cavities of the cavities, the joints of the joints, the seats of the joints of the joints, the openings of the openings, the seats of the openings of the openings, the movements of the movements, the seats of the movements of the movements, the strength of the strength, the seats of the strength of the strength—this constitutes the sixfold limb of knowledge. (Śā. A. 1) Thus, the heart is the seat of the vessels carrying blood and the rest. Furthermore, the heart is the seat of the vessels carrying rasa, because it is the seat of the vessels carrying vāta and the rest. Moreover, the heart is the seat of the vessels carrying blood and the rest because it is the seat of the vessels carrying rasa. "The self, along with its qualities, the mind, and that which is to be contemplated, are situated in the heart" (Sūtra 3.30).
Thus, the "elements" (dhātavaḥ) refer to the constituents such as the sattva, the intellect, and the sense organs.
Regarding the general rule that "alcohol leads to a transformation of the mind," he states the first exception to this: "when *ojas* is not impaired," and so forth.

Here, by the word "heart" (*hṛdaya*), the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties residing therein are designated through metaphorical usage, just as one says, "the benches are shouting. The awakening of the intellect and other faculties is the effect of alcohol in its first stage of intoxication. He then describes the conditions for the occurrence of moderate and intense intoxication: "in the moderate [stage]," and so forth.

"In impaired" means in impairment; when there is slight impairment of the vital energy (*ojas*), there is "middling intoxication. In "severely impaired"—meaning specifically and excessively impaired—it is the "highest," which is the third [type].
With the verse beginning with "In the heart" (hṛdi), he states the general definition of intoxication (*mada*):
"thirst" (*tarṣa*) means longing;
"according to one's being" (*yathāsattva*) means that by nature those belonging to the *rājasa* constituent are *rājasa*, and those belonging to the *tāmasa* constituent are *tāmasa*.
"Citrā" means of various kinds;
"ending in the sleep of delusion" (mohanidrāntā) means having the sleep of delusion as their conclusion.
He states the definition of the first and the others [of the six types of friends], beginning with "one who causes delight" (*praharṣaṇa*).
The phrase "one who shows the qualities of drinks and food" (*pānānnaguṇadarśaka*) means one who correctly makes known the qualities of drinks and food.
Regarding the term "in objects" (*viṣayeṣu*), it refers to the enjoyment of sense objects; "and not incapable" (*na cākṣama*) means one who does not cause incapacity.
"Raving" (*pralāpa*) refers to speech that is either coherent or incoherent.
"Rolling about" (*pracalāyana*) means tossing or whirling.

"Application with its opposite" (*yojanā saviparyayā*) means that the correct application of postures and so forth sometimes occurs, while at other times there is a reversal of the application of postures and so forth, which takes the form of an incorrect application; such is the meaning.

Although three types of intoxication (*mada*) have been mentioned starting with "having transcended the middle intoxication," nevertheless, by demonstrating the extreme censurability of the state immediately following the second intoxication—that is, the stage of not yet having attained the third intoxication—he shows that the third intoxication is utterly reprehensible. The intended meaning is that even the preliminary stage of that third intoxication is extremely censurable, as it serves as the cause for performing all manner of unwholesome acts and so forth.

This state, which is designated by the terms "transgression of the middle intoxication" (*madhyamadātikrama*) and "attainment of the third intoxication" (*tṛtīyamada*), actually denotes only the states that constitute the end of the middle intoxication and the beginning of the third intoxication. Just as in the expression, "When the moon moves between the jar (*kumbha*) and the fish (*mīna*)," the word "between" (*madhye*) refers specifically to the end of the jar and the beginning of the fish—since in reality there is no space between them—so too here, because in the ultimate sense there is no time for a separate second intoxication, the mention of the end of the second and the beginning of the third intoxication is intended solely to express the extreme condemnation of the third intoxication, and not to indicate a fourth intoxication.
"Ending badly" means having an unpleasant conclusion;
"like a broken tree" means he remains fallen like a shattered tree; "future" refers to the subsequent time.
By the passage beginning with "suffering, disease,
and intoxication" (41.51) and continuing with "both in this world and after death," he presents the view of certain [teachers] who revile liquor.
By the expression "having passed away" (*pretya*), meaning in another birth,
he shows the state of being unshakeable by external winds;
with the words beginning "truth" (*satya*), he states his own view.

The meaning is that these defects of liquor, as stated in the opinion of certain authorities, occur only when it possesses qualities such as being unwholesome (*ahita*), and not when it is consumed according to the prescribed rule (*vidhi*) in small quantities.
The term "devoid of rule" (*vidhivarjitam*) is an adverbial modifier.

By demonstrating the similarity of liquor to food, he states its beneficial nature when used according to the rule and its harmful nature when used without the rule—beginning with the words "But... (*kiṃtu*).
That which is joined with reason—taking into account place, time, dosage, and so forth—is auspicious; that which is joined with lack of reason is inauspicious.
He states the effect [of this] through the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of reason, beginning with "the vital breaths" (*prāṇā*):
they are called "vital breaths" because they are the cause of life.
"Unreasonably applied" means applied contrary to the prescribed method;

"reasonably applied elixir" should be understood as follows: just as in the application beginning with "one should give a sesame seed of poison" (Ci. A. 1), the quantity of a single sesame seed possesses the nature of an elixir, so it should be known here.
He states the qualities of liquor consumed according to the prescribed rules, beginning with "joy" (*harṣa*): *harṣa* refers to physical enthusiasm,
and *muda* refers to mental contentment.

By the expression "pauruṣa" (manly) and "āśu" (swift), it means that it produces exhilaration and so forth quickly, without waiting for a transformation; "sukhamadapradam" means bestowing the intoxication of pleasure— that is, an initial state of exhilaration.

Others, however, read "madasukhapradam"; there too, by the words beginning with "rocanam," he describes the qualities of wine, wherein "madasukha" refers specifically to the onset of the first stage of intoxication.

The two functions—inducing sleep in those who have lost their sleep and awakening those who are excessively drowsy—occur solely through the power of promoting proper sleep. Alternatively, it should be understood that for those who have lost their sleep, it induces sleep by causing them to forget excessive anxiety and other causes of insomnia; whereas for those who are excessively drowsy, it acts as an awakener by removing the obstructions in the mental channels (manovahasrotas) and other factors that cause excessive sleep. Furthermore, the meaning is that alcohol itself is the remedy for diseases arising from alcohol, due to its power of producing an effect contrary to its own cause. "Rati" means that which produces sexual pleasure (*ratikāraka*).

"Increasing the attachment to pleasure upon contact with sense objects" means that when there is contact with sense objects such as sound and so forth, it increases both pleasure and attachment. When one who has drunk wine comes into contact with sense objects like sound and so forth, he then feels pleasure even in them; being thus pleased and desiring happiness, he again becomes attached to them.
"Of the aged" (*pravayasām*) means of the elderly; "festival" (*utsavaḥ*) refers to eagerness, that is to say, the longing for sense objects; "delight" (*āmodaḥ*) means joy.

Now, one might object: "Is not pleasure produced by the very nature of the object itself; so what is accomplished by liquor? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] first states that liquor is the agent of a particular kind of delight, beginning with the words "In the five," and so forth.
It should be understood that here, delight (*rati*) is to be adopted precisely because it generates extreme happiness.
Furthermore, "rest" (*viśrāma*) refers to the cause of rest for those afflicted by suffering.
"World of the living" (*jīvaloka*) means the world of those who are alive (62–67).
Regarding the phrase "practiced according to reason," he states the reasoning for the consumption of liquor as follows: "food and drink," and so forth.

In this regard, food is of three types—causing *vāta*, *pitta*, or *kapha*; likewise, drink is also of three types; age is also of three types according to the divisions of childhood and so forth; disease is also of three types by way of the distinctions of mild, moderate, and intense; or alternatively, it is of three types by way of the distinctions of *saumya* (cooling), *āgneya* (fiery), and *vāyavya* (windy); strength is of three types according to the distinctions of superior, inferior, and middling; and time is of three types characterized by cold, heat, and rain. Regarding the threefold nature of *sattva*—pure (*śuddha*), passionate (*rājasa*), and dark (*tāmasa*)—the author determines the result of *yukti* (methodical application), which consists of correct application, by means of the passage beginning with "by which method" (*yayā yuktyā*).

"One who is elevated by the qualities of *sattva* partakes of the qualities of wine"—this is how it should be applied. In that regard, the reasoning with respect to food is as follows: having consumed food that produces *vāta*, one should drink wine that removes *vāta*; likewise, in the case of [food] producing *pitta* or *kapha*, there should be the consumption of food that removes *pitta* or *kapha*.
In this way, the application with respect to drinks and so forth is also explained.

Strong liquor should not be drunk even during the three stages of life—childhood, old age, and youth; however, it may be drunk even in strong form during youth. This application is also made with regard to disease: for mild disease, [one should drink] strong and hot [liquor]; in heat, cold and sweet [liquor]; and in the rainy season, unctuous and digestive liquor.

Furthermore, according to the specific *doṣa*: for *vāta*, unctuous and hot liquor such as that made from molasses (*gauḍika*); for *pitta*, cold and sweet liquor such as that made from sugar (*śārkarā*); and for *kapha*, dry and strong liquor such as that made from honey (*mādhava*).

For it has been said: "Wine made from molasses or flour is generally beneficial for those with a predominance of wind (vāta), whereas that made from sugarcane juice, honey, or dates is for those with a predominance of phlegm (kapha) and bile (pitta).
By the very mention of the humors (doṣas), the constitutional types (prakṛti) such as those dominated by wind are also implicitly included.
Even according to the distinction of *sattva*, one whose *sattva* is predominant may drink even much liquor; however, for those who are *rājasa* or *tāmasa*, it should be only a very small amount.

The meaning is that the minds—referring to the *sattvas*—reach a state of unmanifestness (*avyaktatām*), that is, slight unmanifestness, and in the middle state, they reach a state of complete unmanifestness (*avyaktatām*); the sense is that in the highest state, they become entirely unmanifest.
Some, however, recite the verse beginning with "The rain that awakens the crops," and so forth.

In that context, just as fire—which has gold as its source—reveals the purity or impurity of gold, so too does liquor act in both ways: it is an awakener of the mind and a revealer of the qualities of the mind, [just as it reveals] the forms of gold; or perhaps the reading is "of gold coins" (*rukmāṇām*).
"Manifesting the individual" means manifesting the form (ākāra).
Verses 68–73 state that drinking is of three kinds according to the divisions of *sāttvika* and so forth, beginning with "fragrant," etc.
That which has a beautiful fragrance is *sugandhi*; *gandharva* means "one whose singing is beautiful";
that which has a happy end is *svanta*;
and *sumada* means "well-intoxicated" (*samamada*).

"And not causing the highest intoxication" means it does not produce the highest intoxication; there is never any apprehension of a third stage of intoxication from drinking this liquor. The meaning is that the highest intoxication does not occur in one who possesses *sattva*.
He states the reason for the absence of the highest intoxication: "Due to the quality," and so forth.

"From the conjunction with *sattva*" means from the association with the quality known as *sattva*; the point is that the quality called *sattva*, being illuminating by nature, is not overcome by intoxication, which causes delusion.
He says this very thing in the passage beginning with "sahasā" (suddenly) and so forth;
he describes the drinking of *rājasa* liquor in the passage beginning with "saumyāsaumya" (gentle and ungentle) and so forth.
"Gentle discourse" (*saumyakathā*) refers to that which is connected with the gentle; its opposite is "ungentle" (*asaumya*).

"Clear" and "unclear," "serene" and "unserene," and "variegated"— meaning consisting of various types due to the connection with coherent or incoherent sentences and so forth; by the words "likewise" (tathā) and so on, he describes the *tāmasa* [type of speech].
That which ends in delusion, anger, and sleep is "sammohakrodhanidrāntam" (74–78).

By the word "by whom," those characterized by passion and darkness (*rājasatāmasāḥ*) are referred to; drinking together with them, and through addiction to that [drinking] drinking excessively himself, he incurs the faults of liquor—the faults of the second and third stages of intoxication.
He states those who are to be accepted as being characterized by *sattva*: "those of pleasant character," and so forth;
"those with beautiful faces" means those whose appearance is pleasing.
"Clear" (viśadāḥ) means not turbid;
"increasing the drinking" (āpānaṃ vardhayantīti) means they increase clarity in the drinking, not an addiction to drinking, for that is censured.
Regarding the word "delightful" (manoramaiḥ), the word "more excellent" (sādhīyāṃsaiḥ) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
"Equal to those of virtuous deeds" means that such drinking is attainable by those of virtuous deeds;
"of steady constitution" and so forth refers to those who have previously consumed food, meaning those who have eaten before drinking liquor;

"descendants of liquor-drinkers" means those born into a family of liquor-drinkers—for them, the drinking of liquor does not cause disorder precisely because it is habitual (*sātmya*), just as poison does not affect a *viṣakanyā* (a girl born with innate immunity to poison).

Having described the faults and virtues of drinking intoxicants (madya) in verses 80–87, [the author] explains the types of alcoholism (madātyaya) by means of their causes and so forth, beginning with the word "ūrdhvam" (upward), etc.;
"sambhavam" refers to the cause.

In the passage beginning with "predominantly vāta" (*vātaprāyam*), the word *prāyaḥ*, meaning "mostly" or "in excess," indicates that all the types of alcoholism (*madātyaya*) to be described hereafter are caused by the three *doṣas*.

In the verse beginning with "but that [is] vāta... (*sa tu vāta...*), the term "that" (*sa tu*) refers to the *paittika* (bilious) type. Because the *paittika* alcoholism characterized by an excess of *vāta* is produced by the conjunction of *vāta* and *pitta*, it acts rapidly—just as an external fire joined with wind acts quickly.

In this regard, the established rule is: where the treatment yields immediate results, the condition subsides immediately; yet in the absence of treatment, it kills quickly, like the *śaṅkhaka* or *rohiṇī* diseases.
He states the reason why liquor causes the three *doṣas*: "Of poison," and so forth.
Although liquor is sour while poison is unmanifestly sweet, nevertheless, because of the similarity of many qualities, it is said that those very [qualities] are seen in liquor as well.
In the same way, the final [type of] intoxication means that it is life-taking and causes disease;
"separateness" (pṛthaktva) refers to its distinctness from the other types, such as the wind-based (vātika) and so forth.

By the passage beginning with "bodily suffering" (*śarīraduḥkha*), he states either the general definition of all types of alcoholism (*madātyaya*) or specifically the definition of alcoholism caused by the three *doṣas* (*tridoṣa-madātyaya*). This is because, in the *Rogasaṅgraha*, four types of intoxication (*mada*) are mentioned—due to *vāta*, *pitta*, *kapha*, and their combination (*sannipāta*)—in the following verse: "That which is called intoxication by liquor, that which is born of poison, and that which is born of blood—all these intoxications do not exist apart from the triad of *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha*" (Sūtra-sthāna, chapter 24). Thus, the fourfold nature of intoxication is stated on the basis of its origin from *vāta* and the other *doṣas*.

Therefore, intoxication (mada) has four types, because of the fourfold nature of intoxication; for "intoxication-excess" (madātyaya) is etymologically defined as an intoxication that is excessive (ātyayika).
"Like lightning" means it lasts for only a moment like a flash of lightning;
"tremor" (sphuraṇa) is a slight quivering, while "shaking" (vepana) is a distinct trembling localized in one part.
101–106 He describes the treatment according to the specific aggravation [of the humors]: "All," etc.;
he describes the treatment for when all the doshas are equal: "In the seat of kapha," etc.

Furthermore, the treatment here should be understood as following the sequence of the seats of *kapha*, because it arises from the seat of *kapha* and is first associated with *kapha*, just like *sannipāta* fever.

It states that *kapha* is predominant at the outset by saying "ending with bile and wind"; by this, it implies that [the treatment] begins with *kapha*. Moreover, the type of intoxication (*madātyaya*) produced by a particular kind of wine is pacified most effectively by that very same kind of wine.

Some say that just as primary poison is neutralized by the venom of a fanged creature, so too alcohol is neutralized by a different type of alcohol; however, by the phrase "by that very [alcohol]," he refers back to that same class of alcohol, and therefore it must be understood that the alcohol belongs to that very same class, since he will state immediately thereafter: "and whatever may be beneficial for whom."

Likewise, by the statement, "One should give salted liquor, or that made from flour (*paiṣṭika*), for the pacification of wind," when a wind-type alcoholism (*vātamadātyaya*) has arisen, any kind of liquor may be used, yet specifically *paiṣṭika* is mentioned; furthermore, specific prescriptions such as "with sugar, or that made from sugarcane juice" (*saśarkaraṃ śārkaraṃ vā*) will be applied extensively. Therefore, liquor of that same class or of another class should be administered in cases of alcoholism.
Regarding the phrase "the moistening of the essence of food" (*annarasotkleda*), some read it as "the moistening by sour taste" (*amlarasakleda*).
When sour [substances] are administered to sweeten an alkaline [mixture], why is another sour substance not given? To this he says: "For the alkaline... and so forth.
"Successively" (*uparyupari*) means one after another, even further above; that is to say, it is exceedingly superior.

"Madodayāḥ" refers to thirst and other such states caused by intoxication; some, however, read "jvarādayaḥ," in which case the meaning should be understood as thirst and other states characterized primarily by fever. An "avadaṃśa" is that which is consumed before drinking liquor;
a "dakṣa" is a cock.
Veśavāra is a seasoned meat preparation; it is characterized as previously described, consisting of repeatedly rolled balls of minced meat (pūpavarti) shaped like wicks,
coated with sauce— meaning it is prepared in the form of a sauce-coated "rasapraleha" (a savory lickable confection).
"With aguru-pastes" means with thick applications of aguru;
"dense" means abundant;
"bringing comfort through the heat of confinement" means producing pleasure by means of the warmth generated by being enclosed.
With the verse beginning "bhavya" (117–135), he describes the procedure for the bilious (paittika) fever;
"bhavya" refers to that from the northern region, while others say it is *karmaraṅga*.
*Mārdvīkam* means prepared from the juice of *mṛdvīkā* (grapes).
*Satīna* refers to the round pea (*vartulakalāya*).
"He is freed from disease" means he is freed from the present bile-induced alcoholism (*pittamadātyaya*).

"Krama" refers to the sequence for the gradual introduction of food mentioned immediately after emesis; "residual morbid humors" (doṣaśeṣa) here should be understood as the residual dregs in the digestive tract (koṣṭha); in the verse beginning with "guḍūcī," "rasa" means a decoction (kvātha).

"Tittiripratibhojana" refers to that rasa in which the partridge is the subsequent meal after digestion; one should administer it "without thirst" (anutarṣa), meaning one should have it drunk while observing for thirst at the time of eating; this amounts to saying one should provide it as a post-prandial drink (anupāna). By the words "of one without thirst" and so forth, he states the dosage for this post-prandial drink.

Regarding "of one who is not thirsty" (*anuttarṣasya*): this means that by giving him a drink again and again, his mind is not corrupted—that is, it does not undergo a transformation. By this it is meant that the wine which merely removes the mental distress of thirst is designated as *anutarṣa*; however, wine should not be given until intoxication is reached. "Thirst-quelling" (*tṛṣṇāghna*) refers to a liquid in the form of a cold, astringent decoction.
In the case of *cukrīkā*, *cāṅgerī*, *badarī*, and so forth, one should churn the leaves of the *badarī* and other such plants and take the resulting froth;
*ariṣṭaka* is the *nimba* tree.
136–163 – The treatment for *kapha*-type alcoholism, beginning with scraping (*ullekhana*) and so forth.
In such cases as "water is desired by one who thirsts," the preparation of water according to the sixfold method (ṣaḍaṅga-vidhi) is excellent; likewise,
that which has honey as its primary ingredient is called *mādhava*, and a broth (*yūṣa*) in which the three pungents (*vyoṣa*) predominate is called *vyoṣayūṣa*.
"Nīrasavartitam" means a side dish (vyañjana) known as "dry" (śuṣka), prepared by frying without excessive moisture.
"Vṛṇuyāt" means one should cover or pervade [the dish].
"Ārdrakapeśikāḥ" refers to long slices of fresh ginger; alternatively, there is a reading: "prabhūtārdrakapeṣitam."
In the case of *sauvarcala* and the following recipes, each component such as cinnamon, cardamom, black pepper, and so forth, constitutes one-half part;
the portion of sugar is equal to the portion of the previously mentioned single substance;
and "mixed with pungents" means it is joined with a small amount of spices.
"Śvetā" refers to the grape (*mṛdvīkā*); it should be understood that "śvetā" is the white grape produced in Kashmir. "Kāravī" refers to the small grape.
By the term "peśī" for mango and *āmalaka*, the fruiting grain (the pulp) contained within the fruit is intended.

"Of those whose limbs possess the pleasure of warmth through contraction"—that is, of those whose limbs have warmth and comfort due to their contraction (saṅkoca) and close contact (saṃśleṣa); some, however, say that "contraction" (saṅkoca) refers to saffron (kuṅkuma).
With the words "That which is this," etc., he describes the treatment for alcoholism caused by the combination of all three humors (sānnipātika-madātyaya).

Although thirteen types of *sannipāta* (combined morbidity) involving increased *doṣas* have been mentioned, nevertheless, because all forms of alcoholism (*madātyaya*) arise from the three *doṣas*, this treatment for alcoholism caused by *vāta* and the others that has been described constitutes the treatment for alcoholism arising from a *sannipāta* where one *doṣa* is predominant. Therefore, with reference to the remaining ten types of *sannipāta*—distinguished by two being predominant, one being deficient, or by the variations of medium and excessive intensity, as well as by balanced *sannipāta*—it is stated: "In the case of the tenfold *sannipāta*, it should be differentiated accordingly. In cases of alcoholism produced by the three *doṣas* in inferior, medium, or superior degrees, the treatment must be applied after differentiating them according to whether the *doṣas* are inferior, medium, or superior. However, in the case of balanced *sannipāta*, the treatment for all three combined should be administered.
He states that a treatment producing exhilaration should be administered for the disorder of intoxication (*madātyaya*), beginning with the words "forests" (*vanāni*).
Furthermore, he explains why an exhilarating therapy must be performed in the case of *madātyaya*, beginning with the words "not by agitating" (*nākṣobhya*).
The sense is that a gladdening treatment (*praharṣaṇī kriyā*) should be administered for the sake of mental pleasure and the pacification of the body.
He states the scope and the benefit of the aforementioned application of milk with the verse beginning "by means of fasting" (*laṅghanaiḥ*), etc.

Therein, he further describes the sequence of the milk-based regimen and the sequence of the practice of wine with the verse beginning "when [the body] has been restored by milk" (*payasābhihṛte*), etc.
"Gradually" means by way of the sequence of time; "little by little" means in small increments. 191–198
In contrast to this, he describes the fault in the consumption of intoxicants with the words beginning "vicchinna" and so forth;
"dhvaṃsaka" and "vikṣaya" have characteristics that will be described later,
and these two— dhvaṃsaka and vikṣaya— are also mentioned by Suśruta.

However, some explain the inclusion of *dhvaṃsaka* and *vikṣaya* by means of the following passage: "Indeed, those disorders designated as *pānātyaya* occur in one who suddenly indulges in excessive drinking after having abstained for a long time.
Regarding the treatment of these two, he says: "Of those two," and so forth.
"Action" refers to medical treatment;

by the words "for those two," etc., he demonstrates that destruction (*dhvaṃsaka*) and wasting (*vikṣaya*) are primarily caused by *vāta* due to the exhaustion and weakness [of the body]. "For one who consumes liquor" means for one who partakes of liquor according to the prescribed method.
199–205 He states the fruit of the total renunciation of intoxicants, beginning with "nivṛtta" (restrained) and so forth;
the qualification "jitendriya" (one who has conquered the senses) is specifically intended to apply only to the renunciation of intoxicants.

"By bodily and mental disturbances" means, by virtue of the context, specifically those bodily and mental disturbances produced by the impairment caused by liquor. The sense is that abstinence from liquor is ineffective against bodily and mental disturbances arising from other causes;
thus, "it is not appropriate" means that one does not become free from bodily and mental disturbances merely through the cessation of liquor.
The summary of the chapter beginning with "yatprabhāva" (207–211) is clearly intended as a concise overview of its contents.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Alcoholism," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka Saṃhitā* composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Chapter 25 of the Cikitsāsthāna (91 of 120)]
When a wound arises due to a blow or similar injury to one intoxicated by liquor, the "Chapter on the Two Wounds" (Dvitraṇīya) is taught for the purpose of treating that wound.
1–2. *Para* means liberation (*mokṣa*), and *avara* refers to substances and so forth; he who knows these is the *parāvarajña*.

Regarding the signs and treatment of these two, the cause is also included by means of the signs themselves, since it serves to indicate the disease. Although the *doṣas* are indeed corporeal (*śārīra*), the term "corporeal" is used here in order to exclude [the application of] the term *doṣa* to things such as the moistening of the tendons (*snāyu-kleda*).

He describes the distinction between endogenous (*nija*) and exogenous (*āgantu*) wounds with the verse beginning with "mantra" and so forth: Exogenous wounds are the opposite of endogenous ones in terms of their remedies—such as mantras and other medicines—as well as their causes, such as killing or imprisonment, and even in terms of certain portions of their symptoms. This partial symptom is as follows: an exogenous wound arises first with pain and subsequently provokes *vāta* and the other doshas; whereas in an endogenous wound, *vāta* and the others become aggravated first, and pain arises afterwards, as it has been said:
"An exogenous wound, having arisen first with pain, subsequently brings about the imbalance of *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha*" (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 20).

Since traumatic wounds (*āgantuvraṇa*) belong to a different category, they shall not be discussed here in detail. Therefore, he describes their treatment only in brief: "Of wounds," and so forth. The construction is as follows: for traumatic wounds which persist because their own [endogenous] causes remain, and for endogenous wounds that do not subside through treatments such as mantras, one should act exactly according to the medicines to be described, while observing the strength of the *doṣas*.

Furthermore, the failure to pacify visiting [agantuka] diseases here by means of treatment for visiting diseases should be understood as resulting solely from the persistence of innate [nija] morbid humors (doṣas); for this very reason, the phrase "of the innate causes" is employed here.
By the words beginning with "according to their own," there is an exposition of the etiology, pathogenesis, and so forth of innate ulcers.

Here, by the expression "by their respective causes," [the author] demonstrates that vāta and the other doshas undergo provocation independently; for a dosha vitiated by its own specific cause becomes independent. Furthermore, by the expression "by their respective causes," it is understood that those very factors which are the causes for the provocation of vāta and the others are themselves the producers of the intrinsic (nija) ulcer in this context, and there is no separate, specific cause for ulcers. It should be known, however, that the production of the specific characteristics of an ulcer from the general causes of vāta and the others occurs due to a difference in the pathogenesis (samprāpti).
With the words beginning with "stabdha," he describes the characteristics of wounds caused by Vāta and the other [doshas], as well as the aphorisms for their treatment;
in the phrase "with plasters and affusions," the word "non-oleaginous" (asnigdhaiḥ) is understood from the preceding context;
and "cirakārī" means that which produces a disorder over a long period of time.
And the concise exposition of medical treatment (cikitsāsamāsābhidhāna) is for the sake of easy comprehension alone (sukhagrahaṇārtham).
"Those two," and so forth.
The diversity that creates manifoldness is "diversity-of-manifoldness";
they are thoroughly corrupted, meaning excessively corrupted.

These types of wounds, such as *kṛtya* (curable), *utkṛtya* (requiring excision), and so forth, will be explained further on by the passage beginning with "having cut" (*kṛtyotkṛtya*). Among them, a *kṛtya* wound is one that requires treatment involving incision and other procedures; for an *utkṛtya* wound, however, nothing further needs to be done here other than healing (*ropaṇīya*). Alternatively, *kṛtya* means curable, while *akṛtya* means incurable. Thus, six types beginning with *kṛtya* are stated along with their opposites. Furthermore, seven types beginning with *saṃvṛta* (concealed) are indicated, which, together with their opposites, total fourteen.

*Utsaṅgī* means having flesh that has risen up (*udgatamāṃsa*), being elevated (*utsaṅgī*) with thick margins; alternatively, it refers to having a "hollow" (*utsaṅga*) in the form of a space for pus outside the wound. However, the definition of a malignant ulcer (*duṣṭavraṇa*) stated in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā*—beginning with "In that regard, one that is too constricted (*atisaṃvṛta*) or too dilated (*ativivṛtta*)" (Su.Sū.A. 22)—refers specifically to cases involving excessive constriction and so forth. Here, however, only the states of being constricted or dilated are mentioned; therefore, the inclusion of a malignant ulcer that is constricted (*saṃvṛta*) should be understood here as well.
Having stated that the threefold nature of examination (*parīkṣā*) has been explained, [the author] analyzes it with the words beginning "darśana" and so forth:
although the sense organs (*indriya*) are themselves objects of inference because they transcend the senses, here the term "sense organ" is used to refer to their physical bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

And although fire has been stated to be an object of inference based on the statement, "Fire [is known] by its power of burning" (Vi.A. 4), nevertheless, since fire is indeed understood through direct perception, it is here said that only the verbal testimony regarding fire must be examined, along with its opposite, namely hardness and heat.

Although inference (*anumāna*) was indeed mentioned in the section on examination with the words, "Examination for the wise is twofold: perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference" (Vi. A. 4), and so forth, he states here that it is not included because inference generally has no role [in this specific context]. However, we consider it correct to see that since inference is preceded by perception and other means, inference—along with perception and the rest—is included as a means of grasping supersensible objects (*atīndriya*) and the like. Furthermore, the word "perception" (*darśana*) here refers to direct apprehension; thus, even the examination of a wound by its odor is included.
Although touch is already included by the word "vision" (*darśana*), it is mentioned again here because it is more extensively engaged [in the process].
With the words "the white [discharge] has subsided," etc., he describes ulcers that are severely corrupted.

The characteristics of *ropya* (silver-like) [gems] are to be understood from another tantra; for Bhoja says: "Those that, having been repeatedly heated, become agitated again and again due to internal defects, yet appear as if pure on the outside—these are proclaimed as *ropya*.

Showing that these very [gems], such as the white ones and so forth, become twenty-four in number through further subdivisions based on other causes of differentiation, he says: "Twenty-four," and so on.

The meaning is that they become twenty-four types when differentiated by another factor— namely, the variation in the combination of causes that produce the corruption of the wound, such as the moistening of the tendons (snāyu-kleda) and so forth.
(Verses 24–25) The location is indicated by the words beginning with "tvak" (skin).
The intermediate receptacle is the stomach (koṣṭha);
the indication of its odor is given by the passage beginning with "clarified butter" (sarpiḥ).

They say that *śyāvagandha* is a smell like that of curd and other substances rubbed on copper; however, some read it as *śāva*; *śāva* is the smell of a corpse (*śava*), and the smell associated with sourness is called *amlagandha*.
With the words beginning with *lasīkā*, he describes the secretions (srāva):
He states the twenty-four defects mentioned in another classification: "Due to the moistening of the sinews," and so forth.
Here, the injury from nails or wood is a single cause, whereas the excessive rubbing of the skin and hair constitutes two causes.

The state of being beyond medical treatment is "inaction" (niṣkriyatva). By stating that an incurable disease is "without therapeutic intervention" (nirupakrama), even after having already declared its incurability, [the author] excludes those diseases that are curable with effort or manageable.

Since the treatment consisting of thirty-six therapeutic procedures has reached its proper occasion for discussion, it is mentioned separately first by the words beginning with "of ulcers" (*vraṇānām*) in order to demonstrate the preeminence of purification (*saṃśodhana*).
He states the therapeutic measures (upakrama), beginning with "śophaghna":
the anti-inflammatory measure (śophaghna-upakrama) consists of bloodletting and other methods that will be described hereafter.

Surgical procedure (*śastrakarma*) is of six kinds, beginning with incision (*pāṭana*). Within this very category, the two additional procedures mentioned in the *Śalyatantra*—extraction (*āharaṇa*) and probing (*eṣaṇa*)—are to be included. However, probing is an auxiliary to surgical procedure and not a surgical procedure itself; it is treated separately. Furthermore, he will describe "compression" (*avapīḍana*), which is the application of a paste or similar substance for the purpose of discharging pus, and "cooling" (*nirvāpaṇa*), which is the alleviation of the heat of burning.
"Two decoctions for purification and healing, along with two ointments"—thus there are two decoctions for purification and healing, as well as two ointments for purification and healing.

Regarding the statement "two oils possessing those same qualities," here even *ghṛta* (clarified butter) is included by the term "oil" (*taila*) because of their commonality as unctuous substances (*sneha*). Therefore, although he will later describe four types of oil and *ghṛta* each according to the distinction between purifying and healing, nevertheless, in this context, they should be counted as only two, based on their performing the dual function of purification and healing.
However, the Kashmiris read the text as: "two unctuous substances possessing those same qualities."
Regarding the term *patra* (leaf) in the sense of "covering," one *patra* constitutes the initial procedure; however, covering is of two kinds—external and internal—as will be described later.
*Utsādana* (elevation) is the raising of depressed ulcers, while *avasādana* (depression) is that which causes the reduction of elevated ulcerous flesh.

Regarding "making hard and making soft" in the context of fumigation and ointment: there is fumigation that makes hard and fumigation that makes soft; likewise, ointment should be known as being of two kinds.
They say that dusting powders for wounds are of two types, distinguished by those that improve the color of the skin and those that generate hair.
Thus, there are thirty-six therapeutic measures (*upakrama*); however, sixty measures are mentioned in the *Śalyatantra*, and these too should be understood as included within these very categories.
Now, he describes the treatments for ulcers according to their respective stages: "The premonitory symptoms," and so forth.

Swelling (*śotha*) is indeed the premonitory symptom of an ulcer; because the treatment of swelling is prescribed even before an ulcer has manifested, it is described here as a preliminary treatment for ulcers (*vraṇopakrama*).
By means of decoctions and medicated ghees— that is, by means of decoction-ghees— vijayā and balā [are used].
By "applications" (upanāhaiḥ) is meant warm and thick plasters;
*kiṇva* is the fermenting agent for liquor;
*umā* is *atasī*.
Saudha is milk; snuhīkṣīra is the latex of the thorn-apple; hemakṣīrī is kaṅkuṣṭha;
mukūlaka is dantī.
The word division is *sukumārasya* (for one who is delicate) and *kṛcchrasya* (for one who is not delicate); the connection is that "the weapon is the ultimate means of piercing. 49–54.

Regarding the sixfold surgical procedures mentioned by the words "incision" (*pāṭana*) and so forth, one should understand that they include the additional surgical acts such as incising (*dāraṇa*) described in the *Tisraiṣaṇīya* chapter; therefore, there is no contradiction. (55) He states the distinct scope of incision and the other procedures: "Vascular ulcers" (*nāḍīvraṇāḥ*), etc.
Those gulmas that are fully ripened are to be pierced (surgically),
as are those born of blood; thus, the blood-born gulmas are the diseases of the blood described in the chapter on the "Regimen for Blood."
"Curable by venesection and so forth" refers to those treatable by bloodletting and similar procedures;
"requiring scarification" refers to those that have reached the stage for excision.
Regarding "in the case of afflicting a wound": the application for afflicting a wound should be made without oil, avoiding the opening of the wound.

"Nyagrodha and so forth" refers to what was stated as *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and so on; herein, "strength and so forth" refers to what was taught in the treatment for removing swelling, beginning with "vijayā, madhuka, vīrā," and so on.
With the words beginning "lambāni," he describes the commencement of the ritual union;
"śukti" refers to the jujube fruit.

Regarding the phrase "having made it equal with an equal limb," it should be construed as follows: having made it equal—that is, similar—to another limb that is equal, meaning unaltered, one should join it.
The bandages *kavalikā* and *kuśikā* are to be found in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*,

in the section beginning with "of limbs that have fallen off or been struck," and so forth. Some read "the treatments for constipation (*ānāha*) and so on" as "from its own treatment," meaning from the treatment of erysipelas (*visarpa*) and other such conditions.
68–71 – *Balā*, *guḍūcī*, and so forth.

In this case, *balā* and the other ingredients should be ground together with equal parts of sugar, milk, beeswax, oil, and so forth, and a bolus (*utkarikā*) should be prepared for fomentation (*sveda*). Others, however, state that one should prepare an oil-based unctuous substance (*sneha*) by cooking it with four times the amount of milk and a paste of *balā* and the rest, adding beeswax equal to one-quarter of the oil;
because the oil here remains in a solidified state, it is designated as "oil-sugar" (*sneha-śarkarā*), similar to honey-sugar.
The phrase "with a decoction of the ten roots" (*dvipañcamūla-kvathitena*) should be construed with "water," "milk," "ghee," or "oil."

Regarding the passage beginning with "of two kinds" (dvividhām) and so forth: it is soft (*mṛdvīm*) because of its shoots (*audbhidaiḥ*) which are tender stalks (*mṛdubhir nālaiḥ*), and hard (*kaṭhinām*) because of its metals (*lohaiḥ*).
"To be split" (*pāṭhyam*) means that which is to be probed (*eṣaṇīyam*) and that which is to be incised (*pāṭhyam*).
Regarding verses 80–82, "the leaves of *nimba* and *kolaka*": here, *nimbakolaka* refers to a mild variety of *nimba*; alternatively, there is a reading *kulaka*, where *kulaka* means *paṭola*.
(Verses 83–85).
Having described the characteristics of a clean wound with the words "not excessively red" and so forth, he states the treatment for healing: "Nyagrodha," etc.
By the use of the plural term "decoctions" (kaṣāyāḥ), he indicates that the formulations may be used either individually or collectively as previously mentioned.
The bark of *dārvī* (dārvītvak) is both a purifier of wounds and a healer.
"One should prepare the ghee with those very same substances" means that one should prepare it with the very same ingredients used for the oil; this refers specifically to the ghee.
By the statement "it is healing (ropaṇīya)" and so forth, the meaning is that only a healing ghee should be prepared, and not a purifying (śodhana) ghee.
Regarding "vārkṣa" and so forth: bark produced from a tree is "vārkṣa.
As for "savyadakṣiṇa," it means left and right; the circumambulation on the left is "savya," and the circumambulation on the right is "dakṣiṇa."
Right here, the restriction of the fourteen types of bandaging mentioned by Śalya (in Sūtra 95–96) should be applied;
the breast-milk preparations are those mentioned in the *Ṣadvirecanaśatāśritīya* chapter.
Aśmakāsīsa (black vitriol) and dhātukāsīsa (green vitriol); the downward-moving substances such as trivṛt and others are purgative agents.
Regarding the phrase "in those fit for cutting" (*chedye*), it means in those prepared for excision; and regarding "in those cut" (*klṛpteṣu*), it means in those incised.
To demonstrate the scope of dryness, oiliness, burning, and piercing, as well as the various types of burning substances, he says: "of the delicate ones," and so forth.

"One who knows the distinctions of burns" means one who knows the specific characteristics of burns—such as their oily or dry nature—as well as their forms such as spots or circles; thus, he is "one who knows the distinctions of burns. Regarding "of those [afflicted] by poison and so forth," it refers to those who have consumed poison.

Although alkali (kṣāra) is not mentioned separately among the initial procedures (upakrama), nevertheless, because it performs the function of surgical instruments and fire, it is included within the procedures involving instruments and fire; thus, by the statement "one should also apply alkali," alkali is also prescribed.
"One should saturate" (tarpayet) means one should cause an ointment (lepa) to be applied for the purpose of saturation.
By means of the section beginning with "kakubha," he states three introductory procedures: the production of skin, likewise the restoration of natural color, and likewise the production of hair;
[it is said] that because they take hold of the skin very quickly, they become possessed of skin (*satvacas*).
"Triphalākusumāni" refers to the flowers of the three myrobalan trees;
"latā" is priyaṅgu;
"kāntā" is mañjiṣṭhā.
The best of liquids is mercury, or ghee, which is the union with nectar; [the best of salts is] karparikā-tuttha. 113–119.
The summary of the chapter beginning with "Two types of wounds" (dvau vraṇau) and so forth is clear [in verses] 120–121.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Two Types of Wounds," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka-saṃhitā composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.

[Chapter 26 of Cikitsāsthāna (92 of 120): Following the description of the treatment for diseases categorized as "two-wound" (dvivraṇīya), the treatment for the three vital organs (trimarmīya) is now stated in order to describe the treatment for diseases of the head, bladder, and heart, which are categorized as "three-vital-organ" (trimaṇi).

By the term *trimarma*, diseases localized in the three vital organs (*marma*) and their treatment are denoted; therefore, the therapeutic procedure composed concerning the diseases of the three vital organs is called *trimarmīya-cikitsita*. [Sūtra 1–2] He identifies the three primary vital organs under discussion: "seven more," and so forth.
"With reference to the enumeration of the body" means with reference to what has been stated in the *Śārīra-sthāna* (Śā. A. 7) regarding the enumeration of the body.
He states the reason for the primacy of the vital points (*marman*) such as the heart: "because they are the substratum of the vital breaths" (*prāṇāśrayāt*).
He provides the justification for why the heart and so forth are the substrata of the vital breaths: "those [vital points]," and so on.

Since the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is specifically impaired by the injury of the heart and other organs, the vital breaths are said to be "supported by" the heart and so forth; just as a painting, being damaged when the wall is damaged, is said to be "supported by the wall" because it rests upon it—so too [the vital breaths] rest upon the heart and other organs which serve as their support. For by the word "supported" (*saṃśrita*), the act of resting upon a support is expressed.

Listen to the protection—that is, the treatment—for those great diseases such as urinary disorders (*basti*) and others, for the sake of preserving them; or alternatively, for the sake of preserving the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) residing therein, that is, residing in the bladder and other organs. "Of the great diseases" refers to conditions like *udāvarta* that pervade the major vital points (*marman*) such as the bladder and so forth. "Protection" means medical therapy.
(3–4) He states the causes and other factors for those arising from the bladder and so forth, in their proper order, beginning with the word "kaṣāya": [The text continues: "Kaṣāya... and so on.
By stating "hot and pungent [substances] in the colon," and so forth, he describes the etiology, symptoms, and treatment of udāvarta.

Now, one might ask: how can it be said that the vitiated apāna vāyu causes its own obstruction, when it is expressed by the term "obstruction of māruta"? We reply: this [vāyu], being corrupted and failing to function properly, causes its own obstruction; it is just as the mind itself effects the restraint of the mind.
And it has been said: "The restraint of the senses is the work of the mind; [therefore] its own restraint [is required]" (Śāstradīpikā 1.1).
Furthermore, the term "upward" (*ūrdhva*) means having the nature of moving upward (5–10).
"Anointed with [medicines] that destroy *tailajvara* (oil-fever)" means anointed with *guru* and other substances that destroy *śītajvara* (cold-fever).
Regarding the fruit-candle (*phalavarti*) beginning with "black" (*śyāmā*): *śyāmā* is a variety of *trivṛt*.
That in which there are ten parts of *māṣa* is called "having ten parts of *māṣa*" (*daśabhāgamāṣā*).
"Dvirlavaṇām" means containing two parts of salt;
by the statement "with jaggery," one should provide as much jaggery as is suitable for making a pill (varti).
By the phrase ending with "with yavaśūkas," it is indicated that the second pill must be made with jaggery alone.
Śaṅkhinī, śvetabuhnā,
rāḍha, madanaphala, veśmadhūma, and agāradhūma.
"Rakṣoghna, sarṣapa, karahāṭa, and madana:
in their failure" refers to the non-performance of the tasks for which the powders of these fruit-wicks have been prescribed.
Regarding the "upward-moving" (ūrdhvānuloma) medicine— the emetic and purgative medicines—

he states the addition to the enema according to the distinction of the *doṣas* with the words "when vāta is predominant," and so forth; in upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*), pitta and kapha should be understood as being provoked by vāta alone.
"Saḥ" refers to the previously mentioned enema (basti);
"prasannā" is the clear portion on top of wine.
Guḍasīdhu is a fermented liquor made from jaggery (guḍa).
Regarding the phrase "bhūyo'nubandhe," it refers to a case where, despite the administration of an enema (basti), there is a recurrence or persistence of upward-moving wind (udāvarta).

And this purgation [should be administered] after seven days from the administration of the enema, as it has been stated: "A person who has undergone purgation must certainly avoid the administration of a non-unctuous enema for seven days; once purified by a non-unctuous enema, he may undergo purgation" (Siddhisthāna, Chapter 1).
In the sequence beginning with "dviruttarā" (twice higher), there is a doubling of the substances in each successive stage;
*suvarcikā* is the alkali of *svarjika*.
The ellipsis "drunk with sweet water" is to be supplied;
*ugragandhā* is *ajamodā*.

Regarding the phrase "of the *sthirā* group," which refers to the minor *pañcamūla*, and the phrase "of *śampāka*, *pūtīka*, and *karañja*": here, the word *pūtīka* is an epithet for a specific type of *karañja*.
For instance, Jatūkarṇa states: "Ghee prepared with *āragvadha*, *pūtīka*, *punarnavā*, the *sthirā* group, and so forth... and so on.

"Fruit and root are said to be purgatives" refers to what is stated in the *Dīrghañjīvitīya* chapter (Sūtra-sthāna, chapter 1) regarding the purgative action of plants possessing roots and fruits; alternatively, it refers to what will be explained in the *Kalpa-sthāna* concerning purgative formulations.
By the verse beginning with *hṛdi* (26), having demonstrated the specific name *ānāha*— which is produced by particular causes and symptoms of *udāvarta*— he states the remedy for it.
By the verse beginning with *vyāyāma* (27–31), he describes the various types of dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*) among the diseases localized in the bladder.
With the words beginning "separately" (*pṛthak*), he describes the pathogenesis (*samprāpti*) of dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*) arising from vāta, pitta, kapha, and their combination (*sannipāta*);
and with the words beginning "intense pain" (*tīvrā hi ruk*), he describes the specific symptoms (*rūpa*) of each of the four types [32–35].

By the passage beginning with "viśoṣayet" (one should dry up), [the author] mentions all four types of *aśmarī* (urinary calculi) diseases. In another treatise (*tantrāntara*), calculi are said to be born of Vāta, Pitta, Kapha, and semen (*śukra*). Although all calculi are indeed produced by the three *doṣas*, as it is said: "Just as the wind and the lightning-fire condense celestial waters, so too does heat, together with Vāta, condense the phlegm (*balāsa*) situated in the bladder" (Suśruta Saṃhitā).
Thus it is established by Suśruta (Ni. A. 3); nevertheless, the designation as "born of Vāta" and so forth should be understood as referring to cases where a single doṣa is predominant.

In the case of a stone (aśmarī) born of vāta, when the urine is being dried up by a powerful wind, the *kapha* residing therein is transformed into the form of a stone; this should be understood to apply similarly to a stone born of pitta. For this very reason, Suśruta stated that all stones have *śleṣman* (kapha) as their substrate.

Regarding the production of a stone, he provides an analogy: "Like yellow pigment (*rocanā*) in the bile of a cow"; the use of the plural "in the biles" (*pitteṣu*) is with reference to the multiplicity of bile. 36
