Specific characteristics, such as the shape of a *kadamba* flower and so forth, are to be inferred according to their suitability from the specific humors involved.

Among these, due to *vāta*, the stone has the shape of a *kadamba* flower and is three-lobed; due to *pitta*, it is like a stone and smooth; and due to *kapha* and *śukra*, there is injury from agitation, meaning that through the agitation caused by the stone, an injury occurs in the urinary passage or the bladder.
"Of it" means of the stone;
"due to its removal" means due to the departure from the urinary passage;
"happily" means without pain.
With the words beginning with "eṣā," he speaks of sugar.
"Bhinnamūrtiḥ" means having its form divided due to its atomic nature;
for this very reason, it is said that "it flows out through the urinary passage.
By that wind, the stone (aśmarī), divided into two, three, or many parts, becomes like gravel (śarkarā) as it flows out through the urinary passage.
By the passage beginning with "semen and impurities," the symptoms of dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra) arising from semen are described;
the phrase "located in the receptacle of urine" means situated within the urinary tract.
With the verse beginning with "kṣata," etc., [the author] describes dysuria caused by blood.
"Kṣataja" refers to blood;
"provoked by depletion" means that when semen is depleted due to excessive sexual intercourse, it is driven upward by the *vāyu* (wind) and brought into the bladder,
resulting in "distension," which is the state of the bladder being filled.
Regarding the phrase "in that [blood]," when it is excessively accumulated,
these eight types of urinary obstruction (*mūtraghāta*) mentioned in the *Sūtrasthāna* are here designated by the term *mūtrakṛcchra* and explained.

As for the thirteen types of urinary obstruction (*mūtrāghāta*) to be discussed in the *Siddhisthāna* chapter on the three vital organs (*trimarmīya*), although they were not explicitly formulated in the *Sūtrasthāna*, they should be understood as being included within this category, just like the eleven minor types of skin diseases (*kṣudrakuṣṭha*).

This is the distinction between *mūtrāghāta* (obstruction of urine) and *mūtrakṛcchra* (dysuria): in *mūtrakṛcchra*, the urine flows with difficulty, whereas in *mūtrāghāta*, the urine is dried up or suppressed. Furthermore, in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā*, the distinction between *mūtrakṛcchra* and *mūtrāghāta* is stated by means of a separate chapter.

Others, however, claim that *mūtrāghātas* are merely specific varieties of *mūtrakṛcchra*, and thus include them within the four types of *mūtrakṛcchra* caused by Vāta, Pitta, and so forth, according to their suitability; for that reason, they do not mention *mūtrāghāta* separately.
He describes the treatment for dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra) with the verse beginning "abhyañjana" and so forth;
[it is prepared] with the *pañcamūla* groups starting with *sthira*,
which are designated as "vāta-alleviating" (*vātahara*) in various contexts.
Pattūra, śāliñcaka, aśmabhit, and pāṣāṇabheda—
these and other such substances possess these very same qualities.
The oils and fruits such as *tila*, *umā*, *sphota*, and so forth [are mentioned in verses] 45–48;
"the summer regimen" refers to the rules for the summer season as stated in the chapter on the eighty [disorders].

Although sprinkling and immersion were already mentioned there as being specifically for the cold season (*śiśira*), they are stated again here specifically for the purpose of performing cold-season sprinkling and immersion; [this is done] according to the previous method using *daṇḍairaka*— known as *ahoggala*— along with a decoction and a mixture of honey and sugar.
In the passage beginning "from the cucumber and the safflower," the word "seed" (*bīja*) is to be connected [to each].
Regarding the passage beginning with "kṣāroṣṇa" and so forth:
in cases of difficult kapha-type dysuria (kaphakṛcchra), medicinal drugs and food and drink combined with alkali (kṣāra) and other such substances should be administered;
"vyoṣa" refers to the three pungents (trikaṭuka).
*Truṭi* is cardamom;
*sārasa* is the bird well-known by its own name;
"the size of a *kola*" means a measurement of eight *māṣakas*.
Kaiṭarya, pārvata, nimba, śitivāraka, and śāliñca. 54–57.

"All [the remedies] for wind and so forth," etc.: this very same medicine for wind and the other doshas, when combined, should be administered for dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra) arising from the three doshas. Furthermore, even when the doshas are in equilibrium, the treatment must be performed according to the sequence of the locations of the doshas, starting with vāyu; it should not be done according to the sequence of the locations of kapha as in the case of fever (jvara) arising from the three doshas. The point is that although dysuria may be initiated by all three doshas in equal measure, because it occurs in the location of vāyu, vāyu alone is to be treated first.
Regarding the treatment for a disorder initiated by an irregular combination (*viṣama-sannipāta*), he states: "When [the humors] exceed three," and so forth.
The phrase "exceeding three" is connected in this sequence with the words "in phlegm (*kapha*)," "likewise in bile (*pitta*)," and "likewise in wind (*pavana*). (58)
That therapeutic procedure which is prescribed for the difficult condition arising from *kapha* and *vāta* should indeed be performed together for gravel (*śarkarā*) and stone (*aśmarī*).
Regarding the instruction "one should drink the powder of *kharāśvā* and *ajamodā*," the drinking is to be done with water alone.
Iksuraka is kokilakṣa;
kunduru is known by its own name;
"two parts of triphalā" means two parts for each of the constituent roots of the triphalā.
"By sour substances" means by fermented gruel (*kāñjika*) and the like;
"not by vinegar" means excluding vinegar (*śukta*).

Although wine (*madya*) is already included under the category of "sour substances," it is mentioned again here for the purpose of declaring its excellence as a purifier of the bladder and its superior power in breaking up *aśmarī* (urinary calculi).
"Aśmabhid" means that which breaks stones;
"sitopalā" refers to sugar.

"A surgeon skilled in the science of surgery (śalya-vid) should extract [the stone]" means that one who knows the surgical treatise should draw out the calculus according to the procedure prescribed therein.

Having observed the fault—meaning, having observed the fault to be excessive—one should perform the remedial treatment (*pratikarma*), which is medical therapy (*cikitsita*). *Madhvasanākhyaparṇyau* refers to *madhuparṇī* (guḍūcī) and *asanaparṇī* (aparājitā); others say it refers to *dāruparṇī*.
"In that which arises from combination" means when it is associated with all three *doṣas*;
"bird" (*vihaṅga*) refers to a winged creature.

Regarding the instruction "one should eat," one should consume [the substances] even if they are unprocessed, as in the case of *ghṛtaṃ śvadaṃṣṭrā* and similar formulations, due to their association (*sāhacarya*). Some say that the fresh juice (*svarasa*) of *śvadaṃṣṭrā* should also be eightfold [in quantity]; that is not correct, for among oleaginous substances (*sneha*), the fresh juice is always equal in measure to the oil itself. As stated by Jatūkarṇa: "The oil is four times the amount of the paste (*kalka*); the fresh juice is commensurate with the oil. Therefore, the rule for fresh juice should be understood to apply to all oleaginous substances, just like milk. Regarding the phrase "of *sthirā* and others," the group beginning with *kataka* is to be understood as the group mentioned in the sweet category (*madhuraskandha*) in the eighth chapter of the Vimānasthāna: "...*kataka*, *kāśmarya*... and so forth.
"By that very same procedure" means by the previously mentioned procedure. Therefore, in place of *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *sthirā* and the others should be substituted individually.
"Produced from sweet fruits" refers to oil extracted from fruits such as *madhūka* and *akṣoṭa*.
With the verse beginning "vyāyāma" (76), he describes the unwholesome factors for dysuria;
then, following the sequence starting with etiology, he describes the treatment for heart disease.
"Excessive medical treatment" (*gadāticāra*) refers to the improper management of diseases.
Regarding the phrase "causing heart disease," it is as in the example: "Bhīṣma was the remover of fear and grief for the Kurus. By this, [the rule] *tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari* (Pāṇini 2.2.15) [is applied].

15) By this [statement], the compound here is [to be understood as] "born from heart disease" (*hṛdrogaja*) in the passage beginning with "discoloration" (*vaivarṇya*); because of the expression "born from heart disease," they maintain that discoloration and the other symptoms are complications (*upadrava*) because they occur at a time subsequent to the heart disease. However, those who assert that discoloration and the others are the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of heart disease explain their status as symptoms (*liṅga*) based on the grammatical analysis (*vigraha*) "born from heart disease" (*hṛdrogeṇa saha jāyante*), meaning they arise simultaneously with the heart disease itself.

Although heart diseases have been described in detail in the chapter on "The Head and the Heart" (Sūtra-sthāna 17), they are stated here in brief within the section on treatment; the term *marman* refers to the heart.
With the words beginning with "oil" (*taila*), he describes the treatment in due order; here, it should be understood that the oil and the other ingredients are to be drunk in equal proportions.
Regarding the phrase "of *vayaḥsthā* and *kāyasthā*," this refers to the extraction of the fresh juice (*svarasa*) of *guḍūcī* and *āmalaka*, respectively.
Regarding the term *agryasarpiḥ* (best ghee), the word *agrya* is used here to indicate the preeminence of this specific ghee.

In the context of *vikartikā*— where pain takes the form of cutting in the heart— they say that one should prepare a decoction and add a paste (*kalka*) of *nāgara* and other ingredients into a decoction of *pauṣkara* and other herbs.
In the verse beginning with "pathyāśatī," it should be explained that the paste (kalka) is fried with *yamaka* oil and then drunk with jaggery (*guḍa*), clear wine (*prasannā*), and salt.
Regarding the phrase "two *triphalās*," the second *triphalā* consists of grapes (*drākṣā*), *kāśmarya*, and *parūṣaka*; *truṭi* refers to small cardamom (*sūkṣmailā*).
"Cold" and so forth refers to the treatment for pitta-type heart disease;
"in the case of injury" refers to the treatment for chest injury and emaciation.
Rāsnā is superior;
[the preparation consists of] dates and date-pulp mixed with honey— meaning that after the cooking process is complete, one-quarter part of honey is added.
In the section beginning with "svāduphala" (90–95), the term *svarasāḥ* refers to juices;
the section beginning with "svinna" (96) constitutes the chapter on the treatment of heart disease caused by *kapha*.
The term *śaṅkarāṇi* means "beneficial.

In the case of *udumbara* and so forth, one should add a quarter-part (*pādika*) of the powder of *trivṛt* and the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*) to three parts of a decoction of *udumbara* and other such ingredients; it is said to be "joined with non-cold water," meaning it should be taken with a warm water after-drink (*anupāna*).

"Prescribed by the ritual method" (kalpavidhānadiṣṭam) means prescribed in the context of rejuvenation therapy (rasāyana); by the word "kalpa," minor rejuvenation therapy (kṣudrarasāyana) is intended. "Prāśa" refers to the Cyavanaprāśa, and "Āgastya" is a specific designation for a medicinal electuary (leha).

Regarding the treatment for disorders arising from all three *doṣas* (*tridoṣaja*), the prescription of fasting (*laṅghana*) at the outset is made because the heart is a seat of *kapha*; thus, even when all three *doṣas* are involved, it is considered that *kapha* alone must first be overcome through fasting.
However, regarding the *tridoṣaja* disorder, he states the general rule for treating the predominant *doṣa*: "When [the *doṣa*] is deficient," and so forth.

The meaning of the statement is that, having observed whether the doshas are in a state of deficiency, excess, or equilibrium, one should perform that treatment which is praised for its ability to overcome the predominant dosha. (100) By the verse beginning with "When [the patient] has eaten excessively," etc., the author treats the sannipātika type of heart disease by dividing the commonly occurring colic according to its specific symptoms.
By the words "excessive during digestion" (*bhukte'dhikam*) and so forth, *śleṣma-śūla* (phlegmatic colic) is described;
by "remains [unrelieved]" (*sthitam*), it is meant to be subsided;

by "excessive after digestion" (*jīrṇe'dhikam*) and so forth, *anila-śūla* (windy colic) is indicated; and by "excessive while digesting" (*jīryatyadhikam*), he speaks of *paittika-śūla* (bilious colic).
"By fruits" refers to grapes, *kāśmarya*, and so forth.

By the phrase "in the three [doshas] alone," etc., he describes colic caused by the combination of all three doshas (*sānnipātika-śūla*). "Root purgative" refers to purgation using the roots of *trivṛt* and other such plants.
Regarding this, he states the rationale for purgation: "Generally, [the dosha] is wind," and so forth.
Here, although enema (basti) is appropriate when wind is aggravated, nevertheless, with regard to the stomach (āmāśaya), purgation alone should be administered to cleanse the stomach.
*Kṛmighna* [is mentioned] in the section on the nature of diseases (*Vyādhitārūpīya*).
7) The procedure stated for the removal of worms (103).

While the treatment for hereditary head diseases (*kramāgata-śiroroga*) is yet to be discussed, [the author] first addresses catarrh (*pratiśyāya*), because it is the primary cause of head diseases and is a frequent cause of such ailments.
It is also stated in the *Śālākya*: "Since almost all diseases are caused by *pratiśyāya* (catarrh), therefore the disease *pratiśyāya* is taught first.

Although *pratiśyāya* has indeed been mentioned in the treatment of *rājayakṣma* (consumption), there it was described as a premonitory symptom (*pūrvarūpa*) of consumption; however, the distinction here is that *pratiśyāya* is being discussed as an independent disease.
Dust,
dirt, excessive sleep, sleeping during the day, and frost.
Regarding the phrase "in the defect of condensation" (*saṃstyānadoṣe*), which refers to the defect that has become thickened,
he states the characteristics of the four types of catarrh (*pratiśyāya*) caused by vāta and the other humors in sequence, beginning with "pain in the nose" (*ghrāṇārti*).
The term "disease of the voice" (*svararoga*) refers to hoarseness (*svarabheda*), characterized by a change in the quality of the voice.
In the passage beginning with "heavy due to phlegm" (kaphādguruḥ), the word *guru* is an adjective qualifying itching (*kaṇḍū*). The term *srotasi* refers to the nasal passages (*nāsāsrotasi*).
By the passage beginning with "sarvo 'tivṛddhaḥ" (when excessively aggravated), [the author] describes sneezing and other symptoms born of catarrh (*pratiśyāya*);
here, those who do not list diseases of the mouth consider that the disease of the mouth is already included by the mention of diseases of the head.

The detailed treatment of these conditions, such as malignant coryza (*duṣṭapratiśyāya*) and nasal catarrh (*kṣavathu*), is found in the *Śālākya* and other specialized treatises; however, because this work primarily concerns other subjects, only a brief summary is given here (verses 107–109).
Beginning with "obstruction and injury" (*rodhābhighāta*), he describes the characteristics of malignant coryza and the subsequent conditions, ending with *arjunaloma*, in their proper sequence.
In the passage beginning with "kruddha," the word "sa" refers to *anila* (vāta).
From "mastuluṅgāt," meaning from the brain (*mastiṣka*).
By the passage beginning with "sapitta," he describes *aruṃṣikā*; that [condition] should be known as arising in the head.

Although the symptoms of head diseases are stated here starting with "bhṛśārti" (intense pain) as arising from the occurrence of catarrh (*pratiśyāya*), nevertheless, these same symptoms should be understood to apply to head diseases that arise independently as well;
this should likewise be stated regarding the symptoms of diseases of the mouth and other such areas.
"By all [the humors]" means that when the characteristics of vāta and the others are combined, it becomes a disorder of the three doṣas (tridoṣa);
"emission" refers to the discharge from the mouth.

"Thirst," and so forth, refers to the symptoms of mouth diseases born of *pitta*. Showing that the various mouth diseases described in detail in *Śālākya* are included within these very four types of mouth disease, he says: "Configuration," and so forth. "Configuration" (*saṃsthāna*) refers to the location, such as the lips; "vitiated element" (*dūṣya*) refers to blood and the like; "shape" (*ākṛti*) refers to the clinical sign (*liṅga*); and "name" (*nāma*) refers to [conditions] such as *śītāda*. Due to the distinctions and variations of these factors, they become sixty-four kinds; these are to be understood from the *Śālākya* itself.

In the Suśruta-saṃhitā, sixty-five diseases of the mouth are mentioned; nevertheless, here, following the opinion of Videha, these sixty-four [diseases] are presented according to their respective locations— that is, according to the sections on treatment (119–123).
Because these diseases are located within the mouth, they are indeed included among the types of anorexia (arocaka) and abdominal distension (ānāha).

Although anorexia has already been mentioned in the treatment of *rājayakṣman* (consumption), there is no redundancy here, as the anorexias described in this context are specifically those that arise separately from the anorexias associated with wasting (*śoṣa*).

Here, "aversion" refers to a lack of appetite caused by excessive greed; in this regard, the author demonstrates that the constant practice [of eating] driven by excessive greed is the cause of anorexia.
"Vibaddhasambaddhayutam" means "joined with bonds";
"naikarasam" means "possessing many flavors.
With the verse beginning "nādo 'tiruk" (excessive ringing), he describes the diseases of the ear;

although twenty-eight such diseases are mentioned in the *Śālākya*, it should be understood here that the remaining ones are included within these four ear diseases, as they too are produced by [the imbalance of] vāta and the other humors.
By the passage beginning with "alpastu rāgaḥ," four eye diseases are designated:
*upadeha*, *dūṣikā*,
and *subhṛśoṣṇavāhī*, which is that which discharges excessively hot [matter].
He states the number of eye diseases not previously mentioned: "There are ninety-six eye diseases.

Regarding these eye diseases, there is a disagreement among the teachers: Videha stated seventy-six eye diseases, Karāla stated ninety-six, and Sātyaki stated eighty. This present enumeration follows the opinion of Karāla, as it is said therein: "Twenty-seven are located in the eyelids, and nine are proclaimed to be in the joints."
"Thirteen reside in the white [portion], six diseases arise from the black portion,
twenty-five reside in the vision, and sixteen indeed are all-pervading.
Regarding these, he states the means of knowing them, beginning with "Of those," and so forth.
"Manifestation" is the definition.
He states the reason for not enumerating the various eye diseases in the following passage beginning with "In the sections concerning other [senses]," etc.
With the words beginning with "tejaḥ," he states the definition of baldness (*khālitya*);

by the word "tejas" (heat), the bodily warmth is intended. It should be construed that when this [warmth] is joined with wind (*vāta*) and other humors, it produces baldness and so forth. However, those who read "tejaḥ savātam" explain that by the word "tejas," bile (*pitta*) is also meant.
"Having the luster of Hari" means having the color of Kapila;
"of the hair" refers to the locks of hair;
"for the sake of not being empty" means for the sake of this science of medicine (kāyacikitsā) not being devoid of the diseases designated in the branch of surgery (śālākya).
"Bheṣajasaṅgraha" refers to the treatise that designates medicinal remedies (132–133).
Now, their medical treatments are described in sequence.
The prohibition of smoking in cases of coryza (pratiśyāya) was made with reference to purgative (virecanika) smoke; therefore, the prescription of unctuous (snehika) smoke here is not contradictory.

Regarding the phrase "pāṇisvedaṃ ca upanāhanaṃ ca" (fomentation by the palms and poultices), the term "rodha" in the expression "kṣavathusrāvarodhādau" (in cases such as the obstruction of sneezing and discharge) denotes nasal catarrh (pratīnāha).
The *saṅkara* and other types, as well as the *saṅkaraprastara* and others, are the sudations described in the chapter on sudation (*svedādhyāya*).
*Tarkārī* and *jayantī* [are used] for the drying of the channels, the *śṛṅgāṭaka*, the nose, and the eyes; the *śṛṅgāṭaka* is the junction of the vessels that nourish the nose, ears, and eyes.

Regarding the oil for nasal drops mentioned in the passage beginning with "prabhāvyāje," the phrase "by its heat" means by the heat of goat's milk; in the process of grinding and steaming, they are only slightly moistened.
As for the phrase "with the powder of yaṣṭyāhvā," because the powder of yaṣṭyāhvā is subordinate, it should be one-quarter the amount of the sesame powder.

"One should press it with that very [goat's milk]" means that when the oil has been prepared in this manner, by cooking it ten times with a decoction of the *daśamūla* and other ingredients, the resulting oil becomes *aṇutaila*. Its "subtlety" (*aṇutā*) arises from its ability to follow subtle channels (*aṇusrotas*); and this is achieved here through repeated heating (*bhāvanā*), frequent cooking (*pāka*), and a specific method of pressing.
For it is said in the *Videha*: "The subtlety of oils is produced either through saturation (*bhāvanā*) or through cooking (*pācana*)."
"Even from the massaging of all bodies, [the body] attains the state of being like oil in a small vessel.
With the words "siddhāmla," etc., he describes diet and conduct; "nivātoṣṇapratiśraya" means one who dwells in a windless, warm house.
Regarding the statement "in the case of *pitta*, one should drink ghee prepared [with these]," it is specifically ghee prepared with *śṛṅgavera* (ginger) that should be administered.
The phrase "those which destroy *rakta-pitta*" refers to those treatments mentioned in the chapter on the therapy for *rakta-pitta*.
Regarding "mandapitte" (in mild pitta), it means when pitta is slight (144–148). "Vamana that subdues kapha" means that emesis prepared with substances that subdue kapha should be administered.
"With pungent fruits" means with black pepper, long pepper, and so forth;
"released from cooking" means having fallen away at the conclusion of the cooking process;
and "when the impulse is obstructed" means when the impulse of the catarrh has become weakened.
Regarding "and in swelling," this refers to nasal swelling (nāsāśophe) [verses 149–157].

In the passage beginning with "daśamūla" and so forth, one should cook a peacock— devoid of its feathers and other parts— with each of the ten roots and the other ingredients measured at three palas each, in exactly one droṇa of water.
In this context, one *droṇa* of water is used for decoction and is reduced to one-fourth; thus, it becomes four times the quantity of the *prastha* of ghee.

Furthermore, forty *palas* of the ten roots (*daśamūla*) and so forth, together with one peacock, should be boiled until sixty-four *palas* remain, and this should be added to a *droṇa* measure of water.
Alternatively, whatever amount of liquid results from boiling the ten roots and the peacock combined, four times that amount of water should be added according to the general rule of practice.

"By sweet [drugs]" means by the ten [substances] mentioned in the *jīvanīya* group; for it is the *jīvanīya* substances that are referred to here by the word "sweet" due to their excellence in sweetness (158–165).
"By this very [decoction]" refers to the decoction of *daśamūla* and so forth up to *mayūra*, prepared according to the prescribed method.
By the second mention of *kharjūra*, the fruit of the date palm is intended; as for the *akṣoṭa*, *vātāma*, and others which are products of the northern regions,

although their method of preparation as a decoction (*kvātha*) was already established by the previous rule beginning with "by this very decoction" and so forth, nevertheless, by the statement "again according to the previous procedure" and the phrase "according to availability," it is shown that they are to be used as a paste (*kalka*) alone, as available, and not as a decoction.

Regarding the variations in its application, Jātūkarṇa states: "One should cook ghee with the peacock [meat] boiled in that same decoction, along with three palas each of daśamūla, śreyasī, balā, and madhuka; then, adding one karṣa each of the jīvanīya drugs and milk, one should prepare one prastha of ghee in this very quartet of liquids. According to availability, it may be prepared with jīvaka, bṛṃhaṇa, vāta, āmra, akṣoṭa, triphalā, pūga, madhuka, kharjūra, tālamastaka, tvak, elā, pauṣkara, śvadaṃṣṭrā, tāmalakī, bisa, bhārgī, kaseru, śṛṅgāṭaka, mṛṇāla, rāsnā, sthirā, samaṅgā, śṛṅgī, and ajaḍā. This peacock-ghee (māyūra-ghṛta), through its fourfold administration, acts like nectar for diseases above the clavicle."
Regarding this, showing that mice and other creatures may be used in place of the peacock, he says "by mice" and so forth;
they state that even by a single mouse here—though its size is small compared to the peacock—the ritual accomplishment (*sādhana*) should be performed.
Regarding the phrase "or with boiled [substances]," this refers to milk that has been boiled;
and regarding the phrase "nasal medication (nasya) with ghee," after the administration of the pressed-out extract (avapīḍa), nasal medication with ghee should be given.

Regarding the statement "burning sensation arises from the provocation of *kapha* and *vāyu*," based on the words of Suśruta, cauterization (*dāha*) should be performed on the forehead and temple regions (*lalāṭa-śaṅkha-deśa*) in cases arising from *kapha* and *vāyu*.
For it is stated in the Suśruta Saṃhitā: "In diseases of the head such as *adhimantha* and others, one should apply cauterization to the regions of the eyebrows, forehead, and temples" (Su.Sū.A. 12).

Regarding the phrase "with fragrant substances (*gandha*), *kuṣṭha*, and *tagara*," this refers to fragrances such as *aguru* and others; the exclusion of *kuṣṭha* and *tagara* here is for the purpose of avoiding the discharge of brain matter (*mastuluṅga*).

And it is stated in Śālākya: "If one applies a smoke-wick (dhūmavarti) when nata and kuṣṭha are causing discharge, the brain matter (mastuluṅga) will flow out excessively; therefore, one should not apply them at all.
Vyāghrakaraja means *nakhī* (onion).
Sneezing is that which causes the act of sneezing (180–186).
"Śukta," and so forth, refers to the treatment for diseases of the mouth;
"purity below" refers to purgation;
and "dārvītvak" refers to the bark of the *dārvī* tree.
*Rujāpaha* means that which removes the affliction of disease.
In the formula beginning with *pañcakola*, jaggery (*guḍa*) is double the amount of the combined powder.
*Karkandhūmātrā* refers to a measure of eight *māṣaka*s.
Some read "loha" (iron) in place of "rodhra"; for it is stated in the Śālākya-tantra: "Pāṭhā, rasāñjana, vyoṣa, tejohvā, triphalā, agnika, gṛhadhūma, and yavakṣāra—this powder is indeed 'Kālaka'.
Thus, each of these three formulations beginning with Kālaka individually removes vāta, pitta, and kapha, and are therefore eliminators of the three doṣas.
*Rasakriyā* is the technical term for concentrated *rasa*.

In the passage beginning with "in cases of dryness of the palate," the phrase "one who is not thirsty" prohibits the drinking of even post-prandial ghee for one suffering from thirst when the palate is dry.

Although the drinking of unctuous substances (*sneha*) is generally prohibited in such cases—as stated in Sūtra-sthāna 13: "Those afflicted by thirst and fainting, pregnant women, and those with dryness of the palate"—nevertheless, in this instance, post-prandial ghee must indeed be administered because of this specific prescription.
"Sirākarma" refers to venesection (sirāvyadhana); and according to the statement of Suśruta, that should be performed on the palate and the tongue.
With the verse beginning "tulām," etc., he describes the pills made of khadira and other ingredients.
"Twice the amount of *amarimedas*" refers to two *tulas* of *viṭkhadira*; likewise, there are exactly two *tulas* of *pattanga* (red sandalwood).
In this context, the measurement for *lavaṅga* and the other ingredients is one *pala*.
The diseases of the teeth, mouth, and throat are to be understood as those described in *Śālākya*;
"the ultimate resort" (*parāyaṇa*) means the supreme refuge, that is to say, the best medicine.
Thus ends the treatment of diseases of the mouth.

He describes the treatment for anorexia (arocaka): regarding the four formulations mentioned in the half-verse beginning with "In anorexia" and ending with "kuṣṭha," they should be understood as being applied respectively to anorexia arising from vāta, pitta, kapha, and sannipāta.
In the passage beginning with "215–220 varāṭakāni," the phrase "tadbhasma" refers to the ash produced by burning the varāṭakas; one should cause it to drip, that is, filter it.

"Gandhataila" refers to oil mixed with a paste of fragrant substances, or alternatively, sesame oil infused with fragrant substances. In the context of "kṣārataila" (alkaline oil) beginning with "dried radish" and so forth, the phrase "fourfold honey-vinegar" (*madhuśukta*) means a vinegar in which honey is the primary ingredient, used in a fourfold proportion; and as for vinegar (*śukta*), it is defined as: "curds and other such substances placed in a clean vessel along with jaggery, honey, and ginger..."

"Śukta is that which has stood for three nights in a heap of grain; it is called cukra. Regarding this, some say the juices of *mātuluṅga* and plantain are equal to oil, while others prescribe both honey and *śukta*. In that regard, they state that the honey is equal to oil, but the *śukta* is four times [the quantity]; however, that is not very convincing, because honey is not even mentioned by Jatūkarṇa, since it is already included by the mention of *śukta* itself.

And it is said: "Oil cooked with radish-ash, *śatāhvā*, the two types of alkali (*dvikṣāra*), *vacā*, the four salts, *kuṣṭha*, *dāru*, *rasāñjana*, ginger, *śobhāñjana*, asafoetida, thick birch-bark, and the juices of citron and plantain, along with four times as much fermented vinegar (*śukta*), destroys deafness caused by the resonance of sound, pain, and [afflictions by] spirits. (Sū.
22.221–230) With the words "as soon as it has arisen," etc., he describes the treatment for eye diseases.
*Biḍālaka* is said in *Śālākya* (the science of eye diseases) to be an external application for the eyes;
in the passage beginning with "nighṛṣṭam," the phrase "tadvat" (likewise) means it is a *rasakriyā* (a medicinal extract).
Similarly, "harītakī tadvat" (harītakī likewise) refers to a *biḍālaka* prepared with *harītakī* and clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

Regarding the phrase "in the case of a *sannipāta* [disorder], however, with all [ingredients]": the meaning is that an ointment should be applied using the substances previously mentioned for each individual [dosha], such as vāta and so forth. Regarding the statement "eye-salve [should be used] after three days": this is stated because eye diseases generally reach suppuration (*pāka*) within three days.
The definition of suppuration is given in another treatise: "The eyelids of the eyes become well-formed, and the irritation and tearing are pacified."
"Dull sensitivity, itching, and the symptoms of a matured eye ulcer" [are the signs]; "eye-drops" refers to the irrigation of the eyes with *sumanaḥ* buds and *jātī* flower buds.

White pepper, the seed of the *śobhāñjana* tree, the *plava* (a specific kind of bird), the *prasevaka* (the throat of a bird), and two of each of long pepper and sea-foam— this is the meaning of "two *śāṇas*."
Regarding "in Citrā": in the constellation Citrā, *tāpya* is the mineral; it is the mineral of honey (*mākṣika-dhātu*) produced from the Tāpī river.
*Cakṣuṣyā* is the wild horse-gram (*vanakulatthikā*).
"Flower collyrium" (*pauṣpamañjana*) means *puṣpāñjana*; "for one with unopened eyes" (*abhinnacakṣuṣaḥ*) means for a black snake whose pupils have not yet opened— that is, for a dead black snake.
With the words "Regarding baldness," etc., he describes the treatment for baldness and other such conditions.
"Harilomnī" means one with tawny hair; "sahacara" refers to the *jhiṇṭī* plant;
"in a vessel equal to stone" means in a stone vessel or on a ram's horn. It is placed therein.
"The roots of *ādityaparṇī*": *ādityaparṇī* is *sūryāvarta*,
*kṛṣṇasairīyaka*, *kṛṣṇajhiṇṭī*, *somarājī*, and *bākucī*.
*Śastra* refers to black iron;
*kṛṣṇapiṇḍita-citraka* refers to black *madana* and black *citraka*;
and *ādityapāka* means ripened solely through contact with the rays of the sun.

Here, although "separate portions" (*pṛthagbhāga*) is already established by the plural number in the word *bhāgaiḥ*, the inclusion of the word *pṛthak* is for the purpose of emphasizing that the portion of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) is indeed separate, even though that is established by logical necessity.
Furthermore, although an abundance of paste (*kalka*) occurs here by virtue of the statement itself, it must still be prepared accordingly.
The formulations beginning with "sesame and āmalaka" are for the purpose of coloring the hair.
In the verse beginning with "one should cook with rock salt" (*saindhava*), there is an equal quantity of rock salt, iron powder, and rice;
"pure" means washed;
"in the remaining diseases" refers to thirst, dyspnea, cough, fever, internal hemorrhage (*raktapitta*), and consumption (*śoṣa*), which are mentioned as complications of chronic rhinitis (*pīnasa*).

Regarding the statement "they are indicated for the remaining [conditions] and at the beginning," the word "remaining" (śeṣa) refers here to the diseases arising from the three vital organs (*trimarman*) that have not been previously mentioned. By the phrase "indicated at the beginning," it should be understood that the treatment for these diseases of the three vital organs is presented right here without explicitly listing the specific doshas; furthermore, another [treatment] will be taught in the *Siddhi-sthāna*, meaning it will be explained in the *Siddhi* section concerning the three vital organs.
In verses 262–282,
beginning with "clarified butters taken after meals," etc., he describes the treatment for the specific types [of hoarseness].

Although the characteristics of hoarseness caused by *vāta* and the other [humors] are not mentioned here, they should nevertheless be understood as being exactly those described in the treatment for *rājayakṣman*.

Although treatment has already been mentioned there, it is stated again here— beginning with "by four applications"— because voice disorders (*svarabheda*) are the subject at hand; these refer to the applications of drinking, massage, gargling, and enemas using the oils of *balā*, *rāsnā*, and *amṛtāhvaya* (guḍūcī), which will be described in the section on wind diseases (*vātavyādhi*).
Tryūṣaṇa is prescribed for cough;
Jīvanīya-ghṛta for vātarakta (as will be described later);
and Vṛṣa-ghṛta for the treatment of raktapitta (as stated in the section on its therapy).
The connection is that this is the treatment for curing hoarseness born of pitta;
thus ends the treatment for hoarseness (svarabheda), verses 283–290.
He states [the following] for the purpose of treating [diseases] mentioned and unmentioned: "Vāta, pitta, and kapha...

residing in the bladder, heart, and head," etc. This means that, according to their respective order, due to proximity to those locations, they are to be removed by whichever action among emesis and the others possesses the capacity to extract the nearby doṣa from the sites of vāta and the rest—namely, the bladder and so forth. Thus, they are to be removed by that specific action.

He explains, with an illustration, how it is precisely the wind and other elements, both in their modified and unmodified states, that cause pain to and sustain the body—beginning with the words "adhyātma" and so forth.
"Adhyātma-loka" refers to the world of sentient beings.
Regarding the world,
here in this illustration, phlegm corresponds to the moon and bile corresponds to the sun;
the established principle is that it is afflicted by the [humors] when they are disordered, and maintained by them when they are undisturbed.
Regarding how there is no contradiction when the *doṣas* act together despite their mutual opposition of qualities, he says: "Even by those that are opposed.

This means even by those that are mutually contradictory; for example, the observed mutual destruction of the qualities of *śleṣman*—such as unctuousness (*sneha*), sliminess (*paicchilya*), and heaviness (*gaurava*)—by the opposing qualities of *vāta*, such as dryness (*raukṣya*) and lightness (*lāghava*), does not occur here in the combination of the *doṣas*.

To the question "Why do they not kill?", he says: "Because of their innate nature (*sahajasātmyatvāt*). This means because of their being naturally assimilated (*svābhāvikasātmyībhāvāt*). Assimilation (*sātmyībhāva*) is the state of being non-injurious.

And whether this nature is produced by karma (*karmajanya*) or dependent on the inherent nature of the substance (*vastusvabhāvādhīna*), or even both, it remains nonetheless inconceivable (*acintya*). Furthermore, because it is observed [in experience], no logical sublation (*yuktibādhā*) can prevail here. Therefore, the deviation regarding the mutual impairment of qualities (*guṇopaghātavyabhicāra*) elaborated by the author of the *Candrikā* in the *Suśruta* does not apply.
To provide an example for the non-injury of even contradictory things, he says: "Just as a terrible poison [is neutralized] by the earth."
The summary of those arising from the three vital organs (marmans) is clear.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Treatment of the Three Vital Organs," in the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka Saṃhitā, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Chapter 27 of the Cikitsāsthāna (93 of 120)]

In the chapter on the three vital organs (*trimarmīya*), having observed that many diseases are curable by the five purificatory procedures (*pañcakarma*), the Teacher—recalling [the specific nature of] *ūrustambha* (stiffness of the thighs) as being incurable by those five procedures—taught specifically the treatment for *ūrustambha*. For indeed, from the perception of a contradictory thing, there arises the recollection of its opposite, just as the sight of a mongoose leads to the recollection of a snake.
The term "not deficient" (*ahīna*) implies it is always appropriate [to apply this].
"All together" means combined.

The term "born of the *doṣas* (*doṣaja*)” is for the purpose of excluding mental and exogenous [diseases], since those two are well known to be outside the scope of the five purificatory therapies (*pañcakarma*).

Furthermore, even among those born of the *doṣas*, the five purificatory therapies are not capable of curing what is incurable; therefore, in order to exclude that, he says: "of the curable," and so forth.
The connection is "of that which is to be established" (sādhyasya sataḥ).
The connection is that the teacher, having been asked about the causes and other factors of ūrustambha, spoke further.
Regarding the phrase "in the state of being digested or undigested" (jīrṇājīrṇe), the meaning is "when there is a slight remainder of what has been digested and when there is indigestion."

"Accumulated raw matter" (āmaṃ citaṃ) refers to that which exists in the form of residual chyle; "accumulated raw matter" (āmaṃ sañcitaṃ) is that which adheres to and nourishes the visceral cavity. It should be understood that raw matter accompanied by fat (medasā saha) acts as an obstructer of the *vāta* and other doshas.

Furthermore, when the raw matter moves toward the thighs, it travels together with the three doshas via the vessels (*sirā*) and so forth—namely, through the channels of the veins (*sirā*), arteries (*dhamanī*), and ducts (*srotas*).
Regarding the phrase "the *doṣa* is dominated by fat and strength": the *doṣa* refers to *vāta* and the others when they are obstructed by *āma*.
If the reading is "dominated by *doṣa* and fat," then it is an adjective qualifying *āma*.
Although the mention of the "thighs" (*sakthi*) implies the inclusion of the calves and thighs, their specific mention is for the purpose of demonstrating their particular filling [of the channels].
"Having uncontrolled movement" means having senses that are not under one's own command; "having little prowess" means performing little action or being inactive.
By the simile beginning with "a great lake," [the author] expresses the predominance of *kapha*, which is the primary factor initiating *ūrustambha*.

Although it is stated both here and in the *Sūtrasthāna*—specifically in Sūtra 19—that "ūrustambha arises from the three *doṣas* in an undigested state (*āma*)," nevertheless, because *kapha* is predominant, it is taught here specifically as *kapha*.

For this very reason, [the author] subsequently explains the etymology of the term *ūrustambha* (stiffness of the thighs) and its causal complex by means of the passage beginning with "thigh, phlegm," etc.;
by the phrase "through stability and coldness," he demonstrates that stability and coldness—two qualities of *kapha*—are the causes for the action of stiffening.
Regarding the complication arising from the application of oleation in *ūrustambha*, the author says "by those who suspect [it to be] vāta," and so forth.

The suspicion of *vāta* in this condition arises from observing symptoms identical to those of *vāta*, such as numbness and contraction. The complications resulting from excessive oleation for this condition have been stated by the passage ending with "difficult extraction as well."
The symptoms beginning with "affliction of the calves and thighs" describe a distinct set of causal factors;
however, others maintain that all of these are signs of incurability resulting from the fault of improper application of oleation (snehana) above or below.
"Constantly burning pain" (*śaśvac-cādāha-vedanā*) refers to slight burning pain; others, however, say it refers to pain devoid of burning.
(Verses 17–19) Now, he states the rationale for the prohibition of unctuous enemas (*sneha-basti*) and so forth, beginning with "of that," etc.
Although the defect of oleation (sneha) has already been mentioned, it is nevertheless explained here how that oleation acts as a cause of such defects;
furthermore, it should be understood that head-purgation (śirovirecana) is not introduced here precisely because it is entirely impossible [in this context].
"Oleation" (snehana) refers to the application of unctuous substances through both internal drinking and external massage.

And regarding *bastikarma* (enema therapy), this refers to *snehabastikarma* (oleation enema), because that specifically increases *śleṣman* (phlegm); alternatively, the word *snehana* may be an adjective for *bastikarma*, by which only *anuvāsana* (unctuous enema) is obtained. On the other hand, *nirūha* (non-unctuous enema) is already included by the term *virecana*, which denotes purification. For this very reason, *nirūha* is mentioned here specifically within the description of purificatory therapies incapable of removing the disorder of *ūrustambha*. Explaining in sequence the inability of emesis (*vamana*), purgation (*virecana*), and *nirūha* to remove the aforementioned disorder, he says: "When [the disorder] has reached the seat of *śleṣman*," and so forth.
The phrase "to remove happiness" (*hartuṃ sukham*) should also be applied to what follows by changing the case ending and gender;
"both of them" (*tāv ubhau*) should be applied as before to "to remove unhappiness" (*nirhartum asukhau*);
and [this applies to] all three: wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*).

The phrase "due to the conquest of the root" (*mūlanirjayāt*) is to be construed with both "due to vomiting" (*vamanāt*) and "by means of enemas" (*bastibhiḥ*). By stating "due to the conquest of the root," which means due to the severance of the root, [the author] has shown the scope of cases where emesis and the other treatments are effective;
he now states the scope of cases where they are ineffective, beginning with the words "they are possible" (*śakyāḥ*).
Likewise, because of the stiffness of the *āmameda* (undigested fat), one should understand that emesis and the other treatments lack efficacy in the region of the calves and thighs.
He states another reason for the fact that the disorder of *ūrustambha* (stiffness of the thighs) cannot be removed by emesis and other such measures: "In the seat of Vāta," etc.
"In the seat of Vāta" refers to the seat of Vāta consisting of the calves and thighs;
"due to its coldness" means due to the cold nature of Vāta.
He describes the treatment: "Of that," and so forth;
the meaning is that for this ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs), pacification (śamana) should be performed, not purification (śodhana).

The construction is: "it should effect the depletion (*kṣapaṇa*) and drying (*śoṣaṇa*) of phlegm (*āmaka*) and *kapha*"; therein, "depletion" means eradication in every respect, while "drying" means the evaporation of the liquid portion.
[The plants mentioned are] *vāyasī*, *kākamācī*, *kulaka*, and *kāravellaka*.
The connection is that one should drink these— śālmala and śālmalīveṣṭaka— with honey (verses 25–29).
The five formulations beginning with *musta*, mentioned in half-verses [30–32], remove stiffness of the thighs (*ūrugraha*).
Śārṅgeṣṭā, guñjā, svādukaṇṭaka, and vikaṅkata.
The phrase "as before" (pūrvavat) is connected with what precedes;
it should be construed as "one should drink guggulu that has been soaked in urine," and the word "soaked in water" (jalāplutam) implies "one should drink."
The fruit of the *nyagrodha*,
gold, and *nāgakeśara* (33–38).

He states the situational sequence beginning with "arising from under-nutrition" and so forth, and beginning with "from drying" and so forth; thus, the prescription of oleation is situational. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the general prohibition of oleation prescribed here, because this rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to that.
Pīluparṇī is morata; others say it is a variety of rāsnā.
"With honey" means with one-quarter part honey.
Ajagandhā is ajamodā.
"Twenty *bhallātaka* stones" refers to their physical size;
"two *pala*s" refers to two *pala*s from the total quantity of the *pippalī* and other ingredients.
"Eightfold *kaṭvara*" means that in which there is *kaṭvara* eight times the amount of oil in a *prastha* of oil; *kaṭvara* is buttermilk (*takra*).
Picumarda is *nimba*;
*dravantī* is a variety of *dantī*.
*Tarkārī*, *jayantī*, and *gandhā*— these, along with *aguru* and the others mentioned here, are to be taken; *kuṭheraka* is *parṇāsa*.
"Among those capable of being carried,
at the break of day— that is, in the morning— it is auspicious,
meaning free from predatory aquatic creatures and easy to traverse."

Now, one might ask: how does crossing water cause the depletion of *śleṣman* (phlegm), since it is generally stated that merely coming into contact with water leads to an increase in *śleṣman*? It is explained as follows: because the heat (*ūṣman*) exiting the body is obstructed by the water and forced back inside, the congealed mass of *śleṣman* is broken apart; likewise, through the act of swimming (*prataraṇa*), the *śleṣman* is dispersed. Furthermore, even actions considered similar [to those that increase phlegm] are indeed performed here due to their suitability for the purpose. For it has been said: "Sometimes even an action considered contradictory may be effective" (Ci. A. 30).
To include the treatment of [diseases] not previously mentioned, he says: "Of phlegm," and so forth.

The summary beginning with "the cause" (hetu) refers to the cause for the unsuitability of the [five] actions; it should be understood as the cause for the unsuitability of the five actions, which was stated in the passage beginning with "for the increase of phlegm" (śleṣmaṇo vṛddhaye).
"Of two kinds" means internal and external;
"remedy" means medicine.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Urustambha," in the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka Saṃhitā, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Cikitsāsthāna, Chapter 28 (94 of 120)]

Because of the connection that the provocation of *vāta* occurs through drying (*virūkṣaṇa*) by means of the treatment for *ūrustambha*, the treatment for *vātavyādhi* is stated immediately after *ūrustambha*.

In this regard, regarding the view that "the disease is *vāta* itself" (*vāta eva vyādhiḥ*), *vāta* itself—having reached various corrupted elements (*dūṣya*) and having assumed the form of either the whole body or a single limb—is called *vātavyādhi* because it causes manifold afflictions. However, when the view is that "the disease [arising] from *vāta*" (*vātād vyādhiḥ*), then the disease characterized by a specific combination of the humors (*doṣa*) and corrupted elements (*dūṣya*), taking the form of either the whole body or a single limb due to the vitiation of *vāta*, is called *vātavyādhi*.

Although fevers and other such conditions arise from vāta, they are nevertheless not designated by the term "vāta-vyādhi" (diseases of vāta) in this treatise because they can also occur through other *doṣas* even without vāta.

Furthermore, those disorders of vāta that are covered by *kapha* or *pitta* and ought to be called vāta-vyādhis here, are nonetheless considered to be of the nature of vāta-vyādhis precisely because they cannot exist without the primary vāta.

Nor should it be said that just as diseases born of various [humors] such as Vāta are treated separately, so too should those born of Pitta and Kapha be treated; for diseases produced by Pitta and Kapha, though they arise from various causes, do not possess the same degree of predominance as those born of Vāta. Therefore, a separate treatment is specifically prescribed for those Vāta-born diseases that are most manifest, whereas for the manifest diseases born of Kapha and Pitta, it should be understood that the treatment consists of emesis, purgation, and other measures appropriate for Kapha and Pitta.

In order to make known the modifications of *vāyu*, since the knowledge of modification is necessarily preceded by the knowledge of its essential nature (*svabhāva*), he first describes that very nature: "Vāyu," and so forth.

Although life (*āyus*) consists of the conjunction of the body, the senses, the mind (*sattva*), and the self (*ātman*), nevertheless, because *vāyu* is the predominant factor in such a conjunction, *vāyu* residing in its primary state is indeed called life.
Likewise, considering that *vāyu* is the cause of strength (*bala*), and because it is the support of the body, *vāyu* alone is said to be strength as the cause that supports strength.
The omnipresence and sovereignty of *vāyu* have indeed been established in the *Vātakalākalīya*.
Demonstrating that *vāyu* is the cause of life (*āyus*), he says: "Unobstructed," and so forth.
With unimpeded movement, not abandoning his own path,
and established in his place, he does not stray from the way; remaining in his natural state, he is neither diminished nor increased.
"Free from disease" means being healthy.

With the words beginning with "prāṇa and udāna," [the author] first presents the designations for the sake of conventional usage, and then states the locations and functions of the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth.

"It governs the body" means it sustains it in its respective locations, which will be described as its own locations; in the phrase "food and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes the maintenance of food and other such functions.
"And action" refers to the vital air, *prāṇa*.

Although *prāṇa* and *udāna* share the same location, the chest, they are nonetheless distinct due to the difference in their functions. Just as there is a distinction between the exertion and effort of a lamp-maker and a potter residing in the same house, so too are there distinctions of exertion (*prayatna*), vigor (*ūrja*), enthusiasm (*utsāha*), and so forth. By virtue of these actions such as exertion, the production of effort, vigor, strength, and complexion is described.

In the passage beginning with "svedadoṣāmbuvāhīni" and so forth, it should be understood that the channels carrying sweat (*svedavāhīni*) as well as those carrying water (*ambuvāhīni*) are described separately in the *Srotovimāna* (Vi. A. 5). Furthermore, the channels carrying the *doṣas* (*doṣavahāni*) move throughout the entire body; for it is stated: "Moreover, the channels of vāta, pitta, and śleṣman, which move through the whole body, serve as the pathways for all [other] channels" (Vi.
A. 5). In the phrase "gatītyādau," the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes contraction, extension, and other such functions.
Regarding the term "located in the intestines" (*antrastha*), the meaning is that the intestines (*antrāṇi*) are the site of the downward wind (*apāna*).
"Produces" means "expels," that is to say, she produces both the menstrual flow and the fetus; this is the connection.
He describes what kind of women perform these actions by saying "endowed" (*yuktāḥ*), and so forth; "endowed" means "unimpaired."
"Abiding in their respective places" means abiding in the places as previously described;
because they are of such a nature, therefore the body is maintained by them without affliction.
He describes the pathological effects of the *vātās* (winds) with the words beginning "situated on wrong paths" (*vimārgasthā*).

Regarding the phrase "born from their own locations and functions" (*svasthānakarmajaiḥ*): they afflict the body with diseases produced by those winds that reside in whatever location has been assigned to each specific wind, as well as by those diseases produced by the functions of the winds—such as spitting—that have been described. Alternatively, they may even take away life through a major illness.

In this context, because the wind alone is the primary cause of numerous diseases and necessitates distinct therapeutic measures, its five divisions are mentioned, whereas those of *pitta* and *kapha* are not, as they are of less practical utility in this regard.

For instance, in another tantra, bile (pitta) is also said to be fivefold, distinguished as *pācaka*, *rañjaka*, *sādhaka*, *ālocaka*, and *bhrājaka*; and their locations are stated to be, respectively, the stomach (*jaṭhara*), the heart (*hṛdaya*), the eyes (*dṛṣṭi*), the skin (*tvak*), and the [entire] body. Likewise, phlegm (*śleṣman*) is also fivefold, distinguished as *bodhaka*, *śleṣmaka*, *tarpaka*, *avalambaka*, and *kledaka*; and their locations are, respectively, the heart (*hṛdaya*), the stomach (*āmāśaya*), the tongue (*jihvā*), the head (*śiras*), and the joints (*sandhi*). Furthermore, their functions are separately stated to be, respectively: supporting (*avalambana*), moistening (*kledana*), awakening the sense of taste (*rasabodhana*), nourishing the eyes (*akṣatarpaṇa*), and binding the joints (*sandhisaṃśleṣa*).
The mention of the number and other details here is for the purpose of explaining the wind-diseases under discussion; "of those born from them" refers to the five diseases born from wind,
and "in the Sūtra" refers to the chapter on major diseases (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 20).
"Being described" refers to [conditions] such as *nakhabheda* (nail-splitting) and so forth, being described according to their gross characteristics;
"by synonyms" means by other designations.

But how are those eighty types of *nakhabheda* and so forth taught? It is said: some diseases such as trembling (*vepathu*) and others are mentioned specifically with reference to *vāyu* (wind), while others are mentioned with reference to *vāta* covered [by another humor], as in the passage beginning: "The symptom when [vāta] is covered by pitta is burning sensation (*dāha*), thirst (*tṛṣṇā*), and so forth."
12–14 Now he states the etiology (nidāna): "By dryness," and so forth;
"due to irregular treatment" means due to improper conduct.
In passages such as "doṣāsṛk" (humors and blood), the word *doṣa* also includes feces (*purīṣa*).

*Apataṃsana* refers to falling from elephants and the like, or alternatively, *avataṃsana* refers to the extraction of the bodily constituents (*dhātus*). For it is said by Kharanāda: "That which scrapes excessively due to its sharpness is known as *ullekhana* (scraping); that which excessively extracts the constituents is called *ava(pa)taṃsana*."
"Empty" means void; the meaning is that they are devoid of qualities such as moisture and so forth.
By the phrase "the unmanifest characteristic" (*avyaktaṃ lakṣaṇam*), etc., he describes the premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*).
"The nature of the self" (*ātmarūpam*) refers to the current state of the disease.

"Disappearance and lightness" (*apāyo laghutā*) means the disappearance or departure of the diseases caused by *vāta*, which is to say the lightness of the body due to the cessation of the signs of *vāta* disorders; that is, the bodily well-being. Alternatively, "disappearance and lightness" does not mean the total absence of all *vāta* signs, since the natural signs [of *vāta*] still persist.
Regarding the action of those who are provoked, he says: "contraction," and so forth.

Furthermore, these conditions such as contraction (*saṅkoca*) and so forth are also diseases; for it has been said: "In that context, those [abnormalities] are considered signs of disease at that time, not the diseases themselves" (Ni. A. 8). *Huṇḍana* refers to the inward displacement of the head and other parts. Others, however, define *śirohuṇḍana* as the cracking of the scalp and the splitting of the temples and forehead; *nāsāhuṇḍana* as the destruction of the nose; *akṣihuṇḍana* as the displacement of the eyes; *jatruhuṇḍana* as the constriction of the chest; and *grīvāhuṇḍana* as the stiffness of the neck. He states the cause for the arising of these specific wind-diseases (*vātavyādhi*) with the words beginning "due to the particularity of the cause and location" (*hetusthānaviśeṣāt*).

The specific cause refers to the aggravating factors such as pitta-obstruction and the like; the specific location refers to the visceral cavities and the like, or rather, the specific location produced by the cause. For it has been stated: "But when aggravated, [the doshas], due to the specific nature of the aggravating factors, corrupt the specific tissues to be corrupted" (Vi. A. 6), and so forth. Some, however, read the text as: "and also from the specific location in the body. (20–23)
He describes the differentiation of diseases based on their specific locations: "In that regard, when [the doshas] are located in the visceral cavity," and so forth;
"when aggravated in all limbs" means when they are aggravated throughout the entire body.
"Located in the rectum" means located in the upper rectum; "it is stretched" means it is extended;
"stiffness of what has been eaten" means that stiffness of the limbs occurs in one who has eaten.

The symptoms beginning with "gurvaṅga" (heaviness of the limbs) and so forth are common to both the flesh and the fat; likewise, the symptoms beginning with "bhedo 'sthiparvaṇām" (loosening of the bones and joints) and so forth are common to both the bone and the marrow.

Even though the symptoms are the same, the specific distinction should be inferred from the characteristics of the particular *dhātu* described in the chapter on "Vividhāśitapītīya" (Various Foods and Drinks).
The term "santati" means continuous or accompanied by a sequence.

It releases quickly or binds; thus, at the time of sexual intercourse, it either releases quickly or retains for a long time. Likewise, it causes the fetus to be released quickly or retained for a long time, and produces a deformed fetus—one endowed with various defects such as being maimed.

By the phrase "externally" (*bāhya*) and so forth, the symptoms of *vāta* located in the tendons (*snāyu*), such as external convulsions (*bahirāyāma*) and others, are indicated; these will be discussed further below.
"Mandarukśopham" means with mild pain and mild swelling;
"suptāḥ" means motionless. (24–37)
Now, intending to describe the disorders of vāta that are exceedingly powerful, he speaks of *ardita* (facial paralysis), beginning with the words "excessively increased" (*ativṛddha*).
By the inclusion of the term "excessively increased," he indicates the intense provocation (*prakopa*) of the vāyu.
"Single" means she contracts either the left or the right arm, leg, or knee; she makes her face crooked and distorted;
she walks with a limp; and regarding food, she does not eat evenly with her mouth, but eats miserably from only one side of her mouth—thus she is shallow.
*Jihmeti* means crooked;
*samutkṣipteti* means excessively hurried;
*kaleti* means indistinct.
Regarding the statement "the two ears are afflicted," although this disorder resides on only one side, nevertheless, due to its power, the affliction occurs here in the ears alone.
[Objection: Is it not the case that it affects only half [of the body] and not the whole?

Indeed, when *ardita* (facial paralysis) pervades half of the body, what is the difference between it and *ardhāṅga* (hemiplegia)? We reply: *ardita* does not persist at all times because it is characterized by paroxysmal intensity (*vegitā*), whereas *ardhāṅga* persists by pervading [the body] at all times. For it has been said: "One may be healthy for a while when the onset of *ardita* and similar disorders has passed."
Or rather, one afflicted with the specific symptoms as described [is considered incurable], whereas these [symptoms] do not all occur in only half the body;
by the words beginning with "I think," etc., he describes the *antarāyāma* (intermittent contraction).

"When it enters the internal channels" means that it enters the veins situated within the neck (manyā). "Known as internal extension" (antarāyāma) means that this type of stiffness of the neck is called internal extension; however, another form of stiffness of the neck is to be described as external extension (bahirāyāma), which will be mentioned later.
In other medical treatises, however, stiffness of the neck is stated to be a premonitory symptom (pūrvarūpa) of both types of extension.
"Restrained internally" means it is drawn inward;
"extended externally" means its movement goes outward from the back.
Back" and so forth are the characteristics of external extension; "resting on the back and the neck" means they follow the back and are connected to the neck.
"External" (*bāhya*) is an adjective qualifying the vessels (*sirā*);

furthermore, some read it as "the external vessels located specifically in the back," while others read it as "supported by the *manyā* muscle of the back," taking it as an adjective qualifying the wind (*vāta*).
"Leading behind" means being drawn toward the back;
"agitation" refers to one whose momentum has arisen.
These two types of extension (āyāma) are: external and internal extension, as well as lameness and even hunchbackedness.

By the statement, "The *vāyu* located in the tendons (*snāyu*) causes all diseases of the single limbs," those two [conditions] are said to be caused by *vāyu* residing in the tendons; whereas here they are stated to be caused by *vāta* residing in the vessels (*sirā*). Therefore, because of these two statements, they are indeed caused by *vāta* residing in both the vessels and the tendons.

For it is said elsewhere: "The powerful *vāyu*, the great cause, having dried up the vessels along with the tendons and *kaṇḍarās* that are external and supported by the neck and back, causes affliction externally," and so forth.
He states the characteristics of *hanustambha* (lockjaw) and *saṅkoca* (contraction): "Situated at the root of the jaw," and so forth;
"it causes it to contract" means it causes it to dislocate.

Regarding the phrase "or with the mouth open," the word "or" (*athavā*) here implies that having the mouth closed is also an alternative option. By the term "having steadied" (*saṃstabhya*), one makes the mouth closed by rendering it motionless;
both of these [positions] constitute the stabilization of the jaw (*hanustambha*).
"Muhur" and so forth is the definition of *ākṣepa* (suggestion by anticipation).
The description of the onset of *daṇḍākṣepaka* (convulsive paralysis), beginning with "having thoroughly dried the hands and feet," and so forth.
"Hand, foot, head," and so forth, is the definition of the *daṇḍaka* meter.
He states the common form of [the diseases] beginning with *ardita* and ending with *daṇḍaka*: "One should be healthy," and so forth.
Among *ardita*, *hanustambha*, and the others, wherever a rapid recurrence is observed, that should be known as being included within *ardita*.
Having taken the definition of the slaughter of a faction beginning with "having killed one," and the definition of a single limb beginning with "half."
"Entire body" (*sarvāṅga*) means "arising from the whole body"; this is the definition of all bodily parts (53–55).
"Beginning with the buttocks" (*sphikpūrva*), etc. [refers to the sequence].

First, it seizes the buttocks with stiffness, pain, and piercing sensations; subsequently, it seizes the waist, back, thighs, knees, calves, and feet—this is Gṛdhrasī caused by Vāta. When caused by Vāta and Kapha, however, while possessing the previously mentioned symptoms, it is accompanied by drowsiness and other such signs. Thus, the two types of Gṛdhrasī are explained by the statement: "There are two types of Gṛdhrasī: from Vāta and from Vāta-Kapha" (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 19).
To include the unmentioned varieties of nail disorders and others, he says: "Of the locations," and so forth.
It should be understood that the remaining [diseases], such as *nakhabheda* and others, are to be diagnosed by signs corresponding to the nails, ankles, and so forth, such as splitting and pain.

Some read "by signs corresponding to the names of the locations"; in that case, the sign corresponding to the location of the nail and corresponding to the name "splitting" (*bhedasañjñā*) consists of the cracking of the nail.
In this same manner, for the other disorders caused by wind (vāta-vikāra) mentioned among the great diseases, one should follow the application of symptoms according to their respective locations.
Explaining the association of vāta with pitta and the other doshas, he says "sarveṣu" and so forth;

"pittādyaiḥ" means by pitta, kapha, blood, feces, and so on. Now, one might ask: how can vāta become aggravated when it is obstructed, since an obstructed vāta is actually weakened? To this, he says "vāyoḥ" and so forth.
"Due to the depletion of the elements (*dhātu*)": this means due to the depletion of the essential core (*sāra*).
It becomes aggravated precisely because its momentum is obstructed by an impediment to the path.

Now, while it may be that the wind (*vāta*) is provoked by the obstruction of the path, [the author] asks: "How is it that there is no connection between this [wind] and the obstructing bile (*pitta*) or phlegm (*kapha*)? To this he says: "Wind, bile," and so forth.

Even in the conjunction of the three [humors], he states the predominance of *vāyu*: "For *vāyu* alone, because of its subtlety... Because it acts as the impeller by following subtle pathways, *vāyu* alone is the primary factor among all three *doṣas* according to the logic already stated. Therefore, when provoked, it stirs up *pitta* and *kapha*; even though its own path is obstructed by them, it produces diseases in various locations. Likewise, by casting the *rasa* (nutrient fluid) and other elements here and there, it causes them to dry up. 58–60.

Having shown the aggravation of *vāta* caused by an obstruction (*āvaraṇa*), he states the symptoms produced by specific types of obstructions: "The symptom when [vāta] is covered by pitta," and so forth;
"relief by pungent and similar substances" means relief by pungent, hot, and other qualities that are contrary to *kapha*.
The word "more" (adhika) indicates that even with treatments that alleviate Vāta, there is no greater relief. Regarding the phrase "when located in the muscle" (māṃsage):

since the symptoms of Vāta located in the muscle—whether covered by muscle or having moved into the blood and other tissues—have already been described previously, the distinction here is that the symptoms of Vāta covered by blood and so forth are now being stated.
"Āḍhyavāta" is a designation in Āyurveda for wind (vāta) obstructed by fat (medas);
when it is in its own location, namely the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya), it causes cutting pain, producing what is known as *parikartikā*.
He explains the distinction between the curable and the incurable, beginning with "the loss of the joints," and so forth.

In this context, although conditions such as humpbackedness and lameness are not explicitly detailed here, their characteristics should nevertheless be understood through the extension of the remaining [definitions].
"Khuḍavātatā" and "gulphavātatā" mean wind located in the joints; "majjāsthigā" means produced by wind residing in the marrow and bones—that is, wind situated within the marrow and bones.
"Because of the profundity of the condition" means because it relies upon a profound state; others, however, say that "profundity" refers to having taken root [in the body].

The statement regarding "conditional success"—as to whether they succeed with effort or not—should be understood as referring to the perspective of other physicians. But a master physician, or one equal to a master, certainly succeeds by force; whereas another physician does not necessarily possess unimpeded knowledge in all cases, and for that reason, doubt is expressed. Consequently, it should be understood that there is no ultimate uncertainty regarding the curability of such conditions.
He states the curability of these nine [diseases] due to their lack of complications (*nirupadravatā*)—beginning with "nine," etc.

Although some diseases here are not mentioned by name (*śṛṅgagrāhikayā*), they should be understood as being endowed with the general characteristics of complications (*upadrava*). Alternatively, the complications should be understood as those that will be described later in this chapter, beginning with "heart disease, abscess," and so forth.
He states the action that has reached its proper occasion, beginning with "from the Action [system]" (*kriyāmataḥ*) and so forth.
Regarding the word "only" (*kevala*) in the phrase "only" and so on: "only" means unadulterated (*asaṃsṛṣṭa*);
"without support" (*nirupastambha*) means unobstructed (*anāvṛta*).
By what means? And how should one administer the treatments? He says: "by the drinking of ghee, muscle fat, oil, and marrow.
After the application of these oleaginous drinks, he states what must be done: "Then the person, exhausted by the oleation," and so forth.

The phrase "having comforted one exhausted by oleation" (snehaklāntam) means having reassured one who is weary from drinking oleaginous substances and fatigued by oleation; the term "one should administer oleation" (snehayet) continues [in its application] up until the words "with satiating drinks" (tarpaṇaiḥ pānaiḥ).
"By other [means]" refers to methods such as *kuṭī*, *bhūḥ*, and *sveda* (enclosure, bed, and fomentation), respectively.
"As appropriate" means that in every case, sudation should be preceded by oleation.
He states the benefits of sudation preceded by oleation in the verse beginning with "Oleated and sweated," and so forth.

Although this benefit of sudation preceded by oleation was already stated in the chapter on sudation (Sūtra 14) with the words "by that which is employed preceded by oleation" (*snehapūrvaṃ prayuktena*), it is stated again here because it is relevant to the current context; it connects with the phrase "applied quickly" (*āśu prayojitaḥ*) and means that the diseases of *vāta* do not persist— that is, they do not become chronic.
75–82 – If [it is argued] that "because it is faulty," and so forth.

In this context, Vāyu alone, being without support, is the subject under treatment; however, its state of being *sadoṣa* (vitiated) is logically untenable. Therefore, the state of being *sadoṣa* must be attributed to the therapeutic action (*karman*). Because that action is impure, the Vāyu is not pacified; and the impurity of the aforementioned action here arises from its capacity to generate *mala* (impurity). For it will be stated: "Indeed, *mala* is accumulated by foods that are unctuous, sour, salty, hot, and so forth," and so on.

Alternatively, by the phrase "because of being associated with doṣas" (sadoṣatvāt), the subsequent pacification of vāyu is expressed; as for what was stated regarding its being unassociated and unsupported, that should be understood as pertaining to the time of initiating the treatment.
Furthermore, being associated with doṣas is the cause for performing purification (saṃśodhana) when there is no improvement through the administration of oleation (sneha).
To explain how this state of having impurities (samalatva) arises at a later stage, he says: "snigdha... and so forth.
The phrase "one who is weak should not be purged" means that due to the extreme degree of weakness, he is unfit for purgation;
for instance, in the passage beginning with "those who have indigestion should not be given a non-unctuous enema" (Siddhisthāna, A. 2), one who is excessively weak is mentioned.
Thus, even though such a person is unfit for an enema due to being exceedingly weak, [the author] prescribes a regimen, stating: "by means of digestive and appetizing [drugs]."

Some things are digestive but not appetizing, such as *paṭola*; some are appetizing but not digestive, such as *triphalā*. For it is stated in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā*: "Triphalā destroys *kapha* and *pitta*, cures urinary disorders and skin diseases, is beneficial for the eyes, and is appetizing" (*Su.Sū.A.* 38). Therefore, the term "digestive" (*pācanaiḥ*) has been qualified by the term "appetizing" (*dīpanaiḥ*), meaning by foods that are either [digestive] or combined with those [digestives and appetizers], i.e., foods conjoined with both digestive and appetizing properties.
"And when the fire has arisen" means when the flame is blazing.
He describes the specific action according to the specific location with the passage beginning "In particular... and ending with "...the *avapīḍaka* is recommended below the navel.

Here, "alkali" (*kṣāra*) refers to barley-alkali (*yavakṣāra*), for it is stated: "Barley-sprout (*yāvaśūka*) is for those [drugs] that are laxative, digestive, and destroy hemorrhoids" (Sūtra-sthāna 25). Alternatively, "alkali" may refer to the digestive-stimulating alkali mentioned in the context of the *grahaṇī* [disorders], or it should be understood as the alkali used for the treatment of upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*) described in the *Trimarmīya* chapter, beginning with: "That [alkali], smeared with oil which destroys cold-fever... (Chikitsā-sthāna 26).
"Sweats" and so forth refer to the treatment for wind (vāyu) located in the skin;
"exhilaration" means gladdening the mind;
"one who has eaten after purgation" refers to one who has been given food immediately following a purgative.
The aforementioned action, which produces semen and brings joy,
is for the purpose of arousal; for the production of nourishment, milk processed with white [sugarcane] and other ingredients is beneficial,
as are *aṃśumatī* and *śālaparṇī*.
Regarding "fish": when the *vāta* is aggravated in the region of the navel, fish cooked together with unripe *bilva* fruits should be administered;
and although the aggravation of *vāta* in the navel region has not been explicitly mentioned here, it is to be understood from the presence of colic, piercing pain, and so forth.
Regarding "being twisted": it means being squeezed or wrung.
The poultice should be prepared using only wind-alleviating substances.
For nasal administration and internal consumption, it should be understood that the oil used after meals is specifically processed with black gram (*māṣa*) and rock salt (*saindhava*);
in this case, there is a decoction of black gram and a paste of rock salt.
An *avapīḍaka* of ghee is that where, having drunk the ghee, one eats the food that squeezed it out.
He describes the treatment for facial paralysis (*ardita*) and other conditions: "In facial paralysis," and so forth.
Here, "satiating" (*tarpaṇa*) is a qualification of the nasal medication (*nāvana*); alternatively, "satiating" refers to nourishing therapy (*santarpaṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "the vein between the *kaṇḍarā* and the ankle," venesection should be performed on the vein situated between the *kaṇḍarā* and the ankle.
The plural "gṛdhrasīṣu" (in cases of sciatica) is used because there are different types [of the disease].
"Vyāttānanam" means with the mouth opened wide;
"pradeśinī" is the finger next to the thumb.
To include treatments for which specific details have not been mentioned, he says: "Each individually," etc.

"Location" (sthāna) refers to the receptacle such as the colon (pakvāśaya); "vitiated element" (dūṣya) refers to the constituents such as plasma (rasa) and blood; by the inclusion of the word "etc. (ādi), the coverings (āvaraṇa) are also included.
The specific action, however, which depends on the location and the person to be corrupted, has already been stated by the verse beginning with "one who is in the treasury" (Koṣṭhasthe).
He states the treatment that equalizes all disorders of vāta, beginning with "clarified butter, oil," etc.

In the passage beginning with "for strength" (*balāyai*), there are three separate applications of medicinal substances starting with *balā*; for each of these, four preparations beginning with "goat-head" (*ajaśīrṣa*) are to be prepared separately. Thus, there are twelve formulations.
"At dawn" (*kalyam*) means in the morning;
"of fruits" refers to those originating from sesame oil, such as sesame paste and the like.
Regarding the phrase "pradehas and upanāhas," a *pradeha* is a thin application compared to an *upanāha*.
"With fragrances" refers to *aguru* and other such substances.
In the passage beginning with "rūkṣaśuddha," those afflicted by pure wind (śuddhānilārtāḥ) are those suffering from vāta alone;
"ghṛtamaṇḍa" refers to the uppermost layer of clarified butter.
