A *śukti* is half a *pala*, and a *prakuñca* is one *pala*; likewise, it is prepared with milk boiled with *balā*, *bilva*, and other ingredients, and then cooked with *culukī*, which is a porpoise (*śiśumāra*).
"Pratyagra" means fresh;
"in nasal treatments and drinks" refers to both nasal applications (*nasya*) and oral drinks (*pāna*); "kṛṣṇagandhā bark" refers to the bark of *śobhāñjana*.

"Mahāsneha" refers to the four fats (catuḥsneha); "oil prepared with that" means equal [to the other ingredients], specifically equal to the juice of *nirguṇḍī*. Here, the word "equal" (*sama*) does not mean "together," because the sense of "together" has already been expressed by the instrumental case ending. "Nāḍī" refers to a sinus ulcer (*nāḍīvraṇa*); it should be understood that the five types of sinus ulcers described in the works of Suśruta and others apply here as well.
And *apacī* occurs in regions such as the jawbone, the armpit, and so forth.

Regarding the passage beginning with "the fresh juice of radish" (*mūlakasvarasa*), curd should be placed in the fresh juice of radish mixed with an equal amount of milk. As for the phrase "of that which has become sour," this refers to the state of acidity attained by the radish juice and the other ingredients.
Furthermore, because of the statement "with three *prasthas*," it is indicated that each of the radish juice and the others is measured at one *prastha*.
Indeed, Jatūkarṇa states: "One should cook [it] with curd, radish juice, and milk," and so forth.

Regarding the passage beginning with "with the decoction of the five roots" (pañcamūlakaṣāyeṇa), some say that the decoction of the five roots and water boiled with oil-cake (piṇyāka) should be administered separately; however, we maintain that one should desire only the juice of the oil-cake prepared with the decoction of the five roots itself, which serves as the liquid medium.

And the text is read as: "Having cooked old oil-cake (*piṇyāka*) with a decoction of the five roots (*pañcamūlī*), having strained its juice," and so forth; likewise in Jātūkarṇa: "One should cook old oil-cake in water containing *sthirā* and other [herbs]; in this juice, oil should be prepared with eight times the amount of milk.
Regarding the phrase "with sour liquids," this refers to sour gruel (*kāñjika*), buttermilk (*takra*), and the like.
"With sour fruits" means with acidic fruits such as pomegranate and others.

Regarding the "four applications"—namely those consisting of drinks, ointments, nasal drops, and oil enemas—in the passage beginning with *sahacara* and ending with *mūlakalkāddaśapalam*, a paste (*kalka*) of ten palas of the root of *sahacara* itself is to be administered. However, in the *Jatūkarṇa*, it is stated that here the paste is of the radish (*mūlaka*) alone.
Regarding the passage beginning with *jīrṇe taile*, it means when the oil has been digested after being drunk.
Regarding the preparation of the gruel (peyā) with milk, this is done here because it is suitable for the application; "one-fourth part of *guḍūcī*" refers to twenty-five palas,
and "one-eighth part of *rāsnā*" means that, in relation to the total quantity mentioned, there are twelve and a half palas of *rāsnā* by one-eighth of the [total] eight parts.
"Half a part of goat's milk" means mixed with half as much goat's milk;
"rasa" refers to the juice of *sūrpa-parṇī* (both *mudgaparṇī* and *māṣaparṇī*), that is, its sap.
*Nalikā* is well-known by its own name;
*kaṭuphalā* is *latākastūrī*. Others say it is a fragrant substance called *padyala*, famous in the Deccan (*dakṣiṇāpatha*).
*Turuṣka* is *silhaka*.
Regarding *nakhī* and *svalpanakhī*:

because this oil is fragrant, it is stated that a paste of leaves (*patrakalka*) should be added according to the technical terminology of the *Gandhaśāstra*. As the *Gandhaśāstra* states: "When the powder, the fresh juice, and the flowers have been processed and the oil has cooled after being removed from the heat, wise men add a paste of leaves for the purpose of increasing the fragrance. Therefore, in this case, the paste of leaves such as camphor and others should be added only once the oil has been removed from the heat.
In the passage beginning with "of Amṛtā," *mahāśrāvaṇī* refers to the large *muṇḍitikā*.
Kālā, kālānusārivā, tridaśāhva, and devadāru (157–164).
In the passage beginning with "in a decoction of a thousand parts of rāsnā," the term "haimavatāni" refers to substances originating from the Himalayas, such as agaru, kuṣṭha, kṣemaka, and so forth.
The phrase "elādyaiḥ" refers to those mentioned in the *Amṛtādyā* [chapter], beginning with "elā, māṃsī, nātā," etc.
This "kalpa" (method of preparation), namely the aforementioned *rāsnā*-kalpa, should also be stated for the drugs beginning with *balā*.
"Of bala and the others" refers to bala, prasāriṇī, and aśvagandhā mentioned immediately above (verses 165–166).
In the passage beginning with "vṛṣamūla," there is one *tulā* of aśvagandhā and citraka combined.

"Proven by the prior addition of oil" means it is prepared with the juice of *mūlaka* and so forth, together with the paste (*kalka*) for the oil as previously described, and with a decoction (*kvātha*) of the roots of *vṛṣa* and other ingredients.
Regarding the reading "it is twice as superior," this means that it is twice as excellent as the oil prepared with the decoction of the roots of *vṛṣa* and other ingredients.

Regarding the phrase "with all aromatics" (*sarvagandhaiśca*), this means together with the aromatics mentioned in the *Balātaila* formula; it is known by the name *Mūlakataila*. In that context, he demonstrates that the decoction is prepared using the roots of the *rāsnā* and other ingredients themselves.

In the passage beginning with "in the juice of garlic" (*laśunasvarase*) and so forth, the phrase "by these" (*ebhiśca*) refers to the decoctions of barley and other ingredients mentioned immediately prior.

The expression "prepared many hundreds of times" (*anekaśataśas*) means that it has been accomplished—that is, perfected—many hundreds of times by means of that very same ritual procedure (*vidyānena*).
Now he describes the treatment for Vāta associated with other doshas and so forth: "The treatment is common," etc.

"Common" (sādhāraṇī) means that which is prescribed for Vāta is the same for its association with Pitta and others—that is to say, beneficial even in such combinations. It is not only common when Vāta is combined [with another dosha], but it should also be applied when the channels (srotas) are occluded by Vāta, Pitta, and the rest.
He will explain the occlusion of the channels by Vāta later on.
Some, however, read "vāte pittādibhiḥ"; this reading is easy to understand and expresses a specific action prescribed in the aphorism: "pittāvṛte" and so forth.
By "vyatyāsāt," meaning through alternation, the sense is that one should make what is cold hot, and make what is hot cold.
Regarding the sustaining enemas (*yāpanā-bastis*) to be described in the section on Siddhi,
the statement "one should first conquer pitta" teaches the conquest of pitta specifically because of its rapid action compared to kapha (183–188).
Considering [the pitta] located in the stomach (āmāśaya) to be "kapha," this treatment is intended specifically for kapha associated with vāta;
however, in the statement "purgation [is indicated] when [it is] in the large intestine (pakvāśaya)," the term "kapha" carries over [from the previous context].
Regarding the phrase "when it is pervasive" (sarvatrage), this refers even to pitta that has moved to other locations.

Although, when [the wind] has reached the site of another disorder, an emetic or enema characterized by that specific disorder would be appropriate, nevertheless, he shows by this [verse] that purgation is also indicated there.

Regarding the phrase "when accompanied by phlegm" (*sakaphe*), some read "when the wind has reached the channels of the chest" (*uraḥsrotogate*); in that context, the meaning is "having entered the subtle channels."
Regarding the statement "it destroys urinary disorders (prameha), vāta, and fat," the *mahāsneha*—that is, the fourfold unctuous substance (*catuḥsneha*)—is mentioned right here;

[this applies] as before. As for the phrase "when obstructed by semen," whatever treatment was previously stated for vāta located in the semen should also be performed when vāta is obstructed by semen.
"Ullekha" means scraping or emesis;
"mūtralāni" means diuretics;
"śakṛtā" means by feces.
"Remaining in its own place," and so forth: because a *doṣa* becomes powerful by being nourished in its own location, one should therefore first conquer it with its own specific medicines.
By which specific medicines? He says: "by emetics," and so forth.

"By pacification" means by the very pacification of *kapha* and the other *doṣas*. And this pacification should be understood as occurring either after purification (*śodhana*) or for those cases where purification is not required.
He explains the mutual obstruction of the winds, beginning with the words "mārutānām" and so forth.

Although the formlessness (*amūrtatva*) of wind is stated here in the *Vātakalākalīya*, nevertheless, this "formlessness" denotes a lack of solidity rather than a negation of constituent parts (*avayava*). Consequently, the obstruction of one wind by another in the form of a hindrance to its movement is entirely logical. Indeed, it is observed that when one wind is struck by another, it becomes coiled like a whirlwind even outside [the body]; thus, the mutual obstruction of winds is established, as twenty such obstructions are described in passages such as "Prāṇa obstructs Udāna and the others."

By the statement "Prāṇa envelops Udāna and the others," four veils are indicated; by "and they also envelop Prāṇa," another four; and by "likewise Udāna and the others [envelop] one another," twelve veils are described. Among these, there are three veils when Udāna envelops the three beginning with Vyāna; likewise, there are three when Vyāna and the others envelop Udāna; similarly, there are two when Vyāna envelops Samāna and Apāna, and two when those two envelop Vyāna; and finally, there are two for the mutual enveloping of the remaining two. Thus, the twelve veils combined with the previous eight amount to twenty.

"Of the *ulbaṇas*" means of the increased [defilements]; or alternatively, "of the *ulbaṇas*" means of the five combined which are most manifest. By this, he shows that through the combination of these one, two, three, and so forth, there arises a manifold obscuration due to the distinction of being an obstructive cover (*āvāryāvarakatva*).

By the words "headache" (*śirograha*) and so forth, he mentions the eight afflictions (*āvaraṇa*) that generally occur; then, in order to include the remainder of those not explicitly mentioned, he says "upward-moving karma" (*ūrdhvabhāgikaṃ karma*), which refers to the aforementioned intake of unctuous substances, nasal drops (*nasya*), and so on;
and "dyspnea and so forth" (*śvāsādayaḥ*) refers to dyspnea, hiccups, and the like.
By the phrase "moving upwards" (*ūrdhvagena*), [the author] refers to *udāna*.
To explain the nature of the obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) for the sake of understanding what has not been explicitly stated, he says: "Of these, their own actions," and so forth.

Here, because the stronger [element] obscures those that are to be obscured (*āvārya*), there is a diminution of their own actions; however, for the obscurer (*āvaraka*), by general rule, there is an increase of its own action. Furthermore, by means of the obscuration, the one to be obscured becomes provoked, at which time there is an increase of its own actions—this is the established rule. Others, however, state the rule that there is a diminution of the obscured's own action, while for the obscurer, by general rule, there is an increase.
206–213 – He states the means for knowing the characteristics of the obstructions not previously mentioned, beginning with "having observed the locations," and so forth.
The explanation regarding the increase and decrease of the [doshas'] functions is here also as before.

By the phrase "having observed the locations," it is shown that the morbid transformation of vāta is to be understood through the disorders occurring in the locations previously mentioned for the vātas.

Regarding the statement "hot in sequence and non-hot [in sequence]": although a hot sequence alone is appropriate for vāta, nevertheless, with respect to the location, the vitiated elements such as blood (rakta) and so forth should be known as the cause of the reversal of the sequence.
He states the restoration of disordered *vātas* to their natural state: "One should direct the *udāna* upward," and so forth.
And this application to one's own path for the vital airs (vātās) should be performed by means of the prescribed method of yoga involving actions such as vomiting;

"one should pacify the *samāna*" means one should cause it to reside in the middle of the body. As for "one should apply the *vyāna* in three ways," one should apply it in three ways: upward, downward, and in the middle.

"It is indeed appropriate that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) should be protected and maintained by all four [therapeutic measures]. By this statement, he declares its extreme necessity for protection compared to the other types of wind (*vāta*).

To the question "Why is this one to be protected with such particular care? he replies: "But its stability is certain when it is in its proper place. When this *prāṇa* is in its proper place—that is, in its correct state—its stability, which consists of life itself, is "certain," meaning fixed and assured.
He describes the symptoms of the obstruction of the *prāṇa* and other vital breaths by *pitta*, by *kapha*, and by both *pitta* and *kapha*: fainting, burning sensation, vertigo, and so forth.

Fainting and so forth—fainting, burning sensation, and the rest—as previously mentioned; likewise, "affliction of the heat" (*uṣmaṇa upaghātaḥ*) here should be understood as the impairment of the bodily heat due to the absence of stimulation of the digestive fire when the *samāna* wind is obstructed by *pitta*. "Stiffness in the movement of the limbs" (*gātravikṣepasaṅgaḥ*) refers to the cessation of the movement of the limbs.
Regarding *rajas* (the menstrual flow):
"Mixed obstruction" refers to an obstruction of combined *kapha* and *pitta*. "According to their own [nature]" means according to what is inherent to them;
"by way of being more significant" means by way of predominance.
He states the reason for its greater importance with the words beginning "because of the distinction" (*viśeṣāt*):
"dependent" (*saṃśritam*) means subject to [others],
and "not fully understood" (*aparijñātāḥ*) means not known according to their true nature (*yāthātathyena*).
Even though they have been correctly known, because of indifference— even though they have been known according to reality for a full year— the same [fault] should be applied.
By the verse beginning with *hṛd-roga*, he describes the complications (*upadrava*).
Regarding the phrase *pañcātmakasya* ("of that which consists of five"), it means that [the wind] has five forms through its divisions as *prāṇa* and so forth.
In the passage beginning with *prasamīkṣya*, the intention is that when there is an excess of strength, a mild purgative (*sraṃsana*) should be administered.

The connection [of the phrase] is that it is "highly praised. "Loha" refers to the *bhārgavaprokta* (proclaimed by Bhārgava), namely the *cyavanaprāśa*; for Cyavana is called Bhārgava, as it is stated in the *Āyurvedasamutthāna*: "Bhārgava Cyavana, being lustful and old, underwent a transformation of his physical state" (Ci.A.1, pāda 4).
One should apply the treatment that facilitates the downward movement of *vāta*; this is how it should be understood (vv.
236–245). He demonstrates the difficulty of diagnosing *vāta* and the other doshas through an analogy, beginning with the words "In the world," etc.

In the passage beginning with "destruction" (kṣaya), the obscuration (āvaraṇa) is also already indicated within the context of its relationship to decrease and increase; nevertheless, it is mentioned separately for the purpose of defining its specific characteristics and its medical treatment.
The phrase "in the [treatments] for karma" refers to the medical treatments.
In the summary beginning with "pañcātmanaḥ" (of the fivefold self), the analysis is "pañcātmanaḥ sthānavaśāt" (of the fivefold self by virtue of its locations).
"Dehadhātoḥ" means of the unmodified wind that has the nature of sustaining the body.
Having stated the performance of treatment, he briefly mentions that which must be taken into consideration, beginning with the words "tām" (that [fever]) and so forth.

The dependence on factors such as place (*deśa*) has been explained by us in the *Sūtrasthāna*; it should be inferred according to the distinctions of place and other factors, though it is not elaborated upon here for fear of prolixity.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Vāta Diseases," in the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka Saṃhitā, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Chapter 29 of the Cikitsāsthāna (95 of 120)]
Immediately after the treatment for wind diseases (*vātavyādhi*), the treatment for *vātarakta* is stated, precisely because it is a specific variety of wind disease.
*Vātarakta* is a disease produced by both wind and blood; alternatively, it is simply wind and blood that have reached a particular stage of progression.
By the phrase "equal to fire and wind," he indicates that vātarakta is difficult to cure and acts rapidly;
by the phrase beginning with "salt" (lavaṇa), he states the cause;

and by the phrase "mostly of those who are delicate" (sukumāra), he demonstrates that in a delicate body, vāta and blood (vātaśoṇita) quickly become vitiated through the consumption of causes such as salt and the like.

Those who eat sweet food with pleasure—among these eaters of sweet foods with pleasure, although salt and the like are mentioned here as causes of *vāta-śoṇita* (gout), they should nevertheless be understood primarily as causes of blood vitiation (*śoṇita-doṣa*). As for the cause of wind vitiation (*vāta-doṣa*), it has been stated [elsewhere] beginning with "astringent" (*kaṣāya*) and so forth. Consequently, when salt and the like are combined with astringent and the other tastes, they produce *vāta-śoṇita*. Furthermore, the statement that "salt and the like give rise to *vāta-śoṇita*" should be understood as occurring through the medium of causing blood vitiation, which in turn generates *vāta-śoṇita*.

Regarding the term *aśuddhyā* (due to impurity), some read "due to injury and impurity" (*abhighātād aśuddhyā ca*) as "due to impurity and the imbalance of wind" (*aśuddhyā vātavaiṣamyāt*) at this point, because it was not purified during the time of purification; furthermore,
by the word *ca* (and) in the phrase "due to impurity," [the author] includes the causes of blood vitiation beginning with salt and ending with staying awake.
Here, by listing many causes for the severance of blood and wind, he demonstrates that both of these undergo independent provocation (prakopa) in this context.
"Traveling by means of vehicles drawn by horses and camels" refers to riding on horse-drawn or camel-drawn carriages;
and "in the heat due to excessive travel and unevenness" means during the hot season, due to the imbalance of wind caused by traveling too great a distance.
With the words beginning with "Vāyu," he describes the pathogenesis (*samprāpti*);
"on the path" means in the channel that carries the wind;
"provoked" means that even though the wind has increased due to its own causes, it becomes specifically aggravated by being further obstructed by blood.

For the sake of practical usage, he also mentions the various technical designations well-known in other systems: "khuḍa," and so forth. It is called *khuḍa* because it reaches a small (*khuḍa*) region; by the word *khuḍa*, a joint (*sandhi*) is meant. Because strength (*bala*) exists in this blood due to the obstruction of the wind (*vāta*), it is called *vātabalāśa*. Because it generally occurs among the wealthy (*āḍhya*), it is called *āḍhyaroga*.
He states the specific location of *vātaśoṇita* (blood vitiated by wind) with the words "its location," and so forth.

Although the mention of the hands and feet already implies the inclusion of the fingers, they are mentioned again specifically to demonstrate that the fingers are a particular site of manifestation due to their many joints.
Having established the root— that is, having made it one's basis— he states the reason for the pursuit of the body, beginning with "due to subtlety" (*saukṣmyāt*):
because it follows subtle paths.
He explains the cause for the wind-blood (vātaśoṇita) specifically halting at the joints as it moves through the body, beginning with the phrase "due to its fluidity" and so forth;
"by way of the channels" means by paths in the form of vessels (sirā),
and "due to curvature" means due to the curvature of the joints.
"Combined with bile and so forth" means conjoined with bile, phlegm, and wind arising from other causes;
"therefore" means because of its location in the joints (12–15).
With the verse beginning "excessive sweating" (*svedo'tyartham*), he describes the premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*).

Although excessive sweating and its absence are also mentioned among the premonitory symptoms of *kuṣṭha*, nevertheless, because of the connection with many dissimilar premonitory symptoms, there is certainty that it is a premonitory symptom belonging to one or the other [disease].

Regarding the treatment of *vātaśoṇita* (blood disorder caused by wind), he states the distinction between superficial and deep types for therapeutic purposes: "superficial," and so forth. "Internal support" (*antarāśraya*) refers to that which rests upon deep tissues other than the skin and flesh. "By all the symptoms" means by the combined symptoms described for both superficial and deep *vātarakta*.
And since this third type is indeed included within the types already mentioned as external and internal, vātaśoṇita is stated to be of two kinds in the summary of diseases (rogasaṅgraha).

"Some say that vātaśoṇita is of two types: superficial (uttāna) and deep-seated (avagāḍha); but that is not correct. Why? Because, like kuṣṭha, having been superficial, it becomes deep-seated after some time" (Suśruta, Cikitsāsthāna 5). Since Suśruta refutes this twofold classification, it is not appropriate to consider either of the two supreme teachers, Suśruta or Agniveśa, as lacking authority. Therefore, we shall explain this matter in a way that avoids contradiction. To clarify: when Suśruta states that superficial vātaśoṇita becomes deep-seated like kuṣṭha, he does not assert that *all* superficial cases necessarily become deep-seated. Consequently, for one who claims that it remains superficial exclusively, Suśruta’s statement would indeed be a contradiction. However, that is not the case, because Caraka does not state that it remains superficial exclusively; rather, at the time of its initial manifestation, some cases arise as superficial while others arise as deep-seated. Thus, there is no contradiction between Caraka and Suśruta.

In the passage beginning with "tatra vāte 'dhike" (there, when vāta is predominant), the term "in [the humor] predominant" (*adhike*) is to be understood as recurring for blood (*rakta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*kapha*). By this, an increase of bile, an increase of blood, and an increase of phlegm are to be known.
Regarding "in combinations" (*saṃsṛṣṭeṣu*): this refers to two or three combined, and "in all together" (*samasteṣu*) refers to all four combined when they are predominant.
By the passage beginning with "sirāyām" and so forth, he describes the characteristics of the four [types of swelling] in which vāta and the other [doshas] are predominant:
"āyāmaḥ" means expansion; "śyāvatā" means a dark-brown (śyāva) complexion.
From the words "swelling" (śvayathu) up to "blood" (asṛj), the symptoms of increased blood (udriktarakta) are described.

In the phrase "born from two or three doṣas," the association with excessive blood (adhika-śoṇitānubandha) must also be understood. Therefore, vātaśoṇita should be known as a combination involving an excess of all four [doṣas], including blood.
For this very reason, the ancient commentators have stated that there are forty-five varieties of vātaśoṇita, based on the distinctions of one, two, three, or all [doṣas] being predominant.
However, by Kharanāda, in another context, it is stated to be of thirty-six types;
for it is said: "That which is dominated by vāta with increased blood is considered to be of thirty-five types;
from pitta, it is of thirty types through combination; and from kapha, it is considered to be of ten types."
These subdivisions have not been explained in detail because they serve no further purpose (vv. 24–29).
He now states the division of the *sādhya* and so forth, beginning with "following a single fault" (*ekadoṣānugam*), etc.

Regarding the statement "and for whom there may be complications," although this indicates that [the disease] is curable, it becomes incurable due to the presence of the complications to be described hereafter.

Furthermore, as for what will be said regarding the incurability of the *tridoṣaja* type—namely, "in *vātarakta* born of the three *doṣas*, a *peyā* churned with a churning stick [is prescribed]"—that refers to cases where the symptoms are incomplete or where the *tridoṣaja* type is of recent onset.
[The term] *mūrchāyaḥ* means fainting (*mūrchā*).

"Lameness and paralysis through a single type of *moha* (delusion/confusion)" means that the incurability [of this condition] results from the confluence of other complications, whereas *moha* alone is what renders it incurable. Those who read "by a single *meha*" (urinary disorder) maintain that it is incurable due to the association with *meha*, because the treatments for *meha* and *vāta-śoṇita* (blood vitiated by wind) are contradictory. For the treatment of *vāta-śoṇita* generally consists of sweet and cold remedies, while that for *meha* is the opposite; thus, there is a contradiction in their therapeutic approaches.
"Discolored" (*vivarṇa*) means having an altered complexion; however, discoloration alone is a complication inherent to all types of *vāta*.
He describes the symptoms for the purpose of bloodletting in *vātaśoṇita* (vātarakta), beginning with "the path of the blood" (*raktamārgam*), etc.

The wind (*māruta*) obstructs the path of the blood and settles in the branches and joints (*śākhāsandhiṣu*). Having settled in the branches and joints, and then due to the obstruction of the blood by the wind, they mutually block one another—that is, the blood blocks the wind and the wind blocks the blood. It should be understood that one should remove the blood (*asūn*) from this *vātarakta* by means of painful sensations (*vedanābhiḥ*).
Therefore, the intention here regarding *vātaśoṇita* (blood-wind disorder) is that one should let out the blood;
by the release of blood, the obstruction is removed and the wind (*vāyu*) becomes serene, and from that, the disease ceases—this is the underlying meaning.
"Moving from place to place" means having the nature of spreading to other locations.

Regarding "in the case of bodily exhaustion": it states that even when blood is to be drained for the emaciation of the limbs, excessive drainage leads to a disorder, beginning with the words "deep-seated," etc.;
and regarding "lameness and so forth," this refers to wind-related diseases such as lameness, toe-deformity, and hunchback.
The word "kuryāt" (one should do) is the division [of the sentence];
"by means of the measure" means by the unchanging quantity.

Regarding the two alternatives in the procedure for purgation—namely, "with unctuous substances" or "with dry substances"—purgation with unctuous substances is intended for those who are slightly unctuous, whereas purgation with dry substances is intended for those who are excessively unctuous.

By the term "mild," he prohibits sharp purgation here due to the fear of agitating the *vāta*. The phrase "enema therapy" refers to both the oil enema (*anuvāsana*) and the decoction enema (*nirūha*).
"Generally non-burning" means not burning at all.
"Specifically" (viśeṣam) means a specialized medical treatment;
"external" (bāhyam) means superficial; and "mild" (mṛdu) is an adjective qualifying emesis.
Regarding the defect caused by cold applications in cases where *kapha* or *vāta* is predominant, he says "in cases where *kapha* or *vāta* is predominant," etc.;
it should be understood that here, burning (*vidāha*) arises from the cold application due to the obstruction of heat.
Regarding the defect caused by hot applications in cases where *pitta* or *rakta* is predominant, he says "in cases where *rakta* or *pitta* is predominant," etc.

"Having understood the strength of the *doṣas*, one should act"—this means that having understood the strength of the *doṣas*, one should perform only such treatment as is appropriate; namely, a warm treatment when *vāta* and *kapha* predominate, a cold treatment when blood and *pitta* predominate, and a mixed treatment when they are combined. (42–48) *Nīvāra* is wild rice (*uḍikā*).
"Sauvarcala" refers to the *sūryāvarta* vegetable;
"for the sake of a condiment" (*vyañjanārtham*) means that which is manifested (*vyañjate*) as a means for preparing food,
and this alone is the statement of the abbreviated application.
In detail, through an elaboration [of the topics] from verses 49 to 54,
[the ritual of] Śrāvaṇī Muṇḍitikā [is described].
By the phrase "with milk," since no other liquid is mentioned, the milk itself is four times the quantity of the ghee.

In the formula beginning with *trāyantikā*, by the phrase "with these pastes," the substances ending with *śatāvarī* constitute the paste (*kalka*). There is a decoction (*kaṣāya*) of *kaśeruka*, and each of the liquids such as the juice of *parūṣaka* is equal in quantity to the ghee; this equality also applies to the juice of *vidārī*, because it is stated [in the text] to be the same.

On this point, Jatūkarṇa says: "One should cook ghee with a decoction of four parts each of *parūṣaka*, *kāśmarya*, *kaśeruka*, *vidārī*, *drākṣā*, and *ikṣu* having equal tastes, along with milk, and having ground two parts each of *kākolī*, *tāmalakī*, and *śatāvarī*. This ghee, known as *pārūṣaka*, conquers vāta, blood disorders, erysipelas, and fever when used;
it is called 'prāyogika' because it is to be employed through regular practice. (55–60)
In the passage beginning with "two pentads of roots" (*dve pañcamūle*), *varṣābhū* refers to white *punarnavā*,
also known as *avākpuṣpī* or *adhaḥpuṣpī*;
[this constitutes] the equality of the fats among milk and the other substances.
The Vīras, the Vṛddhis,
the Bhavyas, and others from the northern regions [should ensure] that it is well-concealed, such that there is no contact with wind or other elements.
"In a clean place" means in a pure location (61–70).
In the passage beginning with "raisins," the phrase "with sugar-candy" means with added sugar.
Ṛṣyaproktā, atibalā,
kālā, mañjiṣṭhā, madhuparṇī, and vikaṅkata.
“Dhānvaprātudavaiṣkira” refers to specific types of fat and marrow (71–75).
In the passage beginning with “sthira,” the term “catuḥkṣīra” means fourfold milk.

By the phrase "oil separately, ghee separately," he prohibits cooking them as a mixture. In that dosage where there is three times the quantity of milk and one and a half parts of sugar, it is called *kṣīratriguṇādhyardhaśarkarā*.
A *khaja* is a hand five fingers long, or a churning stick.
In this case, the measure (*mātrā*) to be taken is that of the combined oil and clarified butter;
*aṃśumatī*, *śālaparṇī*,
and *dvisitopala* means it is joined with two palas of sugar (*śarkarā*).
And this quantity of milk is "hot as a stream" (dhāroṣṇa) for those with the highest digestive fire; it has become warm through contact with fire while falling in a stream during the time of milking,
and the urine here is equal in measure to the milk.
The connection is that the powder of *trivṛt* is [mixed with] milk that is warm from the stream;
by "by means of application" (*prayogeṇa*) is meant by repetition. A *basti* (enema) in which milk is the primary ingredient is a *kṣīrabasti*.
Regarding the passage beginning with "madhuyaṣṭyā," one should add one droṇa of water to one tulā of madhuka (liquorice); from this, a decoction measuring one āḍhaka of oil is produced.
*Varī* is *śatāvarī*.
Haṃsapadī is known by its own name; payasyā, arkapuṣpī, vitunnaka, and dhānyaka [are also included].
"From the fourfold application" means from the application of [medicated] drinks, massages, enemas, and nasal drops (88–95).
In the passage beginning with "guḍūcī," each of the *guḍūcī* and other herbs is measured at one hundred *palas*, while each of the *kola* and other ingredients is measured at one *āḍhaka*.
"Of *kāśmarya*s" means of the fruits of the *gaṅgārī* tree;
"universally applicable" (*sārvayaugika*) means applicable in the fourfold administration beginning with drinking;
"productive" (*prasavana*) means that which brings about childbirth.
In the passage beginning with "padmavetasa" (96–109), "phenilā" refers to *upodikā* (a type of aquatic plant),
and "sauvīrasammitam" means that the *sauvīraka* (sour gruel) is equal in quantity to the oil.
One karṣa each of lodhra and the others, and two karṣas of kuṅkuma (110–113).
"Khuḍḍākapadmaka" means that which is known as "small padmaka"; this designation is for the purpose of medical convention.

In the formula beginning with "a hundred parts of liquorice" (*yaṣṭimadhuka*), one hundred *palas* of liquorice should be prepared with ten times its quantity of milk; with that milk reduced to one-fourth, oil should be cooked.
Thus, it is established that [the preparation] is "prepared from a hundredfold decoction" (*śatadhāpāka*) means prepared from one hundred *palas* of madhuka;

and by this instruction for preparing one hundred *palas* of madhuka, he establishes that in the phrase "having made it a hundredfold" (*śataṃ kṛtvā*), the word "hundred" (*śata*) signifies abundance.

Regarding the preparation of one hundred or one thousand decoctions mentioned in the passage beginning with "balākaṣāya," those who observe the depletion of the oil due to excessive heating explain that it should be cooked all at once with a liquid one hundred or one thousand times its quantity. However, we consider that the authoritative teaching of the Teacher is exactly as stated here: the amount of oil to be cooked must be such that it is not entirely consumed during the process of heating, and since milk is present here to increase the oil content, the text remains valid as it stands.

Furthermore, since the cooking is nearly complete when the liquid has evaporated, the extraction of the oil and paste must be performed at this stage; by this means, the quantity of oil becomes equal to the measure of the liquid.
According to the rule that "in recipes beginning with *guḍūcī*, the oil is one-fourth of the liquid," there results one *prastha* of oil.
"Khajita" means churned (mathita).
In the passage beginning with "samadhūcchiṣṭa," substances such as beeswax (madhūcchiṣṭa) and the like constitute the paste (kalka), and water should be added as the liquid.
Regarding this, they say that by the term *piṇḍataila* (lump-oil), it should be understood that the oil must be strained through a cloth;

however, from the statement of Jatūkarṇa, it is inferred that *piṇḍataila* is what is described here as an oil prepared with one *āḍhaka* of sour gruel (*āranāla*), wherein beeswax and other substances are added in place of resin (*sarjarasa*). For it is stated there: "An ointment for massage [prepared] by boiling resin with sour gruel, stirred with a large amount of water, and combined with beeswax and resin.

"By those prepared with sweet [substances]" means by oils prepared with the *jīvanīya* [group of drugs]; in the phrase beginning with "rice," the word "water" (*ambu*) is connected to each of the three [items];
"accompanied by cold water" means sprinkled with cold water.
Regarding the phrase "sprinkled with the water from the moon's rays": it means sprinkled with frosty water;
by the touch of the riverbank (*pulina*), the breeze becomes cool, and [the body] is fanned by that wind upon the bed—[the word] "of the bed" being understood as the ellipsis;
*erakā* is a type of grass (*hoggala*).
"Nirvṛtā" means those which have been steeped in milk; "umā" refers to linseed;
"agracchadāḥ" refers to young leaves.
In the passage beginning with "mūtrakṣāra," "kṣāra" means alkaline water;
"with acids" refers to fermented rice-gruel (kāñjika) and the like;
"romaśa" refers to potassium sulfate (kāsīsa).
Regarding "at dawn" (kalyam), he states what must be done upon waking in the passage beginning with "buddhvā" and so forth;
"one who knows the process of reasoning and exclusion" (ūhāpohavikalpavid) means one who understands the application and rejection of the previously mentioned medical treatments.

The meaning of the verse beginning with "kupita" (provoked) is as follows: when the *vāyu* (wind) becomes provoked due to the obstruction of its channels caused by the excessive increase of either *medas* (fat) or *kapha* (phlegm), then at the outset, oleation (*snehana*) as well as nourishing therapy (*bṛṃhaṇa*) are not recommended.
Regarding this, since oleation and nourishing therapies are prohibited, he states what should be done with the verse beginning with "vyāyāma" and ending with "mākṣikasya ca" (verses 156–159).
In the phrase "gambhīre," it refers to deep-seated or non-superficial vātarakta.
Regarding the statement "the blood is overcome" (*raktam ākrāntam*), meaning it is overwhelmed by *vāyu*, one should treat it with *vāta-vajra* (wind-subduing) measures.
He states what must be done subsequent to this action: "Afterwards, by *vāta*," etc.

When *vāta* is obstructed by *kapha* and *medas*, and once *kapha* and *medas* have been conquered, the treatment that clarifies *vāta-rakta*—namely, the application of oleation (*sneha*) and so forth mentioned right here—should be performed; because it is a disorder of *vāta*, one should conquer it with the therapeutic procedures for *vāta*-related diseases.
And this statement "in the deep" (*gambhīre*) is made to show that this overcoming of blood by wind (*vāta*) generally occurs only in the deep stage of *vātarakta*.

For when *vātarakta* has entered the deep [tissues], there is not much blood, because the second layer of skin, the blood-bearing (*raktadhara*), is the seat of blood. Therefore, blood is powerful only in the superficial [stage], since blood resides in the external locations.
He states the regimen according to the stages—beginning with "raktā" and so forth:
"by the excessive increase of blood and bile," that is, by the excessive increase of *rakta* and *pitta*, it brings about suppuration; the word "vātarakta" is to be understood as the subject.

Regarding the passage beginning with "tayoh" and so forth, he states "kuryāt" and so forth (verses 161–162) to extend the treatment for complications to *vātarakta* caused by increased *pitta* and increased *rakta*, which have undergone suppuration.

In this summary [of the chapter], he presents the causes, the locations (*sthāna*), and so forth, followed by the complications (*upadrava*), and finally the curable, palliable, and incurable conditions—not in their usual order—in order to demonstrate the curability, incurability, or palliability of the disease based on the absence, presence, or slight degree of these complications (vv.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Vātarakta," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā* composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Section on Therapeutics (*Cikitsā-sthāna*).

[Chapter 30 of Cikitsāsthāna (96 of 120)] Following the treatment of vātarakta, the treatment of gynecological disorders (yonivyāpad) is now described, by virtue of being the remaining topic and because it is caused by vāta.
For it has been said: "Indeed, without wind, the womb of women does not become corrupted.

[He is] possessed of divine holy sites (*tīrtha*) such as the Gaṅgā and so forth, and divine medicinal herbs (*auṣadhi*) such as *brahmasuvarcalā*, *aindrī*, and others; thus, he is one who possesses divine holy sites and medicinal herbs.

The "variegated realm" (*citradhātu*) is the realm of manifold colors; he whose nature it is to perceive objects through the knowledge of reality—that is, through correct knowledge—is "one who perceives objects through the knowledge of reality.
This is the "root," meaning the cause.
"Obstruction thereof" means the obstruction of the causes of offspring;
"of them" refers to those [factors] that cause birth from the womb; "origination" refers to the cause of origination, because the term for the cause is applied metaphorically to the effect.

In the section on the summary of diseases, specifically in the chapter on the eight types of abdominal enlargements (*aṣṭodarīya*, Sūtra-sthāna 19), it is stated that [abnormality] arises from improper conduct—that is, from unwholesome diet and lifestyle—and from vitiated *ārtava* (menstrual blood), meaning corrupted *ārtava*.
It further states that "gynecological disorders (*yonivyāpad*) arise from defects in the seed," which refers to the corruption of the seed within the *ārtava*; this [topic] will be discussed later.
"By fate" (*daivāt*) means by the power of past unrighteousness (*adharmavaśāt*).

The causality of these [factors] should be inferred according to their respective suitability from the specific types of causality to be explained later regarding the disorders of the womb (*yonivyāpad*). However, "fate" is a common cause in all cases, to be inferred because an effect is observed even when no specific visible cause is perceived.
In the passage beginning with "vātalāyāḥ," the term "vātalāyāḥ" is used specifically to demonstrate the manifestation of disorders of the female reproductive tract (yonivyāpad) arising from vāta.
The phrase "pipīlikāsṛptim" refers to a sensation resembling the crawling of ants.

The description "saśabdarukphenatanūrūkṣārtava" indicates that even outside the fertile period (anṛtu), such menstrual flow (ārtava) occurs; therefore, this is a disorder of the reproductive tract characterized as vātika-pradara. In the same manner, they describe the paittika, ślaiṣmika, and sānnipātika disorders of the reproductive tract as being paittika-pradara, kaphaja-pradara, and sānnipātika-pradara respectively.

The "blood-source" (raktayoni) mentioned here should be discussed under the technical name *asṛgdara* in the context of medical treatment; therefore, that very condition, which takes the form of *pradara*, is what is intended. However, those who consider *pradara* to be entirely distinct from these morbidities will read a separate section for the treatment of *pradara* later in this chapter, beginning with the words "samaśnantyāḥ," meaning for one who consumes [food] through a combination of wholesome and unwholesome items.

Regarding the passage beginning with "raktapittakaraiḥ" (9–15): even when conception has occurred, blood flows excessively; because of that, her fetus does not remain. This refers to one who has a "bloody womb" (*sāsr̥j raktayoni*). As for those who read "sā aprajā" (she is childless), they explain it thus: "In her case, even when conception occurs, blood flows excessively; she becomes childless due to such excessive bleeding, and this condition is called 'raktayoni,' which is identified by the very fact of excessive discharge of blood."
That which stays in the womb and the uterus is "situated in the womb and uterus" (*yonigarbhāśayastha*); "without menses" (*arajaska*) means without menstrual blood. 16–17.
"Acaraṇā" means "without movement," because there is no movement due to running; "kaṇḍvā" refers to the itching produced by worms in the female organ.
The disorder arising from excessive indulgence in sexual intercourse is called *aticaraṇā*;
"rujan" means causing pain.

"Prior to the time for sexual intercourse" (*ucita-vyavāya-kālāt prāk*) means before engaging in sexual intercourse; [this applies] in cases such as "of a pregnant woman" (*garbhiṇyāḥ*). "Discharge" (*āsrāva*) refers to a discharge distinct from phlegm (*śleṣman*).
She is called "upaplutā" because she is afflicted by diseases of phlegm and wind;
"nṛsaṃvāse" means at the time of sexual union.
Because it is overwhelmed on all sides by the disturbances of vāta and pitta,
it causes the womb to turn upward (pariplutā), thereby producing the upward-moving wind (udāvarta) in the womb.
"Udāvṛtta" means led upwards;
because of the upward movement of *rajas* due to its transformation, she is called "udāvartinī.

Regarding the phrase "of her who is inducing labor at the wrong time" and so forth: for one who causes the fetus to be expelled before the time for delivery has arrived, [the punishment is] a *karṇikā*, meaning a knot shaped like a *karṇikā* (an ear-ornament).
"From roughness" means due to the predominance of the quality of roughness (*rūkṣa-guṇa*);
by the statement "born from vitiated blood," it is shown that here the wind (*vāyu*) also causes the corruption of the [menstrual] flow out of season.
And here, although the destruction of the embryo has been stated in general terms, nevertheless, because the son holds primacy, it should be understood that the designation used is "slayer of a son.

In the passage beginning with "of one who is excessively satiated during sexual intercourse" (vyavāyamatitṛptāyāḥ), it is meant that for a woman who has engaged in excessive intercourse and whose limbs are positioned incorrectly at the time of union, the wind, provoked by food, bends the opening of the womb inward; by the word "bends" (vakrayati), the intention is the turning of the opening inward due to its curvature.
In the passage beginning with "of one staying in the womb," the term *raukṣyāt* means due to the quality of dryness (*rūkṣa-guṇa*);

*mātṛ-doṣāt* means due to the mother's fault, namely her improper conduct (*apacāra*) consisting of the consumption of things that cause the provocation of wind (*vāta*) during the period of gestation.
By the phrase "drying up of the vaginal opening," the designation "dry vagina" (śuṣkayoni) is explained as resulting from the desiccation of the vaginal opening.
She is called "the vomiter" because of the vomiting of semen, as indicated by the passage beginning with "six days," and so forth.

By the general statement "due to a defect of the seed" (*bījadoṣāt*), it should be understood specifically as a defect of the seed in the form of menstrual blood (*ārtava*), because only that defect causes injury to the uterus (*garbhāśaya*).
For it has been said: "When the portion of the seed within her menstrual blood undergoes corruption, then it produces a barren woman" (*Śārīra-sthāna*, Chapter 4).
"One whose womb is afflicted by wind" means one whose uterine cavity is afflicted by wind; "astanī" means having small breasts.
"Unevenly" (*viṣamam*) is an adverbial modifier; the meaning is "in such a way that it becomes uneven.
"One should obstruct" (*viṣṭambhayet*) means one should expand [the seminal flow].
"Meat-swollen" means having flesh that has become swollen.

By the phrase "the womb is afflicted by the *doṣas*," the word *doṣa* refers to the diseases mentioned as the corrupters of the womb; for it has been stated: "Indeed, even diseases receive the designation of *doṣa*" (Viśeṣasthāna, Chapter 6).

Therefore, regarding the expression "from the affliction of the womb, [such as] *pradara* and so forth," they consider *pradara* to be a specific type of *yoni-vyāpad* (womb disorder); thus, they describe *pradara* as a manifestation of *yoni-vyāpad* produced by the *doṣas*. As for those who maintain that *pradara* is distinct from *yoni-vyāpad*, for them there is no contradiction whatsoever in the inclusion of *pradara* here in this list.

Now, having set aside the first four complications, [the author] says "āsām" and so forth, demonstrating the classification of the humors (doṣavibhāga) for the purpose of knowing the symptoms and treatment regarding the remaining sixteen complications, such as those caused by Vāta and the others.
Regarding the phrase "the first two," this refers to those with a blood-stained (*raktayoni*) or menstruation-less (*arajaskā*) womb.

As for the statement "the body [is afflicted] by vāta and so forth," the meaning is that in those cases where the disorders of the womb have been described according to the divisions of vāta and the other *doṣas*, vāta and the others afflict the body with their own respective symptoms; thus, the predominance of vāta and the other *doṣas* in those conditions is logically established. Others, however, say that here the word "body" (*deha*) refers specifically to the location of the womb (*yonisthāna*).
Immediately after the signs [of the disease], he describes the treatment, beginning with "oleation" (snehana), etc.

Although it is already established that oleation and the other [therapies] alleviate *vāta*, the specific qualification "alleviating *vāta*" (*anilāpaha*) is intended to demonstrate oleation and so forth specifically as produced by substances that particularly alleviate *vāta*.
Regarding the phrase "in combined [diseases]," this refers to those born from the conjunction of two [doshas];
"one should establish" means one should establish them after having made them well-settled (*susthitām*).
He describes the method for establishing what is poorly positioned with the words "with the hand," and so forth;
the term "lubricated and fomented" applies throughout,
and "crooked" means bent.
"Open" means with the mouth opened;
"one should turn around" means one should make it closed by turning it all around;
the word "with five" is for the purpose of demonstrating that all ritual actions should be performed with gentleness.

In this context, it should be understood that since emesis and the other therapies are beneficial to the entire body, they certainly possess the capacity to remove diseases located in the female reproductive tract as well;
the remaining procedures will be described hereafter (verses 41–48).

Regarding the phrase "in a decoction of two *droṇas* of *balā*" (*balādroṇadvaye*) and so forth, it means either "in a decoction of two *droṇas* of *balā*" or "in a decoction measuring two *droṇas* of *balā*"; in both cases, the decoction is precisely the measure of two *droṇas*.
[The plant] *payasyā* is *arkapuṣpī*.
The term "parṇī" is connected individually with each of the names mudga, pīlu, and māṣa; among these, pīluparṇī is moraṭā, though some say it is mūrvā;
prasannā is the upper layer of wine, used for "śūla," that is, for pain in the womb (yoniśūla).
"Oil should be retained" means it should be retained in a vagina afflicted by pain;
"and one should introduce it into the vagina" means one should insert it into the vagina using an uttarabasti (urethral/vaginal enema).
"Of the *śyāmā* and others" refers to those mentioned in the *Rogabhiṣagjitīya* chapter, beginning with "The *śyāmā*, *trivṛt*, *caturaṅgula*... (Vi. A. 8).

In the passage beginning with "hatāvarīmūlatulā" (49–62), one should extract as much juice as possible by pressing the roots of *śatāvarī* while they are moist; this juice should be cooked with an equal quantity of milk and ghee along with the pastes (*kalka*) to be mentioned later.
Regarding the phrase "with two parts of *madhuyaṣṭī*," this means using two portions of *madhuyaṣṭī*, or alternatively, using both the aquatic and terrestrial varieties of *madhuyaṣṭī*.
In the passage beginning with "evam eva," the meaning is "mixed with an equal amount of śatāvarī and the four hundred juices"; *kṣīrasarpiḥ* is ghee produced from milk;
and the *jīvanīya* [drugs] serve as the paste (*kalka*) here.
"With the milk of *arka*" means with the latex of the *arka* plant.
The *secyā* (sprinkling vessel) is to be sprinkled [with water];
it is equal to the forefinger in circumference and equal to the forefinger in length.

Regarding the phrase "of *udumbara* fruits" (*udumbara-śalāṭūnām*) and so forth: one should take a *droṇa* measure of *udumbara* fruits together with the five barks (*pañca-valka*) and other ingredients, along with an equal amount of water.

As for the phrase "with exudations" (*niryāsaiḥ*), it should be understood that these refer specifically to the exudations of the *palāśa* tree; furthermore, it should be noted that lac (*lākṣā*) exists apart from the *palāśa*.
"With decoctions containing sugar" means specifically with decoctions made from the young fruits (*śalāṭu*) of the *udumbara* tree and so forth; "vitiated by time" means vitiated after a long period;
"with the milk of the *udumbara*" means with the sap of the *udumbara* tree.
"With its decoction" means with the decoction of that very *udumbara* tree;
"Saurāṣṭrikā" is *tuvarī* clay;
"in goat's urine and milk" means that goat's urine and milk are each twice the amount [of the clay].
*Uttāna* means elevated;
*karīra* is a desert tree,
the *koṣāmra*, known by its own name.
The *jiṅginī* is well known.

In the case of a fever born from the three doṣas combined, one should perform the therapeutic measures for wind (vāta) and the other doṣas as described individually for their respective origins, combined together.
"In a case of *raktayoni* (menorrhagia), etc."—

this means that one should observe the association with blood-colored [discharges], that is, having examined the association with the *doṣas* through the specific characteristics of the blood-colored [discharges].
In the passage beginning with "pāṭhā," *ambaṣṭhā* is a synonym for *pāṭhā*. Others, however, explain that the word "ambaṣṭhā" is repeated for the purpose of including two parts of the *pāṭhā* plant.
For it has been said: "When a substance is mentioned again in a formulation containing ghee or oil..."
"Indeed, twice that amount by weight should be taken by the wise"—
thus [it refers to] *śālmalī-śleṣa*, which is a paste made from *śālmalī* (silk-cotton tree),
and *bāhlīka*, which is saffron.

"By Puṣya" means having extracted [the hair] under the Puṣya asterism; it should be understood that the extraction under the Puṣya asterism here serves as an invisible (transcendental) aid. "Blue, white, and yellow," etc., are qualifiers of the specific defects of the hair-color.

In the passage beginning with "virecanam" (purgation), one should understand that one should drink purgatives such as *trivṛt* and so forth; likewise, it should be applied that one should drink the *mahātiktaka* ghee mentioned in the chapter on skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*).

Regarding the phrase "and what has been said concerning the discharge of the fetus," one should perform the treatment for fetal discharge that was described in the *Jātisūtrīya* chapter (Viśeṣa-sthāna, Chapter 8).
In the passage beginning with "mṛgājāvī," it should be understood that one should drink the blood of deer and other such animals along with curd, sour fruits, and clarified butter.
Alternatively, there is the reading "with sour gruel, honey, and ghee.
Regarding the phrase "oil for the uttarabasti," oil prepared with the *jīvanīya* (vitalizing) drugs should be employed.
In the passage beginning with "in cow's bile," the word "should give" means that one should apply it to the vagina.
"Prāgaticāriṇī" means one who previously transgressed her conduct; in the case of such a woman,
"saṃyāva," "utkārikā," and "dhāraṇa" are prescribed— meaning that for a Vāminī, these are the means for retaining the seed.

"Traivṛta unctuousness" refers to the unctuous substances of ghee, oil, and muscle fat; "this very [substance]" means that *traivṛta* itself [should be used] for the oil enema (*anuvāsana-basti*) and the urethral/vaginal enema (*uttara-basti*).
"Until the time of urination" means one should maintain the binding until the time of passing urine.
He states the reason for performing wind (vāta) therapy in all disorders of the female reproductive tract (sarvayonivyāpad): "Indeed, there is nothing other than wind," and so forth (100–115).
"In *pāṇḍure pradare* means in white leucorrhea;
'saturated by that' means saturated with a decoction of *nyagrodha* bark;
*kaṭumatsyaka* is a small fish (*śapharī*), or a dried fish."

When the seeds—namely, the semen and the blood—are not defective, being endowed with their natural qualities (*kāṅkṣī*, *saurāṣṭrī*, *mṛt*), and when such a union occurs and the soul (*jīva*) enters, women conceive a fetus. This entry of the soul occurs through a favorable conjunction impelled by past karma.

Since the male semen is also a cause for the embryo here, and the embryo is required, he therefore describes the treatment for the semen preceded by its examination— beginning with "the five procedures" (pañcakarma) and so forth;
"indriya" refers to the semen.

The meaning is that if, upon examination of the doshas such as vāta and the others, [the blood] becomes vitiated by their colors, then one should treat it with medicines that pacify vāta and the others, due to its association with the colors of vāta and so forth.

In this context, some recite the passage beginning with "punareva" (once again), which describes the symptoms and treatments for defects of semen (*śukradoṣa*) and so forth. Others, however, declare this to be non-canonical (*anārṣa*), providing the following justification: defects of semen are already treated by the chapter on aphrodisiacs (*vājīkaraṇa*); impotence (*klaibya*) has already been explained in the *Śārīra-sthāna*; therefore, it does not deserve to be mentioned again here. Furthermore, dysuria (*pradara*) has already been treated in the section on disorders of the female genital tract (*yonivyāpatti*). Those who do recite it, however, explain that this is an elaboration upon the brief summary previously stated.
Thus, even though there is a dispute regarding its status as a work of the Ṛṣis, we shall indeed compose some grammar because it is accepted in regions such as Kaśmīra and others.
(Verses 127–132) He states the reason for describing the qualities of semen in the passage beginning with "bījaṃ yasmāt" and so forth.
Since the semen is the seed of the embryo, I shall therefore explain that in sexual intercourse,
exhilaration alone is the source;
that which arises from it is called "pauruṣa" (the male characteristic), for it is by means of the semen alone that a man is manifested.
"Do not engage in sexual intercourse" indicates that even at the proper time for sexual union, one should refrain from it simply because of the obstruction of the flow of semen;
"out of distrust" means out of a lack of confidence.

"I shall speak"— [this refers to] speaking of vitiated semen, meaning semen associated with blood (blood-mixed). In connection with the topic of semen, he states the characteristics of pure semen, beginning with "unctuous" (*snigdha*) and so forth.
Regarding the passage beginning with "māgadhī-amṛtā," *amṛtā* refers to *āmalakī*.
In the phrase "of the bhallātaka," the term "rasāyana" (rejuvenative therapy) is understood to follow.
"By purity alone" means by the purity of semen alone; it is accomplished, that is, it becomes tranquil.

In the passage beginning with "saṅkalpa," the phrase "due to the laxity of the *liṅga*" means because the *liṅga* does not arise; he is one whose resolve and efforts are "moghāni" (futile), that is, fruitless. 154–157.

Because the destruction of wind does not logically entail the destruction of the seed, and because of the total depletion of wind and the other [humors], it should be understood that in the case of the depletion of natural wind and the others, the non-production of semen results precisely from the impairment of the body.
"From excessive indulgence in thorns" means from the overuse of thorns performed for the purpose of increasing the size of the penis (*liṅga*);

some call this fivefold condition "flag-failure" (*dhvajabhaṅga*). Thus, its fivefold nature is according to the divisions of vāta, pitta, kapha, blood, and their combination (*sannipāta*), as previously stated.

Among these: swelling and pain in the penis and so forth are caused by vāta; eruptions and so forth by pitta; growth of flesh and so forth by kapha; fever, thirst, and so forth by blood; and [pain] as if by fire and so forth by *sannipāta*.
Regarding the passage beginning with "jaghanya," the term *pravaram vayaḥ* refers to old age.

Based on the statement that [semen] generally diminishes, this shows that sometimes the semen of even the elderly does not diminish—provided they possess the essence of semen (*śukrasāra*) and consume aphrodisiacs (*vṛṣya*).
He states the cause for the depletion of semen in the elderly: "of the *rasa* and so forth," etc.
Furthermore, these causes, such as the depletion of *rasa*, arise solely from the very nature of old age.
176–180—Regarding the phrase "some say" and so forth: it refers to the occurrence of the collapse and destruction of the banner that will be described as distinct; and these two are incurable.

Up to the point of "by the excision of the testicles," the failure of the virile organ (*dhvajabhaṅga*) has been described; however, that which arises from decay (*kṣayaja*), as stated in the passage beginning with "of the mother and father," refers to how a man becomes impotent (*apumān*) due to his inability to perform the male function with women.
The phrase "arising from causes related to sexual intercourse" is intended to exclude those congenital [diseases] produced by defects in the seed;
"due to a disorder of the elements" means due to an imbalance of the humors (*doṣa*).

With the passage beginning "Daivavyapāśrayam" (191–195), he describes the treatment for impotence caused by malevolent spells (*abhicāra*) and similar factors; and since impotence arising from such causes is mentioned specifically in the context of treatments based on divine means (*daivavyapāśraya*), it must be understood as being included therein.

"By means of *palāśa*, *eraṇḍa*, *mustā*, and so forth" means by means of the established groups beginning with *eraṇḍa* and *palāśa*, and those beginning with *mustā*. Among these, the group beginning with *eraṇḍa* leaves and so on will be described in the text starting from "from the root and leaves of *eraṇḍa*" (*Si. A. 12*) for the purpose of curing (*siddhi*). The group beginning with *mustā* constitutes the palliative enema (*yāpanā-basti*).
Here, the plural number is used for both types of enemas (*vasti*) with reference to the existence of multiple individual instances.

196–203—Regarding that which was previously mentioned under the heading "pradara" (uterine hemorrhage) and so forth as being of the nature of a complication (*upadrava*), some say: "It was previously called *pradara*; however, in the chapter on the treatment of *raktayoni* (menorrhagia), it is designated by the very name *asṛgdara*, described within that same context as a form of *raktayoni* according to the specific differentiation of the doshas, and thus the repeated statement here of the characteristics of *asṛgdara* is not approved by the earlier commentators."
In this regard, even those who read this text explain that "this" refers to a specific division or elaboration of that very [organ];
however, we provide this interpretation because we observe such a reading in many manuscripts:
"situated in the *garbhāśaya*" means connected to the *garbhāśaya* (uterus).

He explains the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the term *asṛgdara* with the words "the provoked wind" (*kupito 'nila*), and so forth. Regarding the phrase "having transgressed the measure of blood" (*raktaṃ pramāṇamutkramya*), it means having made the blood exceed its proper measure; because the wind (*pavana*), having taken up that blood, increases the *rajas* (menstrual flow)—that is, because it increases the *rajas* by joining it with the increased blood—this disease is called *asṛgdara*, since it consists of a mixture of blood and *rajas*. Furthermore, the etymology should be understood here as follows: it is called *pradara* because "it is torn apart" (*pradīryate*), meaning it becomes expanded; and it is called *asṛgdara* because "blood is torn apart in it" (*asṛg dīryate yasmin*). This etymology is also to be understood in this context.

"Not remaining in a single state" means being joined with various states produced by wind (*vāta*); with the words "But the woman," etc., [the author] describes the states produced by these secondary factors (204–224).
In connection with the description of pure menstrual flow (*viśuddhārtava*), he states its characteristics, beginning with "from the month" (*māsāt*) and so forth.

Regarding the term *pañcarātrānubandhī*: it is called *pañcarātrānubandhī* because it persists for five nights due to its manifestation; this is because the duration of the menstrual flow (*ārtava*) is twelve nights. Alternatively, it should be understood that the capacity of the menstrual flow to initiate conception lasts up to twelve nights, but not its actual discharge.
Furthermore, the various colors of the menstrual flow, such as "the color of the *guñjā* fruit" and so forth, arise solely from differences in the woman's constitution (*prakṛti*).

Having now described *pradara* (menorrhagia/leucorrhea) along with its treatment, the author—intending to discuss another female disease, namely defects of breast milk (*stanyadoṣa*), in the context of the exposition on women's diseases—says: "The breast milk of the wet-nurse," and so forth;
"vitiated by Vāta and the others," and so forth, meaning that [the description] is included within the very disorders of Vāta and the other doshas.
Since disciples are of three types, I shall speak accordingly; among these three distinct categories of disciples, for the sake of easy comprehension by those of dull intellect, [it is said]:
"The decoction with ginger"—here, it should be understood that the decoction is prepared using ginger alone. 229–231.
As before, regarding the phrase "beginning with jīvaka," here "beginning with jīvaka" refers to the *jīvanīya* (vitalizing) group.

Having shown the nature of the childhood disorders arising from the consumption of spoiled milk, he states the medicine to be administered as follows: "Doṣā... and so forth. The *doṣas* are wind (*vāta*) and the others; the *dūṣyas* are blood (*rakta*) and the others; the *malas* are feces, urine, sweat, and so forth. These very same *doṣas* and other factors that exist in adults also exist in children; however, the distinction is that when they reach children, the quantity (*mātrā*) of those *doṣas* and other factors is much smaller. Therefore, the sense is that the dosage of medicine should also be small, in consideration of the quantity of the *doṣas* and other factors.
The cessation of emetics and so forth, and so on.

Children are of two types: those who act independently and those who act dependently. Observing this state of dependence among children, the cessation of emesis and other such procedures should be performed. Furthermore, observing a child’s capacity for speech and movement, once independence has been established, a physician learned in the scriptures should employ mild forms of emesis and so forth. Likewise, even palliative medicine should be administered to children in small doses according to the specific disease; this is the meaning of the statement. Alternatively, one may interpret it as follows: observing mildness and dependence in children, the cessation of emesis and other procedures should be ordained; and observing the capacity for speech and movement in children, one should administer palliative medicine in small doses according to the specific disease—this is how the construction should be understood.

With the passage beginning with "sweet" (*madhurāṇi*) and ending with "one should employ" (*prayojayet*), he describes the medicine to be administered to children; this section from verse 282 to 287 is subject to dispute regarding its status as the word of the Sage (*ārṣa*).
With the words "of all disorders" and so forth, he summarizes the meaning stated in the Section on Therapeutics (*Cikitsā-sthāna*).
By the expression "of all disorders," he demonstrates that this aphorism regarding the seeds of treatment applies even to those disorders not explicitly mentioned.
The term "secret" (*rahasya*) means it is to be concealed because it sets forth treatments of extreme utility; it must not be disclosed to anyone who is most wicked.
Now, Dṛḍhabala, demonstrating the scope of his own editorial revisions, says "In this [work]," and so forth.

"Seventeen chapters" refers to the seventeen chapters in the Cikitsāsthāna (Section on Therapeutics). These should be understood as excluding the eight chapters composed by Caraka ending with the treatment of consumption (yakṣmacikitsita), as well as those concerning hemorrhoids, diarrhea, erysipelas, the two types of wounds, and alcoholism.

(Since the supplementary purification (*pariśiṣṭasaṃskāra*) is to be accomplished by means of a super-sensory excellence (*adṛṣṭātiśaya*), the author, demonstrating that very super-sensory excellence of the self, says: "That [is] Śaṅkara," etc.
Now, for the purpose of extending the treatment to diseases both mentioned and unmentioned, he says: "Those diseases which are here," etc.)

"Etadeva" and so forth means that this very medicine prescribed in the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsā-sthāna) becomes the appropriate remedy when applied accordingly with respect to diseases not specifically described by name or form, but generally stated to be caused by Vāta and the other doshas. "Doṣādīn" refers to the doshas, dūṣyas, and nidānas which will be explained later; alternatively, it may refer to the factors mentioned in the Sūtra-sthāna: dosha, medicine, place, time, strength, body, diet, suitability, mental state (sattva), constitution (prakṛti), and age.

Now, as to how this medicine serves as a remedy for diseases not explicitly mentioned, he says: "The doshas, the dūṣyas," and so forth. The *doṣas* are wind (*vāta*) and the others; the *dūṣyas* are blood (*rakta*) and the others; the *nidānas* (causes) are dryness (*rūkṣa*) and the others. Whatever is contrary to these—whether taken individually or collectively—is the beneficial medicine. When properly administered, it certainly subdues both the diseases already mentioned and those not mentioned. "Mentioned" refers to them by name, form, and so on; "not mentioned" refers to those not specified by particular names, forms, and so forth.

By this, he demonstrates that as soon as this [subject] has been established through its opposition to the defects (doṣa) and so forth, then even for diseases not explicitly mentioned, one may understand their respective dosas and other factors and thereby administer medicine that is correctly applied.

Although a medicine that is contrary to the cause (*nidāna*) can only be understood as being contrary to the humor (*doṣa*)—since the provocation of the humor is produced by the cause, and what is contrary to that humor is likewise contrary to the cause (for example, when wind is increased by a dry cause, the remedy "moisture" which is contrary to it is indeed contrary to the cause as well)—nevertheless, the mention here of what is contrary to the cause is for the purpose of demonstrating the application of medicine through partial contrariety to the humor itself.

For example: if the *vāyu* is aggravated in its entirety, then oil, which is the opposite of that *vāyu*, should be administered. However, when the *vāyu* has increased due to cold, one should abandon oil—which is entirely contrary [to the required treatment]—and instead apply a hot medicine as a cause-opposite (*hetu-viparīta*) for the purpose of pacifying that very cold quality, using whatever is beneficial against coldness.
Therefore it is said: "Those learned in medicine pacify diseases caused by heat with cold," and so forth. (Vi. A. 3)

In this context, however, because the *doṣas* and so forth are mentioned, the disease—which consists of a combination of *doṣas* and *dūṣyas*—is also included. By that, even medicine that is contrary to the disease is encompassed;

and by the word "contrary" (*viparīta*) here, what is meant is "opposing," not merely "possessing opposite qualities. Consequently, there is the inclusion of medicines that produce effects contrary [to the disease].

However, that which is considered "identical" for depleted *doṣas* or *dhātus* is actually the opposite, because it produces the increase of those very *doṣas* and so forth that were previously diminished. Therefore, in that case, it is not the *doṣas* and so on that must be counteracted, but rather their depletion; thus, it has been stated that when applied correctly, that which is "opposite" to the depleted state properly restrains the *doṣas* and so on. Consequently, there is no fault in saying that what is identical to the *doṣas* and so on is indeed the opposite. Now, he explains that very correct application (*samyagyoga*) by which a medicine, when joined with it, becomes effective: "Place, time," and so forth.

The teacher himself has provided examples for these applications of place (*deśa*) and so forth, beginning with "from the mouth to the site of the *āmāśaya*" and ending with "even if excessive, it causes no great harm.

Among these, *deśa* is stated to be of the nature of the patient (*ātura-rūpa*) alone; however, the application regarding *deśa* in the sense of the physical terrain (*bhūmi-rūpa*) is already included by the mention of application according to suitability (*sātmya*).
*Kāla* (time) is sixfold, consisting of day, the patient, the medicine, and so on.
In this regard, the time for medicine is tenfold; the dosage of medicine is threefold—small, large, and moderate;

suitability (sātmya) is twofold, pertaining to place and the body; suitability to the disease is indeed included within the medicine itself; suitability to the season is subsumed under time; and the inclusion of dosage and suitability is accomplished through proper administration alone.
That which is unwholesome (*asātmya*) is the opposite of what is wholesome (*sātmya*).

Proper application (*samyagyoga*) means correct usage. Regarding the fault that arises from the opposite [of proper application], he says: "Otherwise, even what is beneficial for these would become otherwise. For these factors—place and so forth—"otherwise" refers to improper application; "even what is beneficial" refers to a medicine that is contrary to the doshas and other factors; "otherwise" means it becomes non-beneficial (*apathya*).

Furthermore, other factors such as strength (*bala*) and constitution (*sattva*), which are included among the ten types of defects (*doṣa*) and so forth and were not mentioned here because they are to be examined [in detail], should be subsumed within those very defects and others.
(293) He provides an example of correct application (*samyagyoga*) with respect to the body, beginning with "from the mouth" (*āsya*), etc.

In the case of "āsyādityādi" (from the mouth, etc.), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used in place of the third case (*tṛtīyā*); thus, medicine administered through the mouth quickly destroys diseases located in the stomach (*āmāśaya*) by means of vomiting and so forth. Likewise, medicine administered through the nose destroys diseases located in the head, and that administered through the anus destroys those located in the large intestine (*pakvāśaya*).
Regarding the external application of medicinal treatments in consideration of specific body parts, he says: "In those [diseases] arising in the limbs of the body," and so forth;
"according to the location" means that poultices (pradeha) and other treatments—such as affusions (pariṣeka), plasters (upanāha), and the like—are to be applied according to the site of the disease.
Having first divided time, [the author] states examples of correct application (samyagyoga) dependent on place and time, beginning with "day, disease, medicine," and so forth.
The word "consideration" (avekṣaṇa) is connected with "day" and the other terms; *avekṣaṇa* means *avekṣā* (consideration).

Here, he illustrates the times for observing the day and so forth in sequence—beginning with "observing the day" and ending with "observing the patient. The meaning of "observing the patient" is that [the treatment] occurs after having observed the specific condition of the patient, whether they are strong or weak. "Without food" means not eating even while undergoing the administration of medicine.

Regarding the examination of medicines and the times for administering them, he says "the times for medicine" and so forth. Here, by the phrase "at the beginning of eating," two times are indicated: namely, [taking medicine] on an empty stomach in the morning, as well as before eating;
and by the phrase "likewise after," two further times are indicated: the time following the morning meal, and another, the time following the evening meal.
That half which is consumed after having first eaten [the other half] is called *muhurmuhurbhakta* (repeated eating).
That which is eaten at every moment during the mealtime is called *sāmudga*.
That which is eaten at both the beginning and the end of the meal is designated as *sāmudga* because, like a casket (*samudga*), it covers the food.

The word "bhuktam" (eaten) is connected individually with each term beginning with "bhuktādi. That which is eaten mixed with food due to contact or preparation is called "antarābhaktam" (intermediate eating). However, that which is eaten in the intervals between morsels is called "bhuktam" (eaten), meaning what is consumed amidst the mouthfuls.

Others, however, read "between morsels" (*grāsagrāsāntare*) and state that there is only one time for medicine; by the word "having eaten," they designate another time for medicine and thereby complete the ten times for medicine. For this very reason, the Teacher has stated only one time in the statement: "But when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is vitiated, [the medicine] is to be taken between morsels. In that context, the medicine which is taken in the interval between one morsel and the next is called "between morsels" (*grāsagrāsāntara*).

The definition of *bhukta* (eaten) is: "that which is eaten together with light food"; that which is consumed in conjunction with light food such as *peyā* (thin gruel) and the like is called *bhukta*.

However, by the statement beginning with "but *sambhojya* [is] with medicinal substances," that food which is used after being prepared with medicinal drugs—whether heavy or light—is denoted by the term *sambhukta*.

However, those who read "in one morsel or between morsels" (*grāse grāsāntare*) explain that when the *prāṇa* is deranged, the two times for administration are during a morsel or between morsels by means of using medicine; they further explain that the phrase "combined with light food" (*laghunānnena saṃyutam*) is a qualification of "to be eaten" (*sambhojyam*).
