They interpret the word "eaten" (*bhuktam*) in the commentary as a qualification of the specific medicine to be used at all times.
This being established, the explanation of the timing for medicine beginning with "when the *apāna* is impaired" (*apāne viguṇe*) is quite clear and need not be stated again.

Although these times are prescribed specifically for particular diseases, they nevertheless constitute the proper times for administering medicine itself when it is subject to defects such as those of the *apāna* wind;
for here, conditions like the impairment of the *apāna* are presented as objects for which medicine is intended.
Therefore, this textual arrangement should be understood to mean that these times apply even to the medicine administered when the *apāna* is impaired, and so forth.

The distinction here is that while time based on the consideration of medicine has been described, time based on the consideration of the disease must now be explained as consisting of the stages of the disease.
Having stated the time regarding medicine, he speaks of the time regarding the disease, beginning with "In fever, gruel," and so forth.

In this context, according to the general rule for gruel, decoction, ghee, milk, and purgation, their administration is prescribed sequentially starting from the first day of the fever up to the sixth day.

The administration of *peyā* (gruel) after the lapse of six days does not entail any contradiction, because it is universally accepted that a general rule is set aside by a specific rule. Therefore, even the administration of *peyā* during the six-day period of decoction-therapy—which might otherwise follow from the statement, "One should treat with gruels at the appropriate time one who has undergone fasting or emesis" (Ci. A. 3)—is not contradictory; furthermore, since the detailed exposition of that verse has already been provided in the *Jvaracikitsita*, it is not repeated here.

"Having observed the time of the disease" means that one should observe the stage of the disease characterized by fever and give *peyā* (gruel) after six days; this refers to the time in consideration of the signs of digestion.
He states the time with reference to the signs of hunger and so forth:
"Hunger arises," meaning the desire to eat; "release of the impulse" means the discharge of feces and other waste.

"Lighness" (laghutā) means purity; "purity of the heart's expression" (hṛdayodgāraviśuddhi) refers to the characteristic of digestion (jīrṇalakṣaṇa), which is the characteristic of digested food. Although this characteristic of digestion has already been mentioned in the *Rasavimāna*, it is nevertheless stated here because it pertains to the present context in view of the [specific] time; thus, it does not incur the fault of redundancy.

By the statement "then the medicine should be taken," one refers to that medicine which is given at dawn as non-food (*ananna*); whereas that which is given after the meal is given only when the morning meal has already been digested (*jīrṇa*). Alternatively, even the medicine that is given after a meal is given only when the food eaten on the previous day has been digested; for otherwise it would be defective (*doṣavat*). Regarding this, some read "dvidoṣavat" (defective with respect to two humors), meaning that it would be associated with two defects both while the food is being digested and once it has been digested.
The original reading, however, is "syāttu doṣavad anyathā."
He explains the proper application of yoga by observing the seasons in their various forms: "Accumulation and so forth," etc.
"Accumulation and so forth" refers to accumulation (*caya*), provocation (*prakopa*), and pacification (*praśama*).

These accumulations and so forth have the following nature: for *kapha*, there is accumulation in the winter (*hemanta*), provocation in the spring (*vasanta*), and pacification in the summer (*grīṣma*), and so on.

That which is to be avoided and that which is to be practiced during the fertile period (*ṛtu*) have been stated; therein, heavy foods and the like are also mentioned as things to be avoided. Therefore, that [topic] should be understood from that very place.
Some recite the verse beginning with "of the procedures" (*upakramāṇām*) along with its half-verse; however, they say that this is not the word of the Sage (*anārṣa*).
He states, with an illustration, the undesirable result of an application that disregards the six types of time already mentioned: "In this way," and so forth.

Just as crops suffer distress or even perish due to unseasonable rain, so too does medicine, though it be of six types, lead to affliction or destruction when administered without regard for the proper time. On the other hand, some recite four verses beginning with "The diseases [are regulated by] seasons, days, nights, and rules," which demonstrate the application [of medicine] with due regard for the time; however, this too is not very well known.
Demonstrating the application of yoga while considering the specific measure [of the medicine], he says: "Not a small amount," and so forth.

Although the specific measure of the medicine has not been stated here by way of individual specification (*śṛṅgagrāhikayā*), nevertheless, one should understand that the medium measure of medicine mentioned here—such as in the passage beginning, "For the variation in the measure of medicine is in accordance with the measure of the *doṣas* and depends on the specific measure of strength" (Viśeṣa-sthāna, Chapter 8)—is to be applied.
Now, explaining the proper application [of treatment] while considering suitability (*sātmya*), he says: "By reason of suitability for whom," and so forth.

"By reason of suitability" means by habituation (*abhyāsa*). The construction is as follows: even if something is unwholesome (*apathya*), if it is suitable (*sātmya*) for a particular person, one does not obtain happiness by abandoning it absolutely;
"absolutely" meaning abandoning it suddenly and in every respect.

By this, he demonstrates that for one who abandons even unwholesome things absolutely because they have become habitual (*sātmya*), happiness does not arise; furthermore, he shows that when wholesome things that have become habitual are abandoned, suffering occurs all the more intensely.
By the word "region" (*deśa*) here, the inhabitants of the region—the people—are intended.
Therefore, by the term "regional habituation" (*deśasātmya*), that which is consumed by persons simply because it originates in that region is understood as common habituation (*sādhāraṇa-sātmya*).

By the inclusion of the term "personality suitability" (*puruṣasātmya*), however, that which becomes a habituation through the practice of a specific individual alone is understood as "person-specific suitability";
whereas that which was previously described as "having qualities opposite to those of the regions and diseases by their own qualities... [is understood as regional suitability].

By the statement, "They desire suitability" (Sūtra, Chapter 6), regional suitability (*deśasātmya*) is explained; that is, suitability for the people living in a particular region is described by virtue of qualities contrary to those of that region. However, the distinction here is that whether or not a quality is actually contrary to the region, it is called "suitability" (*sātmya*) when it becomes habitual for the inhabitants of that region.
As for personal suitability (*puruṣasātmya*), because it varies from person to person and is thus indeterminate, no specific examples have been given by way of individual enumeration.
Therefore, he provides well-known examples of suitability through regional habituation, beginning with "The Bāhlīkas," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "fit for Vaiśvānara," here the word *ucita* denotes habitual practice (*abhyāsa*). The term *tailāmlam* refers to oil and sour [substances].
The expression "to the south" means in the southern region (*dakṣiṇāpatha*).

Regarding the phrase "in the north and the west" (uttare ca paścime ca), the term *uttarapaścime* refers to those [regions]; here, by the word *tat* (those), both the countries and the people are intended.
Therefore, the expression *tatsātmyayuktāni* means "endowed with the suitability for those [countries] and endowed with the suitability for those people" as previously described.
He states the result of the use of what is wholesome (*sātmya*): "For wholesomeness quickly [produces] strength," and so forth;
"even in excess" (*bahv api*) means even in overabundance (*atimātram api*).
He states the fault of one who performs treatment by means of the aforementioned applications alone, without the examination of the location and other factors: "By applications alone," etc.

By the phrase "ignorance of location and so forth," he characterizes the person who, due to ignorance of the location and other factors, administers treatment that is defective with respect to the location and other such variables.

"One fails" means one does not achieve the desired result due to ignorance regarding place (*deśa*) and so forth. Here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of time (*kāla*) and the others already mentioned, as well as age (*vayas*), strength (*bala*), body (*śarīra*), constitution (*prakṛti*), and temperament (*sattva*), which are mentioned in another passage.
To the question "Why does ignorance regarding place and so forth fail? he says: "Age, strength," and so forth.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of [the patient's] constitution (*prakṛti*), strength (*sattva*), and so forth is intended.

Since many distinctions such as age and physical power are considered by physicians to be factors requiring consideration in medical treatment, the meaning is that a treatment performed without regard for place and other such factors does not achieve the desired result.
He states that the general treatment described can also produce specific effects through another method: "In that way, internally," and so forth;
"internal pathways" are those residing in the visceral cavities (*koṣṭha*), while "joint pathways" are those residing in the middle channels (*madhyamārga*).

Regarding the phrase "of those moving secretly": because they reside within the internal junctions (*antaḥsandhi*), the courses of the *doṣas* are unmanifest; thus, even treatments considered contradictory may sometimes occur. "Considered contradictory" means they are known as being the opposite [of what is expected].

Furthermore, it is not only that many differences such as age and strength are recognized, but rather that many variations of the *doṣas* moving secretly through the internal junctional pathways are considered to be observed in treatment. Therefore, one should apply the reasoning that a difference in treatment may occasionally arise from a difference in the *doṣas* that move secretly, and so forth.
He provides an example of performing an action that is considered contradictory, beginning with the words "the bile within" and so forth.

"It is led outside" means it is led out through the external hair follicles; "by hot [means]" means in the manner described, they pacify the hot bile by means of hot treatments such as sudation and the like.
Now, he provides an illustration of the pacification of cold phlegm (*śīta-śleṣman*) by means of cold treatment: "By external [means]," and so forth;
"afflicted" means being obstructed while moving outward.
Then, he states that even an opposing factor can produce a different effect through a specific mode of preparation: "finely ground," and so forth.
"Due to the obstruction of the heat residing in the skin" means due to the obstruction of the heat exiting through the pathways of the skin.
"And otherwise, *aguru* produces coldness" means that even though *aguru* is hot, a thick paste of it, when ground into a solid mass, would produce coldness.
In the context of describing contradictory actions, he provides an example of how one part of a whole may perform a contrary effect relative to the aggregate: "emesis-inducing," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "in substances that have been steamed and eaten, there is likewise a transformation," the meaning of the sentence is as follows: in those very substances that constitute the excrement of a fly, once they have been steamed by the digestive fire within the fly's stomach, there occurs such a transformation—a contradictory action—consisting of both remaining within the fly's body and being present in its excrement, as previously described. The term "steamed and eaten" (*svinnajagdheṣu*) refers to substances that, immediately after being consumed, have been cooked by fire. The term "transformation" (*vikriyā*) refers to a contradictory action;

alternatively, it is stated for the purpose of providing an example of an effect contrary to the previous substance through processing (*saṃskāra*). This is expressed in the passage beginning with "in substances... (*dravyeṣu...*).

In this alternative view, they read "dagdheṣu" (when burnt) instead of "jagdheṣu" (when eaten). In that case, regarding parched grain flour (*lāja-saktu*) within prepared balls (*siddha-piṇḍa*), because it is steamed, its action is contrary to that of parched grain (*lāja*); being heavy, it causes the suppression of the digestive fire (*agni-vadha*) and other such effects. Similarly, when lotus stalks (*utpala-nāla*) are burnt, because they are alkaline, their action is contrary to the cold; it produces actions such as cutting (*chedana*). Such examples should be inferred accordingly. When the reading is "yasmin jagdheṣu," even then, since "eaten" (*jagdha*) occurs after "steamed" (*svinna*), the example should be understood as referring specifically to the ball of prepared flour.
321–325 – He summarizes the result of the investigation, beginning with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt), etc.

The eleven items beginning with the doshas and drugs are enumerated in the chapter on *Upakalpanīya* (Sūtra 15), and twelve are enumerated in the *Vimāna-sthāna*. Therefore, by including those [twelve], the number ten mentioned here would be contradicted. Consequently, it is precisely those ten items—beginning with the doshas and drugs—that were specified by Dṛḍhabala himself in the context of the *nirūha-vasti* by the verse: "Having duly considered the doshas, the drug, the place, the time, suitability, digestive fire, mental disposition (*sattva*), habit (*ukā*), age, and strength" (Śārīra 3), that are to be understood as the ten items referred to here.
The inclusion of the aforementioned group of eleven items to be prepared (*upakalpanīya*) and the group of twelve mentioned in the *Vimāna-sthāna* is contained within this very group of ten.

To explain: among the items to be prepared, those other than these ten—namely the natural constitution (*prakṛti*), the body (*śarīra*), and diet (*āhāra*)—are included. Therein, both the body and the natural constitution are subsumed under the term "place" (*deśa*), which includes the land and the patient; for it is said: "Place consists of the land and the patient" (*Vi. A. 8*). As for diet, it is included precisely by the mention of suitability (*sātmya*).
Furthermore, the twelfth disorder (*vikāra*) listed in the *Vimāna-sthāna* is already encompassed by the mention of the humors (*doṣa*).
In this manner, the inclusion of all the aforementioned items beginning with "upakalpanīya" (preparatory materials) is to be explained.

As for the fact that Āṣāḍhavarma and others, by resorting to the view of a *bahuvrīhi* compound based on non-essential qualities (*atadguṇa*), have explained here that the number ten applies only to those things specifically mentioned as "upakalpanīya," that is neither scripturally authoritative nor logical; for it is not the case that [the number] applies only to those [items] explicitly used, nor merely by their application.
Now, showing what should be done once the disease has been cured by treatment, he says: "Even though it has ceased," and so forth.

It is as if ceased, being ceased, yet having some root in the form of residual defects; it is not ceased entirely, because that would contradict its recurrence through similar causes, and because it is dissimilar to the illustration of the subtle fire.
When [the humors] such as the flesh have diminished and been made into a path—that is, made similar to a path by no longer obstructing the disease—[then the fever subsides].
The word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is an adjective for fire;
by the word "also" (*api*), he shows that even when [the fire] returns due to a slight cause after having been extinguished, it returns all the more inclined toward subsiding.
This being the established state, he states what must be done, beginning with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

"One should continue with the application" means that one should again employ the continuous medicinal treatment; "without fail" means without causing another disease. To the question "For what purpose should one continue? he says: "For the sake of consolidation."
For the sake of strengthening— that is, for the sake of stabilizing— the purpose characterized by the cessation of disease produced by the application of proven medicine;
He states another application concerning the subject of the sequence [of the humors]: "Because of hardness," and so forth.

"Because of hardness" means because of being a compact aggregate in the form of an accumulation of the *doṣas*; "because of deficiency" means because of the provocation [of a humor] even when there is no accumulation. For indeed, provocation of the *doṣas* occurs even during their non-accumulation; for example, of *vāyu* through strenuous physical struggle and the like, of *pitta* through anger and the like, and of *śleṣman* through sleeping during the day and the like. And this provocation during non-accumulation is called "provocation due to deficiency" because it does not result from the increase of dense constituent parts.

Regarding the statement, "The great [dosha], provoked internally, [becomes mild]," the established principle is that it becomes mild due to its hardness and smallness in quantity. For, because of its hardness, the provocation of the accumulated [dosha] generally occurs within [the body]; however, due to its smallness in quantity, there is provocation of the unaccumulated [dosha]. Furthermore, because of its nature of spreading, even that which has a subtle essence of accumulation becomes "great" when it is reduced to a soft and small state—this being the sequence. Therefore, that which was provoked internally due to hardness is brought to a state of softness; and that which was "great" due to its gross state, when provoked, is brought to a state of smallness. Thus, "one who makes the dosha mild" means one who causes only slight morbidity.

Or rather, [it is so] because of hardness— that is, due to the stability created by the connection between the *doṣas* and the *dūṣyas*; or because of its diminished state— that is, even without the aforementioned hardness,
the word "inside" (*antara*) and the word "great" (*mahān*) are connected to both [terms], referring respectively to the non-protruding region of the body and the interior.
For a single person, greatness arises through the accumulation of causes,
just as it occurs for one who eats even wholesome food or employs even beneficial medicine; thus, it persists either by way of gentleness or by way of smallness.

Having understood that "this is beneficial for him" and "this is his medicine," yet realizing that "this disease, due to its magnitude or depth, does not recede at all and he remains submerged," one should, knowing this, cause the increase or the repetition of that very same previously employed application; one should not employ another application based on a different method. "Increase" refers to an excess in dose, while "repetition" refers to constant use.
This point has been stated elsewhere as well: "Yogas, when practiced gradually, conquer even powerful and chronic diseases."
Therefore, a person who is not weary should apply themselves to the practice of yoga when afflicted by a disease.

If a wholesome regimen, though prescribed for constant use, becomes loathed due to that very continuity of use, or if it becomes loathed because of its natural sweetness or its disagreeable nature, even then one should restore that same wholesome regimen to the patient's favor through various methods of preparation—such as fresh juices, decoctions, pastes, and so forth—as well as by the procedures taught in the culinary sciences (*sūda-śāstra*).
For it is observed that even something sweet becomes unpleasant through constant use; however, that which is naturally unpalatable is unpleasant by its very nature.
Here, the word "sweet" (*svādu*) refers to a pleasant taste.
He states the purpose for producing affection— beginning with "due to the favorability of the mind"— as follows:
by providing things such as medicine that are favorable to the mind,
*ūrjā* (vigor) arises, which is mental strength.
The state of enjoying comfort is the administration of medicine in a manner that is not disagreeable.

Here, after explaining what should be done in cases of nausea following purgation—such as when it ends in excessive thirst and other symptoms—he states what should be done for a specific kind of appetite: "out of greed," etc.

In this regard, a person’s taste for a particular thing arises solely from greed; taste may also arise from the elimination of a defect, such as when one who is afflicted by disease develops a taste for a drink. Furthermore, taste may arise through the power of a disease, as in the case of clay in the disease of jaundice (*pāṇḍuroga*). Taste may also arise due to contrast (*vaidharmya*), as in the case of a person accustomed to unctuousness preferring the dry, or one accustomed to sweetness preferring the sour. As it has been said: "Some people, being repelled by sourness, become fond of the association with sweetness" (Suśruta Sūtrasthāna 46). Alternatively, there is only one cause: the contrast with the disease itself; an example of this is the craving for sour and pungent things during phlegmatic fever (*śleṣmajvara*).

The desire produced by each of these factors—greed and so forth—requires a wholesome regimen (*pathyopacāra*) regarding those desires; that is to say, only what is wholesome should be given, not what is unwholesome.

In this regard, if something is both wholesome and an object of desire, then it is excellent. However, when an object of desire is unwholesome, he states what must be done: "One should modify the first through a combination" (*yogena ādyaṃ vikalpayet*).
This means that one should prepare and give the food that is the object of one's wish by means of a medicinal combination (*bheṣajayoga*).

However, others state that there are three types of anorexia here arising from defects such as greed (*laulya*): in the case of anorexia born of greed, treatment consists of wholesome regimens (*pathyopacāra*); in the case of anorexia born of the depletion of the *doṣas*, it is through "yoga," meaning treatment by means of a proper application of therapeutic measures; and in the case of anorexia born of a discordance with the disease, one should prepare the food to be eaten by means of applications counteracting the disease.
Although this [latter] explanation has been given previously, we prefer the former explanation.
The summary beginning with "twenty" and so forth is indeed easy to understand (334–341).

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Gynecological Disorders," in the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka Saṃhitā, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta, son of Śrī Nārāyaṇadatta. [Kalpasthāna]
[Chapter 1 of Kalpasthāna (97 of 120):

Now, in order to describe in detail the various applications of emesis and purgation as prescribed here and there in the Cikitsāsthāna, the Kalpasthāna—which constitutes a section (sthāna) dedicated to formulations (yoga) pertaining to therapeutics—is being expounded.

Although the Siddhisthāna (Section on Success) should also be presented as a branch of therapeutics because enemas (basti) are also prescribed therein, nevertheless, since the procedure for enemas generally occurs only after emesis and purgation within the standard application of the five therapeutic measures (pañcakarman), the Kalpasthāna (Section on Formulations)—which deals with emesis and purgation—is stated immediately after the Siddhisthāna which deals with enemas; it is called Kalpasthāna because "formulations (kalpa) regarding emesis and purgation reside (tiṣṭhanti) in this [section]."

Even though the chapter on pharmaceutical preparations (*kalpa*) generally concerns purgation, its application proceeds preceded by emesis; therefore, because purgation is preceded by emesis, the preparations for emesis (*vamana-kalpa*) must be described first.

Among the preparations for emesis, the preparation of the *madana* fruit is described at the outset, as it is the best among emetic substances. Its superiority will be stated right here [in verse 1–2]: "They declare the *madana* fruits to be the very best among emetic substances because they are free from complications (*anapāyitva*).
Showing the meaning of the word *kalpa*, he says: "Then indeed" (*atha khalu*), and so forth.
Here, the word *atha* refers to what was previously introduced, while the word *khalu* serves to clarify.
"For the purpose of emesis and purgation" means for the sake of inducing vomiting and for the sake of inducing purging;

"of emetic and purgative substances" refers to *madana* fruits and the like, and *trivṛt* and the like; "by others" refers to fermented liquors such as *surā* and *sauvīraka*, and various types of *kovidāra* and so forth.
The qualification of the term "by others" is "by those characterized by the enjoyment of happiness.

Here, "those characterized by the enjoyment of happiness" refers to those for whom the enjoyment is for the sake of happiness; it does not refer to those whose enjoyment is happiness only for the moment. For if it were the latter, there would be no inclusion of such things as the *kovidāra* tree, which provide enjoyment that is not happiness at that very moment.

Without showing the connection of the word *kalpanārtham* with the verb, he explains it for the sake of making its meaning understood: "for the purpose of differentiation (*bhedārtham*) and for the purpose of division (*vibhāgārtham*). In this context, "for the purpose of differentiation" means for the purpose of differentiating the application of emetic and purgative substances; and those various applications are such as "three hundred and thirty formulations have been prepared for the fruits" (Sūtra 4), and so forth. "For the purpose of division" means for the purpose of dividing the substances that will be mentioned here, such as "two parts of the fruits of *pippalī* [are taken] with a decoction of *kovidāra*, etc. (Sūtra 5).

Having concluded the introduction, he states the subject at hand with the words "tadyogānām" (of those applications). The "procedure for action" (*kriyāvidhi*) refers to the method of performing the application of emetic and purgative substances—that is, the means consisting of fresh juices and so forth. The qualification of that procedure is "by easy means" (*sukhopāyasya*); that which has an easy purpose or an easy means is "easy of means," and [the phrase] "for the sake of its proper preparation" means for the sake of its correct instruction.

He analyzes the meaning of the terms *vamana* (emesis) and *virecana* (purgation): "In that regard," and so forth. That which effects the removal of *doṣas* through the mouth is the upper route (*ūrdhvabhāga*); that which effects the removal of *doṣas* through the anus is the lower route (*adhobhāga*).

Showing that even emesis (*vamana*) and purgation (*virecana*) are sometimes designated by the term "purgation" as stated in the *Ṣadvirecanaśatāśritīya*, he says: "Both [emesis and purgation]," and so forth.

This being the case, one should not raise the objection that the designation "purgation" would then also apply to non-unctuous enemas (*nirūha*), like emesis and purgation; for this term "purgation" applies specifically to emesis and purgation through both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), just like the word "lotus" (*paṅkaja*).

Now, having first shown the common effects—such as the liquefaction of the *doṣas*—produced by the application of qualities like heat (*uṣṇa*) and sharpness (*tīkṣṇa*) shared by both emetic and purgative substances, he describes their specific effects, namely emesis and purgation, which are produced by the application of specific attributes such as being composed of the nature of fire and air. He says: "In that regard, hot," and so forth;
"hot" means possessing a hot potency (*uṣṇavīrya*);
"by its own potency" means by its own inherent power (*svaprabhāva*).

"Following the channels" means following the channels that pervade the entire body; this following of the channels throughout the whole body is to be understood as occurring by way of its potency (*vīrya*), not directly.
Because it is fiery in nature, it causes them to "drip," meaning it causes them to melt, and it "cuts," meaning it causes them to be severed.

"Moving about," meaning going here and there; "not becoming attached," meaning not entering into attachment anywhere; "due to its atomic nature and its tendency to flow"—that is, because of its minuteness (*aṇutva*) and its state of being prone to flow (*pravaṇabhāva*). Here, "flowing" refers to the state of being oriented toward moving through the internal channels (*koṣṭha*), and "minuteness" refers to the capacity for movement within the atomic pathways (*aṇumārga*).
"Propelled by *udāna*" means impelled by the *udāna* wind;
"because it consists of fire and wind" means because it possesses an abundance of fire and wind;
"due to the power of its upward portion" means due to its specific power (*prabhāva*) consisting in its capacity to remove disorders located in the upper part of the body.
In this same way, its nature as consisting of water and earth should also be explained.
The phrase "on both sides" means that it is cast upward and downward;
"because of possessing the qualities of both" means because it consists of fire and air, and because it consists of water and earth, it exerts influence over the upper and lower portions.
The phrase "thus is the enumeration of characteristics" means that the essential nature of the substances for emesis and purgation has been stated by the subsequent text.

In this section, the fiery nature (*āgneyatva*) of emetic and purgative substances is established in a general sense by the statement, "because they are fiery, they cause liquefaction. Furthermore, their fiery nature is specifically established for emetic substances by the phrase, "because they consist of fire and air. Thus, since the fiery nature of emetic substances is established both generally and specifically, their fiery quality is preeminent. For purgative substances, however, because their connection to the fiery nature mentioned generally is qualified by the description of their specific qualities—which state they consist of water and earth—their fiery nature is inferior compared to that of emetic substances.

For instance, even in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā*, the fiery nature (*āgneyatva*) of both emesis and purgation is stated in the passage: "By means of its mobility, subtlety, sharpness, heat, and expansiveness, purgation and emesis remove the humors (*doṣas*), provided they are contrary to their natural state" (*Su.Ci.A.* 33).

Regarding what is stated here: if emesis causes upward movement by virtue of its inherent power (*prabhāva*) as an agent that eliminates the upper portion [of the doshas], then the description of the reason—"because it consists of the nature of fire and air"—is not appropriate. This is because an effect that cannot be accounted for through logical reasoning is designated as being produced by *prabhāva*. For it has been said: "Power (*prabhāva*) is said to be inconceivable" (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 26).

That is not so, because here, in the context of the action of emesis, the fact of being composed of air and fire is presented as the cause by virtue of being a quality of the specific potency (*prabhāva*) itself, and not as an independent cause of emesis. For if that were the case, then anything else that is composed of air and fire but lacks the potency to remove the humors located in the upper part of the body would also produce emesis—just as it might occur with a substance possessing a pungent taste (*kaṭuka-rasa*). Therefore, the description of the cause is based solely on the quality of the potency.
In this same manner, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding purgative substances should also be understood.

Now, by way of explaining the locations for the *kalpa* (pharmacological preparations), he makes a formal declaration regarding the six hundred applications of purgatives (*virecana*), preceded by a demonstration of their methods in a manner that is neither too concise nor too detailed—beginning with the words "In that regard, [using] *phala*" and ending with "we shall explain the six hundred formulations of purgatives.

Therein, by means of a specific textual arrangement (*vicchedapāṭha*) ending with *kṛtavedhana*, he demonstrates that those [drugs] are to be employed in the application of emetics (*vamana*), while those beginning with *śyāmā* are to be employed in the application of purgatives.

In this very section on emesis and purgation, many formulations of individual substances—such as *madanaphala* and others for emesis, and *śyāmā* and others for purgation—are described; it is not the case that each single substance alone acts as an emetic or a purgative. Anticipating the concern that by employing a small number of formulations, the administration of emetic and purgative compounds may become easy to grasp and the therapeutic objective may still be achieved, he says: "of various kinds," and so forth, up to "because of the possession of various potencies according to the state of the disease and other factors."

The meaning of this is as follows: Since medicinal substances such as the *madanaphala* fruit are found to arise in various places and times, possess various tastes (*rasa*), various potencies (*vīrya*), various post-digestive effects (*vipāka*), and various specific actions (*prabhāva*); and since medicinal substances used for their processing, such as the *kovidāra*, are likewise observed; and since human beings are seen to be diverse, distinguished by differences in body, humors (*doṣa*), constitution (*prakṛti*), age, strength, digestive fire (*agni*), preference (*bhakti*), suitability (*sātmya*), and the state of disease; therefore, no single substance is suitable for every instance of body, humor, and so forth, nor is it available at all times or in all places. Consequently, for a person characterized by these various differences in body, humor, and so forth, many substances prepared through numerous formulations can be employed according to their respective suitability and availability. Thus, the intention is that it is appropriate to present many substances, such as the *madana* and others, along with their many types of applications.

Because it is perceived—that is, apprehended—the body is manifold through distinctions such as being stout or thin; "inclination" refers to desire; by the word "condition" (*avasthā*), only the state of disease is to be understood here; and by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the constitution (*sattva*) and diet (*āhāra*) are included. He also states another purpose for demonstrating the extensive application of purgatives, beginning with the words "various," etc.
The meaning is that they are for the sake of pleasure, both at the time of application and subsequently, by virtue of their various kinds of fragrance, color, and taste.

Now, one might ask: "From what distinctions do the six hundred applications of the *madanaphala* and other substances arise, such that more applications are not mentioned? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Innumerable," and so forth.

"For the purpose of demonstrating the path for devising [additional] applications" means that this presentation of six hundred applications is intended for physicians capable of conceiving additional applications; by means of it, other applications may also be devised here. The reason why not all applications are mentioned in the text is precisely because they are innumerable and thus impossible to state in full.
The intention is that the statement of six hundred applications without excessive detail is for the sake of practical use by those of duller intellect.

For it has been stated elsewhere: “These [categories] are indeed sufficient for the practical discourse of those of small intellect, and for the knowledge of the unspoken meaning by the wise who are skilled in specific characteristics (*svālakṣaṇya*), inference (*anumāna*), and reasoning (*yukti*)” (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 4).
Now, demonstrating the excellence of the qualities of emetic and purgative substances through the perfection of their place of origin and other factors, he says: “Those,” and so forth.
The word "sampat" (perfection) is connected with each of the four [factors] beginning with place (*deśa*);
it refers to the vessel, the location for storing the medicine,
and the strength of the vigor— that is, the very excellence of one's energy.
Explaining the country and other factors correctly, he says: "In that regard, it is of three kinds," and so forth.

Here, some do not recite the textual passage concerning the characteristics of countries such as *jāṅgala*; however, they claim that this is not the work of the Sage (*anārṣa*) here, on the grounds that it was already recited in the section on the destruction of the countryside (*janapadoddhvaṃsanīya*).

By those, however, for whom the characteristics of the *jāṅgala* and other types of regions— which determine the destruction of the population— are not recited, this very text must indeed be recited here [in this context].
"According to the season" means in a region frequented by the cold season (*śiśira*) and so forth at the appropriate time.
The word "devoid" (virahita) is connected with each [term] beginning with "cemetery" (śmaśāna);
the word "house" (agāra) is connected with "sacrificial ground" (devayajana); and "assembly hall" (sabhā) refers to a place where people gather.
"Not ploughed with a plough" means unploughed (*aphālakṛṣṭe*).
Therein, by the phrase "those which have arisen in due season," the perfection of time is expressed; "arisen in due season" means they have appeared at their own proper time.
By the passage beginning with "upāgatasampūrṇa" and ending with "pratyagrāṇi," the perfection of qualities (*guṇasampad*) is expressed;
"pratyagrāṇi" means they are produced through the possession of complete qualities.
Then, by the passage beginning with "teṣāṃ śākhāpalāśam," he elaborates upon the perfection of time (*kālasampad*).
By the mention of "branches," the inclusion of bark and other parts is also implied.
The phrase "of withered and regrown leaves" is the correct division [of the compound].

By stating "roots in summer or in winter," it indicates the following rule: the roots of those plants that are fiery (*āgneya*) should be taken in summer, and the roots of those that are lunar (*saumya*) should be taken in winter. For it is said elsewhere: "One should collect lunar medicinal herbs during the lunar seasons, and fiery ones during the fiery seasons" (Suśruta Sūtrasthāna 36).
He states the procedure for taking the medicine: "maṅgala... and so forth.
He states the excellence of the vessel: "gṛhītvā... and so forth.
"Situated in a vessel possessing corresponding qualities" means that the vessel's possession of corresponding qualities is due precisely to its having qualities similar to the medicine;
thus, "properly covered" means they are well-sealed.

In brief, he states the substances for maceration and stirring for *madanaphala* and other drugs according to the distinctions of *vāta* and the other *doṣas*: "One should employ them according to the specific *doṣa," and so forth.

*Dhānyāmla* is fermented grain-water (*kāñjika*); *phalāmla* is sour fruit juice such as pomegranate juice; and in the phrase "for *śleṣman*," etc., the word *kaṣāya* is intended to mean a decoction of substances that alleviate *śleṣman*.
"Uddesa" means a brief statement;
in the phrase "substance, body, defects, suitability, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes constitution, strength, and other such factors.
With the words beginning "of emetic substances," he describes the method of administration while first demonstrating the preeminence of the *madanaphala* (emetic nut).
The phrase "due to its non-harmfulness" means that it causes fewer complications compared to other emetic substances.
The word "in between" (*antare*) refers to the middle; this middle should be understood as only a few days occurring between the summer and spring seasons.
In the month of Aśvayuja, during the *muhūrta* called Aśvinī, which is presided over by Mitra among the [deities] beginning with Śiva, Bhujaga, and Mitra— thus, in this *maitra* *muhūrta*,
[the rule applies] to the "palas" of the zodiacal signs (*rāśis*).

Those which possess the fragrance of honey and liquor are to be taken; this is what he shows by the phrase "phalapippalīḥ," meaning the seeds within the fruit of the *madana* tree that have the shape of long peppers (*pippalī*).
In the expression "tāsām" and so forth, the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*), due to its connection with a word expressing completion (*pūraṇavācaka-śabda*).
"Well-protected" means that the protective rites (*rakṣāvidhāna*) have been performed.

Regarding the phrase "having undergone oleation and sudation for two or three days," this prescribes the administration of sudation accompanied by oleation while the massage (*abhyaṅga*) is being performed for two or three days. There is no contradiction with the statement, "A person who has been oleated should be subjected to sudation for at least three days and at most seven days" (Sūtrasthāna, Aṣṭāṅgasaṅgraha 1), because that [latter] refers to the maximum duration of seven nights or three nights for oleation administered via oral intake (*pāna*).

This application of sudation combined with massage and oleation is performed starting from the day following the intake of oil; thus, including the day of rest after the oil intake, the practice of sudation along with massage and oleation completes a period of two or three days. Furthermore, regarding the day of rest after the oil intake, it is stated: "Having rested for one day, having eaten, one should drink [the emetic] for the purpose of vomiting" (Sūtra-sthāna 13). In the same way, here too, he prescribes food that causes the provocation of *kapha*, beginning with the words "on the next day, one should vomit," and so forth.
"Tomorrow" (*śvas*) means on the following day;
"having stayed overnight" (*vyuṣitam*) means having passed the night; "without food" (*nirannam*) is the word division.

By the phrase "not excessively unctuous" (*anatisnigdha*) and so forth, [the author] states that for a person who is not excessively unctuous, emesis should be induced on the very day of emesis, preceded by the drinking of a medicated gruel (*yavāgū*) containing a dose of ghee. Others, however, maintain that for one who is not excessively unctuous, the drinking of the gruel occurs on the preceding day, immediately after having drunk a dose of ghee. As it is said: "When the bodily humors (*doṣas*) of a person have been excited by various delicate foods, and he has been treated with oleation and sudation, emesis administered to him proceeds effectively."

Then, on the following day, in the forenoon at the common time, [one should administer] one of the emetic substances—decoction, paste, powder, or oil—as stated in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā* (Ci. 33): "As much as a fistful with the nails tucked inside," or "as much as one deems appropriate. By this, he indicates that the dosage is not fixed due to differences in strength, the humors (*doṣa*), and other factors.
The separate mention of *yaṣṭīmadhuka* among the group beginning with *kovidāra* is for the purpose of including *kovidāra* and the others in subsequent formulations while excluding *yaṣṭīmadhuka*.

*Kovidāra* is well-known by its own name; it flowers in autumn. *Karbudāra*, however, is *kāñcanāra*; it flowers in spring. *Nīpa* is *kadamba*; *vidula* is *vetasa*; *śaṇapuṣpī* is *ghaṇṭāravā*; *sadāpuṣpī* is *arkapuṣpikā*; *pratyakpuṣpī* is *apāmārga*.

Having let it stand overnight and then crushing it, [the text] states "purified" from the boiled decoction (*śṛtakāṣāya*); this indicates another alternative decoction. Alternatively, the rule for a cold decoction (*śītakāṣāya*) is stated here regarding the drinking of decoctions itself: "a full *śarāva*" is for the sake of auspiciousness, like a full pitcher;
"again and again" means that one should drink the decoction repeatedly as long as the onset of *pitta* does not occur.
It is also stated elsewhere: "Emesis is desired until bile appears; it is half [the dose] of purgation," and so forth.
To provide a remedy for the occurrence of weak force or inadequate action caused by an improper application of emesis, he says: "Of weak force," and so on.

Although the combination of honey and rock salt (*saindhava*) is not used in emetic formulations containing fragrant substances (*ghreya*) and the like, nevertheless, the word "in all" (*sarveṣu*) is intended to indicate the majority of cases.

However, the addition of honey to a hot decoction for emesis is not appropriate due to their incompatibility; for it has been stated: "Honey is incompatible with heat, or [heat] with one afflicted by heat" (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 27). Anticipating this objection, he provides the resolution with the words "nor is there an incompatibility of honey with heat," etc.;
by the phrase "due to the non-return of the undigested," he demonstrates that honey would indeed be incompatible when combined with heat while it is still undergoing digestion.

And because it eliminates the *doṣas*, honey—even though it is incompatible with heat—is desired when used in an emetic formulation; this demonstrates that there is no contradiction precisely because it eliminates the *doṣas*.
In the same way, the non-contradiction of honey with heat in the application of enemas (*basti*) should also be described.
By this, nine formulations are established using nine decoctions made from nine substances, such as liquorice (*yaṣṭīmadhu*) and others.

In the passage beginning with "two parts of *phalapippalī*," three parts of *phalapippalī* should be prepared. Of these, two parts should be strained twenty-one times through a decoction of *kovidāra* and the other [seven] drugs, six times each, according to the procedure for straining alkaline preparations (*kṣāraparisrāvaṇa*).
Furthermore, eight separate decoctions of the eight [drugs] starting with *kovidāra* should be employed for the individual straining process.

With that same decoction from which two parts of the *phalapippalī* have been strained, a dose equal in quantity to the *harītakī* and other ingredients is prepared using one-third part of the *phalapippalī* paste; by means of that very decoction, the dose-formulations are made. Thus, eight formulations of *phalapippalī* are specified according to the dose of the *harītakī* and others. Furthermore, the variation in dosage should be understood as being determined by the variation in the strength of the *doṣas* and other factors.

The phrase "the same as the previous" means that here, the procedure for oleation (*sneha*), sudation (*sveda*), consecration with mantras (*abhimantraṇa*), and so forth, must be performed just as in the preceding formulation.
In the same way, the meaning of the words in other instances should also be understood as before.
Milk prepared by the method of milking with *phalapippalī* is called *phalapippalīkṣīra*; this is one formulation (*yoga*).
"Tenā" means with milk prepared with *phalapippalī*;
"tajjasya" means of the curd produced from that milk and *phalapippalī*;
"uttarakam" means the supernatant liquid (*sara*).
Santānikā is the thickened layer on the surface of milk.
Fruits and the like: there are six, namely the fruits of jīmūtaka, ikṣvāku, dhāmārgava, kuṭaja, and kṛtavedhana.
These five formulations— consisting of the four milk-based formulations together with the ghee-based formulation— are to be stated in the summary of the chapter.
With the verse beginning "of *phalapippalī*s, with a decoction of the fruit and so forth," he describes one olfactory formulation (*ghreya-yoga*).
"By that which has the appearance of flower-dust" means by that which resembles the pollen of flowers; *haridrākṛśara* is a porridge made with turmeric.

"Distilled according to the procedure for *bhallātaka*" means that the fresh juice should be taken by following the method for extracting the oil from *bhallātaka* as described in the section on elixirs (*rasāyana*).
This is one formulation involving molasses (*phāṇita*).
"Or dried in the sun," and so forth, refers to another formulation involving a powder.

In the passage beginning with "twenty powders of *phalapippalī*," it should be understood that there are six applications of the medicinal wick (*varti*), as they are prepared according to the six different decoctions of the *phala* group and so forth.
In the preparation of the wick, its wick-like form should be achieved by cooking it with a decoction four times the quantity [of the powder].

In this case, as well as in the case of the linctuses (leha) and so forth, the addition of honey is appropriate according to the general rule; however, some do not approve of this because they consider it incompatible with the cooking process of the honey. Twenty linctuses are to be understood here, as they are prepared through twenty distinct decoctions of twenty substances beginning with *āragvadha* and *phalapippalī*.
Vṛkṣaka is *kuṭaja*; svādukaṇṭaka is *vikaṅkata*; śārṅgeṣṭā is *guñjā*; suṣavī is *kāravellaka*; dvīpikā is *hiṃsrā*, though others call it *kaṇṭakārī*.
(22) Regarding "in the case of fruit-pippalīs" and so forth, there are twenty types each of *utkārikās* and *modakas*.

*Coraka* is a fragrant substance well-known by its own name; *paripelava* is *kaivartamustaka*; *sthauṇeyaka* is *granthiparṇaka*; *pārāvatapadī* is *jyotiṣmatī*; and *aśokarohiṇī* is a creeper with leaves resembling those of the *aśoka*. Some others, reading "kaṭurohiṇī" here, omit *sthauṇeyaka* and complete the list of twenty with *apākīpādī*, which is known by its own name and prepared according to the method for *utkārikā* as described in the treatises on cookery (*sūdaśāstra*).
By the passage beginning with "with the juice of *phalapippalī*," one formulation for *śaṣkulī* and *apūpa* is given separately;

and by the passage beginning with "by this very method," fifteen formulations are produced because *śaṣkulī* and *apūpa* are prepared separately with the decoction of the fifteen substances beginning with *sumukha*.
Thus, by combining these, there are sixteen distinct formulations for *śaṣkulī* and *pūpa*. [The herbs are:
*poṭā*, *ikṣugandhā*; *daṇḍairaṇḍā*, the shrub known as *gundrā*, or *nala*. (24–25)

Likewise, by the phrase "badara-ṣāḍava" and so forth, ten preparations (yoga) made from jujube fruit (badara) are indicated; "badara-ṣāḍava" refers to a six-flavored preparation (ṣāḍava) made from jujube fruit.
He states synonyms for *madana* for the sake of its practical application: "Madana, karahāṭa," and so forth.
Regarding its "preparation" (*kalpanā*): this preparation belongs to that which has been explained through such synonyms;
and it should be understood that the mention of these synonyms is because they are highly esteemed due to being established in extensive medical practice.
In this way, the purpose for expressing synonyms elsewhere should also be described.

To refute the increase in the number [of recipes] beyond nine and so forth regarding the formulations of *madanaphala*, and for the sake of easy recollection, he states them in summary: "nine formulations," and so on.
And the meaning of this has been explained in its proper place [in verses 28–30].

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Chapter on Madana," in the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka-saṃhitā composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Section on Pharmaceutics (Kalpasthāna).
1 [Kalpasthāna, Chapter 2 (98 of 120)]:

Immediately following the Madana-kalpa, the Jīmūtaka-kalpa is now described; because it is non-toxic and because of its preeminence over substances such as Ikṣvāku and others, the Jīmūtaka is treated first.
In this way, to the extent that there is an excellence in the non-deviation of these [qualities], to that same extent the prior placement is to be understood.
Therefore, the connection of subsequent chapters should be understood as stated right here.
Just as in the case of the *madanaphala* [purgative] where oil, sudation, and so forth come first, the sequence here also is to be inferred through extension (*atideśa*).
By the statement "based on fruits and flowers," [the author] prohibits the administration of emetic therapy using the leaves, stalks, and so forth of the *jīmūta* plant;
the passage beginning with "and *garāgarī*" is an enumeration of synonyms.

Jīmūta and pītaghoṣaka (3) destroy the three doṣas when combined with substances that pacify vāta and so forth as appropriate; likewise, when prepared with substances that pacify vāta and the other doṣas, they become destroyers of the three doṣas.
Regarding the phrase "in hiccups and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes cough and other disorders arising from defects located in the chest.

Regarding the phrase "endowed with the aforementioned qualities and virtues," these should be understood as possessing qualities such as being seasonally appropriate and having full flavor, following the qualities described for *madana* fruits.
"Born in that land" means those produced in the auspicious regions described in the *Madanakalpa*;
"according to the rule" means those gathered according to the procedure described in the *Madanakalpa*.
"Milk and flowers" constitutes one formulation (*yoga*).
The second application begins with the word *nirvṛtte*:

"when [the fruit] has been produced," meaning as soon as the fruit has arisen; there, one should prepare milk with those fruits, and with that milk, one should prepare the *peyā* (thin gruel), starting with the word *romaśe*. This is the third [application].

Regarding "romaśe" (when the fruit has acquired hair): here too, the cream (*santānikā*) produced from milk processed with hairy fruit should be understood as the fourth formulation, beginning with "the supernatant of curd" (*dadhyuttara*). Here also, the whey (*sara*) produced from curds derived from milk processed with fruit in its state of having acquired hair should be understood as the fifth formulation, beginning with "when the milk has been boiled" (*śṛte payasi*).
"Dadhyamla" refers to curd that has reached the state of acidity;
"haritapāṇḍuka" refers to *jīmūtaka* fruits that have attained a greenish-yellow state;
and the phrase beginning with "of those who are aged" constitutes the sixth milk-preparation.

And these formulations, although not explicitly stated as being of the nature of milk due to their connection with milk, are to be included within the category of "the six milk-formulations" (*ṣaṭ kṣīre*) precisely because they are applications of milk (5–7).
By the words "having pressed" (*āsutya*) and so forth, one formulation of liquor (*madirā*) is described.

Regarding the term *āsutyā*, it means having allowed [the mixture] to stand overnight; in this particular yoga, only the ripe fruit of the *jīmūtaka* is intended. Likewise, in the subsequent yogas as well, it should be understood that only the ripe fruit is intended, based on the general rule stating, "the fully ripened fruit is to be taken.
Furthermore, twelve yogas are described according to the twelve varieties of decoction (*kaṣāya*), beginning with "two" and so forth.
"By that very method" refers to the procedure for accomplishment (*sādhanavidhi*) as stated in the *Madanaka-lpa*.

Alternatively, in the passage beginning with "or," there are seven formulations due to the different decoctions (*kaṣāya*) of seven substances starting with *āragvadha*. These seven substances—*āragvadha*, *vṛkṣaka*, *svādukaṇṭaka*, *pāṭhā*, *pāṭali*, *śārṅgeṣṭā*, and *mūrvā*—are those mentioned in the preceding chapter.
8–10: With the words "The measures (mātrās) should be... and so forth, he describes eight applications of the measures.

"Like the *phala* [fruit]" means that just as eight formulations of *mātrā-yoga* are described for the *madana* fruit, so too should they be prepared here; specifically, however, these should be made in the measure of a *kola*, but not in the proportions of the *harītakī* and other fruits as described for the *phala*—this is the meaning.
By the verse beginning with "jīvaka," four formulations are presented, distinguished by their preparation as drinks (*pāna*) or decoctions (*kaṣāya*).
With the words "tathā" and so forth, he states one formulation involving ghee.
The summary of the meaning, beginning with "six [are used] in milk," etc., has already been explained in its proper place (verses 14–15).

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Chapter on Jīmūtaka," in the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka-saṃhitā composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Kalpasthāna.
2 [Kalpasthāna, Chapter 3 (99 of 120)]:
Following the connection and other introductory matters stated in the preceding chapters, the *Ikṣvākukalpa* is now being described.
"I shall describe those for whom the Ikṣvāku ritual is praised"— this is how the passage should be construed.
The explanation of synonyms beginning with "lambā," etc.,
number three.
Thus it is intended; the conceptualization of Ikṣvāku is intended.
With the words "of the flowerless," etc., there is one milk-preparation (*kṣīrayoga*).
"Of the flowerless" means of that which has not yet produced flowers.

"A handful measured by a span" (*prādeśasammitam*) refers to the quantity of a fist made reaching as far as the base of the index finger (*pradeśinī*); thus, in this context, the word "handful" (*muṣṭi*) does not denote a leaf.
From the statement "boiled in a *prastha* of milk," one should prepare the milk by adding the aforementioned quantity of *ikṣvāku* to a *prastha* of milk and pouring in four times as much water.

By the words "in flowers, etc.," he describes four milk-based formulations; regarding *jīmūtaka*, it is said: "When its flower has withered and its fruit is ripe, a gruel (*peyā*) prepared with its milk should be drunk."

It has been stated [in the *Kāśyapa Saṃhitā* 2]: "In the case of a hairy [fruit], a stream of milk; in the case of a hairless one, curd as the superior [ingredient]. Accordingly, here too, the fourfold application (*yogacatuṣṭaya*) must be performed.
By the words beginning with "green," he describes the application for liquor (*surāyoga*).

For green and pale fruits of the *ikṣvāku* species, the application should be made like that of *jīmūtaka*; by the extension of the procedure for *jīmūtaka*, the method described in the text—"having fermented it in the scum of liquor (*surāmaṇḍa*), and having become exhilarated, one should drink what has flowed out"—is also applicable here.
By the words "phalasvarasa" and so forth, the sixth milk-preparation (kṣīrayoga) is described.
"Prepared with three times the milk" means prepared with three parts of milk; that [decoction] should be prepared with four parts of water.
Here, by the word "phala," the fruit of the Ikṣvāku plant is meant.
By the verse beginning with "jīrṇe," the seventh milk-preparation (kṣīrayoga) is described;
by the phrase "madhyoddhṛte" (meaning "when the middle portion has been extracted"),
and [the verse] beginning with "ajākṣīreṇa," the eighth milk-preparation is described.
By the phrase "with buttermilk" and so forth, the preparation with buttermilk is indicated;
"by that" refers to the interior of the *tumbī* fruit (5–10).
With the words beginning with "tumbī," he describes the application of fragrant substances.

"Accustomed to the pleasure of excellence of fragrance" means that his excellence of fragrance consists in being well-scented; by that excellence of fragrance, pleasure was "accustomed"—that is, practiced—by him. The sense is that, having merely smelled a garland whose flowers have been sprinkled with the juice of *ikṣvāku* fruit, he vomits, for he is unaccustomed to foul odors.
With the words "one should consume" and so forth, he describes one method for inducing vomiting.
*Phalamadhyam* means *ikṣvākuphalamadhyam*;

*ikṣvākuphalatailam* is oil prepared with the paste (*kalka*) of *ikṣvākuphala*. This is one and the same oil formulation as before, like that of *jīmūtaka*. Therefore, by following the procedure stated in the passage beginning with "likewise from *jīmūtaka* milk" (Ka.A. 2), one should prepare ghee here by substituting *ikṣvākuphala* for *jīmūtaka*.
With the words "fifty," etc., he describes six *vardhamānaka* yogas.
Starting from fifty, the quantity should be increased by tens using seeds of *Ikṣvāku* until one hundred is reached;
by this, six formulations are produced.
These should be soaked in the decoctions of any one of the six substances beginning with *madanaphala*, crushed, and drunk in their respective order.

Others, however, say that from ten seeds up to fifty seeds, [the amount] should be drunk according to the specific defects and other factors; in this regard, they state that the variation in the yoga arises solely from the different decoctions of *madana* and other such substances.
With the verse beginning "yaṣṭyāhva" and so forth, he describes nine formulations of decoctions (kaṣāya);
therein, *yaṣṭyāhva* (liquorice) is one, and *kovidāra* and the others are eight, as mentioned in the Madanaphala Kalpa.
With the words beginning with "kaṣāyaiḥ" (by decoctions), eight applications characterized by specific measures (*mātrā*) similar to those of *madanaphala* are described.

By the verse beginning with "bilva," one electuary (leha) is described; likewise, by the verse beginning with "kalpa," four electuaries are to be understood at the end. Thus, there are five electuaries.
An "añjali" consists of four *pala*s.

In this context, according to the statement, "From that point, water should be eightfold up to the amount of a *kuḍava*," eight *añjali*s of the decoction of *bilva* root should be added. Then, when reduced to one-fourth, two *kuḍava*s remain.
Phāṇita is half-boiled sugarcane juice;
in place of the phrase "and a fourth part of phāṇita," some read "and three parts of trikaṭuka";
"with ghee" means one part of ghee.
"Half-portioned" (*ardhāṃśikān*) means measuring half of one part each for the *mahājālinī* and the others;

*mahājālinī* is the yellow *koṣātakī*, and *kṛtavedhana* is a variety of *ghoṣaka* known as "jyotsnikā. With the words beginning "as long as it becomes fibrous" (*yāvat syāttantumad*), he describes the characteristics of the cooking of the linctus (*leha*). These characteristics should be understood to apply to other digestive (*pācanīya*) linctuses as well.
"It does not diminish nor does it expand;

one should drink a *pramathyā*," as stated in the treatment of diarrhea (*atīsāra-cikitsita*) following the verse beginning with "long pepper, ginger, coriander" (*pippalī nāgaraṃ dhānyam*, Ci.A.19). This means that one should drink a decoction prepared from any one of the *pramathyās* mentioned therein.
In place of the phrase "and a *pramathyā*," some read "and also a *mantha*" (*manthaṃ cāpi*).

Regarding the phrase "beginning with agnimantha," the four roots— agnimantha, syonāka, pāṭalā, and gambhārī— are each mentioned individually in the section on the *pañcamūla* (five roots) within the context of *rasāyana* (rejuvenation therapy),
verses 15–18.
"With groats," and so forth; this constitutes a single preparation for a stirred drink (mantha).
With the verse beginning "In cases of gulma, fever," etc., he describes a single medicinal formulation with *rasa*; the paste refers to the paste of *ikṣvāku* seeds.
The summary beginning with "payasyāṣṭau" has already been explained.
Here, regarding the fruits— such as the *madana* fruit and others—
although ghee was previously recited in the *Vardhamāna* [meter], it is nevertheless recited later here for the sake of conforming to the meter (*chandaḥ*).
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Chapter on Ikṣvāku," in the Kalpasthāna of the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka Saṃhitā, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Chapter 4 of Kalpasthāna (100 of 120)] Following the stated connection, the *dhāmārgava* procedure is now described.
In that context, the synonyms are stated beginning with "karkoṭakī" and so forth; *dhāmārgava* is [also] called *pītaghoṣaka*.
Regarding the phrase "those which are firm and heavy," the word "maces" (*gadāḥ*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
"By the rule" refers to the rule stated for taking medicine;
with the words "pravāla" and so forth, he states nine formulations.

"Pravālasvarasaḥ" means the fresh juice of coral; here, it should be understood that pills are to be prepared from decoctions of *kovidāra* and other such plants, and these are to be administered as a drink.

By the phrase "in flowers, etc. and so forth, the four milk-based applications prescribed according to the ritual procedure for *jīmūtaka* are indicated, and the fifth, the wine application, is extended by analogy; these are to be understood as those stated in the passage beginning with "The milk [is used] on its flower" (*Ka. A.* 2).
"As before" is connected with what precedes.

By the words beginning with "of those that are old and dry," he states the nine decoction-formulations (*kaṣāya-yoga*); likewise, by the words beginning with "of the *jāti* [flower]," he will state eleven decoction-formulations. Thus, the twenty decoction-formulations to be mentioned in the summary (*saṅgraha*) are completed.

Regarding the phrase "the fruit extracted from the seed-vessel" (*bījakaṇṭhoddhṛtaṃ phalam*): that in which seeds are bound is the "seed-vessel" (*bījakaṇṭha*), and that from which it has been extracted is the "extracted fruit.
Here, the lack of a fixed rule for the prior placement of terms should be understood as being like the compound *āhitāgni* and others.
And such a fruit should be filled with a decoction mixed with jaggery and allowed to steep overnight;

for it is stated in the *Jatūkarṇa*, in the chapter on *Dhāmārgava*: "Nine decoctions of *Kovidāra* and other plants, along with jaggery, should be kept overnight in *Dhāmārgava* fruits from which the seeds have been removed.

Furthermore, emesis is indeed beneficial for those suffering from abdominal tumors (*gulma*) depending on their condition; therefore, the demonstration of emesis here in the context of *gulma* is not contradictory.
By the words "one should give" (*dadyāt*) and so forth, a single yoga of food (*ekānnayoga*) is taught.
And there is one formulation by means of the combination of *dhāmārgava* with honey (verse 9).
With the words "by powders" (*cūrṇaiḥ*) and so forth, he describes one formulation for inhalation (*ghreya*).
In this context, the distinction between the *utpala* and other flowers is not intended to be expressed; for the *utpala*, there is only a single connection with fragrance.
Here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of the *saugandhika*, the lotus (*padma*), and others is meant; it should be understood that these have been infused with abundant powders.

By the passage beginning with "cūrṇīkṛtasya" (of the powdered [drug]) and ending with "goaśvaśakṛdrase" (in the juice of cow and horse dung), two formulations are stated; likewise, together with the ten formulations beginning with "pṛṣata," there are twelve formulations involving dung due to their connection with the dung-juice preparations.
The *pṛṣata* is a spotted deer; the *ṛṣya* has blue testicles; the *kuraṅga* has a restless gait; the *aśvatara* is a mule; and the *śvadaṃṣṭra* is a specific type of animal with four tusks. 11–12.
With the verse beginning "jīvaka," etc., he describes ten electuaries (*lehā*).

*Madhūlikā* is known here as *markaṭahasta*; in these electuaries (*lehāḥ*), the quantity of the powder of substances other than *dhāmārgava* and so forth should be equal [to that of the *madhūlikā*]; and the amount of honey and sugar should be such that the consistency of an electuary is achieved—this being in a case of *kapha* associated with the heat of *pitta*, meaning in *kapha* joined with *pitta* whose quality of heat is active. Others, however, say that by the term "heat of *pitta*" (*pittoṣman*), they mean the fever produced by the heat of *pitta*.
With the words beginning with "dhānya," he describes one formulation of a paste (*kalka-yoga*).
The decoction of coriander and *tumburu* itself is the coriander-*tumburu* soup;
for it is stated by Jatūkarṇa: "A paste with the juice of coriander and *tumburu* is an antidote to poison.
With the words "by species" (*jātyā*) and so forth, he states the eleven types of *kaṣāya* preparations.
*Jāti* is that which produces mental pleasure; others say it is *yūthikā*, while *vṛścīra* is white *punarnavā*.
Mahāsahā, kṣudrasahā, mudgaparṇī, māṣaparṇī, haimavatī, and vacā. 16–17.
With the words beginning "melted in that [ghee]," he describes one formulation involving ghee.
In the summary beginning with "pallave nava," the mention of the inverted order is for the sake of metrical requirements;
"ten and two" means twelve. (19–20)
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Dhāmārgava," in the Kalpasthāna of the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka-saṃhitā, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Kalpasthāna, Chapter 5 (101 of 120)]
Based on the aforementioned relationship, the naming [of the plant] as *vatsaka* is established (1–2).
To facilitate practical usage, he states the names of the *vatsaka* varieties and the distinction between male and female plants, beginning with "atha" and so forth.

In this context, although no distinction in qualities or difference in application has been set forth based on the division of male and female *vatsaka*, nevertheless, even when the female *vatsaka* possesses specific characteristics such as having flowers and fruits, it should be understood that both possess equal qualities for the purpose of ensuring that the cessation of disease occurs without distinction through either one. (3–6) "At the proper time" means at the appropriate time.
"Shushkāni" means dried after being cooked;
by the passage beginning with "teṣām antarnakham," he states nine formulations using decoctions (*kaṣāya*).

Although the formulation of honey (*kṣaudra*) and rock salt (*saindhava*) is prescribed generally for all emetic procedures, nevertheless, here, because of the statement "combined with salt and honey," the preeminence of rock salt is specifically indicated.
7-8. With the words "for eight days" and so forth, he describes five formulations of medicinal powders (*cūrṇa-yoga*).
By the words beginning with "with kṛśara," the application of kṛśara is stated.
And here, because it concerns the powder of *indrayava*, it is stated as such;
the summary verse beginning with "by decoctions" (*kaṣāyaiḥ*) has its meaning already explained.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, named "The Chapter on Vatsaka," in the Kalpasthāna of the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka-saṃhitā, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Kalpasthāna, Chapter 6 (102 of 120): Following the conclusion of the section on emetics, the section on *kṛtavedhana* is now described.
"In severe cases" means in cases of leprosy and other diseases that are exceedingly severe (verses 3–4).
By the phrase "milk and so forth," milk-based formulations are described.

He describes the four milk-preparations and the wine-preparation by extending the rules for the *jīmūtaka* procedure; by the word "milk" (*kṣīra*), there is the inclusion of milk-gruel (*kṣīrakṛtapeyā*), milk-scum (*kṣīrasantānikā*), and the whey of curd (*dadhyuttara*).
Although these are not in the form of milk, they are included under the term "milk" because they are milk derivatives, according to the statement: "Two [preparations] each in milk."

Regarding "of the flowers, etc.": for the flowers and so forth of *kṛtavedhana* (jīmūtaka), one should prepare milk and the other substances according to the procedure stated in the *Jīmūtaka-kalpa*: "When the flower has ripened into fruit, a gruel prepared with milk is to be drunk; when it is hairy, a continuous stream of milk; when it is not hairy, curdled milk.

As in these cases, liquor (*surā*) is also to be prepared as before—that is, just as milk and the other substances are to be prepared according to the procedure of the *Jīmūtaka-kalpa*, so too is the liquor to be prepared.
With the words "of those well-dried" and so forth, he describes nine decoction formulations.
"Like a fruit" means that just as the *madanaphala* is drunk with *yaṣṭīmadhuka* and other ingredients, so too should this [decoction] be drunk; such is the meaning.

Some read the following extract as indicating a linctus (leha) for the remaining nine decoction-formulations: "Having boiled its juice and strained it, one should have the linctus prepared," and so forth. This is consistent with the meaning, and it is stated in the *Jatūkarṇa*: "In this context, there are nine linctuses made from the decoctions of the ripened seeds, like those of the *madana* fruit.
By the words "separately" (*pṛthak*) and so on, he describes thirteen formulations of decoctions.
Thus, there are twenty-two decoctions (kaṣāya-yoga).
The thirteen beginning with *āragvadha*, mentioned in the Madanaphala-kalpa starting from "āragvadha-vṛkṣaka... (Ka.A.1) and ending with *guḍūcī*, are to be understood [as part of this group].

With the verse beginning "Śālmalī," etc., he describes ten *picchā* formulations. Those whose first ingredient is the root of *śālmalī* are called "those beginning with *śālmalī*"; these are the ten plants recited in the *Vimāna-sthāna*, ending with *śālmalī*, *śālmala*, *bhadraparṇī*, *elāparṇī*, *upodīkā*, *uddāla*, *dhanvana*, *rājādana*, and *upacitrā* (Vi. 8). Since these powders are prepared by means of *picchās*, they should be understood as ten formulations. *Śālmala* is a variety of *śālmalī*, or it may be *rohitaka*. *Bhadraparṇī* is *gambhārī*. *Elāparṇī* is *nāgabalā*, though others call it *ahiṃsrā*. *Rājādana* is *kṣīrikā*; *upacitrā* is *dantī*; and *gopī* is *sārivā*.

"Six preparations of wicks (*varti*) like those of the *phala*": by the passage beginning with "the powders of *phala-pippalī* as before" (*Ka.A.* 1), the preparation of wicks described in the *Madanaphala-kalpa* is indicated; likewise here, six preparations of wicks should be made from the powders of *kṛtavedhana*.

By the phrase "and likewise the ghee of the *phala* etc.," the meaning is that fresh butter (*navanīta*) raised from the milk processed with *kṛtavedhana* should be prepared with a decoction of the *phala* and other ingredients, just like the *madanaphala-ghṛta*.
Regarding "eight *kośātakas*" and so forth:

here, when a paste (*kalpa*) is to be prepared with one-fourth part decoction (*kvātha-pādika*), a full portion of *kṣveḍa* (aconite) should be added, while for the fruits and other ingredients, each should be half the portion of the *kṣveḍa*.
With the words "in decoctions" (*kaṣāyeṣu*) and so forth, he states seven meat-preparations.
"Equal" (*samam*) means the meat is equal in quantity to the *kośātakī*.
Here, by the words ending with "one should drink," the six types of meat broths are indicated; by the phrase "with fruits, etc.," one [preparation] using fruits and so forth is indicated;
by the phrase "equal to that, like pippalī," meat is to be used in equal measure with the fruits and other ingredients;
and because of the expression "in the same way," it is to be prepared with a decoction of *kośātakī*.
He describes one formulation involving sugarcane juice, beginning with "kṣveḍam," etc.
The meaning is that one should drink it prepared by mixing it with sugarcane juice (ikṣurasa). For it is stated in the *Jatūkarṇa*: "Kṣveḍa boiled in sugarcane juice.
This is the summary beginning with "two each in milk," and so forth.
"Two and two" makes four; 13–14.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Kṛtavedhana," in the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka-saṃhitā composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Kalpasthāna.
6 [Kalpasthāna, Chapter 7 (103 of 120)]:

Following the preparations for emesis, since the preparations for purgation must now be discussed, and because *trivṛt* is the foremost among purgative substances due to its ease of administration, the *trivṛt*-kalpa alone is described here.
*Śyāmā* is indeed not different from *trivṛt*; therefore, the pharmaceutical preparation (*kalpa*) of *śyāmā* and *trivṛt* is called the *śyāmā-trivṛt-kalpa*.

Although it should be stated that here *trivṛt* with reddish roots (*aruṇamūlā*) is superior, nevertheless, by placing *śyāmā* first in the title of this chapter, [the author] demonstrates the excellence of *śyāmā* due to its quality as a destroyer of impurities (*āśudoṣa*).

Furthermore, whatever formulations (*yoga*) are to be mentioned here should be administered using either the reddish-rooted variety, the dark variety (*śyāmā*), or both, after considering the relative strength or weakness of the humors (*doṣa*), the body, and other factors.
In the passage beginning with "1–2.
For purgation," etc., the term *trivṛnmūla* (the root of *trivṛt*) refers generally to the root of both the black-rooted (*śyāmamūlā*) and the red-rooted (*aruṇamūlā*) varieties.
"By means of synonyms," that is, by means of words that express synonyms; "now," and so forth.

It should be understood that through the addition of drugs that pacify *vāta*, the quality of being a *vāta*-destroyer becomes non-existent, while the existing quality of destroying *kapha* and *pitta* increases;
this is known as "specificity of preparation" (*kalpavaiśeṣya*), meaning a particular mode of formulation.
The phrase "remover of all diseases" (*sarvarogahara*) refers to the removal of diseases arising from all *doṣas*, whether individually or collectively.
He states the distinction between the two types of *trivṛt*: "The root, however, is of two kinds," and so forth.
"Superior" (*mukhyatara*) means that it is the best because it causes no complications specifically in the act of purgation (*virecana*).
Although delicate children are said to be unfit for purgation, it should nevertheless be understood that purgation is beneficial for them when administered according to the prescribed method.
With the words "it might cause delusion" and so forth, he describes the qualities and actions of *śyāmāmūla* (black-rooted turpeth);
