"it would emaciate" means it would cause a depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).

Although the general qualities of medicinal substances, such as being born in fertile soil and so forth, have already been described in the *Madanaka-lpa*, nevertheless, since specific characteristics such as "deep-rootedness" were not mentioned there, they are stated here; and in connection with that, the following is briefly said: "In fertile soil," and so forth;
"in the bright fortnight" (*śukle*) means during the bright half of the month.
"Following the profound" means having entered deeply;
"one should extract the embryo" means one should extract the bone of the root;
"one should deposit it" means one should deposit it according to the prescribed method for storing medicinal substances.

"Having stayed for one day on a diet of only *peyā* (thin gruel)" means that on the previous day he has subsisted solely on *peyā*. Although elsewhere, regarding the days preceding a purgation, the diet is similarly restricted by the statement, "Having eaten oily, warm food and rice with meat broth for three days" (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 13), nevertheless, because there is a specific rule for the day prior to the administration of *trivṛt* purgation, it should be understood that the consumption of *peyā* is intended here.

Furthermore, this very [diet], when prepared with unctuous and warm meat broth as prescribed by that [specific] statement, does not contradict the previously mentioned rule of eating oily, warm meat broth and rice.
With the nine substances beginning with "twelve finger-breadths" (*akṣamātra*) and so forth, he describes nine formulations using the nine [substances] such as *amlā* and others;
the phrase "of those two" refers to *śyāmā-trivṛt* and *aruṇa-trivṛt*.
And it has already been explained previously that there are applications for these two both combined and individually;
"with sour [liquid]" means with *kāñjika*.
With the words beginning "one by one" (*ekaikaṃ*), he describes twelve formulations using rock salt (*saindhava*) and other ingredients.
These twelve substances, beginning with rock salt, are to be understood as those mentioned in the section on groups of salts (*lavaṇaskandha*) in the *Rogabhiṣagjitīya* chapter (Vi. A. 8).

"Together with ginger" (*sanāgaraṃ*) means that the powder of each of these substances, including rock salt and the others, should be taken individually along with ginger, combined with twice the amount of *trivṛt* powder. This mixture is to be drunk.
14–16: With the verse beginning with "pippalī," he describes eighteen formulations for urine using various substances, starting with *pippalī*.
The formula beginning with "madhuka" and so forth is a single application,
and this is one of the two [formulas] mentioned in the *Saṅgraha* under the heading "two in yaṣṭī."
With the words beginning "jīvaka" (17), he describes fourteen formulations, as well as one called "yaṣṭyāhva";
this is one of the two mentioned in the summary [verse] regarding the two [formulations] for yaṣṭi.
Kṣīraśuklā, kṣīravidārī,
indrā, kokilākṣa, payasyā, and arkapuṣpī.
With the words beginning with "kṣīra" (milk), he states seven formulations for milk and other substances.
The *pīlu* fruit from the northern region.
With the verse beginning "lihyādvā madhu" (or one should lick honey), he describes eight electuaries; the first electuary begins with "lihyādvā," and the second begins with "ajagandhā."
The third linctus consists of *ajagandhā*, *ajamodā*, *śyāmā*, *trivṛt*, and so forth; here,
the linctus is prepared from equal parts of sugar and *trivṛt* powder, with the decoction added in a quantity one-quarter of the total.
Regarding the fourth [preparation] beginning with "sakṣaudrām" and so forth:

here, due to the greatness of the formulation (*yogamahiman*), there is a cooking process with honey (*kṣaudrapāka*), and the dosage of the *trivṛt* powder is reduced to one-quarter; this is because the inclusion of cinnamon bark (*tvak*), cardamom (*patra*), and other ingredients serves solely for the purpose of providing fragrance.

By the statement "purgation for the wealthy," he indicates that because of their delicacy, this [formulation] is intended for those who are not habituated to unctuous therapies; for the wealthy are generally delicate and unctuous.

Regarding the fifth [preparation], beginning with "one *kuḍava* part" and so forth, the measure of the *trivṛt* powder is not specified; according to the rule of addition, it should be made one-quarter of the electuary.
For those with depleted pitta or provoked pitta,
he mentions four sugar-based formulations beginning with "śarkarā" (sugar) among the electuaries (lehas), as they are appropriate by extension; here,
it should be understood that even the suppositories (vartī) and other such preparations are likewise made from sugar.
"By this method" means by means of the processing with the juices of sugarcane and other substances, as well as the addition of *trivṛt* powder;
"the sixth electuary" refers to the formula beginning with *pippalī* and *nāgara*;
"the middle" refers to the middle portion of the *amlakapittha* fruit.
"And whatever fruit is sour," such as the citron (*mātuluṅga*) and so forth—
"as before" indicates that the citrons and other such fruits possess the quality of being one *kuḍuba* in measure when their juices are expressed.

By means of the passage beginning with "beverages" (*pānakāni*) and so forth, he states the five formulations starting with the beverage (*pānaka*), in accordance with the principle of extended application (*atideśa*). "Rāga-ṣāḍava" refers to a *ṣāḍava* in which passion (*rāga*) predominates. "By this method" refers to the method previously stated for the electuary (*lehya*).
By the verse beginning with "bhṛṅgailābhyām," he first states the method of satiation (tarpaṇa-yoga); however, the second method of satiation will follow,
which involves *bhṛṅga* and *guḍatvak*.
And with those— namely sugar, *bhṛṅgarāja*, indigo, and *trivṛt*— there is fruit juice, specifically pomegranate juice (34–35).
With the words beginning with "śarkara," the first *modaka* is described;
and in that regard, according to the statement, "In a *modaka*, the jaggery (*guḍa*) is double [the amount]," they desire the jaggery and sugar to be double the quantity of the powder.

Although the formulation beginning with *trivṛcchāṇā* is recited here for the sake of the *modaka*, nevertheless, because this is taken specifically as a linctus (*leha*), it constitutes the eighth linctus (verses 37–39).
The second *modaka* begins with *viḍaṅga* (verse 40).
By the verse beginning with "vyoṣa," the third modaka is described;
this modaka is known as "Abhayādya" in another tantra.

Regarding *mukūlaka* and *dantī*: here, for each individual substance beginning with *mukūlaka*, there is a doubling [of the quantity] and so forth; and the honey should be of such a measure that the bolus (*modaka*) is formed.
Some here state that in this powder composed of *vyoṣa* and other ingredients, the *dantī* and subsequent drugs should be doubled.
The fourth [verse] begins with "pathyā" and so forth.
The fifth modaka is completed by the verse beginning with "trivṛddhaimavatī" (51–55);
"one should envelop" means one should dust it [with the powder].

With the passage beginning "trivṛtāṃ kauṭajam" and ending with "rūkṣāṇām api śasyate," he states that [these] formulations prescribed for the six seasons, including sātala and carmakaśā, are recommended at the end of the rainy season, in autumn.
Although purgation is prohibited during the winter season when cold winds are powerful, nevertheless, this purgation should be understood as prescribed for specific diseases.
Formulations applicable to all seasons, even when no specific season such as spring is mentioned, should be understood as such;
thus, the formulation beginning with *trivṛt* and *śyāmā* is also a formulation for all seasons.

The powder formulation beginning with *tryūṣaṇa* and so forth is the second [method] (verses 56–64). The nourishing (*tarpaṇa*) formulation beginning with *trivṛtā* and *triphalā* and so forth [is the third].
Thus, by means of the application of all seasons, there are two equal applications for satiation.
"Equal sourness" refers to the first ghee; "śyāmā," etc., is the second; "with the decoction of śyāmā and trivṛt," etc., is the third;
and by the phrase "prepared with," etc., he states one formulation involving milk.
When combined with both ghee and milk, or with either ghee or milk alone, there are four formulations consisting of ghee and milk.

By the passage beginning with "trivṛnmuṣṭīn" (66–68), the first type of *surā* is described; by the passage beginning with "surāṃ vā" (69), the second is described. Thus, there are two formulations of *surā*.
That [fermented liquor] in which the *kiṇva* (yeast/fermenting agent) is joined with the *trivṛt* formulation is so designated.
By the words beginning with "yavaiḥ" (69–71), he describes sauvīraka and tuṣodaka;
these two are preparations of kāñjika.
*Kulmāṣa* is the flour of slightly boiled barley;
*palle* refers to a heap of grain and the like;
"mixed with that powder" means mixed with the powder of *trivṛt*.
"In the same way," [referring to] those staying in the enclosure for six days (72–73);
"likewise," etc., [refers to] the ten-day period involving the preparation of *ṣāḍava* and other dishes.

The ten preparations beginning with *ṣāḍava*—namely, *badara-ṣāḍava*, *rāga-leha*, *modaka*, *utkārikā*, *tarpaṇa*, *śāka*, *māṃsa-rasa*, *yūṣa*, and *madya*—are those mentioned in the *Madanakalpa* section [of the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya] by the passage beginning "of *badara-ṣāḍava*, *rāga-leha*... (Ka.A.1).

Having now described one hundred and ten formulations, he states the applications for purgation together with the three preparatory procedures (*kṛtyatraya*) in order to prevent vomiting, beginning with the verse starting "tvakkeśara... and so forth.
The summary beginning with "75–76.
With one sour [substance], etc. has a clear meaning.
Regarding the two [formulas] for *yaṣṭi*, there is one starting with "yaṣṭyāhvaṃ vidhinā" and another starting with "madhuka," etc., among the [formulas] for *jīvaka* and so forth.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Formulation of Śyāmā Trivṛt," in the Kalpasthāna of the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka-saṃhitā, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta. 7–80.

[Kalpasthāna, Chapter 8 (104 of 120)] Immediately following the *śyāmā-trivṛt* procedure, the *caturaṅgula* procedure is now described, due to its commonality with the former in being a mild purgative.
He states synonyms for the sake of common usage— beginning with "āragvadha" and so forth.
It is "especially wholesome" (adhikaṃ pathya), meaning it is particularly beneficial when employed as a purgative in cases such as fever and other ailments.
"At the time of fruition" (phalakāle) means at the appropriate time for their fruition;
"of them" (teṣām) refers to those fruits.
"Bhāra" is an indicator for abundant wealth;
"majjānam" refers to the marrow of fruit.
The first formulation, beginning with "drākṣā" and so forth,
by the phrase "in a child from four years of age up to twelve," prohibits the medicinal application of this formula for those under four years of age and for those over twelve years of age.
The second [method] is with the scum of *surā* liquor;
or else, the third is with *kola-sīdhu*.
The three other formulations ending with "or with sauvīraka" are clear: kola-sīdhu is a fermented liquor made from jujube fruits (kola).
"Or one should likewise drink the paste of *majjan* with the decoction of *trivṛt*"; this is the seventh [formula].
By the words "likewise" (*tathā*) and so forth, the eighth is indicated.
This pair of paste and decoction is indeed stated by Jatūkarṇa as well: "Two [preparations] with the decoctions of *trivṛt* and *bilva*, along with honey and salt."
Therefore, the alternative reading here is not authoritative;
and he will include it in the *Saṅgraha*: "And [the fruits] of the *trivṛt* and the *bilvaka* in the *kaṣāya*.
The ninth is the linctus (leha) beginning with "with decoction" (kaṣāyeṇa), etc.;
the first ghee begins with "caturaṅgulā" (Caturangula), etc.
Regarding "of the marrow," this refers to four finger-breadths of marrow;
by the words "that very [substance]" and so forth, the second type of clarified butter is described.
"By means of the *śyāmā* and others" refers to the nine [drugs] recited in the *Madanakalpa*, beginning with "The *śyāmā*, *trivṛt*, *dantī*... (Ka.A.1).
With the words beginning with "dantī," he describes the *ariṣṭa* formulation;
the connection is "one handful of jaggery" (*guḍasya cāñjalim*). "Remaining for half a month" (*māsārdhamāsastham*) means remaining for one and a half months.
By the verse beginning with "yasya yat," he prescribes other successive methods not previously mentioned;
for indeed, a purgative formulation becomes agreeable when it is pleasant to the heart.
The terms "beverage" (*pāna*) and "food" (*anna*), as well as "delicious" (*hṛdya*) and so forth, are each connected [to the preceding].
The inclusion of "grapes" (*drākṣā*) and so on is evident.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Pharmaceutics of Caturaṅgula," in the Kalpasthāna of the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka-saṃhitā, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta. 17–18.
[Kalpasthāna, Chapter 9 (105 of 120):
Because the Tilvaka chapter does not deviate from the Caturaṅgula chapter, the Tilvaka chapter is expounded immediately after the Caturaṅgula chapter.
"Deprived of the inner bark" means that the inner bark of the *tilvaka* tree is hard; for that reason, it is to be removed.

By the statement "one should let it drip," it should be understood that one should cause it to flow twenty-one times with a liquid six times its weight, because such a method of dripping is seen in the *Madanaphala-kalpa*. Furthermore, the procedure for the infusion (*bhāvanā*) has been explained continuously [in the preceding text].
By the passage beginning with "curd-whey" (*dadhimaṇḍa*) and ending with "one should drink" (*pibet*), five formulations are presented.
One formulation consists of a specific type of *sauvīraka* (sour gruel) beginning with *meṣaśṛṅgī*; another is roasted barley grown in arid land (*maruja*).
With the words beginning with "surām," he describes a formulation involving *surā*;
with the words beginning with "dantī," he describes one *ariṣṭa* formulation.
One āḍhaka each of dantī and citraka should be boiled separately in one droṇa of water; the powder of tilvaka is to be added as an after-paste (āvāpa).
With the words beginning "kampillaka," he describes the application of kampillaka; kampillaka is guṇḍārocanikā.
"Mātrām" means the quantity of *tilvaka* powder— [this is] number ten.
By the words "caturaṅgula" and so forth, the first electuary is described;
according to the procedure stated in the "Caturaṅgulakalpa" as in the verse beginning with "or else with its decoction" (Ka.A.
8), one should prepare this electuary by cooking the powder of trivṛt mixed with jaggery in a decoction of tilvaka.
The second electuary begins with "of triphalā" (triphalāyāḥ),
and the third begins with "of tilvaka" (tilvakasya).
By the phrase "eight times eight" and so forth, clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is first [specified]; "with the nails" means with the nails still present.
Here, because *lodhra*—which is included among the *trivṛt* group—is the principal substance, its portion becomes double.
For it is stated in the *Jatūkarṇa*: "The decoction of *lodhra* is double [the amount] of *trivṛt* and the other ingredients.

If, however, they were in equal proportions, what would be the distinction of this as a *lodhra*-application? Therefore, the explanation as it has been given is correct; furthermore, the salt here should also be exactly one *pala*.
"Beginning with *lodhra*," and so forth, refers to the second ghee;
by the passage beginning with "four-fingered" (*caturaṅgula*), two further ghees are extended by analogy. Thus, there are four formulations using ghee.

Regarding the *caturaṅgula* ghee, it should be understood as described by the passage beginning with "prepared from *caturaṅgula*" (Ka.A. 8), and likewise by the passage beginning with "that same [preparation] of the ten roots" (Ka.A. 8). Similarly, according to the procedure for *caturaṅgula*, there are two types of *lodhra* ghee using *lodhra* and other ingredients (verses 14–16).
The summary of the five [types of ghee] prepared with curd and so forth is clear.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Tilvaka," in the *Kalpasthāna* of the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā*, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Chapter 10 of Kalpasthāna (106 of 120):

Following the *tilvaka-kalpa*, which describes sixteen formulations, the *sudhā-kalpa*—which describes twenty formulations—is now set forth according to the sequence of describing formulations in increasing numerical order. Immediately after this, following the same sequence of describing an even greater number, the *saptalā-śaṅkhinī-kalpa*—which describes thirty-nine formulations—will be described.
Regarding "of purgatives," this refers to purgative substances;
"difficult complication" means that which produces complications difficult to treat;
"therefore" means because of their extreme sharpness and because of the difficulty of their complications.

Regarding the phrase "when there is an alternative route for the path": when another preliminary route exists, *sudhā* (ghee) should not be employed; the meaning is that *sudhā* should only be employed when no other alternative route is possible. In the passage beginning with "pāṇḍuroga" (jaundice), the term *madhumeha* refers specifically to the *prameha* (urinary disorders) in general. However, a specific type of *vātika-madhumeha* is indeed incurable; therefore, the instruction for purgation (*virecana*) directed toward that [incurable type] would be entirely useless. Furthermore, it has already been established in the chapter on the treatment of *prameha* that the term *madhumeha* applies to all types of *prameha* alike.
In that [condition] where the mind is deranged by the increase of the humors— that is, in insanity characterized by a mind deranged by the humors—
one who is "possessed of life" means one who is strong.
"Pre-eminent with many thorns" means that it is superior to the large tree with few thorns because it is not excessively sharp;
"those two" refers to the large trees with few thorns and many thorns.

Although it is stated in the *Madanakaḷpa* that "in autumn, [one should collect] bark, tubers, and milks" (*Ka.A.* 1), nevertheless, the mention of milk here at the end of the cold season (*śiśirānta*) should be understood as an exception (*apavāda*).
The remaining days of the cold season are the "end of the cold season" (*śiśirāntāḥ*), namely the 7th, 8th, and 9th days.

Regarding the phrase "of the *bilva* group, etc.": one should dry the milky latex of *sudhā*—which is contained in a vessel placed over charcoal—over the embers using a decoction of any one of the five roots beginning with *bilva*, making it solid through this drying process. Then, pills the size of a jujube fruit (*kola*) should be prepared, which are to be drunk with any one of the liquids beginning with *sauvīraka*.

Thus, there are seven formulations based on the different types of *sauvīraka* and so forth. Furthermore, in this context, a distinction based on the different decoctions of the *bilva* group is not intended.
With the verse beginning with "sātalām," etc., he states two formulations: a ghee for the pacification of vāta and a variety of meat broth.

Although *sātalā* is already included by the mention of *carmakaśā*, *śyāmā*, and so forth, its separate mention here is for the purpose of declaring the preeminence of even a single *sātalā* when used in conjunction with *sudhā*.
With the verse beginning "tryūṣaṇam," etc., he describes a preparation for a refreshing drink;
"guḍapānakam" means a refreshing drink prepared with jaggery.

With the words beginning with "trivṛtā," he describes the application of the fragrant substance: "having prepared the *rajanī* in cow's urine" means having placed the *rajanī* in cow's urine; "covering the cloth itself" means covering the cloth that has been consecrated according to the prescribed ritual procedure.
With the words beginning with "śyāmā," he describes the method of medicinal electuaries (*lehayoga*).
By the phrase "with the proper measure" (*mātrayā*), he means by a dose that is not excessive.
With the words "one should cause [the patient] to drink" (pāyayet) and so forth, [the author] states three formulations separately using vegetable broth, meat broth, and ghee.
By [the verse] beginning with "cultivated impermanence" (bhāvitānitya), there is the preparation of dried fish and meat;
by [the verse] beginning with "with milk" (kṣīreṇa), there is one [preparation of] ghee.
With the words beginning with "or ghee," he will state one [method];

by the statement "with *āmalaka*s, as in the case of *caturaṅgula*," he extends the procedure for that which was taught in the *Caturaṅgulakalpa*—beginning with "or from the prepared *caturaṅgula*" (Ka.A. 8)—by means of the juice of *āmalaka*.
Regarding the phrase "or one should prepare *surā* in milk," one should prepare the *surā* according to the procedure beginning with "steeped in the milk of the *snuhī* tree."

Regarding the instruction "one should cook ghee as before," the term "as before" refers by proximity specifically to the procedure previously prescribed in the *tilvaka-kalpa* by the passage beginning with "with a paste of *lodhra*" (Ka.A.
9). The compendium beginning with "sauvīraka" and so forth has already been explained.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Sudhā," in the Kalpasthāna of the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka-saṃhitā, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta. 10.21–22.

[Kalpasthāna, Chapter 11 (107 of 120)] Following the very connection established in the preceding chapter, the *Saptalā-śaṅkhinī-kalpa* is now described. In this chapter, the formulations (*yoga*) that are taught are prepared using either *saptalā*, or *śaṅkhinī*, or both together, just like the formulations involving *śyāmā-trivṛt*.
1–3: Regarding "te gulma" and so forth,
"te" refers to *saptalā* and *śaṅkhinī*.

With the passage beginning "four to five finger-breadths" (*akṣamātra*), there are sixteen formulations of *kalka* (pulp) combined with clear wine (*prasannā*) and salt in the decoctions (*kaṣāya*) of *priyāla* and other plants.

Although *maireya* and sugarcane wine (*aikṣava*) are not technically decoctions, they must nevertheless be classified as such because they are included among the many decoctions; thus, they are designated by the summary statement: "the decoctions are sixteen."
By the word *kaṣāya*, a paste-decoction (*kalkakaṣāya*) is intended;
by the words *karkandhu*, *kola*, and *badara*, the three types of jujube fruits are included.
With the words beginning "oil" (*tailam*), the first oil formulation is presented;
in the phrase "with half a part of *trivṛt* and *śyāmā*," the paste of *trivṛt* and *śyāmā* is to be administered along with half a part each of the pastes of *saptalā* and *śaṅkhinī*.
With the words beginning "śaṅkhinī," he describes five oil formulations; thus, there are six oil formulations in total.
Regarding the phrase "that oil is pressed out": one should mix the powder of *śaṅkhinī* and the powder of sesame seeds with a decoction of *harītakī*, press it to extract the oil, and drink that oil.
By the statement "this procedure applies to *atasī* and the others," the author prescribes the use of *atasī* and other seeds in place of sesame seeds.
Regarding "śaṅkhinīsaptalā" and so forth: first is the ghee;

then, by means of a paste (*kalka*) of two substances beginning with *dantī* and *dravantī*, and with half the amount of paste of *saptalā* and *śaṅkhinī*, there is another preparation cooked like the previous ghee—thus there are five ghee formulations (*pañcaghṛtayoga*).
Furthermore, *dravantī* is a variety of *dantī*.
Ajaśṛṅgī, viṣāṇikā, kṣīriṇī, dugdhikā,
masūravidalā, and śyāmalatā [are synonyms].

"With a paste consisting of half a part each of *pratyakparṇī* and *mūṣikaparṇī*" refers to the seventh ghee, prepared with a paste of half a part each from the two groups beginning with *dantī* and from *śaṅkhinī* and *saptalā*; "with a paste of *trivṛt*" refers to the eighth ghee.
In this context, however, because they are the subjects under discussion, a double decoction of *saptalā* and *śaṅkhinī* is prescribed, just as in the case of *lodhra*;

that is, like the *lodhra*-kalpa. Just as three electuaries (*leha*) are described in the *lodhra*-kalpa beginning with "by the method of *caturaṅgula*" (Ka.A. 9), by that [analogy], the application of *saptalā* and *śaṅkhinī* should be made in place of *lodhra*, and likewise the application of wine (*surā*) and the application of *kampilla* should be done as in the *lodhra*-kalpa; here too, the addition of *saptalā* and *śaṅkhinī* must be made in place of *lodhra*.
With the verse beginning "Of *dantī* and *dravantī*," etc., he describes four types of compounding (*sandhāna*).

These four compounds are included in the summary by the statement "five [are] in wine" (*pañca madye*), as they are equivalent to the previously mentioned formulation of wine (*surā-yoga*). Furthermore, it should be understood that substances such as *sauvīraka* are designated here by the term "wine" (*madya*) because they share the common quality of being fermented (*āsūtatva*).

Regarding the phrase "by the method of *dantī* and *dravantī*": by looking ahead to what follows, it extends here the procedure for the *sauvīraka* and *tuṣodaka* which are to be mentioned in the chapter on *dantī* and *dravantī*.

There, it says, "with the decoction of *ajagandhā*, [one prepares] *sauvīraka* and *tuṣodaka*" (Ka.A. 12); therefore, here too, *sauvīraka* and *tuṣodaka* must be prepared from *saptalā* and *śaṅkhinī* combined with the decoction of *ajagandhā*.
In this case, it says: "Likewise, with the decoction of *dantī* and *dravantī* together with *ajagandhā*..."

By the statement, "The gauḍa [ariṣṭa] should be prepared with ajaśṛṅgī; indeed, that is a pleasant purgative" (Ka. A. 12), the procedure for the gauḍāriṣṭa mentioned there is extended by analogy to the one described in the *dantīdravantīkalpa*. The summary beginning with "the decoctions" (*kaṣāyāḥ*) has thus been explained.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Chapter on Saptalā and Śaṅkhinī," in the Kalpasthāna of the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka-saṃhitā, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta. 18–19.
[Chapter 12 of Kalpasthāna (108 of 120):
By way of remainder, the pharmaceutical preparations of *dantī* and *dravantī* are now described.
He states the synonyms for those two: "the teeth," and so forth;
"firm" means being of essential substance.

"Bahalāni" means having thick layers; "hastidantaprakārāṇi" means having the appearance of elephant tusks; "antapūrvopacitāni" means accumulated from the edges inward; and "śyāvatāmrāṇi" means dark-brown and copper-colored respectively—namely, the teeth of *dantī* are dark-brown and those of *dravantī* are copper-colored.

"One should steam them between clay and *kuśa* grass" means that after coating them with a paste of *pippalī* and *madhuka*, wrapping them with *kuśa* grass, and then smearing them with clay, one should subject them to steaming.
Regarding the result of drying them by fire, sun, and steaming, it says: "For fire and the sun destroy their state of being opened."

The quality of these roots of *dantī* and *dravantī*, characterized by their laxative action, has been neutralized by fire and the sun through the processes of sweating and drying; thus, the intention is that the roots of *dantī* and *dravantī* do not cause excessive morbidity.
Their qualities are described by the passage beginning with "sharp and hot" (*tīkṣṇoṣṇāni*).
"The two defects" refers to bile (*pitta*) and phlegm (*śleṣman*).
With the words beginning with "curd" (*dadhi*), he describes seven applications using seven substances.
The word *śīdhu* is connected separately with each of the four [substances], beginning with *priyāla*;
the term *abhiklinna* means "soaked.
In the phrase *gomṛgājarasaiḥ*, the expression *piṇḍamakṣasamaṃ tayoḥ* is also understood to follow.
Here too, there are three formulations with the three juices of cow and the other animals;
by the words "of those two," etc., he describes three unctuous preparations:

one should cook ghee with the paste and decoction of these two, along with an equal portion of *daśamūla* juice, for conditions such as erysipelas (*visarpa*); oil, however, is used as before for conditions such as urinary disorders (*meha*); and the fourfold unctuous preparation (*catuḥsneha*) is used for conditions such as the retention of feces, semen, and flatus.
By the verse beginning with "rase," one electuary (leha) is described;
by the verse beginning with "vātatarṣe," the second is described;
and by the phrase "sa evājagandhayā," the author indicates a specific modification of the previously mentioned electuary, namely the substitution of *ajagandhā* for *ajaśṛṅgī*.
By the words "dantī" and so forth, the third electuary is described;
by the phrase "in parts," meaning the taking of each part individually,
through these applications ending thus, the first group of sixteen is formed.
In the verse beginning with "rase ca" (7-14), the word "evam" (thus) extends by analogy (*atideśa*) the three previously mentioned modes of administration (*lehana*);
the fourth [mode], beginning with "tayoh," refers to those two—the roots of *dantī* and *dravantī*. "Tayoh" means of the two roots of *dantī* and *dravantī*.
Regarding "asṛṣṭe" (when not emitted), it means when [the wound] is bound;
"pāṭayitvā" (having split) and so forth refers to the fifth [method]:
having smeared the interior with a paste (*kalka*)—specifically a paste of *dantī* and *dravantī*—inside the split sugarcane stalk.
By the verse beginning with "mūlaṃ dantī," he describes eight prepared and unprepared meat soups (*rasa*).

Here, the eight [birds] such as the *lāva*, *vartīraka*, and so forth, are mentioned in the following passage: "The *lāva*, the *vartīraka*, the *vārtīka*, along with the *kapiñjala*, the *cakora*, the *upacakra*, the *kakubha*, and the *raktacarmaka*" (Sūtra-sthāna 27). From the individual combination of these, there are eight soups.
With the words "tayor vā api" and so forth, he describes the combination of gruel and meat broth, as well as the combination of black gram soup;
thus, by combining these liquids with the previous formulations, there would be a second group of sixteen [formulations].

With the words "from its decoction" (*tatkaṣāyāt*) and so forth, he describes the formulation of *utkārikā* and the formulation of *modaka*. Regarding "from its decoction," even in the preparation of the *modaka*, the procedure beginning with "three parts from its decoction" is to be followed.
The third [category] consists of intoxicants processed with the three astringent decoctions (kaṣāya); the fourth is the preparation of edible substances, beginning with "dantī" and so forth;
and the fifth begins with "dantī, dravantī, marica," and so on.
"Hemadugdhā" means *svarṇakṣīrī*;
the connection is that one should drink [the preparation] ending with "cūrṇitam" (powdered),
as described in the sixth [verse] beginning with "palam."
And twenty *harītakī* fruits by measure of their form— this formulation, beginning with two *pala* of *dantī*, is known as "Agastyamodaka" in another tantra; it is the seventh.
In this context, a decoction should be prepared from two palas of dantī and half a prastha of drākṣā;
"dantī-kalkam" and so forth is the eighth [formula],
while "śyāmā" and so forth is the ninth.
"Gauḍa" means made from molasses; in the phrase "lipte," the word "ghaṭe" (in a jar) is to be understood as the ellipsis;
likewise, the tenth [type] begins with "dantīdravantyośca" and so forth.
By the word "tathā" (likewise), the application of the plaster made from pippalī and other ingredients mentioned in the previous formulation is extended [to this case].
The eleventh [formulation] begins with "or with ajaśṛṅgī," etc.;
the connection is that an ariṣṭa prepared with molasses (*gauḍa*) should be made using the decoction (*kaṣāya*) of *ajaśṛṅgī*, *dantī*, and *dravantī*.
The twelfth [recipe] begins with "taccūrṇa" (their powder) and so forth;

here, the meaning of the sentence is that one should prepare a liquor (*madirā*) arising from wine (*surodbhavā*), which is made by first employing a fermenting agent (*kiṇva*) using the powder and decoction of those two—*dantī* and *dravantī*—as well as *māṣa*-water. With the words beginning with "ajagandhā," he states two formulations.

In that context, with the decoction of *ajagandhā* and *dantī* and *dravantī*, one should prepare *surā*, *sauvīraka*, and *tuṣodaka*; by the words "another two formulations," he states another pair of methods.

Regarding the phrase "like *lodhra* for those two": just as *surā* was described in the *lodhra*-kalpas by the statement "wine with a *lodhra* decoction" and so forth, and likewise the *kampillaka* formulation was stated by "with a *kampillaka* decoction" (Ka.A. 9), in the same way, by substituting *lodhra* with these two—*dantī* and *dravantī*—the *surā* formulation should be prepared according to the very same procedure for *sauvīraka* and *tuṣodaka*.
Thus ends the third sixteen-verse section (20–35).
The summary of the meaning of this chapter, beginning with the word "danti," is indeed clear.
The construction is as follows: regarding the various types of formulations (yoga) mentioned for the diseases caused by defects in devotion (bhakti-doṣa), three groups of sixteen have been declared;
[these concern] devotion (bhakti) and desire (icchā). (36–40)
Now he states the summary of the contents of the section on the *kalpa* (pharmacology), beginning with "three hundred" and so forth:
"three hundred and fifty-five" means three hundred plus fifty-five formulations.
"Relying primarily" means relying upon fifteen substances—starting from *madanaphala* and ending with *dravantī*—by way of designating them as the primary formulations.

Now, since other substances such as wine (surā) and so forth are also present in these formulations for emesis and the like, he explains why these formulations are designated specifically by their reliance on *madanaphala* and the others: "Because... and so forth.

Although these formulations are prepared using a combination of *madana* and the like along with wine and the like, nevertheless, because the fruits (*phala*) and other primary ingredients are predominant, they are designated as "formulations of the fruits" and so on, rather than as "formulations of wine" and so forth.
"Being subordinate" means being non-primary.

He states the reason for the non-primary status of wine and the other substances: "for they follow those [qualities]," meaning that wine and the others follow intoxication and so forth by way of conforming to effects such as vomiting and purging, and by way of not resisting them.

Now, one might object: "Let those factors which are compatible with emetics (*madanādi*) be considered qualities; however, what about those that are contrary, such as the pungency of *dantī* or the meat-broths and so forth? Likewise, how can cardamom (*elā*) and other such items—which, due to their pleasant aroma, are opposed to vomiting—be qualities for emetics? To this he replies: "Even that which possesses contrary potency (*viruddhavīrya*) does not obstruct these primary [substances].
The meaning is that even though it has a contrary potency, it is a quality because it does not obstruct the intended effect, namely purgation (*virecana*).

For if a substance with contrary potency (*viruddhavīrya*) were not present as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*), it would obstruct the effect of substances such as *madana*; the point is that even when contrary, its failure to obstruct the effect necessarily means it is non-injurious. Having thus stated the assistance in the form of non-obstruction of the effect by the contrary, he states the effect of one with equal potency: "excessive," etc.;
the meaning is that when a substance of equal potency is combined, the capacity for action becomes excessive.

45. Now, substances of equal potency (vīrya) act by increasing the capacity for action; therefore, let there be their combination. But for what purpose are combinations of substances with contrary potencies made? To this he says: "For the sake of attaining desired color and so forth" (iṣṭetyādi). Thus, the application of substances with contrary potencies, such as the madana fruit and others, as well as the application of substances with contrary potencies against contrary diseases, is appropriate (yaugika) in specific cases of vomiting, purgation, or the removal of particular ailments. This is the meaning.

Now he describes the procedure regarding the excellence of potency and other qualities of madanaphala and the rest, beginning with "Furthermore, of these... and ending with "or with those of equal potency.
This means [administering them] with fresh juices or decoctions that possess an equal potency.
He states the effect of the conjunction of potencies that are equal or unequal, beginning with the words "Even of the small," and so forth.

In that regard, even a small quantity [of a substance] attains great efficacy through combination with substances of similar potency (*vīrya*); likewise, even a large quantity may have its action diminished through combination with substances of opposing potency. This reduction of action in a large quantity of medicine is performed for purposes such as filling the digestive tract (*koṣṭha*) when it is blazing with heat. Therefore, this is not purposeless.

Furthermore, the great efficacy of a small quantity should be understood to result from the separation [of substances] of opposing potencies; conversely, the diminution of action in a large quantity is to be known as resulting from the separation of those that are equal or superior in potency.
Thus, from the application of *saṃskāra* (processing) as well, whether the qualities are similar or dissimilar, it is logical that there may be great purposefulness or minimal action;

for even a small amount can have great purposefulness, just as even a tiny measure of an emetic, when applied with oil, serves to remove many morbid humors (*doṣas*). Conversely, the case of a large quantity resulting in minimal action should be cited as an illustration.
Now, demonstrating the formulation of unstated applications by means of the six hundred seed-syllables of the stated applications, he says: "A region," and so forth;
"region" (pradeśa) means a single part.
Now, as to why the yogas are not explained in their entirety, he says: "Because they consist of many substances," and so forth.
The meaning is that because they are innumerable, they cannot be fully described. (49–50)
Now, he describes the characteristics and causes of the sharp, medium, and mild degrees of emesis, purgation, and non-unctuous enemas (nirūha), along with their preliminary procedures: "Sharp," etc.
"Pleasantly" means without causing pain; "unobstructed" means without impediment.

One should administer [the medicine] such that it does not cause excessive exhaustion for a purgative or a non-unctuous enema (nirūha), and such that it does not cause pain in the heart for an emetic; this is to be understood as the characteristic [of a successful administration]. "Without harming" means without causing distress;

"purgative" refers to both emesis and purgation. For it has been said: "Both [emesis and purgation] receive the designation 'purgation' (virecana) because they purge the bodily humors and impurities" (Ka. A. 1).
51–52. With the words beginning "water and fire," he states the cause for its sharpness.
"Endowed with the qualities of place and time" means being possessed of excellent qualities through the attainment of a favorable place and time;
"endowed with oleation and sudation" refers to one who has been well-oleated and well-sudated;
by the words "something" and so forth, he states the causes and characteristics for moderate emesis and other procedures.
By the phrase "by these qualities," [the author] refers back to [qualities such as] rapidity and so forth, as well as being untouched by water, fire, or insects.
By the phrase "of weak potency" (*mandavīrya*) and so on, he states the characteristics and the causes of the mild [drugs].
"Possessing slow velocity" (*mandavegavat*) is the characteristic; the remainder, however, constitutes the cause.
To explain the application of the sharp (*tīkṣṇa*) and other [purgatives] according to their respective degrees of purification, he says: "Incomplete," and so forth.

These two—medium and mild purification—are considered impure for strong individuals because they do not completely eliminate the morbid humors (*doṣa*); therefore, they are [regarded as] non-purifications.

By describing the reason as "because it removes defects that are not complete," he indicates that when the two [types of purification], being of moderate and slight strength respectively, remove only partial defects due to the greater strength [of the poison] and thus become moderate or slight purifications, they are nonetheless considered "correct purifications" (*samyak-śuddhi*).

The meaning of the passage beginning with "moderate" (*madhya*) is that for one of moderate strength, moderate purification is required, while for one of inferior strength, mild purification is required.

By using the term "required" (*prayojya*), he shows that even though these may be incorrect purifications in terms of their efficacy, they must be performed according to the strength [of the patient]; thus, with respect to those of moderate and inferior strength, those two [purifications] function as correct purifiers.

Regarding the classification by intensity (tīkṣṇatva) and other factors for the purpose of purification, he states the prescription of intensity and so forth: "Intense (tīkṣṇa), moderate (madhya)," and so on.

The characteristics of intense and other diseases correspond respectively to the characteristics of being all [symptoms], moderate, or slight. A disease characterized by all symptoms is "intense" (tīkṣṇa); one characterized by moderate symptoms is "moderate" (madhya); and one characterized by slight symptoms is a "mild" (mṛdu) disease.
By the term "considering the strength" (*balāvekṣī*), it is shown that if the strength is great when the disease is acute, only then should a strong purification (*tīkṣṇa-śodhana*) be performed.
(58) Regarding the specific procedure to be followed during the administration of emesis, he says: "It should be given," and so forth.

When emesis has been induced in this manner but the morbid humors (doṣas) have not been fully expelled, medicinal drugs for the purpose of further emesis should be administered repeatedly until the appearance of bile (pitta). That is to say, emesis should be given repeatedly as long as the bile is not seen;
for emesis is considered properly administered when it concludes with the appearance of bile.
For it has been said: "Emesis is desired until the appearance of bile; it is half [the dose] of purgation" (Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 1).
Furthermore, demonstrating the exceptions and the appropriate indications for the repeated administration of medicine, he says: "In cases of strength," and so forth.

Medicine should be administered again even to a person with strong *doṣas* [if necessary]; however, when the *doṣas* and the person are both of weak strength, one should entirely avoid medicine for the purpose of purification (*śodhana*). The meaning is that one should not perform purification.
By the word "or" (*vā*), it is shown that for a person and *doṣas* of medium strength, purification is not to be avoided altogether, but may be administered once.

Regarding the phrase "when [the medicine] has been expelled" (*nirhṛte*) and so forth, [it means] when the medicine intended for the purpose of eliminating the *doṣas* has been expelled. If it is said that [the medicine] has departed or been digested even without having eliminated the *doṣas*, then since this is stated with reference to emesis (*vamana*), it follows that one need not wait for the time of digestion for emesis; thus, it should be stated as "unripe emesis" (*apakvaṃ vamanaṃ*) and so on.
The state of being "like digested" (jīrṇasadṛśatā) in the case of emesis should be understood through its lack of causing agitation and its tendency toward maturation;
one should administer another [medicine], meaning that immediately after drinking the medicine for the purpose of emesis, one should give it on that very same day.

Regarding the administration of other medicines to counteract the failure (*ayoga*) of emetic applications, he explains with justification why one should not wait for the time of digestion (*pākakāla*): "Uncooked," and so forth (verse 62).
Having stated what must necessarily be done in the case of emesis, he now speaks regarding purgation as well: "When the laxative has been drunk," and so forth.
"When the medicine has been vomited"— that is, when only the purgative medicine has been vomited—
"again" means on that very same day.
Regarding what should be done when only a small amount of morbid humors (*doṣa*) has been removed by purgation, he says: "one with kindled digestive fire," and so forth.

By the phrase "possessing firm oleation qualities" (*dṛḍhasnehaguṇa*), it is meant that when the quality characterized by oleation is not firmly established in the body, then this medicine should not be administered; rather, oleation itself must first be performed. For if purgation is administered again while the body is insufficiently oleated, it leads only to improper application (*ayoga*), resulting in an incomplete purification (*duḥśuddha*), which is to say, an impurity due to improper application.
When the next day has arrived— that is, on the following day— or according to the reading "śvo bhūyaḥ" (on the next day again),
[the patient] is purged slowly by means of foods that are "anulomana" (downward-moving), because the accumulated doshas have ripened and are thus unobstructed and abundant.
And here, fearing excessive application (atiyoga) in one whose doshas have already been mobilized, he does not permit the administration of purgation again.
To provide a remedy for the remaining doshas that have been left over by emesis and purgation, he says: "By emetics," and so forth.
Here, the plural number is used with reference to the multiplicity of the digestive forces;
"immeasurably" means that there, food— such as gruel and the like— is neither consumed nor digested in its entirety.

Regarding the drinking of decoctions between meals: those who read the text as "according to measure" (pramāṇataḥ) explain that even when the food is perfectly pure, one should drink between meals for the purpose of pacifying defects that cause a coating in the stomach.
Regarding the preparation of mild purification, he says: "The weak," and so forth.
Because that which was previously purified is weak, a mild medicine should be administered; for with a sharp one, there would be loss of strength and excessive action (atiyoga). 67
He states the suitability for the application of mild medicine: "It is better," and so forth.
"Drunk repeatedly" means that being drunk repeatedly results in little affliction.
"Better" (śreyaḥ) refers to its superiority, which should be understood in comparison to sharp [medicines] that cause excessive complications.

"And not too sharp" means that what is excessively sharp should not be administered to those who are weak and so forth; for an excessively sharp [remedy], upon reaching those who are weak and such, would quickly produce a risk to life.
Regarding what should be done in the case of a weak person with many *doṣas*, he says: "Even one who is weak," and so on.
"Much or little" means repeatedly, even in small measure;
he states the reason why such [practices] remove great faults: "For if they are not removed, the faults will surely destroy him. (69)

Regarding the passage beginning with "of whom" (*yasya*), it refers to one for whom the downward-cleansing medicine (*ānulomika-virecana-auṣadha*) moves upward; such a person one should cause to drink the "downward-cleansing medicine"—this is the ellipsis.
"Purified by mouthfuls" (*kavalaiḥ śuddham*) means having the mouth and throat cleansed by mouthfuls.
"By that" (*tena*) refers to the warm water having been drunk.
Regarding what should be done when there is a suspicion of *atiyoga* (excessive purgation), he says: "When well-purged," and so forth.
"Well-purged" means having been properly expelled [of the impurities] in the correct measure.
The term *sodgāram* refers to the state of being cooked by the upward movement of gases (*udgāra*).

By this, it is shown that even when a proper purgation has occurred, if any portion of the medicine remains, one should extract it on that very day; for if even that single part of the medicine were not digested, it would result in an excessive purgation (*virecanātiyoga*).
By the words beginning with "kadācit" (sometimes), he states the reason for the non-advancement of the purgative.

Although the specific action to be taken in this case has not been explicitly stated, nevertheless, having perceived the obstruction of the medicine by phlegm due to heaviness and other factors, one should infer that the continued non-action of the medicine until the end of the night is to be tolerated; thus the course of action is to be inferred.
"It proceeds" means that the medicine, accompanied by defects, proceeds.

(74) Regarding "dry," etc.: due to inadequate administration, when the medicine has been digested, or has become obstructed, or has moved upward, another purgative containing oil and salt should be administered.
With the verse beginning "thirst and delusion" (tṛṇmoha), he describes the symptoms and treatment for a medicine that is obstructed by pitta.
The phrase "they occur while it is being digested" means that thirst and the other symptoms arise while the medicine is undergoing digestion.
76–77. With the verse beginning "lāla" and so forth, [the author] states the symptoms and treatment for a medicine that is obstructed by phlegm (kapha).
In the passage beginning with "susnigdha," the term *avirecita* means slightly purged;
*snehaja* refers to phlegm (*śleṣmā*) produced by the administration of oleation (*sneha*); and *saṅga* refers to the obstruction of the humors (*doṣasaṅga*).
By that fasting, through the very ripening of the *doṣas*, the pacification of excessive *śleṣman* and the pacification of the obstruction of the *doṣas* are brought about; this is the meaning.
(78) He states the specific sequence for the application of drying (*rūkṣa*) and other therapies prior to the administration of purgation, along with its rationale, beginning with "drying" (*rūkṣa*).

Regarding the statement "having first administered a *basti*," they intend by the word *basti* a *snehabasti* (oil enema); however, a *nirūha* (decoction enema) is not intended here because it aggravates *vāta*, and furthermore, because the administration of purgation is prohibited immediately after a *nirūha*. For it has been said: "From the administration of a *nirūha*, there may be danger from *pavana* (wind)" (*Siddhisthāna*, A. 1), and likewise: "A person who has been purged must certainly avoid the administration of a *nirūha* for seven days."

"Once purified by a *nirūha*, one should undergo purgation" (Siddhisthāna 1); however, by the term *basti*, both the *nirūha* and the oil enema (*snehabasti*) are included. As for the statement that the *nirūha* produces *vāta*, this refers specifically to its habitual use when devoid of an oil enema; whereas its general quality of subduing *vāta* is stated by the very aphorism: "The enema is the foremost among those that alleviate *vāta*" (Sūtrasthāna 25).

The prohibition of purgation immediately following a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) is a general rule; therefore, its exception by a specific injunction is entirely appropriate. Furthermore, the purgation prescribed here after the enema will occur only seven days after the administration of the enema; thus, there is no contradiction, as it has been set in motion and directed toward its commencement.
By the phrase "those who eat dry food" (*rūkṣāśanā*) and so forth, he states that even those requiring oleation (*snehya*) should not be purified (*śodhanīya*) except in cases of disease.
The term "constantly active" (*karmanityāḥ*) means those who constantly perform activities such as physical exercise.

Regarding "those who eat incompatible food" (*viruddhāśanādayaḥ*), the meaning is that they tolerate the humors (*doṣa*) resulting from incompatible food, overeating, and indigestion; thus, these factors—being of the nature of humors—do not produce a morbid transformation (*vikāra*) in them. Furthermore, incompatible food, overeating, and so forth are designated by the word "humor" (*doṣa*) because they generate the humors.

"Not in a non-disorder" means that one should not purge those [humors] when a disorder exists that can be cured solely by purification; this same point is stated elsewhere: "The provocation of humors that have not been provoked is not recommended, like striking stones that are already stuck together on top of one another.
Concluding the stated procedure, he says: "Knowing thus," and so forth;
"to those fit for purgation" means to those who are suitable for purgative therapy;
and in the passage beginning with "loss of [consciousness]," the word "whose" refers to the person undergoing purification.

One might object: "Since this purification (saṃśodhana) is a disorder equal to poison, why should it be practiced? To this he says: "It must necessarily be drunk at the [proper] times. The meaning is that when a disease is to be treated by purification, it must necessarily be administered; therefore, because it is an indispensable duty in specific conditions, purification cannot be avoided.

Now, as for this measurement of purification (śodhana) mentioned in some places as being one *karṣa* and so forth, that does not apply to all persons; rather, showing that such measurement should be understood to apply to those who are of middling constitution, age, and strength, he says "dravya... and so on.
By the phrase "taking that as the basis" (*tanmūlamālambya*), he means taking the stated measure as the seed for inferring unstated measures.
He speaks for the sake of providing an option, saying: "their state of being more or less is to be determined"; the meaning is that the excess or deficiency of the medicinal dose is to be determined.
86. Introducing the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as it is employed in all treatises, [the author], while defining it, says: "The six [atoms] are destructible," and so forth.
They say that the *trasareṇu* (a mote of dust) is destructible; others, however, call dust (*dhūli*) destructible.
Regarding the statement, "Eight red mustard seeds are [equal to] two rice grains," the word "red" (*rakta*) is an adjective qualifying the mustard seeds.
"Two of those [rice grains] are a *dhānyamāṣa*"; thus, two rice grains would constitute one *dhānyamāṣa*.
"Those four," however, refers to four barley grains; others, however, say that four *māṣas* are an *aṇḍikā*.
Three māṣakas are one śāṇa.

In this system of measurement, a *pala* consists of forty-eight *māṣakas* according to the *māna* standard; that same *pala* is equal to sixty-four *māṣakas* according to the ten-*raktikā* standard, because ten *raktikās* are equal to twenty-four *dhānya-māṣakas*. Consequently, sixty-four *māṣakas* of the ten-*raktikā* standard, when multiplied by twenty-four *dhānya-māṣakas*, result in exactly one thousand five hundred and thirty-six *dhānya-māṣakas*. Thus, there is an equivalence between the *pala* measure consisting of forty-eight *māṣakas* (each being thirty-two *dhānya-māṣakas*) and the *pala* measure consisting of sixty-four *dhānya-māṣakas* of the ten-*raktikā* standard.
In the Suśruta-saṃhitā as well: "In that regard, twelve *dhānyamāṣas* constitute one *svarṇamāṣaka*, and sixty-four of those make one *pala*" (Suśruta, Cikitsā-sthāna).
31) Thus it has been established;

therefore, sixty-four *māṣakas* multiplied by twelve *dhānya-māṣas* become seven hundred and sixty-eight *dhānya-māṣas*. In this way, the measure of a *pala* and so forth according to Suśruta is half of the measure stated by Dṛḍhabala. Likewise, even in the Suśruta, a *māṣa* consists of five *raktikās*; they say that the measure of Dṛḍhabala is the Māgadha standard, while the measure of Suśruta is the Kāliṅga standard.
In the *Jatūkarṇa*, however, six *guñjās* are said to constitute one *māṣaka*.
"Double that amount is desired for liquids," and so forth.

Although here the doubling of liquids is stated in a general sense, nevertheless, according to the observation of other treatises (*tantra*), the doubling of liquids is specified only from the *kuḍava* measure onwards; for it is said: "In measures beginning with the *raktikā*, as long as one has not reached the *kuḍava*..."

In the *Jatūkarṇa* it is also stated: "The measure for liquids and moist substances is declared to be the same as for dry ones. Furthermore, regarding the doubling of liquids, the doubling rule for *raktikā*s and so forth was previously established by the Teacher himself when, in the context of the *Suniṣaṇṇaka-cāṅgerī-ghṛta*, he reinforced the doubling of liquids within the technical *prastha* by stating: "In this case, thirty palas plus two palas should be understood as a *prastha*" (Ci. A. 14). Thus, it has already been demonstrated that the rule of doubling applies to *raktikā*s and other units.

The doubling of the dose applies only to that substance for which both dried and fresh forms are available for use; it is not stated that there is a doubling of the dose for that which is always used only in its fresh state. As it is said elsewhere: "Vāsā, kuṭaja, kūṣmāṇḍa, śatapatrī, sahā, amṛtā, prasāraṇī, aśvagandhā, śatapuṣpā, and sahācara..."
"They should always be applied moist; for them, there shall be no doubling.
This means that for other [substances], after performing the doubling, one should take two measures of the *māna*.
He states another technical rule: "Even in a liquid preparation," and so forth.
This means that in the preparation of an unctuous substance (*sneha*) or similar items where a liquid is to be employed, water should be used wherever a specific liquid is not mentioned.

Furthermore, since the mention of "feet" (*pāda*) signifies one-fourth part, the meaning of "and that" (*saḥ*) is established by common worldly usage; nevertheless, it is stated again for the sake of clarity.
In passages such as "of water, fat, and medicinal herbs," the rule "fat is four times the medicinal herb" means that the fat is four times the paste (*kalka*);
and since the word "water" (*toya*) is indicative of any liquid, the rule "water is four times the fat" means that the liquid is four times the fat.

However, where a specific measure for water and other ingredients has been stated, it must be performed exactly as prescribed, according to the statement: "But when [a measure] is specifically indicated, that very one [must be used]" (Su.Ci.A.
He now states the definition of the threefold cooking of medicated fats (sneha-pāka), beginning with the words "sneha-pāka" and so forth.

"Equal to the paste" means when the resin has reached a state of consistency equal to the paste first added during cooking; "like *saṃyāva*"—here the word *saṃyāva* refers to a lump made of equal parts of ghee, jaggery, and wheat flour; "while it is crumbling," and so forth, describes the characteristic of a firm cooking stage (*kharapāka*).
"In the process of breaking" means it is sinking; while existing, it undergoes a state of being rolled up due to the pressure of the fingers.
He states the subject matter concerning *kharapāka* and so forth with the verse beginning "khara" (104).
Some recite the verse beginning with "kāliṅga," but they declare that to be non-Vedic (*anārṣa*).

The section beginning with "the meaning of the Kalpa" (105) is a summary of the meaning of the locations; the "meaning of the Kalpa" is that which was stated in [verse] 1, beginning with "for the sake of the Kalpa, for the sake of differentiation."

The perception of purification (*śodhana-saṃjñā*)— stated in [verse] 1 of the *Kalpasthāna* as "or both [are used] because they purge the impurities of the body," etc.— is a distinct cause for its administration; and the qualities of place (*deśa*) and so forth, stated in [verse] 1 as "in that regard, hot, sharp, and expansive," etc., and "in that regard, the place (*deśa*), however," etc., [are also factors].
The qualities of fruits and other substances have been stated in the very same manner as the pharmaceutical preparations for *madanaphala* and others;
the six hundred formulations were mentioned in the passage beginning with "three hundred and fifty-five.
The reason for these variations was explained in the first chapter by the verse beginning with "for the sake of the pleasure of enjoyment" (*upabhogasukhārtham*).
The names refer specifically to the *madanaphala* and other such substances, and these have been mentioned in each respective chapter.

Their characteristics as sharp, moderate, or mild are described in the passage beginning with "easily [administered], quickly [acting], and of great force" (*Ka. A. 12*). Furthermore, the regimen according to the specific condition is stated in the passage beginning with "it should indeed be given before the previous [dose has passed]" (*Ka. A. 12*).
The remainder is easy to understand.
(106–107) Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Dantī and Dravantī," in the *Kalpasthāna* of the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of Caraka composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
12 [Section on Success] [Section on Success, Chapter 1 (109 of 120)]

Immediately after the section on cosmology (kalpasthāna), the section on accomplishment (siddhisthāna) is stated by way of remainder; that is, the section which expresses accomplishment is the "section on accomplishment."

By the term *siddhi* (success/attainment), what is meant here is the success in the form of curability by medicine regarding complications (*vyāpada*) arising from improper administration of emesis and other therapies. It is called the *Siddhisthāna* (Section on Success) because it denotes the causes of such success. Alternatively, through the metaphorical identification of cause and effect, the word *siddhi* refers here directly to the causes of success—namely, emesis and the other procedures themselves. For it has been stated: "We shall teach in the *Siddhis* [this section] the correct application of therapeutic actions, as well as the means for remedying those actions that have gone astray" (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 4).

Nor should it be argued that, by virtue of the etymological derivation of the term *siddhisthāna* (the section on success), the other sections such as *cikitsāsthāna* (the section on therapeutics) would also incur the designation *siddhisthāna*; for this name applies here alone through both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍhi*) usage, and not elsewhere.

Furthermore, even when the term *siddhisthāna* is mentioned, it is specifically the "success of treatment" (*kalpanāsiddhi*) that is stated first, because of its primacy in expressing the entire range of considerations required for the *siddhisthāna*, such as the conceptualization of the five therapeutic procedures (*pañcakarma*).

Having introduced the twelve questions of the disciple beginning with "What is the conceptualization? and so forth, he explains them in their proper order for the purpose of illuminating the teacher's intellect in accordance with those questions;
as it was said by Bharadvāja: "The intellect of a teacher who has been properly questioned by a disciple with an uncorrupted disposition and a serene inner self shines forth."

In this regard, the first question is: "What is the conceptualization (kalpanā) said to be for the five types of enemas? The second is: "And what is the sequence (krama)? The third is: "Furthermore, what is the indicator (liṅga) regarding those [enemas] that have been performed, those not performed, and likewise those performed excessively? The fourth is: "What is the number (saṅkhyā)? The fifth is: "What qualities (guṇa) does the enema possess? The sixth is: "In whom and which type of enema [is indicated]? The seventh is: "What is to be avoided at the time of each procedure? The eighth is: "Once performed, how long is the period of restriction (parihārakāla)? The ninth is: "By what means does the enema fail to enter when being administered? The tenth is: "By what means does it enter quickly? The eleventh is: "And by what means does it take a very long time to enter? The twelfth begins with: "Which [conditions] are curable," and so forth.

Although there is no room for the question beginning with "curable" (*sādhya*) and so forth— since diseases that are not curable do not subside by the aforementioned medicines when administered according to their respective indications— nevertheless, this question should be understood as referring to cases where the medicine itself is improperly applied, despite being designated as the appropriate treatment.

In this context, the term *kalpanā* refers to the formulation of the five components of the therapeutic procedure (*pañcakarmāṅga*). Therefore, he first stated the application of oleation and sudation as the five components of the procedure;
this is the answer to the first question. Regarding the phrase "at least three days" (*tryahāvara*) and so forth:
"at least three days" (*tryahāvara*) means one who has become oleated (*snigdha*) by means of oleation performed over a period of three days or for three days, such that it is the minimum duration.
"Seven days" means being oleated for a period extending over seven days;
"extremely oleated" means being oleated for a period extending over seven days by way of the limit of time for the excellence of oleation.

Thus, in the view that oleation is performed as a preliminary limb of purification (*śodhana*) due to an extension of time, one is oleated for up to seven days; however, in the view where there is no extension of time, the meaning is that one should be oleated for three days and then subjected to sudation (*saṃsvedana*).
He states, with supporting reasoning, that the seven-day period for oleation (*snehana*) should not be exceeded: "Not beyond this," and so forth.
"Beyond this" means beyond seven days.
To the question "Why do they not prescribe it longer? he replies: "Because it would become habitual (*sātmyībhavet*)," and so forth.

The meaning is that oil therapy administered after seven days does not produce excessive unctuousness (snehana) in the body because it has become habitual through its seven-night application; thus, the dose of oil which achieves unctuousness when used for seven days is precisely the habitual dose. However, a higher dose that has not yet reached the state of habituation must indeed be administered even beyond seven nights. But the Vaidyas, when a person has not been sufficiently oleated after seven nights, allow a brief rest and then administer the oil again with a higher dose.

This three-day oleation and seven-night oleation have been mentioned according to the distinction between soft and hard bowel habits, as it is said: "A person with a soft bowel habit becomes oleated by the consumption of clear [unmedicated] substances in three nights, whereas a person with a hard bowel habit becomes oleated in seven nights" (Sūtra-sthāna 13).

Now, if the rule is that one with a hard bowel (krūrakoṣṭha) becomes oleated within seven nights, then how can it be said here—by the statement "they do not prescribe oleation beyond this"—that there is no oleation even after seven nights? We reply: True, one with a hard bowel becomes oleated in exactly seven nights; however, they become oleated by the dose of unctuous substance administered in consideration of their hard-bowelled condition. But when an insufficient dose is administered, then they do not become oleated even after seven nights.

As for the statement in another tantra, "The administration of oleation is prescribed for three six-nights or nine nights," by which oleation is enjoined even beyond seven nights—that is certainly not the intention of the Teacher. Alternatively, that [statement] should be explained as referring to the application of excessive doses that have not become habitual after seven nights, since here the use of oleation beyond seven nights is prohibited, or rather, because the use within three days is prohibited, they say that the Teacher permits oleation even in a single day through the immediate (sadyas) administration of oleation.

Although the duration for the maximum degree of oleation regarding the medium-sized bowel has not been explicitly stated, nevertheless, according to the medium method, it should be understood that the oleation of the medium-sized bowel occurs within five days.

As for the interpretation offered by some, namely, "For one with a soft bowel (mṛdukoṣṭha), oleation should not be administered after three days because it has become habitual (sātmyībhāvāt)," this does not satisfy us. For the teacher has stated that the state of habituation is accomplished specifically within seven days; therefore, if a person with a soft bowel does not become oleated after three days due to the administration of an excessively small dose of unctuous substance, then the oleation should be continued for even more days.

He states the fruit of oleation (sneha) as a constituent of purification: "Sneha destroys vāta," and so forth. He states the fruit of sudation (sveda) preceded by oleation: "Of one who has been oleated," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in subtle [doshas]," this refers to even subtle ones.

Now, he describes separately the diet appropriate for emesis for one who is to be treated with emetics, and the diet appropriate for purgation for one who is to be treated with purgatives, beginning with "grāmyaudaka... and so forth.
Regarding the dietary regimen for one requiring purgation, beginning with the words "by means of tastes" (*rasaiḥ tathā*) and so forth:

here, when the connection is made with the term *utkleśanīya* (to be provoked), it should be understood as the provocation of *pitta* alone. Alternatively, the term *utkleśanīyaḥ* does not even follow [from the previous context]; therefore, the remainder is that one should "eat" with tastes and soups (*yūṣa*) that do not increase *kapha*.

This post-purgative meal should be known to last for three days; however, for the purpose of emesis, the post-emetic meal lasts for only one day. For it has been said: "After a person has rested for three nights following oleation, they should drink [the emetic]."
"Having eaten unctuous, liquid, and hot rice with meat broth for three days,
and having rested for one day, he should eat similarly again and then drink an emetic" (Sūtra-sthāna 13).

He states the rationale for when one who requires emesis (*vāmanīya*) should instead be treated with excessive phlegm (*śleṣmottara*), and when one who requires purgation (*virecanīya*) should instead have their phlegm reduced (*alpakapha*): "In one with excessive phlegm," etc.
He states the reason for the opposite of what was previously mentioned: "Below," etc.

When phlegm (kapha) is diminished, emetic medicine that has been drunk passes downwards even without inducing vomiting; however, when phlegm is increased, purgative medicine administered moves upwards and results in vomiting—this is the meaning.

Now, he provides the answer to the question regarding the sequence: "Emesis should be given to one who has been oleated. This means that on the day of drinking the emetic, the emesis should be administered after the patient has been oleated by means of an oil massage (*abhyaṅga*). As for oleation produced by drinking [the emetic], it need not be mentioned again since it has already been stated previously. Others, however, say "to one in whom the qualities of oleation have arisen," as it is said [in the source]. It should be administered according to the procedure described in the *Madanaka-lpa*.
He states what is to be done after the emesis: "Of the one who has vomited," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase beginning with "peyādiḥ," which will be explained later in the verse starting with "peyāṃ vilepī," after describing the procedure for emesis, he states the procedure for purgation: "of one who has been oleated" (snigdhasya), etc.,
and "whose body has been well-fomented" (susvinnatanuḥ) means whose body has been properly subjected to sudation.

Furthermore, this sequence of oleation and sudation, which constitutes a limb of purgation, should also be performed after the administration of emesis and following the sequence of liquid gruels (*peyā*) and so forth, even when purgation follows immediately after emesis. As it has been stated: "Having administered soft foods according to the sequence, one should again treat the patient with oleation and sudation and then administer purgation. Moreover, regarding the three-day interval of light meals for the purpose of purgation following oleation, since that has already been explained as part of the description of the therapeutic procedures, it is not restated here in full detail, but should be understood according to the method prescribed in the *Kalpasthāna*.
"Most suitable" means that, in consideration of bodily defects and other factors, whatever purgative is therapeutically appropriate should be administered.
He describes the sequence of post-emetic and post-purgative therapies beginning with gruel (*peyā*), etc.: "gruel (*peyā*), thick gruel (*vilepī*," and so forth.
*Yavāgū* is [a thin gruel] with many grains;
*vilepī* is a thin liquid.
For it is said: "Maṇḍa is devoid of grains; peyā is endowed with grains;
yavāgū should have many grains; and vilepī is thin and liquid.

Here, *akṛtayūṣa* (unprepared soup) is that which is not seasoned with fats, salt, and so forth, while *kṛtayūṣa* (prepared soup) is that which is seasoned with fats, salt, and so forth; in this same way, the distinction between prepared and unprepared applies to *rasa* (broth) as well.
As it is stated in the *Sūdaśāstra*: "All food that is without fat and salt is to be known as 'unprepared' (*akṛta*); that which is seasoned with salt, fat, and pungents is 'prepared' (*kṛta*).

The term "three times" (*tris*) refers to throughout the three meal-times; "twice" (*dvis*) refers to two meal-times; and "once" (*ekaśas*) refers to a single meal-time. Furthermore, these terms beginning with "three times" are each to be connected with the categories of drinks and so forth (*peyā* etc.).

And these three options, beginning with "three times," should be understood respectively according to the degree of purity of the primary element (the *pradhāna*). Therefore, for one whose primary element is pure, the gruel (*peyā*) and so forth should be administered three times each. Thus, for three meal-times [after the day of vomiting], gruel is given; after that, for three meal-times, thin porridge (*vilepī*); after that, for three meal-times, cooked food accompanied by both prepared and unprepared soup; and after that, for three meal-times, cooked food with both prepared and unprepared broth. In this manner, starting from the evening of the day of vomiting, the sequence of gruel and so forth is completed in seven nights over twelve meal-times.

This same sequence is to be applied even to the preparations [of the diet], as stated starting from "Then, in the evening, of red śāli rice grains... and continuing up to "...at the twelfth meal-time" (Sūtra 15).

Although the division of time for the soup (*yūṣa*) and the meat-broth (*rasa*) is not explicitly set forth here, nevertheless, the division of time for the soup—referring to that which was not prepared during the first three periods of the day but was prepared during the latter three—and likewise for the meat-broth, must be described.
In this way, the sequence of *peyā* and so forth twice over, as well as the sequence of *peyā* and so forth taken singly, should be described.

Although at one time, during the sequence beginning with *peyā*, no temporal distinction between prepared and unprepared soups (*yūṣa*) and broths (*rasa*) is obtained, nevertheless, it should be understood that at that very same time, the state of being prepared or unprepared regarding the soups and broths is determined by their slight degree of processing.

Because weakness of the digestive fire (*agnimāndya*) can arise from the agitation caused by the excessive entry of morbid humors (*doṣa*) when the primary purification has occurred, it should be understood that in such cases the sequence beginning with *peyā* is maintained for a long duration.
Furthermore, the characteristics of the primary purification and so forth will be explained later.
Demonstrating by means of an illustration how the sequence beginning with gruel (peyā) serves to kindle a weakened digestive fire, he says: "Just as," and so forth.
He states the characteristics of the purity of the primary element and so forth, beginning with the words "jaghanya" (inferior), etc.

Purgation that occurs with four urges is considered inferior (*jaghanya*); that which occurs with six is middling (*madhyama*); and that which occurs with eight is excellent (*pravara*). Regarding enemas (*virecana*), ten [applications] are for the inferior, twenty (twice ten) for the middling, and thirty (thrice ten) for the excellent—this is the meaning.

Having thus described the classification into inferior and so forth based on the number of urges, he now states the inferior, middling, and excellent nature of the purgative according to the quantity of morbid humors (*doṣa*) respectively, beginning with "prasthas tathā" and so on.
In a mild purgative, the dose is double a *prastha*; in a moderate one, it is triple; and in a superior one, it is quadruple.

Here, by the word *prastha*, thirteen and a half *palas* are meant; for it is stated in another treatise: "In emesis, in purgation, and likewise in bloodletting, the wise say that a *prastha* consists of thirteen and a half *palas*."

Emesis is desired to end with the appearance of *pitta*, being half the measure of purgation; that is, whatever quantity has been declared for purgation according to the division into inferior, moderate, and superior, emesis should be known as half of that, respectively, according to its own division into inferior, moderate, and superior. However, the fact that emesis ends with *pitta* and purgation ends with *kapha* should be understood as inherently implied within the threefold classification of purification.
