When the morbid humor (doṣa), having been expelled through four urges and measuring one *prastha*, reaches the end with pitta, and the signs of proper purification by emesis are observed, then that is the minimum degree of purification (*jaghanyā śuddhi*). When, in the case of purgation, the morbid humor measuring two *prasthas* is expelled through ten urges and the end with *kapha*—the sign of proper application of purgation—is observed, then that constitutes the minimum degree of purification for purgation. In this same way, for medium and superior purification as well, the sign of proper application should be understood as reaching the end with *pitta* in emesis and reaching the end with *kapha* in purgation.

Following the description of the faults regarding speed, number, and measure, the mention here is for the purpose of establishing the characteristics of correct purification (*samyak-śuddhi*) and purification by signs (*laiṅgika-śuddhi*), such as ending with the elimination of *pitta*. Therefore, the claim that there are four types of purification mentioned here for emesis and purgation—namely, that which is based on time (*āntikī*), that which is based on speed (*vaigikī*), that which is based on measure (*mānikī*), and that which is based on signs (*laiṅgikī*)—is entirely unacceptable to us; rather, there is only one type of purification, which is that based on signs.

In that regard, one should understand that in emesis (*vamana*), the state of ending with bile (*pittāntatva*) and the signs to be described later in the text beginning with "Kapha [is expelled] in due order" apply; likewise, in purgation (*virecana*), the state of ending with phlegm (*kaphāntatva*) and the signs to be described later in the text beginning with "Purification of the channels and the sense organs" apply.

Therefore, the objection raised here by Āṣāḍhavarmā—namely, "The signs of proper purification have been stated according to their characteristics, their measure, the force of the urges, and the emergence of the *doṣas*; is this [set of criteria] to be taken individually or collectively?"—is already refuted by the fact that it was not even accepted as a valid challenge.
However, the refutations of other [opinions] regarding this matter have not been written here for fear of prolixity.
Furthermore, the threefold classification of purification as inferior and so forth should be established here according to whether it pertains to inferior, middling, or superior faults.
As for the mention of the characteristics of inferior and other types of purification in terms of "impetuosity" (*vega*), that should be understood as referring to what occurs most frequently.

The distinction between inferior and other grades of purification is ultimately based on the difference in the quantity of morbid humors (doṣa) expelled. Thus, when in emesis there is a discharge of two *prastha*s of humor through eight bouts, that is indeed excellent purification (*pravara-śuddhi*); when in emesis there is a discharge of one and a half *prastha*s of humor through six bouts, that is middling purification (*madhya-śuddhi*); and when there is a discharge of one *prastha* of humor through even four bouts, that is only inferior purification (*jaghanya-śuddhi*). This should be illustrated in the same way for purgations (*virecana*) as well. That in which the discharge of bile (*pitta*) occurs at the end is called "ending with bile" (*pittānta*); likewise, "ending with phlegm" (*kaphānta*) should be explained in the same manner.

Therefore, that which is to be stated as the characteristic of successful emesis by the verse beginning with “In sequence: phlegm, bile, and then wind,” as well as that which is to be stated as the characteristic of successful purgation by the verse beginning with “The arrival of feces, bile, phlegm, and wind,” is not contradictory to this [present statement].

In that context, the arrival of wind (vāyu) which is mentioned at the end should be understood as an indicator of the end of pitta and the end of kapha; for when pitta and kapha have been completely eliminated from their respective receptacles, the wind alone circulates. By that circulation of the wind alone, the end of pitta and the end of kapha are known.

Objection: If this matter has already been stated by the very passage beginning with “Kapha [is expelled] gradually,” then why is it stated here again that they say emesis ends with pitta and purgation ends with kapha? We reply: This is stated here for the purpose of demonstrating the correspondence with the state of ending with pitta and so forth within the three grades of purification—mild, moderate, and intense—which are being explained through the distinctions of impulse, number, and the quantity of the doshas. For if the characteristics of the correct administration of those emesis and purgation were not stated here, a student might fall into the error of thinking that even when a person has a powerful dosha, if the impulse and quantity arise during a mild purification and the state of ending with pitta does not occur, it is still a mild purification. The same logic may be applied to other cases as well.
Regarding what must be done when a specific quantity of morbid matter (doṣa) has been expelled through emesis or purgation, he says: "two or three," and so forth.

By using the expression "two or three" in an indefinite sense, he shows that the amount of waste matter is immeasurable. In the case of emesis, however, "having drunk"—meaning, excluding the medicine that was drunk during emesis—the remainder is to be measured.
Now, he provides the answer to the question beginning with "And what [is there] in regard to the performed and the unperformed," etc., in due order, starting with "In sequence," and so forth.

By the word "in sequence" (*kramāt*), [the author] demonstrates that the arrival of *kapha* and the other humors by bypassing the stated order is not the characteristic of a correct administration of therapy. For when *pitta*, having moved upward from *kapha*, arises, then even though there is the arrival of *pitta*, there is no purification (*śuddhi*); rather, purification occurs only when *pitta* located in the lower part of the stomach (*āmāśaya*) brings about emesis. And that bringing forth of *pitta* occurs only after the bringing forth of *kapha*. Thus, the meaning of the term "in sequence" should be explained here even in the context of the characteristics of a correctly performed purgation (*virecana*).
"Duśchardite" and so forth describe the symptoms of vomiting caused by improper application [of emetics];
"tṛṇmoha" and so forth are the signs of excessive vomiting.
Here, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of complexion, voice, and so forth is intended;
furthermore, the loss of sleep here is caused solely by the provocation of wind (vāyu).
"Clarity of the channels," and so forth, refers to the characteristics of a proper purgation;
"vitality and digestive fire" means a sharp digestive fire;
and "freedom from disease" means the disappearance of disorders produced by the morbid humors (doṣas) that were to be expelled by the purgation.
The meaning of the passage beginning with "and acquisition" (prāptiśca) has already been explained in another place.
The meaning is that there may be a characteristic of discord caused by improper application of yoga, and not the downward movement of wind (vātānulomya).
The passage beginning with "kaphāsra" describes the symptoms of excessive purgation (virekātiyoga);
the word "kṣaya" (depletion) is to be connected individually with each of the factors, such as phlegm (kapha), blood (asra), and so forth.

Having described the characteristics of correct administration (*samyagyoga*) and so forth as they arise in the context of the formulations for emesis (*vamana*) and purgation (*virecana*), he now states the formulation for enemas (*bastikalpanā*): "When the meal is digested," and so forth.

On the eighth day for one who has followed the procedure of gradual dietary restoration (*saṃsarjana-krama*) over seven days, once the meal has been consumed, the drinking of clarified butter (*sarpiḥ-pāna*) or an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) should be administered on the ninth day. Regarding these two alternatives, the rule is as follows: if purgation (*virecana*) is to be performed immediately after emesis (*vamana*), then the drinking of clarified butter is given on the ninth day; however, if an enema is to be administered immediately after purgation, then the unctuous enema is to be given on the ninth day.

Immediately following the *vamana* (emesis), the drinking of clarified butter (*sarpiḥ-pāna*) on the ninth day was not previously mentioned; therefore, it is now shown that the drinking of clarified butter occurs at the same time as the oil enema (*anuvasana*), which is to be performed after the purgative (*virecana*) as part of the *nirūha* procedure. Consequently, the drinking of clarified butter should not be considered a constituent part of the *nirūha*. Furthermore, the ninth day here should be understood starting from the day of purification (*śodhana*). As stated by Jatūkarṇa: "On the ninth day after purification, there is the drinking of unctuous substance (*sneha-pāna*) or an oil enema (*anuvasana*). Likewise, it is also stated in the Suśruta: "When seven nights have passed since the purgation, for one whose strength has been restored..."
"A non-unctuous enema should be properly administered to one who has consumed prepared food and is fit for an unctuous enema" (Suśruta Cikitsā-sthāna 37).

Furthermore, regarding the sequence of gradual dietary advancement (*rasa-saṃsarjana*) mentioned in the *Uttarabasti-cikitsita* following the sequence of gruels (*peyā*) and so forth—that must be performed at the conclusion of all therapeutic procedures in order to return to a natural diet, not merely upon the completion of the acts of emesis or purgation. Therefore, it is appropriate here that the drinking of ghee and the administration of an unctuous enema occur on the ninth day for one who has not yet undergone the gradual dietary advancement. As for what is stated by Bhadraśaunaka: "One whose meal is digested, who is cheerful, who has drunk oil, and whose digestive fire is strong..."

It has been stated: "Once thoroughly purified, the person should then be given an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) after one month"; this does not contradict [the previous rule], as that statement refers either to a prior occasion for an unctuous enema or to a specific type of disease. Furthermore, there are many commentaries on this point by the authors of the *ṭīkā*s, such as Aṅgiri, Saindhava, Jejjhaṭa, Īśvarasena, and others; however, the interpretations of others have been refuted simply by pointing out their flaws.
The phrase "with the body smeared with oil" is intended to show that the application of unctuous substances occurs even through massage (*abhyaṅga*).

In this context, although sudation (*sveda*) has not been explicitly mentioned, it is indeed implied by its being preceded by the five procedures (*pañcakarma*); as it is said: “One should perform the five procedures for those whose morbid humors (*doṣa*) have manifested, by means of oleation (*sneha*) and sudation” (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 2).

Regarding the phrase "one should administer [the enema] after three days," this refers to three days after the day of the non-unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*); thus, according to the sequence to be described, the non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*) should be administered one day, two days, more than that, or on the very same day as the oleation.

By the phrase "not for one who is excessively hungry," it is indicated that for one who is excessively hungry, a *nirūha* enema leads to over-action (*atiyoga*) and upward movement [of the doshas]. In this regard, a follow-up meal consisting of meat broth (*dhanva-rasa*) is entirely appropriate, because—unlike purgation—it does not cause a dulling of the digestive fire (*agni-māndya*) and is strength-promoting. As stated by Bhoja: "For one whose body has been purified from the head down by a *nirūha*, why is meat-broth and the like prescribed as food, and why is the post-purgation diet (*saṃsarga*) like that for one who has undergone purgation?"

"Purgation destroys the digestive fire because it overwhelms its seat, but an enema does not do so; therefore, it kindles the fire. Thus, showing that the meal—whether consisting of meat broth (*rasa*) and so forth, or thin gruel (*peyā*) and so forth—should be administered according to the state of the humors and the strength of the fire, he says: "or, having considered the strength of the humors, as is appropriate"; by "strength," he means the strength of the digestive fire.
With the words beginning "naras tataḥ," [the author] describes the follow-up enema (*anuvāsana*) for one who has undergone a non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*).

By the word "niśi" (at night), he shows that the *anuvāsana* performed on the same day following a *nirūha* must be administered specifically at night; however, others maintain that during the cold season (*śīta*) and spring (*vasanta*), the *anuvāsana* should not be given at night to one who has just received a *nirūha*. Furthermore, by the word "niśi," they show that for one who has been *nirūḍha* on that very day, the *anuvāsana* should be given in the evening; thus, they say it should be administered either at night or during the day according to the specific divisions that will be described below.
By the statement "fit for an oil enema" (*anuvāsanārha*), it is indicated that if the digestive fire (*pāvaka*) is moderate or weak, then the oil enema should not be administered on that very day.

For this very reason, Jatūkarṇa states regarding the second day alone: "Then, after three days have passed since the decoction enema (*nirūha*) and [the patient] has awakened from sleep and eaten, the oil enema (*anuvāsana*) is given. Hārīta also says: "Having observed the night has dawned, one should then administer the oil enema according to the strength or weakness [of the patient].
The statement "one who has just received a decoction enema should be given an oil enema" refers to a person afflicted by the agitation of *vāta* produced by the decoction enema.

By the word "at night" (*niśi*), he shows that the oil enema (*anuvāsana*) prescribed for the vicinity of night is indeed distinguished by a different time through a division of time, stating "in the cold," and so forth.
By the word "cold" (*śīta*), both the *śiśira* and *hemanta* seasons are included. "During the day" (*divā*) refers to the daytime portion near night, and also to the night near day.

By one who is protecting against the faults (*doṣa*), having observed the faults, and by one who protects through the avoidance of faults; those faults which were proclaimed regarding the drinking of oleaginous substances (*sneha*) in the chapter on oleation—beginning with the passage, "When phlegm is predominant, [one should drink] during the day in the cold season" (Sūtra-sthāna 13)—those very same faults that arise from taking oleaginous substances at an improper time also arise from an oil enema (*anuvāsana*) performed at a time contrary to what has been prescribed. This is what is meant.

Whatever administration of oleation (sneha-pāna) was prescribed in the chapter on oleation according to specific conditions such as the predominance of vāta or pitta during the night or the day, that should also be understood here, because the principle is the same and one part implies the other.

Regarding the passage beginning with "pratyāgate ca" (and when [the oil] has returned), the term "anuvāsanīye" refers to the unctuous enema (*anuvāsana-sneha*). The phrase "vyuṣitāya" means that for one who has spent the night without any complications, food should be given during the day; likewise, food should also be given in the evening.
Following the unctuous enema, he states the time for the subsequent unctuous enema: "tryahe vā" (or after three days), and so forth.

In this case as well, the determination of three or five days is as previously stated. Furthermore, this time for the non-unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) must be understood as being administered on the very day of the purgative (*nirūha*), provided the *anuvāsana* is to be given immediately. Others, however, read: "On the second, third, or fifth day thereafter, one should administer the *anuvāsana*. They explain it thus: "On the second, third, or fifth day thereafter, one should administer the *anuvāsana*. In this regard, the rule is that the *anuvāsana* on the second day is for those with excessively strong wind (*vāta*); on the third day for those whose wind is not excessively increased; and on the fifth day for those in whom phlegm (*kapha*) and bile (*pitta*) have increased.

The daily administration of *anuvāsana* enema is also stated by Hārīta; for his statement says: "Having observed the excessive manifestation of vāta day after day, they prescribe the enema. It is also stated in the Suśruta-saṃhitā: "A physician should administer an oil enema (*snehabasti*) every day to one who is dry and has abundant vāta;
for others, he should do so every third day, out of fear of impairing the digestive fire" (Su.Ci.A. 37).

Here too, by the passage beginning with "But one who is rough and constant" and ending with "and those afflicted by Vata day by day" (Siddhi Ayurveda 4), the author will prescribe an oil enema every two days; therefore, the reading "on the second or third day" is correct. As for the claim that "the word *dvyaha* here denotes merely a connection with two days, not the completion of a two-day period, and thus, starting from the oil enema administered on the first day, the subsequent oil enema is obtained when the third day is complete," that is refuted. Likewise, in the case of "three days" (*tryaha*), it should be understood that only the connection with the third day is intended.
Now, he states the rules for non-unctuous enema (anuvasana) according to the specific doshas, beginning with "one, and likewise three," and so forth.

This is the answer to the question, "How many [doshas]? Furthermore, the answer to the question regarding their number will follow later with the verse beginning, "Thirty are considered [to be involved] in clinical procedures.
Although non-unctuous enema is not prescribed for kapha and pitta, this should nevertheless be understood as referring to cases where kapha and pitta are associated with vata.
Furthermore, by the phrase "or again," [the author] indicates that one should administer nine or eleven [pulses] for *vāta*;

by the phrase "odd numbers," he prohibits the administration of even numbers such as two, four, six, and so on. It should be understood from the words of the Great Sage (*maharṣi*) that the administration of odd numbers is beneficial here precisely because of its inherent power, as in: "On even days, those desiring a son should cohabit" (*Śārīra-sthāna*, A. 8). The underlying rationale for this has not been stated by the Teacher here, out of fear of excessive prolixity.

As for that which will be stated [later] regarding the administration of even-numbered enemas (yugmabasti) in the passage beginning with, "Three, five, or four, or else six," that should be understood as referring to the administration of even-numbered enemas performed for the purpose of oleation (snehana) as an ancillary part of the decoction enema (nirūha). However, in this context, the administration of odd-numbered enemas is intended as the primary procedure for the non-unctuous enema (anuvāsana); thus, there is no contradiction.

By this, the argument raised by Āṣāḍhavarmā—namely, "The administration of odd-numbered enemas, which is the cause for the effect of the decoction enema, has not been mentioned here and was previously prohibited; furthermore, he speaks of unctuous substances such as 'one, or three,' etc., at the end of the regimen"—is to be understood as refuted.

Furthermore, by the terms "odd" (*ayugma*) and "alternately" (*punar vā*), the meaning is that where an *anuvāsana* is to be administered according to the rule of recurrence, it should be performed as an odd number and interspersed with *nirūha*s; thus, after administering *nirūha*s in the stated number, the oil (*sneha*) should be given in the stated number.

The employment of an odd number, however, by way of a middle rule (*madhyavidhayā*), includes intervals of two or four days and so forth; therefore, he states that this does not contradict the number of *anuvāsana*s to be mentioned later.

It is also stated by Jatūkarṇa: "When the non-unctuous enema (nirūha) has been digested, one should administer the unctuous enema (anuvāsana) to the patient who has eaten, on the second day at the latest, or on the fifth, or likewise on the eleventh; for those with [predominance of] Vāta and other doshas, it is said that the interval may be reduced to two, three, four, or more days.
Now, he states the time that must necessarily be observed between the non-unctuous enema and the purgation, beginning with the verse: "The person who has been purged," and so forth.
By the word "necessarily" (*avaśyam*), it is shown that even in a disease curable in a single day, the cutting [of the vein] must necessarily be performed on the seventh day.

Although, according to the *Siddhi* chapter on the five procedures (*pañcakarman*), an enema (*nirūha*) is strictly prohibited immediately after purgation (*virecana*), and likewise purgation is prohibited for one who has received an enema, nevertheless, that prohibition applies only to that specific time; therefore, this statement is intended to preclude the possibility [of performing it] on the third, fourth, or subsequent days.

As for the statement that the prescription for *nirūha* on the ninth day—immediately following the time for the subsequent *anuvāsana* after purgation—is intended to show that there would otherwise be no possibility of administering the *basti* earlier than that; this is not correct. For this is the rule regarding the sequence of dietary restoration (*saṃsarjana-krama*) dependent upon purification by *anuvāsana*. When the sequence of *peyā* and so forth is completed in three days due to prior purification, then because the *anuvāsana* is given on the fourth day, the *nirūha* would necessarily follow on the fifth or sixth day. Therefore, this statement is made to preclude such a possibility.

However, there is no sequence of gradual dietary restoration (*saṃsarjana-krama*) immediately following a non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*); therefore, after administering unctuous therapy for three days, the application of purgation is indeed appropriate.
Regarding the reason for avoiding both non-unctuous enemas and purgation for up to seven days (rather than just within the first seven days), he says: "For that [dosha] of his," and so forth;
[if administered too soon], it would expand and thus cause injury.
The meaning is that one should not harm the body, which was previously rendered empty through purification (*śūnya-śodhana*), by performing purification (*śodhana*) once again.

As for what is stated in another treatise (*tantrāntara*)—"Purgation (*vireka*) may be administered up to seven days, and after that, a non-unctuous enema (*nirūhaṇa*)"—that should be understood as referring to the sequence of purification performed according to the method of *saṃsarga*. Furthermore, the completion of the seven-day period in that context should be explained as being for the purpose of avoiding the optional alternatives regarding the *saṃsarjana* diet, unctuous substances (*sneha*), and so forth.
Regarding the question, "What are the qualities of the enema (basti)?", the answer begins with "The enema stabilizes youth," and so forth;

this refers to the qualities of the non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana), whereas the author will describe the qualities of the unctuous enema (anuvāsana) in the passage beginning with "In the body, by means of the non-unctuous enema... and so on.
"Vayaḥsthāpayitā" means one who establishes or maintains youth (*vayas*). Its quality of establishing youth arises from its capacity to purify the channels (*srotas*).
Because it accomplishes all objectives, even contrary effects such as the reduction of stability are achieved through the application of specific medicinal formulations.
By the phrase "harmless for children, the elderly, and the young," its superiority over emesis and purgation is expressed, for those two are contraindicated for children and the elderly.

The quality of removing all diseases (*sarvagadāpahatva*) is to be understood through the term "pacification" (*saṃśamana*); since the statement "it should pacify all disorders" refers to the removal of all diseases by means of purifying the *doṣas*, there is no tautology. Alternatively, the distinction is that "all disorders" (*sarvān vikārān*) refers to disorders in all their stages.
With the words beginning with "in the body" (*dehe*), he describes the qualities of non-unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*).

By the statement "when the passage has been purified by a non-unctuous enema (nirūha)," it is shown that only when the passage has been cleansed by a nirūha does an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) produce the qualities as described; it does not do so through the mere administration of oil. Regarding the word "oil" (*taila*) here, some take it as an indication for any unctuous substance (*sneha*), including ghee (*ghṛta*); however, we consider it more appropriate to understand that "oil" alone is intended here because it is the primary agent for pacifying Vāta. For it is stated here that [the enema] produces coldness from heat, and ghee is not hot. Furthermore, although other unctuous substances—excluding marrow—are authorized for use in anuvāsana, they are not permitted here because ghee is not considered a primary agent in this context.

In the passage beginning with "paramasti," the term "substance" (dravya) refers to the cause; and that cause is to be understood through the pacification of wind (anila). Some read, "There is no action here other than latent impression" (nānvāsanāt kiñcid ihāsti karma); this explains that the function of oil itself is indeed the cause. Regarding the phrase beginning with "snehena," oil used for non-unctuous enema (anuvāsana) should be known as processed by cooking; for uncooked oil is prohibited by the statement: "One should not administer unripe (ama) oil, for it would cause secretions in the rectum" (Sūtrasthāna, A. 4).

In this case, when oil and wind—possessing contrary qualities—are combined, it is due to the specific potency (*prabhāva*) of the substance that the oil alone subdues the wind, and not the wind the oil. Although the quality of subtlety (*aṇutva*) exists in both oil and wind, nevertheless, here by virtue of its potency, the oil—being connected with the subtle components of the wind through its unctuousness (*sneha*) and other properties—conquers the wind. Thus, although subtlety is common to both, here it produces an effect that is contrary [to what might be expected]. To illustrate how the oil performs the aforementioned action, he says: "In the root," and so forth.

By means of the primary analogy and the non-unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*), [the author] demonstrates that the rectum, which is to be directly satiated, is the root of the body. For it is said by Parāśara: "The rectum is the root of the body;

the vessels (*sirā*) are established therein, and reaching as far as the head, they nourish the entire body. Likewise, the meaning is that through the non-unctuous enema, a man shall be endowed with strength, virility, and so forth, and shall possess offspring.
He states the general benefits of both *nirūha* and *anuvāsana* enemas: "Those who are stiff," and so forth.
"Broken" (*bhagna*) refers to those with fractured bodies; "afflicted" (*rugṇa*) refers to those with dislocated joints; and "lack of relish for food" (*bhaktānabhinandana*) refers to anorexia.
"Afflictions caused by Vāta" means complications produced by Vāta;
"those with diminished sense faculties" means those whose semen (*śukra*) is excessively depleted.

In this context, one should follow the underlying meaning that *anuvāsana* (oil enema) is indicated for cases of pure Vāta and the like, while *nirūha* (decoction enema) is indicated for types of non-appetite resulting from food aversion.

Now follows the answer to the question regarding in which conditions and by what means an enema (basti) should be administered—beginning with the verse "In those overcome by heat" (*uṣṇābhibhūteṣu*) and so forth.

Although one might have simply stated "in those overcome by heat" (*uṣṇābhibhūte*) and "in those overcome by cold" (*śītābhibhūte*), the author uses the term "in all cases" (*sarvatra*). By doing so, he demonstrates that even in cases of being overcome by the qualities of unctuousness, dryness, heaviness, or lightness, an enema prepared with drugs possessing the opposite qualities should be administered.
He states the diseases that must be constantly purified: "In cases of leprosy, urinary disorders, and so forth.
Here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of loss of appetite, drowsiness, elephantiasis, and others.
"In those who are fat" means in those who possess excess fat (medasvin).
"Not for those with diminished tissues" (kṣīṇakṣata): those with diminished [tissues] should be understood as those suffering from consumption (rājayakṣman) and similar ailments.
"Those to be purified" refers to those who cause [the humors] to be expelled;
and "those whose lifespan is bound to their defects" refers to those who lose their lives by the mere act of purifying and removing [those defects].
Describing the vast scope of the enema's praise, he again provides the answer to the question "What are the qualities of the enema? with the verse beginning "śākhāgatā" and so forth.

By the phrase "located in the branches, the trunk, and the vital points" (marmas), the three types of disease pathways—branches and so on—are included. Indeed, by the term "born in the vital points" (marmajas), there is an inclusion by association of those diseases arising in the joints, which reside in the middle disease pathway; for here, the vital points, bones, and joints are stated to be the middle disease pathway.
Furthermore, by the word "all" (sarva) in the phrase "above all," the three aforementioned disease pathways are also included according to their divisions into upward, downward, and transverse.

By the term "arising from all parts and limbs," there is the inclusion of what was previously mentioned, even through the distinction of localized versus systemic involvement of all limbs. Regarding the phrase "superior to wind" (*vāyoḥ param*), it means that there is nothing superior—that is, more excellent—than wind.
By this, although both phlegm (*kapha*) and bile (*pitta*) are also causes of disease, it is nevertheless stated that wind alone is the most important.
He states the reason for the preeminence of wind in the passage beginning with "feces, urine," and so forth.

In the phrase "pittādi," the word "ādi" (and so forth) includes *kapha*. (Note that *kapha* is not included by the word *mala* [impurity]). By the word *mala*, the impurities of the other *dhātus* (tissues), such as feces and the like, are included. By the word *āśaya* (receptacle), the receptacles known as *prasāda* (pure essences) distinct from the *malas*, as well as the *dhātus* themselves, are included. The term "performing dispersal and aggregation" means performing separation and union. By this it is meant that since *vāyu* alone effects the conjunction and disjunction of the *doṣas*, *malas*, and *dhātus*, therefore *vāyu* alone is the primary factor in all diseases, which consist of the union of *doṣas*, *dūṣyas* (vitiated tissues), and excretory waste (*viṇmala*).

Alternatively, does the word *āśaya* (receptacle) connect with each [of the products] such as feces (*viṭ*) individually, while the location-holder is understood through the location itself? And is it by the very conjunction and separation of feces and so forth that the inclusion of all substrates of disease occurs?
Let it be so; since *vāta* is thus predominant, he asks "What [follows] from this?
and says: "Of that," etc., meaning the primary medicine. As it has been stated: "Enema (*basti*) is the foremost among those things that alleviate *vāta*" (Sūtra 25).
Therefore, it is entirely logical that enema (basti) constitutes half of medical treatment, as well as the entirety of medical treatment.
In this regard, he describes the characteristics of the enema (basti) when it has been administered and when it has not, in sequence—beginning with "at the navel" and so forth.

"Having stirred" means having agitated; "having moistened the body" means having pervaded the body with its essence in the form of *vīrya* (potency), for it is said: "By its *vīrya*, the enema draws out the *doṣas* from the feet to the head" (Suśruta Cikitsā-sthāna, Chapter 35).
By the word "sneha" (unctuousness), "essence" (sāra) is intended; as in: "The body [perishes] from the depletion of sneha" (Ci. A. 8).
"Properly" means without remainder, "comfortably" means without causing any disorder.
Having described the characteristics of the correct application of the enema at that time, he now speaks of what occurs at a subsequent time, beginning with the words "prasṛṣṭa" and so forth.

Regarding the reading ‘āmayalāghavāni’ instead of ‘āśayalāghavāni’ here, the word ‘vā’ (or) should be understood after ‘rogopaśāntiḥ’ (the alleviation of disease); by this, ‘rogopaśāntiḥ’ refers here to the alleviation of those disorders that are curable by non-unctuous enemas (nirūha). 41.
"Syāt" and so forth describe the symptoms of insufficient enema (basti-ayoga); "not properly purged" means it has been purged by an insufficient dose.
He states the symptoms of excessive administration of enemas by means of extension [of the rule], beginning with the words "the sign," etc.
He states the characteristics of the correct application of an oil enema (anuvāsana), beginning with "it returns," etc.;
"unobstructed" means without attachment,
[referring to] the bodily constituents (dhātus) such as blood and the rest.
The persistence of dreams and the persistence of sleep are created; thus they are unbound.
The characteristics of excessive application (*atiyoga*) of the *anuvāsana* enema beginning with the word "adha" include dryness and roughness of the body due to the lack of oleation,
as well as nausea and other such symptoms.
He states the time for returning out of appropriate affection, beginning with the words "yasya" and so forth.
"Yāmān" means for the watches (of the night);

"sa viśuddhadehaḥ" means that, due to the correct application of the oil enema procedure (*anuvāsana-prayoga*), he is free from complications arising from the enema; "āśvāgate" means having returned quickly. "Another [enema] should be administered" means that at that very time, another unctuous substance (*sneha*) should be given.
Again, he states the justification for the giving of affection: "For affection does not cause one to be loved if it does not persist" (46).
Now he states the specific answer to the question regarding the number: "Thirty," and so forth.
The designations *karman*, *kāla*, and *yoga* should be understood respectively as referring to the groups of thirty, sixteen, and eight enemas (*basti*).
Regarding the phrase "time (*kāla*) is half of that," the word "half" (*ardha*) does not denote an equal division; therefore, half of thirty becomes sixteen.
With the words "sānvasanāḥ" and so forth, he explains the classification of the non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) and unctuous enemas (anuvāsana) for the [twelve] actions and so on:

"sānvasanāḥ" refers to those which are given after one unctuous enema has been administered; thus, through the individual association with the unctuous enema, there are twelve non-unctuous enemas, making twenty-four enemas in total, as stated previously at the beginning.

"Subsequent" (*parataḥ*) means that after twelve *nirūha* enemas, there should be six *nirūhas* interspersed (*antaritāḥ*) by [other treatments]; thus, twelve *bastis* are to be completed. "Five at the end, middle, and beginning" (*parādimadhyāḥ*) refers to those five oleation (*sneha*) enemas which are distributed at the end, middle, and beginning. In this context, there are two *sneha* enemas at the beginning and two at the end; with one *anuvāsana* (oil enema) placed between three *nirūhas*, there are thus five *sneha* enemas in total.

As for those who maintain that the oil enema (*anuvāsana*) should be administered on the very same day as the decoction enema (*nirūha*), according to their view, there is one at the beginning and one at the end on another day, thus making five in total; in this way, the administration of the *anuvāsana* during both the main therapeutic period (*karma-kāla*) and the others should be explained as being either on the day of the *nirūha* or on a subsequent day. Furthermore, when administering *nirūhas* separated by a single oil enema, one need not fear the agitation of *vāta*, because the *nirūhas* given during the therapeutic periods and so forth are in the form of *yāpanā-basti*s; since these are inherently unctuous (*snigdha*), they do not cause *vāta* agitation.

Although these [categories] such as *karman* and so forth are not employed in the specific sections of the treatise (*śāstra*), nevertheless, this terminology of *karman* and so on is intended solely for the purpose of technical usage within that science, just like the designations *yamaka*, *mahācchapa*, and so on. Therefore, the claim that a text explaining *karman* and the other categories is non-Vedic (*anārṣa*) because such terminology is not seen in use within the treatise is refuted; furthermore, the terminology of *karman* and so forth exists even in other systems (*tantra*).

For instance, Jatūkarṇa states: "There are thirty enemas (bastis), consisting of sixteen, eight, and six applications of action (karma-kalā-yoga); there are twelve non-unctuous enemas (nirūhas) interspersed with unctuous ones, and six and three [others]; those beginning with one unctuous application end with five, three, and one. Hārīta also says: "The wise declare that the action consists of thirty [applications]," and so forth.
Some authorities state that the application of these actions and others is for the [pacification of] vāta and the other doshas. 47–48.
With the words "three, five," and so forth, he describes the unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) for the purpose of oleation.

Regarding this, those who read "of vāta and the others" (*avātādikānām*), for them the word "and the others" (*ādi*) includes both pitta and kapha as well. Furthermore, the use of the plural number is justified because, through a *bahuvrīhi* compound with attributive significance (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi*), it refers to vāta, which possesses a plurality of qualities.

As it is stated in the *Kuṣṭhanidāna*: "When vāta and the others are vitiated" (*Ni.a.* 5); likewise, in the *Kiyantaḥśirasiya* chapter as well, plurality is indicated by the phrase "of vāta and the others, and of rasa and the others" (*Sū.a.* 17).
However, others read it as "of those in whom vāta is predominant."

In this context, the administration of four or six unctuous substances—even when given in pairs—is not contradictory, because this [administration] is performed for the purpose of oleation as an ancillary part of the *nirūha* enema. However, regarding the administration of an odd number, since it is prescribed for the *anuvāsana* enema as its primary feature by the rule "one should give an odd number of enemas," there is no contradiction due to the difference in scope. This is because the *anuvāsana*, which has oleation as its objective, must be concluded with an odd-numbered administration once the oleation process is complete. Alternatively, "odd" (*ayugma*) refers to the numbers themselves according to the traditional interpretation; thus, five options are prescribed here: three, five, three and four (making seven), five and four (making nine), and five and six (making eleven).
In another tantra, the administration of unctuous enemas in pairs is stated, as follows: "One should administer two or even three unctuous enemas to a person who is dry and has an excess of *vāta*;
having recognized that the body has become unctuous, one should thereafter administer a non-unctuous enema" (*Suśruta Saṃhitā*, Cikitsā-sthāna 37).
By the word "channels" (*srotas*), the obstructed vessels are indicated.

Now, he describes the formulations for head-purgation (śirovirecana) in their proper sequence, as well as the signs of improper administration and excessive administration, beginning with the words "viśuddha... and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "of one whose body is purified": this refers here to the fact that head-purgation (*śirovirecana*) must be preceded by purification, which is to be accomplished through the five types of therapeutic procedures (*pañcakarman*). Therefore, this sequence should be understood as applicable even to a person who has not been purified by emesis and so forth, provided that head-purgation alone can be successfully administered. The term *snigdha* means [the body] has been treated with oil massage (*abhyaṅga*), head-baths (*śirobasti*), internal potions, and so on; *talasvedita* means it has been fomented over the palms of the hands.
The phrase "three times, twice, or once" should be applied appropriately on that very day, depending on the threefold strength of the defects (doṣas), such as their predominance.
"Clarity of the senses" means the sharpness of the eyes and other faculties toward their respective objects;
"and he would see darkness" means he would see everything pervaded by gloom.

He states the connection [of the following] as a supplementary discussion regarding the treatment for excessive (atiyoga) and deficient (ayoga) application: "It may be a nourishing drink," and so forth.
By the phrase "soft and liquid," the treatment for excessive application is indicated;
by "but sharp again, not in deficiency," it is meant that in the case of deficient application, a sharp head-purgative (śirovirecana) should be administered once more.
50–52 – He concludes the exposition on the application of the five therapies with the words beginning "Thus, in the case of the patient," and so forth.

By the statement "the happiness of the afflicted and the healthy," it should be understood that the application of the aforementioned fivefold therapy (*pañcakarma*) is a cause of happiness because it removes disease in the afflicted and increases strength and longevity in the healthy. Furthermore, the commencement of the fivefold therapy for the healthy is to be known as already declared in the *Sūtrasthāna* beginning with the words, "In the first month of Mādhava" (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 7).

He provides the answer to the question, "Once [the procedure] has been performed, for how long is there a period of avoidance? with the words beginning with "kālas tu" (but as for the time), etc. It means that the period of avoidance should be twice as long as the duration of time occupied by the application of enemas (*basti*) and so forth; for this reason, it is stated that one must avoid [certain things] for a period double that time. Here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), emesis (*vamana*), purgation (*virecana*), and head-evacuation (*śirovirecana*) are included. By explaining enemas first, he demonstrates their primary importance.
54. The answer to the question “What is to be avoided? begins with “atyāsana,” etc.; *āsana* refers to the state of being seated.
Standing means staying upright; moving means traveling by means of chariots, horses, and so forth.

These have been described here as the most prominent [factors]. Therefore, even those such as anger and excessive reflection, which are prohibited in the preparation of emetics and other applications, must certainly not be indulged in.
The answer to the question beginning with “being led forth” (*praṇīyamāna*) and so on is [the verse] beginning with “when bound” (*baddha*) and so on.
When the eyes are closed and [the breath] is directed unevenly, it does not go forth because it is obstructed by the parts of the rectum;

thus, by the passage beginning with "it does not exit easily," the answer to the question "and after a long time, by what? is given: "it does not exit easily" means that it comes out after a long time and having caused pain.
"Enveloped by defects" means obstructed by a powerful defect;
"small" means of small measure;
"of little potency" means having mild potency due to the absence of hot, salty, and other such qualities.
By the phrase "and when [it] has arrived," he states the reason for the swift arrival.

When vāta is excessively increased, the unctuous substance (sneha), being obstructed by the vāta, does not reach its destination (the receptacle) and consequently returns quickly; furthermore, a person with weak anal sphincters is unable to retain the unctuous substance, as the weakness of the anus results from the debility of the closing folds (saṃvaraṇī-valī). 56.

The answer to the question beginning with "sādhyāḥ" (curable) is as follows: "by fat and phlegm," etc., meaning by fat (*medas*) or by phlegm (*kapha*). Here, having observed colic and other symptoms, one might administer oleation (*sneha*) under the mistaken impression that it is pure *vāta*, failing to recognize the presence of an occlusion (*āvaraṇa*); for this very reason, the term "unwise" (*abudha*) is used.

It is also stated elsewhere: "When the wind (vāyu) is aggravated by the obstruction of the channels, or when it is excessively increased by fat (medas) or phlegm (kapha), nourishment with oleation is not recommended at the outset.
The term "not being reflected upon" means not being correctly understood.
He states the reason for the very fact that [the object] is not being correctly known: "by means of one another," and so forth;
here, by the word *roga*, the *doṣa* (humor/defect) is intended.

Because their pathways are mutually obstructed, they become difficult to grasp; likewise, being vitiated and coalesced by the *dhātus* such as blood and the rest, they become difficult to discern. And when not recognized, they do not reach pacification through their own respective remedies. By "their own respective remedies" is meant those remedies for a single *doṣa* that are independent of other *doṣas*, *dhātus*, or causes such as the obstruction of the pathways. Indeed, such a remedy is simply not appropriate for those [conditions] existing in that state; therefore, non-pacification is entirely logical. Thus, having understood the mutual obstructions of the *doṣas* as well as the specific types of coalescence with the *dhātus*, one must pursue the detailed analysis (*prapañca*) of the disease.
Now, he states the failure [of treatment] when the disease has been diagnosed but increases due to improper application and other factors by the physician: "And all," etc.

"Contrary time" means that which is administered at an improper time, and "due to incorrect application" means because the medicines are not prepared or administered accordingly; for instance, it is the established doctrine that medicine should be consumed once it has been properly digested,
and that only a medicine which is thus correctly applied succeeds.
With the words "praśnān" and so forth, he summarizes the meaning of the chapter.
And the summary is clear:

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Successful Formulation of Preparations," in the Siddhisthāna of the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka-saṃhitā composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Siddhisthāna, Chapter 2 (110 of 120)]

When the conceptual framework is established, there arises a desire to know regarding the engagement in and withdrawal from the five types of action for one who has understood their application; therefore, in order to demonstrate that, the "Success regarding the Fivefold Action" (*pañcakarmīyasiddhi*) is stated.
Success regarding the fivefold action is the success composed with reference to the knowledge of the objects of engagement in and withdrawal from the fivefold action.
With the words beginning with "yeṣām" (of whom), he summarizes the subject matter of the chapter and makes his formal declaration:

by the phrase "for whom the five actions are not to be performed," he indicates that those for whom these actions—both individually and collectively—are not to be performed will be described separately.
By the words beginning with "caṇḍa," [the author] states the objects that fall outside the scope of all five types of therapeutic action (*pañcakarma*).

Although in the chapters on "The Destruction of the Country" (*Vi.a.3*) and "The Conquest of Disease by Medicine" (*Vi.a.8*), those who are beyond reproach and incurable have already been declared as not to be treated, they are nevertheless mentioned again here because they are relevant to the present context.

In the case of the "violent" (*caṇḍa*) and others, the administration of medicine is prohibited because it is impossible; in the case of the "ungrateful" (*kṛtaghna*) and others, medicine does not succeed simply due to the power of their unrighteousness (*adharma*), and moreover, by treating such unrighteous persons, only unrighteousness results—thus, desisting from treatment is enjoined.

"One who hates a virtuous king and physicians" means one who hates both a virtuous king and physicians; alternatively, "virtuous" (*sat*) is an adjective qualifying both the king and the physicians, and thus "one hated by such [persons]" (*sadādidveṣyaḥ*) refers to a person who is hostile toward them by chance, namely an atheist (*nāstika*).
"Deprived of instruments" means lacking the necessary tools;
"an enemy" refers to one who harms the physician, whereas one who merely hates the physician is not necessarily harmful—this is the distinction.
"One who is conceited about being a physician" is one who considers himself a physician.
"Incurable by physicians" means not dependent on physicians;
"by all" refers to emetics and other such measures, as well as pacifying treatments and the like;
"of these" refers to those other than the violent (caṇḍa) and so forth.

Now, demonstrating that even those diseases which are currently fit for treatment may become unsuitable for the five therapeutic procedures (*pañcakarman*) due to differences in their state caused by the combination of factors such as the disease itself, he says: "First, those unfit for emesis," and so forth.
The phrase "first, those unfit for emesis" (*avamya ādau tāvat*) is intended to indicate what was previously introduced.
The word *prasakta* is connected individually with sexual intercourse (*maithuna*) and the others.
*Saṃvṛtakoṣṭhaḥ* means one whose abdominal cavity has been reduced by wind; some say it means "one whose abdominal cavity is pervaded by wind.
In that context, he states the reason for not administering emetics as previously described, beginning with the words "of one who is wounded" (*kṣatasya*).

The obstruction of breath is death; others say it is the loss of strength. By reading "fatigue and so forth" as a separate term, he shows that the obstruction of breath is of a lesser degree compared to the former [death].
In the phrase "fear of cutting and injury from wind-blood," "cutting of blood" (raktaccheda) refers to the letting of blood (raktamokṣa).
"Of one who is delicate" means one with a soft body;
"because it draws out the heart" means because it injures the heart;
"the same as that" refers to the defect mentioned previously regarding those suffering from upward-moving *raktapitta*.
He describes emesis even in conditions where it is generally prohibited, beginning with the words "In all [conditions]," and so forth.

Although at the end of this chapter he will state that emesis is forbidden in all the aforementioned conditions, nevertheless, it should be understood here that emesis must certainly be performed according to the prescribed method.

Having stated that "the remaining [diseases] are fit for emesis," he further demonstrates that conditions such as chronic rhinitis (pīnasa) and others also fall within the scope of emesis, thereby showing that emesis is particularly appropriate for them; this same principle should be understood when he subsequently points out other subjects for purgation and so forth.

By the term "most important" (*pradhānatama*), the author causes one to grasp that portion of the text which demonstrates its preeminence, as stated in part in the chapter on major diseases (*mahārogādhyāya*) beginning with "the breaking of the embankment of a field" (*kedārasetubhede*, Sūtra 20). Therefore, that fragment of the text which was stated there—"Physicians consider emesis (*vamana*) to be indeed the most important among all therapeutic measures for *śleṣman* (phlegm), because it enters the stomach (*āmāśaya*) from the very beginning and extracts the root of the morbid *śleṣman*; when *śleṣman* has been conquered therein, even the disorders of *śleṣman* located within the body reach pacification, just as when the embankment of a field is broken, the rice, *ṣaṣṭika* grains, and other crops, though flooded by water, undergo desiccation; so it is here"—is to be connected here [to the present context]. Likewise, regarding the preeminence of purgation (*virecana*) and similarly regarding the preeminence of enemas (*basti*), if he will state a fragment of the text demonstrating the preeminence mentioned in the chapter on major diseases as a partial illustration, it should be applied there by supplying (*adhyāhāra*) that text.
He states the contraindications for purgation: "Those who are not to be purged," and so forth.

"Subhagakṣataguda" refers to one with a subhaga-guda (a naturally well-formed anus) and one with a kṣata-guda (an injured anus); others, however, say that "subhaga" means one who has been raised in comfort.
Those with a ruptured anus, those with an uncovered rectum, and those beginning with those afflicted by wounds up to pregnant women are listed among the contraindications for emesis;
[if these subjects undergo] "purgation," it is implied that it will produce pain.
The phrase "one suffering from downward hemorrhage (*adhobhāgaraktapitta*) likewise" means that [the treatment] would kill [the patient] due to excessive discharge.
In the phrase "due to desire, etc.," the word "etc. includes grief, anger, and so forth.

In this context, non-discharge and scant discharge are considered *ayoga* (deficiency); for it has been said: "Deficiency consists in [discharge] occurring in the reverse order, or not occurring at all, or occurring only slightly" (Siddhi-sthāna, Chapter 6).
The defects of yoga (ayogadoṣa) include those to be described hereafter, such as displacement (vibhraṃśa), hiccups (hikkā), and stiffness (stambha);
"defect of undigested matter" (āmadoṣa) refers to conditions such as visūcikā caused by the defect of āma;
and "fecal receptacle" (purīṣakoṣṭha) refers to a digestive tract obstructed by feces and the like.
Regarding the statement "spoken concerning difficult emesis," it refers to the defects previously mentioned in the section on emesis (vv.
He now states those who are especially fit for purgation, beginning with "kuṣṭha" and so forth.
In the case of *visūcikā*, purgation should be understood as necessary at a later stage for the purpose of eliminating the remaining morbid humors.
Regarding those who should not be given non-unctuous enemas (*anāsthāpya*): "Those who should not be given [enemas]," and so forth.
By the term *madhumeha*, all types of *prameha* are included;
*dūṣyodara* refers to *sannipātodara*; and *yāna* refers to vehicles such as chariots and the like.
The word "enema" (*basti*) is to be supplied after "burns";
the word "of the sense organs" (*indriyāṇām*) is to be supplied after "disorder" (*vibhraṃśam*);
and "it should rise upward" means it should emerge through the mouth and other [orifices].
They say that for those who are intoxicated or unconscious, there would be a complication (*vyāpad*)—namely, a complication characterized by intoxication and fainting.

In cases such as abdominal obstruction (*baddhodara*), enema (*basti*) is prohibited for those suffering from flatulence; therefore, the prescription of *nirūha* enemas, along with oil enemas (*anuvāsana*), in the passage beginning with "to one who is unctuous and suffering from abdominal obstruction" and ending with "the *nirūha* with *anuvāsana*" (Ci. A. 13), remains consistent. Others, however, maintain that within the chapter on abdominal diseases itself, the mention of "one with abdominal obstruction" refers specifically to cases of abdominal disease with constipation (*savibandha*); thus, the general prohibition of *nirūha* for *baddhodara* here does not contradict that [specific] view. 14–15.
He states those who should be specifically excluded: "In all limbs," and so forth;
[here] pain, emaciation, and stiffness are connected with the buttocks and other such parts.

In the presentation of those for whom non-unctuous enema (ananuvāsana) is contraindicated, "one who has eaten" is mentioned among those for whom unctuous enema (anāsthāpya) is contraindicated; the inclusion of "one who has not eaten" is for the purpose of excluding that case. The distinction is that because it is not obstructed by food, the unctuous enema moves upward when administered on an empty stomach, whereas the decoction enema (nirūha) does not. Furthermore, because the oil in an unctuous enema is characterized by its subtle nature and tendency to spread, it is administered in the evening; thus, due to fasting for that duration, it moves upward through the body which is then empty.

Although *anuvasana* (unctuous enema) is prescribed by the rule, "In cases of colic and lack of appetite for food" (*Siddhi-sthāna*, A. 1), nevertheless, its prohibition here in the context of *aruci* (anorexia), which is included within the causes of lack of appetite for food, is not contradictory; for while *anabhinandana* (lack of relish) is merely a lack of faith caused by *vāta*, *aruci* is always a state of non-desire. Furthermore, mere *vāta*-disease is characterized by lack of faith, whereas one afflicted by pure *vāta*-disease is fit for *anuvasana*.

By the phrase "like the uprooting of a tree," he demonstrates the textual passage from the chapter on major diseases (*mahārogādhyāya*) that proclaims the primacy of the non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*); namely, "Just as when the root of a tree is cut, the destruction of the trunk, branches, aerial roots, flowers, fruits, leaves, and so forth is inevitable" (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 20). And by the phrase "like watering the root of a tree," he includes the textual passages proclaiming the primacy of the unctuous enema (*anuvasana*) as previously stated in the section on pharmaceutical preparations (*kalpanāsiddhi*), beginning with: "For just as a tree watered at its root... (Śārīra Sthāna, Chapter 1), and so on. (17–19)
He states those who are unfit for head-evacuation (śirovirecana): "Those unfit for head-evacuation," and so forth.
"Desirous of drinking" means desirous of drinking unctuous substances (sneha) and the like. "Exhausted from drinking" refers to one afflicted by a disease requiring further drinking on another day.
"Out of season" refers to the cold, hot, and rainy seasons.
On a "bad day" (*durdina*) means on a day covered by clouds.
"When the head-purgative has been administered" means when they have been made to drink unctuous substances (*sneha*).
A "cripple" (*kuṇi*) is one with a bent hand; a "bed-crawler" (*pīṭhasarpī*) is a lame person.

In the passage beginning with "out of season" (*anṛtau*) and "on a cloudy day" (*durdine*), by the phrase "due to the defects of cold" (*śītadoṣāt*), it is indicated that [the oil] administered during the cold season or on a cloudy day causes putridity of the nose, whereas that administered during summer or the rainy season causes diseases of the head. Others, however, explain "out of season and cloudy day" as referring to a cloudy day that is not part of the rainy season. With the verse beginning "head, teeth," etc., [the author] specifically describes those who are fit for head-purgation (*śirovirecana*).
The term "stiffness" (*stambha*) is connected with the head, teeth, and neck.
Here, *pīnasa* refers to chronic rhinitis (*pakvapratiśyāya*); thus, there is no contradiction, as nasal evacuation (*śirovireka*) is contraindicated for acute rhinitis.

*Apatantraka* is indeed a specific variety of *apatānaka*, characterized by loss of consciousness (*niḥsañjña*); for it has been stated: "That which is unconscious is *apatantraka*" (Sūtra-sthāna, chapter 9).

The *śūlaharṣacālā* [plants] are used in conjunction with the tooth; *akṣirājī* (also known as *netrarājī*) is a specific eye disease. Even in cases of a wind disorder (*vātavikāra*), purgation is appropriate here precisely because it eliminates the phlegm and wind that have reached the site through their respective locations.

"Like a reed-stalk attached to *muñja* grass": just as a reed-stalk (*īṣikā*, *śarikā*) attached to the parts of the *muñja* grass is pulled out without damaging the *muñja*, so too the matured morbid humor (*doṣa*) is removed from the head; this is the meaning.
(22) Head-purgation (*śirovirecana*) is prohibited outside the proper season (*anṛtu*); he states its prescription according to specific conditions, beginning with "the rainy season" (*prāvṛṭ*), etc.
"In others" refers to the winter, summer, and rainy seasons.
By the mention of "urgent cases," he prohibits [the use of medicinal substances] for non-urgent diseases.

Regarding urgent cases as well, for the purpose of counteracting cold and other such factors, he says: "by the application of artificial qualities"; the application of artificial qualities should be performed as described in the chapter on the physician's victory over disease (*rogabhiṣagjitīya*).
Showing the counteraction of heat and other factors according to specific times such as summer, he says: "In summer, in the forenoon," and so forth (verse 23).

Having stated the summary of the chapter's meaning, and having established [the conditions] both as being unsuitable for emesis and the like, and as being suitable for emesis and the like, he says "nor exclusively" and so forth, in order to preclude any certainty regarding the cessation or engagement in emesis and the like.
"One should adhere" means one should form a firm conviction.
By the phrase "it is to be reasoned out," even that which is not explicitly stated is to be inferred by the intelligent;

by this statement, he excludes those who lack intelligence. For it has been said: "Therefore, for the intelligent, there is reasoning through inference and exclusion (*ūhāpoha*), but for one of small intellect, it is better simply to follow what has been stated" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.8).
Now, as to why following what has been stated is indeed the highest good, and why one should not make an absolute determination [to that effect], he says: "For [an action] arises," and so forth.

This means that depending on the power of place, time, and strength—i.e., due to differences in place and so on—an action that is to be done might become something not to be done; that is, what was declared as a duty might become something that should not be performed. Likewise, an action that is normally avoided might become something to be done due to a particular circumstance.

He provides an illustration of even a prohibited act being performed due to the influence of a specific condition, such as emesis and so forth, in the passage beginning with "vomiting, heart disease," etc., [stating] "in its own treatment. By the phrase "indicated after reaching a particular condition" in the chapter on the treatment of vomiting, he demonstrates that there is no contradiction, because the prescription of what is otherwise prohibited applies only to a specific state according to the principle of general rule and exception (*utsargāpavāda*). In this same manner, the prescription of emesis and other acts in other contexts where they are exceptions should also be reconciled as referring to specific conditions.
Concluding the matter that has been established through reasoning and stated, he says: "Therefore," and so forth.

Even though the instruction of the treatise exists, one should perform even what is not explicitly stated by means of one's own intellect following the treatise. As it has been said: "Just as a begging bowl is to a mendicant, or a seed to a farmer, even a small sūtra serves for the acquisition of vast knowledge by those who possess intelligence" (Viśeṣa-sthāna, Chapter 8).

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Successful Application of the Five Purificatory Procedures," in the *Siddhisthāna* of the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā*, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Siddhisthāna, Chapter 3 (111 of 120)]

Having explained in the preceding chapter the scope and other details regarding the administration of emesis and so forth, the *Bastisūtrīyasiddhi* is now stated for the purpose of describing in detail the preparation of enemas as mentioned in the *Kalpanāsiddhi*.
The *Bastisūtrīyasiddhi* is the treatise composed concerning the aphorism (*sūtra*) that prescribes the procedural requirements (*itikartavyatā*) for the enema (*vasti*).
Regarding "of the abode of the Lord of Wealth" (dhaneśāyatana), which refers to the Himalaya; "the bladder for men" (bastirnarebhyaḥ), and so forth—these are the ten questions.
The "eye" (netra) is the tube (nalikā).

Regarding the question "What is the source (yoni) and what are the qualities (guṇa) of the enema (basti)?": here, *basti* refers to the bladder-sack (*bastipuṭaka*); *yoni* refers to the place of origin or the receptacle for the unctuous substance (*sneha*). Thus, the detailed exposition of the non-unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*)—including its method of administration and dosage—must be stated here. Therefore, the question regarding the procedure (*kalpa*) of the non-unctuous enema is to be understood as intended here. However, when the reading is "or what [is the rule] for the unctuous substance" (*snehasya vā kaḥ*), then it means: what is the protocol for the unctuous substance administered on the day following a decoction enema (*nirūha*)? And that meaning is indeed consistent with the subsequent text.
"What enemas are beneficial for whom" means: for which types of persons are enemas of which origins beneficial?
(3–5) "Having examined," etc.

In this context, it should be explained that the eleven items mentioned in the *Upakalpanīya* chapter—namely the defects (*doṣa*) and so forth, as well as the medicines (*bhaiṣajya*) and other factors—and the ten objects of examination mentioned in the *Rogabhiṣagjitīya* chapter, are all subsumed within these very ten [defects] that are said to be examined here. Furthermore, this inclusion of unmentioned items has already been stated by us in the *Yonivyāpattika* chapter and should be followed with due consideration. Having observed this with prior knowledge, all procedures—including emesis and the rest—become beneficial when they are applied with regard for the defects and other such factors.
The answer to the question, "Of what is his eye composed? is as follows: "Gold," and so forth; *trapu* is tin, and *rīti* is brass (*pittala*).

"With horns" means with the horns of buffaloes and the like; "with beautiful pericarps" means with well-arranged pericarps. Some read "with three pericarps," and the state of having three pericarps will be explained further on.
The answer to the question "Of what measure and form? is as follows: "Six," and so forth.

In that regard, from one year up to six years, [the measure] is six finger-breadths; for a twelve-year-old, the eye becomes eight finger-breadths; for a twenty-year-old, the eye becomes twelve finger-breadths.

Here, by stating the sequence out of order, it is shown that there is no variation in the measurement of the nozzle (*netra*) before six years of age or after twenty years of age, whereas there is a variation in the measurement of the nozzle after six years of age. Consequently, after six years of age, there is an increase of one-third of an *aṅgula* per year, and after twelve years of age, there is an increase of half an *aṅgula* per year; in this way, the stated measurement is fulfilled. As for the different measurements of the nozzle mentioned in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*, they should simply be disregarded because they do not cause significant contradiction.

For it is stated there: “The nozzle for those one year old, eight years old, and sixteen years old should be six, eight, and ten *aṅgulas* long respectively; for those over twenty-five years of age, it should be twelve *aṅgulas*. (Suśruta Cikitsā-sthāna, Chapter 35).
The fact that these nozzles have channels capable of passing *mudga* beans and so forth should be understood according to the respective lengths of six, twelve, and eight *aṅgulas*.

Here, by the word *karkandhu*, the small *śṛgāla-badarī* (fox-jujube) is intended; for it is stated in the Suśruta: “The aperture should be the size of the stone of a *kola* fruit. (Suśruta Cikitsā-sthāna, Chapter 35).

However, for the taking of large jujube fruits (*bṛhadbadara*), the tip [of the vessel] should be the size of the little finger; it is not fit to carry those. Seeing such a contradiction, some take the marrow of the jujube stone to be what is meant here by the word *karkandhu*.
*Satīna* refers to round peas (*vartulakalāya*).
The phrase "covered with a wick" (*vartyāpihitāni*) means that the openings must be covered with a wick in order to prevent the entry of other substances.

"According to age" means that the nozzle (*netra*) should be made with a circumference equal at both the base and the tip, using the thumb and the little finger respectively, for one who stands in the age for which the nozzle was prescribed.
With the words "straight," etc., he states the qualities of the nozzle;
"smooth" means not rough.

By the phrase "having the mouth of a pill" (*guṭikāmukha*), he indicates that because the mouth is circular, it is not sharp-edged. One *karṇikā* (projection) should be made at the tip for the purpose of preventing the [tube] from entering too deeply into the eye; there are two for the purpose of securing the enema bag (*basti*).
The answer to the question "From what [substances] and with what qualities is the enema (basti) prepared? is as follows: "jāradgava" and so forth—*jāradgava* means derived from an old bull.
*Basti* refers to the bladder;
*naṣṭasira* means one from whom the network of veins has been removed;
*vigandha* refers to one whose foul odor has departed.
"Reddened by decoctions" means colored by the infusion of medicinal extracts.

"Having observed the age, according to what is appropriate" means that whichever enema has the suitable dosage for a particular stage of life, as previously described according to the distinctions of age, that should be attached to his nozzle.
By this, the answer to the question "For whom is which enema? is provided.
He states the alternative procedure for when a bladder is unavailable: "In the absence of a bladder," and so forth.
"Plavaja" refers to a bird with a pouch-like throat known as the "plava."
The *aṅkapāda* is the leather-thrush (*carmacāṭaka*); its skin is to be taken for the purpose of the bladder.
This is the answer to the question beginning with "the procedure for the non-unctuous enema" (*nirūhakalpa*), namely: "suitable for an asthāpana enema," and so forth.

"In the bright fortnight" (śuklapakṣe) is stated because the bright fortnight is praised for all undertakings; however, Hārīta has prescribed the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) specifically for this. For it is said: "The procedure should be performed during the dark fortnight; those learned in the scriptures state that at birth, all diseases are destroyed and become well-subdued. In the bright fortnight the gods are born, while in the dark fortnight the asuras and all diseases are born. Therefore, the treatment of disease should always be carried out during the dark fortnight.
"One-pointed" (ekāgram) means having a mind focused solely on the application of the enema (basti). 12
By the words beginning with "balām," he describes the procedure for the enema (basti);
here, the measure of one pala applies to each individual substance, including both the three myrobalans (triphalā) and the five roots (pañcamūlī).
"Phalas" refers to *madana* fruits; and here, eight of them are used according to their very form.

In this context, regarding the herbs such as *bala* and others, according to the standard procedure for decoction (*kvātha*), the total weight is sixty-six *pala*s plus eight *madana* fruits. Because of the rule "the decoction is equal to the substance to be decocted," there is a large volume of decoction. Furthermore, even when three layers (*puṭa*) are administered in an enema (*basti*), since the rule is to give ten *pala*s of decoction per layer, only thirty *pala*s are ultimately utilized. Although the remainder is useless, nevertheless, because of the words of the Great Sage, a decoction prepared exactly as the specified quantity is stated here becomes efficacious; therefore, this should not be questioned. For it has been said: "The way they act is the means" (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 26). Alternatively, this was stated for the purpose of illustrating the proportional division of the quantity of the decoction substance actually used; thus, in accordance with that, one should take only as much of the substance to be decocted as is suitable for preparing the decoction actually required.
Each of the ingredients beginning with *yavānī* should be one *picu* per *pratinirūha* enema; a *picu* is a *karṣa* of oil—that is, of ghee or sesame oil—since this has been stated previously.
Furthermore, this dosage of oil should be understood as applying to a person of normal constitution (*prakṛtistha*), according to the rules that will be explained later.

By the phrase "according to reason (yuktyā) [and] honey and rock salt," he shows that the measurement of honey and rock salt is not fixed with respect to the base substance and other factors; the word "and" (ca) indicates that the measurement of meat broth, milk, cow urine, and so forth is also not fixed. We shall demonstrate the established rules for the measurement of these later, in the section on the measurement of decoctions (kaṣāya).
Regarding the term "having caused to exhale" (ucchvāsya), one intends the exit of wind produced by the impact of the substance through the act of exhalation;
"without folds" (nirvalīkam) is an adverbial modifier of the action.
"Placed at the tip of the nozzle" means it is applied to the opening of the nozzle-tip in order to first prevent the escape of the liquid and so forth.

"With the body smeared with oil" implies that, by association with the application of oil (*abhyaṅga*), sudation (*sveda*) is also to be understood; thus, the meaning is "one whose body has been anointed and fomented. For it is stated elsewhere: "One should administer a non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*) to one whose body has been anointed and fomented" (Su.Ci.A.
38). He now describes the procedure for the bed, which arises from the context, beginning with "the person on the bed," etc.

The two alternatives—either with the head level or slightly lowered—should be performed according to the patient's preference; alternatively, for a person whose waist region is elevated, the bed should be made level, while for one with a low waist, the head should be raised. In this way, the enema (basti) will properly follow the body of those two.
"With the left" means with the left side; the purpose of lying on the left side is as will be stated later in the passage beginning with "For [the digestive fire] resides in the left.
The connection is that, having prepared the person with all the aforementioned qualities, one should administer it.
He was lying down in such a way that his own arm served as a pillow; "pillow" (upadhāna) here means a cushion,
and "the other" (itarat) refers to the right thigh and shank.

Having extended the left thigh and contracted the right thigh over it—meaning with the left thigh spread out and the right thigh drawn in—one should insert [the nozzle] into the lubricated anus to the extent of one-fourth of the tube; "one-fourth" refers to the entire portion delimited by the septum (karṇikā);
"along the spinal column" means having directed it following the spinal column.

In the passage beginning with "akampana" (non-trembling), "kampana" means shaking; "vepana" means trembling; and "lāghava" means quickness of action. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the grasping and squeezing of the bladder and other such actions are included.

Here, by demonstrating [the procedure] while performing it—specifically through the phrase "having squeezed once and given"—he prohibits repeated squeezing after resting, as that would generate wind (*vāyu*).
He states the fault of horizontal resolve and so forth, beginning with the word "tiryak" (horizontally).
If there is a lateral application [of the enema], it does not flow; it holds back, and there is an obstruction of the anal folds. Because of that, the stream does not pass;
it causes excessive stiffness. Thus, the enema causes stiffness of the body, which is to say, a numbness of the physical frame.

If it is slightly salty, it is called *tanu* (thin) or *ayoga* (non-application); or, if it is thick (*sāndra*) yet only slightly salty, it is the opposite of *tanu*. It makes a person emaciated (*kṣāma*). If it is excessively salty, it is called *atimātra-lavaṇa* (excessive salt).
"Therefore" means that because faults have been demonstrated in the aforementioned methods,
it is "well-reasoned" (suyukta) to be devoid of animal-like mental application (*tiryakpraṇidhāna*) and the like, as well as devoid of coldness and so forth.

Regarding the passage "one should give first," some say it is not of Vedic origin (*anārṣa*); however, since this meaning is observed in other tantras, this reading is indeed correct. For it is stated in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*: "Having first given an *akṣa* of rock salt and two *palas* of honey, one should stir them in a vessel with the palm [of the hand]" (*Su.Ci.A.* 38), and so forth.
Furthermore, in the phrase "him again with liquids" (*punardravaiḥ tam*), the word "liquids" (*drava*) refers to a decoction (*kvātha*).
He states the purpose of that which was mentioned regarding lying on the left side, beginning with "vāmāśraye" and so forth:

Because the *grahaṇī* and the rectum (*guda*) have their seat on the left side, for one who sleeps on the left side, the *grahaṇī* and the rectum remain in their natural state (*prakṛtistha*). When the rectum is in its natural state, through the proper contact of the rectum with the bladder (*vasti*), pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs; likewise, the folds (*valaya*) become relaxed. Consequently, the enema (*basti*) enters easily. It should be understood that because the *grahaṇī* and the rectum are in their natural state, the enema, having pervaded them, easily nourishes the *grahaṇī*.
