Regarding the passage beginning with "viḍvāta," etc.: when the enema has been administered after drawing out the nozzle and releasing it during the forceful movement of feces and flatus,
the patient should lie on his back with a pillow placed beneath him.
He states the purpose of performing this [practice] as follows: "One attains vigor," and so forth. (25)

The passage beginning with "one [enema] draws down" (*eko 'pakarṣati*) and so forth refers to the prescription for administering one or more enemas according to the distinctions of the doshas, such as vāta and the rest; it should not, however, be explained as meaning that in a case of all three doshas, the first [enema] conquers vāta, the second conquers pitta, and the third conquers kapha. This is because, by the statement "the first, being unctuous and warm, along with meat, [is used] for vāta," and so forth, he will establish the numerical restriction specifically according to the distinctions of vāta and the other doshas.

Thus, one enema draws the wind (vāyu) from its own path, while the second draws the bile (pitta) from its own path; it should be understood that these two [enemas] conquer bile alone, whereas all three together conquer phlegm (kapha). Regarding the phrase "from its own path," this means from its own location.

Although it has been stated that an enema conquers only the dosha located in the colon (pakvāśaya), nevertheless, by the power of specific enema procedures, the removal of doshas even from the locations of pitta and so forth is declared. Therefore, generally there is the removal of doshas situated in that [colon], and by specific prescriptions, there is the removal of doshas situated in other locations.
This meaning is also stated in the *Jātūkarṇa*: "An enema should be administered once for each of the locations of the *vāyu* and other [doshas].

Here it is said that the second [enema] removes *pitta* and the third removes *kapha*. Nevertheless, even the first and second possess the capacity to remove *pitta* and *kapha*; however, because the removal of *pitta* is performed by the second and the removal of *kapha* by the third due to their proximity to the respective locations, it is stated that "the second removes *pitta* and the third removes *kapha*."

Although enema therapy is easily administered for pitta and kapha, nevertheless, this administration of enema should be understood to apply when pitta or kapha are either obstructed by vāta or associated with vāta; for it is stated in the Suśruta Saṃhitā: "Enema is recommended for vāta, pitta, kapha, and blood" (Su.Ci.A.

35). Regarding the phrase "when the śāli rice, etc., is digested," it means that the application of the non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) and its unguent should be performed once they have been digested and reside within the gastrointestinal tract.
In this case, the consumption of thin meat broth and similar foods is intended for the protection of the digestive fire (*agni*) which has been slightly impaired by the non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*);

however, the sequential regimen of gruels (*peyā*) and so forth is not employed here, because, unlike in the case of purgation, there is no emesis involved. For this very reason, Suśruta, having omitted the sequence of gruels, prescribed a sequence beginning with meat broth for the purpose of nourishment (*paribṛṃhaṇa*). By this, he indicates that when a non-unctuous enema is administered for the purpose of scraping (*lekhana*), an oil enema (*anuvāsana*) should be performed on that same day for the purpose of nourishment.

For this very reason, even though [the oil] is established through conceptualization, the necessity of performing the unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) on that same day is stated by the verse: “Therefore, the man is fit for the subsequent unctuous enema” (*Siddhi-sthāna*, A. 1). It is also stated in *Jatūkarṇa*: “When the evening meal has been digested, one should administer an unctuous enema for the sake of nourishment,” using oil equal to one-quarter part of the decoction used for the non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*). This means that if the *nirūha* consists of twenty-four *pala*s, the oil should be six *pala*s; this is the maximum dose for an unctuous enema. For it is said elsewhere: “The maximum is declared to be six *pala*s, while the medium dose should be three *pala*s.”

"The smallest dose for an oil enema (anuvāsana) is one and a half palas, divided into three parts. In the *Suśruta Saṃhitā* as well, this very same measure for the oil in an oil enema is stated according to the classification of doses.
He states the procedure for the purpose of preventing the rapid return of the oil: "Slightly," and so forth.
Furthermore, while the patient's body is held upright with the toes of the feet pointing upward, a retention time of one hundred measures (mātrā) should be performed.
Regarding the non-unctuous enema (nirūha), they consider the retention time for one lying supine to be thirty mātrās;
"the pair of toes" refers to the joint of the phalanges;
"one should pull" means one should draw [the enema back].
The statement "one should attend to sleep" is for the purpose of prohibiting other activities.
Now, defining the proportions of the decoction and the oil for that threefold non-unctuous enema (nirūha) consisting of twelve *prasṛta*s, he says: "The parts," and so forth.

By the phrase "five parts of the decoction," it is meant that in every case—whether in one with aggravated doshas or in a healthy person—for a non-unctuous enema of the twelve-*prasṛta* type, there are five parts of decoction; thus, there are five *prasṛta*s of decoction. He then states the difference in measurement for the oil according to the specific dosha and in the healthy state: "In pitta," and so forth.

In the case of *pitta*, the sixth part [of the dose] is for oil; likewise, when a person is in their natural state and healthy, it is the sixth part—meaning that here, the "sixth" is that which completes the number six. Thus, the sixth part of twelve *prasṛtas* becomes two *prasṛtas*.
By the word "oil," ghee, sesame oil, and so forth are included. However, when *vāta* is increased, it is the fourth part; the fourth part of the oil amounts to three *prasṛtas*.
"One-eighth part" means one and a half *prasṛtas*.

Regarding this matter, Hārīta states: "There are five parts of the decoction and the sixth part is of the oil; however, when pitta is predominant or in a healthy person, it should be that much; for vāta, it is a fourth part; for kapha, it is an eighth part; and when [kapha] has gone to excess, there is an alternative."

This quantity of oil should be applied even in a Nirūha enema where the quantity is deficient, according to the stated proportions for the decoction and the oil; however, no specific rule for the quantity of the remaining ingredients—madhuka-paste and rock salt—is mentioned here, as their amounts are also not fixed due to variations in the patient's constitution and other factors. Therefore, the total of twelve *prasṛta*s for honey and the other ingredients should be completed by using one *prasṛta* each for honey and so forth, according to the constitution and other factors; in this regard, based on the authority of Jatūkarṇa, there are always two *palas* of paste used.

For it is stated there: "In the twenty-fourth chapter, two *palas* of the substances to be ground, a small amount of honey and rock salt (*saindhava*), the oil to be mentioned later, and the remainder of the decoction [are used]; in the case of Vāta, six *palas* of oil for one in good health; four *palas* of ghee in Pitta, and three *palas* of oil in Kapha. Rock salt, however, is measured at one *karṣa*; since it is stated in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā*: "Having taken one *akṣa* of rock salt and two *prasṛtas* of honey" (Su.Ci.A. 38), and Hārīta says: "Honey should be given in the measure of one *prasṛta*, and they say a second [measure] of one *akṣa* of salt"—by this method, the preparation of rock salt and honey is established.

The filling of the portion filled with the aforementioned decoction, oil, paste, honey, and rock salt should be performed by means of an *āvāpa* (additive). Although not mentioned here, the *āvāpa* to be used—consisting of meat broth, milk, cow urine, and so forth, according to the specific doshas such as Vāta and others—should be understood from what will be stated later. For it will say: "In the case of Vāta, one unctuous and hot non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*) [is prescribed]; in Pitta, two sweet and cold ones with milk; and in Kapha, three pungent, hot, and sharp ones with cow urine; beyond these, no more should be administered."
Hārīta also said: "One should employ oil, jaggery, meat broth, milk, sour substances, urines, and rock salt—all these together with the fruit of *madana*—in the application of a *nirūha* enema.

As for what is stated in another treatise regarding the filling of twelve *prasṛta*s according to the specific division of each substance, it is as follows: "First, having added one *akṣa* of rock salt and two *prasṛta*s of honey..."
Then, having thoroughly stirred it, one should add three *prasṛta* measures of oil; once the oil has become a single mass, one should throw in one *prasṛta* measure of the paste (*kalka*);
and when that has fully blended, one should add a decoction (*kaṣāya*) measuring four *prasṛta*.
"And at the end, one should add an infusion (*āvāpa*) measured at two *prasṛtas*;

thus, a well-prepared enema (*basti*) becomes twelve *prasṛtas* in volume" (Suśruta Cikitsāsthāna 38). This [statement] refers specifically to the treatment of Vāta, because oil (*sneha*) subdues Vāta. However, regarding the four *prasṛtas* of decoction (*kaṣāya*) mentioned here, that is indeed approved by our own treatise.
As for what others read: "In the sequence of honey, oil, paste (*kalka*), decoction (*kaṣāya*), and infusion (*āvāpa*)," [our view remains as stated].
"Three, six, two, ten, and three *palas* for those suffering from wind (*vāta*);
four, four, two, ten, and four for bile (*pitta*);
and six, three, two, ten, and three for phlegm (*kapha*)—this is the non-unctuous enema (*nirūhaṇa*). This is indeed approved by us, as it conforms to our own treatise.
30—Now, demonstrating the dosage of *nirūha* according to the distinction of age, he says: "Nirūha... and so forth.

In the first year of a child’s life, the decoction and other ingredients for the non-unctuous enema (nirūha) should be prescribed according to the stated measurements in *palas*. Thereafter, there is an increase of half a *prasṛta* every year. Thus, by the twelfth year, the enema consists of six *prasṛtas*. From the twelfth year up to the eighteenth year, with an annual increase of one *prasṛta*, the measure reaches twelve *prasṛtas*. By the statement "beyond twelve," [the author] prohibits the use of enemas of greater volume accepted by some, which cause great harm; as is recorded in Hārīta as the opinion of certain authorities: "Half an *āḍhaka* is the maximum measure"; likewise in Suśruta: "Some say twelve *prasṛtas*, while others say thirty *palas," and so forth.
To demonstrate the measurement of the enema (basti), he says: "up to seventy," and so forth.
"That [measurement] up to seventy" refers to the twelve-prasṛta measure, which applies up to the age of seventy;
"like a sixteen-year-old" refers to the ten-prasṛta standard.
Demonstrating that the aforementioned *prasṛta* measure applies to both children and the elderly, he states another distinction therein: "In the case of a simple enema (*nirūhamātra*), etc.
For children and the elderly, the enema should be administered with the aforementioned measure of one *prasṛta*; specifically, their enema should be mild.
He will describe the procedure for making a sharp enema mild as follows: "Sharpness [is removed] by means of urine, *pīlu*, fire (ash), salt, alkali, and mustard seeds."
"What is appropriate for the occasion should be performed, as well as gentleness with milk and other such things" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 7).
Now he provides the answer to the question, "What is the rule for the bed? with the verse beginning "not too high," and so forth.

The distinction is that the rule for the bed previously mentioned pertains to that specific occasion, whereas this one pertains to subsequent times. "Pradhānamṛdvāstaraṇa" means a covering that is both excellent and soft; "upapanna" means furnished or provided with such a covering.
"Head facing east" is because of the statement: "The gods reside in the eastern direction; for the sake of their worship, [the head] should face east" (Suśruta Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 19).

The rules for preparing soups and other foods are prescribed according to the sequence of kapha, pitta, and vata; alternatively, they should be explained in accordance with the digestive fire (agni) as appropriate.
Demonstrating that the aforementioned rules must be applied to the procedures to be described hereafter, he says "In all [cases]," etc.
This is "the first," meaning it is primary—that is to say, it is the general rule (autsargika); by this, he indicates that there will be exceptions (apavāda) to it through specific prescriptions.
The answer to the question beginning with “What are the bastis? is as follows: “Of the two groups of five roots,” and so forth.
In this case, the meat is equal in quantity to the ten roots;
the *rasa* is a decoction (*kvātha*), and the sour liquid is fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*) or similar substances.

The phrase "with previous grinding" (sapūrvapeṣya) indicates that it should be combined with the paste (kalka) prescribed for *balā* and the like, while the mention of "combined with the three unctuous substances" (trisneha) serves as a reminder of the established rule for all enemas (basti) regarding the exclusion of marrow (*majjan*). For it is stated elsewhere: "The unctuous substance intended for enema should be understood as being of three types, excluding marrow."

Regarding the phrase "of the *sthirā* group" and so forth: although *madhu* (honey) and *saindhava* (rock salt) are already obtained through the general rule for administering enemas (*basti*) that has been stated, they are mentioned again here to ensure that oils and other substances do not predominate in this case; alternatively, their mention here may be for the purpose of recalling the general injunction. This same principle should be applied elsewhere as well when something already obtained through a general rule is mentioned again, such as in the passage beginning with "the root of *eraṇḍa*" and so on, where *palāśā*, *śaṭī*, and "short roots" constitute the *pañcamūla* of the *sthirā* group.
A *kaṃsa* is an *āḍhaka*;
"a measure of an *akṣa* by a part" means a measure of an *akṣa* by one part;
"half of a hundred from a goat" means it becomes fifty *palas*.
"Having ground" refers to [the preparation] combined with a paste of *balā* and so forth (35–45).
"Of *yaṣṭyāhvaya*" and so forth are four [formulas] for *pitta*, whereas the five previously mentioned are for *vāta*.
In this context, the preparation of the milk is accomplished solely by means of the technical rule for cooking milk (*kṣīrapākaparibhāṣā*).
From the words "yaṣṭyāhva-lodhra" up to "jīvanīya," there is one formulation;
here, the paste (*kalka*) consists of the life-sustaining (*jīvanīya*) drugs.

In this context, coolness is the general rule, and it is especially beneficial for those with soft bowels due to its suitability for *pitta*. Following this same principle, one should understand that coolness applies to other *pitta*-alleviating enemas as well.

Regarding the phrase "two karṣas" and so forth, the [herbs] such as *anantā*, *utpala*, *sārivā*, and the five roots of grass (*tṛṇapañcamūla*)—namely, "the roots of *śara*, *ikṣu*, *darbha*, *kāśa*, and *śālī*" (Ca.Ci.A.1.Pā.1)—are as stated in the text.
"Devoid of water" means boiled until only milk remains;
"rājakaśeru" is simply *kaśeru*;
"with *saindhava*" means with a small amount of *saindhava* salt.
In the passage beginning with "sasārivā," *śītapākī* means *śītalī*;
*madhuyaṣṭitailam* is oil prepared with *madhuyaṣṭi*; and *uttamāṅga* refers to the head.
46–55: Four enemas for kapha beginning with *koṣātaki*, as well as *śārṅgeṣṭā* and *guñjā*.

In this case, although the quantity may exceed [the standard] due to the ten *prasṛtas* of decoction as well as the paste (*kalka*), honey, and so forth, one should nevertheless prepare the medicinal compound in this very manner and administer exactly twelve *prasṛtas* of enema (*basti*), because a quantity exceeding that is prohibited.

In the case of *paṭola* and so forth, water should be prepared with the drugs starting from *paṭola* up to *pippalī*, and a second [enema] should be administered as before. For a patient suffering from *kapha*, a third [enema] should be prepared as an alkaline solution (*kṣāra*) using the two groups of five roots (*pañcamūla*) and other ingredients;
the alkali is *yavakṣāra*.

In the passage beginning with "rāsnā," *śampāka* is *caturaṅgula*, and *tiktā* is *kaṭurohiṇī*; here, the decoction of *piṇḍītaka* is also included as an additive (*āvāpa*) by which it enters [the formulation]; *piṇḍītaka* is *madana*.

The construction [of the verse] is as follows: even for those who have been excessively emaciated by dry (rūkṣa) medicines, this [formula] bestows strength when administered in these diseases such as leprosy (kuṣṭha), etc. (vv. 56–64). The formula beginning with *punarnavā* pertains to all combinations of vāta and other [doshas].
Vṛścīra, white punarnavā,
grains, and fruits— these constitute "grains and fruits"; this is prepared with two āḍhakas of milk and water, meaning it is combined with equal parts of milk and water totaling two prasthas.
Demonstrating the specific formulation and number of the aforementioned enemas that pacify vāta and other doshas, he says: "unctuous and hot," etc.;
"one" means there is indeed only one pouch.

Regarding the phrase "and with milk" (*payasā ca*), the pungency, heat, and sharpness associated with the milk should be understood as resulting precisely from its combination with substances that alleviate *kapha*, and not because the milk itself possesses those qualities.

By the statement "they should not be administered," he prohibits the administration of a fourth enema as prescribed in other treatises, which is excessively harmful to the body; as stated in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*: "The second, third, or fourth [enema] should be given as appropriate."

"However, when the signs have been correctly established and [the patient] has reached [the point of recovery], one should withdraw the enema" (Su.Ci.A.32); by this, the fourth administration is stated.

Now, he describes the specific post-prandial food according to the distinctions of Vāta and the other doshas, as well as the oil enema (anuvāsana), beginning with "In the case of Vāta, with meat broth," and so forth.

*Pratibhojana* refers to eating immediately after a *nirūha* enema. For *vāta*, an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) with *bilva* oil is prescribed; for *pitta*, one prepared with *jīvanīya* drugs; and for *kapha*, one prepared with *madana* fruits.

Here, the *bilva* oil and others are explained as those which will be described later. Thus, one should understand that the *bilva* oil mentioned in the section on complications of oleation (*sneha-vyāpad-siddhi*) starting with "the ten roots" (*daśamūlam*, Si. A. 4), the *jīvanīya* group mentioned in the *yamaka* formulation starting with "jīvantī and madana" (Si. A. 4), and likewise the *madana* oil mentioned starting with "or with *madana* fruits combined with sour substances" (Si. A. 4), are all intended here.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Success of the Enema Formula," in the Siddhisthāna of the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka-saṃhitā, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.

[Siddhisthāna, Chapter 4 (112 of 120)] In the previous section on Siddhi, bilva oil and other substances were specified for the purpose of massage (*abhyaṅga*) and unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*); since this section is a *siddhi* concerning those, the subsequent chapter is called "The Siddhi on Complications of Unctuous Substances" (*snehavyāpatsiddhi*). This *siddhi* describes the medicinal treatments for complications arising from unctuous substances used for unctuous enemas (*ānuvāsanika*) as well as their respective disorders. 1–2.
He states what is to be discussed in this chapter: "The unctuous enemas," and so forth.

This means that the unctuous substances (snehas) to be employed for enemas are those mentioned in this verse. As for the other matters not to be elaborated upon here—which were to have been stated by the passage beginning with "the unctuous enema and the decoction enema" (snehabastiṃ nirūhaṃ ca)—they are not to be spoken of in detail, and thus they were not promised [to be discussed].

In the passage beginning with "daśamūlam" (the ten roots), *bhūtīka* refers to *kattṛṇa* or *yavānikā*; *kākanāsā* is the fruit of *vāyasī*, though others say it is a different substance known as *vāsāphala* or *kāyuyāṭuṭī*.
They state that this [oil] made with the *bilva* present in the *daśamūla* is called *bilvataila*.
In the passage beginning with "of marshy animals" (*ānūpānām*), the phrase "likewise" (*tadvat*) refers to the previous decoction;
*śatāhvā* and so forth constitute another formulation,
while "with rock salt" (*saindhavena*) constitutes yet another formulation.
With the verse beginning "jīvantīm," etc., this *yamaka* enema is presented;
this *yamaka* was previously designated by the name "jīvanīya" in the preceding chapter.

"According to availability" means that one should use sandalwood and so forth as they are obtained; "oil-based" (tailapāda) refers to that [ointment] in which oil constitutes one quarter, as prescribed in the treatment for fever.

Regarding the passage "or with *madana* fruits combined with sour substances" (9–12), here *madana* serves as the paste (*kalka*), while the sour liquids such as fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*) and others serve as the liquid medium;
this is known as *madanataila*.

The *bilvādi* group is the *daśamūla*; and here, the *daśamūla* should be administered both as a decoction and as a paste, for it has been stated: "When neither a decoction nor a paste is specifically prescribed, one should add them from that [relevant] group. Regarding the phrase "with phlegm-subduing [drugs]," this refers to the phlegm-subduing medicines mentioned in the previous chapter, or alternatively, to *trikaṭu*, *pañcakola*, and so forth.
In the passage beginning with "viḍaṅga" (13–17), the phrase "with these made into a paste" refers to those [substances] to be mentioned later; *latā* is *mañjiṣṭhā*, and *gaurī* is *haridrā*.
"Snehabasti bestows strength" means that the unctuous enema (snehabasti) prepared with these oils [is so described].
Verses beginning with "vātapitta... describe the complications (vyāpada) of the unctuous enema.

These complications are said to occur when oleation (*sneha*) is administered through improper application (*mithyāyoga*); for it was indeed stated that "complications arise from [medicines] wrongly applied. Therefore, there is no occasion here for complications resulting from the under- or over-application of oleation; furthermore, complications arising from the under- or over-application of non-unctuous enemas (*anuvāsana*) have already been discussed in the section on pharmaceutical preparations (*kalpanā*). Their remedy is as follows: for one who has been excessively oleated, a purificatory enema (*śodhana-basti*) is indicated, whereas for one who is not oleated at all, the administration of an unctuous enema (*sneha-basti*) alone is to be understood. This has been mentioned here incidentally, as it was stated in the passage beginning with: "Therefore, one who has undergone a purificatory enema should be oleated, and one who has been oleated should undergo a purificatory enema. (25)

He states the causes for the six types of *vyāpad* in their respective order: "cold," and so forth. "Heavy" (*guru*) means possessed of heaviness. "Having little strength when there is an accumulation of feces" (*varcaḥsañcaye 'lpabala*) means that when the waste matter has accumulated, one has little strength and is incapable of expelling the accumulation of feces.

The word "covered by them" (tairāvṛta) should be applied individually to each of the five, beginning with wind. Furthermore, "due to being overcome" means that because the path is obstructed by wind and the other [elements], it does not go; likewise, because its qualities are overwhelmed by that dominant wind and so forth, it does not come, as it is not unobstructed—since the upward path is blocked by food.
Its characteristics: the symptoms of [the channels] obstructed by vāta and the other doshas will be described in due order as body aches and so forth.
By "bindings," it means specifically the binding of the sides.

Furthermore, these [symptoms] such as stiffness arise solely through the power of the unctuous substance (sneha) obstructed by vāta; therefore, they do not occur at all prior to the administration of unctuous substances.
26–28: *Rāsnā-taila*, prescribed by the verse beginning with "In a decoction of a thousand parts of *rāsnā*" (*Ci. A. 28*), is stated to be used for wind diseases (*vātavyādhi*);
and they say that *pītadru-taila* is to be prepared with liquids such as *pītadru* and *sauvīraka*.
"From those two" means from rāsnā and yellow druta-taila (29–31).
The fruit oil (phala-taila) should be understood as being exactly as previously described.
Regarding "by the signs of *āma*": by the characteristics of *āma*, such as lassitude (*ālasya*) and so forth;

"the procedure prescribed for *āma*" refers to that which is ordained [in the text] beginning with, "One should again induce emesis when the *āma* is vitiated and overwhelmed by food" (Viśeṣa-sthāna, Chapter 2), and so on, and this [procedure] is to be followed.

In the passage beginning with "snehaṃ viḍāvṛtam," the term "with wicks" (vartibhiḥ) refers to fruit-wicks (phala-vartibhiḥ). Some, however, read it as "with enemas" (bastibhiḥ). Regarding "śyāmābilvādīni": this refers to *śyāmā*, the *bilva* group, and the ten roots (*daśamūla*); alternatively, the nine drugs mentioned in the Kalpa section beginning with *śyāmā* are also included here. By means of these, the preparation of both the non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*) and the unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) is to be understood.
By "removing udāvarta" is meant the treatment for udāvarta as described in the chapter on the three vital organs (trimarmīya), verses 36–37.

The triad of causes beginning with "when one has not eaten" should be understood as the reasons for the upward movement of the unctuous enema (snehabasti). Although previously only the administration [of medicine] while fasting was declared as the cause, nevertheless, because they share the same effect and because of the similarity in their treatment, "an empty rectum" and "excessive pressure" are also stated here as causes; furthermore, an empty rectum causes the unctuous substance to move upward by failing to provide downward resistance.
"From the upper apertures" means from the mouth, nose, and so forth;
"goes" means it emerges.
By the word "also," he indicates that the emergence from the mouth and other openings occurs only occasionally.
"Tatsiddhataila" means combined with oil prepared from urine, śyāmā, and other ingredients; "sānuvāsana" means that an oil enema (anuvāsana) should also be administered using that same prepared oil;
"āgacchata" means that at the very moment of its arrival, measures such as immobilization (stambha) and so forth should be performed.

Stupor [is treated] by means of fanning, cold water sprinkling, and so forth; "constriction of the throat" refers to the pressing of the throat to prevent upward movement [of vomit]. The "anti-emetic measures" intended here should be understood as those described in the treatment of vomiting (Ci. A. 20), beginning with "In the case of mental trauma, however, things agreeable to the mind... and ending with "...[these] are easy to conquer. (38–40)

Having explained the administration of unctuous substances (sneha) when obstructed by wind (vāta) and other factors, he now describes the case where the unctuous substance should not be administered: "For one who has no complication," and so forth. This means that even if it has not fully emerged, it should not cause the aforementioned symptoms such as stiffness (stambha) and pain (rug).
"Slightly emerged" (alpaḥ) means having emerged only a little; "slightly obstructed" (āvṛtaḥ) means being blocked only slightly.
He states the reason why even when the oil is obstructed, complications such as stiffness do not arise: "due to dryness" (*raukṣyāt*).

This means that because the body is exceedingly dry at that time, the retained unctuous substance (*sneha*) does not cause any disorder. "Neglecting it" (*upekṣya*) means that the aforementioned treatment for unctuous substances obstructed by Vata should not be performed there. It is also stated elsewhere: "Even after a day and night, the unctuous substance returning [from the obstruction] is not corrupted; it produces the benefits of an enema (*basti*), though once digested, it may have diminished efficacy. (Suśruta Saṃhitā, Cikitsā-sthāna 37).
Having explained the remedies for complications that have arisen, he now describes the diet appropriate for non-complicated *anuvāsana* enemas, beginning with "yuktasneham" and so forth;
the meaning of "yuktasneham" is that the oil should not be spoiled (*avyāpannasneham*).
The rule that "service and eating [should occur] after three days" is general;
however, in cases such as those involving grains and so forth, water should be prepared according to the sixfold procedure (*ṣaḍaṅgavidhi*).
"Kalyam" means at dawn;
"sneha-ajīrṇam" refers to the undigested portion of the unctuous substance that acts as a coating within the digestive tract (42–45).
He states those who are fit for daily non-unctuous enemas (anuvāsana): "Those who are constantly dry," and so forth;

those whose vāta is located in the groins and hips, as well as those whose vāta is upward-moving (udāvṛtta), are "those with upward-moving vāta in the groins and hips"; "fit" means they are fit for non-unctuous enemas.

And it is stated elsewhere: "The physician should administer an oil enema daily to one who is parched and has an excess of wind; for others, however, he should do so every third day out of fear of injury to the digestive fire" (Suśruta Saṃhitā, Cikitsā-sthāna 37).
With the words beginning with "eṣām" (of these), [the author] explains the rationale for administering it daily or every third day.

Regarding the statement "it digests the oil in three days": it means that the oil which coats the colon (*pakvāśaya*) is digested by the heat that has emerged outward; even though there is no such direct contact with the oil from the fire situated above, nevertheless, its digestion must be understood as occurring through the mixed components of the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*) itself. By using the word "generally" (*prāyas*), he indicates that digestion may also take five days; thus, the previously mentioned administration of oil every five days for one with weak digestion (*mandāgni*) should be understood [as applicable]. For it is said: "After three days, or two days, or on the fifth day, one should be given an unctuous enema (*anuvāsya*)" (Siddhisthāna, Chapter 10). 46–47
"Raw" means uncooked;
"one should administer" refers to the non-unctuous enema (anuvāsana); "one should leave a residue" means one should not administer it until it is completely exhausted.
"By means of the rectum and the throat" refers to non-unctuous enemas (anuvāsana) and oral intake;
"immediately thereafter" means at the same time;
"it would vitiate both vāta and agni"—here, the vitiation of vāta should be understood as being caused by the production of indigestion (ajīrṇa) and by the obstruction of vāta.

48–49 He states the fault in administering a *nirūha* and an *anuvāsana* without mutual interval: "Whether it be an oil enema (*snehavasti*) or a *nirūha*, etc."— the phrase "only one" means that they are not separated by the other.
"Disturbance" refers to the disturbance of *kapha* and *pitta*.

"Fear from *vāyu* due to *nirūha*" means that through excessive purification of the body by continuous administration of *nirūha*, fear arises from *vāyu*. "One who has been *nirūḍha* should be oleated" means that once the channels have been purified by *nirūha* and the *kapha* and *pitta* have been overcome, an unctuous enema (*snehabasti*) should be practiced. Likewise, one should be given an oil enema (*anuvāsana*), for only after being properly oleated by an oil enema is one fit for a *nirūha*.

He states that when administered in this manner, oleation (sneha) and non-unctuous enema (nirūha) act as destroyers of the three doṣas; this occurs because vāta is conquered by oleation and kapha and pitta are conquered by the non-unctuous enema—thus he says "sneha-śodhana... and so forth.
Here, "śodhana" (purification) is intended to mean the non-unctuous enema (nirūha).
He describes, in due order, the scope, the dosage, and the benefits of the specific non-unctuous enema known as *mātrābasti*: "The action," and so forth.
Here, "action" (*karma*) refers to activities such as moving a ball, while "exertion" (*vyāyāma*) refers to activities such as drawing a bow;
this is indicated for one afflicted by wind (*vāta*), that is, one suffering from a wind-related disorder.
"Daily" means every day;

"of the small dose" refers to that which is to be digested within half a day. For it has been said: "The superior, middling, and small doses of oil wait respectively for a full day and night, a full day, and half a day until digestion" (Sūtra-sthāna 13).

In another tantra, the three measures of oil alone have been stated by way of specific quantities; as it is said: "The maximum dose should be six *pala*s, the medium should be three *pala*s, and the minimum should be one and a half *pala*s—thus are the three doses for an oil enema (*anuvāsana*).

Furthermore, the measure for the enema (*basti*) has also been stated by Suśruta; as in the section on *anuvāsana*: "A variation of that [dose], reduced by half and half again, is the 'dose-enema' (*mātrā-basti*), which is not to be avoided."

By this, the dosage enema (*mātrābasti*) measuring one and a half *palas* is described; for in that context, a fatty enema (*snehavasti*) of six *palas* is prescribed, whereas an oil enema (*anuvāsana*) of three *palas* is intended as being easy to manage due to the absence of restrictive rules regarding diet and conduct.

In the section on *saṅgraha*, by the mention of "edibles" (*bhojya*), grains, ginger, water, and so forth are also to be included. The phrase "daily indeed" (*dhruvaṃ yehā*) means they are to be used as daily enemas (*anuvāsana*);
thus the procedure has been stated, which is the meaning expressed in the passage beginning with "but one should not administer raw [food]" (*na tvāmaṃ praṇayet*).

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Successful Management of Complications Arising from Oleation Therapy," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka Saṃhitā*, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta. 55–56.

[Siddhisthāna, Chapter 5 (113 of 120)] In connection with the discussion on the successful management of complications arising from oleation (*sneha*), the *Netrabastivyāpatsiddhi*—the successful management of complications related to the nozzle (*netra*) and the bladder-sack (*basti*)—is now described. This includes the management of complications occurring in the nozzle, those occurring in the bladder-sack, and those resulting from improper application of the nozzle; thus, it is the "Success in Managing Complications of the Nozzle and Bladder. Furthermore, it includes the management of complications involving a defective nozzle or bladder-sack, which should be avoided once they are recognized as being impaired.
1–3 He says that very thing: "Short," and so forth.
In the description of the defects of the eyes, the word "eight" is used for the purpose of showing that the unmentioned defects, such as roughness and so on, are included within these very [eight].
Because of the similarity in their agency with respect to the state of being worn out (*jīrṇa*), roughness (*karkaśatva*) is not separately mentioned;
the same [principle] applies elsewhere as well. The purpose for mentioning number (*saṅkhyā*) here must be described;
it is subtle (*tanu*) and thin (*kṛśa*).
Non-attainment and so forth should be understood, respectively, in relation to the short eye and the others;
"over-penetration" (atigati) is deep entry,
and "agitation" (kṣobha) is the moving here and there of that which has entered the anus.
"Gudapīḍā" refers to the pain in the anus resulting from contact with the liquid from a bladder that has emerged through a lateral opening;
"jihmā" means crooked or curved.

*Viṣama* means irregularly shaped; *sthūla* means excessively large in dimension; *jālika* means having many minute pores; *vātala* means vitiated by wind (*vāta*), which is determined here by the presence of frothiness and other such signs following the administration of oleation (*sneha*) and similar treatments;
*snigdha* means oily; *atisnigdha* means excessively oily; *klinna* means moist; and *śīrṇāvayava* means having decayed or disintegrated parts.
The eight defects, such as irregular movement and so forth, correspond respectively to the [eight] conditions beginning with unevenness:

*visratva* is the state of having a raw, fleshy odor; *daurgrahya* is the state of being difficult to grasp; *cyuti* is falling from the hand; and *adhāryatva* refers to the bladder (*vasti*), which, due to its moisture, is unfit for holding—this is the unsuitability of the bladder-bag for retention.
"Excessive inflation" (*savātatā*) and other such defects are said to be produced by faults in the administrator;
among them, "excessive inflation" occurs when the enema (*basti*) is tied without allowing for respiration, or when it is administered without leaving any residue,
or even when the administration is too rapid due to its rapid discharge.
"Thrown upward" (*utkṣiptatva*) means thrown upwards;
"sideways" (*tiryak*) refers to aiming sideways.
"Cut off" (*ulluptatva*) here should be understood as the fault of crushing, wherein after having made an interruption to the crushing, one crushes again.
"Tremblingness of the eye" means excessive protrusion of the eye; "external [application]" refers to medicine that has not entered the rectum.
And its slowness consists in not reaching the colon; for this arises from mild compression, while excessive speed arises from deep penetration, which is caused by excessive compression.
He states the treatments for each of these complications individually, beginning with "without making [the patient] breathe," and so forth.

Although these instances such as not allowing the patient to breathe were already prohibited previously by such statements as "having well secured [the head] and made [the patient] breathe so that there are no wrinkles" (*Siddhisthāna*, Chapter 3), they are nevertheless repeated in this section for the purpose of prescribing the treatment for complications that may arise if such procedures are performed through negligence.
The passage beginning with "drutam" and so forth is read as a single continuous section, because even though it was set aside, it produces the same fault.

The word *sahasā* should be separated [from the following] as *niṣkṛṣṭe sahasā*. However, even without force (*asahasā*), the extraction causes injury; *bastistambha* is the stiffness of the *vasti*, that is, the urinary bladder, or it refers to those accompanied by *vāta*-relieving enemas (*basti*).

Regarding the fault of lateral positioning (*tiryak-praṇidhāna-doṣa*), although it ought to be explained [separately], another substance that blocks the nozzle opening is mentioned because it causes a similar injury: "when the opening is covered by a fold or tied. This means that when the nozzle is inserted laterally and the opening is covered by a fold, or likewise when the nozzle is bound by a thread or other material attached to the enema substance (*basti-dravya*), the enema substance does not enter. One should withdraw that laterally inserted nozzle and insert it straight, and having cleared the obstructed opening, one should insert it—this is how it should be applied.

When there is an interruption midway—that is, when a cessation occurs in the middle—the wind is struck back at the anus; thus, the air produced by the interruption of the pressure is repelled from the anus.
The ten roots beginning with bilva (daśamūla); the purgative substances beginning with śyāmā and trivṛt (śyāmādi).

"Excessively well-prepared" (*atimātrapraṇīta*) means prepared repeatedly; others, however, say that "excessively well-prepared" refers to that which is difficult to introduce. Although excessive preparation does not occur when [the enema] is placed over a tied *karṇikā* (plug), nevertheless, due to the pressure on the *karṇikā*, it should be understood as an excessive introduction because of the resulting pressure on the rectum.
This refers to the *picchābasti* (mucous enema) which will be described later (verses 15–16).

The view that [the enema] does not reach the colon because it does not digest [the medicine] occurs when there is excessive pressure or when it remains in the stomach; this should be understood as resulting from sluggish digestion, excessive pressure, and obstruction by Vāta. However, the medicine reaching the throat occurs due to intense pressure and lack of obstruction.

This complication was mentioned in the previous chapter in the context of administering an oil enema (anuvasana) without food; the distinction here, however, is that it is understood as being caused by excessive pressure in the case of both decoction enemas (niruha) and oil enemas.

In this case, when [the medicine] does not move from the abdomen, enema or purgation should be administered; however, when it has gone to the throat, measures such as pressing the throat should be understood [to be applied].
(17–18) "By that" in the summary means by a physician who is skilled in the aforementioned medicines.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Successful Treatment of Complications Arising from the Eye and Enema," in the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka-saṃhitā, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
Chapter 5.

[Siddhisthāna, Chapter 6 (114 of 120)] In connection with the discussion on the successful management of complications (*vyāpatsiddhi*), the successful management of complications arising from emesis (*vamana*) and purgation (*virecana*) is also stated. However, the successful management of complications of enema (*basti*) is described later, because enema is preceded by emesis and purgation. Thus, by the description of the successful management of complications of enema, the preeminence of enema among the therapeutic procedures (*karma*) is also indicated here. The preeminence of enema is expressed by the statement: "Therefore, they say that enema is half of treatment; some even say that enema is the entirety of treatment" (Siddhisthāna, Chapter 1).

And here, because emesis and purgation are intended as treatments for future complications, the correct procedure for them is stated; therefore, the description of the rules for emesis and purgation does not deviate from the sūtra. In the passage beginning with "atha" (now), the word "samyak" (correctly) is an adjective qualifying the procedure.
Regarding the phrase "of upward and downward [movements]," this refers to emesis and purgation;

"impurities" (doṣas) refers to complications; and although the procedure for these two cleansing therapies has been stated here and there—in the chapters on pharmaceutical preparations, successful administration, and the necessary equipment—nevertheless, this is stated here for the purpose of explaining specific details not previously mentioned. Furthermore, because of that context, the matter already stated there is also repeated here. In all cases, what has not been explicitly stated should be understood from such instructions as, "one should not administer purgation to those who are excessively unctuous," and so forth.
Showing the general time suitable for purification, he says: "Excessively hot," and so forth.
This should be understood according to the respective order [of seasons], such as summer and the others.
"In that interval" means among the seasons beginning with summer;
"the rains and so forth" refers to the rainy season (*prāvṛṭ*), autumn (*śarat*), and spring (*vasanta*).
These are "common" to them, meaning they are common to heat, rain, and cold—that is to say, their heat, rain, and cold are not yet fully manifested.

Showing the divisions of the months beginning with the rainy season (*prāvṛṭ*), he says: "The rainy season (*prāvṛṭ*) consists of *śuci* and *nabhas*, etc. Here, *śuci* and *nabhas* refer to the months of Āṣāḍha and Śrāvaṇa.
The months of Kārttika and Mārgaśīrṣa are Ūrjasaha;
Phālguna is Tapasya; and Caitra is Madhu.

Regarding purification (*śodhana*): when purification is to be performed, this aforementioned division of seasons beginning with the rainy season (*prāvṛṭ*) applies; however, in the context of the regimen for the healthy (*svasthavṛtta*) or the production of bodily tissues (*rasotpatti*), the sequence of seasons consists of the rains, autumn, winter, the cool season (*śiśira*), spring, and summer, as stated in the chapter on diet (*āśitīya*). Having thus distinguished these seasons beginning with the rainy season and established them according to the aforementioned division of months, one should administer the purificatory therapy.

By this very division of the seasonal sequence for the purificatory measures mentioned above, the Caraka-saṃskāra also—in the chapter on the non-suppression of urges (*Navegāndhāraṇīya*)—states that purification such as emesis (*vamana*) and so forth occurs during Caitra, Śrāvaṇa, and Agrahāyaṇa through the passage beginning with "In the first month of Mādhava" (Sūtra Sthāna, A. 7). Likewise, in the Rogabhiṣagjitīya (Vimāna Sthāna, A. 8), the seasonal sequence starting from the rainy season (*prāvṛṭ*) and excluding the cold season (*śiśira*) is stated as being subsidiary to purification. Therefore, while the sequence beginning with the cold season (*śiśira*) applies to considerations regarding the production of the strength of the bodily constituents (*rasa-bala*) and to the performance of healthy regimens (*svastha-vṛtta*), the sequence beginning with the rainy season (*prāvṛṭ*) applies to the administration of purification. Thus, this sequence beginning with the rainy season was devised by the Teacher for its suitability to purification, but it is not absolute.

As for those who claim that on the southern bank of the Gaṅgā the sequence begins with the rainy season (*prāvṛṭ*) and on the northern bank it begins with the cool season (*śiśira*), in their view the text "with regard to purification" (*śodhanaṃ prati*) would be untenable. Therefore, even if by means of such passages as "The rain-cloud rains more abundantly on the southern side of the Gaṅgā;

by that [water] the two seasons known as *varṣā* and *prāvṛṭ* are established for them," a real seasonal sequence based on geographical difference were being asserted, nevertheless, that is not what the Teacher intends here. And this point has already been explained in the Sūtrasthāna itself.

This instruction regarding the timing for purification (*śodhana*) should be understood to apply to non-urgent diseases; however, in the case of an urgent disease, one may indeed proceed with purification even during an excessively hot season, provided that measures such as cooling applications (*ūṣma-pratikāra*) have been taken. For this matter has already been stated in the *Rogabhiṣagjitīya* chapter: "But in the case of an urgent procedure, one may certainly disregard the season by employing artificial qualities," and so forth. (Vi. A. 8, verses 5–6)

Regarding the passage beginning with "of the actions" (*karmaṇām*), the phrase "in the intervals" (*antareṣu*) means that after emesis (*vamana*), when purgation (*virecana*) is to be performed, or after purgation, when enema (*basti*) is to be performed, oleation (*sneha*) and sudation (*sveda*) must be performed again according to the prescribed method; the meaning is that the five procedures (*pañcakarma*) are not to be carried out by means of a single application of oleation and sudation alone.

Furthermore, the statement "one should employ oleation at the end" means that upon the completion of the purification procedures (*saṃśodhana-karma*), one should administer pacifying oleation (*saṃśamanīya-sneha*) for the purpose of avoiding the exhaustion produced by those purifications.
"Neither too unctuous" means persons whose bodies are not excessively unctuous (8).
When purgation is necessary, he says "neither... and so forth, demonstrating the purgative that produces the correct effect for both those who are too unctuous and those who are not unctuous enough.

"Snehavirecana" means an unctuous purgative. It is prescribed for one who is not excessively unctuous (*anatisnigdha*), in order to prevent the failure of the purgative when administered to someone who is insufficiently unctuous. For one who is excessively unctuous (*atisnigdha*), a unctuous purgative—due to the excess of unctuousness—cannot eliminate even the displaced doshas because it moves with excessive force; instead, those doshas, having been displaced from their seats by that purgative, settle back into the channels (*srotas*). To prevent this, a dry (*rūkṣa*) purgative that ensures a proper administration should be given; this is the underlying intent. 9
He states the collection of materials for the correct application of purification (saṃśodhana) in the verse beginning with "snehasvedopapannena" and ending with "mātrāvat.
The state of being "of appropriate dose" (mātrāvat) should be understood as the quality of having a small dose, which will be described later in the passage beginning with "alpamātraṃ mahāvegam.

"With a one-pointed mind" means with a mind focused solely on purification; for if the mind is distracted by desire and other such things, there would be improper application (ayoga) due to the obstruction of the [purificatory] force.

By demonstrating the fruit of oleation (sneha) and sudation (sveda) through numerous examples beginning with "from a lubricated vessel" (snigdhāt pātrāt), he indicates that oleation and sudation must necessarily be performed; [the term] "without effort" (ayatnena) means with little exertion.
"They are driven forth" means they are drawn out;
"it causes to flow everywhere" means it draws out the fluid situated throughout the entire body.

By the example of fire, the proper removal of the *doṣas* from a person with unctuous limbs is described; by the third example, however, the result of unctuousness (*sneha*) and fomentation (*sveda*) combined is stated.
"Afflicted" means withered;
"having been agitated" means having been thoroughly agitated by contact with caustic substances and fire.

Having described the fruits of oleation and sudation as previously stated within the exposition of the complete requirements for the proper application of purification (śodhana), he now states the defect resulting from the contravention of the rule "when [the previous treatment] has been digested" (jīrṇe pītam), which follows in sequence: "In the state of indigestion (ajīrṇa), exhaustion increases. When purification is administered while in a state of indigestion, great exhaustion occurs and the opposite effect ensues:
emesis goes downward and purgation goes upward.
He explains what was stated as "in moderate measure" with the words beginning "alpamātram":
"alpamātraṃ mahāvegam" means that even though it is present in a small measure, it possesses a praiseworthy great intensity;
"avikārī" means that even in the event of a complication (*vyāpatti*), it causes only slight alteration.
"Endowed with measure" (mātrāvat) means possessing a recommended measure.

Although the pleasant taste and other qualities are not themselves the result of the measure, they are nevertheless included here because the excellence of the measure depends on specific factors such as the substance and its processing; for in this context, the excellence of the measure consists in its being inherent in the substance that serves as the substratum for the pleasure and so forth. Alternatively, it should be understood that this definition of "endowment with measure" is prescribed specifically for purification therapies of this kind.
He explains what was stated as "with a one-pointed mind" by saying "having shaken off," etc.
(verse 17). He states how one should eat on the day prior to emesis and purgation by saying "the person," etc. (verse 18).
Although this was stated previously, it is mentioned again here by virtue of the context with the intention of specifying a particular detail:
"pātu" means desiring to drink;
the word should be divided as "dravabhūyiṣṭham."
The connection is that one should consume light and non-cold food after administering purgation (*virecana*).
He states the justification for such a diet with the words beginning "utkliṣṭa" and so forth;
the distinction is that [the patient] has aggravated *kapha* in relation to emesis (*vamana*), whereas in relation to purgation, he has only a small amount of *kapha*.

Although the signs of purification following emesis and purgation have already been mentioned, they are stated again here beginning with "of one who has drunk the medicine," etc., for the purpose of specifying the remaining medicinal substances, impurities, and other particulars.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: when Pitta is followed by Kapha, one should say that the Doshas have been expelled upwards; and when fecal matter (Vish) and Pitta are seen followed by Kapha, one should say that the Doshas have been expelled downwards. This is the conclusion with Kapha for purgation (Virecana), and the conclusion with Pitta for emesis (Vamana), which has already been explained previously.

Since this conclusion with Pitta or Kapha may occur even in an incomplete purification due to the sequential persistence of the Doshas, he states other characteristics associated with these two: "If there is leanness and debility, yet lightness [of the body]. (19–20)

Regarding what must be done when, in the course of a purgative administration (*virecana-yoga*), the medicine remains partially undigested even though signs of purification (*śuddhi-lakṣaṇa*) have appeared, he says: "Then one should cause the remaining medicine to be vomited. The meaning is that once the signs of purification have arisen, upon perceiving that some medicine remains, one should induce vomiting to prevent an excessive action of the purgative (*virecana-atiyoga*); however, this does not mean that vomiting should be induced simply because there is no lightness (*alāghava*). Even if other signs of purification besides lightness are observed, the vomiting of the remaining purgative medicine should not be performed.
Regarding what must be done during the administration of an emetic medicine (*vamana-auṣadha*), he says: "In case of numbness," and so forth.

In the administration of emetic medicine, as long as stiffness and the obstruction of wind persist, emesis must be induced even if there is no eructation. This defines the limit for emesis: "until lightness and thinness of the *kapha* [occur]. Regarding the fault of administering emesis beyond lightness and thinness due to negligence, it says: "an emergency may arise thereafter"; "emergency" (*āpad*) here refers to the symptoms of excessive administration (*atiyoga*).
Others, however, say that by the words "in cases of torpor" (*staimitye*) and so forth, even the emetic action of a purgative medicine is described according to its specific state (*avasthika*).
He states the result of emesis as described, beginning with "When vomited, [the patient] increases," etc.,
by not observing the signs of proper digestion; that is, failing to observe the signs of the proper digestion of the purificatory medicine, which will be described later—
those being the signs of digested medicine.
He explains the appropriate sequence of the gruel (peyā) and so forth for one who has been purified by stating "by the two purifications" (*saṃśodhanābhyām*), etc.

Although a dullness of digestive fire (*agnimāndya*) may occur even in one who has undergone a non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*), such a dullness of fire does not occur in the case of a *nirūha*-treated patient that would necessitate the administration of the gruel sequence; therefore, the dual number is used in the phrase "by the two purifications" in order to exclude the *nirūha*.

As for the increase of the digestive fire (*agni-vṛddhi*) mentioned in the description of proper purgation by the verse "The fire [of digestion] is vigor" (*Si.A.* 1), that is an increase of the fire relative to the previous state of diminished fire caused by the excessive suppression resulting from the agitation of the purgative drugs; therefore, there is no contradiction with the statement here that "the fire reaches a state of dullness.
[Now, he] states the scope regarding *tarpaṇa* (satiating therapy) and so forth, beginning with "In *kapha* and *pitta*," etc.
Regarding "pure and little":
when [the purification] is not perfectly pure, in the sequence of nourishment (tarpaṇa) and so forth, one should give clear *tarpaṇa* in place of *peyā*, and thick *tarpaṇa* in place of *vilepī*.
He states the signs of digested medicine, beginning with "anuloma":
*ūrjaḥ* is strength;
*indriyaśuddhiḥ* is the clarity of the sense organs.
The purity of eructation consists precisely in its being devoid of the scent of medicine and so forth.
Regarding what kind of medicine causes a disorder, he says: "At the wrong time," and so on.
Whether small or excessive, or both small and excessive,
it is "not cultivated" (abhāvita) if it has not been processed by its own juices or by substances of equal potency.
He states the complications manifested by deficient or excessive administration of purification therapies, beginning with "distension" (*ādhmāna*) and so forth.

(These conditions, such as distension and the rest, do not necessarily occur at the conclusion of deficient or excessive administration; rather, they are mentioned separately because they function as secondary complications.
The meaning of the sentence is that these complications arise from the deficiencies of the attendants and others, and occur due to either deficient or excessive administration.

Among these, distension (*ādhmāna*) arises from deficient administration (*ayoga*); cutting pain (*parikartikā*), however, arises from excessive administration (*atiyoga*); discharge (*srāva*) arises from deficient administration; cardiac seizure (*hṛdgraha*) also arises solely from deficient administration, as does the seizure of the limbs (*aṅgagraha*). Extraction of the vital essence (*jīvādāna*) arises from excessive administration. Dislocation (*vibhraṃśa*), moreover, should be described as threefold, based on the distinctions of prolapse of the rectum (*gudabhraṃśa*), loss of consciousness (*sañjñābhraṃśa*), and loss of [normal] characteristics such as itching (*kaṇḍū*) and so forth. Prolapse of the rectum and loss of consciousness are produced by excessive administration, while the remaining type of dislocation is produced by deficient administration. Complication (*upadrava*) is also produced solely by deficient administration, and exhaustion (*klama*) is likewise produced by deficient administration.
Furthermore, the distinction between these [doshas] as being produced by under-application (ayoga) or over-application (atiyoga) will become clear in the subsequent section of the text.

Although underutilization (*ayoga*), overutilization (*atiyoga*), and misutilization (*mithyāyoga*) have been mentioned in various places as causes [of complications], nevertheless, here one does not consider misutilization (*mithyāyoga*) in the context of emesis and purgation. This is because the movement of the *doṣas* occurs in only four ways: excessive movement (*atipravṛtti*), improper movement (*asamyakpravṛtti*), non-movement (*apravṛtti*), or scant movement (*alpapravṛtti*). Among these, non-movement and scant movement are indeed subsumed under underutilization (*ayoga*). Furthermore, even that movement which occurs in a contrary direction (*prātilomyena*) is also strictly included within underutilization, because it fails to expel the *doṣa* that was intended to be expelled. For it will be stated: "Underutilization consists of movement in a contrary direction or insufficient movement."
29–30 He states the nature of excessive application (atiyoga), deficient application (ayoga), and proper application (yoga): "Yoga," and so forth;
"excessive application" means proceeding beyond what is required for purification.

"By way of reverse order" means the administration of emesis by means of purgation, or purgation by means of emesis. This administration in reverse order is generally classified as "inappropriate therapy" (*ayoga*) precisely because it fails to eliminate the intended morbid humor (*doṣa*); furthermore, since neither slight elimination nor total non-elimination is acceptable, it is established that [the humor] moves upward immediately.
He states how there is a lack of application (*ayogatva*) through the occurrence of this [process] in reverse order, beginning with the words "by way of reverse order" (*prātilomyena*).
It should be construed as: "Because they remove [the afflictions] incompletely by way of reverse order, they are designated as 'non-application' (*ayoga*).
Demonstrating that in the removal [of afflictions] by reverse order there is indeed the removal of the fault of incompleteness, he says "with difficulty" (*kṛcchreṇa*), and so forth.

The meaning is that in the case of taking [the medicine] in reverse order (*pratiloma*), the entire defect does not persist, or it persists only slightly; thus, the idea is that the removal of the incomplete defect is established in the case of taking it in reverse order. Regarding the reading "when it comes with difficulty and only slightly," the word *yat* indicates the reason (*hetu*); in the previous reading, the word *vā* indicates the reason.

Deficiency (ayoga) and excess (atiyoga) of emesis and the other procedures have been stated as the causes [of complications such as flatulence]; therefore, he first describes the etiology, signs, and treatment for those two causes, deficiency and excess—beginning with "having drunk the medicine" and so forth.
Regarding the word "jīrṇe" (when digested): when the medicine has been digested, one should drink again on that very same day.

"There may be danger from excessive application" means that there could be an over-application due to either the previous medicine not having been digested or the administration of a new medicine; therefore, one should administer a mild dose. This establishes the rule: one should give a sharp (strong) dose to those with a heavy digestive tract and great strength, and a mild dose to those with a light digestive tract and weak constitution.
He speaks again regarding the scope for administering emesis and purgation: "But emesis [should not be given]" and so forth;
the meaning is that if it is drunk again, it would kill [the patient].
He describes the application (*ayoga*) characterized by slight manifestation according to its different causes, beginning with "asnigdha" and so forth:
"asnigdhasya" means one who is not properly oleated;
"rūkṣasya" means one who is not even slightly oleated.
"Anava" means [the mind] having its vigor diminished due to being worn out;
"nirhartum" means to remove it completely;
"vibhraṃśam" means the capacity for perverse activity.
38–39 He states another application: "of one who has been lubricated and fomented," and so forth;
"digested" (*jīrṇam*) means it has been digested due to its small quantity and because of the intensity of the digestive fire.

"In the raw" (*āme*) means when the disorder (*doṣa*) is undigested; "having been drunk" (*pītam*) is the ellipsis to be supplied here. Those diseases explained by these three characteristics of under-dosage (*ayoga*) are not produced by a different set of causal factors nor do they require a different treatment; therefore, they were not mentioned previously in the section on complications arising from under-dosage. The same should be understood for the diseases to be described as having the characteristics of over-dosage (*atiyoga*), as it was stated: "If the medicine has been drunk but one is not purified," and so forth; or else, as stated later in the passage beginning with "that oil," etc.
"One should cause to drink" means one should administer a purificatory treatment;
"with the products of the desert" (dhānvaiḥ) means with the meat juices of desert-dwelling animals and birds.

He states the causes and other factors of excessive administration (*atiyoga*): "excessively sharp," and so forth. This collection of factors applies specifically to the excessive administration of purgation (*virecana*); for it is precisely in one with a soft bowel (*mṛdukoṣṭha*) and one who is hungry that this [purgative] is administered excessively through the sequential removal of feces, bile, and phlegm. The collection of factors for the excessive administration of emesis (*vamana*) is to be inferred by this same example. Alternatively, by the very term "excessively sharp," the excessive sharpness of the emetic agent itself is stated as a cause of excessive administration; and the removal of feces, bile, and phlegm should be understood as occurring appropriately and sequentially in both purgation and emesis. "One should scrape out the remaining medicine" refers to the immediate treatment (*tādātvikī cikitsā*).
The term "mṛdu" (mild) is connected with both emesis and purgation;
regarding the *vaṭa* and others, these are the *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *kapītana*.
Those that arrest the stool are the six [drugs] beginning with *priyaṅgu* and *anantā*, as mentioned in the chapter on the hundred purgatives (*Ṣadvirecanaśatāśritīya*).
Eating sour fruits in front [of the patient] serves to remove the stiffness of the tongue caused by salivation;
"emerged" (*niḥsṛtām*) is an adjective qualifying the tongue, used in the context of excessive application.
Regarding verses 52–56, he explains how the sequence beginning with gruel (peyā) is applied even in cases of excessive administration: "Once vomited," and so forth;
it should be understood that "excessively vomited" and "excessively purged" result from over-administration.

Explaining the causes, symptoms, and treatments for the disorders of *ayoga* (under-treatment) and *atiyoga* (over-treatment), such as flatulence (*ādhmāna*) and others, respectively, he says: "Of one with many *doṣas*," and so forth.

These disorders do not necessarily arise from *atiyoga* and *ayoga* alone, because they are merely complications (*upadrava*). For this very reason, in the *Upakalpanīya* chapter, these ten disorders are set forth in the passage beginning with "One should recognize these complications caused by *atiyoga* and *ayoga*" and "Flatulence, cutting pain (*parikartikā*)," etc. (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 15).
58–60 He describes *parikartikā* with the words beginning "with unctuous [substances]," and so forth.

The passage beginning with "having reached the rectum, yellow [matter]... is appropriate for the cutting pain (*parikartikā*) resulting from excessive purgation (*virecana*), but not for the cutting pain resulting from excessive emesis (*vamana*). Furthermore, in the *Upakalpanīya* chapter, distension (*ādhmāna*) and other symptoms are explicitly stated to arise only from deficient or excessive application of emesis; therefore, although not mentioned there, cutting pain (*parikartikā*) in the case of an emetic complication must be inferred by this very example. It is also stated in another treatise: "That which is cutting pain in purgation is the scraping of the throat in emesis; that which is downward discharge in purgation is the secretion of phlegm in emesis" (Suśruta Saṃhitā, Cikitsā-sthāna 34). Thus, some explain that distension and the other symptoms are to be understood as arising from deficient or excessive application of both emesis and purgation.
"Having quickly expelled the morbid humor (doṣa)"—this complication arises from excessive emesis (vamanātiyoga).
In this case, treatments such as fasting (laṅghana) and so forth should be understood as intended for the digestion of undigested matter (āma), even though there is already excessive [emesis].

For a person who is emaciated or has a soft bowel (mṛdukoṣṭha), the treatment consisting of fasting, digestive measures (pācana), and the like, which is prescribed based on the etiology (samprāpti) described here, should indeed be undertaken.

He states what is to be done during the stage of *āma* (undigested matter), beginning with "When the *āma* is digested," etc., up to "alkaline and sour [food] that is light is recommended. Regarding diarrhea (*atīsāra*), it has been stated: "Cumin, *kola*, curd, sour [gruel], ginger, and combined with alkaline salt... [and so forth].
"Ghee" (Ci. A. 19); it should be understood that a small dose is recommended.
Regarding the term *puṣpakāsīsa*, some take the word "flower" (*puṣpa*) to include astringent substances such as the flowers of *dhātakī* and others.
With the words "a small amount" (*alpam*) and so forth, he describes evacuation (*parisrāva*).

Regarding the statement "one should pacify or even cause emesis" (*śamayed vāmayed api*), the rule is that pacification (*śamana*) is for minor morbidity (*alpa-doṣa*), while emesis (*vamana*) is for excessive morbidity (*bahu-doṣa*) or when the morbidity has moved upward (*ūrdhvagata-doṣa*).
In the phrase "or even cause emesis," the word "furthermore having been oleated" (*snehitaṃ punar*) is also to be connected.
Powders, fermented liquors (āsava), and decoctions (ariṣṭa) are to be understood as being used in the treatment of malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī) and hemorrhoids (arśas), etc. (verses 68–70).
By the verse beginning with "pītauṣadhasya," [the author] describes cardiac oppression (hṛdgraha).
"He should not fall into confusion therein" means that one who is afflicted by the seizure of the heart (*hṛdgraha*) should not fall into the delusion of thinking, "This person is dying.

Furthermore, administering emetics to one who has fainted is difficult to perform; therefore, emetics should be administered at the very onset of fainting. Alternatively, even during fainting, emesis should be induced by such means as inserting a finger [into the throat].
"Afflicted by bile-fainting" (*pittamūrchārtam*) refers to one suffering from fainting produced by the predominance of the bile humor (*pitta*).
"Excessive emesis" refers to one who causes excessive discharge for the purpose of inducing vomiting.

"Otherwise, in the case of pitta or kapha" means that when pitta or kapha cause pain in the heart, one should employ a regimen contrary to unctuous, sour, and salty [substances], such as dry, bitter, pungent, and so forth.

By the verse beginning with "pītauṣadhasya" (of one who has taken medicine), he describes the seizing of the limbs (*aṅgagrahaṇa*) as being caused by both under-treatment (*ayoga*) and over-treatment (*atiyoga*); or, the dosha obstructed by phlegm (*kapha*) again seizes the limbs; or, in one who has been purified (*śuddha*), the aggravated wind (*māruta*) seizes the limbs through stiffness and other symptoms. (76–77)
With the words "extremely sharp" and so forth, he describes the extraction of vital fluid (*jīvādāna*);
"of one with slight defects" means of one with minor faults;
"having thoroughly churned" means having agitated the blood itself.

"Jīva" refers to blood in the form of the element that is the cause of life. Some blood arises from the agitation of *rakta-pitta* (blood-bile), while other blood is "living blood" (*jīva-śoṇita*). To examine the distinction between these, he says: "By that [one should determine] food," and so forth, up to "one should indicate the *pitta* located in the blood"—that is to say, *rakta-pitta*.
Regarding the term "āvāna" (steaming):
in the case of *pitta*, specifically when there is *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorder), a washed cloth becomes discolored; however, when *jīvaśoṇita* (vital blood) is present, the cloth remains pure.

This examination is intended solely for the purpose of distinguishing the treatment: in *raktapitta*, one should apply treatments that alleviate *raktapitta*; but upon seeing *jīvaśoṇita*, one should perform the treatment prescribed in the verse beginning with "For one afflicted by thirst, fainting, and intoxication," and so forth.

Regarding "that which is beneficial in case of excessive [bleeding]," this should be understood as that which was stated in the very same context: "One should arrest it with very cold sprinklings, immersions, and so forth.

Because it quickly reaches the vital principle (*jīva*), it immediately attains the nature of blood due to the power of the blood itself; in the verse beginning "fresh blood is dark" (*sadyaskam asṛk śyāmam*), *śyāmā* refers to the *priyaṅgu* plant.
From verse 78 to 84,
beginning with "the rectum is prolapsed" (gudaṃ bhraṣṭam), he describes the disorder characterized by prolapse of the rectum (vibhraṃśa).
Regarding the term "with astringents" (kaṣāyaiḥ), it means with substances having an astringent taste (kaṣāya-rasa).
With the words beginning with "sāma," he describes the treatment for the impairment of consciousness in the form of the impairment of perception:
*sāma* means consoling;
*gāndharva-śabda* means song.
These two types of failure (vibhraṃśa) are produced by excessive application (atiyoga);
with the words "when... and so forth, he describes the third type of failure produced by deficient application (ayogaja).
"It remains ending in feces" means that it remains after having removed only the waste matter (mala).
The phrase "ending with medicine" means that only the medicine remains after emesis;
"does not carry away" means it does not eliminate [the doshas]. This technical term "vibhraṃśa" (disturbance) refers to complications.
"Just as medicine [is prescribed] according to the disease" means that the medicine is contrary to [the condition of] itching and so forth.
By the passage beginning with "drunk by one who is unctuous," he describes *stambha* (suppression).

"Covered by mildness" means that because of the mildness of the medicine, it is covered by the *doṣas*; this should be construed as meaning that it would stabilize those [humors] displaced from their own locations.
"Deserving of sharpness" (*sauhārda*) means that after fasting (*laṅghana*) and digestion (*pācana*), one deserves a sharp enema (*basti*) or sharp purgation (*vireka*). This is the meaning.
By the words beginning with "rūkṣam" (dry), he describes the complications (*upadrava*).

Although distension (*ādhmāna*) and the like are also indeed complications, nevertheless, because they have already been included under different designations, it is only colic (*śūla*) and the others that are designated by the term "complication."

These conditions, such as colic (*śūla*) and others, are primary; although they do not take the form of complications because they arise at a later stage, they are nevertheless referred to by the term "complication" (*upadrava*). This is as in the statement: "Smoking may produce complications" (*Sūtra-sthāna*, chapter 5). Alternatively, it should be understood that these are complications of the disease known as *ayoga* (improper administration). With the words beginning with "of one who has been oleated" (*snigdhasya*), he describes exhaustion (*klama*).

Having aggravated the *kapha* and *pitta*, and having obstructed the *vāta* by those very two, the medicine—accompanied by drowsiness and other symptoms—would cause exhaustion; therefore, it should "scrape away" (*ullikhet*), meaning that medicine should scrape away both the *kapha* and the *pitta*.
Having shown the summary of the chapter's subject matter with the words "ityetā" and so forth, he states the cause for the occurrence of complications:
"one should properly administer purification. This means that one should administer purification in such a way that complications do not arise at all.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Successful Management of Complications of Emesis and Purgation" (or "The Successful Management of Complications of Purificatory Therapies"), in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka Saṃhitā*, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Siddhisthāna, Chapter 7 (115 of 120)]

Since enema (*basti*) occurs immediately after emesis and purgation, and since the successful management of complications from purification therapies follows that, the successful management of enema complications is discussed next. Here, the term *basti* refers specifically to the non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*), because it is the complications of that alone which are to be described.
There are five questions, beginning with "What are they? and "How many? (1–2).

The answer to the first question, beginning with "not excessive" (*nātiyogau*), refers to deficient application (*ayoga*) and excessive application (*atiyoga*); the meaning of this will become clear in the very explanation of these twelve complications (*vyāpad*).

"Arising from improper application" means that they arise from improper application (*asamyagyoga*) of the non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*), consisting of under-application (*ayoga*), over-application (*atiyoga*), and wrong application (*mithyāyoga*).
By this statement, which identifies the general cause, the answer to the question regarding their origin is provided.

Here, through the improper application of the enema procedure, under-application and over-application—which are forms of complications—prevent the removal of morbidities, which is the function of the *nirūha*. Furthermore, exhaustion and other such symptoms, though born of under- and over-application, are mentioned here separately because they have specific causes, characteristics, and treatments; just as in the context of purification therapies (*saṃśodhana*), distension (*ādhmāna*) and other symptoms, though born of under- and over-application, are stated separately.

Some read "from excessive application, exhaustion, distension," and so forth, as well as "these ten are the complications of enema," and so forth; in that case, the meaning should be understood according to the explanation given in the preceding chapter. However, the previous reading alone is definitive; for in the passage beginning with "of these," etc., the specific causes to be described individually are already included by the word *rūpa* (form/manifestation), since even a cause is indeed a *rūpa* by virtue of being indicative of the [condition].
