"In the guru-koṣṭha" means in a *krūra-koṣṭha* (hard bowel) or a bowel filled with impurities (*mala-pūrṇa-koṣṭha*).
The word "alpa" (small dose) is connected individually with each [of the following]:

"of the warm *pramathyā*"—that is, the application of that *pramathyā* which is warm among the *pramathyās* mentioned in the treatment of diarrhea; it has already been established in the section on diarrhea that "*pramathyā*" is a technical term (*saṃjñā*) for a digestive decoction (*pācana-kaṣāya*) as established by the tradition of Ayurveda.

"Having known the time" means having recognized the state suitable for purgation (*virecana*); in the phrase "possessing wine and the like as urine," the word "and the like" (*ādi*) includes sour gruel (*sauvīraka*), fermented rice-water (*tuṣodaka*), and so forth;

"with fresh paste" (*saprākpeṣya*) means accompanied by the medicinal paste (*kalka*) prescribed for enemas (*basti*) such as those made from *bala* and other ingredients mentioned in the *Bastisūtra*.
"One should bring that [enema]" refers to the case where the enema is obstructed and fails to act;
having thus described non-action (ayoga), he now describes excessive action (atiyoga) with the verse beginning "In one who has been oleated and fomented," and so forth.
"Excessive application" (*atiyujyate*) means one becomes a perpetrator of excessive administration (*atiyoga*);

"should be equalized by purification" (*śodhanābhyāṃ samā bhavet*) means it should be balanced by the treatment prescribed for the symptoms of excessive emesis (*vamana*) and purgation (*virecana*). Regarding the specific treatment for the burning sensation (*dāha*) arising from excessive enema (*basti*), he says: "Pṛśniparṇī," and so forth.
In this context, the dissolution of the paste (kalka) into the five liquids such as milk and others,
as well as the clear extracts (prasāda) of grapes and so forth, should be understood as being prepared according to the procedure for cold infusions (śītakaṣāya).
By the words "when there is a remnant of *āma*" and so forth, he describes exhaustion (*klama*).
It should be construed that when a remnant of *āma* remains, the *doṣa* is provoked by the administered non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*).
Here, by the word *doṣa*, both pitta and kapha, together with *āma*, are meant as those obstructing the channels.

It causes fainting because it provokes [the humors] by obstructing the channels; it blocks the path because it obstructs the channels in the body. As for those who maintain that the word *doṣa* here refers exclusively to *kapha*, in their view, the presence of burning sensations (*sadāhatva*) would be untenable even in the case of exhaustion (*klama*).
In the passage beginning with "vacā," the term *mūrchitāḥ* means "steeped";
*kṣārān* and *dīpanān* refers to those [alkalines and digestive stimulants] prescribed in the treatment of *grahaṇī* and elsewhere;

*dāśamūlikam* refers to what is stated in [Siddhi-sthāna, Chapter 3]: "The juice of the two groups of five roots (*pañcamūla*) combined with acid," or alternatively, that which is prepared from a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*).
The *mādhutailika* type, which will be described [in verses] 15–20 starting with "of little potency" (*alpavīrya*), etc., indicates flatulence (*ādhmāna*).

"Obstructed path" means the downward path has been blocked; that [wind] obstructs the vital air (anila), and the vital air, because its path is obstructed, causes distension (ādhmāna)—thus "affliction of the vital points" (*marmapīḍana*) is a qualification of the distension. "It obstructs the heart with piercing pains" means it pervades the heart with piercing pains.

"By means of *śyāmā* fruit and so forth" refers to the nine [substances] beginning with *śyāmā* and the six beginning with "fruit," as stated in the *Kalpasthāna*. Here, the word "smoke" (*dhūma*) refers specifically to house-smoke (*gṛhadhūma*).
Furthermore, the amount of jaggery (*guḍa*) used here is just enough to be suitable for making the wick (*varti*).

In the phrase "the thumb of the hand" (*karāṅguṣṭha*), the mention of the "hand" (*kara*) is for the purpose of excluding the big toe of the foot; furthermore, even in the second enema (*varti*) described by the words "or else," molasses (*guḍa*) should be added to ensure its consistency as an enema, and a *nirūha* (non-unctuous enema) should be prepared with *bilva* and other ingredients, as stated in the verse beginning: "Containing *bilva* root, *trivṛt*, *dāru*, barley, jujube, and horse-gram."
In the passage beginning with "saraletyādi" and ending with "siddham," the word "oil" (*tailam*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
With the verse beginning "mṛdvityādi," he describes hiccup (*hikkā*).
"Excessively expelling" means expelling the *doṣas* through excessive application (*atiyoga*).
"Curing hiccups" refers to the medicinal remedies prescribed for the treatment of hiccups.

Now, although enema (*basti*) is prohibited in cases of hiccups by the statement: "In those afflicted by persistent vomiting, spitting, cough, dyspnea, and hiccups, the upward-moving *vāyu* may lead the enema upward" (Sūtra-sthāna 2), nevertheless, because unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) is beneficial here in specific types of hiccups, the unctuous enema described starting with "bala, sthirā, etc. is faultless.

The term *vātanut* (wind-alleviating) is connected with "smoke" (*dhūma*) and the other [therapies] by changing its gender; therefore, only those smokes and so forth that are beneficial for wind (*vāta*) are to be employed here.
With the verse beginning "excessively sharp" (*atitīkṣṇa*), he describes the reaching of the heart (*hṛtprāpti*).
The state of being well-distended (*savātatva*) of the bladder should be understood through its complete emptying and so forth;
the state of being improperly compressed should be understood as that which causes [the urine] to reach the heart;
and the "mass of salt" (*lavaṇaskandha*) is that described in the chapter on "Victory over Diseases and Physicians" (*rogabhiṣagjitīya*).
"With wind-alleviating [drugs]" refers to the ten roots (daśamūla) and so forth;
by the verse beginning with "vātamūtra" and so forth, he describes the upward movement [of the urine].
When the bladder has been inserted, if one observes a disorder in the form of fainting as the bladder moves upward, one should perform measures such as sprinkling water on the face;
"one should shake it in the air" means one should shake it while it is unsupported.
And it should be understood that one should cause [the victim] to tremble by means of cows, donkeys, and so forth;
likewise, even by other unmentioned methods of causing terror.
He explains how the constriction of the throat should be performed: "so that he does not die."
He states the purpose of constricting the throat: "Because of the obstruction of *prāṇa* and *udāna*, the *apāna* follows its well-established path," and so forth.

By the constriction of the throat, the *apāna*—due to the obstruction of *prāṇa* and *udāna*—comes to follow its well-established path; the meaning is that it takes on the nature of moving toward the rectum. Consequently, it leads the enema fluid, which has been directed upward, downward. It should be understood, however, that by the obstruction of *prāṇa* and *udāna*, the *apāna*—being pressed by those two—returns to its own natural course.

However, some read "yāvat prāṇoparodhāt hi," where the meaning is that the pressure on the throat should be applied until there is obstruction of the breath; "kramukam" means betel nut; "śiraḥsthe" means when it is situated in the head, that is, in a portion of the bladder.
"Pracchādyam" means that which is to be smeared (ālepanīya).
With the verse beginning "snigdhasvinna" (32–39), he describes *pravāhikā*.

In the phrase "it produces [the condition] described by the symptoms of *pravāhikā* and *atīsāra*, [administered as] purgative and carminative," the term "purgative" (*śodhanīya*) refers to substances such as *trivṛt* and other purgatives; "carminative" (*ānulomika*) refers to those combined with milk and sugarcane juice which facilitate downward movement; and "diet" (*vṛtti*) refers to the sequential regimen beginning with thin gruel (*peyā*).
With the words beginning with "durbale" (weak), he describes headache; "tanuḥ" means not dense.
"Tadvihata" means provoked by a non-unctuous enema (nirūhabasti);

it is "struck upwards in the head" because, following an upward course, it is obstructed in the head. As for those who read "ūrdhvaṃ vidhāvati," in their view, the meaning is that it runs higher and higher.
Regarding the phrase "one should purge this," the word "head" (śira) is to be supplied as the object, or alternatively, the reading is "anuvirecayet."

It should be understood that one should administer an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) after consuming sharp and carminative food; or rather, the meaning is that the unctuous enema itself should be accomplished by means of sharp and carminative [substances].
By the verse beginning with "with oleation and sudation" (*snehasvedaiḥ*), he describes bodily pain (*aṅgārta*).

"Without having prepared [the body]" means that one should not apply oil and sudation to the body; if one administers [the enema] in excess, it will cause pain for the "humors" (doṣas)— this is the remainder of the sentence—
thereby producing affliction in one whose abdomen has become stiff and constricted.

Although an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) is generally administered even after one has eaten, the specific mention of "after eating" indicates that the enema should be given immediately following the meal.
With the verse beginning with "mṛdu," etc., [the author] describes parikartikā.
"Due to the purgation by enema" means because of the drawing action of the enema by sharp *vāyu*;
"manifestly sour" (*vyaktāmla*) is an epithet of the enema.
With the words "In the case of pitta diseases," etc., he describes *parisrāva*.
"It diminishes" (*kṣiṇoti*) means it destroys.
"This procedure" (*eṣa kalpaḥ*) refers to the procedure for processing with milk mentioned in the section on the fresh stalks of the *śālmalī* tree.
They call *suvarcala* *suniṣaṇṇaka*;
*karbudāra* is *kāñcanāra*.

Now, since the mildness and sharpness of enemas (basti) have been prescribed in various places, he states the group of substances that produce mildness and sharpness for the sake of understanding them: "Sharpness," and so forth.
*Pīlu* is the fruit from the northern region (*auttarapathika*). Some read *bilva* in place of *pīlu*. "At the appropriate time" means in the state already described.
He describes the efficacy of enema (basti): "From the feet," and so forth;
"situated in the receptacle of digested food" means located precisely within the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya).

"It takes [the doshas] by means of its vigor" means by its power inherently connected to its own nature; such vigor exists specifically in the enema (basti). Therefore, unlike the enema, applications such as *pācana* (digestive) therapies do not possess the capacity to conquer the morbid humors (*doṣas*) located throughout the entire body on that very same day;
"situated in space" (*khastha*) means situated in the ether (*ākāśa*).

In the *Suśruta*, however, it is stated: "By its potency, the enema draws up the doshas from the feet to the head, just as the sun, situated in the sky above the digestive tract, draws up the juices from the earth" (*Su.Ci.A.* 35).
Now, demonstrating by means of an illustration how an enema (basti) extracts only the waste portion even when the body contains both waste and pure constituents, he says: "Just as," and so forth;
"from that which has been liquefied" means from that which has been melted by oleation (sneha) and sudation (sveda); "wastes" refers to the humors (doṣas) and feces (purīṣa).
65. This is the summary beginning with "these [are they]":

since these complications arise from the improper application of enemas (*basti*), therefore, one who employs enemas after having understood them in their entirety does not err; the meaning is that he does not encounter complications of the enema.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Successful Management of Complications of Enemas," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā*, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Section on Success (*Siddhisthāna*).

[Siddhisthāna, Chapter 8 (116 of 120)] Now, the Siddhi concerning the *prasṛta* formulations is being stated precisely because it describes the enemas that pacify complications arising from enema therapy (*bastivyāpad*). A "siddhi" is that which is composed with reference to those formulations characterized by the term *prasṛta*; therefore, the formulations characterized by *prasṛta* must certainly be discussed here as well.
"These" refers to those that will be mentioned further on;
therefore, there is no necessity for a rule characterized by what has already been introduced regarding the matters to be stated in the remainder of the chapter.
"For those who are delicate" refers to being endowed with qualities such as thinness;
"prasṛta" is two palas.

Regarding the phrase "the three from honey, oil, and ghee," these are to be combined; furthermore, the enema (basti) here should be administered using only the substances as they have been specified. Therefore, the procedure for preparing unmentioned pastes (kalka) and so forth does not apply according to the rules for other types of enemas. Where an enema is prescribed with a fixed proportion of specific ingredients, there is no room for the general measurement of enema substances. However, where only a portion is mentioned, the authority for the quantity of substances applies by virtue of their being part of the *nirūha* formulation. The addition of rock salt (*saindhava*) must certainly not be omitted; and the roots of *bilva* and others constitute the *daśamūla*.
It dispels wind; thus, this enema (basti) destroys wind. 4–6. *Hapuṣākārṣa*.
In the passage beginning with "paṭola" and so forth, regarding the phrase "of water," it means from the decoction;

and regarding "mixed with a paste of mustard seeds," although the specific measure of the paste (kalka) is not stated here, nevertheless, since a paste of two palas is prescribed for a twelve-prasṛta nirūha enema, here, by that same proportion, in a five-prasṛta enema, it becomes one pala less six parts. In this manner, the determination of the paste is established even where the measure is not explicitly mentioned elsewhere.
In the verse beginning with "viḍaṅga," the word "phala" refers to the fruit of the madana plant.

In passages such as "ākhuparṇī, dantī, payasyā," etc., although the decoction of *payasyā* and the others is not explicitly mentioned, nevertheless, because one *prasṛta* measure is prescribed for each of them together with other liquids, it follows that the decoction of *payasyā* and the others is to be measured at one *prasṛta* each.
"Vṛṣatvakṛt" means that which causes the increase of semen (śukra).

Regarding the passage beginning with "śvadaṃṣṭrā," each of the three substances—śvadaṃṣṭrā and the others—should be measured at one *prasṛta*; thus, together with the *taila* and *surāsava*, five *prasṛtas* in total should be filled. *Surāsava* is an *āsava* prepared from *surā*.

He states what should be performed at the conclusion of the applications of mild enemas (mṛdu-basti): beginning with the word "mṛdu" and ending with "a sweet pratyāsthāpana is desired," where "sweet" refers to that prepared from substances such as grapes (drākṣā) and the like.
Some maintain that "pratyāsthāpana" (re-administration) refers to the very same day; it is called pratyāsthāpana because it is administered with the aim of establishing [the medicine] anew.
In the passage beginning with "vātopasṛṣṭasya" (of one afflicted by vāta), the term "uṣṇaiḥ" (with hot [substances]) is an adjective qualifying the enema (*basti*).
"Dāhādayaḥ" (burning sensations, etc. refers to burning, delusion, thirst, and so forth, which are produced by *vāta* and *pitta*.

By stating "taddhi... (for that... and so on, the author demonstrates that the administration of *trivṛt* with grape juice is beneficial for both *pitta* and *vāta* when they cause burning sensations and other such symptoms.
*Kulmāṣas* are foods made of barley and other grains that have been half-boiled.
He describes the treatment for the types of diarrhea caused by the improper administration of enemas (basti-mithyāprayoga), beginning with the words "If it is sāma" (sāmaṃ cet) and so forth.

This means one should pass stool in such a way that it is *sāma*. By this, this type of diarrhea—characterized by the passage of *āma* alone, distinct from fecal matter—is stated first among the six types of diarrhea to be described here, which are produced by undigested matter (*āma*), feces (*śakṛt*), wind (*vāta*), blood (*rakta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*kapha*).
The term *kuṇapa* refers to that which has the odor of a corpse (*śava-gandha*).
The word "afflicted" (*yukta*) is to be supplied [with the preceding]; "ghana" means *mustaka*.
He describes dysenteries (*atisāra*) caused solely by feces and other such factors, beginning with "feces and flatus," etc.
"Matured" (*pakva*) means free from *āma*.

Here, by the word *āma*, what is intended is the undigested essence of food (*āhārarasa*) itself, which, due to weakness of the digestive fire (*agnidaurbalya*), acts as a coating within the abdominal cavity (*koṣṭha*). As it is said elsewhere: "That which resides in the stomach (*āmāśaya*) remains undigested due to the weakness of the bodily fire."
"The first element of food is designated as *āma*.

[This is done] "by those belonging to its own class," meaning by groups of medicinal substances that collect feces, alleviate wind (*vāta*), stabilize the blood, and remove bile (*pitta*) and phlegm (*kapha*); or alternatively, by the specific medicinal substances for feces and so forth that will be described individually later on.
He states the divisions of diarrhea with the words "of the six," and so forth.
Regarding the word "of these" (*eṣām*), it refers to those already mentioned.
Others, however, say that there are six types arising from the displacement of the enema (*bastivibhraṃśaja*); yet the previous explanation alone is correct.
21 He states their complications, beginning with "śūla" (pain), etc.
He states the treatment for the aforementioned types of diarrhea: "In that case, in the presence of undigested matter (āma)," and so forth.
Regarding the term *antarapāna*, they call it a digestive (*pācana*) drink;
by this term "digestive," the previously mentioned digestive formulation beginning with "that [decoction] of *ghana* and *ativiṣā*" is intended here.
"Combined with vyoṣa, sour, and salty substances" means prepared through the combination of vyoṣa, sour, and salty substances (verse 23).

Regarding "with vātaghna [drugs]" and so forth, *vātaghna* refers to the ten roots (*daśamūla*); and the group of astringent drugs (*grāhivarga*) is exactly as described in the chapter on the six hundred purgatives (*ṣaḍvirecanaśatāśritīya*).
Regarding this, Jatūkarṇa says: “An enema with feces containing swelling-alleviating and astringent substances”; and the *daśamūla* itself is indeed the swelling-alleviator.

Furthermore, an oil enema (*snehabasti*) prepared with sweet, sour, and salty substances is recommended; this means an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) made from oils processed with sweet, sour, and salty ingredients.
Regarding "in *samīraṇa*," this refers to diarrhea caused by wind alone (24). Regarding "in blood," when blood is being discharged in diarrhea, an enema with blood should be administered.
Regarding "in the case of pitta," this means that when diarrhea caused by pitta is occurring, the enema prepared with decoctions and other such ingredients is indeed [the treatment].
He now describes the treatment for the combination of humors (saṃsarga), beginning with the words "feces" and so forth.

When the feces (*śakṛt*) and *āma* are mixed as primary [components], or when the wind (*vāyu*) and *āma* are mixed; by that [word] "tena" (by that), it refers to the non-primary *āma* being mixed separately with the stool and the wind. Here, "tena" is to be explained as before.

Among these mixtures, that which is indicated by the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) should be understood as secondary due to its small quantity, while that indicated by the locative case (*saptamī*) is to be known as primary because of its large quantity.
"Tayoḥ" refers to bile (*pitta*) and blood (*asṛj*).

Regarding the phrase "of the two combined": when [the two] are joined by a single measure, the term "internal drink" (*antarapāna*) is understood to apply up to the point where it says "combined with *vyoṣa*, astringent, and salt" in the context of *kapha*.

In the passage beginning with "by *vāta*... seventy," the phrase "sweet, sour, and astringent enema" means that an enema prepared from decoctions and other substances such as sweet ones should be administered.

In the passage beginning with "of feces and blood" (*śakṛcchoṇitayoḥ*), when there is mutual contact—that is, when feces are mixed with blood or blood is mixed with feces—the two-fold combination of bile and feces, as well as blood and bile, should be explained in the same way.

Regarding the phrase "by feces, bile, and blood," the meaning is that [the humors] are combined with each of the [three] starting with feces; and "in the state of being overwhelmed by phlegm" (*kaphavimūrcchite*) means being mixed with phlegm as the secondary element.
Introducing the treatment for combinations not previously mentioned, he says: "The combinations of three, four, etc.
This refers to the combinations of *āma* and the other factors in the form of triads, tetrads, and pentads.

"In this very way one should formulate" means that one should formulate [the medicine] by combining the primary [ingredients] and so forth; likewise, one should also prepare the medicine for them according to the aforementioned medicinal formulas—this is the meaning.

Furthermore, if these variations were to be written out, they would result in excessive bulk due to their great number of subdivisions; since they are easy for an intelligent person to distinguish on their own, they are not written here.
Thus, extending by analogy (atideśa) the necessity of performing such differentiation through intelligence regarding other diseases as well, he says: "It is prescribed for all diseases."

This systematic arrangement regarding all diseases is intended to be according to the teacher’s approval as far as possible. In that regard, concerning the disease of *grahaṇī* where all six [factors] beginning with *āma* are present, combinations (*saṃsarga*) are formulated in this manner; and where three *doṣas* are present, or four including blood (*śoṇita*), there their mutual combinations must be formulated for the purpose of determining the specific medicinal treatment.
Regarding the effect produced by the combination of the sixfold collection beginning with *āma*, he states: "Simultaneously," and so forth.
"Simultaneously" means at one and the same time; "of the six" means of the six [factors] when they have come together.
"The six tastes" refers to that which is produced by the combined six tastes.
"Nirāmāṇām" means of the five [substances], excrement and so forth, which are devoid of "āma";
"ṣāḍrasikaḥ" means prepared by the combination of the six tastes. 35.
He states the medicine common for all types of diarrhea: "udumbara," etc.
Regarding the reading "raktamūlibhiḥ" instead of "raktaśālibhiḥ," others say that "raktamūlī" refers to *raktairaṇḍa*.
"Boiled in water" means boiled in water according to the six-fold method (*ṣaḍaṅga-vidhāna*).
"Unripe *udumbara* fruit" refers to the young fruit of the *udumbara* tree; "it would become gruel" refers to [gruel made from] sugarcane and so forth—
namely, those included among the five grass roots (*tṛṇapañcamūla*), excluding *śara*, such as sugarcane, *kuśa*, *kāśa*, and rice roots.

"With rice grains such as *śāli* and so forth" means with the fresh grains of red *śāli* rice and the like; here, the gruel (*yavāgū*) should be prepared with curd and other ingredients acting as the liquid medium.
He states the medicine described in detail in brief: "And here there are," etc.;
"drinking" refers to digestive drinks;
and "enema" refers specifically to an enema that is unctuous, sour, salty, and sweet.

In the phrase "mārute," [it refers to] diarrhea caused by Vāta (mārutātisāra); likewise, in other instances such as "pitte" and so forth, it should be understood as diarrhea caused by Pitta and the like (pittādijātisāra).

In the expression "astringent and Vāta-alleviating," the word "medicine" (bheṣaja) is to be supplied as the ellipsis; and that medicine consists precisely of the aforementioned enemas (vasti) and other forms.
Regarding "digestive therapy for undigested matter (āma), drinking [decoctions]," the meaning is a drink prepared from substances such as cavya, ghana, and ativiṣā used for digestion.

"Picchāsṛgbastis" refers to picchā-bastis and asṛg-bastis; "uktam" means that which has been stated both directly and by way of extension (*atideśa*) regarding the combination of three or more [substances];
and "miśram" (mixed) refers to these very same [substances] combined together individually.
Regarding the phrase "arising from the combination of two or more [doshas]," this refers to diarrhea produced by the conjunction of three or four doshas.
Because of the specific predominance [of one dosha] among them, the very nature of the treatment varies according to the relative strength or weakness of those combinations.

This is precisely what is meant by the statement that, depending on the relative strength [of the doshas], even when many [doshas] are weak and there is no opposing factor, the enema (*basti*) alone is the primary medicine; such is the remainder of the meaning.

This is the summary of the contents of the chapter beginning with "prāsṛtikā," including the complications (vyāpada) and the treatments for them; the complications arising from the administration of mild enemas (mṛdu-basti), such as numbness and other symptoms, have been described, as well as the therapeutic procedures for those very complications.
Non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) have been described in the treatment of diarrhea;
the preparation of meat-juice (rasakalpa) has been provided for cases of diarrhea through the treatment indicated for meat-juice;
and medicated ghee has been mentioned starting with the verse beginning "udumbara... and so forth.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Success of Preparations Containing a Prasṛta Measure," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā*, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Section on Success (*Siddhisthāna*).

[Siddhisthāna, Chapter 9 (117 of 120)] Immediately following the *Prāsṛtayogīyā* [siddhi], the *Trimarmīyā Siddhi* is now stated for the purpose of demonstrating the remedial treatment using enemas (*basti*) for complications arising from diseases affecting the three vital organs (*trimarman*). Furthermore, the section on the administration of enemas continues from the previous chapter after the discussion of the management of complications. Alternatively, since the treatment for enema complications was already established in the preceding chapter, and since diseases of the three vital organs can also arise from such complications, the *Trimarmīyā Siddhi* is taught here to demonstrate their treatment based on prior knowledge.

The diseases to be discussed in this chapter have not been mentioned in the *Trimarmīya-cikitsita* (the treatment of the three vital spots) for fear of excessive prolixity; they are now set forth here.
In this context as well, by the word "marmas," the diseases located in the vital spots are meant; the successful treatment concerning them is the *Trimarmīya-siddhi*.

It has been stated that there are one hundred and seven vital points (*marman*) enumerated according to the body's constituents; these are situated within the flesh, vessels, ligaments, bones, and joints. The term "trunk" (*skandha*) refers to what follows immediately [the head]. And here, by the term "branches" (*śākhā*), the two arms and the two legs are meant, because they are like branches. The blood and other bodily elements (*dhātu*) are not included here by the term "branches," because those elements exist even in the trunk; therefore, forty-four vital points are located in the branches, while the remainder are located in the trunk.

As stated in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*: "Of these, eleven are located in each leg; by this, the other leg and the two arms are explained; there are twelve in the abdomen and chest, fourteen in the back, and thirty-seven above the neck" (*Su. Śā. A.* 6). Furthermore, the specific classification of each of these vital points (*marman*) has been stated in detail in the *Suśruta* itself, beginning with the section on the "sole-heart" (*talahṛdaya*) (*Su. Śā. A.* 6), which should be followed accordingly. He now states the defining characteristic of the one hundred and seven vital points, which distinguishes them from non-vital regions of the body: "Of these," and so forth.

"Due to the specific nature of the binding of consciousness" means that the element of consciousness (cetanā-dhātu) is bound specifically to the vital points (marmas). Furthermore, this binding of consciousness in the vital points is inferred to be caused by past karma (adṛṣṭa), since a specific intensity of pain is observed when those vital points are afflicted.

"Because the branches depend on that": since the branches themselves depend on the trunk, the meaning is that a *marman* (vital point) directly dependent on the trunk is more critical than those dependent on branches which themselves depend on the trunk. Furthermore, the dependence of the branches on the trunk is due to the fact that they are damaged when the trunk is damaged, as well as because they are nourished by the sap and other nutrients produced by the trunk itself. Moreover, it is only the *marmans* situated in the trunk that are immediately fatal, not those residing in the branches; thus, the trunk holds primacy.

As stated in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā*: “The *śṛṅgāṭakas*, the *adhipati* [vessel], the two *śaṅkhas*, the throat, the head, the anus, the heart, the bladder, and the navel—these, when struck, indeed cause instantaneous death” (*Su. Śā. A.* 6).
The connection is that the heart, the bladder, and the head are the most vital [parts].
He states the reason for its greater importance: "Because the body has that as its root.

"Because it has that as its root" means because it is dependent upon it. And thus, he will demonstrate the heart's support of the body with the passage beginning, "There are ten vessels in the heart," and ending, "like spokes from the hub," even though other vital points (*marmans*) are also specifically said to be the supports of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*); as it is said: "They say there are exactly ten abodes in which the vital breaths are established."

By the statement, "The two temples, the three vital points, the throat, blood, semen, ojas, and the rectum" (Sūtra-sthāna 29), although the temples and so forth are indeed seats of the vital breaths (*prāṇāyatana*), they do not serve as the primary substrates for the body in the same way that the heart and other organs do. Therefore, even though their status as seats of the vital breaths is equal, because of the specific distinction of being the primary substrates of the body, it is here stated that the heart and others alone possess primacy. Furthermore, the heart and others are the substrates of the vital breaths in a manner that the temples and others are not; for it has been said: "Regarding the enumeration of the body, one hundred and seven vital points (*marman*) have been mentioned; among these..."

"The sages declare that the vital points (*marmāṇi*), the bladder, the heart, and the head are the primary [seats], for they are the supports of the life-breaths (*prāṇa*); by afflicting these, Vāta and the other humors afflict the life-breaths as well" (Suśruta Saṃhitā, Śārīra-sthāna, Chapter 6).

Others, however, show that the supports of the life-breaths such as the temples (*śaṅkha*) are included within the heart and so forth due to their proximity; but that view has been disregarded because it lacks a scriptural basis.

"Ten vessels" refers to the ten vessels that carry *ojas*. These are those explained in the chapter on the Ten Great Roots (*Arthadaśamahāmūlīya*) beginning with: "In the heart, ten great roots are attached" (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 30). "Prāṇa and apāna" refer to inhalation and exhalation; however, some say that prāṇa and apāna are simply the two aforementioned types of wind (*vāta*). Regarding this, although they say that apāna has its seat specifically in the penis, the pelvis, and so forth, nevertheless, because it conforms to the heart without being separate from it, it is said to be "situated in the heart."
The mind (*manas*) is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*);
it is consciousness (*cetanā*) denoted by the term "the Great" (*mahat*),
which is a specific modification of the intellect (*buddhi*).

"The great elements" refers to the subtle great elements connected with the self; all of this is established in the Sāṅkhya system and should be followed as it is explained in the *Śārīra*, where it is stated in another passage: "The sixfold limb is consciousness, the sense faculties, and the five objects."

"The Self, along with its qualities, the mind, and that which is to be contemplated, are situated within the heart" (Sūtra 30). These are the topics mentioned in this verse; furthermore, the inclusion of additional subjects should be understood as being subsumed within those already stated. Alternatively, they are mentioned here by way of a summary of the entire treatise.

Just as the ten vessels (*dhamanī*) and so forth are supported within the heart, he illustrates this by means of the following analogy: "They are established like spokes from the hub" (*nābhyāmarā iva pratiṣṭhitāni*). Here, "hub" (*nābhi*) refers to the nave of a wheel, and "spokes" (*arāḥ*) refer to the wooden rods situated between the rim and the nave of a wheel. Just as the spokes are connected to the hub of the wheel and are affected by its injury—since they are rooted in it and thus connected to it—in the same way, the vessels and other organs are also related to the heart. Alternatively, there is a reading *nābhyāmaparā*, which means "like others [connected] to the umbilical cord of the embryo" (*garbhanābhyāmaparā iva*); some explain this as *arā ivāpare*.
The implication is that by this [statement], it is established that even the vessels (*dhamanī*) and other structures located in other regions are dependent upon the heart.
He states their dependence on the head with the words "in the head," etc.

Although the channels (*srotas*) that carry the sense organs and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) exist in other regions as well, nevertheless, they are especially bound together in the head; he demonstrates this through the simile, "like rays from the sun."
The fact that the aforementioned channels have the head as their locus is inferred from the observation of specific injury resulting from injury to that [head];
they state that the bladder has the body as its locus— by the passage beginning with "But the bladder," etc.,
which establishes its location in the middle of the rectum and so forth, he demonstrates that the rectum and other parts have the bladder as their locus.

The "foundation" (pratiṣṭhā) of the water-carrying channels means their location; just as the ocean is the place where rivers are filled, so too the bladder is the place of rest for the water-carrying channels. "Rooted in those" means connected to them by those [channels] designated as *marmas*. For the channels themselves do not possess the status of *marmas*; rather, either the term "channel-marma" refers to the inclusion of the vessel-*marmas* (*sirā-marmas*), or the channels connected to the *marmas*, or the channels that nourish the *marmas*, are what are designated by the term "channel-marmas."

Because the destruction of that which is supported follows from the destruction of its support—since the destruction of the supported occurs due to the destruction of the support—it is logical that the destruction of the body results from the destruction of any one of the [vital organs] such as the heart.

That the body is supported by the heart should be understood precisely through its dependence on the ten principal vessels (*dhamani*) and other structures that constitute the primary origin of the body.
"From injury" means from some kind of pathological alteration.
4–5 He describes, in sequence, the diseases arising from trauma to the heart and other organs: "In that regard," etc.;
*klomāpakarṣaṇam* refers to a pain characterized by the sensation of being pulled out from the *kloman*.
*Veṣṭana* is a sensation on the head in the form of being bound;
*kuṇḍala* is a sensation in the bladder in the form of a coil;
*upastambha* is likewise of the bladder.
In the "Therapeutics," specifically in the "Therapeutics of the Three Vital Organs" (trimarmīyacikitsita),
there are the "Procedures for Treatment" (sacikitsitavidhāna), which include the methods of therapeutic action.
He states, with supporting reasoning, the primacy of enema (*basti*) in the protection of the vital points (*marman*): "But these... and so forth.

Since wind (*anila*) alone is the cause for the provocation of both pitta and kapha when they are inactive, therefore, even in a disorder born of kapha and pitta, wind is the underlying factor; and even in a disorder born of wind itself, wind is the independent cause. Consequently, by one who wishes to protect the vital points in all disorders, the vital points must be protected from that very cause, which is wind.

Likewise, it is said that the root of *prāṇa* is the cause of life, which consists of unvitiated *vāyu*, whereas vitiated *vāyu* is destructive to *prāṇa*. Therefore, even the vital points (*marmans*) must be protected from *vāta* for the sake of preserving life;

and because [these] are most effectively treated by enema (*basti*), they are "most curable by enema" compared to other treatments. For it has been stated: "Enema is the foremost among those things that alleviate *vāta*" (Sūtra Sthāna, Chapter 25).

Furthermore, regarding the two categories of non-unctuous enemas (*anuvāsana-skandha*), as stated in the *Rogabhiṣagjitīya*: "Non-unctuous enema, however, is simply oil (*sneha*); it is of two kinds—stationary (*sthāvara*) and mobile (*jaṅgama*)" (Vimāna Sthāna, Chapter 8)—these two categories of non-unctuous enema are to be understood.
The word "here" (iha) means in the place of success;

"having reflected with the intellect" means having reflected with the intellect upon the ten factors such as the doshas and medicines, and having reflected with the intellect upon the treatment for wind diseases, one should apply it—this is the meaning.
He speaks specifically regarding the treatment for piercing the vital points (*marmabhedacikitsita*): "Furthermore," and so forth;
in the phrase "when the heart is afflicted by *vāta*," the word "by *vāta*" is to be supplied as the ellipsis;
and in the expression "of salts" (*lavaṇānām*), the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).

"Anyatama" means one among others, as in "the most excellent"; "hṛdya" means agreeable to the mind. That which is disagreeable to the heart because its flavor is loathsome is precisely what is not agreeable to the mind; furthermore, it is stated in the *Trimarmīya-cikitsita* that such [unwholesome] action causes heart disease.

In the phrase "smoke and so forth" (*dhūmādīni*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes fomentation by sprinkling (*pariṣeka*), poultices (*upanāha*), and the like. Regarding the statement "in the bladder, however," it should be understood from the context that this refers to when [the bladder] is vitiated by Vāta. Furthermore, it has already been established that even in cases of vitiation by Pitta and Kapha, Vāta alone is the primary factor; therefore, vitiation by Kapha and Pitta is also implied.
"Vartis" refers to medicinal suppositories made from fruit-pulp.

“By the *śyāmā* group and so forth” refers to the *śyāmā* group previously mentioned in [Viśeṣasthāna 8] as “of *śyāmā*, *trivṛt*, *caturaṅgula*, *tilvaka*, *mahāvṛkṣa*, *saptalā*, *śaṅkhinī*, *dantī*, and *dravantī*.

“The *bilva* group” refers to the great *pañcamūla*; alternatively, it should be understood as the *bilva* group mentioned in [Siddhisthāna 7]: “containing the root of *bilva*, *trivṛt*, *dāru*, barley, jujube, and horse gram.
Another [preparation] is the paste of *hapuṣā* and so forth, boiled in milk with the roots of the *śara* group and so forth.
An oil prepared with *kharāśvā*, *ajamodā*,

and *pītadāru* is used for an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) in that same decoction enema (*nirūha*); however, some say that "oil extracted from the heartwood of *sarala* and prepared with *pītadāru*" refers to the oil prepared with *pītadāru*.
The *tailvaka-sarpis* is as stated in the *tilvaka-kalpa*;
in the [formula] beginning with *śatāvarī*, "two *sārivās*" refers to *anantamūla* and *śyāmā*;
[and] *śreyasī* is *rāsnā*.
Upakuñcikā, kṛṣṇajīraka, śitivāraka, śāliñca,
aśmabhedaka, and pāṣāṇabhedaka.
The meaning is that it should be administered as an *uttarabasti*, because of the procedure for the *uttarabasti* which will be described hereafter;
the meaning is that the *nirūha* should be administered in place of the *nirūha*.
Demonstrating the meaning stated in prose through verse, he further says with the words "something in the heart" (*kiñcit hṛdaye*) and so forth:
the avoidance of afflictions (*ābādhavarjana*)— meaning the avoidance of causes that injure the vital points (*marman*)—
and the adherence to the regimen for the healthy (*svasthavṛttānuvartana*), become protective precisely by way of nourishing the heart and other [organs].
"Removal of arisen suffering" (utpannārtivighāta) means the counteracting of arisen diseases of the vital points (*marmaroga*).

Following the discussion on the enemas that protect the vital points, the author says "hereafter," etc., while showing the diseases located in the vital points along with their treatments, which had not been previously mentioned.
He describes the heart disease known as apatantraka: "When enraged," and so forth;
"above its location" refers to being above the location of vāta.
"Stabdha-akṣa" (fixed eyes) or "nimīlana" (closing of eyes): he either has fixed eyes or his eyes are closed;

"niḥsañjña" (unconscious) means that at the time of the onset of the disease, having stiffened his vision and destroyed consciousness, he makes a gurgling sound with his throat and becomes unconscious.

"Mohaṃ vṛte punar" (again, when the heart is obstructed) means that when the heart is again obstructed by wind—specifically by wind associated with phlegm—he falls into a state of delusion. Some call this very condition "apataṅka."

On this point, Jatūkarṇa states: "In apatantraka, there is pain and pressure in the heart, head, and temples, bending of the body, convulsions, delusion, stiffness of the eyes, inability to close them, difficult breathing, and moaning.

Alternatively, they describe apatantraka as being of two types: from vāta and from kapha. Among these, by the phrase "that which is unconscious is apatantraka," the kapha-born type is indicated; and by the phrase "they say [the other] is severe due to vāyu," they mean that the apatantraka produced by vāyu is indeed called apatānaka.
Its severity (dāruṇatva) is to be explained as resulting from its being initiated by a violent (dāruṇa) vāta.
Likewise, in the Suśruta-saṃhitā, the chapter on Vātavyādhi (12–15) mentions them as such:
"in those dhamanīs which carry consciousness."
"With barley-decoction water" means with water boiled with barley according to the six-fold method (*ṣaḍaṅgavidhi*).
That therapeutic procedure which cures heart disease and subdues *vāta* and *kapha* is beneficial in *apatantraka*.

Regarding the statement "cleansing therapies (*śodhana*) are not beneficial in their entirety," the intention is that one should administer a small enema (*nirūha*) for the purpose of cleansing; for if a large cleansing enema were administered, it would cause agitation of the *vāta*.
Some recite the definition of *tandrā* (drowsiness) and its treatment beginning with the words "sweet and unctuous" (*madhurasnigdha*), etc.;

Having described diseases of the heart, he speaks of diseases of the bladder, beginning with "mūtraukasāda" and so forth; and it has been established in the *Trimarmīya* chapter that these urinary disorders (*mūtradoṣas*) are indeed distinct from dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*).
By the passage beginning with "pitta, kapha," etc., he describes *mūtraukasāda* (obstruction of urine).
It is implied that this condition is produced by vāta-kapha, pitta-vāta, and the three doṣas combined (*saṃhata*).

Regarding the term *saṃhate*: redness and yellowness of color are caused by pitta; whiteness of color by kapha; and the presence of the characteristics of both kapha and pitta by kapha and pitta together; while vāyu, however, is always present as a concomitant factor.

In this case, the provocation of the wind (*vāyu*) is caused solely by obstruction; therefore, the treatment for pitta and kapha alone has been stated by the phrase "one should conquer [them] with those that remove pitta and phlegm," the sense being that the victory over wind occurs precisely through the conquest of its obstruction. (27–28) "Pain without a cause" (*animittaruḥ*) refers to pain whose cause is not perceived.
Regarding "mūtravairecanīm" (the urine-purgative): this refers to the formulation consisting of the ten drugs that purify the urine.
As for "hiṅgudviruttaram," it is as stated in the verse beginning with "dviruttaraṃ hiṅguvacā" (Ci. A. 26); that in which asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) is doubled is called *hiṅgudviruttaram*. (29–31)
"Of one who has urinated" means one who has experienced the urge to urinate; that is to say, one possessed by the urge to urinate.
"Ejaculated" means fallen from its own place.
"Agitated by wind" means dispersed by wind.
The *kṛcchra* characterized by these other symptoms is indeed distinct from *mūtrakṛcchra*, because the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) differ slightly.
The term "a little" (*kiñcit*) means a small amount;
"with heavy genitals due to residual urine" (*uccheṣaguruśephasaḥ*) means that the penis becomes heavy due to the presence of increased residual urine.
"Having the appearance of wind," and so forth, refers to the symptoms of depletion (*saṅkṣaya*).
"Having the appearance of wind" means being endowed with the characteristics of *vāta*.
"Due to suppression" means due to the obstruction of the urge to urinate.
"By heat" means by the heat of bile (*pitta-ūṣman*);
"drying up" means that the *vāta* itself, accompanied by heat, dries up the urine.
By the phrase beginning with "due to obstruction of the movement," he describes *vātakuṇḍalikā*.

Due to the obstruction of the flow of urine, the wind (vāyu) moves upward and discharges urine while being broken, twisted, or coiled within the bladder or the urinary passage. "Broken" means struck back; "twisted" means curved; "coiled" means remaining in a whirling state. Such a manifestation of the wind occurs specifically in the urinary passage; this describes the characteristics of *vātakuṇḍalikā*—beginning with the words "stiffening" (*saṃstambha*) and so forth—and "breaking" refers to a pain in the form of a splitting sensation.

One should understand that [the disease] is produced by vitiated *vāta* and *kapha*, resulting in a red glandular swelling (*rakta-granthi*). "Obstruction of feces" (*viḍ-vighāta*) means the cessation of stool;
by the verse beginning with "rapid journey" (*drutādhva*), etc., [the author] describes *basti-kuṇḍala*.

If the enema bag is turned upward (udvṛtta), meaning its opening is facing away, or if it is squeezed by the hands or other means, or if its opening is blocked by phlegm (śleṣman), it does not succeed; likewise, it does not succeed when the bile (pitta) is aggravated.
"Unobstructed aperture" means its opening is not blocked;
"coiled" means made circular.
He states the characteristics of that which is circular in the passage beginning with "it may be in the bladder," and so forth.
32–48 – He describes the treatment, beginning with "the predominance of the doshas," and so forth.
The meaning is that one should overcome [the condition] by employing applications that alleviate dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra), after having observed the predominance of the [specific] doṣas.
It has been stated that one should administer the *uttarabasti* (urethral/vaginal enema); following that, he describes the procedure for the *uttarabasti*: "The flower-tube," and so forth.

"Flower-tube" (*puṣpanetra*) is the technical name for the tube of the *uttarabasti*. It is called *uttarabasti* because it is administered through the upper passage (*uttaramārga*), or alternatively, because of its superior quality (*śreṣṭhaguṇatayā*).

It is equal to the stalk of the flower of the *jātyaśvaghana*; that is, its tip is similar to the stalk of the flowers of both the *jāti* and the *aśvaghana*. For it is said in the *Hārīta-saṃhitā*: "Likewise, [the tip] is like the stalk of the *kunda*. *Aśvaghana* is the *karavīra* (oleander).
"Having a hole the size of a mustard seed" means having a hole large enough for a mustard seed to pass through.

"Having two rings" (*dvikarṇika*) means there is one ring on one side for the purpose of binding the bladder, and another ring at the tip, six finger-breadths from the beginning, which is the length of the penis; or alternatively, the reading is "having three rings" (*trikarṇika*).

And having determined the quantity of unctuous substance according to the specific age—as the aforementioned unctuous substance is for a twenty-five-year-old—one must apply a reduction based on the differentiation of ages below that point. For it is stated in the Suśruta-saṃhitā: "The maximum measure of unctuous substance is declared here to be one *prakūñca*; for those under twenty-five years of age, it is determined by the physician's judgment" (Su.Ci.A. 37). Regarding the term "in a healthy person" (*hṛṣṭe*), meaning in one who is firm: if the probe (*śalākā*) should pass through without obstruction, then a flower-tube (*puṣpanetra*) equal in size to the penis should be inserted.
First, an exploration with a probe is performed for the purpose of ascertaining the path;

just as [the nozzle] is inserted into the anus with qualities such as steadiness of the eye, so too it should be done in the penis. If the nozzle enters beyond the measurement of the phallus, it will injure the bladder.
Regarding the term *ūne* (in deficient cases), it refers to when [the oil] has entered only slightly according to the measure of the rectum (ślokas 50–57).
With the verse beginning with *pippalī*, etc., [the author] describes a wick (*varti*) that induces the movement of the oil which has remained overnight (*vyuṣita*) yet does not emerge.

And this wick (varti) should be made hard by cooking with jaggery (guḍa), so that it becomes smooth at its posterior half—as stated in the root text; "resembling a thumb" means that when being inserted into the anus for the purpose of inducing the flow of oil, it should be made equal in size to a thumb;
"by those two" refers to the penis and the anus once the wick has been applied.

Extending by analogy the characteristics of what should be used, what should be avoided, complications, and correct administration as they apply to the *uttarabasti* (urethral/vaginal enema) just as they do to the *anuvāsana* (oil enema), he says: "The procedure for the *ānuvāsanika*," etc.
(verses 58–61).
Regarding the administration of the *uttarabasti* to women during the menstrual period, which was previously mentioned as the general rule, he now prescribes it specifically for that time.
He states the reason for giving [the medicine] during the period of menstruation (ārtava-kāla), beginning with "garbhāsana" and so forth.
"Garbhāsana" means the seat of the embryo, that is, the uterus (garbhāśaya); others, however, say it refers to the vagina (yoni).
"Ādatte" means she properly receives [it].
"Apāvṛta" means that which has the covering of accumulated dust and form removed.

"Of the measure of a flower-stalk," and so forth; "carrying a flow of mung beans" means a channel through which mung beans can pass should be inserted into the birth canal to a depth of four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*). This procedure for lubricating the birth canal is to be performed only on women who have reached puberty. However, when lubricating the urinary tract, an insertion of two finger-breadths (*dvyaṅgula*) is to be performed only on women who have reached puberty.

Because of the small size of a young girl, the introduction of only one finger should be performed for the purpose of applying [medication] to the urinary tract; however, for young girls, [the application] is not given at all to the birth canal, because their birth canal remains closed. The wick (*varti*) should be thicker; thus, for the purpose of returning the oleaginous substance (*sneha*), the wick should be made thicker, and the dosage of the oleaginous substance here is to be understood as that stated by Suśruta: "In this case, a *prasṛta* of the oleaginous substance is measured by the root of one's own fingers" (Su.Ci.A. 37).

In order to explain the detailed exposition on the three vital organs (*trimarmīya*) for the sake of knowing the disorders of the head that arise through sequential transmission, he says: "Therefore," and so forth.
"Severe" (*dāruṇa*) means that it acts quickly;
"he lives for no more than three days," and so forth—this is the specific power (*prabhāva*) of *śaṅkhaka*.

By the statement, "one should perform treatment after having rejected [it]," it is meant that as soon as this disease has arisen, medical treatment must be undertaken preceded by a formal rejection [of the prognosis].
With the verse beginning with "rūkṣa" (dry), etc., he describes hemiplegia (*ardhāvabhedaka*).
*Avaśyāya* means frost (*hima*).

"Resembling a weapon and a fire-drill" means resembling the cutting of a weapon and the friction of a fire-drill; *araṇi* is the wood used for producing fire. Alternatively, by means of the fire-drill (*araṇi*) as the cause, fire itself is indicated here;

this is the supreme dose of the fourfold unctuous substance (*catuḥsneha*). And the supreme dose is that which is metabolized over a day and night—clarified butter (*ghṛta*) that has been aged for ten years.

Some say that *upanāha* is a type of head-compress (*śirobasti*), which is called *māstiṣka*; for in another treatise, the *māstiṣka* is described as a variety of head-compress, stating: "For the *māstiṣka*, an eight-finger-width strip [is used], while for the *basti* it is twelve fingers," and so forth. The procedure for the head-compress is to be known from *Śālākya*: "A leather strip twelve fingers wide, equal in length to the head, should be tied with a cloth-wick at the forehead—the site of the ear-tie—after wrapping it with cloth, and then smeared with a paste of black gram."

Then, one should administer lukewarm oil prepared according to the specific disease, pouring it up to the hairline; one should retain it for ten, eight, or six finger-breadths' duration in cases of Vata and the other doshas, respectively, until the nose becomes moist.
"One should massage one thousand measures [of oil] upon a single part, such as the shoulder, until it is free from pain;

for one who has been properly treated with oleation, the maximum duration of its use is seven days. Likewise: "Having stretched a piece of leather over the head so that it is eight finger-breadths high, one should wrap it around the head and below it, and then smear it with a paste of black gram (māṣa)."
"While the patient is seated and motionless, one should fill [the head] with lukewarm oils and retain them for the sake of pacifying pain for one watch (yāma) or even half a watch;
this head-poultice (śirobasti) conquers diseases of the head arising from wind," and so forth.

"Or its burning" (dahanaṃ vā asya) refers to burning with a reed stalk (*śarakāṇḍa*) or similar means on the forehead and the temple regions (*lalāṭa-śaṅkha-pradeśa*), based on the authority of other tantras;
this should be understood as what is prescribed as the medical treatment (*cikitsita*), and it is that which is commended here—thus it should be applied.
The brain is the marrow located in the head;
being liquid, it flows— that is, it moves.

And this form of *sūryāvarta* arises from an abnormal and discordant combination (*vikṛti-viṣama-samavāya*) of the *doṣas* and *dūṣyas*; therefore, no other disorder becomes like this, nor does its pain increase specifically under the heat of the sun and not under the heat of fire—this too should be understood as being caused by its specific power (*prabhāva*). Regarding the reading "maintaining the three unctuous substances" (*tri-sneha-dhāraṇam*), they say it refers to the common application of oil, ghee, and muscle fat.
The *lāva* and other such birds are described as *viṣkira* (scattered-feeders) [in verses 79–83].
*Manyā* refers to the two vessels (veins) of the neck; *ghāṭā* is the posterior part of the neck; and *paścāt* refers to the back.
And that [pain] resides in the eyes, eyebrows, and temples; having pervaded the temples and other areas, it becomes fixed.
In another medical treatise, they call this Anantavāta "Anyatovāta.
It is to be treated with the destruction of the *sirā* (veins) by means of *arkāvarta* and *nāśana* procedures—that is, by venesection—and with medicinal remedies for *sūryāvarta* and *nāśana*.
*Nastaḥkarma* (nasal therapy) is the treatment common to all diseases of the head.
Regarding the reason for performing *nastaḥkarma* in cases of head diseases, he states: "For [the nose] is the gateway," and so forth.
By means of that path in the form of the nose,
"that" refers to the medicine given through the nose;
"pervading" means having pervaded the head.
Regarding those [treatments] for diseases of the head (śirogada):
following the discussion on diseases of the head, he states the necessary distinctions regarding nasal therapy (nastaḥkarma) that must be explained, beginning with "nāvanam" and so forth.

The methods beginning with *nāvana* (nasal medication) are described in the section on therapeutics (*cikitsā-sthāna*). Here, in the *Suśruta*, five types of nasal therapy (*nastaḥ-karma*) are mentioned, excluding *dhūma* (fumigation): "That [nasal therapy], though twofold, has five varieties; namely: *nasya*, *śirovirecana*, *pratimarśa*, *avapīḍa*, and *pradhamana*" (Ci. A. 40).

However, in this [text], *śirovirecana* is included by the very term *nāvana*; as it is said: "Nasal medication (*nāvana*) is traditionally held to be of two kinds: oleating (*snehana*) and purifying (*śodhana*). Therefore, the meaning stated in the *Suśruta* is indeed included here.

Regarding the statement that *avapīḍa* (pressed-out preparation) is both purificatory (*śodhana*) and constipating (*stambhana*), some authorities maintain that pacifying (*saṃśamana*) action is also included among the functions of *avapīḍa*; however, that [pacifying action] should be subsumed under constipation itself.

It is called *avapīḍa* because the paste and other ingredients are administered after being pressed out. By this, the inclusion of the paste of rock salt, long pepper, and so forth—which is administered for the purpose of head-purgation (*śirovirecana*)—is also established.
Furthermore, by the statement "for *dhmāpana* (fumigation) indeed purifies the channels of the body," he demonstrates that *dhmāpana* serves exclusively the purpose of head-purgation.

In the phrase "śamanādika" (beginning with pacification), the word *śamana* includes that which is produced by application (*prāyogika*). By this, there is the inclusion here of the unctuous (*snehanika*), purgative (*virecanika*), and smoking (*dhūma*) [medications] administered through the nose; however, the smoke intended for oral consumption is not a nasal medication (*nasya*), as it serves both purposes. The definition of *pratimarśa*, which serves the purposes of both unctuousness and purification, will be stated later in the passage beginning with, "One should apply a finger of unctuous substance into the nose."
He states the threefold nature of the previously mentioned five types of nasal therapy (nastaḥkarma) with the words beginning "evam" (thus), etc. "Karma" refers to nasal therapy;

by mentioning pacification (śamana), suppression (stambhana) is also included; by nourishment (tarpaṇa), oleation (snehana) is subsumed; and whatever other sub-varieties are taught in other treatises are also included within these very categories.
He states the scope for the triad of procedures beginning with purgation (virecana): "stambha" and so forth;
"tarpaṇa" refers to nourishment by means of oleation (sneha).

"Likewise, it is recommended for those who are fit" means it is recommended for those fit for fumigation (*dhūma*) and inhalation (*dhamāpana*). Among these, those fit for fumigation have been explained in the *Sūtrasthāna*. However, those fit for inhalation (*dhamāpana*) should be understood as those mentioned under the description of the qualities of inhalation by the phrase "purification of the bodily channels" (*dehasrotoviśodhana*), namely those such as *abhiṣyanda* (excessive secretions) and *apasmāra* (epilepsy), whose channels require purification.

He describes the powder for head-evacuation (śirovirecana) and its procedure: "The medicinal substances beginning with fruits," etc. This refers to the sevenfold head-evacuative materials mentioned in the *Rogabhiṣagjitīya* chapter—namely, fruits, leaves, roots, tubers, flowers, exudates, and barks.
One should prepare a powder; that is, one should prepare the powder for the purpose of blowing it into the nose (*pradhamana*) and for the purpose of pressing it into the nostrils (*avapīḍana*).
The section on sweet substances (madhura-skandha) has also been explained in the chapter titled "The Victory over Diseases through Physicians" (rogabhiṣagjitīya).
He states the procedure for nasal administration (*nastaḥkarma*): "When the sun is in the east," and so forth.

The rule is that it should be done in summer when the sun is in the east, but in winter when the sun is at the meridian. Furthermore, this applies to one who has already performed the necessary daily duties (*prākkṛtāvaśyaka*), meaning one who has completed the required tasks such as the evacuation of impurities.
"Thus for one lying down" means that for one lying with the head slightly lowered,
one should administer [the medicine] equally through both nostrils;
"the tube" (*praṇāḍī*) refers to the nozzle used for administering the nasal medication.

Regarding the phrase "according to the prescribed method" (*yathāvidhi*), this refers to smoke-inhalation (*dhūmapāna*) that is free from defects such as improper dosage; after first describing the rationale for smoke-inhalation, he states the procedure for inhaling smoke, beginning with "by means of sudation" (*svedana*) and so forth, as well as the method for insufflation (*pradhmāpana*) which has been previously mentioned and will also be described later starting with "with a tube six finger-breadths long" (*ṣaḍaṅgulayā*).
The phrase beginning with "one whose head has been purged" (*viriktaśirasam*) applies generally to all types of purgation;
"in the three" refers to the [doshas] such as vata and so forth,
and "purified by purgation" (*virekaśuddha*) means purified by head-purgation (*śirovireka*).

The phrase "one indulges in that which aggravates the [specific] doṣa" should be applied accordingly; that is to say, one should administer treatment in accordance with the diseases produced by untimely head-purgation (śirovirecana). (98–110)
"Nāvanam" means "snehana," which refers to nasal therapy (nasya) for the purpose of oleation;
"sveda-ādi" is the division [of the list];
and "ghṛtam kṣīram" refers to ghee and milk for the pregnant woman to overcome vāta and for the nourishment of the fetus.
Regarding the passage beginning with "jvara" (fever) and so forth:

for those afflicted by fever and other such conditions, oleation and nasal drops (nāvana) would cause blindness (timira); likewise, they would cause blindness in a drinker of alcohol. To this, he states the treatment, beginning with "rūkṣaiḥ" (with dry substances) and so forth.

They call *śītāñjana* "stream-born collyrium" (*srotoñjana*); or rather, *śītāñjana* is a collyrium made from bitter substances. As it is stated in the *Śālākya*: "Scraping (*lekhana*), healing (*ropaṇa*), and also clarifying (*prasādana*): healing should be performed with a bitter substance, clarifying with a sweet one, and the wise person should effect scraping with pungent, sour, salty, and other [substances]."

"Because it is cooling, it pacifies [the eye]; because it is bitter and dry, it quickly dries it up"—here, "with dry substances" refers to collyriums (*añjana*) and the like, and "application" (*lepa*) means an ointment applied to the eyes. *Puṭapāka* should be understood as either a scarifying (*lekhanīya*) or a pacifying (*śamana*) treatment that removes disorders arising from eye-irrigation (*akṣitarpaṇa*). Indeed, in the science of *Śālākya*, *puṭapāka* is said to be of three types—emollient (*snehana*), scarifying (*lekhanīya*), and clarifying (*prasādana*). Its specific procedure has not been elaborated upon here, as it belongs to another section.

In order to demonstrate that both types of action—those accomplished by massage (*pratimarśa*) and those by nasal medication (*nāvana*)—are applicable here, the previously mentioned procedure for *nāvana* is reiterated: "oleation," and so forth.

Others maintain that these two actions are reiterated specifically for all nasal treatments (*nastaḥkarma*), and they state that in this context, there is an inclusion of the previously mentioned oleation and pacification (*śamana*).

Regarding its purpose, he describes the procedure for *pratimarśa*— which consists of oleation and purification and is free from harm— that is, devoid of complications— in the verse beginning with "into the nose," and so forth.
"Snehāṅgulim" means a finger filled with oil;
"sarvadā" means in all seasons;
"dārḍhyakṛt" means that which produces firmness in the skull and other parts of the head.

This *pratimarśa* (nasal drop) should be understood as being of a small quantity of oil and administered without snuffing, and it may be used at all times. However, that which consists of a large quantity of oil is not for constant use.

As it has been said: "One should know the quantity of *pratimarśa* by the amount of oil poured through the nose that reaches the mouth with only slight snuffing. Likewise: "A person should not drink [the oil] during a *pratimarśa*, for fear of causing a flow from the throat."
"As long as the oil remains in the mouth, that shall be its measure. Thus,
the summary beginning with "three" and so forth has a clear meaning.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Successful Treatment of the Three Vital Organs," in the Siddhisthāna of the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka Saṃhitā, composed by Śrī Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Siddhisthāna, Chapter 10 (118 of 120):

Since this chapter on the three vital organs (*trimarmīyā*) sets forth many diseases, the "Success of Enemas" (*bastisiddhi*) is now declared for the purpose of setting forth enemas that are beneficial against those many diseases;
here, by the word *basti*, the "enemas of success" (*siddhibasti*) to be described later are intended.
"Of the perfected ones" (siddhānām) means those for whom the results are well-known;
"in those various [conditions]" refers to the diseases of wind (vāta) and so forth that will be described hereafter.

"Siddhim" means the accomplishment of the enema (*basti*), or alternatively, the treatise that describes the enema. He now states the procedure for the enema and its benefits, which constitute the constituent parts of the enema to be explained, beginning with "baladoṣa... and so forth.

In this context, it should be explained that by taking the powers (*bala*) and so forth according to their primary importance, all examinations are encompassed; furthermore, this matter—which was already stated in the passage beginning with "having examined the defects and the medicines" (*Si. A. 3*)—is stated again here by virtue of the specific topic, namely, by means of the respective groups of medicines as prescribed for each particular disease.

Regarding the phrase "svān svān" (each their own): enemas intended for the pacification of specific diseases through specific drugs and medicinal formulations—such as those using *āśvapa*, *parṇa*, or *tarpaṇa*—achieve their depleting effect more rapidly than other depleting medicines because they are administered for the purpose of depletion itself. Likewise, an enema prepared with nourishing substances also brings about nourishment more quickly than other nourishing treatments. 4–5

Regarding the removal of *doṣas* by means other than purification (*śodhana*) while depending on enemas (*basti*), he states the disadvantage [of such alternatives] in the passage beginning with "even though" (*satyapi*):

because of administering purgatives (*virecana*) with drugs such as pungent ones (*kaṭuka*), there occurs pain, eructation (*udgāra*), nausea (*utkleśa*), unpalatability (*ahṛdyatva*), and pains in the digestive tract (*koṣṭha-rujā*); all these arise. Among these, the pain arises precisely from the agitation caused by the pungent taste and so forth. The point is that these disadvantages do not occur in the case of an enema (*basti*).

By the term "purgation" (vireka), both emesis (vamana) and purgation are to be understood; alternatively, emesis is not mentioned here because its scope is entirely distinct from that of enemas (basti). However, since purgation is applicable even when the morbid humors (doṣa) reside in the colon (pakvāśaya)—which is the primary site for enemas—it is with reference to purgation alone that the preeminence of the enema is stated here. He declares the preeminence of the enema regarding cases where purgation is not indicated, etc., with the words beginning "those who are not to be purged."

In the passage beginning with "those two," the explanation should be understood according to their respective order: the child has not attained the [mature] elements (*dhātu*) nor attained strength, while the old man has lost the elements and lost his strength. Because they are in such states, these two are not to be purged;
yet, for one who acts for the sake of all, it is a means of removing faults without harm and providing nourishment, and so forth.

He states the different types of enemas: "Anuvāsana," and so forth; "prepared with suitable medicinal substances" means prepared with medicines that either alleviate heat-related afflictions or alleviate cold-related afflictions.
8–10 He describes the diseases that require purification: "Those who are obese," and so forth;
"those who are also to be purified" means those who are fit for purification due to having a great abundance of *doṣas*.

"Those whose life-span is bound to the *doṣas*": those such as emaciated or extremely weak individuals whose life-span is bound to the *doṣas*—in the form of impurities (*mala*) and so forth—residing in the body; for it has been said: "The consumptive patient releases his limbs even from the discharge of feces; how much more so one who is purged with a dose that requires strength? (Ci. A. 8, vv. 11–12).
Regarding the specific preparations for enemas (bastis) based on the particular purpose, he states "in aphrodisiac therapy" (*vājīkaraṇe*) and so forth.

Although the addition of honey to the enema is already obtained by the previously mentioned general rule, it is stated here again for the sake of adding it in a greater quantity and for the sake of its being indispensable. The phrase "because it does not conflict with the bodily constituents" (*dhātūnām avirodhāt*) is connected with what precedes it. Therefore, among the sour substances and others used in a preparation, that which does not conflict with the bodily constituents should be given, while that which does conflict with the constituents should not be given. The meaning is: whatever is not incompatible with the disease and the patient's constitution should be given to that person.

Furthermore, because water is the source of taste (*rasayonitva*), it is said that "water is hot"; since water is the source of taste, it should be administered in all enemas while being hot for the purpose of nourishing the taste residing in the entire bladder. This water, however, is not seen to be added directly into the enemas; rather, it should be employed in the grinding of medicinal pastes (*kalka*) and the like. Alternatively, this should be understood here simply by the authority of that statement. Or else, this word "water" is an indicator for any liquid (*drava*); therefore, this justification applies specifically to the administration of liquids such as sour substances (*amla*). The fact that sour substances and the like are sources of taste is established precisely through their connection with liquids.

Others, however, maintain that hot water alone is specifically prescribed for this purpose, and they assert it should be administered as a *cūrṇabasti* (powder enema); a *cūrṇabasti* is one that is given using only a liquid medium. It is also stated in another treatise (*tantrāntara*) as follows: "A *cūrṇabasti* consisting of *rāsnā*, *vacā*, *bilva*, *śatāhvā*, *elā*, *pūtīka*, *kṛṣṇā*, *phala*, *dāru*, and *kuṣṭha*, along with rock salt, sour substances, hot water, and oil, is indeed desired as a destroyer of colic.

By the verse beginning with "suradāru" (Cedrus deodara), he describes the additives (*āvāpas*) for enemas (*bastis*), which are to be added according to the requirements of the *doṣas* and other factors, either individually or in combination;
the phrase "those which" refers to those things combined with decoctions (*kaṣāyas*). The meaning is that these are the substances to be added to the enemas.

Regarding the statement "sharp [therapies] for those with long-standing, firm strength," this refers to the application of sharp substances as mentioned here; conversely, for those who are not long-standing or do not have firm strength, one should employ *anuvāsana* and *nirūha* enemas. In the case of *anuvāsana*, the addition of decoctions (*kaṣāya*) is solely for the purpose of preparing the unctuous substance (*sneha*), yet the inclusion of *śatāhvā* and other such ingredients must certainly be performed even in *anuvāsana*. As it is stated elsewhere: "Pippalī, madana, kuṣṭha, śatāhvā, madhuka, and vacā..."
"One should grind [the ingredients] with the proper measure and add the *āvāpa* (supplementary additives) for the oil enema (*anuvāsana*).

(15–17) With the words "of the previously established enemas" (*pūrva-siddhānāṃ bastīnām*) and so forth, he states the subject matter promised by the phrase "with half-verses" (*ardhaślokaiḥ*) and so on, namely the enemas (*basti*).

In the phrase "in diseases" (*vyādhiṣu*), the word "disease" (*vyādhi*) should also be understood as referring to the "humors" (*doṣa*); "frequently" (*bahuśaḥ*) means in many instances for each individual disease and humor;
and "with parts equal in potency" (*vīryasamaiḥ bhāgaiḥ*) refers to the constituent parts of the substances whose potencies are not mutually impaired.
Vardhamānaka and eraṇḍa are "endowed with the essence of meat," meaning they contain the juice of meat;
vañjula is vetasa, and vānīra is a variety thereof.
Tuṅga, punnāga, alarka, mandāra, ekāṣṭhīlā, and pāṭhā.
Kuṭannaṭa is *kaivartamustaka*; others say it is *tagara*.
Kṣveḍa is *kṛtavedhana*. 18–24.
*Dravantī* is a species of *dantī*; *prakīryā* is *karañja*;
*nīlinī* is *nīlabuhnā*, though others call it *nīlāñjanikā*.
Regarding the phrase "these [are] rich in semen and flesh," "these" refers to the four previously mentioned.
Piṇḍītaka, madana, raktamūlī,
samaṅgā, taruṇī, ārāmataruṇī, or navamālikā.
Up to the end of verse 31 with the phrase "taṇḍulīyakayuktayā," two types of *parisrāva* (strained decoctions) have been described.
*Kāṇḍekṣu* is large cane; *poṭagala* is *hoggala*.
Regarding "with blue lotuses and so forth" (*utpalādibhiḥ*), blue lotuses and the like refer to specific water-born flowers such as the *nalina* and *saugandhika*.
From *karbudāraḥ* and *kāñcanāraḥ*, through *vidulaḥ*, *vetasaḥ*,
and ending with *kovidārajaiḥ*, the second [section] on cutting is concluded.
The second [type] is for inducing purgation by means of the fibers of the *śālmalika* tree, ending with that [verse].
*Aśvāvarohikā* is *aśvagandhā*, *aśvakarṇa*, or *ikṣuraka*; however, according to the view of Jatūkarṇa, *aśvāvarohaka* is *aśvakarṇa*.
The four beginning with *nyagrodha* are *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *plakṣa*.
"By that very procedure" means by the procedure of the previous yoga;
these two [trees] are for the *atiyoga*.
Regarding "in the taking of life": this refers to the flow of living blood.
From the words "go-avyaja" (cow, goat, sheep) up to "praśasyate" (is praised), the third enema regarding the administration of living organisms (*jīvādāna*) is described.

Although this enema is prescribed by half a verse (*ślokārdha*), the promise that they are "prescribed by half-verses" should be understood as referring to those [enemas] that are mostly prescribed by half-verses. Alternatively, even here, the prescription is established by the half-verse beginning with "go-avyaja," while the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for it is stated by the preceding half-verse. Furthermore, the description of the procedure occurs even beyond a single half-verse, as is observed in other formulations.
The word division is "raktapitte" (in cases of raktapitta). These two [substances] are recited together in the compendium by the phrase "two in raktapitta.
Somavalka is vitkhadira.
To explain the preparation of enemas not previously mentioned, he says "in cases of gulma, diarrhea," and so forth;
"with their respective medicines" means with drugs that are antagonistic to each specific disease.

"One should prepare various types of formulations" means that, according to the prescribed method involving the addition of medicinal substances and so forth, one should prepare appropriate formulations— such as those intended for abdominal tumors (gulma) and other conditions— to be used as enemas (basti).
The summary beginning with "the three triplets" is quite clear.
"Those with few medicines and few afflictions" (alpauṣadhakleśāḥ) means those who have few medicines and few afflictions (46–48).
