Thus ends the tenth chapter, named "The Success of Enemas" (bastisiddhi), in the Āyurvedadīpikā, a commentary on the intent of the Caraka-saṃhitā composed by the venerable Cakrapāṇidatta, within the Section on Success (siddhisthāna).
10 [Siddhisthāna, Chapter 11 (119 of 120)]:

In the previous *siddhis*, the results for the clinical applications were prescribed by the Teacher; therefore, in order to determine the qualities of those results, as well as to demonstrate the measures for enemas (*basti*) such as those for elephants which were not previously mentioned, the "Success of the Measure of Results" (*phalamātrāsiddhi*) is now stated.

Although the description of the administration of enemas for elephants and other animals is irrelevant to the present context, nevertheless, the dosage of the enema itself is being established here as being applicable to elephants and others due to its suitability (*yaugikatayā*). Therefore, this chapter, which establishes the fruits [of treatment] as well as the dosages for enemas in elephants and other animals, is titled "The Success of Dosages for Fruits and Others" (Phalamātrāsiddhi).

To explain the qualities of fruits and other substances used in enema formulations, he relates a historical account (*itihāsa*) of past events, beginning with the words "The Blessed One," and so forth.
The historical account (itihāsa) is indeed provided as a means of honoring the text by way of its traditional authority (saṃhitā-dharma), and for the purpose of demonstrating its venerability.

"The excellence of the fruit-enema" (phala-basti-varatva) refers to the superiority of the fruit-enema among [other types]; regarding its determination or ascertainment, the phrase "among fruits and so forth" refers to substances such as *madana*, *jīmūtaka*, and others.

Although in the *Kalpa* section it is stated that *jīmūtaka* removes the disorder of bile (*pitta*), nevertheless, according to the statement here, its primary action is inferred to be the removal of phlegm and bile (*kapha-pitta*).
Because of its mild potency (*mṛdu-vīryatā*), it "breaks" [the doshas]— meaning it does not excessively break them—
and thus it is a remover of the doshas by means of enema (*basti*).
In passages such as "kṛtavedhana" and so forth, it should be understood that [the phrase] "it quickly removes kapha and pitta" is to be supplied.

By means of this statement regarding the dispute among sages, the intended meaning (tātparya) to be known is that the qualities and defects of jīmūtaka and other such substances are thereby described.
[The passage continues with] "praśaśaṃsa" and so on.
Regarding fruits such as the *jīmūtaka* and others,
having taken as her objective the perception of their defects and virtues,
[she is called] *sarasvatī*, which means speech.
"Free from defects and devoid of qualities" means that it is nothing at all, whether in terms of having defects or having qualities.

Thus, even when there is a slight connection with defects, that which abounds in qualities is here "universally applicable" (*sārvayaugika*) in the applications for the pacification of disease; by the phrase "opposed to all maladies," he expresses the universal applicability of *madana*.
"Quick-acting" means that it brings about the swift removal of defects;
therefore, it is obtained because of its excellence among fruits, and thus the *madanaphala* fruit is so called, not the fruit of *jīmūtaka* or other such plants.

"Performing the qualities of all therapeutic actions" (*sarvakarmaguṇakṛt*) means that it performs the quality of all actions—such as emesis and so forth—namely, the removal of morbid humors (*doṣa*) and the like. Alternatively, it performs all therapeutic actions such as lightening (*laṅghana*) and nourishing (*bṛṃhaṇa*), as well as qualities such as strength and digestive fire;
it moves downward from the navel to the anus, and thus it governs (*tantrayate*) and sustains (*dhārayate*).
Regarding the phrase "due to obstruction":

because of the cause of provocation, [the vāta] remains within its own site (*svāśaya*) and generally undergoes provocation right there; the point is that any provocation of vāta in another location is rooted in that very [original] site, and it attains pacification through the pacification of the root vāta residing in the *pakvāśaya* by means of enema (*basti*).
When their roots and continuations have been severed, the disorders located in the remaining sites are pacified;
this has already been established previously through such analogies as "like cutting the root of a tree.
By means of this enema (*basti*), that which is achieved is the conquest of the disorders residing within the specific regions by way of conquering their roots.
It should be understood that what was previously stated—that the potency of an enema spreads from the feet to the head and that this potency destroys all disorders—is indeed applicable here;
however, it should be noted that in this instance, the answer has been given specifically in accordance with the student's question, while keeping the potency itself concealed.
In the passage beginning with "Then, having approached," it should be construed that he asked about the treatment for elephants and other animals.

"Disease-dispelling" (*roganud*) is an adjective qualifying the action; thus, the meaning is that the action—namely, the treatment—is "disease-dispelling," meaning it is the most excellent medical therapy for removing disease.

He spoke of the enema (*basti*); that is, he declared the enema alone to be the most excellent for removing the diseases of elephants and others. Subsequently, when the procedure for that enema was again asked by the disciple, he replied with the words beginning "from goats and deer" (*ājoraṇa*), and so forth—this is the construction.
"Uraṇaḥ" means a ram; "meṣaḥ" means a sheep; "bastiḥ" means a bladder or a pouch; "jaradgavaḥ" means an old bull.
"Those who contemplate the means for that" refers to those whose minds are intent upon accomplishing the enema (basti) with elephants and so forth.
"The cubit (aratni) and the hand (hasta) respectively" means that, in due order, the measure of the nozzle (netra) for elephants and the others is one cubit and so on.
"Introducing one-fourth part" means introducing one-fourth of the eye [of the pestle].
"Among cows and so forth" refers to the various types of cattle; the use of the plural is correct because it includes cows, buffaloes, and horses.
However, for the elephant, there is an increase, meaning that by doubling two *āḍhakas*, it becomes one *droṇa*.

"Anuvasana is one-eighth [of the dose]" means that for the anuvasana enema, one-eighth part of the fatty substance (sneha) should be administered compared to the quantity of the decoction enema (nirūha) previously described for goats and other animals.
This "alternative formulation" refers to a specific calculation; the dosage for elephants will be explained later as being greater.
By the passage beginning with "tālajaṃ tālaphalam tathaiva" (23–26), that which is beneficial for cows is described.
Now, demonstrating those who are always fit for enema therapy, he says "Then Agniveśa," and so forth;
"beneficial" means beneficial for those who are always fit [for it],
such as merchants and traders.

He states the reason for the constant illness of those previously mentioned— from "dvijo hi" up to "paṇyajīvinaḥ," ending with "na ceṣṭate dehahitam"— this [passage] should be understood as applying throughout.
"Out of consideration for others" means out of consideration for other people who are the king's dependents;
"intent on civility toward men" means intent on showing courtesy to men;
"cleansing" refers to the washing of the body.

"Paṇāṅganā" means a prostitute; "due to greed for continuous buying, selling, and so forth" means due to greed for uninterrupted buying, selling, and the like. He speaks of others who are likewise constantly afflicted: "at improper times," and so forth.
Nirhāra is the expulsion of impurities and the like (28–30). *Punarnavā* and so forth constitute a *nirūha* enema; *nikumbhā* is *dantī*.
"Great roots" refers to the five roots beginning with *bilva* (*pañcamūla*).
"With *nikumbha* oil" means with oil prepared from the decoction and paste of *nikumbha*.
In the passage beginning with "balā," the phrase "with *kaliṅgaka* and so forth" refers to those mentioned here: "*kaliṅga*, *kuṣṭha*, *madhuka*, *bilva*, etc."

The three oils—those from *bilva*, *śatāhvā*, and *phala*—are for use as an oil enema (*anuvāsana*). Furthermore, an oil prepared with a decoction of the *jīvanīya* (life-promoting) drugs should be used as an enema;
likewise, for a child, a *jīvanīya* decoction mixed with oil and devoid of salt should be administered as a non-unctuous enema (*nirūhaṇa*).

By stating that even the non-unctuous enema (anuvāsana) prepared with life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs is for the infant alone and no other, [the author] declares that the enema is suitable for both children and the elderly; furthermore,
he calls it "param," meaning supreme.
The summary beginning with "phalakarma" (the fruit of action) and so forth is clear.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Successful Treatment of Dosages," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka Saṃhitā*, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta.
[Siddhisthāna, Chapter 12 (120 of 120)]

By the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the establishment of the urethral enema (*uttarabasti*) is stated; the "establishment of the urethral enema" (*uttarabastisiddhi*) refers to the successful application of the superior (*uttara*) or excellent enemas.

In order to demonstrate the scope of the enemas (basti) about to be described—the collection of diseases produced by improper treatment—he first states the correct regimen, beginning with "atha khalu" and so forth.

The phrase "by emesis and the rest" refers to emesis (vamana), purgation (virecana), decoction enema (nirūha), and head-purgation (śirovirecana). However, not all that will be described, such as the sequence of gruels (peyā) and so forth, applies to both the decoction enema and the head-purgation; therefore, this sequence does not apply to these two, as indicated by the expression "muktasandhānabandhana," meaning the binding of joints that were previously loosened.
"Emaciated constitution" (kṛśāśaya) refers to one whose internal receptacle is free from morbid humors (doṣa);

"incapable of remedial treatment" (pratīkārāsahiṣṇu) refers to one unable to endure actions such as loud speaking; alternatively, it may refer to one incapable of undergoing procedures such as emesis.
The connection is that one should protect such a person from every kind of improper conduct (apacāra).
The mention of the three examples beginning with the "young egg" (taruṇāṇḍa) is intended so that at least one of them may be familiar to someone.

Regarding the instruction "one should treat with *rasottara*," *rasa* here refers to meat broth (*māṃsarasa*); thus, it means by means of a sequence starting with gruel (*peyā*) and so forth, where the broth is predominant—this is the gradual progression. Alternatively, one should treat with the sequence of gruel and so forth between the emesis and the purgation, whereas in the case of a non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*), one should treat with that which has broth as the predominant element; such is the established rule.

In that regard, it has already been established previously that for a non-unctuous enema (nirūha), the sequence of meat-broth and so forth is prescribed in consideration of a slight impairment of the digestive fire (agnimāndya); or rather, he describes the very sequence of practicing meat-broth (rasābhyāsakrama) by means of that [diet] beginning with liquid gruel (peyā) which is rich in meat-broth at a later time—starting with the words "unctuous, sour, sweet, and pleasing," and so on.

This sequence of practicing meat-broth (rasābhyāsa) is to be understood as intended for the purpose of providing natural nourishment and strengthening the body—which has been cleansed by the root purification therapies—once it is no longer necessary to perform subsequent procedures such as purgation. Others, however, describe a sequence of unctuous, sour, and prepared broths specifically for the purpose of flavoring the gruel and other items within the *peyākrama* itself.

In this context, sour and sweet tastes are employed first to pacify the vāta located in the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya); likewise, sour and salty tastes are used for the purpose of kindling the digestive fire situated above that; thereafter, sweet and bitter tastes are used to pacify pitta; and subsequently, astringent and pungent tastes are used to pacify the kapha situated above the pitta. This is the sequence.
Furthermore, in this case as well, only those two tastes that are antagonistic [to the disorder] are employed in combination;
the application of these four pairs of tastes occurs precisely within the sequence beginning with thin gruel (peyā).
Thus, the attainment of food containing all flavors through twelve meal-times is to be understood as the supreme method;
"mutually," and so forth,
means "of those that are mutually antagonistic," that is, those which counteract one another.

"One should employ them alternately" means that after employing one pair, one should employ another pair so as to return to the natural state; thus, one should bring about a return to the natural mode of eating. Regarding the practice of tastes, he states another method: "of the unctuous and the dry," and so forth.

The meaning is that after consuming an unctuous (snigdha) taste, one should employ a dry (rūkṣa) one; or after consuming a dry one, an unctuous one—in this sequence, one should lead toward the natural diet (*prakṛtibhojana*).

Here, "unctuous" and "dry" are introduced merely as examples; therefore, the practice of alternating pairs of tastes such as heavy and light (*guru-laghu*) and so forth should also be understood here.

Alternatively, the practice of alternating pairs of tastes is demonstrated by the phrase "thereafter [the] astringent and pungent"; however, by the passage beginning with "of those mutually antagonistic," the practice of alternating each respective antagonist with another is stated.

He describes the characteristics of a person whose health has been restored through the practice of the sequence beginning with *peyā* (thin gruel) and the gradual habituation to tastes: "capable of everything," and so forth;
"capable of everything" means capable of habituating to all tastes.

"Non-attachment" (*asaṃsarga*) means the absence of the impulse of clinging; alternatively, the reading is "unattached" (*nirāsaṅga*), meaning one who is not obstructed by restricted objects and is capable of all activities.
Regarding the phrase "born from that" (*tajjā*) and so forth, they should be understood respectively as bodily afflictions such as pain from speaking loudly and the like.

From speaking loudly, there is pain in the upper body; from the jolting of a chariot, pain throughout the entire body; from excessive walking, pain in the lower body; from sitting too long, pain in the middle of the body; from eating during indigestion, diseases arise from *āmadoṣa*; from unwholesome food, diseases arise from the *doṣas*; from sleeping by day, diseases arise from *śleṣman* (phlegm); and from sexual intercourse, diseases arise from depletion (*kṣaya*).
Here, the passage beginning with "speaking loudly" is for the most part self-evident.
Because excessive speech and unsystematic discourse are equivalent to speaking loudly, the illustration is as follows:
*piṇḍikodveṣṭana* is a sensation of twisting in the calves (*jaṅghāpiṇḍikā*),
and *sirādhamanīharṣa* is the swelling or throbbing of the veins and arteries (*sirādhamanī*).

When it is said "arising from the jolting of a chariot," there would be the possibility of [disorders] such as laxity of the joints; therefore, to exclude those, he says: "there may be pain in the buttocks, sides, groins, scrotum, waist, and back. In the phrase "due to indigestion and overeating" (*ajīrṇādhyaśanābhyām*), since eating during indigestion (*ajīrṇāśana*) acts as the cause of disorders arising from *āma*, "overeating" (*adhyaśana*)—though not explicitly mentioned in the aphorism—is included. Likewise, because eating at irregular times (*viṣamāśana*) produces disorders similar to those produced by eating unwholesome food (*ahitāśana*), "eating at irregular times"—though also not explicitly mentioned in the aphorism—is included.
"As if being torn away, as if being cut off"—
this refers to their "accomplishment" (siddhi); that is to say, the means for achieving the aforementioned modifications, which is to say, the medicine (bheṣaja).

"Emesis without residue" means the complete expulsion of undigested food. Regarding "urinary disorders," etc.: when urinary disorders and the like arise from sexual intercourse, one should prepare oil with milk using the decoction and paste of the two groups—the Vidārigandhādi and Jīvanīya—and administer it as an uttarabasti (urethral/vaginal enema).

He describes the sustaining enemas (*yāpana-basti*) with the words beginning "and the sustaining ones" (*yāpanāśca*), etc., up to "to be administered at all times" (*sarvakālaṃ deyā*); by this, he shows that the previously mentioned non-unctuous enemas (*nirūha*) are not for all times. And the administration of these [sustaining enemas] at all times is not contradictory, because they sustain life—that is, they cause it to persist for a long duration—therefore they are called sustaining enemas (*yāpana-basti*).
In the phrase "mustādi" and so forth, the term *khaṇḍaśaḥ klṛptāni* means prepared in pieces;
*pādajāṅgalarasam* means with one-quarter part of the meat-broth of wild animals, specifically the broth of wild animals as described along with the decoction made from milk.

*Tulyamadhughṛtaḥ* refers to that in which the honey and ghee are in equal measure. By this, it is meant that whatever quantity of ghee would be given here according to the previously established rules for the enema (*basti*), that same quantity of honey should also be administered.
In this enema, the enema should be prepared according to the same dosage proportions for enemas mentioned previously;
here, milk takes the place of the decoction,
and *śatakusumā* refers to *śatapuṣpā*.
"Along with Saindhava" means with a small amount of Saindhava;
"the root of Eranda," etc., is the second [recipe];
similarly, "Sahacara," etc., is the third.
The phrase "in that manner" (*tadvat*) refers to the previous method of administering enemas (*basti*).
Similarly, the fourth [type] begins with "the large one" (*bṛhatī*) and so forth.

Furthermore, there is no explicit mention of the results for this enema; rather, the results should be understood from the general statement to be mentioned later: "Thus these enemas and oleation therapies have been described."

The fifth [group] begins with *balā*, *atibalā*, and *vidārī*; the sixth begins with *balā*, *atibalā*, and *rāsnā*; and in the phrase "of dried radishes," the term "two *prasṛtas*" is understood to carry over.

"Nirūhapramāṇaśeṣaṃ kaṣāyam" means a decoction (kaṣāya) of the quantity remaining after the standard measure of a *nirūha* enema; thus, the five *prasṛta* measures of the five decoctions to be administered in three enema-pouches (*puṭaka*) will be established.

Here, the decoction must be prepared according to the technical rules for decoctions (*kvātha-paribhāṣā*). Furthermore, the application should be construed as follows: "One should administer an enema prepared from the decoction remaining after the standard measure of a *nirūha*, combined with *madhuka*, *madanaphala*, and other ingredients."

The seventh [group] begins with *hapuṣā* and so forth; "stiff," "dry," and furthermore "scraped" and "pounded" refer to the *mustā* and other drugs previously mentioned, which the Kashmiris recite in this section.
The eighth begins with *hrasvapañcamūlī* and so forth;
the ninth begins with *balātibalāpāmārga* and so forth;
and the tenth begins with *balāmadhuka* and so forth.

In this context, after the decoction of *balā* and the other ingredients has been boiled with fresh milk until only the milk remains, the eleventh preparation beginning with *śāliparṇī* and the twelfth beginning with *sthirā* should be prepared.
By the words "erakā, hoggala, kalpa," and so forth, three [types of practitioners] who are designated by extension (atideśika) are mentioned.

Among the twenty-nine enemas (bastis) to be described hereafter, each according to its own formulation, the thirteenth begins with "satittiri," the fourteenth begins with "dvipañcamūlī," and the fifteenth begins with "mayūramapittapakṣa."
With the words "And this is a kalpa," and so forth, he states the one hundred and fifteen [verses] that are extended by analogy (atideśika).

In this regard, there are twenty formulations with the *viṣkira* birds, as stated in the passages beginning with "the quail (*lāva*) and the *vartīraka*" and "the *vartaka* and the *vartikā*" (Sūtra, Chapter 27); although the peacock is also listed among the *viṣkiras*, it is not counted here because it has already been mentioned previously. There are thirty formulations with the *pratuda* birds, as stated in the passage beginning with "the woodpecker (*śatapatra*)" (Sūtra, Chapter 27). Likewise, there are twenty-nine with the *prasaha* animals, as stated in the passage beginning with "the cow, the donkey, the mule... (Sūtra, Chapter 27). Twenty-seven aquatic creatures, such as the swan (*haṃsa*) and others, have been mentioned, and with these, there are twenty-seven formulations. With the fish, such as the *rohit* and others, there are nine. Thus, the total becomes one hundred and fifteen.
The term "akṣīra" (milkless) is connected with the *rohit* and others;
it is the sixteenth among those to be counted individually, such as the *godhā*, *nakula*, and so forth, while the phrase "any one of the *kūrma* and others" is the seventeenth.
Here, eleven [animals] beginning with the tortoise (*kūrma*) and the crab (*karkaṭa*) are recited;
among them, that which is generally performed by the tortoise enters into each individual calculation,
whereas the ten enemas (*basti*) performed by the crab and others— being included under the term "and so forth" (*ādi*)— should be understood as being extended by analogy (*atideśika*).
The eighteen [signs] beginning with the bull (go-vṛṣabha) and the goat (aja) are the male signs;
the nineteenth, beginning with the crab (karkaṭa), is the female sign.
By the phrase "these are the enemas," the enemas described in the preceding text—beginning with "any one of the kūrma [group]," etc.—are referred back.
Regarding "uccaṭaka," etc.: *uccaṭā* is well-known by its own name; *ikṣuraka* is *kokilākṣa*;
and the twentieth [enema] begins with *daśamūlī*, etc.
By the passage beginning with "deer and gallinaceous birds" (*mṛgaviṣkira*), there are fifty-nine transference-based (*ātideśika*) formulations (*yoga*).

Among these, there are seventeen from the deer (*mṛga*) group mentioned in [Sūtra 27], beginning with "the *pṛṣata*, the *śarabha*, the *rāma*," and so on; seventeen from the gallinaceous (*viṣkira*) birds; nineteen from the nineteen types of birds such as the *lāva* and others, excluding the peacock and the cock; nine from the marsh-dwellers (*ānūpa*) such as the *sṛmara* and others; fourteen from the burrow-dwellers (*bileśaya*) such as the white and black four-tusked ones (*caturdaṃṣṭra*);
and the twenty-first consists of honey, clarified butter, and so forth.
The twenty-second [chapter] begins with "sadyoghṛtataila" and so forth;
the twenty-third begins with "madhutaila" and so forth;
likewise, the twenty-fourth begins with "tadvanmadhughṛtābhyām" and so forth.
These six formulations mentioned thus far should be known as *mādhutailika* because they are primarily composed of honey and oil.

Some do not recite the formula beginning with "the two groups of five roots" (*dvipañcamūlī*), and they state that it should not be included here because it exceeds the prescribed number and because it is already recited in the *Siddhi-sthāna* of the *Basti-sūtra*.
Showing the three unctuous substances for the purpose of the three oil enemas (snehabasti), he says: "From here onwards," etc.
*Mattākṣa* is the cuckoo;
*jīvañjīva* is the pheasant (which dies at the sight of poison).
Puṣkarākṣa is a particular kind of swan;
Brahmaghoṣa is the sound of the Vedas.
These, beginning with Brahmaghoṣa, act as invisible aids for the purpose of depriving the Rākṣasas and others of their prowess.
19(1) The second oil begins with *bala* and so forth.
The third unctuous substance consists of one hundred palas of sahacara and palaśa, and so forth; [the herbs] are sahasravīryā, dūrvā,
varāṅga, and guḍatvak.

Regarding the terms "cooked a hundred times" (*śatapāka*) and "cooked a thousand times" (*sahasrapāka*), some authorities maintain that these refer to a single cooking process using a liquid medium one hundred or one thousand times the quantity of the oil (*sneha*).

The intended meaning is that they have been observed to serve both purposes; thus, even in the case of oil enemas (*snehavasti*) and decoction enemas (*nirūha*), they perform the objectives of both oleation (*snehana*) and purification (*śodhana*).
He states what is to be avoided during *yāpana* enemas, beginning with "physical exercise" (*vyāyāma*), etc.
With the verse beginning "Śikhigo-narda," etc., he provides a summary of the previously mentioned enemas (bastis); the purpose of this summary has already been explained.
The meaning of "these twenty-nine" is that these individually specified enemas, when combined with the oleaginous substances (snehas), become twenty-nine in total.
He states the total number: "two hundred and sixteen.
And this is clearly fulfilled exactly as we have explained it.
"Exceedingly excellent" (*ativṛṣam*) means possessing the increase of semen (*śukra*).
"And paralyzed" means paralyzed by honey.
Regarding what should be done when the *yāpanā-basti* does not proceed, he says: "Because of its softness," and so forth (verse 29).
He states the fault in the excessive application of *yāpana-basti* with the verse beginning "śopha," etc. (verse 30).
This describes the treatment for swelling and other such conditions, beginning with the verse "ariṣṭa... and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "tasmāt" (therefore): because swelling and other symptoms are observed when *yāpana* [purgatives] are used in excessive amounts, one should not employ them habitually out of a sense of casual indulgence (*prasaṅga*). One should not practice their use as a matter of routine.
"He should protect them from those" means he should protect them from harms such as those arising from loud speech and the like.

Now, demonstrating the etymology of the term *siddhisthāna* (the section on successful treatment) and summarizing the meaning of the sentence as expressed by that term, he says: "Of actions," and so forth.

"Calamities arising from improper performance" refers to the complications produced by the incorrect application of emesis and other therapies. Furthermore, the remedy for complications such as those of emesis is presented as the primary purpose of the *siddhisthāna*. Consequently, it is entirely appropriate that even the description of the preparation of emetics and other procedures in this section serves the purpose of preventing future complications of emesis and the like.
Having completed the entire section on Siddhi (therapeutics), he concludes the treatise: "Thus, [the work] beginning with the chapters...
and ending with "...the speech of the sage Ātreya," meaning that which follows the words of the sage Ātreya.
He states the fruit of studying this tantra, beginning with "long life," and so forth.
"Trivarga" refers to dharma, artha, and kāma;
"puṣkala" refers to mokṣa. Alternatively, "puṣkala" is an adjective qualifying the trivarga;
"siddhi" refers to the accomplishment of what is to be achieved through the application of medical treatment.
"Reciting according to the prescribed method" refers to the method of recitation described in the chapter on "The Physician’s Victory over Disease" (Rogabhiṣagjitīya).

For one who recites these one hundred and twenty chapters in this manner, the attainment of long life and other benefits arise solely through the power of the merit (*dharma*) produced by such recitation, as well as through the practice of the science preceded by the understanding of the treatise generated by that recitation.
Having first demonstrated the refinement of this treatise through logical reasoning, Dṛḍhabala, pointing out Caraka and himself as the two refiners of the treatise, says: "He expands," and so forth.

Since, when subjects are presented in a treatise—either by being initially explained with excessive detail or by being stated only briefly—a correct understanding of the meaning does not arise, it is appropriate for a refiner to act in order to eliminate the defects of such excessive detail or brevity; therefore, this supreme system has been refined by Caraka.

Because the previous text was excessively extensive and so forth, its designation as a *tantra* should be understood as being intended solely for the sake of the earlier audience; however, with regard to the intention of the present-day audience, it should be known as the editor’s own editorial refinement (*saṃskāra*).
And it has been said: "That which is stated in brief overcomes [the mind], while that which is stated at length is not grasped;
therefore, setting aside both brevity and prolixity, one should refine the treatise from the very beginning."
Showing that the Caraka-saṃskāra was incomplete, Dṛḍhabala states— "That," and so forth— making the ancient [text] new again through expansion, condensation, and other means;
"the third part" (tribhāgaḥ) refers to a one-third portion.

This "incompleteness by one-third" is stated because the distance [between the two locations] is not great; therefore, it should not be raised as an objection that the forty-one chapters established by Dṛḍhabala cannot constitute one-third of a total of one hundred and twenty chapters.

To demonstrate his own origin from the excellent region of Pañcanada-pura, and to show that his own refinement is achieved through the meaning brought from other systems, he says: "Having [received it] from many," and so forth.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: from the *tantras*—namely the *Suśruta*, *Videha*, and other treatises—he gathered a "collection of special gleanings" (*viśeṣoñchaśiloccaya*), meaning a collection of specific features that exceed the meanings stated by Caraka; having taken those from other *tantras*, Dṛḍhabala completed this work—which possesses no deficiency in words or meaning, is free from the faults of a treatise, and is adorned with the twenty-six methodological principles of a *tantra*—by means of seventeen chapters on medicinal herbs, along with their preparations and formulations.

In this context, *uñcha* is the gathering with a winnowing basket of grains and other seeds that have fallen on the ground; *śila*, however, is the picking up of what has fallen scattered in the form of ears of grain and so forth.

By this, he shows that the essential portion of the Tantras was compiled by the teachers of the *Caraka* school, while he himself has filled it out by making the remainder the supplement (*pariśiṣṭa*), such that the words are not deficient and the meaning is not deficient—thus, [the work is] "neither deficient in word nor deficient in meaning."

The fourteen defects of a treatise (*tantra-doṣa*), such as "repetition," "poorly composed," "inclusion of sutras," and "lack of sequence" as stated in the *Rogabhiṣagjitīya*, are avoided; [it is] by means of the principles of treatise (*tantra-yukti*)— as will be described— which are manifold, meaning they are endowed with various meanings and logical methods.
He states the very principles of the treatise (*tantrayukti*), beginning with "In that regard" (*tatra*) and so forth.

*Adhikaraṇa* (subject matter) is that object with reference to which an author proceeds to act; for example, in the passage beginning "When diseases become obstacles" (*Sūtra-sthāna*, chapter 1), Āyurveda was composed by the great sages with reference to diseases and so forth—thus, "diseases" is the *adhikaraṇa*.
*Yoga* (connection) is the joining together, the unification of separate words.

To provide an illustration: it is as follows—the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*). Among these, the proposition is: "This embryo is born of the mother"; the reason is: "because an embryo cannot arise without a mother"; the example is: "a gabled house" (*kūṭāgāra*); the application is: "just as a gabled house is produced from a collection of various materials, so too is the formation of the embryo"; and the conclusion is: "therefore, this [embryo] is born of the mother. This is the connection of the propositions; in the same way, other meanings of the connections should also be explained.

The meaning of "cause" (*hetvartha*) is that which is stated in one place and applies elsewhere. For example, it is said with reference to *vāta*: "The practice of similar qualities (*samānaguṇābhyāsa*) is indeed the cause of increase for the *dhātus*" (Sūtra 12). Although it should have been stated there as "of *vāta*," by using the word "of the *dhātus*," it is understood that just as for *vāyu*, so too for *rasa* and the others, the practice of similar qualities is the cause of increase.
The term *padārtha* means the meaning of a word (*pada*), the meaning of two words, or the meaning of many words.

In this context, by the term *dravya* (substance), ether (*ākāśa*) and the other [elements], with consciousness (*caitanya*) as the sixth, are denoted. The meaning of two words (*pada*) is as follows: for example, the meaning of the two words "science of life" (*āyurveda*) is a treatise (*tantra*) that makes life known. In the same way, the meaning of multiple words (*padāni*) may also be cited.

A "portion" (*pradeśa*) is that which, because of the vastness of the subject matter, cannot be expressed in its entirety and is therefore expressed by way of a single part; for example: "This has been stated as a portion of the adjunctive drinks (*anupāna*), intended for general use" (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 27), and so forth.
*Uddeśa* (enunciation) is a concise statement; for example, "knowledge of causes, signs, and medicines" (*Sūtra* 1.1), by which there is an enunciation of all that is to be expressed in Āyurveda.

*Nirdeśa* (explanation) is the detailed exposition of what was stated in brief; for example, the further elaboration of causes, signs, and medicines beginning with "at all times, of all entities... and ending with "thus the cause has been stated" (*Sūtra* 1.20), which constitutes the elaboration of the cause, and so forth.

The "vākyaśeṣa" (supplementation of a sentence) refers to that which, for the sake of brevity, is not explicitly stated as a word by the Teacher in a sentence but is supplied through implication; for example, in the statement "the activity of causal factors" (*pravṛttir hetubhāvānām*, Sūtra 16), the word "exists" (*asti*) is supplied, and likewise in the phrase "with juices born of arid lands" (*jāṅgalajai rasaiḥ*), the word "meat" (*māṃsa*) is supplied.
These very words are made into supplements (*śeṣāḥ*) within sentences, which are understood even though they have not been inserted.

"Prayojana" (purpose) is that for the sake of which one acts with desire; for example: "The purpose of this treatise is said to be the restoration of the equilibrium of the bodily constituents" (*dhātusāmyakriyā coktā tantrasyāsya prayojanam*, Sūtra 1).

*Upadeśa* (instruction) is the teaching of an authoritative person (*āpta*); for example: "One should first apply oleation (*sneha*), and immediately thereafter sudation (*sveda*)" (Sūtra-sthāna 13), and so forth.

*Apadeśa* (explanation) is the statement of a reason (*hetu*) for the purpose of establishing a proposition (*pratijñāta-artha*); for example: "One should know that water [arises] from wind, place from water, and time from place, by their very nature, because they are unavoidable" (Vimāna-sthāna 3), and so forth. In this context, the statement of the reason for the proposition is: "because they are unavoidable."

*Atideśa* (extended application) is defined as a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) whereby, for the sake of clarifying a certain matter, it is established that even though a specific point has not been explicitly stated, another related point should be understood in the same way; for example: "Whatever else may be honored here that has not been mentioned, Ātreya always approves of that as well" (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 8). *Arthāpatti* (presumption) is that which is obtained by implication from what has not been explicitly stated; for example, the prohibition of eating curd at night implies by implication that one should eat it during the day.

*Nirṇaya* (conclusion) is the formal determination of a matter after it has been investigated; for example, having conducted an investigation into the fourfold nature of medicinal substances and so forth, it is stated: "That which was described in the previous chapter as the sixteen-fold medicine is sufficient for health when applied according to the proper method" (Sūtra-sthāna, Chapter 10).

*Prasaṅga* (consequence/reiteration) is the restatement of a previously mentioned point because it has entered into the context or for similar reasons; for example, after stating at the outset, "In that regard, excessive seeing of visible objects by those with extreme visual power is *atiyoga*," [the author] later restates that very same point with the words, "From hearing excessively loud sounds, or from not hearing at all," and so forth.

*Ekānta* (certainty/exclusivity) is that which is stated with a restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇa*); for example, "endogenous [diseases] arise from bodily humors," or "the three-fold [mixture] causes purgation," and so forth.

*Anaikānta* (inconsistency) is the non-determination of either alternative, as in: "For those who die from illness despite being without medicine, it does not follow that all of them would have recovered had they been provided with medicine" (Sūtra 10), and so forth.

*Apavarga* (exception) is the partial exclusion of what has been prescribed in its entirety; as in: "One should not eat stale food, except for meat, green vegetables, dried greens, fruits, and edible delicacies" (Sūtra 8).

For here, having established a general prohibition against eating stale food, the consumption of meat and other such items—even if stale—is specifically prescribed as an exception; this is called *viparyaya* (contradiction), which is an example of an exception drawn from what was set aside. For instance: "The things mentioned in the section on etiology do not agree with him, while their opposites do" (Ni. A. 3). A *pūrvapakṣa* (prior position) is a statement that subverts the meaning of a proposition; for instance, the proposition "one should not eat fish with milk," which is then countered by the statement "one should not eat any fish at all with milk, except for the cilicima fish" (Sū. A. 26). This subverts the original intended meaning.

The author of the Sūtra, after prescribing a rule, describes it as follows: "The channels of excretion are obstructed by vitiated humors (doṣas) that have exceeded their proper measure. In this context, by the word "vitiation" (duṣṭi), the Teacher intends both the deficiency and the excess of the humors; he explains this as: "One should recognize the increase of humors by heaviness, and the decrease of humors by lightness."

"One should understand the purifiers of the impurities through the renunciation of attachment" (Sūtra-sthāna 7). However, some say that "vidhāna" refers to the exposition of the subject matter according to the sequence of the context; for example, the exposition of chyle, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen in accordance with the order of their production.

This is called "anumata"—the acceptance [of a view] by not refuting the opinion of certain authorities. For instance, after presenting the opinion of certain authorities in such passages as, "Some say that the procedure for inducing the expulsion of the fetal membranes in the case of a retained fetus is palliative" (Śārīra-sthāna 8), it is accepted by not being prohibited.

Explanation (*vyākhyāna*) refers to that which is explained though it is not an object of any [ordinary] cognition, such as: "In the first month, the embryo is coagulated, defiled by all the elements, consisting of phlegm, with an unmanifest form" (*Śārīrasthāna* 4), and so forth—this is the exposition of a meaning unknown to people like us.

Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is a cognition whose object is undetermined due to a desire for specific details, such as: "Some consider the mother and father to be the cause of birth; others consider inherent nature, the creation of another, or chance."

The doubt expressed by the passage beginning with “(Sūtra 11)” and so forth is what is called *atītāvekṣaṇa* (reference to the past), which refers precisely to that which has already occurred; for example: “That hut and that bed also alleviate fever” (Cikitsā-sthāna, Chapter 3), where one refers to the hut and other items prescribed in the chapter on sudation (*sveda*) that have already passed. *Anāgatāvekṣaṇa* (reference to the future) is the accomplishment of a purpose by taking a future procedure as authoritative; for example: “Alternatively, [the use] of bitter ghee,” and so forth, which is stated by way of reference to the future. *Svasañjñā* (specific technical name) is the name assigned by the authors of the treatises for the sake of conventional usage; for example, names such as *jentāka*, *holāka*, and so forth.

*Ūhya* (that which is to be inferred) refers to that which is not explicitly mentioned in the text but is taught as something to be reasoned out through wisdom; for example: "Whatever substance, even if enumerated, one considers to be unsuitable [for a particular purpose], that one should exclude" (Viśeṣa 8).
*Samuccaya* (combination) refers to that which is prescribed by way of stating "this and this"; for example: "The color and the accent," etc. (Sūtra 1).
*Nidarśana* (illustration) refers to an example that serves as a common ground for the understanding of both the ignorant and the learned; for example: "Just as the nectar is known," etc. (Sūtra 1).

An etymological explanation (*nirvacana*) is an illustration accessible to the intellect of the learned; for example: "The cause of the passing away [of diseases] is known to be like that of ever-moving time" (Sūtra 16).

This is the distinction between an illustration (*nidarśana*) and an etymological explanation: an illustration is a subject common to the understanding of both the ignorant and the wise, whereas an etymological explanation is to be understood only by the intellect of the learned. Alternatively, an etymological explanation is a derivation (*nirukti*), such as: "Because it spreads in various ways (*vividhaṃ sarpati*), it is therefore designated as 'visarpa'" (Cikitsā 21), and so forth.
*Niyoga* is an injunction characterized by the necessity of performance; for example: "Even when overcome by sweat and fainting, this medicinal bolus must not be abandoned" (Sūtra 14), and so forth.

*Vikalpa* is the statement of an alternative; for example: "Either water with *sāra* grass or water with *kuśa* grass" (Cikitsā 6), and so forth. *Pratyutsāra* is the refutation of another's position through logical reasoning; for example, Vāryovida says: "Beings are born from *rasa*, while diseases are said to arise from *rajas*" (Sūtra 25), to which Hiraṇyākṣa objects: "For the self is not said to be born of *rajas*," and so forth.

*Uddhāra* (extraction/rescue) refers to the establishment of one's own position after having refuted the opposing position; for example, the establishment of one's own position through such statements as: "Indeed, those very factors that produce prosperity in a person, those same factors may bring about misfortune and disease" (*Sūtra-sthāna*, chapter 25).
*Sambhava* (possibility) refers to that which is possible within a given context; for example, the possibility of moles, freckles, and dark spots occurring on the face, and so forth.

Thus, these thirty-six *tantrayuktis* have been explained by Bhaṭṭāraka Haricandra. However, he has also explained four other *tantrayuktis* known as *paripraśna* (inquiry), *vyākaraṇa* (explanation), *vyutkrāntābhidhāna* (transposed statement), and *hetvākhyā* (statement of reason). Since these are not explicitly mentioned in the *Tantra*, they must be subsumed within those already listed.

Among them, *paripraśna* is included in *uddeśa* (enumeration); *vyākaraṇa* is included in *vyākhyāna* (exposition); *vyutkrāntābhidhāna* is a variety of *nirdeśa* (specification); and as for the term *hetu*, those means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) that were mentioned are included within *hetu* (reason).

The commentary consists of fifteen types; there are seven kinds of conceptualization, twenty-one bases of meaning, seventeen habitual tendencies, and fourteen defects of the system (*tantra*); since these have been explained in the *Uttaratantra*, they were not written down here by the Teacher.

Now, having introduced the *tantrayukti*s (the methodological principles of the treatise), he explains their application within the treatise itself, beginning with the words "In a treatise stated both in brief and in detail," and so forth.

By the phrase "stated in brief" (*samāsābhihite*), he demonstrates that not all *tantrayukti*s necessarily occur in a treatise that is extremely concise; alternatively, the connection is that they are seen [only] partially in one stated in brief.
Demonstrating the function of the *tantrayukti*s (methodological principles) by means of an illustration, he says "just as" (*yathā*) and so forth.

Just as the sun causes a contracted lotus grove to expand, so too do the *tantrayukti*s expand the condensed portions of meaning within the treatise (*tantra*); he shows that they cause expansion through awakening by means of the illustration of the sun. By means of the illustration of the lamp, however, he shows that just as a lamp illuminates that which is already present but concealed by darkness, so too do the *tantrayukti*s such as the logical reason (*hetu*) illuminate the meaning that is already present but hidden.
Intending that these two objectives are to be accomplished by the principles of the Tantras (tantrayukti), it has been said: "They are for the purpose of awakening and illumination.
He states the fruit of the practice of the authentic treatise [in verses] beginning with "Even in a single...
He describes the faults and virtues regarding the incorrect and correct understanding of the treatise [in verses] beginning with "Misapprehended... (durgṛhītam...).

Just as a weapon, if poorly grasped, brings about the severing of one's own hand and so forth, so too a scripture, if poorly grasped, brings about one's own ruin through the application of false medicine; or just as a weapon, if well-grasped, provides protection from thieves and the like, so too a scripture, if well-grasped, effects the protection of oneself and the patient.

Therefore, they recite the verse beginning with "tasmādetāḥ" as an exposition within the *Uttara-tantra*, specifically in the section on logic and grammar (*yuktivyākaraṇa*); however, the elders declare this to be non-Vedic (*anārṣa*), because this very *Uttara-tantra* is not of Vedic origin within the *Agniveśa-tantra*.
(49–50) He states the fruit of studying the *Tantra* [in general] in the passage beginning with "idamakhilam": [The text continues: "All this... and so forth.
"Undistressed in mind" means one whose mind does not waver from the meaning of the treatise;
"constant in practice" refers to one for whom medical treatment must be performed at all times;
he is the giver of happiness and life—or rather, the giver of a life in the form of happiness, a "giver of happy life."

Regarding the phrase "dhṛtyādi" (beginning with fortitude): he whose qualities of fortitude, mindfulness, and intelligence have been accumulated is "one who has increased his qualities of fortitude, mindfulness, and intelligence.
Some recite three verses beginning with "yasya dvādaśasāhasrī," but that is irrelevant to the context.
The son of Nārāyaṇa, the worthy minister of the kitchen of the Lord of Gauḍa,
a man of noble conduct born into the renowned Lodhravalī lineage after the venerable Bhānu, the illustrious Cakrapāṇi, holds the office of author here.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Success of the Subsequent Enema," in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary on the intent of the *Caraka-saṃhitā*, composed by the illustrious Cakrapāṇidatta.
